question: On 4 February 1976 a nineteen-year-old army recruit at Fort Dix, New Jersey collapsed and died after leaving his sickbed to complete a forced five-mile night march. When the CDC identified the strain of influenza recovered from him, one alarming feature drove federal officials to act within weeks. What did the strain look like?
answer: a close genetic relative of the 1918 pandemic virus
choices: a close genetic relative of the 1918 pandemic virus
a laboratory hybrid that had escaped a research freezer
a bird flu that had never before infected a human
a completely new virus with no relatives in any archive
context: The recruit's name was Private David Lewis, and the strain was a swine influenza (H1N1) that at the time looked closely related to the virus that had killed roughly 50 million people worldwide in 1918-19. That single family resemblance is what turned an isolated barracks death into a national programme. Source: History News Network, The Last Great Swine Flu Epidemic; Ford Presidential Library, The Swine Flu Immunization Program of 1976.

question: President Gerald Ford went on national television flanked by Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin urging every American to be vaccinated against swine flu, and in about ten weeks roughly 45 million Americans took the shot. By the normal end of the 1976 flu season, worldwide surveillance had returned a specific verdict on the strain first found at Fort Dix. What had surveillance found about that strain outside the barracks?
answer: not a single case of the same strain had been reported anywhere else in the world
choices: not a single case of the same strain had been reported anywhere else in the world
roughly 30,000 Americans had died of it before winter's end
it had reached Europe about a year later than the campaign had predicted
it had mutated into a milder strain partway through the campaign
context: By the normal end of flu season, not one case of the same strain had been reported anywhere else in the world. The confident official forecast was simply wrong. A useful contrast is the 1957 Asian flu, for which the vaccinologist Maurice Hilleman actually did forecast a real pandemic in time - showing that these calls can go either way. Sources: Emerging Infectious Diseases 12(1), Reflections on the 1976 Swine Flu Vaccination Program; History News Network.

question: By late 1976 CDC surveillance had detected an excess of Guillain-Barre syndrome - an ascending paralysis - in swine flu vaccine recipients at roughly one extra case per 100,000 doses. On 16 December 1976 the federal government took a specific action in response to that safety signal. What did the government do?
answer: suspended the vaccination program nationwide
choices: suspended the vaccination program nationwide
recalled every unused dose from doctors' offices
prosecuted the vaccine manufacturers for negligence
rewrote the vaccine's ingredient list within the week
context: The programme was never reinstated at scale, and the Department of Health, Education and Welfare formally ended it in March 1977. The 1976 episode cuts three ways in a single breath, all true at once: an official pandemic forecast was wrong; a rare harm WAS detected by the surveillance system; and the government DID act on that signal and stop. The last two are what a working safety system is supposed to look like. Sources: CDC Museum, 1976 Swine Flu Vaccination Program; Emerging Infectious Diseases 12(1).

question: Between 1978 and 1981, American families filed nine lawsuits in all over injuries they blamed on the DTP shot, the combined diphtheria, tetanus and whooping-cough vaccine given to babies. Then lawyers began arguing that a maker could be made to pay even where nobody could show it had been careless. By the mid-1980s, how many of these suits were being filed each year?
answer: More than two hundred
choices: More than two hundred
About twenty
About sixty
More than two thousand
context: The sums demanded climbed with the count: the average claim rose from about $10 million in 1978 to $46.5 million by 1984. Insurers answered by withdrawing cover from vaccine makers or charging premiums the makers could not pay. Source: grokipedia.com/page/National_Childhood_Vaccine_Injury_Act, 'Pre-1986 Vaccine Liability Crisis'.

question: By 1984 insurers were either refusing to cover American vaccine makers or charging premiums the makers could not afford, and firms began quitting the childhood vaccine business altogether. Every American baby was meant to get the DTP shot. By the middle of the 1980s, how many American companies were still making it?
answer: One
choices: One
Four
Seven
Twenty
context: The College of Physicians of Philadelphia's History of Vaccines project states that by the end of 1984 only one U.S. company still manufactured DPT, and other vaccines were losing manufacturers too; Grokipedia dates the low point about a year later, at one or two producers. Either way, the supply of a vaccine every American child was expected to receive rested on a single firm. Sources: historyofvaccines.org, vaccine-injury-compensation programs page; grokipedia.com/page/National_Childhood_Vaccine_Injury_Act.

question: Since the 1986 Act, an American family that believes a vaccine injured their child petitions the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, where an officer called a special master decides the case and no jury sits. When the hearing opens, who argues the case against the family?
answer: Lawyers from the Department of Justice
choices: Lawyers from the Department of Justice
Lawyers from Health and Human Services
Lawyers from the Food and Drug Administration
Lawyers from the Centers for Disease Control
context: The respondent is the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and the attorneys across the table come from the Justice Department's Civil Division, Office of Vaccine Litigation. HHS reviews the medicine, DOJ argues the case, the court decides what to pay: three roles, all inside the federal government. The manufacturer is not in the room. Sources: justice.gov/civil/vicp; hrsa.gov/vaccine-compensation/about.

question: In 1976 the United States set out to vaccinate the whole country against swine flu. On 8 April the Federal Insurance Company told Merck it would stop covering the firm against injury claims from 1 July, and no maker would release a dose without cover. Congress passed a law on 10 August to get the shots moving. What did that law do?
answer: It put the government itself on the hook for injury claims
choices: It put the government itself on the hook for injury claims
It ordered the insurers to keep covering the makers
It set a legal limit on what an injured person could claim
It gave the makers a cash grant to pay their premiums
context: Assistant Secretary Theodore Cooper had told the White House on 2 June 1976 that indemnity legislation was necessary. About 45 million Americans were then vaccinated, and 362 cases of Guillain-Barre syndrome were reported in the six weeks after vaccination; the CDC put the excess at roughly one extra case per 100,000 people vaccinated. So 1986 was not the first time the federal government stepped between an injured citizen and a vaccine maker. It was the first time it made the arrangement permanent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_swine_flu_outbreak.

question: The awards handed down in the vaccine court are not paid by the companies. They come from a federal trust fund filled by an excise tax collected on doses sold in America, so the person being vaccinated is funding the scheme that would compensate them. Most people describe that tax as a flat 75 cents a shot. It is not flat. What changes the amount?
answer: The number of diseases the shot prevents
choices: The number of diseases the shot prevents
The number of doses in the childhood schedule
The price the manufacturer charges for it
The number of claims that vaccine has drawn
context: HRSA's own example: a trivalent influenza vaccine is taxed 75 cents because it prevents one disease, while measles-mumps-rubella is taxed $2.25 because it prevents three. The Treasury collects the tax and manages the Vaccine Injury Compensation Trust Fund's investments. Source: hrsa.gov/vaccine-compensation/about.

question: Ronald Reagan signed the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act into law on 14 November 1986. When a president signs a bill he often issues a written statement alongside it, setting down what he thinks of what he has just approved. What does Reagan's statement say about the new vaccine compensation programme?
answer: That he had serious reservations and signed it reluctantly
choices: That he had serious reservations and signed it reluctantly
That it was the most important children's health law in years
That he expected it to end vaccine injury lawsuits for good
That he had wanted it widened to cover injured adults too
context: He objected that the programme would be 'administered not by the executive branch, but by the Federal judiciary,' and that under it 'there continues to be the opportunity for very substantial and inequitable differences in liability judgments awarded similarly situated plaintiffs.' He also noted that it could not start until Congress passed a separate funding measure, which is why the vaccine court did not open for business until 1 October 1988, almost two years after his signature. One oddity: the act was never a standalone law, so the statement is officially titled 'Statement on Signing the State Comprehensive Mental Health Plan Bill'. The vaccine act is Title III of that bill, Public Law 99-660. Sources: presidency.ucsb.edu, Reagan signing statement of 14 November 1986; hrsa.gov/vaccine-compensation/about.

question: When a special master decides a vaccine claim in a family's favour, the fund pays their unreimbursed medical and rehabilitation bills with no limit at all, and lost future earnings with no limit either. Two items do have a ceiling: pain and suffering, and the payment made when a child dies. Both were written into the 1986 Act and have never been raised for inflation since. What is that ceiling?
choices: $2.5 million
context: The uncapped medical and lost-earnings awards are the strongest thing supporters of the programme can point to. The death benefit is the opposite case: a family whose child dies receives a flat sum fixed in 1986 dollars and never indexed, which is among the most-cited arguments for reform. Sources: hrsa.gov/vaccine-compensation/about; compensation table and 'Proposed Reforms' at grokipedia.com/page/National_Childhood_Vaccine_Injury_Act.

question: Hannah Bruesewitz was left with a seizure disorder after a DTP shot given to her as a baby. Her parents turned down the vaccine court's judgment and sued the maker's successor in a Pennsylvania court, testing how much of the 1986 Act's shield really held. On 22 February 2011 the Supreme Court ruled 6-2 against them, in an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia. Which kind of claim did that ruling shut out of American courts?
answer: A claim that the vaccine could have been designed more safely
choices: A claim that the vaccine could have been designed more safely
A claim that the vaccine was made wrongly at the factory
A claim that the maker hid what it knew about a risk
A claim that the warning given to the parent was inadequate
context: Scalia wrote that 'provided that there was proper manufacture and warning, any remaining side effects, including those resulting from design defects, are deemed to have been unavoidable.' In plain English: in an American court you cannot argue that a safer version of the vaccine could have been designed. The other three claims in this question are the doors the Act deliberately left open, along with failure to comply with FDA requirements. Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justice Ginsburg; Justice Kagan took no part. Sources: Bruesewitz v. Wyeth (law.cornell.edu/supct/html/09-152.ZO.html); retained-liability categories at grokipedia.com/page/National_Childhood_Vaccine_Injury_Act.

question: The National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, the court the 1986 Act put between injured families and vaccine makers, reported on 1 September 2025 that 28,991 petitions had been filed since it opened in 1988, that 12,339 were paid, and that roughly $5.4 billion had gone out. Campaigners quote that total in both directions. The Health Resources and Services Administration, the federal agency that runs it, adds one line about how most of that money was awarded. What does that line say?
answer: Most came from settlements in which the government never concluded the vaccine caused the injury
choices: Most came from cases in which a special master ruled the vaccine had caused the injury
Most came from claims the government conceded after its own doctors reviewed them
Most came from settlements in which the government never concluded the vaccine caused the injury
Most came from injuries already on the programme's published list of recognised harms
context: HRSA's wording: 'Approximately 60% of all compensation awarded by the VICP comes as result of a negotiated settlement between the parties in which HHS has not concluded, based upon review of the evidence, that the alleged vaccine(s) caused the alleged injury.' Of 25,593 petitions adjudicated by that date, 12,339 were compensated and 13,166 dismissed. Finding the true total is oddly hard: the Justice Department's own VICP page still reported about 9,500 people paid and $4.5 billion, stamped as updated in January 2023, two arms of one government roughly a billion dollars apart. Sources: hrsa.gov/vaccine-compensation/data; justice.gov/civil/vicp.

question: A family bringing an injury claim in the vaccine court the 1986 Act created still needs a lawyer, and in an ordinary injury suit that lawyer's pay comes out of the winnings. Congress forbade that arrangement here: by statute, a lawyer in a vaccine case may not take a share of the family's award, nor charge the family any other fee. So who pays that lawyer, and when?
answer: The programme pays them, win or lose
choices: The programme pays them, win or lose
The programme pays them only if the family wins
The manufacturer pays them, win or lose
The manufacturer pays them only if the family wins
context: HRSA: attorneys 'are eligible for reasonable attorneys' fees, whether or not the petitioner is awarded compensation by the Court, if certain minimal requirements are met,' and 'by statute, attorneys may not charge any other fee, including a contingency fee.' The Justice Department adds that fees are available on denied claims so long as the claim was filed in good faith and with a reasonable basis. Sources: hrsa.gov/vaccine-compensation/data; justice.gov/civil/vicp.

question: Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented in Bruesewitz v. Wyeth, decided by the Supreme Court in 2011, where the majority read the 1986 Act to bar one whole class of lawsuit against vaccine makers. Writing for herself and Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, she argued that the country loses more than a source of damages when such cases can no longer be brought. What did she say the majority's reading left behind?
answer: A vacuum in which no one ensures makers keep up with new science
choices: A vacuum in which no one ensures makers keep up with new science
A backlog of claims the special masters could never hope to clear
A patchwork of state rules that would differ from court to court
A shortage of expert witnesses willing to testify against makers
context: Sotomayor wrote that the majority's reading 'leaves a regulatory vacuum in which no one ensures that vaccine manufacturers adequately take account of scientific and technological advancements,' and that 'absent a clear statutory mandate to the contrary, there is no reason to think that Congress intended in the vaccine context to eliminate the traditional incentive and deterrence functions served by state tort liability.' That is two justices of the Supreme Court on the record, not an activist's assertion. The answer on the other side is equally concrete: the shield kept manufacturers in the business, and the vaccine court demands less proof, costs the family less and moves faster than a jury trial. Source: Sotomayor, J., dissenting (law.cornell.edu/supct/html/09-152.ZD.html).

question: Section 300aa-27 of the 1986 Act is headed 'Mandate for safer childhood vaccines.' It orders the Secretary of Health and Human Services to promote vaccines that cause fewer and less serious reactions, and to send Congress a report describing what has been done. In 2017 a group called the Informed Consent Action Network asked for copies of those reports under freedom-of-information law, and sued in 2018 when none arrived. How did the department answer in court?
answer: It said its searches had located no such records
choices: It said its searches had located no such records
It said the reports were exempt from release as internal advice
It said the reports had gone to Congress and were not kept
It said the request was too broad for it to process
context: HHS's answer of 27 June 2018: 'The Department's searches for records did not locate any records responsive to your request.' The stipulation records that the Immediate Office of the Secretary, which holds the Secretary's official correspondence file including reports to Congress, searched its document tracking systems and the indexes of Secretarial correspondence at the Federal Records Centers. The case was dismissed with prejudice, so-ordered by Judge Jesse M. Furman on 9 July 2018. Read it exactly: this is a no-records-found response, not a confession. ICAN's own press release went further, saying HHS never once filed a report, and that stronger sentence is the group's characterisation and not the government's. One footnote: the lawyer who signed that suit against the department was Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who as of 2025 is the Secretary of Health and Human Services. Source: ICAN v. DHHS, No. 1:18-cv-03215-JMF (S.D.N.Y.), Document 18, filed 9 July 2018.

question: Cosmologists needed a light source they could recognize across billions of light years -- a 'standard candle' bright enough to see and identical enough to trust. Type Ia supernovae fit the job because every one detonates under very nearly the same trigger condition. What triggers a Type Ia?
answer: A white dwarf pushed near the Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4 solar masses
choices: A white dwarf pushed near the Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4 solar masses
A massive star running out of fuel and collapsing on its iron core
Two neutron stars spiralling in and merging under gravity
A cloud of hydrogen igniting fusion at the centre of a new star
context: Type Ia supernovae come from white dwarfs (Earth-sized stellar remnants) that pull in matter from a companion until they approach ~1.4 solar masses; at that threshold, set by quantum mechanics, the star reignites runaway fusion and detonates. Because the threshold is the same everywhere, each explosion peaks at nearly the same true brightness (with a small correction from the shape of the fading light curve). Sources: rubinobservatory.org exploding-stars guide; Berkeley Lab.

question: Through the 1990s two rival teams -- Saul Perlmutter's Supernova Cosmology Project and Brian Schmidt's High-z Supernova Search Team -- raced to hunt down distant Type Ia supernovae. What did both teams SET OUT to measure?
answer: How fast gravity was slowing the universe's expansion
choices: How fast gravity was slowing the universe's expansion
Whether space itself was pushing galaxies apart
The mass of the invisible halos holding galaxies together
The exact age of the oldest globular clusters
context: Everyone in the field assumed the universe's expansion had to be slowing under the combined gravity of all its mass; the only open question was how much. Both teams designed their surveys to pin the deceleration DOWN. The surprise result -- that the expansion is speeding up -- was one nobody was looking for, which is a big part of why it was believed. Source: NobelPrize.org 2011 physics press release.

question: In 1998 both supernova teams published the same startling number. The distant Type Ia supernovae they had observed came in about 10 to 15 percent fainter than they should have if the universe were doing the expected thing. What did that faintness force them to conclude?
answer: The expansion of the universe is speeding up, not slowing down
choices: The expansion of the universe is speeding up, not slowing down
There is far more dark matter in galaxies than anyone had guessed
The universe is much younger than the ages of its oldest stars
Distant galaxies contain far less hydrogen than nearby ones
context: Fainter means farther. The distant supernovae sat about 10-15 percent farther away than a decelerating universe allows -- the light had been climbing away from us longer than gravity alone would predict, which meant space itself had been stretching faster over time, not slower. Sources: Riess 1998 (Astronomical Journal); Perlmutter et al. 1999 (Astrophysical Journal); Riess Physics Reports review.

question: Adam Riess and his High-z colleagues did not celebrate their 1998 result. Instead they spent years trying to KILL it -- running follow-up studies aimed at the two most respectable escape routes that could explain the missing brightness without any acceleration. Which pair of loopholes did they most seriously chase?
answer: Grey intergalactic dust, and ancient supernovae being intrinsically dimmer
choices: Grey intergalactic dust, and ancient supernovae being intrinsically dimmer
Gravitational lensing by hidden black holes, and cosmic-ray damage to the CCDs
Atmospheric absorption at high altitude, and a systematic Hubble-constant error
Neutrino oscillation in transit, and background quasars biasing the redshifts
context: The two respectable ways to explain the missing brightness without any dark energy were (1) some grey dust floating in intergalactic space that dimmed distant light uniformly, and (2) 'evolution' -- the idea that supernovae born in the young universe were intrinsically dimmer than modern ones. Riess's follow-up work over years failed to find either effect at the size required. Only THEN did the acceleration result become unavoidable. Sources: Riess stsci.edu darkEnergy page; Riess 2000 review at DePaul.

question: The 1998 supernova result was so strange it needed a name. At a physics meeting an astrophysicist proposed a deliberately neutral phrase for the acceleration's unseen cause -- chosen precisely so the name would NOT smuggle in an answer to what was actually causing it. Who coined the term, and what was it?
answer: Michael Turner called it 'dark energy'
choices: Michael Turner called it 'dark energy'
Alan Guth called it 'inflation'
Fritz Zwicky called it 'missing mass'
Fred Hoyle called it 'the steady state'
context: Turner, of the University of Chicago, coined 'dark energy' in 1998. He later explained he wanted a term that did not assume the answer was Einstein's cosmological constant, or vacuum energy, or something else -- 'dark' because we cannot see it, 'energy' as the most generic word he could pick. The name stuck. Sources: en.wikipedia.org Michael_S._Turner; news.uchicago.edu dark-energy-explained.

question: Two very different unseen things are usually mixed up. One pulls galaxies together and shows up in their rotation curves and gravitational lensing; the other pushes space itself apart and was found by the 1998 supernova surveys. Roughly what fraction of the total energy of the universe is the PUSHING one?
answer: About 68 percent
choices: About 68 percent
About 27 percent
About 5 percent
About 95 percent
context: Best-fit Planck-mission numbers: dark energy ~68 percent, dark matter ~27 percent, ordinary matter (stars, gas, dust, us) ~5 percent. Two utterly different unknowns dominate the cosmic budget: dark matter holds structures together, dark energy pushes space apart. Getting them mixed up is one of the classic freshman-astronomy errors -- the 95 percent trap counts BOTH dark components together. Sources: science.nasa.gov building-blocks; en.wikipedia.org Dark_matter.

question: Mathematically the simplest description of dark energy is a term Albert Einstein wrote into his field equations in 1917 and then abandoned when Edwin Hubble showed the universe was expanding. Which term was that?
answer: The cosmological constant, Lambda
choices: The cosmological constant, Lambda
The Planck length
The Schwarzschild radius
The Chandrasekhar limit
context: Einstein originally added Lambda to his 1917 field equations to permit a static universe, since a purely gravitating universe would collapse. Once Hubble's redshifts showed space was in fact expanding, Einstein dropped it. The 1998 supernova result revived it -- a positive Lambda behaves exactly like a uniform energy density with negative pressure, which is what dark energy has to be. Whether dark energy IS a plain Lambda or something dynamical (called 'quintessence') is what modern surveys like DESI are testing. Sources: Carroll dark energy review (ipac.caltech); Physics Today.

question: One obvious first guess for what dark energy might BE: the quantum vacuum carries a leftover energy density that pushes space apart. When particle physicists actually compute how big that vacuum energy should be and compare it with what cosmology measures, the mismatch is famously called 'the worst theoretical prediction in the history of physics'. How wrong is the calculation?
answer: Off by about 120 orders of magnitude
choices: Off by about 120 orders of magnitude
Off by about 10 orders of magnitude
Off by about 30 orders of magnitude
Off by roughly a factor of two
context: Depending on the cutoff scheme the number is quoted as ~120 (Planck-scale cutoff) or ~56 orders of magnitude -- either way it is the largest mismatch between theory and experiment in physics. It is called the vacuum catastrophe, or the cosmological constant problem, and nobody has a persuasive solution. The other famous quote about the cosmological constant -- that Einstein called it his 'biggest blunder' -- is secondhand from George Gamow (1956) and may never have actually been said. Sources: Scientific American cosmological-constant piece; Carroll dark energy review.

question: On 6 October 1995 two astronomers announced the first planet ever found orbiting an ordinary Sun-like star -- 51 Pegasi b, about 50 light years away, discovered with a spectrograph called ELODIE. Who made the announcement?
answer: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz
choices: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz
Geoffrey Marcy and Paul Butler
Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail
David Charbonneau and Timothy Brown
context: Mayor and Queloz used the ELODIE spectrograph on the 1.93 metre telescope at Haute-Provence. Marcy and Butler (Lick Observatory) confirmed the planet within a week. Wolszczan and Frail had found the first exoplanets of ANY kind in 1992 (a later rung explains what kind of host); Charbonneau and Brown come later, as the first to catch an exoplanet transit. Mayor and Queloz shared half of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. Sources: astrobites.org 51 Pegasi b; NASA exoplanets Nobel piece.

question: Several other observing groups already had spectrographs sensitive enough to have caught 51 Pegasi b before 1995. Why did they miss it?
answer: They assumed giant planets need long orbits, so they sampled each star too slowly to catch a 4-day signal
choices: They assumed giant planets need long orbits, so they sampled each star too slowly to catch a 4-day signal
Their large telescopes had atmospheric distortion that smeared out any short-period Doppler wobble
They believed hot giants would show up first as transits, so they weren't running Doppler surveys
They were watching only pulsars, following Wolszczan and Frail's 1992 timing-signal method
context: This is a classic scientific parable: the instruments were ready, but a theoretical expectation shaped what the data were allowed to show. Groups revisited their old measurements after 1995 and found the signal had been there. Sources: Hot Jupiters review (arXiv 2102.05064); Youth-plus-experience Mayor-Queloz history paper.

question: 51 Pegasi b was the first planet found around a normal Sun-like star -- but not the first exoplanet ever. Three years earlier, in January 1992, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail had used the giant Arecibo dish to announce two planets orbiting an even stranger host. What kind of host?
answer: A millisecond pulsar spinning hundreds of times a second
choices: A millisecond pulsar spinning hundreds of times a second
A cool red dwarf flare star in a nearby cluster
A pair of white dwarfs orbiting each other closely
A young protostar still wrapped in its birth disk
context: Wolszczan and Frail found the planets around PSR B1257+12, a millisecond pulsar about 2,300 light years away, by detecting tiny irregularities in its otherwise metronome-precise pulse arrivals -- gravitational tugs from the planets. A Jodrell Bank team had to retract a competing pulsar-planet claim from the same era after they realized they had botched Earth's orbital eccentricity. Sources: en.wikipedia.org PSR B1257+12; space.com 25-year anniversary.

question: The radial-velocity wobble gives astronomers only a MINIMUM mass for a planet, because the true mass depends on the unknown tilt of the orbit. A transit measurement adds something the wobble cannot give. What?
answer: The planet's radius, from the depth of the dip
choices: The planet's radius, from the depth of the dip
The star's chemical composition, from its spectrum
The distance to the star system, from parallax
The planet's surface temperature, from its color
context: A transit's depth is the ratio of the planet's disk to the star's disk, which gives the planet's RADIUS directly. Combine radius (from transit) with mass (from radial velocity plus a known tilt near 90 degrees for transiting planets) and you get the planet's DENSITY, which tells you whether the world is rock or gas. This is why the two methods together are so powerful. Sources: hao.ucar.edu HD 209458 page; en.wikipedia.org HD 209458 b.

question: During a transit a sliver of the star's light passes THROUGH the planet's atmosphere on its way to Earth and picks up that atmosphere's absorption fingerprints. In 2002 Charbonneau's team used the Hubble Space Telescope to detect the first such fingerprint on a world orbiting another star, HD 209458 b. What element did they identify?
answer: Sodium
choices: Sodium
Iron
Helium
Neon
context: Charbonneau's team used the STIS spectrograph on Hubble to catch extra absorption in the yellow sodium D lines at 589.3 nanometres during transit -- the first detection of an atmosphere on a planet outside our Solar System. Later missions like Kepler and TESS turned the transit method into a census: the count of known exoplanets went from zero in 1994 to thousands in one working lifetime. Sources: en.wikipedia.org HD 209458 b; aanda.org sodium detection.

question: In 1825 at Sandhurst, William Sturgeon built the first practical electromagnet: a bent iron bar the weight of a pocket watch, wound with a coil of bare copper wire and hooked to one battery cell. That seven-ounce lump could pick up a real load of iron - and dropped it the instant the switch opened. About how much did Sturgeon's little magnet lift?
answer: Nine pounds
choices: Nine pounds
Half a pound
A hundred pounds
One ton
context: Roughly twenty times the magnet's own weight. Break the circuit and the load fell instantly - the soft iron released the moment the current stopped, which is what makes an electromagnet a switch and not just a magnet. Source: lindahall.org Scientist of the Day, William Sturgeon.

question: William Sturgeon's 1825 electromagnet used BARE copper wire wrapped straight onto a horseshoe of soft iron. To keep the current from short-circuiting through the iron itself, Sturgeon coated the iron with something before he wound the wire on. What did he coat it with?
answer: Varnish
choices: Varnish
Wax
Rubber
Silk
context: Insulated wire did not yet exist. Varnishing the CORE, not the wire, was a working man's shortcut - and it capped how many turns you could pack on, because the bare wire loops still had to lie in one loose layer. That is exactly the limit Joseph Henry broke a few years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org William Sturgeon.

question: In upstate New York around 1830, Joseph Henry found a way to stack many more turns of wire around an iron core than any previous experimenter. Reportedly his wife Harriet handed over strips of her petticoat for the job. What material did Henry use to insulate his wire, turn by turn?
answer: Silk
choices: Silk
Cotton
Wax paper
Rubber
context: Silk was thin, tough, and a fine insulator; wrapping each strand let Henry pack hundreds of tightly stacked turns onto a single core, multiplying the field. Source: madehow.com Joseph Henry biography.

question: In 1831 Joseph Henry demonstrated at the Albany Academy a machine using about a mile of wire strung around a large lecture room. A battery at one end worked a distant electromagnet at the other end, which struck a small object every time the circuit closed. What did the distant magnet strike, giving the world its first working demonstration of a principle Samuel Morse later built a business on?
answer: A bell
choices: A bell
A rotating drum
A pen against paper
A wire filament
context: The bell was audible proof that a weak current at one end could work a strong action at the other - the working principle of the electric telegraph, five years before Morse patented his version. Source: edisontechcenter.org Joseph Henry.

question: By 1831 Joseph Henry's silk-wrapped magnets had grown into monsters. The one he built for Yale College the same year could hold up a genuinely startling load - a world record at the time. Roughly what weight did the Yale electromagnet lift?
answer: Two thousand pounds
choices: Two thousand pounds
One hundred pounds
Twenty tons
Fifty pounds
context: 2,063 pounds, to be exact. Henry's insight was that lifting power scales with turns times current, not wire thickness - which is why silk-wrapped layers of thin wire beat bare wire in a single loose layer. Source: britannica.com Joseph Henry.

question: Samuel Morse's transcontinental telegraph would not have worked without a small iron-lever device Joseph Henry pioneered, sprinkled every few miles along the wire. What did each of these devices do to the fading electrical signal?
answer: Re-boosted it with a fresh battery
choices: Re-boosted it with a fresh battery
Stepped it up to a higher voltage
Stored it briefly in a capacitor
Spun a wheel to redraw it on paper
context: The device is called a relay: a tiny incoming current energises a coil whose field pulls an iron lever that closes a second circuit powered by a fresh local battery, sending a full-strength copy down the next span. Because a soft iron core drops its magnetism the instant the current stops, the lever releases cleanly - the whole point. Relays are the ancestor of every switching element in a computer. Source: technicshistory.com The Relay.

question: A steel nail, a metre of insulated wire and one AA battery is the whole kit for the kid version of Sturgeon's experiment: wind the wire round the nail, touch the ends to the cell, and count the paperclips the nail picks up. Add ten more turns and count again - what will the count usually do?
answer: Go up
choices: Go up
Stay the same
Go down
Reverse the nail's ends
context: Field strength scales with turns times current (ampere-turns) - more turns, stronger magnet, more paperclips. Safety note: a shorted AA cell heats up fast, so keep each test short. This is a direct measurement of the same law Henry used in 1831. Source: energizer.com Science Center telegraph project.

question: On 19 September 1783 in the forecourt at Versailles, Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette watched three animals become the first passengers in the history of flight, going up under a Montgolfier balloon. Which three?
answer: a sheep, a duck and a rooster
choices: a sheep, a duck and a rooster
a cat, a dog and a pigeon
a rabbit, a hen and a mouse
a goat, a raven and a hare
context: Eight minutes and about three kilometres later all three came down alive. The crowd around the palace numbered in the tens of thousands. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/hot-air-balloon-rooster-sheep-duck-first

question: The sheep that flew at Versailles in September 1783 -- the first passenger in the history of flight -- was given a name that made its own joke about the trip. What was the sheep called?
answer: Montauciel
choices: Montauciel
Papillon
Bellerophon
Icare
context: Montauciel means 'Climb-to-the-sky'. The duck and the rooster were never named for the record. On landing the rooster had a hurt wing -- from being kicked by the sheep, not from the descent. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/hot-air-balloon-rooster-sheep-duck-first

question: The Montgolfiers picked the Versailles crew as an experiment with a comparison group built in. The duck went up because it was already known to survive at altitude; the rooster went because it was a bird that does not fly high. Why was the sheep on board?
answer: as a physiological stand-in for a human
choices: as a physiological stand-in for a human
as the heaviest weight they could safely lift
as an animal sacred to Louis XVI's household
as an animal that lies still where a goat would thrash
context: The whole point of sending live animals was to test whether a person could survive the ascent; the sheep, with its size and cardiovascular arrangement, was thought to be the closest living gauge. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/hot-air-balloon-rooster-sheep-duck-first

question: The Montgolfier brothers were paper makers from Annonay who were wrong about their own machine. They burned damp straw and wool under the balloon's mouth and named the imaginary lift 'Montgolfier gas'. What did they mistakenly believe was doing the lifting?
answer: the smoke itself
choices: the smoke itself
the sound of the fire
the burning shoe leather
the paper of the envelope
context: The real reason the balloon rose is density: heating air spreads its molecules apart, so a given volume weighs less than the cooler air outside, and the outside air pushes the lighter parcel up. No 'Montgolfier gas' is involved. Source: https://www.chm.bris.ac.uk/~paulmay/webprojects2003/hetherington/final/montgolfier_bros.html

question: On 27 August 1783 Jacques Charles's first unmanned hydrogen balloon, Le Globe, drifted north from the Champ-de-Mars and came down in the village of Gonesse -- where the local farmers thought it was a monster from the sky. What did they do to it?
answer: they tore it apart with pitchforks and knives
choices: they tore it apart with pitchforks and knives
they chained it to a plough and tried to lead it home
they set it alight with torches and threw it in the river
they wrapped it in blankets and carried it to the parish priest
context: By legend Louis XVI later issued a proclamation reassuring peasants that any future balloon coming down in a field was harmless. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/the-first-hydrogen-balloon-launch

question: On 21 November 1783 two men lifted off from the Chateau de la Muette in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon and drifted about nine kilometres over Paris in roughly twenty-five minutes -- the first free human flight in history. Who were they?
answer: Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes
choices: Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes
Joseph-Michel Montgolfier and Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier
Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert
Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace
context: The Montgolfier brothers themselves never flew: Louis XVI first proposed sending condemned prisoners, but Pilatre de Rozier pressed for the honour of a free man to be first, and d'Arlandes went with him. Source: https://vintageaviationnews.com/warbird-articles/today-in-aviation-history-first-documented-free-flight-of-humans.html

question: On 1 December 1783 Jacques Charles flew a hydrogen balloon with Nicolas-Louis Robert from the Tuileries in Paris. After Robert alighted, Charles went up alone to about three thousand metres -- and never flew again. What drove him down for good on that solo ascent?
answer: a pain in his ears so severe he could not bear it a second time
choices: a pain in his ears so severe he could not bear it a second time
a leak in the hydrogen bag that nearly caught fire
a bird strike that punctured the envelope near the crown
a squall that carried him almost to the Channel coast
context: At three kilometres up the outside air pressure is low; the higher-pressure air trapped behind the eardrum pushes outward against it. Charles had discovered altitude ear-pain before anyone had a theory of it. Source: https://www.amusingplanet.com/2023/01/jacques-charles-and-first-hydrogen.html

question: The two rival balloons of 1783 needed opposite controls. To make a hot-air balloon rise, its pilot fires the burner; to make it descend, he opens a vent. A hydrogen balloon carries no burner. To make a hydrogen balloon climb, what does its pilot do?
answer: drop ballast overboard
choices: drop ballast overboard
release gas from a valve at the crown
uncover the envelope so sunlight can warm the gas
shift the pilot's weight forward in the basket
context: Once the gas is sealed in, the only way to make a hydrogen balloon lighter mid-flight is to throw weight over the side; the only way to make it heavier is to let gas out, which is the descend action. Modern weather balloons follow the hydrogen family: they simply swell as they rise into thinner air, and finally burst. Source: https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/Balloon_Flying_Handbook_FAA-H-8083-11B/bfh_chapter_2.pdf

question: Ernst Abbe's 1873 rule says a light microscope cannot separate two points closer together than about HALF the wavelength of the light being used. Visible light runs roughly from 400 to 700 nanometres. Roughly what does that make Abbe's wall for a microscope working with ordinary visible light?
answer: Around 200 nanometres
choices: Around 2 nanometres
Around 20 nanometres
Around 200 nanometres
Around 2 micrometres
context: Half of visible wavelengths (roughly 400-700 nm) puts Abbe's diffraction limit near 200 nm - about the size of the smallest bacterium. For sixty years after 1873 that number decided which objects biology could see at all. Source: https://svi.nl/DiffractionLimit

question: Abbe's 200-nanometre wall did not just make certain objects fuzzy - it made them invisible. From roughly 1873 to the early 1930s, three important biological objects sat on the wrong side of the wall. Which of the following list is entirely made of objects too small for any light microscope of that era to resolve?
answer: A virus, a ribosome, the gap between two nerve cells
choices: A typical bacterium, a red blood cell, a human hair
A virus, a ribosome, the gap between two nerve cells
A mitochondrion, a plant chloroplast, a pollen grain
A yeast cell, an amoeba, a paramecium
context: A virus is roughly 20-100 nm, a ribosome about 25 nm, a synaptic cleft about 50-100 nm - all under Abbe's ~200 nm wall. The other lists are objects the light microscope had already resolved comfortably before 1873. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6937598/

question: If Abbe's wall is set by wavelength, one honest way past it is to stop using visible light and use a wave with a much shorter wavelength. In 1931 Max Knoll and his student Ernst Ruska built the first lens that focused a beam of subatomic particles, and by 23 September 1933 Ruska had a prototype producing images at about 12,000x - beating the best light microscope. Which particles was the beam made of, treated in the lens as waves?
answer: Electrons
choices: Electrons
Protons
Neutrons
Positrons
context: Electrons behave as waves with wavelengths thousands of times shorter than visible light, so a good electron lens beats the best light microscope by orders of magnitude on resolution. Ruska received half of the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for the invention - fifty-odd years after the fact. Source: https://www.tu.berlin/en/about/history/people-portraits/ernst-ruska

question: In 1999 Stefan Hell's STED microscopy overlaid a second, doughnut-shaped beam on a normal fluorescence spot and beat 200 nm resolution with ordinary visible light. Headlines said Hell had broken Abbe's diffraction limit. What did the Nobel committee later say his trick had actually done to that limit?
answer: Left the diffraction limit intact, but shrunk the region that emits any light
choices: Broken the diffraction limit, which is now known to be wrong
Left the diffraction limit intact, but shrunk the region that emits any light
Replaced the diffraction limit with a new limit set by the sample thickness
Bypassed the limit only for samples cooled below liquid-helium temperature
context: Hell's STED (stimulated emission depletion) does NOT violate Abbe's law - the light being collected still diffracts. What Hell controls is WHICH molecules are allowed to emit at a given instant. The doughnut-shaped depletion beam switches off fluorescence at the rim, so only molecules in the tiny dark centre are left free to glow; the emitting region is far smaller than the diffraction-limited spot itself. Headlines said 'broke the limit'; the physics says 'dodged it'. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/popular-chemistryprize2014.pdf

question: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went jointly to Stefan Hell, Eric Betzig, and William Moerner for super-resolved fluorescence microscopy. Betzig's technique (PALM, 2006) attacked Abbe's wall from the OTHER side: instead of switching most molecules off, he let only one lone molecule glow at a time. Its image on the camera is still a fat 250 nm diffraction blur. What did Betzig then do to that blur to get nanometre precision?
answer: Computed the CENTRE of the blur to within a few nanometres, then repeated
choices: Sharpened it with a smaller aperture lens
Computed the CENTRE of the blur to within a few nanometres, then repeated
Ran the blur through an ultraviolet phase filter to shrink it
Cooled the sample until the blur froze to a single point
context: The blur itself is diffraction-limited, but if only one molecule is glowing you can fit its point-spread function and place its centre to a few nanometres. Do it thousands of times with different lone molecules and the dots draw a picture no lens could form. Betzig and Harald Hess demonstrated PALM in 2006; W.E. Moerner had shown the underlying single-molecule fluorescence a decade earlier. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1500784112

question: The Nazi program that killed disabled Germans was filed on paper as the 'Charitable Foundation for Curative and Institutional Care.' Insiders called the program simply 'T4.' What is the code T4 short for?
answer: Tiergartenstrasse 4, the office's street address
choices: Tiergartenstrasse 4, the office's street address
Tabelle 4, a patient-classification tier
Truppe 4, a Waffen-SS staff unit
Toedlich 4, an internal terminal-case grade
context: The office sat at Tiergartenstrasse 4 in the Tiergarten borough of Berlin; the villa itself no longer stands, and a plaque set into the pavement marks the spot. The whole horror sits inside one small fact: a killing program named after an address, filed under a charitable foundation. The bureaucracy did the work of the euphemism. Sources: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, 'Aktion T4.'

question: The 1933 German sterilization law did not spring from nothing. Historians of the drafting can name the specific document its authors leaned on and cite by name. What was the German law's relationship to the American eugenics movement?
answer: It closely followed Harry Laughlin's American Model Eugenical Sterilization Law
choices: It closely followed Harry Laughlin's American Model Eugenical Sterilization Law
It was copied word-for-word from the 1927 US ruling Buck v. Bell
It was written by American consultants sent over by the Rockefeller Foundation
It was drafted in explicit opposition to American practice as too permissive
context: Laughlin ran the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, on Carnegie and Rockefeller money; the University of Heidelberg awarded him an honorary doctorate in 1936 for his work. This is where the science-bank lane sits: the moral scandal is the medical pedigree, and it runs backward across the Atlantic. Sources: USHMM 'Biological State' overview; Wikipedia entry on the 1933 law.

question: The 1933 Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring took effect on January 1, 1934, and sterilized roughly 360,000 Germans by the outbreak of war in 1939. What special body did the law create to order those sterilizations?
answer: Erbgesundheitsgerichte, special Genetic Health Courts
choices: Erbgesundheitsgerichte, special Genetic Health Courts
Rasse- und Siedlungshauptamt, the SS Race and Settlement Office
Reichsgesundheitsamt, the national health office
Ahnenerbe, Himmler's ancestral-research institute
context: By the end of the Reich in 1945 the total reached roughly 400,000 people sterilized. The Genetic Health Courts were empowered to use force. The other three bodies are all real Nazi-era institutions from adjacent racial-policy work, which is exactly the bank's point: the sterilization apparatus had its own dedicated court system. Sources: USHMM 'Biological State' article; Wikipedia, 'Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring.'

question: Aktion T4 killed for two years without any statute, no parliamentary debate, no legal proclamation at all. The only paper that authorised it was a short private letter typed on Hitler's personal stationery. What did Hitler do with the DATE on that letter?
answer: He signed it in October 1939 and backdated it to September 1, 1939, the day the war began
choices: He signed it in October 1939 and backdated it to September 1, 1939, the day the war began
He signed it on September 1, 1939, and post-dated it to January 1, 1940
He left the date blank so any official could fill it in later
He signed it on the day of the Munich Agreement, September 30, 1938
context: Doctors had been refusing to participate in the killings without written cover; the backdated page on Hitler's private stationery gave them one. Two years of killing ran on a single unpublished letter, never a law, never a debate, never a vote. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Backdated Order Authorizes Euthanasia Program.'

question: The letter did not name the doctors on the ground; it named the two officials who would run the whole apparatus and give them cover. Who were those two men?
answer: Philipp Bouhler, head of Hitler's Chancellery, and Karl Brandt, Hitler's personal physician
choices: Philipp Bouhler, head of Hitler's Chancellery, and Karl Brandt, Hitler's personal physician
Reinhard Heydrich, head of the SD, and Rudolf Hess, Deputy Fuehrer
Heinrich Himmler, Reichsfuehrer-SS, and Albert Speer, then a junior architect
Hermann Goering, head of the Luftwaffe, and Joseph Goebbels, Propaganda Minister
context: Brandt was later hanged at Nuremberg on the strength of the Doctors' Trial evidence. The chain of authority ran through a personal physician and a chancellery clerk, not through health ministers or army generals -- part of why the atrocity could stay filed as private and 'charitable' for years. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia.

question: The killing was carried out in six specific institutions, most of them old castles or converted psychiatric hospitals, and the internal Nazi records name all six. Which set of place names lists the T4 killing centres accurately?
answer: Grafeneck, Brandenburg, Hartheim, Sonnenstein, Bernburg, Hadamar
choices: Grafeneck, Brandenburg, Hartheim, Sonnenstein, Bernburg, Hadamar

Wannsee, Wewelsburg, Nuremberg, Bayreuth, Berchtesgaden, Obersalzberg
context: The other distractor sets are, in order, the Aktion Reinhard extermination camps, the largest concentration camps, and famous Nazi meeting sites -- adjacent but different categories. Keeping the six T4 sites separate is how the medical program stays separately visible from the war-and-camps history. Source: USHMM map, 'Euthanasia Centers, Germany 1940-1945.'

question: In June 1945 an American investigating officer, Charles Dameron, broke open a steel safe at the Hartheim killing centre and pulled out a 39-page brochure the T4 office had produced. The document recorded the number 70,273. What did that figure count?
answer: Gassing deaths tallied month by month across the six centres
choices: Gassing deaths tallied month by month across the six centres
Names of doctors employed at the six killing centres
Reichsmarks spent transporting patients to the centres
Patients transferred from ordinary hospitals into T4 care
context: The same brochure calculated the 'savings' the deaths represented, in Reichsmarks of food and care not spent. The internal accounting is the fact that historians point at when they want to show the difference between a horror and a horror ADMINISTERED. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Hartheim killing centre'; Grokipedia, 'Hartheim killing centre.'

question: In the summer of 1941, with two years of killing on the books, T4 was stopped in its centralized form. What stopped it was not a court, an election or a foreign army but a sermon delivered from a Catholic pulpit in Muenster on August 3, 1941. Who preached it?
answer: Bishop Clemens August von Galen
choices: Bishop Clemens August von Galen
Cardinal Michael von Faulhaber of Munich
Pastor Martin Niemoeller of Berlin
Pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer of Finkenwalde
context: The three distractors are all real, prominent German churchmen active under the regime. Copies of the Galen sermon were printed and passed hand to hand; British aircraft later dropped them over German troops as leaflets. Galen was not arrested -- Hitler judged an open clash with the Catholic Church too costly -- though lower priests who read the sermon from their pulpits were persecuted. Sources: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; History Place transcript of the sermon.

question: Three weeks after the Muenster sermon, on August 24, 1941, Hitler ordered T4's centralized killings halted. It looks like a neat cause and effect. What is the SECOND fact that any honest account of the halt has to name?
answer: The internal projected quota for T4 had also just been reached
choices: The internal projected quota for T4 had also just been reached
The German army was on the verge of victory over the Soviet Union
Bouhler and Brandt had resigned in protest against the killings
The Nuremberg racial laws had been amended to exclude the disabled
context: The Galen sermon plainly did move public opinion; it was the most effective public protest against any Nazi policy. But the T4 office had also hit its projected numbers by August 1941, and the killing simply continued in a decentralized form. Both facts belong in the same rung: teach the sermon's real power and refuse the false lesson that one sermon by itself STOPS such a thing. Sources: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, 'Aktion T4.'

question: After August 1941 the centralized gassings ended but the killing did not. Doctors and nurses in ordinary hospitals across Germany went on killing patients until 1945, using lethal injections and deliberate starvation. What did the T4 apparatus itself call this next phase?
answer: Wilde Euthanasie -- 'wild euthanasia'
choices: Wilde Euthanasie -- 'wild euthanasia'
Endloesung -- 'final solution'
Sonderbehandlung -- 'special treatment'
Umsiedlung -- 'resettlement'
context: Local hospital directors set the pace; central control was less visible; the killing spread instead of stopping. Combined estimates for T4 plus wild euthanasia across Germany, Austria and occupied Europe reach 250,000-300,000 dead. The other three terms are real Nazi euphemisms from adjacent programs. Sources: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia; Britannica, 'T4 Program.'

question: The American army psychiatrist Leo Alexander investigated the Nazi medical crimes for the Nuremberg prosecutors and then wrote a warning to his own profession in the New England Journal of Medicine on July 14, 1949, titled 'Medical Science under Dictatorship.' Where did Alexander locate the ORIGIN of everything he had just documented?
answer: In a subtle shift among physicians toward accepting that there is such a thing as a life not worth living
choices: In a subtle shift among physicians toward accepting that there is such a thing as a life not worth living
In direct orders from Hitler that individual doctors were physically compelled to obey
In a national economic collapse that made hospitals close and patients starve on their own
In a single peer-reviewed 1932 paper that all Nazi doctors were required to read
context: Alexander's exact sentence: 'It started with the acceptance of the attitude, basic in the euthanasia movement, that there is such a thing as life not worthy to be lived.' The rest, he argued, followed. The bank keeps this rung last because it is the reason the whole ladder sits in a science bank rather than a history one -- physicians hold a special power, and that power turns on premises so small they can be missed. Sources: Alexander, NEJM, 14 July 1949; Foundation for Economic Education, 'From Small Beginnings.'

question: In 1837 Theodor Schwann sat at dinner with the botanist Matthias Schleiden, who was describing the little round bodies he kept finding inside plant cells. Schwann had seen the same bodies in animal tissue. What did the two men do next?
answer: They left the table and went straight to a microscope
choices: They left the table and went straight to a microscope
They wrote to Robert Brown in London for his opinion
They wrote the claim up for print before testing it
They put the question off until the next field season
context: They compared plant and animal tissue at the microscope that same evening. Schleiden published the claim for plants in 1838 and Schwann extended it to animals in 1839, so a single claim now covered an oak, a frog and a boy. The dinner itself is documented, but the neat line usually quoted from it -- that the cell is the unit of all organic structure -- is a traditional retelling rather than a transcript, which is why this rung is marked as legend. Sources: Wikipedia, Theodor Schwann; Hektoen International, 'The beginnings of cell theory: Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow'.

question: Matthias Schleiden took his degree in 1827 and set up a practice in Hamburg. It went badly, he abandoned it, and eleven years later he published the paper arguing that every plant is built out of cells. What had his Hamburg practice been?
answer: Law, as a courtroom advocate
choices: Law, as a courtroom advocate
Medicine, as a town physician
Pharmacy, as a shop druggist
Surveying, as a land measurer
context: Schleiden qualified in law in 1827 and opened his Hamburg practice; a severe depression ended the career, and he turned to botany instead. He lived from 5 April 1804 to 23 June 1881, and his 1838 paper 'Beitraege zur Phytogenesis' argued that all plants are built of cells. Sources: Wikipedia, Matthias Jakob Schleiden; Embryo Project Encyclopedia, 'Matthias Jacob Schleiden (1804-1881)'.

question: In 1831, seven years before Matthias Schleiden argued that plants are built of cells, the Scottish botanist Robert Brown stripped the outer skin from an orchid flower and found one opaque spot sitting inside cell after cell. He sent a report on it to the Linnean Society of London. What did Brown's report claim about the spot?
answer: He named it and left its purpose an open question
choices: He named it and left its purpose an open question
He named it and called it the store of the cell's food
He named it and called it the seed of a new cell
He named it and took it for a bubble raised by his lens
context: Brown called the spot the areola, or nucleus -- the name it still carries -- and offered the Linnean Society no guess at all as to what it did. The name arrived decades before anyone could say what the thing was for. Earlier sightings exist: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek drew a 'lumen' in salmon red blood cells, and Franz Bauer described the structure in 1804. Source: Wikipedia, Cell nucleus.

question: Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann got the big claim right: plants and animals alike are built of cells. But both men were wrong, in the same way, about where a NEW cell comes from -- neither thought a cell already present had anything to do with it. How did they think a new cell arose?
answer: It crystallised out of a formless fluid in the tissue
choices: It crystallised out of a formless fluid in the tissue
It budded from a starch grain lying in the tissue
It was spun out of fine fibres by the tissue itself
It swelled from a droplet the blood left in the tissue
context: Schwann's third tenet held that living cells formed in ways similar to the formation of crystals: a nucleus deposited around a granule, the cell hardening out of the surrounding juice the way a crystal hardens out of syrup. Starch grains as the parents of new cells was a real rival proposal of the same decades, from Francois-Vincent Raspail. Sources: Wikipedia, Theodor Schwann; OpenStax Microbiology 3.2, 'Foundations of Modern Cell Theory'; Wikipedia, Francois-Vincent Raspail.

question: Matthias Schleiden, who had argued in 1838 that every plant is built of cells, believed a new cell could only appear in a liquid of one exact composition -- and he wrote that composition down like a cook's recipe. What three ingredients did he insist the liquid had to contain?
answer: Sugar, gum and mucus
choices: Sugar, gum and mucus
Starch, resin and water
Salt, chalk and lime
Oil, albumen and blood
context: The imaginary juice had a name -- cytoblastema, a structureless granular fluid out of which new cells were supposed to arise independently of any existing cell. Schleiden wrote out the sequence too: 'The mucous portion condenses into round corpuscles, and the liquid transforms into jelly... and the cell is completed.' He also renamed Robert Brown's nucleus the cytoblast, or cell builder, believing it formed first and the cell condensed around it. Sources: Embryo Project Encyclopedia, 'Matthias Jacob Schleiden (1804-1881)'; Wordnik, cytoblastema.

question: In April 1855 the Berlin pathologist Rudolf Virchow printed four Latin words -- omnis cellula a cellula, every cell from a cell. Textbooks still quote the line, though the version that stuck reads omnis cellula e cellula. The essay ran in volume eight of the Archiv fuer pathologische Anatomie und Physiologie. What was Virchow's own connection to that journal?

choices: He had founded it and was its editor
He had helped found it but never edited it
He had trained under its founding editor
He had never published in it before
context: Virchow had founded the Archiv and edited it, and the cell essay ran on pages 3-39 of his own eighth volume. He actually wrote the phrase as 'Omnis cellula a cellula'; the 'e cellula' form is the one that stuck. Sources: Internet Archive scan of Virchow 1855, Archiv fuer pathologische Anatomie und Physiologie vol. 8; University of Wuerzburg, 'Virchow in Wuerzburg'; Britannica.

question: Robert Remak and Rudolf Virchow were appointed to the Berlin faculty in the same year, 1847, and worked in the same laboratory. In 1852 Remak published his case that animal cells multiply by division; three years later Virchow pressed the same idea so forcefully that it became textbook truth. What had Virchow's own position on cell division been before he took it up?
answer: He had doubted the evidence for cell division

He had thought cell division a plant-only affair
He had backed the formless-juice account of new cells
He had backed the starch-grain account of new cells

The two men were appointed to the Berlin faculty in the same year, 1847, and worked in the same laboratory. Sources: Marine Biological Laboratory, 'Seeing Cells'; Wikipedia, Rudolf Virchow; Ribatti, 'An historical note on the cell theory', Exp Cell Res 2018.

question: Robert Remak finished his medical degree in Berlin in 1838, but Prussian law barred Jews from teaching at its universities. He petitioned King Friedrich Wilhelm IV directly in 1843 and was refused; Alexander von Humboldt kept pressing the king on his behalf, and in 1847 a special royal order finally let him teach -- the first Jew to do so at the University of Berlin without renouncing his faith. What did that hard-won post come with?
answer: A post with no salary and no laboratory
choices: A post with no salary and no laboratory
A full salary but no students to teach
A laboratory shared with the anatomy chair
A stipend paid privately by Humboldt
context: Remak funded his own research out of his general practice and his teaching fees. He waited another twelve years, to 1859, to be made associate professor (Extraordinarius), and was never made a full professor (Ordinarius). In 1856 he lost the Berlin chair of pathology to Virchow and afterwards gave up research for medical practice; he died suddenly at fifty, on 29 August 1865. Sources: Dictionary of Scientific Biography via encyclopedia.com; Hektoen International, 'Robert Remak remembered'; MacTutor Biographies, Remak.

question: After Rudolf Virchow's 1855 essay made 'every cell from a cell' famous, Robert Remak wrote to him pointing out how closely it resembled his own published work of 1852. Virchow brushed the letter aside. Three years later, in the preface to a book, Virchow gave a reason why he had owed Remak no citation at all. What was the reason?
answer: That the 1855 piece had been an editorial, not a paper
choices: That the 1855 piece had been an editorial, not a paper
That Remak's paper had never named the process itself
That the Latin phrase had been common property for years
That he had reached the same conclusion first, back in 1847
context: Virchow argued in the 1858 preface that his 1855 publication had been merely an editorial piece rather than a scientific paper, and that there had therefore been no need to cite Remak. The historian Paul Weindling documents the stronger claim that Virchow plagiarised Remak's notion that all cells come from pre-existing cells -- that is a historian's characterisation, not a court finding. The documented facts stand on their own: Remak published the evidence in 1852, Virchow published the slogan in 1855 without citing him, and Virchow then declined to cite him on the grounds that the piece was an editorial. Sources: OpenStax Microbiology 3.2; Wikipedia, Robert Remak.

question: Every one of your cells came from a cell that divided, and that one from another, back without a break -- no cell in you was ever built from scratch. In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo did the counting properly and put your total at about 30 trillion cells. Their tally held a surprise: about nine of every ten of those cells belong to a single lineage, one family line of cells descended together. Which lineage is it?
answer: The blood-forming lineage
choices: The blood-forming lineage
The muscle-forming lineage
The skin-forming lineage
The bone-forming lineage
context: The blood-forming lineage -- the hematopoietic one -- accounts for roughly 90% of the total. Blood cells are small and enormously numerous, so counted one by one you are mostly blood. The 30-trillion figure is Sender, Fuchs and Milo's 2016 revision in PLOS Biology (3.0 x 10^13 human cells). Every one of those cells sits at the end of an unbroken chain of divisions, and a 2024 study put the far end of that chain -- LUCA, the last ancestor every living thing on Earth shares -- at about 4.2 billion years ago. Sources: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLOS Biology 2016; Wikipedia, Abiogenesis.

question: Rudolf Virchow's rule -- every cell from a cell -- covers every cell alive today, but not the first one: that cell had to come from chemistry that was not alive, and how it did is still unsolved. The most famous attempt on the problem is Stanley Miller and Harold Urey's 1952 experiment, which sparked a mixture of methane, ammonia and hydrogen and got amino acids out of it. Why do scientists no longer think that settles how life began?
answer: Earth's early air was probably not the mixture they used
choices: Earth's early air was probably not the mixture they used
Their spark was far stronger than any natural lightning
The amino acids they made are not the kinds life uses
No one else has ever managed to repeat the experiment
context: Miller and Urey used a strongly reducing mixture; current scientific consensus holds the primitive atmosphere was only weakly reducing or neutral, which shrinks both the amount and the variety of amino acids that could actually have formed that way. The experiment itself worked and has been repeated -- the objection is to the recipe of the air, not to the result. And amino acids are a long way short of a cell: the transition from non-life to life has not been observed experimentally, and the derivation of LUCA from simple components is far from understood. Nobody yet knows. Source: Wikipedia, Abiogenesis.

question: At Emperor Napoleon III's state banquets in the 1850s, the story goes, his most honoured guests were given cutlery of one particular metal while the ordinary guests around the table made do with gold and silver. Which metal was reserved for the guests of honour?
answer: Aluminium
choices: Platinum
Aluminium
Palladium
Rhodium
context: The anecdote is widely repeated but should be treated as reputed, not documented. In the 1850s aluminium really was, ounce for ounce, the most expensive metal on Earth; gold and silver were common by comparison. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/aluminum-common-metal-uncommon-past/  (Legend.)

question: Aluminium is not rare. It is about 8% of the Earth's crust by mass and the commonest metal in it, ahead of iron. Yet for centuries no one held a piece of aluminium metal. What paradox did early chemists run into?
answer: Its oxygen bond is stronger than any wood-or-charcoal furnace on Earth can break
choices: Its atoms are so light they float out of hot ore as vapour and cannot be caught
Its oxygen bond is stronger than any wood-or-charcoal furnace on Earth can break
Its ore lies only deep on the sea floor, on ridges no 19th-century miner could reach
It is chemically bonded to gold in the crust, and no chemist could separate the two
context: Aluminium is the third most abundant element in the crust after oxygen and silicon, and the most abundant metal, but its bond to oxygen is so tight that the wood-and-charcoal furnaces that freed iron and copper for millennia simply cannot free aluminium. Source: https://www.chemicool.com/elements/aluminum.html

question: In 1827 a young German chemist reduced aluminium chloride with hot potassium metal and produced the first reliably reproducible sample of aluminium: a dull grey powder. A year later he shocked the field by making urea in a flask from starting materials no living thing had touched. Who was he?
answer: Friedrich Wohler
choices: Justus von Liebig
Friedrich Wohler
Robert Bunsen
August Kekule
context: Wohler followed up Hans Christian Orsted's 1825 attempt (which no one else could reproduce) and produced a fine grey powder on 22 October 1827. In 1828 he synthesised urea from ammonium cyanate, breaking the barrier between 'organic' and 'inorganic' chemistry. Source: https://rinconeducativo.org/en/recursos-educativos/friedrich-wohler-first-isolate-beryllium-and-aluminium-metal/

question: At the 1855 Paris Exposition Universelle, visitors filed past twelve small ingots of a silvery-white metal placed beside the French Crown Jewels and labelled 'silver made from clay'. Emperor Napoleon III had paid for their production, hoping to arm his soldiers with lightweight equipment. What was the metal, and who made the ingots?
answer: Aluminium ingots, produced by Henri Sainte-Claire Deville by reducing aluminium chloride with sodium
choices: Magnesium ingots, produced by Humphry Davy in London using a giant electrical battery
Aluminium ingots, produced by Henri Sainte-Claire Deville by reducing aluminium chloride with sodium
Titanium ingots, produced by William Gregor by carefully purifying black beach sand
Beryllium ingots, produced by Louis Vauquelin by reducing beryl in a bloomery fire
context: Deville, funded by Napoleon III, swapped Wohler's expensive potassium for cheaper sodium and by 1855 could pour ingots. His twelve bars were the sensation of the exposition and set beside the crown jewels; the 'clay' in the label was bauxite. Source: https://vedantaaluminium.com/blog/a-brief-history-of-aluminium-part-2/

question: On 6 December 1884 the Washington Monument was topped out with a cast pyramid of one metal, 100 ounces, about 8.9 inches tall. Before it was carried up, the pyramid was sent to Tiffany's jewellery store in New York and left in the display window for two days, so that visitors could later say they had stepped over the top of the Washington Monument. What was the metal?
answer: Aluminium
choices: Platinum
Silver
Aluminium
Tungsten
context: Frishmuth of Kensington cast the 100-ounce pyramid; the whole capstone commission cost about $225. Tiffany's kept it in the window for two days, valuable enough to sit there like a precious stone, and the National Park Service still notes the story. Source: https://www.tms.org/pubs/journals/jom/9511/binczewski-9511.html

question: In 1886, working independently within months of each other, two 22-year-old chemists on two different continents hit on the same trick and turned aluminium from an emperor's toy into a bulk industrial metal. The trick was to dissolve alumina in molten cryolite, so it melts far below its own melting point, and then run electric current through it. Who were the two young men, and what is the process still called?
answer: Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Heroult in France; the Hall-Heroult process
choices: Justus von Liebig in Germany and August Kekule in France; the Liebig-Kekule process
Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Heroult in France; the Hall-Heroult process
Humphry Davy in England and Michael Faraday in France; the Davy-Faraday process
William Perkin in England and Louis Pasteur in France; the Perkin-Pasteur process
context: Hall filed his American patent in July 1886; Heroult had filed a French patent in April 1886 for essentially the same idea. It is one of the classic cases of simultaneous independent discovery, and it dropped aluminium's price by two orders of magnitude within a generation. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/paul-heroult-and-charles-m-hall/

question: Freeing aluminium from ore by the Hall-Heroult route is one of the most electricity-hungry operations in industry; melting old cans and window frames back down needs far less energy. What fraction of the primary-smelting energy does recycling take, and what has that meant for the aluminium already produced?
answer: About 5%; roughly three-quarters of the aluminium ever produced is still in productive use
choices: About 30%; roughly half of the aluminium ever produced is still in productive use today
About 50%; nearly all the aluminium ever produced has been landfilled after a single use
About 15%; only a small share of the aluminium ever produced still remains in circulation
About 5%; roughly three-quarters of the aluminium ever produced is still in productive use
context: Recycling aluminium takes roughly 5% of the energy of primary smelting, a 95% saving. Aluminium buildings and vehicles have working lives of decades, and the metal is repeatedly re-melted, so around 75% of the almost billion metric tons of aluminium ever made is still in service. Source: https://international-aluminium.org/landing/aluminium-recycling-saves-95-of-the-energy-needed-for-primary-aluminium-production/

question: Dive 713 to the Galapagos Rift in February 1977 carried pilot Jack Donnelly and two named scientists -- Jack Corliss of Oregon State and Tjeerd van Andel of Stanford. What fields did the two of them work in?
answer: geologists and geochemists
choices: geologists and geochemists
marine biologists and ecologists
oceanographers and marine zoologists
microbiologists and physiologists
context: The whole cruise was funded by the National Science Foundation and staffed by geologists and geochemists -- not a single biologist was aboard when the vent ecosystem was found. The rule of biology got overturned by rock hunters. Source: https://www.whoi.edu/feature/history-hydrothermal-vents/discovery/1977.html  (Legend.)

question: On dive 713 in February 1977, the geologists aboard Alvin radioed up a nickname for the very first vent site they saw -- a nickname that stuck in the record and is still used today. What did they call it?
answer: Clambake 1
choices: Clambake 1
Poseidon Field
Riftia Ridge
Site Alpha
context: The name came from clusters of white bivalves up to 30 centimetres long spread across roughly 50 metres of fresh lava. Riftia is the tube worm genus discovered later; Poseidon is the tallest chimney at a completely different field found decades on; Site Alpha is a distractor. Source: https://divediscover.whoi.edu/archives/ventcd/vent_discovery/thediscovery/trail_77_page5.html

question: The Galapagos Rift ecosystem sat 2.5 kilometres down in permanent darkness, and it was thriving. Every biology textbook of 1977 taught one universal rule about where the energy for animal life must ultimately come from -- a rule this scene broke. Which rule?
answer: all food chains begin with photosynthesis
choices: all food chains begin with photosynthesis
all life ultimately runs on free oxygen
only sunlit surface water can support large animals
no ecosystem can live on inorganic chemistry alone
context: Photosynthesis at the base of the food web was treated as universal. Chemosynthesis itself was not new -- Sergei Winogradsky described chemosynthetic bacteria in the 1880s -- but no one had ever seen a whole ECOSYSTEM built on it independent of the sun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis

question: If sunlight is not the meal on the Galapagos Rift, what is? At the base of the vent food web, bacteria pull energy out of one dissolved chemical in the vent fluid and use it to build sugar. Which chemical are they eating?
answer: hydrogen sulfide
choices: hydrogen sulfide
carbon dioxide
liquid methane
dissolved iron
context: This is chemosynthesis: 18 H2S + 6 CO2 + 3 O2 -> C6H12O6 + 12 H2O + 18 S. The bacteria oxidise the sulfide and fix the CO2 into sugar, producing solid sulfur instead of oxygen. Sergei Winogradsky described chemosynthetic bacteria in the 1880s -- what 1977 overturned was that a whole ECOSYSTEM could run on it without the sun. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis

question: The 1977 cruise was geological, so the ship carried almost no biological preservatives. When the one student's small bottle of formaldehyde ran out and the crew still had giant clams and tube worms coming up, what did they preserve the specimens in?
answer: Russian vodka bought on the way through Panama
choices: Russian vodka bought on the way through Panama
shipboard isopropyl alcohol from the medical kit
ice-chilled seawater in sealed glass jars
diesel fuel drawn from the engine room
