context: The vodka story is a widely retold expedition anecdote -- flagged legend. Isopropyl alcohol is too dilute and denatures proteins wrong; iced seawater rots specimens fast; diesel would destroy tissue outright. The point of the rung is the improvisation, not the chemistry. Source: https://scienceblog.com/t-deep-sea-dive-hydrothermal-vents-ecosystem-without-sunlight/

question: One vent animal made the puzzle unmissable: Riftia pachyptila, the giant tube worm, reaches three metres long and grows faster than any other known marine invertebrate. Dissect an adult and one whole body system is simply not there. Which system does an adult Riftia lack?
answer: a digestive tract
choices: a digestive tract
a circulatory system
a nervous system
a body cavity
context: Adult Riftia has no mouth, no gut and no anus -- it cannot eat anything. It does have a heart, nerves and a coelom. That is exactly what made the animal such a good clue: whatever was feeding it was not being swallowed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftia_pachyptila  (Legend.)

question: In a Harvard seminar, Meredith Jones of the Smithsonian was describing the mouthless Riftia and mentioned finding crystals of pure elemental sulfur inside the worm. A first-year graduate student stood up in the audience and solved it on the spot. Who was she?
answer: Colleen Cavanaugh
choices: Colleen Cavanaugh
Lynn Margulis
Rosalind Franklin
Ruth Patrick
context: Cavanaugh jumped up during the talk, announced she had it, and Jones handed her a specimen to work on. She would be lead author on the 1981 Science paper that pinned the mechanism down. Source: https://loe.org/shows/segments.html?programID=10-P13-00007&segmentID=8  (Legend.)

question: Colleen Cavanaugh's 1981 paper, published while she was still a graduate student, pinned down how the giant Galapagos tube worm Riftia pachyptila stays alive at all. What did she find living inside the worm, and where?
answer: sulfur-oxidising bacteria packed into a spongy organ called the trophosome
choices: sulfur-oxidising bacteria packed into a spongy organ called the trophosome
archaea in the plume tissue metabolising methane from the vent fluid
symbiotic algae in the plume doing chemosynthesis in the dark
digestive bacteria hiding in a tiny vestigial gut along the trunk
context: The trophosome fills most of the trunk and houses billions of sulfur-oxidising bacteria plus stored sulfur granules -- the worm is essentially a farm and the trophosome is the field. The red plume is highly vascularised and packed with haemoglobin that ferries hydrogen sulfide and oxygen down to the tenants. Cavanaugh, C.M.; Gardiner, S.L.; Jones, M.L.; Jannasch, H.W.; Waterbury, J.B. (1981). 'Prokaryotic Cells in the Hydrothermal Vent Tube Worm Riftia pachyptila Jones: Possible Chemoautotrophic Symbionts.' Science 213(4505): 340-342. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleen_Cavanaugh

question: On December 4, 2000, Alvin was diving on the Atlantis Massif near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge when it lit up a field unlike anything found before: white carbonate chimneys, the tallest 60 metres high, driven by no magma at all. What is that field called?
answer: Lost City
choices: Lost City
Clambake 2
Snake Pit
Rainbow
context: Lost City is alkaline, its fluids only 40-90 C, and it is powered by SERPENTINIZATION -- seawater reacting with olivine in mantle rock to produce hydrogen and methane, no magma heat needed. Its chimneys are aragonite, brucite and calcite. Snake Pit and Rainbow are real Mid-Atlantic vent fields but different sites. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_City_Hydrothermal_Field

question: Three men sheltered in Apollo 13's lunar module, and its lithium hydroxide canisters -- the cartridges that scrub carbon dioxide from the air -- were filling up. The dark command module up front had canisters of its own. Why could the men not swap them in?
answer: They were square; the lunar module's sockets were round
choices: They were square; the lunar module's sockets were round
They were spent, saturated on the outbound coast
They ran on command module power, and it was gone
They were stowed behind panels no one could open
context: NASA's own mission summary says it flatly: 'Square command module canisters adapted to LM's round openings by using plastic bags, cardboard and tape.' Because the crew were sheltering in Aquarius, Aquarius's own cylindrical canisters saturated first -- and the cubic spares sitting a few feet away simply would not go in. Robert 'Ed' Smylie of NASA's Crew Systems Division led about sixty engineers who had under two days to design an adapter from nothing but what was already aboard; they worked from a computer printout of the onboard inventory, not from the box of parts dumped on a table in the film. Smylie's summary: 'You can't put a square peg in a round hole, and that's what we had.' He died on 21 April 2025, aged 95. Sources: nasa.gov/missions/apollo/apollo-13-mission-details/ ; Space Center Houston CO2-scrubber infographic; AP obituary via gvwire.com (17 May 2025); hackaday.com (18 May 2025) for the printout.

question: Apollo 13 never landed on the Moon. Yet Jim Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert came home holding a human record that stood for more than fifty-five years, until another crew finally passed it in April 2026. Which record?
answer: the greatest distance from Earth ever reached by humans
choices: the greatest distance from Earth ever reached by humans
the greatest number of hours humans have spent in lunar orbit
the greatest speed at which humans have ever re-entered
the greatest number of days an Apollo crew spent in flight
context: 400,171 km -- 248,655 miles. Nobody set out to set it; it fell out of an emergency, a side effect of the wide loop that carried the crippled ship home. It stood until the Artemis II crew passed the mark on 6 April 2026. Sources: NASA news release, 'NASA's Artemis II crew eclipses record for farthest human spaceflight'; Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'.

question: Fifty-six hours out and 330,000 km from Earth, something let go in Apollo 13's service module. The crew heard the bang. But the first specific fault they named to Houston was not a noise and not a leak -- it was an instrument reading. Which one?
answer: a voltage drop on the Main B electrical bus
choices: a voltage drop on the Main B electrical bus
a master alarm from the guidance computer
a low-quantity warning on the hydrogen tank
a pressure surge in the descent-stage helium
context: The tank let go at 55:54:53 mission elapsed time (14 April 1970, 03:08 UTC). Twenty-six seconds later Jack Swigert reported the trouble, and Jim Lovell followed by naming it: 'We've had a Main B Bus undervolt.' Worth noticing what that means about how a spacecraft is diagnosed: the first hard evidence of the worst accident in crewed spaceflight was a sagging bus voltage on a meter -- an electrical symptom of an oxygen tank rupture nobody could see. Source: Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'.

question: Jim Lovell looked out of Apollo 13's window and saw gas streaming away into space. Nobody aboard knew yet what had failed, and Houston was still sorting the readings. What did the crew first believe had happened to them?
answer: a meteoroid had punched through the hull
choices: a meteoroid had punched through the hull
a fuel cell had ruptured inside its bay
the docking hatch seal had blown open
a helium tank's burst disc had let go
context: A bang plus visible venting looks exactly like something arriving from outside, so the crew's first hypothesis was a meteoroid strike. The trouble was inside the ship. The other options here are not inventions: the descent stage's helium tank pressure had been suspect since before launch and kept climbing, and Mission Control predicted when its burst disc would give way -- it did, at 108:54, harmlessly and on schedule. Two of the three fuel cells did die, but as a consequence of losing the oxygen, not as its cause. Sources: Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'; NASA Apollo Flight Journal, Apollo 13 Day 3.

question: With carbon dioxide climbing, CAPCOM Joe Kerwin read Apollo 13 a shopping list of things already aboard: two command module canisters, a roll of grey tape, one lunar module cue card, and two liquid cooling garments -- the water-cooled underwear worn beneath a spacesuit. Houston did not want the crew to put those on. It wanted one piece of that kit. Which piece?
answer: the plastic bags they were stowed in
choices: the plastic bags they were stowed in
the water tubing sewn through them
the rubber seals around their collars
the cotton liners fitted inside them
context: Kerwin's list, read up at 090:09:17 mission elapsed time: 'two Command Module lithium hydroxide canisters, a roll of the gray tape, the two LCGs, because we're going to use the bags from the LCGs, and one -- one LM cue card.' Two details of the popular telling get corrected by the primary transcript: the garments were wanted for their stowage bags, not to be worn or cut up, and the famous 'plastic cover ripped off a flight manual' is, in the transcript, a lunar module cue card. Source: NASA Apollo Flight Journal, Apollo 13 Day 4 Part 4, 'Building The CO2 Adapter'.

question: Apollo 13's crew taped their carbon dioxide adapter together from a command module canister, a cue card and a roll of grey tape. In the middle of the square canister's face sat a bypass opening that would let air slip past the lithium hydroxide instead of through it, and Joe Kerwin read up a short list of things aboard that would plug it. What did the crew push into that hole?
answer: a towel
choices: a towel
a sock
a wet wipe
a wad of tape
context: The bypass matters because of what it does to the flow: unless it is blocked, air takes the easy route and never has to pass through the lithium hydroxide, so the scrubber does nothing however well it is taped. Kerwin's offer, at 090:44:13 mission elapsed time: 'we recommend that you either use a wet wipe, or cut off a piece of sock and stuff it in there, or you could probably even crumble up some tape.' The crew reached for a towel instead, and Kerwin answered, 'Sounds good.' So the sock of the popular telling was one of three suggestions from the ground, not the part that actually flew -- and the physics point survives either way. Once the adapter was running, carbon dioxide partial pressure fell from about 15 mmHg and 'remained below 2mm Hg for the remainder of the Earth-return trip.' Sources: NASA Apollo Flight Journal, Apollo 13 Day 4 Part 4, 'Building The CO2 Adapter'; Universe Today interview with Jerry Woodfill, who designed the caution-and-warning system.

question: About thirty hours out, Apollo 13 traded the path it launched on for a course that would reach the Fra Mauro highlands. After the tank blew, Mission Control's first order was a 34-second burn to put the ship back on that abandoned path -- a path that brings a ship home with no further burn at all. What supplies the turn?
answer: the Moon's gravity, bending the ship into a loop home
choices: the Moon's gravity, bending the ship into a loop home
the Earth's gravity, hauling the ship back once it slows
the Sun's gravity, drawing the ship around a wide arc
the ship's own speed, coasting it around and home
context: That path has a name: a free-return trajectory, aimed so that the Moon's own gravity does all the work of turning the ship around. Space historian Andrew Chaikin: 'the moon's gravity will bend your flight path around the moon in a kind of a figure-8 loop, and send you back to Earth.' Apollo 13 had traded it at about 30:40 mission elapsed time for a 'hybrid' trajectory that reached the Fra Mauro landing site -- and on that hybrid path, coasting without an engine would have missed Earth by roughly 2,600 miles. Being off free return is precisely why a burn was not optional. (The 2,600-mile figure is history.com citing Chaikin; the free-return swap is in the NASA/Wikipedia mission record.) Sources: history.com, 'Apollo 13 slingshot around the Moon'; Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'.

question: Two burns brought Apollo 13 home: a short one to restore a safe return path, and a longer one of four minutes twenty-three seconds that cut about twelve hours off the trip and moved the splashdown to where the recovery ships were waiting. The service module's big engine sat directly behind the wrecked bay and was never trusted again. What fired both burns?
answer: the lunar module's descent engine, built to land on the Moon
choices: the lunar module's descent engine, built to land on the Moon
the lunar module's ascent engine, built to leave the Moon
the lunar module's steering thrusters, fired in long bursts
the command module's own thrusters, fired in long bursts
context: Both burns used the lunar module's descent propulsion system -- the engine designed to set Aquarius gently onto Fra Mauro, now pushing a whole docked spacecraft. Burn one fired at 61:29:43.49 for 34.23 seconds. Burn two, called PC+2 because it came two hours past pericynthion (the closest point of the lunar flyby), fired at 79:27:38.95 for 4 minutes 23 seconds and added about 860.5 ft/s, moving the splashdown from the Indian Ocean to the South Pacific. Sources: Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'; AmericaSpace, 'We Show You on the Mains'; Grokipedia, 'Free-return trajectory' (860 ft/s = 262 m/s).

question: In 1965 NASA more than doubled the voltage of the ground equipment at Kennedy Space Center, so that oxygen tanks could be filled and emptied faster on the pad. Every part of Apollo 13's oxygen tank 2 that would carry that current was requalified to the new level -- except one, which nobody caught for five years. Which part was left at the old rating?
answer: the two thermostatic switches that guarded the heaters
choices: the two thermostatic switches that guarded the heaters
the motor windings of the stirring fan inside the tank
the quantity sensor that read the tank's fill level
the heating elements coiled along the tank's inner wall
context: The switches were built to a 1962 specification of 28 volts -- the spacecraft's own DC bus voltage -- while the 1965 revision put ground supply at 65 volts. Beech Aircraft, which made the tank, installed switches not rated for 65 volts, and the mismatch then sat sealed inside a tank where no flight instrument could ever see it. The Cortright board's verdict is a sentence about engineering, not luck: the accident 'was not the result of a chance malfunction in a statistical sense but, rather, it was the result of an unusual combination of mistakes coupled with a somewhat deficient and unforgiving design.' The board then finished the experiment by changing the hardware: for Apollo 14 NASA added a third oxygen tank in a different bay, fitted thermostats that could survive ground voltage, removed the stirring fans from the tanks altogether and sheathed the internal wiring in stainless steel -- a redesign that slipped the launch from October 1970 to January 1971. Sources: NASA history, '50 Years Ago: Apollo 13 Review Board Report'; Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'; Grokipedia agrees the thermostats were not updated for the 28V-to-65V change.

question: Coming home, Apollo 13's path drifted shallow and needed one more correction -- but the lunar module's guidance computer was switched off, so there was nothing to aim by except the window. Jim Lovell flew the attitude by hand while Fred Haise worked the throttle. What did the two of them use as their aiming mark?
answer: the crescent Earth, its lit horn on the reticle
choices: the crescent Earth, its lit horn on the reticle
a pair of bright stars in the overhead window
the Sun's disc centred in the optical telescope
the Moon's limb crossing the hatch window frame
context: Haise described the sight picture at 103:50:21: they would hold 'the partial Earth, the lit portion laying in the top half of the COAS with the cusp laying right on the Y-Y line' -- the crescent Earth parked in a gunsight reticle with its horn on a crosshair. The burn came at about 105:18:32, roughly 14 to 15 seconds at 10 percent throttle for 7.6 ft/s. Haise afterwards: 'I'd say I put in maybe about six or seven inputs. I don't think it ever got off more than a couple of needle widths.' Source: NASA Apollo Flight Journal, Apollo 13 Day 5 Part 3, 'The Manual Course Correction Burn'.

question: Two weeks before launch, technicians at Kennedy could not empty oxygen tank 2, so they switched its internal heaters on for about eight hours to boil the liquid oxygen away, watching the tank's temperature readout the whole time. The readout showed nothing abnormal. Inside, the heater tubes may have reached 540 degrees C, burning the insulation off the wiring. How did the gauge miss that?
answer: its scale simply stopped a little above room temperature
choices: its scale simply stopped a little above room temperature
it sampled the gas at the vent, not the metal of the tubes
it was calibrated for flight, not for ground power runs
it averaged each reading over a full hour of running
context: The tank's temperature readout topped out at about 29 degrees C (85 degrees F). While the heater tubes climbed toward 540 degrees C, the needle sat pinned at its maximum and every technician watching it saw a perfectly normal tank. The instrument meant to catch the problem was blind to the size of it -- and the tank was then loaded and flown with bare wire inside. It is a lesson worth carrying out of the story: an instrument reading 'normal' can mean the fault is off the end of the scale. (Date note: the sources disagree on exactly when the boil-off ran -- Wikipedia and the Cortright account give 27 March 1970, NASA's fiftieth-anniversary piece dates the detanking problem to 25 March, PopSci says 30 March -- so the stem keeps to 'two weeks before launch'.) Sources: Wikipedia 'Apollo 13' ('The temperature gauge only read to 29 degC'); NASA history, '50 Years Ago: Apollo 13 Review Board Report' ('undetected because temperature gauges maxed out at 85 degF').

question: No one had ever brought an Apollo command module back to life from cold and dead, because no one had ever meant to try. Ken Mattingly -- pulled off the crew two days before launch over a rubella exposure -- flew the command module simulator with flight controller John Aaron, and in under two days the two of them wrote a 39-page checklist of about 400 steps, to be executed once, cold, correctly. What were they hunting for, run after run?
answer: an order of switch throws that would not overdraw the batteries
choices: an order of switch throws that would not overdraw the batteries
a sequence that would not overheat the guidance computer
a start-up that skipped the wrecked service module entirely
a path through the panels the crew could follow in the dark
context: John Aaron set the power budget and Mattingly flew the simulator until he found an order of switch throws that fitted inside it -- a job that would normally take three months, finished in under two days. AmericaSpace: 'Mattingly and Swigert plunged into a 39-page, 400-step checklist, which established every switch throw and keystroke needed to bring Odyssey back from the dead.' The arithmetic was brutal: the command module's three re-entry batteries held about 40 amp-hours each -- and one of the three was only about half charged -- against the 70 to 80 amp-hours a normal re-entry draws. Aaron had also cut the lunar module's draw from roughly 60 amps to about 12, and the crew even ran the umbilical backwards to feed lunar module power into command module battery A. Mattingly, who was grounded because he was the only astronaut in either crew without immunity, never developed rubella at all, and later flew Apollo 16. Sources: AmericaSpace, 'Our Finest Hour: Remembering Apollo 13, 50 Years On' part 4; Universe Today, 'Charging the batteries'; Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'.

question: Apollo 13's lunar module, Aquarius, had oxygen to spare -- more than twenty-eight pounds of it were still aboard when the crew finally cast it off. What ran dangerously short was water, and not because three men were thirsty: Aquarius cooled its electronics by throwing water overboard into vacuum, and early projections had the supply running out about five hours before re-entry. How did losing that water take the heat with it?
answer: it froze in a plate's pores, then went straight to vapour and blew away
choices: it froze in a plate's pores, then went straight to vapour and blew away
it soaked up the heat and was pumped out warm through a hull valve
it was sprayed into the vacuum, where it flashed at once into steam
it ran to radiator panels on the hull and boiled away in the sunlight
context: The device is called a sublimator. Water is fed into porous plates that are open to space; because the pressure out there is below water's triple point, an ice layer forms in the pores, and hot coolant flowing past the plate makes that ice sublimate straight from solid to vapour and blow overboard, carrying the heat away with it. Every watt the electronics burned was therefore paid for in water thrown into space. So the crew drank less -- about 6 fluid ounces (200 mL) each per day, roughly a fifth of normal -- and the three of them lost 31.5 pounds between them, Lovell alone 14. The arithmetic came out on the right side: Apollo 13 splashed down with 28.2 pounds of water still aboard, about 9 percent of the supply. Note what was never the crisis: there were still 28.5 pounds of oxygen left at jettison. Carbon dioxide, electrical power and water nearly killed them. Air never did. Sources: NASA Apollo Experience Report, 'Lunar Module Environmental Control Subsystem' (NTRS 19720013195); nasa.gov Apollo 13 mission details; Wikipedia 'Apollo 13'.

question: Two weeks before launch, oxygen tank 2 refused to empty: eighty psi of gaseous oxygen down the vent line still left the liquid sitting at about 92 percent full. That refusal is why technicians reached for the heaters, and the heaters are why the wiring cooked. The Cortright board traced the trouble back to October 1968. What had gone wrong then?
answer: a crew hoisted an oxygen shelf with a bolt still in and dropped it two inches
choices: a crew hoisted an oxygen shelf with a bolt still in and dropped it two inches
technicians overfilled an oxygen tank on the test stand and vented it for an hour
a welder rebuilt a fill line and left a bead of metal in the pipe
a fitter installed a stirring fan backwards and never pulled it out
context: The shelf was being lifted out of Apollo 10's service module for modification, and one retaining bolt had not been removed. The shelf caught, then dropped about two inches. Engineers calculated the loads, judged that nothing had been damaged, and the tank went into Apollo 13's service module in November 1968. The board concluded that the jarring probably displaced a fill-tube assembly that had been loose since it was manufactured at Beech's Boulder, Colorado plant -- which is exactly why the tank could not be emptied normally seventeen months later, which is why the heaters were run, which is why the insulation burned off the wires. This is what failure analysis buys you: not a villain, but a chain, published so the next crew does not fly it. Sources: NASA history, '50 Years Ago: Apollo 13 Review Board Report'; PopSci Vintage Space, 'The recipe for Apollo 13's disaster'.

question: In Syracuse in the third century BC, Archimedes reportedly boasted that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could shift one particular object of astonishing size. What did he name?
answer: The whole Earth
choices: The whole Earth
The Great Pyramid at Giza
Mount Etna in Sicily
The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
context: The line survives as 'Dos moi pa sto, kai tan gan kinaso' -- 'Give me a place to stand and I shall move the Earth.' It is quoted by Pappus of Alexandria in Book VIII of his Synagoge, written c. AD 340, roughly 500 years after Archimedes died; it appears nowhere in Archimedes' own surviving writings. Sources: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Archimedes ; math.nyu.edu/Archimedes/Lever/LeverIntro.html  (Legend.)

question: Plutarch tells a story to satisfy King Hiero II of Syracuse, who wanted proof Archimedes' lever principle could really do practical work. Archimedes drew a fully loaded warship out of the water by himself, using one hand-worked mechanical device. Which device does Plutarch name?
answer: A compound pulley
choices: A compound pulley
A large screw-jack of his own design
A windlass turned by a single crank
A system of iron levers braced against the quay
context: Plutarch's Life of Marcellus reports Archimedes drew the loaded ship single-handed with a compound pulley -- a block-and-tackle in which each extra sheave trades force for a longer haul of rope. Athenaeus tells a rival version in which the ship was the enormous Syracusia and the launch used a different device -- the two ancient sources disagree, so this is late story, not eyewitness fact. The point that survives it: pulleys, like levers, buy force by spending distance. Sources: worldhistory.org/Syracusia ; tmindset.substack.com/p/he-didnt-pull-harder  (Legend.)

question: In his treatise On the Equilibrium of Planes, Archimedes did not tell a story about the lever -- he PROVED it, in the geometric style of Euclid. What did his proof establish about two weights on the two arms of a balanced lever?
answer: They balance when weight times arm-length is equal on each side
choices: They balance when weight times arm-length is equal on each side
They balance only when both weights are exactly equal
They balance when the heavier weight sits on the longer arm
They balance when the total length of both arms equals the fulcrum's height
context: On the Equilibrium of Planes, Book I, Propositions 6 and 7: magnitudes balance at distances inversely proportional to their weights. Formally, w*d = w'*d'. Archimedes derives it from a handful of Euclid-style postulates, the first being that equal weights at equal distances balance. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Equilibrium_of_Planes ; mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Archimedes_on_statics

question: Archimedes' lever law hides a stern accountant. If a child on a seesaw pushes down with only one tenth the force needed to lift her heavier friend, the law lets her win -- but only if she pays a price on her own end. What price?
answer: Her end must travel ten times as far as her friend rises
choices: Her end must travel ten times as far as her friend rises
Her end of the bar must weigh ten times more than her friend's end
She must push in ten smooth, timed bursts to build enough momentum
The fulcrum must be lubricated to shed ten-tenths of the friction
context: This is the force-distance trade, and it is a statement of conservation of energy: work in equals work out. Every simple machine -- lever, pulley, wedge, ramp, screw, wheel-and-axle -- multiplies force only by demanding a matching multiplication of distance. None of them creates energy; each spends it differently. Kid-replicable: balance a ruler on a pencil with coins on each end, slide the pencil off-center, and feel the trade in your fingers. Sources: openstax.org/books/physics/pages/9-3-simple-machines ; energyeducation.ca/encyclopedia/Simple_machine

question: A separate legend about Archimedes -- that at the siege of Syracuse in 212 BC he set Roman warships on fire with focused sunlight -- has been tested by MIT students in 2005 and by MythBusters in 2010, aiming hundreds of mirrors at a stationary wooden mock-up. What did the modern tests actually produce?
answer: Smoke and scorching but no sustained blaze
choices: Smoke and scorching but no sustained blaze
A clean, fast fire exactly as the legend describes
Nothing at all -- the mirrors never focused enough light
An explosion strong enough to shatter the mock-up
context: The 'burning mirrors' story is not mentioned by Polybius, Livy, or Plutarch -- the earliest historians of the siege -- and first surfaces centuries later. The MIT 2.009 team scorched a wooden hull after ten still, cloudless minutes at 30 metres; MythBusters got smoulder from bronze mirrors on a replica ship in San Francisco Bay but no sustained fire. With moving ships and damp timber in a real sea-battle, the effect collapses. A useful reminder that a story about Archimedes is not the same thing as a proof by Archimedes. Sources: livescience.com/8383 ; web.mit.edu/2.009_gallery/www/2005_other/archimedes/10_Mythbusters.html  (Legend.)

question: Take Archimedes' boast at his word and run the arithmetic. Suppose he wants to shift Earth (mass about 6 x 10^24 kg) by a single centimetre with an ordinary lever, his own body weight on one end. Which move does the lever law itself DEMAND -- and which are wrong turns a kid might reach for?
answer: Push his own end through a distance and a time vastly beyond a human life
choices: Push his own end through a distance and a time vastly beyond a human life
Set the fulcrum closer to Earth than to himself, to shorten his own arm
Push down faster, converting his motion into extra force
Add a second lever in series to double the mechanical advantage for free
context: The arithmetic is exact. To lift Earth by 1 cm at a mechanical advantage set by weight-ratio ~10^23, Archimedes' end of the lever would have to sweep through roughly 10^21 metres -- far larger than the Milky Way -- and at any human walking pace that takes vastly more than the age of the universe. The other three are the classic force-distance confusions: shortening HIS arm makes the trade worse, not better; pushing faster changes power, not the force the law requires; and chaining two levers just spends the same distance twice -- no simple machine ever creates energy. Which is why the boast is poetry, not engineering -- but the LAW it rests on is exactly right, and still runs every crowbar, wheelbarrow, and pair of scissors in the kitchen. Sources: openstax.org/books/physics/pages/9-3-simple-machines ; math.nyu.edu/Archimedes/Lever/LeverLaw.html

question: A steel nail dropped in a bucket sinks at once - steel is eight times heavier than water for its size. Yet a cargo ship of the same steel floats. What keeps it up?
answer: Its hull traps so much air that the whole ship averages lighter than water
choices: Its hull traps so much air that the whole ship averages lighter than water
Its curved plates spread the ship's weight over a far wider patch of sea
Sea salt makes water dense enough to hold up steel plate of any size
Its paint seals the hull so completely that water never soaks the steel
context: Steel's specific gravity is about 7.8 - roughly 7,800 kilograms per cubic metre against water's 1,000 - so a solid lump of it sinks every time. A ship gets around that by shape alone: the hull encloses an enormous volume of air, dragging the AVERAGE density of the whole vessel below 1. Grokipedia puts it exactly this way: 'steel ships, despite steel's high specific gravity of around 7.8 relative to water, achieve an effective specific gravity below 1 through their large enclosed volume of air.' Nothing about the steel changed - the vessel's average did. Source: Grokipedia, 'Buoyancy' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Buoyancy

question: A raw egg lowered into a glass of tap water sinks to the bottom. Stir in five spoonfuls of salt, lower the same egg back in, and it rides at the surface. The egg itself was never altered. What did the salt do?
answer: It packed extra weight into every cupful of water
choices: It packed extra weight into every cupful of water
It thickened the water enough to hold the shell up
It filled the water with bubbles that cling to the shell
It settled into a dense layer for the egg to rest upon
context: A raw egg is slightly denser than tap water, so it sinks. Dissolved salt adds mass to the water without adding much volume, and three to six tablespoons stirred into a warm glass push the water's density past the egg's. Density is just weight for a given amount of space - and a thing floats when the fluid around it is denser than it is. This one costs nothing to run in a kitchen tonight, and the point is worth watching for: the egg is the same egg. The FLUID is what you changed. Source: Science Buddies / Scientific American, 'Salty Science: Floating Eggs in Water' - https://www.sciencebuddies.org/stem-activities/salty-science-floating-eggs-in-water

question: Hold a sealed steel drum under the sea and it fights you the whole time, the still water shoving it back toward the surface. Let go and it goes. What sets the size of that upward push?
answer: The weight of the seawater the drum takes the place of
choices: The weight of the seawater the drum takes the place of
The weight of the seawater standing in a column above it
The weight of the drum and everything sealed inside it
The depth beneath the surface at which the drum is held
context: This is Archimedes' principle, set down in his work On Floating Bodies in the 3rd century BCE: a fluid pushes UP on anything wholly or partly immersed in it with a force exactly equal to the weight of the fluid that body DISPLACES - that is, shoves out of the way. Written out, F_B = rho_f x V x g, where rho_f is the fluid's density, V the displaced volume and g gravity. Seawater runs about 1,025 kilograms per cubic metre, so one cubic metre displaced yields about 10,056 newtons - roughly 1.025 tonnes of upward shove from a box of water a metre on a side. The object floats if its weight is less than that push and sinks if it is greater. Source: Grokipedia, 'Archimedes' principle' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Archimedes'_principle

question: Galileo Galilei was 22 when he wrote a short 1586 treatise called La Bilancetta - 'The Little Balance'. In it he takes up the familiar account of how the gold in a royal wreath was tested, in which the wreath is dunked in water and the spilt water measured. What was his verdict on that method?
answer: A crude thing, far from scientific precision
choices: A crude thing, far from scientific precision
An ingenious trick, but fit only for a craftsman
A sound test that later copyists garbled badly
A tale invented to flatter the king who ordered it
context: Galileo's phrase is exact: he calls the dunk-and-measure story 'a crude thing, far from scientific precision' - too rough, he thought, for a mathematician of Archimedes' rank. He then offered a replacement he believed was the real thing: 'a method came to my mind which very accurately solves our problem. I think it probable that this method is the same that Archimedes followed, since, besides being very accurate, it is based on demonstrations found by Archimedes himself.' Worth knowing honestly: the wreath episode appears nowhere in Archimedes' surviving On Floating Bodies, which is two books of pure geometry and never mentions a crown at all. It reaches us only through Vitruvius's De Architectura, written in the 1st century BCE - nearly two centuries after Archimedes died around 212 BCE - and the bath scene is likely apocryphal. Sources: Chris Rorres, 'The Golden Crown: La Bilancetta' - https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/bilancetta.html ; Grokipedia, 'On Floating Bodies' - https://grokipedia.com/page/On_Floating_Bodies

question: Chris Rorres, the mathematician who reconstructed the crown problem, ran the celebrated bath test on paper: 1,000 grams of pure gold lowered into a bowl 20 centimetres across, then a 1,000-gram wreath cut with silver lowered into the same bowl, the water level read off each time. His verdict was that Archimedes could never have caught a goldsmith this way. Where does the test break down?
answer: The two water levels differ by under half a millimetre
choices: The wet metal carries off a spoonful of water every dunk
The two water levels differ by under half a millimetre
The two metals shove aside water within a grain of each other
The bowl's rim holds back a tenth of what should spill over
context: Gold packs 19.3 grams into every cubic centimetre; silver only 10.5, barely half. So 1,000 grams of pure gold fills about 51.8 cubic centimetres, while the same 1,000 grams of a wreath that is 70% gold and 30% silver fills about a quarter more room. Dunk each in a bowl 20 centimetres across - a cross-section of 314 square centimetres - and the levels rise 0.165 cm for the gold and 0.206 cm for the wreath: a difference of 0.41 millimetres, thinner than a credit card. Rorres calls it 'much too small a difference to accurately observe directly or measure the overflow,' and told Scientific American: 'The volumetric method works in theory so it sounds right but when you actually try it you find that the real world gets in the way.' Wetting and spilling are real nuisances too - but they are not what sinks this test. The numbers were hopeless before anyone touched the bowl. Sources: Chris Rorres, 'The Golden Crown' - https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/CrownIntro.html ; Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: Archimedes Coined the Term Eureka! in the Bath'

question: Galileo's Little Balance never cuts or melts the metal. Hang 1,000 grams of pure gold from one arm and a 1,000-gram wreath cut with silver from the other, and in air the beam sits perfectly level. Now lower both until they hang under water. The beam tips. By how much do the two now disagree?
answer: About 13 grams
choices: About 13 grams
About 2 grams
About 48 grams
About 115 grams
context: Submerged, the alloyed wreath reads 935.2 grams and the pure gold 948.2 - 'an imbalance of 13.0 grams,' as Rorres puts it, and he notes that 'Scales from Archimedes' time could easily detect' a gap that size. The bulkier wreath loses more apparent weight because it shoves aside more water. Galileo stated the rule himself: 'solid bodies that sink in water weigh in water so much less than in air as is the weight in air of a volume of water equal to that of the body.' The same fraud that hid inside a fraction of a millimetre of water level shows up as 13 whole grams on a beam - and you can run the principle at home with a kitchen scale and a mug: weight in air minus weight in water, divided by water's density, gives you any object's volume without touching it. Sources: Chris Rorres, 'The Golden Crown' - https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/CrownIntro.html ; 'The Golden Crown: La Bilancetta' - https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/bilancetta.html

question: In a still tank the water squeezes a hanging block from every direction at once - top, bottom and all four sides. Yet the block is shoved upward, and not at all sideways. Which property of still water produces that?
answer: Its pressure grows with depth, so the lower faces are pressed hardest
choices: Its pressure grows with depth, so the lower faces are pressed hardest
It clings to a solid's underside and drags it upward as it settles
It is slightly elastic, and springs back against whatever compresses it
It refuses to leave a gap, and rushes underneath whatever hangs in it
context: Water does not 'know' what it displaced - there is no bookkeeping. Pressure in a still fluid rises with depth as P = rho_f x g x h + P_0. The block's bottom face sits deeper than its top, where the water squeezes harder, while pressures on opposite side faces are equal and cancel completely. Only the vertical mismatch survives, and Grokipedia states the result: 'the upward force on the bottom exceeds the downward force on the top by an amount equal to rho_f g h A.' Add that mismatch up over the whole surface and it comes out EXACTLY equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. The fourth choice is horror vacui - 'nature abhors a vacuum' - which serious people held for centuries and which is not what is happening here. Source: Grokipedia, 'Archimedes' principle' (Physical Mechanism / Buoyant Force Components) - https://grokipedia.com/page/Archimedes'_principle

question: Helium weighs 0.178 kilograms per cubic metre; the sea-level air around it weighs about 1.2. A helium balloon tugs its string toward the ceiling. Carry that balloon into a chamber - imagine its skin stiff enough not to burst - pump out every trace of air, and let go of the string. What does it do?
answer: It falls straight to the floor
choices: It falls straight to the floor
It climbs faster than it did before
It hangs exactly where it was let go
It climbs at the same steady rate
context: Lift on a balloon is L = (rho_air - rho_gas) x g x V - the weight of air shoved aside minus the weight of the gas inside. Pump the air out and rho_air goes to zero: there is nothing left to displace, no push at all, and the balloon's own small weight simply pulls it down. That is the whole point. Buoyancy is not a water law, it is a FLUID law, and air is a fluid; a helium balloon rises for the identical reason a cork held underwater does - the stuff it shoves aside outweighs it. A hot air balloon carries no helium whatever: its burner simply thins the air inside the envelope to about 0.9 kilograms per cubic metre against the 1.2 outside. Source: Grokipedia, 'Buoyancy' (Balloons and Lighter-Than-Air Craft) - https://grokipedia.com/page/Buoyancy

question: Around 402 AD Synesius of Cyrene wrote to the teacher he had studied under in Alexandria, asking for an instrument to be built: a sealed tube 'which has the shape of a flute', weighted at one end so that it floats upright, its side scored with 'notches in a perpendicular line' - by which, he wrote, 'we are able to test the weight of the waters'. That letter is the earliest surviving description of a hydrometer. Which Alexandrian was he writing to?
answer: Hypatia of Alexandria
choices: Theon of Alexandria
Hypatia of Alexandria
Pappus of Alexandria
Diophantus of Alexandria
context: Hypatia of Alexandria - mathematician, astronomer and head of the Neoplatonist school in that city - had taught Synesius, and he went on writing to her for years afterward. His Letter 15, around 402 AD, asks her for 'a cylindrical tube, which has the shape of a flute and is about the same size,' carrying 'notches in a perpendicular line, by means of which we are able to test the weight of the waters.' That letter is the earliest surviving written description of the instrument we now call a hydrometer. And it is Archimedes' principle turned into a dipstick: the sealed tube always weighs the same, so it sinks only until the water it has shoved aside weighs exactly what the tube does, then stops. A dense water supplies that weight in very little volume, so the tube rides HIGH; in a thin one it must go deep to find the same weight of liquid. The reading is simply where the surface cuts the stem. You can build a rough one tonight: a drinking straw sealed at one end with a blob of modelling clay inside it will float upright in a glass. Mark where the water cuts the straw, then stir in salt and watch the mark climb. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Hydrometer' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Hydrometer ; Synesius, Letter 15 - https://www.livius.org/sources/content/synesius/synesius-letter-015/

question: Galileo marked the arm of his Little Balance at the point for pure gold and the point for pure silver, then wound steel wire around it at those marks and fine brass wire through the gap between, so that a reading came out as a count of turns of wire. How did he count them?
answer: He drew a stiletto over the wires, counting by ear and touch
choices: He drew a stiletto over the wires, counting by ear and touch
He counted them under a polished lens of Venetian glass
He pressed damp paper along the wires and counted its marks
He struck the arm and counted the notes the wire bands rang
context: In Galileo's own words: 'take a most sharp stiletto and pass it slowly over the said wires. Thus, partly through our hearing, and partly through our hand feeling an obstacle at each turn of wire, we shall easily count said turns.' The brass wire was wound too fine to count by looking, so he read his own instrument as a series of ticks - by sound and by feel. It is a reminder of what precision measurement actually costs: the principle is the easy half, and building something that can genuinely READ the difference is the hard half. Source: Chris Rorres, 'The Golden Crown: La Bilancetta' - https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/bilancetta.html

question: In 2003 Jeffrey Bierman and Eric Kincanon lowered a smooth flat block onto the floor of a tank and sealed it there, so that not a drop of water could reach underneath it. Then they filled the tank and measured the force the water exerted on the block. What did their measurements show?
answer: The water pressed the block down, harder with every centimetre added
choices: The water lifted the block by the weight it shoved aside, as always
The water lifted the block, but with barely half the usual force
The water pressed the block down, harder with every centimetre added
The water pushed neither way, its forces cancelling all around
context: This is the documented exception, called the bottom (or side) case. Wikipedia states it plainly: 'This occurs when a side of the object is touching the bottom (or side) of the vessel it is submerged in, and no liquid seeps in along that side. In this case, the net force has been found to be different from Archimedes' principle, as, since no fluid seeps in on that side, the symmetry of pressure is broken.' With nothing pushing up from beneath, only the column above pushes - downward - and the force needed to lift the block rises LINEARLY with the depth of water over it. Bierman and Kincanon's conclusion in The Physics Teacher (September 2003) was that the principle must be stated for an object SURROUNDED by fluid, not merely submerged. 'Weight of displaced fluid' was always shorthand for pressure acting on every face; it was never a law about displacement itself. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Archimedes' principle' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes%27_principle ; J. Bierman & E. Kincanon, 'Reconsidering Archimedes' Principle,' The Physics Teacher 41, 340 (2003)

question: Steel is far denser than water - much heavier for its size - and a steel needle dropped point-first sinks at once. Lay the very same needle down flat and gently on still water and it rides there instead. Its weight and its volume are unchanged. What is holding it up?
answer: Surface tension, which wins out only at sizes of a few millimetres
choices: Surface tension, which wins out only at sizes of a few millimetres
Air pressure, which presses harder on the water than on the needle
Viscosity, which slows a slim shape falling through water to a crawl
Static charge, which builds between polished steel and pure water
context: Water has a capillary length of about 2.7 millimetres at 20 C. Below that scale, surface tension - the water surface behaving like a stretched skin - supplies extra upward force along the meniscus, enough to hold up steel at roughly 7,800 kilograms per cubic metre. Which effect wins is set by the Bond number, Bo = (delta-rho x g x R^2) / sigma; when Bo is far below 1, surface tension outweighs displacement entirely. Pure Archimedes assumes surface tension can be ignored, and for anything sizeable it can - but for small enough objects it cannot. Two rungs, two limits: the tidy rule holds beautifully in the middle of its range and stops being the whole story at both ends. Try it with a sewing needle and a bowl of water. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Archimedes' principle' (Refinements for Non-Ideal Conditions) and 'Buoyancy' (Incompressible Objects) - https://grokipedia.com/page/Archimedes'_principle ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Buoyancy

question: Svante Arrhenius won Sweden's first Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903, for his theory that salts dissolved in water break apart into free electrically charged particles. That theory was already complete in the doctoral thesis he defended at Uppsala in 1884. What grade did the Uppsala examiners give that thesis?
answer: Fourth class, the lowest pass
choices: Fourth class, the lowest pass
Third class, a middling pass
Second class, a strong pass
First class, the highest pass
context: His examiners thought loose ions drifting about in water was absurd, so the thesis that became a Nobel Prize scraped through with the lowest passing mark Uppsala could award. On 10 December 1903 the citation honoured 'the extraordinary services he has rendered to the advancement of chemistry by his electrolytic theory of dissociation'. Chemistry was his career; climate was the side quest. Source: Grokipedia, 'Svante Arrhenius' (sections 'Nobel Prize in Chemistry' and 'Academic Training and Influences').

question: On 15 November 1894 the geologist Arvid Hogbom read a paper in Uppsala to the Swedish Chemical Society, with Svante Arrhenius in the audience. Hogbom's work was accounting, not physics: he tallied what puts carbon dioxide into the air -- volcanoes, hot springs -- against what takes it out -- weathering rock, the ocean. Then one human source turned out to rival the natural ones. Which one?
answer: Coal burned in factory furnaces
choices: Coal burned in factory furnaces
Limestone burned in cement kilns
Timber burned in cleared forests
Peat burned in cottage stoves
context: Hogbom's ledger was bookkeeping, and the coal fires of the 1890s already showed up in it as an entry comparable to the volcanoes. The possibility that changing that gas might change the temperature of the ground came up in the discussion after his talk -- and Arrhenius, sitting there, went home and started calculating. His job was to put a temperature on Hogbom's accounts. Source: Grokipedia, 'Svante Arrhenius'; Spencer Weart, 'The Carbon Dioxide Greenhouse Effect', American Institute of Physics (history.aip.org/climate/co2.htm).

question: Svante Arrhenius owned no instrument for measuring how strongly carbon dioxide soaks up heat, so he borrowed the numbers from the American astronomer Samuel Langley, who had measured heat radiation arriving through the atmosphere at many different angles from a single object in the sky. What had Langley aimed his instrument at?
answer: The Moon
choices: The Moon
The Sun
Venus
Jupiter
context: Langley had measured the heat coming from the Moon through different thicknesses of air. Arrhenius also leaned on about 780 humidity readings from around the world, Dr Buchan's temperature charts from the HMS Challenger voyage reports, and latitude-by-latitude cloudiness surveys. The first calculation of greenhouse warming was built, in part, out of moonlight. Source: Michael de Podesta, 'Arrhenius 1896: First Calculation of Global Warming', Protons for Breakfast, reading the 1896 paper directly.

question: Guy Stewart Callendar stood before the Royal Meteorological Society in February 1938 and argued that the world had warmed and that human carbon dioxide was the reason. He held no degree in meteorology or climatology whatever; the climate work was a hobby, done at home by hand. What was his actual profession?
answer: A steam technologist, writing tables for turbine engineers
choices: A steam technologist, writing tables for turbine engineers
A colliery chemist, assaying coal for the Yorkshire pits
A marine surveyor, certifying hulls for the merchant fleet
A railway signals inspector, timing the northern lines
context: His formal title was steam technologist to the British Electrical and Allied Industries Research Association, and with his father Hugh Longbourne Callendar he produced 'The Callendar Steam Tables', the standard reference engineers used for turbine and boiler design. He did his climate arithmetic by hand at home, in a house he shared with his wife and two young daughters. Source: Grokipedia, 'Guy Stewart Callendar' ('Education', 'Engineering Roles'); Nautilus, 'The Part-Time Climate Scientist'.

question: Guy Stewart Callendar, blind in one eye since a childhood accident, was kept out of the fighting in the First World War. In the Second he helped build and patent FIDO: rows of petrol burners lit along British airfield runways, swallowing thousands of gallons of fuel for a single aircraft. What did those burning runways accomplish?
answer: They burned the fog away so bombers could land
choices: They burned the fog away so bombers could land
They melted the ice off the strips in winter
They lit the strips without lamps a raider could see
They dried the mud so heavy bombers would not sink
context: FIDO stood for Fog Investigation Dispersal Operation, and it consumed 3,000 to 5,000 gallons of petrol for a single aircraft operation -- an extravagant way to buy a crew a visible runway. The man who first showed the world was warming spent the war setting runways on fire. Source: Grokipedia, 'Guy Stewart Callendar' ('Wartime and Technical Contributions').

question: Svante Arrhenius spent most of 1895 covering paper with thousands of hand calculations: the globe cut into ten-degree latitude bands from 70 north down to 50 south, every band worked for all four seasons, at carbon dioxide levels running from two-thirds to three times the amount then in the air. He was not thinking about industry at all. Which puzzle had set him going?
answer: What had buried Europe under ice and then let it go
choices: What had buried Europe under ice and then let it go
Why the Sun's output rises and falls over centuries
Why the deep ocean stays near freezing at every latitude
How the tropics hold nearly the same heat all year
context: Arrhenius wrote in the 1896 paper that 'there exists as yet no satisfactory hypothesis that could explain how the climatic conditions for an ice age could be realised in so short a time.' Carbon dioxide was his candidate answer. Other explanations were genuinely live in 1896 -- James Croll's orbital variations, a varying Sun, volcanic dust veils, continental uplift -- and every cell of his grid was worked by hand. Source: Arrhenius (1896), quoted in Michael de Podesta, 'Arrhenius 1896: First Calculation of Global Warming', Protons for Breakfast; Grokipedia, 'Svante Arrhenius'.

question: Svante Arrhenius's finished tables carried one headline: double the carbon dioxide in the air and the ground warms about five or six degrees Celsius. But his tables did not spread that warming evenly over the globe -- one part of the world took several times the average. Where did his numbers pile the heat up?
answer: Up in the high latitudes near the poles
choices: Up in the high latitudes near the poles
Out over the warm tropical oceans
Across the dry continental interiors
Up in the high mountain ranges
context: His tables gave up to 10-12 degrees Celsius of warming at high latitudes for a doubling -- and, running the calculation the other way, 18-32 degrees of cooling there if the gas were halved. The poles swing hardest in both directions. That lopsidedness fell out of pen-and-paper arithmetic in 1896 and later work kept it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Svante Arrhenius' ('Quantitative Models and Predictions').

question: Svante Arrhenius had just calculated that doubling the air's carbon dioxide would warm the ground five or six degrees Celsius, and industry was pouring carbon dioxide out year after year. So he worked out the timescale that decides everything: at the rates of his own day, how long would the doubling take?
answer: Perhaps three thousand years
choices: Perhaps three thousand years
Perhaps three hundred years
Perhaps thirty thousand years
Perhaps a hundred years
context: 'Perhaps three thousand years' is why Arrhenius never wrote a word of alarm. Human emissions in 1896 ran about 0.5 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide a year; the figure today is roughly 37 gigatonnes. He got the physics of the calculation broadly right and the speed of the world's industry catastrophically wrong -- which is a different kind of error, and worth telling apart. Source: Spencer Weart, 'The Carbon Dioxide Greenhouse Effect', AIP (history.aip.org/climate/co2.htm); Protons for Breakfast.

question: Svante Arrhenius, the first person to put a number on how much extra carbon dioxide would warm the ground, wrote in his 1908 book 'Worlds in the Making' about what that warming would mean for the people who lived through it. What did he say the world could expect from it?
answer: Milder, more settled climates for mankind
choices: Milder, more settled climates for mankind
Higher, rougher seas over the harbour towns
Wider, drier deserts across the grain lands
Fewer, weaker plagues across the crowded cities
context: Arrhenius wrote that by the increasing carbonic acid in the atmosphere 'we may hope to enjoy ages with more equable and better climates' -- 'equable' meaning steadier, less extreme -- and looked forward to it 'for the benefit of rapidly propagating mankind'. Milder Swedish winters, and the next ice age postponed. The first man ever to compute greenhouse warming wanted it to happen. That fact cuts against lazy stories in both directions: he was no prophet of doom and no doubter of the physics, just a chemist with a number. Source: Arrhenius, 'Worlds in the Making' (1908), p. 63; fragments quoted at The Climate Historian; full text at Project Gutenberg ebook 69022.

question: In 1900 the Swedish physicist Knut Angstrom set out to test Svante Arrhenius, and handed the measuring to his laboratory assistant, a man recorded only as Herr J. Koch. Koch shone infrared heat rays through a 30-centimetre tube of carbon dioxide, took away a third of the gas, and found the absorption barely moved. Physicists treated that as the end of the matter. But Koch's tube held much less gas than the air standing over any patch of ground. How long would his tube have needed to be?
answer: About 250 centimetres
choices: About 250 centimetres
About 90 centimetres
About 700 centimetres
About 2,000 centimetres
context: Roughly eight times longer than the tube he used: Koch was testing a slice of air, not a sky. He reported the absorption changing by no more than 0.4 percent; modern recalculation puts the real change nearer 1 percent, so his number was somewhat too small as well. Angstrom concluded the band was already saturated and extra carbon dioxide could do nothing, American meteorologists picked the result up through the Monthly Weather Review in June 1901, and the carbon dioxide theory went quiet for some forty to fifty years. This was honest experiment honestly believed, not suppression -- Arrhenius fought back in the open with a scathing reply in Annalen der Physik in 1901, and the field simply judged the experiment stronger than the calculation. It judged wrong. Source: RealClimate, 'A Saturated Gassy Argument'; Spencer Weart, AIP.

question: Guy Stewart Callendar told the Royal Meteorological Society in February 1938 that the world's land had warmed about three-tenths of a degree in fifty years and that rising carbon dioxide was why. Sir George Simpson, director of the British Meteorological Office, answered that the agreement 'must be taken as rather a coincidence' -- and behind the brush-off lay a serious scientific objection, not spite. On what grounds did Simpson object?
answer: The air's temperature is set by air moving up and down, not by radiation
choices: The air's temperature is set by air moving up and down, not by radiation
The records came from towns that had grown up around the thermometers
Water vapour absorbs the same heat and swamps what carbon dioxide does
The oceans would soak up any extra carbon dioxide within a few years
context: Simpson said the atmosphere 'was not in a state of radiative equilibrium', that its temperature 'was determined almost entirely by the movement of the air up and down', and that therefore 'One could not... calculate the effect of changing any one factor in the atmosphere.' On that narrow point he was right -- Callendar's calculation did ignore convection. Callendar did not quit: six more papers across 1938-39, hand-updated datasets into the 1950s, and a 1949 estimate of about 2.1 degrees Celsius for a doubling. The effect now carries his name. Source: Grokipedia, 'Guy Stewart Callendar' ('Contemporary Skepticism and Critiques'); Nautilus; Science History Institute.

question: Gilbert Plass redid Svante Arrhenius's arithmetic in 1956 with modern infrared measurements, put the warming from doubled carbon dioxide at about 3.6 degrees Celsius, and predicted carbon dioxide would climb roughly 30 percent over the century. He already had the mathematics for how heat rays travel through air, because of the day job he had been doing. What work had handed Plass those methods?
answer: Infrared work on heat-seeking missiles for Lockheed
choices: Infrared work on heat-seeking missiles for Lockheed
Infrared work on night-vision scopes for the Army
Infrared work on submarine detectors for the Navy
Infrared work on furnace controls for a steel maker
context: The radiation mathematics that revived Arrhenius came out of missile guidance. Plass also warned that climate change could become 'a serious problem to future generations -- although not for several centuries.' The wartime and postwar leap in infrared spectroscopy is what made a better answer possible at all -- one caution: some accounts credit early electronic computers for the 1956 numbers and others deny it, so treat that detail as disputed. Source: RealClimate, 'The carbon dioxide theory of Gilbert Plass'; Spencer Weart, AIP.

question: Knut Angstrom's laboratory was not imagining things: his assistant Herr J. Koch shone heat rays through a 30-centimetre tube of carbon dioxide, took away a third of the gas, and measured the absorption falling by less than half a percent -- modern recalculation makes the true change about one percent, still tiny. In a tube of air like that, carbon dioxide really does soak up nearly all the heat there is to soak up. And yet the planet warms when carbon dioxide is added to the air. Why does that extra gas warm it, when Koch's measurement stands?
answer: Heat escapes from thin cold air high up, and extra gas lifts that escape level higher and colder
choices: Heat escapes from thin cold air high up, and extra gas lifts that escape level higher and colder
Heat escapes near the tops of the clouds, and extra gas thickens the clouds that do the radiating
Heat escapes through gaps beside the absorbed band, and extra gas slowly closes those gaps
Heat escapes into the oceans first, and extra gas slows how fast the sea gives it back
context: The ground is not what cools the planet. Heat finally leaves for space from the thin, cold upper air, where there is almost no water vapour to compete. Add carbon dioxide and the level from which that last escape happens moves further up -- higher means colder, colder means radiating less energy away, and the planet must warm until the balance is restored. Saturation lower down changes nothing, 'since it is the layers from which radiation does escape that determine the planet's heat balance.' Weart adds the sting: 'a 1% change in that delicate balance would make a serious difference in the planet's surface temperature.' Source: RealClimate, 'A Saturated Gassy Argument' Parts I and II; Spencer Weart, AIP.

question: Svante Arrhenius's 1896 paper put the warming from doubled carbon dioxide at five to six degrees Celsius -- the first number anyone had ever attached to the question. Ten years later, in a paper called 'The Probable Cause of Climate Fluctuations', he came back to that headline figure of his own. What did he do with it?
answer: He cut it himself, to about two degrees Celsius
choices: He cut it himself, to about two degrees Celsius
He raised it to nearly ten degrees Celsius
He withdrew it and called the method unsound
He defended it and blamed rival instruments
context: The 1906 revision came down to about 1.6 degrees Celsius, or 2.1 degrees once water-vapour feedback was counted. Scientists today argue over a range of roughly 1.5 to 4.5 degrees for a doubling, with a central estimate near 3 -- so Arrhenius's own second answer lands inside an argument that is still running, and his first one runs hot. The first number was wrong; the method was right; both halves are the lesson, and the man who corrected him first was himself. Source: Grokipedia, 'Svante Arrhenius'; Arrhenius (1906), 'Die vermutliche Ursache der Klimaschwankungen', English translation via Friends of Science.

question: On 21 October 1638, during a violent storm, worshippers at the Sunday afternoon service in St Pancras church at Widecombe-in-the-Moor on Dartmoor reported an object entering the building, hovering, splitting in two, and exploding. Four were killed and the roof was torn open. What did they say they saw?
answer: A great ball of fire
choices: A great ball of fire
A blade of white light
A pillar of black smoke
A cloud of blue sparks
context: The Great Thunderstorm of Widecombe, one of the oldest detailed accounts of what is now called ball lightning. Contemporaries smelled brimstone (sulphur) and blamed the devil; the Reverend George Lyde was mid-service. The word for the phenomenon did not exist yet - 'ball lightning' as a scientific term came much later.

question: The reports of what we now call ball lightning are eerily consistent across centuries and continents: a glowing sphere drifting horizontally about a metre off the ground at walking pace, lasting a handful of seconds, sometimes ending with a bang. Roughly how big are the reported spheres?
answer: About the size of a grapefruit or a soccer ball
choices: About the size of a grapefruit or a soccer ball
About the size of a wristwatch face or smaller
About the size of a compact car or larger
About the size of a marble or a coin
context: The Wikipedia summary of accumulated eyewitness accounts puts the typical diameter at 10 to 30 centimetres - grapefruit to soccer ball. Other consistent features across the reports: a lifetime of a few seconds, horizontal drift at a few metres per second, an ozone or sulphur smell, and occasional passage through a closed window. Pea-sized and metre-sized events are on record but they are the tails, not the middle.

question: On 6 August 1753 in St Petersburg, an academician was in his own house measuring atmospheric electricity with an insulated iron rod, following up Benjamin Franklin's kite work. During the storm, a discharge reported to have been ball lightning appeared, struck him in the head, and killed him instantly. Who was he?
answer: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
choices: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov
Alessandro Volta
Luigi Galvani
context: Richmann's engraver companion was knocked unconscious; a red spot was left on Richmann's forehead, his left shoe blown open, and the doorframe was torn from its hinges. He is generally considered the first person killed while doing electrical research - and one of the first documented cases of ball lightning taking a life. Franklin's kite experiment had made the topic fashionable that decade; the danger was not.

question: Ball lightning is often confused with a phenomenon sailors have named for centuries: St Elmo's fire. But the two look and behave differently. What is the single giveaway that tells them apart?
answer: St Elmo's fire stays attached to a mast or a wingtip; a ball drifts free
choices: St Elmo's fire stays attached to a mast or a wingtip; a ball drifts free
St Elmo's fire only happens on the ocean; a ball only happens on land
St Elmo's fire lasts several hours; a ball only lasts a few seconds
St Elmo's fire glows red; a ball almost always glows a pale blue
context: Sailors named it after St Erasmus of Formia (Elmo), patron saint of Mediterranean sailors; it appears on the mastheads of ships in strong storm fields, and modern pilots sometimes see it flickering on the windshield frame or wingtips. Sprites and blue jets are also real, but they occur high above thunderclouds and last only milliseconds. Will-o'-the-wisp is a marsh-gas phenomenon over boggy ground with no connection to storms.

question: For nearly three centuries after Widecombe, science had no instrument record of ball lightning at all. In July 2012 a team led by Ping Yuan at Northwest Normal University in Lanzhou finally captured one, from about a kilometre away on the Qinghai Plateau, using video and slitless spectrographs. How did they get the recording?
answer: By luck: they were pointing their instruments at ordinary lightning and the ball appeared in the frame
choices: By luck: they were pointing their instruments at ordinary lightning and the ball appeared in the frame
By design: they had been chasing storms for years with the specific goal of catching ball lightning
By reconstruction: they built one in a lab and photographed it as a controlled demonstration
By review: an amateur mailed them an old photograph and they identified the object in it
context: A cloud-to-ground strike about a kilometre away kicked off a glowing sphere that drifted a few metres, changed colour from purple to orange to white to red, and faded in under two seconds - all in the field of view of a camera and a spectrograph aimed at normal lightning. Published in Physical Review Letters in 2014. Spectrographs spread light into its component wavelengths so the elements emitting it can be identified.

question: The 2012 Qinghai recording produced the first ever spectrum of natural ball lightning - the elements emitting its light, read straight out of its glow. Three emission lines dominated. Which set of elements did the spectrum show?
answer: Silicon, iron, and calcium - the elements of the soil below the strike
choices: Silicon, iron, and calcium - the elements of the soil below the strike
Nitrogen, oxygen, and argon - the elements of the surrounding air
Hydrogen, helium, and lithium - the light elements of the upper atmosphere
Carbon, sulphur, and phosphorus - the elements of nearby organic matter
context: The elements emitting the ball's light were the elements of the ground it hovered above, not of the air it hovered in. That is the strongest single piece of physical evidence yet for any theory of what ball lightning IS.

question: Frederick Madison Allen treated a hundred diabetics at the Rockefeller Hospital from 1914 to 1918, when a child diagnosed with diabetes rarely lived a year. His regimen was the best medicine had, and it kept a few of them alive into 1922. What was it?
answer: 400 to 500 calories a day, nearly all fat and protein
choices: 400 to 500 calories a day, nearly all fat and protein
Six pints of water a day, to wash the sugar out
Two hours of hard exercise a day, to burn the sugar off
A pint of minced ox pancreas, swallowed each day
context: Allen's wards were known as the starvation rooms. They smelled of acetone, the odour of patients burning their own fat and muscle for fuel. Children cried for food, and their parents knew that feeding them would kill them faster. It bought months, not years - but for a handful of patients those months were exactly enough to still be breathing when insulin arrived. Sources: Rockefeller University Hospital historical vignette (ccts.rockefeller.edu); diabetes.co.uk on Frederick Madison Allen.

question: Elizabeth Hughes, a U.S. Secretary of State's daughter, reached Toronto in August 1922 weighing forty-five pounds after years of starvation dieting. Insulin gave her fifty-eight more years, and she went to Barnard College. What did she do about the diabetes for the rest of her life?
answer: Kept it secret from almost everyone she knew
choices: Kept it secret from almost everyone she knew
Campaigned for diabetes research all her life
Wrote a memoir of her months in Toronto
Returned each year to be examined by Banting
context: She died in 1981 at seventy-three, having hidden her diabetes from nearly everyone she ever met. Her mother's letter begging Banting to take her had read: 'She is pitifully depleted and reduced. She is five feet tall and weighs less than fifty pounds.' She had been living on as little as 300 to 800 calories a day; on insulin she was put on 2,500 a day, a pint of cream among them, and gained ten pounds in five weeks and sixteen in two months. Note what insulin is and is not: it replaces a hormone the body has stopped making, so it must be injected for life. Diabetes was not defeated in 1922 - it stopped being a death sentence and became a condition you manage. Teddy Ryder, five years old and twenty-seven pounds when Banting first treated him on 10 July 1922, put it in his thank-you letter: 'I am a fat boy now and I feel fine.' He lived more than seventy years on insulin. Sources: University of Toronto insulin collections (collections.library.utoronto.ca); Diabetes UK on Elizabeth Evans Hughes; Hektoen International on Toronto Sick Kids in the 1920s.

question: Frederick Banting and Charles Best spent the summer of 1921 in a hot Toronto attic, operating on dogs to test an idea about the pancreas. Extracts spoiled, animals died, and by midsummer their dogs had run out. How did they keep the experiments running?
answer: They bought strays off Toronto's streets for one to three dollars
choices: They bought strays off Toronto's streets for one to three dollars
They took ten at a time from the city pound on a police permit
They borrowed dogs from the veterinary college for a week each
They wired Macleod in Scotland to ship ten more from Aberdeen
context: Work had begun on 17 May 1921 with a pancreatectomy on a dog. The medical building had no air conditioning, the summer was brutal, and the early preparations were so impure they threw the animals into convulsions. In their notebooks the two men called the extract 'isletin'. (A popular retelling says Banting sold his car to buy more dogs; that one could not be verified in the Canadian Medical Hall of Fame, Western University or U of T records - the street dogs are documented.) Source: Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, University of Toronto, 'The Summer of 1921'.

question: Charles Best and Edward Clark Noble, two new Toronto graduates, were both handed to J.J.R. Macleod's laboratory for the summer of 1921. They agreed to split it, one shift each, and tossed a coin for who went first. Best won. Noble never worked a day on the insulin experiments. Why not?
answer: Best had grown good at the surgery, and switching hands seemed unwise
choices: Best had grown good at the surgery, and switching hands seemed unwise
Banting quarrelled with Noble and had him kept out of the attic
Macleod called the second shift off when the extracts kept spoiling
Noble took a post in Montreal before his own shift came round
context: The toss was only ever about who went FIRST. By the time Best's month was up he had become skilled at the operations, it seemed unwise to switch, and the second shift simply never happened. Noble's own turn came thirty-one years later: in 1952 a patient mailed him Madagascar periwinkle leaves, sold as a tea for diabetes. He forwarded the envelope to his brother Robert - and that lead produced the cancer drug vinblastine. Sources: 'Almost famous: E. Clark Noble, the common thread in the discovery of insulin and vinblastine', CMAJ (PMC137361); Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, U of T.

question: Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering took the whole pancreas out of a dog in Strasbourg in 1889. Within twenty-four hours its urine ran five percent sugar, and the pancreas was suddenly the organ that governed sugar in the blood - a fact nobody could turn into a medicine for thirty-two years. Why had the two men opened the dog up in the first place?
answer: To settle a bet that no dog could live without one
choices: To settle a bet that no dog could live without one
To test the pancreatic islets Paul Langerhans had described
To learn whether surgeons could spare it in people
To trace the sweet smell on a dying diabetic's breath
context: Von Mering, echoing Claude Bernard, held that a dog could not survive without its pancreas. Minkowski took the other side and did the surgery himself. The dog lived - and inside a day it was pouring sugar into its urine, five percent of it. Paul Langerhans had drawn the little islands of cells scattered through the pancreas back in 1869 without knowing what they were for. After 1889 every researcher knew the organ mattered; for thirty-two years none of them could get the substance out of it intact. Sources: Pediatric Endocrine Society, historical tidbit on Oskar Minkowski; Mayo Clinic Proceedings.

question: Frederick Banting spent the evening of 30 October 1920 in his rented room in London, Ontario, preparing a student lecture on the pancreas, and could not sleep afterwards. At two in the morning he got up and wrote twenty-five words in his notebook, misspelling two of them. What did those words tell him to do?
answer: Tie off the pancreatic ducts of dogs and extract what survives in them
choices: Tie off the pancreatic ducts of dogs and extract what survives in them
Transplant a healthy dog's pancreas into one whose own had been cut out
Chill a whole pancreas until its juice went quiet, then grind it down
Feed dogs nothing but fat for weeks and measure the sugar in their urine
context: The note reads: 'Diabetus [sic]. Ligate pancreatic ducts of dogs. Keep dogs alive till acini degenerate leaving Islets. Try to insolate [sic] the internal secretion of these to relieve glycosuria.' Banting was a 29-year-old orthopaedic surgeon with a failing practice at 442 Adelaide Street, teaching part-time. He took the idea to J.J.R. Macleod on 7 November 1920; Macleod thought it speculative and said so - then gave him an attic laboratory, about ten dogs and two months of a student's time. The notebook is held by the Academy of Medicine, Toronto. Sources: Western University heritage project; Canadian Medical Hall of Fame.

question: On 30 July 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best injected their pancreas extract into a vein of dog 410, a terrier whose pancreas they had cut out weeks before, and its blood sugar fell from .20 to .12 percent within hours. But a few hours of lowered blood sugar is not a life. On 6 December 1921 they began a second test, on another dog with no pancreas at all, one they had named Marjorie - test dog 33 in the notebooks. What did the injections do for her?
answer: Kept her alive and steady for about seventy days
choices: Kept her alive and steady for about seventy days
Held her steady nine days, then failed when it spoiled
Worked only while she was injected every two hours
Pulled her round so far that in three weeks she needed none
context: A dog with no pancreas, living roughly seventy days on injections, was the proof that mattered: it was the missing SUBSTANCE, not the missing organ, and a substance can be given back. Watch how the story gets told, though. Popular accounts, Grokipedia among them, put the first success on 27 July 1921, with extract from dog 92 injected into a dog named Marjorie and blood sugar falling from 0.44 to 0.14 percent. The University of Toronto's primary-document exhibit disagrees on every particular: 30 July, dog 410, .20 to .12 percent; dog 92 was a later laboratory pet, kept from 11 to 31 August; Marjorie was test dog 33. Dog 406 followed on 1 August, and dog 408 got repeated 'isletin' injections from 3 to 7 August. Repetition in respectable places is not sourcing - the notebooks are. Source: Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, University of Toronto, 'The Summer of 1921'.

question: At the end of January 1922 James Collip walked into Frederick Banting and Charles Best's laboratory and told them he had cracked the purification of the extract, and that he would share the method with J.J.R. Macleod alone. Banting lost his temper. What did he do?
answer: Grabbed Collip by the overcoat and sat him down hard in a chair
choices: Grabbed Collip by the overcoat and sat him down hard in a chair
Swept the flasks off Collip's bench and smashed the day's batch
Went to Macleod that evening and demanded Collip be dismissed
