Walked out and did not enter the laboratory again for a month
context: Banting told Collip it was a good job he was so much smaller, or he would 'knock hell out of him'. Best physically restrained him, and an uneasy agreement a few days later kept the four men working together. The discovery that saved millions of children was made by a team that could barely stand each other. Sources: Science History Institute biography of Banting, Best, Collip and Macleod; The Conversation, 'The discovery of insulin: a story of monstrous egos and toxic rivalries'.

question: For years, researchers hunting the pancreas's blood-sugar hormone had ground up fresh glands, injected the result into diabetic dogs, and got almost nothing for it. Frederick Banting's plan began by tying off a dog's pancreatic ducts and then leaving the animal alone for weeks before he took the gland out at all. What was the waiting for?
answer: The juice-making part of the gland withers, and that juice wrecks the hormone
choices: The juice-making part of the gland withers, and that juice wrecks the hormone
The islets swell and multiply once the duct is blocked, raising the yield
The gland's fat clears away, so alcohol can pull the hormone free of it
The gland's blood drains out, and blood breaks the hormone down fastest
context: The paper that set it off was Moses Barron's, in the November 1920 Surgery, Gynecology and Obstetrics (vol. 31, pp. 437-48): block the pancreatic duct and the acinar cells that make the digestive juice waste away, while the islets of Langerhans survive. The pancreas makes trypsin, which digests protein - and the hormone is a protein. Every earlier extractor had been mashing the hormone together with the enzyme built to destroy it. Banting's leap was to let the gland dismantle its own weapon first. Sources: Western University heritage project; Grokipedia, Frederick Banting.

question: James Bertram Collip, a biochemist, joined the Toronto work in December 1921 with one job: pull the hormone in Banting and Best's pancreas extract clear of the crowd of other proteins that came out of the gland with it. In late January 1922 he told them he had it. What was his method?
answer: Driving the alcohol past ninety percent, so the other proteins fell out
choices: Driving the alcohol past ninety percent, so the other proteins fell out
Boiling the extract briefly, so the other proteins cooked and settled
Straining it through unglazed clay fine enough to hold proteins back
Freezing it solid, so the other proteins crystallised and lifted off
context: Alcohol precipitation: past roughly 90 percent concentration the contaminating proteins can no longer stay dissolved and drop out of solution, while the hormone stays in. Nothing exotic - a solvent, a concentration, and the patience to find the point where the two behave differently. It was the step that turned a dog-laboratory curiosity into a medicine you could put in a child. Sources: Science History Institute biography of Banting, Best, Collip and Macleod; Grokipedia, Frederick Banting.

question: The scene most often told about insulin has Frederick Banting, Charles Best and James Collip moving down a hospital ward of children in diabetic comas, injecting one after another, the first child waking before they reached the last bed. Historians working on the insulin centennial call that a retelling rather than a record. What does the record actually show for October 1922 at Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children?
answer: Elsie Needham, aged eleven, was brought back from a diabetic coma
choices: Elsie Needham, aged eleven, was brought back from a diabetic coma
Teddy Ryder, aged five, was brought back from a coma in one night
Elizabeth Hughes, aged fifteen, was brought back from a coma by Banting
Leonard Thompson, aged fourteen, was brought back from a coma twice
context: Elsie Needham was the first patient anywhere brought back from a diabetic coma. The newspaper report ran: 'The child was unconscious several days, and little hope was held for recovery...has responded to the treatment wonderfully well.' By the end of December 1922, ten patients had been revived from complete comas out of about fifty treated. The historian Michael Bliss called it 'a reprieve from death almost without precedent in the history of medicine.' The true version is astonishing enough without the ward walk. Sources: Defining Moments Canada, 'Diabetic Resurrections' (sharedhistories.ca); Hektoen International on Toronto Sick Kids.  (Legend.)

question: Leonard Thompson was carried into Toronto General Hospital on 2 December 1921, sixty-five pounds and drifting in and out of diabetic coma. On 11 January 1922 he became the first human being ever injected with Banting and Best's pancreas extract. What did that first injection do?
answer: His blood sugar barely moved, and an abscess rose where the needle went in
choices: His blood sugar barely moved, and an abscess rose where the needle went in
His blood sugar fell to normal in a day, and the ketones left his urine
His blood sugar crashed so low that the doctors had to feed him sugar
His blood sugar held for a week, then climbed higher than before
context: The most famous cure of the century failed on its first try. The record notes only 'a slight lowering of blood sugar', and the contaminants in the extract produced an allergic reaction and an abscess at the injection site. Treatment was stopped. Twelve days later, on 23 January, Thompson was given Collip's purified extract: his blood sugar dropped to normal within a day, the ketones cleared from his urine, and he began gaining weight. He lived thirteen more years, dying on 20 April 1935 of bronchopneumonia. He was living on 450 calories a day when he was admitted. Sources differ on his age at that first injection - thirteen or fourteen. Sources: Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, U of T, 'Leonard Thompson'; University of Toronto insulin collections; Wikipedia, Leonard Thompson (diabetic).

question: The 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, announced on 25 October, went to Frederick Banting and to J.J.R. Macleod. Banting was enraged: Charles Best had worked beside him at the bench all through the summer of 1921, and Macleod had spent part of that summer on holiday in Scotland. What did Banting do?
answer: Telegrammed Best to say he was splitting his half of the money with him
choices: Telegrammed Best to say he was splitting his half of the money with him
Wrote to Stockholm asking that Best's name replace Macleod's on it
Published a letter naming Best as the discovery's second author
Told the university he would resign unless Best was given a chair
context: Macleod then split his own half with James Collip. Banting was thirty-two, and remains the youngest person ever to win the Nobel in Physiology or Medicine. The easy version makes Macleod a freeloader, and it is not true: he supplied the dogs, the laboratory, the assistant and the blood-sugar method, recruited Collip, directed the follow-up work, and announced 'insulin' to the world on 3 May 1922. The Nobel Committee cited exactly that division - Banting's initiative in conceiving the duct-ligation experiment, Macleod's facilities and direction. Banting still boycotted his lectures and called for his resignation; Macleod left Canada in 1928. The 2021 Toronto centennial monument deliberately carries all four names. Sources: Grokipedia, Frederick Banting; Wikipedia, Frederick Banting; Science History Institute.

question: Perth, 1984. Barry Marshall was certain a spiral bacterium in the stomach caused ulcers, and Australia's specialists would not listen. Proving a germ causes a disease means making it sicken a healthy body. That July, Marshall solved the problem. What did he do?
answer: He drank a beaker of the bacterial culture himself
choices: He drank a beaker of the bacterial culture himself
He fed the bacterial culture to a pen of piglets
He paid medical students to swallow the culture
He bred a strain of mice that carried the bacteria
context: It was about 50 ml of alkaline peptone water carrying a four-day-old culture, roughly a billion organisms, swallowed on an empty stomach after 400 mg of cimetidine to knock his stomach acid down. The Nobel presentation speech of 10 December 2005 put it flatly: 'In the absence of a suitable animal model, Marshall decided to drink a bacterial culture containing Helicobacter.' (Grokipedia 'Barry Marshall'; Nobel Prize presentation speech by Prof. Staffan Normark, 10 Dec 2005, nobelprize.org)

question: For most of the twentieth century doctors treated an ulcer by calming the stomach's acid, never by killing anything. Bertram Sippy's regimen, standard from 1915, had patients swallowing the same soothing stuff hour after hour, all day long, with alkaline powders in between. What were they swallowing every hour?
answer: Mixtures of milk and cream
choices: Spoonfuls of thin honey
Mixtures of milk and cream
Cups of warm barley water
Bowls of boiled white rice
context: The dictum behind the whole regime was surgeon Karl Schwarz's 1910 line: 'no acid, no ulcer.' Sippy's hourly milk and cream gave way to antacids, and from 1976 to the acid blocker cimetidine, taken in practice forever. The Lasker Foundation's 1995 citation says the bacterial idea 'challenged half a century of entrenched belief' about where ulcers come from. (Grokipedia 'Timeline of peptic ulcer disease and Helicobacter pylori'; Lasker Foundation 1995 award citation, laskerfoundation.org)

question: In July 1984 Barry Marshall, an Australian doctor trying to prove a bacterium causes ulcers, swallowed a beaker of the bugs on an empty stomach. Within days he was nauseated, vomiting in the mornings, waking clammy, and breathing so foully that his family noticed. On day ten a colleague passed an endoscope and took a biopsy. What did the biopsy show?
answer: Raw inflammation across the lining, but no ulcer
choices: A deep ulcer already bleeding at the stomach outlet
A lining that looked normal despite all the symptoms
Raw inflammation across the lining, but no ulcer
A ring of small ulcers spreading into the intestine
context: Gastritis means inflammation of the stomach lining; an ulcer is a crater eaten right through it. Marshall's own paper is deadpan: 'A mild illness developed, which lasted 14 days. Histologically proven gastritis was present on the tenth day after the ingestion of bacteria, but this had largely resolved by the fourteenth day.' The infection cleared mostly on its own and he finished it off with tinidazole. He gave himself gastritis, not an ulcer, and the story is worth telling correctly. (Marshall BJ, Armstrong JA, McGechie DB, Glancy RJ, 'Attempt to fulfil Koch's postulates for pyloric Campylobacter', Med J Aust 1985;142(8):436-439, PMID 3982345)

question: In 1981 at Royal Perth Hospital, pathologist Robin Warren showed a young doctor named Barry Marshall a list of patients whose stomach biopsies carried curved bacteria. One name stopped Marshall: a woman on his own ward who had been in severe stomach pain for months, with no diagnosis. His team had already settled on a course of action for her. What was it?
answer: A referral to a psychiatrist and antidepressant tablets
choices: A transfer to surgery to remove part of her stomach
A referral to a pain clinic for long-term painkillers
A ward regimen of hourly milk and alkaline powders
A referral to a psychiatrist and antidepressant tablets
context: Marshall's Nobel autobiography says the team had made the referral 'in desperation'. Her only abnormal finding was a redness in the stomach and Warren's bacteria on the biopsy slide. This is what the acid-and-nerves theory looked like from a hospital bed: when the tests found nothing, the patient's mind became the diagnosis. Marshall met Warren in the second half of 1981, in the basement pathology department, where Warren drank strong black coffee and smoked small cigars. (Barry J. Marshall, 'Biographical', NobelPrize.org)

question: Every specialist had the same objection to Barry Marshall and Robin Warren: the stomach is a vat of hydrochloric acid, so nothing can live in it. Helicobacter pylori manages anyway. It corkscrews down into the thick mucus layer on four to six sheathed flagella, and it manufactures an enzyme called urease, which splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. How does that reaction save the bacterium?
answer: The ammonia it makes neutralises the acid right around it
choices: The ammonia it makes neutralises the acid right around it
The carbon dioxide it makes forms a gas shell around it
The ammonia it makes tells the stomach to make less acid
The ammonia it makes stiffens the mucus into a hard shell
context: The urea is already there in the stomach's fluid, so the bug carries its own antacid factory. The ammonia raises the pH in a bubble tight around each bacterium, while the flagella drive it out of the open acid and down into the mucus, where the pH is close to neutral anyway. 'The stomach is sterile' had been an assumption, not a measurement, and nobody had gone looking hard enough to catch it out. (Grokipedia 'Helicobacter pylori'; Grokipedia 'Barry Marshall')

question: When doctors believed that too much stomach acid was what ate an ulcer, the boldest cure was to stop the stomach making acid at all. Lester Dragstedt's operation severed the vagus nerve, the wiring that tells the stomach to pour acid out. American surgeons were performing over 100,000 ulcer operations a year at the 1960s peak, and between a fifth and a third of those patients were left with a permanent complication. What happened to them afterwards?
answer: Food raced through the gut, leaving them faint after meals
choices: Bile washed back up into the stomach, sickening them daily
Food raced through the gut, leaving them faint after meals
The stomach lining thinned until it bled at the slightest strain
The stomach emptied so slowly that meals sat in it for hours
context: Surgeons called it dumping syndrome. With the vagus nerve cut, and often the acid-signalling bottom of the stomach removed as well, the stomach lost its grip on the pace of digestion, so a meal dumped into the small intestine all at once: nausea, sweating and collapse after eating. That was the standard of care for a stubborn ulcer, performed on tens of thousands of people a year, on a theory Barry Marshall and Robin Warren would overturn. (Grokipedia 'Timeline of peptic ulcer disease and Helicobacter pylori')

question: Robin Warren, a pathologist at Royal Perth Hospital, could see spiral bacteria clinging to his stomach-biopsy slides; nobody could grow them in a dish. Through 1981 and into 1982 Barry Marshall seeded plate after plate and every one came back empty. Then one batch came back covered in colonies of exactly the organism Warren had been watching under his microscope. As Marshall tells it, what had happened to that batch?
answer: It had been left in the incubator over the Easter holiday
choices: It had been left in a cold room instead of the incubator
It had been mislabelled and seeded twice from one sample
It had been left in the incubator over the Easter holiday
It had been carried across town to a colleague's laboratory
context: The Nobel Foundation's presentation speech tells it straight: 'Many fruitless attempts were made. During the Easter 1982 holiday, the agar plates were left in the incubator by mistake, and when they were inspected after the holiday they contained numerous colonies consisting of the same bacterium that Warren had observed under his microscope.' The routine was to bin a plate after two days; this slow, fussy organism needed longer, and the long weekend gave it the time. Helicobacter researchers call Easter 1982 the bug's birthday, though the sources disagree over whether it was Easter Sunday, 11 April, or Easter Monday, 12 April, which is why the story is best told as Marshall tells it rather than pinned to a day. (Nobel Prize presentation speech, Prof. Staffan Normark, 10 Dec 2005, nobelprize.org; Grokipedia 'Robin Warren' vs Grokipedia 'Timeline of peptic ulcer disease and Helicobacter pylori')

question: By 1982 Barry Marshall had more than a hunch about his stomach bacterium: a study of a hundred consecutive endoscopy patients at Royal Perth Hospital had turned it up in every single duodenal-ulcer patient. He sent the abstract to the Gastroenterological Society of Australia, which turned it down, and that October a Perth meeting heard the data and largely shrugged. Then Royal Perth Hospital acted. What did the hospital do to Marshall?
answer: It refused to renew his contract for the next year
choices: It refused to renew his contract for the next year
It barred him from endoscoping his own ulcer patients
It struck him from the roster of teaching physicians
It cut off his access to Warren's biopsy slides
context: Marshall's own account of how the objection worked, from his Nobel autobiography: 'When the work was presented, my results were disputed and disbelieved, not on the basis of science but because they simply could not be true. It was often said that no one was able to replicate my results. This was untrue but became part of the folklore of the period. I was told that the bacteria were either contaminants or harmless commensals.' The refusal was not pure stupidity: in 1954 Edwin Palmer had published a study in Gastroenterology reporting no bacteria at all in gastric biopsies, so the field had a printed reason to stop looking. (Barry J. Marshall, 'Biographical', NobelPrize.org; Grokipedia 'Barry Marshall'; Grokipedia 'Timeline of peptic ulcer disease and Helicobacter pylori')

question: In 1985 Barry Marshall published the experiment in which he had swallowed a beaker of stomach bacteria himself. It ran in the Medical Journal of Australia under the title 'Attempt to fulfil Koch's postulates for pyloric Campylobacter', with three co-authors. The abstract's opening sentence describes the man who swallowed the bacteria, and never names him. What does the paper call him?
answer: 'A volunteer'
choices: 'A volunteer'
'A physician'
'The subject'
'The author'
context: The full sentence reads: 'A volunteer with histologically normal gastric mucosa received pyloric campylobacter by mouth.' Marshall, Armstrong, McGechie and Glancy are on the title page; none of them is identified as the volunteer. Koch's postulates are the nineteenth-century checklist for blaming a germ for a disease, and the fourth is the hard one: take the organism you grew in the laboratory and show that it produces the same disease in a fresh, healthy host. Marshall had been trying to meet it with pigs, which took the bacteria happily and never got sick. (Med J Aust 1985;142(8):436-439, PMID 3982345, onlinelibrary.wiley.com)

question: In July 1984 Barry Marshall swallowed a beaker of Helicobacter pylori to prove the bug could sicken a healthy stomach. Writing about it decades later in his Nobel autobiography, Marshall named one step he had skipped before he drank, and did not excuse himself for it. Which step had he skipped?
answer: He never put the experiment to the hospital's ethics committee
choices: He never had the culture screened for other disease organisms
He never asked the hospital's senior physicians for approval
He never put the experiment to the hospital's ethics committee
He never arranged for a second doctor to monitor him afterwards
context: His own words: 'I didn't discuss it with the ethics committee at the hospital. More significantly, I didn't discuss it in detail with Adrienne. She was already convinced about the risk of these bacteria and I knew I would never get her approval. This was one of those occasions when it would be easier to get forgiveness than permission.' An ethics committee is the panel that must approve any experiment on a human being, the experimenter included; the Nuremberg Code of 1947 made informed consent the bedrock. Defenders say he risked only himself. Critics say he could not know that in advance, and he conceded as much: 'I was taken by surprise by the severity of the infection.' (Barry J. Marshall, 'Biographical', NobelPrize.org)

question: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren were right: the stomach bacterium they had chased, Helicobacter pylori, is behind over 90% of duodenal ulcers, and killing it cures them. Then epidemiologists went looking for the same bacterium in ordinary healthy people, and found it in roughly half of all living humans, about 44% of adults today. Of everyone carrying it, what share ever develops peptic ulcer disease?
answer: Between one in ten and one in five
choices: Between one in three and one in two
Between two in three and three in four
Between one in ten and one in five
Between one in a hundred and one in fifty
context: About 80% of carriers never show a single symptom. The Nobel presentation speech says it plainly: 'Half of humanity is infected, but luckily most people have no symptoms.' That is the mature version of the discovery: H. pylori is necessary for most peptic ulcers and not sufficient by itself, and what decides which carriers get sick is still argued over. The same bug turned out to be, in the Lasker citation's words, 'the world's most common chronic infection', and the World Health Organization classed it a Class I carcinogen in 1994 for its role in stomach cancer. (Grokipedia 'Helicobacter pylori'; Nobel Prize presentation speech 2005; Lasker Foundation 1995 citation)

question: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren won the argument, and an ulcer is now treated as an infection. The 2024 first-line regimen runs fourteen days of bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole plus a fourth agent, and killing the bacterium cures the ulcer. Yet for a duodenal ulcer that fourth agent alone carries on for another four to eight weeks, long after the bug is dead. What is it doing in those extra weeks?
answer: Switching off the stomach's acid pumps so the sore can close
choices: Switching off the stomach's acid pumps so the sore can close
Coating the sore with a film that shields it from digestion
Prompting the lining to lay down protective mucus faster
Blunting the nerve signal that drives the stomach to churn
context: Acid was never irrelevant; it simply was not the cause. Helicobacter pylori is what lets the sore open, and stomach acid is what keeps working at it, so the antibiotics remove the cause while the acid drug buys the wound the quiet weeks it needs to close. The full course has a name: bismuth quadruple therapy, meaning a proton pump inhibitor alongside bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole. A proton pump inhibitor is a drug that switches off the pumps in the stomach wall that pour acid out. Karl Schwarz's 1910 dictum 'no acid, no ulcer' turned out to be half right: the acid was not the culprit, but it was still doing damage, and the century of doctors who fought it were fighting something real. (Grokipedia 'Helicobacter pylori', citing the American College of Gastroenterology 2024 guidelines)

question: On 6 June 1822 at a fur post on Mackinac Island, a gun went off at close range into a young voyageur named Alexis St. Martin. Army surgeon William Beaumont expected him to die -- but as St. Martin healed, the edge of a hole in one organ knitted directly to the edge of the hole in his skin, leaving a permanent window into that organ. Which organ was it?
answer: the stomach
choices: the stomach
the liver
the small intestine
the left lung
context: The permanent opening from stomach to skin is called a gastric fistula. St. Martin survived roughly a year of terrible convalescence, and the fistula gave Beaumont something no anatomist had ever had: a live human stomach he could see and reach into during work. The distractors were all real casualties of the same wound -- St. Martin's lung was pierced and his ribs broken -- but only the stomach fused to the skin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_St._Martin.

question: Beaumont wanted to know how fast a working human stomach dissolves different foods. He worked out a simple method: attach a piece of beef, or bread, or raw cabbage to something long and slender, lower it through the fistula, wait a set number of minutes, then haul the sample back up and look. What did he attach the food to?
answer: a length of silk thread
choices: a length of silk thread
a curved glass rod
a hollow tin capsule
a coiled copper wire
context: The silk thread built the first table of digestion times in a living human. The distractors are all real digestion apparatus used by other people: Lazzaro Spallanzani (1780) had swallowed food in linen bags and later hollow wood or metal tubes; Rene Reaumur (1752) had used a kite that swallowed a metal tube with a sponge to soak up its gastric juice; and modern gut-transit studies use radio-opaque capsules. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Beaumont.

question: Watching the exposed stomach day after day, Beaumont noticed it did not always behave the same way -- some hours the lining flushed red, other hours it paled, and the rate of work varied wildly. When he cross-checked those readings against a diary of St. Martin's daily life, he became the first person to demonstrate one particular link in a living human being. Which link?
answer: that anger and fear measurably slow digestion
choices: that anger and fear measurably slow digestion
that spicy foods eat holes in the stomach lining
that a cold drink stops digestion for the hour
that a sleeping stomach makes no juice at all
context: On one recorded occasion of violent temper Beaumont even saw yellow bile back-flowing into a stomach where it should not have been. It is the first direct human evidence of what we now call the gut-brain link. The distractors are all real and interesting physiological facts -- but not what the fistula proved. Source: sciencehistory.org -- Probing the Mysteries of Human Digestion.

question: Beaumont's 1833 book Experiments and Observations on the Gastric Juice made him the father of American gastric physiology. But it rested on roughly a decade of experiments performed almost entirely on a single dependent man. What was the ARRANGEMENT that bound Alexis St. Martin to submit to those experiments?
answer: he signed a written contract as Beaumont's paid servant
choices: he signed a written contract as Beaumont's paid servant
he was placed by a court in Beaumont's legal custody
he agreed to a life-annuity in exchange for public displays
he enlisted in the US Army under Beaumont's direct command
context: St. Martin was illiterate, poor, and had no other way to feed his family; the signed contract made him Beaumont's servant, obliged to submit to experiments on demand. He ran off home to Quebec for the first time in September 1825, and Beaumont spent something like twenty years trying to get him back. Presented, not preached: an epochal piece of science rests on real ethical weight, and the kid gets to weigh it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_St._Martin.

question: Alexis St. Martin lived with the fistula in his side for 58 years and outlived Beaumont by 27 -- Beaumont died in 1853 from a fall on icy steps in St. Louis; St. Martin died in Quebec in 1880 at age 78. His family, fearing that anatomists would dig up his body for the famous stomach, took an unusual step to spoil the prize. What did they do?
answer: they let the body decompose above ground before burial
choices: they let the body decompose above ground before burial
they sealed the coffin under a slab of imported granite
they had his stomach removed and cremated before the wake
they hired armed men to guard the grave for a full year
context: A rotted body is worthless to a museum, so the family's tactic was cruder and cheaper than the alternatives -- and it worked. The distractors are all real nineteenth-century anti-'resurrectionist' tactics (heavy iron mortsafes, night watchtowers over new graves, and cremation) that other families used against the grave-robbing trade that fed the anatomy schools. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_St._Martin.

question: Paris, February 1896. Henri Becquerel wraps a photographic plate in black paper, sets uranium salts and a metal cross on top, and waits for sun. Clouds arrive for a week. He shoves it in a drawer, and on 1 March develops it anyway. What is on the plate?
answer: Silhouettes of the crystals and cross, blazing through it
choices: Silhouettes of the crystals and cross, blazing through it
Nothing - uniformly blank, like any unexposed plate
A faint fog across it, with no distinct shapes
The outline of the wooden drawer, in stray light
context: A week of cloud, one careful null-check, one accidentally momentous developing tray. Becquerel presents the plate to the French Academy of Sciences on 2 March 1896. Source: aps.org, March 1, 1896: Henri Becquerel Discovers Radioactivity.

question: Before the drawer, Henri Becquerel had a definite theory: sunlight would first charge his uranium crystals up, and they would then re-emit stored solar energy as penetrating rays. The cloudy week and the developed plate falsified that idea. What did the drawer force him to conclude instead?
answer: The uranium needs no light or heat - it emits on its own, constantly
choices: The uranium needs no light or heat - it emits on its own, constantly
The paper wrapping had been secretly leaking light onto the plate
The uranium was itself glowing invisibly from a nearby X-ray source
The developing chemicals produced the images from the plate's defects
context: Becquerel's initial hypothesis was WRONG - and only survived contact with the drawer because he developed the plate anyway. The corrected picture: spontaneous emission by the atom itself. Source: ans.org, Henri Becquerel's Discovery of Radioactivity.

question: In April 1901 Henri Becquerel walked to a lecture in Paris with a small glass tube of radium in his waistcoat pocket, resting against his chest for a few hours. About two weeks later the skin over that pocket ulcerated in the exact shape of the tube; the wound took months to heal. Becquerel published the observation - and it is remembered as the starting point of which field?
answer: Radiotherapy, the medical use of radiation against tumours
choices: Radiotherapy, the medical use of radiation against tumours
Radiography, the diagnostic imaging of bones and organs
Radiometric dating, the age-reading of rocks by decay clocks
Radio-astronomy, the reading of the sky in radio wavelengths
context: Becquerel's paper on his own burn (1901) prompted the first clinical trials with radium - a pharyngeal carcinoma was treated in Vienna in 1902. The observation was made on his own body: the test-it-yourself thread runs even through this. Source: vidyaenews, That Accidental Burn.

question: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu reached Constantinople in 1717, her face scarred and her brother dead of the same disease. She wrote home describing Turkish women at 'engrafting parties' who opened a vein with a needle and rubbed something in to protect the healthy from what she had just survived. What went into the cut?
answer: pus from another person's smallpox sore
choices: pus from another person's smallpox sore
powder scraped from a cowpox scab
juice pressed from willow bark
ash from a sickroom fire
context: This is variolation, not vaccination -- it used LIVE human smallpox and gave the patient a real (usually milder) case, immunising the survivor. Jenner's cowpox vaccine did not exist for another 79 years. Source: Hektoen International; Montagu's 1 April 1717 letter to Sarah Chiswell.

question: Boston, 1716. The Puritan minister Cotton Mather did not learn engrafting from a book. An enslaved West African man in his household rolled up a sleeve, showed him a small round scar, and told him the procedure had been done where he came from. What was the man's name, as Mather recorded it?
answer: Onesimus
choices: Onesimus
Titus
Boston
Prosper
context: Mather bought Onesimus from his congregation in 1706 and gave him a Greek New Testament name. Mather only came to trust the procedure after questioning other West Africans and reading Turkish reports; by the 1721 epidemic he was its loudest advocate. Source: Rush University.

question: In the 1721 Boston epidemic, most of the doctors refused to try engrafting. One physician, Zabdiel Boylston, tried it and did the thing that mattered most: he kept a written tally of every person he treated and every death. Of his 282 inoculated Bostonians about 2 percent died; of the 5,759 who caught the disease the natural way, roughly what percentage died?
answer: about 14 percent
choices: about 14 percent
about 3 percent
about 40 percent
about 60 percent
context: Boylston counted 6 deaths among 282 inoculated versus 844 deaths among 5,759 who caught natural smallpox. It is one of the earliest quantitative comparisons in medicine -- numbers, not authority, decided the argument. He presented the volume to the Royal Society in London in 1726. Source: James Lind Library.

question: Zabdiel Boylston's arithmetic did not settle the Boston argument peacefully. Around three in the morning on 14 November 1721, someone hurled a lit grenade through the front window of Cotton Mather, the minister who had backed the procedure. What kept it from killing anyone in the house?
answer: the fuse jarred loose when the shell hit the floor
choices: the fuse jarred loose when the shell hit the floor
a servant kicked the shell back out the window
the powder inside was old and refused to catch
the shell landed in a basin of washing water
context: A note was tied to the grenade: 'Cotton Mather, you dog, dam you: I'l inoculate you with this; with a Pox to you.' The impact snapped the fuse off, so the powder never fired. Mather kept campaigning. Source: Washington Post; Boston Post-Boy contemporary reporting.

question: Engrafting was neither free nor entirely safe. Because the technique used LIVE smallpox taken from an actual sore, the inoculated person came down with a real case of the disease. About what portion of the engrafted died of the treatment itself?
answer: one or two in a hundred
choices: one or two in a hundred
about five in a hundred
about ten in a hundred
about one in five
context: Variolation killed 1 to 2 percent of those treated, against about 30 percent for natural variola major in the wild -- a real medical trade-off, roughly a 1-in-50 chance of the treatment killing you against a 1-in-3 chance if the disease found you naturally. This is the sharp distinction from Jenner's later cowpox vaccination, which used a different virus and was much safer. Source: WHO smallpox monograph.

question: An engrafted patient did not just get a milder personal case -- they came down with real, transmissible smallpox for a stretch while the sores formed and healed, and could seed an ordinary outbreak in the town. What practical rule did that force communities to build around the procedure?
answer: keep the engrafted apart from the healthy until the sores had scabbed and dried
choices: keep the engrafted apart from the healthy until the sores had scabbed and dried
confine the whole household under quarantine for a full month after the cut
perform the procedure only in a pest-house set outside the town walls
require the inoculated to wear a marked cloth in public until they had healed
context: In practice this meant about one to two weeks of isolation for the inoculated person themselves. Several colonies eventually restricted or banned the practice because the rule was hard to enforce -- a scientific and ethical problem Jenner's cowpox vaccine, which did not shed smallpox, would later escape. Source: Massachusetts Historical Society.

question: London, 9 August 1721. Six condemned inmates of Newgate Prison were promised a royal pardon if they would submit to being engrafted with smallpox in front of physicians of the Royal College. The event was called the 'Royal Experiment.' How did the surgeon place the smallpox matter into each prisoner's body?
answer: by cutting incisions into both arms and the right leg of each
choices: by cutting incisions into both arms and the right leg of each
by a single deep cut into the left shoulder of each
by four shallow scratches arranged across the chest
by pricking the sole of each foot with a loaded needle
context: Charles Maitland did the cutting, using three sites per prisoner to raise the chance the graft would take. All six lived; they were pardoned and released around 6 September 1721. Hans Sloane organised the trial; Mead and Jurin were among the observing physicians. Source: Indiana University Libraries.

question: In 2011 a Cornell social psychologist published nine experiments claiming that undergraduates could sense the future. On each trial the students had to guess which of two curtains on a screen would hide an erotic image, and they picked correctly slightly more often than chance BEFORE the computer had chosen where to put it. Who was the researcher?
answer: Daryl Bem
choices: Daryl Bem
Stuart Ritchie
Uri Simonsohn
Brian Nosek
context: The paper was titled 'Feeling the Future: Experimental Evidence for Anomalous Retroactive Influences on Cognition and Affect'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daryl_Bem

question: Daryl Bem's 2011 precognition paper landed in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the flagship journal of the American Psychological Association's social-personality wing. Why did publishing it THERE, specifically, deliver the shock rather than a fringe parapsychology outlet publishing the same nine experiments?
answer: It was the field's flagship, so the field owned the result
choices: It was the field's flagship, so the field owned the result
The journal had a larger circulation than any rival
Only that journal would let Bem keep his raw data private
The journal offered faster peer review than its competitors
context: The Journal of Personality and Social Psychology is the American Psychological Association's flagship for its wing; a fringe journal publishing 'psi is real' would have been dismissed, but the flagship publishing it meant mainstream psychology's own gatekeepers had waved it through. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Personality_and_Social_Psychology

question: Stuart Ritchie, Richard Wiseman and Chris French re-ran Daryl Bem's ninth precognition experiment three times, at three different universities, using Bem's own computer program. What did the three replications actually turn up?
answer: No effect at all in any of the three
choices: No effect at all in any of the three
A larger effect than Bem reported
The same effect only for female students
An effect that ran in the opposite direction
context: Three careful replications, three flat lines. In the crisis-year vocabulary that would follow, this is the standard shape of a psychology finding that lived only in its first author's data. Source: https://www.badscience.net/2011/04/i-foresee-that-nobody-will-do-anything-about-this-problem/

question: The replication of Daryl Bem's precognition experiments by Stuart Ritchie, Richard Wiseman and Chris French was refused by the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, by Science Brevia and by Psychological Science, in each case without ever being sent to a peer reviewer. On what stated grounds did all three refuse it?
answer: It was a replication rather than a new finding
choices: It was a replication rather than a new finding
It failed a statistical pre-check by the editor
The authors did not yet hold tenure at their universities
The topic was too speculative for a serious journal
context: The stated policy 'we do not publish replications' was the file-drawer machine caught operating in daylight. The paper eventually appeared in the open-access journal PLoS ONE as 'Failing the Future'. Source: https://www.badscience.net/2011/04/i-foresee-that-nobody-will-do-anything-about-this-problem/

question: After three journals had refused the replication of his precognition paper without review, the British Journal of Psychology finally sent it out to two referees. The authors were suspicious about the identity of the second referee and later got confirmation of who it had been. Who WAS that second referee?
answer: Daryl Bem, the original paper's author
choices: Daryl Bem, the original paper's author
The paper's original statistical consultant
A senior parapsychology researcher at Duke
The Cornell psychology department's chair
context: Bem confirmed to the authors afterwards that he had been asked to referee the replication of his own paper. The editor rejected the authors' request for a third referee. Source: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/b9vvmMn2kF76aThHn/follow-up-on-esp-study-we-don-t-publish-replications

question: Eric-Jan Wagenmakers and colleagues reanalyzed the numbers in Daryl Bem's 2011 precognition paper and produced the technical finding that swung the crisis harder than any failed replication. Which of these reanalyses was WAGENMAKERS's specific move?
answer: A Bayesian reading of Bem's own data actually favoured no psi effect
choices: A Bayesian reading of Bem's own data actually favoured no psi effect
The nine significant results out of ten were too clean given the effect sizes
The reported effect vanished once optional stopping was corrected for
The precognition trials were underpowered to detect the reported effect
context: Wagenmakers and colleagues also flagged that Bem had reported one-sided p-values where two-sided were required. The 'too clean' finding came later from Gregory Francis and Uli Schimmack independently. The lesson psychologists took: the toolkit itself was overstating evidence, not just in this paper. Source: https://web.stanford.edu/class/psych201s/psych201s/papers/Wagenmakers-etal-2011-bemComment.pdf

question: In a 2017 Slate interview about his precognition work, Daryl Bem gave an unusually candid answer that many observers read as close to an admission of what would soon be called p-hacking. He described his data as 'a point of persuasion' and added a specific line about a habit most scientists at least pretend to have. What did Bem say he had 'never really worried about'?
answer: Whether the findings would replicate
choices: Whether the findings would replicate
Whether the participants took the task seriously
Whether the effect had a physical mechanism
Whether his coauthors agreed with him
context: The full Bem quote to Slate: 'I used data as a point of persuasion, and I never really worried about, will this replicate or will this not.' Historians of psychology now date the discipline's replication crisis from his 2011 paper. Source: https://ivy0.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-on-parapsychology

question: Paris, 1903. A glass flask falls from a high shelf in the laboratory of the French chemist Edouard Benedictus and hits the tiled floor. He goes to sweep up the shards - and there is nothing to sweep. What has the fallen flask done?
answer: Cracked all over but is still holding its shape
choices: Cracked all over but is still holding its shape
Bounced off the tiles undamaged
Fused itself onto the tile in one piece
Shattered into a fine glass powder
context: The flask had been sitting on the shelf for months. Something invisible was holding the shards in place. Source: Wikipedia, 'Edouard Benedictus' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edouard_Benedictus).

question: Benedictus wrote the odd flask up in his notebook and then, for six years, did nothing with it. The accident sat waiting for a use. What finally sent him back to the flask in 1909?
answer: Newspaper reports of drivers cut by broken car windshields
choices: Newspaper reports of drivers cut by broken car windshields
A French navy commission to build reinforced portholes
A private prize offered for a stronger sort of drinking glass
A friend's gift of a new type of French laboratory flask
context: The 1909 patent followed reports of drivers and passengers cut by flying glass in the earliest automobile accidents. Retellings name particular victims, but the trigger was the newspaper coverage itself. Sources: McGill OSS; Wikipedia, 'Edouard Benedictus'.

question: In 1911 Benedictus founded the company to sell his new safety glass. He gave the product a Latin-flavored brand name that stuck. The name became a licensed brand across Europe, is still stamped into vintage car windshields today, and outlived Benedictus by decades. What did he call it?
answer: Triplex
choices: Triplex
Cristallo
Argento
Fortis
context: The 1911 Societe du Verre Triplex. The name licensed across Britain and Europe and became almost synonymous with laminated safety glass. Source: McGill OSS, 'What is Safety Glass?' (https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/history-you-asked/what-safety-glass).

question: The whole point of the invention had been to keep drivers from being cut by their windshields - and yet carmakers of the 1910s judged Benedictus's safety glass too expensive to fit as standard. Then the Great War broke out and gave the material its first real mass market. Where did Triplex glass first prove itself at scale?
answer: In the eyepieces of Allied gas masks
choices: In the eyepieces of Allied gas masks
In submarine periscopes
In field-hospital operating-theatre skylights
In the observation slits of tanks
context: A cracked-but-whole eyepiece is exactly what you want between a soldier's face and a chlorine cloud. The gas-mask contract made the material affordable enough for carmakers to consider afterwards. Source: Lexology, 'Serendipitous Invention - Safety Glass' (https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=cdd91c2f-0d25-4b27-937f-f0d30b460fb1).

question: At the end of the 1920s Henry Ford finally forced laminated safety glass into the American car, ordering it as standard on the Ford Model A - but he paid for it on only one pane of the car, and the rest stayed ordinary plate glass until 1931. Which pane got the safety glass first?
answer: The windshield
choices: The windshield
The rear window
The driver-side window
All four side windows
context: The Model A (1927-31) was the first Ford production car with laminated safety glass, and Ford put it only in the windshield - the pane a driver's face would hit first in a crash. Side and rear windows stayed plate glass on most Model As until 1931. Source: Model A Ford Garage, 'Model A and B Safety Glass' (https://www.fordgarage.com/pages/craiglewisglass.htm).

question: Walk out to a parked car tonight. The modern windshield is a Benedictus descendant: two sheets of glass with a clear plastic interlayer that lets it craze but hold in the frame. That interlayer is no longer collodion - the whole industry now uses a tougher, clearer plastic bonded permanently between the panes. What is the modern windshield interlayer made of?
answer: Polyvinyl butyral, known as PVB
choices: Polyvinyl butyral, known as PVB
Cellulose acetate, known as CA
Polystyrene, known as PS
Polycarbonate, known as PC
context: PVB replaced cellulose nitrate in the 1930s (nitrocellulose yellowed badly in sunlight and was flammable). A modern windshield is glass-PVB-glass, engineered so that in a crash it crazes into a web and STAYS IN THE FRAME. The side and rear windows are a completely different fix - tempered rather than laminated - which is why they burst into pebbles instead. Source: Wikipedia, 'Polyvinyl butyral' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyvinyl_butyral).

question: In March 1949 a BBC radio broadcast used the vivid phrase 'this big bang idea' - the name that would stick to the leading cosmological theory for the rest of the century. Who spoke the phrase on air that night?
answer: Fred Hoyle, then a leading proponent of the rival steady-state cosmology
choices: Fred Hoyle, then a leading proponent of the rival steady-state cosmology
Georges Lemaitre, the Belgian priest whose primeval-atom paper Hubble later cited
Edwin Hubble, whose redshift-distance measurements first showed cosmic expansion
George Gamow, whose team calculated a hot early universe and its relic radiation
context: Hoyle was a co-author of the steady-state theory; he spoke on the BBC Third Programme on 28 March 1949 and later said he chose the phrase for its striking visual image over radio. The name did not catch on until the 1970s, after the theory it named had won. Source: Kragh 2013, 'Big Bang: the etymology of a name', Astronomy & Geophysics 54(2).

question: Everyone repeats that Fred Hoyle coined the phrase 'big bang' as an insult to mock a theory he opposed. Historian of science Helge Kragh went back to the surviving broadcast texts and Hoyle's own words to check the story - and reported which finding?
answer: The derision story is popular but poorly supported; Hoyle denied any mocking intent and the record does not back it up
choices: The derision story is popular but poorly supported; Hoyle denied any mocking intent and the record does not back it up
The broadcasts confirm the mockery in Hoyle's own tone of voice, preserved in a BBC recording from that night
Hoyle later admitted in a 1989 interview that the mockery had been a rehearsed script written by a BBC producer
Bondi and Gold jointly wrote the mocking line and slipped it into Hoyle's script without telling him first
context: In a 1989 interview Hoyle explained he was 'constantly striving over the radio, where I had no visual aids, nothing except the spoken word, for visual images' and needed a phrase to distinguish the two rival pictures. The much-repeated 'meant it as an insult' story is a corrected misconception. Source: Kragh, Astronomy & Geophysics 54 (2013); Nature news, 'How did the Big Bang get its name?' (2024).

question: What made the 1948 rival cosmology science and not taste was that it made a sharp, testable prediction about the deep sky: because the universe was supposed to look the same at every era, the population of very distant (and therefore very old) radio sources had to look statistically like the nearby one. Through the 1950s Martin Ryle's Cambridge surveys tested exactly this - and reported what?
answer: Far too many faint (distant) radio sources for a universe that always looked the same
choices: Far too many faint (distant) radio sources for a universe that always looked the same
Far too FEW faint radio sources, as if the deep sky were emptier than the nearby one
A ring of bright radio sources at one preferred distance, ruling out both models at once
A perfectly uniform count of radio sources at every distance the survey managed to sample
context: In his 1955 Halley Lecture at Oxford, Ryle stated bluntly that the results 'cannot be explained in terms of a steady-state theory.' Quasars, discovered soon after, sealed it: they sit only at large redshifts, meaning they were common only in the distant past. Ryle shared the 1974 Nobel Prize partly for this work. Source: Ryle 1955 Halley Lecture; Britannica, 'Extragalactic radio source'.

question: After the 1965 relic-heat discovery finished steady state as mainstream cosmology, Fred Hoyle did not concede. He kept publishing rescue variants of his rejected theory - including a 'quasi-steady state' model - for the rest of his life. This stubbornness is often held against him. What is the honest coda most historians add before closing the case?
answer: Hoyle was magnificently right about a different, huge question: that the elements heavier than helium are cooked inside stars
choices: Hoyle was magnificently right about a different, huge question: that the elements heavier than helium are cooked inside stars
Hoyle later privately renounced the C-field in a letter to Bondi that surfaced only after his death in 2001
Hoyle's rescue variants each made a fresh prediction that was verified by later satellite surveys of the microwave sky
Hoyle's late-life papers were reviewed by Ryle himself, who signed off on their mathematical soundness in print
context: In 1957 Hoyle co-authored the B2FH paper 'Synthesis of the Elements in Stars' with Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, and William Fowler, establishing stellar nucleosynthesis. Fowler alone received the 1983 Nobel Prize for that work; Hoyle was pointedly omitted, a decision widely regarded as a snub. Theories rarely die because their authors give up. Source: Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle, Rev. Mod. Phys. 29, 547 (1957).

question: The phrase 'big bang', spoken on air in March 1949 by a leading opponent of the theory it named, took a surprisingly long time to become the standard label for the theory itself. In roughly what decade did the phrase finally catch on with working cosmologists?
answer: In the 1970s, well after the theory it named had already been vindicated by the microwave hiss
choices: In the 1970s, well after the theory it named had already been vindicated by the microwave hiss
In the 1950s, during the same run of Cambridge radio surveys that first embarrassed the rival
In the 1960s, right after the theory's central prediction was confirmed at Bell Labs
In the 1980s, after Fowler's Nobel Prize for stellar nucleosynthesis restored Hoyle's standing
context: Historian Helge Kragh documents that early Big Bang theorists did not much use the phrase; Gamow and colleagues stuck with 'primeval atom' and 'dynamic evolution' for years. The rival's insult (that wasn't an insult) only became the theory's own name once the theory had already won. Source: Kragh 2013, Astronomy & Geophysics 54(2).

question: In November 1915 Albert Einstein finished the field equations of general relativity and expected the first exact solutions would take years. Within weeks a letter arrived from an artillery lieutenant on the Russian front who had solved them by hand between shell-trajectory calculations. Who wrote the letter?
answer: Karl Schwarzschild
choices: Karl Schwarzschild
Hermann Minkowski
Max Planck
David Hilbert
context: Schwarzschild's letter is dated 22 December 1915. He closed it: 'the war is kindly disposed toward me, allowing me... to take this walk into this your land of ideas.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Schwarzschild

question: The Russian-front artillery lieutenant who mailed Einstein the exact solution was over forty when he volunteered, and he did not live to see the war end. What killed him five months after Einstein received the letter?
answer: a skin disease he caught at the front
choices: a skin disease he caught at the front
a shell burst during a ballistic test
typhus in a field hospital
a stray bullet on patrol
context: The disease was pemphigus, a rare autoimmune condition. Schwarzschild was invalided home in March 1916 and died on 11 May 1916, aged 42. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Schwarzschild

question: Neither Einstein nor Schwarzschild ever used the phrase 'black hole' for the collapsed object at the centre of the Schwarzschild solution. The two-word name did not stick until an American physicist began using it in lectures in 1967, and it spread from there. Who made the phrase stick?
answer: John Archibald Wheeler
choices: John Archibald Wheeler
Robert Oppenheimer
Fritz Zwicky
Freeman Dyson
context: The phrase had already appeared at a 1963 Dallas astrophysics conference and in a 1964 AAAS meeting report; Wheeler popularised it, he did not coin it. He said an audience member suggested it after hearing him say 'gravitationally completely collapsed object' one too many times. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Archibald_Wheeler

question: In 1930, on the boat from India to England to take up a Cambridge scholarship, a 19-year-old worked out with pencil and paper that a burnt-out star above about 1.44 solar masses cannot hold itself up against its own gravity. Whose calculation was it?
answer: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
choices: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
Georges Lemaitre
Fritz Zwicky
Lev Landau
context: The 1.44-solar-mass ceiling is now called the Chandrasekhar limit. Above it, electron degeneracy pressure loses to gravity. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrasekhar_limit

question: On 11 January 1935 at the Royal Astronomical Society, the young Chandrasekhar presented the mass ceiling above which a white dwarf must keep collapsing. Then Arthur Eddington -- the hero of the 1919 eclipse expedition, at the height of his authority -- rose to speak next. What did Eddington do?
answer: attacked the result in public as physically meaningless
choices: attacked the result in public as physically meaningless
endorsed the result as the calculation of the decade
asked for a private repeat in Cambridge before commenting
sat silent and refused to react
context: Eddington believed some unknown physics would prevent unlimited collapse -- not a stupid position at the time. He later called the work 'stellar buffoonery' at Harvard. Chandrasekhar was right; his Nobel came in 1983, forty-eight years after that RAS meeting. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrasekhar%E2%80%93Eddington_dispute

question: For decades sceptics argued that gravitational collapse to a singularity was an artefact of assuming perfect spherical symmetry -- a real star, with lumps and spin, would find some way to avoid it. In a 1965 paper in Physical Review Letters, one mathematician proved that once a trapped surface forms, the singularity is unavoidable regardless of symmetry. Whose theorem?
answer: Roger Penrose
choices: Roger Penrose
Stephen Hawking
Kip Thorne
John Wheeler
context: Penrose used null geodesics to show that once light rays cannot escape outward, the future ends in a singularity. He shared the 2020 Nobel for this result. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose%E2%80%93Hawking_singularity_theorems

question: Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel with two astronomers whose teams spent decades in Chile and Hawaii tracking individual stars -- especially one with a 16-year orbit -- whipping around an invisible ~4-million-solar-mass object at the heart of our galaxy. Who shared the prize with him?
answer: Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez
choices: Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez
Kip Thorne and Rainer Weiss
Vera Rubin and Sandra Faber
Saul Perlmutter and Brian Schmidt
context: The tracked star is S2 (also called S0-2). At closest approach in May 2018 it was clocked at 2.55% of the speed of light. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagittarius_A*

question: On 10 April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released its picture of M87*, and on 12 May 2022 the one at the centre of the Milky Way. It looks like a photograph but is not: radio dishes on four continents recorded raw data onto hard drives that had to be physically flown to central labs, and the picture was reconstructed from what those signals did when they were combined. What are you actually looking at in the image?
answer: the shadow cast on the hot gas around the hole
choices: the shadow cast on the hot gas around the hole
the hole itself, seen against black sky
an artist's rendering fitted to numeric data
a heat map of X-rays from the accretion disc
context: A black hole emits no light, so it cannot be seen directly. Gravity bends light from the surrounding hot glowing gas and leaves a dark central region -- the shadow -- roughly 2.6 times wider than the event horizon itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_Horizon_Telescope

question: A smashed egg never unscrambles itself. Ludwig Boltzmann argued in the 1870s that no LAW of nature actually forbids the unsmashing - the real reason is simpler than a law. What did he say the real reason is?
answer: scrambled arrangements vastly outnumber tidy ones
choices: scrambled arrangements vastly outnumber tidy ones
friction drains the energy needed to reverse motion
gravity locks liquid yolk to the floor once it touches
atoms in a broken egg forget where they started
context: This is Boltzmann's statistical reading of the second law: entropy 'always' rises because tidy configurations are astronomically outnumbered by messy ones. Tidy is not forbidden, just wildly improbable. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-Boltzmann.

question: Ernst Zermelo pressed a second attack using a recent theorem of Henri Poincare: any bounded mechanical system must EVENTUALLY return arbitrarily close to its starting state. So entropy cannot really rise forever. Boltzmann's answer did not disprove the theorem - he reshaped the second law itself. What did his reply say about a spontaneous decrease in entropy?
answer: it is not forbidden, only astronomically improbable
choices: it is not forbidden, only astronomically improbable
it is impossible in any closed system by pure logic
it is a measurement artefact of imperfect thermometers
it occurs continuously but averages out over long times
context: Poincare's recurrence time for a real gas is so unimaginably long that no observer would ever see it. Boltzmann's move turned the second law from an absolute prohibition into a statistical near-certainty. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/statphys-Boltzmann.

question: Einstein's paper was a prediction; someone had to actually do the measurement. In 1908-1909 a French physicist patiently tracked those jittering grains under a microscope and pulled Avogadro's number out of the numbers - a result that effectively ended the argument over atoms. Who did that experiment?
answer: Jean Perrin
choices: Jean Perrin
Paul Langevin
Marie Curie
Ernst Rutherford
context: Perrin's Brownian-motion work won him the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics. His careful measurements matched Einstein's formula and yielded Avogadro's number - even Ostwald conceded atoms after Perrin's data. Source: advlabs.aapt.org/bfy/files/AJPBrownianPaper.pdf.

question: Boltzmann took his own life on 5 September 1906 at Duino, near Trieste, less than two years before Perrin's data settled the atomic question. A popular story blames despair over the atom fight - but Boltzmann's own record contains something else, independently documented, that the story quietly omits. What is it?
answer: a long history of severe depression, with earlier attempts
choices: a long history of severe depression, with earlier attempts
a stroke suffered at Duino only weeks earlier
a specific medication side effect noted by his physician
a heart condition his family had long concealed
context: Boltzmann had earlier suicide attempts and rapid mood swings consistent with what would today be called bipolar disorder. Historians agree the true cause cannot be settled; the 'despair over rejection' narrative is a repeated story, not a documented finding. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Ludwig_Boltzmann.

question: October 1970. Margaret Borlaug drives an hour out to the wheat fields near Toluca to find her husband and tell him a newspaper in Oslo had called that morning: he had won the Nobel Peace Prize. What was Norman Borlaug's first reaction?
answer: He thought it was a hoax
choices: He thought it was a hoax
He fainted in the field
He refused the prize
He asked for a translator
context: The call had come from a reporter at the Norwegian paper Aftenposten rather than through official channels, so Borlaug assumed someone was pulling his leg and kept working. Source: World Food Prize extended biography.

question: Norman Borlaug did not invent short wheat. In 1953 he got hold of a semi-dwarf line an American agronomist named Cecil Salmon had shipped home after World War II from occupied Japan. What was that Japanese variety called?
answer: Norin 10
choices: Norin 10
Kanto 107
Sonora 64
Marquis 44
context: Gonjiro Inazuka released Norin 10 in Japan in 1935; Salmon collected it in 1946 for the USDA; Orville Vogel at Washington State bred it further and passed seed to Borlaug in 1953. Its Rht1 and Rht2 genes now sit in more than seventy percent of the world's commercial wheat. Sources: Wikipedia 'Norin 10 wheat', 'Cecil Salmon', 'Orville Vogel'.

question: The claim you hear about Norman Borlaug - that he 'saved a billion lives' - is an ESTIMATE, not a measurement. This ladder checks its own heroes. Who put that figure into print, and where?
answer: Gregg Easterbrook, in a 1997 Atlantic essay
choices: Gregg Easterbrook, in a 1997 Atlantic essay
The Nobel committee, in the 1970 citation
Paul Ehrlich, in a 1990 retraction
The World Food Programme, in a 1985 report
context: Easterbrook's January 1997 essay 'Forgotten Benefactor of Humanity' introduced the billion-lives figure, and the agricultural economist Dennis Avery echoed it. A defensible estimate is not the same thing as a measurement, and the bank marks its own hero-numbers as such. Source: The Atlantic archive.

question: In his 1970 Nobel lecture in Oslo, Norman Borlaug refused to declare the food problem solved. He warned that 'the frightening power of human reproduction must also be curbed' and insisted on one flat sentence about what his kind of work could never be. What did he say there are none of, in agricultural production?
answer: Miracles
choices: Miracles
Shortcuts
Free lunches
Final answers
context: 'There are no miracles in agricultural production.' The man who had just been called the Father of the Green Revolution used his acceptance speech to say the pressure would return unless yields kept rising - the honest verdict of the man who had broken the prophecy. Source: Nobel Prize lecture, 11 December 1970.

question: Cap a syringe with your finger and push the plunger -- the air inside resists you and shoves it back out. In the 1660s Robert Boyle gave that resistance a memorable name. What did he call it?
answer: the spring of the air
choices: the spring of the air
the weight of the atmosphere
the horror of the vacuum
the elasticity of the aether
context: Boyle published New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air in 1660. 'Spring' meant elastic push-back -- the same word we still use for a metal coil. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/robert-boyle/

question: In the 1660s Robert Boyle -- with the young Robert Hooke, who built the glassware -- proved that doubling the squeeze on trapped air shrinks it to half its size. Their apparatus was a J-shaped glass tube, with air sealed into the short closed arm. What did they pour down the long open arm to do the squeezing?
answer: mercury
choices: mercury
water
molten wax
olive oil
context: Mercury is dense enough that a modest column of it presses hard, and it is a liquid at room temperature that does not stick to clean glass -- ideal for a pressure column. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/full-boyle/

question: The rule that doubling the pressure on a gas halves its volume is famous under Robert Boyle's name -- but Boyle himself did not claim it as his own idea. He credited a hypothesis put to him by two other English natural philosophers who had done the measurement first. Whom did he name?
answer: Richard Towneley and Henry Power
choices: Richard Towneley and Henry Power
Isaac Newton and Christopher Wren
Edmund Halley and John Flamsteed
Isaac Barrow and John Wallis
context: Boyle called it 'Mr Towneley's hypothesis' in print in 1662, and said Hooke had already verified it in August 1661. Giving the two Lancashire experimenters public credit is the point of the story: Boyle's law was not solely Boyle's. Source: https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jappl.1999.87.4.1543

question: In France the same gas-law is not called Boyle's law. It bears the name of a French physicist who found it independently in the 1670s -- and who added the condition Boyle had left unsaid, that the temperature must be held constant. What is the French name for the law?
answer: Mariotte's law
choices: Mariotte's law
Pascal's law
Gay-Lussac's law
Fresnel's law
context: Edme Mariotte (1620-1684). Without the constant-temperature clause the rule fails: warm the gas up and it will expand even under the same squeeze. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle's_law

question: When Robert Boyle published his air-pump experiments, a philosopher fired back in 1661 with a book titled Dialogus physicus de natura aeris, arguing that a true empty space was impossible in nature and that Boyle's evacuated glass must simply be leaking. Which philosopher was the attacker?
answer: Thomas Hobbes
choices: Thomas Hobbes
John Locke
Henry More
Ralph Cudworth
context: Hobbes -- yes, the Leviathan Hobbes -- treated the air-pump as a threat to his whole plenum-based natural philosophy. Boyle answered him with more experiments rather than more argument. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2021/entries/hobbes-science/

question: A Jesuit contemporary of Boyle, Franciscus Linus, refused to accept that the evacuated glass was really empty. He proposed an invisible substance still filling the space and defying the pump. What Latin name did he give it?
answer: the funiculus
choices: the funiculus
the plenum
the aether
the horror vacui
context: Funiculus is Latin for 'little rope' -- Linus imagined it as a stretched thread. Distractors: plenum = Descartes's fully-packed cosmos; aether = the light-carrying medium killed off by Michelson-Morley 1887; horror vacui = the Aristotelian idea that nature abhors a vacuum. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2021/entries/hobbes-science/

question: For seventy years after Boyle no one could explain WHY the trapped air pushed back. In 1738 a Swiss mathematician wrote out the answer in a book called Hydrodynamica: air is mostly empty space, tiny particles are flying about, and pressure is the drumming of those particles on the walls -- halve the space and every wall gets hit twice as often. Whose picture was that?
answer: Daniel Bernoulli
choices: Daniel Bernoulli
Leonhard Euler
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
Robert Hooke
context: Bernoulli derived Boyle's law from a billiard-ball model of gas, a century before anyone could see a molecule. The kinetic theory of gases would not be fully worked out until Maxwell and Boltzmann in the 1860s and 70s. Source: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/bernoulli-proposes-kinetic-theory-gases

question: To prove that living things depend on air, Robert Boyle put flies, snails, eels, mice and birds inside his evacuated glass. A hundred years later travelling lecturers had turned that same demonstration into the paid showpiece of an evening's entertainment. In 1768 an English painter caught the scene by candlelight, with the lecturer staring straight out of the canvas at the viewer. Which painter?
answer: Joseph Wright of Derby
choices: Joseph Wright of Derby
William Hogarth
Thomas Gainsborough
George Stubbs
context: The painting is An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump (1768), National Gallery, London. The bird under the bell jar is a white cockatoo; a child watches, frightened. Wright specialised in candlelit scenes of the new scientific culture -- his Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery hangs as a pair with this one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Experiment_on_a_Bird_in_the_Air_Pump

question: In 1912 the British Army had a problem: rifle barrels kept eroding and pitting after repeated firing. Sheffield metallurgist Harry Brearley was hired to solve it. While hunting a tougher gun-barrel alloy he stumbled onto something else entirely. What was that unexpected result?
answer: A steel that would not rust
choices: A steel that would not rust
A bronze that would not tarnish
An iron that would not spark
A nickel that would not oxidise
context: The tougher gun barrel eluded him; the corrosion-resistant alloy did not. Brearley called what he had 'rustless steel'; the world soon adopted a different name for it. Source: Sheffield Museums, Burngreave Voices; Wikipedia, Harry Brearley.

question: The popular telling of Harry Brearley's discovery has him wandering past a scrap pile and noticing one sample refusing to rust in the rain. Brearley's own account is more mundane: the true clue came from a routine bench step he ran on every new alloy before inspection. What was that step?
answer: Polishing then etching with nitric acid
choices: Polishing then etching with nitric acid
Quenching in oil then tempering
Heating red-hot then hammering thin
Dipping in hydrochloric acid to descale
context: Brearley polished and etched every new alloy with nitric acid to bring out its crystalline structure under a microscope; on this alloy the acid simply refused to bite. The scrap pile is folklore; the etching bench is the record he left. Source: Wikipedia, Harry Brearley; The Hexagon on Brearley.

question: The real reason Brearley's alloy resists nitric acid, sea spray and rain is what happens on its surface the moment it meets the atmosphere. A film only a few nanometres thick forms where a specific metal in the alloy reacts with the outside world. What is that ultrathin film made of?
answer: Chromium oxide
choices: Chromium oxide
Aluminium oxide
Iron oxide
Titanium oxide
context: Above roughly 10.5 to 12 percent chromium in the alloy, that 1-to-5-nanometre chromium-oxide layer forms so readily and so uniformly that it seals the metal from further attack. Metallurgists call it a passive film. Source: Viox on stainless passivation; Nature 415, Why stainless steel corrodes.

question: Scratch a chrome-plated car bumper hard enough and the shiny plating peels off, exposing bare iron that starts to rust the next morning. Scratch a stainless-steel knife the same way and no rust appears. What is the stainless alloy's self-healing trick?
answer: Regrow the protective film from atoms in its bulk
choices: Regrow the protective film from atoms in its bulk
Sacrifice a zinc layer that wears down in the iron's place
Flow a polymer coating back over the scratch
Re-deposit a copper film from dissolved ions
context: Chromium atoms from deep inside the alloy migrate to the fresh wound and react with air to lay down a new passive film in minutes. Zinc galvanising is a different (sacrificial) trick used on cheaper steel; a plated coating has no reservoir behind it and simply wears through. Source: Viox on stainless passivation; Wikipedia on galvanization.

question: Brearley was not the first person on Earth to make a chromium-iron alloy. Two years before his 1913 cast, a German researcher had already published a study titled A Study of Iron-Chromium Alloys with Special Consideration of their Resistance to Acids, arguing that chromium above roughly 12 percent made steel passive. Which claimant was that?
answer: Philipp Monnartz
choices: Philipp Monnartz
Hans Goldschmidt
Adolf Martens
Wilhelm Borchers
context: Monnartz (with W. Borchers as co-author) held the priority on the mechanism itself in the scientific literature. Frenchman Leon Guillet had made nearly the same alloys years earlier without noticing their corrosion resistance. What Brearley did that the others had not was recognize what he was holding and drive it into a saleable product. Source: worldstainless.org History of Stainless Steels.

question: In October 1912, ten months before Brearley's Sheffield cast, engineers at Krupp in Germany filed a patent on a different variant of the same idea: a chromium-nickel alloy branded 'Nirosta'. Which two Krupp metallurgists did the work behind that patent?
answer: Benno Strauss and Eduard Maurer
choices: Benno Strauss and Eduard Maurer
Adolf Martens and Emil Heyn
Friedrich Krupp and Alfred Krupp
Hans Goldschmidt and Wilhelm Borchers
context: Strauss and Maurer developed the austenitic (chromium-nickel) family between 1909 and 1912, opening a whole second branch of the alloy tree that Brearley's chromium-only recipe did not. Multiple independent teams converged on the same continent at nearly the same moment. Source: worldstainless.org History of Stainless Steels.

question: Eastern Washington is scarred with bare rock canyons, giant potholes and a dry cliff (Dry Falls) 3.5 miles wide and taller than Niagara. In 1923 the geologist J Harlen Bretz published a shocking claim about what carved it. What did he say?
answer: It was cut by a single catastrophic flood.
choices: It was cut by a single catastrophic flood.
A slow river that has since dried up ground it out.
Ordinary glacial meltwater carved it over many summers.
Wind-driven sandblasting shaped it during ice-age dry periods.
context: Bretz's paper was 'The Channeled Scabland of the Columbia Plateau,' Journal of Geology, 1923. He named the landscape the Channeled Scablands and called the culprit the Spokane flood. The three losing options here were among the real alternatives senior geologists offered against him at the 1927 Cosmos Club meeting. Source: EWU digital archives.

question: The geological establishment did not just dismiss Bretz - they had a principled reason. Charles Lyell had rebuilt geology on 'uniformitarianism' (present processes at present rates) precisely to escape an older kind of explanation. Which older kind of explanation had Lyell's principle been designed to banish?
answer: Appeals to a biblical Flood carving the land in one event
choices: Appeals to a biblical Flood carving the land in one event
Werner's Neptunism, which said all rock had settled out of a primeval ocean
Cuvier's successive catastrophes, each wiping the earth and prompting a new creation
Ussher's chronology, which dated the earth to about 4004 BC
context: Neptunism, catastrophism and Ussher's short chronology were all real rivals uniformitarianism displaced - but the specific one Lyell hammered was 'flood geology'. That is why Bretz's giant flood sounded to older geologists like a step backwards: the critics were defending a principle that had done geology enormous good. Source: HistoryLink, Bretz biography.

question: Bretz had the landforms - the scoured channels, the dry cataracts, the giant potholes. But he had one crippling gap that his critics kept pressing him on. What could he not answer?
answer: Where a body of water that large could have come from
choices: Where a body of water that large could have come from
How to date the basalt rocks beneath the channels
Whether the rocks beneath the channels were basalt
Why erosion channels appear on a plateau at all
context: It was Wegener's gap: right about the pattern, silent on the source. Bretz had no water source, which is exactly what a skeptical geologist demands you supply. Source: encyclopedia.com, J Harlen Bretz.

question: On 12 January 1927 J Harlen Bretz was invited to present his hypothesis at the Cosmos Club in Washington DC, at a meeting of the Geological Society of Washington. What actually happened at that meeting?
answer: Six pre-arranged rebuttals from senior geologists followed his talk
choices: Six pre-arranged rebuttals from senior geologists followed his talk
The society voted on the spot to expel him for pseudoscience
A single friendly commentator praised the paper and closed the session
The chair adjourned the meeting before Bretz could speak
context: Several were US Geological Survey officers. The alternatives offered were all respectable science of the day: ordinary glacial meltwater, subglacial streams, slow river incision, wind erosion, marine submergence. Bretz later called it an ambush by invitation. Source: Washington History magazine.

question: The missing water source was found not by Bretz but by USGS geologist Joseph Thomas Pardee, working on the former floor of Glacial Lake Missoula in Montana. In 1940 Pardee presented a set of landforms 5 to 10 metres tall on the old lake bed. What were they?
answer: Giant current ripples the shape of stream-bed ripples but enormous
choices: Giant current ripples the shape of stream-bed ripples but enormous
Terminal moraines dumped where a stalled ice lobe had stood
Ice-shove ridges pushed up along the former lake shore
Strandlines cut by a lake level that had fallen slowly over centuries
context: Moraines, ice-shove ridges and strandlines are all real Pleistocene landforms another glacial geologist could reasonably have proposed.
