The ripples were the tell: only a single sudden torrent draining the lake could sculpt streambed-shape ripples that tall. Pardee thus supplied Bretz's missing water; both share the credit. Source: Baker, GSA Today (1995), 'Joseph Thomas Pardee'.

question: Once the flood was accepted, geologists counting rhythmic silt beds along the Columbia and Snake valleys found the flood had not happened once but dozens of times - one railway cut near Missoula records 29 separate events. What kept refilling Glacial Lake Missoula between floods, so it could burst out again and again?
answer: A lobe of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet advancing back across the Clark Fork valley
choices: A lobe of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet advancing back across the Clark Fork valley
Seasonal snowmelt from the surrounding Bitterroot mountains alone
A rerouted Columbia River repeatedly spilling into the basin
Post-flood tectonic uplift damming the outlet each time
context: The ice dam - a lobe of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet - kept re-blocking the Clark Fork, the lake refilled behind it (up to 2,500 cubic km, 650 m deep), then the dam floated free and failed again. Each cycle left one graded rhythmite couplet; the 29-unit section is one of the longest records. At peak, the discharge was roughly ten times the combined flow of all the world's rivers. Source: IAFI, Missoula Flood Rhythmites; glaciallakemissoula.org.

question: In 1979, at the age of 96, J Harlen Bretz was awarded the Geological Society of America's Penrose Medal, the society's highest honour. What did he reportedly say to his son after the ceremony?
answer: 'All my enemies are dead, so I have no one to gloat over.'
choices: 'All my enemies are dead, so I have no one to gloat over.'
'The Lord vindicates the patient man in due season.'
'A medal proves nothing; a stratigraphic column proves everything.'
'I was wrong on the details and glad to be corrected.'
context: Bretz outlived his critics by decades. The real lesson is not 'the establishment was stupid' - it is that geology had to make room for rare, enormous events alongside slow ones. Victor Baker's 1978 Science paper then used Bretz's landform vocabulary to read the giant outflow channels of Mars. Source: Wikipedia, J Harlen Bretz; Baker, Science (1978).

question: In the summer of 1827 the Scottish botanist Robert Brown floated pollen of the wildflower Clarkia pulchella in water under his microscope. Hour after hour, the tiny particles in the water kept doing the same thing. What were they doing?
answer: Jittering in endless zigzags, never settling
choices: Jittering in endless zigzags, never settling
Drifting to the rim and clumping into a ring
Swelling slowly until they burst apart
Sinking to the bottom and lying still
context: Brown had just been made the British Museum's first Keeper of Botany, and he was trying to learn how plants fertilise. The motion never stopped and never tired -- a dance with no dancer. It would take eighty years to say what was pushing. Source: Grokipedia, 'Brownian motion'; Grokipedia, 'Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)'.

question: Robert Brown could have published the jiggling particles as a curiosity and left it there. Instead he spent weeks trying to demolish the very explanation he had reached for first -- the one he liked best. What had Brown first suspected was causing the motion?
answer: A vital force stirring inside living matter
choices: A vital force stirring inside living matter
Warm currents rising through the water
The water quietly drying at the edges
An electrical attraction between the specks
context: Brown was studying plant fertilisation and the particles had come out of pollen, so his first thought was that he was watching life itself at work in the male sex cells. Then he went hunting for the evidence that would kill it. Attacking your own favourite idea first is the whole method in one move. Source: Grokipedia, 'Brownian motion'.

question: Robert Brown had watched tiny particles jitter endlessly in water, and he wanted to know whether the motion needed anything living. He ground up whatever he could reach and dropped the dust into water: window glass, lava, obsidian, pumice, meteorites, manganese, arsenic, asbestos. For one sample he wanted dust as dead and as ancient as dust can be, and used scrapings from a fragment of an ancient monument. Which monument?
answer: The Sphinx
choices: The Sphinx
Stonehenge
The Parthenon
Trajan's Column
context: 'Rocks of all ages' was Brown's own phrase, and his list ran on through stalactites, volcanic ash, nickel, bismuth and antimony. He also tried pollen that had sat in alcohol for eleven months and dust shaken from plants pressed and dried for over a century. Every single sample jiggled. The Sphinx entry is a scraping taken from a fragment of the monument, not a piece Brown chipped off himself. Source: Brown's 1828 pamphlet, quoted in Resonance 10(9), ias.ac.in; Britannica, 'Brownian motion'; brianjford.com/wbbrowna.htm.

question: Almost every retelling says Robert Brown watched pollen GRAINS dancing in his drop of water. Put the same preparation under a modern microscope and the retelling falls apart: a Clarkia pulchella grain is 50 to 100 micrometres across and sits there like a boulder. So what was actually doing the jiggling?
answer: Far smaller particles released from inside the grains
choices: Far smaller particles released from inside the grains
Bubbles of air trapped against the grain surfaces
Dust that had settled on the slide from the room
Fibres shed by the cloth Brown wiped his lens with
context: The microscopist Brian J Ford re-measured the dancing specks and put them at roughly 2 micrometres -- about one fiftieth the width of the grain that released them. The famous story is told wrong nearly everywhere; the true version is more interesting, because it means the effect never depended on pollen at all. Source: Grokipedia, 'Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)'; brianjford.com/wbbrowna.htm.

question: By 1828 Robert Brown had produced the same restless motion from pollen, from window glass, from powdered metal and from stone scraped off ancient monuments, and he wrote the whole thing up for the Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal. He closed the pamphlet with the line he is remembered for. What did Brown write?
answer: That he was unable to account for the motion
choices: That he was unable to account for the motion
That a vital principle pervades all fine matter
That his own lenses were producing the effect
That heat in the water must be the hidden cause
context: Brown's exact words: extremely minute particles of solid matter, 'whether obtained from organic or inorganic substances, when suspended in pure water, or in some other aqueous fluids, exhibit motions for which I am unable to account.' He had already sealed his slides, suspended water droplets in oil to exclude draughts, and watched long enough to rule out evaporation -- so he knew what it was NOT. Stopping where the evidence stops is a virtue, not a failure. Source: Brown 1828, quoted in Britannica, 'Brownian motion' and Resonance 10(9), ias.ac.in.

question: Robert Brown's name is on the motion, but he was not the first to see it. The Dutch physician and plant physiologist Jan Ingenhousz had reported the same restless jiggling in 1785 -- forty-two years earlier -- and then never followed it up. What was Ingenhousz peering at when he noticed it?
answer: Fine coal dust floating on alcohol
choices: Fine coal dust floating on alcohol
Pollen grains floating on rainwater
Chalk powder stirred into warm oil
Ground pepper floating on still water
context: Ingenhousz was studying evaporation at the time, noted the jiggling in 1785, and moved on. Brown's contribution was never the sighting -- it was the control and the generality: he showed the motion in living and dead matter alike, and made it mean something. In science the credit usually goes to whoever turns an observation into a result. Source: Grokipedia, 'Brownian motion', Historical Background.

question: Some historians doubted Robert Brown could really have seen what he described in 1827: his instrument was a single tiny bead of glass, not a modern compound microscope. In 1992 the microscopist Brian J Ford settled the doubt. What did Ford do?
answer: Borrowed Brown's own microscope and repeated the 1827 experiment
choices: Borrowed Brown's own microscope and repeated the 1827 experiment
Reground a replica lens to Brown's published specification
Photographed Clarkia pollen through the best Victorian optics
Traced Brown's notebooks to check what he claimed to see
context: Ford borrowed the surviving single-lens Bancks microscope from the Linnean Society's collections, mounted the lens on a video camera, and filmed the particles jiggling through Brown's own 1827 glass. When the question is 'could he really have seen it?', the answer is to go and look -- and you can: any decent school microscope shows the same jitter in milk or diluted ink. Source: brianjford.com/wbbrowna.htm.

question: Ludwig Boltzmann, the Austrian physicist behind the kinetic theory of heat, spent years locked in a dispute with the editor of Germany's leading physics journal -- not over his mathematics, which nobody disputed, but over what he was permitted to say his equations were ABOUT. What did the editor keep demanding?
answer: That atoms be called convenient constructs, never real things
choices: That atoms be called convenient constructs, never real things
That heat be called a fluid, never a form of motion
That entropy be called a bookkeeping term, never a quantity
That his gas laws be called approximations, never laws
context: Ernst Mach's positivism held that physics may speak only of what is perceived, so atoms were economical shorthand rather than things. Wilhelm Ostwald's 'energetics' went further: only energy is 'genuinely real', and 'matter is nothing but a complex of energy factors'. The fight was not a seminar debate -- it decided what a working scientist was allowed to print. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'; Grokipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'; Foundations of Chemistry, 'Wilhelm Ostwald's Energetics 1'.

question: Albert Einstein's 1905 paper turned the restless jiggling of microscopic specks in water into a prediction anyone with an ordinary microscope could check. Do not measure how FAST the particle moves, Einstein said -- measure how far it has strayed from its starting point after one minute, then two, then three. What did Einstein predict that straying distance would do?
answer: Grow as the square root of the elapsed time
choices: Grow as the square root of the elapsed time
Grow in direct proportion to the elapsed time
Grow as the square of the elapsed time
Grow at first, then level off at a fixed distance
context: Why abandon speed? Because the path doubles back on itself so often that any speed you measure just depends on how often you look -- there is no honest value to report. Einstein's rule was that the mean SQUARED displacement grows in proportion to time -- <r^2> = 6Dt in three dimensions -- so the distance itself creeps up like the square root of time, not straight up like a steadily pushed object. He supplied a number to check: a particle a thousandth of a millimetre across, in water at 17 C, should wander about 6 micrometres in a minute. And he named in advance what would sink him: 'had the prediction of this movement proved to be incorrect, a weighty argument would be provided against the molecular-kinetic conception of heat.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Brownian motion', Einstein's 1905 Theory; Einstein 1905 (Furth/Cowper translation), damtp.cam.ac.uk; Physics Today quick study.

question: Jean Perrin set out in 1908 to test Einstein's prediction by plotting the wanderings of thousands of identical specks. He rubbed gamboge -- the bright yellow resin painters use as a pigment -- under distilled water, spun it for months in a centrifuge to sort out spheres all of one size, then began recording positions. How did Perrin actually take the readings?
answer: Two men at the microscope, dotting the granules every 30 seconds
choices: Two men at the microscope, dotting the granules every 30 seconds
A clockwork camera exposing a fresh plate every 30 seconds
A rotating drum tracing each granule's shadow onto paper
A student counting granules crossing a ruled line each minute
context: Perrin's own words: '[We took] turns at the microscope, each dotting the granules every 30 seconds at the call of the other.' A camera lucida threw the granule's image onto squared paper so the dot could be marked; one recorded run lasted 24 minutes and produced 48 dots. Two people, a stopwatch and a pencil -- that is what counting atoms looked like. Source: Perrin, quoted at uvachemistry.wordpress.com; Charlotte Bigg, 'A Visual History of Jean Perrin's Brownian Motion Curves', cak.ehess.fr; encyclopedia.com, 'Jean Baptiste Perrin'.

question: The French physicist Jean Perrin followed his Brownian measurements with a book: 'Les Atomes', published in 1913 and written not for specialists but for the ordinary reader, at a time when the reality of molecules was still disputed. What did Perrin fill it with?
answer: Thirteen unrelated methods, all returning the same number
choices: Thirteen unrelated methods, all returning the same number
Thirteen photographs of single granules at high magnification
Thirteen years of his own laboratory notebooks in full
Thirteen objections from the anti-atomists, answered one by one
context: Brownian displacement, sedimentation equilibrium, gas viscosity, the blueness of the sky, radioactivity, blackbody radiation -- routes with nothing in common, all handing back the same magnitude. Perrin's own Brownian value was 7.05 x 10^23, about 17 per cent above today's 6.022 x 10^23: not precise, but unmistakably the right size. Agreement between independent methods is stronger evidence than precision from one. The Nobel committee gave him the 1926 Physics Prize 'for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter, and especially for his discovery of sedimentation equilibrium'. Source: S. Psillos, 'Moving Molecules Above the Scientific Horizon', users.uoa.gr; Perrin translated at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/perrin.html; nobelprize.org.

question: Wilhelm Ostwald had spent two decades arguing that chemistry needed no atoms at all -- only energy was 'genuinely real', and matter was nothing but a complex of energy factors. Then in 1908 Ostwald brought out the fourth edition of his chemistry textbook. What had changed in it?
answer: He wrote that the particulate nature of matter was now proved
choices: He wrote that the particulate nature of matter was now proved
He added a chapter defending energetics against Perrin
He removed every reference to Boltzmann's kinetic theory
He proposed a new experiment to settle the question
context: Ostwald credited Perrin's Brownian-motion work by name. The most formidable anti-atomist in Europe read the evidence and changed his mind in print, in a textbook students would read. That is what the method is supposed to do to people -- and how rarely it does is exactly why this one is worth remembering. Source: J. Chem. Educ., 'Perrin's Experiment Handed Ostwald Avogadro's Constant', pubs.acs.org; Grokipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'.

question: Carved on Ludwig Boltzmann's headstone in Vienna is the formula he was mocked for: S = k log W, which tallies the invisible arrangements that could have produced a visible state -- and means nothing at all unless the invisible things exist. In 1900 another physicist borrowed that exact expression to derive the law of the glow that hot objects give off. Who?
answer: Max Planck
choices: Max Planck
Wilhelm Wien
Walther Nernst
Paul Ehrenfest
context: Planck borrowed Boltzmann's entropy expression in 1900 to derive the blackbody law -- the law of how a hot object glows -- and stumbled into quantum theory without meaning to. So the equation Boltzmann was mocked for, a tally of microscopic possibilities that is meaningless unless the microscopic things are there, became the seed of the next century of physics. Boltzmann insisted for an entire career that atoms are real things, and did not live to see the argument settled: he took his own life at Duino near Trieste on 5 September 1906, one to two years before Jean Perrin's measurements arrived, his doctor having recently diagnosed neurasthenia and told him to stop intellectual work. Wikipedia states the vindication plainly: 'Only a couple of years after Boltzmann's death, Perrin's studies of colloidal suspensions (1908-1909) confirmed the values of the Avogadro constant and the Boltzmann constant, convincing the world that the tiny particles really exist.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'; Wikipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'.

question: The random-walk mathematics behind Robert Brown's jiggling particles turned out to describe a smell crossing a room, ink spreading through water, and an ion finding a channel in a cell membrane. But someone had written that mathematics down first, for a completely different purpose: on 29 March 1900 a doctoral student defended a Sorbonne thesis using the same random process, five years before Einstein. What was that student modelling?
answer: The wandering of prices on the Paris stock exchange
choices: The wandering of prices on the Paris stock exchange
The spread of an epidemic through a crowded city
The drift of artillery shells around their target
The errors made by surveyors mapping France
context: Louis Bachelier's thesis 'Theorie de la speculation' defined Brownian motion mathematically before any physicist did, and even derived its link to the heat equation -- and nobody in physics noticed. Norbert Wiener made it rigorous in 1923. Perrin, staring at his own dot-to-dot plots, realised they lied about scale: between any two 30-second dots the true path is just as crinkled, giving 'a curve without a tangent'. Benoit Mandelbrot cited that passage when he coined the word fractal. Source: Wikipedia, 'Louis Bachelier'; Grokipedia, 'Brownian motion'; Images des Mathematiques, CNRS.

question: On 3 June 1845 horn players rode an open railway wagon behind a locomotive on the new Utrecht-Maarssen line, holding one unchanging note, while musicians with trained ears stood beside the track. What did they report hearing?
answer: Higher by about a half-tone coming in, lower going away
choices: Higher by about a half-tone coming in, lower going away
Lower by about a half-tone coming in, higher going away
Higher by about a half-tone coming in, higher going away
The same pitch coming in, the same pitch going away
context: The wagon was doing about forty miles an hour - an incredible speed for its day - and that gave a pitch change of roughly five percent, just large enough for trained ears to judge with the techniques of 1845. German sources record that the runs were repeated on 5 June. Source: KNMI, 'Doppler-experiment Buys Ballot 160 jaar geleden'; Utrecht University Muurformules, 'Professor Buys Ballot investigates the Doppler Effect'; German Wikipedia, 'Christoph Buys Ballot'.

question: In 1845 Christophorus Buys Ballot sent horn players down the Utrecht-Maarssen line on an open railway wagon, holding one steady note for trained ears at the trackside, to settle Christian Doppler's claim about what a source's motion does to pitch. What did he expect to prove?
answer: That Doppler was wrong, and no shift existed at all
choices: That Doppler was wrong, and no shift existed at all
That Doppler was right, and his rule exact
That the shift needed ears trained to catch it
That the shift tracked loudness, not speed
context: He got the opposite of what he wanted. Buys Ballot did not believe Christian Doppler and built the railway run to refute him; the Utrecht mural page that commemorates the trial states the outcome flatly - Buys Ballot turned out to be wrong, and Doppler's theory was right. The Oostkrant account puts it the same way: he had expected he could disprove the effect, and instead his own trumpeters showed it exists. The hostile witness had built the best confirmation the theory ever received. Source: Utrecht University Muurformules, 'Professor Buys Ballot investigates the Doppler Effect'; Oostkrant, 'Experiment van Buys Ballot'.

question: Christophorus Buys Ballot's first attempt to test Christian Doppler's pitch-shift claim, with horn players on a moving railway wagon, came in February 1845 and collapsed before it produced any usable result. What wrecked it?
answer: Hail and snow that stopped the players from playing
choices: Hail and snow that stopped the players from playing
Ice on the rail that held the locomotive to a crawl
Frost in the valves that choked the horns' tone
Wind at the trackside that carried the note away
context: Hail and snow disrupted the February trial and the musicians could not play properly, so he waited for the milder month of June and ran it again on 3 June 1845 - the attempt that worked. Most popular accounts blur February and June into one date; there were two attempts, and February was the washout. Source: David D. Nolte, 'The fall and rise of the Doppler effect', Physics Today (March 2020), pp. 30-35; date corroborated by KNMI, 'Doppler-experiment Buys Ballot 160 jaar geleden'.

question: An ambulance comes straight down a long street toward you, siren wailing, passes within a few metres and drives on away. The siren itself never changes the note it makes. Track the pitch you hear from first to last: what does it do?
answer: Steady high all the way in, an abrupt drop as it passes, then steady low
choices: Steady high all the way in, an abrupt drop as it passes, then steady low
Steady low all the way in, an abrupt rise as it passes, then steady high
A slow, even slide downward from the first sound to the very last
One unchanging pitch throughout, only growing louder then quieter
context: Take this one outside. The siren's own note is constant; only the frequency arriving at your ear changes, so what you hear is a plateau, a step, and a second plateau - never a slide. The closer the vehicle passes to you, the more abrupt that step becomes. Listen for it at the next ambulance and you will not be able to un-hear it. Source: OpenStax/Lumen University Physics Vol. 1, section 17.7 'The Doppler Effect'; ScienceABC, 'Why Does An Ambulance Siren Sound Different As It Passes By?'

question: In Christophorus Buys Ballot's 1845 railway trial the horn was held to one note while the wagon ran at about forty miles an hour, yet a listener at the trackside heard that note arrive noticeably high. Nobody had touched the horn. Why did the note reach the ear higher than it left the horn?
answer: Each crest set out from nearer the listener than the last, arriving crowded together
choices: Each crest set out from nearer the listener than the last, arriving crowded together
The wagon squeezed the air ahead of it, so the sound crossed that air faster
The wagon dragged the nearby air forward, carrying the sound bodily along with it
The sound arrived louder as the wagon closed, and a loud note reads as a high one
context: This is the whole of the Doppler effect for sound: the source chases its own sound. Ahead of the wagon the wavefronts bunch into a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency at your ear; behind it they spread out. Doppler had worked this out on paper three years earlier; the trumpeters made it audible. Source: Grokipedia, 'Doppler effect' - 'when the source moves toward the observer, the wavefronts bunch together, resulting in a shorter wavelength and higher frequency'.

question: In December 1955 Shigeo Satomura, at Osaka University, aimed a beam of 3 MHz ultrasound at a patient's chest and found the echo coming back with its frequency shifted - a Doppler shift, from something inside the body that was moving. In a beating chest almost everything moves, so what was doing it was not obvious; in 1962 Kanemasa Kato pinned it down. What was throwing the shifted echo back?
answer: The red blood cells streaming through the heart
choices: The red blood cells streaming through the heart
The valve leaflets snapping open and shut
The muscle walls thickening with each beat
The vessel walls flexing with each pulse of blood
context: Kato showed in 1962 that the returning signal came from the moving red blood cells themselves, with the frequency tracking how fast they flowed. Satomura had published the method in December 1955 - 'A new method of the mechanical vibration measurement and its application' - working at the Institute of Scientific and Industrial Research with the cardiac physicians T. Yoshida and Yasaharu Nimura at Osaka University Hospital; he died in 1960, aged 41, before the field he founded grew up. Colour Doppler now paints the shift straight onto the screen: blood flowing toward the probe is drawn red, blood flowing away is drawn blue, and a fast jet squirting backwards through a diseased valve shows as a chaotic mosaic - so a leaking heart valve can be seen, and roughly sized, without opening a chest. Source: K. Kaneko, Cardiovascular Ultrasound (BioMed Central, 2015), 'Shigeo Satomura: 60 years of Doppler ultrasound in medicine'; Johnson Francis, 'Basic Principles of Colour Doppler Echocardiography'.

question: Jupiter takes about twelve years to go once round the Sun. On 6 October 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced the first planet ever found circling an ordinary Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi - a world of about Jupiter's mass, detected purely as a rhythmic wobble of some 57 metres per second in the star itself. How long did that world take to go once round its star?
answer: About four days
choices: About four days
About four months
About four years
About forty years
context: 4.23 days. A Jupiter-mass world hugging its star was something nobody's theory of planet formation had predicted. Mayor and Queloz read the wobble from 35 measurements over 114 days with the ELODIE spectrograph on the 1.93-metre telescope at Haute-Provence Observatory. The radial-velocity method has since confirmed over a thousand planets, roughly a fifth of the 6,000-plus known worlds; ESPRESSO on the VLT now reads stellar motions of about 10 centimetres per second - walking pace, measured across light years. Source: Grokipedia, '51 Pegasi', 'Michel Mayor', 'Doppler spectroscopy'.

question: Christian Doppler's 1842 Prague paper was titled 'On the Coloured Light of the Double Stars', and in it he pushed his rule out of sound and into light: the colours of paired stars, he argued, came from their motion toward and away from Earth. He then described what a white star would look like as its approach speed climbed higher and higher. What did he say we would see?
answer: Green, then blue, then violet, and finally invisible
choices: Green, then blue, then violet, and finally invisible
Orange, then red, then deep red, and finally invisible
Yellow, then orange, then blue, and finally invisible
Violet, then blue, then green, and finally invisible
context: That part of the paper was wrong, for two independent reasons: a star's colour is set overwhelmingly by its surface temperature (hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths and look blue-white, cooler ones glow red), and the orbital speeds of the double stars actually observed are far too small to move a colour visibly - you would need an enormous fraction of the speed of light. Doppler also assumed light waves were longitudinal, like sound; they are transverse. His frequency-shift derivation, though, was sound. He read the paper on 25 May 1842 to the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences in Prague, with five members present. Source: English Wikipedia, 'On the coloured light of the binary stars and some other stars of the heavens'; Grokipedia, 'Doppler effect', 'Starlight'; David D. Nolte, Physics Today (March 2020).

question: A traffic officer points a radar gun at a car coming toward him. The gun sends out a radio wave at about 24 gigahertz, catches the echo off the car and reads the change in frequency. When engineers wrote the formula that turns that change into a speed, they had to divide by two. Where does that factor of two come from?
answer: The wave is shifted twice, once at the moving car and again on the bounce back
choices: The wave is shifted twice, once at the moving car and again on the bounce back
The wave travels the distance twice, out to the car and back to the gun
The gun sends two waves and compares them, which doubles the raw reading
Only half the car's motion lies along the beam, the rest across it
context: The moving car is both a receiver and a re-transmitter: it meets the outgoing wave already shifted, and the echo it throws back is shifted a second time on its way to the gun. That is why the speed formula reads v = (change in frequency x wavelength) / 2. Handheld guns typically run continuous-wave K-band around 24 GHz. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radar speed gun'.

question: By 1848 Christian Doppler's application of his rule to starlight looked dead. Real stars move far too slowly to shift a colour any human eye could catch, and a star's colour is set overwhelmingly by its surface temperature anyway. Then the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau changed one thing about what an observer should look for, and the dead idea became a working measuring instrument. What did he say to watch instead of the overall colour?
answer: The narrow dark lines in a star's spectrum, shifted from their usual places
choices: The narrow dark lines in a star's spectrum, shifted from their usual places
The total brightness of the star, dimming and brightening with its motion
The width of the star's spectrum, stretched or squeezed at both ends
The polarisation of the starlight, twisted by the star's motion toward us
context: The Fraunhofer lines - narrow dark absorption lines sitting at fixed, known wavelengths. Fizeau saw in 1848 that motion would displace those sharp lines even where no eye could ever see a whole star change hue, and that single reframing turned a discredited idea into a measuring instrument. Christian Doppler never saw it work: tubercular, he travelled to Venice in November 1852 hoping a milder climate would help, and died there on 17 March 1853, aged 49. Source: Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy', 'Hippolyte Fizeau', 'Christian Doppler'.

question: On 14 May 1868 William Huggins told the Royal Society of London that in February he had measured the speed of Sirius - the first time anyone had measured the speed of a star at all. He put it at roughly 40 kilometres per second, receding. Sirius is in fact closing on us at about 5.5 kilometres per second, so Huggins had the size and even the direction wrong. What is the likeliest source of that error?
answer: He had not subtracted the Earth's own orbital motion around the Sun
choices: He had not subtracted the Earth's own orbital motion around the Sun
He had not allowed for the Sun's own drift through the local stars
He had measured a faint companion in the same field, not Sirius itself
He had trusted a reference standard that had drifted since its making
context: Earth swings round the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second, and Huggins does not appear to have subtracted it. What he had found, on 24 February 1868, was the F line - a hydrogen line - in the spectrum of Sirius, displaced toward the red. Reported figures for his velocity vary between about 40 and 50 km/s. David Nolte's verdict is that the importance of the Sirius measurement was more psychological than scientifically accurate: wrong in size and even in sign, it still convinced the scientific community that the optical Doppler effect was real, which is exactly what the idea needed. Source: David D. Nolte, 'Orion's Dog: The Serious Science of Sirius', Galileo Unbound (4 Sept 2023); OpenStax/Pressbooks Astronomy 17.4.

question: In 1872 Camillo Golgi became chief physician at a hospital for the chronically ill near Milan. The post came with patients but no laboratory, and he still meant to make single brain cells visible. Where did he do the work that produced his stain in 1873?
answer: In the kitchen of his own apartment at the hospital
choices: In the kitchen of his own apartment at the hospital
In the hospital mortuary, between his night rounds
In his old laboratory at the University of Pavia
In a rented room over a pharmacy in Milan
context: Golgi had no funding and no institute. At the Pio Luogo degli Incurabili in Abbiategrasso he fitted out the kitchen of his apartment as a rudimentary laboratory and worked there, reportedly by candlelight. In February 1873 he wrote to his friend Nicolo Manfredi: 'I am delighted that I have found a new reaction to demonstrate even to the blind the structure of the interstitial stroma of the cerebral cortex.' He published the recipe on 2 August 1873 in the Gazzetta Medica Italiana-Lombardia and called it la reazione nera -- the black reaction. Sources: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6388087/ ('set up there, in the kitchen of his apartment, a rudimentary laboratory'); Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camillo_Golgi; grokipedia.com/page/Camillo_Golgi

question: Camillo Golgi's black reaction picked out a scattering of nerve cells in full, every branch traced to its tip. He read those pictures as proof of a claim about the brain and defended it for the rest of his life. What did he claim he was looking at?
answer: One continuous net, the cells all fused together
choices: One continuous net, the cells all fused together
A crowd of separate cells, each ending on its own
A mass of tubes carrying fluid from the ventricles
A jelly of fibres held in place by glue cells
context: This is reticular theory: nerve cells fused into one continuous diffuse network -- a single nerve organ, which for Golgi explained why the brain acts as one thing rather than as millions of scraps. He never gave it up. The stain that produced those pictures works by precipitating microparticles of silver chromate inside a cell, rendering it black and complete -- body, dendrites, axon, even dendritic spines, in three dimensions -- against a light yellow background. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron_doctrine; grokipedia.com/page/Neuron_doctrine; grokipedia.com/page/Golgi's_method

question: By 1921 physiologists knew that a nerve ending stops just short of the muscle it commands, and Otto Loewi wanted to know how the order gets across. He set two frog hearts beating in separate baths of salt solution. Only the first still had its vagus nerve attached, and he stimulated that nerve until the first heart slowed. What did he do next?
answer: Poured the first heart's bath over the second heart
choices: Poured the first heart's bath over the second heart
Chilled the second heart's bath until its beat stopped
Ran a fine copper wire from one heart to the other
Stitched a vagus nerve onto the second heart too
context: The second heart -- with no nerve attached to it at all -- slowed too. Something dissolved in the fluid had carried the message. Loewi named the unknown substance Vagusstoff, 'vagus stuff'. It turned out to be acetylcholine, the first neurotransmitter ever identified: Henry Dale had isolated acetylcholine as a chemical back in 1914 without knowing the body used it as a messenger, and Loewi's purification work confirmed the identification in 1926. Loewi and Dale shared the 1936 Nobel Prize. Physiologists had a nickname for the whole quarrel about how signals cross -- 'soup versus sparks'. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagusstoff; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Loewi; grokipedia.com/page/Otto_Loewi

question: Between 1877 and 1887 four anatomists, working separately, each concluded that the branches of nerve cells do not, as a rule, join. One of them kept a microscope in a museum on the coast, went to Pavia in April 1886 to learn Golgi's black reaction, and turned it on creatures hauled from the sea. Who was he?
answer: Fridtjof Nansen, known for the Fram's drift across the Arctic ice
choices: Fridtjof Nansen, known for the Fram's drift across the Arctic ice
Thomas Huxley, known for taking Darwin's side against Wilberforce
Ernst Haeckel, known for his plates of embryos and radiolarians
Elie Metchnikoff, known for the cells that swallow invading microbes
context: Nansen was a curator at the Bergen Museum before the Arctic made his name; he sailed the Fram into the polar pack in 1893 and let it drift. He learned the black reaction at Pavia in April 1886, applied it to creatures from the fjords, and wrote in his 1887 monograph, italics and all: 'direct anastomosis between the processes of the ganglion cells does not exist, as a rule.' He worked with a Zeiss achromatic microscope and packed 389 references into the monograph. The other three of the four doubters were Edward Schaefer, who had said much the same of jellyfish mantles in 1877, and Wilhelm His (October 1886) and August Forel, who reached the same conclusion independently by other routes. Huxley, Haeckel and Metchnikoff all bent over sea creatures under a microscope too, but the sentence about nerve endings was Nansen's. Cajal was not the first to doubt the net -- he was the one who made the doubt impossible to ignore. Source: Ortwin Bock, 'Cajal, Golgi, Nansen, Schaefer and the Neuron Doctrine', Endeavour 37(4), 2013.

question: In 1897 Charles Sherrington was writing the nervous-system chapters of Michael Foster's physiology textbook and had no name for the place where one nerve cell hands its signal on to the next. Nobody had ever seen one; no microscope of the day could resolve it. He asked the classical scholar Arthur Verrall for a Greek coinage and got 'synapse'. What image does the Greek behind the word describe?
answer: A clasp, which fastens two things
choices: A clasp, which fastens two things
A bridge, thrown across a gap
A weld, where two metals run together
A seam, sewn along a torn edge
context: Verrall built it from synaptein -- syn, 'together', plus haptein, 'to fasten'. The word names a fastening; the thing it names turned out to be a gap the two cells never close. Sherrington put the coinage into the seventh edition of Foster's Textbook of Physiology in 1897, naming a structure that no instrument of the day could resolve -- it sat in the textbooks for more than half a century before anyone laid eyes on it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synapse; Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013.

question: Santiago Ramon y Cajal had Golgi's stain and still could not settle the argument. In the tissue everyone was studying, each cell's branches were wrapped in fatty myelin and tangled among a hundred neighbours, so no single cell could be followed to its ending. Cajal's answer was to change the specimen rather than the chemistry. What did he put under the stain instead?
answer: Bird embryos and newborn animals
choices: Bird embryos and newborn animals
Spinal cords from the abattoir
Frogs and salamanders from ponds
Human brains taken at autopsy
context: Embryonic and very young tissue has simple, un-myelinated branches the stain handles cleanly, and Cajal worked heavily on bird and pigeon embryos. In his own words: 'Since the full-grown forest turns out to be impenetrable and indefinable, why not revert to the study of the young wood in the nursery stage?' Of what followed he wrote: 'Realizing that I had discovered a rich field, I proceeded to take advantage of it, dedicating myself to work, no longer merely with earnestness, but with fury.' Sources: Scientific American, 'The Father of Modern Neuroscience Discovered the Basic Unit of the Nervous System'; Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013 (Cajal, Recollections of My Life).

question: The black reaction has a defect nobody has fully explained even now. Drop a block of nervous tissue into the silver and most cells simply refuse it: only about one cell in twenty to one in a hundred turns black. A method that misses ninety-odd percent of its targets sounds broken. Why does staining a few cells beat staining them all?
answer: A slice thick enough to hold a whole cell would be a black smear if every cell stained
choices: A slice thick enough to hold a whole cell would be a black smear if every cell stained
The unstained cells stay pale, giving a built-in scale for the stained ones
Only dying cells resist the silver, so the picture shows healthy tissue alone
Sparing most cells leaves enough silver in the bath to run the block again
context: To follow one cell's branches to their tips you need a thick slice, because the cell is a three-dimensional thing. If every cell in that thickness went black you would be looking at a wall of ink. Sparseness turns the forest into a few visible trees. Why only 1-5% of cells take the stain is still unknown; Bock calls it a defect that 'has turned out to be an advantage', and the PMC review of Golgi's original slides calls it 'the still unexplained secret of its revelatory power'. Sources: Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013; grokipedia.com/page/Golgi's_method; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6388087/

question: The man who demolished Golgi's theory did it with Golgi's own tool. Santiago Ramon y Cajal did not invent the black reaction -- in Madrid around 1887 the physician Luis Simarro, freshly back from Paris, laid silver-stained slides of nervous tissue under his eyes and Cajal was captivated. He then reworked Golgi's protocol. What was his change?
answer: Running the tissue through the silver a second time
choices: Running the tissue through the silver a second time
Replacing the silver with a gold chloride of his own
Passing a current through the bath to speed the soak
Adding a second dye to stain the background blue
context: Cajal called it 'double impregnation', and paired it with altered submersion times and solution strengths to drive the stain deeper into the block; he later added a photosensitive variant using pyrogallic acid as the reducing agent. Sources differ on the fine protocol -- Grokipedia describes it as two brief immersions rather than one prolonged exposure -- but the second pass through the silver is the safe framing. The date of the Simarro meeting is genuinely uncertain: it is usually given as November 1887, yet a surviving preparation handwritten and dated by Cajal himself reads 1886. Sources: Science History Institute, 'A Cold Day in Stockholm'; Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013, citing Juan de Carlos of the Cajal Institute; grokipedia.com/page/Santiago_Ramon_y_Cajal

question: Santiago Ramon y Cajal was arguing that nerve cells are separate units, each branch ending free, against a field that held they fused into one net. He published in Spanish, in journals the German anatomists who ran that field did not read, and for years his work went nowhere. In October 1889 he travelled to the German Anatomical Society's meeting in Berlin, where the men who could end his obscurity would all be in one room. What did he bring?
answer: His own microscopes, loaded with his slides
choices: His own microscopes, loaded with his slides
His collected papers, translated into German
His best preparations, blown up as photographs
His letter of introduction from Camillo Golgi
context: He set them up and made the Germans look down the eyepieces themselves. Cajal wrote afterwards: 'Finally, the prejudice against the humble Spanish anatomist vanished and warm and sincere congratulations burst forth.' His most interested listener was Albert Koelliker, 'the venerable patriarch of German histology', who was impressed enough to learn Spanish in order to read Cajal's papers. Source: Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013, quoting Cajal's autobiography.

question: On 11 December 1906 Camillo Golgi rose in Stockholm to deliver his Nobel lecture. He was sharing that year's prize in physiology or medicine with Santiago Ramon y Cajal, who had used Golgi's own stain to argue that nerve cells are separate units, each ending free -- the neuron doctrine. Cajal was sitting in the hall; the two had met for the first time five days earlier. What did Golgi do with the podium?
answer: Attacked the neuron doctrine as a theory already going out of favour
choices: Attacked the neuron doctrine as a theory already going out of favour
Conceded that Cajal's embryo work had settled the question for good
Offered a compromise in which each of the two theories was half right
Spoke only about his malaria work and left the nervous system alone
context: Golgi titled the lecture 'The neuron doctrine: theory and facts'. He called the doctrine 'generally recognized to be going out of favour', argued that the apparent gaps between cells were artifacts of incomplete impregnation of his own stain, rejected Cajal's law of dynamic polarization, and declared: 'I cannot abandon the idea of a unitary action of the nervous system.' A prize is not a proof. Golgi was 63 and reticent, Cajal 54 and ebullient; they met exactly once in their lives, in Stockholm on 6 December 1906, and never became friends -- Golgi had arrived believing Cajal too ill to travel and was startled to find him there. Sources: Science History Institute, 'A Cold Day in Stockholm'; nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1906/golgi/lecture/; Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013.

question: On 12 December 1906 Santiago Ramon y Cajal gave his own Nobel lecture in the hall where he had sat the day before listening to Camillo Golgi, as he put it, 'trembling with impatience'. He answered with a single sentence about the fused, continuous net Golgi still defended. What did he say about it?
answer: That it would be convenient and economical, but nature does not care
choices: That it would be convenient and economical, but nature does not care
That it explained the brain's unity, but broke down in the embryo
That it would make learning and memory physically impossible in a brain
That it had been abandoned years ago by every anatomist in Germany
context: Cajal granted that a continuous network 'would be very convenient and very economical', and then: 'nature seems unaware of our intellectual need for convenience and unity.' Elegance is not evidence. Privately he was furious at what he saw as odious errors and deliberate omissions. On being permanently yoked to his opponent he wrote in Recollections of My Life: 'What a cruel irony of fate to pair, like Siamese twins united by the shoulders, scientific adversaries of such contrasting character!' Sources: Science History Institute, 'A Cold Day in Stockholm'; Bock, Endeavour 37(4) 2013.

question: Otto Loewi's most repeated story is that the two-heart design came to him in a dream. He woke, scribbled a note, and in the morning could not read his own handwriting; the next night the idea returned and he got up and went straight to the laboratory. It is one of science's favourite anecdotes, and historians hold it at arm's length. On what grounds?
answer: Loewi told it decades later himself, and he liked to sensationalise
choices: Loewi told it decades later himself, and he liked to sensationalise
Two of his laboratory assistants published a conflicting account
The institute's logbooks for that week were destroyed in the war
No frog heart of the period could have survived until morning
context: The story comes from Loewi's own autobiographic sketch, written long afterwards: 'The night before Easter Sunday of that year I awoke, turned on the light, and jotted down a few notes on a tiny slip of thin paper. Then I fell asleep again. It occurred to me at six o'clock in the morning that during the night I had written down something most important, but I was unable to decipher the scrawl.' He called that the longest day of his life. The discovery is solid; the midnight dash is a memoir, not a lab notebook. Loewi was 'known to be a storyteller with a tendency to sensationalize' and probably did not in fact run the experiment in the small hours -- and his own sketch dates it to 1920 while the experiment is universally dated 1921. Treat it the way Kekule's snake-dream should be treated: as the discoverer's own later telling. Sources: encyclopedia.com (Loewi's autobiographic sketch); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Loewi; neuroscientificallychallenged.com, 'History of neuroscience: Otto Loewi'.  (Legend.)

question: A light microscope bottoms out at about 200 nanometres -- a nanometre is a billionth of a metre -- which is why eighty years of argument about whether nerve cells fuse could not be settled by looking harder. In 1954 Sanford Palay and George Palade turned an electron microscope on the junction and measured the gap at roughly 20 nanometres: two membranes running parallel and never merging. Their pictures also showed something waiting on the sending side. What was it?
answer: A crowd of tiny round sacs pressed against the membrane
choices: A crowd of tiny round sacs pressed against the membrane
A dense tangle of fine protein threads spanning the gap
A ring of open pores punched clean through the membrane
A knot of fine tubules spiralling away into the cell body
context: Synaptic vesicles -- sacs roughly 40 nanometres across, holding the chemical messenger and queued at the membrane to dump it into the cleft. The cleft itself is about 20 nanometres wide (some sources give 20-40): the two cells come within about a ten-thousandth of the width of a human hair and still do not touch. The instrument decided the argument, not the argument. Cajal had been dead for twenty years. Sources: Sotelo, 'The History of the Synapse', The Anatomical Record 2020; 'The discovery of synaptic vesicles', J Cell Biol 168(1); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_synapse; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron_doctrine.

question: In 1959 Edwin Furshpan and David Potter put electrodes into a giant motor synapse in a crayfish -- a synapse being the junction where one nerve cell passes its signal to the next. A chemical hand-off across such a junction costs a lag of half a millisecond or more. Furshpan and Potter measured almost no lag at all. What had they found?
answer: A junction whose channels join the two cells' insides directly
choices: A junction whose channels join the two cells' insides directly
A messenger far faster than any chemical known at the time
A junction where the two membranes had fused into one sheet
A spark jumping the gap through the salt fluid around it
context: An electrical synapse. At a gap junction the two membranes close to 2-4 nanometres and channels called connexons -- six connexin subunits each -- link the two cells' cytoplasm directly, so current simply flows across with almost no delay, against the 0.5-4.0 millisecond lag at a chemical synapse. Golgi was not wrong about everything: genuine cytoplasmic continuity between nerve cells does exist. It is just the exception, not the rule he claimed -- which is why working neuroscientists state the neuron doctrine as 'almost always separate' rather than as an absolute. Source: Furshpan and Potter, 'Transmission at the giant motor synapses of the crayfish', J. Physiol. 145: 289-325 (1959); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_synapse; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron_doctrine.

question: Otto Loewi's proof that nerves signal chemically -- stimulate the vagus nerve of one frog heart until it slows, pour that heart's bathing fluid onto a second heart with no nerve attached, and the second slows too -- was beautiful and, for years, unreliable. Other labs got nothing; Loewi himself often got nothing; the doubt held up acceptance of chemical signalling for decades. What had quietly been helping him?
answer: An unheated room in winter, which slowed the chemical's breakdown
choices: An unheated room in winter, which slowed the chemical's breakdown
A well on the institute grounds whose water was unusually pure
Unusually large frogs, far bigger than other laboratories used
Hearts taken within a minute of the kill, fresher than most
context: Loewi used Rana esculenta frogs in February or March -- the season when inhibitory vagal fibres predominate -- and his laboratory was unheated, so acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that destroys the messenger, worked slowly and enough Vagusstoff survived the transfer to reach the second heart. Warm rooms and the wrong season destroyed the effect before it could be measured. The luck does not make the result false, but it does show why an experiment that will not repeat is a problem rather than a proof -- and why replication is a skill, not a formality. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagusstoff; neuroscientificallychallenged.com, 'History of neuroscience: Otto Loewi'; sciencedirect.com topic page, 'Vagusstoff'.

question: Sadi Carnot opens his 1824 book on steam engines with a warning about England. Take her steam engines away, he writes, and you take away her coal and her iron, dry up every source of her wealth, and annihilate that colossal power. Destroying which of England's possessions, he adds, would perhaps be less fatal to her than that?
answer: Her navy.
choices: Her colonies.
Her banks.
Her navy.
Her canals.
context: Carnot's own words: 'To take away to-day from England her steam-engines would be to take away at the same time her coal and iron. It would be to dry up all her sources of wealth... to annihilate that colossal power. The destruction of her navy, which she considers her strongest defense, would perhaps be less fatal.' He was not praising England so much as frightening France. Post-Napoleonic France was losing badly to Britain in steam, and French engines were running at roughly 3 percent efficiency. The spark seems to have come from an 1821 visit to his father Lazare, then exiled in Magdeburg, where the two talked about imported British engines and their appalling waste of fuel. SOURCE: Sadi Carnot, 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire' (Thurston translation), UChicago excerpts PDF; Grokipedia 'Carnot heat engine' and 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: Sadi Carnot was a French army engineer, not a professor, and in 1824 he went after two questions about the steam engine that had defeated everyone before him. One was whether some working substance other than steam - alcohol, mercury, sulphur - would do the job better. What was the other?
answer: Whether there is any upper limit to the power a fire can give.
choices: Whether friction can go on making fresh heat without any limit.
Whether there is any upper limit to the power a fire can give.
Whether the work comes from the steam's pressure or from its heat.
Whether a hotter furnace or a bigger boiler yields the greater work.
context: MacTutor puts his pair of questions this way: 'whether there was an upper limit to the power of heat, and secondly whether there was a better means than steam to produce this power.' Nobody had settled either one. The answers he found - yes, there is a hard ceiling, and no, no substance beats any other - are the whole of the book, and between them they founded a science. SOURCE: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Sadi Carnot'; Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: In June 1824 Sadi Carnot, a 28-year-old French army engineer, paid a Paris printer himself for 600 copies of his 118-page book 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire'. Pierre-Simon Girard presented it to the Academie des Sciences and reviewed it favourably in the Revue encyclopedique that July. What became of the 600?
answer: Eleven years on, the copies had still not sold out.
choices: Bachelier reprinted it twice before Carnot died in 1832.
Most of it was bought up by British engine builders.
Eleven years on, the copies had still not sold out.
Most of it burned in the 1832 cholera precautions.
context: Girard's review, in the Revue encyclopedique of 26 July 1824, was warm - but it 'did not comment on the highly original reasoning which Carnot had employed to achieve his results,' and nobody followed it up. Between 1824 and 1834 the book was mentioned in print only twice, leaving aside the 1824 reviews and the obituaries. By 1835 the original edition still had not sold out; by 1845 the booksellers had forgotten it entirely. The copies were not lost or destroyed - they simply sat there, while Kelvin and Clausius later built the second law of thermodynamics out of a secondhand account of the argument. The 600-copy figure comes from the surviving printer's bill, reproduced in Robert Fox's critical edition. SOURCE: MacTutor 'Sadi Carnot'; Sophia Rare Books first-edition description; Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: Sadi Carnot sat the competitive examination for the Corps des Ponts et Chaussees, the elite corps of French state engineers, in 1819. He passed it, and the corps refused him admission anyway. Historians name one likely reason, and it had nothing to do with his marks. What was it?
answer: His father Lazare, Napoleon's minister, was living in exile.
choices: His colonel at Metz would not release him from active service.
His father Lazare, Napoleon's minister, was living in exile.
He would not swear the Bourbon oath of loyalty to Louis XVIII.
He was over the age limit Paris imposed on the corps' entrants.
context: Lazare Carnot had been a revolutionary and a Napoleonic minister, and the Bourbon Restoration exiled him to Germany in 1815. Historians read Sadi's rejection as inherited suspicion rather than any failure of merit - Grokipedia's wording is 'likely owing to this familial taint rather than merit deficiencies', so treat it as the historians' best reading, not a proven fact. In 1828 Carnot resigned his army commission outright, giving up any pension, in order to work on heat in private. SOURCE: Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: By 1850 William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) and Rudolf Clausius were building the second law of thermodynamics on Sadi Carnot's argument - and both admitted in print that they had never read Carnot's book. Clausius: 'I have not been able to obtain a copy of this work.' How had the argument reached them?
answer: Emile Clapeyron had recast the whole argument in an 1834 memoir.
choices: Hippolyte Carnot had circulated his brother's 1832 notebook widely.
Pierre-Simon Girard's 1824 review had spelled out the reasoning.
Emile Clapeyron had recast the whole argument in an 1834 memoir.
James Joule's 1845 experiments had rediscovered the same ceiling.
context: Kelvin's 1848 footnote: 'Having never met with the original work, it is only through a paper by M. Clapeyron... that the Author has become acquainted with Carnot's Theory.' Clapeyron's 1834 memoir in the Journal de l'Ecole Polytechnique recast the reasoning and drew the first pressure-volume diagram of the cycle - and that copy of a copy is what sat in the libraries and kept the argument alive. Pierre-Simon Girard had reviewed the book favourably back in 1824, but his review said nothing about the reasoning, and nobody followed it up. Sadi's brother Hippolyte finally got him reprinted in 1878, with a facsimile of Sadi's handwritten sheet on the mechanical equivalent of heat, and wrote: 'But the only work he completed is the one we publish for the second time. It will be enough to ensure that his name is not forgotten.' SOURCE: CarnotCycle, 'How Kelvin and Clausius discovered Carnot's ideas', quoting Thomson 1848 and Clausius 1850; MacTutor 'Sadi Carnot'; arXiv:2508.17027; Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: Sadi Carnot needed a picture for something nobody had words for; he apologised in a footnote for the expressions he was obliged to invent. He compared an engine to a waterfall driving a mill wheel. A waterfall's power, he said, depends on two things: how much water comes down, and the height it falls through. In the comparison, what stands in for the height?
answer: The temperature gap between the furnace and the cold body.
choices: The pressure the boiler holds back before the valve opens.
The temperature gap between the furnace and the cold body.
The weight of coal shovelled into the firebox every hour.
The volume of the cylinder swept out by the moving piston.
context: Carnot verbatim: 'we can compare with sufficient accuracy the motive power of heat to that of a waterfall. Each has a maximum that we cannot exceed... The motive power of a waterfall depends on its height and on the quantity of the liquid; the motive power of heat depends also on the quantity of caloric used, and on what may be termed... the height of its fall, that is to say, the difference of temperature of the bodies between which the exchange of caloric is made.' And the sting he draws out of it: 'the production of heat alone is not sufficient to give birth to the impelling power: it is necessary that there should also be cold; without it, the heat would be useless. And in fact, if we should find about us only bodies as hot as our furnaces, how can we condense steam?' An engine in a room as hot as its own firebox is a waterfall with no height. SOURCE: Sadi Carnot, 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire' (Thurston translation), UChicago excerpts PDF.

question: Sadi Carnot concluded that the working substance in an engine makes no difference whatever to what it can deliver, and he pushed the point to its extreme: a machine with no steam and no vapour in it at all can still be a heat engine, driven by nothing but heating and cooling. What did he offer as his example?
answer: A metal bar, which lengthens when heated and shrinks when cooled.
choices: A magnet, which weakens when heated and strengthens when cooled.
A glass rod, which bends when heated and straightens when cooled.
A tight spring, which slackens when heated and stiffens when cooled.
A metal bar, which lengthens when heated and shrinks when cooled.
context: Carnot verbatim: 'A solid body - a metallic bar for example - alternately heated and cooled increases and diminishes in length, and can move bodies fastened to its ends.' His general proposition is the reason it works: 'The motive power of heat is independent of the agents employed to realize it; its quantity is fixed solely by the temperatures of the bodies between which is effected, finally, the transfer of the caloric.' He named the fluids inventors were chasing - 'Vapors of all substances capable of passing into a gaseous condition, as of alcohol, of mercury, of sulphur, etc., may fulfill the same office as vapor of water' - and then stated it flatly: 'wherever there exists difference of temperature, motive-power can be produced.' SOURCE: Carnot, 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire' (Thurston translation), UChicago excerpts PDF; the 'independent of the agents' sentence also quoted in Kostic, Entropy 27(5):502 / arXiv:2501.15787.

question: Two centuries after Carnot, the best heat engine humanity builds is the combined-cycle gas power station: just over 60 percent of the fuel's heat leaves as electricity, against 20 to 30 percent for the petrol engine in a car. It reaches that by stacking two engines, so that the exhaust of the first serves as the furnace of the second. What is the second engine?
answer: A steam plant: the exhaust boils water to drive a second turbine.
choices: A steam plant: the exhaust boils water to drive a second turbine.
A Stirling engine: the exhaust warms sealed air in a hot cylinder.
A thermoelectric panel: the exhaust makes current with no moving parts.
A hot-air turbine: the exhaust heats compressed air to spin the blades.
context: Everything else is worse: petrol (Otto) car engines manage about 20-30 percent, diesels 30-40, conventional steam power plants 30-40. The second engine of a combined-cycle station is an ordinary steam plant: the gas turbine's exhaust boils water, and a steam turbine takes a second bite at the same fuel's heat, so the most advanced power station on earth still finishes with the machine Carnot was writing about in 1824. Every one of them sits under Carnot's line, and engineers climb toward it in exactly the two ways Carnot allows - push the hot side UP (superheated steam, higher turbine inlet temperatures, nickel superalloy blades, internal blade cooling and ceramic coatings that let a blade survive it) or pull the cold side DOWN. There is no third move; no gearing, lubricant, fuel or boiler size will do it. SOURCE: Grokipedia 'Carnot cycle'; ASME landmark brochure on Carnot's Reflections.

question: Carnot's ceiling comes down to one line: the best efficiency any engine can reach is 1 minus the cold temperature divided by the hot temperature. A student boils water at 100 degrees Celsius, dumps the exhaust into a 25-degree room, works out 1 minus 25 over 100, and announces a ceiling of 75 percent. No steam engine ever built between those two has come within shouting distance of it. Where did the student go wrong?
answer: Both temperatures have to be counted from absolute zero, in kelvin.
choices: The rule gives the efficiency of one stroke, not of a whole cycle.
The rule describes the steam alone, not the engine wrapped round it.
Both temperatures have to be counted from absolute zero, in kelvin.
Both temperatures must be read inside the cylinder, not outside it.
context: In kelvin, 100 C is 373 K and 25 C is 298 K, so the real ceiling is (373 - 298) / 373 = 20.1 percent - and the engines of Carnot's own day were managing three to five. Against freezing water at 273 K it rises to about 27 percent. Counting from the freezing point of water instead of from absolute zero is not a small error; it is measuring a waterfall's height from a line drawn partway up the cliff. The same formula also kills a favourite fantasy: to set the efficiency to 1 you would need the cold side sitting at absolute zero, so a '100 percent efficient engine' is not a hard engineering target but a physical impossibility - the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law in disguise. SOURCE: Wikipedia, "Carnot's theorem (thermodynamics)"; Grokipedia 'Carnot cycle' and 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: Sadi Carnot argued that no engine of any design can beat a perfectly reversible one - an engine that wastes nothing, so it can be run backwards through the same steps it ran forwards. He supposed the opposite: a super-engine that DOES beat it, between the same furnace and the same cold body. One further move turned that supposition into 'an unlimited creation of motive power', which Carnot ruled 'inadmissible'. What was the move?
answer: He spent part of the super-engine's work on driving the reversible engine backwards.
choices: He spent part of the super-engine's work on driving the reversible engine backwards.
He set the reversible engine running forwards beside the super-engine, and compared them.
He let the reversible engine run backwards, driven by nothing but its own output.
He coupled the reversible engine to the super-engine in a ring, each feeding the other.
context: Carnot verbatim: if such an engine existed you could spend part of its output driving a reversible engine backwards to restore the starting conditions, and 'this would be not only perpetual motion, but an unlimited creation of motive power without consumption either of caloric or of any other agent whatever. Such a creation is entirely contrary to ideas now accepted, to the laws of mechanics and of sound physics. It is inadmissible.' The theorem this establishes is the uncomfortable one: every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs is exactly as efficient as every other, 'regardless of the working substance employed or the operation details'. Better gears, better oil, better metal, a different fuel, a bigger boiler - none of it moves the ceiling. SOURCE: Carnot, 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire' (Thurston translation), UChicago excerpts PDF; Wikipedia "Carnot's theorem (thermodynamics)"; Grokipedia 'Carnot cycle'.

question: The engine that reaches Carnot's ceiling has to be perfectly reversible - able to run backwards through exactly the states it ran forwards through, wasting nothing on the way. Engineers who worked out what a real machine would need in order to manage that found something badly disappointing about the perfect engine. What is it?
answer: It must run infinitely slowly, so it delivers no power at all.
choices: It must be rebuilt after each cycle, so it can never run twice.
It must be infinitely large, so it can never actually be built.
It must be perfectly sealed, so its own friction slowly cooks it.
It must run infinitely slowly, so it delivers no power at all.
context: A reversible process is quasi-static: it 'proceeds infinitely slowly to maintain equilibrium.' Reversible isothermal heat transfer 'requires infinitely slow processes and vast heat exchangers... resulting in zero net power output over finite time.' Real power costs real waste - that is the trade, not a failure of engineering. There is a second, more honest ceiling for engines that actually have to produce something: in 1975 Curzon and Ahlborn showed that an engine run for MAXIMUM POWER rather than maximum efficiency tops out at 1 minus the square root of (cold over hot), and that endoreversible figure tracks real power stations far better than Carnot's bound does. Chambadal and Novikov had reached it independently in 1957, hence the mouthful 'Chambadal-Novikov-Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency'. SOURCE: Grokipedia 'Carnot cycle' and 'Carnot heat engine'; Energy Conversion and Management, 'On the Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency and its connection with the efficiencies of real heat engines'; Stanford PH240 note on endoreversible thermodynamics.

question: Everything Sadi Carnot published rests on caloric: the theory, inherited from Lavoisier, that heat is a weightless invisible fluid which pours from hot bodies into cold ones and is never used up. Caloric is false, and a false premise usually wrecks the argument built on it. Yet scholars of thermodynamics call believing it in 1824 reasonable rather than stupid. What made caloric so hard to catch out with the engines of that day?
answer: Those engines wasted so much heat that nearly all of it came out the far end, and the shortfall hid inside experimental error.
choices: Those engines wasted so much heat that nearly all of it came out the far end, and the shortfall hid inside experimental error.
No thermometer of the day could be trusted near a furnace's temperature, so nobody could measure the heat going in.
Lavoisier had weighed caloric on a balance, and laboratories across Europe had repeated the result for thirty years.
No boiler of that period could be sealed tightly enough to stop heat leaking through its walls, so every trial disagreed.
context: Run the numbers: at about 3 percent efficiency, the heat leaving an engine was about 97 percent of the heat going in. The missing sliver was smaller than the instruments of 1824 could resolve, so 'caloric is conserved' was an experimentally indistinguishable hypothesis - not a superstition, a hypothesis nobody could yet test. And it is precisely the belief that handed Carnot his waterwheel: if heat is a fluid that falls through without being consumed, then only the height of the fall can matter. The physicist M. Kostic calls it 'a fortunate misconception leading to the critical analogy with the waterwheel.' Carnot was wrong about what heat IS and right about the limit - and the published argument really is a caloric argument, not a tidied-up modern one. SOURCE: M. Kostic, '2024 Key Reflections on the 1824 Sadi Carnot's Reflexions and 200 Year Legacy', arXiv:2501.15787 / Entropy 27(5):502; Wikipedia and Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: Cholera killed Sadi Carnot in Paris in 1832, at 36, and under the epidemic rules most of his papers went to the fire; his brother Hippolyte saved one notebook. In it Carnot had thrown over caloric, the fluid theory of heat his published book rests on: 'Heat is simply motive power, or rather motion that has changed form. It is a movement among the particles of bodies.' Then, in the same notes, he went further, and put a claim on paper that no one else would publish for another twenty years. What was that claim?
answer: He priced the trade: 2.70 units of heat spent for one unit of work.
choices: He fixed absolute zero at 267 degrees below the freezing of water.
He priced the trade: 2.70 units of heat spent for one unit of work.
He plotted the first pressure-volume diagram of an engine's cycle.
He tabulated the specific heats of eleven gases, one by one.
context: Carnot's note, verbatim: 'From some ideas I have formed on the theory of heat, the production of one unit of motive power requires the destruction of 2.70 units of heat.' Turned into the units of his day, that is one kilocalorie for about 370 kilogram-metres, against the modern value of 427 - inside roughly 12 percent, from a man with no laboratory of his own, about two decades before James Joule measured it. His notes even propose friction experiments very like the ones Joule went on to perform. None of it was printed in his lifetime; it waited until Hippolyte's 1878 edition, which carried a facsimile of the handwritten sheet. The first pressure-volume diagram of the cycle was Emile Clapeyron's, in 1834. SOURCE: Wikipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'; New World Encyclopedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'; MacTutor 'Sadi Carnot'; Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot' on the cholera burial and the surviving notebook; arXiv:2508.17027 on the 1878 edition.

question: Carnot's engine is reversible, so you can drive it the wrong way: pay in work and it will carry heat from the cold side to the hot side. That machine is a refrigerator, and the same two temperatures set its ceiling. Take a fridge holding its box at 271 kelvin in a kitchen at 312 kelvin. At best, how much heat can one joule of work shift out of that box?
answer: About seven joules.
choices: About one joule.
About seven joules.
About seventy joules.
About a tenth of a joule.
context: The reversed Carnot cycle's coefficient of performance for cooling is T_cold / (T_hot - T_cold): 271 / (312 - 271) = 271 / 41, about 6.6. Nothing is being created - the fridge is not making energy, it is MOVING it, and paying one joule for the privilege of moving six and a half. Run the same machine to warm a house instead and the figure is T_hot / (T_hot - T_cold), better still, which is exactly why a heat pump beats an electric bar heater: the bar heater can only turn one joule of electricity into one joule of warmth. Carnot himself stressed that his cycle's reversibility let the engine run backwards. Notice the shape of it - widen the temperature gap and an engine gets better, but a fridge gets worse. SOURCE: Grokipedia 'Carnot cycle' (reversed cycle, both COP formulas and this worked 271 K / 312 K example); Grokipedia 'Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot'.

question: On May 2, 1927, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that Virginia could sterilize Carrie Buck against her will. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote the majority opinion, and he ended it with a single sentence that has followed the ruling ever since. What was that sentence?
answer: Three generations of imbeciles are enough.
choices: Three generations of imbeciles are enough.
Separate but equal is inherently unequal.
The power to tax involves the power to destroy.
A thing is worth what it will bring in the market.
context: Buck v. Bell, 274 U.S. 200 (1927). The sentence closes Holmes's majority opinion and is the ruling's most-quoted line. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/274/200

question: The Buck v. Bell ruling was 8-1, with a single Justice voting no. That Justice was Pierce Butler -- and his 'no' vote is unusual in the Supreme Court record for one reason. What did Butler do with his dissent?
answer: He filed no opinion at all -- the record is blank.
choices: He filed no opinion at all -- the record is blank.
He wrote a dissent longer than the majority opinion.
He read his dissent aloud from the bench.
He resigned from the Court in protest weeks later.
context: Butler was the Court's only Catholic and its lone dissenter, but he wrote nothing to explain his vote. His silence has been debated by legal historians ever since. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/buck-v-bell-1927/

question: Carrie Buck's school record before the Colony was ordinary -- she was a normal student in a foster home. What actually put her in the Virginia Colony for Epileptics and Feeble Minded, at 17, was a specific event the state used against her. What was the event?
answer: a pregnancy after she said she was raped
choices: a pregnancy after she said she was raped
a fight at school that ended in expulsion
a diagnosis of epilepsy from a family doctor
a theft charge brought by a neighbor
context: Carrie said the rapist was the nephew of her foster parents, the Dobbs family. She was committed to the Colony to keep the pregnancy quiet and out of the household. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie_Buck

question: Carrie Buck was not the first woman Colony superintendent Albert Priddy had sterilized. He had been performing the operation for years. What Priddy did with Buck's case that he had not done with the others was a deliberate legal move. What did he do?
answer: he pushed the case up to test Virginia's new 1924 law
choices: he pushed the case up to test Virginia's new 1924 law
he refused to operate until a court ruling came
he stopped keeping written records of surgeries
he asked the governor for a personal exemption
context: Priddy brought the case as a deliberate test of the 1924 Eugenical Sterilization Act. He wanted the Supreme Court to bless the statute before he continued -- a manufactured appeal. Priddy died in 1925 during the litigation and was replaced by John Bell, which is why the case bears Bell's name. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/buck-v-bell-1927/

question: Eugenics Record Office field worker Arthur Estabrook testified at trial that Carrie's baby daughter Vivian was feebleminded. He had examined her once, when she was about seven months old. What did the test he gave a seven-month-old actually consist of?
answer: he held a shiny coin in front of her eyes
choices: he held a shiny coin in front of her eyes
he watched her reach for a bright rattle
he measured the circumference of her skull
he timed how long she watched a picture
context: Estabrook later described the exam as a standard infant assessment: he offered a coin and read her tracking as below average. On that observation of a seven-month-old the Court's 'third generation' rested. Source: https://dnalc.cshl.edu/view/15837-Vivian-Dobbs.html

question: The lawyer the court appointed to defend Carrie Buck was named Irving Whitehead. When historian Paul Lombardo dug into the case decades later, he found something disqualifying about Whitehead that had never been raised at trial. What was it?
answer: he had sat on the Colony's board and backed sterilization
choices: he had sat on the Colony's board and backed sterilization
he had never argued before the Supreme Court in his life
he was superintendent Priddy's own brother-in-law
he had been paid secretly by Virginia, not by the family
context: Whitehead was a former Colony board member and a personal supporter of the sterilization program. Lombardo documented that at trial he failed to cross-examine aggressively, conceded key facts, and called no witnesses for Buck. The defense was run by a man on the other side. Source: https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/buck-v-bell-1927/

question: The legal engine of Holmes's Buck v. Bell opinion was an analogy. He argued that the power the state was using to sterilize Carrie Buck rested on a broader power the Court had already blessed in an earlier case. Which power did he stretch to reach forced sterilization?
answer: compulsory vaccination, upheld in Jacobson v. Massachusetts
choices: compulsory vaccination, upheld in Jacobson v. Massachusetts
the wartime military draft, in the Selective Draft Law Cases
state quarantine power, in Compagnie Francaise v. Louisiana
