state limits on women's work hours, in Muller v. Oregon
context: Holmes leaned on Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905), the compulsory-vaccination case, writing: 'The principle that sustains compulsory vaccination is broad enough to cover cutting the Fallopian tubes.' A public-health precedent about smallpox shots was stretched into a surgical one. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/274/200

question: In 1942, in Skinner v. Oklahoma, the Supreme Court struck down an Oklahoma statute that mandated a forced vasectomy after three felony convictions. The ruling used a narrow constitutional ground -- narrow enough to leave the deeper eugenic precedent alone. Which ground did the Court use?
answer: equal protection -- larcenists sterilized, embezzlers not
choices: equal protection -- larcenists sterilized, embezzlers not
cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment
due process -- the surgery was ordered without a hearing
double jeopardy -- the sentence had already been served
context: Justice Douglas wrote the majority. Oklahoma sterilized three-time thieves but exempted embezzlers -- an inconsistency Douglas called irrational. The equal-protection framing let the Court avoid ruling on eugenic sterilization itself, so Buck v. Bell was untouched. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skinner_v._Oklahoma

question: In the same decade the Virginia Colony was locking up Southern women for 'feeblemindedness,' other American doctors were finding real medical causes for symptoms that looked like it. Charles Stiles was tracking one cause across the rural South; Joseph Goldberger was tracking another with diet studies. Which pair were they finding?
answer: hookworm and pellagra
choices: hookworm and pellagra
tuberculosis and rickets
scarlet fever and diphtheria
malaria and yellow fever
context: Charles Stiles's hookworm campaign showed a soil-borne parasite was sapping the energy and cognition of poor Southerners. Joseph Goldberger's controlled diet trials proved pellagra was a nutritional deficiency (later identified as niacin), not a hereditary defect. Serious contemporary science was pointing at causes the Colony ignored. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Buck-v-Bell

question: Victoria Gray, a mother of four from Mississippi, had spent her life in and out of hospitals with sudden, crippling pain that could last for weeks. Which inherited blood condition was tormenting her?
answer: sickle-cell disease
choices: sickle-cell disease
hemophilia
leukemia
cystic fibrosis
context: In 2019 she became the first US sickle-cell patient dosed in the trial that would become Casgevy; since her infusion she has reported no crises and no hospital stays. Source: Wikipedia, 'Victoria Gray (patient)'; NPR, March 2023.

question: The whole illness that turns red cells into rigid crescents that jam in capillaries comes down to a single amino-acid swap in one chain of the hemoglobin protein. At position 6 of the beta-globin chain, which normal amino acid is replaced by valine?
answer: glutamic acid
choices: glutamic acid
lysine
methionine
cysteine
context: The negatively-charged glutamic acid is swapped for the neutral, hydrophobic valine; that one hydrophobic patch lets hemoglobin S molecules stack into stiff fibres that deform the red cell into its crescent shape. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sickle cell disease'.

question: The odd-shaped red cells that give sickle-cell disease its name have their crescent form only when one specific condition drops in the tissues. Under what condition do the cells stiffen and jam in the capillaries?
answer: low oxygen
choices: low oxygen
high salt
cold temperatures
high blood pressure
context: In low-oxygen conditions (working muscles, high altitude, or the tissues generally), hemoglobin S molecules stack into stiff fibres inside the red cell and warp its shape. That is why exercise, illness or altitude can trigger a crisis. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sickle cell disease'.

question: In 1949 the chemist Linus Pauling and his team ran hemoglobin from sickle-cell patients and hemoglobin from healthy people through an electric field. They saw the two forms drift to different places on the gel -- the first time any human illness had been tied directly to a single defective protein. What phrase did Pauling coin for the new category of illness he had opened up?
answer: molecular disease
choices: molecular disease
genetic disorder
protein defect
chromosomal illness
context: The paper -- 'Sickle Cell Anemia, a Molecular Disease' -- appeared in Science on 25 November 1949 (Pauling, Itano, Singer, Wells). Vernon Ingram narrowed the defect to the single amino-acid swap in 1956. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sickle Cell Anemia, a Molecular Disease'.

question: The new CRISPR therapy for sickle-cell disease is often mis-described as 'fixing the broken gene'. In fact it does not touch the mutated hemoglobin gene at all. Instead it goes after a completely different gene, called BCL11A. What does the therapy actually do to BCL11A?
answer: Silences it, so the fetal form of hemoglobin comes back on
choices: Silences it, so the fetal form of hemoglobin comes back on
Boosts it, so adult hemoglobin production doubles
Replaces it with an edited working copy
Adds a second copy from a healthy donor
context: BCL11A is a transcription factor that switches off fetal hemoglobin (HbF) after birth. Casgevy uses CRISPR-Cas9 to cut BCL11A's red-cell-specific enhancer; with the switch broken, HbF returns and takes over the job the sickling adult hemoglobin was failing at. Source: NEJM, 'Exagamglogene Autotemcel for Severe Sickle Cell Disease' (2023).

question: The world's first-ever CRISPR therapy approval landed at one regulator ahead of the rest. Which agency granted Casgevy its first authorisation, in November 2023?
answer: the UK's MHRA
choices: the UK's MHRA
the US FDA
the European Medicines Agency
Japan's PMDA
context: The UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy for both sickle-cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia in November 2023. The US FDA followed for sickle-cell in December 2023 and for beta thalassemia in January 2024. Source: MHRA news release, November 2023.

question: The bank is careful to state Casgevy's real numbers, not slogans. In the pivotal trial, how many of 31 evaluable sickle-cell patients went at least 12 consecutive months with no severe vaso-occlusive pain crisis?
context: 29 of 31 -- a real, cited number, not a marketing figure. The 2 who missed the primary endpoint still had major reductions in crisis frequency. Source: NEJM 2023, 'Exagamglogene Autotemcel for Severe Sickle Cell Disease'.

question: The triumph is stated straight, and so is the price tag. What is the US list price for a single Casgevy treatment course?
answer: about $2.2 million
choices: about $2.2 million
about $85,000
about $12 million
context: The conditioning chemotherapy required before infusion is also harsh and can cause infertility. Both the cure and the cost are stated as facts, not as a rebuttal to each other. Source: NPR Health Shots, March 2023.

question: On the same day the FDA approved Casgevy for sickle-cell disease -- 8 December 2023 -- it also approved a rival gene therapy from bluebird bio. That rival takes a different technical route: instead of using CRISPR to cut a switch, it uses a virus to ADD a modified beta-globin gene. What is it called?
answer: Lyfgenia
choices: Lyfgenia
Zolgensma
Luxturna
Kymriah
context: Lyfgenia (lovotibeglogene autotemcel) uses a lentiviral vector, not CRISPR. Zolgensma treats spinal muscular atrophy, Luxturna treats an inherited blindness, and Kymriah is a CAR-T cancer therapy -- all real gene therapies, none for sickle cell. Source: FDA press announcement, 8 December 2023.

question: Before any CRISPR was possible, doctors had one drug that worked on sickle-cell by the same broad idea Casgevy exploits: raising the amount of fetal hemoglobin in the patient's red cells, so the sickling form was diluted. What is that older drug?
answer: hydroxyurea
choices: hydroxyurea
penicillin
deferoxamine
erythropoietin
context: Hydroxyurea (also called hydroxycarbamide) has been standard sickle-cell therapy for decades; it turns fetal hemoglobin back on pharmacologically instead of by editing DNA. The other three are real drugs used in sickle-cell care but for different jobs (infection prevention, iron overload, anemia). Source: Wikipedia, 'Hydroxycarbamide'.

question: Drop a piece of raw liver into a beaker of drugstore hydrogen peroxide and it does not just fizz. It erupts, throwing up a column of foam that climbs over the rim in seconds -- no flame, no spark, nothing added but the peroxide. What is trapped inside all those bubbles?
answer: Oxygen gas, torn out of the peroxide
choices: Oxygen gas, torn out of the peroxide
Hydrogen gas, torn out of the peroxide
Carbon dioxide, driven out of the liver
Water vapour, boiled off as the mix warms
context: Raw liver is loaded with catalase, an enzyme that splits hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into water and oxygen gas; the escaping oxygen is what inflates the foam. Catalase sits in nearly every air-breathing organism, concentrated in liver, kidney and red blood cells, where it destroys the peroxide those cells make as a by-product of their own chemistry. TRY IT: add dish soap to strong peroxide and the same reaction gives the classroom 'elephant's toothpaste' column -- which comes out hot, around 75 C, because the peroxide's breakdown releases heat all by itself. Either a mineral salt (potassium iodide) or a spoonful of living baker's yeast will start it, and neither is used up. Sources: Scientific American, 'The Liver: Helping Enzymes Help You!'; Wikipedia, "Elephant's toothpaste".

question: Raw liver dropped into drugstore hydrogen peroxide erupts into foam -- the work of an enzyme in the meat called catalase. Boil a second piece of the same liver, cool it, and drop it in: the beaker barely stirs. Nothing was rinsed away. What did the boiling do?
answer: It warped the catalase out of its working shape
choices: It warped the catalase out of its working shape
It drove the iron out of the catalase's core
It boiled off the water the catalase needs to work
It sealed the meat against the peroxide
context: Boiling denatures catalase. Heat unravels the enzyme's folded three-dimensional structure, and the active site -- a narrow channel about 3 nm deep leading down to an iron-bearing heme -- is deformed, so hydrogen peroxide can no longer dock. Every atom is still present; only the shape is gone. Enzymes are catalysts, and for a catalyst built of protein, shape IS function. Scientific American's version of this test just microwaves the liver for 20 seconds and the bubbling largely stops. That same physics is why a very high fever is dangerous: between roughly 40 and 44 C human enzyme systems begin to malfunction as proteins unfold and clump, with heatstroke core temperature around 41-42 C. Sources: Scientific American, 'The Liver: Helping Enzymes Help You!'; Grokipedia, 'Catalase'; Hashim, 'Clinical biochemistry of hyperthermia', Annals of Clinical Biochemistry 2010.

question: Each catalase molecule carries just four working sites, and each site takes one peroxide molecule at a time -- grab it, split it, let go, reach for the next. No partner, no stored energy, no shortcut. Yet a cube of raw liver turns a beaker of drugstore peroxide into a foam column in seconds. Chemists have clocked a single catalase molecule at work. How many peroxide molecules does one get through in a second?
answer: About 40 million
choices: About 4,000
About 400,000
About 40 million
About 4 billion
context: Catalase (EC 1.11.1.6) decomposes up to about 40 million molecules of hydrogen peroxide per second per enzyme molecule (~4 x 10^7 s^-1) -- one of the highest turnover rates known for any enzyme. It is a tetramer: four identical subunits of roughly 60 kDa, each carrying one iron-bearing heme, and each active site sits at the bottom of a narrow hydrophobic channel about 3 nm deep that lets H2O2 in and shuts larger molecules out. It is found in nearly all aerobic organisms and lives inside cell compartments called peroxisomes. Source: Grokipedia, 'Catalase'.

question: On 27 July 1823 at the University of Jena, Johann Wolfgang Doebereiner aimed a jet of hydrogen at a lump of spongy platinum with no flame anywhere near it. The platinum glowed red-hot and the hydrogen caught fire. What did Doebereiner build out of it?
answer: A pocket lighter for making flame on demand
choices: A pocket lighter for making flame on demand
A safety lamp for the tunnels of coal mines
A furnace for smelting platinum from its ore
A burner for filling army hydrogen balloons
context: Doebereiner's lamp: zinc granules in roughly 25% sulfuric acid generate hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2); opening a stopcock sends a jet onto a platinum sponge at the nozzle, which glows red-hot and lights the gas. Close the stopcock, pressure builds, the acid falls away from the zinc, and the flame dies. Doebereiner -- a coachman's son and self-taught apothecary's apprentice -- owed his Jena professorship to the backing of the poet Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who bought one of the first lamps, funded the platinum research and wrote a poem in its honour. Doebereiner filed no patent on it. Grokipedia records roughly 20,000 units in use in Germany and Britain by 1828; the largest maker, Heinrich Gottfried Piegler of Schleiz, kept building them until about 1880. Friction 'Lucifer' matches were not patented until 1826 -- the lighter beat the match to market. Doebereiner also proposed the element 'triads' around 1829, foreshadowing the periodic law. Source: Grokipedia, "Doebereiner's lamp".

question: From the 1975 model year American cars carried a new catalyst pack in the exhaust -- alumina beads coated with platinum and palladium -- that turned carbon monoxide and unburned fuel into carbon dioxide and water. Garages soon found some of these converters stone dead, and no cleaning would bring one back. What had killed them?
answer: One tank of leaded petrol
choices: One tank of leaded petrol
One tank of petrol cut with kerosene
One tank run down to fumes
One tank of the new unleaded petrol
context: Burning leaded petrol produces elemental lead plus lead oxide, chloride and bromide. The lead alloys with the platinum-group metals while its compounds coat the catalyst surface. The UN Environment Programme states flatly that a converter 'can be destroyed by a single tankful of leaded fuel'; a Ford patent puts it bluntly: lead 'will deactivate catalysts formed from materials such as platinum, palladium, ruthenium, rhodium, iridium'. Poisoned metal cannot be regenerated in a garage -- the part is replaced. Other real catalyst poisons: sulfur, phosphorus and zinc from burnt engine oil, silicon from coolant leaks. The 1975 units were two-way oxidation converters (about 74% CO and 68% hydrocarbon reduction) that did almost nothing about nitrogen oxides; the three-way design, which adds rhodium to turn NOx back into plain nitrogen, arrived with the 1981 model year. The converter mandate is what forced unleaded petrol across America. The last country selling leaded petrol was Algeria, which stopped in July 2021. Sources: UNEP, 'Inside the 20-year campaign to rid the world of leaded fuel'; Grokipedia, 'Catalytic converter'; US Patent 4,372,748 (Ford Motor Co.).

question: By the 1830s chemists had a heap of results nobody could file: sulfuric acid turning starch into sugar syrup, blood making hydrogen peroxide foam, platinum lighting gas with no flame. Writing his annual survey of chemistry in 1835, Joens Jacob Berzelius argued that all of these were one phenomenon and gave it a definition sharp enough to test. What did he insist the mysterious agent must do?
answer: Hasten the reaction, yet end unaltered in quantity and quality
choices: Hasten the reaction, yet end unaltered in quantity and quality
Hasten the reaction by giving up heat stored in its own bonds
Hasten the reaction while being consumed in step with the product
Hasten the reaction only while held above its melting point
context: Berzelius named the class CATALYSIS, from the Greek katalysis, 'loosening', defining it as 'the property of exerting on other bodies an action which is very different from chemical affinity', the agent hastening the reaction while emerging unaltered in quantity and quality. He had already called Doebereiner's 1823 platinum result 'the most brilliant' of its year and cited it as the founding example. Berzelius also coined isomerism (1830), protein (1838) and allotropy (1841), introduced the modern element symbols, and published the first table of atomic weights in 1814. FORGOTTEN FIRST: the British chemist Elizabeth Fulhame got there 41 years earlier. Her 'An Essay On Combustion with a View to a New Art of Dying and Painting' (1794), the fruit of fourteen years of experiments, showed that many oxidations run only when water is present, that the water directly participates, and that it is handed back and detectable at the end -- the exact 'consumed then returned' logic. Wikipedia's article on catalysis says outright that the concept 'was invented by chemist Elizabeth Fulhame'. Earlier observations Berzelius was gathering: Gottlieb Kirchhoff's acid-and-starch syrup (1811) and Louis Jacques Thenard's discovery that blood breaks down hydrogen peroxide (1818). Sources: Grokipedia, 'Joens Jacob Berzelius'; Grokipedia, 'Catalysis'; Wikipedia, 'Elizabeth Fulhame'.

question: Fritz Haber pulled ammonia out of ordinary air in his Karlsruhe laboratory in 1909, but his catalysts were osmium and uranium. At BASF, Alwin Mittasch hunted for a replacement by brute force: thirty small high-pressure reactors running side by side, each packed with two grams of a different recipe, all tested under identical conditions at once, through thousands upon thousands of runs. Which material came out on top?
answer: Fused iron ore, with alumina and potash added
choices: Fused iron ore, with alumina and potash added
Fused nickel ore, with alumina and potash added
Fused copper ore, with alumina and potash added
Fused tungsten ore, with alumina and potash added
context: The winner was fused magnetite (Fe3O4) promoted with alumina (structural -- it holds the surface area open) and potassium oxide (electronic -- it helps split the tough nitrogen molecule), plus lime and silica. Cheap, abundant, and as good as osmium; it is still in use, nearly unchanged, today. Mittasch's parallel mini-reactor programme, begun in 1909, was arguably the first high-throughput catalyst screen (Grokipedia says over 20,000 formulations by 1912; Wikipedia's Mittasch article says roughly 10,000). Credit splits two ways: on 2 July 1909 Haber and his English collaborator Robert Le Rossignol ran off roughly a pint of liquid ammonia over five hours at about 200 atmospheres and 500-600 C -- that was the demonstration. Carl Bosch made it industrial: the first carbon-steel reactor tubes burst after about 80 hours as hydrogen attacked the metal, so Bosch designed a double-walled converter with a replaceable soft-steel liner, patented in 1911, its vents still called 'Bosch holes'. Oppau made its first ammonia on 9 September 1913. Vaclav Smil's ESTIMATE, from nitrogen-response curves and not a measured constant, is that the resulting fertiliser underwrites roughly 40-50% of the world's food supply. Haber took the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, Bosch the 1931. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of the Haber process'; Wikipedia, 'Alwin Mittasch'.

question: Hydrogen peroxide sitting quietly in a bottle breaks down so slowly you would wait days to see a bubble. Sprinkle in a spoonful of manganese dioxide powder and the same bottle foams over within seconds -- and the powder can be filtered out afterwards, dried, and used on the next bottle just as well. What did the powder change?
answer: The height of the energy barrier the molecules must climb
choices: The height of the energy barrier the molecules must climb
The temperature at which the reaction becomes possible
The amount of energy the reaction gives off in total
The mixture of products the reaction finally settles into
context: This is the rail that kills the magic. A catalyst opens an ALTERNATIVE pathway with a lower activation energy -- a lower pass over the same mountains -- and ends unchanged. It does not touch the destination: the standard Gibbs energy change is identical with or without it, and catalysts have no effect on where a reaction's equilibrium sits. A catalyst that shifted equilibrium would violate the second law of thermodynamics. In a reversible reaction it speeds the forward and reverse rates in proportion, so the system reaches the SAME equilibrium sooner. Two things a catalyst can never do: supply energy, or make a thermodynamically impossible reaction happen. 'It lowers the temperature the reaction needs' is the subtly wrong cousin -- the reaction was always possible at that temperature; it was simply too slow to see. Quantitative comparisons put the manganese-dioxide-catalysed peroxide breakdown at over 2,000 times the uncatalysed rate; potassium iodide does the same job dissolved rather than as a solid, with iodide ions acting as an intermediate. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Catalysis'; Wikipedia, 'Catalysis'.

question: Irving Langmuir worked at General Electric's laboratory in Schenectady, measuring how gases settle onto clean surfaces -- hydrogen and oxygen onto tungsten filaments, and onto glass, mica and platinum. Between 1916 and 1918 he turned the result into an equation by setting the rate of arrival equal to the rate of departure, and the surface chemistry that followed won him a Nobel Prize. What did Langmuir find a gas does when it lands on clean metal?
answer: It sticks in a layer exactly one molecule thick
choices: It sticks in a layer exactly one molecule thick
It dissolves inward and spreads through the metal
It gathers into droplets at the coldest points
It drifts across until it finds a crack to fill
context: Langmuir showed that adsorption occurs in MONOMOLECULAR layers on a clean surface, and derived the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, theta = Kp/(1 + Kp), by equating the rates of adsorption and desorption. He separated chemisorption -- strong, site-specific bonding, oxygen on tungsten at about 160 kcal/mol -- from physisorption, the weak van der Waals kind. He won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and was the first industrial scientist ever to take one; he also coined the word 'plasma' in 1927. The consequence: if only the outermost single layer of atoms can take part, surface area is the entire game -- which is why catalysts are built as sponges, powders and honeycombs rather than solid blocks. A modern converter uses a cordierite ceramic honeycomb with typically 400 to 900 cells per square inch. The catalytic cycle runs adsorption -> surface reaction -> desorption of product -> catalyst regenerated, and the two classic surface mechanisms are Langmuir-Hinshelwood (both reactants adsorb on adjacent sites, then react) and Eley-Rideal (one adsorbs, the other strikes it straight out of the gas). Sources: Grokipedia, 'Irving Langmuir'; Grokipedia, 'Catalysis'; Grokipedia, 'Catalytic converter'.

question: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland worked out where CFCs finally end up. The refrigerant gases are so unreactive that nothing at ground level touches them, so they drift upward for decades, until ultraviolet light in the stratosphere snaps a single chlorine atom loose. That one atom goes on destroying ozone molecule after ozone molecule and is never used up. What happens to the chlorine atom on each pass?
answer: It takes an oxygen from ozone, then a loose oxygen atom takes that one away
choices: It takes an oxygen from ozone, then a loose oxygen atom takes that one away
It splits an ozone molecule in two, then drifts free of both halves
It bonds to an ozone molecule, then breaks loose when the cold deepens
It swaps places with an oxygen in ozone, then a second chlorine frees it
context: Cl. + O3 -> ClO. + O2, then ClO. + O -> Cl. + O2. Net: two ozone molecules gone per cycle and the chlorine handed back intact, so one atom destroys thousands before it is finally scavenged. This is the purest possible statement of 'changed by nothing, changing everything' -- and here it is a catastrophe rather than a benefit. Catalysts are not automatically the good guys; the same trick that feeds the world through an iron catalyst tears the ozone layer apart through a chlorine atom. Molina and Rowland's seminal work is where the cycle was worked out. Source: Grokipedia, 'Catalysis' (Basic Examples).

question: Orotic acid is one of the most stubborn molecules in biochemistry. Left in plain water at room temperature, half of a sample takes 78 million years to shed its carbon dioxide -- a half-life longer than the whole span since the last dinosaurs died. Your cells run that exact step constantly, with one enzyme doing the work. In 1995 Anna Radzicka and Richard Wolfenden measured how long the enzyme needs. How long?
answer: About 18 milliseconds
choices: About 18 microseconds
About 18 milliseconds
About 18 seconds
About 18 minutes
context: Radzicka and Wolfenden, 'A proficient enzyme', Science 1995, 267(5194):90-93. Orotic acid decarboxylates spontaneously with a half-time of 78 million years in neutral water at room temperature; the enzyme orotidine 5'-monophosphate decarboxylase does the same transformation with a half-time of 18 milliseconds. That is a rate enhancement of about 10^17 -- the most proficient pure protein catalyst known in nature. And the enzyme puts in no energy and is consumed by nothing: it simply opens a lower pass over the same mountain. The same paper reports dimethyl phosphate hydrolysing spontaneously with a half-time of 130,000 years. Sources: Radzicka A, Wolfenden R, Science 1995 (PubMed 7809611); Wikipedia, "Orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase".

question: Catalase, the liver enzyme that rips hydrogen peroxide apart, is one of the fastest enzymes ever measured. In 2025 a single-molecule study using protein electrochemistry watched individual catalase molecules at work. What caps the speed of one of them?
answer: How fast peroxide molecules can drift into its reach
choices: How fast peroxide molecules can drift into its reach
How fast the iron at its core can reset between splits
How fast its products can clear the narrow channel
How tightly the peroxide clings once it has landed
context: Catalase is classed as a diffusion-limited or 'catalytically perfect' enzyme: its bottleneck is physics, not chemistry -- the substrate simply cannot arrive any faster. A 2025 single-entity protein-electrochemistry study confirmed this for individual catalase molecules. A caution on the numbers: the theoretical diffusion ceiling for k_cat/K_m in water is about 10^8-10^9 M^-1 s^-1, while catalase's measured bimolecular rate constant is around 10^7 M^-1 s^-1 -- APPROACHING that ceiling rather than sitting on it. Carbonic anhydrase, triose phosphate isomerase, superoxide dismutase and acetylcholinesterase are the other textbook diffusion-limited enzymes. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Diffusion-limited enzyme'; Grokipedia, 'Catalase'.

question: In a sealed outbuilding on his London estate in 1797, Henry Cavendish set out to measure the tiny gravitational pull between two lead balls. His own body heat inside the shed would have stirred the air enough to swamp the signal. How did he read the result?
answer: through a telescope from outside the room
choices: through a telescope from outside the room
with his ear pressed to a listening tube
by attaching a long paper pointer that stuck out through a slot in the wall
with a mirror rigged to reflect down a chimney
context: The man who had to leave the room to take his own measurement. Cavendish's shed sat in his garden at Clapham Common; he took 17 patient measurements between August 1797 and May 1798. Source: APS News, 'June 1798: Cavendish weighs the world'.

question: Henry Cavendish called his 1797-98 project 'weighing the world'. What single number did he actually publish in his Philosophical Transactions paper for the whole planet?
answer: its mean density, in multiples of the density of water
choices: its mean density, in multiples of the density of water
its total mass, measured in tons of iron
the gravitational pull at its surface, in units of feet per second
the length of its diameter, measured in English miles
context: Cavendish's 1798 paper in the Philosophical Transactions was titled 'Experiments to determine the Density of the Earth.' From that single number you can get the mass; from the mass and the size, everything else. Source: Grokipedia -- Cavendish experiment.

question: The apparatus in Cavendish's shed was not his own invention. It had been designed and built by a shy Yorkshire country rector, who died in 1793 before ever using it and whose kit reached Cavendish second-hand through Francis Wollaston. Name the builder.
answer: John Michell
choices: John Michell
Joseph Priestley
Erasmus Darwin
Nevil Maskelyne
context: Michell had spent years planning the experiment; when he died, the balance had never been fired. Cavendish quietly rebuilt it and kept close to Michell's plan. Source: FamousScientists.org -- John Michell.

question: In June 1798 Cavendish published his answer for 'weighing the world' -- the ratio of Earth's mean density to that of water -- in a 57-page paper in the Philosophical Transactions. Which value did he print?
context: The modern accepted value is 5.514. Cavendish had come within about 1.2% of the right answer, from a garden shed, in 1798. Baily's 1821 re-average of Cavendish's own tables gave 5.448; Maskelyne's earlier Schiehallion result had been about 4.5. Source: American Journal of Physiology, Vol. 307 (2014) -- 'Cavendish and weighing the world'; APS News, June 2008.

question: Cavendish had run 29 individual measurements before publishing his density number for Earth. In 1821 the astronomer Francis Baily sat down and re-averaged Cavendish's tables by hand. What did Baily find?
answer: a small arithmetic slip in Cavendish's own average
choices: a small arithmetic slip in Cavendish's own average
a systematic bias caused by a warped suspending wire
a transcription error introduced by the printer of the paper
no mistake at all -- the tables checked out perfectly
context: Cavendish had published 5.48; Baily's corrected average from the same 29 measurements was 5.448, actually closer to the modern 5.514. John Henry Poynting confirmed the re-check decades later. Source: APS News, June 2008.

question: Physics textbooks usually say the Cavendish experiment of 1797-98 measured big G, the gravitational constant. Historians of physics point out that this is not quite right: Cavendish himself never used the letter G or the term. Who actually extracted G from his data, and when?
answer: Alfred Cornu first extracted G from Cavendish's data in 1873
choices: Alfred Cornu first extracted G from Cavendish's data in 1873
Isaac Newton had already extracted G in his 1687 Principia
James Clerk Maxwell first extracted G while editing Cavendish's notebooks in the 1870s
John Henry Poynting first extracted G when re-checking Cavendish's 29 measurements
context: Cavendish never used the letter G or the term 'gravitational constant'. Newton's law of gravity had a constant of proportionality no one had yet measured; Cornu (with Baille) supplied a value in 1873, and the symbol G came into common use in the late nineteenth century. Cavendish's own quarry was density. Source: 'Historical Notes: The Gravitational Constant', arXiv 2306.06411.

question: The Yorkshire rector who designed Cavendish's torsion balance also wrote a letter to the Royal Society in November 1783, describing an object no one would name for two hundred years. What did John Michell propose in that letter?
answer: a star so massive that its escape velocity would exceed the speed of light
choices: a star so massive that its escape velocity would exceed the speed of light
an invisible planet beyond Saturn whose pull would explain cometary orbits
a comet composed entirely of ice that returns every seventy-six years
a moon of Venus that would eventually be detected by improving telescopes
context: Michell called such an object a 'dark star'. He reasoned that if a star were about 500 solar masses, no light could ever leave it. It is the first written black-hole idea in the scientific literature. Source: APS News, November 2009 -- 'John Michell anticipates black holes'.

question: In 1925 a 25-year-old graduate student at the Harvard College Observatory, Cecilia Payne, finished her PhD thesis on the spectra of hundreds of stars and reached a conclusion nobody wanted. What did she find the Sun -- and the other stars -- to be made of, overwhelmingly?
answer: Mostly hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements
choices: Mostly iron, a hot version of the Earth's core
Mostly hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements
Mostly carbon and oxygen in roughly equal parts
Mostly heavy metals held together by gravity
context: Payne's 1925 Harvard PhD thesis, 'Stellar Atmospheres,' concluded that the Sun and other stars are composed overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium -- together about 98 percent of a star's mass -- the two lightest elements in the universe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Payne-Gaposchkin

question: In December 1919 a first-year Cambridge student, Cecilia Payne, sat through a lecture by the astronomer Arthur Eddington on his recent expedition to Principe. She wrote it down almost word-for-word and switched from botany to physics on the spot. What had Eddington's expedition just done?
answer: Confirmed Einstein's theory of general relativity
choices: Measured the distance to the Andromeda galaxy
Discovered a new planet beyond Neptune
Confirmed Einstein's theory of general relativity
Proved that the Sun rotates on its axis
context: Eddington's May 1919 eclipse expedition to Principe measured starlight bending around the Sun -- the first observational confirmation of general relativity. Payne, born in England in 1900, was so overwhelmed by his December 1919 lecture that she left botany for physics. Source: https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/the-young-female-astronomer-who-worked-out-what-the-sun-is-made-of/4021693.article  (Legend.)

question: Cecilia Payne finished the physics course at Cambridge but walked away with no degree -- Cambridge would not grant degrees to women at the time. In 1923 she crossed the Atlantic to Harvard on a fellowship from observatory director Harlow Shapley, and in 1925 she became the first person, of any sex, to earn a PhD in astronomy from Harvard. But Harvard, too, would not grant a doctorate to a woman. Which institution formally awarded her the degree instead?
answer: Radcliffe College
choices: Radcliffe College
Wellesley College
Bryn Mawr College
Smith College
context: Payne's 1925 doctorate -- the first astronomy PhD ever granted at Harvard -- was formally issued through Radcliffe College because Harvard would not confer a doctorate on a woman. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Payne-Gaposchkin  (Legend.)

question: Payne did not go out and take her own photographs. She read hundreds of stellar spectra off glass plates already sitting on shelves at Harvard College Observatory -- the same shelves where a team of women 'computers,' led by Annie Jump Cannon, had spent years sorting stars by the shapes of their spectra. Which famous star catalogue supplied the spectra Payne worked from?
answer: The Henry Draper Catalogue
choices: The Bonner Durchmusterung
The Bright Star Catalogue
The Henry Draper Catalogue
The Yale Parallax Catalogue
context: Payne applied Saha's ionization equation to hundreds of stellar spectra taken from the Henry Draper Catalogue at Harvard College Observatory, connecting Saha's theory with the spectral classification system built by Annie Jump Cannon and Harvard's women 'computers.' Source: https://astrobites.org/2018/12/03/the-stuff-of-stars/

question: Payne's key theoretical tool was a 1920 equation from the Indian physicist Meghnad Saha. Astronomers before her had been reading the strength of a spectral line as 'how much of this element is present.' Saha's equation showed that reading was mostly wrong -- line strength actually depends on something else about the star. What?
answer: The temperature of the star's outer atmosphere
choices: The rotation speed of the star on its axis
The distance from the star to the Earth
The temperature of the star's outer atmosphere
The strength of the star's surface magnetic field
context: Saha's 1920 ionization equation showed that a spectral line's strength depends mainly on the star's temperature, because heat strips electrons from atoms and changes which lines the atom can even make. Correcting for temperature is what let Payne read hundreds of stellar spectra and see hydrogen's true abundance. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saha_ionization_equation

question: Once Payne applied Saha's temperature correction to hundreds of stellar spectra, the numbers she got back for hydrogen dwarfed anything astronomers had assumed. Roughly what factor did her result raise hydrogen's abundance by, relative to what earlier readings had said?
answer: About a million times more abundant
choices: About ten times more abundant
About a hundred times more abundant
About a thousand times more abundant
About a million times more abundant
context: Payne's analysis showed hydrogen was about a million times more abundant in stars than had been assumed, and helium about a thousand times more abundant. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2015/01/cecilia-payne-gaposchkin-universe-changed

question: Harlow Shapley sent Payne's thesis draft to Henry Norris Russell of Princeton -- the most powerful astronomer in America -- for review. Russell wrote back a short, blunt verdict on her hydrogen number. How did his letter characterize the finding?
answer: As a result that was clearly impossible
choices: As a bold but premature conjecture
As a result that was clearly impossible
As a promising line worth further work
As the natural extension of his earlier calculations
context: Russell wrote to Payne that 'it is clearly impossible that hydrogen should be a million times more abundant than the metals.' Arthur Eddington was skeptical as well. Source: https://physicsworld.com/a/cecilia-payne-gaposchkin-the-woman-who-found-hydrogen-in-the-stars/  (Legend.)

question: Russell's letter had come back calling Payne's hydrogen number 'clearly impossible,' and Harlow Shapley was afraid the whole thesis would be rejected outright. Under that pressure, Payne kept her calculated abundances in the text but tucked in a single hedging sentence about them. Which sentence did she insert into the published thesis?
answer: 'The enormous abundance derived for these elements is almost certainly not real.'
choices: 'The enormous abundance derived for these elements is almost certainly not real.'
'The strength of the hydrogen lines has probably been overestimated by the plates.'
'A revised temperature scale would very likely bring these numbers back into line with the Earth.'
'The excess of hydrogen appears to be a peculiarity of the hottest stars alone.'
context: At Russell and Shapley's urging, Payne inserted the sentence 'The enormous abundance derived for [hydrogen and helium] is almost certainly not real' into the published thesis -- but she left the calculated numbers themselves standing. The finding was softened in prose, never in the data. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2015/01/cecilia-payne-gaposchkin-universe-changed  (Legend.)

question: Four years after Payne's muffled thesis, in 1929, Henry Norris Russell published his own paper, 'On the Composition of the Sun's Atmosphere,' in the Astrophysical Journal. Reaching the same hydrogen-dominant conclusion by a different route, he gave a specific composition for the solar atmosphere by volume -- and much of the public credit for the discovery drifted to him. Which breakdown did his 1929 paper publish?
answer: About 60 parts hydrogen, 2 helium, 2 oxygen, 1 metallic vapors, 0.8 free electrons
choices: About 60 parts hydrogen, 2 helium, 2 oxygen, 1 metallic vapors, 0.8 free electrons
About 40 parts hydrogen, 20 helium, 10 oxygen, 5 metallic vapors, 2 free electrons
About 30 parts hydrogen, 30 helium, 5 oxygen, 3 metallic vapors, 1 free electrons
About 90 parts hydrogen, 1 helium, 1 oxygen, 0.5 metallic vapors, 0.2 free electrons
context: Russell, 'On the Composition of the Sun's Atmosphere,' Astrophysical Journal vol. 70, p. 11 (1929) -- four years after Payne's thesis. He estimated the Sun's atmosphere as roughly 60 parts hydrogen by volume, 2 helium, 2 oxygen, 1 metallic vapors, and 0.8 free electrons -- publicly settling that hydrogen was by far the dominant element, four years after Payne had said so. Source: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1929ApJ....70...11R/abstract

question: Payne's hydrogen result turned out to be load-bearing for two of twentieth-century science's biggest ideas at once. A hydrogen Sun is a Sun that can shine by fusing hydrogen into helium -- and one major cosmological model predicts the universe should be dominated by those same two lightest elements. Which cosmological model did her abundance result quietly line up with?
answer: A hot Big Bang, with the universe expanding from an early hot dense state
choices: A hot Big Bang, with the universe expanding from an early hot dense state
A steady-state cosmology in which new matter is continuously created
A cold, static Newtonian universe of fixed unchanging size
A cyclic universe endlessly bouncing between crunches and rebirths
context: A hot Big Bang predicts that the young universe emerged overwhelmingly as hydrogen and helium, with heavier elements forged later inside stars. Payne's 1925 result -- stars are made of that same primordial mix -- became load-bearing for both stellar physics (hydrogen fusion) and modern cosmology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Payne-Gaposchkin

question: Cambridge, early 1932: James Chadwick has been firing a mysterious 'beryllium radiation' at a slab of paraffin wax and watching protons come flying out of it, hard. In about a fortnight of near-continuous work at the Cavendish, he identifies what the beam is really made of, and sends a letter to Nature. What was the particle?
answer: the neutron
choices: the neutron
the positron
the muon
the neutrino
context: Chadwick's letter to Nature was titled 'Possible Existence of a Neutron' and appeared in February 1932. The full paper in the Proceedings of the Royal Society followed. It closed the book on twelve years of hunting inside the Cavendish Laboratory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Chadwick.

question: James Chadwick's target was a slab of paraffin wax. Paraffin is a hydrocarbon -- carbon and hydrogen -- and he chose it not for the carbon but for the hydrogen. What property of hydrogen made it the ideal target to fire the mystery radiation at?
answer: its nucleus is a lone proton with nothing else attached
choices: its nucleus is a lone proton with nothing else attached
it is the lightest element, so its atoms move fastest at room temperature
its nucleus has the largest cross-section of any element
its electrons are the most loosely bound of any element
context: That is what makes hydrogen the cleanest target imaginable. If the mystery beam kicks a recoiling nucleus out of the wax, and that nucleus is bare, the recoil speed maps straight to the beam without complications from the rest of an atom. That is the trick. It is why Chadwick used it -- and why the Joliot-Curies had used it before him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: James Chadwick was not the first to run the paraffin-wax experiment. In January 1932, two months before his letter, a team in Paris did it and reported the same recoiling protons -- but reported that the radiation causing them was gamma rays. Who were they?
answer: Irene and Frederic Joliot-Curie
choices: Irene and Frederic Joliot-Curie
Marie and Pierre Curie
Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn
Gerty and Carl Cori
context: Irene Curie (Marie's daughter) and Frederic Joliot published the paraffin result in Comptes Rendus in January 1932. They went on to a Nobel of their own in 1935 for the discovery of induced radioactivity -- they were superb experimentalists. Their miss on the neutron was a wrong prior about what the radiation had to be, not sloppy work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: Chadwick had hunted a neutral, roughly proton-mass particle for about twelve years before 1932 -- because his own boss had already predicted one in a famous lecture back in 1920. Which physicist gave that lecture?
answer: Ernest Rutherford
choices: Ernest Rutherford
Niels Bohr
Werner Heisenberg
Arthur Eddington
context: Rutherford's 1920 Bakerian Lecture to the Royal Society sketched a neutral particle of roughly proton mass, arguing it would explain how heavy nuclei hold together and could slip past their electric charge. Chadwick took the sketch as a research programme and ran it for a decade -- until the Joliot-Curies handed him the clue by misidentifying it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: Within seven years of James Chadwick's paper, physicists were splitting uranium with slow neutrons. A slow proton fired at uranium is turned away long before it reaches the nucleus. What property of the neutron lets it walk in where the proton cannot?
answer: it carries no electric charge to be repelled by
choices: it carries no electric charge to be repelled by
it is much smaller than a proton in size
it decays into a photon before it arrives
it moves faster than any proton the lab could make
context: A proton fired at a uranium nucleus meets a wall of Coulomb repulsion -- 92 protons pushing back. A slow neutron feels nothing until it is right at the nuclear surface, where the short-range strong force grabs it. Otto Hahn, Fritz Strassmann and Lise Meitner used that fact to split the nucleus in 1938-39, and the world changed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron.

question: On 7 December 1854, at Douai, a French chemist rose to give the formal inaugural address for the brand-new science faculty at Lille. Talking to students about to head into factories and dye-works, he told them: 'in the fields of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind.' Who said it?
answer: Louis Pasteur
choices: Louis Pasteur
Jean-Baptiste Dumas
Marcelin Berthelot
Claude Bernard
context: The line is from Pasteur's printed 7 December 1854 inaugural address for the new Lille faculty of sciences, delivered at Douai. Original French: 'dans les champs de l'observation, le hasard ne favorise que les esprits prepares'. Dumas, Berthelot and Bernard were all leading French scientists active in the 1850s. Source: Louis Pasteur, Wikiquote (https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur).

question: In that same 1854 Lille address, Pasteur illustrated 'the prepared mind' by pointing to a Scandinavian scientist who had spotted a tiny compass needle twitch beside a battery wire during a lecture. Every student in the room saw the same wobble. Only one saw why it mattered - because his research programme had been aimed at exactly this question for years. Which scientist was Pasteur crediting?
answer: Hans Christian Orsted
choices: Hans Christian Orsted
Jons Jacob Berzelius
Johan Georg Forchhammer
Heinrich Christian Schumacher
context: Orsted had spent years expecting a link between electricity and magnetism, and in 1820 the anomaly finally arrived. A prepared mind is not a lucky mind - it is a mind with an expectation already loaded, waiting for an anomaly to fit. Berzelius was the great Swedish chemist of the era, Forchhammer a Danish geologist-chemist, Schumacher a Danish astronomer - all contemporaries. Source: APS News, 'July 1820: Orsted & Electromagnetism' (https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2008/07/1820-oersted-electromagnetism).

question: On 6 April 1938 the young DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett went to the lab freezer for a heavy steel cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas. He opened the valve and nothing came out. Most chemists would have written it up as a leak and moved on. Plunkett instead did one boring routine thing that revealed the discovery of Teflon. What single check did he run first?
answer: He weighed the whole cylinder on a lab balance
choices: He weighed the whole cylinder on a lab balance
He tested the valve with a soap-bubble sniffer
He heated the cylinder to release trapped gas
He rinsed the valve with hot solvent
context: The cylinder still weighed the same as when it had been full - so nothing had actually leaked. Plunkett sawed it open and found a slippery white powder inside. Remove the lab balance and there is no anomaly to notice. Source: Science History Institute, Roy J. Plunkett (https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/roy-j-plunkett/).

question: In 1913 the Sheffield metallurgist Harry Brearley was hunting a longer-lived steel for British gun barrels. Along the way he cast a chromium alloy that turned out to be the wrong hardness for the guns. The alloy might have been thrown out as a failure - but one routine step Brearley never skipped when examining a sample gave the alloy away. Which routine step?
answer: He etched every polished sample with nitric acid
choices: He etched every polished sample with nitric acid
He dropped every sample into a flame test
He struck every sample with a spring-loaded hammer
He bent every sample in a vise to failure
context: Etching with acid is how a metallurgist brings out the grain structure under a microscope. Brearley's sample stubbornly refused to etch - and that refusal is the moment stainless steel was noticed. Source: Nautilus, 'The Father of Modern Metal' (https://nautil.us/the-father-of-modern-metal-235939).

question: In 1968 the 3M scientist Spencer Silver produced an adhesive that stuck lightly, then peeled off cleanly and could be re-stuck. For about six years he could not find anyone at 3M who could name a use for it. Silver had a favourite phrase for what he had made, and he used it in every in-house pitch. How did he describe his invention?
answer: A solution waiting for a problem to solve
choices: A solution waiting for a problem to solve
A better rubber cement for schoolrooms
A cheap replacement for masking tape
A promising future aerospace adhesive
context: Six or seven years later Silver's colleague Art Fry needed a bookmark for his church hymnal that would not damage the page - and Silver's 'solution' finally had its problem. Post-it Notes shipped in 1980. Source: C&EN, 'Spencer F. Silver' (https://cen.acs.org/acs-news/Spencer-F-Silver-inventor-of-sticky-note-adhesive-dies-at-80/99/web/2021/05).

question: Newton's apple appears in William Stukeley's 1752 Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life. Kekule's benzene-ring-as-snake dream appears in an 1890 speech he gave to the German Chemical Society. Careful historians of science rank both stories as the same KIND of source. Which kind?
answer: A late self-told anecdote, not a contemporary record
choices: A late self-told anecdote, not a contemporary record
A passage from the discoverer's own contemporary correspondence
A rival chemist's diary written the same year as the discovery
A signed eyewitness deposition taken at the time
context: Stukeley wrote up Newton's story from a conversation about sixty years after the alleged event; Kekule told the snake-dream story roughly twenty-five years after already publishing the benzene structure. Retold discovery stories smooth themselves with age - the older the retelling and the more famous the teller, the tidier the story gets. That does not prove them false; it means treat them as testimony, not evidence. Sources: History.com on Stukeley; contemporary essays on the Kekule dream.  (Legend.)

question: In 1930, a nineteen-year-old sailing from India to England filled his shipboard notebooks working out what happens to a burnt-out star -- and found that above about 1.4 times the Sun's mass, no such star can hold itself up. Who was he?
answer: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
choices: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
Homi Bhabha
Meghnad Saha
Jagadish Chandra Bose
context: All four are real Indian physicists of that generation. Chandrasekhar was on his way to graduate work at Cambridge. Source: Wikipedia, Chandrasekhar limit.

question: An ordinary white dwarf star has burned through its nuclear fuel and cannot rely on heat to hold itself up against gravity. What DOES prop it up?
answer: A quantum rule that forbids two electrons from occupying the same state
choices: A quantum rule that forbids two electrons from occupying the same state
The star's rotation, spinning fast enough to fling matter outward
A magnetic field strong enough to counter its own gravity
Gravitational potential energy released as the star gradually shrinks
context: This is the Pauli exclusion principle. Squeeze electrons close and they shove back -- 'electron degeneracy pressure' -- with a push that has nothing to do with temperature. The slow-shrinkage idea (Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction) was the pre-quantum guess for what powers stars, and it fails for white dwarfs.

question: Chandrasekhar's addition to the old white-dwarf theory came from one specific piece of physics that others had left out. What did he put in?
answer: Special relativity
choices: Special relativity
General relativity
The uncertainty principle
Quantum tunneling
context: As the crushed electrons are driven toward light speed, their outward push stops growing fast enough to keep pace with gravity, so support fails above a definite mass -- the ceiling.

question: At the Royal Astronomical Society meeting on 11 January 1935 in London, Chandrasekhar presented his mass ceiling. Whose talk had been scheduled immediately after his -- and blindsided him by demolishing the theory in front of the room?
answer: Arthur Eddington
choices: Arthur Eddington
James Jeans
Edward Milne
Ralph Fowler
context: Chandrasekhar had seen the program and knew Eddington would speak next, but the content had not been shared. Eddington was the most famous astrophysicist alive at the time. Chandrasekhar left depressed.

question: Eddington's published objection to Chandrasekhar's mass ceiling (The Observatory, 1935) was famously short. What did he actually write?
answer: 'There should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way.'
choices: 'There should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way.'
'Chandrasekhar's arithmetic is beyond reproach; his physics is not yet.'
'Above such a mass, the star must first shed matter to save itself.'
'The equation is correct but the boundary conditions of a real star will never touch it.'
context: The consequence Eddington could not accept: above the limit, nothing was left to halt total collapse -- a star crushed to a few kilometers or to a point. He preferred to think the equation itself must be wrong. Only the first is his real 1935 quote.

question: In January 1932 -- one month before Chadwick discovered the neutron -- a Soviet physicist independently guessed that at extreme density stellar cores would behave like gigantic atomic nuclei, and estimated a limiting mass around 1.5 suns. Who was he?
answer: Lev Landau
choices: Lev Landau
Yakov Zeldovich
George Gamow
Igor Tamm
context: Landau was working with only protons in his atomic-nucleus picture because he did not yet know neutrons existed. After Chadwick's discovery he became the first to speculate seriously about a star made entirely of neutrons. All four names are real Soviet-era physicists.

question: You clamp a square metal plate at its centre, sprinkle fine sand across it, and draw a violin bow along one edge. In 1787 Ernst Chladni published a whole book of what the sand does. What does the sand do?
answer: heaps itself into sharp symmetrical lines
choices: heaps itself into sharp symmetrical lines
slides off the plate entirely
vibrates as a fine mist above the plate
clumps into one mound at the bow contact
context: The book was 'Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges' ('Discoveries in the Theory of Sound'). You can reproduce it at home with a cookie sheet, table salt, and a phone speaker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Chladni

question: Halfway through a Chladni demonstration -- bow going steadily, note held constant -- the presenter presses one fingertip firmly onto a spot near the centre of the plate. What happens to the sand pattern?
answer: the whole pattern reorganises around the finger
choices: the whole pattern reorganises around the finger
the pattern instantly vanishes
the pattern stays put and the sand ignores the finger
the sand jumps toward the finger and clings there
context: Your finger cannot move up and down, so wherever it presses the plate the plate cannot vibrate. Physicists call that a forced node. The plate settles into the next standing-wave shape that respects the new constraint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chladni_figures

question: Chladni was not the first person to see the figures. On 8 July 1680 an English natural philosopher bowed a flour-covered glass plate, sketched the shapes that appeared, and then never followed it up. Who was he?
answer: Robert Hooke
choices: Robert Hooke
Isaac Newton
Christiaan Huygens
Robert Boyle
context: Hooke recorded the effect and moved on; Chladni turned the curiosity into a research programme with hundreds of catalogued shapes. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2017/07/first-experiments-chladni-figures

question: Michael Faraday redid Chladni's experiment in 1831 with a much lighter dust than sand -- powdered lycopodium spores. The pattern was the exact inverse of Chladni's: the powder gathered in the loudest-moving regions, not the quiet ones. What was sorting the spores the opposite way?
answer: tiny air currents stirred up by the vibration
choices: tiny air currents stirred up by the vibration
static electricity from the friction of the bow
the plate's own magnetic field
the shape of grain in the metal itself
context: This is called acoustic streaming: the vibrating surface pumps circulating air currents that carry the light spores to the antinodes. Repeat the experiment in a vacuum and the inverse pattern does not form -- Faraday's confirming test. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/279629673_Convection_and_fluidization_in_oscillatory_granular_flows_The_role_of_acoustic_streaming

question: In 1808 Chladni demonstrated the sand figures in Paris. Napoleon Bonaparte watched, was fascinated, and the following February the Institut de France announced a prix extraordinaire of 3,000 francs for anyone who could derive the mathematics of a vibrating elastic plate. Only one serious mathematician ever entered. Who?
answer: Sophie Germain
choices: Sophie Germain
Simeon Denis Poisson
Pierre-Simon Laplace
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
context: Poisson was elected to the Academy, which made him a judge rather than a contestant, and no one else was willing to try -- Lagrange had said the problem would need a new branch of analysis. Germain, barred from the Ecole Polytechnique for being a woman, worked from smuggled lecture notes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Germain

question: Sophie Germain's first submission to the Institut prize was rejected for mathematical errors. Her second earned only an honourable mention. She won the grand prize in 1816, the first woman ever to take a Paris Academy grand prize -- but the winning memoir was still not entirely correct. Who later supplied the last piece?
answer: Gustav Kirchhoff, who corrected the boundary conditions
choices: Gustav Kirchhoff, who corrected the boundary conditions
Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who redid the derivation from scratch
Simeon Denis Poisson, who withdrew his own competing paper
Pierre-Simon Laplace, who signed off on it as it stood
context: Germain had leaned on an incorrect expression from Euler, and her boundary conditions were wrong. Kirchhoff (later famous for the circuit laws) supplied the correct ones. The Academy did not invite her to the award ceremony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Germain

question: Chladni set off a second controversy the learned world would not touch. In 1794 he published a book arguing that the stones peasants kept reporting to fall from the sky were not local -- they came from beyond the Earth. The case was closed his way after a spectacular fall on L'Aigle in Normandy on 26 April 1803. Who investigated that fall for the French Academy of Sciences?
answer: Jean-Baptiste Biot
choices: Jean-Baptiste Biot
Antoine Lavoisier
Georges Cuvier
Pierre-Simon Laplace
context: Lavoisier had died on the guillotine in 1794, the same year Chladni's book appeared; Cuvier and Laplace were French Academy figures of the same period, but the L'Aigle investigation went to Biot. Thousands of stones fell in broad daylight in front of hundreds of witnesses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorite

question: Clair Patterson's rock measurements kept coming out as nonsense, and he traced the trouble to lead getting into everything: the air of his laboratory, the dust, the benches, the glassware. Then he sampled something with nothing to do with the experiment at all, and found lead in that too. What had he sampled?
answer: The hair on his own head
choices: The ink in his notebook
The snow on the roof outside
The hair on his own head
The coins in his pocket
context: During his doctoral research Patterson found lead contamination pervasive throughout his laboratory -- including in his own hair. The world itself was dirty enough to ruin the measurement, so before he could weigh the age of the old world he had to build a clean one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Clair Patterson, who measured lead for a living, tested fish two ways: fresh, and out of a tin. Fresh fish carried about 0.3 nanograms of lead per gram. The canned fish carried 1,400 -- thousands of times more. What was the extra lead coming from?
answer: The lead solder sealing the can's seams
choices: The lead solder sealing the can's seams
The lead pipes in the cannery's water
The tin plating flaking off the steel
The lead-based ink printed on the label
context: The official laboratory that had measured the same comparison reported a rise of only 400 to 700 nanograms per gram -- Patterson found 1,400. He was not only catching industry: he was catching the regulators' own numbers running low. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: By 1953 Clair Patterson knew the lead ruining his measurements was coming from the room, not the rock, so at Caltech he built one of the first ultra-clean laboratories in the world: every piece of apparatus acid-washed, every entry point sealed. He also refused to use the chemicals his suppliers shipped him in the state they arrived. What did he do to them first?
answer: Re-distilled every one of them himself
choices: Diluted them tenfold before any use
Filtered them through fresh charcoal
Froze them and poured off the top
Re-distilled every one of them himself
context: Careful with the credit: Patterson built one of the first ultra-clean LABORATORIES in 1953, but the modern laminar-flow cleanroom was invented by the physicist Willis Whitfield at Sandia National Laboratories in 1960, seven years later. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'; Wikipedia, 'Cleanroom'.

question: The rock Clair Patterson chose for dating the Earth was the Canyon Diablo meteorite, and it does not sit in one piece: some 30 tonnes of fragments have been picked up across northern Arizona, the biggest a 639-kilogram lump now standing in a visitor centre. Why is it scattered rather than whole?
answer: The asteroid exploded on impact and blasted out a crater
choices: The parent body broke apart high in the atmosphere
The asteroid exploded on impact and blasted out a crater
Glaciers dragged the pieces apart over 50,000 years
Collectors sawed the single mass up for museums
context: The roughly 50-metre asteroid blasted out Meteor Crater in Arizona about 50,000 years ago, and the 639-kilogram Holsinger Meteorite sits in the crater's visitor centre. Canyon Diablo also carries three mineral phases -- sulfide, metal alloys and silicates -- with sharply different uranium and lead contents, which is exactly the spread an isotope analysis needs. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Canyon Diablo (meteorite)'; Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'.

question: Nobody had measured the lead in the air in 1750, or 1850, or 1900 -- the instruments did not exist. Clair Patterson wanted those numbers anyway, so he went hunting for a place that had recorded each year's air and stored it, layer on layer, ever since. Where did he go?
answer: To Greenland, to drill out a core of ice
choices: To California, to core bristlecone pines
To Switzerland, to dredge a lake bed
To Greenland, to drill out a core of ice
To London, to sample old chimney soot
context: Patterson analysed cores from Camp Century in Greenland in 1964 and from Antarctica in 1965. Snow falls, traps the dust and gases of its year, and is buried by the next year's fall -- so a column of ice is a dated archive of the air, read downwards. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'; Wikipedia, 'Ice core'.

question: Clair Patterson set out to measure how long ago the Earth formed, and the obvious material was lying under his feet by the tonne. He ignored it and worked on meteorites instead. What is wrong with using the Earth's own rocks to time the Earth's beginning?
answer: The surface is endlessly remade, so rock records its last reset
choices: The surface is endlessly remade, so rock records its last reset
The core's heat boils lead out of the crust, leaving it unreadable
Earth's magnetic field scrambles the lead isotope ratios in crust
Uranium is far too rare in crustal rock to leave a usable signal
context: The planet separated into core, mantle and crust, and plate tectonics, weathering and hot water circulating through rock have mixed and remade the surface ever since. A meteorite is debris from the same formation event that was never recycled -- so its clock has been running, untouched, from the beginning. Source: Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'.

question: In 1956 Clair Patterson published his answer for the age of the Earth -- 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million -- read out of the lead in meteorites. The textbooks of the day carried roughly 3.3 billion. Seventy years of sharper instruments have gone by since. What has become of Patterson's figure?
answer: Later work has shifted it by only about ten million years
choices: Later work halved it once radioactive heating was allowed for
Later work doubled it when far older meteorites turned up
Later work dropped it when the Apollo Moon rocks came back
Later work has shifted it by only about ten million years
context: The modern consensus is 4.54 plus or minus 0.05 billion years -- Patterson's 1956 value was 4.55 plus or minus 0.07, and the two should not be blurred. The same lead-lead technique, sharpened, now dates the oldest solids in the Solar System to 4,567.35 plus or minus 0.28 million years. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'; Wikipedia, 'Lead-lead dating'.

question: Clair Patterson read the lead in Greenland ice layer by layer down the column, the deepest layers he reached having been laid down long before any industry existed. By 1969 the result was public. Set against those deep pre-industrial layers, what had the lead done in the most recent ice?
answer: Risen more than two-hundredfold
choices: Risen by about a tenth at most
Risen more than two-hundredfold
Fallen to roughly half its level
Held steady the whole way up
context: Lead levels in Greenland ice had increased by a factor of over 200 since pre-industrial times. The same ice carries older spikes matching Roman-era mining and war, alongside industrial-era rises in copper, cadmium and zinc -- human lead pollution is genuinely thousands of years old, which is precisely why fixing the natural baseline mattered so much. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ice core'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Robert Kehoe was the field's leading authority on lead in the human body, and for decades the Kettering Laboratory he directed at the University of Cincinnati held what one account calls an almost complete monopoly on lead toxicity research -- its studies were the ones everybody cited when they wanted to know whether leaded petrol was safe. Who paid for that laboratory?
answer: General Motors, DuPont and the Ethyl Corporation
choices: The Rockefeller, Carnegie and Guggenheim foundations
The Public Health Service, the Army and the Navy
General Motors, DuPont and the Ethyl Corporation
Ford, Firestone and the Goodyear Tire Company
context: Charles Kettering hired Kehoe at General Motors in 1924; Kehoe became chief medical adviser of the Ethyl Corporation, maker of the leaded petrol additive, in 1925 and held the post until he retired, and he directed the Kettering Laboratory from 1930. His scientific position was that lead in humans was normal and low-level exposure harmless. Source: Wikipedia, 'Robert A. Kehoe'.

question: Robert Kehoe's argument was that the lead in human bodies had always been there. To test it, Clair Patterson compared bone from 1,600-year-old Peruvian burials with modern bone, and found the modern bone carrying between seven hundred and twelve hundred times more lead. One objection was obvious: perhaps ancient bone simply loses what it holds over sixteen centuries. How did Patterson close that hole?
answer: He measured barium and calcium too, and those had not shifted
choices: He measured barium and calcium too, and those had not shifted
He measured a hundred more burials from the same cemetery
He sealed the ancient bone in clean glass for a year first
He compared the burials with Roman bone of the same age
context: Barium and calcium are chemically similar to lead and are taken up by bone in the same way, so if old bone leaked its contents they should have fallen too. They had not. Only lead had moved -- which is what a control is for. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Clair Patterson had built the ultra-clean laboratory, fixed a natural baseline for lead by measuring ancient bone, deep ocean and deep ice, and published the measurements other researchers worked from. In 1971 the National Research Council assembled a panel on airborne lead contamination. What happened to Patterson when the panel was put together?
answer: He was left off it entirely
choices: He was made its chairman
He was asked to review its draft only
He resigned from it after two meetings
He was left off it entirely
context: After criticism from the lead industry Patterson was also refused contracts by several supposedly neutral research organisations, including the United States Public Health Service. When he did reach an NRC panel in 1978 he refused to sign its consensus and filed a 78-page minority report arguing that controls on leaded fuels, water systems, food containers, paints and glazes should start immediately. Source: Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Every radioactive clock has the same weak point: to read it you must know how much of the end product was already sitting in the sample at the start, before any decay began -- and nobody was there to write it down. Clair Patterson got round that by measuring several samples together and plotting them as a straight line, an isochron. Which feature of the plot hands him the starting amount?
answer: The point where the line crosses the axis
choices: The steepness of the line across the plot
The point where the line crosses the axis
The average position of the plotted points
The spread between the outermost points
context: Because several samples are plotted together, no assumption is needed about the initial amount of the decay product -- it falls out of the intercept instead of being guessed. Better still, the method grades itself: points on a straight line give you an age, and scatter tells you an assumption has failed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Isochron dating'.

question: Robert Kehoe went further than claiming human bodies had always carried lead: he held that the species had adapted to it, the way a body adapts to anything it lives among. Clair Patterson answered him in one sentence. What did he say?
answer: Humans have worked lead for a few thousand years, an instant on the Darwinian scale
choices: Humans store lead in their bones, which no species adapted to a poison would do
Humans adapted to the lead in their food, never to the lead pouring from engines
Humans have worked lead for a few thousand years, an instant on the Darwinian scale
Humans take up lead exactly as other primates do, showing no special resistance
context: Kehoe's paradigm, laid down at the Surgeon General's conference of May 1925, was that leaded petrol should be stopped only if someone could show that an actual danger resulted from it -- in the absence of clear evidence of risk, no risk of significance. Patterson's counter had two edges. Against the adaptation claim he set the clock: a few thousand years was only an instant on the Darwinian time scale. And he went after the word itself: 'normal' merely means average, so it should be replaced by 'typical' -- what is commonplace is not therefore harmless. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert A. Kehoe'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: Leaded petrol did not leave American pumps because one man won an argument: Clair Patterson supplied the measurement and forced the question, but the phase-out took twenty years of regulation, finishing in 1986. One step mattered more than any argument about health -- from the 1975 model year, new American cars had to burn unleaded fuel, because lead wrecked a device they now carried. Which device?
answer: The catalytic converter
choices: The catalytic converter
The electronic ignition module
The fuel injector
The turbocharger
context: The EPA issued regulations to reduce lead in petrol from 1973, the accelerated phase-out finished in 1986, and leaded fuel was fully banned for American road vehicles on 1 January 1996. Average blood lead in American children fell from 13.7 micrograms per decilitre in 1976 to 3 by 1991. Patterson died on 5 December 1995, the year he received the Tyler Prize; minor planet 2511 carries his name. Algeria, the last producer, stopped in July 2021, and the UN declared the global end of leaded petrol that August. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Tetraethyllead'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: In September 1904 a Berlin commission chaired by the psychologist Carl Stumpf -- a vet, a circus manager, a cavalry officer, teachers, and the Berlin zoo director -- inspected a horse tapping arithmetic answers with his hoof. What did they conclude?
answer: That no trickery was involved
choices: That no trickery was involved
That the owner was hiding a hand signal in his sleeve
That an assistant behind the fence tapped answers first
That the horse had memorised a sound cue per number
context: The horse was Clever Hans. The commission was right that no one was cheating -- and the wonder of the story is exactly that: no fraud existed, and everyone (horse, owner, commission, crowd) was honestly baffled. The trick was hidden inside the questioner's own body, and the commission was not designed to look there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Clever Hans belonged to a man who charged no admission, believed every hoof tap, and taught the horse arithmetic in his own backyard. Who was he?
answer: A retired gymnasium mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten
choices: A retired gymnasium mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten
A retired cavalry officer named Oskar Pfungst
A circus impresario named Carl Stumpf
A veterinary surgeon named Bernhard Schillings
context: Von Osten was also an amateur horse trainer and a phrenologist -- he genuinely believed animals could be taught to reason, and Hans was his life's project. That earnestness is why the fraud investigators kept coming back empty-handed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: The Berlin crowds were shown Clever Hans doing far more than adding small numbers. Which trio of skills was in his advertised repertoire?
answer: Fractions, telling the time, and spelling German
choices: Fractions, telling the time, and spelling German
Reading Latin, naming coins, and identifying flags of nations
Counting audience members, naming days of the week in French, and reciting the alphabet
Recognising written names, solving simple equations, and telling temperature
context: Hans's public act also included multiplication, division, tracking the calendar, and distinguishing musical tones -- all through hoof taps and small head movements. The bigger the repertoire, the harder any single-trick explanation had to work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: In 1907 Oskar Pfungst, a student at the Psychological Institute at the University of Berlin, redesigned the tests around two knobs he could turn independently. Between them, they cracked the case. What were the two things Pfungst varied?
answer: Whether Hans could see the questioner, and whether the questioner knew the answer
choices: Whether Hans could see the questioner, and whether the questioner knew the answer
The size of the audience, and the temperature of the room
The breed of horse used, and the language of the question
The distance to the questioner, and the volume of the crowd
context: Pfungst blindfolded Hans, changed questioners, and quietly slipped some questioners the right answer and others a wrong one. Von Osten's honesty had passed every earlier test for cheating -- but no earlier test had checked the questioner's knowledge, only their intent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Oskar Pfungst's decisive numbers, published in 1907, are the ones every experimental-psychology course still teaches. Given a questioner Hans could see who knew the right answer, Hans was right on 50 of 56 trials -- 89%. Given a questioner Hans could not see, how did his score change?
answer: It collapsed to 2 of 35 -- about 6%
choices: It collapsed to 2 of 35 -- about 6%
It stayed near 28 of 35 -- about 80%
It fell to roughly 16 of 35 -- about 45%
It rose to 33 of 35 -- about 94%
context: Six percent is roughly what you would expect from a horse tapping until told to stop; the previous 89% had never been about the horse's counting. The score tracked what the human in the room knew, not what the horse knew. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Once Pfungst knew the questioner was the source of the answer, he watched them closely as Hans tapped. What was the tiny movement the questioners made -- the movement Hans was reading?
answer: A small upward jerk of the head on the correct tap
choices: A small upward jerk of the head on the correct tap
A quiet shift of weight from one foot to the other
A whistled note too high for humans to hear
A finger twitch on the reins the horse could feel
context: Posture tension built up as the taps neared the right count and released with that small head jerk. Hans stopped on the release, because the release was what he had learned to look for.
