Every human in the room was giving him the answer without knowing they were doing it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: Pfungst then tried something braver: he put himself in the questioner's chair, knowing the cue and trying not to give it. What happened when he ran the trial?
answer: He emitted the cue involuntarily anyway, even while trying to suppress it
choices: He emitted the cue involuntarily anyway, even while trying to suppress it
He suppressed it easily and Hans got every answer wrong
He suppressed it easily and Hans still got most answers right
He emitted a bigger cue than the untrained questioners had
context: This is why Wilhelm von Osten had never been caught by any earlier commission: not because he was hiding a signal, but because the signal was hiding from him. It is also the reason honest people can still bias an experiment, and why sincerity is not a protection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clever_Hans.

question: In 1993, Wheeler, Jacobson, Paglieri and Schwartz ran an experiment on 'facilitated communication' -- where an assistant physically supports a non-speaking client's hand at a keyboard. In some trials the client and the facilitator were shown DIFFERENT pictures. Whose picture did the typed answer name?
answer: The facilitator's picture, essentially every time
choices: The facilitator's picture, essentially every time
The client's picture, essentially every time
Neither, because the typing became unreadable
Both pictures in equal proportion across the trials
context: The trap is Clever Hans's, eighty-nine years later. The facilitators were not lying -- like von Osten, they believed. The test worked because it made the human in the room ignorant of the target answer. That single design idea, born of a horse, still catches the same illusion whenever it reappears. Source: Wheeler et al., 'An experimental assessment of facilitated communication', Mental Retardation 31(1), 1993.

question: Jupiter's moon Io ducks into Jupiter's shadow once every 1.769 days, so the blackouts tick like a pendulum. At the Paris Observatory, Ole Romer logged about 140 of them and found they would not keep to the table. What was the pattern in the drift?
answer: Early when Earth was near Jupiter, late when it was far.
choices: Early when Earth was near Jupiter, late when it was far.
Later and later, by a little more with every orbit.
Early whenever Jupiter stood high in the night sky.
On time for Io, but hours out for the outer moons.
context: Romer and his colleagues timed the eclipses on Christiaan Huygens' new pendulum clocks, good to about fifteen seconds a day. Io's orbit takes 1.769 days, about 42.5 hours, so the eclipses recur like a ticking pendulum -- which is exactly what makes a drift of whole minutes impossible to miss. A moon used as a clock. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light'.

question: In Two New Sciences (1638) Galileo Galilei describes two men standing less than a mile apart, each holding a lantern covered by his hand, uncovering it in turn. He ran it himself. What did Galileo report?
answer: He could not tell, only that light must be extraordinarily rapid.
choices: He could not tell, only that light must be extraordinarily rapid.
He saw a clear delay, and put light at some ten miles a second.
He saw no delay at all, and declared light plainly instantaneous.
He gave up when the lanterns proved far too dim to see at all.
context: Galileo's own conclusion was that light is, if not instantaneous, extraordinarily rapid -- an honest report of a test that failed. The historian Carl Boyer later calculated that the lantern method at best established a lower limit of about 60 miles per second for light: true, and useless. Isaac Beeckman had proposed a version nine years earlier, watching a cannon flash reflect off a mirror about a mile away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light, citing Galilei, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences (Crew and de Salvio trans.) p.43, and C. B. Boyer, Isis 33:1 (1941) p.24.

question: Ole Romer went on record before the fact. In September 1676 he named a coming eclipse of Io and said the printed tables had its time wrong. On the night, the Paris Observatory logged Io's emergence from Jupiter's shadow at 5:35:45 in the morning -- late, exactly as Romer had said. How far off the tables had he said it would be?
answer: About ten minutes late.
choices: About ten minutes late.
About half a minute late.
About one hour late.
About four hours late.
context: Romer explained the reason to the Academie Royale des Sciences on 21 November 1676 -- after the event, not before it; the prediction itself was made in September. Sources differ on the day of the eclipse (Grokipedia gives 9 November, Wikipedia 16 November), so the reliable facts are the year, the roughly ten-minute delay, and that he said it first. A prediction made in advance and checked in public is what turns a pattern into science. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light', cross-checked against en.wikipedia.org.

question: James Bradley had spent three years stuck. Hunting for stellar parallax, he had found instead that every star traces a tiny annual ellipse, and he could not say why. The most-told story of his breakthrough puts him on a sailing boat on the Thames in 1728. What does the story say he noticed?
answer: The masthead flag swung round when the boat turned, not the wind.
choices: The masthead flag swung round when the boat turned, not the wind.
The wake stayed dead straight while the boat swung beneath it.
The sails filled harder on one tack than the other in one breeze.
The gulls overhead slid backwards as the boat gathered way.
context: Wikipedia flags the Thames story as famous but possibly apocryphal, so treat it as a story, not a document. What it points at is real and is called aberration: Bradley told the Royal Society in January 1729 that an observer must tilt the telescope forward while Earth moves, exactly as a person running through vertical rain tilts the umbrella forward. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bradley.  (Legend.)

question: In 1667 the Accademia del Cimento of Florence ran Galileo's lantern trial again in earnest: two lanterns set about a mile apart, observers watching for any lag between one lantern's uncovering and the other's answering flash. They reported no delay at all. About how long was the delay they were hunting?
answer: About eleven millionths of a second.
choices: About eleven millionths of a second.
About eleven thousandths of a second.
About one fiftieth of a second.
About one tenth of a second.
context: Light covers a mile in about 5.4 millionths of a second, and the lantern protocol needs the round trip, so the lag was near eleven millionths of a second -- eleven microseconds. Human reaction time is tens of thousands of times too slow. The experiment was beaten by biology, not by bad technique, which is why the next real advance came from the sky instead of the hilltop. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light, citing Foschi and Leone, Perception 38(8):1251-1259 (2009).

question: Ole Romer explained his finding to the Academie Royale des Sciences in Paris in November 1676, and the next month an account of it reached print in the Journal des scavans -- the public announcement of the most talked-about measurement of the century. What form did that printed announcement take?
answer: An anonymous six-paragraph notice, written in the third person.
choices: An anonymous six-paragraph notice, written in the third person.
A signed forty-page memoir with his full tables of eclipses.
A letter from Cassini setting out his assistant's claim.
A single engraved plate with a caption and no text at all.
context: Romer never produced a formal mathematical description of his own discovery. The English translation of those six unsigned paragraphs ran in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society in 1677. The most famous measurement of the seventeenth century was announced by an author who did not sign his name to it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light'.

question: Textbooks that credit Ole Romer with a figure like 227,000 kilometres per second are quoting somebody else's arithmetic, done later and with someone else's numbers. Romer himself published no speed at all. What he gave was a duration. What did that time measure?
answer: The time light needs to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit -- about 22 minutes.
choices: The time light needs to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit -- about 22 minutes.
The time light needs to travel from the Sun out to Earth -- about 11 minutes.
The time light needs to cross the whole of Jupiter's shadow -- about 22 minutes.
The time light needs to travel from Jupiter across to Earth -- about 40 minutes.
context: Romer's 22 minutes was generous: light crosses one astronomical unit in 499 seconds, so the full diameter takes about 998 seconds -- roughly 16.6 minutes. Christiaan Huygens is the man who turned the minutes into a speed, in his Traite de la Lumiere: 110,000,000 toises per second, which converts to about 212,000-220,000 km/s, some 27 percent low. The error was not Romer's timing but the era's Earth-Sun distance -- Cassini's 1672 figure was about 140 million km against the true 149.6 million. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light' and 'Speed of light'; en.wikipedia.org for the toises figure.

question: Hippolyte Fizeau, 1849: a limelight beam leaves a tower at his father's house in Suresnes, runs 8,633 metres to a mirror on Montmartre and back, and on both legs it must slip between the teeth of a wheel carrying 720 of them. Fizeau wound that wheel from a crawl up to dozens of turns a second, watching the mirror's answering flash. What happened to that flash as the wheel sped up?
answer: It vanished at one wheel speed, and returned at double that.
choices: It vanished at one wheel speed, and returned at double that.
It dimmed steadily as the wheel sped up, and never returned.
It arrived doubled, as two separate flashes a moment apart.
It broke into a flicker too fast for any eye to follow.
context: At 12.6 turns a second the wheel moved by half a tooth while the light was away, so a tooth stood where the gap had been and the beam was cut off; at 25.2 turns a full tooth passed, a gap stood where a gap had been, and the flash came through. From the wheel's rate and the 17,266-metre round trip Fizeau got about 313,000 km/s, roughly 4 to 5 percent high -- and the first value for light's speed that owed nothing to astronomy. Marie Alfred Cornu reran the same wheel from 1872 to 1876, pushing to the 21st-order extinction and recording the turns electrically: 300,400,000 m/s, 0.2 percent high. Fizeau is one of the 72 names around the Eiffel Tower, and the only one of them still alive when it opened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fizeau%27s_measurement_of_the_speed_of_light_in_air.

question: James Bradley and Samuel Molyneux spent 1725 to 1728 pointing a zenith sector straight up at the star gamma Draconis, hunting stellar parallax -- the tiny yearly shift that would finally prove Earth moves, and that must reach its extremes six months apart, in June and December. Bradley did find a yearly shift, about 20 arcseconds either side of the star's true place. What told him it was not parallax?
answer: Its extremes fell in March and September, three months out.
choices: Its extremes fell in March and September, three months out.
Its extremes came six months apart, but swung the wrong way.
Its extremes came eighteen months apart, not twelve months.
Its extremes arrived a month later with each passing year.
context: The effect is aberration, and it has a second signature parallax cannot fake: it does not shrink with the star's distance. Bradley announced the cause in January 1729 -- you must tilt the telescope forward while Earth moves, as a runner tilts an umbrella into vertical rain -- and from that tilt he stated that light 'is propagated as far as from the Sun to the Earth in 8 minutes 12 seconds'. The modern figure is 8 minutes 19 seconds. He also found light travels 10,210 times faster than Earth moves in its orbit; the modern value is 10,066 times. He was hunting one thing and settled another. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Bradley and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberration_(astronomy).

question: Francois Arago proposed the decisive test in 1838 and his failing health stopped him running it: compare light's speed in air with its speed in water. The corpuscular theory of light and the wave theory made opposite predictions about the denser medium, so the result would kill one of them. On 27 April 1850, in his own Paris apartment, Leon Foucault spun a mirror at 600 to 800 turns a second with a small steam engine and ran the comparison. What did he find?
answer: Light runs slower in water, by very nearly a factor of 1.33.
choices: Light runs slower in water, by very nearly a factor of 1.33.
Light runs faster in water, by very nearly a factor of 1.33.
Light runs at the same speed in both, as far as he could measure.
Light runs slower in water, but by less than a tenth of a percent.
context: The water path threw the returning image 0.469 mm off centre, the air path only 0.375 mm -- and that ratio is water's refractive index, 1.33. Isaac Newton's corpuscular theory required light to speed UP in the denser medium; the wave theory required it to slow DOWN. Foucault announced to the French Academy on 6 May 1850, seven weeks before Hippolyte Fizeau published the same result on 17 June. One measurement, one dead theory. In 1862, with a folded baseline of only about 20 metres indoors at the Paris Observatory, Foucault got 298,000 +/- 500 km/s, backing Urbain Le Verrier's insistence that the accepted figure was several percent too high. Source: Grokipedia, 'Foucault's measurements of the speed of light'.

question: Giovanni Domenico Cassini ran the Paris Observatory and Ole Romer worked under him. Cassini rejected the finite-speed explanation outright, blaming the wandering eclipse times on irregularities in the moons' own orbits, and Robert Hooke called the evidence inconclusive. Then Cassini published his revised tables of Jupiter's satellite eclipses in 1693. What did those tables contain?
answer: Corrections of up to fourteen minutes, keyed to where Earth stood.
choices: Corrections of up to fourteen minutes, keyed to where Earth stood.
New orbital periods for all four moons, shortened to absorb the drift.
Two predicted times for every eclipse, an early one and a late one.
Io dropped from the tables, leaving only the outer three moons listed.
context: Cassini used the effect while denying its cause. Note what the record does not say: there was no vote, and no fifty-year rejection by the Academy. Cassini personally opposed the explanation -- having himself floated a finite speed in 1675 and then dropped it -- and Hooke thought the evidence thin. Consensus is not truth; the test decides. The honest version of this story is smaller and stranger than the legend. Source: Grokipedia, 'Romer's determination of the speed of light'.

question: Albert Michelson had chased light's speed since 1878, when he was a 26-year-old instructor spinning a mirror at the US Naval Academy; asked why he gave a lifetime to one number, he said 'because it's so much fun.' On Mount Wilson in 1926 he spun an eight-sided mirror 528 times a second and fired the beam to a reflector some 35 kilometres away. A speed is a distance over a time, so his answer was only as good as that 35 kilometres. How did they pin down the line between the peaks?
answer: Surveyors taped the whole line along the ground in invar, tape length by tape length.
choices: Surveyors taped the whole line along the ground in invar, tape length by tape length.
Surveyors triangulated the line from three summits by theodolite, angle by angle.
Surveyors fixed each end by sextant star sightings, night after night at both peaks.
Surveyors chained the line with steel Gunter chains, down one slope and up the other.
context: The US Coast and Geodetic Survey did the taping, and invar is a nickel-steel alloy that barely expands with heat -- which is why it, and not steel, went into the tape. The line came out good to about one part in 500,000, and the 1926 run gave 299,796 +/- 4 km/s, within about a thousandth of a percent of today's value. Sources disagree on the far peak's name, so the distance is the safe fact. Michelson had been the first American to win a Nobel Prize in a science, in 1907. He never stopped: in 1929, with Francis Pease and Fred Pearson, he began a mile-long tube near Santa Ana, California, with the air pumped out so that not even the atmosphere could slow the beam, 233 series of measurements planned. He died on 9 May 1931 with 36 of them finished, and that posthumous value, 299,774 +/- 11 km/s, reached print in 1935. Source: Grokipedia, 'Albert A. Michelson'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_A._Michelson.

question: For three centuries the speed of light was something you went out and measured, from Ole Romer's eclipsing moons to Louis Essen's resonant cavities, which by 1950 had the figure pinned to within a few kilometres per second. Then in 1983 the 17th General Conference on Weights and Measures ended the chase -- not with a finer measurement, but with a decision. What did the conference decide?
answer: To define the metre as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
choices: To define the metre as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
To define the metre as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of krypton-86's orange light.
To define the metre as the distance light travels in one 300-millionth of a second.
To define the metre as 1,553,163.5 wavelengths of cadmium's red spectral line.
context: Defining the metre that way fixed the speed of light at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, with zero uncertainty -- it is now a defined constant, not a measured one. Every experiment since 1983 that claims to measure the speed of light is really measuring the metre. The second is defined separately, by caesium, so it is the metre that rides on light and not the other way round. Louis Essen's cavity resonators, the last era of genuine measurement, had reached 299,792.5 +/- 3.0 km/s by 1950. Three centuries of ever-finer measurement ended not in a better number but in a decision. Source: Grokipedia, 'Speed of light'.

question: Here is a claim that sounds like crankery and is not: nobody has ever measured the one-way speed of light. Every experiment ever performed -- Hippolyte Fizeau's wheel, Leon Foucault's mirror, Albert Michelson's mountain beam -- times a round trip, out and back. To time a one-way journey you would need a clock at each end. Why has no experiment ever managed it?
answer: Any way of synchronising two distant clocks assumes the answer.
choices: Any way of synchronising two distant clocks assumes the answer.
No clock can resolve a gap as short as the light's own crossing time.
No two clocks can be built to run at exactly the same rate for long.
Earth's own motion adds an unknown amount to every one-way path.
context: Send a light signal to synchronise the two clocks and you have assumed light's one-way speed; carry a clock slowly across and you have assumed how motion affects clocks. The arithmetic is simple: if the outward speed is c+ and the return speed is c-, experiment can pin down only their harmonic mean, 2*c+*c-/(c+ + c-), which is the c everyone quotes. Light could go instantly one way and at half speed back, and nothing observable would change. Albert Einstein made equal-in-both-directions a definition in his 1905 paper, not a measurement. This is mainstream physics stating its own open loophole out loud. Source: Grokipedia, 'One-way speed of light'.

question: Isaac Newton, writing in Opticks (1704), reported Ole Romer's eclipse timings and then put a question of his own to the observers: as Io slid into Jupiter's shadow and out again, did the edge of that shadow come out coloured? They told him it did not. What did Newton conclude?
answer: That light of every colour crosses space at the same speed.
choices: That light of every colour crosses space at the same speed.
That Jupiter's shadow is too blurred at the rim to show colour.
That the eye cannot register colour in so faint a light.
That colour is made in the prism and not carried by the light.
context: If red light outran blue, the edge of the shadow would arrive fringed with colour, one colour reaching the eye before the other. No fringe, no difference in speed -- a second discovery got for free out of someone else's data. Newton also reported Romer's result as 'seven or eight minutes' for sunlight to reach Earth; the modern figure is 8 minutes 19 seconds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light, citing Newton, Opticks (1704), Prop. XI.

question: Two electrochemists, Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons, told the world on 23 March 1989 that they had produced nuclear fusion in a jar of water on a bench. Where did they make the announcement?
answer: At a press conference at the University of Utah
choices: At a press conference at the University of Utah
In a peer-reviewed paper in the journal Nature
At the American Physical Society meeting in Baltimore
In a keynote lecture at Caltech
context: The story's first flaw is baked into the setting: the announcement skipped the step where somebody checks. No paper had been peer-reviewed and no outside lab had seen the data. Source: undsci.berkeley.edu/cold-fusion-a-case-study-for-scientific-behavior/publication-by-press-conference

question: The Fleischmann-Pons cell that supposedly produced tabletop fusion was startlingly simple. A rod of what metal, dipped in heavy water with a platinum wire and a running current, was the heart of the apparatus?
answer: Palladium
choices: Palladium
Uranium
Beryllium
Tungsten
context: Palladium can soak up hundreds of times its own volume in hydrogen isotopes. Fleischmann and Pons believed deuterium packed inside the palladium lattice might be forced close enough to fuse; their calorimeter said more heat was coming out than electricity was going in. Source: interestingengineering.com/science/the-pons-fleischmann-experiment

question: Palladium can soak up hundreds of times its own volume in hydrogen. Fleischmann and Pons bet that packing DEUTERIUM into the palladium lattice would squeeze the nuclei close enough to fuse. What does a deuterium nucleus carry that ordinary hydrogen does not?
answer: An extra neutron
choices: An extra neutron
An extra proton
An extra electron
A muon in place of its electron
context: Ordinary hydrogen is a single proton; deuterium is a proton plus a neutron. Two deuterium nuclei fusing is a real reaction, the same one that powers experimental hot-fusion reactors - the extraordinary claim was that squeezing them into palladium could force it at room temperature. The muon-swap distractor is a real different low-temperature fusion process, muon-catalyzed fusion, which Steven Jones at BYU studied for real. Source: interestingengineering.com/science/the-pons-fleischmann-experiment ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_E._Jones

question: Within days of the 1989 Utah announcement, physicists raised an unnerving objection. If the excess heat had really come from a fusion reaction at the reported rate, what SHOULD the apparatus and the room around it have shown?
answer: A neutron flux fatal to anyone standing next to it
choices: A neutron flux fatal to anyone standing next to it
A cell melted into a puddle of palladium
Heavy water boiled off in seconds
A bench magnetised for weeks afterwards
context: Real deuterium-deuterium fusion emits neutrons, and to produce the claimed heat you would need roughly a trillion of them per second per watt. Two unharmed chemists at the bench were themselves the counter-evidence: the human body, right there, was a detector. Source: large.stanford.edu/courses/2015/ph241/chung2

question: Richard Petrasso and colleagues at MIT published a critique in Nature in 1989. They looked at the gamma-ray peak Fleischmann and Pons had shown as their nuclear fingerprint. What was wrong with it?
answer: It had no Compton edge - every real peak from that detector shows one
choices: It had no Compton edge - every real peak from that detector shows one
Its linewidth was twice the detector's resolution, not a sharp line
Its energy matched a known background line from the room, not deuterium fusion
It appeared in the spectrum even when the current to the cell was off
context: The Compton edge is a ridge in the spectrum caused by gamma photons scattering off electrons inside the detector itself; every genuine gamma peak from that kind of detector carries one. Petrasso also found the peak's linewidth was about half of what the instrument allowed - too narrow, not too wide - a second tell that the peak was spurious. Source: nature.com/articles/339667b0 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compton_edge

question: In the weeks after the Utah press conference, what did the world's physics and chemistry labs actually do?
answer: More than a hundred labs on four continents tried to replicate the experiment
choices: More than a hundred labs on four continents tried to replicate the experiment
They waited politely for the referees at Nature to render a verdict
They referred the claim to the United Nations for independent review
They ignored it as too extraordinary to be worth their time
context: Some groups reported early positive signals; those signals faded as calorimetry and stirring were tightened. That is what the immune system of science looks like at speed - the check does not know or care whether the original claim was honest or fraudulent. Source: interestingengineering.com/science/the-pons-fleischmann-experiment

question: The 1989 story effectively ended at the American Physical Society meeting in Baltimore on 1 May. Speaking for a Caltech team that had built a more careful version of the cell, Nathan Lewis reported what?
answer: None of the five nuclear fingerprints - heat, neutrons, gammas, tritium or helium
choices: None of the five nuclear fingerprints - heat, neutrons, gammas, tritium or helium
A small but real excess heat that could not yet be explained
A signal roughly ten times smaller than the Utah claim
That his own apparatus had not yet been sensitive enough to test
context: Eight of the nine leading speakers at the session judged the Utah claim dead. A US Department of Energy panel that November reached the same conclusion; a second DOE panel in 2004 was still unpersuaded that any nuclear mechanism had been demonstrated. Source: calteches.library.caltech.edu/3782/1/Goodstein.pdf

question: Why did Fleischmann and Pons rush to a press conference instead of waiting for peer review? A rival researcher at Brigham Young University was working on a related low-energy neutron claim, and the two groups had actually agreed to submit papers to Nature simultaneously. Who was the BYU rival?
answer: Steven Jones
choices: Steven Jones
Freeman Dyson
Edward Teller
Luis Alvarez
context: Jones's real subject was muon-catalyzed fusion, a genuine and different low-temperature process. The two groups planned to file simultaneously on 24 March 1989; the University of Utah went to the press one day earlier to secure patent priority - the very race that removed the checks that would have saved them. Source: everything-everywhere.com/a-history-of-cold-fusion ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_E._Jones

question: A small research community has kept working on excess-heat experiments in palladium-deuterium and nickel-hydrogen systems, renaming the field to avoid the 1989 baggage. What name does that community publish under today?
answer: Low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR)
choices: Low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR)
Muon-catalyzed fusion
Inertial confinement fusion
Magneto-hydrodynamic fusion
context: In 2023 the US agency ARPA-E funded roughly $10 million of LENR proposals. The mainstream position remains that no nuclear mechanism has been demonstrated - and the bank says exactly that, without pretending the file is sealed by decree. Source: popsci.com/science/cold-fusion-low-energy-nuclear-reaction

question: Two identical fresh glow sticks are cracked at the same moment. One is dropped into a mug of hot tap water; the other is stood upright in a home freezer. Which pair of outcomes will actually happen?
answer: The hot one blazes brighter and burns out fast; the frozen one dims but lasts for days
choices: The hot one blazes brighter and burns out fast; the frozen one dims but lasts for days
The frozen one blazes brighter, because cold concentrates the dye
Both die within a minute, because the chemistry needs mild room temperature
The hot one dies at once; the frozen one glows brighter than at room temperature
context: Temperature is a volume-and-speed knob on the reaction; the TOTAL amount of light emitted is roughly fixed, and heat only spends it faster. This is the kid-testable heart of chemiluminescence, and it works with any two supermarket glow sticks. Source: Wikipedia, Glow stick.

question: In 1928 the German chemist H. O. Albrecht reported that a certain then-obscure compound would glow bright blue when dropped into alkaline hydrogen peroxide. Under what name did that compound go on to become famous, half-recognised today by every crime-drama viewer?
answer: Luminol
choices: Luminol
Fluorescein
Rhodamine
Methylene blue
context: Luminol (C8H7N3O2) had been synthesised in Germany in 1902 but was not given the name 'luminol' until 1934. Albrecht's 1928 paper was the first record of its blood-catalysed blue glow, the observation on which every modern forensic use rests. Source: Wikipedia, Luminol.

question: In a darkened crime-scene room, technicians spray a luminol solution across a floor scrubbed clean of blood years earlier, and the floor lights up in faint blue patches for about thirty seconds. What specific component of blood is actually catalysing that glow?
answer: The iron atoms locked inside haemoglobin
choices: The iron atoms locked inside haemoglobin
The sodium salt dissolved in the plasma
The DNA released from broken cells
The proteins of the white immune cells
context: The iron in a red-cell haemoglobin molecule is what oxidises the luminol; it survives ordinary scrubbing because the iron ions stay bound to microscopic residues down in the grain of the wood or the pores of the concrete. Source: Wikipedia, Luminol.

question: Luminol spray lights up any bloodstain still present, no matter how well it was scrubbed, yet forensic manuals insist on calling it a PRESUMPTIVE test only, never proof. Which grated kitchen root is the classic false-positive offender, glowing just as brightly when the spray hits it?
answer: Horseradish
choices: Horseradish
Ginger
Turmeric
Carrot
context: Horseradish is packed with the plant enzyme peroxidase, which catalyses the same luminol-plus-peroxide reaction that blood iron does. Household bleach, copper metal, and cigarette residue also trigger it. A positive luminol result is a LEAD for the lab to follow, never a verdict on its own. Source: Wikipedia, Luminol.

question: In 1910 a lab opened at Cold Spring Harbor on Long Island with a peculiar way of gathering evidence. It sent trained field workers out with notebooks to do one specific thing. What did the ERO's field workers actually do?
answer: walk up to strangers' doors and record family 'defects'
choices: walk up to strangers' doors and record family 'defects'
collect blood samples in city hospitals for analysis
test schoolchildren for reading and math problems
count immigrants at Ellis Island for the Census
context: The Eugenics Record Office collected 'family history' cards through door-to-door interviews and letters. That data -- gathered by a stranger with a notebook, filed on a card -- became the evidence base cited in court and legislature. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics_Record_Office

question: The Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor opened in 1910 and ran for the next 29 years. It was directed for most of that time by a working biologist with real academic credentials -- which was part of the whole point of putting the office where they put it. Who was that biologist?
answer: Charles Davenport
choices: Charles Davenport
Thomas Hunt Morgan
H.J. Muller
Luther Burbank
context: Davenport (1866-1944), Harvard-trained zoologist, founded the ERO under the Carnegie Institution and led it until his retirement. His credentials as a legitimate biologist gave the office cover, which is exactly why he was chosen. Source: https://collections.countway.harvard.edu/onview/exhibits/show/galtonschildren/galton-s-children/charles-b--davenport

question: The Eugenics Record Office was not paid for by fringe money. It was paid for by three of the most respectable philanthropies in America -- the same institutions funding legitimate science at the time. Which trio bankrolled the ERO?
answer: Mary Harriman, the Rockefeller Foundation, and Carnegie
choices: Mary Harriman, the Rockefeller Foundation, and Carnegie
J.P. Morgan, Andrew Mellon, and the Guggenheim Foundation
the Vanderbilts, the Astors, and Cornelius Bliss
Henry Ford, the DuPonts, and the Whitney family
context: Mary Harriman, widow of the railroad fortune, paid for the initial 80-acre farm and building in 1910. The Rockefeller Foundation added support. The Carnegie Institution of Washington absorbed the ERO and paid the salaries until 1939. The funding list is the argument: this was mainstream American science philanthropy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics_Record_Office

question: The ERO's superintendent, Harry Laughlin, went a step beyond scientific papers. In 1922 he published a document that a state legislature could adopt with barely any change and pass into force. What did Laughlin publish that year?
answer: a Model Eugenical Sterilization Law
choices: a Model Eugenical Sterilization Law
a Model Marriage Restriction Act
a Model Immigration Screening Statute
a Model Institutional Commitment Bill
context: The Model Law appeared in Laughlin's 1922 book Eugenical Sterilization in the United States. It named nine categories -- feeble-minded, insane, criminal, epileptic, alcoholic, blind, deaf, deformed, indigent -- and gave a legislature ready-to-file statute language. Source: https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/eugenical-sterilization-united-states-1922-harry-h-laughlin

question: Virginia's 1924 Eugenical Sterilization Act -- the law tested in Buck v. Bell -- was built directly on Laughlin's 1922 template. Beyond Virginia, what is the documented reach of laws built on Laughlin's template by the mid-1930s?
answer: roughly 18 other states passed laws built on it
choices: roughly 18 other states passed laws built on it
only Indiana and Michigan fully adopted the wording
no other state adopted it before World War II
over 40 states passed identical versions of it
context: A one-office document from Long Island became a template for roughly 18 additional state laws by the mid-1930s. By 1956, twenty-four states had sterilization laws on the books and had collectively sterilized more than 59,000 Americans. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Sterilization_Act_of_1924

question: Between 1920 and 1924 Harry Laughlin testified three times before the House Committee on Immigration and Naturalization. Chairman Albert Johnson was so impressed he added Laughlin to the committee's official staff under a specific title. What was Laughlin's title on the committee's staff?
answer: Expert Eugenics Agent
choices: Expert Eugenics Agent
Chief Statistical Advisor
Special Immigration Consultant
Deputy Committee Counsel
context: Laughlin's data purported to show that inmates in mental institutions were disproportionately from southern and eastern Europe. His statistics were later shown to be flawed, but they were used to justify the 1924 Johnson-Reed Immigration Act's national-origin quotas -- one of the most consequential immigration statutes in U.S. history. Source: https://hpsrepository.asu.edu/bitstream/handle/10776/8271/PeLaughlinHHRGA.xhtml;sequence=1

question: The ERO was not brought down by protesters, by a court, or by a rival lab. In 1935 the Carnegie Institution sent a visiting committee to review the office's science, and in 1939 Carnegie's new president Vannevar Bush acted on their report. What did the committee's report say about the ERO's science?
answer: that the work was seriously wanting scientifically
choices: that the work was seriously wanting scientifically
that the data collection was sound but the interpretation weak
that the office needed to modernize its statistical methods
that the research was ahead of its time and needed patience
context: The 1935 Carnegie visiting committee called the ERO's work mostly 'second or third rate.' In 1939 Bush -- later famous for organizing wartime U.S. science -- forced Laughlin's retirement and closed the office by December 31, 1939. It is the rare case of an institution auditing itself out of existence. Source: https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/eugenics-record-office-cold-spring-harbor-laboratory-1910-1939

question: In 1936 an ancient European university awarded Harry Laughlin an honorary degree, its citation praising his work in what it called 'the science of racial cleansing.' He accepted the degree by mail rather than by traveling to receive it in person. Which university awarded it?
answer: the University of Heidelberg
choices: the University of Heidelberg
the University of Berlin
the University of Vienna
the University of Leipzig
context: The University of Heidelberg was among the German universities that fully aligned with the Nazi regime. Laughlin's acceptance letter to Carl Schneider survives; in it he called the honor 'doubly valued' because Germany was 'the human seed-stock' of America. Source: https://dnalc.cshl.edu/view/11198-H-Laughlin-letter-to-C-Schneider-acknowledging-honorary-degree-from-the-University-of-Heidelberg.html

question: Three months after Laughlin accepted his Heidelberg degree, he helped found a new American foundation with money from textile heir Wickliffe Draper -- the Pioneer Fund, incorporated in 1937. The Fund's very first project brought material out of Nazi Germany and put it in front of American audiences. What did the Pioneer Fund distribute in American churches and schools?
answer: the Nazi eugenics propaganda film Erbkrank
choices: the Nazi eugenics propaganda film Erbkrank
a Nazi Party racial-hygiene short film called Opfer der Vergangenheit
Fritz Lenz's German-language textbook on racial hygiene
pamphlets from the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute in Berlin
context: Erbkrank ('The Hereditary Defective') was produced by the Rassenpolitisches Amt to prepare Germany for its euthanasia program. Draper obtained the film from that office and, through the newly incorporated Pioneer Fund, sent it into American schools and churches -- the same year the Fund was created. Laughlin served as the Pioneer Fund's first president. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pioneer_Fund

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, a cathedral canon at Frombork, kept his astronomy book back nearly thirty years. A stroke left him paralysed, and the recorded account says a printed copy reached him the day he died, 24 May 1543. What did the book claim about the Earth?
answer: It is one of six planets circling a motionless Sun
choices: It is one of six planets circling a motionless Sun
It sits still while the Sun and planets circle it
It stands still while the planets circle the Sun
It rests inside nested crystalline spheres of aether
context: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium made the Earth one planet among six -- Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn -- circling a fixed Sun once a year while spinning daily on its own axis to give day and night. Copernicus composed it between about 1520 and 1541, after circulating a short outline by 1514. The deathbed copy is the recorded account, not an eyewitness scene: the date survives through a letter from his friend Bishop Tiedemann Giese to Rheticus, and Grokipedia notes the viewing 'remains unverified beyond contemporary reports'. Of the wrong choices, the third is Tycho Brahe's later compromise and the fourth is Aristotle's cosmos. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Nicolaus Copernicus' and 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'.  (Legend.)

question: Mars drifts steadily eastward against the stars night after night. Then for about seventy days it slows, halts, and loops backward, before resuming its eastward march. What produces the loop?
answer: Earth, on the faster inside track, sweeps past Mars
choices: Earth, on the faster inside track, sweeps past Mars
Mars rides a small circle carried on a larger one
Mars truly halts and doubles back along its path
Mars circles the Sun while the Sun circles the Earth
context: EarthSky puts it as passing a slower car: 'As you pull alongside and pass it -- from your vantage point in the faster car -- the slower car may appear to move backwards for a moment.' Earth laps the Sun in a year and Mars in nearly two, so Earth catches and overtakes it about every 780 days. The small-circle-on-a-larger-one answer is Ptolemy's epicycle -- the patch heliocentrism replaced for the loops, though Copernicus kept other small circles elsewhere; the last choice is Tycho Brahe's later compromise, which reproduces the same loops from a standing Earth. Go check it yourself: Mars had no retrograde at all in 2026, and the next runs from about 10 January to 1 April 2027, starting some six weeks before Earth passes between Mars and the Sun on 19 February 2027. Sources: EarthSky, 'What is retrograde motion?'; Almanac.com, 'Mars Retrograde'; Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'.

question: Georg Joachim Rheticus, a young Wittenberg mathematician, arrived at Frombork in 1539 and became the only pupil Nicolaus Copernicus ever took. The old canon's manuscript had sat unpublished for decades and would not reach a printer until 1541. Yet in 1540 Rheticus had a book of his own printed at Danzig. What was in it?
answer: A short summary of the theory, his Narratio Prima
choices: A short summary of the theory, his Narratio Prima
A survey of Ptolemy's Almagest beside the new theory
A book of tables for finding the planets nightly
A record of the observations Copernicus had made
context: The Narratio Prima ('First Narration'), printed at Danzig in 1540, was a trailer -- it let the world react before the real book existed in print. The reception was good enough that Rheticus carried the complete manuscript to the Nuremberg printer Johannes Petreius in 1541 and supervised the press, until academic duties pulled him away and oversight passed to Andreas Osiander. That handover mattered more than anyone expected. Source: Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'.

question: As De revolutionibus went through the press at Nuremberg in 1543, an unsigned preface appeared at the very front, ahead of Copernicus's own dedication -- so early readers took it for his own words. Andreas Osiander, the Lutheran theologian supervising the final printing, had slipped it in without asking. What did that preface tell readers?
answer: That the hypotheses need not be true, or even probable
choices: That the hypotheses need not be true, or even probable
That the author had died before the book was finished
That the Church had already examined and approved it
That Wittenberg mathematicians had checked the sums
context: Osiander's 'Ad lectorem de hypothesibus huius operis' ('To the reader concerning the hypotheses of this work') sold the model as a mere calculating device: 'it is not necessary that the hypotheses be true, or even probable; but this one thing suffices, that they provide calculations that agree with observation.' Copernicus had argued the opposite -- that this is how the heavens actually are. Osiander was Petreius's theological consultant and supervised the final printing stages; Grokipedia records that he inserted the preface 'without Copernicus's knowledge or consent'. Source: Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'.

question: Nicolaus Copernicus was a working cathedral administrator at Frombork, not a full-time observer. Across his whole career he logged only about twenty-seven astronomical observations of his own, with a quadrant and a triquetrum, good to five or ten arcminutes at best. So where did the numbers filling his book come from?
answer: Centuries-old records from Ptolemy and from al-Battani
choices: Centuries-old records from Ptolemy and from al-Battani
Nightly measurements made for him by his pupil Rheticus
A century of records kept by the canons of Frombork
Sightings he commissioned from the university at Krakow
context: The revolution came out of recomputation, not out of new looking. Copernicus used no innovative instruments and built the book on Ptolemy's centuries-old records and on data from Islamic astronomers such as al-Battani. That is worth holding on to: the same numbers everyone already had, rearranged, gave a different universe. Source: Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' -- 'roughly 27 personal astronomical observations spanning his career, primarily conducted at Frombork using simple instruments like quadrants and triquetra'; 'no innovative instrumentation'; 'citing figures like al-Battani'.

question: For seventy-three years after it was printed in 1543, De revolutionibus circulated freely. Copernicus had dedicated it to Pope Paul III, praising him for reforming the calendar; a summary of the theory had reached the papal court in 1533 without objection; and Jesuit colleges taught the model under Christoph Clavius. Then in 1616 the Congregation of the Index suspended it 'until corrected'. Why did Rome act then and not in 1543?
answer: Galileo was now pressing heliocentrism as physical fact
choices: Galileo was now pressing heliocentrism as physical fact
Protestant reformers had begun attacking it from Wittenberg
A new printing had dropped Osiander's unsigned preface
The Jesuit colleges had stopped teaching the model
context: This is the corrected misconception: the book drew no condemnation at all in 1543, and the earliest hostility came from Protestant reformers, not from Rome. The 1616 suspension was also an edit, not a ban -- in 1620 the Index specified NINE sentences, the ones stating heliocentrism as certain rather than hypothetical, to be omitted or changed; owners struck them out by hand and wrote the approved wording in the margins, after which the book could be read legally. It came off the Index Librorum Prohibitorum entirely only in 1835. Sources: Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'; Cambridge HPS, 'Starry Messenger: Copernicus's Book'.

question: In 1959 Arthur Koestler called De revolutionibus 'the book that nobody read' -- a masterpiece printed in perhaps four or five hundred copies and, he said, left unopened. Owen Gingerich spent three decades tracking down first editions and examining them himself, and in 2002 published a census of 277 surviving copies. What did he find inside them?
answer: Dense working annotations by sixteenth-century astronomers
choices: Dense working annotations by sixteenth-century astronomers
Printers' variants marking three distinct early issues
Owners' bookplates from a dozen cathedral libraries
The same nine sentences struck out by hand in each
context: Gingerich's An Annotated Census (2002) located 277 first editions, most of them thick with the marginal working notes of sixteenth-century astronomers -- which is how he refuted Koestler's jibe. The habit of going and looking for yourself is the point: Koestler asserted, Gingerich counted. The physical object was a folio of about 26 x 19 cm, six preliminary leaves plus 196 numbered leaves, over 140 woodcut diagrams, printed at Nuremberg by Johannes Petreius in an estimated run of 400-500 copies. Source: Grokipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'.

question: Copernicus was not the first to move the Earth. Around 280 BC Aristarchus of Samos argued that the Sun and the stars stand still while the Earth circles the Sun, and he even had the reply to the missing star-shift: the Earth's orbit stands to the sphere of stars as a centre point stands to its surface. His own book is lost, and survives only because Archimedes summarised it. Copernicus named him in an early draft. What became of that mention?
answer: Copernicus struck it out before the book went to press
choices: Copernicus struck it out before the book went to press
The printer Johannes Petreius cut it from the proofs
It survived into the printed first edition of 1543
Osiander moved it into his own unsigned preface
context: An early unpublished manuscript of De revolutionibus mentions Aristarchus; the passage was removed before publication. Archimedes preserved the ancient claim in The Sand Reckoner: Aristarchus supposed 'the fixed stars and the sun remain unmoved, that the earth revolves about the sun in the circumference of a circle'. Aristarchus had also anticipated the parallax answer -- Earth's orbit is to the stars 'as the centre of the sphere bears to its surface'. Source: Wikipedia, 'Aristarchus of Samos'.

question: Copernicus moved the Earth, but he kept the ancient rule that every heavenly motion must be a perfect circle swept at a steady rate. That cost him: he still needed extra circles -- small ones riding on larger, and circles swung off centre -- up to forty-eight of them across the planets. Set against Ptolemy's tables, how good were his predictions?
answer: About the same, within roughly ten arcminutes
choices: About the same, within roughly ten arcminutes
Rather better, within roughly one arcminute
Rather worse, off by roughly a whole degree
Better for Mars, worse for Mercury and Venus
context: This is the honest caveat, and it is the interesting part. Copernicus won nothing on precision -- his predictions ran 'typically within 10 arcminutes for major planets', comparable to Ptolemy's, with Mars residuals still 20-30 arcminutes. Wikipedia is blunt: the ideas 'were not markedly easier to use than the geocentric theory and did not produce more accurate predictions of planetary positions'. He won on structure: the arrangement forced the planets into one order and made retrograde loops a consequence rather than a patch. Note also that the famous '34 circles' figure belongs to the earlier Commentariolus, not to this book. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Nicolaus Copernicus' and 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'; Wikipedia, 'Copernican heliocentrism'.

question: For decades, readers of De revolutionibus took the unsigned preface at the front of the book for Copernicus's own words. Andreas Osiander had in fact written it, and Johannes Kepler proved so and published the fact in 1609. What was Kepler's evidence?
answer: A handwritten note in Hieronymus Schreiber's own copy
choices: A handwritten note in Hieronymus Schreiber's own copy
A ledger entry in the printer Johannes Petreius's books
A letter from Bishop Tiedemann Giese to the city council
A confession Osiander left among his theological papers
context: Kepler read an annotation in Schreiber's copy naming Osiander as the author, then demonstrated it methodically and published it in 1609. The two men closest to Copernicus had reacted with fury at the time: Rheticus said that if he knew for certain Osiander had done it, 'he would rough up the fellow', and Bishop Tiedemann Giese urged the Nuremberg city council to issue a public correction. The council never did. Sources: Wikipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'; early-astronomy-um.org on Kepler's 1609 publication.

question: From December 1725 James Bradley and Samuel Molyneux aimed a twelve-and-a-half-foot zenith sector, built by George Graham and fixed to a chimney stack at Kew, at Gamma Draconis, a star that passes almost overhead from London. They were hunting the six-month shift a moving Earth should cause. The star did move, about twenty arcseconds a year -- but southward from September to March and back again, ninety degrees out of step with the shift they wanted, and every star did the same whatever its distance. What had they found?
answer: Starlight arriving tilted because the observer is moving fast
choices: Starlight arriving tilted because the observer is moving fast
Air above the telescope bending starlight with the seasons
The chimney stack shifting as the year warmed and cooled
The Earth's axis slowly wobbling against the fixed stars
context: This is the aberration of starlight, and the flash of insight came from watching how rain slants for a walker (Grokipedia records the analogy as a boat on the Thames). Light has a finite speed and the observer is racing sideways, so the telescope must be tilted slightly into the motion. The angle is v/c -- Earth's roughly 30 km/s against light -- giving about 20.5 arcseconds. Bradley presented it to the Royal Society in a letter to Edmond Halley on 18 December 1728, published 1729. Two payoffs at once: the first direct physical proof that the Earth moves, 186 years after Copernicus's book, and a speed of light of about 301,000 km/s against the modern 299,792.458. Sources: Grokipedia, 'James Bradley'; Wikipedia, 'Aberration (astronomy)'.

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, drafting the Commentariolus by 1514, worked back through Ptolemy's planetary machinery -- fourteen centuries old, and still the arrangement Europe used to predict the sky. One piece of it he refused to accept, and his answer was to rebuild the heavens: the system that needed this device was, he wrote, 'neither sufficiently absolute nor sufficiently pleasing to the mind'. The device was the equant. What did the equant do?
answer: It set an off-centre point about which the planet sweeps evenly
choices: It set an off-centre point about which the planet sweeps evenly
It set a small circle riding steadily round the planet's great one
It set the great circle's centre at a point beside the standing Earth
It set the planet's circle turning at a tilt to the Sun's yearly path
context: Ancient astronomy ran on one rule: every heavenly motion is a circle swept at a steady rate. In Ptolemy's system the Earth stood still while each planet rode a small circle, the epicycle, carried round a great circle, the deferent -- and the equant was one further point, sitting off from that great circle's true centre. The equant saved the appearances by quietly breaking the rule it was meant to serve: the planet's motion is uniform as seen from that one arbitrary point and non-uniform from every other, including the real centre of its own circle. Copernicus wrote in the Commentariolus, by 1514: 'these theories were not adequate unless certain equants were also conceived; it then appeared that a planet moved with uniform velocity neither on its deferent nor about the center of its epicycle. Hence a system of this sort seemed neither sufficiently absolute nor sufficiently pleasing to the mind.' The wrong choices are Ptolemy's other real devices: the epicycle, the eccentric deferent whose centre sits away from the Earth, and the tilted planes that carry the planets north and south of the Sun's yearly path. The Commentariolus ends by counting the cost of his fix: 'Altogether, therefore, thirty-four circles suffice to explain the entire structure of the universe and the entire ballet of the planets.' Sources: Copernicus, Commentariolus, trans. Edward Rosen; Wikipedia, 'Equant'.

question: Tycho Brahe's naked-eye instruments at Uraniborg were the best in the world, good to about one arcminute, and they showed no six-month shift in any star. If the Earth really swung across a vast orbit, that pushed the stars out to at least seven hundred times the distance from the Sun to Saturn. Tycho then measured the apparent discs of ordinary third-magnitude stars and worked out, at that range, how big each one would have to be. What did he get?
answer: A star as wide as the Earth's whole orbit
choices: A star as wide as the Earth's whole orbit
A star a hundred times the width of the Sun
A star about the width of the Earth itself
A star the size of the Moon's orbit at most
context: Tycho's figure was that each such star would be 'at least as big as the orbit of the Earth, and of course vastly larger than the Sun'. His verdict on the geometry: 'Deduce these things geometrically if you like, and you will see how many absurdities...' -- so he built a compromise instead, with the Moon and Sun orbiting a stationary Earth and the five planets orbiting the Sun. Copernicus's own answer had been written down decades earlier, as Assumption 4 of the Commentariolus: the distance from Earth to Sun 'is imperceptible in comparison with the height of the firmament'. To Tycho that was special pleading. It was right. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Tycho Brahe'; Grokipedia, 'Stellar parallax'; Copernicus, Commentariolus.

question: Friedrich Bessel had to pick one star out of thousands and hope it lay near enough to shift. He chose 61 Cygni on a clue from Giuseppe Piazzi, who in 1804 had catalogued it as a freak -- 'the Flying Star', crossing the sky at over five arcseconds a year, faster than any other star the naked eye can see. Bessel took about a hundred measurements of it at Konigsberg over 1837-38. Why was Piazzi's freak a good bet?
answer: Nearby stars slide fastest against the far ones behind them
choices: Nearby stars slide fastest against the far ones behind them
A star sliding that fast must be small, and small stars lie near
Only the nearest stars are catalogued finely enough to show it
A star sliding that fast must lie in the Milky Way's near disc
context: Proper motion is distance's giveaway: the nearer a star, the faster it appears to slide against the far ones behind it, the way near trees race past a train window while distant hills barely move. A star can also simply be moving fast through space, which is why the clue is a bet and not a proof -- but it was a good bet. Bessel worked the heliometer built by Joseph von Fraunhofer and got 0.3136 arcseconds, plus or minus 0.020 -- about a third of an arcsecond -- for a distance he reported as roughly 10.3-10.4 light years. Gaia DR3 now gives 286.005 milliarcseconds and 11.40 light years, so he was within about ten per cent on the first try. He was not alone by much: Thomas Henderson had observed Alpha Centauri from the Cape of Good Hope in 1832-33 but held back over calibration worries and published only in 1839, and Struve chased Vega from 1835. Bessel published in 1838 and took the prize -- 295 years after the book. Sources: Grokipedia, '61 Cygni' and 'Stellar parallax'.

question: In a beach town, ice-cream sales and drowning deaths climb together on the same days and fall together on other days. A newspaper columnist blames the ice cream. What third thing is really driving BOTH of them up and down?
answer: Hot weather
choices: Hot weather
The tourist board's advertising
A rise in local shark sightings
The federal minimum wage
context: Hot weather sends people to the ice-cream counter AND into the water. When one thing drives BOTH of two others up together, statisticians call it a 'confounder' -- and finding the confounder is the whole game. Source: Wikipedia, 'Correlation does not imply causation.'

question: Children with bigger shoes read at a higher level than children with smaller shoes. A shoemaker announces that buying kids bigger shoes will make them better readers. What has he missed?
answer: Older kids just have bigger feet and stronger reading
choices: Older kids just have bigger feet and stronger reading
Extra shoe weight forces better posture at the desk
Reading slowly stretches the bones of the foot
Better readers buy more expensive, better-fitting shoes
context: The classic teaching example of a confounder: AGE drives both foot size and reading level. Compare only 8-year-olds to 8-year-olds and the correlation vanishes. Source: standard textbook example, cited in Matthews R. 'Storks Deliver Babies' (2000).

question: In 2000, statistician Robert Matthews published a mock-serious paper in Teaching Statistics called 'Storks Deliver Babies (p = 0.008)' -- showing a real, statistically significant correlation across 17 European countries between the number of stork pairs and the number of human births. The correlation vanished once one hidden variable was accounted for. What was it?
answer: The land area of each country
choices: The land area of each country
The average winter temperature
The percentage of Catholics in the population
The number of chimneys per capita
context: Bigger countries just have more of both -- more storks and more babies. Once you divide by area, the correlation collapses. Matthews wrote the paper as a teaching example after complaining that the usual textbook cases (shoe size and reading level) were too obviously confounded to make students think. Source: Matthews, R., 'Storks Deliver Babies (p = 0.008),' Teaching Statistics 2000.

question: Medieval Europeans noticed that sick people had almost no lice on them, and concluded that lice must be keeping folks healthy. In fact the lice were reacting to something the illness ITSELF did to the body -- so the arrow ran the other way. What did the illness do that drove the lice off?
answer: Raised the body's temperature with fever
choices: Raised the body's temperature with fever
Changed the smell of the sweat glands
Slowed the flow of blood in the skin
Thickened the outer layer of the scalp
context: Lice are very sensitive to temperature and abandon a feverish body in search of a cooler host. The correlation between 'no lice' and 'healthy' was real; the causal arrow was upside down. This is the textbook shape of REVERSE CAUSATION. Source: Brainly / standard reverse-causation examples.

question: A 1999 study in Nature by Richard Stone and Graham Quinn reported that babies who slept with a night light on were far more likely to become nearsighted -- a finding that terrified new parents. Two 2000 Nature follow-ups by Jane Gwiazda and Karla Zadnik found no such link. What hidden third factor had fooled the first study?
answer: Nearsighted parents were the ones using night lights
choices: Nearsighted parents were the ones using night lights
The first study double-counted premature babies
The bulb wattages had never been controlled for
Children's daily screen time had climbed in parallel
context: Nearsightedness is strongly heritable, so children of nearsighted parents were more likely to become nearsighted whether or not the light was on. The night light was tracking the parents, not causing the eye. Source: ScienceDaily, 'Night Lights Don't Lead To Nearsightedness, Study Suggests' (2000).

question: For decades, observational studies said women who took hormone therapy after menopause had fewer heart attacks, and it became standard advice. On 9 July 2002 the randomized Women's Health Initiative trial was halted three years early because ONE specific arm of the study was showing MORE heart disease, stroke and blood clots than placebo. Which arm?
answer: Combined estrogen plus progestin
choices: Combined estrogen plus progestin
Estrogen alone at half dose
A soy-based plant hormone
Vitamin D plus calcium
context: About 8,500 women had been randomised to the combined arm. The confounder that had fooled the earlier observational studies was 'healthy-user bias': the women who chose hormone therapy were already healthier, wealthier and better screened than those who didn't -- so their fewer heart attacks looked like a drug effect but were really a lifestyle effect. Source: PMC, 'The Controversial History of Hormone Replacement Therapy.'

question: Randomising who gets a treatment is medicine's single strongest tool against the kind of lie that fooled hormone therapy for decades. What specifically does randomisation DO that plain observation cannot?
answer: Severs the link between the treatment and every other patient trait
choices: Severs the link between the treatment and every other patient trait
Guarantees the sample is large enough for statistical significance
Ensures the results will be published in a top medical journal
Removes any placebo effect from the treated group entirely
context: When a coin decides who gets the drug, income, health habits, motivation and screening frequency all balance out between the two groups on average -- so any difference at the end is due to the drug, not to WHICH patients chose the drug. That's what breaks 'healthy-user' bias. Source: Wikipedia, 'Randomized controlled trial.'

question: Even the inventor of the randomized trial fooled himself once. In the late 1950s statistician Ronald Fisher publicly argued that cigarettes might NOT cause lung cancer -- proposing instead a single hidden factor that caused both the smoking habit AND the disease. What did Fisher blame?
answer: A shared genetic 'constitution' behind both
choices: A shared genetic 'constitution' behind both
Coal-tar pollution from Britain's industrial cities
A wartime shortage of fresh milk and dairy fat
Emotional stress left over from two world wars
context: Fisher cited twin studies showing identical twins had more similar smoking habits than fraternal twins, and interpreted this as genetic. He was also a heavy pipe smoker and a paid consultant to the tobacco industry, and he was wrong. The lesson isn't that Fisher was a villain but that expertise doesn't exempt anyone from motivated reasoning. Source: Priceonomics, 'Why the Father of Modern Statistics Didn't Believe Smoking Caused Cancer.'

question: The smoking-and-cancer case was actually won WITHOUT randomizing anyone to smoke. In October 1951, epidemiologists Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill mailed a questionnaire to every doctor in Britain and followed the roughly 40,000 who replied for decades. Which line of evidence from that cohort was the most decisive?
answer: A dose-response curve, with risk falling when doctors quit
choices: A dose-response curve, with risk falling when doctors quit
One unusually large lung-cancer cluster in a single hospital
A statistical link between doctor age and pipe brand
Wartime rationing records showing tobacco use had fallen
context: Dose-response -- more of X, more of Y, and REMOVE X and Y falls -- is one of Bradford Hill's nine famous 'viewpoints' for turning a correlation into a cause (strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, and analogy). Source: Embryo Project, 'The British Doctors' Study (1951-2001).'

question: Software developer Tyler Vigen runs a website that pairs unrelated real-world series to make the point that any two things can look connected if you check enough pairs. His most famous pair -- correlating at roughly r = 0.947 across ten years of U.S. data -- links per-capita cheese consumption with WHAT?
answer: Deaths from becoming tangled in bedsheets
choices: Deaths from becoming tangled in bedsheets
Divorces in the state of Maine
Films Nicolas Cage appeared in that year
The height of the winning New York marathon runner
context: All four options are real examples from Vigen's Spurious Correlations project -- Maine divorces vs margarine consumption, Nicolas Cage films vs swimming-pool drownings, and so on. The point is that with thousands of series to compare, coincidences at r = 0.9 or better are unavoidable. Source: Errorstatistics.com, 'Spurious Correlations: Death by getting tangled in bedsheets and the consumption of cheese.'

question: Lightning flashes across the valley and you wait for the bang. The light reaches your eyes almost instantly; the sound is still crawling toward you. Storm-watchers turn that lag into a rangefinder by counting the seconds after the flash. How does the count turn into a distance?
answer: One kilometre for every three seconds counted
choices: One kilometre for every three seconds counted
One kilometre for every ten seconds counted
Three kilometres for every second counted
Ten kilometres for every three seconds counted
context: Light crosses the gap at about 300,000 km/s -- effectively instantly -- while sound plods along at about 343 m/s, so the seconds you count are almost entirely the sound's journey. Divide by three for kilometres, or by five for miles: nine seconds of counting puts the strike roughly 3 km away. The trick has a built-in range limit, though. Thunder normally carries only about 16 km (10 miles), so past that you see the flash and the count simply never ends. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thunder' ('roughly 5 seconds per mile or 3 seconds per kilometer'; audible range up to 10 miles) and 'Velocity of Sound' (343 m/s in dry air at 20 C); NWS JetStream, 'The Sound of Thunder'.

question: A lightning bolt's return stroke slams current back up its channel at up to a third of the speed of light, and it does it in a few millionths of a second, heating the air it passes through. Compared with the visible surface of the Sun, how hot does that channel get?
answer: About five times as hot
choices: About five times as hot
About the same temperature
About a tenth as hot
About a hundred times as hot
context: Roughly 30,000 K. The NWS puts it as 'as hot as 54,000 F (30,000 C), a temperature that is five times the surface of the sun,' with peak currents of 10-30 kA. The air cannot get out of the way fast enough, so it blows outward faster than sound and forms a cylindrical shock wave that radiates sideways off the channel before decaying into ordinary sound -- that shock wave is the bang. Right beside the channel the overpressure tops 100 atmospheres, and about 1 psi is enough to break glass, which is why a very close strike can crack walls or blow out windows. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thunder'; NWS JetStream, 'The Sound of Thunder'.

question: Thunder from a storm on the horizon does not bang - it rumbles, and the rumble can run on for tens of seconds after a flash that lasted a heartbeat. What stretches the noise out so long?
answer: The far end of the bolt's path is heard seconds after the near end
choices: The far end of the bolt's path is heard seconds after the near end
The low notes in the bang lag behind the high notes over that distance
Wind trapped inside the storm cloud bangs against its walls repeatedly
The vacuum left along the bolt's path collapses in stages, one by one
context: A distant or long branching channel is kilometres of crooked path, so sound from the near end arrives first and sound from the far end straggles in behind it; the overlapping arrivals smear into a rumble that can run for tens of seconds, sitting low at 20-120 Hz with real energy below 20 Hz. A strike close overhead is a short, straight, near-vertical channel, so it all lands at once: one sharp crack or snap, over in under two seconds. Pitch has nothing to do with it -- Pierre Gassendi established back in 1635 that low notes and high notes travel at exactly the same speed. The two losing options are real history: Aristotle held that thunder was wind striking or trapped inside a cloud, and as late as the 19th century scientists proposed that lightning left a vacuum behind it whose collapse made the noise. Source: Grokipedia, 'Thunder'; NWS JetStream, 'The Sound of Thunder'; en.wikipedia 'Thunder' (historical explanations); fr.wikipedia 'Vitesse du son' on Gassendi.

question: A lungful of party-balloon helium turns a grown man's voice into a cartoon squeak - a trick with real physics inside it. What does the helium actually do?
answer: Helium carries sound three times faster, tuning the throat higher
choices: Helium carries sound three times faster, tuning the throat higher
Helium makes the vocal cords themselves vibrate three times faster
Helium is so light that only the higher notes survive the trip out
Helium chills the throat, tightening the cords like a guitar string
context: Sound runs at about 1,007 m/s in helium at 20 C against about 343 m/s in air, so the notes the throat and mouth amplify shift upward while the cords buzz on as before. The rule cuts the other way too: sound manages only about 259 m/s in carbon dioxide at 0 C, and about 200 m/s on Titan, cold and heavy with methane at -179 C. Titan is also where thunder runs out: Cassini's radio and plasma instrument found no lightning across 126 close flybys from 2004 to 2017, and the Huygens probe's microphone recorded no thunder on the way down. Source: Grokipedia, 'Velocity of Sound'; Grokipedia, 'Thunder' (Cassini, Huygens).

question: A thunderstorm arrives on a 35-degree August afternoon and you count the seconds between flash and bang exactly as you would in a January storm. Air pressure, it turns out, cannot spoil that count: raise the pressure and the air's density rises in step, and the two cancel exactly. So what does the August heat do to it?
answer: The sound arrives sooner, so the storm is farther off than you counted
choices: The sound arrives sooner, so the storm is farther off than you counted
The sound arrives later, so the storm is closer than you counted
Nothing - heat is cancelled by a change in density, exactly as pressure is
Nothing - the speed is fixed by what air is made of, not by how warm it is
context: Temperature is the knob, not pressure. The speed in air is about 331 m/s at 0 C and about 343 m/s at 20 C, gaining roughly 0.6 m/s for every degree Celsius -- the working rule is c = 331 + 0.6T. More precisely it equals 20.05 times the square root of the absolute temperature in kelvin, giving 0.59 m/s per degree near 15 C. At constant temperature the speed really is independent of pressure, and it is independent of the sound's frequency and amplitude as well. So on a hot afternoon the bang gets to you sooner, and a flat three-seconds-per-kilometre count slightly underestimates how far off the storm is. Source: Grokipedia, 'Velocity of Sound'; T. B. Gabrielson, 'Background and Perspective: William Derham's De Motu Soni', Acoustics Today, January 2009.

question: William Derham, a country parson in Upminster, Essex, had spent months in his church tower timing cannon fired twelve miles away, and he had a speed-of-sound figure good enough to send to the Royal Society. He did not trust it. What did he do before he published?
answer: He walked six miles of dark tidal sands, firing muskets at every mile
choices: He walked six miles of dark tidal sands, firing muskets at every mile
He hired a second observer to repeat every timing from the tower
He measured the twelve miles again with a surveyor's chain and staff
He wrote to Isaac Newton and asked him to check the arithmetic
context: In his own words: 'I made a journey to Foulness Sands on our Essex Coast... Upon this plain I measured off only six miles... At the end of almost each mile I made experiments by the firing of muskets, not without great peril to my life from the influence of the sea and the darkness of night. From these experiments I found that all my former observations were most exact and true, to wit, that sound traverses one mile in 9 1/4 half seconds.' Nine and a quarter half-seconds per mile works out to 1,142 feet per second -- about 348 m/s, within a couple of per cent of the modern figure. Checking your own result before anyone else can is the oldest scientific virtue there is. Source: W. Derham, 'De Motu Soni', Philosophical Transactions vol. 26 (1708-1709), translated in T. B. Gabrielson, Acoustics Today, January 2009.

question: William Derham, rector of Upminster in Essex, published his speed-of-sound work in 1708 after months in his church tower, twelve and a half miles from the artillery ground at Blackheath - far enough that a cannon's report took a full minute to arrive. Earlier experimenters had timed such shots against a free-swinging pendulum and had all come out far too fast. Derham, who had written his own book on clockmaking, used a tuned pendulum clock instead. What did that clock give him that a swinging weight could not?
answer: A tick he could hear every half second, so both eyes stayed on the muzzle flash
choices: A tick he could hear every half second, so both eyes stayed on the muzzle flash
A dial he could read in the dark, so no lantern spoiled his night vision
A spring that ran for hours, so one winding covered a whole evening
A face divided into quarter-seconds, so he could split the count finer
context: He took the time by ear and kept both eyes at his telescope, trained on the distant muzzle flash. That was exactly what had beaten his predecessors: Pierre Gassendi in 1635 got about 478 m/s and Marin Mersenne about 448 m/s, both watching a free-swinging pendulum with one eye and watching for the flash with the other, over baselines too short to absorb a timing slip. The 17th-century graveyard of numbers runs Gassendi ~478 m/s, Mersenne ~448, Boyle ~365, Borelli and Viviani ~350, against a true figure near 343. Derham's long line and audible tick gave 1,072 Parisian feet per second, about 348 m/s. Source: T. B. Gabrielson, Acoustics Today, January 2009; Grokipedia, 'William Derham'; en.wikipedia 'Speed of sound' for the early figures.

question: In 1738 the Académie des Sciences sent Cassini de Thury, Maraldi and the abbé de Lacaille out with cannon to pin down the speed of sound along a line twenty-eight kilometres long, from the tower of Montlhéry to the pyramid of Montmartre. Every earlier campaign had been spoiled by the same enemy: a following breeze hurried the sound along, and a headwind held it back. How did they get the wind out of their number?
answer: They fired from both ends of the line and averaged the two runs
choices: They fired from both ends of the line and averaged the two runs
They measured the wind with flags at both ends and subtracted it
They waited for nights when the air along the line was dead still
They laid the line across the region's usual wind, not along it
context: The baseline was 14,636 toises, about 28.5 km. A tailwind speeds one shot exactly as much as it slows the other, so averaging the two directions kills the bias by design rather than by correction -- the wonder here is the design, not the number it produced. Their verdict: 'The sound travels 173 toises (337.2 m) in one second, day and night, in clear or rainy weather,' and they added that the intensity or force of the sound changes nothing about its velocity. Reduced to 0 C the campaign gives 332 m/s, within one per cent of the modern value. Reciprocal firing is harder than it sounds: repeating it in Holland in January 1823, Gerrit Moll reported that 'the report of the shots of Zevenboompjes was not heard at all at the station of Kooltjesberg. But at Zevenboompjes all the shots of Kooltjesberg were distinctly heard.' Wind bending sound rays up over the heads of upwind listeners explains it -- George Stokes proposed the refraction in 1857 and Osborne Reynolds proved it two decades later; until then the leading rival was John Tyndall's 'flocculence', invisible turbid blobs in the air supposedly scattering the sound away. Source: fr.wikipedia 'Vitesse du son'; handwiki 'Physics:Speed of sound'; Moll & Van Beek, Phil. Trans. 114 (1824), quoted in T. B. Gabrielson, Acoustics Today, January 2009.

question: Jean-Daniel Colladon spent October 1826 on Lake Geneva trying to hear a bell struck under a boat thirteen kilometres away. Ducking his own head under the surface worked, but only out to about two kilometres. So he built a listening device instead, and through it the far bell came in as loudly as a bell two hundred metres off sounds to a man with his head in the water. What had he built?
answer: A five-metre tin tube, closed at the bottom and full of air
