He had been laboratory superintendent at Beddoes's Pneumatic Institution since 2 October 1798, aged nineteen, and ran the 160-odd inhalation sessions between April and June 1799. The subject of every one of them was Davy. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy ; Public Domain Review, 'O, Excellent Air Bag: Humphry Davy and Nitrous Oxide' — https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/o-excellent-air-bag-humphry-davy-and-nitrous-oxide

question: Edmund Davy was working as assistant to his cousin Humphry in the Royal Institution basement in October 1807, when the first burning globules broke up through the potash crust. Years afterwards Edmund set down what his cousin did at that moment. What did Humphry do?
answer: He danced about the room and had to be calmed.
choices: He danced about the room and had to be calmed.
He fainted and was carried up to the street.
He shut the crucible and sat down without a word.
He ran out to fetch witnesses from the lecture hall.
context: Edmund Davy's account: as the globules 'burst through the crust of potash, and take fire as they entered the atmosphere, he could not contain his joy — he actually danced about the room in ecstatic delight; some little time was required for him to compose himself sufficiently to continue the experiment.' Treat this as testimony rather than transcript: the words are Edmund's, recalled long afterwards and printed second-hand in John Ayrton Paris's 'The Life of Sir Humphry Davy' (London, 1831). They are not Humphry's own record of the moment. Humphry had made Edmund, his younger cousin, his lecture assistant that same year. Sources: Chemistry World, 'Potassium' podcast transcript — https://www.chemistryworld.com/podcasts/potassium/3005912.article ; todayinsci, 'Edmund Davy — Biography' — https://todayinsci.com/D/Davy_Edmund/DavyEdmundBio.htm  (Legend.)

question: Davy dropped one of his new potassium globules into a dish of water. It caught fire on contact and went on burning for several seconds. Where in the dish did the burning globule sit?
answer: On the top of the water, riding the surface as it burned.
choices: On the top of the water, riding the surface as it burned.
On the bottom of the dish, under the water as it burned.
Just below the surface, held in a shell of gas as it burned.
Against the wall of the dish, at the waterline as it burned.
context: Potassium is less dense than water, so the globule floats while it burns — one of the very few metals that will. Davy also noticed the two new metals parted company as they cooled: potassium 'remained fluid at the temperature of the atmosphere' when first made, while sodium 'became solid on cooling, and appeared having the lustre of silver.' Both are soft enough to cut, and both tarnish the instant air touches them. Sources: ChemTeam, 'Davy Discovers Sodium and Potassium' (Davy's 1807 text) — https://www.chemteam.info/Chem-History/Davy-Na&K-1808.html ; Chemistry World, 'Potassium' podcast — https://www.chemistryworld.com/podcasts/potassium/3005912.article

question: On Boxing Day 1799 Humphry Davy sealed himself inside an airtight box and breathed twenty quarts of nitrous oxide every five minutes for an hour and a quarter, then took twenty quarts more from a silk bag on his way out. The box had been built for him by one of the most famous engineers in the country. Who built it?
answer: James Watt, of steam-engine fame.
choices: James Watt, of steam-engine fame.
John Rennie, of canal-aqueduct fame.
Richard Trevithick, of locomotive fame.
Thomas Telford, of iron-bridge fame.
context: The steam-engine man built the sealed box; Davy climbed in. Coming out of it he declared: 'Nothing exists but thoughts! The world is composed of impressions, ideas, pleasures and pains!' He got the poets to try the gas too. Robert Southey wrote to his brother Tom, 'O, Tom! Such a gas has Davy discovered, the gaseous oxyd! O, Tom! I have had some; it made me laugh and tingle in every toe and finger-tip... O, excellent air-bag!' Samuel Taylor Coleridge said it felt like 'that which I remember once to have experienced after returning from the snow into a warm room', and admitted he 'could not avoid... beating the ground with my feet.' Sources: Public Domain Review, 'O, Excellent Air Bag' — https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/o-excellent-air-bag-humphry-davy-and-nitrous-oxide ; Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy

question: Potash and soda had beaten every chemist who attacked them — even charcoal, which had been pulling metals out of ores since the Bronze Age, left the ash exactly as it found it. Then Humphry Davy ran his battery's current through molten potash, and metal came up out of the ash. What was the current itself doing to the compound?
answer: It tore the oxygen off by sheer electrical force, hauling it to the far wire.
choices: It tore the oxygen off by sheer electrical force, hauling it to the far wire.
It made hydrogen inside the melt, and that hydrogen took the oxygen off.
It fed phlogiston into the ash, and the loaded ash let its metal go.
It poured caloric through the ash until the heat shook the metal loose.
context: Potash and soda are ashes, and the metal in them grips its oxygen so hard that no fire, acid or charcoal reduction of the day could pry it loose. Every older method worked by setting one substance to fight another for the oxygen; electricity broke the deadlock because it does the chemistry with raw electrical force instead. Davy generalised the point into a theory — chemical affinity IS electrical attraction — and it paid. In roughly eighteen months he isolated potassium and sodium (1807), then calcium, magnesium, strontium, barium and boron (1808): more chemical elements than any other single person in history. His decompositions also 'proved that the earths — previously considered irreducible elements — were oxides of metals... establishing electrolysis as a fundamental tool for element discovery.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy

question: Within a year of 1815 Davy's wire-gauze lamp was going down into coal pits all over Britain, and pit owners were working seams that had been too dangerous to touch. A patent on the design would have paid Davy for the rest of his life. What did he do about one?
answer: He never filed one, and let anyone copy the design free.
choices: He never filed one, and let anyone copy the design free.
He filed one and handed the fees to the miners' widows.
He filed one but then let it lapse after a single year.
He left the filing to the Royal Society, which held it.
context: Asked why he had never taken out a patent, Davy answered: 'My good friend, I never thought of such a thing: my sole object was to serve the cause of humanity; and if I have succeeded, I am amply rewarded in the gratifying reflection of having done so... More wealth could not increase either my fame or my happiness.' What he received instead of royalties: the Royal Society's Rumford Medal in 1816, about £2,000 worth of silver plate raised by public subscription among the coal owners, and a baronetcy in 1818. Sources: Royal Society, 'Sir Humphry Davy and the coal miners of the world' (Phil. Trans. A 373:20140288) — https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsta/article/373/2039/20140288 ; Wikipedia, 'Davy lamp' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_lamp

question: Davy's 1815 lamp caged an oil-wick flame inside a cylinder of wire gauze, so that firedamp — the miners' name for methane — could pass in through the holes and burn inside the cage without the fire escaping to the seam outside. Miners soon found the caged flame did a second job for them, and some lamps carried a small metal gauge inside for reading it. What did the flame tell them?
answer: It stretched taller and burned blue when firedamp rose.
choices: It stretched taller and burned blue when firedamp rose.
It shrank back and burned orange when firedamp rose.
It flattened out and burned green when firedamp rose.
It guttered and threw black soot when firedamp rose.
context: The lamp was a gas detector nobody had set out to design. Miners read the flame's height against the little metal gauge inside the gauze to judge how much firedamp was in the air — and if the flame went out altogether, the oxygen was running short and it was time to leave. The lamp told you the air was killing you before it killed you. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Davy lamp' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_lamp ; Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy

question: Humphry Davy is remembered for pulling calcium, magnesium, strontium and barium out of lime, magnesia, strontia and baryta in 1808 — four 'earths' that every chemist's list, Lavoisier's included, had printed as elements. Through that spring he was stuck: his current freed metal out of the earths and lost it again in the same instant. Then a letter reached him from the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who had hit on a way to hold the metal. What did Berzelius tell Davy to do?
answer: Run the current into the lime through a pool of mercury, which takes the metal up.
choices: Run the current into the lime through a pool of mercury, which takes the metal up.
Run the current into the lime through a bed of charcoal, which soaks the metal up.
Run the current into the lime under a layer of oil, which shuts the air off it.
Run the current into the lime inside a sealed jar, which keeps the metal dry.
context: Berzelius and Magnus Martin af Pontin had decomposed lime by electrolysing it in contact with mercury: the mercury takes up the new metal as an amalgam, so it cannot escape. Davy took the hint, electrolysed lime with mercuric oxide to make a calcium amalgam, then boiled the mercury off to leave the silvery metal behind. Honest credit where it is due — Davy was the first man to hold the pure metals, but the mercury-cathode trick was not his idea. For the 30 June 1808 announcement one of the Royal Institution's enormous 600-plate voltaic batteries was wheeled into the lecture theatre in front of fashionable London. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy ; Chemistry LibreTexts, 'The Alkaline Earth Elements' — https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Inorganic_Chemistry/Chemistry_of_the_Main_Group_Elements_(Barron)/04:_Group_2_-_The_Alkaline_Earth_Metals/4.01:_The_Alkaline_Earth_Elements

question: Davy's wisdom teeth came in badly in 1799 and his gums were inflamed; he found the pain faded after three or four breaths of nitrous oxide. In his 580-page 'Researches' of 1800, written at twenty-one, he set the clue down in print: since the gas 'appears capable of destroying physical pain, it may probably be used with advantage during surgical operations in which no great effusion of blood takes place.' What became of that sentence?
answer: Surgeons ignored it and went on cutting conscious patients for forty more years.
choices: Surgeons ignored it and went on cutting conscious patients for forty more years.
Surgeons took it up inside a decade, first in Bristol and then in London.
The Royal College of Surgeons forbade the gas as too dangerous to breathe.
Beddoes tried it on his own patients and published the results in 1802.
context: Davy's own note of the clue: 'In cutting the unlucky teeth called dentes sapientiae, I experienced an extensive inflammation of the gums, accompanied with great pain... On the day when the inflammation was most troublesome, I breathed three large doses of nitrous oxide. The pain always diminished after the first three or four inspirations.' The printed suggestion simply sat there. Surgery went on being done on screaming, conscious, held-down patients until the mid-1840s — the answer had been published, and nobody tested it. Sources: Davy, 'Researches, Chemical and Philosophical; Chiefly Concerning Nitrous Oxide' (1800), via Wood Library-Museum of Anesthesiology — https://www.woodlibrarymuseum.org/rare-book/davy-h-researches-chemical-and-philosophical-chiefly-concerning-nitrous-oxide-or-dephlogisticated-nitrous-air-and-its-respiration-1800/ ; the toothache passage via Pocket Dentistry, 'Discovery, History, and Evolution of N2O/O2 Sedation' — https://pocketdentistry.com/1-discovery-history-and-evolution-of-n2oo2-sedation/

question: On 16 November 1812 a fragment of nitrogen trichloride exploded in Humphry Davy's face. He wrote that week: 'It is not safe to experiment upon a globule larger than a pin's head. I have been severely wounded by a piece scarcely bigger.' His eyes healed, but for months he could not write for himself, and in March 1813 he took on an assistant — a twenty-one-year-old bookbinder's apprentice who had sat in on his lectures, bound his own notes of them into a book by hand, and posted it to him. Who was the apprentice?
answer: Michael Faraday.
choices: Michael Faraday.
William Wollaston.
William Brande.
John Dalton.
context: Michael Faraday was appointed laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution on 1 March 1813, and shortly afterwards the two of them were injured together in yet another nitrogen trichloride explosion. Davy sent his warning to John George Children: 'It must be used with great caution... My sight, however, I am informed, will not be injured.' He was right — he had recovered by April 1813, and he was never blinded. Handle the famous line 'Faraday was Davy's greatest discovery' with care: reputable sources render it as something that 'has been said', not as a documented quotation from Davy. Pierre Louis Dulong, the Frenchman who first made the compound, was less lucky than either of them: he lost two fingers and an eye to it. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphry_Davy ; IET Archives, 'Michael Faraday' — https://www.theiet.org/membership/library-and-archives/the-iet-archives/biographies/michael-faraday ; Britannica, 'Michael Faraday' — https://www.britannica.com/biography/Michael-Faraday

question: In 1810 Humphry Davy told the Royal Society that the choking greenish-yellow gas chemists called oxymuriatic gas was no compound at all. He had failed, with his batteries and with everything else he had, to pull one particle of oxygen out of it. It was an element in its own right, and he named it chlorine, from the Greek for greenish-yellow. The result also demolished one of Antoine Lavoisier's central rules — and Lavoisier, unluckily, had built that very rule into the name he gave oxygen, two Greek roots stating what he took the element's essential work to be. What do those roots say oxygen does?
answer: It forms acids.
choices: It forms acids.
It forms alkalis.
It forms salts.
It forms water.
context: 'Oxygen' is Lavoisier's coinage from Greek roots meaning acid-former. He was certain that oxygen is what makes an acid an acid, and he wrote the claim straight into the element's name. Davy's chlorine killed the rule: if chlorine is an element, then muriatic acid — the classic screaming-strong acid — is nothing but hydrogen and chlorine, with no oxygen in it at all. The great chemist had named the element after a job it turned out not to do, and chemists have been stuck with the name ever since. Davy proposed instead that hydrogen is the thing acids have in common, which is closer to right, though it never explained why methane, stuffed with hydrogen, is not an acid. (Hydrogen's own name is built the same way: water-former.) Carl Wilhelm Scheele had first made the gas back in 1774 by dripping hydrochloric acid onto manganese dioxide, and Davy wrote in his follow-up paper, read 21 February 1811, 'As I have named that elastic fluid Chlorine...'. Sources: ChemTeam, 'Early acid base theories: Lavoisier and Davy' — https://www.chemteam.info/AcidBase/Early-Acid-Base.html ; ChemTeam, 'Davy on Chlorine' (Davy's 1811 Phil. Trans. text) — https://www.chemteam.info/Chem-History/Davy-Chlorine-1811.html ; Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy

question: Coal miners worked by candle-flame in air laced with firedamp — the methane that seeps out of a cut seam — and the flame that let them see was the thing that killed them. Testing flames in closed vessels through the autumn of 1815, Humphry Davy found that a flame will not run down a metal tube narrower than about a seventh of an inch, and will not cross a fine wire gauze at all. So he caged an ordinary oil-wick flame inside a cylinder of gauze pierced with thousands of holes to the square inch: gas walks in and burns inside the cage, and the fire does not walk back out. Why can the flame not get through the holes?
answer: The wires drain heat from the burning gas faster than the fire can spread.
choices: The wires drain heat from the burning gas faster than the fire can spread.
The wires carry the flame's charge away, and a flame without charge dies.
The mesh splits the flame into threads too thin to keep themselves alight.
The mesh holds a film of moisture that quenches the fire at every hole.
context: Metal carries heat away fast. The gauze pulls heat out of the burning gas quicker than the gas can carry the fire forward, chilling it below the temperature at which methane will ignite — so the flame burns right up to the mesh and stops dead there. The same cooling is why a flame will not run down a metal tube narrower than about a seventh of an inch, roughly 3.6 mm. Davy's gauze cylinders carried something like 625 to 6,400 holes per square inch. He had a working prototype by 9 November 1815 and read the paper to the Royal Society that same day. This is Davy's own test, and it is one you can watch rather than take on trust: with an adult present, hold a piece of fine metal mesh flat over a candle flame and the flame flattens against it instead of climbing through. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Humphry Davy' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Humphry_Davy ; Wikipedia, 'Davy lamp' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davy_lamp

question: Anders Celsius did not simply say 'water boils at this mark'. He wrote a fussy little clause into his 1742 definition. What condition did he insist on for the boiling point?
answer: Mean barometric pressure at sea level
choices: Mean barometric pressure at sea level
That the water be freshly distilled
That the thermometer be immersed a full inch
That a rolling boil, not a simmer, be reached
context: Boil the same pot on a mountain top and the water boils cooler; Celsius's fine print protected his scale from that. It was Fahrenheit and Celsius together who turned temperature from a feeling into a number strangers could compare. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anders_Celsius.

question: Fahrenheit's zero is famous, but historians of science treat the numbers as the less important half of what he built. His real gift was a piece of hardware, first perfected around 1721, that meant two observers in two different cities could take a reading and mean the same thing. What piece of hardware?
answer: A mercury-in-glass thermometer
choices: A mercury-in-glass thermometer
An alcohol-in-glass thermometer with a fixed bore
A bimetallic-strip thermometer
A linseed-oil-in-glass thermometer
context: Alcohol thermometers of the day drifted and boiled off too easily; Fahrenheit's mercury column was reproducible enough to trade between labs. Consistent instruments are what turn private impressions into shared measurements. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Gabriel_Fahrenheit.

question: Take any gas in a sealed rigid vessel and slowly cool it, then plot pressure against temperature. You get a straight line sloping down. Draw that line for oxygen, for nitrogen, for helium: three straight lines. If you extend them all downward on paper, what do the lines do?
answer: They meet at one point on the temperature axis
choices: They meet at one point on the temperature axis
They fan out to three different points
They curve away from each other before crossing
They flatten into three parallel horizontal lines
context: That shared meeting point is where pressure would fall to zero. Every gas that has ever been measured tells the same story, and that is the geometric ghost of absolute zero, showing up in the arithmetic long before anyone got near the temperature itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero.

question: A common line in schoolbooks says absolute zero is the temperature at which 'all motion stops'. Modern physics says that line is wrong. What actually survives at zero kelvin?
answer: A residue of zero-point energy
choices: A residue of zero-point energy
A ghost of chemical bonding heat
A trickle of nuclear decay warmth
A leftover jitter from cosmic rays
context: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle forbids a particle from having a perfectly known position and a perfectly known momentum at the same time, so it cannot sit perfectly still even in principle. Zero kelvin is the point of minimum possible energy, not zero energy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero.

question: The third law of thermodynamics says absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps. This is not a note about weak fridges; it is a statement about the shape of every cooling method ever invented. What do they all share?
answer: Each step removes only a fraction of what is left
choices: Each step removes only a fraction of what is left
Each step removes a fixed number of joules
Each step warms the fridge back up by a degree
Each step is halted by a small quantum leak
context: Halve, halve, halve: you approach the floor as an infinite sequence with a limit. A better fridge cuts a bigger fraction; it still cannot cut down to nothing. This is why the record has kept dropping without ever landing at zero. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_zero.

question: On 10 July 1908 in his Leiden laboratory, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes ran the last stage of a cascade cooler and watched a colourless liquid drip out of the tap for the first time. Three years later, sinking a mercury sample in that same liquid, he found electrical resistance vanishing entirely: superconductivity. What gas had he just learned to liquefy?
answer: Helium
choices: Helium
Hydrogen
Neon
Nitrogen
context: It boils at about 4 kelvin at atmospheric pressure. His cryogenic lab held the world record for cold for decades, and the Nobel Prize followed in 1913. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heike_Kamerlingh_Onnes.

question: In 2021 a team dropped a cloud of rubidium atoms down a 122-metre tower in Bremen, using a magnetic trap to focus the atoms as if with a lens. During the free-fall the atom cloud held a temperature that beat every previous record by orders of magnitude. What did they measure?
answer: About 38 picokelvin
choices: About 38 picokelvin
About 38 microkelvin
About 38 millikelvin
About 38 nanokelvin
context: 38 trillionths of a kelvin, held for about 2 seconds in a Bose-Einstein condensate. For scale, the coldest known natural place, the Boomerang Nebula, sits around 1 kelvin: billions of times warmer than the lab record. Sources: phys.org/news/2021-10-coldest-temperature38-picokelvins.html ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boomerang_Nebula.

question: For most of the twentieth century, the kelvin was defined by pinning one number to a physical setup: the triple point of pure water, sealed inside a special glass cell. On 20 May 2019 the SI abandoned the water cell entirely. What now sets the size of a kelvin?
answer: An exact value of the Boltzmann constant
choices: An exact value of the Boltzmann constant
An exact value of the speed of light
An exact value of Avogadro's number
An exact value of Planck's constant
context: 1.380649 x 10^-23 joules per kelvin, exact by decree. Temperature is now defined by a constant of nature rather than by a jar of water: no substance sits between you and the number. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin.

question: In the 1930s two German Nobel laureates in physics campaigned to have Einstein's relativity thrown out of German universities as 'Jewish physics'. Which pair led that campaign?
answer: Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark
choices: Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark
Max Planck and Arnold Sommerfeld
Erwin Schroedinger and Peter Debye
Max von Laue and Walther Nernst
context: Lenard (1905 Nobel, cathode rays) and Stark (1919 Nobel, the Stark effect) attacked relativity as 'juedische Physik' and pushed for a 'German' physics rooted in what they called Aryan experimental style. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-2-pro-nazi-nobelists-attacked-einstein-s-jewish-science-excerpt1/

question: In the foreword to his four-volume physics textbook (Munich, 1936-37), Philipp Lenard put the doctrine of Deutsche Physik in one line. What did he claim decides what counts as science?
answer: race and blood
choices: race and blood
mathematical rigour
practical experience
national tradition
context: Lenard wrote that science, like everything man creates, is determined by race and by blood. The textbook Deutsche Physik in vier Baenden was published by J.F. Lehmann in Munich, 1936-1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philipp_Lenard

question: On 7 April 1933 the new Nazi government passed a law that emptied German universities of professors with a Jewish grandparent or a record of political opposition. Which law?
answer: the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service
choices: the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service
the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour
the Law Against the Overcrowding of German Schools
the Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring
context: Enacted two months after Hitler was appointed chancellor. By 1938 roughly a quarter of Germany's physicists had lost their positions, and eleven past or future Nobel laureates -- including Max Born and James Franck -- were among the emigres. Source: https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/scientific-exodus/

question: Johannes Stark was appointed in April 1933 to a post that let him decide who was hired and paid across German physics; he also ran the country's main research-funding body. Which institute did he take over as president?
answer: the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt
choices: the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt
the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics
the Prussian Academy of Sciences
the Fraunhofer Gesellschaft
context: Germany's national standards institute. Stark served as its president 1933-1939 and simultaneously ran the Notgemeinschaft der Deutschen Wissenschaft, the main research grant body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Stark

question: The proof that Deutsche Physik was never really about ancestry: on 15 July 1937 Johannes Stark used the SS newspaper Das Schwarze Korps to smear an 'Aryan' German physicist as a 'white Jew' -- because that physicist taught modern theoretical physics. Whom did he attack?
answer: Werner Heisenberg
choices: Werner Heisenberg
Max von Laue
Arnold Sommerfeld
Pascual Jordan
context: Stark's article said Heisenberg should be made to 'disappear'. Heisenberg had defended Einstein's relativity in his teaching. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Heisenberg

question: In 1936 Werner Heisenberg co-signed a petition of German physics professors defending modern physics against the Deutsche Physik attacks. Who were his two co-authors?
answer: Hans Geiger and Max Wien
choices: Hans Geiger and Max Wien
Max Planck and Arnold Sommerfeld
Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner
Walther Nernst and Peter Debye
context: Geiger (of the Geiger counter) and Max Wien organised the petition with Heisenberg; it argued that abstract theory is where practical power comes from -- Heisenberg pointed at Maxwell's equations, pure mathematics that produced radio. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-0348-9008-3_49

question: Heisenberg was not saved by argument. In 1938 his mother appealed to Heinrich Himmler's mother -- the two families knew each other through a Bavarian hiking club. On 21 July 1938 Himmler wrote two letters clearing Heisenberg, on one condition. What was he allowed to teach only if he obeyed it?
answer: relativity, so long as he never credited Einstein by name
choices: relativity, so long as he never credited Einstein by name
quantum mechanics, so long as he called it a German discovery
any physics he liked, but only to SS-vetted students
atomic theory, so long as he swore loyalty to Hitler personally
context: The rescue was a family connection, not a triumph of reason: Heisenberg's maternal grandfather and Himmler's father had been fellow rectors in the same Bavarian hiking club. Heisenberg stayed in Germany and led the wartime nuclear effort. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Heisenberg ; https://www.thenewatlantis.com/publications/the-most-dangerous-possible-german

question: On 18 September 1933, chairing the opening of the German Physical Society congress at Wuerzburg, one physicist compared the Nazi rejection of relativity to the Church's silencing of Galileo -- and closed his address with Galileo's own line, in Italian. The audience applauded. Which physicist gave that address?
answer: Max von Laue
choices: Max von Laue
Werner Heisenberg
Max Planck
Arnold Sommerfeld
context: Von Laue ended with 'Eppur si muove' -- 'and yet it moves'. He did it in public, in 1933, as chairman of the society, and remained one of the very few senior German physicists to defy the regime openly for the rest of the Reich. Source: https://live-center-for-science-technology-medicine-society.pantheon.berkeley.edu/current-events/max-von-laue-1879-1960-champion-of-freedom

question: Germany had led the world in theoretical physics before 1933. The verdict on Deutsche Physik was written not in argument but in what the physics it demanded could no longer do. Which task fell outside its reach?
answer: compute a nuclear reaction
choices: compute a nuclear reaction
explain the electric motor
predict a planet's orbit
measure the speed of light
context: A physics that rejected relativity and quantum mechanics could not describe the atomic nucleus. The men who could -- Born, Franck, Bethe, Meitner and dozens more -- were the ones the Reich had driven out; that emigration handed the theoretical lead to Britain and the United States. Source: https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/online/5299/The-scientific-exodus-from-Nazi-Germany

question: James Dewar built the first vacuum flask in 1892, and he was not thinking about picnics. What was he actually trying to hold?
answer: Liquefied gases at extremely low temperatures
choices: Liquefied gases at extremely low temperatures
Molten iron for casting laboratory tools
Radioactive salts for glow experiments
Live bacterial cultures at body temperature
context: The flask was cryogenic laboratory kit. Dewar had been forcing gases to their liquid state for years, and it was expensive work -- he needed a way to keep them liquid long enough to study. He first showed the flask at the Royal Institution on Christmas Day 1892. The picnic flask is a spin-off; it was never designed for soup. Source: https://www.rigb.org/explore-science/explore/collection/james-dewars-vacuum-flask

question: James Dewar sealed one glass chamber inside another and pumped the air out of the gap. With the gap empty, heat had almost no way to cross -- almost. One way to move heat still worked even through the vacuum. Which one?
answer: Radiation
choices: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
Evaporation
context: Conduction hands heat molecule to molecule; convection carries it in a moving fluid. Take the molecules out of the gap and both stop. Radiation is photons -- infrared light -- and it happily crosses a vacuum. That is the road the silvering has to handle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask

question: The walls of a Dewar flask are pretty close to perfect -- vacuum takes out two heat-transfer roads, silvering handles the third. And yet a flask of coffee does eventually cool. Where does most of the leaking heat actually get out?
answer: Through the neck and stopper
choices: Through the neck and stopper
Straight through the silvering on the inner wall
Along the seam where the glass was blown
Out the base, where the flask sits on the table
context: There is no vacuum at the neck -- the two chambers have to be joined somewhere. That is where conduction and convection get back in. It is why the lid matters more than the walls, and why an open flask empties its heat fast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask

question: Two German glassblowers, Reinhold Burger and Albert Aschenbrenner, took the laboratory flask, built a rugged consumer version with a protective outer casing, and ran a public contest to name it -- won in 1904 by a resident of Munich with 'Thermos', from the Greek word for heat. Dewar was furious and took them to court to claim the rights. How did the case end?
answer: Dewar lost the case outright
choices: Dewar lost the case outright
Dewar won a share of every flask ever sold
The court ordered the Germans to change the name
The two sides settled and split the profits
context: Dewar had never patented the flask -- he viewed it as a scientific instrument, not a product, and had already been through the exhausting Nobel v. Abel & Dewar cordite patent fight in 1893-1895. No patent, no case. It cost him the fortune the Thermos company went on to make. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_flask ; https://gizmodo.com/how-the-thermos-corporation-cheated-the-inventor-of-the-1420505076

question: In September 2011, Dutch psychologist Diederik Stapel made headlines: thinking about meat, he claimed, makes people more selfish. Something about HOW that claim reached the public was itself a warning sign. What was it?
answer: It went out via press release before any journal saw the paper
choices: It went out via press release before any journal saw the paper
It contradicted his own earlier published work on empathy
It was released in six different languages at once
It was posted anonymously on an academic board
context: Tilburg University sent out the press release on the meat finding a day before Stapel's own junior researchers took their concerns to the department head. Sources: 24oranges.nl coverage; Science, Dutch University Sacks Social Psychologist.

question: Diederik Stapel's fabricated data survived peer review for years and passed through many co-authors. Who finally caught him?
answer: Three of his own junior researchers
choices: Three of his own junior researchers
A Nature editor filing a records request
A rival lab that failed to replicate the study
A university auditor doing a routine check
context: The three students were the least powerful people in the building. They had noticed he always handed them finished datasets nobody had watched him collect and discouraged questions about where the numbers came from. Source: Scientific American blog, Reluctance to Act on Suspicions.

question: When Diederik Stapel's three junior researchers finally compared the files he had handed them, they found the specific pattern that made the fraud undeniable. What did they find?
answer: Identical rows of scores in two different studies
choices: Identical rows of scores in two different studies
Standard deviations mathematically impossible for the sample
Timestamps predating the experiments themselves
Signatures forged in his own handwriting
context: Real data drawn from different people cannot produce byte-identical rows. Duplication is one of the classic tells investigators check for, along with the GRIM test and Benford's law. Source: Levelt Committee report, University of Groningen.

question: Confronted about where his data came from, Diederik Stapel first claimed he had special access to schools that had run his surveys for him. When the rector asked him to produce contacts at those schools, what did Stapel admit?
answer: The schools did not exist
choices: The schools did not exist
The teachers had lost the paperwork
The children had answered anonymously
The recordings had been destroyed
context: That admission -- not any statistical test -- ended his career. He had invented the data from scratch, without ever collecting anything. Source: Levelt Committee final report, 28 November 2012.

question: The three junior researchers did not go straight to the press or to Diederik Stapel. They went first to their department head -- deliberately at a conference in a foreign city so he could not be tipped off. Who was that department head?
answer: Marcel Zeelenberg
choices: Marcel Zeelenberg
Daryl Bem
Brian Nosek
Roy Baumeister
context: They approached Zeelenberg in London so Stapel could not be immediately warned. Zeelenberg took the evidence to Tilburg's rector, Philip Eijlander, and formal investigations opened at three universities within days. Source: Wikipedia, Diederik Stapel.

question: The Stapel case exposes a general structural weakness in a research group that a kid can learn to spot from outside. What was the structural feature that made his fraud possible for so long?
answer: One person was the sole source of every dataset
choices: One person was the sole source of every dataset
The group published only in low-ranked journals
The group refused to preregister its studies
The group used only undergraduate students as subjects
context: Every study ran through Stapel's hands, and no co-author ever met a participant. Any arrangement where one person controls the only copy of reality is a fraud waiting to happen, however trusted that person is. Source: Levelt Committee report; Academia.edu, Changes in Publication Culture.

question: The Levelt Committee issued its final report on Diederik Stapel on 28 November 2012. How many of his publications did the committee identify as containing fabricated or manipulated data?
answer: At least 55
choices: At least 55
At most 5
Around 500
About 12
context: The eventual retraction count reached 58 papers, including a 2011 Science paper on disorder and stereotyping that was retracted on 1 December 2011. Graduate students had built entire doctorates on results that were never real. Sources: Wikipedia, Diederik Stapel; Retraction Watch, 2015.

question: A schoolteacher in Cologne published a small book in 1827 giving the rule every physics class now uses: the current through a wire scales with the voltage across it. When no university offer followed, he resigned his teaching post. His name is now stamped on every resistor. Which man?
answer: Georg Simon Ohm
choices: Georg Simon Ohm
Alessandro Volta
Andre-Marie Ampere
Michael Faraday
context: Ohm's 1827 book 'Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet' was received coldly; he resigned his Cologne post in March 1828 and did not get a chair of physics (Munich) until 1852, less than two years before his death. Sources: Wikipedia Georg Ohm; MacTutor History of Mathematics.

question: In Prague in 1842 Christian Doppler proposed that a wave's pitch depends on whether the source is approaching or receding. In the same paper he tried to apply the idea to something in the night sky, and he was wrong: the motion involved is far too slow to produce the shift he claimed. Which claim did he get wrong?
answer: the colours of double stars
choices: the colours of double stars
the phases of Venus
the paths of comets
the parallax of Mars
context: Doppler's 1842 paper to the Royal Bohemian Society was titled 'On the coloured light of the double stars and certain other stars of the heavens'. The principle was right; the stellar-colour application was wrong. Source: Wikipedia Christian Doppler.

question: Georg Ohm hoped for a university chair for a quarter of a century after his 1827 book on the galvanic circuit was met with a shrug. The chair, when it finally came in 1852, was at which German university?
answer: Munich
choices: Munich
Heidelberg
Gottingen
Leipzig
context: Ohm was appointed to the chair of physics at the University of Munich on 1 October 1852 and died in July 1854, less than two years into the post he had wanted his entire adult life. Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics.

question: In February 1845 a Dutch meteorologist set out to disprove Doppler on the newly opened railway line near Utrecht. He had listeners with trained pitch on the ground write down what they heard as an open railway carriage passed at speed. Who did he put on the carriage to hold the calibrated pitch?
answer: a band of trumpeters
choices: a band of trumpeters
a string quartet
a barrel-organ crew
a choir of boy sopranos
context: Christophorus Buys Ballot's 1845 experiment on the Utrecht-Maarssen line put trumpeters on an open flatcar and heard the pitch drop about a half-tone as it passed. He had aimed to refute Doppler and ended up confirming him. Sources: KNMI; Utrecht mural formulas project.

question: Doppler's principle was right for sound but he had no way to test it on starlight. In 1848, unaware of the 1842 German paper, a French physicist independently proposed the same shift should show up as a displacement of spectral lines in the light of moving stars. Who?
answer: Hippolyte Fizeau
choices: Hippolyte Fizeau
Leon Foucault
Francois Arago
Augustin Fresnel
context: Fizeau's 1848 proposal is why the shift is sometimes called the Doppler-Fizeau effect. Sources: Wikipedia Hippolyte Fizeau; MacTutor History of Mathematics.

question: Svante Arrhenius defended his Uppsala doctoral thesis in May 1884 arguing that dissolved salts split into charged ions in water on their own, with no current applied. The examiners passed him. What grade did they give the thesis itself?
answer: fourth class, the lowest pass
choices: fourth class, the lowest pass
first class, the highest honour
second class with distinction
third class, a routine pass
context: The thesis was graded fourth class (non sine laude approbatur); the oral defence was raised to third class (cum laude approbatur). The grades did not qualify him to teach at university level. Sources: Wikipedia Svante Arrhenius; DiVA Uppsala biography.

question: Nineteen years after his Uppsala examiners graded that thesis fourth class, the same idea about ions won Arrhenius the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Ostwald, van 't Hoff and Clausius had championed him from outside long before the local establishment did. What did Arrhenius call Ostwald in his 1903 Nobel lecture?
answer: the theory's enthusiastic godfather
choices: the theory's enthusiastic godfather
the prophet of chemistry
the father of ions
the master of Riga
context: Arrhenius's 1903 Nobel lecture credited Wilhelm Ostwald as the theory's 'enthusiastic godfather'. Pattern across Ohm, Doppler and Arrhenius: not persecution but a gap between the claim and the community's ability to test or use it. When the gap closes, the name ends up printed on the instrument. Source: Nobel Prize 1903 Chemistry ceremony speech.

question: At 9:05 a.m. on Monday 10 September 1984, geneticist Alec Jeffreys lifted a wet X-ray film from a developing tank in his Leicester lab. He was five minutes away from the discovery that would make his name. What was his reaction in the first seconds?
answer: Disgust -- he thought the film was a mess.
choices: Disgust -- he thought the film was a mess.
Alarm -- he thought the samples had been swapped.
Boredom -- he thought the film showed nothing new.
Relief -- he thought the probe had finally worked.
context: His exact words were 'God, what a mess.' Then, he says, 'I stared a bit longer -- and the penny dropped... an absolute Eureka moment. It was a blinding flash. In five golden minutes, my research career went whizzing off in a completely new direction.' At 8:55 that morning, by his own account, he had absolutely no idea the work had any practical use at all. (Genetics Unzipped podcast transcript, geneticsunzipped.com/transcripts/2020/3/26/the-accidental-discovery-of-dna-fingerprinting -- direct Jeffreys quotes; time and date corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: The X-ray film that started DNA fingerprinting was not a human experiment at all. Alec Jeffreys was testing how widely his new DNA probe worked, so the human lanes sat in the middle of a row of samples from other living things. What else was on that film?
answer: DNA from a cow, a grey seal and tobacco.
choices: DNA from a cow, a grey seal and tobacco.
DNA from a rabbit, a mouse and wheat.
DNA from a horse, a herring and barley.
DNA from a dog, a fruit fly and maize.
context: Jeffreys wanted to know whether his probe would pick out the same kind of repeated DNA across wildly different species -- a mammal, a sea mammal, a plant. The human barcode was an accident sitting in the middle of somebody else's experiment. (labxchange.org/library/items/lb:LabXchange:793cf91f:html:1, 'The Eureka Moment That Revolutionized Crime Solving', caption to the original autoradiograph)

question: Three lanes on Jeffreys' film held human DNA: his lab technician Jenny Foxon had volunteered a sample, and so had her mother and her father. Reading her column of bands against theirs is what turned a routine morning into a discovery. What did Jeffreys find in Jenny Foxon's pattern?
answer: It was unlike anyone else's, yet every band showed up in one parent.
choices: It was unlike anyone else's, yet every band showed up in one parent.
It was unlike anyone else's, and no band showed up in either parent.
It matched her mother's pattern band for band, as a daughter's does.
It sat exactly halfway between her mother's pattern and her father's.
context: Unique to her, and visibly inherited: that single combination is what makes a barcode both an identifier and a family record, and it is why the technique could later be used on families as well as on suspects. Jeffreys called the images 'rather fuzzy-looking barcode-like patterns', and admitted the first ones were 'pretty blurry and horrible'. (timeshighereducation.com/features/the-small-scientist/407947.article, 'The small scientist')

question: Alec Jeffreys spotted the first DNA barcode on an X-ray film on the morning of 10 September 1984, and within the hour he and his colleague Victoria Wilson had written out a list of jobs it might do. At his first public talk about the discovery, Jeffreys suggested one of those jobs and part of the audience laughed out loud. Which job did they laugh at?
answer: That it could be used to catch criminals.
choices: That it could be used to catch criminals.
That it could settle who a child's father was.
That it could tell whether twins were identical.
That it could track wild animals in the field.
context: In 1984 the idea that a smear of bands on a film could identify a murderer sounded like science fiction; within four years it had convicted one. The list Jeffreys and Wilson wrote that hour covered paternity disputes, crime-scene identification, telling whether twins were identical, and tracking wild animals -- a fingerprint cannot tell one identical twin from the other, because the two carry the same barcode. Jeffreys' wife Sue added the use nobody in the lab had thought of: immigration cases. (timeshighereducation.com/features/the-small-scientist/407947.article; the laughter from theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation, Ian Cobain, 'Killer breakthrough'; the wife's suggestion corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: Alec Jeffreys was not looking for a way to identify people. Since about 1980 he had been hunting stretches of DNA that differ a lot from person to person, because the markers he already had barely differed at all and were useless to him. Useless for what job?
answer: Tracing an inherited illness through a family.
choices: Tracing an inherited illness through a family.
Matching a transplant donor to a patient.
Working out how common a blood group was.
Telling whether a tumour had spread.
context: To follow a disease gene down through a family you need a nearby marker that a parent and child can be told apart by; Jeffreys' earlier single-letter markers were nearly identical in everybody, so they could not be tracked. He gave up on them and went hunting wildly variable DNA instead -- and the identification barcode fell out as a by-product. The Guardian later described the experiment that produced it as a failed one. (grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys; theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation)

question: Alec Jeffreys went hunting for spots in the DNA where people differ a lot, and minisatellites delivered: at one such spot a person may carry thirty copies of a short motif in a row, the next person twenty-five, a third eighteen. Those counts change up to ten thousand times faster than ordinary DNA. What makes them so unstable?
answer: The copies mis-align when chromosomes pair off, and the pair swaps unequal lengths.
choices: The copies mis-align when chromosomes pair off, and the pair swaps unequal lengths.
The copying enzyme stutters along the row and slips in an extra copy or two.
Repair enzymes patch the row more sloppily than they patch the rest of the DNA.
Radiation and chemicals strike the row far more often than they strike the rest.
context: One person may carry thirty copies at a spot where another carries twenty-five and a third eighteen. Those counts change up to ten thousand times faster than ordinary DNA: when eggs and sperm are made, the identical copies mis-align as the paired chromosomes line up, and the pair then swaps unequal lengths, so a row gains or loses copies. That instability is exactly why the barcodes differ so much between people. (grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys -- 10-15 bp core motifs, mutation rates up to 10,000x baseline via unequal meiotic exchange, myoglobin gene; repeat-count example quoted from Jeffreys at geneticsunzipped.com)

question: In April 1985 a fifteen-year-old boy, Andrew Sarbah, was stopped at the British border; officials said his passport was fake and another boy had been put in his place. His mother and three undisputed brothers and sisters were in Britain, but the father he claimed was in Ghana and out of reach. Alec Jeffreys rebuilt the missing father's barcode without using Andrew at all. From what?
answer: The bands his brothers and sisters had that their mother lacked.
choices: The bands his brothers and sisters had that their mother lacked.
The bands his brothers and sisters shared with their mother.
The bands his mother had that none of her children did.
The bands all three of his brothers and sisters had in common.
context: Any band in a child that is absent from the mother has to have come from the father, so the three undisputed siblings between them rebuilt most of a man who was never tested. Nearly half of Andrew's bands matched that reconstructed profile. The Home Office dropped the case and he stayed; the family's solicitor was Sheona York. This immigration dispute -- not a crime -- was the technique's first real-world use, and Jeffreys credits his wife Sue with spotting that application. (thebiotalkmagazine.com/the-first-immigration-dispute-case-resolved-by-dna-fingerprinting/; corroborated at grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: In August 1986 Leicestershire police brought Alec Jeffreys samples from two linked murders near the village of Narborough. They already had a seventeen-year-old, Richard Buckland, who had confessed to one of the killings, and they wanted the DNA to prove he had done the other one too. Jeffreys worked through the night. What did the film show?
answer: One man had committed both crimes, and it was not Buckland.
choices: One man had committed both crimes, and it was not Buckland.
One man had committed both crimes, and that man was Buckland.
Two different men had done them, and one of them was Buckland.
Two different men had done them, and neither one was Buckland.
context: The very first use of DNA in a murder inquiry cleared the only suspect the police had -- a suspect who had confessed. They did not believe it: the test was repeated, then run a third time. One officer's reported reaction has stuck to the case -- the senior investigating officer is said to have muttered, 'One minute we got the guy, and the next we've got Jack shit.' Buckland, who had learning difficulties, had been in custody more than three months, and became the first person in the world exonerated by DNA. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation; grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys, which dates the exclusion to early 1987, so the exact month is uncertain)

question: Two linked murders near the Leicestershire village of Narborough had left police with no suspect they could prove. So they tried something no force anywhere had attempted: a letter to every man born between 1953 and 1970 who lived or worked in the villages, asking him to come and give blood. Centres in a school and a council office ran morning and evening sessions three days a week, and after eight months 5,511 men had given a sample. How many of the men asked said no?
answer: Just one of them.
choices: Just one of them.
Just over forty.
Nearly two hundred.
More than a thousand.
context: Every man had to bring proof of identity to the session. The screen -- locally nicknamed 'the blooding' -- was the first mass DNA screen anywhere in the world, and after all that it found nobody: 5,511 samples, one refusal, no match. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation; 'the blooding' is the title of Joseph Wambaugh's 1989 book on the case, cited at grokipedia.com/page/Colin_Pitchfork)

question: The Narborough blood screen found nobody, because the man police wanted never sat it. Colin Pitchfork, a 27-year-old cake decorator at a Leicester bakery, paid a workmate, Ian Kelly, 200 pounds to give blood in his name -- and every man at the test centre had to show proof of identity at the door. How did Pitchfork get Kelly past it?
answer: He put Kelly's photograph into his own passport.
choices: He put Kelly's photograph into his own passport.
He sent Kelly in with his younger brother's passport.
He had Kelly copy his signature onto a bakery works pass.
He gave Kelly a driving licence he had reported lost.
context: The Guardian published a formal correction on 8 June 2016 confirming the doctored passport was Pitchfork's own, not Kelly's -- many retellings get this backwards. The excuse Pitchfork gave Kelly was a lie: that he had already sat the test once as a favour to a friend with an indecent-exposure conviction and could not sit it again. Pitchfork drove Kelly to the school himself and waited outside. On 1 August 1987 Kelly let it slip over a pint with bakery workmates in the Clarendon in Leicester; six weeks later, on 18 September, one of the drinkers, Jackie Foggin, passed it to a local policeman, and both men were in custody within a day. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation and its published 8 June 2016 correction; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Pitchfork)

question: On 22 January 1988 Colin Pitchfork was convicted at Leicester Crown Court -- the first murder conviction in the world obtained through DNA, and the case that made the new technique famous in courtrooms everywhere. Yet no judge and no jury in that trial ever examined the DNA evidence. What kept it out?
answer: Pitchfork pleaded guilty, so the prosecution never leaned on it.
choices: Pitchfork pleaded guilty, so the prosecution never leaned on it.
The judge ruled the technique too new for a jury to weigh.
The defence and the prosecution agreed to leave it aside.
Jeffreys' laboratory films had been damaged before the trial.
context: The courtroom reputation of DNA evidence was built by a case that never argued it. Because Pitchfork pleaded guilty, the prosecution did not have to rely on the science and no court examined it -- the testing, the assumptions and the odds all went unchallenged. (theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation: 'Pitchfork's guilty pleas meant that DNA evidence was not relied upon by the prosecution, and this new science was not tested by the court')

question: Reputable accounts of the Pitchfork match quote the odds very differently: one in ten million at a single band position in one telling, one in 250 million in another, one in 700 million in a third -- the same test on the same man. That spread is not sloppy reporting; all three are quoting the same kind of figure. What does a DNA 'match' number actually state?
answer: How rare that band pattern is in the population it is compared against.
choices: How rare that band pattern is in the population it is compared against.
How likely it is that the suspect, and not someone else, left the sample.
How many people in the whole country carry the same repeat counts.
How rarely that band pattern turns up in the police database itself.
context: A match is a probability statement, not a photograph and not a certainty in the way an old ink fingerprint was sold as one. Change the database you compare against, or change what you assume about how many close relatives the suspect has, and the number moves with it -- which is why three careful sources can print three different odds for one man. Jeffreys' original multilocus method was estimated at one in a million million or lower, but that figure rests on the same kind of assumption. (grokipedia.com/page/Colin_Pitchfork, which reports the 1-in-10-million, 1-in-250-million and 1-in-700-million figures in different sections; grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys)

question: In November 2012 Lukis Anderson, a homeless man in San Jose, California, was charged with the murder of a millionaire and faced a possible death sentence: his DNA was under the victim's fingernails. Anderson had spent that entire night in a hospital bed under continuous supervision, and could not have been anywhere near the house. How did his DNA get there?
answer: The paramedics who had treated him that day answered the murder call.
choices: The paramedics who had treated him that day answered the murder call.
A blanket from the hospital ward he was on was taken to the house.
An officer who had searched him earlier searched the house as well.
The victim had picked up a bottle Anderson discarded that morning.
context: The same ambulance crew that had picked Anderson up earlier that day responded to the murder scene hours later, carrying his cells on their hands and equipment. He spent about five months in jail before anyone worked it out. Modern tests amplify DNA from a handful of cells, and that sensitivity created a brand-new way to be wrong: in a 2016 Journal of Forensic Sciences study, pairs of volunteers shook hands for two minutes and then one of them picked up a knife -- the other person's DNA turned up on 85% of the samples, and in five of them the person who had never touched the knife came out as the only or the major contributor. (scientificamerican.com/article/when-dna-implicates-the-innocent/; firelawblog.com/2013/06/28/dna-transfer-by-ems-personnel-leads-to-wrongful-arrest/; Cale et al., DOI 10.1111/1556-4029.12894)

question: By 2009 Britain's national DNA database held profiles taken from roughly 800,000 people who had been arrested and then never charged with anything. Alec Jeffreys, who invented the technique, said those people were being 'branded as criminals', and told the government: 'My genome is my property. It is not the state's.' What became of those profiles?
answer: A European court ruled the retention unlawful and most were destroyed.
choices: A European court ruled the retention unlawful and most were destroyed.
Parliament reviewed the retention rules twice and left them unchanged.
The Home Office kept them and added everyone arrested afterwards.
Police kept them on file but were barred from ever searching them.
context: The European Court of Human Rights ruled the blanket retention of innocent people's profiles unlawful, and the UK's Protection of Freedoms Act 2012 required most of them destroyed; Jeffreys backed the reform. The inventor of the tool spent years arguing publicly about what the state may keep of you -- an argument about power, not about whether the science works. (dailymail.com/news/article-1170130/Drop-innocent-national-database-says-DNA-pioneer.html, 'branded as criminals'; grokipedia.com/page/Alec_Jeffreys for the quotation, the ~800,000 figure and the ECtHR ruling; theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/jun/07/killer-dna-evidence-genetic-profiling-criminal-investigation)

question: A confession looks like the end of an argument. The Innocence Project has counted 375 people in the United States freed by DNA testing after a jury had already convicted them, having served an average of fourteen years each. In what share of those 375 cases had the innocent person confessed, or made statements against himself?
answer: Twenty-nine per cent of them.
choices: Twenty-nine per cent of them.
Three per cent of them.
Eleven per cent of them.
Sixty per cent of them.
context: Nearly three in ten. Those 375 exonerations add up to 5,284 years of imprisonment between them; the first was Gary Dotson's in 1989. Confessions are not the only courtroom evidence that failed: in 2015 the FBI and the Justice Department reviewed 268 trials in which FBI examiners had told juries that a crime-scene hair matched the defendant, and found erroneous statements favouring the prosecution in 257 of them -- 96%. Thirty-two of those defendants had been sentenced to death, and 26 of the 28 examiners involved had given flawed testimony or written flawed reports. Bite-mark comparison has been similarly discredited. Both were in routine use while DNA was still the new and doubted thing. (innocenceproject.org/dna-exonerations-in-the-united-states/; fbi.gov press release on microscopic hair analysis; washingtonpost.com, 18 April 2015)

question: Before 1982 the insulin keeping diabetics alive was scraped out of slaughterhouses: eight ounces of it could take two tons of pig parts. On 24 August 1978 a Genentech team led by David Goeddel announced real human insulin grown in a vat. What had they gotten to manufacture a human hormone?
answer: Escherichia coli, an ordinary gut bacterium
choices: Escherichia coli, an ordinary gut bacterium
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, brewer's yeast
Chinese hamster ovary cells, a mammalian line
Human pancreas cells, taken from donors
context: Bacteria fold the whole hormone badly, so Goeddel and Dennis Kleid chemically synthesized the genes for insulin's A chain and B chain SEPARATELY, expressed each in E. coli, purified both and joined them chemically into bioactive human insulin. A bacterium could read a human gene at all because the codebook of life is shared. The FDA approved the product in October 1982 and Eli Lilly sold it as Humulin, the first recombinant-DNA medicine; by the mid-1990s fermentation yields passed 10 grams per litre. Source: Grokipedia, 'Genentech' and 'History of genetic engineering'; Wikipedia, 'Insulin (medication)'.

question: Scurvy research stalled for over a century because nobody could give the disease to a laboratory animal: rats, mice and dogs stayed healthy on the worst diets going. In 1907 Axel Holst and Theodor Frolich finally produced it in one, and that animal is how Albert Szent-Gyorgyi went on to isolate vitamin C itself in 1928. Which animal was it?
answer: The guinea pig
choices: The guinea pig
The ferret
The rabbit
The hamster
context: Guinea pigs, unlike rats, cannot make their own vitamin C, and that is the only reason the model worked: Holst and Frolich had the first non-primate animal model of a human deficiency disease. Szent-Gyorgyi's curative experiments on scorbutic guinea pigs let him isolate and characterize ascorbic acid in 1928. James Lind had shown as early as 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, that citrus cured scurvy - he split twelve sick sailors into six pairs and gave each pair a different remedy, and only the citrus pair recovered fast - but nobody yet knew what was in the fruit. Source: Grokipedia, 'Scurvy', 'Guinea pig', 'Albert Szent-Gyorgyi', 'James Lind'.

question: Scurvy killed more sailors than combat did in the age of sail: teeth loosening, old wounds splitting open, men dying within sight of land. The ship's dog on the same rotten rations never got it. The difference is not the diet - a human simply has to get vitamin C from food. Why can't we make our own?
answer: The gene for the pathway's last enzyme is still in us, wrecked
choices: The gene for the pathway's last enzyme is still in us, wrecked
The gene was deleted from our line entirely, leaving no trace
The pathway is intact but a human liver runs it far too slowly
We break the vitamin down as fast as the liver can build it
context: The enzyme is L-gulonolactone oxidase, GULO, and it performs the last step of vitamin C synthesis. Nishikimi and colleagues cloned and mapped the dead human copy in 1994: it sits on chromosome 8p21 and is called GULOP - a pseudogene, meaning a gene still present in the genome but disabled. Compared with the working 12-exon rat gene, only about five of the twelve exon counterparts survive in ours; the rest are simply gone. Source: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'L-gulonolactone oxidase'; Nishikimi et al. 1994; Inai, Ohta & Nishikimi 2003.

question: Almost every mammal builds its own vitamin C in the liver. Humans cannot, and neither can any primate descended from the ancestor in which that ability broke, about 63 million years ago. But the primate order is older than the accident: one whole branch of it split away before the damage was done, and its members still manufacture their own supply. Which primates are they?
answer: The lemurs and lorises
choices: The lemurs and lorises
The gibbons and siamangs
The marmosets and tamarins
The baboons and mandrills
context: Lemurs and lorises belong to Strepsirrhini, which parted from Haplorhini - the branch holding monkeys, apes and us - at about the time the enzyme was lost. Strepsirrhines kept it. The ability has been lost more than once elsewhere on the tree, too: guinea pigs lost theirs separately within the last 20 million years, some bats have lost it while other bats have not, and in several passerine bird lines it appears to have been lost repeatedly and possibly regained. Same handicap, different scars. Source: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'L-gulonolactone oxidase'.

question: Cytochrome c is the small protein that passes electrons down the line inside every breathing thing, from baker's yeast to a blue whale, and it runs about 104 amino acids long. Line the human version up against yeast's and 44 of those 104 positions differ. Line the human version up against a chimpanzee's. How many differ?
answer: Zero of the 104
choices: Zero of the 104
Six of the 104
Nineteen of the 104
Thirty-one of the 104
context: The human and chimpanzee sequences are identical, letter for letter. A rhesus monkey differs from a human at one amino acid; baker's yeast at 44. Across more than thirty species tested in one study, 34 of the 104 positions were identical in every single species. Counts shift with the alignment method and published sources disagree on the exact figures, so the ORDER of the distances is the sturdier fact, not the numbers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cytochrome c'; Biology LibreTexts 19.1.1, 'Taxonomy'.

question: Cytochrome c does not work alone. It hands its electrons to a partner enzyme, cytochrome oxidase, and the two must fit each other like a key in a lock. Researchers took human cytochrome oxidase and, instead of its usual human partner, offered it the cytochrome c of a wheat plant - a different kingdom of life altogether. What came of the swap?
answer: The wheat protein worked, as did every other cross-species pairing tested
choices: The wheat protein worked, as did every other cross-species pairing tested
The wheat protein worked, but no other cross-species pairing tested did
The wheat protein worked only after chemists patched its docking surface
The wheat protein did not work, though closer relatives' versions all did
context: Human cytochrome oxidase reacted with wheat cytochrome c in vitro, and the same held true for every pair of species tested. A human enzyme accepted a plant's protein as its working partner across more than a billion years of separation - the same interchangeability that let a bacterium build a human hormone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cytochrome c'.

question: A retrovirus makes its living by pasting its own genes into the DNA of a cell it infects. Now and then it hits a sperm or an egg cell rather than an ordinary one, and the insert is then copied into every cell of every descendant forever, a passenger that can never be evicted. Reading the human genome, geneticists count roughly 98,000 such inherited viral elements and fragments. What share of your DNA is old virus?
answer: Somewhere between five and eight percent
choices: Somewhere between five and eight percent
Somewhere between one and two percent
Somewhere between thirty and forty percent
Somewhere between fifty and sixty percent
context: Published estimates for endogenous retroviruses run from about five to eight percent of the genome, with some estimates as low as three percent, across roughly 98,000 elements and fragments. About 90% of them are solo LTRs - stripped of every open reading frame, the burnt-out shell of a virus with the engine gone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Endogenous retrovirus'.

question: Gregor Mendel grew and crossed peas from 1856 to 1863 and worked out that inherited traits are carried by discrete, stable factors. He published the result in 1866 in the proceedings of the Brunn natural history society. What became of the paper?
answer: It sat unread for a generation, until three botanists hit on it in 1900
choices: It sat unread for a generation, until three botanists hit on it in 1900
It was reprinted in London in 1875 and fought over by breeders for a decade
It was answered in 1869 by a rival who held that peas were a special case
It was taught in German universities from 1872 as the new law of heredity
context: Mendel ran his pea experiments from 1856 to 1863 and published 'Versuche uber Pflanzenhybriden' in 1866, formulating segregation and independent assortment. Hugo de Vries in the Netherlands, Carl Correns in Germany and Erich von Tschermak in Austria each rediscovered it independently in 1900 - a full generation later, and eighteen years after Darwin's death. Darwin had published On the Origin of Species in 1859 with no account of heredity at all; the answer he needed was already sitting in print. Source: Grokipedia, 'Mendelian inheritance' and 'History of genetics'.

question: Roughly 98,000 pieces of ancient retrovirus sit in the human genome and almost all of them are inert wreckage, stripped of their genes and going nowhere. A few were not junked. One retroviral gene - the one for the envelope protein a virus normally uses to fuse itself into a cell - was kept and put to work, and the proteins it makes are called syncytins. What job does a virus's fusion gene do in a human body today?
answer: It fuses cells into the placental layer that feeds and shields a fetus
choices: It fuses cells into the placental layer that feeds and shields a fetus
It fuses muscle cells into the long fibres that pull on a limb
It joins bone-eating cells into the units that remodel a skeleton
It fuses the egg and the sperm together at the moment of conception
context: Intact retroviral envelope proteins called syncytins are responsible for the formation and function of the syncytiotrophoblast - the placental layer that handles nutrient exchange and separates the fetus from the mother's immune system. A gene an ancient virus carried in now does a job in every human pregnancy. Muscle-fibre fusion and bone-remodelling cell fusion are real processes too; they just are not this gene's work. Source: Wikipedia, 'Endogenous retrovirus'.

question: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans all have 24, and so did the ancestor we share with them. In 1991 J. W. IJdo and his colleagues sequenced two cloned stretches of DNA taken from band 2q13 of human chromosome 2. What did they find sitting there?
answer: Telomere repeats, the caps that finish a chromosome's ends, running head to head
choices: Telomere repeats, the caps that finish a chromosome's ends, running head to head
Centromere repeats, the alpha satellite a spindle grips, in two blocks side by side
Ribosomal gene clusters, the factories that build protein machinery, stacked in rows
Transposons, the sequences that copy themselves about, packed denser than anywhere else
context: IJdo's team cloned two allelic cosmids, c8.1 and c29B, each carrying two inverted arrays of the vertebrate telomere repeat head to head: 5'(TTAGGG)n-(CCCTAA)m 3'. Telomeres cap the ENDS of chromosomes; these were stranded mid-chromosome, at a band that sits near the base of the long arm. Human chromosome 2 also carries the remains of a second, dead centromere - the pinched waist a chromosome is hauled around by - further down the same arm, and a chromosome normally has exactly one. Jorge Yunis and Om Prakash had matched the banding patterns nine years earlier, in 1982, concluding that 18 of the 23 human pairs are virtually identical to the ancestral hominoid ones. Source: IJdo et al. 1991, PNAS 88:9051; Yunis & Prakash, Science 215:1525 (1982); Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Chromosome 2'.

question: Yeast and people last shared an ancestor roughly a billion years ago. In 2015 Kachroo, Marcotte and their colleagues ran a brutal test: they knocked out 414 yeast genes the cell cannot live without, one at a time, and dropped the matching HUMAN gene into each empty slot. Each yeast then either lived or died. How many of the 414 human genes kept the yeast alive?
answer: Nearly half of them
choices: Nearly half of them
About one in twenty
Only three of them
All but a handful
context: 47% of the 414 essential yeast genes could be successfully 'humanized', the human version keeping the yeast alive across roughly a billion years of divergence. Sequence similarity only partly predicted which ones would work: replaceability tracked MODULES, with genes serving the same cellular process tending to be similarly replaceable. Source: Kachroo et al., 'Systematic humanization of yeast genes reveals conserved functions and genetic modularity', Science 348:921 (2015).

question: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859 and the objections came fast, from every direction. In June 1867 the engineer Fleeming Jenkin reviewed the book anonymously in the North British Review; Darwin later said Jenkin had done him more service than any of his other critics, and answered him at length the following year. What had Jenkin argued?
answer: If a child comes out midway between its parents, a rare advantage is diluted away
choices: If a child comes out midway between its parents, a rare advantage is diluted away
If the Earth cooled from a molten ball, it is far too young for all this to have happened
If selection built the eye, the half-made eye it passed through would have been useless
If species truly change, the rocks should hold intermediates that nobody has dug up
context: Jenkin argued that if heredity blends, a rare beneficial variation is halved in every generation of interbreeding until it is swamped out of existence long before selection can build on it. Darwin conceded the point and offered pangenesis in 1868 - every cell of the body throwing off granules he called gemmules - specifically to give inheritance discrete particles that could resist swamping. He credited Jenkin in correspondence with more service than his other critics. The other three objections are real ones Darwin also faced. Source: Grokipedia, 'Fleeming Jenkin' and 'Blending inheritance'.

question: A retrovirus that pastes itself into a sperm or egg cell leaves its own DNA at one fixed address in the chromosome, and every descendant inherits it at that same address. In 2001 M. Barbulescu and colleagues checked one such insert - a HERV-K provirus, the virus's DNA settled in for good - at a single address in humans, chimpanzees, bonobos and gorillas. Three of the four carried it. Which one came up empty?
answer: The humans
choices: The humans
The chimpanzees
The bonobos
The gorillas
context: At the human address there was no provirus at all: the locus carries an intact, uninterrupted pre-integration site - the sequence as it reads before any virus lands. So the shared-insertion evidence is not a one-way story, because an absence can be checked against the branching order just as a presence can. For scale, of 211 HERV-W loci examined, 123 are shared by every catarrhine primate from humans to rhesus macaques, and calling a locus truly orthologous required a minimum of 500 matching nucleotides of flanking sequence on each side. Source: Barbulescu et al., Current Biology 2001; Grandi et al., PMC5775608.

question: In 1962 Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling noticed that the amino-acid differences in hemoglobin between two lineages pile up at a roughly steady rate - a molecular clock. It has since been caught running at odd speeds: tube-nosed seabirds tick at about half the rate of many other birds, turtles at an eighth the rate of small mammals or slower. But there is a deeper limit than uneven ticking, one that would still hold if every lineage ticked at exactly the same rate. What is it?
answer: Molecular data alone cannot supply an absolute date, only a count of changes
choices: Molecular data alone cannot supply an absolute date, only a count of changes
Molecular data alone cannot tell a selected change from one that merely drifted in
Molecular data alone cannot separate a true mutation from a sequencing error
Molecular data alone cannot be read from a lineage that left no living descendants
context: Molecular data alone contains no information on absolute times: a clock has to be calibrated against independent evidence, in practice a fossil date. Francisco J. Ayala flagged changing generation times as a further limiting factor, and 'relaxed' molecular clocks using Bayesian and MCMC methods were built to cope with the rate variation. Divergence DATES from a molecular clock are statistical inference, not direct evidence; the branching ORDER is far more secure than the numbers hung on it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Molecular clock'.

question: Every second the Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium. Weigh what comes out and it is about 4 million tonnes lighter than the hydrogen that went in. Where did those 4 million tonnes go?
answer: They left the Sun as sunlight.
choices: They left the Sun on the solar wind.
They left the Sun as sunlight.
They sank into the core as heavy ash.
They were carried off as loose neutrons.
context: The other 596 million tonnes are still there, as helium. Only the missing 0.71 percent leaves, and it leaves as light: four hydrogen nuclei weigh 4.03130 atomic mass units, the helium nucleus they make weighs 4.00268, and the 0.02862 that goes missing is the sunshine on your arm. Each such reaction pays out 26.7 million electron-volts, in a core running at about 15 million kelvin. Sources: Grokipedia 'Sun' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Sun); OpenStax Astronomy 2e 16.2 (https://openstax.org/books/astronomy-2e/pages/16-2-mass-energy-and-the-theory-of-relativity).

question: Lise Meitner, exiled from Berlin, spent Christmas 1938 at Kungalv in Sweden, puzzling over a letter from her old partner Otto Hahn.
