Her nephew Otto Frisch arrived; he took to the snowy woods on skis, she kept pace on foot, and they argued it out as they walked. Where did they do the calculation?
answer: On scraps of paper, on a tree trunk.
choices: On scraps of paper, on a tree trunk.
In the margins of Hahn's letter, on a ski.
On a notepad from Frisch's pack, on a rock.
In their heads, on paper that evening.
context: A Nobel-grade physics result, worked out sitting on a log in the snow. Meitner was 60 and had been driven out of her Berlin laboratory that summer; Frisch was visiting from Copenhagen. Accounts of the visit fix it to the Christmas 1938 holiday, though the exact day varies between tellings. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: On 19 December 1938 Otto Hahn wrote from Berlin to Lise Meitner with a result his chemistry could find but not explain: he and Fritz Strassmann had bombarded uranium with neutrons, and one substance that came out behaved chemically like barium. Why was barium the impossible answer?
answer: Barium is barely half the weight of uranium.
choices: Barium is heavier than uranium, not lighter.
Barium cannot be made radioactive at all.
Barium is a gas that should have boiled away.
Barium is barely half the weight of uranium.
context: Barium is element 56; uranium is element 92. The nucleus had not been chipped or nudged - it had come apart near the middle. Physicists at the time expected neutron bombardment to push uranium up the table into new heavy elements; Enrico Fermi and Irene Joliot-Curie had both read their own results that way. Hahn's chemistry was sound, but he had no physics to explain it, which is why he wrote to Meitner. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch had just explained what Otto Hahn's chemistry could not, and realised the process had no name. At Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, Frisch borrowed the word 'fission' from William Arnold, an American biologist down the corridor. What did that word already mean in Arnold's field?
answer: The splitting of one cell in two.
choices: The splitting of one cell in two.
The splitting of one chromosome in two.
The splitting of a DNA strand in two.
The splitting of a fertilised egg in two.
context: Arnold said 'fission.' The word for splitting atoms was borrowed straight out of cell biology, by a physicist who could not think of one himself. Frisch and Meitner mailed their papers to Nature on 16 January 1939; the note explaining the split appeared on 11 February. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: Two answers competed for what keeps the Sun alight before fusion was known. Coal that size would burn out in a few thousand years, so Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz proposed instead that the Sun is slowly collapsing under its own gravity, shrinking 40 metres a year - good for about 100 million years. Which science killed both?
answer: Geology - rock laid in liquid water 4 billion years ago.
choices: Astronomy - stars like the Sun alight for 10 billion years.
Biology - fossil beds recording 500 million years of life.
Geology - rock laid in liquid water 4 billion years ago.
Physics - radium's heat warming the Earth for billions of years.
context: The rocks demanded a Sun billions of years old, and neither coal nor collapse could supply one. The squeeze troubled Charles Darwin badly: natural selection needed the longer clock too, and physics was refusing to give it. Both sides were arguing honestly from good arithmetic; the missing piece was a power source nobody had imagined yet. Source: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 16.1 'Sources of Sunshine: Thermal and Gravitational Energy' (https://openstax.org/books/astronomy-2e/pages/16-1-sources-of-sunshine-thermal-and-gravitational-energy).

question: On the tree trunk at Kungalv, Lise Meitner did the one sum that mattered: she weighed the two fragments against the uranium nucleus they had come from. The gap was absurdly small - about one-fifth the mass of a single proton. Put through E=mc2, what did that one-fifth of a proton come out as?
answer: About 200 million electron-volts, every split.
choices: About 200 thousand electron-volts, every split.
About 200 million electron-volts, every split.
About 27 million electron-volts, every split.
About 3 billion electron-volts, every split.
context: You can check her arithmetic yourself: a proton is 938 million electron-volts of mass, and 200 divided by 938 is 0.21 - one-fifth, exactly as she said. The picture she and Frisch used was the liquid-drop model, the nucleus as a wobbling charged droplet held by surface tension until the protons' mutual shoving wins and it pinches in two. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: Fission a whole tonne of uranium-235 and the ash left behind weighs 999 kilograms: a full kilogram of metal has left as energy, and a good enough scale would in principle catch it missing. Chemistry loses mass the same way, only far less of it. Burn a thousand tonnes of coal - how much mass goes missing there?
answer: About half a gram.
choices: About half a milligram.
About half a kilogram.
About half a gram.
About fifty kilograms.
context: 0.53 grams, from a thousand tonnes. This is why chemists spent three centuries weighing reactions and concluded that mass is exactly conserved - they were wrong, but by an amount no balance on Earth could see. Sources: radioactivity.eu.com 'Nuclear energy: 200 million electronvolts!' (https://radioactivity.eu.com/articles/nuclearenergy/fission_energy); Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: In 1932 John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton fired protons at lithium and split it into two alpha particles - the first time anyone weighed E=mc2 on a laboratory bench. Splitting the lithium was only half the test. The equation turns a shortfall in weight into an energy, so the weights of the nuclei going in and coming out had to be known in advance, and known precisely. Whose measurements supplied them?
answer: Francis Aston's, from his mass spectrograph.
choices: J.J. Thomson's, from his positive-ray plates.
Francis Aston's, from his mass spectrograph.
Arthur Dempster's, from his mass spectrometer.
Theodore Richards's, from his atomic weights.
context: Aston's numbers said 0.0186 atomic mass units had gone missing in the split, which E=mc2 turns into 17.3 million electron-volts. The alpha particles came out carrying 17.2. Agreement to within about half a percent, in 1932 - and a Nobel Prize for Cockcroft and Walton in 1951. A prediction is only a test if the number exists before the experiment runs. Source: Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: Otto Frisch went back to Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen in January 1939 to check his aunt's arithmetic against an instrument. His problem: the uranium sample was also throwing out alpha particles by the million, drowning the rare splits in a constant crackle of counts. How did Frisch arrange to see only the splits?
answer: He set the detector's threshold above any alpha pulse.
choices: He shielded the chamber in lead and counted the drop.
He chilled the chamber until the alpha activity fell.
He compared uranium against thorium in the same chamber.
He set the detector's threshold above any alpha pulse.
context: A fission fragment carries so much more energy than an alpha particle that its pulse is in a different league - so Frisch simply set the bar where nothing but a split could clear it. On 13 January 1939 the pulses came through at the size his aunt's scrap of paper had predicted. The arithmetic survived contact with an instrument. Sources: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission); Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner).

question: The Sun cashes in mass by sticking small nuclei together; a reactor cashes in mass by breaking big ones apart. Opposite operations, one equation - because how tightly a nucleus grips each of its own particles climbs as nuclei get bigger, reaches a peak of about 8.8 million electron-volts per particle, and then falls away again. Which nucleus sits at that peak?
answer: Iron-56.
choices: Carbon-12.
Lead-208.
Iron-56.
Silicon-28.
context: That grip is called binding energy per nucleon, and its single peak at iron-56 decides everything: below iron, sticking nuclei together pays; above iron, breaking them apart pays. Nothing on either side of the peak can profit by going the other way. Typical nuclei run a mass shortfall of about 0.9 percent against their loose parts. Source: Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, working in Berlin, pulled barium out of neutron-bombarded uranium and could not say why it was there. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, both driven into exile, worked out what had happened and sent the explanation to Nature in January 1939. The Nobel committee then ruled on who had discovered fission. How did it rule?
answer: It gave the Chemistry prize to Otto Hahn alone.
choices: It gave the Chemistry prize to Otto Hahn alone.
It split the Chemistry prize between Hahn and Strassmann.
It gave the Physics prize to Meitner and Frisch.
It split the Physics prize between Hahn and Meitner.
context: The 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Otto Hahn alone, 'for his discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei.' Meitner had supplied the physics that explained the barium and Frisch had measured the energy release at the bench; the committee named neither. The paper trail: Hahn and Strassmann submitted theirs on 22 December 1938 and it appeared on 6 January 1939; Meitner and Frisch mailed theirs to Nature on 16 January, their note ran on 11 February 1939, and Frisch's measurement followed on 18 February. Sources: Grokipedia 'Lise Meitner' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Lise_Meitner); Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_nuclear_fission).

question: A hospital PET scanner is a ring of crystals watching a patient who has been given a fluorine-18 tracer. The tracer sends out positrons; each positron meets an electron somewhere in the tissue, and two photons leave that spot back to back. Every photon of every pair reads 511 thousand electron-volts, and never any other value. Why 511?
answer: It is the electron's own mass, written as energy.
choices: It is the electron's own mass, written as energy.
It is the gamma ray fluorine-18 gives off as it decays.
It is the smallest photon energy the vacuum permits.
It is the energy the crystal ring is built to catch.
context: Total conversion - 100 percent of the mass gone, no ash, no residue. An electron is 511 keV of mass; a positron is another 511; annihilate the pair and you get 1.022 MeV of light and nothing else. A PET scanner is a machine built to catch exactly that pair: a fluorine-18 tracer emits a positron that travels about 0.6 mm through tissue before it finds an electron, and a ring of crystals watches for two 511 keV photons hitting opposite detectors within about 6 to 12 nanoseconds. The annihilation happened somewhere on the line joining them. Sources: Grokipedia 'Positron emission tomography' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Positron_emission_tomography); Grokipedia 'Mass-energy equivalence' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Mass%E2%80%93energy_equivalence).

question: On Christmas Eve 1968, three astronauts came around the far side of the Moon on Apollo 8's fourth orbit -- pointed carefully at the lunar surface for a mapping run. Their cameras were NOT aimed at the blue-and-white world that suddenly swung up over the horizon. One of them grabbed a fresh magazine of 70 mm colour film in a hurry and got frame AS08-14-2383. Which astronaut took the shot?
answer: William Anders
choices: William Anders
Frank Borman
James Lovell
Michael Collins
context: Frank Borman was the commander; James Lovell was the CMP; Anders was the LMP and mission photographer. Michael Collins flew on Apollo 11, not 8. On Apollo 8 the flight plan had them shooting the lunar surface, not Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise.

question: In the Earthrise frame it looks as if Earth is climbing above a still lunar horizon. It isn't -- something else is doing the moving. What actually carried Earth across the crew's window during Apollo 8?
answer: The command module's own orbital motion and attitude
choices: The command module's own orbital motion and attitude
The Moon rotating under the spacecraft
Earth's own libration wobble
A tilt in the lunar rotational axis
context: The Moon turns once per lunar month -- far too slow to lift Earth visibly in seconds. Libration is a small wobble of the Moon (not of Earth); the lunar axis tilt is small and irrelevant here. Apollo 8's own sweep around the Moon carried the view across the horizon. From a fixed spot on the near side, Earth does not rise or set at all -- only a moving spacecraft gets an Earthrise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise.

question: For half a century most books told it this way: Frank Borman took the first black-and-white frame, and only THEN did Anders scramble for colour film and get the famous shot. In 2018 NASA Goddard visualiser Ernie Wright rebuilt the whole scene from the onboard voice tape and the spacecraft's motion. What did his reconstruction actually show?
answer: Anders took all three frames
choices: Anders took all three frames
Lovell had taken the first frame
Borman took two of the three frames
The first frame was exposed after Earth was already up
context: Wright matched the voice loop (Anders spotting Earth, asking Lovell to hand him colour film, exposing the frames) to the spacecraft attitude data. Frank Borman himself later publicly accepted the correction -- even the eyewitnesses had been wrong until the record was re-derived from data. Historian Andrew Chaikin helped popularise the analysis. Source: smithsonianmag.com/who-took-legendary-earthrise-photo-apollo-8; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthrise.

question: The Earthrise print that hangs on classroom walls shows Earth rising 'up' over a level grey landscape. That composition is not the frame as Anders exposed it -- NASA and the press adjusted it before releasing it. What was done to the original?
answer: It was rotated about 90 degrees clockwise
choices: It was rotated about 90 degrees clockwise
It was flipped left-to-right
It was colourised from black-and-white
It was stitched together from two separate exposures
context: In the raw frame the lunar horizon runs VERTICALLY down the side and Earth sits off to the LEFT -- that is what Anders actually saw through the window. Turning the print 90 degrees clockwise gave a familiar 'sunrise' composition. The image was genuine colour Ektachrome, not colourised. Source: planetary.org/space-images/earthrise.

question: Babylonian astronomers, staring at centuries of clay-tablet eclipse records, pulled out a hidden rhythm: if you know one eclipse, you know another one, one particular stretch of time later. That cycle was named the saros. How long is it?
answer: about 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours
choices: about 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours
about 76 years, one Halley's Comet lap
about 100 years, one long human life
about 12 years, one Jupiter orbit
context: The saros is exactly 223 synodic months, which works out to roughly 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours. After that stretch the Sun, Earth, and Moon return to almost exactly the same geometry, and a very similar eclipse repeats. Babylonian astronomers used it as a genuine prediction tool. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saros_(astronomy) ; https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-news/how-did-the-ancients-predicted-eclipses-the-saros-cycle/

question: The saros brings back nearly the same Sun-Earth-Moon geometry, but each eclipse in the same series lands somewhere different on Earth than the one before. Where does the NEXT eclipse in a saros series fall relative to the one you just saw?
answer: it lands about a third of the way around the world westward
choices: it lands about a third of the way around the world westward
it lands at the same city, but starts about 8 hours later
it lands at Earth's opposite pole from the previous one
it fails to reach the ground and passes entirely in space
context: The saros is 223 synodic months, but that works out to 18 years, 11 days AND 8 hours -- and 8 hours is a third of a day, so Earth has spun an extra 120 degrees when the geometry lines back up. Each successive eclipse in the same saros lands about 120 degrees westward. Stack three saroses -- an interval called the exeligmos, about 54 years and 33 days -- and the shadow comes back near the same longitude. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saros_(astronomy) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeligmos

question: The Moon reaches the new-moon position roughly every 29.5 days, yet solar eclipses only occur a couple of times a year, not every month. What geometric fact of the Moon's orbit is responsible?
answer: its orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to the ecliptic
choices: its orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to the ecliptic
its orbit is a near-perfect circle instead of an ellipse
its orbit runs backwards compared to Earth's spin
its orbit passes directly over the Earth's poles
context: The Moon's orbit is inclined about 5.145 degrees to the ecliptic. At most new moons the Moon passes above or below the Sun's disk as seen from Earth. Only when a new moon falls near one of the two nodes -- the two points where the Moon's tilted orbit crosses Earth's -- can its shadow actually reach the ground. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit_of_the_Moon ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclipse_season

question: The Moon's disc from Earth looks almost exactly the same size as the Sun's -- which is why totality is a knife-edge and why sometimes an eclipse leaves a bright ring of Sun uncovered instead. Two numbers about the Sun and the Moon happen to match with remarkable precision, making the coincidence work. Which pair?
answer: the Sun is ~400 times wider AND ~400 times farther than the Moon
choices: the Sun is ~400 times wider AND ~400 times farther than the Moon
the Sun is 100 times wider AND 100 times more massive than the Moon
the Sun is 10 times hotter AND 10 times brighter than the Moon
the Sun is a billion times wider AND a billion times older than the Moon
context: The Sun is roughly 400 times wider than the Moon and, by pure accident, roughly 400 times farther from Earth, so the two look almost the same size in the sky. When the Moon is near the far end of its slightly elliptical orbit it looks too small to cover the Sun entirely, and totality becomes an annular ('ring') eclipse. No other moon in the solar system pulls off this trick. Sources: https://earthsky.org/earth/total-solar-eclipses-are-a-coincidence/ ; https://theconversation.com/explainer-what-is-a-solar-eclipse-33019

question: The Apollo 11, 14, and 15 astronauts left corner-cube arrays sitting on the lunar surface. Observatories on Earth still fire laser pulses at them and time the round-trip, now to the millimetre. That decades-long record shows one thing about the Moon that has an interesting consequence for eclipses. What?
answer: the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm each year
choices: the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm each year
the Moon is falling closer by about 3.8 cm each year
the Moon's orbit is tightening into a perfect circle
the Moon rotates on its axis faster than once thought
context: Lunar laser ranging (best current value about 3.83 cm per year) shows the Moon slowly retreating -- a consequence of ocean tides on Earth transferring rotational momentum. Total eclipses therefore have an expiry date: eventually the Moon will look too small in the sky to ever cover the Sun completely, and only annular eclipses will remain. Meanwhile a kid with a clock and NASA's published eclipse tables can time contact to the second and check the prediction against the sky personally. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_Ranging_Retroreflector ; https://earthsky.org/tonight/wayward-moon-receding-from-earth/

question: Arthur Eddington, a Cambridge astronomer and a Quaker, refused on religious grounds to fight in the First World War. In July 1918 a tribunal that had already refused to renew his exemption gave him one last hearing, and he walked out free. On what condition?
answer: That he lead an eclipse expedition the following year
choices: That he lead an eclipse expedition the following year
That he compute tables for the Nautical Almanac
That he join a magnetic survey of the northern isles
That he take farm work of national importance
context: The letter that did it came from Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal, who told the tribunal that the total eclipse of 29 May 1919 was of exceptional importance and that Eddington was the right man to lead the British expedition. So the Quaker who would not fight Germans was released on the condition that he go and test a German's theory, six months after the armistice. Sources: Scientific American, 'The 1919 Solar Eclipse and General Relativity's First Major Triumph'; Grokipedia 'Arthur Eddington'.

question: The Royal Greenwich Observatory sent two parties across the Atlantic for the eclipse of 29 May 1919. Arthur Eddington drew Principe, an island in the Gulf of Guinea, and took one companion: Edwin Cottingham, who was no astronomer at all. What was Cottingham's trade?
answer: A clockmaker, to keep the machinery running
choices: A clockmaker, to keep the machinery running
A carpenter, to repair the telescope mountings
A photographer, to develop the plates by night
A surveyor, to fix the site's exact longitude
context: Edwin Turner Cottingham was a clockmaker, brought along because the instruments ran on clock drives that had to track the sky exactly while a plate was exposed. The other party, Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin, went to Sobral in northeastern Brazil. Eddington and Cottingham left England on 8 March 1919 aboard the SS Anselm and reached Principe on 23 April, setting up at Roca Sundy, a cocoa plantation about 500 feet above the sea. Before they sailed, Cottingham is said to have asked Frank Dyson what it would mean if they measured twice Einstein's predicted deflection; Dyson answered, 'Then Eddington will go mad, and you will have to come home alone.' That exchange is reported secondhand. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Royal Observatory Greenwich; Smithsonian Magazine.

question: Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal, proposed the starlight test in 1917 and picked his date years ahead. Catching a bend of under two seconds of arc needs a crowd of stars standing close beside the covered Sun, and most eclipses put the Sun in a thin patch of sky. Where would the eclipsed Sun stand on 29 May 1919?
answer: Inside the Hyades, a cluster in Taurus
choices: Inside the Hyades, a cluster in Taurus
Inside the Pleiades, a cluster in Taurus
Inside the Beehive, a cluster in Cancer
Inside the Butterfly, a cluster in Scorpius
context: The Sun sits in Taurus in late May, and on 29 May 1919 it stood in the Hyades, an unusually rich field of BRIGHT stars, promising many measurable points close to the Sun's edge instead of the usual handful. The Pleiades lie in Taurus too, a few degrees off the Sun's yearly path; that day the Sun was among the Hyades. Totality also ran up to 6 minutes 51 seconds along the track, one of the longest of the twentieth century. Dyson had proposed the test in 1917 after failing to find any displacement at all on plates from the eclipse of 1905. Sources: Wikipedia 'Solar eclipse of May 29, 1919'; Royal Observatory Greenwich.

question: In 1911 Albert Einstein published a first prediction for the bending of starlight past the Sun - about 0.87 seconds of arc - worked out before he had finished general relativity. In November 1915, with the full theory, he recomputed it and got 1.75, exactly twice as much. The 1911 figure was worse than merely wrong. What was the trouble with 0.87?
answer: It was exactly what Newton's own mechanics gave
choices: It was exactly what Newton's own mechanics gave
It was too small for the cameras of that decade
It held only near the Sun's poles, not its equator
It assumed the ray crossed the Sun's atmosphere
context: Treat light as fast particles with weight, falling under Newtonian gravity, and you get a bend of roughly 0.87 seconds of arc. The German mathematician Johann Georg von Soldner had computed a figure of about this size in 1801, more than a century before Einstein - so Einstein's own first answer was Newton's answer, and any measurement of it would have decided nothing. Only the completed field equations of November 1915, which add the curvature of space itself to the falling, doubled the figure and made an eclipse able to choose between three worlds: no bend at all, the Newtonian half-value, or Einstein's. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Wikipedia 'Eddington experiment'; T. Sauer, 'Soldner, Einstein, Gravitational Light Deflection and Factors of Two', Annalen der Physik (2021).

question: In 1919 British astronomers photographed a total eclipse to see whether the Sun bends starlight passing close by. The test came down to two photographs of one star field: one during totality, with the eclipsed Sun among those stars, and one at night, with the Sun far away. On the eclipse plate the stars were neither missing nor dimmed - each sat a little off the spot it held on the night plate. Which way had they moved?
answer: Outward, away from the Sun's centre
choices: Outward, away from the Sun's centre
Inward, toward the Sun's centre
All one way, as if the field had slid
Apart, the whole group spread wider
context: Light passing the Sun bends TOWARD it, so the star it came from appears shoved the other way - outward, away from where it really sits. The shift was biggest for stars closest to the Sun's edge and fell off with distance, and it was that falloff, not any single star, that the least-squares fit actually measured. The other three answers are not silly: a uniform slide would mean a mis-set plate, and a general spreading would mean the plate scale had changed with temperature. Those were exactly the objections raised against the result. Source: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: Erwin Finlay-Freundlich, a young Berlin astronomer, meant to photograph the total eclipse of 21 August 1914 from the Crimea and settle Einstein's claim that the Sun bends starlight. His own observatory director refused to pay for the expedition, so Einstein went out and found the money himself. Who put it up?
answer: Gustav Krupp, an arms and steel magnate
choices: Gustav Krupp, an arms and steel magnate
Carl Duisberg, a dye and drug magnate
Emil Rathenau, an electrical magnate
Robert Bosch, a motor-parts magnate
context: Freundlich's own observatory director had refused to pay for the trip, so Einstein found the money from the arms manufacturer Gustav Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach. Weeks later Krupp's country was at war with Freundlich's host country: he was interned as an enemy alien, his instruments were seized, and he was freed only in a prisoner exchange, leaving them behind. Sources differ on the exact dates. The failure saved Einstein - at that moment his published prediction was still the 1911 value, and a successful 1914 measurement would have contradicted him. Sources: Wikipedia 'Erwin Finlay-Freundlich'; Encyclopedia.com 'Erwin Finlay Freundlich'; St Andrews eclipse-history project.

question: At Sobral in Brazil a British party photographed the eclipse of 29 May 1919 to test whether the Sun bends starlight. Their main instrument was a 13-inch astrographic telescope - a camera for photographing star fields - focused the night before. As the tropical morning heated up, its steel tube and mirror expanded, and during totality the telescope sat out of focus; its nineteen plates came back with stars like smudges rather than points. The Sobral number that carried the day came from somewhere else. From what?
answer: A 4-inch lens borrowed from a Jesuit astronomer
choices: A 4-inch lens borrowed from a Jesuit astronomer
A 6-inch refractor lent by a Brazilian observatory
A spare astrograph shipped out from Greenwich
A wide-field camera built during the voyage
context: The 4-inch lens had been lent by Father Aloysius Cortie and packed almost as an afterthought. Seven of its plates were usable and gave a deflection at the Sun's edge of 1.98 seconds of arc; Eddington's Principe plates gave 1.61. Both sit near Einstein's figure and far above the Newtonian one - but the error bars were large. Stephen Hawking later remarked that the size of the error was about the size of the effect being measured, so the honest claim is not that the eclipse proved relativity; it is that the half-size Newtonian rival was excluded, and precision came only later. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Royal Observatory Greenwich; St Andrews eclipse-history project.

question: At Sobral in Brazil the main instrument for the eclipse of 29 May 1919 was a big astrographic telescope, a camera built for photographing star fields. It lost focus during totality, and its nineteen plates came back with smeared stars. Charles Davidson and Andrew Crommelin, the Greenwich astronomers who had made the exposures, did not sail for home: they stayed in Brazil until 22 July. What were they staying for?
answer: To re-shoot the same field with the same telescope in the same spot, so its distortion would cancel
choices: To re-shoot the same field with the same telescope in the same spot, so its distortion would cancel
To have the astrograph's mirror reground at an observatory in Rio, so it would hold its focus
To measure the smeared plates in Brazil, so the long voyage home could not disturb them further
To photograph a second eclipse crossing Brazil later that year, so the trip would not be wasted
context: An eclipse plate proves nothing on its own: the shift only shows up when you set it beside plates of the same stars taken with the Sun elsewhere in the sky. Davidson and Crommelin returned to Sobral on 9 July and re-photographed that star field at night, from 11 to 18 July, with the same instrument standing on the same ground - so that whatever distortion the optics introduced would appear in BOTH sets of plates and cancel out in the comparison. That is what good practice looks like when you suspect your own instrument. Eddington had no such luxury: his Principe plates had to be compared against check plates taken at Oxford, a weaker comparison. Sources: St Andrews eclipse-history project; Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: In 1980 the philosophers of science John Earman and Clark Glymour charged Eddington's team with confirmation bias. Of the three sets of 1919 eclipse photographs, the one set that came out near the Newtonian half-value - about 0.93 seconds of arc - was the set thrown away, and the two that came out near Einstein's were the ones published. Men who wanted Einstein to be right, they said, had discarded the data that said otherwise. The charge was answered from the surviving 1919 material. How?
answer: The plates were re-measured by Harvey and Clements, and the discarded set no longer favoured Newton
choices: The plates were re-measured by Harvey and Clements, and the discarded set no longer favoured Newton
The logbook was re-read by Crommelin's biographers, and it listed those plates as unusable
The referee reports were re-read by historians, and they had urged that the set be dropped
The check plates were re-measured by Woolley's staff, and they showed the astrograph had shifted
context: In 1979 the original 1919 plates were pulled out of storage at the Royal Greenwich Observatory. Geoffrey Harvey and E. D. Clements re-measured the star positions on a modern plate-measuring machine, and Andrew Murray re-reduced the data with new astrometric software. The 4-inch plates came out at 1.90 plus-or-minus 0.11 seconds of arc - and the discarded astrograph plates at 1.55 plus-or-minus 0.34, near Einstein's value rather than Newton's. The exclusion had been justified by a real, measurable instrument fault, not by wishful thinking. That re-measurement was already finished in 1979, the year before Earman and Glymour published; Daniel Kennefick set the two side by side in Physics Today in 2009. This is the honest shape of the story: the accusation was serious, and it was answered by going back to the evidence. Sources: Kennefick, 'Testing relativity from the 1919 eclipse - a question of bias', Physics Today (2009); Kennefick, 'Not Only Because of Theory', arXiv:0709.0685.

question: The bias story has Arthur Eddington, who believed in general relativity, choosing which Sobral plates to keep. Daniel Kennefick went back to the surviving records of the Sobral data reduction to see who had actually done the measuring and the arithmetic. Whose hand fills the notebooks?
answer: Frank Dyson's, and Eddington learned the Sobral numbers by letter
choices: Frank Dyson's, and Eddington learned the Sobral numbers by letter
Andrew Crommelin's, with Dyson signing the results at the end
Eddington's, though only after a second measurer had checked
Charles Davidson's, with the plates re-measured later at Oxford
context: Dyson's handwriting runs all through the Sobral reduction notes and Eddington's does not; Eddington first heard the Sobral results in a letter Dyson sent him. And Dyson was the sceptic of the pair - he described the outcome as contrary to his expectations. The man who supposedly wanted the answer was not the man who chose the data. Sources: Kennefick, Physics Today (2009); Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: The 1919 plates carried error bars about as large as the effect they were measuring. The number was pinned down at the next good eclipse: 21 September 1922, a camp at Wallal on the coast of Western Australia, a cloudless sky, more than a hundred stars photographed around the covered Sun, and a deflection of 1.72 seconds of arc. Whose party made that measurement?
answer: William Campbell's party from Lick Observatory
choices: William Campbell's party from Lick Observatory
Charles Perrine's party from Cordoba Observatory
John Evershed's party from Kodaikanal Observatory
Andrew Crommelin's party from Greenwich Observatory
context: Campbell and Robert Trumpler worked with a 16-inch instrument at Wallal and got 1.72 plus-or-minus 0.11 seconds of arc from over a hundred stars - far more stars than 1919 managed, under a clear sky, with no ruined telescope. Campbell had been openly sceptical of relativity beforehand and accepted the finding once the plates were measured. A careful person should say the deflection was nailed down HERE, in 1922, by an independent team that expected a different answer - not in 1919. Sources: Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'; Grokipedia 'Tests of general relativity'.

question: Eddington needed a total eclipse because the Sun's glare drowns any star close enough to its edge for the bend to show. The same deflection is now measured without waiting for an eclipse at all, and pinned far tighter than any photographic plate managed. What replaced the eclipse?
answer: Radio telescopes tracking quasars as the Sun drifts past them
choices: Radio telescopes tracking quasars as the Sun drifts past them
Space telescopes observing from above the atmosphere's blur
Coronagraphs that mask the Sun's disc inside the telescope
Infrared cameras that see stars through the solar glare
context: Very Long Baseline Interferometry watches compact quasars as the Sun passes near them in the sky. Radio waves are not drowned by the Sun's light, so there is no eclipse to chase, no cloud to fear, and no photographic plate to smudge. Analyses of quasar observations in the early 2000s confirmed the predicted deflection to within 0.03 percent; a 2004 analysis of roughly two million observations of 541 radio sources reached 0.1 percent, and a 2005 Very Long Baseline Array experiment on four quasars gave the curvature parameter as 0.9998 plus-or-minus 0.0003. Sources: Grokipedia 'Tests of general relativity'; Grokipedia 'Eddington experiment'.

question: In 1936 Albert Einstein published a short paper in Science, written reluctantly after a Czech amateur named Rudi Mandl pestered him for months, showing that a star lying almost exactly behind a nearer star would have its light bent into a ring or double image. What did Einstein say in that paper about the chance of ever seeing it?
answer: That it was so improbable no one would ever observe it
choices: That it was so improbable no one would ever observe it
That the next total solar eclipse would confirm it decisively
That Palomar's coming 200-inch telescope would find one easily
That radio telescopes might catch it long before optical ones did
context: Einstein's note ('Lens-Like Action of a Star by the Deviation of Light in the Gravitational Field', Science 84, 506) closes with the line that 'there is no great chance of observing this phenomenon'. In a letter to the Science editor he added that the note had little value but he was submitting it to satisfy Mr Mandl. The alignment of two stars needed for a visible ring seemed effectively impossible.

question: Within a year of Einstein's pessimistic 1936 paper, the Caltech astronomer Fritz Zwicky wrote a two-page reply in Physical Review pointing out exactly what Einstein had missed. What did Zwicky, in that 1937 note, point to as the ideal gravitational lens?
answer: Entire galaxies, which he called extragalactic nebulae
choices: Entire galaxies, which he called extragalactic nebulae
Close binary stars, whose combined mass would double the deflection
Globular clusters, whose stars share a common velocity
The Milky Way's own bulge, acting on any distant quasar
context: Zwicky's 1937 notes in Physical Review (vol. 51, pp. 290 and 679) argued that a galaxy would lens far more often and far more strongly than any star, and -- his real punchline -- that measuring the bending of background light would let astronomers weigh the lensing galaxy directly, mass included, whether that mass shone or not. The idea was ignored for forty years. Zwicky died in 1974, five years too early to see it confirmed.

question: In 1979 Dennis Walsh, Robert Carswell and Ray Weymann were using the 2.1-metre telescope at Kitt Peak to look at a pair of very close quasars called Q0957+561, and they made the discovery that turned Einstein's toy calculation into a working instrument. What made them realise the pair was actually ONE quasar seen twice, rather than a genuine physical pair?
answer: The two objects had essentially identical optical spectra and matching redshifts
choices: The two objects had essentially identical optical spectra and matching redshifts
The pair was flickering exactly in phase, minute by minute, on both telescopes
One image sat inside the disc of a foreground galaxy at the same distance
A radio survey found no counterparts, which no real quasar pair could explain
context: Two real quasars, being separate objects, would show at least small differences in their spectra and redshifts. Walsh's pair matched to within measurement error at z = 1.41 -- one source, split around an intervening giant elliptical galaxy at z = 0.36. Q0957+561 (the 'Twin Quasar') was the first confirmed gravitational lens. Today astronomers use exactly Zwicky's trick to map dark matter: where the background sky bends and no visible mass is present, invisible mass has to be.

question: In 1887 Heinrich Hertz was proving that Maxwell's electromagnetic waves were real by making sparks jump across a gap. When ultraviolet light from one spark happened to fall on the metal knobs of the second gap, what did that second spark do?
answer: It jumped the gap far more readily
choices: It jumped the gap far more readily
It shrank unless the gap was darkened
It turned from blue-white to deep red
It wandered to the rim of the knob
context: Hertz wrote the effect down, did not measure it and did not try to explain it, and went straight back to his waves - the puzzle then sat for eighteen years. Presenting Einstein's Nobel Prize in 1922, Svante Arrhenius described exactly what Hertz had seen: an electrical spark between two spheres 'does so more readily if its path is illuminated with the light from another electrical discharge.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'; Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 award ceremony speech (S. Arrhenius, 10 December 1922), nobelprize.org.

question: In 1888 Wilhelm Hallwachs stood a clean zinc plate on an insulating stand, wired it to a gold-leaf electroscope so that the two leaves hung apart, and put a NEGATIVE charge on the plate. Then he shone ultraviolet light on the zinc. What did the leaves do?
answer: They fell shut as the charge drained away
choices: They fell shut as the charge drained away
They spread even further apart
They held still until the lamp was moved
They fluttered in time with the lamp
context: Now charge the same plate POSITIVELY and the ultraviolet does the opposite - the leaves spread FURTHER apart, because the plate keeps losing negative charge and grows more positive still. That asymmetry is the whole clue: light is knocking negative things out of the metal. This is a demo a school can still run with a zinc plate, a bit of sandpaper, an electroscope and a UV lamp. Between 1888 and 1891 the Russian physicist Alexander Stoletov took the effect apart with proper instruments and built the first photoelectric cell out of it - an ancestor of the solar cell. Sources: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 award ceremony speech, nobelprize.org; Wikipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'; Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'.

question: In 1902 Philipp Lenard sealed a light-sensitive metal plate in a pumped-out glass tube, faced it with a collector, and added a reverse voltage he could crank up until even the fastest escaping electrons fell short - which told him how fast they flew. Then he lit the plate with one lamp, turned ever brighter. What did the extra brightness change?
answer: The number of electrons leaving, but never their top speed
choices: The number of electrons leaving, but never their top speed
The top speed of the electrons, but never their number
Both the number leaving and their top speed, in step
Neither, until the lamp's colour was changed as well
context: The reversal in one line: brightness sets HOW MANY electrons come out; frequency - the colour - sets HOW FAST. A wave should do exactly the opposite, since cranking up a wave ought to shove harder. That is why a feeble blue lamp can free electrons from a metal a blazing red lamp cannot touch. The reverse voltage that just turns back the fastest electron has a name worth keeping - the stopping voltage - and it becomes the key measurement later in this story. Source: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect'.

question: In late May 1905 Albert Einstein wrote to his friend Conrad Habicht about four papers he had in hand that year: one on radiation and the energy properties of light, one on the size of atoms, one on the jittering of tiny particles in water, and an electrodynamics of moving bodies - the paper the world now calls special relativity. Einstein called exactly one of the four 'very revolutionary'. Which one?
answer: The one on radiation and light
choices: The one on radiation and light
The one on the size of atoms
The one on jittering particles
The one on moving bodies
context: Not relativity. In the letter Einstein said the first paper 'deals with radiation and the energy properties of light and is very revolutionary'; of relativity he said only that 'the fourth paper is only a rough draft at this point, and is an electrodynamics of moving bodies which employs a modification of the theory of space and time.' The one he thought would overturn physics was the light paper - and he was right, though it took twenty years and a man trying to destroy it. Source: Einstein to Conrad Habicht, May 1905, quoted in Walter Isaacson, 'Einstein: His Life and Universe' (Simon & Schuster, 2007), p. 93.

question: Robert Millikan needed an absolutely clean face of sodium or potassium - metals that corrode the instant air touches them. So he sealed the workshop inside the vacuum: the metals rode on a wheel, a magnet outside drove a knife inside that shaved off a fresh slice, and the wheel turned the clean face into the light beam, the tube never once opened. He made that tube of quartz, not ordinary glass. Why quartz?
answer: Ordinary glass blocks ultraviolet light
choices: Ordinary glass blocks ultraviolet light
Ordinary glass glows under a strong beam
Ordinary glass leaks gas into a vacuum
Ordinary glass melts near an arc lamp
context: 'A machine shop in vacuo' was Millikan's own phrase for the thing. The knife was worked from outside by a magnet precisely so nothing ever had to be opened to the air, and the wheel then presented the fresh, unoxidised face to the beam. Quartz was not a luxury: ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet, and ultraviolet was the light Millikan needed to reach the metal. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Robert Millikan'; Rick Dower, 'Millikan Photoelectric Analysis', QuarkNet.

question: Classical wave theory made one prediction about light striking metal that anybody could go and check: an electron sitting in a faint passing wave has to soak up energy little by little until it has enough to break free, and with a dim enough lamp that soaking should take seconds, even hours. Experimenters hunted for the wait with the dimmest lamps they could build. What did they find?
answer: Electrons came out at once, with no measurable wait at all
choices: Electrons came out at once, with no measurable wait at all
Electrons came out instantly from warm metals, later from cold ones
Electrons came out after a wait that shrank as the lamp was brightened
Electrons came out after a wait, but far shorter than predicted
context: Emission begins within about 10^-9 second - a billionth of a second - of the light arriving, even at very faint intensities, and no measurable lag has ever turned up. The missing time lag is one of the four empirical facts the wave picture could not survive, alongside the sharp threshold colour below which nothing happens at all no matter how bright the lamp. This is what a good test looks like: the theory named a number, someone went and looked for it, and it was not there. Source: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect' ('Key Characteristics' and 'Classical Wave Theory Failure').

question: Light lands on a metal plate and electrons come flying out - the effect Heinrich Hertz stumbled on in 1887 and left unexplained. In 1905 Albert Einstein took it up in a paper he titled 'On a Heuristic Viewpoint Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light'. What did he propose light was doing?
answer: Arriving in countable packets, each swallowed whole by one electron
choices: Arriving in countable packets, each swallowed whole by one electron
Riding the ether in a steady stream that pushes on electrons inside
Travelling as tubes of electric force with its energy bunched in front
Spreading as a wave whose energy an electron gathers until it escapes
context: In Einstein's own words, the energy of a spreading light ray is 'not distributed continuously over ever-increasing spaces, but consists of a finite number of energy quanta' which 'can be absorbed or generated only as a whole.' That 'only as a whole' is the entire mechanism: one packet, one electron, no part payments. Every metal charges a fixed toll to release an electron - its work function - and whatever the packet has left over becomes the electron's speed: K_max = hv - phi. Below the threshold frequency phi/h a packet simply cannot pay the toll, and a brighter lamp sends only MORE packets, never bigger ones - which is why below that threshold colour a metal gives up no electrons at all, not at twice the brightness, not at a thousand times. Two footnotes: the third choice above is real science - J. J. Thomson, who had found the electron, proposed 'tubes of electric force' in 1903 to save the classical field, an honest attempt that still could not produce a sharp threshold. And Einstein never once wrote the word 'photon'; he said 'light quanta'. The American chemist Gilbert N. Lewis coined 'photon' in a letter to Nature on 18 December 1926, from the Greek phos, light. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Photoelectric effect' and 'Photon'; Einstein 1905 quoted at kathylovesphysics.com.

question: Philipp Lenard came away from his 1902 measurements convinced of something strange: the light was not supplying the escaping electron's energy at all. Until about 1911 nearly every physicist in Europe held the picture he built on that conclusion - it was the respectable, mainstream reading of the effect. Where, on Lenard's picture, did the electron get the energy to fly out?
answer: It took the energy from inside the atom, where it already sat waiting
choices: It took the energy from inside the atom, where it already sat waiting
It took the energy from the metal's heat, gathered to a point by the light
It took the energy from the ether, stirred into motion by the light
It took the energy from the charge on the plate, unlocked by the light
context: Lenard's trigger hypothesis, in his own words: in emission 'the light plays only the role of triggering [the release of] a motion which already exists with full velocity inside the atoms of the body' - light as 'the fuse in firing a loaded gun.' It was not a stupid idea; it followed from what he had actually measured, and serious people believed it for a decade. That is the point worth carrying away: the consensus of expert physicists was the wrong answer, and only a better test settled it. Sources: M. Niaz et al., 'Reconstruction of the history of the photoelectric effect...', Science Education (2010), Wiley; kathylovesphysics.com.

question: Robert Millikan shone one colour of light after another on his freshly shaved metal, and for each he measured the stopping voltage - the reverse voltage just big enough to turn back even the fastest electron. Running a mercury arc from 2399 to 5461 angstroms, he plotted stopping voltage against frequency and got a dead-straight line. He had already measured the electron's charge himself, in the oil-drop experiment, so the slope of that line handed him a second number to about half a percent - a constant that had come out of an entirely different corner of physics. Which constant?
answer: Planck's constant
choices: Planck's constant
Boltzmann's constant
The electron's mass
The speed of light
context: The slope of stopping voltage against frequency is h/e. Millikan's own oil-drop value for the electron's charge was 1.592x10^-19 coulombs, good to 0.2%, which turned that slope into h = 6.57x10^-27 erg-second (6.57x10^-34 joule-second), accurate to about 0.5%; the modern value is 6.626x10^-34. Planck's constant, first pulled out of a completely different phenomenon, measured all over again from a straight line on a graph of light knocking electrons out of sodium. Two unrelated windows onto nature giving the same number is about the strongest evidence physics ever offers. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Robert Millikan'; Rick Dower, 'Millikan Photoelectric Analysis', QuarkNet.

question: Robert Millikan expected Einstein's 1905 light-quantum equation to break. He spent ten years testing it - measuring the stopping voltage, colour by colour, on faces of sodium and potassium shaved clean inside his sealed vacuum - and in January 1916 he published a verification of the equation good to about half a percent. What did that same paper say about the light-quantum idea behind it?
answer: That the theory behind the equation seemed at present wholly untenable
choices: That the theory behind the equation seemed at present wholly untenable
That his own results had converted him to it, against his expectations
That the measurements left the theory neither proved nor disproved
That the whole question should be left to the theorists to sort out
context: Millikan printed the confirmation and refused the picture in the same breath - and the honest record matters more than a tidy conversion story. He had gone in hostile on stated grounds, calling Einstein's hypothesis 'bold, not to say reckless': a lump of light that stays put in one place violates the very idea of an electromagnetic disturbance, and the picture 'flies in the face of the thoroughly established facts of interference.' Of Einstein's equation he wrote that it 'cannot in my judgment be looked upon at present as resting upon any sort of a satisfactory theoretical foundation,' even though 'it actually represents very accurately the behavior' of the effect; and flatly, 'Yet the semi-corpuscular theory by which Einstein arrived at his equation seems at present to be wholly untenable.' He accepted the EQUATION and rejected the PHOTON. At Einstein's seventieth-birthday celebration in 1949 he summed it up: 'I spent ten years of my life testing that 1905 equation of Einstein's, and, contrary to all my expectations I was compelled in 1915 to assert its unambiguous experimental verification in spite of its unreasonableness since it seemed to violate everything that we knew about the interference of light.' His 1950 autobiography went softer, saying his data 'scarcely permits of any other interpretation than that which Einstein had originally suggested' - a kinder account of himself than what he actually printed in 1916. Arrhenius credited him at the 1922 Nobel ceremony all the same: 'Einstein's law of the photo-electrical effect has been extremely rigorously tested by the American Millikan and his pupils and passed the test brilliantly.' Einstein's citation reads 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect' - relativity is not in it, and Einstein was not in the room ('Being too remote from Sweden, Professor Einstein could not attend the ceremony'). Millikan received his own Nobel Prize in 1923. Sources: Millikan, Physical Review, January 1916, and Phys. Rev. 7 (1916) 355-388, quoted in the National Academies biographical memoir chapter 'Bold, Not to Say Reckless'; Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 award ceremony speech, nobelprize.org; Grokipedia, 'Robert Millikan'.

question: By 1923 Einstein's equation had been verified and most physicists still would not swallow the packet. Arthur Compton fired sharp X-rays from a molybdenum tube at a thin block of graphite and read the scattered beam angle by angle on a rotating crystal spectrometer. Beside the line at the original wavelength sat a second line that had no business existing: on the wave picture, bouncing light off an electron cannot change its colour at all. What had become of that second line's wavelength?
answer: It was longer, and longer still at wider scattering angles
choices: It was longer, and longer still at wider scattering angles
It was shorter, and shorter still at wider scattering angles
It was longer at narrow angles and shorter at wide ones
It was shifted by the same amount at every angle
context: The shift followed delta-lambda = (h / m_e c)(1 - cos theta) exactly - about 0.041 angstrom at 135 degrees - which is precisely what you get by treating the X-ray as a particle carrying momentum and letting it bounce off an electron like one billiard ball off another. Longer wavelength means less energy: the packet came away poorer because it had paid the electron, which recoiled with the difference. Compton used a Coolidge tube with a molybdenum target (the K-alpha line at 0.71 angstrom), a calcite crystal and an ionisation chamber, and shared the 1927 Nobel Prize with C. T. R. Wilson. Source: Grokipedia, 'Compton scattering'.

question: In February 1924 Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater made the last serious attempt to keep light a pure classical wave. To do it they were willing to pay an extraordinary price: one of the deepest rules in physics would hold only as a statistical average over many events, and would be allowed to fail outright in any single collision between light and an electron. Which rule were they giving up?
answer: The conservation of energy
choices: The conservation of energy
The conservation of charge
The constancy of light's speed
Newton's third law of motion
context: Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger killed the Bohr-Kramers-Slater theory in April 1925 with a test aimed straight at its weak point: put one counter on the scattered X-ray and another on the recoiling electron, and see whether they fire together. If energy is conserved in each individual collision, they must. They did. The price of 1925 precision: a timing resolution near a millisecond, 66 coincidences logged over five hours of which 46 were expected as accidents, an excess with about a 1-in-400,000 chance of being luck, and more than a year spent hand-reading over 3 kilometres of 1.5-centimetre film. Their conclusion: 'One must therefore probably assume that the light quantum concept possesses a high degree of validity.' Bohr took the loss cleanly, writing to Fowler that 'there is nothing else to do than to give our revolutionary efforts as honourable a funeral as possible.' Max von Laue's verdict: 'Physics was saved from being led astray.' Bothe won the 1954 Nobel Prize for inventing the coincidence method. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Bothe-Geiger coincidence experiment'; Walther Bothe, 'The Coincidence Method', Nobel Lecture 1954, nobelprize.org.

question: The Indian summer monsoon failed almost completely in 1877, and the famine that followed swept across Madras Presidency and the Deccan. Roughly how many people did the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 kill?
answer: More than ten million
choices: More than ten million
About sixty thousand
About four thousand
About two hundred
context: The 1877 monsoon failure was the trigger; British relief policy made it worse. The scale of the disaster is what drove the Government of India to demand a way of predicting the monsoon in advance. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1876%E2%80%931878

question: For generations, fishermen along the coast of Peru had a name for a warm current that arrived in December and killed the anchovy fishing. They called it El Nino, and the name means what?
answer: The Christ Child
choices: The Christ Child
The great fever
The empty net
The southern wind
context: El Nino is Spanish for 'the boy' and specifically for the infant Christ, because the warm water usually shows up around Christmas. Peruvian fishermen named the phenomenon centuries before oceanographers connected it to anything larger. See https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/elnino/what-is-el-nino

question: After the 1877 famine and the collapse of the first monsoon-prediction attempts, in 1904 the British sent to Simla a Cambridge Senior Wrangler who had spent his academic career on electromagnetism and the dynamics of spinning tops, and who had never worked a day in weather. Who was he?
answer: Gilbert Walker
choices: Gilbert Walker
Henry Blanford
John Eliot
Norman Lockyer
context: Walker was Senior Wrangler in the Mathematical Tripos in 1889 and had published on projectile flight and gyroscopes. The India Meteorological Department was struggling to predict the monsoon and the government thought a first-class mathematician might succeed where the meteorologists had failed. Blanford was the man Walker eventually succeeded via Eliot; Eliot was Walker's immediate predecessor at Simla; Lockyer was the sunspot-cycle theorist whose forecasts had failed publicly in 1877. See https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gilbert-Walker

question: Gilbert Walker set a room full of Indian clerks to computing correlation coefficients by hand between weather records from stations all over the world. What kind of pattern fell out of the arithmetic that made Walker famous in the end?
answer: A pressure see-saw across the Pacific: when Tahiti is high, Darwin is low, and back
choices: A pressure see-saw across the Pacific: when Tahiti is high, Darwin is low, and back
A twenty-two-year cycle in monsoon rainfall matching the double sunspot cycle
A three-year lag between North Atlantic hurricanes and Bay of Bengal cyclones
A drift in the Himalayan snowline that predicted the following summer's rain
context: Walker named this see-saw the Southern Oscillation and published it through the 1920s. He could describe it in exquisite statistical detail but could never explain WHY it happened, and for decades most meteorologists treated it as a numerical curiosity rather than a real physical thing. The distractors are all patterns that were seriously proposed at the time. See https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gilbert-Walker

question: For forty years Gilbert Walker's Southern Oscillation and the fishermen's warm current sat in separate literatures, and neither could be explained. In 1969 the Norwegian-American meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes finally joined them together. What did Bjerknes argue?
answer: The two are one coupled system: the tropical air and the tropical ocean drive each other
choices: The two are one coupled system: the tropical air and the tropical ocean drive each other
The two are downstream signals of the eleven-year sunspot cycle acting on the tropics
The two are triggered by large tropical volcanic eruptions in the preceding year
The two are seasonal responses to the Himalayan snowpack melting in early summer
context: Bjerknes showed that Walker's pressure see-saw in the air and the warm water off Peru are two faces of the same event: the trade winds and the ocean push each other. He named the great east-west overturning of the equatorial atmosphere the WALKER CIRCULATION, after the man whose numbers no one had trusted. The other three options are real hypotheses that had been floated for either the Southern Oscillation or the fishermen's current before 1969. See https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/insurance/the-el-nino-southern-oscillation-enso-discovery-and-dynamics.html

question: In the normal, non-El-Nino state of the equatorial Pacific, the trade winds blow steadily from east to west and drag warm surface water toward Indonesia. The wind is holding one whole side of an ocean higher than the other. Roughly how much higher does the sea surface stand at Indonesia than off Peru?
answer: About half a metre
choices: About half a metre
About twelve metres
About four centimetres
About five metres
context: Half a metre is the standing tilt maintained by the trade winds alone. Cold, nutrient-rich water wells up along the South American coast to replace what the winds have blown west, and that upwelling is what feeds the anchovy fishery. See https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/elnino/what-is-el-nino

question: Jacob Bjerknes noticed that whenever the equatorial trade winds slackened, the sea off Peru also warmed. He argued this was not a coincidence but a self-driving loop, which is now called the Bjerknes feedback. In one sentence, how does the loop close?
answer: Weaker winds let warm water slide east, and the extra warmth in the east weakens the winds further
choices: Weaker winds let warm water slide east, and the extra warmth in the east weakens the winds further
Stronger winds pile warm water in the west, and the cooling east strengthens the winds further
Volcanic aerosols cool the tropics, which strengthens the winds and cools the east further
Melting polar ice freshens the Pacific surface, which stalls the winds and warms the east further
context: That runaway is why the system FLIPS between states instead of drifting: cause and effect chase each other around the loop until it saturates. The Bjerknes feedback remains the cornerstone of El Nino theory today. See https://www.moodys.com/web/en/us/insights/insurance/the-el-nino-southern-oscillation-enso-discovery-and-dynamics.html

question: For her fourth-grade science fair Emily Rosa put a cardboard screen between herself and each practitioner, with two holes for their hands. She flipped a coin, then held her hand over one of theirs. What did she ask each practitioner to do?
answer: say which of their hands felt her energy field
choices: say which of their hands felt her energy field
guess the outcome of the coin flip in advance
diagnose a hidden illness through the screen
match their pulse to a metronome she tapped
context: Emily Rosa was nine when she designed the test after seeing a video of practitioners claiming to sense a Human Energy Field. Each practitioner ran ten trials. Source: Wikipedia Emily Rosa; Washington Post, 7 April 1998.

question: Twenty-one practitioners took Rosa's test, ten trials each, 280 trials in all. If they could genuinely feel a hand a few inches away they should have scored well above 5 out of 10. What did they average?
answer: 4.4 out of 10
choices: 4.4 out of 10
8.7 out of 10
9.6 out of 10
6.3 out of 10
context: The correct-hand count was 123 of 280, an average of 4.4 out of 10; chance alone would give an expected 5. Source: 'A close look at therapeutic touch', JAMA, 1 April 1998.

question: The paper 'A close look at therapeutic touch', co-authored by Emily Rosa, her mother Linda, Larry Sarner and Stephen Barrett, ran on 1 April 1998 in one of the world's most-cited medical journals. Rosa was recorded as the youngest research-paper author it had ever published. Which journal was it?
answer: the Journal of the American Medical Association
choices: the Journal of the American Medical Association
the New England Journal of Medicine
the British Medical Journal
Annals of Internal Medicine
context: The journal's editor George Lundberg defended running it: 'Age doesn't matter. It's good science that matters, and this is good science.' Sources: PubMed 9533499; Wikipedia George D. Lundberg.

question: In 2012 a six-year-old girl named Emily Whitehead had leukemia that had come back twice and stopped answering chemotherapy. Doctors at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia tried something no child had ever received: they took a particular kind of immune cell out of her own blood, rewired it in a lab, and put it back to hunt the cancer. She has been cancer-free ever since. Which immune cell did they rewire?
answer: T cells
choices: T cells
B cells
NK cells
Macrophages
context: Emily was infused on 17 April 2012 by Dr Stephan Grupp's team at CHOP, using the CTL019 construct developed by Carl June's group at the University of Pennsylvania. All four choices are real immune cells that kill or target other cells - the trick is that CAR-T uses T cells specifically because of their targeting receptor. B cells make antibodies; NK cells are natural killers with broad targets; macrophages engulf debris and pathogens. Source: chop.edu Emily Whitehead 10-year celebration.

question: A T cell only kills what it can SEE - what its receptor recognises on another cell's surface. Leukemia cells are the body's own cells, so an ordinary T cell walks straight past them. To fix that, engineers welded a synthetic receptor onto Emily Whitehead's T cells that locked onto a specific protein studded across the surface of B cells (including the leukemic ones). What is that protein called?
answer: CD19
choices: CD19
HER2
ACE2
PD-1
context: CD19 sits on the surface of B cells at every stage of their development, which makes it a clean target for B-cell leukemias and lymphomas. HER2 is a breast-cancer target; ACE2 is the receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter cells; PD-1 is a T-cell 'off switch' that checkpoint-inhibitor drugs release. Source: FDA tisagenlecleucel approval, Aug 2017.

question: The lab-built receptor that gave Emily Whitehead's T cells a new pair of eyes for finding leukemic B cells is called a CAR - the 'C' is a word borrowed from Greek mythology. In the myth, the beast it names had the head of a lion, the body of a goat, and a serpent for a tail; it terrorised Lycia until the hero Bellerophon killed it from the back of Pegasus. Which mythological creature is the receptor's 'C' named after?
answer: Chimera
choices: Chimera
Hydra
Cerberus
Minotaur
context: CAR = Chimeric Antigen Receptor. The word 'chimeric' comes from the Chimera of Greek myth, a creature stitched together from a lion, a goat, and a snake - which is exactly what the receptor is: an antibody head fused to a T-cell signalling tail. Hydra was the many-headed serpent killed by Heracles; Cerberus the three-headed dog guarding the underworld; the Minotaur the bull-headed man of the Cretan labyrinth - all Greek monsters, but only the Chimera gave English the word for mismatched parts spliced into one. Source: pubmed 29451276 tisagenlecleucel review.

question: Days after her infusion, Emily Whitehead's fever spiked, her blood pressure crashed, and she was moved onto a ventilator in intensive care. The engineered cells were working - but working so violently that her body was flooded with immune signalling molecules called cytokines. Doctors ran blood tests and found ONE cytokine in particular running at extraordinarily high levels. Which one?
answer: Interleukin-6
choices: Interleukin-6
Tumor necrosis factor alpha
Interleukin-2
Interferon gamma
context: This is now called cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and IL-6 is its signature - the specific cytokine measured off the charts in Emily's blood and the one the team decided to target. TNF-alpha, IL-2 and interferon gamma are all real immune cytokines, released in various inflammatory conditions, but IL-6 was Emily's runaway signal. Source: Penn Medicine 'A Port in the Storm'.

question: Emily Whitehead's team knew Emily was dying and did not have time to design a new drug. Carl June, the trial's lead scientist, happened to know an existing antibody drug that blocked the IL-6 receptor - because his own daughter took it for juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. The team ordered it, gave it to Emily in the ICU, and her fever broke within hours. What was the drug?
answer: Tocilizumab
choices: Tocilizumab
Rituximab
Infliximab
Adalimumab
context: Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds and blocks the IL-6 receptor. It had been approved for rheumatoid arthritis; nobody had ever given it to a child in a CAR-T crisis before Emily. The FDA later formalised its emergency role by approving it for CAR-T-associated CRS on the same day it approved Kymriah in 2017. Rituximab targets CD20; infliximab and adalimumab target TNF-alpha - all real antibody drugs, none of them IL-6-receptor blockers. Source: AACR interview with Carl June, 2020.

question: On 30 August 2017 the FDA approved the CAR-T therapy that saved Emily Whitehead as a marketed drug, developed by Carl June's group at the University of Pennsylvania and licensed to Novartis. It was the first therapy of its kind ever cleared in the United States, and the first including a gene-therapy step. What is the drug's trade name?
answer: Kymriah
choices: Kymriah
Casgevy
Herceptin
Humira
context: Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel) was approved for patients up to age 25 with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; the pivotal trial showed an 83% remission rate within 3 months. Casgevy is the 2023 CRISPR sickle-cell therapy; Herceptin is trastuzumab (a HER2 breast-cancer antibody); Humira is adalimumab (a TNF blocker for autoimmune disease). Source: FDA tisagenlecleucel approval, 30 Aug 2017.

question: Rudolf Clausius wrote the second law of thermodynamics in 1854 as one plain sentence with no mathematics in it at all - eleven years before he invented the word 'entropy'. His sentence names one thing that never happens on its own. What?
answer: Heat passing from a colder body to a warmer one.
choices: Heat passing from a colder body to a warmer one.
Heat being turned entirely into work by an engine.
A wheel turning forever with no fuel at all.
Energy vanishing entirely as two surfaces rub.
context: Clausius's sentence: heat can never pass from a colder to a warmer body 'without some other change, connected therewith, occurring at the same time.' That last clause is why a refrigerator is legal - it drives heat the wrong way only by running a compressor and dumping heat out the back. He published the statement in German in 1854 and in English in 1856, and only coined the word 'entropy' in 1865. Turning heat entirely into work is also impossible, but that is Lord Kelvin's version of the second law, not Clausius's. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'; Wikipedia, 'Second law of thermodynamics'.

question: Scramble an egg and you can never unscramble it. An egg is nothing but molecules colliding. Take a single collision between two molecules and run it backwards. What do Newton's laws say about the reversed collision?
answer: They allow it, since a reversed collision is just as legal.
choices: They allow it, since a reversed collision is just as legal.
They forbid it, since the equations pick out one direction.
They allow it, but only for perfectly elastic collisions.
They forbid it, since momentum runs one way through time.
context: At the level of single collisions the laws of motion are time-symmetric: run any one of them backwards and it is still a legal collision. Nothing in the forces forbids an egg unscrambling. What stops it is the statistics of enormous numbers - the chance of a system stumbling back into a low-entropy condition falls off exponentially as the system gets bigger, and everyday objects hold something like a million million million million particles. The arrow is a matter of odds, not of law. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'; Wikipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'.

question: Rudolf Clausius, whose work on heat had turned up a quantity with no name, went looking for one in 1865. He kept a standing rule for naming important scientific quantities, and he followed it here. What was the rule?
answer: Go to the ancient languages, so the name means one thing everywhere.
choices: Go to the ancient languages, so the name means one thing everywhere.
Build it from plain German, so any careful reader could follow it.
Ask a classical scholar for a fresh term each time one is needed.
Borrow from the engine shop, so engineers would know it at once.
context: Clausius's rule, in his own words: 'I prefer going to the ancient languages for the names of important scientific quantities, so that they may mean the same thing in all living tongues.' So he built 'entropy' from Greek en, 'in', plus trope, 'transformation' - literally transformation-content, which is nearly what he had been calling the quantity all along in German: Verwandlungsinhalt, transformation content. He shaped the new word to echo an older one too, and said so in the same 1865 memoir: 'I have intentionally formed the word entropy so as to be as similar as possible to the word energy, since both these quantities are so nearly allied in their physical significance that they might be called twins.' The word reached English by 1868, through Peter Guthrie Tait's 'Sketch of Thermodynamics', the first English textbook on the subject. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'; Grokipedia, 'Entropy'.

question: Rudolf Clausius ended his 1865 paper, the one that gave the world the word 'entropy', not with a summary but with two bare sentences and nothing else - one about the universe's energy, one about its entropy. What are they?
answer: The energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.
choices: The energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.
The energy of the universe is constant; the entropy of the universe tends to zero.
The energy of the universe is falling; the entropy of the universe is rising.
The entropy of the universe is constant; the energy of the universe tends to a maximum.
context: In the German: 'Die Energie der Welt ist constant. Die Entropie der Welt strebt einem Maximum zu.' The first sentence is the first law of thermodynamics - energy is never created or destroyed - and the second is the second law. Clausius delivered the paper as a lecture on 24 April 1865, then printed it as his ninth memoir in Poggendorff's Annalen der Physik. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'; pro-physik.de, 'Der Geburtstag der Entropie'.

question: Before Rudolf Clausius, heat was caloric: an invisible fluid that seeped from hot bodies into cold ones, and serious people worked with it for decades. Count Rumford, overseeing the boring of cannon in Munich, wrote up one thing he saw in that workshop. What did Rumford report?
answer: The friction made heat without end, however long the work ran.
choices: The friction made heat without end, however long the work ran.
The chips gave off more heat than the barrel they came from.
The barrel grew hot only where the borer had already passed.
The heat came faster from a sharp borer than from a blunt one.
context: Rumford's boring shop kept producing heat for as long as the work went on, with no sign of the metal's supply running dry - and a fluid that a body holds a store of cannot pour out without end. Caloric was not a silly idea: it was the working theory of serious people, and it accounted well enough for how heat flows from hot things to cold ones. Rudolf Clausius's 1850 paper replaced the fluid with heat as the motion of the particles themselves, and it is from that paper that the line of work leading to entropy runs. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius', section 'Thermodynamics and Heat Theory'.

question: Textbooks often gloss entropy as 'disorder' - a messy bedroom, a jumbled sock drawer. Physicists who actually use the quantity say that gloss misleads, because entropy is not a judgement about tidiness at all. It is a number you get by counting. In a box of gas, counting what?
answer: The particle configurations that match what you measure from outside.
choices: The particle configurations that match what you measure from outside.
The particles moving faster than the average speed inside the container.
The collisions the particles make against the container walls each second.
The units of energy already lost from the gas into its surroundings.
context: What you can measure from outside - energy, volume, temperature, particle number - is called the macrostate. One exact set of positions and momenta for every particle is a microstate. The multiplicity W is how many microstates would look identical from outside, and entropy is S = k ln W, with k about 1.38 x 10^-23 joules per kelvin. The fundamental assumption is that every available microstate is equally likely, so a system drifts to whichever macrostate owns the most of them. That is why 'disorder' is the wrong word: entropy is a count, not a verdict on how something looks. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy', section 'Statistical Mechanics Formulation'.

question: A hot frying pan left on the counter goes cold on its own. That cooling is the kind of one-way event Rudolf Clausius built the second law around. What became of the energy the pan held?
answer: All of it is still there, but hardly any could now be turned into work.
