choices: All of it is still there, but hardly any could now be turned into work.
All of it is still there, and any of it could still be turned into work.
Most of it was used up, and the remainder went into the kitchen air.
Most of it turned into entropy, which is the thing the cooling made.
context: Clausius stated the first law in the very same 1850 paper that started all this: energy is conserved through every irreversible process. Entropy does not track energy going missing; it tracks energy becoming unavailable. Clausius's own gloss on entropy was 'the amount of thermal energy unavailable for conversion into mechanical work.' That is also why 'entropy means things wear out' is subtly wrong - nothing is lost, it is only spread. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy'; Grokipedia, 'Rudolf Clausius'.

question: The phrase 'arrow of time' is not ancient. Arthur Stanley Eddington coined it in his 1927 Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh, published the next year as The Nature of the Physical World, and he gave a working test along with it: a way to look at any physical process and say which end of it is the future. Follow the arrow, he wrote, and you should find one thing increasing. What?
answer: More and more of the random element in the state of the world.
choices: More and more of the random element in the state of the world.
More and more heat gathered into fewer and hotter places.
More and more of the world's mass converted into radiation.
More and more separation between the fast and the slow molecules.
context: Eddington's sentence: 'If as we follow the arrow we find more and more of the random element in the state of the world, then the arrow is pointing towards the future.' By 'random element' he meant what statistical mechanics counts - the drift towards the vastly more numerous configurations - not untidiness. He also ranked the second law above every other law of nature, saying it holds the supreme position among them: a theory that disagrees with Maxwell's equations, he argued, may just be bad news for Maxwell's equations; a theory contradicted by observation may only mean the experimentalists bungled it; but a theory found to be against the second law has no hope at all. He restated the passage in New Pathways in Science (1935), so some books date it to 1935. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arrow of time'; JILA, University of Colorado, Eddington quotation page.

question: In Vienna's Zentralfriedhof, a single line of physics is carved on Ludwig Boltzmann's gravestone, above his bushy-bearded marble bust: S = k log W. It is the formula his life's work is remembered for, tying entropy to W, the count of microscopic possibilities. But in 1877 Boltzmann proposed only that entropy is PROPORTIONAL to that count; he never supplied the constant k, and he never wrote the equality down. Who first wrote the equation in the form now carved on his stone?
answer: Max Planck.
choices: Max Planck.
Rudolf Clausius.
Josef Loschmidt.
Ernst Zermelo.
context: Planck introduced the constant and wrote S = k log W in a paper presented on 14 December 1900, 'On the theory of the law of the energy distribution in the normal spectrum' - and then named the constant after Boltzmann. So the equation on Boltzmann's grave is Planck's. Boltzmann lies in Group 14C, grave 1, in the same cemetery as Beethoven, Brahms, Schubert and the Strauss family. Source: Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'; Atlas Obscura, 'Boltzmann's Grave in Vienna'.

question: In 1872 Ludwig Boltzmann believed he had derived one-way time from mechanics alone. He defined a quantity H from the spread of molecular speeds in a gas and proved that H can only fall, never rise. Four years later Josef Loschmidt - a Vienna colleague and a close friend, not a rival - published the objection that has bothered physicists ever since: do one thing to the gas, he said, and H would have to climb. Do what?
answer: Reverse the velocity of every molecule all at once.
choices: Reverse the velocity of every molecule all at once.
Remove every molecule travelling faster than the average.
Halve the volume of the container in a single stroke.
Heat one wall of the container while cooling the other.
context: In German it is the Umkehreinwand, the 'reversal objection'. Boltzmann answered in two parts. First, odds: states with falling entropy do exist, but the probability of a drop shrinks exponentially with the size of the drop, which for anything of everyday size crushes it to nothing - he conceded that some starting points behave improperly, and claimed only that by far most do not. Second, beginnings: the arrow exists because the system started in a low-entropy condition, which is a fact about initial conditions rather than about the equations. Ernst Zermelo raised the other great objection in 1896 - a bounded system must eventually return close to where it began - and Boltzmann answered with the waiting time, on the order of 10^(10^23) years for an ordinary quantity of gas. Loschmidt was no enemy: his measurements of molecular sizes helped draw Boltzmann into kinetic theory in the first place. Source: Wikipedia, 'Loschmidt's paradox'; Grokipedia, 'Ludwig Boltzmann'; Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'.

question: A freezer makes ice and breaks no law of physics. Earth pulls off something comparable on a planetary scale, and Sean Carroll counts the exchange in photons: for every visible photon the Sun delivers, Earth radiates about twenty infrared ones back into space. What does that photon trade amount to?
answer: More entropy leaves than arrives, and the surplus pays for order down here.
choices: More entropy leaves than arrives, and the surplus pays for order down here.
More energy leaves than arrives, and the shortfall is what drives the winds.
Less energy leaves than arrives, and the surplus is stored in the deep ocean.
Less entropy leaves than arrives, and the deficit is taken up by living things.
context: Carroll's line: 'the Earth needs to radiate twenty low-energy (long-wavelength, infrared) photons for every one high-energy (short-wavelength, visible) photon it receives.' The Sun runs at about twenty times Earth's average temperature, which is what sets that exchange rate. Earth radiates back into space exactly as much energy as it receives, so the energy books balance and the first law is untouched - but roughly twenty times as much entropy leaves as arrives. Sunlight is energy in a low-entropy, useful form; infrared radiated back to space is the same energy at much higher entropy. That outgoing entropy is what pays for local order on the planet. The freezer runs on the same accounting: it is not a closed system, and it pumps more heat out through the coils at the back than it ever took out of the box, so the compressor's waste heat pays for the ice. Source: Sean Carroll, 'Evolution and the Second Law', Preposterous Universe, 7 May 2009; Energy Education, University of Calgary, 'Second law of thermodynamics'.

question: Roger Penrose has put numbers on how strange the beginning was. Measured in units of Boltzmann's constant, the entropy of the universe today runs to something like 10^103, most of it locked inside black holes. At the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, the estimate is around 10^88 - fifteen orders of magnitude lower. The forward direction of time traces back to that fantastically improbable start. So why did the universe begin with entropy that low?
answer: No accepted explanation exists, only an assumed starting condition.
choices: No accepted explanation exists, only an assumed starting condition.
Inflation flattened the early universe and drove its entropy down.
Gravity gathered the first matter and held its entropy down.
The Big Bang's heat erased whatever entropy came before it.
context: Physicists call it the past hypothesis, and it is a boundary condition put in by hand rather than a result derived from anything. Wikipedia lists it among the unsolved problems in physics: why did the universe have such low entropy in the past, giving us the distinction between past and future? Inflation is the near-miss answer - it does explain the early universe's smoothness, but not its low entropy, and why the pre-inflationary state was so extraordinarily ordered remains unresolved. Today's total is dominated by black holes through the Bekenstein-Hawking area formula. Source: Wikipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'; Grokipedia, 'Entropy as an arrow of time'.

question: In 1852 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, published 'On a Universal Tendency in Nature to the Dissipation of Mechanical Energy' and carried the engine room's rules out to the whole cosmos: everything, eventually, evens out to one tepid temperature with nothing left to drive anything. That picture is called the heat death of the universe. Lee Smolin is one of several physicists who doubt it, and his reason is gravity. Take energy away from a gravitationally bound clump - a star radiating into empty space - and what does the clump do?
answer: Its parts speed up, so it draws tighter and grows hotter still.
choices: Its parts speed up, so it draws tighter and grows hotter still.
Its parts slow down, so it settles into an even, cooling calm.
Its parts speed up, but the clump swells outward as it does.
Its parts drift apart, so the clump thins out and fades away.
context: Physicists call it negative specific heat: take energy out of a gravitationally bound system and its components speed up, which is the reverse of what a gas in a box does. Gravity gathers matter into stars and galaxies rather than smoothing it out, so Smolin's point is that a gravitating universe does not even out - it fragments into ever more structured and heterogeneous pieces. He is not alone in doubting the heat death. Max Planck wrote that the phrase 'entropy of the universe' has no meaning, because it admits of no accurate definition. Laszlo Tisza wrote that if an isolated system is not in equilibrium, we cannot associate an entropy with it. Hans Buchdahl objected to 'the entirely unjustifiable assumption that the universe can be treated as a closed thermodynamic system.' Heat death also assumes the expansion continues indefinitely, which depends on dark energy behaving as expected. Hermann von Helmholtz had carried Thomson's idea to the cosmos in an 1854 lecture, 'On the Interaction of the Natural Forces.' Nobody knows how this one ends. Source: Wikipedia, 'Heat death of the universe'; Grokipedia, 'Heat death of the universe'.

question: You can run a genetics test on a cat from the pavement, without touching the animal: just find one whose coat is a patchwork of orange and black. Roughly 99.9% of calico cats share one trait, and the exceptions turn up about once in 3,000 cats. What does that patchwork coat let you predict?
answer: That the cat is female
choices: That the cat is female
That the cat is male
That the cat is deaf
That the cat is long-haired
context: About one calico in 3,000 is male, and he is almost always XXY -- carrying two X chromosomes plus a Y (Klinefelter syndrome) -- and usually sterile. The orange-and-black patchwork needs two X chromosomes to be a patchwork at all, which is why the coat doubles as a sex test you can run from twenty feet away. Go try it: find a calico or a tortoiseshell, predict 'female', then ask the owner. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Calico_cat

question: In 1961 Mary Lyon bred female mice carrying a different version of the same coat-colour gene on each of their two X chromosomes, then looked at how their fur turned out. What she read off those coats became the rule for every female mammal. What did Lyon propose each cell does early on?
answer: Shuts down one of its two X chromosomes at random
choices: Shuts down one of its two X chromosomes at random
Discards one of its two X chromosomes at random
Reads its two X chromosomes in alternating turns
Halves the output of both of its two X chromosomes
context: From 'Gene Action in the X-chromosome of the Mouse', Nature 190:372 (1961). Lyon's rule: the choice is made once, early, and every daughter cell of that cell keeps the same X switched off forever. So the coat is a map of which X won where -- each patch is the descendants of one embryonic cell. She was not working on cats at all; the calico is simply the version you can see from the street. Sources: nature.com/articles/190372a0; grokipedia.com/page/X-inactivation

question: In 1809 Jean-Baptiste Lamarck argued that traits built during a life get handed on -- a giraffe's neck stretched by reaching. In 1888 August Weismann docked the tails of mice, bred them, docked the pups' tails, and carried on for five generations and 901 mice. What was born at the end?
answer: Mice with full-length tails in every generation
choices: Mice with full-length tails in every generation
Mice with shorter tails in each generation
Mice born tailless by the fifth generation
Mice with stumpy or kinked tails in some litters
context: Every single pup, across all five generations and all 901 mice, was born with a full tail. This is why 'Lamarck was right after all' -- the most common thing said about epigenetics -- is wrong. What epigenetics shows is different in kind: not a trait built by use and handed down, but a regulatory setting altered by environment, sitting on a genome whose sequence is untouched, and usually wiped clean between generations. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/August_Weismann; grokipedia.com/page/Transgenerational_epigenetic_inheritance

question: A neuron in your brain fires electrical signals. A liver cell strips poisons out of your blood. A beta cell in your pancreas makes insulin, the hormone that lets your body take up sugar, and almost no other cell makes a drop of it. All three grew by division from the one fertilised egg you started as. So what actually differs between your neuron and your liver cell?
answer: Which genes are held shut by a chemical tag
choices: Which genes are held shut by a chemical tag
Which genes were cut out as the cell specialised
Which chromosomes the cell kept as it divided
Which genes were rewritten into a new sequence
context: This is what the machinery is actually for -- not inheritance, but memory inside one body. Your neuron and your liver cell carry byte-identical DNA: nothing was thrown away and nothing was rewritten. What differs is which genes carry a chemical tag holding them shut, and that annotation is copied every time the cell divides. It is why the insulin gene runs in the beta cells of the pancreas and nowhere else. The mark is how a cell remembers what it is. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics

question: Conrad Waddington coined 'epigenetics' in 1942, for the machinery running between the genes an animal inherits and the body it grows. Nobody yet knew what a gene was made of, and he had no mechanism to offer. In 1957 he published what he had instead, and it turned out to be right. What was it?
answer: A drawing of a ball rolling down a valleyed hill
choices: A drawing of a ball rolling down a valleyed hill
A drawing of a switchboard wiring one gene to another
A drawing of a clock whose gears turn each tissue
A drawing of a ladder each cell climbs rung by rung
context: Waddington's 'epigenetic landscape' (1957): a hilly terrain scored with branching valleys, down which a cell rolls toward its fate. Nudge it early and it takes a different valley; once it is deep in one, it stays. He had a metaphor and no chemistry whatsoever -- the methyl tags that fill in the picture were not proposed as the heritable off-switch until the 1970s. The word arrived a generation before the mechanism. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics

question: A calico cat wears three colours, and only two of them are the X-chromosome story. Orange versus black is settled on the X, patch by patch, in the way Mary Lyon described in mice. The white is not on the X at all: it comes from an ordinary gene, piebald spotting, sitting on a chromosome that has nothing to do with sex. So why is a white patch white?
answer: Pigment cells never migrated into that patch of skin
choices: Pigment cells never migrated into that patch of skin
The pigment cells there lack the enzyme that makes colour
The pigment is made but never reaches the hair shaft
The pigment bleached out of those hairs before birth
context: The orange-versus-black choice does sit on the X: a 154,000-letter deletion upstream of the gene ARHGAP36 flips a pigment cell from making black eumelanin to orange phaeomelanin, and X-inactivation decides which cell gets which. The white is a second system stacked on top -- the autosomal piebald spotting gene (S) blocks pigment cells from migrating into parts of the skin while the embryo is forming, so hair grows there with no pigment cells beneath it at all. Two independent systems on one cat, and only the orange-and-black mosaic is the X-inactivation story. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Calico_cat

question: Robert Waterland and Randy Jirtle worked with a mouse strain whose pups are normally born yellow, fat, and prone to diabetes and tumours -- the fault of a parasitic jumping gene wedged beside the coat-colour gene, which nothing ever switches off. In 2003 they shifted those litters toward brown, lean, healthy pups by changing nothing but what the pregnant mothers were fed -- not one letter of the pups' DNA was altered. What went into the food?
answer: Folic acid, vitamin B12 and choline
choices: Folic acid, vitamin B12 and choline
Vitamin D, calcium and phosphate
Vitamin C, zinc and magnesium
Extra protein, iron and fish oil
context: Waterland & Jirtle, Molecular and Cellular Biology 23:5293 (2003). Folic acid, vitamin B12, choline chloride and betaine are methyl donors -- raw material for the tags that hold a gene shut. Loading the pregnant mothers' diet with them shifted the pups toward brown pseudoagouti (P = 0.008; 39 supplemented pups against 30 unsupplemented) -- a shift in the odds across the litters, not a switch that turned every pup brown. The jumping gene is an intracisternal A particle retrotransposon, and when its hidden promoter goes untagged it drives agouti protein everywhere. Even untreated, genetically identical littermates in one cage vary widely in coat colour, waistline, glucose tolerance and tumour risk -- because the tag landed differently in each embryo. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC165709/

question: A methyl group -- one carbon and three hydrogens -- parked on a cytosine base can hold a gene switched off for the life of a cell, and not one letter of the DNA sequence underneath is altered. But a dividing cell unzips its double helix and builds a fresh strand beside each old one, and the fresh strand comes out bare: no tags at all. Both daughter cells still end up with the same genes switched off. How does the pattern survive the copying?
answer: An enzyme reads the old strand and tags the new one to match
choices: An enzyme reads the old strand and tags the new one to match
An enzyme re-tags the whole helix from scratch each division
Small RNAs guide the tags back onto the bare new strand
Proteins packed around the DNA carry the pattern instead
context: The enzyme is DNMT1, the maintenance methyltransferase. After replication it finds a half-tagged double helix -- old strand marked, new strand bare -- and writes the matching tags onto the new strand, so the annotation survives division while the letters stay identical. The tag itself is 5-methylcytosine, a methyl group on the fifth carbon of cytosine; about 1% of all bases in a vertebrate body cell carry one, spread across roughly 28 million CpG sites in the human genome. Rollin Hotchkiss spotted 5-methylcytosine in calf thymus DNA in 1948, five years before anyone knew DNA's shape. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Epigenetics

question: The Dutch hunger winter of 1944-45 became one of the best-documented natural experiments in human biology, because scientists working decades later could say how deep the hunger ran in each separate month of a pregnancy: the food allowed to an adult in the occupied west averaged 652 calories a day from December 1944 to April 1945, with monthly lows near 364. Roughly 4.5 million people were sealed inside the German blockade and some 20,000 died. Where do those month-by-month figures come from?
answer: The Dutch ration ledgers kept through the occupation
choices: The Dutch ration ledgers kept through the occupation
German ration decrees issued for the occupied west
Diaries that Dutch families kept through the winter
Red Cross surveys carried out after the liberation
context: The ledgers survived the war, and they are why that winter is a laboratory and not only a tragedy. Official adult rations ran about 1,800 calories a day for most of the occupation, fell to roughly 1,400 by October 1944, dropped below 1,000 in November, and slid to about 500 by April 1945 -- every figure written down as it happened. The famine also had a sharp start and a sharp end, and the Wilhelmina Gasthuis hospital in Amsterdam never stopped recording the course of each pregnancy and the size of each baby and placenta. Out of that paperwork came the Dutch Famine Birth Cohort: 2,414 people born there between November 1943 and February 1947 -- some exposed in early, mid or late pregnancy, some conceived after the food came back as built-in controls -- followed in six waves from about age 50 to age 74. Nobody would ever be allowed to run this experiment. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Dutch_famine_of_1944-1945; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7934722/

question: Bastiaan Heijmans and colleagues drew blood in the 2000s from Dutch men and women who had been in the womb during the hunger winter of 1944-45, and measured the chemical tags on one gene, IGF2 -- sixty years after the food ran out. Two exposure groups were compared: 60 people conceived during the famine, and 62 who met it only in the last months before birth. Which group's DNA still showed a difference?
answer: Only those conceived during the famine
choices: Only those conceived during the famine
Only those who met it late in pregnancy
Both groups, to about the same degree
Both groups, but only in the men
context: Heijmans et al., PNAS 2008: the periconceptional group carried about 5.2% LOWER methylation at the IGF2 differentially methylated region than their own brothers and sisters. The late-gestation group showed no difference at all. Keep the claim its true size -- one imprinted gene, a roughly 5% shift, measured in blood. This is not 'the famine rewrote their DNA'; the sequence was never touched. What it does show is a window: a few weeks around conception, while the embryo is setting its annotations, left a chemical trace still readable six decades later. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2579375/

question: In 1976 the epidemiologists Ravelli, Stein and Susser pulled the military induction records of some 300,000 nineteen-year-old Dutch men and sorted them by when in the womb the hunger winter had caught them -- a winter when official rations fell to about 500 calories a day. Men whose mothers had starved in EARLY pregnancy were more likely than unexposed men to be obese at nineteen. What about the men whose mothers had starved in the last months and just after birth?
answer: They were significantly less likely to be obese
choices: They were significantly less likely to be obese
They were about as likely to be obese as the rest
They were more likely to be obese, but only slightly
They were even more likely to be obese than the rest
context: Ravelli GP, Stein ZA, Susser MW, New England Journal of Medicine 295:349 (1976). Early exposure raised obesity rates on the order of 1.3-fold; late exposure lowered them significantly. One famine, two opposite answers, decided entirely by which weeks of development the hunger hit -- which is why 'starvation makes you thin' is the wrong lesson to draw from the Dutch winter. Followed into old age, the exposed cohort shows raised rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and coronary heart disease, and accelerated biological ageing on epigenetic clocks -- yet cognitive function at 18 looked unaffected. The damage was specific, not global. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/934222/

question: Carl Linnaeus described a toadflax whose flowers came out radially symmetric, like a star, instead of the usual two-lipped snapdragon shape -- and the odd form has bred true ever since, for 250 years. In 1999 Pilar Cubas, Coral Vincent and Enrico Coen examined Lcyc, the gene that sets flower symmetry in that plant. What did they find at Lcyc?
answer: An intact gene, drenched in methyl tags and silent
choices: An intact gene, drenched in methyl tags and silent
An intact gene, blocked by a protein clamped over it
A single changed letter, halfway along the gene
A missing gene, deleted from one chromosome
context: Cubas, Vincent & Coen, Nature 401:157 (1999). The sequence of Lcyc in the peloric toadflax is fine; the gene is simply methylated into silence. The methylation is heritable, it travels with the odd flower, and plants occasionally revert to normal flowers as Lcyc quietly loses its tags. An epimutation -- a heritable change with no change in the letters -- passing down since before the American Revolution. Plants do this; so do nematode worms, where small RNAs carry silencing for at least three generations and, under continuous reinforcement, for as many as eighty. Mammals mostly do not. Source: nature.com/articles/43657

question: When Bastiaan Heijmans's team went looking for a chemical mark left on Dutch adults by the famine they had been carried through, they did not compare them with the Dutch population at large, or with a matched sample of strangers. Each exposed person was set against a brother or sister of the same sex, born to the same two parents. What made a sibling the necessary comparison?
answer: How heavily that gene is tagged runs strongly in families
choices: How heavily that gene is tagged runs strongly in families
Brothers and sisters share the same adult diet and habits
Only siblings could be traced through the hospital records
Blood drawn on the same day gives a fairer measurement
context: Methylation at the IGF2 control region is strongly heritable, so two unrelated people can differ for reasons that have nothing to do with any famine. Only a sibling holds the family background steady while the exposure varies. That choice is what makes the 2008 result worth anything: the control group was picked to kill the most obvious rival explanation before a single measurement was taken. Sixty exposed adults, each set against their own brother or sister. The design is the finding. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2579375/

question: The babies carried through the Dutch hunger winter of 1944-45 grew up and had children of their own -- a second generation who never went hungry. In 2013 Veenendaal and colleagues weighed those children at birth and followed their health into adulthood, testing whether the famine had reached one generation further down. What did the two measurements show?
answer: No change in birth weight, and none in adult health
choices: No change in birth weight, and none in adult health
Lower birth weight, and more diabetes in adulthood
Lower birth weight, but no change in adult health
Normal birth weight, but more diabetes in adulthood
context: Veenendaal et al., BJOG 2013: no transgenerational effect of prenatal famine exposure on the birth weight of the F2 generation, and no differences in adult health between the F2 groups. A few scattered signals exist -- children of famine-exposed fathers ran somewhat heavier -- but nothing that establishes a mark being handed down, and anyone who tells a child otherwise is ahead of the data. Notice too how the counting works, because it deflates most grandchild claims: when a pregnant woman is exposed, her fetus is exposed directly, and the egg or sperm cells already forming inside that fetus are exposed directly too. Three generations touched at once. Genuine inheritance only begins in the generation after that. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23346894/

question: A mammal embryo does not keep the chemical annotations -- the methyl tags -- it inherits. It strips them off twice: first in the cells that will become eggs and sperm, then again in the hours and days after fertilisation. By the blastocyst stage, a few days in, roughly 80 to 90% of the tags across the whole genome are gone. What happens to the father's genome in that second wipe, and what happens to the mother's?
answer: An enzyme scrubs the father's genome; division dilutes the mother's
choices: An enzyme scrubs the father's genome; division dilutes the mother's
An enzyme scrubs the mother's genome; division dilutes the father's
A single enzyme strips both genomes, at the same rate and moment
Division alone dilutes both genomes over the embryo's first days
context: In the mouse zygote the enzyme TET3 actively strips up to about 90% of the methylation from the father's genome before the first division. The mother's genome loses its tags a different way, passively: the maintenance enzyme DNMT1 is shut out of the nucleus, so the tags are simply not copied onto the new strands and thin out as the cell divides. Imprinted regions are the deliberate exception -- about 150 genes, IGF2 among them, where only one parent's copy runs and the marks are protected from the wipe. That exception is exactly why a famine mark could still be read at IGF2 sixty years on, and why, at most other genes, a mark in a grandmother has no obvious road to a grandchild in mammals. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Transgenerational_epigenetic_inheritance

question: Once a year, at midday on the longest day, the townspeople of Syene in southern Egypt watched something happen to a certain deep well that never happened on any other day. What did they see?
answer: Sunlight reached the water at the very bottom
choices: Sunlight reached the water at the very bottom
The water level dropped by exactly one hand
A flock of ibises circled the rim at noon
The stone lining rang faintly like a bell
context: At the summer solstice at Syene (near modern Aswan) the Sun stood so nearly overhead that light reached straight down to the water and a vertical rod cast no shadow at all. That observation is the seed of the whole measurement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Eratosthenes.

question: On that same solstice noon, far to the north in Alexandria, Eratosthenes set his own vertical rod. This one did throw a shadow. He measured the angle between the rod and the sunbeam and found it close to 7 degrees and 12 minutes. What did he do with that angle?
answer: He recognized it as one-fiftieth of a full circle
choices: He recognized it as one-fiftieth of a full circle
He doubled it to get the tilt of the Earth's axis
He subtracted it from ninety to get the latitude of Syene
He divided it by the height of the rod to get the Sun's distance
context: 7 degrees 12 minutes goes into 360 degrees exactly fifty times. That single ratio is the whole trick: the arc between the two cities is one-fiftieth of the Earth's meridian. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference.

question: The 5,000-stadia figure did not come from a surveying chain. Who was actually paid to produce it?
answer: Bematists, professional pacers trained to walk with an even step
choices: Bematists, professional pacers trained to walk with an even step
Priests of Isis who counted temple flagstones between shrines
Naval crews rowing a measured barge up the Nile
Astronomers timing sunrise from paired hilltops
context: Bematists were paid step-counters used across Alexander's world; caravan-day estimates filled in where they did not walk. It is one of history's great answers built on a foot count. Source: aps.org/apsnews/2006/06/eratosthenes-measures-earth.

question: Eratosthenes wrote up his whole method in a book called On the Measurement of the Earth. Every copy is lost. Why do modern historians still know how he did it?
answer: Cleomedes summarized the method centuries later in a surviving textbook
choices: Cleomedes summarized the method centuries later in a surviving textbook
The original scroll was recovered from the ashes of Herculaneum in 1752
Ptolemy quoted the full derivation in the opening of his Almagest
A stone-carved copy still stands in the ruins of Syene
context: Cleomedes' handbook On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies preserves the simplified account. That is why some historians treat the famous well detail with caution: it is Cleomedes, not Eratosthenes, telling us. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eratosthenes; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Eratosthenes.

question: Any classroom today can rerun Eratosthenes without a boat or a caravan. What is the minimum kit two schools need to reproduce the whole result?
answer: A vertical stick at each school and a phone call at local noon on the same day
choices: A vertical stick at each school and a phone call at local noon on the same day
A telescope at each school and a shared observation of the same star at midnight
One weather balloon released simultaneously from each school
A GPS receiver at each school and a stopwatch
context: Each school records its shortest noon shadow, converts the ratio to an angle, and the difference in angles times the north-south distance gives the whole planet's circumference. Every summer the eratosthenes-project.eu network runs it in hundreds of classrooms. Source: school-education.ec.europa.eu; astro.princeton.edu/~dns/teachersguide/MeasECAct2.html.

question: Eratosthenes' geometry only works cleanly if two things are true: that the Sun sits exactly over Syene on the solstice, and that Syene lies exactly due south of Alexandria. Neither is true. What actually happens?
answer: The two mistakes push the answer in opposite directions and partly cancel
choices: The two mistakes push the answer in opposite directions and partly cancel
The two mistakes both shrink the answer, and only luck kept him near the truth
The two mistakes both grow the answer, and later scholars had to divide it down
Only the second matters; the first has no effect on the geometry
context: Syene sits about 37 km north of the Tropic of Cancer (so the Sun is not truly overhead) and roughly 3 degrees of longitude east of Alexandria's meridian. The errors partly offset, and that lucky cancellation is a large part of why the number came out so respectable. Source: geo.hunter.cuny.edu/~jochen/gtech201/lectures/lec6concepts/datums; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference.

question: Textbooks often say Eratosthenes measured the Earth to within one percent. Serious historians are more careful. What is the honest reason his exact accuracy cannot be pinned down today?
answer: Scholars do not know which length of stadion he was using
choices: Scholars do not know which length of stadion he was using
Alexandria's ancient position on the coast has since moved a full degree
The Earth's true circumference was only nailed down after 1990
His original numerical result was scrubbed by later editors
context: Estimates of one stadion run from about 157 metres to about 185 metres. That range gives Earth circumferences from roughly 39,375 km up to 46,100 km, against a true value near 40,075 km. The honest claim is 'within a few percent,' not 'he nailed it.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference; home.adelphi.edu/~bradley/HOMSIGMAA/Walkup.pdf.

question: Beyond Eratosthenes' shadow trick and Posidonius' Canopus sighting, ancient thinkers proposed at least one more sizing method that used the sky's own clock. Which was it?
answer: Timing a single lunar eclipse from two widely separated cities
choices: Timing a single lunar eclipse from two widely separated cities
Counting the days a caravan needed to circle a fixed mountain
Comparing the depth of a well dug at the coast against one dug inland
Watching how a star's rising point shifted along the horizon each dawn
context: That is one of the real ancient sizing methods: two cities note the moment a lunar eclipse begins, and the time difference between their local clocks gives the longitude arc between them, a fragment of the whole planet. The other real ancient approaches were Posidonius' Canopus star method from two ports and the simple horizon geometry of a distant ship's hull sinking before its mast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_circumference; aps.org/apsnews/2006/06/eratosthenes-measures-earth.

question: Almost all water is ordinary H2-16O, but roughly one water molecule in every 500 carries oxygen-18 instead of oxygen-16. Oxygen-18 is still chemically oxygen and behaves the same in reactions -- so what makes it different from oxygen-16?
answer: It carries two extra neutrons, so it is heavier
choices: It carries two extra neutrons, so it is heavier
It carries two extra protons, so it is a different element
It carries two extra electrons, so it is negatively charged
It is missing two neutrons, so it is lighter
context: That is the definition of an isotope: same element (protons unchanged), different neutron count, so different mass but the same chemistry. Oxygen-16 has 8 neutrons; oxygen-18 has 10. The whole ladder rests on that tiny mass difference. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_isotope_ratio_cycle.

question: A cloud drifts off the ocean and rains itself out mile after mile. As it does, each fresh raindrop coming down is a little richer in oxygen-18 than the drop before. What property of the two water molecules drives that sorting?
answer: H2-18O is heavier, so it evaporates less readily and condenses more readily
choices: H2-18O is heavier, so it evaporates less readily and condenses more readily
H2-18O carries a small electric charge, so it clings to airborne dust and salt ions
H2-18O forms a stronger hydrogen bond, so it clumps into larger droplets
H2-18O absorbs sunlight more strongly, so it warms up and rises before H2-16O
context: Fractionation, driven by mass. The two extra neutrons in oxygen-18 make H2-18O slightly harder to lift into the air and slightly easier to pull back out of a cloud. Result: vapour is isotopically light, first rain is isotopically heavy, and what remains in the cloud gets lighter and lighter as it rains itself out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core.

question: In June 1952 the young Danish physicist Willi Dansgaard collected rain right through a two-day Copenhagen storm and measured the ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 hour by hour. When he plotted it up, the isotope ratio was tracking one specific thing about the cloud each drop had fallen from. What was he actually reading?
answer: The temperature of the cloud the rain fell from
choices: The temperature of the cloud the rain fell from
The altitude the raindrop had started falling from
The distance the storm had travelled inland
The age of the water vapour in the cloud
context: A thermometer you could pour into a bottle. Because the sorting is sharper the colder it gets, the isotope ratio in a raindrop encodes the temperature at which it condensed. Dansgaard later extended the idea to Greenland snow -- the same reading, frozen and stacked layer by layer. The rapid climate flickers he and Hans Oeschger later found in those cores are named Dansgaard-Oeschger events. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willi_Dansgaard.  (Legend.)

question: Harold Urey had discovered deuterium -- hydrogen with an extra neutron -- back in 1931 and won the 1934 Nobel in Chemistry for it. In the late 1940s he realised the same oxygen-isotope sorting is locked in when a sea creature crystallises its shell. What did that turn a fossil shell into?
answer: An instrument recording the temperature of the sea it grew in
choices: An instrument recording the temperature of the sea it grew in
A radioactive clock giving the year the animal died
A pressure gauge showing how deep the seafloor was
A magnetic compass pointing to the ancient pole
context: A dead animal becomes an instrument. Calcium carbonate crystallising in seawater takes up oxygen-18 slightly more readily when the water is cold, so the ratio fossilised in the shell is a paleothermometer. Urey's insight seeded the whole field of stable-isotope paleoclimatology and set up his student Cesare Emiliani's foraminifera work a few years later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Urey.

question: Rain gets isotopically LIGHTER the further inland it falls and the higher up the mountain it lands, because the heavy molecules keep dropping out first. So the tap water in a valley carries a different isotopic signature from the tap water on a mountain peak. What body tissue records the water a specific person actually drank while growing up?
answer: Tooth enamel and hair keratin
choices: Tooth enamel and hair keratin
Bone marrow and spleen tissue
Liver tissue and stomach lining
Muscle fibre and lymph nodes
context: Enamel locks in the oxygen isotopes of childhood drinking water and never remodels; hair records the last few months. When researchers analysed the tooth enamel of Otzi the Iceman, the signature pointed to the South Tyrol village of Feldthurns just north of Bolzano as where he grew up, with later years in valleys about 50 km farther north. The water in you is signed by the clouds over the place you grew up. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_hydrology; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otzi.  (Legend.)

question: Willi Dansgaard argued snow is rain's archive: every winter's layer freezes in its isotope ratio, and if you drill straight down you read climate layer by layer back through time. In July 1966 the US Army's Camp Century project in northwest Greenland pulled the first long ice core to reach bedrock, 1,387 metres down. Later Antarctic cores went far deeper still -- the EPICA Dome C core in Antarctica reached bedrock at 3,260 metres. Roughly how far back in time does its usable climate record extend?
answer: About 800,000 years
choices: About 800,000 years
About 8,000 years
About 80,000 years
About 8 million years
context: Camp Century in 1966 was the first bedrock-reaching ice core, 1,387 m of Greenland ice read layer by layer. The polar deeps went further: Vostok reached about 3,769 m and roughly 420,000 years; EPICA Dome C reached about 3,260 m and pulled a usable climate record extending back roughly 800,000 years -- nearly a million winters of stacked snow, each layer's isotope ratio a temperature reading. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core.

question: When you drill an ice core, you are not only reading oxygen isotopes in the frozen water. Tiny bubbles are trapped in the ice at every depth, and those bubbles are not a proxy at all -- they are literal samples of ancient air, sealed at the moment that year's snow packed down. What did those bubbles directly measure about the atmosphere at the Last Glacial Maximum, compared with the air just before the industrial era?
answer: Carbon dioxide was about 30 percent lower
choices: Carbon dioxide was about 30 percent lower
Oxygen was about 30 percent lower
Nitrogen was about 30 percent higher
Water vapour was about 30 percent higher
context: A bubble in a polar ice core is a literal sample of Ice Age air. Direct measurement, no model in between: CO2 at the Last Glacial Maximum was roughly 30 percent below its pre-industrial value. The isotopes of the surrounding ice give the temperature at the same layer, so the two records sit side by side. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_core.  (Legend.)

question: In 1955 Cesare Emiliani, a student of Harold Urey, measured oxygen-18 in the calcite shells of tiny sea creatures called foraminifera pulled from deep-sea cores. Reading the ratio the way Urey had taught him, Emiliani reported that Caribbean sea-surface temperatures had swung by about how much across the great ice-age cycles?
answer: About 6 degrees Celsius
choices: About 6 degrees Celsius
About 2 degrees Celsius
About 10 degrees Celsius
About 15 degrees Celsius
context: Emiliani turned a jar of microscopic shells into a record of glacial cycles -- the first quantitative paleotemperature curve for the deep sea. The interpretation was not the whole story (see the next rung), but the measurement itself opened a new era of paleoclimatology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesare_Emiliani.

question: Cesare Emiliani had read the oxygen-18 signal in foraminifera shells as a direct thermometer of ancient ocean water. In 1967 the British paleoclimatologist Nicholas Shackleton published a Nature paper reanalysing exactly the same kind of measurement and argued the signal was being driven mostly by something else instead -- same numbers, different meaning. What was Shackleton saying the shells were actually recording?
answer: How much light water was locked up in continental ice sheets
choices: How much light water was locked up in continental ice sheets
The salinity of the surface ocean during each glacial
The abundance of plankton food across each cycle
The pH of the deep ocean over the last million years
context: When a glacial cycle locks huge volumes of isotopically light water into ice sheets, the ocean left behind gets heavier -- and every shell crystallising in it does too. Shackleton showed that effect dominates Emiliani's signal. Same measurement, wrong interpretation, fixed by a better one -- and it made the record MORE useful, tying the deep-sea shells directly to global ice volume. Source: nature.com/articles/215015a0 (Shackleton, Nature 215:15-17, 1967).  (Legend.)

question: Natural background tritium in rain sits at only about 5 to 10 tritium units. In the late 1950s and early 1960s atmospheric nuclear-weapons tests spiked tritium in rainwater worldwide by two to three orders of magnitude, with peaks near 1,000 TU. In the decades since, what have hydrologists most commonly done with that global tritium spike?
answer: Used it to date whether a well's water fell as rain before or after the bomb era
choices: Used it to date whether a well's water fell as rain before or after the bomb era
Used it to map how quickly rainwater from the 1960s reaches deep aquifers today
Used it to check whether a glacier's youngest ice was laid down after 1963
Used it to trace bomb-era fallout patterns from the prevailing winds
context: The bomb pulse. A weapons-test scar turned into a hydrologist's dating tool: tritium is radioactive hydrogen with a half-life of about 12.3 years, so water coming out of a well with essentially no tritium fell before about 1953; water carrying a clear bomb-pulse signal fell after, and the decay of the spike puts a decade-scale age on it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritium.  (Legend.)

question: In May 2020 Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley flew SpaceX's Dragon Endeavour with a sequin-covered toy apatosaurus, Tremor, tied inside the cabin. Crews have carried such a toy since the earliest flights, and it does a job. What does Tremor show them?
answer: It lifts off its string the instant they go weightless.
choices: It lifts off its string the instant they go weightless.
It swings toward the nose when the thrusters fire.
It presses flat to the wall as the g-force peaks.
It spins on its string if the capsule starts rolling.
context: Tremor was a Ty Flippables apatosaurus chosen by Behnken's and Hurley's sons, Theodore, 6, and Jack, 10. It began floating the moment Dragon Endeavour reached orbit, and at the station it met the crew's own plush 'Little Earth'. Yuri Gagarin is credited with starting the tradition in 1961, releasing a pencil inside Vostok 1 to catch the exact instant; Snoopy flew as the indicator on Artemis I. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Zero-gravity indicator'; Space.com, 'SpaceX "stowaway" revealed by crew as sons' dinosaur toy "Tremor"'.

question: A pen hangs in the air beside an astronaut aboard the International Space Station, 400 kilometres above the Pacific. Nobody is holding it and nothing is touching it, yet it stays exactly where she left it. Why does the pen stay put?
answer: Everything around it falls toward Earth at the same rate.
choices: Everything around it falls toward Earth at the same rate.
There is no gravity in space to pull it downward.
The station's speed cancels out the pull of gravity.
It is far too distant for Earth's gravity to reach.
context: NASA puts it plainly: 'The spacecraft, its crew and any objects aboard are all falling toward but around Earth. Since they are all falling together, the crew and objects appear to float.' The station never hits the ground because the curve of its fall matches the curve of the Earth. What is missing up there is not gravity but WEIGHT — the space journalist James Oberg defined weight as 'the resistance of gravitational attraction by an anchored structure or a counterforce'. Take away the floor's push and you feel nothing, even while gravity keeps pulling at nearly full strength. Sources: NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'; Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: The International Space Station circles about 400 kilometres above the ground, roughly the distance from London to Paris but straight up instead of along the ground. Compared with the pull you feel on your kitchen floor, how strong is Earth's gravity out where the astronauts work?
answer: About 90 per cent as strong.
choices: About 90 per cent as strong.
About 50 per cent as strong.
About 10 per cent as strong.
About 1 per cent as strong.
context: Gravity at that altitude measures about 8.69 metres per second squared, against 9.81 at the surface. The Open University states it directly: 'The gravitational field on the ISS is approximately 89% of that on the Earth's surface.' NASA rounds it to 'about 90 percent of what it is on the planet's surface.' So the popular phrase 'zero gravity' is not a small exaggeration — it is wrong about the one thing it names. Sources: Open University OpenLearn, 'Is there any gravity on the ISS?'; NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'.

question: Isaac Newton asked readers to picture a cannon on a mountain so tall its summit rises above the atmosphere, aimed dead level at the horizon. He imagined packing in more and more powder, so each ball flew farther before landing: one mile, two, five, ten, a hundred, a thousand. Then one ball never came down at all, and Newton drew its path. Where does it finish?
answer: Back at the mouth of the cannon it was fired from.
choices: Back at the mouth of the cannon it was fired from.
A quarter turn short of the cannon, and still climbing.
Stalled high above the far side of the turning Earth.
Far beyond the cannon, spiralling wider on every lap.
context: The diagram on page 6 puts the cannon at point V and labels three paths: VD, which falls back almost at once; VE, a longer ellipse that loops partway round before striking the ground; and VF, the circle that carries the ball the whole way round and home to the muzzle. Newton's own words run: 'We may therefore suppose the velocity to be so encreased, that it would describe an arc of 1, 2, 5, 10, 100, 1000 miles before it arrived at the Earth, till at last exceeding the limits of the Earth, it should pass quite by without touching it.' That escape case is described in the text but is NOT drawn on the diagram. ACCURACY RAIL: the scene is from A Treatise of the System of the World, drafted about 1685 and published posthumously in 1728, a year after Newton's death — not in the Principia proper. Voltaire retold the whole scenario for general readers in his Letters Concerning the English Nation (1733), using it to demolish the rival Cartesian vortex theory across Europe. Source: Grokipedia, 'Newton's cannonball'.

question: The International Space Station carries its crew around the world at about 17,500 miles per hour, some ten times the speed of a rifle bullet. How many sunrises does an astronaut aboard pass through in a single twenty-four hours?
answer: Sixteen.
choices: Sixteen.
Forty.
Four.
Two.
context: One lap takes about ninety minutes — Wikipedia's figure is 92.9 minutes, or 15.5 orbits a day — at roughly 7.66 kilometres per second, 28,000 km/h, on an orbit running from a perigee of 413 km to an apogee of 422 km. Human bodies cannot run on a ninety-minute clock, so the station keeps Greenwich time and the crew pull the window shades down in order to sleep on a normal twenty-four-hour schedule. Sources: NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'; NASA Earth Observatory, 'Sunset from the International Space Station'; Wikipedia, 'International Space Station'; Grokipedia, 'Free fall'.

question: You do not need a rocket to be weightless. On the first steep plunge of a big rollercoaster, riders are for a second or two exactly as weightless as an astronaut aboard the space station. Which of these puts an ordinary person into that same real weightlessness?
answer: A lift racing down its shaft with the cable cut.
choices: A lift racing down its shaft with the cable cut.
A submarine sinking fast with its ballast tanks flooded.
A parachutist descending under a fully open canopy.
An airliner holding a shallow, perfectly steady dive.
context: A cut cable leaves the lift and everyone inside it accelerating downward together with nothing pressing back — the identical condition an astronaut is in, except that theirs never ends. Orbit is simply free fall that does not stop; NASA's point is that the crew are not floating in an absence of gravity but falling in it. The other three descents all have something still holding the body up: the open canopy's drag, the water around the submarine's hull, and the wings of the steadily diving airliner each push back, so the person inside still weighs what they always did. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Free fall'; Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: Blue Origin's New Shepard carries passengers above 100 kilometres, high enough to count officially as space, where they unbuckle and float for about three minutes before strapping back in for the ride home. Crews aboard the International Space Station, circling at 400 kilometres, float for months. What would New Shepard have to gain before its passengers could do the same?
answer: Enough sideways speed to keep missing the ground.
choices: Enough sideways speed to keep missing the ground.
Enough thrust to climb four times higher than it does.
Enough altitude to leave the last of the air behind.
Enough fuel to keep its engine burning far longer.
context: Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo gives four to five minutes of floating near 100 kilometres, and neither vehicle goes fast enough sideways to orbit, so both simply fall back down — Newton's cannonball fired with too little powder. There are clean numbers for how much sideways speed is enough: circular orbital speed just above the surface is about 7.9 kilometres per second, and escape speed is about 11.2 — exactly the square root of two times as fast. Same cannon, same mountain; only the muzzle speed differs. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'; Grokipedia, 'Newton's cannonball'.

question: NASA's weightlessness training aircraft, which crews call the Vomit Comet, climbs at about forty-five degrees with everyone aboard pressed at nearly twice their normal weight, then cuts its thrust and pushes over the top about eight kilometres up. For the next twenty-five seconds every person and loose tool inside floats. Over that stretch, what path is the aircraft tracing through the air?
answer: The exact arc a stone would follow if you threw it.
choices: The exact arc a stone would follow if you threw it.
A circle of one fixed radius, held all the way over.
A curve flattened at the top to hold one steady speed.
A curve steepened at the top to match the cabin's weight.
context: The pilot flies the aircraft along the path a thrown object would take on its own, so the aeroplane and everyone inside it fall together and nothing presses on anybody. The pull-out at the bottom costs another twenty seconds at about 1.8 g. The original was a modified KC-135 military tanker flying thirty to forty parabolas per sortie over the Gulf of Mexico from the 1960s until it retired in 2004; NASA then flew a C-9B Skytrain II from 2005 to 2014. ESA's Airbus A310 Zero-G, flown by Novespace out of Bordeaux-Merignac since 2015, does thirty-one parabolas a mission. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: Some experiments need only seconds of weightlessness, so engineers buy those seconds by dropping the experiment down a tall evacuated shaft. NASA's shaft at the Glenn Research Center runs 155 metres deep and yields 5.18 seconds. Germany's ZARM tower in Bremen is much the same height, and a plain drop there gives 4.74 seconds, yet ZARM can deliver 9.3 seconds from that same tower. How?
answer: It fires the capsule upward first, so it floats going up too.
choices: It fires the capsule upward first, so it floats going up too.
It pumps the shaft to a harder vacuum, cutting the drag.
It releases the capsule from a cradle already moving downward.
It brakes the capsule magnetically, stretching out the fall.
context: A thrown ball is weightless on the way up exactly as it is on the way down, so catapulting the capsule from the bottom of the shaft buys the rise as well as the fall — nearly double the time from the same building. The capsules come to rest in polystyrene granules that hold the impact to about 30 g. NASA's Zero Gravity Research Facility has been running since 1966. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness'.

question: NASA never calls conditions aboard the space station zero gravity; the word it uses is microgravity. That is not only because nine-tenths of Earth's pull still reaches up there — the pull is also not quite the same at every point inside the station. Which effect chiefly accounts for that difference?
answer: An astronaut's feet sit nearer Earth than their head, so they are pulled harder.
choices: An astronaut's feet sit nearer Earth than their head, so they are pulled harder.
The station's metal hull shields its innermost modules from part of the pull.
The station's own mass tugs loose objects toward its heaviest section.
The Sun pulls hardest on whichever end of the station is turned toward it.
context: That head-to-feet difference is a tidal, or gravity-gradient, effect, and it has been measured: about 0.384 microgravities per metre at 400 kilometres. Add the drag of the thin air and the nudges of astronauts pushing off the walls, and the leftover acceleration on a quiet day comes to roughly one millionth of Earth's gravity (10^-6 g) — small, but not nothing, and that is where the 'micro' comes from. NASA flags the popular error by name: microgravity 'is sometimes called zero gravity, but this is misleading.' Gravity cannot be screened off by any hull; the station's own mass and the distant Sun do pull as well, but the measured gradient that gives 'microgravity' its name is the head-to-feet one. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness'; Grokipedia, 'Weightlessness'; NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'.

question: Four hundred kilometres up is normally called space, but the International Space Station is not in a true vacuum: enough thin gas remains to drag on it, and the station sinks about two kilometres lower every month. Docked Progress and Cygnus freighters have to fire their engines six to twelve times a year to shove it back up. That sinking is not steady, though. What makes the station fall fastest?
answer: The Sun reaching the peak of its activity cycle.
choices: The Sun reaching the peak of its activity cycle.
The Moon swinging closest to Earth at perigee.
The station gaining mass as freighters and modules dock.
The station passing over the tropics twice each orbit.
context: At solar maximum the upper atmosphere heats and puffs outward, so the station runs into thicker gas at the same altitude and the drag can double or triple. Day to day the loss runs roughly 50 to 100 metres of altitude; the station's own thrusters can perform the reboost when no freighter is docked. Sources: Wikipedia, 'International Space Station'; The Planetary Society, 'How NASA plans to deorbit the International Space Station'.

question: In 1907 Albert Einstein was sitting in a chair in the Bern patent office when a single thought struck him. It startled him, he said, and he called it in German the happiest thought of his life; it grew into general relativity. Lecturing in Kyoto in December 1922 he repeated the thought exactly as it had come to him. What was it?
answer: If a person falls freely, he will not feel his own weight.
choices: If a person falls freely, he will not feel his own weight.
If a clock is carried fast enough, its hands must run slow.
If light carries energy, a beam must bend as it passes the Sun.
If space is truly empty, nothing in it can say which way is up.
context: Einstein's telling, from the Kyoto address of 14 December 1922: 'I was sitting in a chair in the patent office at Bern when all of a sudden a thought occurred to me: "If a person falls freely he will not feel his own weight." I was startled.' In German he called it 'der glucklichste Gedanke meines Lebens' — the happiest thought of my life. His sharper published formulation ran: 'For an observer falling freely from the roof of a house, the gravitational field does not exist.' That one sentence became the equivalence principle. TESTIMONY, NOT RECORD: the patent-office moment survives only in Einstein's own recollection, told fifteen years afterwards. Source: Stanford Gravity Probe B, 'Einstein's Spacetime'; Einstein's Kyoto address, 14 December 1922.  (Legend.)

question: Michael Faraday left his London Sunday school at thirteen with reading, writing and arithmetic and nothing more. In 1805, aged fourteen, he was apprenticed for seven years to a tradesman on Blandford Street. Where did the boy get the science that made him a chemist?
answer: From the books brought into the shop to be bound.
choices: From the books brought into the shop to be bound.
From evening classes at a London hospital.
From a tutor his master hired for him.
From a chemist's shop where he swept at night.
context: The tradesman was the bookbinder George Riebau of Blandford Street, and Faraday was fourteen when the seven-year apprenticeship began in 1805. Everything he learned came off the workbench: he read the volumes that passed through his hands to be bound. Source: Grokipedia, Michael Faraday (Early Life and Education); Wikipedia, Michael Faraday.

question: In September 1821 Michael Faraday stuck a magnet upright in a lump of wax at the bottom of a deep basin, filled the basin with mercury, and hung a wire so its tip dipped into the mercury beside the magnet. Then he sent a current down the wire. What did the wire do?
answer: It travelled round and round the magnet, endlessly.
choices: It travelled round and round the magnet, endlessly.
It sprang upright and stood there, quite rigid.
It glowed red and melted the wax beneath it.
It leapt clear of the mercury and hung still.
context: It was the first device ever built that turned electricity into continuous motion. His notebook for 3 September 1821, describing a cruder first attempt, records only: 'Very satisfactory, but make more sensible apparatus.' He built the basin version the next day. He later mailed pocket-sized working models to colleagues across Europe, where the little motors became fashionable novelty gifts; his own original apparatus does not survive. Source: Royal Institution, 'The birth of electric motion'; IEEE Spectrum, '200 Years Ago, Faraday Invented the Electric Motor'.

question: The Royal Institution still keeps the iron ring, 170 mm across and 32 mm thick, that Michael Faraday spent some ten working days winding with cotton-insulated copper in its basement in 1831. The copper was ordinary wire from an everyday trade. What had it been made for?
answer: Wire made for ladies' bonnets.
choices: Wire made for ladies' bonnets.
Wire made for corset stays.
Wire made for umbrella ribs.
Wire made for fishing tackle.
context: Bonnet wire, wound by hand onto a lump of soft iron in a basement, was the first electric transformer ever built, and the object itself survives in the Royal Institution's collection. Source: Royal Institution collection, 'Michael Faraday's ring-coil apparatus'.

question: Michael Faraday, an apprentice in a London shop with no laboratory of his own, read Jane Marcet's 'Conversations on Chemistry', a book written as a dialogue for young readers, and said long afterwards that it 'came as the full light in my mind'. What did the boy do with the chemistry he found in it?
answer: He tested her chemistry with his own cheap experiments.
choices: He tested her chemistry with his own cheap experiments.
He checked her chapters against the other books in the shop.
He set her chemistry to memory and recited it nightly.
He copied the whole book out by hand for his own shelf.
context: Writing to Auguste De La Rive on 2 October 1858, Faraday set out the rule he had taught himself as a boy: he would 'trust a fact' but 'always cross examined an assertion'. When his own cheap experiments agreed with Marcet's book, he said, 'I felt that I had got hold of an anchor in chemical knowledge.' Source: Faraday to Arthur-Auguste De La Rive, 2 October 1858, Epsilon letter archive.

question: In 1812 Michael Faraday, a twenty-year-old apprentice, attended the last four lectures Humphry Davy gave at the Royal Institution and wrote up every one of them in full. He then sent Davy the notes, with a letter asking for scientific work. What landed on Davy's desk?
answer: A hand-bound volume of three hundred-odd pages.
choices: A hand-bound volume of three hundred-odd pages.
A printed pamphlet of some forty-odd pages.
A leather case of sixty numbered cards.
A fair copy on twenty large folded sheets.
context: He bound his own lecture notes into a book, because binding books was his trade. It worked: Faraday was appointed chemical assistant at the Royal Institution on 1 March 1813. The post was open because Davy's eyesight had been damaged by an exploding sample of nitrogen trichloride and because the previous assistant had been dismissed after a fight. Sources disagree on the page count -- Bence Jones, describing the surviving volume, says 386 small quarto pages, Grokipedia says 313, Wikipedia says 300. Source: Bence Jones, 'The Royal Institution' (Project Gutenberg); Grokipedia, Michael Faraday.

question: In January 1836 Michael Faraday built a wooden cube twelve feet on a side in the Royal Institution's lecture room, stood it on glass insulators, and covered it with copper netting and bands of tin foil. He climbed inside carrying lighted candles while a machine charged the outside hard enough to throw sparks. What happened to the flames?
answer: They stood perfectly still.
choices: They stood perfectly still.
They bent towards the netting.
They flared up and burned blue.
They guttered out at once.
context: A gold-leaf electrometer left inside never twitched either, although the outside of the cage reached a potential high enough to ignite alcohol. Charge spreads over the outside of a conductor and leaves the inside untouched. Faraday wrote the work up in the Eleventh Series of 'Experimental Researches in Electricity', received by the Royal Society on 30 November 1837. Source: Grokipedia, Faraday cage (Early Experiments); Wikipedia, Michael Faraday.

question: Michael Faraday was a Sandemanian, a Christian who held that Scripture forbade the heaping up of riches and worldly reward. He refused the knighthood the Crown offered him, twice refused the presidency of the Royal Society, and refused burial in Westminster Abbey, where England lays its great men. Where does he lie instead?
answer: In the dissenters' section of Highgate Cemetery.
choices: In the dissenters' section of Highgate Cemetery.
In the churchyard of his Sandemanian meeting house.
In the vault beneath the Royal Institution.
In the parish ground at Hampton Court Palace.
context: Dissenters were Christians who worshipped outside the Church of England, and Highgate Cemetery keeps a section for them; that is where Faraday lies. He had said he would rather remain 'plain Mr Faraday to the end', and the Royal Society first asked him to be its President in 1857. Westminster Abbey carries only a memorial plaque for him, near Isaac Newton's tomb. Queen Victoria did persuade him to accept one thing: a rent-free grace-and-favour house at Hampton Court in 1858, where he died on 25 August 1867. Source: Wikipedia, Michael Faraday; Grokipedia, Michael Faraday (Later Years; Advisory Roles and Honors).

question: Michael Faraday rushed his 1821 rotation experiment into print in a journal he was editing himself, naming nobody else. William Hyde Wollaston had tried the same rotation in the Royal Institution laboratory, with Humphry Davy watching, and his apparatus had failed. Within a week Davy -- Faraday's own mentor, and President of the Royal Society -- was accusing him of plagiarism. Faraday went to see Wollaston. What did Wollaston tell him?
answer: That what others thought of Faraday's conduct was Faraday's affair.
choices: That what others thought of Faraday's conduct was Faraday's affair.
That the credit was his, and he would say so at the Royal Society.
That what Davy had said of the business he would not contradict.
That he wanted his own name added to the paper's next printing.
context: Wollaston's reply ran: 'As to the opinion which others may have of your conduct, that is your concern, not mine; and if you fully acquit yourself of making any incorrect use of the suggestions of others, it seems to me that you have no occasion to concern yourself much about the matter.' Davy was less generous. At a Royal Society meeting on 6 March 1823 he said publicly that 'we owe to the sagacity of Dr. Wollaston, the first suggestion of electro-magnetic rotation', and that Wollaston would have found it himself had his apparatus not failed. Faraday was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1824 with exactly one vote against him, believed to be Davy's; the other Fellows overruled him. Source: Frank James, Davy Notebooks Project, Lancaster University; MacTutor, Michael Faraday.

question: On 29 August 1831 Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of insulated copper onto opposite halves of a soft iron ring. One coil ran to a battery of ten pairs of plates. The other, with no battery in its circuit at all, ran to a sensitive galvanometer. When did that galvanometer's needle move?
answer: Only as the battery was joined or broken.
choices: Only as the battery was joined or broken.
Only while the battery current ran steadily.
Steadily at first, then fading away slowly.
Only once the iron ring had grown warm.
context: That 'only at make and break' behaviour is the law itself: a steady magnetic field induces nothing, and only a changing one drives a current. Faraday's earlier attempts had all used static arrangements -- a magnet sitting near a closed loop, a steady current in a neighbouring wire -- which is much of why the hunt took him about ten years. He was not alone in seeing it: Joseph Henry, teaching at the Albany Academy in New York, observed induction independently and had some results earlier, but published only in July 1832, after Faraday's paper of 24 November 1831. Today mutual induction is credited to Faraday, self-induction to Henry, and the unit of inductance is the henry. Source: Grokipedia, Faraday's law of induction; Smithsonian Institution Archives, 'Electromagnetism'.

question: In the autumn of 1831 Michael Faraday mounted a copper disc a foot across on a brass axle and set it spinning between the poles of the Royal Society's great magnet. Sliding contacts touched the disc at its rim and at its centre and ran to a galvanometer. What did the needle do?
answer: It swung right over and held there, turn after turn.
choices: It swung right over and held there, turn after turn.
It kicked once and dropped straight back to zero.
It trembled in time with each turn of the disc.
It crept over slowly and then sank back again.
context: This came only weeks after the two-coil iron ring of 29 August 1831. The needle swung ninety degrees or more, and unlike every earlier result the current did not die away: keep turning the handle and it keeps flowing. Reverse the spin, or flip the magnet, and the current reverses. That disc is the ancestor of every generator in every power station. Faraday's induction law also runs every transformer on every pole and every electric motor from a hairdryer to a locomotive. Source: IEEE Milestones Wiki, 'Faraday's Discovery of Induction'; Joseph Henry Project, Princeton, 'Faraday Unipolar Generator'.

question: Michael Faraday showed in 1836 that charge sits on the outside of a conductor and leaves the inside untouched, and you can test that in a kitchen. Seal a switched-on mobile phone in a plastic bag, wrap the bag completely in aluminium foil, and ring the number: nothing. Leave the bag out, so the foil lies straight against the phone, and the call gets through. Why does the bare-foil version fail?
answer: The foil then acts as an extension of the phone's antenna.
choices: The foil then acts as an extension of the phone's antenna.
The foil then earths itself through the phone's metal case.
The foil then heats slightly and stops blocking the signal.
The foil then carries too little charge to shield anything.
context: The same principle is why a microwave oven's door carries a metal mesh with holes smaller than the microwaves it must hold in, and why a car body protects the people inside it during a lightning strike. Source: University of Iowa Physics instructional demonstrations 5B20.35 'Faraday's Cage - Radio' and 'Cell Phone and Aluminum Foil'; Wikipedia, Faraday cage.

question: Michael Faraday's mathematics never reached trigonometry -- he could manage only the simplest algebra, and no calculus at all -- yet for thirty years he worked on magnetic and electric forces that nobody could see. Having no equations to write, what did he put on paper instead?
answer: Curved lines of force, drawn through empty space.
choices: Curved lines of force, drawn through empty space.
Tables of measured forces, to four decimal places.
Scale drawings of every piece of his apparatus.
Geometric figures built with a compass and rule.
context: Faraday treated those lines as physically real -- tensile lines of stress distributed continuously through space -- not as a bookkeeping trick. That is the idea of the FIELD: space itself carries the action, instead of a magnet reaching across a void. Do not inflate the story into 'no education' -- he read constantly and lectured for over thirty years, giving nineteen series of the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures between 1827 and 1860. Source: Wikipedia, Michael Faraday; Grokipedia, Michael Faraday (Field Theory).

question: James Clerk Maxwell took the diagrams Michael Faraday had drawn of magnetic and electric action and recast them as the equations physicists still use today. Faraday himself could manage only the simplest algebra and had never reached trigonometry. What was Maxwell's own written verdict on him?
answer: That he was in reality a mathematician of a very high order.
choices: That he was in reality a mathematician of a very high order.
That he was a superb observer who left the mathematics to others.
That his drawings were a useful crutch for an untrained mind.
That his instinct had outrun his training at every single step.
context: Maxwell titled his first great electromagnetic paper, in 1855, 'On Faraday's Lines of Force', and wrote of Faraday that he was 'in reality a mathematician of a very high order -- one from whom the mathematicians of the future may derive valuable and fertile methods.' Source: Wikipedia, Michael Faraday (Maxwell quote); Grokipedia, Faraday's law of induction.

question: One of the best-loved stories about Michael Faraday has the Prime Minister, William Gladstone, ask what use his electrical toy could possibly be, and Faraday answer, 'One day, sir, you may tax it.' No letter, newspaper or biography from Faraday's own lifetime carries the tale. Which checkable date shows the story cannot be true as told?
answer: Gladstone first became Prime Minister the year after Faraday died.
choices: Gladstone first became Prime Minister the year after Faraday died.
The same exchange appears in a French almanac printed in 1789.
Britain had already been taxing electricity since the year 1852.
Faraday's electrical work was all done before Gladstone was born.
context: Faraday died on 25 August 1867, and William Gladstone did not become Prime Minister until 1868 -- so the story's own casting breaks on a date anyone can look up. Snopes can find the tale in no account by Faraday or by any contemporary -- no letter, no newspaper, no biography -- and it surfaces only well after his death; it is also told with the answer 'Of what use is a new-born baby?'. It looks invented later to score a point against short-sighted politicians. Faraday is worth loving without it -- and checking a beloved story against a date is exactly what he would have done. Source: Snopes fact-check, 'Michael Faraday Tax Quote'; Grokipedia, Michael Faraday.  (Legend.)

question: Michael Faraday lit a single candle at the Royal Institution in December 1860 and gave six lectures on it -- his last Christmas course for children. He began by telling them why he had picked so plain a thing. What did he tell them a candle was?
answer: The open door into the study of natural philosophy.
choices: The open door into the study of natural philosophy.
The oldest instrument that natural philosophy ever had.
The little sun that every household keeps indoors.
The one machine a child could take wholly to pieces.
context: Six lectures -- two in December 1860, four in January 1861 -- to houses averaging 650 children, the biggest, 740, at the fifth. He opened the first one with 'And now, my boys and girls, I must first tell you of what candles are made.' Faraday's reason for giving a whole course to one object: there is 'no better, there is no more open door by which you can enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.' It was his last Christmas series; he had run a candle course before, and gave nineteen series in all. He did not start the tradition either -- the Royal Institution's Managers founded it in 1825, and John Millington gave the first course. Source: Faraday, The Chemical History of a Candle, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org; Project Gutenberg pg14474); Homerton College Library, 'Faraday and the Christmas Lectures'; Royal Institution, '200 years of the Christmas Lectures'.

question: Faraday's showstopper prop was a cracked tallow candle raised from the warship Royal George, which sank in 1782; divers reached the wreck fifty-seven years later, so it had lain all that time in salt water. Faraday lit it in front of the children. What did it do?
answer: It lit and burned as steadily as a new one.
choices: It lit and burned as steadily as a new one.
It guttered out in a cloud of steam and smoke.
It burned with a green flame from the sea salt.
It crumbled into a wet powder as it warmed.
context: The Royal George went down on 29 August 1782; Colonel Pasley's salvage operations began in August 1839. Faraday: 'It has been sunk in the sea for many years, subject to the action of salt water... though it is cracked about and broken a good deal, yet, when lighted, it goes on burning regularly, and the tallow resumes its natural condition as soon as it is fused.' His prop table also held a plaited wick that never needs snuffing, paraffin candles made from paraffin out of the Irish bogs, and a wax sent to him from Japan.
