Source: Faraday, Lecture I and its footnote (en.wikisource.org).

question: The flame of a candle sits at the top of the wick, but every scrap of fuel is down in the solid stick below, and nobody carries it up by hand. Faraday told the children the fuel travels 'not in a careless way, but very beautifully in the very midst of the centre of action.' What carries it up to the flame?
answer: Capillary attraction, drawing melted wax up the wick.
choices: Capillary attraction, drawing melted wax up the wick.
The wick burning steadily downward into the wax.
Hot air from below, pressing the melted wax up.
The flame boiling wax off the open pool's surface.
context: Capillary attraction is the same pull that walks water up the corner of a paper towel or into a lump of sugar -- try it in a saucer tonight. The wick is a pump, not the fuel: the flame's heat melts a pool, the pool climbs the wick, and only at the top does it turn to vapour and burn. Nothing solid ever burns in a candle. Source: Faraday, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org).

question: Faraday closed the last of the lectures with a wish that had nothing to do with chemistry. He hoped his young listeners might, in their own generation, 'be fit to compare to a candle' -- and then said exactly what he meant by it. In what way were they to be like one?
answer: By shining as lights to those about them.
choices: By shining as lights to those about them.
By burning steadily and wasting nothing.
By giving warmth to the house that keeps them.
By making light from the plainest stuff there is.
context: The documented closing words: 'all I can say to you at the end of these lectures (for we must come to an end at one time or other) is to express a wish that you may, in your generation, be fit to compare to a candle; that you may, like it, shine as lights to those about you; that, in all your actions, you may justify the beauty of the taper by making your deeds honourable and effectual in the discharge of your duty to your fellow-men.' He was sixty-nine, and this was the last Christmas course he ever gave. Source: Faraday, Lecture VI, closing paragraph (en.wikisource.org); Homerton College Library.

question: Michael Faraday left school with nothing but reading, writing and arithmetic. At fourteen he was apprenticed to the London bookbinder George Riebau and read the books he was binding. In 1812 he got tickets to Humphry Davy's Royal Institution lectures and took 313 pages of notes. What did he do with them?
answer: Bound them into a book and sent it to Davy, asking for work.
choices: Bound them into a book and sent it to Davy, asking for work.
Bound them into a book and sold it to buy chemical gear.
Bound them into a book and gave it to his master Riebau.
Bound them into a book and kept it as his private course.
context: 1805: aged fourteen, apprenticed to Riebau for seven years. Jane Marcet's 'Conversations on Chemistry' (1806) lit the fuse. 1812: 313 pages of notes on Davy's lectures, bound by the apprentice's own hands and posted to Davy with a letter asking for a job. Davy took him on as chemical assistant on 1 March 1813. Faraday's lifelong interest in flames began with the miners' safety lamp he worked on with Davy in 1815-16 -- confined combustion and explosive firedamp, life-or-death flame science that fed straight into the lecture bench thirty years later. Source: Grokipedia: Michael Faraday.

question: Set a candle burning where nothing disturbs it and a neat cup forms at the top: a pool of melted wax inside a solid rim that never lets the pool spill over. Michael Faraday made the children look hard at that rim -- something shapes it every second the candle burns. What keeps the rim solid?
answer: Rising air, which cools the outer edge fastest.
choices: Rising air, which cools the outer edge fastest.
The wick, drawing wax hardest from beneath it.
The flame, whose heat is weakest at the edges.
The wax skin, setting as soon as it stops moving.
context: Faraday: 'As the air comes to the candle it moves upwards by the force of the current which the heat of the candle produces, and it so cools all the sides of the wax, tallow, or fuel, as to keep the edge much cooler than the part within.' Spoil the symmetry and the cup fails: 'If I made a current in one direction, my cup would be lop-sided, and the fluid would consequently run over'; 'there will be a guttering round about it because of the irregularity of the stream of air and the badness of the cup which is formed thereby.' That is all guttering is -- a broken cup. Source: Faraday, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org).

question: Faraday set the children a test you can run tonight with one candle. Hold a strip of paper flat and push it straight through the middle of the flame, keeping it level, then pull it out after a moment and look at it. Where has it scorched?
answer: In two bands, with the middle barely marked.
choices: In two bands, with the middle barely marked.
In one solid black band right across it.
In a single burnt line down the centre.
In an even brown scorch from edge to edge.
context: Two scorch marks mean two hot zones, and that means the flame is hollow -- a dark cone of unburnt vapour sits down the middle of it. Faraday: 'put the piece of paper right across the middle of the flame... you will find that it is burnt in two places, and that it is not burnt, or very little so, in the middle.' Run it with a grown-up, in still air, and pull the paper straight out. Source: Faraday, Lecture II (en.wikisource.org).

question: The candle course became a book in 1861 and has never been out of print since; it has been turned into at least nineteen languages. In Japan a fourth-grade teacher handed a copy to a boy named Akira Yoshino, who has said it taught him why a candle burns and why it has a wick. What did Yoshino grow up to invent?
answer: The lithium-ion battery.
choices: The lithium-ion battery.
The blue light-emitting diode.
The flash memory chip.
The quartz wristwatch.
context: Faraday spoke the candle lectures; he never wrote them out as a book. We have the exact words because a young chemist in the audience, William Crookes, took them down: Crookes serialised the 1860-61 course in his own weekly, Chemical News, in early 1861, and Griffin, Bohn and Company issued it as a book that March: 'A Course of Six Lectures on the Chemical History of a Candle... delivered before a juvenile auditory at the Royal Institution of Great Britain during the Christmas holidays of 1860-1. Ed. by William Crookes.' (Faraday had given a candle course earlier as well, but the book everyone reads is the 1860-61 one -- it is never dated 1848.) Crookes's preface opens: 'From the primitive pine torch to the paraffin candle, how wide an interval!' The book has been translated into at least nineteen languages. Akira Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the lithium-ion battery, and has said the book made him understand why a candle burns and why it has a wick. Sources: Grokipedia, The Chemical History of a Candle; Homerton College Library; NobelPrize.org interview material; Japan Times, 12 Nov 2019.

question: Faraday blew a candle out gently, so that a white trail rose off the smoking wick and hung there in the still air. He then brought up a lighted taper -- a thin candle -- to within two or three inches of the wick, close but nowhere near touching it. What did the children see?
answer: A train of fire ran down the trail and relit the wick.
choices: A train of fire ran down the trail and relit the wick.
The trail flared once and died, the wick staying cold.
The trail blew apart and snuffed out the taper itself.
The trail bent toward the taper and glowed faintly.
context: Faraday: 'you will observe a train of fire going through the air till it reaches the candle.' What the fire runs down is wax vapour -- which is the proof that a candle burns vapour, not the wick and not the solid wax. This is the trick to run at the dinner table: blow the candle out gently so the white trail stays whole, hold still air, and have a grown-up carry the flame. Source: Faraday, Lecture I (en.wikisource.org; Project Gutenberg pg14474).

question: The middle of a candle flame is dark. Faraday pushed a bent glass tube down into that dark centre, then ran the far end of it out into the room, well clear of the candle. What did he show the children next?
answer: He lit the far end, and a second flame burned there.
choices: He lit the far end, and a second flame burned there.
He led the far end into lime-water, which turned milky.
He caught a cold white smoke there that would not light.
He found the tube choked with soot within a minute.
context: Faraday's own words: 'I will arrange another tube carefully in the flame... where we will light it, and obtain absolutely the flame of the candle at a place distant from it.' Then the punchline to the children: 'Talk about laying on gas -- why, we can actually lay on a candle!' The dark centre is fuel that has not yet reached enough air; pipe it away and it will burn wherever you choose to light it. Source: Faraday, Lecture II (en.wikisource.org).

question: Hold a cold dry glass over a burning candle and it fogs. Faraday collected those drops and told the children the candle had made water -- 'nothing but water' -- and then refused to let them take his word for it. He dropped a lump of potassium, Humphry Davy's metal, onto the liquid he had caught. What did the potassium do?
answer: It caught fire on the surface and burned away.
choices: It caught fire on the surface and burned away.
It sank through the liquid and lay there unchanged.
It fizzed quietly and left a white crust behind.
It clouded the liquid to a milky white.
context: Faraday on the drops: 'we find that that part of the product is just water -- nothing but water.' Potassium takes fire on water, so the test settled it in front of the audience: 'See, it takes fire, and burns in just the same manner.' The scale is the startling part -- 'A pint of oil, when burnt fairly and properly, produces rather more than a pint of water' -- because the hydrogen locked in the wax leaves as water vapour. In a later lecture Faraday took that same water apart again on the bench with a battery and two platinum plates, collecting twice the volume of hydrogen as oxygen. Never handle potassium; the cold spoon held over a flame is the safe half of this experiment, and it fogs every time. Source: Faraday, Lectures III and IV (en.wikisource.org).

question: Michael Faraday, in the last of the six lectures, put the children themselves in the candle's place: 'In every one of us there is a living process of combustion going on very similar to that of a candle.' A slow burning, he meant, inside every child in the room -- and he would not leave it there as a fine saying. He proved it at the bench, using his own breath. What did he do?
answer: He breathed through clear lime-water until it turned milky.
choices: He breathed through clear lime-water until it turned milky.
He breathed on a cold glass until it fogged with water.
He breathed into a jar and the candle inside it went out.
He breathed on a glowing splint until its ember flared up.
context: Faraday at the bench: 'you see how white and milky the water is getting' -- the very same change the candle's own product had made earlier in the course, when he bubbled the gas off the flame through lime-water. Carbonic acid, he called it; we call it carbon dioxide, and the flame and the children watching it were both pouring it into the room. His arithmetic: a man converts 'as much as seven ounces of carbon into carbonic acid' in a day, while 'a milch cow will convert seventy ounces, and a horse seventy-nine ounces, solely by the act of respiration.' For the whole city his printed page reads '5,000,000 pounds, or 548 tons, of carbonic acid... in twenty-four hours' -- do that division yourself and the two figures do not agree, since five million pounds is about 2,200 tons. The 548 tons looks to be the weight of the carbon inside the gas rather than the gas itself. Check a printed number when you can, even one of Faraday's. Source: Faraday, Lecture VI (en.wikisource.org).

question: A candle gives a soft yellow light you can read a book by. A gas jet in a laboratory can burn hotter than that candle and still light almost nothing -- its flame is pale and nearly colourless. Faraday told the children the difference is not the temperature. What is actually glowing in a candle flame?
answer: Grains of solid carbon, glowing white-hot.
choices: Grains of solid carbon, glowing white-hot.
Sodium from the burning wick, glowing yellow.
Droplets of unburnt wax, glowing as they rise.
Grains of ash off the wick, glowing yellow.
context: Faraday: 'All bright flames contain these solid particles.' The heat inside the flame decomposes the wax vapour and sets carbon free; the grains rise, glow white-hot, give the light, and then mostly burn away. Where air mixes with the gas BEFORE it burns, no grains ever form: 'you see how pale and blue the flame is... the difference is solely due to the solid particles not being separated before the gas is burnt.' Hold a cold spoon in the flame and you catch those same grains as soot -- the light and the black smudge are the same stuff. Source: Faraday, Lecture II (en.wikisource.org); Grokipedia flame-structure section.

question: On Earth a candle flame is a teardrop -- every one you have ever seen. NASA burned candles inside a sealed glovebox aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia in June 1992, about seventy tests in all, to watch what a flame does in orbit. What did they see?
answer: A small blue ball, standing off the wick.
choices: A small blue ball, standing off the wick.
A small yellow ball, sootier than on Earth.
A thin blue ring circling the wick.
A teardrop as always, only dimmer.
context: NASA states it plainly: 'Gravity-driven buoyant convection causes a candle flame to be teardrop-shaped' on Earth, whereas in microgravity 'the flame is spherical, soot-free and blue.' The candles burned in the glovebox on Columbia's USML-1 mission in June 1992 -- about seventy tests -- and the report found the flame 'becomes and remains hemispherical and blue (apparently soot-free)' with a large standoff distance from the wick, concluding 'that a candle can burn indefinitely in a large enough ambient of air in microgravity.' The strangest detail: as such a flame died, its TIP was the last part to survive -- the exact opposite of a candle on Earth, where the base is the most reactive part. Sources: NASA, 'Candle Flame - 1g vs Microgravity' (nasa.gov); Ross & Dietrich, 'Candle Flames in Microgravity: USML-1 Results' (ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20030075810).

question: In 1975 Matthew Kluger, Daniel Ringler and Miriam Anver injected desert iguanas with the bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila and let the sick animals move freely around an enclosure. Within hours the infected lizards' body temperatures had risen by about two degrees. What did the sick iguanas do?
answer: Basked under a hotter lamp
choices: Basked under a hotter lamp
Curled into a tight ball to trap heat
Panted rapidly to draw in warmer air
Buried themselves under the sand
context: A lizard cannot heat itself from the inside; if it wants to be warmer it has to go and find heat. The paper appeared in Science on 11 April 1975 under the flat title 'Fever and survival'.

question: The Rogers Commission spent months on the Challenger investigation and the piece of evidence Richard Feynman produced on live television was famously humble. What was the object he pulled out of a glass of ice water on the witness table on 11 February 1986?
answer: a scrap of rubber from the shuttle booster's O-ring
choices: a scrap of rubber from the shuttle booster's O-ring
a thin foil sample from the external tank's insulation
a slice of the ceramic tile from the orbiter's underside
a shard of the mirror from the crew cabin's periscope
context: Feynman had asked for the ice water in advance and brought the sample himself. Foil, tile and mirror are all real shuttle components, but the failure was in the rubber seal between two segments of the right solid rocket booster.

question: The Challenger launched on the morning of 28 January 1986. Every previous shuttle had lifted off at 53 degrees Fahrenheit or warmer, but that morning the pad had sat overnight in a hard Florida freeze. Roughly what was the launch temperature?
answer: about 36 degrees Fahrenheit
choices: about 36 degrees Fahrenheit
about 45 degrees Fahrenheit
about 22 degrees Fahrenheit
about 42 degrees Fahrenheit
context: The air at liftoff was 36 F, some 15 F colder than any previous launch; overnight pad temperatures had bottomed out in the 20s and the right booster joint, sitting in shade, is estimated to have been near 28 F. Source: NASA weather logs cited in AccuWeather retrospective.

question: The night before the Challenger launch, engineers at one of NASA's major shuttle contractors held a teleconference with mission control and pushed hard against launching in freezing weather -- their initial written recommendation was NO LAUNCH. Which contractor's engineers made that call?
answer: Morton Thiokol
choices: Morton Thiokol
Rockwell International
Aerojet General
Martin Marietta
context: Morton Thiokol built the Solid Rocket Boosters in Utah; the teleconference of 27 January 1986 pitted Thiokol engineers Roger Boisjoly and Arnold Thompson against senior managers in a caucus that eventually reversed the no-launch call. The other three are real shuttle contractors of the era -- Rockwell International built the orbiter, Aerojet made rocket motors, Martin Marietta built the giant external tank -- each of which could plausibly have been the one to object.

question: One contractor engineer, Roger Boisjoly, spoke first and hardest against launching Challenger in the cold; his own recollection of the teleconference the night before is one of the case's plainest quotes. In freezing weather, he warned, the seals would be what?
answer: hard as rocks and would not seal in time
choices: hard as rocks and would not seal in time
several sizes too small to close the joint
brittle enough to shatter on the first vibration
slippery with condensation and unable to hold
context: Boisjoly showed photographs of grease blow-by from earlier cold-weather flights and argued that a stiff O-ring cannot spring back into a flexing joint fast enough to keep hot gas contained. Thiokol management overruled him in a caucus the engineers were shut out of.

question: Feynman came to the Rogers Commission suspicious of NASA's official failure numbers, so he asked managers and working engineers separately for the odds that a shuttle mission would end in catastrophe. Management said about 1 in 100,000 launches. What did the engineers say?
answer: between 1 in 50 and 1 in 200
choices: between 1 in 50 and 1 in 200
between 1 in 500 and 1 in 1,000
between 1 in 2,000 and 1 in 5,000
between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 25,000
context: Feynman himself put the odds near 1 in 100. Management's 1-in-100,000 number implied a shuttle a day for 300 years without an accident -- a public-relations figure, not an engineering one. This factor-of-a-thousand gap between the two decks of the same building is the deeper finding Feynman was after.

question: General Donald Kutyna, a fellow Rogers Commissioner, gave Feynman the crucial hint about cold but wrapped it in a story to protect the person who had actually given HIM the data. By Kutyna's own account, what everyday object did he say had leaked or failed on him one cold morning?
answer: the carburetor of a car he was restoring in his garage
choices: the carburetor of a car he was restoring in his garage
the door seals of the refrigerator on his back porch
the rubber gaskets of the garden hose he had left outside
the front tire of the bicycle he kept in the garage
context: Kutyna's later telling: he showed Feynman a car engine, mentioned that its little O-rings leaked when the weather turned cold, and asked whether the same thing could happen on a shuttle. The BBC's 2013 film 'The Challenger' revealed that Sally Ride had quietly passed Kutyna NASA test data showing the shuttle rings stiffened when chilled -- her role kept secret to protect her source, and made public only after her death in 2012.

question: Feynman insisted his own dissent be published as Appendix F of the Rogers Commission report. Its final sentence is one of the most quoted lines in modern engineering: 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for ...' -- how does it end?
answer: nature cannot be fooled
choices: nature cannot be fooled
the numbers cannot be argued
the hardware cannot be persuaded
the sky itself keeps the score
context: The full Appendix F line: 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.' It belongs to Feynman's minority appendix, not to the commission's main report. The other three choices are plausible-sounding alternates invented here as distractors -- none of them is Feynman's line.

question: The sociologist Diane Vaughan spent years digging into how the Challenger launch was approved and published her findings in 1996 as 'The Challenger Launch Decision.' Her book has since given every engineering-failure classroom the same short phrase for the pattern it describes. What is that phrase?
answer: normalization of deviance
choices: normalization of deviance
erosion of vigilance
drift of the acceptable
collapse of oversight
context: Vaughan traced how each flight that came back with singed rubber and did not blow up nudged the acceptable damage line a little further out; the joint was 'flying', so the damage must be tolerable. 'Normalization of deviance' is now standard usage in engineering failure analysis. The other three are plausible-sounding coinages invented here, not real terms of art.

question: MYTH CORRECTION: nearly every viewer who watched Challenger's plume live in 1986 will say the shuttle 'exploded' -- but the Rogers Commission's own reconstruction says something more precise. What actually destroyed the orbiter?
answer: aerodynamic forces tore the orbiter apart after the external tank ruptured
choices: aerodynamic forces tore the orbiter apart after the external tank ruptured
the main engines detonated when the fuel line ruptured in the joint failure
a chain reaction in the solid rocket booster's own propellant blew the stack apart
an internal cabin fire ignited by the electrical system consumed the orbiter first
context: The failed joint sent a jet of hot gas that burned through a strut and ruptured the external tank. The tank's hydrogen and oxygen burned in the open air -- the bright cloud viewers remember -- and the orbiter itself, still intact for a moment, tumbled sideways at high speed and was torn apart by aerodynamic loads of about 20 g. The crew cabin survived intact through breakup and fell more than two minutes to the ocean. Told soberly because the truth is grimmer than 'it exploded'.

question: At the 1974 Caltech commencement, Richard Feynman told graduates about South Sea islanders who, after the war, built runways with fires along the sides, a wooden hut, and a man sitting in it with two wooden pieces on his head like headphones and bars of bamboo sticking out like antennas -- and waited for the airplanes to land. What did Feynman name that kind of failure?
answer: cargo cult science
choices: cargo cult science
pathological science
the Dunning-Kruger effect
publication bias
context: Feynman: they 'follow all the apparent precepts and forms of scientific investigation, but they're missing something essential, because the planes don't land.' Source: Caltech, 'Cargo Cult Science' (1974). Langmuir's 'pathological science' (1953) is a real, closely related idea covered in the N-rays ladder; Dunning-Kruger and publication bias are real but distinct.

question: Richard Feynman opened his 1974 Caltech commencement with one sentence he called the first principle of scientific thought. Everything after it, he said, follows from getting this one right. What did he say the first principle is?
answer: You must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.
choices: You must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.
You must state, up front, what would prove your own theory wrong.
You must never rest a claim on an authority bigger than the evidence.
You must weigh a bold new claim against the weight of ordinary practice.
context: The line lives in the address's core section on integrity: after you've stopped fooling yourself, 'it's easy not to fool other scientists.' The distractors are Popper-flavored, Sagan-flavored and Bacon-flavored paraphrases -- adjacent to Feynman's line but not it.

question: In 'Cargo Cult Science' Richard Feynman tells about the physicist Millikan, who first measured the charge on the electron with falling oil drops. Feynman says Millikan's answer is off by a small amount -- and pins the error on one specific wrong constant Millikan had used in the analysis. Which constant was wrong?
answer: the viscosity of air
choices: the viscosity of air
the density of the oil
the acceleration of gravity
the electric field between the plates
context: The oil-drop analysis needs air's viscosity to convert a falling droplet's terminal velocity into its radius; Millikan used a value that was slightly wrong, so his final electron charge came out about 0.6 percent low. Feynman: 'It's a little bit off, because he had the incorrect value for the viscosity of air.' The other three are real inputs to the oil-drop calculation, any of which a re-reader could plausibly finger.

question: 'Cargo Cult Science' was first spoken as a Caltech commencement address in June 1974. About a decade later it escaped into ordinary English as a phrase. How did most readers first meet it?
answer: as the closing chapter of Feynman's 1985 memoir 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!'
choices: as the closing chapter of Feynman's 1985 memoir 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!'
as the opening chapter of his 1963 undergraduate lecture volumes
as a 1979 essay in Physics Today under Feynman's byline
as a segment of the 1983 BBC television series 'Fun to Imagine'
context: The 1974 address was reprinted as the final chapter of the memoir (Norton, 1985), and the book's bestseller run is what carried the phrase into common use. 'The Feynman Lectures on Physics,' Physics Today, and 'Fun to Imagine' are all real Feynman venues, but not where 'cargo cult science' broke out.

question: In 'Cargo Cult Science' Feynman studies the history of measurements of the electron's charge after Millikan and notices something strange: each new value is a tiny bit bigger than the one before it, creeping upward instead of jumping to the true answer. Feynman says the mechanism is a habit of the experimenters. What was that habit?
answer: They hunted hard for errors only when a value strayed far from the previous one.
choices: They hunted hard for errors only when a value strayed far from the previous one.
They quietly discarded any drop whose fall time did not fit the pattern.
They let the lead experimenter review every data sheet before it was written up.
They sent papers with unusual values back for a second round of measurements.
context: Feynman's exact diagnosis: 'When they got a number that was too high above Millikan's, they thought something must be wrong -- and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong. When they got a number closer to Millikan's value they didn't look so hard.' Not fraud, he stresses -- honest people, one-sided error-hunting. The three distractors are real bad-lab habits, but not what Feynman named here.

question: In 'Cargo Cult Science' Feynman praises a man named Young, who ran a corridor experiment on rats. The rats kept picking the right door long after the food was moved, so Young hunted the hidden cue. The cue turned out to be something the rats could sense as they ran. What did Young change to kill the cue?
answer: He rebuilt the whole corridor floor out of loose sand.
choices: He rebuilt the whole corridor floor out of loose sand.
He repainted the doors in identical shades of grey.
He rebuilt the corridor without any right-angle turns.
He wiped every wall with a fresh solvent before each trial.
context: Feynman: 'He finally found that they could tell by the way the floor sounded when they ran over it. And he could only fix that by putting his corridor in sand.' Painting doors, straightening the maze, and neutralizing scent are real controls in real rat studies -- but the SOUND cue is the one Young caught and killed.

question: Feynman spends a long paragraph on the Young rat-corridor study for a specific reason. He is not praising Young for finishing a good study -- he is pointing to what happened to it afterward in the rat-research literature. What was Feynman's actual complaint?
answer: Later rat experiments neither cited Young nor used the controls he had proved were needed.
choices: Later rat experiments neither cited Young nor used the controls he had proved were needed.
Later reviewers re-ran the numbers and the sound cue vanished as a statistical fluke.
Young's own follow-up paper walked back the finding after his department head objected.
The journal that had accepted Young's paper was shut down within a year of printing it.
context: Feynman: 'The subsequent experiment, and the one after that, never referred to Mr. Young. They never used any of his criteria of putting the corridor on sand, or being very careful.' The FIELD went on running rat experiments without the one control Young had proved was needed -- the bamboo-antenna failure in a lab coat.

question: In 'Cargo Cult Science' Feynman describes a duty stricter than ordinary honesty: after publishing a result you must report every alternative that could make you wrong, every check that didn't quite work, everything you cannot rule out. He gave this duty a short memorable phrase. Which phrase did he use?
answer: leaning over backwards
choices: leaning over backwards
showing your working
opening the notebook
burning the bridges
context: Feynman: 'It's a kind of scientific integrity, a principle of scientific thought that corresponds to a kind of utter honesty -- a kind of leaning over backwards.' The other three are plausible-sounding idioms invented here as distractors, not real Feynman terms.

question: To show that a technically true claim can still be dishonest, Feynman quotes an advertisement for Wesson cooking oil: the ad boasts that the oil does not soak through food. Feynman says the statement is literally true and still misleads. Why?
answer: At that temperature no oil soaks through food, so Wesson has claimed no real advantage.
choices: At that temperature no oil soaks through food, so Wesson has claimed no real advantage.
The test was run on baked, not fried, food, so no oil was hot enough to soak in.
The word 'food' in the test meant a strip of blotting paper, not any real food.
The company had rewritten the ad after the FDA required a factual correction.
context: Feynman: 'The fact that should be added to that advertising statement is that no oils soak through food, if operated at a certain temperature.' A true sentence framed to imply Wesson is unusual -- when the whole category behaves the same way -- is exactly the dishonesty scientists must avoid, even when every word they publish is technically correct.

question: Richard Feynman closed the 1974 Caltech commencement address with a single wish for the graduating class. What did he wish them?
answer: the good luck to be somewhere free enough to keep that integrity
choices: the good luck to be somewhere free enough to keep that integrity
the patience to keep testing a claim long after their first result
the humility to publish a negative result as loudly as a positive one
the discipline to state up front what would prove them wrong
context: Feynman's closing sentence: 'May you have the good luck to be somewhere where you are free to maintain the kind of integrity I have described.' The word 'luck' concedes what the rest of the address had already implied -- that the freedom to be honest is not a guaranteed feature of a job in science; institutions can and do punish it. The three distractor wishes are Feynman-adjacent virtues (patience with replication, publishing null results, pre-registering falsifiers) but none are what he actually chose to end on.

question: Feynman took the phrase 'cargo cult' from real Melanesian religious movements that grew after WWII, whose followers built airstrips and mock control towers to summon the American cargo back. One movement, centered on a figure called John Frum, is still practiced today. On which South Pacific island did it take root?
answer: Tanna, in Vanuatu
choices: Tanna, in Vanuatu
Guadalcanal, in the Solomons
Bougainville, in Papua New Guinea
New Britain, in Papua New Guinea
context: The John Frum movement on Tanna (in what is now Vanuatu) grew in the 1930s and swelled after the wartime American presence -- villagers still march every February 15, John Frum Day. Feynman's telling is a stylized parable, not fieldwork; the real religion is a serious anti-colonial movement, not the joke his metaphor sometimes suggests. Guadalcanal (Solomons) and New Britain (PNG) were major WWII Pacific sites; Bougainville is another Solomons island where cargo-style movements also arose.

question: Firework makers load a shell meant to burst red with strontium salts, and a shell meant to burst green with barium salts. What is actually making the colour when the shell goes off?
answer: The metal atoms themselves giving off light
choices: Heat-proof dyes surviving the burn
Glowing soot particles tinted by the salts
The metal atoms themselves giving off light
Coloured smoke off the paper casing
context: The colouring compounds are no side ingredient - they can be 10 to 60 percent of a firework composition. The salt takes in heat from the burning star and gives light back out at the wavelengths that belong to that particular metal ion: strontium red, barium green, copper blue, sodium yellow. Nothing survives the fire as a pigment; the element itself is the colour. (Grokipedia: Pyrotechnic colorant.)

question: Put a few grains of ordinary table salt on a clean wire and hold it in a gas flame - a test anyone can run at a kitchen stove. The flame changes the moment the salt reaches it. What does it do?
answer: Flares yellow-orange
choices: Flares lilac-violet
Flares yellow-orange
Flares apple green
Flares brick red
context: That colour is almost the whole of the light: sodium's pair of lines at 589.0 and 589.6 nanometres. The other three answers are real flame colours of real elements - potassium gives lilac-violet, barium apple green, calcium brick red - which is exactly what makes the test useful. Try it on a gas hob with a clean nichrome wire, and clean the wire between samples, or the last thing you touched shows up instead of the thing you meant to test. (Grokipedia: Flame test.)

question: The old low-pressure sodium street lamps - the deep orange ones over motorways and car parks - were among the most efficient ever built, up to 200 lumens per watt, and they got that way through the same physics that makes a pinch of salt flare in a gas flame. Stand under one at midnight. What has the lamp taken away?
answer: Colour - every surface can only give back that one orange
choices: Colour - every surface can only give back that one orange
Sparkle - nothing under it glints the way it does by day
Depth - everything looks flattened against the tarmac
Detail - fine print and sharp edges blur into a haze
context: Colour is reflected light, and that lamp gives a surface nothing to reflect but 589-nanometre yellow, so everything can only come back as some shade of it. It is the chemistry bench's own sodium fingerprint, running over a car park all night. White LED lamps have nearly finished replacing them - if an orange street still survives near you, go and stand in it before it goes. (Wikipedia: Sodium-vapor lamp.)

question: Robert Bunsen was hunting the faint colours that different salts give to a flame, and the gas lamps of the 1850s were his obstacle: they burned with a luminous yellow glow that swamped everything he wanted to see. The burner he designed for his Heidelberg laboratory beat that glow and still reached about 1500 degrees C. How did it get rid of the yellow?
answer: It mixed air into the gas before the gas burned
choices: It burned the gas at a much lower pressure
It fed the flame pure oxygen from a side tap
It passed the gas through charcoal first
It mixed air into the gas before the gas burned
context: A luminous flame is yellow because it is full of glowing soot - carbon specks that never met enough air. Bunsen's tube takes air in through adjustable slits at the base, so gas and air arrive at the top already mixed: the carbon burns completely, the soot never forms, and the flame goes almost invisible in daylight. The instrument was designed around the obstacle. (Wikipedia: Bunsen burner; Grokipedia: Robert Bunsen.)

question: The burner on every school chemistry bench carries Robert Bunsen's name, but in late 1854, with Heidelberg's new laboratory still half-built, Bunsen wrote out his design principles and handed them to Peter Desaga, the university's mechanic. What was waiting when the laboratory opened a few months later?
answer: Fifty finished burners, ready for his students
choices: Fifty finished burners, ready for his students
One prototype, made for Bunsen's own bench
A patent for the burner in Desaga's own name
A crate of parts for the students to build
context: Desaga was the Heidelberg university mechanic, and he turned a page of design principles into fifty working instruments in a few months, ready for the opening in early 1855. Bunsen specified it, Desaga built it, and neither of them invented the premixed gas burner outright - Michael Faraday had already worked on similar principles in an earlier burner. Bunsen refused to patent his inventions, including his carbon-zinc battery, so that anyone could use them. (Wikipedia: Bunsen burner; Grokipedia: Robert Bunsen.)

question: A single firework shell can carry red stars from strontium and green stars from barium - those metals emitting their own particular wavelengths - and alongside them brilliant white stars and gold trailing sparks. What is making the white and the gold?
answer: Hot solid particles glowing across every colour at once
choices: Hot solid particles glowing across every colour at once
A second metal emitting so many lines they blur together
Burning gases fluorescing above the coloured stars
Smoke scattering the burst's light back in all colours
context: Two entirely different mechanisms burn inside the same shell. Strontium and barium give line emission - a few sharp wavelengths belonging to the ion. The white stars are magnesium and aluminium powder giving incandescence: they simply get hot enough to glow, throwing out a smooth continuous spectrum with no lines in it at all, which the eye reads as white. The gold sparks are specks of charcoal incandescing at around 1000 degrees C. (Grokipedia: Pyrotechnic colorant.)

question: Sodium is the saboteur of the flame test: it rides in on dust, sweat, tap water and fingerprints, and the smallest trace floods a flame with a glare that buries potassium's fainter signature. Testing a salt for potassium, what does a chemist hold between the eye and the flame?
answer: A square of cobalt blue glass
choices: A square of cobalt blue glass
A square of ruby red glass
A square of amber brown glass
A square of bottle green glass
context: Cobalt glass swallows sodium's yellow at 589 nanometres and passes potassium's faint violet line at 404, so the colour a chemist actually came for steps out from behind the contamination; didymium glass does the same job more selectively. The lesson underneath is the one textbooks skip - a test sensitive enough to name an element from an invisible trace is also sensitive enough to be wrecked by a fingerprint. (Grokipedia: Flame test; Wikipedia: Cobalt glass.)

question: Bunsen and Kirchhoff claimed their spectroscope could catch a quantity of a substance far too small to weigh, and rather than argue about it they staged a demonstration. In the far corner of a room of 60 cubic metres they set off 3 milligrams of a sodium salt, then watched a flame burning at the other end of the room. What happened at that far-off flame?
answer: It turned yellow and held that colour for minutes
choices: It flickered yellow for a second as the blast passed
It turned yellow and held that colour for minutes
It stayed clear until they fanned the air towards it
It dimmed slowly as the sodium smoke thickened
context: After a few minutes the flame turned yellow, showed a strong sodium line, and did not fade for ten minutes - meaning air carrying less than one twenty-millionth of its weight in sodium was enough to see. They ran it again with 0.3 grams of barium chlorate, stirring the room's air, in the paper's own words, by means of an open umbrella. The same paper puts the limit at less than one three-millionth of a milligram of sodium salt. (Kirchhoff and Bunsen, 'Chemical Analysis by Observation of Spectra', 1860.)

question: Pyrotechnicians will tell you blue is the hardest firework colour of all. The blue in a copper star comes from copper(I) chloride, emitting in bands at 420 to 450 nanometres. Push the star hotter to make it brighter and you do not get a deeper blue: you get a washed-out whitish tint. What has the extra heat done?
answer: Torn the copper chloride apart into copper and chlorine
choices: Torn the copper chloride apart into copper and chlorine
Boiled the copper chloride out of the star as vapour
Shifted the copper chloride's bands across into green
Fused the copper chloride into a copper oxide instead
context: The blue comes from a molecule, not an atom, and that is the whole problem: copper(I) chloride falls apart above roughly 1500 degrees C. So blue lives in a narrow window - the star must burn hot enough to glow brightly but cool enough to leave the emitter intact. Lose that balance and what is left is incandescent white with a hint of blue in it. A deep saturated blue is the mark of a maker who found the window. (Grokipedia: Pyrotechnic colorant.)

question: A flame gives sharp bright lines, but in 1859 nobody could say what those lines really belonged to - the metal in the sample, the compound holding it, the mineral it was dug out of, or the fire doing the burning. Bunsen and Kirchhoff spent two years testing it every way they could contrive, and their 1860 paper rests on what the runs showed. What was it?
answer: The lines belonged to the metal alone, unmoved by the rest
choices: The lines belonged to the metal alone, unmoved by the rest
The lines belonged to the metal, but shifted with its compound
The lines belonged to the metal, but shifted with the flame used
The lines belonged to the mineral more than to the metal in it
context: In their words, the compound the metal came in and the kind of flame used 'had no influence on the position of the spectral lines corresponding to the individual metals.' That negative result is what turns a colour into a name: if the lines never move, the pattern identifies the element and nothing else about the sample. It is the logic of a fingerprint - useless unless it is the same fingerprint every time. (Kirchhoff and Bunsen, 1860.)

question: On 10 May 1860 Robert Bunsen boiled a residue out of the mineral water of the Maxquelle spring at Bad Duerkheim, carried it to his flame, and Gustav Kirchhoff watched through the prism. What did they see in that spa-water residue?
answer: Two blue lines no catalogued element could claim
choices: Two blue lines no catalogued element could claim
Two red lines no catalogued element could claim
A green line no catalogued element could claim
A violet line no catalogued element could claim
context: Between them Bunsen and Kirchhoff had already catalogued the line patterns of every element then known, and this pair matched nothing in it: 455.5 and 459.3 nanometres, sitting near a blue line of strontium. Bunsen named the new element caesium, from the Latin caesius, the word the ancients used for sky-blue. It was the first element in history discovered by its light - it existed as two blue lines long before it existed as anything you could hold. Carl Setterberg, working under Bunsen at Heidelberg, finally got beads of the metal in 1882, twenty-two years later. (Grokipedia: Caesium; Bunsen and Kirchhoff, 1861.)

question: Bunsen's spectroscope could name an element from an invisible trace, but no chemist in 1860 would accept a colour as proof of a new one, so Bunsen had to put the salt itself on a balance. He boiled 44,000 litres of Bad Duerkheim mineral water - about forty tonnes - down to 240 kilograms of brine, then worked that down further. What weight of caesium chloride did the forty tonnes finally yield?
answer: About 7 grams
choices: About 70 kilograms
About 7 kilograms
About 700 grams
About 7 grams
context: 7.3 grams of caesium chloride, with 9.2 grams of rubidium chloride alongside it: two teaspoons of salt out of forty tonnes of spa water. This is the half of discovery nobody puts on the poster - the instrument found the element in an evening, and then Bunsen spent months boiling a tanker-load of water to satisfy the chemists. From crumbs like these they still estimated atomic weights, and their rubidium figure of 85.36 sits within a tenth of a percent of the modern 85.47. (Wikipedia: Caesium; Bunsen and Kirchhoff, 1861.)

question: In 1835 the French philosopher Auguste Comte, in the nineteenth lesson of his Cours de philosophie positive, went looking for an example of knowledge permanently out of human reach and settled on the stars: one fact about them, he argued, could never be established by any means whatever. Within about twenty-five years he had been overtaken. Which fact?
answer: The chemical make-up of the stars
choices: The distance out to the nearest stars
The chemical make-up of the stars
The speed of the stars across the sky
The temperature of a star's surface
context: Comte's claim, in the standard English rendering, runs close to this: we may determine their shapes, distances, sizes and motions, but we shall never be able by any means to study their chemical composition. Bunsen and Kirchhoff answered it inside the same 1860 paper that made the flame test exact, writing that spectrum analysis 'opens to chemical research a hitherto completely closed region extending far beyond the limits of the earth and even of the solar system.' The point is not that Comte was a fool - he was a serious thinker reasoning from what instruments then existed. The point is that a test outranks anyone's certainty about what cannot be done. (Hearnshaw, 'Auguste Comte's Blunder', JAHH 13 (2010) 90; Kirchhoff and Bunsen, 1860.)

question: By the 1870s the flame-and-prism test was ordinary working equipment: mineralogists, metal works and analysts named elements from their line patterns every day and trusted the result. Nobody could say why a given element gives those particular lines and no others. The explanation arrived roughly fifty years after the test did, when Niels Bohr published his model of the atom in 1913. What did Bohr say the lines were?
answer: Electrons dropping between fixed energy levels
choices: Atoms vibrating at their own natural frequencies
The ether ringing around the atom like a bell
Electrons dropping between fixed energy levels
Electrons orbiting at speeds set by atomic weight
context: Each drop releases a photon of one definite energy, and energy fixes frequency, so one drop means one exact colour. Different elements have differently spaced levels, which is the whole reason the pattern is a fingerprint at all. Shown Balmer's formula for hydrogen's lines, Bohr said that everything became clear. Notice the order: the test was in daily industrial use for half a century before anyone understood it. A method can be reliable long before it is explained. (Wikipedia: Bohr model.)

question: Alexander Fleming came back from two weeks away in September 1928 to his lab at St Mary's Hospital, Paddington, and worked through a stack of forgotten Staphylococcus plates left on the bench. On one, a fuzzy blue-green mould had taken hold. What had happened to the staph colonies nearest it?
answer: They had dissolved into a clear ring
choices: They had dissolved into a clear ring
They had grown thicker than the rest
They had turned blue-green like the mould
They had spread right over the mould
context: He did not wash the plate. He kept it, subcultured the mould, and photographed it. In that photograph the mould colony is about 20 mm across with a band of wrecked staph around it, and the colonies further out are only stunted (0.8-1.7 mm) rather than killed (0.4-0.8 mm near the mould) -- a gradient, not a clean on/off line. Fleming's caption was simply 'Photograph of a culture-plate.' The plate itself survives in the British Museum collection. Date note: Fleming's most-quoted line puts the moment on 28 September 1928, but the laboratory record points to 3 September; his first surviving notebook entry on the mould is 30 October 1928. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; Asimov Press, 'The Penicillin Myth'.

question: By 1940 Howard Florey's Oxford team needed Penicillium mould grown by the gallon, and wartime Britain had no factory and no money to build one. Norman Heatley found his culture vessels in the wards of the Radcliffe Infirmary. What was he farming the mould in?
answer: Hospital bedpans
choices: Hospital bedpans
Hospital kettles
Hospital washbasins
Hospital specimen jars
context: Porcelain bedpans turned out to be near-perfect shallow culture vessels -- but bedpans were scarce in wartime, so Heatley designed a stackable rectangular ceramic version and had J. Macintyre and Company of Burslem, in the Staffordshire potteries, make 500 of them; the first 174 were collected on 22 December 1940 and seeded three days later. He tested sugars, salts, malts, alcohol and even Marmite in the growth broth before brewing yeast turned out to cut incubation time by a third. Two women factory hands were hired at two pounds a week to tend the vessels. Sources: Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin'; University of Oxford Medical Sciences Division, 'The lasting legacy of Norman Heatley'.

question: Alexander Fleming's plate gave him a ring of dissolved staphylococci and nothing he could isolate, measure or hand to another laboratory. Over the following months at St Mary's he did the work that let him name penicillin in 1929. What did he do?
answer: He filtered the mould out of the broth and tested the liquid alone
choices: He filtered the mould out of the broth and tested the liquid alone
He crushed the mould colony and rubbed the paste across fresh plates
He injected the mould broth into infected mice and watched them recover
He crystallised the substance out and weighed the doses he needed
context: He grew the mould on the surface of nutrient broth for five or six days at room temperature, then poured the broth through filter paper. What came through was a clear, straw-coloured liquid with no mould in it at all -- he called it 'mould juice'. It still destroyed staphylococci, streptococci and pneumococci; subcultures taken from inside the clear zone came back sterile; his 1929 paper reports it still strongly inhibiting staph and strep when watered down eight hundredfold, while leaving human white blood cells unharmed in the dish. So the killer was a SUBSTANCE the mould leaked into the liquid, not the mould itself -- and in 1929 he named that substance penicillin. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; Fleming, Br J Exp Pathol 10(3):226-236 (1929).

question: Most bacteriologists in 1928 would have tipped a mould-contaminated Staphylococcus plate straight into the disinfectant tray as a ruined experiment. Alexander Fleming kept his, and one reason was that years before he had already watched something else dissolve bacteria in front of him. What was it?
answer: A drop of his own nasal mucus, during a cold
choices: A drop of his own nasal mucus, during a cold
A drop of his own blood, from a cut finger
A drop of his own sweat, after a hot ward round
A drop of pus, from a wounded soldier's dressing
context: In November 1921, with a head cold, Fleming let a drop of his own nasal mucus fall onto a bacterial plate and saw the bacteria around it dissolving. He isolated the agent, found it also in tears, saliva and egg white, and named it lysozyme in a 1922 Proceedings of the Royal Society paper. Clinically lysozyme was nearly useless -- it dissolved a harmless bug, Micrococcus lysodeikticus, and not real pathogens -- but it is exactly why, seven years later, a spoiled staph plate looked to him like an opportunity instead of a wasted week. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alexander Fleming' (Discovery of Lysozyme).

question: Alexander Fleming gave penicillin its name in a paper he published in June 1929 in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology. He had run his mould broth against a range of bacteria, and the paper's title spelled out the particular job he was recommending penicillin for. What job did the title recommend?
answer: Clearing a plate of rivals so the fussy influenza bacillus could grow
choices: Clearing a plate of rivals so the fussy influenza bacillus could grow
Keeping stored laboratory cultures from spoiling on the shelf
Sterilising surgical instruments between one operation and the next
Treating patients whose throats were crowded with streptococci
context: The full title was 'On the Antibacterial Action of Cultures of a Penicillium, with Special Reference to their Use in the Isolation of B. influenzae'. Penicillin barely touches Gram-negative bacilli, the influenza bacillus among them -- so adding it to a plate wipes out the staph and strep that would otherwise smother that fussy organism and lets it grow alone. This is the forgotten half of the story: the headline use Fleming proposed was penicillin as a LABORATORY TOOL, with antiseptic possibilities mentioned only in passing. The paper ran in a specialist journal read by bacteriologists rather than by clinicians, and drew few citations in its first decade. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; paper text at PMC2048009.

question: Through the whole of the 1930s almost nobody chased penicillin. Harold Raistrick, a biochemist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, took Alexander Fleming's strain in 1932, pulled a crude active extract out of it, and quit when the stuff kept destroying itself during extraction. Meanwhile the attention of medicine went elsewhere entirely, and penicillin sat unused for a decade. What had medicine turned to instead?
answer: Gerhard Domagk's Prontosil and the sulfa drugs
choices: Gerhard Domagk's Prontosil and the sulfa drugs
Paul Ehrlich's Salvarsan and the arsenic compounds
Selman Waksman's streptomycin and the soil antibiotics
Joseph Lister's carbolic acid and the phenol antiseptics
context: Raistrick worked with P. W. Clutterbuck and R. Lovell and had every reason to succeed; crude penicillin simply lost its potency within about ten to fourteen days at room temperature and was destroyed by the heat of evaporation. Surface fermentation on shallow trays yielded micrograms per litre at purities often under 0.001%, and nobody knew penicillin's chemical structure until 1945 -- so all anyone could do was measure zones on agar and guess. Prontosil and the sulfa drugs that followed from 1932 were stable, synthesisable and reliable, and medicine's attention went to them. The other three choices are real rivals of the era: Salvarsan (1909) cured syphilis but was arsenic and worked on one bug; carbolic acid (1860s) cut post-operative infection from around 45% to under 15% but was far too toxic to inject; streptomycin arrived in 1943, after penicillin. Source: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'.

question: Albert Alexander, the Oxford policeman who in February 1941 became the first person given a real course of penicillin, appears in most tellings as a gardener who scratched his face on a rose thorn and could not stop the infection that followed. His own family said the rose bush was not what happened. What opened the wounds on his face?
answer: A German air raid on a police station
choices: A German air raid on a police station
A fall from a roof while chasing a thief
A kick from a horse in the police stables
A crash of his police car in the blackout
context: Alexander had been sent to help the Southampton police during the Blitz. At 5:50 p.m. on 30 November 1940 a German air raid hit the police station, killing a sergeant and injuring two constables -- one of them Alexander, whose facial lacerations came from the blast. His family later called the rosebush version 'a bit of wartime propaganda': a gentler story to tell than 'the Luftwaffe did it' while the bombing was still going on. The rose thorn is the legend; the blast is the documented record. Sources differ on his exact age (43, 44 or 45) and even which force he served in, so those details are not worth keying to. Sources: The Conversation, 'Guns, not roses -- here's the true story of penicillin's first patient'; Hektoen International, 'Albert Alexander: Unsung hero of penicillin'.

question: At 11 in the morning on Saturday 25 May 1940 Howard Florey's Oxford team injected eight mice with a dose of Streptococcus certain to kill them, and gave penicillin to only four. Norman Heatley stayed at the bench all night, and his diary records that by 3:45 a.m. every untreated mouse was dead and all four treated ones alive; Florey called the result a miracle. They ran it again on the Tuesday with sixteen mice. What did that bigger run show about the treated mice?
answer: They lived several days, but all were dead by day nineteen
choices: They lived several days, but all were dead by day nineteen
They lived only if the first dose came within an hour
They lived, but passed the infection on to healthy mice
They lived, and stayed healthy for the rest of their lives
context: Heatley's diary: 'I stayed at the lab until 3:45 a.m., by which time all four control animals were dead.' Two of the treated mice got a single 10 mg dose and two got 5 mg at intervals; one of those four died two days later, and in the larger Tuesday run the treated mice survived several days but were all dead within nineteen. The honest reading is that the DOSE, not the principle, was the limit -- and the team said so. What made any of it possible was Ernst Chain's alumina adsorption column, which concentrated the active substance roughly a hundredfold, plus Heatley's assay for measuring potency and his 'reverse extraction' -- flipping the acidity to pull penicillin back out of an organic solvent into water, first with ether and then with the less flammable amyl acetate. Sources: Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin' and 'Norman Heatley'; Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'.

question: On 12 February 1941 Charles Fletcher, a research student under Howard Florey, began the first real course of penicillin on Albert Alexander, an Oxford policeman dying at the Radcliffe Infirmary with abscesses across his head and one eye already cut out. Within a day the fever fell and the wounds began to dry - and the Oxford team's entire stock of the drug was running out. What did they do to keep the doses coming?
answer: They recovered penicillin from his urine and re-injected it
choices: They recovered penicillin from his urine and re-injected it
They recovered penicillin from the mould trays a week early
They cut every dose in half and stretched the stock further
They gave him raw mould broth once the pure stock was gone
context: Alexander got an initial 200 mg (about 10,000 units) intravenously, then 100 mg every three hours; his temperature fell, the discharge from his wounds declined, his appetite returned, and by 17 February his remaining eye had normalised. Fletcher recorded 'obvious resolution of the abscesses... importantly, there had been no sort of toxic effect during the five days.' Penicillin passes out of the body largely unchanged, so the team recovered unprocessed drug from his urine and re-dosed him -- and still ran out after about five days. He relapsed in early March and died on 15 March 1941. The drug worked; there was not enough of it. (Dose figures vary by source: Wikipedia's page on Alexander gives 160 mg.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin'; Hektoen International, 'Albert Alexander: Unsung hero of penicillin'.

question: In 1941 Howard Florey and Norman Heatley carried the problem to a United States Department of Agriculture laboratory in Peoria, Illinois, where Andrew Moyer multiplied the yield roughly tenfold by feeding the mould corn-steep liquor, a sludge left over from milling corn. What the lab still lacked was a Penicillium that made more of the drug in the first place, and in 1943 it found one growing on something mouldy in Peoria itself. On what?
answer: A cantaloupe melon
choices: A cantaloupe melon
A rye bread loaf
A sack of onions
A leather work boot
context: The strain was catalogued as NRRL 1951, a Penicillium chrysogenum (now Penicillium rubens); grown in deep tanks it produced up to about a hundred times more penicillin than Fleming's original mould, and essentially all industrial penicillin since descends from it. The team then broke its DNA on purpose and screened the survivors: X-rays gave mutant X-1612 at about 300 mg per litre, ultraviolet light gave Q-176, and feeding the culture phenylacetic acid switched output to penicillin G at about 550 mg per litre -- directed evolution with a lamp and a filing system, years before anyone could read a gene. WHO found the cantaloupe, and where, is genuinely unsettled: a Peoria fruit market appears in some accounts and a garbage can in the USDA's own timeline, and the local credit to lab technician Mary K. Hunt, 'Moldy Mary', is lab lore the primary record does not confirm. Sources: The Scientist; USDA Agricultural Research Service, 'Penicillin: Opening the Era of Antibiotics'; Wikipedia, 'History of penicillin'.

question: Penicillin blocks the last step in building a bacterium's wall -- the cross-links that lock it together as the cell divides. Drop the drug into a flask of staphylococci dividing hard and within hours the cells swell and burst; drop the same dose into a flask where growth has already stalled and almost nothing happens. What tears the growing cells apart?
answer: The cell's own wall-chewing enzymes carry on demolishing from inside
choices: The cell's own wall-chewing enzymes carry on demolishing from inside
The cell's dividing membrane pinches through the softened wall
The cell's wall-building enzymes pile material on until it splits
The cell's water pumps race as it divides and force the wall open
context: With no new cross-links going in, the cell's own wall-remodelling autolysins keep chewing, water floods in, and a GROWING bacterium bursts under its own internal pressure -- which is why penicillin does almost nothing to a colony that has already stopped growing. The enzyme it jams is DD-transpeptidase, one of the penicillin-binding proteins; the beta-lactam ring mimics the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of the wall's building block, and once it snaps open onto the enzyme's active-site serine it is welded there permanently. Your own cells have no peptidoglycan at all -- no wall of that kind to sabotage -- which is exactly why penicillin can be injected into a person. Bacteria counter-punch with beta-lactamase, an enzyme that hydrolyses the ring open first; Edward Abraham and Ernst Chain described it in E. coli in 1940, before penicillin had ever been given to a human being. Nobody knew the drug's shape until Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin confirmed the four-membered ring by X-ray crystallography in 1945. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Penicillin'; Wikipedia, 'Penicillin'.

question: Norman Heatley built the assay that measured how strong a penicillin batch was, found the vessels to grow the mould in when wartime Britain had no factory, and worked out how to pull the drug back out of solvent -- all of it inside Howard Florey's Oxford department, on work the war kept quiet. When the 1945 Nobel Prize for penicillin was announced in Stockholm, Heatley's name was not on the list. What kept it off?
answer: The prize's rules cap a single award at three winners
choices: The prize's rules cap a single award at three winners
The prize's rules bar work still sealed as a war secret
The prize's rules allow just one winner from any laboratory
The prize's rules pass over anyone without a medical degree
context: A Nobel Prize may be split at most three ways, so once Fleming, Chain and Florey were on it there was no fourth place left to give Heatley -- a rule of the prize, not a judgement on his work. The Assembly announced it on 25 October 1945 and the ceremony followed on 10 December in Stockholm, the three men sharing it equally. Oxford's own answer came in 1990: an honorary Doctorate of Medicine, the first the university had awarded in its 800-year history to someone who was not medically qualified -- given to the bench chemist who never treated a patient. Heatley called it 'an enormous privilege since I am not medically qualified' and described himself as 'a third rate scientist whose only merit was to be in the right place at the right time'. Henry Harris summed the whole story up in one line: 'Without Fleming, no Chain or Florey; without Florey, no Heatley; without Heatley, no penicillin.' Fleming's own verdict on his half of it: 'I did not invent penicillin. Nature did that. I only discovered it by accident.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'Discovery of penicillin'; Wikipedia, 'Norman Heatley'; Engines of Our Ingenuity No. 601.

question: In late 1921 Alexander Fleming was standing over a culture plate of a yellow coccus bacterium when a single drop from his own body fell onto it by accident. Days later he saw a wide clear circle where every bacterium around that drop had dissolved into jelly. Which of his body's own fluids had accidentally dripped onto the plate?
answer: his own nasal mucus
choices: his own nasal mucus
his own tears
his own saliva
his own sweat
context: The clear halo Fleming saw was the body's own germ-killer at work. Later he and his assistant V.D. Allison would find the same enzyme in tears, saliva, blood serum and human milk - so all three distractors are real body sources of lysozyme, not fake. But the accidental drop that day in 1921 came from Fleming's nose. Sources: Scientific American, Penicillin Wasn't Alexander Fleming's First Major Discovery; Wikipedia, Lysozyme.

question: After the accidental discovery, Fleming and his assistant V.D. Allison spent months chasing the bacteria-dissolving enzyme wherever it might hide. They found small amounts in tears, saliva, blood serum, and other body fluids. But one everyday kitchen substance turned out to be packed with the enzyme in far greater concentration than any human fluid. Which substance was it?
answer: egg white
choices: egg white
olive oil
honey
vinegar
context: Egg white is one of the richest natural sources of lysozyme known - a hen packs the enzyme around her yolk to defend the embryo from bacteria. Fleming named the enzyme itself 'lysozyme' (from Greek lyso, to dissolve, plus zyme, enzyme) and gave the sensitive yellow test bacterium the name Micrococcus lysodeikticus - 'the one that shows the dissolving'. Source: Scientific American; Wikipedia, Lysozyme.

question: Fleming spent seven years working on lysozyme and could never turn it into a medicine. Concentrating it did not help; injecting it did not help. There was one fundamental biological reason the enzyme was doomed as a broad antibiotic. What was it?
answer: It dissolved only harmless bacteria and left the ones that cause serious human disease alone
choices: It dissolved only harmless bacteria and left the ones that cause serious human disease alone
It broke down human tissues just as easily as it broke down bacterial cells
It survived in the bloodstream for only a few seconds before being destroyed
It only worked when combined with an acid the human body could not produce
context: Lysozyme cuts a specific sugar bond in peptidoglycan - the mesh that makes up the cell wall of many gram-positive bacteria - but the truly dangerous pathogens (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus and most others that kill people) either have walls it cannot crack or protective outer layers that block it. Seven years of chasing a natural germ-killer and coming up short is exactly why, in 1928, when Fleming saw another clear halo - this time around a mould contaminant on a Staphylococcus plate - he did NOT reach for the wash bucket. Sources: Science History Institute, Alexander Fleming; Wikipedia, Lysozyme.

question: A steel paperclip is nearly eight times denser than water, and dropped in point-first it goes straight to the bottom. Lay that same clip down flat on still water, though, and it stays put. What is holding the paperclip up?
answer: The water's top layer, pulled taut like a skin
choices: Buoyancy, shoving aside its own weight of water
A bubble of air caught in the bend of the wire
The water's top layer, pulled taut like a skin
An oily coating on the steel that water avoids
context: This is surface tension, and it is not buoyancy: steel runs 7.75-8.05 g/cm3 against water's 1.00 g/cm3, so displacement is nowhere near enough. Water molecules cling to each other so hard that the top layer behaves like a stretched elastic sheet, about 0.0728 newtons per metre at 20 degrees C. The clip sits in a shallow dimple the surface makes under its weight. Break that surface and it drops at once. Grokipedia uses a steel razor blade as the same example, floating because careful placement avoids breaking the surface. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Steel'; Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Floating and Immersed Objects').

question: A steel paperclip has been resting on the water in a glass for a full minute without stirring. Touch a toothpick dipped in dish soap to the water at the far side of the glass, well away from the clip. What happens next?
answer: It sinks to the bottom almost at once
choices: It sinks to the bottom almost at once
It drifts to the far rim and floats on
It stays put until the water is stirred
It dips under, then bobs back up flat
context: One drop, and it is gone. The soap does not make the water heavier and does not attack the steel - it destroys the surface. Surfactant molecules gather at the interface and cut surface tension by 50-90%: pure water measures about 72 mN/m, a typical dish-soap solution about 30-40 mN/m. Halve the tension and the surface can no longer hold up eight-times-denser steel. Run it yourself with a glass of water and one drop on a toothpick. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Role of Surfactants'); Vedantu, 'Detergents and Surface Tension'.

question: A soap bubble is a film of liquid closed around a puff of air, and once it leaves the wand nothing holds it in shape - no mould, no frame, no hand. Still it settles into the same shape every time: a ball. Why is a free bubble a sphere?
answer: No other shape wraps that air in less film
choices: No other shape wraps that air in less film
Air outside presses on it evenly from all sides
The charge on the film spreads out and rounds it
The film's own weight settles it into a ball
context: A sphere is the smallest possible surface around a given volume, and a liquid skin pulls until nothing smaller is on offer - which is why a free drop of water and a soap bubble are round for the same reason. A bubble has TWO surfaces, inner and outer, so its inside is over-pressurised by 4*gamma/r - exactly double a plain droplet's 2*gamma/r. The relation is Young-Laplace, from Thomas Young (1805) and Pierre-Simon Laplace (1806). Source: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Pressure Differences and Curvature', 'Soap Films and Bubbles').

question: Water molecules cling to one another - that clinging is why water gathers into drops instead of spreading into mist. Yet water deep in a glass behaves nothing like the water at the very top, which acts as though a stretched sheet lay across it. What makes that topmost layer different?
answer: Nothing tugs at them from above, so their pull runs down and out
choices: Nothing tugs at them from above, so their pull runs down and out
The weight of the whole atmosphere squeezes them flat from above
They move far faster than the molecules below and barely cling
They sit colder than the water below, so they cling much harder
context: A molecule down in the bulk is pulled equally in every direction by its neighbours, and the forces cancel to nothing. A molecule at the top has neighbours only below and beside it, so the pull is unbalanced and the whole surface is dragged inward, contracting like stretched elastic. Water's version is anomalously strong for so small a molecule, about 0.0728 N/m at 20 degrees C, because hydrogen bonds grip far harder than the van der Waals forces holding oils and hydrocarbons together. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Basis in physics: cohesion'); Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Molecular Causes').

question: Dip one corner of a paper towel into a saucer of water and the water climbs up into the dry paper against gravity. Stand a narrow glass tube in the same saucer and the water climbs that too - the narrower the tube, the higher it goes. Why does the water rise?
answer: Water grips the glass more strongly than it grips itself
choices: Water grips the glass more strongly than it grips itself
Air pressing on the saucer squeezes water into the tube
Evaporation at the top drags the column along behind it
The narrow tube walls pinch the water and force it upward
context: Capillary action. Water wets glass, sticking to the wall harder than to itself, and the surface drags a column up behind it. James Jurin established the law experimentally in 1712: h = 2*gamma*cos(theta)/(rho*g*r), so the rise is inversely proportional to the tube's radius. Halve the tube and you double the climb; a tube of 0.1 mm radius lifts water about 15 cm. Test it tonight with a paper-towel corner in a saucer of coloured water. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Capillary action'; Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Capillary Rise in Tubes').

question: Benjamin Franklin carried a teaspoon of olive oil out to Mount Pond on Clapham Common in London, where the wind had the whole pond rough, and poured it on. He set down what happened in a letter of 7 November 1773 that was read to the Royal Society. What did that one teaspoon do?
answer: It spread until half an acre lay smooth as a looking-glass
choices: It spread until half an acre lay smooth as a looking-glass
It drew the ripples into a ring of ridges around one spot
It gathered into a single lens about the size of a plate
It broke into ribbons and sank out of sight in a minute
context: Franklin wrote it up to William Brownrigg on 7 November 1773; the letter was read to the Royal Society and printed in Philosophical Transactions in 1774 as 'Of the Stilling of Waves by Means of Oil'. He hedged the size himself - perhaps half an acre - and he never did the arithmetic. Do it with his own numbers: half an acre is 2,420 square metres, a teaspoon about 2 x 10^-6 cubic metres, and the division gives 9.9 x 10^-10 metres, a thickness that would wait more than a century for anyone to explain. Sources: Royal Society of Chemistry Education, 'Franklin's teaspoon of oil'; Founders Online, 'Benjamin Franklin to William Brownrigg, 7 November 1773'; Grokipedia, 'Langmuir-Blodgett film'.

question: Dish soap does not make water heavier and it does not attack steel. What it does is cut the water's surface tension - the strength of that skin-like pull - from about 72 millinewtons per metre down to nearer 35, and that alone drops a floating paperclip to the bottom of the glass. Soap does it by crowding up into the very top layer of the water and shouldering the water molecules apart. What drives a soap molecule up into the surface in the first place?
answer: One end of it loves water and the other cannot stand it
choices: One end of it loves water and the other cannot stand it
It weighs far less than water and simply floats to the top
It carries a charge the water shoves away from itself
It is a coil that unwinds where the water meets the air
context: Soap molecules are amphiphilic: a water-loving head and a water-hating tail. The tails cannot stand being surrounded by water, so the molecules pile up at the surface with the tails sticking out, wedging between the water molecules and breaking their grip on one another. Surface tension falls by 50-90%. It is also why soapy water WETS things that plain water beads off. Source: Grokipedia, 'Surface tension' ('Role of Surfactants').

question: Scatter ground pepper across a plate of water and the flecks sit where they land. Touch one drop of dish soap to the middle of the plate and the pepper does not drift - it is flung to the rim in an instant, even the flecks already sitting a hand's width out at the edge. What flings them?
answer: The untouched water around them, pulling the surface outward
choices: The untouched water around them, pulling the surface outward
The soap spreading beneath them and shoving them ahead of it
A current rising in the middle of the plate and pushing out
The pepper's own oils, loosened the moment the soap arrives
context: The Marangoni effect: liquid flows FROM low surface tension TOWARD high. The soap makes a weak patch in the middle, and the strong untouched water all round it wins the tug-of-war and hauls the surface - and the pepper - outward. James Thomson, Lord Kelvin's brother, first spotted the effect in 1855 watching the 'tears of wine' crawl up a wine glass; it is named for Carlo Marangoni, whose 1865 doctoral thesis at Pavia was on a drop of liquid spreading over another liquid. Build the raft version: a notched card with a dab of soap in the notch shoots forward, pulled by the higher tension in front of it. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Marangoni effect'; Scientific American, 'Surface Tension Science: Build a Raft Powered by Soap'.

question: Germany's universities refused Agnes Pockels a place for no reason but her sex; her younger brother Friedrich posted her his Gottingen physics textbooks instead. By 1882, at twenty, she had built her own instrument for measuring the pull of a water surface: a metal trough some seventy centimetres long, filled to the brim, with a metal strip that slid across the top to sweep it clean. How did she read the strength of the pull?
answer: A button hung from a balance, weighed as it tore free of the water
choices: A button hung from a balance, weighed as it tore free of the water
A narrow tube stood in the trough, read for how high water climbed
A dropper tip watched closely, timed for how long a drop hung on
A small float set on the surface, watched for how deep it sank in
context: The 'Schieberinne', or slide-trough: a rectangular metal trough about 70 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2 cm deep, filled to the brim; a movable metal strip laid across the surface to sweep it clean and squeeze a film into a measured area, its position read off a ruler; and a disc about 6 mm across hung from an apothecary's balance and lifted until the water film tore free. Pockels dated her own start in a note: '1882: I have developed the Schieberinne.'
