Sources: Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels'; TU Braunschweig, 'Who was Agnes Pockels?'; Europa-Universitat Flensburg, 'The slide trough on the model of Agnes Pockels'.

question: Agnes Pockels had no university post, no laboratory and no way to publish. In January 1891 she wrote in German to Lord Rayleigh in England, one of the most eminent physicists alive, opening with: 'My Lord, - Will you kindly excuse my venturing to trouble you with a German letter on a scientific subject?' What did Rayleigh do with her letter?
answer: Had his wife translate it and sent it on to Nature to be printed
choices: Had his wife translate it and sent it on to Nature to be printed
Repeated all of her measurements for two years before naming her
Wrote back urging her to apply to a German university at once
Published her findings himself, with a footnote of thanks to her
context: Rayleigh's wife translated the letter, and he forwarded it to Nature with a covering note asking the editor to find space for the work of a German lady who, with very homely appliances, had arrived at valuable results on the behaviour of contaminated water surfaces. It ran as 'Surface Tension', Nature vol. 43, pp. 437-439, 1891. He later asked her to build him a trough of his own. (TU Braunschweig dates the letter 1890 and Wikipedia 10 January 1891; the Nature volume year is firm.) Sources: A. Pockels, 'Surface Tension', Nature 43, 437-439 (1891); Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels'; Chemistry World, 'Pockels' trough'.

question: The story usually told about Agnes Pockels is that she stumbled on her results while washing up - a lucky housewife at the sink. Brigitte Van Tiggelen, a historian of chemistry, has said she never heard anyone explain Lord Rayleigh's or Irving Langmuir's interest in surface films by their washing-up. Pockels worked a purpose-built trough for years. When a step in her own procedure began skewing her readings, what did she do?
answer: Wrote to Lord Rayleigh herself to report her own mistake
choices: Wrote to Lord Rayleigh herself to report her own mistake
Set the flawed run aside and began the whole series again
Rebuilt her trough to a new design before measuring again
Asked her brother Friedrich to check the figures over first
context: The kitchen-sink story is a distortion worth naming. Van Tiggelen's point is that nobody explains Rayleigh's or Langmuir's interest in surface films by their washing-up, and Pockels deserves the same reading: she worked a purpose-built instrument, published fourteen papers, and policed her own work - she caught her own procedural oversights and wrote to Rayleigh to correct them. She was also the one who established that apparatus cleanliness governs whether surface measurements replicate at all, the rule every later worker in the field had to obey. Rayleigh thought enough of her to ask her to build him a trough of his own. Source: Science History Institute, 'Agnes Pockels and the Kitchen Sink Myth'.  (Legend.)

question: Babies born more than eight weeks early were dying of hyaline membrane disease, their lungs stiff and refusing to stay open, and nobody knew why. In 1959 Mary Ellen Avery, a young researcher at Harvard, built a modified Wilhelmy balance - an instrument that measures the pull of a liquid surface - and tested the lung washings of nine infants who had died of the disease. What did the washings show?
answer: The washings did nothing at all to the water's pull
choices: The washings did nothing at all to the water's pull
The washings cut the pull to almost nothing at once
The washings cut the pull, then lost it within minutes
The washings pulled far harder than plain water did
context: The foam simply was not there. Healthy lung washings are strongly surface-active; these were not active at all, which identified the missing substance and pointed straight at replacement therapy. Avery had learned to build the balance after visiting John Clements at the US Army Chemical Center in Maryland, and worked with the experimental biologist Jere Mead; the pull-a-plate-off-the-water measurement is a direct descendant of Agnes Pockels's trough. Published in the American Journal of Diseases of Children, 1959. Sources: Harvard Countway Library, 'The Story of Surfactant'; Harvard Magazine, 'Brief life of Mary Ellen Avery'; 'Historical perspective on surfactant therapy', Seminars in Fetal and Neonatal Medicine.

question: Pour a trace of oil onto clean water in Agnes Pockels's trough, then slide the strip across to squeeze that oil into a smaller and smaller patch, reading the area off a ruler as you go. For a long way the surface pull barely shifts. Then, at one particular area, it changes abruptly. Pockels worked out what that sudden change meant. What had happened to the oil?
answer: It had been pressed down to a single molecule in thickness
choices: It had been pressed down to a single molecule in thickness
It had been squeezed out past the ends of the sliding strip
It had rolled up into visible lenses riding on the surface
It had stiffened into a solid skin under the strip
context: Divide the volume of oil by the area at which the pull jumps and you have the room one molecule takes up. Pockels put it near 20 square angstroms; modern Langmuir monolayers of fatty acids give a limiting area per molecule of 20-25 square angstroms. She was right. Lord Rayleigh ran the same idea from the other end in 1890, dropping a known volume of olive oil on a clean tray and dividing by the area it spread to, and got a film 1.6 nanometres thick. In 1932 Irving Langmuir won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for surface chemistry built on a trough refined from her design; that same year Technische Hochschule Braunschweig gave Agnes Pockels an honorary doctorate in engineering, the first woman it ever so honoured. The Colloid Society had given her the Laura R. Leonard Prize in 1931. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Agnes Pockels'; Grokipedia, 'Langmuir-Blodgett film'.

question: Deep in the lungs every breath ends in millions of microscopic air sacs, each lined with a film of liquid. The pressure inside a wet sac works out as twice the surface tension of that lining divided by the sac's radius. If that lining were plain water, pulling at about 70 millinewtons per metre, breathing would fail within minutes. What would happen to the air sacs?
answer: The smallest sacs would empty themselves into the larger ones
choices: The smallest sacs would empty themselves into the larger ones
The largest sacs would burst and tear their neighbours open
Every sac would swell until the lung could not be emptied
Liquid would be pulled out of the sacs and flood the airways
context: Work the law through: halve the radius and you double the pressure, so the smallest sac carries the HIGHEST pressure and would blow its air into its bigger neighbours until the lung was a few slack bags. Pulmonary surfactant, roughly 40% DPPC, drops the alveolar lining from water's ~70 mN/m to about 25 mN/m at equilibrium and below 1 mN/m when the sac is small and its molecules are crowded together. Tension that falls as the sac shrinks is exactly what stops the small sacs draining into the big ones. Babies born before about 28-32 weeks have not made enough of it yet, which is what made hyaline membrane disease a killer. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pulmonary surfactant'; Young-Laplace P = 2*gamma/r.

question: In 1852 at Cambridge, a physicist shone sunlight through blue-violet glass onto a glass of quinine solution and watched an eerie blue glow appear where the invisible beam entered. He wrote up the effect as 'On the Change of Refrangibility of Light' and coined the word we still use for it. Who was he?
answer: George Gabriel Stokes
choices: George Gabriel Stokes
William Henry Bragg
James Clerk Maxwell
Michael Faraday
context: Stokes coined 'fluorescence' in a footnote on p.479 of his 1852 paper (Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc.), noting that opalescence was named after opal so this deserved a mineral-based name too -- after fluorspar (calcium fluoride), which does the same thing. The 'Stokes shift' between absorbed and emitted wavelengths still carries his name. Source: mindat.org (David Carter); royalsocietypublishing.org rsta.2020.0105.

question: You can rerun Stokes's 1852 quinine experiment at home in five minutes, no lab needed -- his glass of quinine was, essentially, a common drink. Which drink glows electric blue under an ultraviolet blacklight?
answer: Tonic water
choices: Tonic water
Milk
Apple juice
Coca-Cola
context: Tonic water contains quinine (originally as a malaria treatment; the classic gin-and-tonic came out of British India). A cheap UV torch and a bottle of tonic water give the eerie blue Stokes saw. Source: mindat.org David Carter, 'George Gabriel Stokes and the phenomenon of fluorescence'.

question: An ultraviolet blacklight makes a highlighter blaze visibly on paper -- but a red lamp cannot make anything glow blue, no matter how bright. Stokes noticed the same asymmetry in his quinine glass and wrote the rule for it. Why does the trick work one way and not the other?
answer: The re-emitted photon always carries less energy than the absorbed photon
choices: The re-emitted photon always carries less energy than the absorbed photon
The re-emitted photon always carries more energy than the absorbed photon
The re-emitted photon carries exactly the same energy as the absorbed photon
The re-emitted photon carries a random fraction of the absorbed photon's energy
context: This is Stokes's rule, and the energy gap is now called the Stokes shift. The excited molecule sheds a little energy as vibration (heat) before re-emitting, so the outgoing photon is redder (longer wavelength, lower energy) than the incoming one. UV can push electrons hard enough to give off visible light; red light cannot push them hard enough to give off blue. Source: edinst.com 'What is the Stokes shift?'.

question: Glow-in-the-dark stars on a bedroom ceiling keep glowing for hours after the light goes off, but a highlighter under a UV torch goes dark the instant you switch it off. The two glows share the same physics up to a point, then split. What is the difference in name?
answer: The bedroom stars are phosphorescent, the highlighter is fluorescent
choices: The bedroom stars are phosphorescent, the highlighter is fluorescent
The bedroom stars are fluorescent, the highlighter is phosphorescent
Both are fluorescence, but at different temperatures
Both are phosphorescence, but at different brightnesses
context: Fluorescence releases the absorbed energy within nanoseconds; phosphorescence traps the energy in a spin-forbidden 'triplet' state that leaks slowly, so the glow can persist for seconds, minutes or hours. Modern glow-in-the-dark toys use doped strontium aluminate, much brighter than the older zinc sulphide, and no longer any radium (a story that cost the Radium Girls their lives). Source: sciencenotes.org and patsnap eureka on phosphorescence.

question: A fluorescent tube and a modern white LED bulb are the same trick twice. In each case light of one colour is generated and a coating on the glass converts it into visible white light. What is the primary invisible or single-colour light that a fluorescent tube's coating actually converts?
answer: Ultraviolet from excited mercury vapour
choices: Ultraviolet from excited mercury vapour
Infrared from a heated tungsten filament
X-rays from a tiny built-in Geiger tube
Microwaves from a low-power magnetron
context: An electric discharge inside a fluorescent tube excites mercury vapour, which emits at 254 nm in the deep ultraviolet; the phosphor on the glass absorbs those UV photons and re-emits visible light (Stokes's rule, again). A common white LED does the same with a blue InGaN chip under a yellow Ce:YAG phosphor -- the leftover blue plus the phosphor's yellow mixes to white. Sources: rp-photonics.com; digikey.com on Ce:YAG.

question: For decades a Japanese chemist collected the jellyfish Aequorea victoria by the tens of thousands off Washington state and isolated a protein that fluoresces bright green. Splicing its gene beside another gene turns any living cell into a self-labelling lantern, and cell biology became something you could film. Nobel 2008 with Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien. Who did the isolation?
answer: Osamu Shimomura
choices: Osamu Shimomura
Shinya Yamanaka
Susumu Tonegawa
Akira Suzuki
context: Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) let biologists watch a neuron fire, a tumour spread, or a virus enter a cell in real colour. Chalfie showed it worked as a genetic tag; Tsien engineered a rainbow of variants (cyan, yellow, red) so multiple processes could be tracked at once. Source: nobelprize.org chemistry 2008.

question: The Hungarian obstetrician Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths in his hospital maternity ward in 1847 by making the doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime -- but the medical establishment mocked him rather than thanked him, and he lost his post. Where did he die in 1865, at forty-seven?
answer: In a lunatic asylum outside the city
choices: In a private surgery in Budapest
On a ship bound for New York
In a lunatic asylum outside the city
At his family estate in the countryside
context: Semmelweis was committed to the asylum at Oberdoebling, outside Vienna, and died on 13 August 1865, two weeks after admission, of an infected wound. His hand-washing conclusion was correct and it did not save him. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/ignaz-semmelweis/

question: In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener argued that the continents had once been joined and were drifting apart, matching coastlines and fossils on either side of the Atlantic. Geologists rejected the idea for about fifty years. What was the one thing he could NOT tell his critics?
answer: Any force strong enough to move a continent
choices: The names of the two former super-continents
Any force strong enough to move a continent
The direction the continents were drifting
The century in which the split had ended
context: Wegener proposed tidal effects and centrifugal forces from Earth's rotation as the drivers, and geophysicists showed those forces were orders of magnitude too weak. The objection was scientifically legitimate; the personal ridicule was not. Vindication came in the 1960s with symmetrical seafloor magnetic stripes -- decades after Wegener died on the Greenland ice sheet in November 1930. Source: https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2019/01/alfred-wegener-theory-continental-drift

question: In 1984 an Australian physician named Barry Marshall could not convince colleagues that bacteria caused stomach ulcers -- the settled view was stress and excess acid. Ethics rules would not let him deliberately infect a patient. What did he do next that made his name?
answer: He drank a culture of the bacteria himself
choices: He wrote to the New England Journal of Medicine demanding a debate
He drank a culture of the bacteria himself
He resigned his post in protest and left medicine
He tested the bacteria on stray dogs in a Perth kennel
context: In late July 1984 Marshall drank a beef-broth culture containing about a billion Helicobacter pylori. Within days he developed acute gastritis; endoscopy confirmed the infection. In 2005 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2005/marshall/interview/

question: Semmelweis, Wegener and Marshall were all right about their conclusions and each was rejected for a stretch of years. The temptation is to say the establishment was simply stupid. But the pattern is more useful than that. What did each of the three lack, in his own moment, that gave his critics a genuine reason to hold back?
answer: A complete argument for WHY his conclusion had to be true
choices: A complete argument for WHY his conclusion had to be true
The willingness to publish his findings in a real journal
The support of at least one working colleague in his field
A method for gathering the data that he had presented
context: Semmelweis had no germ theory and could not say what invisible thing hand-washing removed. Wegener could name no force that could move continents. Marshall's bacteria contradicted the established acid-and-stress model of the stomach. In each case the dissenter had the right conclusion and an incomplete argument -- and that is what real dissent usually looks like from inside. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_reaction_to_Ignaz_Semmelweis

question: The whole point of the Semmelweis-Wegener-Marshall pattern is what it teaches about deciding a scientific dispute. What actually settles the question, according to the tradition the pattern belongs to?
answer: A test that could lose for either side, and someone willing to run it
choices: A test that could lose for either side, and someone willing to run it
A prediction that matches whatever the later data turn out to be
A mechanism that only the original lab has managed to reproduce
A theory elegant enough that a counter-example seems unlikely
context: The mark of a real dispute is that somebody proposes an experiment that could lose. Franklin's 1784 blindfolded trial killed Mesmerism; Marshall's beaker settled the ulcer question in his own body; Eddington's 1919 eclipse gave general relativity a way to fail on the sky. A prediction that can be reshaped after the data, a result no other lab can reproduce, or a theory whose beauty is treated as evidence -- none of these can settle a real dispute. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Report_of_the_Commissioners_charged_by_the_King_with_the_Examination_of_Animal_Magnetism

question: Nikolai Vavilov spent decades building in Leningrad the world's first great collection of crop seeds, so that whatever else happened his country would keep its food supply. The Stalinist state, under Lysenko's ascendancy, arrested him in August 1940. How did the botanist who spent his life on food security actually die?
answer: Of hunger in a Soviet prison at Saratov
choices: Executed by firing squad in a Moscow courtyard
Killed in a bombing raid on Leningrad
Of hunger in a Soviet prison at Saratov
Of typhus in a Siberian labour camp
context: Vavilov died on 26 January 1943 in the NKVD prison at Saratov, on a diet of mashed cabbage and mouldy flour. The seed bank in Leningrad survived the siege because his colleagues starved to death guarding the stocks rather than eat them. Lysenkoism remained official Soviet science until 1965. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-tragedy-of-the-worlds-first-seed-bank/

question: In October 2020 three epidemiologists -- Sunetra Gupta of Oxford, Martin Kulldorff of Harvard, and Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford -- published the Great Barrington Declaration, calling for a different lockdown policy. In a private email the same month, Francis Collins, the head of the NIH, asked Anthony Fauci for what?
answer: A quick and devastating published takedown of the declaration
choices: A quick and devastating published takedown of the declaration
An invitation for the three authors to a Bethesda seminar
A formal ethics investigation of the three universities
A joint statement of areas of agreement with the authors
context: Collins's email, released later under the Freedom of Information Act, called the three authors 'three fringe epidemiologists' and asked Fauci for a 'quick and devastating published takedown of its premises.' In April 2025 one of the three, Jay Bhattacharya, was sworn in as the 18th Director of the NIH -- the same institution whose head had asked for the takedown. Source: https://www.theblaze.com/news/fauci-email-francis-collins-great-barrington-declaration

question: Richard Feynman closed his 1974 Caltech commencement address, later published as 'Cargo Cult Science,' with a line that has become the motto of the whole dissent-and-repair tradition. What did he tell the graduates was the first principle?
answer: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool
choices: The first principle is that a theory must forbid something -- one that fits every result forbids nothing
The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool
The first principle is that a good experiment is worth a thousand expert opinions
The first principle is that if you cannot explain it to a freshman, you do not truly understand it
context: Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science,' Caltech commencement address, 1974. The full line reads: 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself -- and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you've not fooled yourself, it's easy not to fool other scientists.' The other three options are real principles from the wider tradition -- Popper's falsifiability, the experimenter's proverb, and a Feynman-adjacent teaching test -- but none of them is the Cargo Cult line. Source: https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/3043/

question: On 26 March 1851, under the dome of the Pantheon in Paris, Leon Foucault hung a 28 kg lead bob on a 67-metre wire. The crowd watched the swing do something never before demonstrated in a room. What did they see?
answer: The plane crept round and knocked over pegs set in a floor ring
choices: The plane crept round and knocked over pegs set in a floor ring
The bob slowed to a halt despite no visible source of friction
The bob swung higher and higher as the dome quieted the air
The swing quickened whenever the crowd pressed near the wire
context: The pendulum swung in a fixed plane, but the floor and the whole city rotated underneath it, so the plane appeared to sweep round the ring hour by hour and topple pegs one by one. It was the first time a person could walk into a room and watch the Earth turn -- until then, Earth's rotation had only been inferred from astronomy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foucault_pendulum

question: The year after the pendulum, in 1852, Foucault built a second instrument to make the same point without any swing at all -- a rapidly spinning wheel, suspended so its axis stayed fixed in space while Paris turned underneath. He coined a Greek-rooted name for it that we still use. What is that name?
answer: The gyroscope
choices: The gyroscope
The heliostat
The spectroscope
The chronometer
context: Foucault felt his pendulum was too easily explained away, so he built a spinning-wheel apparatus whose axis stayed fixed while the Earth rotated, and named it 'gyroscope' from Greek gyros (circle) and skopein (to see) -- literally 'a device to see the turning.' The instrument is now inside every phone, drone, and spacecraft. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foucault's_gyroscope

question: In 1936 Frances Oldham, a young Canadian pharmacologist, applied to work in E. M. K. Geiling's laboratory at the University of Chicago. The reply offering her the post began 'Dear Mr. Oldham.' She wrote to her McGill supervisor, Dr. Stehle, asking whether she ought to correct the mistake before accepting. What did Stehle tell her to do?
answer: Sign her name, add 'Miss' in brackets, and go.
choices: Sign her name, add 'Miss' in brackets, and go.
Write back correcting the error, then accept.
Turn it down and apply again under her full name.
Say nothing about it until she reached Chicago.
context: Stehle's exact words were 'Don't be ridiculous. Accept the job, sign your name, put Miss in brackets afterwards, and go!' She did. Kelsey never learned whether the mix-up mattered: 'to this day, I do not know if my name had been Elizabeth or Mary Jane, whether I would have gotten that first big step up. My professor at Chicago to his dying day would never admit one way or the other.' That Chicago training is what put her, twenty-four years later, at the FDA desk where the thalidomide application landed. Source: Frances O. Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.12-13 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: The application Richardson-Merrell filed to sell thalidomide in America is the file Frances Kelsey held up for more than a year. Looking back decades later, Kelsey measured it against the applications of her own time - 150 to 200 volumes each, and a volume, she said, is 'the size of a metropolitan phone book.' How many volumes was the whole thalidomide file?
answer: Four.
choices: Four.
Fourteen.
Forty.
Ninety.
context: Four volumes, for a drug already being swallowed nightly across Europe. Thin files were normal in 1960: under the law then in force a company had to show only that a drug would not poison you, so there was not much to file. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.48 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Frances Kelsey had been a medical officer at the FDA for barely a month when her supervisors handed her two applications meant to break her in gently - 'this is a very easy one,' they told her of the sedative, 'there will be no problems with sleeping pills.' That sedative was thalidomide, and she held it up for over a year. The other was for a rectal enema called Lavema. What did Kelsey do with that one?
answer: She approved it, and it went on sale.
choices: She approved it, and it went on sale.
She held that file up too, for months.
She passed it to another reviewer instead.
She turned it down for want of animal data.
context: 'It did get marketed, so I must have approved it,' Kelsey said. She was not a reflexive no-sayer: handed two files the same month, she cleared one and stopped the other, and the difference was the evidence in front of her. She had started at the FDA on 1 August 1960; thalidomide reached her in early September, only her second assignment. Her comment on the supervisors' prediction: 'I never got another one quite like that one.' Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.49 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Through 1961 Richardson-Merrell's contact man telephoned Frances Kelsey again and again about the thalidomide file she had now kept open for a year. On one of those calls, she recalled, he stopped arguing about the science and stated outright why the company was in such a hurry. What reason did he give?
answer: Christmas was their best sales season for sedatives.
choices: Christmas was their best sales season for sedatives.
A rival American firm was about to file the same drug.
Their European patent was close to running out.
Their whole stock of tablets was close to expiring.
context: Kelsey's account: 'There was, for example, the time they kept calling me, and they just came right out and said, "We want to get this drug on the market before Christmas, because that is when our best sales are."' They had aimed at the 1960 season, missed it, and were watching a second Christmas go by. She did not move. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.63 and 74 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: A letter in the British Medical Journal of 31 December 1960, headed 'Is Thalidomide to Blame?', described four patients who had taken the drug nightly for over a year and developed prickling numbness spreading from their feet. Nobody at Richardson-Merrell pointed Frances Kelsey to it; she found it herself, browsing at her desk weeks late. What had held it up?
answer: A mail strike had delayed the FDA's journals.
choices: A mail strike had delayed the FDA's journals.
Her supervisors had routed it to another officer.
The journal had printed it in a late supplement.
The FDA library bound issues before circulating them.
context: Kelsey: 'Although this issue had been published on 31 December 1960, there was a problem with delivery of our journals - I think it was a mail strike - and the journal did not reach us until late January or early February.' The letter was written by Dr. A. Leslie Florence, a Scottish general practitioner (BMJ 1960;2(5217):1954). A mail strike delayed the clue that stopped the drug - and it reached her at all only because she read the journals herself, through no official channel. Sources: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.55 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; Florence AL, BMJ 1960 - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2098660/

question: Frances Kelsey's first objection to the thalidomide application was not about a symptom or a dose - it was about the kind of evidence in the file. She read Richardson-Merrell's clinical section, the reports on patients who had already been given the drug, and judged that it could not carry the claims the company had built on it. What did Kelsey say was wrong with those reports?
answer: They were testimonials rather than well-executed studies.
choices: They were testimonials rather than well-executed studies.
They counted patients but never followed them past a month.
They came from doctors the company itself had paid.
They described European patients only, never Americans.
context: In her words the reports 'were more in the nature of testimonials rather than well-designed, well-executed studies,' and 'the claims made in the NDA for thalidomide were too glowing for the support in the way of clinical back-up.' A doctor vouching for a drug is not the same as anyone measuring it - which is exactly the distinction Congress would write into American law two years later. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.52-54 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Three people at the FDA reviewed the thalidomide file: Frances Kelsey as medical officer, Jiro Oyama as pharmacologist, and Lee Geismar as chemist. 'All three of us found problems,' Kelsey said - and she spent the rest of her life correcting the story that she had stood alone. What did Geismar find?
answer: Mistakes in the company's translations of the German data.
choices: Mistakes in the company's translations of the German data.
An impurity in the sample tablets the company had sent.
A dose in the file ten times the one used in Europe.
A German study the application had quietly left out.
context: Geismar had trained in Germany and could read the original German submissions, so she caught errors in Richardson-Merrell's translations. The lone-heroine version of this story is the legend, and Kelsey never told it that way: accepting the President's Award in 1962 she said she was taking it 'on behalf of a lot of different federal workers. This was really a team effort.' Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.51-52 and p.79 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: By early 1961 Frances Kelsey had a British report on thalidomide - a sedative already taken nightly across Europe - describing four patients left with prickling numbness that spread from their feet to their hands. Kelsey could not say what the drug was doing inside the body, and its makers had years of European sales to point to. She kept the American application open anyway. What was her reason?
answer: Nerve damage is not what a simple sleeping pill should do.
choices: Nerve damage is not what a simple sleeping pill should do.
Four cases from one practice outweighed Europe's sales record.
The numbness matched a known reaction to other sedatives.
A drug taken nightly for years needed years of testing.
context: Her own sentence is the hinge of the whole review: 'the peripheral neuritis did not seem the sort of side effect that should come from a simple sleeping pill.' Peripheral neuritis is damage to the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. Kelsey did not know what thalidomide did. She knew it was doing something a sleeping pill has no business doing, and that was enough to keep asking. The report was Dr. A. Leslie Florence's letter in the British Medical Journal of 31 December 1960. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), p.55 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Under the 1938 law Frances Kelsey worked with, the FDA had sixty days to act on a new drug application; if the agency raised no objection - or simply forgot the deadline - the drug became approved automatically. Kelsey had no power to reject thalidomide. She had one procedural move that started those sixty days over again, and she used it from 10 November 1960 onward for more than a year. What was the move?
answer: Declaring the application incomplete.
choices: Declaring the application incomplete.
Referring the file to an outside panel.
Demanding a fresh set of animal tests.
Objecting in writing to her division chief.
context: Kelsey: 'if we had no objection or if we forgot that the 60 days had elapsed, the drug automatically became approved.' Ruling the file incomplete restarted the clock, and she did it over and over for fourteen months. She never had the power to say no to thalidomide - only the power to keep saying not yet. Source: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.49-50 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; corroborated at https://grokipedia.com/page/Frances_Oldham_Kelsey

question: Frances Kelsey spent the war years on the hunt for a malaria drug, and with a colleague she ran her own experiment on quinine in rabbits, measuring how a pregnant mother and her embryos each handled the drug. Years later, Richardson-Merrell assured the FDA that thalidomide never reached an unborn child - so a pregnant woman could take it safely. What had Kelsey's rabbits shown her?
answer: The mother rabbits broke quinine down poorly, and the embryos not at all.
choices: The mother rabbits broke quinine down poorly, and the embryos not at all.
Quinine crossed into the embryos, which cleared it as fast as adults.
Pregnancy sped the breakdown of quinine in mother and embryo alike.
Quinine gathered in the embryos' bones and leaked out after birth.
context: 'We found that during pregnancy there was less ability in the mother to break down the quinine and that the embryo rabbits had no ability at all to do so until after birth.' The work came out of the WWII antimalarial program - with the Dutch East Indies lost, about 90 percent of the Allies' quinine supply had vanished, and a crash program screened over 14,000 candidate compounds. Note how fast Kelsey deflates her own result: 'This is not something we discovered. In fact, after we thought that we had done so, we found that it had been discovered after the First World War.' Her one-sentence principle: 'When you give a drug to a pregnant woman you are exposing, in fact, two people to the drug, the mother and the child.' Sources: Kelsey, 'Autobiographical Reflections' (FDA), pp.25-29 and p.61 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: Under the 1938 law Frances Kelsey had to work with, an American drugmaker had to demonstrate exactly one thing about a new drug before selling it: that it would not poison you. The Kefauver-Harris amendments, signed by President Kennedy on 10 October 1962 - seven months after Richardson-Merrell withdrew its thalidomide application - added a second thing every maker now had to prove. What was it?
answer: That the drug actually did what the label claimed.
choices: That the drug actually did what the label claimed.
That the drug had been tested on pregnant animals.
That the drug had been approved abroad already.
That the drug could not be taken in a fatal dose.
context: Public Law 87-781 demanded 'substantial evidence' of effectiveness, and the statute spelled out what would count: 'adequate and well-controlled investigations, including clinical investigations, by experts qualified by scientific training and experience.' Testimonials were explicitly no longer enough. Richardson-Merrell had withdrawn its application on 8 March 1962, and Kelsey was careful about the credit: 'There is nothing that would lead me to think we had requested the withdrawal. I think Merrell withdrew it of their own accord when they were finally convinced that there really was a problem.' Sources: Grokipedia 'Kefauver-Harris Amendment' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Kefauver%E2%80%93Harris_Amendment; Kelsey (FDA), p.68 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: On 30 November 1961 it was Richardson-Merrell's own contact man who telephoned the FDA with the news: the German maker was withdrawing thalidomide, because Widukind Lenz, a Hamburg pediatrician, had tied it to babies born with severely shortened limbs. Frances Kelsey said she was very surprised. In more than a year of holding the file she had never predicted that particular harm. On what, then, had her objections rested?
answer: That no one had yet produced evidence the drug was safe.
choices: That no one had yet produced evidence the drug was safe.
That the German safety reports covered too few patients.
That the drug's chemistry resembled a known poison.
That nobody had followed the numbness cases to the end.
context: Kelsey: 'I remember very well when he called... I was - I admit it - very surprised. This was what we had been wanting to make sure would not happen with the drug and it appeared it had.' And then the honest note the whole story turns on: 'Our objections... were really on theoretical grounds, largely based on the fact that there was no evidence that it was safe.' She was not clairvoyant. She refused to assume safety, which is a different and repeatable thing. Lenz first suspected the drug on 11 November 1961, telephoned Chemie Grunenthal on 16 November demanding withdrawal, and presented at a Dusseldorf conference on 18 November, having found that 41 of 46 mothers of affected babies had taken it early in pregnancy. The Australian obstetrician William McBride reached the same conclusion independently; his letter ran in The Lancet on 16 December 1961, two weeks after this phone call. Sources: Kelsey (FDA), p.66 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; Widukind Lenz, 'The History of Thalidomide,' 1992 UNITH Congress - https://www.thalidomide.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Dr-Lenz-history-of-thalidomide-1992.pdf; James Lind Library, McBride WG (1961) - https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/mcbride-wg-1961/

question: Thalidomide was never approved for sale in the United States - and yet Richardson-Merrell had been shipping it for over a year, as 'investigational' samples handed out to doctors, a channel the 1938 law barely covered. The list of investigators the company filed with the FDA named some thirty or forty doctors. How much of the drug had actually gone out?
answer: About 2.5 million tablets, to more than a thousand doctors.
choices: About 2.5 million tablets, to more than a thousand doctors.
About 90,000 tablets, to roughly three hundred doctors.
About 250,000 tablets, to roughly six hundred doctors.
About 12 million tablets, to some eight thousand doctors.
context: The tablets reached an estimated 15,000-20,000 patients, over 600 of them pregnant. Seventeen affected babies were confirmed born in the United States; in about half of those cases the drug had come from overseas, and the FDA could tie ten to the American samples. Kelsey later described what the other doctors had been told: that the drug 'was about to come to market and that they need not bother much about keeping records.' The 'clinical trial' was a sales program, and the FDA learned its real scale only after the withdrawal. America's win here was scale, not perfection - say it plainly. Sources: Kelsey (FDA), pp.58, 71-72, 75 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download; Grokipedia 'Frances Oldham Kelsey' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Frances_Oldham_Kelsey; Smithsonian Magazine - https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/woman-who-stood-between-america-and-epidemic-birth-defects-180963165/

question: Thalidomide exists in two mirror-image forms of the same molecule. One is the sedative that puts a person to sleep; the other is the one that disrupts a baby's development in the womb. Once chemists understood this, an obvious rescue suggested itself - make and sell only the harmless mirror form. That rescue is impossible. Why?
answer: The body converts one mirror form into the other within hours.
choices: The body converts one mirror form into the other within hours.
Only the harmful mirror form can be made in useful quantity.
No known method can separate the two mirror forms at all.
The sedative mirror form stops working once it is purified.
context: In blood serum the two forms interconvert with a half-life on the order of an hour, so a purified single-form thalidomide would scramble back into a mixture inside the patient. The clean-version fix that sounds obvious was chemically impossible from the start. The drug did come back, under strict control: the FDA approved thalidomide in July 1998 for erythema nodosum leprosum, a complication of leprosy, and in May 2006 for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. Kelsey's own comment on its return: 'even the worst of drugs may be used under certain circumstances where the risks are justified.' Same molecule, different question. Sources: Tokunaga et al., Scientific Reports 2018 - https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-35457-6; StatPearls, 'Thalidomide' - https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557706/; Kelsey (FDA), pp.14-15 - https://www.fda.gov/media/89162/download

question: The 1962 law born out of the thalidomide affair raised the standard of proof an American drugmaker had to meet before it could sell a new drug. Economist Sam Peltzman later counted the genuinely new drug compounds introduced in the United States each year, before the law and after it. What did his count show?
answer: A fall from about 43 a year to about 16.
choices: A fall from about 43 a year to about 16.
A rise from about 16 a year to about 43.
A steady rate of about 40 a year throughout.
A fall from about 90 a year to about 60.
context: Peltzman's count is the second edge of this story, and both edges are true. Demanding proof is what kept thalidomide away from American mothers. Demanding proof also costs time that sick people do not always have: critics of the 1962 amendments point to a 'drug lag' in which new therapies reached European patients years before American ones. The point is not that the regulator is always right - Kelsey herself said her objections were theoretical. The point is that a claim with no evidence behind it is not yet knowledge, whoever is making it and whichever answer you were hoping for. Source: Grokipedia 'Kefauver-Harris Amendment', Criticisms and Controversies - https://grokipedia.com/page/Kefauver%E2%80%93Harris_Amendment

question: Benjamin Franklin's printed recipe for a storm kite is homely and exact: two light strips of cedar tied in a cross, a sharp wire rising a foot above the wood, and a covering he chose because it would still be whole after an hour of rain. What did he stretch across the cross?
answer: A large thin silk handkerchief.
choices: A large thin silk handkerchief.
A light square of oiled canvas.
A thin sheet of dressed calfskin.
A fine panel of woven linen.
context: Franklin's own recipe, printed in the Pennsylvania Gazette of 19 October 1752: 'a small Cross of two light Strips of Cedar' with 'a large thin Silk Handkerchief' tied to the four corners, and 'a very sharp pointed Wire, rising a Foot or more above the Wood.' Silk rather than the paper of a child's kite, because paper tears apart once a storm soaks it and this kite had to survive the whole downpour. The instrument that asked the sky a question was a handkerchief, two sticks and a wire. Sources: Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 19 Oct 1752, quoted at the Benjamin Franklin Historical Society (benjamin-franklin-history.org/kite-experiment/); Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: Franklin's storm-kite instructions tell the flier exactly what to watch for as the thundercloud arrives, and it is neither a flash nor a bang. Before the rain has even reached the kite, the hemp twine gives the first sign. What does it do?
answer: Its loose fibres stand out from it in every direction.
choices: Its loose fibres stand out from it in every direction.
It glows faintly with a pale light along its length.
It grows warm enough to feel through a glove.
It stiffens and draws itself taut as a bar of iron.
context: Franklin's words: when a thundercloud comes over, 'the loose Filaments of the Twine will stand out every Way, and be attracted by an approaching Finger.' The order matters and is usually retold backwards. The fibres separate BEFORE the rain arrives; only afterwards, once 'the Rain has wet the Kite and Twine,' does the fire 'stream out plentifully from the Key on the Approach of your Knuckle.' Sources: Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 19 Oct 1752, quoted at The Franklin Institute (fi.edu) and the Benjamin Franklin Historical Society.

question: In the famous engravings of the kite flight, a small boy stands at Benjamin Franklin's elbow holding the string. There really was an assistant that day, his son William, and the two of them were the only people present. How old was William?
answer: Twenty-one.
choices: Sixteen.
Twenty-one.
Twenty-eight.
Thirty-four.
context: William Franklin was twenty-one, a grown man, and he and his father were the only witnesses — no independent observer ever attested to the experiment. In 2023 the Brazilian researcher Breno Arsioli Moura examined seven nineteenth-century illustrations of the kite flight and catalogued their errors, among them lightning shown striking the kite, Franklin shown gripping the conducting string with his bare hand, and William drawn as a young child. The picture is the myth's delivery vehicle. Sources: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment; Moura, 'Picturing Benjamin Franklin's Kite Experiment in the Nineteenth Century,' Science & Education (2023).

question: Every picture of Benjamin Franklin's kite flight shows a bolt of lightning slamming into it, and the Franklin Institute says a real strike would probably have killed him. No bolt came. What did arrive was charge, drawn quietly off the cloud and down the rain-soaked hemp twine, until fire streamed from the key to a knuckle held near it. The charge went no further, because what Franklin held beyond the key was not twine. What was it?
answer: A dry silk ribbon.
choices: A dry silk ribbon.
A waxed leather strap.
A short glass rod.
A dry cedar stick.
context: Franklin's instructions put the flier 'within a Door, or Window, or under some Cover, so that the Silk Ribbon may not be wet.' The conducting hemp twine ended at the key, and past the key he held nothing but that ribbon: wet twine carries a charge, dry silk does not, so the storm stopped at the key. Silk, glass, wax and dry wood were the insulators every electrician of the century reached for — Franklin chose the one that could be tied to a line and held in a fist. The rest of the famous picture is wrong too. The Franklin Institute states it flatly: 'Franklin's kite was not struck by lightning. If it had been, he probably would have been electrocuted, experts say.' There was no strike and no flash at the kite at all — the sharp wire above it drew charge silently off a passing thundercloud, and the whole safety of the thing rested on one dry ribbon. Sources: Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 19 Oct 1752, quoted at the Benjamin Franklin Historical Society (benjamin-franklin-history.org/kite-experiment/); The Franklin Institute (fi.edu); Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: European towns met a thunderstorm by sending men up the bell towers to haul on the ropes. In 1784 Johann Fischer of Munich counted what the custom had cost over thirty-three years: bell towers struck 386 times, 103 ringers killed at the ropes. What did the towns believe the peal did to the storm?
answer: That its sound broke the thunderstorm apart over the town.
choices: That its sound broke the thunderstorm apart over the town.
That its sound drove the hail out of the cloud before it fell.
That its sound turned the storm aside toward open country.
That its sound drew the lightning safely into the bell metal.
context: Fischer's 1784 Munich study was titled 'A Proof that the Ringing of Bells during Thunderstorms may be more Dangerous than Useful.' Across the thirty-three years from 1750 to 1783 he counted bell towers struck 386 times and 103 ringers killed on the ropes. The belief was cast into the metal itself: many church bells carry the motto fulgura frango, 'I break the lightning' — the peal was thought to shatter the storm overhead, so the worse the sky looked, the harder the men pulled. Bans on storm-ringing followed in France. This is the world Franklin's rod walked into: a remedy against lightning that reliably killed the men who worked it. Sources: Fischer (Munich, 1784), as reported at The History Blog (thehistoryblog.com/archives/43119) and campaners.com.

question: A spark at a key proved little by itself; electricians drew sparks from rubbed glass globes in drawing rooms all over Europe. So Benjamin Franklin did bench physics in a thunderstorm. He ran the charge off the kite line into a Leyden jar, the glass bottle electricians used for storing a charge, then spent it on an ordinary laboratory demonstration. What did the storm's charge do?
answer: It set a dish of alcohol alight.
choices: It set a dish of alcohol alight.
It swung a compass needle aside.
It boiled a spoonful of water.
It melted a thin lead wire.
context: Franklin charged a Leyden jar from the key and used the collected charge to run ordinary bench demonstrations, including igniting spirits — alcohol — exactly as electricians did with charge from a rubbed glass globe. That identity, not the spark, was the discovery: the fire from the sky behaved in every way like the fire made on a laboratory bench. Source: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: Two years before any kite, Benjamin Franklin sent Peter Collinson in London a way to find out whether storm clouds carry electricity, and printed it without ever having tried it, leaving the risk to whoever built it first. What did the 1750 letter describe?
answer: A sentry box on a high tower, a man inside on an insulating stand under an iron rod.
choices: A sentry box on a high tower, a man inside on an insulating stand under an iron rod.
A copper wire on an arrow shot up into a cloud base and traced to a jar below.
A ring of iron posts round a field, wired together to catch the storm as it crossed.
A tall mast raised out at sea, where ships were struck far oftener than buildings.
context: Franklin to Peter Collinson, 'Opinions and Conjectures,' 29 July 1750: a sentry box on a high tower or steeple, a man standing inside on an insulating stand of wood and glass, and a sharp-pointed iron rod 20 to 30 feet long rising from the roof; the observer would present a key or an electroscope to the rod's wire to see whether the cloud was charged. He published the dangerous design two years before anyone ran it. It reached France because Buffon demonstrated Franklin's electrical experiments to King Louis XV in March 1752 and Dalibard translated Franklin's book into French — which is how a Philadelphia printer's design ended up standing in a field outside Paris. Sources: Founders Online (Franklin to Collinson, 29 July 1750); Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment; Physics Today, 'Benjamin Franklin and lightning rods.'

question: Benjamin Franklin was not the only man who thought of flying a kite at a storm. On 7 June 1753 at Nérac in France, Jacques de Romas flew his own, and instead of waiting for rain to make plain hemp conduct he had woven a metal wire into the string. Franklin's line gave sparks a man could draw with his knuckle. What did de Romas record from his?
answer: Sparks about ten feet long, heard cracking across the town.
choices: Sparks about ten feet long, heard cracking across the town.
Sparks about a hand's breadth, hissing on and off for a minute.
A single spark that burned a hole clean through his wooden reel.
A steady blue glow that ran along the wire as the cloud passed.
context: De Romas recorded sparks roughly three metres long, with explosions loud enough to be heard in the town. He and Franklin devised the kite version independently, and only one of them is remembered. The figures come from de Romas's own report. Sources: Wikipedia, Jacques de Romas; Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment.

question: At Marly-la-Ville north of Paris, a 40-foot iron rod an inch thick and sharpened at the top stood on a wooden platform insulated by wine bottles, built to Benjamin Franklin's published design and ready a full month before the kite ever flew. When the storm broke on 10 May 1752, Thomas-François Dalibard, who had built it, was away. Someone else stood at the rod between two and three that afternoon and drew the sparks, the first any human hand had pulled from a thundercloud. Who?
answer: Coiffier, a retired dragoon.
choices: Coiffier, a retired dragoon.
Raulet, the village priest.
Buffon, the royal naturalist.
Nollet, an abbé and electrician.
context: Dalibard's assistant Thomas-François Coiffier, a retired dragoon, drew the crackling sparks between two and three in the afternoon of 10 May 1752. The village priest, Father Raulet, was fetched to confirm it with an electroscope and reported bluish flames, a sulfurous smell, and shocks like a Leyden jar; Dalibard reported the result to the Académie Royale des Sciences three days later, on 13 May. The design had reached France because Buffon demonstrated Franklin's electrical experiments to King Louis XV in March 1752 and Dalibard translated Franklin's book into French. The first human being ever to pull sparks out of a thundercloud was not a scientist but a retired soldier standing in for one, and it happened a month before Franklin's kite: the proposal had outrun the proposer. Sources: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment; Physics Today, which calls him 'a retired French dragoon.'

question: St Petersburg, 6 August 1753. Georg Wilhelm Richmann, a professor repeating Franklin's storm experiments, had wired his roof to an iron bar a foot long standing over a vessel of brass filings. He was watching from a foot away when a globe of blue and whitish fire about four inches across struck his forehead; he fell backwards without the least outcry, and an instant later came an explosion like a small cannon. Franklin's rod recipe insisted on one thing Richmann's apparatus did not have. What?
answer: A conductor carrying the charge down into damp earth.
choices: A conductor carrying the charge down into damp earth.
A copper chain looping from the bar across to the chimney.
A pane of glass set between the bar and the roof timbers.
A silk cord held between the observer and the metal.
context: Franklin's recipe in Poor Richard's Almanack for 1753, 'How to secure Houses, &c. from LIGHTNING,' specifies an iron rod 'of such a Length, that one End being three or four Feet in the moist Ground, the other may be six or eight Feet above the highest Part of the Building.' The damp earth is the load-bearing part: the charge must be given a path that is not the building, and not the man. Richmann's bar had none. Franklin printed the Academy's account of the death in his own Pennsylvania Gazette on 5 March 1754. The autopsy is worth knowing because the usual retelling is wrong: there was no burn on him at all and his hair was 'not in the least burned' — only an oval red mark on the forehead 'about the Bigness of a Rouble' and his left shoe torn in two places. The Academy's engraver, Sokolov, was thrown to the floor by the blast, his clothes burned by flying wire fragments, and survived; his description of the four-inch glowing globe is the first reliable scientific report of ball lightning. Nothing in this story is a thing to try. Sources: Pennsylvania Gazette, 5 March 1754 (todayinsci.com); Grokipedia /page/Georg_Wilhelm_Richmann; Poor Richard's Almanack 1753 via the Pennsylvania Center for the Book.

question: On 15 May 1777 lightning damaged the gunpowder magazine at Purfleet in Essex even though Franklin's pointed conductors stood on it. Benjamin Wilson, a portrait painter who had also won the Royal Society's highest medal for work on electricity, argued that blunt rounded conductors were safer, and he settled it with spectacle rather than argument: a 47-metre charge generator of foil and pasteboard hung on silk threads from the ceiling of the Pantheon on Oxford Street, fired at a scale model of the arsenal, with King George III watching, in the middle of Britain's war with Franklin's America. What did the King do next?
answer: He had blunt knobs fitted to the roof of his own palace.
choices: He had blunt knobs fitted to the roof of his own palace.
He had blunt knobs fitted to every powder magazine in England.
He had the Royal Society withdraw its report on Purfleet.
He had Wilson appointed his adviser on the whole question.
context: George III had the pointed conductors on the Queen's House (Buckingham House) replaced with blunt knobs, and the Dictionary of National Biography records the king declaring that Wilson's experiments were enough to convince 'the apple-women in Covent Garden.' A question about the shape of a metal tip had become a loyalty test in the middle of the American Revolution. The best-known line of the affair is probably apocryphal: the President of the Royal Society, Sir John Pringle, is said to have answered his king, 'Sire, the prerogatives of the President of the Royal Society do not extend to altering the laws of nature,' and resigned — the Institute of Physics presents that as 'one version of the story' and the Whipple Library calls it likely untrue. London wits put the quarrel in verse: 'Whilst you, great George, for knowledge hunt, / And sharp conductors change for blunt, / The nation's out of joint: / Franklin another plan pursues, / And all your thunder useless views, / By sticking to his point.' Sources: IOP Spark, 'When lightning conductors were political' (citing Heilbron, Elements of Early Modern Physics, 1982); Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Wilson, Benjamin'; Whipple Library Books Blog.

question: The kite is the most retold experiment in American science, and Benjamin Franklin never described it in his autobiography. His only word on it at the time was a short third-person notice in the Pennsylvania Gazette of 19 October 1752 that gave instructions for building the kite without ever saying he had flown one. The vivid version, the key and the spark and the storm-soaked twine, reached print fifteen years afterwards. Whose account was it?
answer: Joseph Priestley's history of electricity, written from talks with Franklin.
choices: Joseph Priestley's history of electricity, written from talks with Franklin.
William Franklin's sworn recollection, set down long after the event.
Peter Collinson's published memoir of his American correspondents.
Thomas-François Dalibard's preface to his French edition of Franklin.
context: The vivid version first appears in Joseph Priestley's History and Present State of Electricity (1767), fifteen years later, from conversations with Franklin; Priestley dated the flight 15 June 1752, while other accounts say 10 or 24 June. How far the doubt goes, and where it stops: Tom Tucker's Bolt of Fate (2003) argues the flight was a hoax staged for scientific reputation, and Carl Van Doren called the story 'dim and mystifying in fact.' Michael Brian Schiffer answers that 'It is doubtful that Franklin would have crafted a piece of fictional science, for he appreciated the penalty that the gentlemanly establishment of natural philosophy would have meted out had the fraud been exposed.' Most historians accept that some version happened. The rod, by contrast, is documented, dated and installed — on his own Philadelphia house in the autumn of 1752, and on Christ Church's spire and the Academy of Philadelphia by early 1753. It is unquestionably his, and it unquestionably worked. Sources: Grokipedia /page/Kite_experiment ('Modern Skepticism'); National Constitution Center, 'The great debate about Benjamin Franklin and his kite.'

question: Joseph Fraunhofer's guardians signed the orphan over to a Munich mirror-polisher who underfed him and forbade him candlelight to read by. On 21 July 1801 the workshop roof fell in; the fourteen-year-old lay buried for hours, and others beside him died. Being dug out made him famous. What did that fame win him?
answer: A prince who bought out his contract
choices: A prince who bought out his contract
A guild that named him master early
A professor who hired him as helper
A parish fund that paid for school
context: Prince-Elector Maximilian IV Joseph of Bavaria personally oversaw the rescue, and his help was concrete rather than ceremonial: money, textbooks on mathematics and physics, funds to buy an optical grinding machine, cash to buy out the remainder of the six-year apprenticeship, and an annual allowance to live on while he studied. He also forced the employer to allow the boy time to read. Fraunhofer had been orphaned in 1798 — his mother died of malnutrition and hardship, his father later the same year from the effects of his trade. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer' (Birth and Family Background; Apprenticeship and Early Hardships) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Joseph_von_Fraunhofer ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_von_Fraunhofer

question: Joseph Fraunhofer split sunlight with prisms of the finest glass in Europe. You do not need one. A single ordinary object in most houses will fan a sunbeam into its whole range of colours and throw them across a white wall. Which one?
answer: The shiny side of a CD
choices: The shiny side of a CD
The bowl of a steel spoon
A pane of window glass
A magnifying glass lens
context: An ordinary pressed CD or DVD is a diffraction grating: a spiral of microscopic pits under a thin metal layer, ruled so finely that light of different wavelengths bounces off at different angles. Fraunhofer built the first grating in 1821 by stretching about 260 fine parallel wires across a frame, then moved to ruling grooves with a diamond point on a screw-driven dividing engine — spacings near 0.003 mm, over 8,000 lines to the inch, the finest around 10,000. He gave gratings away to leading scientists across Europe and was the first person to measure the wavelength of a spectral line with one. Go further: the strongest solar dark lines — his A, B and C groups near the red end — are visible to the naked eye through even a basic spectroscope. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' — https://grokipedia.com/page/Fraunhofer_lines ; Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer' (Development of the Diffraction Grating); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffraction_grating

question: Split sunlight with a prism and you get what everyone had always seen: a smooth band running red to violet, each colour melting into the next. In 1814 Joseph Fraunhofer sent sunlight through a narrow slit and a prism of his own flint glass, then examined that band closely. It was not smooth. What did he find in it?
answer: Hundreds of sharp dark lines
choices: Hundreds of sharp dark lines
A doubled band, one above the other
Bright lines standing out along it
A violet end that faded out early
context: Fraunhofer mapped roughly 574 of them and lettered the strongest A through K, ordered from the red end toward the blue, publishing an engraved plate of the spectrum in his 1817 memoir in the Annalen der Physik after first presenting the work to the Munich Academy in 1815. Contemporaries said the lines were simply flaws in his glass — streaks or bubbles casting shadows; he killed that objection by getting the identical lines out of several different instruments. And he was not the first to glimpse dark bands: William Hyde Wollaston saw some in 1802 but read them as natural boundaries separating one region of colour from the next. Fraunhofer's contribution is the systematic, measured map, not first sight. On what caused the lines he said plainly that he could not explain them, and the cause stayed unknown for the rest of his life. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines'; Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy' (Early 19th-Century Solar Spectrum Observations); Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer'

question: The instrument Joseph Fraunhofer aimed at the Sun in 1814 was no toy: a narrow slit, a tube to straighten the beam, a prism of flint glass and a small eyepiece, the whole thing mounted on a surveyor's stand so he could measure the angle of anything he saw. He was not an astronomer and had no question about the sky. The apparatus existed to serve his trade. What was his trade?
answer: Making telescope lenses for observatories
choices: Making telescope lenses for observatories
Grinding spectacles for Munich's opticians
Casting mirrors for Bavaria's lighthouses
Surveying the roads and borders of Bavaria
context: Fraunhofer was measuring how sharply each batch of his own glass bent each colour — its refractive index and its dispersion — so that he could grind lenses that brought all the colours to one focus. The marks he found in the Sun's spectrum that day became exactly what he needed: fixed, unmoving reference colours to calibrate instruments against. The fingerprint hidden in sunlight was found during quality control. His own summary of himself: 'In all my experiments I could, owing to lack of time, pay attention to only those matters which appeared to have a bearing upon practical optics.' The stand was a modified surveyor's theodolite. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Joseph von Fraunhofer' (Invention of the Spectroscope); Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy'; quotation from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_von_Fraunhofer

question: Robert Bunsen wanted a laboratory flame he could control exactly. About 1854, with the Heidelberg instrument-maker Peter Desaga, he built the burner that still carries his name: a metal tube with sliding collars near the base that let air mix into the gas before it burns. Slide those collars open and the flame changes. How?
answer: It turns hotter and almost invisible
choices: It turns hotter and almost invisible
It turns cooler and bright yellow
It turns hotter and bright orange
It turns cooler and thick with soot
context: Open collars give a sootless, non-luminous flame reaching about 1,500 °C. That mattered enormously. An ordinary gas or oil flame glows yellow with light of its own and drowns out whatever you drop into it; a flame with almost no light of its own finally let a chemist see the sample's colours instead of the fire's. You can watch the same change on a gas hob at home — the lazy yellow flame that sooties a pan versus the near-invisible roaring blue one. Source: Grokipedia, 'Robert Bunsen' (Laboratory Inventions) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Bunsen

question: Joseph Fraunhofer lettered the strongest dark gaps in the Sun's spectrum A through K and measured each one's position more finely than anyone before him. The pair he called D sat in the yellow — at exactly the colour that one element blazes, hard and unmistakable, when a chemist drops a pinch of it into a flame. Which element?
answer: Sodium
choices: Sodium
Potassium
Lithium
Calcium
context: The D pair sits at 589.0 nanometres (D2) and 589.6 nanometres (D1) — precisely where neutral sodium in a laboratory flame emits its bright yellow doublet. Nobody could shake the coincidence, and for decades nobody could explain it. Test it yourself: table salt is sodium chloride, and a few grains dropped into a gas flame will pull that same hard yellow out of it. Source: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' (Prominent Lines and Associations) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Fraunhofer_lines

question: At Heidelberg in 1859 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen burned one substance after another in a colourless flame and looked at each through a prism. Every element threw up its own set of bright lines. Then they pushed on it, changing everything about the fire and the sample they could think to change. What did that do to an element's lines?
answer: They stayed in exactly the same places every time
choices: They stayed in exactly the same places every time
They stayed put, but each compound added new lines
They stayed put until a hotter flame nudged them
They slid toward the blue as the flame grew hotter
context: Fixed and unforgeable — a barcode per element, the same lines whatever the flame or the temperature. Their spectroscope was a darkened box with adjustable slits, a hollow prism filled with carbon disulfide and viewing telescopes, and the published sensitivity was brutal: they could detect sodium below one three-millionth of a milligram and lithium below nine millionths of a milligram. Source: Grokipedia, 'Robert Bunsen' (Spectroscopic Discoveries) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Robert_Bunsen

question: Joseph Fraunhofer could not say whether his dark lines were made inside the Sun or in Earth's air on the way down, and he admitted it. Both happen. The two broad bands he lettered A and B, far out at the red end, are not solar at all: they are cut into the sunlight in its last few seconds of travel, by one gas in the air above your head. Which gas?
answer: Oxygen
choices: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Water vapour
context: The A band at 759.4 nm and the B band at 686.7 nm are telluric — 'of the Earth' — produced by molecular oxygen in our own atmosphere, and they are broad molecular bands rather than the sharp atomic lines the Sun contributes. Nitrogen dominates the air by volume but stays almost silent in the visible spectrum. Water vapour leaves telluric bands of its own elsewhere, which is part of why astronomers put telescopes on dry mountaintops and in orbit. Source: Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' (Naming Conventions; Prominent Lines and Associations table) — https://grokipedia.com/page/Fraunhofer_lines

question: Gustav Kirchhoff heated a platinum wire white-hot in a flame until it glowed with a perfectly smooth band of colour, no lines in it anywhere. Then he put a cool, thin gas between that wire and his prism — a gas whose own bright lines, when it was made to glow, he already knew by heart. What did the gas do to the smooth band?
answer: Cut dark lines exactly where its bright ones fall
choices: Cut dark lines exactly where its bright ones fall
Added its bright lines on top of the smooth band
Dimmed the band evenly, from the red to the violet
Left the band smooth but pushed it toward the red
context: The same element that had thrown bright lines in a flame now cut dark ones in the identical places: a gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it emits. Kirchhoff set that out as three laws of spectroscopy — a hot solid, liquid or dense gas radiates at all wavelengths and gives a continuous spectrum; a thin gas excited to glow emits at specific wavelengths only, giving bright lines; and continuous light passed through a cooler thin gas comes out with dark lines cut in exactly those places. Apply it to the Sun — a blazing dense body shining up through the thinner, cooler gas above it — and Fraunhofer's hundreds of dark lines become a roll-call of the elements in the Sun's outer layers, readable from a bench in Germany. Kirchhoff presented the underlying thermodynamic principle, that a body absorbs at each wavelength as well as it emits, to the Berlin Academy on 15 December 1859, and showed the same year that the Sun contains sodium — the answer to a coincidence chemists had puzzled over for decades. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Kirchhoff (three laws); Grokipedia, 'Gustav Kirchhoff' (Laws of Spectroscopy; Law of Thermal Radiation)

question: A story told of Gustav Kirchhoff, and well attested: his banker was unimpressed to hear that Kirchhoff could now read which metals lie in the Sun. What earthly use, he asked, is a metal nobody can ever fetch down? In 1862 the Royal Society awarded Kirchhoff its Rumford Medal, and the prize money reached him from London. He carried the coins to the bank. What did he say as he handed them over?
answer: That here, at last, was gold from the Sun
choices: That here, at last, was gold from the Sun
That the Sun had made him a rich man
That London had fetched it down for him
That he would spend it all on new prisms
context: The Rumford Medal money arrived from London as gold sovereigns. The telling on record has the banker ask 'of what use is gold in the Sun if it cannot be brought to Earth?' and Kirchhoff deposit the sovereigns with the words 'here is gold from the Sun.' This is a well-attested anecdote rather than a minuted fact — the usual account names neither the banker nor the original recorder. There was a cost on the other side of that work: Kirchhoff's eyes were damaged by years of staring into bright spectra, and a fall left him on crutches or in a wheelchair for much of his life. He lectured until he retired in 1886 and died on 17 October 1887. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Kirchhoff ; Grokipedia, 'Gustav Kirchhoff' (Later Appointments and Retirement)  (Legend.)

question: Auguste Comte, the French philosopher whose Cours de philosophie positive set out to map where human knowledge must stop, picked out one question about the stars and wrote that we could never learn its answer by any means whatever. He died in 1857 sure of it. The answer came two years later. Which question had he closed forever?
answer: What the stars are made of
choices: What the stars are made of
How far away the stars lie
How the stars first formed
Whether stars have planets
context: Comte died on 5 September 1857. Kirchhoff showed that the Sun contains sodium in 1859 — the man who called the question permanently unanswerable missed the answer by two years. His claim is usually reported as allowing that we may determine the stars' forms, distances, sizes and motions while holding their chemical composition beyond reach, though the exact wording varies between translations; a widely circulated English rendering runs 'We shall never be able by any means to study their chemical composition.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Comte ('Other views'); English rendering via https://libquotes.com/auguste-comte ; death date from Grokipedia, 'Auguste Comte' (Later Years and Death); sodium in the Sun 1859 from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Kirchhoff

question: By the 1860s the spectroscope had become astronomy's sharpest tool. William Huggins wanted still more from it. In 1868 he lined up Sirius's dark lines against the lines of the same elements burning in his own laboratory, and found the star's lines sitting slightly off - displaced a little toward the red. From that small displacement Huggins pulled out a number nobody had ever measured for a star. What had he measured?
answer: Its speed toward or away from Earth
choices: Its speed toward or away from Earth
Its distance from Earth in light-years
The temperature of its glowing surface
The age of the star since it first lit
context: This was the first radial-velocity measurement from a stellar spectrum. Sources disagree sharply on the figure Huggins reported — Grokipedia gives about 9 km/s, Wikipedia's Huggins article records only a redshift in 1868 with no number, other historical accounts differ, and Huggins revised his own value later — so the method and the date are the solid facts, not the speed. The same trick later handed Edwin Hubble an expanding universe, and today it finds planets by the tiny wobble they impose on their star. Be honest about the limits: a spectrum still cannot give you a star's distance or its age, and a single line is read three ways at once — Doppler broadening from heat and turbulence, Stark broadening from charged particles' electric fields, Zeeman splitting in a magnetic field. Reading a spectrum is a chain of inference, not a photograph. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of spectroscopy' (1860s–1890s); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Huggins ; Grokipedia, 'Fraunhofer lines' (Spectral Properties; Solar and Stellar Analysis)

question: Albert Einstein never accepted one quantum prediction: two particles made together stay linked, so measuring one tells you at once what the other will say, however far apart they have been carried. Writing to his friend Max Born in March 1947, Einstein gave the idea a name that physicists have used ever since. What did he call it?
answer: Spooky action at a distance
choices: Spooky action at a distance
Ghostly signals across the void
Telepathy between distant twins
Instant conspiracy of the pair
context: Einstein wrote it in German: 'spukhafte Fernwirkung', from 'Spuk', a haunting. 'Spukhaft' means ghostly or eerie rather than spooky in the cartoon sense, so the famous English phrase is a little softer than what he actually said. His sentence to Born was that he could not seriously believe in quantum mechanics, because the theory could not be reconciled with the idea that physics should represent a reality in space and time, free from spooky action at a distance. Sources: Born-Einstein Letters, 3 March 1947, quoted at en.wiktionary.org, 'spooky action at a distance'; Sabine Hossenfelder, backreaction.blogspot.com, 'What did Einstein mean by spooky action at a distance?'

question: On 4 May 1935 the New York Times ran the headline 'EINSTEIN ATTACKS QUANTUM THEORY.' The paper behind it, by Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, would not reach Physical Review for another eleven days. How had the newspaper got the story?
answer: Podolsky had given the contents to a reporter
choices: Podolsky had given the contents to a reporter
Rosen had described the work in a public lecture
Bohr had mentioned the argument in Copenhagen
The journal's own office had tipped off a reporter
context: Boris Podolsky also drafted the published English text, and Albert Einstein never saw it before it was submitted. On 19 June 1935 Einstein complained to Erwin Schrodinger that the essential thing had been, so to speak, smothered by formalism. The most famous paper with Einstein's name on it is therefore one he neither wrote nor approved, and he was annoyed at Podolsky for handing the contents to the press. Sources: plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-epr/ (authorship and the 19 June 1935 letter); 'The Advent and Fallout of EPR', ias.edu/ideas/2013/epr-fallout; New York Times, 4 May 1935.

question: Physical Review, 15 May 1935. Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen described two particles prepared together and then carried far apart. Measure the first, they argued, and you can predict what the second will give with certainty, without ever touching it. From that, what did the three of them conclude about quantum mechanics?
answer: It was incomplete, with something missing from it
choices: It was incomplete, with something missing from it
It was inconsistent with its own mathematics
It described crowds of particles, never single ones
It was correct but could never be tested at all
context: Their criterion of reality, verbatim: 'If, without in any way disturbing a system, we can predict with certainty (i.e., with probability equal to unity) the value of a physical quantity, then there exists an element of reality corresponding to that quantity.' The paper's title asks the question outright: 'Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?' Their answer was no. The picture they preferred was of particles leaving the source already carrying their answers, like twins setting out from home with sealed envelopes. Sources: Physical Review 47, issue 10, 777-780, 15 May 1935; plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-epr/.

question: For twenty-nine years after Einstein's 1935 challenge, nobody could see how to settle the quarrel over entangled particles by measurement; it looked like a matter of taste. Then in 1964 John Stewart Bell published 'On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen Paradox,' written on a year's leave from work that had nothing to do with quantum foundations.
