What was Bell's actual profession?
answer: Accelerator theory at CERN in Geneva
choices: Accelerator theory at CERN in Geneva
Radio astronomy at Jodrell Bank
Low-temperature physics at Leiden
Reactor engineering at Chalk River
context: Bell submitted the paper in November 1964, during a year's leave spent at Stanford, the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Brandeis. His paid work was accelerator and particle theory, first at Harwell on machines like the synchro-cyclotron and then at CERN from 1960; quantum foundations was the hobby he kept up on the side for years. The paper appeared in Physics Physique Fizika, volume 1, issue 3, pages 195-200. Sources: Grokipedia 'John Stewart Bell' and 'Bell's theorem'; physicsworld.com, 'John Bell and the most obscure journal in physics'.

question: John Clauser spent years at Berkeley building the first machine that could actually decide between Einstein's picture of entangled particles and quantum mechanics, and he has said plainly which result he was hoping for when he switched it on. What was Clauser rooting for?
answer: Einstein's side of the argument to come out right
choices: Einstein's side of the argument to come out right
Niels Bohr's side of the argument to come out right
A third answer neither side had thought to predict
A violation stronger than quantum mechanics allows
context: Clauser, verbatim: 'Before Stu Freedman and I did the first experiment, I also personally thought that Einstein's hidden-variable physics might actually be right, and if it is, then I wanted to discover it.' His own data refuted his own hope, and he reported it anyway - which is what the method asks of you. He later titled his Nobel lecture, delivered on 8 December 2022 at Stockholm University, 'Experimental Proof That Nonlocal Quantum Entanglement is Real'. Sources: caltech.edu/about/news/proving-that-quantum-entanglement-is-real (Caltech Q&A with Clauser); Grokipedia 'John Clauser'.

question: John Stewart Bell's 1964 move was to turn a matter of taste into arithmetic. Any theory in which each particle leaves the source already carrying its own answers, he showed, must obey a strict limit on how strongly the two detectors' results can match, and quantum mechanics predicts breaking that limit. The two pictures do not disagree everywhere, though. When does the gap between them open?
answer: When the two detectors are turned to different angles
choices: When the two detectors are turned to different angles
When the two particles are more than a metre apart
When the same pair is measured over and over again
When both detectors are read at the very same instant
context: Bell's 1964 inequality reads |P(a,b) - P(a,c)| <= 1 + P(b,c), where P is the correlation between two detector settings. Quantum mechanics predicts the singlet correlation E(a,b) = -cos(theta) between the angles, and that curve breaks the bound for some angle choices. Set both detectors to the SAME angle and both pictures predict perfect matching, which is precisely why the argument had gone nowhere for twenty-nine years. The version experimenters actually use is the CHSH inequality of 1969, |E(a,b) + E(a,b') + E(a',b) - E(a',b')| <= 2, written by John Clauser, Michael Horne, Abner Shimony and Richard Holt. Quantum mechanics tops out at 2 times the square root of 2, about 2.828 - a ceiling proved by Boris Tsirelson in 1980, and nobody yet knows why nature stops at that particular number. Sources: Bell, Physics Physique Fizika 1, 195-200 (1964); Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt, Physical Review Letters 23, 880 (1969); Cirel'son, Letters in Mathematical Physics 4, 93-100 (1980); Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem'.

question: John Stewart Bell's 1964 paper is now treated as the most important ever written on the foundations of quantum mechanics. It landed in Physics Physique Fizika, a magazine run out of Bell Labs by Philip Anderson and Bernd Matthias, who read every submission themselves and shut the whole thing down after four years. What did that magazine hand its authors that no physics journal hands them now?
answer: Ten cents for every word they got in print
choices: Ten cents for every word they got in print
A share of what the issue earned in sales
A decision on the paper within one week
The right to print the work elsewhere too
context: Physics Physique Fizika ran three volumes and folded in 1968. Anderson recalled that Bell's paper simply 'came in', unsolicited. Almost nobody thought the subject was worth working on: Abner Shimony's first reaction to Bell's paper, in his own words, was 'I thought, "Here's another kooky paper that's come out of the blue"', and when he and Michael Horne missed a conference abstract deadline Shimony told him, 'It doesn't matter. Nobody is working on this sort of thing. This is so far out.' Sources: physicsworld.com, 'John Bell and the most obscure journal in physics'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics,_Physique,_Fizika; American Institute of Physics oral history, 'Entanglement and experiment, part 2'.

question: John Clauser's senior faculty at Columbia had warned him that testing quantum physics would destroy his career, and Richard Feynman told him the effort was tantamount to professing a disbelief in quantum physics. Clauser built the machine anyway, and in 1972 the Berkeley result came in on the side of quantum mechanics. By Clauser's own account, what did the Columbia faculty say then?
answer: That he had wasted money and should do real physics
choices: That he had wasted money and should do real physics
That the answer was known and he had proved nothing
That he should now chase the loopholes still open
That the gamble had paid off and he should press on
context: Clauser's verbatim account: 'My faculty at Columbia told me that testing quantum physics was going to destroy my career'; 'Caltech's Richard Feynman was highly offended by my impertinent effort and told me that it was tantamount to professing a disbelief in quantum physics'; and afterwards, 'When I reconnected with my Columbia faculty, they all said, "We told you so! Now stop wasting money and go do some real physics."' Not everyone discouraged him: Charles Townes, the maser and laser laureate, backed the Berkeley project, and Eugene Commins freed up his graduate student Stuart Freedman to build it. On 4 October 2022 the Royal Swedish Academy awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics to John Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger 'for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science'. Sources: caltech.edu/about/news/proving-that-quantum-entanglement-is-real; AIP oral history, 'Entanglement and experiment, part 2'; Grokipedia 'John Clauser'.

question: Testing Bell's inequality needs pairs of photons that are genuinely entangled, and in 1972 no such source could be bought. At Berkeley, Stuart Freedman and John Clauser built one: it threw off two photons at a time, one green at 551.3 nanometres and one violet at 422.7, flying back to back with their polarizations, the tilt of their light waves, locked together. What was doing the throwing?
answer: Calcium atoms falling down a two-step cascade
choices: Calcium atoms falling down a two-step cascade
A crystal splitting single photons into pairs
Sodium vapour excited by a pulsed flashlamp
Mercury atoms struck by a beam of electrons
context: Stuart J. Freedman and John F. Clauser, 'Experimental Test of Local Hidden-Variable Theories', Physical Review Letters 28, 938-941, published 3 April 1972. The calcium atoms ran a J=0 to J=1 to J=0 radiative cascade; polarizers were set at angles including 22.5 and 67.5 degrees, and the two ends stood a few metres apart in one room (Clauser has described them as about ten feet apart, and published figures for the separation disagree, so 'a few metres' is the safe statement). The measured violation was delta = 0.050 plus or minus 0.008 against a local-hidden-variable limit of delta <= 0, about six standard deviations. Honest caveat: the photomultipliers caught well under one pair in a hundred, so the conclusion still leaned on the assumption that the pairs they caught were representative of the ones they missed. Sources: link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.28.938; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem' and 'John Clauser'; caltech.edu Q&A with Clauser.

question: In 1982 at Orsay, Alain Aspect's team had to change each analyzer's setting while the photons were still in flight: a flip every ten nanoseconds, a hundred million times a second, across a twelve-metre baseline. The switch they built had no moving parts at all. What did the deflecting?
answer: An ultrasonic standing wave inside water
choices: An ultrasonic standing wave inside water
A high voltage applied across a crystal
A magnetic field wrapped round a glass rod
A second laser crossing the photon's path
context: Alain Aspect, Jean Dalibard and Gerard Roger, Physical Review Letters 49, 1804 (December 1982), Institut d'Optique at Orsay. The acousto-optic switches - ultrasonic standing waves in water - redirected each beam roughly every 10 nanoseconds, while a photon needed about 40 nanoseconds to fly the 12-metre separation, so each setting was fixed after the photons had already left the source. The two switches were run at deliberately mismatched frequencies, near 40 and 48 MHz, so the two ends could never fall into step. The run gave a 5-sigma violation. Aspect's earlier 1982 result with fixed two-channel polarizers (Aspect, Philippe Grangier and Gerard Roger, PRL 49, 91) had already measured S = 2.697 plus or minus 0.015 against the local-realist ceiling of 2, a violation of more than 40 standard deviations. Source: Grokipedia 'Aspect's experiment'.

question: By 2015 the escapes left in Bell tests were nearly all shut, but one stubborn worry remained: whatever picks the detector settings might itself be correlated somehow with the particles about to be measured. In 2018 a Vienna-led team on La Palma handed that job to two telescopes aimed at quasars on opposite sides of the sky, whose light had been travelling for 7.8 and 12.2 billion years. What property of that ancient light chose the settings?
answer: The colour of each photon
choices: The colour of each photon
The brightness of each photon
The polarization of each photon
The arrival time of each photon
context: Rauch and colleagues, 'Cosmic Bell Test Using Random Measurement Settings from High-Redshift Quasars', Physical Review Letters 121, 080403 (August 2018). The William Herschel Telescope and the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo read each arriving photon's wavelength, red or blue of a dividing line, and used that to set the detector. Any local-realist conspiracy would have had to be arranged at least 7.8 billion years before the Earth existed. A 2017 forerunner (Handsteiner and colleagues, PRL 118, 060401) used light from Milky Way stars about 600 light-years away, and on 30 November 2016 the BIG Bell Test let more than 100,000 volunteers worldwide tap over 90 million unpredictable bits into phones and computers to set entangled atoms, photons and superconducting devices in 12 laboratories on five continents; every platform showed a violation. The 2015 loophole-free runs came first: Ronald Hanson's Delft group entangled electron spins in diamond 1.3 kilometres apart, Krister Shalm's NIST team ran detectors 184 metres apart with roughly 90 per cent efficient superconducting nanowires, and Marissa Giustina and Anton Zeilinger's Vienna team reached a local-realism probability of 3.74 x 10^-31. NIST even reran its test with setting-bits drawn from popular movies, television shows and the digits of pi, so nobody could claim its random-number generator was in on the conspiracy. Sources: iqoqi-vienna.at, Cosmic Bell Experiments; nature.com/articles/s41586-018-0085-3; nist.gov news release, November 2015; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem'.

question: Bell violations are real: two distant results match more often than any theory in which each particle left the source carrying its own answers can allow. That has tempted people to sketch a telephone from it - hand one crew the partner particles, fly them to Mars, and signal home the instant you measure. Whether the scheme works turns on one question. What does a single crew's own column of results look like, whatever the far crew does to theirs?
answer: Pure coin flips, with no pattern in them at all
choices: Pure coin flips, with no pattern in them at all
Pure coin flips until the far crew starts measuring
A bias that tracks the angle of the far crew's dial
A faint bias, identical in every run ever done
context: This is the hard limit, and nothing in any Bell experiment sends anything faster than light. Each side's own statistics are completely unchanged by what the distant experimenter chooses to measure - formally, they are the partial trace over the other subsystem - so no message can ride the entanglement. The correlation becomes visible only when the two lists of outcomes are brought together and compared, and that comparison has to travel over an ordinary channel at light speed or slower. The first rigorous proof is Philippe Eberhard's 1978 paper 'Bell's Theorem and the Different Concepts of Locality'; Eberhard and Ronald Ross extended it to quantum field theory in 1989. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-communication_theorem; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem', no-signaling assumption.

question: A common one-line summary of John Stewart Bell's theorem is that particles cannot be carrying hidden instructions after all. That is too strong, and Bell knew it: one hidden-variable theory reproduces every quantum prediction, Bell violations included, and it was published twelve years before his paper. David Bohm's 1952 pilot-wave theory gives every particle a definite position at every moment. What lets it slip past the theorem?
answer: Its guiding wave answers to the whole arrangement at once
choices: Its guiding wave answers to the whole arrangement at once
Its guiding wave can run backwards in time to the source
Its particles learn the detector settings in advance
Its particles each carry a copy of the wave with them
context: Stated precisely: Bell's theorem rules out LOCAL hidden variables, not all hidden variables. Bohm's guiding wave depends instantaneously on the whole configuration, so the theory is openly nonlocal, reproduces every quantum prediction including the Bell violations, and the theorem leaves it standing. Bohm's 1952 spin reformulation of the EPR setup is also the version Bell actually analysed. The field had earlier lost about two decades to a wrong proof: John von Neumann published a theorem in 1932 claiming that no hidden-variable theory could reproduce quantum statistics, and it discouraged the whole line of inquiry until it was shown to rest on a false assumption about how such a model must handle non-commuting observables. Sources: Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem', Impact on Local Hidden Variable Theories and Nonlocality sections; plato.stanford.edu/entries/qm-bohm/; Bub, 'What is wrong with von Neumann's theorem on no hidden variables'.

question: John Stewart Bell's theorem has one escape left that no experiment can ever close: a local theory can still match quantum mechanics exactly if you give up a single assumption Bell had taken for granted. Asked about that escape by Paul Davies on BBC radio in 1985, Bell named the price it demands and said he would not pay it. What did Bell say the escape costs?
answer: The complete absence of free will
choices: The complete absence of free will
A separate physics for living matter
A world that splits at each measurement
An influence running backwards in time
context: Physicists call this escape superdeterminism. Bell, in the 1985 BBC Radio 3 interview with Paul Davies, said it 'involves absolute determinism in the universe, the complete absence of free will', describing a world in which 'our behavior, including our belief that we are free to choose to do one experiment rather than another' is 'absolutely predetermined, including the "decision" by the experimenter to carry out one set of measurements rather than another'. Gerard 't Hooft's cellular-automaton interpretation is its main modern defence, so the position still has serious holders. Meanwhile the violation has become a working tool rather than a curiosity: because a violation certifies that two boxes are not running on pre-set instructions, it underpins device-independent quantum key distribution - Dominic Mayers and Andrew Yao proposed self-testing apparatus in 1998, and Umesh Vazirani and Thomas Vidick published the first unconditional security proof in Physical Review Letters in 2014 - along with certified randomness generation. Sources: Davies and Brown, 'The Ghost in the Atom' (1986), edited transcript of the 1985 BBC Radio 3 interview with Bell; Grokipedia 'Bell's theorem'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Device-independent_quantum_cryptography.

question: In 1763 an English country clergyman, the Reverend Edward Stone of Chipping Norton, wrote to the Royal Society about a simple bitter remedy for fever he had tested on around fifty of his parishioners. Where did he say he had got the remedy?
answer: From the bark of a willow tree
choices: From the bark of a willow tree
From dried mint leaves and honey
From the roots of a common nettle
From boiled rowan berries
context: Stone's letter, dated 25 April 1763 and printed in Philosophical Transactions, described drying the bark, powdering it, and dosing it every four hours until the fever broke. Source: Royal Society, 'From plant extract to molecular panacea: a commentary on Stone 1763'.

question: Nineteenth-century chemists broke willow bark down and pulled out its active ingredient. In 1826 the French pharmacist Henri Leroux isolated it in pure form; two years later the German Johann Buchner independently did the same thing. What did they call the compound?
answer: Salicin
choices: Salicin
Digitalin
Atropine
Morphine
context: The Italian chemist Raffaele Piria then made salicylic acid from salicin in 1838. By the 1870s salicylic acid was a real fever and rheumatism drug - and a real stomach-burner. Source: Pharmaceutical Journal, 'A History of Aspirin'.

question: Salicylic acid, the drug pulled out of willow bark, actually WORKED on fever and rheumatism in the 1870s. There was just one problem so bad that patients kept quitting the drug rather than keep taking it. What was the problem?
answer: It burned the stomach lining
choices: It burned the stomach lining
It turned the skin bright yellow
It tasted so sweet it caused vomiting
It stopped working after a single dose
context: The bare acid was harsh going down and harsh coming back up. Improving that side effect, not inventing the painkiller, is what Bayer's chemists set out to do in the 1890s. Source: McGill OSS, 'Forget the Willow Bark Extract - Go For Aspirin'.

question: On 10 August 1897 at Bayer's laboratory in Elberfeld, a young chemist named Felix Hoffmann tacked a small chemical group onto salicylic acid to muzzle the harsh acid until the body released it inside. What did Hoffmann add?
answer: An acetyl group
choices: An acetyl group
A hydroxyl group
A chloride ion
A sulphate group
context: The result was acetylsalicylic acid, sold from 1899 as Aspirin. The 'a' in Aspirin marks the added group, 'spir' comes from the meadowsweet Spiraea ulmaria (also a source of salicin), and '-in' was a standard drug suffix. Bayer registered the trademark on 6 March 1899. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Aspirin'.

question: The story of who really invented aspirin at Bayer is contested. The head of the pharmaceutical laboratory said afterwards that he had directed Hoffmann's bench work, but his name was written out of Bayer's official history around 1934 under the Nazi regime, and he only published his own account in 1949 after surviving Theresienstadt. Who was he?
answer: Arthur Eichengrun
choices: Arthur Eichengrun
Fritz Haber
Paul Ehrlich
Emil Fischer
context: Eichengrun was a Jewish chemist; a 1999 re-examination by the historian Walter Sneader argued he was the true director of the aspirin project. Bayer's official history still names Hoffmann. Source: Wikipedia, 'Arthur Eichengrun'.

question: Aspirin was on shelves everywhere by 1900, but nobody actually understood WHY it stopped pain, fevers and swelling. That answer did not arrive for another seventy-four years. In 1971 a British pharmacologist worked out over a single weekend what the drug does inside a cell, and it won him the 1982 Nobel Prize. Who was he?
answer: John Vane
choices: John Vane
Alexander Fleming
Frederick Banting
James Black
context: Vane showed aspirin blocks the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX), which manufactures prostaglandins - the local chemical signals of pain, fever and inflammation. He shared the 1982 Nobel with Bergstrom and Samuelsson. Source: Nobel Prize 1982 in Physiology or Medicine.

question: There is one very strange thing about aspirin printed on every heart-attack-prevention label. A tiny 81 mg tablet keeps the blood from clotting for about ten days per dose, while a normal-size headache aspirin wears off in hours. What quirk of the cells aspirin acts on explains this?
answer: Platelets have no nucleus and cannot rebuild the disabled enzyme
choices: Platelets have no nucleus and cannot rebuild the disabled enzyme
Platelets store the drug in granules and leak it out over days
Platelets divide only once every ten days regardless of dose
Platelets absorb aspirin faster than any other cell in the body
context: Aspirin acetylates a serine in cyclooxygenase and shuts it off for good. Most cells simply build fresh enzyme; platelets, having no DNA, cannot. So the antiplatelet effect lasts a platelet's ten-day life, while a headache dose fades as the body clears the drug. Source: Tulane, 'Antiplatelet Drugs'.

question: The commonest tablet in the house carries one warning that specifically singles out children and teenagers with a fever or a viral illness. A rare but very severe reaction of the brain and liver, first described in 1963, is why aspirin is not given to them. What is the reaction called?
answer: Reye's syndrome
choices: Reye's syndrome
Guillain-Barre syndrome
Kawasaki disease
Wilson's disease
context: After the FDA required a warning label in 1986, US cases dropped from hundreds a year to a handful. Adult aspirin is common; children with a fever get paracetamol or ibuprofen instead. Source: American Family Physician, 'Aspirin Use in Children for Fever or Viral Syndromes'.

question: In 2011, two virology labs - Ron Fouchier's at Erasmus Medical Center in Rotterdam and Yoshihiro Kawaoka's at the University of Wisconsin - took H5N1 bird flu (deadly to people but almost never spreading between them) and modified it. They wanted to know what changes would let the virus jump from one mammal to another through the air. Which animal did both teams use as the mammalian test?
answer: Ferrets
choices: Ferrets
Rhesus monkeys
Guinea pigs
Cotton rats
context: Ferrets are the standard model for human influenza: their airways and their sneeze produce a virus-transmission pattern very close to a human's. Both teams passed H5N1 repeatedly through ferrets until it spread cage-to-cage through the air. The exercise deliberately built the thing everyone was afraid of in order to study it. Source: cidrap.umn.edu Fouchier H5N1 study.

question: In late 2011 the manuscripts describing the airborne H5N1 experiments were submitted to Science and Nature. The US federal panel that reviews dual-use life-sciences research took a step almost unheard-of in basic biology: it recommended that the papers be published only with key methodological details REDACTED, so anyone reading them could not rebuild the exact virus. What is that panel called?
answer: NSABB
choices: NSABB
NIAID
FDA
NAS
context: NSABB = National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity. On 30 March 2012 the NSABB reversed its recommendation and the papers were published in full, but the redaction request itself was a milestone. NIAID is Fauci's institute inside NIH; the FDA regulates drugs and devices; the NAS is the National Academy of Sciences, an honorary body. Source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov H5N1 Moratorium Controversy.

question: The bank's answer to that steel-man is that the benefit is speculative but the risk is documented. Laboratory escapes of dangerous pathogens have happened repeatedly. In 1978 smallpox escaped a lab in Birmingham, England and killed a medical photographer named Janet Parker - after the virus had already been driven out of the wild. What technical route did the virus travel to reach her office?
answer: An air duct
choices: An air duct
A shared coffee mug
A contaminated needle
A door handle
context: Janet Parker's darkroom was connected to Henry Bedson's smallpox lab on the floor below by an air duct. The Shooter Inquiry concluded that was the most likely route, though the exact transmission mechanism is still debated. Parker died on 11 September 1978 - the last recorded smallpox death. Bedson took his own life days later. A pathogen only has to get out once, and the people who bear the cost were never asked. Source: en.wikipedia.org 1978 smallpox outbreak.

question: No clock in 1600 could time a falling rock — drop one and it is down before you can say 'now.' Galileo Galilei wanted the law of falling anyway, so he weakened the fall itself, stretching a one-second drop into many. What did he build?
answer: A grooved wooden beam propped up at one end
choices: A grooved wooden beam propped up at one end
A water tank with a wax ball sinking through it
A well shaft with a bell sounding at the bottom
A silk cord with weights knotted along it
context: Galileo gives the recipe in Two New Sciences: a piece of wooden moulding 'about 12 cubits long, half a cubit wide, and three finger-breadths thick' (roughly 5.5 m), with a channel 'a little more than one finger in breadth' cut along its edge, made 'very straight, smooth, and polished' and lined with parchment 'as smooth and polished as possible.' Down it he rolled 'a hard, smooth, and very round bronze ball,' with one end of the beam raised one to two cubits. The ramp changes none of the physics — it only dilutes gravity until a human being can watch it happen. Which means you can run his experiment tonight with a marble, a tilted board and a phone stopwatch. Source: Galileo, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, Third Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dialogues_Concerning_Two_New_Sciences/Third_Day.

question: On 2 August 1971, on the airless Moon and before a live television camera, Apollo 15 commander David Scott said one reason they had got there was 'a gentleman named Galileo, a long time ago.' He held out one object in each hand and let both go at the same instant. What was he holding?
answer: A geology hammer and a falcon feather
choices: A geology hammer and a falcon feather
A wrench and a strip of gold foil
A rock sample and a nylon flag scrap
A drill bit and a paper checklist page
context: The aluminium geology hammer weighed 1.32 kg and the falcon feather 0.03 kg, and Scott released them from about 1.6 m. They hit the dust together. Scott: 'Which proves that Mr. Galileo was correct in his findings.' CapCom Joe Allen, over applause in Houston: 'How about that!' Modern versions are brutally finer: the MICROSCOPE satellite (2016-17) compared two test masses of different composition falling in orbit and found no difference to about one part in 10^15 — a hundred trillion times finer than anything Galileo could see. Sources: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, EVA-3 close-out — apollojournals.org/alsj/a15/a15.clsout3.html; NASA Science, 'The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop'.

question: Vincenzo Viviani, the old Galileo's assistant, tells that at nineteen the boy sat in Pisa Cathedral around 1583 watching a hanging lamp swing, and thought its wide swings and its small ones took the same time. No clock of that day could mark seconds. What does Viviani say he timed the swings against?
answer: His own pulse, felt at the wrist
choices: His own pulse, felt at the wrist
The chant of the priests at the altar
A candle burning down past its marks
A count whispered under his breath
context: Careful: Viviani's Racconto istorico is the ONLY source for this scene, and he wrote it some seventy years after the date he gives — so treat it as his telling, not as Galileo's own record. The idea itself went somewhere real. Galileo built a pulsilogon, a pendulum instrument for measuring a patient's pulse rate, and used pendulums rather than water clocks for short intervals — the boy who timed a lamp by his pulse ended up building a machine to time pulses by a swing. In 1641-42, blind and under house arrest, he dictated the design of a pendulum clock with an escapement, aiming for an error under fifteen seconds a day; his son Vincenzo built a model of it in 1649, after his father's death. You can test the claim yourself with a weight on a string: pull it far, pull it a little, and count. Sources: Museo Galileo, 'Pisa — Following the path of Galileo'; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo_Galilei.  (Legend.)

question: Galileo needed to compare how long each roll down the ramp took, finer than any clock of 1600 could tell. Above the bench he set a large vessel of water with a thin pipe soldered into its bottom, and caught the thin jet in a small glass for exactly the length of each descent. What did he then do with each glassful?
answer: Weighed it on a very accurate balance
choices: Weighed it on a very accurate balance
Poured it into a tube marked in degrees
Counted the drops it had caught
Set it beside the last glass and eyed the level
context: In his own words: 'the water thus collected was weighed, after each descent, on a very accurate balance; the differences and ratios of these weights gave us the differences and ratios of the times.' Notice what he never does — he never measures a second. He measures weights of water, and lets the RATIOS carry the physics. That is the trick worth stealing: when you cannot measure the quantity you want, measure something strictly proportional to it. Source: Galileo, Two New Sciences, Third Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dialogues_Concerning_Two_New_Sciences/Third_Day.

question: Apollo 15's lunar module was named Falcon, and David Scott wanted a real falcon feather to drop beside his hammer. In January 1971 Scott, Jim Irwin and Al Worden went and collected two feathers in person, and carried them to the Moon. Where did the feathers come from?
answer: The mascot falcon of the US Air Force Academy
choices: The mascot falcon of the US Air Force Academy
A peregrine falcon project at Cornell University
A falconry ranch outside Houston, Texas
The raptor collection of the Smithsonian Institution
context: The crew visited the Academy at Colorado Springs; the bird is reported to have been a falcon named Baggin. Two feathers went to the Moon and only one came back into the story — Irwin accidentally stepped on the other, to Scott's annoyance. The feather Scott dropped is still lying on the lunar surface where it fell in 1971, undisturbed, with no air to stir it. Sources: Royal Museums Greenwich, 'The strange things humans have left on the Moon'; Atlas Obscura, 'Object of Intrigue: The Falcon Feather on the Moon'.

question: Galileo Galilei rolled his bronze ball from rest down the parchment-lined groove, measuring each descent against the water caught from his jet clock. Then he cut a single descent into four equal stretches of time and asked how far the ball had travelled during each stretch on its own. The four distances were not equal — they grew as four whole numbers. What were they?
answer: 1, 3, 5, 7 — the odd numbers in order
choices: 1, 3, 5, 7 — the odd numbers in order
1, 2, 3, 4 — the counting numbers in order
1, 2, 4, 8 — the doubling numbers in order
1, 4, 9, 16 — the square numbers in order
context: This is Corollary I of the Third Day. Add those four stretches up and the TOTAL distance runs 1, 4, 9, 16 — the square of the elapsed time. Double the time, quadruple the distance; triple the time, nine times the distance. The speed grows as the plain counting numbers while the distance grows as their squares, and the pattern is the same whatever the ball weighs and whatever the tilt of the beam. Galileo: 'in such experiments, repeated a full hundred times, we always found that the spaces traversed were to each other as the squares of the times, and this was true for all inclinations of the plane.' Source: Two New Sciences, Third Day, Corollary I (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — en.wikisource.org.

question: Tourists in Pisa Cathedral are still shown a hanging lamp and told it is the very one whose swinging the teenage Galileo studied. Antonio Favaro, who edited Galileo's complete works, went to the cathedral records to check the claim. What did he find?
answer: The lamp on show was hung in 1587, after the date claimed
choices: The lamp on show was hung in 1587, after the date claimed
The lamp on show was recast from an older one in 1650
The cathedral hung no lamps at all before the year 1600
The records name a different church across the square
context: The story puts the scene around 1583, so the lamp visitors are shown had not yet been hung. It is the wrong lamp. Museo Galileo notes that a smaller, plainer votive lamp that DID hang in the cathedral in Galileo's day survives, kept now in the Aulla Chapel of the Monumental Cemetery next door. So the famous object is legend even if the observation behind it may still be his — which is exactly the habit worth learning: check the date on the exhibit, not just the label. Sources: Museo Galileo, 'Pisa — Following the path of Galileo'; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo_Galilei.

question: Aristotle's rule about falling bodies was not a vague feeling, and Galileo quotes it exactly in Two New Sciences: let an iron ball of one hundred pounds and a ball of one pound fall together from a height of one hundred cubits, and the heavy one reaches the ground first. On Aristotle's rule, how far had the one-pound ball fallen at the moment the heavy ball landed?
answer: One cubit
choices: One cubit
Ten cubits
Fifty cubits
Ninety cubits
context: A hundredfold weight meant a hundredfold speed, so the small ball has barely started when the big one is finished. Salviati's reply is one flat line: 'I say that they arrive at the same time.' Galileo also doubted the rule had ever been checked: 'I greatly doubt that Aristotle ever tested by experiment whether it be true that two stones, one weighing ten times as much as the other... would so differ in speed.' Aristotle had reached the rule by deduction from his theory of the elements — reasoning downward from a system, rather than dropping anything. Source: Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — galileoandeinstein.phys.virginia.edu/tns_draft/tns_061to108.html.

question: Every school book shows Galileo Galilei dropping two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, yet his own works, letters and manuscripts never mention that tower once. Somebody did drop pairs of objects from it and write the results down, though — fifty years later. Vincenzio Renieri, who took over Galileo's mathematics chair at Pisa, dropped wood against lead from the leaning bell tower in March 1641 and sent his numbers to Galileo, by then blind, who had the letter read aloud to him. What did Renieri report?
answer: The lead beat the wood down by nearly two metres
choices: The lead beat the wood down by nearly two metres
The wood beat the lead down by nearly two metres
The lead beat the wood down by about a hand's breadth
The lead and the wood struck the pavement together
context: About three braccia, in Renieri's own measure — and in the other pair he dropped, a cannonball against a musket bullet, the bigger lead ball beat the smaller by about one palmo, roughly 25 cm. Wood loses badly to lead in air; nothing here looks like the storybook picture of two balls landing as one. And the tower is the famous one: the Leaning Tower IS the bell tower of Pisa's cathedral, one building under two names — so the documented Pisa drop was made from the very tower the legend borrows, fifty years too late and with the wrong answer for the story. The tower legend itself rests on a single source: Vincenzo Viviani, who became Galileo's assistant in 1639, some fifty years after the supposed event, drafted his life of Galileo in 1654, and saw it printed only in 1717 — sixty-three years after he wrote it, seventy-five after Galileo died. Viviani's line: Galileo 'showed this by repeated experiments made from the height of the Leaning Tower of Pisa in the presence of other professors and all the students.' One suggestion is that the story was born in 1641 itself, in a blind old man's reminiscence prompted by Renieri's letter, and Viviani wrote it down thirteen years later. The scholarly fight is live: Alexandre Koyré (Études galiléennes, 1939) called the drop a myth and held that Galileo's real method was mathematics plus inclined planes; Stillman Drake (Galileo at Work, 1978) thought a Pisa demonstration plausible and in character. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment; 'Vincenzio Renieri and the Law of Falling Bodies,' KCKCC e-Journal 7:1 (2013).

question: The drop test that IS documented came before Galileo ever taught at Pisa. In 1586 Simon Stevin and the Delft lawyer Jan Cornets de Groot climbed the Nieuwe Kerk and released two lead balls together, one ten times heavier than the other, from about thirty feet up. Stevin wrote up the result that same year: the light ball did not lag. How did the two men judge that the balls arrived together?
answer: They listened for one impact sound or two
choices: They listened for one impact sound or two
They timed each ball against a swinging pendulum
They counted the beats of their own pulses
They lined the fall up against a nearby window frame
context: Partly by ear, from the sound of the strikes on the boards — a single knock, not two. Stevin's own words in De Beghinselen der Weeghconst (1586): 'Let us take... two lead balls, one ten times heavier than the other, and let them fall together from 30 feet high. That will show that the light ball does not take longer to fall than the heavy one, but they fall together at the same time. This proves that Aristotle was wrong.' His partner was no physicist: Jan Cornets de Groot was a Delft lawyer and burgomaster — and the father of Hugo de Groot (Grotius), who grew up to found modern international law. Stevin called him 'the highly educated and diligent researcher of the mysteries of nature.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_tower_experiment; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment.

question: Giovanni Battista Riccioli, a Jesuit astronomer in Bologna, set out to disprove Galileo's law of fall, and dropped balls from the Torre degli Asinelli — nearly a hundred metres of tower. His timer was a pendulum, but a man watching a falling ball cannot also watch a swinging weight. How did Riccioli get the pendulum's beat to his observers?
answer: A chorus of his fellow Jesuits chanted in time with it
choices: A chorus of his fellow Jesuits chanted in time with it
A brother by the pendulum struck a bell at each swing
A row of novices on the stair passed each count down
A priest at the window tapped a drum at every swing
context: Human beings as a metronome. Francesco Maria Grimaldi and Cassiani stood at the summit and Riccioli on the pavement below, each separately writing on his own sheet the number of pendulum strokes a fall took — a blind-comparison habit worth copying. Riccioli set out to refute Galileo and confirmed him instead, then published the confirmation anyway in the Almagestum Novum (1651): about 15 Roman feet in the first second, 60 in two, 135 in three. He also printed the runs that did NOT flatter the theory. A wooden ball and a lead ball of the same weight (2.5 ounces each) fell together, and when the lead had covered 280 Roman feet the wood had made only 240; two clay balls of the same size, one 10 ounces and one 20, were released together and the lighter was still at least 15 feet up when the heavier struck the pavement. He named air resistance and density as the cause rather than quietly binning the data. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Riccioli; Christopher M. Graney, 'Anatomy of a fall,' Physics Today 65(9), 36 (2012).

question: No clock of 1600 could split a second, but the historian Stillman Drake argued that Galileo had a finer instrument: his own ear. On Drake's reconstruction Galileo tied movable gut frets across the ramp, so the bronze ball gave a small bump as it crossed each one. What was he listening for?
answer: The bumps falling into an even rhythm
choices: The bumps falling into an even rhythm
The bumps crowding closer as the ball ran on
The gaps between the bumps stretching out
The bumps coming in pairs, two close then a gap
context: Once the frets are set right, the marks on the beam ARE the distances at equal times — the ball times itself. Be careful with this one: it is Drake's reconstruction, not a procedure Galileo ever describes. What makes it plausible is the household. Galileo's father, Vincenzo Galilei, was a professional lutenist and music theorist who ran his own experiments on string tension and pitch, and Galileo played the lute well; a trained musician's sense of beat resolves differences far finer than any 1600 clock, which could not split a second at all. And there is hard evidence he really ran the ramps: his surviving motion folios carry raw measured numbers, not just polished prose — 107v on naturally accelerated motion, 114 and 116v on the inclined plane, groove and ball, including a setup on folio 116 where a deflection at the foot of the ramp launched the ball horizontally. Try it: tape pencils across a tilted board and slide them until the clicks come evenly. Sources: Stillman Drake, Galileo at Work (1978); 'Reconstructing Galileo's Inclined Plane Experiments for Teaching Purposes'.  (Legend.)

question: In Two New Sciences Galileo's spokesman Salviati offers to break Aristotle's rule without dropping anything at all. Suppose, he says, a large stone falls with a speed of eight and a small one with a speed of four. Now tie the two stones together and let the pair fall as a single body. What does Salviati say Aristotle's rule is forced to say about the pair?
answer: It must fall slower than eight, yet it outweighs the eight-stone
choices: It must fall slower than eight, yet it outweighs the eight-stone
It must fall faster than eight, yet its parts each fall slower
It must fall at four, yet nothing has been taken from it
It must fall at twelve, yet no stone was seen to fall so fast
context: Verbatim: 'if a large stone moves with a speed of, say, eight while a smaller moves with a speed of four, then when they are united, the system will move with a speed less than eight; but the two stones when tied together make a stone larger than that which before moved with a speed of eight. Hence the heavier body moves with less speed than the lighter.' The slow stone must drag on the fast one, so the pair is slower than eight; but the pair is heavier than either, so on the same rule it must be faster than eight. Aristotle's physics contradicts itself before anyone climbs a tower — cost of apparatus: nothing. Source: Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — galileoandeinstein.phys.virginia.edu/tns_draft/tns_061to108.html.

question: Galileo Galilei never claims two balls land perfectly together in air. In Two New Sciences his spokesman Salviati grants that when a hundred-pound ball and a one-pound ball are dropped together from a great height the heavy one really does win — by about two finger-breadths. It is exactly the admission an Aristotelian would seize on. How does Salviati answer it?
answer: He asks why two fingers should hide Aristotle's ninety-nine cubits
choices: He asks why two fingers should hide Aristotle's ninety-nine cubits
He asks why two fingers should outweigh a rule Aristotle never tested
He asks why two fingers in air should settle what a void would show
He asks why two fingers should be charged to weight and not to the air
context: Verbatim: 'you find, on making the experiment, that the larger outstrips the smaller by two finger-breadths... now you would not hide behind these two fingers the ninety-nine cubits of Aristotle, nor would you mention my small error and at the same time pass over in silence his very large one.' Aristotle's rule had the small ball one cubit down out of a hundred; Galileo's own error is two finger-breadths. Sagredo reports his own trial in the same dialogue: a cannon ball of one or two hundred pounds beat a half-pound musket ball by less than a span over a 200-cubit drop. Naming your own error out loud, in print, and then measuring it honestly against the rival's, is the move the whole book is built on. Source: Two New Sciences, First Day (Crew & de Salvio trans.) — galileoandeinstein.phys.virginia.edu/tns_draft/tns_061to108.html.

question: Galileo Galilei, newly holding the mathematics chair at Pisa around 1590, wrote a treatise he never published, De motu antiquiora. In it he records dropping a wooden block against a lead ball from a height, and then sets out the model that in his view explained what he had recorded — a model it would take him decades to abandon. What did that model say?
answer: That a body sinks through air by its density, as through water
choices: That a body sinks through air by its density, as through water
That each body hurries to the natural place of its element
That a falling body carries a force impressed on it at the start
That the air closing in behind a body keeps driving it down
context: The lead landed first, and the young Galileo believed his eyes: denser bodies, he concluded, genuinely do fall faster through a medium like air. The model is Archimedean — a body sinks through air much as it sinks through water, according to its density in the medium — and it is still half-Aristotelian, because the medium is still doing the deciding. The mature claim, that all bodies fall alike where there is nothing to resist them, does not appear until a letter to Paolo Sarpi in 1604, and the finished law waits until Two New Sciences in 1638, nearly fifty years after the treatise. The man who broke Aristotle's physics started out believing a version of it, and needed decades and a ramp to talk himself out of it. His Pisa post was no prize either: the mathematics chair from December 1589 on a renewable three-year term at 60 scudi a year, among the lowest salaries in the university while medical professors earned more than ten times as much. He was fined for skipping lectures, quarrelled publicly with the Aristotelians, and left in 1592 for Padua at 160 ducats. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment; grokipedia.com/page/Galileo_Galilei.

question: On the night of 7 January 1610 in Padua, Galileo Galilei aimed his homemade tube at Jupiter and noted three faint points strung in a neat line beside it -- ordinary fixed stars, he assumed. Over the next nights they shifted their places, and on 13 January a fourth joined them. What were they?
answer: Four bodies circling Jupiter itself
choices: Four bodies circling Jupiter itself
Four stars that Jupiter was drifting past
Four small planets sharing Jupiter's path
Four comets drawn in toward the planet
context: His own words for the first night: 'three little stars, small but very bright, were near the planet.' On 8 January he wrote, 'I found a very different state of things, for there were three little stars all west of Jupiter' -- and fixed stars do not rearrange themselves overnight. By 15 January he had settled it. The whole discovery took about one week of clear nights, and these were the first moons ever seen circling another world. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; NASA, '415 Years Ago: Astronomer Galileo Discovers Jupiter's Moons')

question: The Milky Way had been a soft smear of light across the night sky for as long as people had looked up, and the old catalogues had no better word for it than milk. In 1609 Galileo Galilei turned his magnifying tube on the band. What did it show the band to be?
answer: A mass of countless separate faint stars
choices: A mass of countless separate faint stars
A vast cloud lit by the stars inside it
A trail of fine vapour high in the air
A gap in the sphere of stars, glowing beyond
context: Galileo's line: 'the Galaxy is nothing else but a mass of innumerable stars planted together in clusters.' The same trick worked on every smudge the old catalogues called a 'nebulous star' -- Praesepe, the Beehive, turned out to be 'not a single star but a mass of more than forty starlets.' And the sky got crowded overnight: the Pleiades, six stars to the naked eye, showed more than forty through the tube, and around Orion's belt and sword he added eighty stars nobody had ever recorded. Point good binoculars at the Pleiades tonight and you can repeat the whole experiment. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; Wikipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius')

question: In January 1610 Galileo Galilei watched four faint points beside Jupiter shuffle from one side of the planet to the other and back, night after night, never straying far from it. Educated Europe had been taught several rules about the heavens, and the astronomers who trusted his report saw at once that this sight had destroyed one of them. Which rule?
answer: That every body in the heavens turns about the Earth
choices: That the heavens never alter from one age to the next
That every body in the heavens turns about the Earth
That every body in the heavens keeps one steady pace
That each planet rides on a crystal sphere of its own
context: Here was a second centre of motion -- four objects visibly going round something that was plainly not the Earth -- and you did not need mathematics to see it, only a tube and a clear night. That is why four faint dots detonated a worldview. (Grokipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius'; Grokipedia, 'Copernican Revolution')

question: On 30 November 1609 Galileo Galilei aimed his tube at the crescent Moon, and he went on drawing it night after night until 18 December, then worked the sketches up into watercolour paintings. Those drawings answered a question the schools had thought closed for centuries. What was the Moon's face actually like?
answer: Rugged and pitted, like the surface of the Earth
choices: Rugged and pitted, like the surface of the Earth
Smooth and polished, like a ball of clear crystal
Flat and still, like a wide sheet of water
Bright and stained, like a disc of beaten silver
context: His own words: the Moon is 'full of inequalities, uneven, full of hollows and protuberances, just like the surface of the Earth itself.' Those watercolours were the first realistic pictures of the Moon ever made -- and made the hard way. His design showed a patch of sky only about fifteen arcminutes across, against the full Moon's thirty, so he could see roughly a quarter of the Moon at a time and had to build the drawings up patch by patch, through a keyhole. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; Linda Hall Library, 'Mapping the Moon: Early Telescopic Observations'; Rice University Galileo Project, 'Making a Galilean Telescope')

question: Galileo Galilei had tutored the young Cosimo II de' Medici in mathematics from 1605 to 1608. When his four new points of light needed a name, Galileo called them the Medicean Stars, after Cosimo's family. On 4 September 1610 the flattery was repaid. What did Cosimo hand him?
answer: A salaried court post in Florence with no teaching at all
choices: A salaried court post in Florence with no teaching at all
A teaching chair at Pisa with a seat in the Medici household
A lifetime pension from Venice with a printing licence attached
A share of every tube sold across the Medici lands
context: Court mathematician and philosopher in Florence, at 1,000 florins a year -- double his Padua salary -- and free of lecturing entirely. The discovery doubled as a job application, and the naming was the covering letter. The bank tells this straight rather than tidying it away: patronage was how science got paid for in 1610. (Grokipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius')

question: Hans Lipperhey, a spectacle-maker in Middelburg, petitioned the Dutch States General on 2 October 1608 for a thirty-year patent on a device he called a kijker -- a looker. Less than a year later, on 25 August 1609, Galileo Galilei was demonstrating a tube of his own to Venetian officials, magnifying eight or nine times; he pushed it to about twenty for the Jupiter nights. How did Galileo come by his instrument?
answer: He heard a description of it and worked out the optics himself
choices: He heard a description of it and worked out the optics himself
He bought one from a Dutch merchant and copied its lens spacing
He was sent a finished kijker by a friend in the Netherlands
He read the patent drawings, which the Dutch had printed in full
context: Galileo did not invent the telescope, and he never claimed to have invented the lens arrangement -- he heard in 1609 that such a thing existed, reasoned out how it had to work, and ground his own lenses. He eventually reached about thirty times. Correcting this one matters: the myth of a lone inventor hides the real skill, which was making a rumour into a working instrument better than anyone else's. (Grokipedia, 'Hans Lipperhey'; Grokipedia, 'Refracting telescope'; Wikipedia, 'Galileo Galilei')

question: Look at a thin crescent Moon on a clear night and you can often see the whole dark disc faintly filled in -- a dim ashen glow where there should be nothing but night. Galileo Galilei set down an explanation for it, and it has held up ever since. What lights the Moon's dark side?
answer: Sunlight bounced off the Earth
choices: Sunlight bounced off the Earth
Sunlight bent around the Moon's edge
A faint glow of the Moon's own
Starlight gathered from the whole sky
context: It is called earthshine, and the consequence is the striking part: the Earth shines in the Moon's sky exactly the way the Moon shines in ours. The Earth is behaving like one more heavenly body, not a different kind of thing altogether. Go out on the next young crescent and check it yourself -- the ashen glow is easy to see with no instrument at all. (Wikipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius'; Kitchin et al., 'On the Earthshine depicted in Galileo's watercolors of the Moon', arXiv:1707.05314)

question: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are printed on every modern chart of Jupiter, and everyone assumes Galileo Galilei chose them. He did not. He called the group the Medicean Stars, and in his own notes the four are only I, II, III and IV, counted outward from the planet. Where did the mythological names come from?
answer: Simon Marius, a rival, prompted by Johannes Kepler
choices: Simon Marius, a rival, prompted by Johannes Kepler
Johannes Kepler alone, in a letter printed at Prague
Cosimo II de' Medici, over Galileo's own objection
The astronomers of Rome, a century after Galileo's death
context: Marius printed the names in Mundus Iovialis in 1614, following Kepler's suggestion. They did not become the standard scientific designations until the middle of the twentieth century -- more than three hundred years later. Until then, working astronomers wrote Jupiter I, II, III and IV, exactly as Galileo had. (Grokipedia, 'Galilean moons'; Grokipedia, 'Simon Marius')

question: In July 1610 Galileo Galilei saw Saturn flanked by two small companions, and rather than publish before he was sure he sent the claim to Johannes Kepler on 30 July as a scrambled anagram: smaismrmilmepoetaleumibunenugttauiras. Unscrambled it read 'I have observed the highest planet to be triple-bodied.' Kepler would not wait for the key and tried to unscramble it himself. What did Kepler conclude Galileo had found?
answer: Two moons circling the planet Mars
choices: Two moons circling the planet Mars
Two moons circling the planet Venus
A fifth moon circling the planet Jupiter
A pair of stars circling each other
context: Kepler's misreading was 'Salve umbistineum geminatum Martia proles' -- hail, twin offspring of Mars. Mars does have two small moons, though nobody would actually see them for another two and a half centuries. Saturn beat Galileo in the end: in December 1612 the two companions were simply gone, and he wrote, 'Has Saturn devoured his own sons?' (The rings had turned edge-on; Earth crossed the ring plane on 17 February 1613.) He sketched Saturn again in 1616 and never solved it. Christiaan Huygens did, in 1655, with a telescope he ground himself. (Springer, 'The scientific significance of planetary ring systems'; Mental Floss, 'How A Misinterpreted Anagram Predicted The Moons of Mars'; The Oikofuge, 'Galileo, Disappearing Rings, And The Seasons Of Saturn')

question: Along the creeping line of lunar sunrise, Galileo Galilei saw bright specks kindle in the darkness -- points already lit while all the ground around them was still in night. He worked out that they were mountain peaks catching the Sun early. Then he did something nobody had ever done to another world: he put a number on their height, more than four Italian miles, when no mountain on Earth, he wrote, reaches even one. What did he measure to get that number?
answer: The distance from a lit peak to the shadow line
choices: The distance from a lit peak to the shadow line
The time from a peak's first light to full sunrise
The width of the notch a peak cut in the Moon's rim
The brightness of a peak against the dark around it
context: His own words: 'more than 4 Italian miles; but in the Earth there are no mountains which reach to the perpendicular height even of one mile.' Geometry, performed on a world he could never visit, from a shadow. Modern measurement says he was close to right. You can start the same investigation tonight: any decent binoculars show the ragged sunrise line and the specks kindling ahead of it, and the Moon looks best not when it is full but when that line is crossing the middle of the disc. (Wikisource, 'The Sidereal Messenger of Galileo Galilei'; Wikipedia, 'Sidereus Nuncius')

question: Dark blotches crossed the face of the Sun and came back on a schedule, which was awkward for a Sun that everyone agreed was perfect and unchanging. The Jesuit Christoph Scheiner, writing under the pen name 'Apelles hiding behind the painting', argued they were swarms of tiny planets passing in front of the Sun, leaving the Sun itself spotless. Galileo Galilei answered that they were marks on the Sun's own surface, and pointed to one thing the blotches did that settled it. What did they do?
answer: They squashed into thin slivers near the Sun's edge
choices: They squashed into thin slivers near the Sun's edge
They came back darker after each trip across the face
They always crossed along one single straight path
They kept exactly the same spacing from one another
context: That squashing is called foreshortening, and it is the giveaway: a mark painted on a turning sphere gets compressed as it swings toward the edge, while a body floating in front of the Sun would keep its shape all the way across. Galileo published the argument as Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari in Rome in 1613. So the last perfect thing in the sky both turns and blemishes. WARNING: never point a telescope, binoculars or your own eyes at the Sun -- solar observation is done by projecting the image onto paper. (Wikipedia, 'Letters on Sunspots'; Linda Hall Library, 'Optics: Telescopes and Technological Change')

question: A captain far out at sea could work out how far north he was, but nothing aboard told him how far east or west he had sailed -- a gap that had been drowning ships for a century. Philip III of Spain offered 6,000 ducats and a lifetime pension to whoever closed it. From 1615 Galileo Galilei pressed Jupiter's moons on the Spanish court: they slide into the planet's shadow on a schedule predictable years ahead, the outermost coming round in about sixteen and a half days. Around 1616 he even built the celatone, a helmet with a telescope mounted on it for holding Jupiter steady on a heaving deck. What were a navigator at sea and an astronomer back home meant to compare?
answer: The local clock times at which each of them saw the eclipse begin
choices: The local clock times at which each of them saw the eclipse begin
The lengths of time for which each of them saw the eclipse last
The heights above the horizon at which each of them saw Jupiter
The background stars against which each of them saw Jupiter sit
context: Two people anywhere on Earth can watch the same eclipse of the same moon at the very same instant; compare the local time each of them reads off, and the difference gives the difference in longitude. The moons are a clock hung in the sky where everybody can see it. Spain said no, and kept saying no through resubmissions in 1620, 1629 and 1631. In 1636 -- old, going blind and under house arrest after his trial -- Galileo petitioned the Dutch States General instead. Their committee reached the same verdict as Spain's but sent him a gold chain anyway, and the Inquisition forbade him to accept it. (Grokipedia, 'Celatone'; Grokipedia, 'History of longitude'; Grokipedia, 'Longitude rewards')

question: In January 1610 Galileo Galilei pointed a homemade 20-power telescope at Jupiter for the first time. Night after night he watched something no one before him had recorded, and he wrote it up in a 24-page pamphlet, Sidereus Nuncius, that sold out across Europe. What was he watching?
answer: Four small points of light that shifted position
choices: Rings of ice and rock encircling the planet
A great red spot as wide as three Earths
Four small points of light that shifted position
A trail of comets sweeping past the planet
context: Galileo first observed Jupiter on 7 January 1610 and saw three points; a fourth appeared soon after. He watched them almost nightly through March 1610. Sidereus Nuncius (March 1610) announced Jupiter's four largest moons -- now called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. He named them the 'Medicean stars' to court Medici patronage. Source: https://www.loc.gov/collections/finding-our-place-in-the-cosmos-with-carl-sagan/articles-and-essays/modeling-the-cosmos/galileo-and-the-telescope/

question: Between September 1610 and February 1611, Galileo made a second telescopic observation that was more damaging to Ptolemy's Earth-centred system than the moons of Jupiter had been. Which planet did he watch cycle from thin crescent through full disk and back to crescent again -- a pattern the Ptolemaic layout physically cannot produce?
answer: Venus
choices: Mercury
Venus
Mars
Saturn
context: In the Ptolemaic arrangement Venus rides on an epicycle roughly between Earth and Sun, so it can never show more than a narrow sickle. Galileo saw a FULL cycle of phases, from crescent through gibbous to full and back. That result is incompatible with Ptolemy -- though it is consistent with Tycho Brahe's geo-heliocentric compromise as well as with Copernicus. Source: https://www.cabinet.ox.ac.uk/galileos-most-decisive-telescopic-observation-phases-venus-1610-23-0

question: On 26 February 1616 Cardinal Robert Bellarmine summoned Galileo and delivered a formal admonition. What did Bellarmine tell him he was and was not allowed to do with the Sun-centred system?
answer: He could treat it as a mathematical hypothesis but not hold or defend it as physically true
choices: He could treat it as a mathematical hypothesis but not hold or defend it as physically true
He could publish only in Latin and only outside the Papal States
He could hold it privately but not teach it to any student under thirty
He could defend it only if he first submitted every draft to the Inquisition
context: Two days earlier, on 24 February 1616, the Inquisition's eleven theologian-qualifiers had graded the proposition that the Sun stands still at the centre of the world 'formally heretical.' Bellarmine's admonition, on 26 February, told Galileo he could use heliocentrism as a calculating device (hypothesi) but could not claim it was physically true. Source: https://www.tau.ac.il/education/muse/museum/galileo/prohibition_helioce.html

question: Galileo's own flagship physical argument for the Earth's motion, presented in Book Four of the Dialogue, turned out to be wrong. He proposed that a specific everyday phenomenon was mechanical proof of Earth's combined daily spin and yearly orbit -- and dismissed the older astrological explanation as superstition. Which phenomenon did he try to explain this way?
answer: The ocean tides
choices: The ocean tides
The passage of the trade winds
The scouring of river valleys
The great earthquakes of Sicily
context: Galileo argued that ocean tides were water sloshing in the basins as Earth's daily rotation and yearly orbit combined -- his headline proof of motion. He waved off the Moon's gravitational pull on the seas as astrology. Newton would later show the Moon's pull was in fact the main driver. The heretic on trial was right about his conclusion (Earth moves) and wrong about his best argument for it. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/galileo/

question: Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems was published in Florence in February 1632. Pope Urban VIII had once been Galileo's friend and even supplied him with a favourite theological argument -- that God could produce any effect on Earth by any means He chose. In the Dialogue, whose mouth did Galileo put that Urban-argument into?
answer: Simplicio, the slow-witted Aristotelian
choices: Salviati, the sharp Copernican character
Sagredo, the intelligent Venetian layman
Simplicio, the slow-witted Aristotelian
An anonymous narrator addressing the reader
context: The Dialogue is a three-way conversation among Salviati (the Copernican), Sagredo (the open-minded layman) and Simplicio (the Aristotelian whose name suggests 'the simpleton'). Urban VIII, reading his own favourite argument in Simplicio's mouth, took it as personal mockery, and the Inquisition machinery moved against Galileo shortly after. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialogue_Concerning_the_Two_Chief_World_Systems

question: On 22 June 1633 the Roman Inquisition delivered its sentence. Galileo was made to kneel and abjure heliocentrism, and the Dialogue was placed on the Index. The formal wording of the verdict was more specific than simple 'heresy.' What was he actually convicted of?
answer: Vehement suspicion of heresy
choices: Formal heresy of the first degree
Vehement suspicion of heresy
Contempt of the Inquisition's officers
Wilful violation of the 1616 admonition
context: The sentence of 22 June 1633: 'we pronounce, judge, and declare, that you, the said Galileo ... have rendered yourself vehemently suspected by this Holy Office of heresy, that is, of having believed and held the doctrine (which is false and contrary to the Holy and Divine Scriptures) that the sun is the center of the world, and that it does not move from east to west, and that the earth does move, and is not the center of the world.' He was made to abjure on his knees the same day. Source: https://hti.osu.edu/sites/default/files/documents_in_the_case_of_galileo.pdf

question: After the sentence Galileo was allowed to retire in December 1633 to his villa at Arcetri, outside Florence, where he lived under house arrest for the rest of his life. Going blind, he wrote there his greatest work in physics -- the foundation Newton would build his mechanics on. Where was that book, Discourses on Two New Sciences, actually printed in 1638?
answer: At Leiden in the Dutch Republic
choices: In Rome, quietly, with a Papal licence
In Florence, by his own students
At Leiden in the Dutch Republic
In Venice, under a false author's name
context: The manuscript was smuggled out of Italy and printed in 1638 at Leiden by Louis Elzevir, safely beyond the Inquisition's reach. Galileo went completely blind that same year and died at Arcetri on 8 January 1642. The Church's ban on heliocentric books was only slowly un-written: the general prohibition dropped in 1758, Pius VII allowed printing in Rome in 1822, and the Dialogue itself was struck from the Index in 1835. Source: https://www.biography.com/scientists/galileo

question: On 31 October 1992 Pope John Paul II addressed the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, closing a commission he had convened in 1980 to re-examine the Galileo case. He conceded the theologians of 1633 had made a mistake about Scripture and natural science. What did the 1992 address NOT do, contrary to many newspaper headlines the next day?
answer: It did not annul the 1633 sentence or declare Galileo innocent
choices: It did not annul the 1633 sentence or declare Galileo innocent
It did not reopen any other Index of Forbidden Books rulings
It did not apologise on behalf of Pope Urban VIII by name
It did not lift ecclesiastical review of astronomy texts in seminaries
context: John Paul II acknowledged that the theologians had erred about the relationship of Scripture to natural science, and called for the old misunderstanding between science and faith to be put in the past. He did NOT formally annul the 1633 sentence and did NOT declare Galileo innocent -- a caveat many contemporary press reports missed and still miss. Source: https://www.pas.va/en/magisterium/saint-john-paul-ii/1992-31-october.html

question: A steady 40 mph wind twisted the Tacoma Narrows deck to pieces on 7 November 1940. As the roadway pitched, Tacoma News Tribune editor Leonard Coatsworth was thrown against the curb, crawled to the tower, and had to leave something behind in the car. What did he leave behind?
answer: A cocker spaniel named Tubby
choices: A cocker spaniel named Tubby
His leather briefcase
His press camera
His portable typewriter
context: Coatsworth drove onto the bridge around 10:00 a.m. with the family dog. Professor Frederick Farquharson tried to rescue Tubby around 10:55 a.m. but the terrified dog bit him and he had to back away; Tubby went down with the deck. Source: WSDOT, https://www.wsdot.wa.gov/tnbhistory/collapse.htm

question: The men who built the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in 1940 already had a nickname for it on opening day, because whenever the wind rose the roadway rippled like a slow ocean swell and drivers saw the car ahead vanish behind a crest. What did they call the bridge?
answer: Galloping Gertie
choices: Galloping Gertie
The Whipping Post
Windy Bridge
The Skinny Lady
context: Construction workers coined the nickname during the build. The rolling motion was vertical and had been present for months before the November collapse; that morning it changed character into a violent twist. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_(1940)

question: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge stretched 2,800 feet across the water on a main span so slim it looked like a ribbon. How deep was the deck girder that carried the roadway?
answer: Eight feet
choices: Eight feet
Forty feet
Twelve feet
Twenty-five feet
context: Designer Leon Moisseiff made the deck 39 feet wide and only 8 feet deep, giving a span-to-depth ratio of about 350 to 1: nearly twice as slender as any long-span bridge before it. That slimness was the point of the design and the reason the deck could twist so easily. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_(1940)

question: For four months after opening, the Tacoma Narrows deck had only rolled up and down. On the morning of 7 November 1940 the motion suddenly changed character, and within an hour the bridge was gone. What did the deck begin doing that morning that it had not done before?
answer: Twisting so hard the two lanes went in opposite directions
choices: Twisting so hard the two lanes went in opposite directions
Sagging in the middle under its own weight
Whipping side to side against its cables
Swaying gently in long slow arcs
context: The standard account is that a cable band slipped at midspan and unbalanced the deck; the new mode was torsional, with one lane rising while the other fell. Photographs show tilt angles reaching about 45 degrees before the suspenders let go around 11:00 a.m. Source: WSDOT, https://www.wsdot.wa.gov/tnbhistory/collapse.htm

question: For half a century, physics textbooks reprinted the Tacoma Narrows film as their classic example of one specific concept. In 1991 K. Yusuf Billah and Robert Scanlan published a paper in the American Journal of Physics naming the books that had it wrong. Which concept did the textbooks wrongly attach to the collapse?
answer: Classical forced resonance
choices: Classical forced resonance
Metal fatigue in the cables
The Bernoulli effect on the deck
Vortex-shedding drag
context: The paper was titled 'Resonance, Tacoma Narrows Bridge Failure, and Undergraduate Physics Textbooks'. It named the actual books and showed that the bridge's failure was not the swing-being-pumped kind of resonance most students were taught. Source: Billah and Scanlan 1991, American Journal of Physics, https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Resonance,-Tacoma-Narrows-bridge-failure,-and-Billah-Scanlan/937cd56aca1ebe07044f87f96630cda82f723d0c

question: At the Tacoma Narrows on 7 November 1940 the wind blew steadily from one direction, yet each twist of the deck grew larger than the last until the suspenders snapped near 45 degrees of tilt. Engineers now call the real mechanism aeroelastic flutter, or negative damping. How does aeroelastic flutter feed a steady wind's energy into a bigger and bigger twist?
answer: Air peeled off the tilted deck and locked in step with the twist
choices: Air peeled off the tilted deck and locked in step with the twist
Vortices spun off the towers arrived in step with the wobble
Long ocean swell shoved the roadway upward in bursts
Suspender cables stored and released energy like rubber bands
context: Instead of bleeding energy away, the structure's own motion pumps itself out of a steady flow: as the deck tilts, the way the air separates from its solid flanks changes and shoves harder on the next twist. Above roughly 35 mph the amplitude grew without limit. Some engineers (e.g., Larsen 2000) argue vortex shedding locked onto the torsional mode, so the settled claim is 'self-excited aeroelastic instability, not classical forced resonance', not one tidy equation. Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge_(1940)

question: Humphry Davy pulled a new metal out of sodium hydroxide in 1807: silvery, soft enough to slice with a knife, and kept under oil because bare air tarnishes it. Drop a pea-sized lump of sodium into a bowl of water and it hisses and fizzes at once. Where in the bowl is the lump while it reacts?
answer: Riding on the surface of the water
choices: Riding on the surface of the water
Resting on the bottom of the bowl
Hovering halfway down in the water
Pinned against the side of the bowl
context: Sodium's density at 20 C is 0.9688 g/cm3 - just under water's - so a lump of it FLOATS while it reacts, skating on the gas it makes. It melts at only 98 C, which is why the racing lump often turns into a molten ball. Davy isolated it in 1807 by electrolysis of sodium hydroxide; because it tarnishes in air by combining with oxygen, sodium is stored under oil or inert gas. Source: Wikipedia 'Sodium' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium

question: Sodium is a metal that catches fire the moment it touches water. Chlorine is a yellow-green gas heavy enough to sink into low ground, and in April 1915 the German army, with Fritz Haber directing the cylinders, opened 5,730 of them at Ypres to kill French troops where they stood. React those two elements together and the result is a harmless white solid found in almost every kitchen. Which one?
answer: Table salt
choices: Table salt
Baking soda
Icing sugar
Corn starch
context: The two elements: sodium, a silvery metal soft enough to cut with a knife, isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807; chlorine, a gas with a density of 3.2 g/L against air's ~1.2 g/L, which Davy named in 1810 from the Ancient Greek chloros, 'pale green', for its colour. Carl Wilhelm Scheele made the first detailed study in 1774 by reacting manganese dioxide with hydrochloric acid, recording 'the bleaching effect on litmus, the deadly effect on insects, the yellow-green colour'. At the Second Battle of Ypres on 22 April 1915 the German army released 168 long tons of chlorine from 5,730 cylinders along a 6.5 km front - a 'strange green cloud of death' that tore a 6 km gap in the French line; Fritz Haber proposed using the heavier-than-air gas and supervised the cylinder installation. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sodium', 'Chlorine', 'Second Battle of Ypres'.

question: Tip a spoonful of table salt onto a dark plate tonight and look at the grains under a hand lens. They are not shapeless specks: every grain has grown into the same regular form, the same one the mineral takes when miners cut it out of the ground as halite. What form is it?
answer: Tiny cubes
choices: Tiny cubes
Slim needles
Flat plates
Round pellets
context: Halite (rock salt / table salt) forms isometric crystals whose habit is 'predominantly cubes', with perfect {001} cleavage in three directions at right angles and a Mohs hardness of only 2.0-2.5 - softer than a copper coin. Its unit cell measures a = 5.6404 A, so the cube you can see on the plate is the inner arrangement enlarged roughly ten million times. Bonus for the lens: 'hopper crystals', cube skeletons, form when the edges grow faster than the faces during rapid crystallisation. Source: Wikipedia 'Halite' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halite

question: Sodium is a metal that bursts into flame on water; chlorine is a gas that kills what breathes it. Combine the two and children sprinkle the result on their food without a thought. Nothing was added and nothing was taken away: the same two kinds of atom are all that is there. What did the sodium and the chlorine do to each other?
answer: One electron moved from each sodium to a chlorine
choices: One electron moved from each sodium to a chlorine
One pair of electrons ended up shared between them
All the outer electrons pooled into a common sea
Each atom kept its own and they clung together weakly
context: The give-away in one line: a sodium atom hands over its single outer electron (Na -> Na+ + e-) and a chlorine atom takes it (Cl + e- -> Cl-). What sits in the shaker is not sodium and chlorine ATOMS at all but sodium and chloride IONS - same nuclei, one electron moved, and every property changes. The three wrong options are all real bonding pictures, just not this one: the shared pair is the covalent bond, the common sea is metallic bonding, and weak clinging is van der Waals attraction. Source: Grokipedia 'Ionic bonding' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Ionic_bonding

question: Chemists write table salt as NaCl, which reads like a recipe for a couple: one sodium locked to one chlorine, that pair repeated over and over through the grain. When X-rays finally showed the inside of a salt crystal, the couples were nowhere to be found. What is the real arrangement?
answer: An endless grid, every sodium ringed by six chlorines
choices: An endless grid, every sodium ringed by six chlorines
Chains of four atoms repeating, laid side by side
Flat sheets of sodium alternating with sheets of chlorine
Linked rings of eight atoms with hollow gaps between
