context: Solid sodium chloride is a face-centred cubic array of chloride ions with sodium ions filling every octahedral hole - coordination number 6 for BOTH ions, each sodium ringed by six chlorides and each chloride by six sodiums, repeating to the edge of the grain. Wikipedia states it flatly: there are 'no discrete NaCl molecules' in the solid. Chloride ionic radius 167 pm, sodium 116 pm, lattice constant a = 564.02 pm. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sodium chloride' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride ; Grokipedia 'Ionic bonding'.

question: Drop a salt crystal into water and it comes to pieces within seconds - 360 grams of salt will vanish into a single litre. That crystal is a rigid grid of charged particles, ions, clamped together by an enormous electrical grip. A water molecule carries no net charge at all: measure one and it comes out electrically neutral. So what lets water get hold of those ions and haul them apart?
answer: Each molecule is lopsided: one end negative, one end positive
choices: Each molecule is lopsided: one end negative, one end positive
Water molecules link into chains that pull by hydrogen bonding
Water molecules are small enough to wedge in between the ions
Water's own molecules split into charged pieces that swap places
context: Water does it the other way from salt, and unfairly. Oxygen's Pauling electronegativity is 3.44 against hydrogen's 2.20 - a difference of 1.24 - so oxygen SHARES the electrons but pulls harder, leaving oxygen partially negative and each hydrogen partially positive. The molecule is bent, which stops the two pulls cancelling: the gas-phase H-O-H angle is 104.48 degrees, the O-H bond length about 0.96 A, and the net dipole moment 1.8546 D. Salt's solubility is 360 g/L at 25 C. Sources: Wikipedia 'Properties of water', 'Electronegativity', 'Sodium chloride'; Grokipedia 'Chemical polarity'.

question: Gilbert N. Lewis filled his lecture notes from about 1902 with atoms drawn as little cubes, an electron possible at each corner, and he kept the sketch to himself for fourteen years. When he finally published 'The Atom and the Molecule' in 1916, he set down what a chemical bond between two atoms actually is. What did he propose a bond to be?
answer: A pair of electrons shared between the two atoms
choices: A pair of electrons shared between the two atoms
A single electron passed from one atom to the other
An attraction between the two atoms' opposite poles
A set number of affinity units each atom must satisfy
context: Lewis's cubes were a teaching doodle in unpublished notes, 'in which the corners of the cube represented possible electron positions'; in that picture a single bond is two cubes sharing an EDGE (two shared electrons) and a double bond two cubes sharing a FACE (four). Walther Kossel, son of the Nobel laureate Albrecht Kossel, published the rival give-and-take (ionic) picture independently in the same year, 1916 - both men reaching the octet from opposite ends. Irving Langmuir coined the term in 1919, not 1916, and the word was 'covalence': in the Journal of the American Chemical Society of 1 June 1919 he wrote, 'we shall denote by the term covalence the number of pairs of electrons that a given atom shares with its neighbors.' Merriam-Webster dates the exact phrase 'covalent bond' to 1939. Lewis's shared pair had no physics under it until Walter Heitler and Fritz London worked out the hydrogen molecule in 1927 - 'the first successful quantum mechanical explanation of chemical bonding', eleven years after the drawing. Lewis himself was nominated for the Nobel Prize 41 times and never won one; he coined the word 'photon' in 1926 and produced the first pure sample of heavy water in 1933. On 23 March 1946 a graduate student found his body under a laboratory workbench at Berkeley; he had been working with liquid hydrogen cyanide and had returned from lunch with his old rival Langmuir 'in a dark mood'. Sources: Wikipedia 'Gilbert N. Lewis', 'Cubical atom', 'Covalent bond', 'Walther Kossel'; Grokipedia 'Gilbert N. Lewis'.

question: W. Lawrence Bragg and his father were the first people ever to read the inside of a crystal with X-rays, and the crystal they read was common salt. Bragg then announced that salt holds no NaCl molecules at all: the equal numbers of the two atoms fall out of how the crystal packs, not from atoms pairing off. Henry E. Armstrong, an old-guard chemist, fired back in Nature in 1927 with a one-page piece headed 'Poor Common Salt!'. How did he swat the physicists' picture aside?
answer: He said that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry
choices: He said that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry
He said X-rays could see only the crystal's outer faces
He said the salt in the experiment must have been impure
He said the molecules were hiding inside the pattern
context: Sodium chloride was the first crystal structure ever determined by X-ray diffraction, published in 1913 by W. Lawrence Bragg with his father W. H. Bragg ('The Structure of Some Crystals as indicated by their Diffraction of X-rays', Proc. Roy. Soc.); it showed crystals are repeating ATOMIC lattices, not stacks of molecules. Von Laue, Friedrich and Knipping had only discovered X-ray diffraction by crystals in April 1912. Father and son shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics; Lawrence was 25 and remains the youngest science laureate ever. Bragg had written: 'In sodium chloride there appear to be no molecules represented by NaCl... it is a result of geometry and not of a pairing-off of the atoms.' Armstrong's furious reply protested 'the unjustified aspersion of the molecular character of our most necessary condiment'. Flagged as legend because the exact wording of his chess-and-geometry line is corroborated through a secondary source rather than the Nature page itself. Sources: H. E. Armstrong, 'Poor Common Salt!', Nature 120, 478 (1927) - https://www.nature.com/articles/120478b0 ; wording corroborated via RSC Chem. Educ. Res. Pract. accepted manuscript; OUPblog centenary piece; Wikipedia 'William Lawrence Bragg'.

question: Turn a tap down to a thread-thin stream, then hold beside it a comb you have just dragged through your hair: the stream bends toward the comb. Rubbing loaded the comb with extra electrons, so it is negatively charged, and a friend explains the bend at once - water must carry a positive charge, and opposite charges attract. Now test that explanation. Rub a glass rod until it carries a POSITIVE charge and hold it beside the stream instead. Which way does the stream go?
answer: It bends toward the rod, just as it did toward the comb
choices: It bends toward the rod, just as it did toward the comb
It bends away from the rod, the opposite way to before
It runs dead straight, unmoved by the positive rod
It bends toward the rod only while the tap runs fast
context: The stream is attracted either way. Water molecules simply rotate, turning whichever end suits toward whatever charge is nearby, so a negatively charged comb and a positively charged glass rod both pull the stream over. A kid who reasons 'the comb is negative, so it pulls the positive water' has the wrong model, and the glass rod is the test that exposes it - which is exactly what a second, opposite trial is for. You can run both tonight with a comb, a glass rod and a wool sleeve. Sources: Saint Mary's University Physics Demos, 'Bending Water with Static Electricity' - https://demos.smu.ca/demos/e-n-m/62-bending-water ; Rutgers Chemistry demo, 'Polarity - Bending of a Liquid Stream'.

question: Sodium dropped into water makes hydrogen, the heat of the reaction sets that hydrogen alight, and the lump bangs - that is how every textbook explained the classroom demonstration for a century. In 2015 Philip Mason and Pavel Jungwirth filmed a drop of sodium-potassium alloy meeting water at 10,000 frames a second, and within the first millisecond, well before any flame, the film showed something the old story leaves no room for. What happened to the drop in that first millisecond?
answer: Metal spikes shot out of the drop in all directions
choices: Metal spikes shot out of the drop in all directions
A shell of steam lifted the drop clear of the water
The drop flattened into a thin disc before it burned
A blue glow spread through the water round the drop
context: Electrons leave the metal into the water almost instantly, leaving positive metal ions packed side by side; they repel one another past the Rayleigh instability limit and the drop tears itself apart in a 'Coulomb explosion', which then exposes fresh metal and makes the whole thing worse. The camera ran at 10,000 frames per second - 400x slow motion. A demonstration performed in schools for over a century was not fully explained until 2015, which is a standing reminder that 'everyone knows why' is not the same as 'somebody checked'. Source: Mason, Uhlig, Vanek, Buttersack, Bauerecker & Jungwirth, 'Coulomb explosion during the early stages of the reaction of alkali metals with water', Nature Chemistry (2015) - https://www.nature.com/articles/nchem.2161 ; corroborated at Chemistry World and C&EN.

question: Linus Pauling proposed electronegativity in 1932 - a single number for how hard an atom pulls on the electrons it shares. Fluorine tops his scale at 3.98 and caesium sits at the bottom at 0.79. Sodium and chlorine differ by 2.23 and the bond is filed as ionic; oxygen and hydrogen in water differ by 1.24 and the bond is filed as covalent. The cut-off between the two names sits at 1.7. Where does 1.7 come from?
answer: From agreement among chemists; nothing in nature changes at 1.7
choices: From agreement among chemists; nothing in nature changes at 1.7
From a jump in bond behaviour; measurements cluster right at 1.7
From Pauling's X-ray work; salt crystals fixed the line at 1.7
From molten-salt experiments; current flows only above 1.7
context: Pauling's scale 'characterizes a bond along the continuous scale from covalent to ionic bonding' - it is a spectrum, not two boxes. Fluorine is the highest at 3.98 and caesium the lowest at 0.79. Textbooks 'generally' call a difference above 1.7 predominantly ionic and above 2.0 near-complete transfer, but those cut-offs are conventions, not nature. Covalent character is greatest between atoms of similar electronegativity: H-H is the perfectly even case, H-Cl the lopsided one, water sits at 1.24 and sodium chloride off the end at 2.23. The honest words are 'mostly ionic' and 'mostly covalent'. Sources: Wikipedia 'Electronegativity', 'Covalent bond'; Grokipedia 'Ionic bonding'.

question: James Cloyd Downs patented a cell in 1924 that runs table salt backwards: molten sodium chloride with a current pushed through it between a carbon rod and an iron shell, chlorine gas bubbling off one and molten sodium metal running off the other. To keep the bath liquid near 600 C instead of 801 C, two-thirds of it by weight is calcium chloride - so there is more calcium in the pot than sodium. Yet almost none of that calcium comes out as metal. Why?
answer: Calcium ions take up electrons less readily than sodium ions
choices: Calcium ions take up electrons less readily than sodium ions
Calcium ions carry two charges and barely move in the melt
Calcium metal dissolves back into the melt as fast as it forms
Calcium ions cannot reach the iron shell where the metal forms
context: In the Downs cell (invented 1923, patented 1924) the reactions are 2Cl- -> Cl2(g) + 2e- at the carbon anode and 2Na+ + 2e- -> 2Na(l) at the iron cathode: green gas out one side, molten silvery metal out the other, the two lethal elements pulled back out of the seasoning. The bath runs at about 33.2% NaCl to 66.8% CaCl2, which drops the melting point to roughly 600 C. Calcium's standard reduction potential (-2.87 V) is more negative than sodium's (-2.71 V), so the sodium ions collect the electrons first and the calcium mostly stays in the melt; the little calcium that does come out is the main impurity in Downs-cell sodium and is removed afterwards. Source: Wikipedia 'Downs cell' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downs_cell

question: On 13 January 1920 the New York Times ran an editorial mocking Robert H. Goddard, a Clark College physics professor who had suggested a rocket could reach the Moon. Its sneer became the most-quoted line in science reporting. What did it say Goddard lacked?
answer: the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools
choices: the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools
the training given freely in technical colleges
the patience learned in any working laboratory
the arithmetic taught in first-year engineering
context: The piece was unsigned, ran in the 'Topics of the Times' column, and was titled 'A Severe Strain on Credulity'. The same paper had run a straight, respectful news story the day before, on 12 January 1920, headed 'Believes Rocket Can Reach the Moon' -- it reported the claim, then ridiculed it twenty-four hours later. The editorial also jabbed that doubting the professor would mean denying 'a fundamental law of dynamics, and only Dr. Einstein and his chosen dozen, so few and fit, are licensed to do that.' The press called Goddard the 'Moon man' and the 'rocket man' for years afterward. Sources: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?' (Air & Space Quarterly, Summer 2026); Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'.

question: On 16 March 1926, on his Aunt Effie's snowy farm at Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert H. Goddard flew the world's first liquid-fuel rocket. There was no ignition switch -- one assistant had to set it going by hand and get clear fast. How did he light it?
answer: he held up a blowtorch on the end of a long pole
choices: he held up a blowtorch on the end of a long pole
he touched a burning taper down through the frame
he fired a signal flare at the base from cover
he dropped a lit rag onto the launch stand and ran
context: The assistant then, in historian Kevin Schindler's phrase, 'ran like heck.' Esther Goddard was filming, but her camera could shoot only seven seconds at a time and the rocket sat roaring on its frame so long that the film ran out before it lifted -- there is no film of the first liquid-fuel rocket flight. Goddard's diary the next day: 'It rose 41 feet & went 184 feet, in 2.5 secs., after the lower half of the nozzle burned off,' and 'It looked almost magical as it rose.' Roughly 60 mph. The launch site is now the ninth fairway of the Pakachoag Golf Course, marked by a four-foot granite obelisk. Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'; Clark University Goddard Collection.

question: On 17 July 1969, the morning after Apollo 11 lifted off, the New York Times printed a short item headed 'A Correction' -- forty-nine years after it had mocked the physicist Robert H. Goddard. Experiment, it said, had confirmed the findings of Isaac Newton, and it closed: 'The Times regrets the error.' What did the correction say was now established?
answer: that a rocket can work in a vacuum as well as in air
choices: that a rocket can work in a vacuum as well as in air
that a rocket can carry a man beyond Earth's gravity
that a rocket can be steered across hundreds of miles
that a rocket can lift more than its own weight in fuel
context: The correction in full: 'Further investigation and experimentation have confirmed the findings of Isaac Newton in the 17th Century, and it is now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum as well as in an atmosphere. The Times regrets the error.' Watch the date: Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969 and landed on 20 July, so the paper corrected itself the morning after the LAUNCH, not after the landing. Goddard did not live to see it; he had died decades earlier. Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'.

question: Robert H. Goddard's 1919 Smithsonian paper ran to 69 pages, nearly all of it sober mathematics on reaching extreme altitudes. What set the newspapers off was about eight lines on the next-to-last page, where he sketched a way to prove a rocket had actually reached the Moon. What did those eight lines propose?
answer: setting off flash powder on the Moon's dark face for a telescope
choices: setting off flash powder on the Moon's dark face for a telescope
bouncing a wireless signal off the Moon and timing its return
sending a mirror to catch sunlight and flash it back to Earth
sending a camera around the Moon and bringing the film back
context: Goddard's own wording: 'The only reliable procedure would be to send the smallest mass of flash powder possible to the dark surface of the moon in such a way that it would be ignited on impact. The light would then be visible in a powerful telescope.' Eight lines at the back of a technical monograph -- and they produced years of ridicule. The paper was 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes', Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections Vol. 71 No. 2 (1919). Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'.

question: The 1920 editorial charged that Robert H. Goddard did not grasp action and reaction, and needed 'something better than a vacuum against which to react.' The test that settled it was already five years old: in 1915 at Clark, Goddard had sealed something inside an evacuated chamber, set it off, and watched which way it moved. What had he sealed in there?
answer: a loaded pistol
choices: a loaded pistol
a firecracker
a signal flare
a flash-powder charge
context: When the pistol fired inside the vacuum chamber, the escaping gases pushed it the opposite way -- exactly as they would in open air. In a second 1915 experiment Goddard fired small rockets inside a vacuum tube he had bent into a ring; they worked perfectly well. The editorial of 1920 was written against an experiment that already existed and was five years old. Source: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?', quoting NASA historian James Anderson.

question: The 1920 editorial was not simply stupid -- it applied to rockets something genuinely true of a different engine. A jet airliner really cannot operate above the atmosphere; put a jet engine in a vacuum and it stops dead. Why does a jet engine need the air it flies through?
answer: it scoops the oxygen it burns straight out of that air
choices: it scoops the oxygen it burns straight out of that air
it needs the air outside for its exhaust to push against
it relies on air rushing past to keep its blades cool
it depends on outside air pressure to hold its flame steady
context: A jet is air-breathing: no air, no oxygen, no fire. A rocket carries its own oxidiser along with its fuel, which is exactly why it works where a jet cannot. The 1920 writer took a true fact about one kind of engine and applied it to the wrong kind. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rocket engine' -- 'Rocket vehicles carry their own oxidiser, unlike most combustion engines such as pulse engines or jet engines, so rocket engines can be used in a vacuum.'

question: A 1929 launch from the Auburn farm went badly wrong: Robert H. Goddard's rocket climbed about ninety feet, nosed over, crashed and set the grass alight. Neighbours thought an aeroplane had come down and called for help, and the state fire marshal banned him from launching there again. The flight was still a first in the history of science, because of what it carried. What was aboard?
answer: a camera, a thermometer and a barometer
choices: a camera, a thermometer and a barometer
a compass, a stopwatch and a hygrometer
a clock, a magnetometer and a spectroscope
a thermometer, a hygrometer and an electroscope
context: They were the first scientific instruments ever launched by a rocket. The crash also put Goddard back in the papers -- the next day's headline read 'MOON ROCKET MISSES TARGET BY 238,799 1/2 MILES' -- and that coverage caught Charles Lindbergh's attention. Lindbergh met Goddard at Clark on 23 November 1929, and the Guggenheim grant approved in July 1930 funded the rest of his career. Sources: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'; Grokipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard'; TIME, 'Rocket Scientist Robert Goddard' (headline).

question: The whole 1920 error sat in one sentence: Robert H. Goddard, the editorial said, needed 'something better than a vacuum against which to react.' The writer took it for granted that a rocket must shove against something in the world around it. Goddard's sealed-chamber test had already shown the rocket still moved with nothing around it. So what does a rocket shove against?
answer: the hot gas it throws backwards out of its own nozzle
choices: the hot gas it throws backwards out of its own nozzle
the walls of the chamber where its own fuel burns
the Earth's gravitational field, which it pushes away
the shock front its burning fuel drives out ahead of it
context: This is Newton's third law, stated in the Principia of 1687: 'to every action there is always opposed an equal reaction.' The engine shoves hot exhaust backwards and the exhaust shoves the rocket forwards, just as hard. The propellant is the partner, not the atmosphere -- which is why the editorial's demand for 'something better than a vacuum' was asking for something a rocket never needed. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Newton's laws of motion' (third law and the rocket-propulsion worked example); Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Who Was the Original Rocket Man?'.

question: Robert H. Goddard's 1915 chamber experiments at Clark answered more than the question 'does a rocket still work with no air around it?' They also settled what the surrounding atmosphere actually does to an engine's push. What did his measurements show?
answer: thrust rose in the chamber -- the air had been cutting it
choices: thrust rose in the chamber -- the air had been cutting it
thrust fell in the chamber -- the air had been adding to it
thrust held steady -- the air made no measurable difference
thrust varied -- the air helped some fuels and hurt others
context: A rocket's performance actually decreases under atmospheric pressure. The thrust equation carries a pressure term, A_e(p_e - p_amb): as the outside pressure falls, thrust rises. At the Earth's surface that pressure thrust can be reduced by up to 30 percent, depending on engine design. Air is not the rocket's partner -- air is in the way. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard' ('his experiment demonstrated that a rocket's performance actually decreases under atmospheric pressure') and Wikipedia, 'Rocket engine'.

question: Momentum is mass times velocity, and in a closed system the total never changes. Newton's third law is that same bookkeeping seen as forces: every push comes with an equal push the other way. Read carelessly, the two pushes look like they should cancel, leaving nothing to move at all. Yet the rocket accelerates. Where does the cancelling argument go wrong?
answer: the two forces act on two separate bodies, the gas and the rocket
choices: the two forces act on two separate bodies, the gas and the rocket
the two forces act at two separate moments, one just after the other
the two forces act along two separate lines, so they never truly oppose
the two forces act on two separate parts of the same rocket body
context: A common misconception is that action and reaction cancel one another; because they act on distinct bodies, their effects are independent and each body accelerates on its own. One force acts on the exhaust gas, the other on the rocket. It is the same bookkeeping that makes a rifle recoil into your shoulder and lets a swimmer who shoves water backwards travel forwards. Source: Grokipedia, 'Newton's laws of motion'.

question: Robert H. Goddard's 1919 Smithsonian paper -- the very document the New York Times was reviewing when it declared he did not understand reaction -- carries in its early pages a formula for the top speed a rocket can reach. Only two things fix that ceiling: the share of the rocket's mass that is fuel, and one property of the engine. Which property?
answer: how fast the gas leaves the nozzle
choices: how fast the gas leaves the nozzle
how much thrust it makes at lift-off
how much fuel it burns each second
how long the engine keeps firing
context: Goddard's formula was v = c(1-k) ln(M/(M-m)): c is the speed of the exhaust gas, k the inert, non-propellant share, and M and M-m the rocket's mass before and after the burn. Thrust never appears in it, nor burn time -- and neither does the air. He built the whole derivation from conservation of momentum alone: the forward impulse on the rocket equals the backward momentum of its exhaust, with no atmosphere anywhere in it. The proof the editorial said he lacked was sitting inside the document the editorial was reviewing. He was also not the first to get there: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, a deaf Russian schoolteacher who taught himself physics in Moscow's public libraries after scarlet fever took his hearing at about nine, had derived the same rocket equation in 1903 and analysed rocket propulsion specifically in vacuum conditions. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard' and 'Konstantin Tsiolkovsky'; Goddard, 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes', Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections Vol. 71 No. 2 (1919).

question: The rice plant itself makes plenty of beta-carotene in its green leaves. Yet the milled grain a child eats is essentially white and carries almost none. Why does the grain end up with almost none, when the leaves make plenty?
answer: The pathway is switched off in the endosperm
choices: The pathway is switched off in the endosperm
The pathway is destroyed when the outer bran is milled away
The pathway runs only in green tissue that sees sunlight
The pathway is blocked by phenolic compounds in the husk
context: The endosperm never expresses the enzymes that would carry the carotenoid chain to completion, so a food that dominates half the world's plates carries almost no provitamin A. This is why children living mainly on white rice go blind. Source: goldenrice.org/Content2-How.

question: Two European plant scientists spent about eight years finishing an inserted pathway so that rice endosperm would produce beta-carotene, and published the result in Science in January 2000. Who were they?
answer: Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer
choices: Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer
Norman Borlaug and M. S. Swaminathan
Marc Van Montagu and Jeff Schell
Mary-Dell Chilton and Robert Fraley
context: Potrykus (ETH Zurich) and Beyer (Freiburg) began the work in the early 1990s and finally succeeded in 1999; the paper was Ye et al., Science 287:303-305 (2000). All four pairs are real names from twentieth-century crop and plant-genetics work. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingo_Potrykus; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11880581.

question: To finish the beta-carotene pathway in a rice grain, the original Golden Rice team borrowed exactly two enzyme genes from outside rice. One came from a soil bacterium (Erwinia uredovora). The other, a phytoene synthase, came from a common European garden flower. Which one?
answer: Daffodil
choices: Daffodil
Marigold
Sunflower
Tulip
context: The daffodil gene (Narcissus pseudonarcissus) supplied phytoene synthase; the bacterial crtI carried the intermediate on to beta-carotene. Together they wake the pathway back up inside the endosperm. Marigold and sunflower are real carotenoid-rich plants -- honest wrong picks. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11880581.

question: The world's first look at Golden Rice on the front of a major American magazine was the July 31, 2000 cover of Time, showing Ingo Potrykus standing among rice plants. What did the cover line promise?
answer: This rice could save a million kids a year
choices: This rice could save a million kids a year
The grain that will end world hunger forever
One seed that could feed a billion people
A modified crop that could beat malnutrition
context: The kids in the headline were the roughly 250,000-500,000 children the WHO estimated go blind each year from vitamin A deficiency, about half of whom die within twelve months. Source: time.com/archive/6598226; who.int/data/nutrition/nlis.

question: A fair, specific criticism of the 1999 prototype was that its beta-carotene dose (about 1.6 micrograms per gram) was too low for rice alone to meet a child's daily vitamin A need. In 2005 Syngenta and colleagues (Paine et al., Nature Biotechnology) answered that objection with a second-generation line that produced roughly 23 times more carotenoid. What one change did the trick?
answer: They replaced the original psy gene with the maize version
choices: They replaced the original psy gene with the maize version
They added a third enzyme borrowed from the carrot pathway
They increased the copy number by growing the line in polyploid rice
They fortified the milled grain with synthetic beta-carotene after harvest
context: Maize (Zea mays) phytoene synthase massively outperformed the original in tissue-culture screens. Golden Rice 2 reached about 37 micrograms/g of carotenoid (~84% beta-carotene). The dose objection was answered nearly two decades before the plant was allowed to be grown. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15793573.

question: On August 8, 2013, a Philippine government field trial of Golden Rice at Pili, in Camarines Sur province, was only weeks from harvest. What ended it before harvest?
answer: Roughly four hundred protesters uprooted the plot by hand
choices: Roughly four hundred protesters uprooted the plot by hand
A typhoon flattened the plot the day before harvest
Regulators quietly pulled the permit and had it plowed under
A rice-blast fungal outbreak wiped the trial out
context: Data collection was set back months. Field reports differ on exactly who was in the crowd, so the record simply says protesters. This was one of a handful of GM trials destroyed by direct action worldwide that decade. Source: science.org, 'Activists Destroy Golden Rice Field Trial'.

question: In late June 2016, Sir Richard Roberts of New England Biolabs organized an open letter signed by a large group of Nobel laureates at launch, asking one specific organization to stand down on Golden Rice. Which organization was named -- and roughly how many laureates signed at launch?
answer: Greenpeace, about 107 laureates

Friends of the Earth, about 80 laureates
IFOAM Organics International, about 50 laureates
ETC Group, about 40 laureates
context: The launch press event was held June 30, 2016 at the National Press Club in Washington; more laureates added their names over the following months. Greenpeace's public reply was that Golden Rice had 'failed' after 20 years -- the letter's point was that 20 years of blocking was what produced the delay. The other three groups are real organizations that have campaigned against GM crops. Source: sciencealert.com, '107 Nobel Laureates Just Signed a Letter Slamming Greenpeace'.

question: In April 2024 the Philippine Court of Appeals revoked the 2021 commercial permit for Golden Rice, invoking the country's constitutional precautionary principle. The revocation came through a specific extraordinary environmental writ, created in Philippine law for cases where an environmental harm crosses jurisdictions. What is the writ called?
answer: The Writ of Kalikasan
choices: The Writ of Kalikasan
The Writ of Amparo
The Writ of Habeas Data
The Writ of Continuing Mandamus
context: 'Kalikasan' is Filipino for 'nature'. The writ was created by the Philippine Supreme Court in 2010 for large-scale environmental cases. Amparo (life/liberty/security), Habeas Data (privacy), and Continuing Mandamus (ongoing agency compliance) are all real Philippine constitutional writs -- just aimed at different harms. The court's Golden Rice ruling cited conflicting scientific views on long-term safety. Source: phys.org, 'Philippine court blocks GMO golden rice production over safety fears'.

question: Charles Goodyear had mixed rubber with anything he could beg, and every batch still went to sticky goo in summer heat. In 1839, at a Woburn factory he was closing, a scrap of his rubber-and-sulphur mix carelessly touched a hot stove. What did it do?
answer: It charred and stiffened like a piece of leather.
choices: It melted into a bright pool across the iron.
It puffed up and gave off a choking white smoke.
It charred and stiffened like a piece of leather.
It cracked apart into small brittle black flakes.
context: Goodyear's own 1853 memoir gives the moment in one quiet sentence, written of himself in the third person: 'He was surprised to find that the specimen, being carelessly brought in contact with a hot stove, charred like leather.' What made that astonishing was that gum-elastic 'always melted when exposed to a high degree of heat.' Note what is NOT in his account: no rage, no flung sample, no general store, no frying pan. The popular retellings added those and they contradict each other (Lemelson-MIT has locals mocking him in a store until an animated gesture lands the sample on a potbellied stove; Wikipedia's own vulcanization article has him 'accidentally drop the mixture in a hot frying pan'). It happened at the old Eagle India Rubber works at Woburn, Massachusetts, which Goodyear was visiting for the purpose of shutting the manufacturing down. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 117-119, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good; myth versions at lemelson.mit.edu/resources/charles-goodyear and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanization.

question: Charles Goodyear died in 1860, deep in debt. Thirty-eight years later Frank Seiberling founded a rubber works in Akron, Ohio and named it after him: a dead stranger whose family had no stake in it. What did the firm make?
answer: Horseshoe pads, poker chips and bicycle tires.
choices: Raincoats, boot soles and surgical tubing.
Horseshoe pads, poker chips and bicycle tires.
Automobile tires, inner tubes and rubber floor mats.
Fire hoses, drive belts and printing rollers.
context: Frank Seiberling founded the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company in Akron on 29 August 1898. He simply borrowed the name; the firm had no connection to Charles Goodyear or to his family, and cars barely existed yet, so before there were automobiles to sell to it made bicycle and carriage tires, rubber horseshoe pads and poker chips. Goodyear himself had earned nearly $163,000 from the patent but owed far more. He died on 1 July 1860, aged 59, at the Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York: he had been travelling to see a dying daughter and was told on arrival that she was already dead, and collapsed. His estate stood at roughly $200,000 in debt, and his son Charles Jr. untangled the books and paid the creditors. Five years before that he had managed both extremes in a single year: debtors' prison in England and again in France, over debts run up staging lavish rubber displays at the Paris Exposition Universelle, and induction into the French Legion of Honour while he was imprisoned. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodyear_Tire_and_Rubber_Company; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Goodyear (citing Charles Slack, 'Noble Obsession', 2003, pp. 210, 213, 226, 230, 234-5); connecticuthistory.org, 'Charles Goodyear and the Vulcanization of Rubber'.

question: In 1839, at a rubber works in Woburn, Massachusetts, Charles Goodyear watched a scrap of his mixture char on a hot stove instead of melting to goo, and he saw at once that it mattered. He held it up to his own brother and the other rubber men in the room. How did they take it?
answer: They shrugged it off as one more of his experiments.
choices: They demanded he repeat it in front of a chemist.
They offered to buy the mixture from him on the spot.
They put it down to the stove, not to the mixture.
They shrugged it off as one more of his experiments.
context: Goodyear's memoir is blunt about the reception: 'The occurrence did not at the time appear to them to be worthy of notice; it was considered as one of the frequent appeals that he was in the habit of making, in behalf of some new experiment.' The men in that room knew the rubber trade, and they had watched Goodyear cry wolf over promising scraps for years. It is one of the sharpest lessons in the history of discovery: the most important moment in rubber happened in front of witnesses who were qualified to judge it, and they judged it worthless. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), p. 119, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: For five years Charles Goodyear mixed rubber with every powder and liquid he could get, and the money ran out long before the answer came. He sold the family furniture and boarded his wife and children with neighbours; two of his small sons died in those years. In the worst of it, what were the Goodyears living on?
answer: Frogs they caught and half-frozen potatoes they dug.
choices: Clams they raked at low tide and greens they boiled.
Frogs they caught and half-frozen potatoes they dug.
Salt fish and beans bought on credit at the village store.
Acorns they gathered and eels they speared in the creek.
context: Goodyear was jailed for debt repeatedly, on both sides of the Atlantic, and came close to killing himself with his own chemistry: while secretly running his nitric-acid process he 'came near being suffocated by generating a large quantity of gas in a close room; he, however, escaped with a course of fever.' The frogs-and-potatoes winter is the low point of a five-year stretch in which he had no laboratory, no chemical training, and no income, and it is the reason the stove is not really a story about luck. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Goodyear (citing Diana Ross McCain, 'It Happened in Connecticut', 2008, p. 82); Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), p. 107.

question: Sulphur was no secret ingredient in the rubber trade. Mr. Chaffee had stirred it into rubber at the Roxbury company years before Charles Goodyear's stove, and neither he nor the company thought the result worth a second look. Goodyear names one plain practical thing that had kept sulphured rubber out of the shops. What was it?
answer: The goods themselves gave off a strong sulphur smell.
choices: The sulphur cost more than the rubber it went into.
The goods themselves gave off a strong sulphur smell.
The goods stained everything they touched bright yellow.
The sulphur crumbled back out of the rubber in weeks.
context: Goodyear's wording: 'the obnoxious odor of sulphur in the goods was an effectual barrier to their reception in the market.' Of Chaffee's earlier trial at Roxbury he writes that 'the effects were not deemed worthy of notice, either by that company or himself.' Half the answer to the greatest materials problem of the age was already lying around in the industry, and the trade had walked past it because the product smelled bad. What was missing was heat, and someone still looking. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 113-114, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: Charles Goodyear's 1844 patent calls for twenty-five parts rubber to five parts sulphur, held near 270 degrees Fahrenheit. Raw rubber is a tangle of very long molecule chains, wound around one another but each chain a separate strand, and rubber like that turns to goo in summer heat. Goodyear could not account for why so little sulphur cured it. What was the sulphur doing to those chains?
answer: Building short bridges from one chain across to another.
choices: Welding the chains end to end into far longer chains.
Coiling each chain into a spring that grips its neighbours.
Wedging fine hard grains into the gaps between the chains.
Building short bridges from one chain across to another.
context: Chemists call such a bridge a CROSS-LINK. The reactive spots on a rubber chain are its allylic C-H bonds, hydrogens on carbons sitting next to a C=C double bond; vulcanization swaps some of those for short chains of one or several sulphur atoms running across to a cure site on a DIFFERENT chain, with hundreds or thousands of carbons between one bridge and the next. The segments between bridges can still stretch and recoil, so the rubber stays springy, but whole chains can no longer slide past one another and flow. It also runs one way only: vulcanized rubber is a thermoset, so you cannot melt it down and recast it the way you can a plastic. Goodyear's actual recipe is in the patent: 'I take twenty-five parts of india-rubber, five parts of sulphur, and seven parts of white lead,' heated between 212 and 350 degrees Fahrenheit but 'for the best effect approaching as nearly as may be to 270.' Nobody then could say what the white lead was doing; it was acting as what chemists now call an activator. Turn the sulphur far up instead, to somewhere between 25 and 80 percent, and the springy solid becomes rigid black ebonite, the hard rubber Charles's brother Nelson Goodyear developed in 1851 for combs, bowling balls, clarinet mouthpieces and car battery cases. Same reaction, different dial setting. Sources: US Patent 3,633 (15 June 1844), patents.google.com/patent/US3633A/en; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanization; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_vulcanization; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebonite; Akiba, 'Vulcanisation and crosslinking in elastomers', Progress in Polymer Science 22(3):475-521 (1997).

question: Before the stove, Charles Goodyear thought he had already won. He boiled his rubber goods in quicklime and water, which tanned the gum and killed its stickiness, and the finish brought him acclaim as far away as Europe. Then Goodyear found the flaw himself, and it wiped the process out. What had he found?
answer: A drop of weak acid turned the rubber soft again.
choices: A night of hard frost cracked the goods right through.
A week in strong sun bleached and powdered the surface.
A drop of weak acid turned the rubber soft again.
A rag soaked in lamp oil lifted the finish clean off.
context: The quicklime bath 'appeared to have the effect of tanning the gum, and destroying its viscous property' -- and then a drop of weak acid neutralised the alkali and the rubber went soft again. Goodyear broke his own triumph, which is the first scientific virtue: the person you most need to be skeptical of is yourself. The graveyard of his other fixes is just as instructive. Magnesia, up to a pound of it to a pound of gum, gave him rubber that came out WHITE, a genuine novelty since 'no India rubber goods except black had before that time been made in the United States,' but it did not last. Quicklime stirred straight into the gum was 'too powerfully caustic to be worked by hand.' And his nitric-acid 'acid gas' process cured only the skin: a US Government mail-bag order made with it was treated across the trade as the test of the invention, and the bags rotted in the warm season because the acid had 'not changed far below the surface.' The compound he happened to test on the stove was the same one that had decomposed in those mail-bags. Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 100-110, 115-118, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: The hot stove had charred Charles Goodyear's sample, and a charred scrap looks like a ruined one. To see it again he held a similar piece of rubber-coated cloth in front of an open fire, and it charred once more. One detail in that scorched cloth told him he was right after all. What was it?
answer: A narrow band at the burn's edge, firm and springy and whole.
choices: A round patch at the very centre, firm and springy and whole.
A narrow band at the burn's edge, firm and springy and whole.
A thin skin across the whole face, firm and springy and whole.
A scatter of small spots in the char, firm and springy and whole.
context: In his own words: 'The same effect, that of charring the gum, followed; but there were further and very satisfactory indications of ultimate success... as upon the edge of the charred portions of the fabric, there appeared a line, or border, that was not charred, but perfectly cured.' That thin band is the whole discovery. It proved heat had a RIGHT amount, not only a wrong one, which turned the remaining problem from 'what should I add?' into 'how hot, and for how long?' He also established that 'India rubber could not be melted in boiling sulphur at any heat ever so great, but always charred.' And the stove did not hand him a process: he moved his family to Lynn to get at the steam power of Messrs. Baldwin & Haskins, then moved back to Woburn, where 'he now pursued his inquiries and experiments for some months quite alone, until the desired result was obtained.' Months more, working by himself, before he 'felt himself amply repaid for the past.' Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), p. 119, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: The mixture Charles Goodyear had on the stove in 1839 was rubber and sulphur, and in his own memoir he is blunt that the sulphur was not his idea. He had bought the right to it, on paper, in February 1839, months before the stove. Who had he bought it from?
answer: Nathaniel Hayward, the foreman of the Woburn works.
choices: Mr. Chaffee, a manufacturer at the Roxbury company.
William Brockedon, an English painter and inventor.
Nathaniel Hayward, the foreman of the Woburn works.
Nelson Goodyear, his own brother and partner.
context: Hayward had been putting sulphur into the solvent and drying the goods in the sun, a trick he called solarizing. Goodyear: 'It was through him that the writer received the first knowledge of the use of sulphur as a drier of gum-elastic.' He bought Hayward's claim and the patent issued on 24 February 1839, months before the stove -- and then drew the line himself, in print: 'It should be remarked that this claim was for the use of sulphur, and not for the heating or vulcanizing process, subsequently discovered by the writer.' Hayward had even warned him not to use sulphur crude, 'because its effects were so powerful when used in a minute quantity.' This is the honest shape of the story: Goodyear did not invent the ingredient, he bought it, and what he added was the heat and the years of looking. Sources: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 112-114, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Hayward.

question: Charles Goodyear knew exactly how his discovery looked from outside: a failed hardware merchant with no chemical training, rescued by a hot stove. In his memoir he grants the no-training part, then flatly refuses the word 'accident', reaching instead for one famous story to explain the difference. Which story?
answer: Isaac Newton and the falling apple.
choices: Archimedes and the overflowing bath.
Isaac Newton and the falling apple.
James Watt and the boiling kettle.
Benjamin Franklin and the storm kite.
context: His sentence: 'Like the falling of an apple, it was suggestive of an important fact to one whose mind was previously prepared to draw an inference from any occurrence which might favor the object of his research. While the inventor admits that these discoveries were not the result of scientific chemical investigations, he is not willing to admit that they were the result of what is commonly termed accident; he claims them to be the result of the closest application and observation.' Elsewhere he states the principle flat out: what cannot be found by research 'will most likely be discovered by accident, if at all, and by the man who applies himself most perseveringly to the subject, and is most observing of every thing relating thereto.' He had the receipts, too. Years earlier he had daubed nitric acid on a piece of rubber drapery only to strip bronze decoration off it, threw the discoloured piece away as worthless, and later found it cured; he calls the two episodes 'parallel cases.' The same man having the same kind of luck twice is the tell that it was not luck. (Newton's apple is itself an anecdote Newton told late in life, not a documented event -- which makes Goodyear's borrowing of it a story about a story.) Source: Charles Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic and Its Varieties' (1853), pp. 96, 104, 119-120, archive.org/details/gumelasticitsva121853good.

question: In the autumn of 1842 the English rubber manufacturer Thomas Hancock was handed a few small scraps of a marvellous new rubber, brought over from America by an agent of its inventor. Hancock turned the scraps over and caught a faint smell of sulphur on one of them. What did he decide the smell meant?
answer: That someone had dusted sulphur on to send him the wrong way.
choices: That the sulphur had rubbed off the packing on the voyage.
That the sulphur was a preservative to stop the gum rotting.
That sulphur had been mixed in as a filler to save money.
That someone had dusted sulphur on to send him the wrong way.
context: The scraps reached Hancock through his friend William Brockedon. Hancock's own 1857 narrative: 'Some time in the early part of the autumn of 1842, Mr. Brockedon showed me some small bits of rubber that he told me had been brought by a person from America, who represented himself as the agent of the inventor.' The agent's story was that the secret lay in a cheap new solvent, which was a blind alley. Then came the sentence that matters: 'The first named had a slight smell of sulphur, and I thought that a little sulphurous powder had been rubbed on to mislead.' The one real clue was literally under his nose and he filed it as a deliberate decoy -- then spent months getting there the hard way anyway. He melted sulphur in an iron vessel, noting its melting point 'was only about 240 [F], which I knew would not be injurious to the rubber,' and dipped in half-inch slips of sheet rubber; by the third immersion the tan colour had gone right through, and on the fourth one slip came out 'perfectly changed,' while the ends of the others nearest the fire were 'turning black, and becoming hard and horny.' His verdict on how unguessable it all was: 'I believe I may confidently affirm that it was not previously known even that rubber would absorb sulphur, and no degree of chemical knowledge, no analogy of reasoning on the relative nature of the two substances would ever have suggested or anticipated the possibility of such a result.' Source: Thomas Hancock, 'Personal Narrative of the Origin and Progress of the Caoutchouc or India-Rubber Manufacture in England' (1857), pp. 91-92, 102-104, archive.org/details/personalnarrati00hancgoog.

question: Charles Goodyear cooked his first vulcanized rubber at Woburn in 1839. Thomas Hancock, in England, did not see a scrap of the American material until the autumn of 1842, and worked backwards from it to a sulphur-and-heat process of his own. Both men then filed patents within months of each other, Goodyear in the United States on 30 January 1844. Who was first onto the register, and by how much?
answer: Hancock, by about ten weeks: he filed on 21 November 1843.
choices: Hancock, by nearly a year: he filed on 15 February 1843.
Goodyear, by about six weeks: Hancock filed on 13 March 1844.
Hancock, by about ten weeks: he filed on 21 November 1843.
Goodyear, by only three days: Hancock filed on 2 February 1844.
context: Hancock filed on 21 November 1843 and enrolled his full specification on 30 May 1844; Goodyear filed in the United States on 30 January 1844 and was granted US Patent 3,633 on 15 June 1844. So the Briton's claim genuinely precedes the American's ON PAPER, while the American's working discovery in 1839 precedes both -- which is why the honest answer to 'who invented vulcanization?' is not a single name. Goodyear refused to fight it out in print: he 'has intentionally omitted all mention of the English patent for the vulcanization of caoutchouc, enrolled by Thomas Hancock on the 30th May, 1844, and also from expressing any views or opinions in relation to the circumstances under which this patent was taken out, lest he might possibly do some injustice to Mr. Hancock or his partners.' An English court tested the question in 1855 (Hancock v. Moulton); Goodyear attended, chemists testified that a sample could not have revealed how it was made, and Hancock prevailed. Hancock also had what Goodyear never did -- a factory. He had invented the rubber 'masticator' in 1820 and ran Charles Macintosh & Co.'s works, and by 1857 could report that 'solid twelve-inch cubes have been done at our works, vulcanized throughout,' while Goodyear worked in attics and borrowed mills with his wife and children helping. One last honesty: neither man knew WHY it worked. Goodyear conceded the results 'have not yet been satisfactorily accounted for,' and cross-linking as an explanation arrived decades later. The word itself was an afterthought too: Hancock had been calling it merely 'the change' until Brockedon, a painter and not a chemist, proposed 'vulcanization' after Vulcan. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hancock_(inventor); patents.google.com/patent/US3633A/en; Goodyear, 'Gum-Elastic' (1853), pp. 88, 119-120; Hancock, 'Personal Narrative' (1857), pp. 11-12, 107-108, 112.

question: LIGO's two detectors, rebuilt and far more sensitive, caught the first gravitational wave anyone had ever detected on 14 September 2015 at 09:50:45 UTC. Where did that morning fall relative to LIGO's science run?
answer: Four days before it began, with the machines in shakedown
choices: Four days before it began, with the machines in shakedown
Four days after it began, with the machines fully calibrated
Four months in, during the run's most sensitive stretch
On its last night, hours before a planned shutdown
context: The upgraded detectors had begun engineering run ER8 on 17 August 2015, and the formal O1 science run was not due to start until 18 September. The first gravitational wave ever detected arrived on 14 September - four days before the observatory was officially open for business. Source: Wikipedia, 'First observation of gravitational waves' (GW150914): the detectors were operating in 'engineering mode'; LIGO/Virgo, arXiv:1602.08492, 'Localization and broadband follow-up of GW150914' (ER8 began 17 August; O1 scheduled for 18 September).

question: Marco Drago, a young Italian postdoc at the Max Planck Institute in Hannover, was the first human ever to see a gravitational wave: an automatic email brought him two graphs of it. About an hour later, what did Drago do?
answer: Emailed the collaboration asking if anything could have faked it
choices: Emailed the collaboration asking if anything could have faked it
Phoned Hanford to have the mirrors re-locked and rechecked
Logged the trigger as noise and went back to his own work
Sent the graphs to an astronomer to hunt for the source
context: Each link opened a graph that looked like the traces ornithologists use to record birdsong. Drago's first move was not celebration but suspicion - he asked the whole collaboration whether anyone knew of anything that could have produced a false signal. The automatic trigger had already fired within about three minutes of the wave passing, at 09:54 UTC. Source: INFN Scienza per Tutti, interview with Marco Drago ('Onde Gravitazionali | Intervista a Marco Drago'); Wikipedia, GW150914.

question: LIGO's laser does not cross its arms once. Mirrors bounce it back and forth until the light has travelled about 1,120 kilometres, and when the wave passed on 14 September 2015 that whole path stretched and squeezed. How big was the change the machine measured?
answer: About a thousandth of the width of a proton
choices: About a thousandth of the width of a proton
About a tenth of the width of a hydrogen atom
About a hundredth of the width of a human hair
About a thousandth of the width of a red blood cell
context: The peak strain was 1.0 x 10^-21 - a fraction, not a fixed length, so the figure only means something once you say which path it is measured over. Wikipedia puts the proportion this way: it is like the distance to the nearest star outside the Solar System changing by one hair's width. Source: Wikipedia, GW150914 (change of about a thousandth of a proton's width over the 1,120 km effective span); LIGO/Virgo discovery paper, arXiv:1602.03837 / Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 061102.

question: In 1967 Rainer Weiss - an MIT dropout who had come back as a lab technician - was teaching general relativity there when his students asked him to explain how Joseph Weber's bar detectors were supposed to catch a gravitational wave. He could not. What did Weiss do about it?
answer: Set the class the problem of designing the simplest possible detector
choices: Set the class the problem of designing the simplest possible detector
Invited Joseph Weber to MIT to explain the bars to the class himself
Dropped the subject from the course until the claims were settled
Wrote to Joseph Weber asking for the raw data behind his detections
context: Weiss's own answer to his own homework problem was an L-shaped laser interferometer with free-hanging mirrors. He wrote it up in 1972 in an internal MIT report, 'Electromagnetically Coupled Broadband Gravitational Antenna', and LIGO grew out of that report; he shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics with Barry Barish and Kip Thorne. Source: MIT News, 'Q&A: Rainer Weiss on LIGO's origins'; Science/AAAS, 'Meet the college dropout who invented the gravitational wave detector'; Wikipedia, 'Rainer Weiss'.

question: Two black holes, one about 36 times the mass of the Sun and one about 29, spiralled together and merged 1.3 billion light-years from Earth. The hole they left behind weighed about 62 solar masses - but 36 and 29 make 65. Roughly three Suns' worth of mass had gone somewhere. Where did it go?
answer: It left as ripples in spacetime, spreading outward through space
choices: It left as ripples in spacetime, spreading outward through space
It was blasted out as a burst of gamma rays and hard X-rays
It went into the spin of the new hole, which whirls faster for it
It became heat in the gas and dust swirling around the pair
context: This was GW150914, heard by LIGO on 14 September 2015. About 3.0 solar masses were radiated away as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second - mass turned directly into the energy of the wave. The pair lay roughly 1.3 billion light-years off, so that wave had been on its way for 1.3 billion years before it reached the mirrors. Source: LIGO/Virgo discovery paper, arXiv:1602.03837 (36 and 29 solar masses, final mass 62, 3.0 solar masses radiated, luminosity distance 410 Mpc).

question: LIGO runs two identical machines, one at Livingston, Louisiana and one at Hanford, Washington, 3,002 kilometres apart. On 14 September 2015 the same trace registered at Livingston 6.9 milliseconds before it registered at Hanford. What did the size of that lag establish?
answer: Something had swept in from the sky, crossing both sites at light speed
choices: Something had swept in from the sky, crossing both sites at light speed
A tremor had travelled through the crust from Louisiana to Washington
The two sites' atomic clocks had drifted apart over the summer
A storm front had crossed the country, hitting each detector in turn
context: Light needs about 10 milliseconds to cross 3,002 km, so a 6.9 ms offset is exactly what a wavefront arriving at an angle from the sky produces. Nothing local can imitate that: a truck, a quake or a storm cannot show up at two sites separated by less than the light-travel time between them. Source: Wikipedia, GW150914 (time delay 6.9 (+0.5, -0.4) ms; sites 3,002 km apart; peaks seen at Livingston first).

question: In September 2010 LIGO recorded a strong signal that seemed to come from the constellation Canis Major, and the team nicknamed it the Big Dog. They analysed it for six months, wrote the discovery paper, and voted unanimously to submit it. Then, on 14 March 2011, with about 300 of them packed into a room in Arcadia, California, they opened a sealed envelope: the signal was a deliberate fake, known in advance to only four people in the whole collaboration. How had the fake been planted?
answer: By shaking the detectors' mirrors
choices: By shaking the detectors' mirrors
By writing it into the recorded data
By modulating the laser's frequency
By seeding it in the analysis code
context: A hundred more watched the envelope opening by video link. Only four LIGO scientists were ever allowed to know when such a blind injection had been made - which is why, when a real signal arrived in September 2015, the very first thing the collaboration did was run a chain of internal emails confirming that no injection, scheduled or unscheduled, had been made that morning. Source: LIGO Scientific Collaboration, 'Blind injection stress-tests LIGO and Virgo's search for gravitational waves' (ligo.org/news/blind-injection.php); Wikipedia, GW150914.

question: For a few thousandths of a second, as two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses fell together in 2015, the merger's peak output reached about 3.6 x 10^49 watts. Set that against every star in the observable universe shining at once: how did the merger compare?
answer: It was greater than all of that starlight put together
choices: It was greater than all of that starlight put together
It was about equal to one large galaxy's starlight
It was a millionth of that starlight, but concentrated
It was about what the Sun radiates in its lifetime
context: And not one photon of it was light. The wattage is agreed across sources; the multiple is not - LIGO's own science summary says more than ten times all the starlight in the observable universe, Wikipedia says fifty times, Grokipedia says about two hundred. So the honest claim is the one all three support: greater. Source: Wikipedia, GW150914 (3.6 x 10^49 W); LIGO Scientific Collaboration science summary for GW150914; Grokipedia, 'First observation of gravitational waves'.

question: Albert Einstein had predicted gravitational waves in 1916, working them out of his own field equations. Twenty years later, in June 1936, he and Nathan Rosen mailed Physical Review a manuscript titled 'Do Gravitational Waves Exist?'. What answer did the two of them give to their own title?
answer: That the waves are not physically real at all
choices: That the waves are not physically real at all
That the waves cannot escape the body that makes them
That the waves are real but far too weak to detect
That the waves form only near very dense stars
context: Working with the full nonlinear field equations, Einstein and Rosen ran into what looked like a singularity and read it as proof that the waves were not physically real - twenty years after Einstein had predicted them himself. The manuscript reached Physical Review on 1 June 1936. He had already corrected himself once on this subject: an error in the 1916 derivation was fixed in a 1918 paper, which produced the quadrupole radiation formula. Source: Daniel Kennefick, 'Einstein Versus the Physical Review', Physics Today; Grokipedia, 'Sticky bead argument'; Einstein 1916 (SPAW 688-696) and 1918 (SPAW 154-167).

question: In 1936 Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen sent Physical Review a paper on gravitational waves whose conclusion the editor, John Tate, found suspicious enough to send out to an anonymous referee - the cosmologist Howard Percy Robertson, who returned ten pages of criticism. Einstein and Rosen had hit a point where their maths blew up - a singularity - and had built their conclusion on it. What did Robertson show they had got wrong?
answer: They had read a quirk of their own coordinates as a feature of spacetime
choices: They had read a quirk of their own coordinates as a feature of spacetime
They had used an approximation where the blow-up demanded the full equations
They had dropped a factor of two from the formula for radiated energy
They had assumed a spherical source, which radiates nothing at all
context: Tate returned the manuscript with Robertson's report on 23 July 1936. A coordinate singularity is a bookkeeping artefact: choose different coordinates and it vanishes, because nothing physical is happening at that point. Robertson was right, and the paper's conclusion did not survive it. Source: Daniel Kennefick, 'Einstein Versus the Physical Review', Physics Today ('Einstein and Rosen mistook a coordinate singularity for a physical one').

question: Albert Einstein was furious that Physical Review's editor, John Tate, had sent his 1936 manuscript to a referee. He wrote to Tate on 27 July that he saw no reason to address 'the - in any case erroneous - comments of your anonymous expert', withdrew the paper, and never submitted there again. That October his assistant Leopold Infeld talked the problem through at Princeton with Howard Percy Robertson - the referee himself - and the two found the mistake. When Infeld brought it to him, what did Einstein do?
answer: Said he had found an error himself the night before - then reversed the paper
choices: Said he had found an error himself the night before - then reversed the paper
Thanked Infeld for the correction - then pulled the paper from print entirely
Disputed the correction for years - then published the paper word for word
Handed the whole problem to Infeld - then never wrote on the waves again
context: Einstein rewrote the paper to the opposite conclusion, retitled it 'On Gravitational Waves', and published it in the Journal of the Franklin Institute in January 1937. He later thanked Robertson for his help. Apart from a single letter to the editor in 1952, he never published in Physical Review again. Source: Daniel Kennefick, 'Einstein Versus the Physical Review', Physics Today (Einstein's letter to Tate of 27 July 1936 quoted verbatim; Infeld's October 1936 discussions with Robertson).

question: Joseph Weber built the first gravitational-wave detector, a resonant aluminium bar, and in 1969 announced he was catching waves - which for a while made him one of the most famous scientists alive. Nobody else could reproduce it: Richard Garwin's bar gave one probable-noise pulse in six months, and Heinz Billing's team at the Max Planck Institute built a copy in 1972 and saw nothing. David Douglass then went through Weber's own analysis program and found the flaw. What was it?
answer: It allowed for noise of random amplitude but not of random phase
choices: It allowed for noise of random amplitude but not of random phase
It counted every coincidence twice, once for each end of the bar
It compared the bars against a clock that drifted through the night
It discarded the quietest hours, when the bar was most sensitive
context: Weber's specific detections did not hold up; the claims were discredited through the 1970s, he lost his main funding in 1987, and he argued for them to the end. He also founded the entire field - it was a student's question about Weber's bars that sent Rainer Weiss looking for a better instrument. Source: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Weber'; Aeon, 'How Joe Weber's gravity ripples turned out to be all noise'; Science/AAAS, 'Remembering Joseph Weber, the controversial pioneer of gravitational waves'.

question: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor used the 305-metre Arecibo dish in 1974 to find a pulsar orbiting another neutron star every 7.75 hours - a natural clock in a binary system. Timing its pulses year after year gave physics the first indirect evidence that gravitational waves exist, and won the two men the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics. What in the timing was the evidence?
answer: The orbit winding tighter, the two stars falling closer every year
choices: The orbit winding tighter, the two stars falling closer every year
The pulses running early and late as passing waves stretched the gap
The pulses reddening as they climbed out of the companion's gravity
The pulsar's beam bending as it swept past the companion each orbit
context: Their timing showed the 7.75-hour orbit tightening - the period dropping 76.5 millionths of a second a year, the orbit's long radius shrinking about 3.5 metres - as the pair steadily loses energy. The rate matches Albert Einstein's quadrupole radiation formula of 1918 to within 0.2%. Hulse and Taylor never detected a wave - their 1993 Nobel citation reads 'for the discovery of a new type of pulsar, a discovery that has opened up new possibilities for the study of gravitation'. They watched a binary bleed energy at precisely the predicted rate; PSR B1913+16's two stars will merge in about 300 million years. Source: Wikipedia, 'PSR B1913+16'; Grokipedia, 'First observation of gravitational waves'.

question: By the 1950s gravitational waves were in the equations, but Nathan Rosen, who had written a 1936 paper on them with Albert Einstein, still insisted they carried no energy and so could do nothing at all. At the Chapel Hill conference of 1957 Richard Feynman answered him with a thought experiment: two beads threaded on a stiff rod, free to slide along it. What did Feynman say a passing wave would do to that rod?
answer: Rub the beads along it and warm it by friction
choices: Rub the beads along it and warm it by friction
Ring it at its own resonant note, like a struck bell
Slide the beads to one end and leave them there
Stretch it lengthwise while the beads stayed put
context: Feynman's own phrasing, from his 1962-63 Caltech Lectures on Gravitation: the mass 'in accelerating up and down will rub the stick, and therefore by friction make heat.' Heat means work was done, and work done means the wave carries real energy. Hermann Bondi later published a version of the argument. Rosen never gave way - he was still publishing objections to the bead argument in 1979. The Chapel Hill conference (18-23 January 1957) was organised by Bryce DeWitt and Cecile DeWitt-Morette and paid for by the industrialist Agnew Bahnson. Source: Grokipedia, 'Sticky bead argument'; Wikipedia, 'Chapel Hill Conference' and 'Sticky bead argument'.

question: On 17 August 2017 two neutron stars collided in the galaxy NGC 4993, about 140 million light-years off, and their gravitational wave rolled through the detectors for about 100 seconds. The Fermi telescope caught a gamma-ray burst from the same patch of sky 1.74 seconds behind the wave, and more than 70 observatories swung around to look. What did comparing those two arrival times establish?
answer: That gravity and light travel at the same speed
choices: That gravity and light travel at the same speed
That gravity outruns light across open space
That gamma rays are slowed by the gas they cross
That gravity acts instantly, with no travel time
context: The event was catalogued as GW170817, the burst as GRB 170817A. Set a 1.74-second gap against 140 million years of travel and the two speeds match to about one part in 10^15: the measured difference lies between -3 x 10^-15 and +7 x 10^-16 of the speed of light. The wave itself ran about 100 seconds, some 3,000 cycles. Source: Wikipedia, 'GW170817' (detection 17 August 2017 at 12:41:04 UTC; GRB 170817A 1.74 +/- 0.05 s later; ~100 s signal, ~3,000 cycles; host galaxy NGC 4993 at about 140 million light-years; more than 70 observatories).

question: In 1907 Albert Einstein sat in the Bern patent office, writing a review article on relativity, when an idea struck him — one he later called 'the happiest thought of my life.' What was the thought?
answer: That a man falling freely would not feel his own weight.
choices: That a man falling freely would not feel his own weight.
That a moving clock must tick slower than a resting one.
That mass and energy are two names for one thing.
That light travels at the same speed for everyone.
context: Einstein put the insight into print that same year, in 'On the Relativity Principle and the Conclusions Drawn from It' (Jahrbuch der Radioaktivitaet und Elektronik, 1907). The famous phrase is his own later retelling, not a 1907 notebook entry — the same way Newton's apple comes from Newton's late-life anecdote. In an unpublished 1920 manuscript he wrote that 'for an observer in free-fall from the roof of a house there is during the fall — at least in his immediate vicinity — no gravitational field,' and in a 1922 lecture in Kyoto he said, 'If a man falls freely, he would not feel his weight. I was taken aback. This simple thought experiment made a deep impression on me.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Equivalence principle'; Wikipedia, 'Einstein's thought experiments'.

question: On 2 August 1971, with a television camera running, Apollo 15 commander David Scott stood in the lunar dust, a hammer in one hand and a falcon feather in the other. He said he had come to test what Galileo claimed about falling objects, and let go of both. What happened?
answer: The feather struck the dust with the hammer.
choices: The feather struck the dust with the hammer.
The feather floated for a full minute first.
The feather landed a clear half-second later.
The feather drifted sideways out of the shot.
context: Scott's words on live television: 'Well, in my left hand, I have a feather; in my right hand, a hammer. And I guess one of the reasons we got here today was because of a gentleman named Galileo, a long time ago, who made a rather significant discovery about falling objects in gravity fields. And we thought where would be a better place to confirm his findings than on the Moon.' At 167:22:43 mission elapsed time he said 'How about that!' — CapCom Joe Allen answered 'How about that!' to applause in Houston — then 'Which proves that Mr. Galileo was correct in his findings.' NASA logs the objects as a 1.32-kg aluminium geological hammer and a 0.03-kg feather, 'observed to undergo the same acceleration and strike the lunar surface simultaneously.' The same equality has been tested far more finely than a Moon drop: Lorand Eoetvoes's torsion balance found no difference between materials to about one part in a billion by 1908, and the French MICROSCOPE satellite, letting cylinders of two different alloys fall side by side in orbit, pushed that to about one part in 10^15 in 2022. Source: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, 'EVA-3 Close-out'; NASA Science, 'The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop'; Grokipedia, 'Lorand Eoetvoes'; Wikipedia, 'MICROSCOPE (satellite)'.

question: Einstein asked readers to picture a man sealed in a windowless chamber drifting far from any star, when a powerful being grabs a rope fixed to the roof and hauls with a steady force, so the chamber gathers speed evenly. What does the inside of that chamber then look like?
answer: Exactly like a room standing still in a gravitational field.
choices: Exactly like a room standing still in a gravitational field.
Exactly like a room falling freely toward a distant planet.
Exactly like a room spinning slowly about its own axis.
Exactly like a room where every object has gained mass.
context: This is the equivalence principle: inside a sealed box, being hauled along at a steady acceleration and standing at rest in a gravitational field give identical results, so no experiment performed inside can tell them apart. The equivalence is only local, and Einstein knew it. Make the box big enough and the difference shows: objects falling in a real planet's field are all aimed at its centre, so their paths slowly converge, while under a rope's uniform pull they stay parallel. That converging is the tidal effect — and it is exactly what the curvature of spacetime means. Source: Wikipedia, 'Einstein's thought experiments'; Grokipedia, 'Equivalence principle'.

question: Every schoolbook has Galileo Galilei climbing the Leaning Tower of Pisa around 1590 to drop two balls of different weight and prove they fall together. Historians trace the whole story back to one single source. What is it?
answer: A life of Galileo written by his student Vincenzo Viviani.
choices: A life of Galileo written by his student Vincenzo Viviani.
A passage in Galileo's own book Two New Sciences (1638).
The transcript of Galileo's trial before the Inquisition.
A letter from the astronomer Johannes Kepler in Prague.
context: Viviani wrote it in 1654, twelve years after Galileo died, and it was not published until 1717. Galileo never described doing the drop himself. What he did publish were his inclined-plane experiments, which slowed falling down enough to time it, and in Two New Sciences (1638) his thought experiment about two stones tied together. Most historians treat the tower drop as a thought experiment rather than a physical test — which is exactly why David Scott repeating it on the Moon in 1971, in front of a television camera, mattered. Source: Wikipedia, 'Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Equivalence principle', which calls the cannonball account 'legendary and unverified'.

question: David Scott carried two falcon feathers to the Moon on Apollo 15 and had meant to try the hammer-and-feather drop privately first, before doing it for a live television audience. He ran out of time and, as he later put it, 'we just winged it.' What had he been worried about?
answer: That static charge would stick the feather to his glove.
choices: That static charge would stick the feather to his glove.
That the hammer would bounce up and tear his suit open.
That the feather would be crushed flat inside its pouch.
That the camera would be aimed the wrong way entirely.
context: Scott told the Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal: 'I had a friend who was a professor at the Air Force Academy. Their mascot's the Falcon. And we had the (LM) Falcon. So that was indeed, a falcon feather from an Air Force Academy bird. In fact, I had two of them. I was going to try it, first, to see if it worked — because of static charge... Didn't have time, so we just winged it. And it worked!' The lunar module was named Falcon, so the feather was, as Scott said on air, 'appropriately, a falcon feather for our Falcon.' The demonstration was CapCom Joe Allen's idea. Analysts later identified the bird as a small gyrfalcon and the feather as a primary flight feather about 30.5 cm long. One of the two feathers is still lying on the Moon. Source: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Journal, 'EVA-3 Close-out'.

question: In 1911 Einstein squeezed a testable number out of the sealed-box argument alone — the claim that a steadily accelerating box and a box sitting in gravity cannot be told apart. Starlight grazing the edge of the Sun, he calculated, should be bent by about 0.83 arcseconds, an arcsecond being a 3600th of a degree. In November 1915 he finished general relativity and ran the calculation again. What became of the prediction?
answer: It doubled, to about 1.75 arcseconds.
choices: It doubled, to about 1.75 arcseconds.
It stayed put, at about 0.83 arcseconds.
It halved, to about 0.42 arcseconds.
It grew tenfold, to about 8.3 arcseconds.
context: The 1911 paper was 'On the Influence of Gravitation on the Propagation of Light' (Annalen der Physik), and its number came from the equivalence of gravity and acceleration alone, with no curvature of space in it at all. The finished theory added that curvature and doubled the answer — which is what made the 1919 eclipse a genuine three-way test: no deflection at all, about 0.87 arcseconds if light were simply a Newtonian particle falling, or 1.75 if Einstein's full theory held. Sobral's four-inch backup telescope returned 1.98 plus or minus 0.18 arcseconds, and Eddington's Principe plates 1.61 plus or minus 0.45. The result was announced on 6 November 1919. Source: Grokipedia, 'General relativity' and 'Eddington experiment'; Wikipedia, 'History of general relativity'.
