question: Einstein's sealed chamber, hauled by a rope so that it steadily gathers speed, handed him a second prediction in 1911 — this one about clocks rather than light. Picture two identical clocks inside it, one bolted to the floor and one to the ceiling. What did Einstein conclude they must do?
answer: The floor clock must run slow against the ceiling clock.
choices: The floor clock must run slow against the ceiling clock.
The ceiling clock must run slow against the floor clock.
Both must run slow against a clock left outside the box.
Both must keep perfect step until the hauling stops.
context: He reasoned it from light. A beam sent up from the floor arrives at a ceiling that has been picking up speed away from it the whole time the light was in flight, so it arrives shifted down in frequency — fewer waves arriving each second, which is a slower clock. If acceleration and gravity truly cannot be told apart, gravity must do the same thing: a clock deeper in a gravitational field runs slow. Einstein published this four years before general relativity existed. One consequence, worked out much later: because clocks run slower deeper in the well, the Earth's core is in effect about 2.5 years younger than its surface, accumulated over 4.5 billion years. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'; Wikipedia, 'Gravitational time dilation'.

question: The International Space Station orbits about 250 miles up, and everything aboard floats — the crew, their tools, blobs of drinking water. NASA puts the strength of Earth's gravity at that altitude at a particular fraction of its strength down on the ground. What fraction?
answer: About 90 per cent of its strength at the ground.
choices: About 90 per cent of its strength at the ground.
About 50 per cent of its strength at the ground.
About 10 per cent of its strength at the ground.
About 1 per cent of its strength at the ground.
context: NASA's own wording: 'At that altitude, Earth's gravity is about 90 percent of what it is on the planet's surface.' The crew float not because gravity has let go of them but because they are falling — 'the spacecraft, its crew and any objects aboard are all falling toward but around Earth.' The station is moving sideways at 17,500 miles per hour, fast enough that the ground curves away beneath it as fast as it drops, so it keeps missing. Everyone aboard is in exactly the state Einstein pictured from his desk in 1907: falling freely, and feeling no weight at all. Source: NASA, 'What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)'.

question: In 1959 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka set out to catch gravity's effect on time inside a single building: gamma rays from iron-57 fired up and down the 22.5-metre tower of Harvard's Jefferson Physical Laboratory. The shift they were hunting was five hundred times smaller than the natural width of the very spectral line they had to read it against. What did they do to drag a signal that small into view?
answer: They mounted the gamma-ray source on a vibrating loudspeaker coil.
choices: They mounted the gamma-ray source on a vibrating loudspeaker coil.
They cooled both source and detector with a bath of liquid helium.
They pumped every last trace of air out of the tall tower shaft.
They averaged ten thousand separate runs taken over four years.
context: The coil ran at about 74 hertz with a peak speed of roughly 0.10 millimetres per second, swinging the source gently toward and away from the target and sliding a Doppler shift back and forth across it until the absorption dipped — and the speed at which it dipped measured the gravitational shift. Predicted fractional shift: 2.5 x 10^-15. Measured: -(2.56 plus or minus 0.25) x 10^-15, agreement to about 10 per cent, announced in April 1960 and sharpened to the 1 per cent level by 1964. Einstein's 1911 prediction about clocks had waited forty-nine years for somebody to build a test delicate enough to check it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'.

question: Kelly Foyle and Philip Freeman put a blunt question to the bowling-ball-on-a-rubber-sheet demonstration of general relativity: what makes the sheet sag in the first place? Earth's gravity pulls the ball down — so the demonstration is explaining gravity by using gravity. Foyle and Freeman do not throw the fabric away; they published a repair that gets Earth's gravity out of the job. Which repair is theirs?
answer: Stretch the fabric upward over a laboratory flask.
choices: Stretch the fabric upward over a laboratory flask.
Blow air up from beneath to hold the fabric domed.
Pull the fabric down with a magnet instead of a weight.
Freeze the sagged fabric solid and lift the ball out.
context: Foyle and Freeman's words: 'what causes the fabric to sag? The massive ball at the centre of the fabric is being pulled down, but by what? ... gravity in the analogy is being caused by gravity outside the analogy. We are explaining gravity using gravity.' Bending the fabric upward over a flask or funnel gives the same curvature with Earth's gravity no longer doing the work, and they recommend laying strips of tape on it rather than rolling marbles, since a rolling marble is being accelerated by its own weight and the slope — 'this use of a bent fabric is in fact a demonstration of force and potential, not of the effect of geometry.' The sheet is not worthless, and this is the honest part: a sagging trampoline really is curved, and you can measure it yourself. Tape out a triangle and its interior angles no longer add to 180 degrees; trace a circle with a pin and string and its circumference is no longer 2 x pi x r. Source: K. Foyle & P. Freeman, 'General Relativity: Beyond the Bowling Ball and the Trampoline', OAPT Newsletter, 23 November 2020.

question: Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock, and relativity pulls it two ways at once: weaker gravity that high up makes it gain about 45 microseconds a day, while its orbital speed makes it lose about 7, for a net gain of roughly 38 millionths of a second. Engineers correct for that. If they simply did not bother, how far would your position drift?
answer: By about 10 kilometres a day.
choices: By about 10 kilometres a day.
By about 10 metres a day.
By about 10 centimetres a day.
By about 10 kilometres a century.
context: Thirty-eight microseconds sounds like nothing, but GPS finds you by timing radio signals that travel at the speed of light, so a clock error of 38 millionths of a second is already more than ten kilometres of position error — and it piles up again the next day, and the next. Gravitational time dilation is not a curiosity for physicists; it is a correction sitting inside the phone in your pocket. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'; R. Pogge, 'Real-World Relativity: The GPS Navigation System', Ohio State University.

question: General relativity swaps the pull of gravity for a bending of spacetime, and spacetime has two halves. A mass curves the space around it, so a radio signal passing nearby has further to travel; it also stretches time nearby, so a clock ticks slower. Both effects are real and both have been measured. For everyday gravity — a thrown ball, a falling apple, you standing on the ground — what does each of the two halves actually contribute?
answer: The warping of time — the warping of space adds very little.
choices: The warping of time — the warping of space adds very little.
The warping of space — the warping of time adds very little.
The warping of time and of space, in roughly equal measure.
The warping of space when a body moves, of time when it rests.
context: The classroom rubber sheet, dented into a funnel by a bowling ball, is a picture of bent space — and Kelly Foyle and Philip Freeman call that the analogy's worst failure, because the sheet shows the small effect and hides the big one: 'almost all our everyday experiences of gravity (i.e. throwing a ball or being stuck to the Earth) are due to the warping of TIME in general relativity and not the warping of space. The warping of time gives us essentially Newton's gravity, while the effect of curvature of space is quite small and makes a difference only in extreme cases, such as the discrepancy in the precession of Mercury's orbit.' Nor does the split depend on whether the object happens to be moving: an object sitting still is still travelling through time, and that is the direction the curvature bends. The space curvature is real, though, and it has been caught: a radio signal from the Cassini spacecraft passing close to the Sun in 2002 arrived late, because there was genuinely further to go, pinning the space-curvature parameter to general relativity's value within about 20 parts per million. Source: K. Foyle & P. Freeman, OAPT Newsletter, 23 November 2020; Grokipedia, 'Tests of general relativity'.

question: Set air resistance aside. A person who has just stepped off a diving board is, in general relativity, following a geodesic — the straightest path available through curved spacetime, travelled with no force acting and no acceleration at all. That leaves an awkward question about the person sitting still in the poolside chair. What is happening to them?
answer: They are being shoved off that straightest path by the chair.
choices: They are being shoved off that straightest path by the chair.
They are following an even straighter path through spacetime.
They are held motionless by the Earth's gravitational pull.
They are being pulled down and pushed up in perfect balance.
context: Foyle and Freeman put it plainly: 'Setting aside air friction, a falling object experiences no forces at all and follows a straightest line path through curved spacetime,' while 'the chair is constantly pushing you away from a straightest line path through spacetime.' That is why the falling person feels nothing at all — the sensation you call your weight is the chair, the floor or the ground interrupting a free fall. It is also why the curvature has to be in spacetime and not in space alone. Drop three balls off a cliff, one released from rest and two thrown horizontally at different speeds: the two thrown balls start off in the same direction in space but land at different distances, and the dropped ball has no direction of motion at all yet still falls. One strip of tape on a curved sheet cannot produce three different paths. Only a spacetime picture can, because even the ball released from rest is still travelling through time. Source: K. Foyle & P. Freeman, OAPT Newsletter, 23 November 2020.

question: Isaac Newton was uneasy about his own gravity: a force reaching instantly across empty space, touching nothing on the way. In a 1690 letter to Christiaan Huygens, Nicolas Fatio de Duillier proposed a replacement, and Georges-Louis Le Sage arrived at the same idea independently in 1748. Physicists took it seriously for two hundred years. How did they say gravity worked?
answer: Unseen corpuscles stream in from all sides, and bodies shade one another.
choices: Unseen corpuscles stream in from all sides, and bodies shade one another.
Whirlpools of fine matter sweep bodies along, and planets ride the swirl.
An ether presses on all bodies, and thins in the gap between any two.
The distant stars fix each body's inertia, and heaviness follows from it.
context: Le Sage called the streams 'ultramundane corpuscles' — arriving from beyond the known world, from every direction at once. Two bodies each block a little of the rain falling on the other, so each is pushed into the other's shadow: gravity as a shove from outside rather than a tug from within. Serious people argued over it for two centuries. James Clerk Maxwell, and later Henri Poincare, killed it by working out that the collisions would heat the Earth by something like 10^26 degrees every second. The rival accounts were real too. Isaac Newton's Principia (1687) made gravity a force acting instantly across any distance — which sits badly with a universe where nothing outruns light. Mach's principle held that inertia is defined relative to all the mass in the universe. What finally replaced them all is the sentence John Archibald Wheeler wrote with Kenneth Ford in Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics (1998, p. 235): 'Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.' Nothing in that sentence pulls on anything. Source: Grokipedia, 'General relativity' and 'Equivalence principle'; Wikipedia, 'Le Sage's theory of gravitation'; J. A. Wheeler with Kenneth Ford, Geons, Black Holes, and Quantum Foam: A Life in Physics (1998), p. 235.

question: From 1946 to 1948, US Public Health Service doctors ran a study in Guatemala on 1,308 prisoners, soldiers, psychiatric patients and sex workers. What made this a category apart from the Tuskegee study?
answer: The researchers gave the subjects the disease on purpose, through infected partners and inoculation
choices: The researchers gave the subjects the disease on purpose, through infected partners and inoculation
The researchers withheld a working cure from subjects who already had the disease
The researchers paid the subjects to hide a positive diagnosis from their own families
The researchers recorded symptoms in secret and never admitted subjects to a hospital
context: Tuskegee (1932-1972) followed 399 Black men in Alabama who ALREADY had syphilis and were left untreated. Guatemala INFECTED healthy people on purpose - through arranged contact with infected sex workers, scarification of the skin, and direct injection. The distinction is the whole point of the ladder: withheld vs. gave. Source: Presidential Commission for the Study of Bioethical Issues, 'Ethically Impossible: STD Research in Guatemala from 1946 to 1948' (September 2011).

question: From 1946 to 1948, twenty-three Nazi doctors stood in the dock at Nuremberg for lethal camp experiments; the verdict laid down a ten-point code that a whole profession would live by. What single requirement does the first point of that code make of every human research study?
answer: The voluntary, informed consent of every human subject before enrollment
choices: The voluntary, informed consent of every human subject before enrollment
A written approval from an independent ethics board before enrollment
The right of any subject to a copy of their own medical records
A ban on any experiment that carries any risk of death to a subject
context: This is the opening line of the Nuremberg Code, delivered in the verdict of the Doctors' Trial in August 1947: 'The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.' In exactly those same years, the Guatemala researchers were inoculating captive people who could not consent. Amy Gutmann's later Bioethics Commission noted that some Guatemala researchers said at the time 'we could not do this in our own country' - they knew. Independent ethics-board review came later (US IRBs via the 1974 National Research Act); a subject's right to their own records is a records-law question, not a Nuremberg point; and Nuremberg does NOT ban all risk of death - it requires that risk be proportionate and that the subject consent.

question: The Guatemala study stayed buried for 62 years after the last subject was inoculated. In 2010 the whole file finally came to light. Who opened the box, and where was it sitting?
answer: A Wellesley medical historian, reading the director's own donated papers at the University of Pittsburgh
choices: A Wellesley medical historian, reading the director's own donated papers at the University of Pittsburgh
A Justice Department lawyer, subpoenaing sealed Public Health Service records in Washington
A Guatemalan journalist, tracing a survivor's family medical file back to the original clinic
A State Department archivist, cataloguing declassified 1940s diplomatic cables from Central America
context: Susan M. Reverby was researching Tuskegee. John C. Cutler had directed the Guatemala study AND later worked on Tuskegee; he donated his papers to the University of Pittsburgh, where he was a faculty member, and died in 2003. Reverby read the Guatemala records in his own file, presented findings in January 2010, and the story broke that autumn. President Obama and Secretary Clinton apologized to Guatemala on 1 October 2010; the 2011 Bioethics Commission report was titled 'Ethically Impossible.' The record survived because a dead man donated his own crime to a university library, and a scholar with a library card opened the box.

question: In 1705 Edmond Halley published a book on comets in which he compared the paths of the bright comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 and reached one bold conclusion. What did he claim about those three apparitions?
answer: They were the same object returning about every 76 years
choices: They were the same object returning about every 76 years
They were three fragments of a single shattered world
They were harmless streaks in the upper atmosphere
They were signals sent by a nearby unseen star
context: Halley's Synopsis Astronomia Cometicae (1705) compiled 24 comet observations; he used Newton's gravity to argue the 1531, 1607, and 1682 comets shared an orbit, and predicted the next return for 1758. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: Edmond Halley predicted in 1705 that the comet he had traced through three apparitions would return in 1758. He never saw the appointment kept -- because of what?
answer: He had died in 1742, sixteen years before it came back
choices: He had died in 1742, sixteen years before it came back
He had gone blind by the year of his prediction
He was on a ship and clouds hid the sky for weeks
He was exiled to Prussia and forbidden to observe
context: Halley died in 1742, well before the 1758-9 return. The French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille later attached his name to the comet in 1759. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: In November 1758 Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute told the Paris Academy how far Jupiter and Saturn would delay Halley's comet. They named mid-April 1759 for perihelion and stated their uncertainty openly. About how big a window did they admit their answer might be off by?
answer: About a month
choices: About a month
About three days
About half a year
About two full years
context: Clairaut reported to the Academy on 14 November 1758 that the giant planets would delay the comet by about 618 days, giving a perihelion of mid-April 1759 with a stated month of uncertainty. It arrived 13 March 1759 -- a month early, and inside the declared error. Teaching error bars without the word. Source: cosmosmagazine.com/science/mathematics/the-comet-calculator-nicole-reine-lepaute/

question: Clairaut's team told the Paris Academy in November 1758 that Halley's comet would reach the Sun around mid-April 1759, and astronomers across Europe began sweeping the winter sky for it. On Christmas night, 25 December 1758, a Saxon amateur near Dresden picked it up first. What did he do for a living?
answer: He was a farmer with a homemade telescope
choices: He was a farmer with a homemade telescope
He was a Lutheran organist and part-time engraver
He was a schoolmaster's assistant in a village outside Dresden
He was a wandering surveyor for the Saxon mines
context: Johann Georg Palitzsch (1723-1788) recovered the comet on the night of 25 December 1758 -- the first sighting of a comet whose return had been predicted. Charles Messier picked it up independently in January 1759. Source: blogs.otago.ac.nz/emxphi/halleys-comet-and-christmas-day/

question: In March 1986 ESA's Giotto probe flew close enough to the nucleus of Halley's comet to photograph it. The bright thing in the sky is gas and dust boiled off a lump of ice and rock about 15 by 8 by 8 kilometres. How reflective is that lump?
answer: It reflects only about 4 per cent of the light hitting it -- darker than coal
choices: It reflects only about 4 per cent of the light hitting it -- darker than coal
It reflects about 60 per cent -- close to fresh snow
It reflects about 25 per cent -- roughly the colour of dry sand
It reflects almost none, because the surface glows red-hot
context: Giotto's cameras showed a peanut-shaped nucleus roughly 14.4 x 7.4 x 7.4 km with an albedo near 0.04. The glowing 'comet' is the coma -- sunlight scattering off gas and dust the dark nucleus sheds when the Sun warms it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: Halley's comet swept past the Sun in 1986, but the show from Earth was faint because Earth and the comet were on opposite sides of the Sun at perihelion. The next return on 28 July 2061 is expected to be far brighter. What geometry makes the 2061 pass a good one?
answer: Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet at perihelion, close and lit
choices: Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet at perihelion, close and lit
A close pass by Jupiter has shortened the comet's period by several years
The nucleus has grown by accreting material in the outer solar system
The comet will pass inside Earth's orbit for the first time on record
context: In 1986 the comet reached perihelion on the far side of the Sun from Earth, making it one of the poorest apparitions on record. On 28 July 2061 Earth will be on the same side of the Sun as the comet, so the fully sunlit coma will be much closer and much brighter. The nucleus does not grow between passes -- it loses mass each perihelion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

question: Yuval Noah Harari took an Oxford doctorate in 2002 and still teaches at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, but the world knows him for Sapiens (2011) and Homo Deus (2016), which sold tens of millions of copies. What academic field was he actually trained in?
answer: Medieval and military history
choices: Medieval and military history
Molecular neuroscience
Development economics
Comparative literature
context: His doctoral thesis was on Renaissance military memoirs, c. 1450 to 1600, and he won the Society for Military History's Moncado Award for outstanding articles in 2011. A historian became a futurist; the bank keeps the distinction. Source: Wikipedia 'Yuval Noah Harari'; Hebrew University faculty page.

question: In an essay published on 24 February 2017 and drawn from his book Homo Deus, Yuval Noah Harari coined a name for a coming category of people. Not merely without jobs, in his words, but without the possibility of one. What did he call them?
answer: The useless class
choices: The useless class
The surplus workers
The idle citizens
The forgotten majority
context: Harari's essay 'The rise of the useless class' ran at ideas.ted.com and paraphrased a passage from Homo Deus. He presented it as a danger to head off, not a policy to enact. Source: ideas.ted.com, 24 February 2017.

question: In Homo Deus, Yuval Noah Harari gives his 'useless class' a verbatim definition, listing three kinds of worth it will lack. Which three does he name?
answer: Economic, political or artistic
choices: Economic, political or artistic
Personal, familial or spiritual
Genetic, moral or educational
Cognitive, physical or emotional
context: Full quote: 'people devoid of any economic, political or even artistic value, who contribute nothing to the prosperity, power and glory of society.' Every noun measures output. The bank shows the sentence and lets the kid decide what to make of the vocabulary. Source: Homo Deus (2016).

question: In Homo Deus, Yuval Noah Harari sets one question as, in his words, 'the most important question in 21st-century economics'. It begins 'What should we do with all the ____ people, once we have highly intelligent non-conscious algorithms that can do almost everything better than humans?' Fill the blank.
answer: Superfluous
choices: Superfluous
Redundant
Displaced
Discarded
context: 'What should we do with all the superfluous people...' - the language of surplus applied to human beings. Harari says he is warning; his critics answer that the choice of word is itself the turn, whatever the intent. Source: Homo Deus (2016).

question: Speaking about liberal democracy at a public talk, Yuval Noah Harari argued the whole system rests on ideas from a particular earlier century - and, in his words, 'especially the idea of free will' - which he thinks was a useful approximation now expiring. WHICH century's ideas did he name as the ones the system rests on?
answer: The eighteenth century
choices: The eighteenth century
The sixteenth century
The nineteenth century
The twentieth century
context: Harari's claim is not that free will is real or unreal; it is that BELIEVING in it was, until now, a practical shortcut for treating humans as too complicated to decipher. Source: Harari public talks and interviews on liberal democracy and big data.

question: Yuval Noah Harari insists his warnings are things he is describing, not endorsing. On the record, his critics answer that the DECISIVE turn is not in his conclusions but in his word choices. Which family of words do those critics point to?
answer: The vocabulary of surplus inventory
choices: The vocabulary of surplus inventory
The language of technocratic determinism
The framing of humans as data
The rhetoric of inevitability
context: Both readings are on the record and the bank lets the reader judge. Critics argue that words like 'superfluous' and 'useless' pre-decide how the reader learns to see the people so labelled, however the framing is presented. Source: reviews and criticism collected on Harari's Wikipedia page and Brownstone Institute article.

question: On a dark October night in 1707, a British fleet under Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell drove full sail into the rocks of the Isles of Scilly. Four warships were lost and estimates of the dead run from 1,400 to over 2,000 sailors. What piece of navigation had the fleet gotten catastrophically wrong?
answer: Their longitude, so they did not know how far west they were
choices: Their longitude, so they did not know how far west they were
Their latitude, so they did not know how far north they were
Their compass declination, so all their bearings were rotated
Their depth soundings, so they missed a rising shoal
context: The sailing masters believed themselves safely out at sea. In fact the fleet had drifted much farther east than dead reckoning could tell them. The disaster gave political weight to the campaign that produced the Longitude Act. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scilly_naval_disaster_of_1707.

question: Seven years after the Scilly disaster, Parliament put a bounty on the longitude problem: 20,000 pounds, the equivalent of many millions in today's money, enough to make a working man rich for life. What accuracy did the 1714 Longitude Act demand of a method to earn that full prize?
answer: Within half a degree, tested by a voyage to the West Indies
choices: Within half a degree, tested by a voyage to the West Indies
Within one degree, tested by a voyage across the English Channel
Within one minute of arc, tested by any voyage in European waters
Within one nautical mile, tested by a voyage around the world
context: The 1714 Longitude Act set 20,000 pounds for a method accurate to half a degree after a West Indies voyage, with smaller graduated prizes for coarser methods. The full 20,000-pound sum was never officially paid out to anyone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison.

question: The trick a good clock buys a navigator has nothing to do with speed and everything to do with time. If a captain carries a timekeeper still set to home port, and he watches the Sun peak where he stands, the difference between the two clocks tells him how far around the world he has come. How much longitude does one hour of that difference correspond to?
answer: 15 degrees of longitude
choices: 15 degrees of longitude
1 degree of longitude
60 degrees of longitude
One full time zone regardless of latitude
context: The Earth turns 360 degrees every 24 hours, so 15 degrees an hour, or one degree every four minutes. A kid with a wristwatch left on home time and a stick's shortest shadow can find her own longitude by this rule. Source: explorersweb.com/longitude-john-harrison.

question: So why not just hand the captain a good land clock and be done? Even the finest pendulum timekeepers of 1720 fell apart at sea for one plain physical reason. What ruined the pendulum?
answer: A pitching deck disturbed its swing on every wave
choices: A pitching deck disturbed its swing on every wave
Salt air rusted the case shut within one Atlantic crossing
Sailing near the poles weakened gravity below what the pendulum needed
The iron of the ship's hull magnetized the escape wheel
context: A pendulum needs a still, level base and a constant swing length; a ship offers neither. Christiaan Huygens' 1660s sea-going pendulum trials had failed for exactly this reason two generations earlier. Source: hautehorlogerie.org/en/watches-and-culture/watchmaking-knowledge/encyclopedia/john-harrison.

question: John Harrison came to horology by an odd route: he was a self-taught Yorkshire joiner from a village with no watchmaking tradition at all. His earliest movements did something no London workshop would have dreamed of. What was strange about the very gears inside them?
answer: They were cut from lignum vitae, an oily tropical wood that lubricates itself
choices: They were cut from lignum vitae, an oily tropical wood that lubricates itself
They were made from boxwood pinions, cut on a lathe and greased with beeswax
They were carved from close-grained European oak, soaked in linseed oil against swelling
They were cast from bell bronze salvaged from village churches
context: Clock oils of the 18th century thickened in cold and thinned in heat, throwing off rates. Harrison sidestepped the problem by choosing a wood whose own natural oils let it run dry, with no added lubricant at all. Some of his early Barrow-on-Humber tower clocks still keep time today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison; momentousbritain.co.uk/go/John_Harrison.

question: In 1761 the Royal Navy carried H4 to Jamaica aboard HMS Deptford for its official trial. The voyage took 81 days. When they checked the watch against local astronomical time on arrival, how far off had it run?
answer: About five seconds slow, roughly one nautical mile of longitude
choices: About five seconds slow, roughly one nautical mile of longitude
About five minutes fast, roughly sixty nautical miles of longitude
About one full hour fast, roughly 900 miles of longitude
It had stopped entirely on the fourth week
context: The rules demanded accuracy to half a degree, or 30 nautical miles. H4 came in more than 60 times better than that. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison.

question: H4 had crushed its Jamaica trial. When Harrison came to the Board of Longitude expecting his prize, what did the Board actually do?
answer: They called the result a lucky one and demanded a second sea trial
choices: They called the result a lucky one and demanded a second sea trial
They paid the prize but forbade the design to be copied
They awarded the money to the Astronomer Royal Nevil Maskelyne
They referred the whole question to the French Academie des Sciences
context: A second trial to Barbados in 1764 was as good or better. The Board still balked, arguing that one handmade watch, six years in the building, was not yet a reproducible method. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison; barringtonwatchwinders.com.

question: The record on the 20,000-pound Longitude Prize itself is often told wrong. What actually happened to that particular sum?
answer: It was never officially awarded to anyone
choices: It was never officially awarded to anyone
It was paid to Harrison in full in 1765 after the Barbados trial
It was split between Harrison and Maskelyne in 1773
It was awarded to Larcum Kendall for his working copies of H4
context: In 1773, at age 80, Harrison received 8,750 pounds by a separate act of Parliament, after his son's appeal reached King George III, who had personally tested H5 at Kew for ten weeks. The original Longitude Act prize went unclaimed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harrison.

question: Tie a band around your upper arm and let the arm hang. The veins of your forearm rise into ropes, and along each rope sit small firm knots that were not there before. William Harvey put this trick in his book so that any reader could run it on himself, no knife needed. What is each knot?
answer: A valve set inside the vein
choices: A valve set inside the vein
A gland that filters the blood
A muscle that pinches the vein
A swelling where two veins join
context: Harvey's next step, Chapter 13: press a finger on the vein just below a knot and stroke the blood away toward your hand. That stretch stays empty, while above the knot the vein is well distended; lift the finger and it refills at once. He chose this demonstration because a reader needed no corpse and no scalpel to check him. Source: Robert Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. XIII (1628 text).

question: Following Galen of Pergamon, European physicians taught for fourteen centuries that blood was never recycled: the body manufactured it fresh, all day long, out of the food just digested, sent it out along the veins, and let the flesh soak it up and consume it. Which organ did they name as the factory?
answer: The liver
choices: The liver
The heart
The spleen
The stomach
context: In Galen's picture the liver turned chyle absorbed from the gut into blood and charged it there with 'natural spirit', and the veins carried it one way to the parts, which used it up. That is why a Galenist felt no need for a return trip: nothing came back, because nothing was left. Source: 'Galen and the beginnings of Western physiology', Am. J. Physiol. Lung Cell Mol. Physiol.

question: Galen's system had a problem in the middle of the heart: blood had to cross from the right chamber into the left, and the wall between them is thick muscle. For fourteen centuries anatomists taught one confident answer to that difficulty. How did they teach that the blood made that crossing?
answer: Seeped through pores in the wall too fine to see
choices: Seeped through pores in the wall too fine to see
Travelled out through the lungs and back again
Was carried across by the beating of the wall
Was made fresh in the left chamber out of air
context: Nobody ever saw those pores, because the wall (the interventricular septum) is solid. Blood really does cross by going out through the lungs and back — the pulmonary transit, described by Ibn al-Nafis in the 13th century, by Michael Servetus in 1553 inside a book of theology, and by Realdo Colombo in 1559. None of the three saw the full body-wide circuit. Sources: Am. J. Physiol. Lung Cell Mol. Physiol., 'Galen and the beginnings of Western physiology'; J. Appl. Physiol., 'Ibn al-Nafis, the pulmonary circulation, and the Islamic Golden Age'.

question: Frankfurt, 1628. The bookseller William Fitzer took William Harvey's 72-page Latin manuscript to a licensed printing shop. It came back so badly set that the shop bound in an errata leaf — the page where a printer lists his own misprints — running to 126 corrections in the book that would end fourteen centuries of Galen. The craftsmen were mediocre, but Harvey had made it worse. What was his share of the fault?
answer: His handwriting, cramped and atrocious
choices: His handwriting, cramped and atrocious
His Latin, crammed with new coinages
His revisions, sent in after typesetting
His hurry, pressing the shop to finish
context: Fitzer had eight licensed shops in Frankfurt to choose from, and by one historian's judgement all of them were mediocre craftsmen; the book came out on thin, unsightly paper in poor type. But the misprints came chiefly from Harvey's hand, which the same historian calls 'atrocious, crabbed' — cramped, jammed together, hard for a compositor to read. The result: 126 corrections for 72 pages, nearly two to a page. The book that ended Galen's fourteen centuries came into the world as a cheap, typo-riddled pamphlet. Sources: 'William Harvey's Anatomy Book and Literary Culture', PMC2175066; Worcester College Library, 'One of the two greatest books of seventeenth-century science'.

question: William Harvey named the creatures that taught him the most: 'toads, frogs, serpents, small fishes, crabs, shrimps, snails, and shell-fish.' Their hearts beat slowly enough for him to follow one whole beat with the naked eye, and he caught a change a warm-blooded heart moves far too fast to show. What did the heart do at the instant it squeezed?
answer: It turned paler than when it lay at rest
choices: It turned paler than when it lay at rest
It turned a deeper red than when at rest
It swelled a little but held its colour
It darkened only where the great veins entered
context: In fishes and other cold-blooded animals Harvey saw the heart go paler as it moved and deepen to blood-red as it rested. The slow beat gave him something else as well: he could separate the squeeze of the small upper chamber (the auricle, today called the atrium) from the squeeze of the big lower one (the ventricle) — in a warm-blooded animal the whole sequence is gone in an instant. Source: Robert Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. II.

question: William Harvey opened the left ventricle of a corpse and found it held two or three ounces when full. He allowed that only a fraction of that leaves with each beat — a fourth, a fifth, perhaps only an eighth. Then he counted the pulse: more than a thousand beats in half an hour. He multiplied the ounces by the beats. What did his half-hour total come to?
answer: More blood than the entire body contains
choices: More blood than the entire body contains
About a tenth of what the body contains
Rather less than the liver makes in a day
About what a man loses in a mortal wound
context: Harvey's own line, in Willis's translation: 'Multiplying the number of drachms propelled by the number of pulses, we shall have either one thousand half ounces, or one thousand times three drachms... sent from this organ into the artery — a larger quantity in every case than is contained in the whole body!' The Latin gives five hundred ounces in half an hour. CORRECTION WORTH KNOWING: the famous '540 pounds an hour' in modern textbooks is NOT Harvey's figure. It comes from later writers assuming two ounces a beat at 72 beats a minute; Harvey used about thirty-three beats a minute and half an ounce at most, and his punchline was a comparison, not a weight. Sources: Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. IX (Fordham Modern History Sourcebook); Latin text, Truman State University.

question: William Harvey bound a band around a volunteer's upper arm, as tight as the man could bear: below it the pulse died away and the hand went cool and pale. Then Harvey eased the band to a middling tightness — snug now, but no longer choking the arm — and watched. What did the forearm and hand below it do?
answer: They swelled and turned warm to the touch
choices: They swelled and turned warm to the touch
They swelled harder but stayed cold and pale
They stayed slack while the swelling rose above
They stayed cold and slack until the band came off
context: The tight band shut everything, deep arteries included, so the hand below it went cool and pale while the arm above stayed warm and full. The middling band still let the arteries — which lie deeper and push harder — force blood in, while the surface veins stayed pinched shut, so blood piled into the forearm and could not get out: warm, swollen, the veins engorged. Blood arrives by artery and leaves by vein, and release the band and the veins empty in the direction of the heart, not the hand. Sources: De Motu Cordis ch. XI; James Lind Library review of Harvey's experimentation.

question: Harvey did not discover the valves in the veins. His own teacher at Padua, Hieronymus Fabricius, had published life-size engravings of them in 1603, a quarter of a century before De Motu Cordis, and had even shown that a finger pressed on a bound vein made them act. Fabricius simply read them as doing a different job. What did he think the valves were for?
answer: Holding the blood back so each part got an even share
choices: Holding the blood back so each part got an even share
Squeezing the blood onward, like pumps in the wall
Straining impurities out of the blood as it passed
Sealing the vein shut wherever it had been wounded
context: Fabricius published them as De Venarum Ostiolis (Padua, 1603), with copperplate engravings, and read their purpose as retarding the blood so it would be distributed evenly to the parts. Harvey asked the different question — not what they do, but what they are FOR — and saw that a one-way gate only makes sense if the traffic is one-way, toward the heart. Sources: Britannica, 'De Venarum Ostiolis'; Nature 135, 567 (1935) review of Franklin's facsimile.

question: William Harvey laid open a living snake — a cold-blooded creature whose heart beat slowly enough to watch stroke by stroke — and took hold of the great trunk vein, the vena cava. He pinched it shut. What did he see in the seconds that followed?
answer: The heart and the aorta both drained and went pale
choices: The heart and the aorta both drained and went pale
The heart swelled dark while the aorta went pale
The heart and the aorta both swelled and darkened
The heart paled while the aorta stayed full and dark
context: The vena cava is the trunk that carries blood back to the heart; the aorta is the great artery leading out of it. Harvey then moved the pinch to the aorta instead and got the opposite result: the heart swelled and became engorged. Two pinches, two opposite results — blood comes in by one door and leaves by the other. Source: De Motu Cordis ch. X, summarised in Revista Argentina de Cardiologia, 'William Harvey (IV) De Motu Cordis'.

question: Harvey's circuit needed one link he could never point to: somewhere in the body's tissue, blood had to pass from the smallest arteries into the smallest veins. Chapter 7 of De Motu Cordis is where he faces that gap, and he spends a single phrase on it. What did he write?
answer: That it passed through hidden porosities, as fluid seeps through a kidney
choices: That it passed through hidden porosities, as fluid seeps through a kidney
That vessels too fine for the eye must join the arteries to the veins
That the flesh drank the blood up and then passed it on to the veins
That the heart's force drove the blood clean through the solid tissue
context: His Latin is 'pulmonum caecas porositates' — the hidden porosities of the lungs — with 'the minute inosculations of vessels', compared to fluid seeping through a kidney or a liver. He did not predict the capillaries and did not name them; he marked the hole in his own argument and left it open, which is what an honest case looks like. Sources: Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. VII; J. Appl. Physiol., 'Historical Perspective: Harvey's epoch-making discovery of the Circulation'.

question: William Harvey died on 3 June 1657 with the last link of his circuit still unfound. Four years later Marcello Malpighi turned a microscope on the lung of a living frog — and the living lung defeated him: he could see blood moving through vessels far finer than the eye can resolve, but he could not follow them to their ends. What did Malpighi do next?
answer: He dried the lung and traced the network in the dead tissue
choices: He dried the lung and traced the network in the dead tissue
He injected coloured wax and cut the dried lung into slices
He ground a stronger lens and watched the living lung again
He compared the frog's lung against the lung of a drowned dog
context: What he mapped were the capillaries — thin-walled vessels joining the smallest arteries to the smallest veins — published in 1661 as De pulmonibus observationes anatomicae. Harvey's circuit was closed four years after his death, by an instrument he never owned. Sources: 'Marcello Malpighi and the Discovery of the Pulmonary Capillaries and Alveoli' (Thoracic Key / Int. J. Cardiol.); '1661 in science'.

question: John Aubrey knew William Harvey personally, and set down what Harvey told him about the years after De Motu Cordis appeared in 1628 — 72 pages of Latin arguing that the blood runs a circuit and comes back to the heart it left. What did Aubrey record that publishing it cost him?
answer: His patients left him, and men thought him crack-brained
choices: His patients left him, and men thought him crack-brained
His fellow physicians barred him from the College's lectures
His pupils deserted him, and studied under a rival
His rivals printed a book naming him a butcher
context: Aubrey, in Brief Lives: 'I have heard him say, that after his book of the circulation of the blood came out, that he fell mightily in his practice, and that 'twas believed by the vulgar that he was crack-brained; and all the physicians were against his opinion.' Physicians of the period were long reported to have said they would 'rather err with Galen than proclaim the truth with Harvey' — a saying repeated for centuries with no named speaker behind it, so take it as tradition, not as testimony. General acceptance took roughly twenty years; Thomas Hobbes remarked that Harvey was the only modern author whose doctrine was established in his own lifetime. Sources: John Aubrey, Brief Lives (Internet Archive); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey.

question: Harvey could not measure exactly how much blood the left ventricle throws out with each squeeze, and he said so plainly. In Chapter 9 he offers a range — a fourth of the chamber, a fifth, a sixth, 'or even but the eighth part' — and then runs the whole calculation on the smallest figure in that range, and on a stingy guess for the chamber's size as well. Why build the argument on his own lowest numbers?
answer: Because a total impossible even at the lowest guess cannot be argued down
choices: Because a total impossible even at the lowest guess cannot be argued down
Because the lowest guess was the one Galen's followers already granted
Because a lower total stayed within what the liver was thought to make
Because the lowest guess was the only figure he had actually weighed
context: Harvey ran the same sum on animals with the same deliberate stinginess: allow only a single scruple per beat in a sheep or a dog, and half an hour still throws about three and a half pounds into the aorta — while the whole animal holds not above four pounds. An argument built on your opponent's most favourable assumptions is one he cannot rescue by haggling over the measurement. Source: Robert Willis translation of De Motu Cordis ch. IX (Fordham Modern History Sourcebook).

question: The Chinese researcher who announced the first gene-edited human babies in November 2018 gave the twin girls pseudonyms to protect their identity. What are the pseudonyms the world now knows them by?
answer: Lulu and Nana
choices: Lulu and Nana
Lily and Rose
Yin and Yang
Ada and Grace
context: A third gene-edited child, given the pseudonym Amy, was born the following year. The researcher was He Jiankui of Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen. Source: sciencealert.com, 'China Quietly Confirms a Third CRISPR-Edited Baby'.

question: He Jiankui aimed his CRISPR edit at a single named gene -- the one whose product sits on a T cell's surface and serves as the doorway most strains of HIV use to get inside. Some people are born with a mutation that inactivates it and are highly resistant to HIV. Which gene was the target?
answer: CCR5
choices: CCR5
CXCR4
TP53
BRCA1
context: He was copying the natural CCR5-delta-32 variant. Even a perfect knockout only blocks R5-tropic HIV strains; X4-tropic strains use a different co-receptor (CXCR4) and would go around the edit entirely. Source: academic.oup.com/jlb/article/6/1/111.

question: He Jiankui justified his experiment by pointing out that the twins' father was HIV-positive. Bioethicists and IVF doctors answered that an ordinary existing procedure had already made father-to-child transmission essentially a non-issue for serodiscordant couples. Which procedure had quietly done that job?
answer: Sperm washing before fertilization
choices: Sperm washing before fertilization
PrEP for the mother during conception attempts
Timed intercourse during the father's undetectable viral load
IVF using donor sperm from an HIV-negative donor
context: Sperm washing separates HIV particles from the sperm before IVF and has been standard practice for decades in HIV-serodiscordant couples. He was editing healthy embryos against a risk ordinary medicine had already solved. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_washing.

question: He Jiankui set out to reproduce the natural protective mutation CCR5-delta-32 -- a specific 32-base-pair deletion many people inherit. When the twins were sequenced, what actually came out?
answer: Brand-new mutations no one had ever studied in humans
choices: Brand-new mutations no one had ever studied in humans
A clean copy of the delta-32 deletion on both alleles
The delta-32 deletion on one allele in each girl only
No detectable edit on either allele in either girl
context: Lulu ended up heterozygous: one normal CCR5 and one carrying a 15-base-pair in-frame deletion. Nana had a 4-base-pair deletion on one allele and a single-base insertion on the other. Those variants are not found in nature; their consequences are unknown -- and the girls can pass them on. Source: Kiran Musunuru thread; journals.plos.org, 'Gene-edited babies: what went wrong'.

question: On November 28, 2018, three days after his YouTube announcement, He Jiankui walked onstage at the Second International Summit on Human Genome Editing at the University of Hong Kong and defended his work before a hall of about seven hundred colleagues. In their formal statement, how did the summit's own organizers describe what he had done?
answer: Unexpected and deeply disturbing
choices: Unexpected and deeply disturbing
A courageous first step in a hard field
Regrettable but scientifically defensible
Consistent with international norms
context: The condemnation was near-universal, but the language mattered: the objection was not to gene editing as such, it was to secrecy, invalid consent, and untested edits on healthy embryos who cannot consent for themselves or their descendants. Source: hongkongfp.com, 'Hong Kong conference slams deeply disturbing baby gene-editing claim by Chinese scientist'.

question: On December 30, 2019, the Nanshan District People's Court of Shenzhen sentenced He Jiankui to three years in prison and a three-million-yuan fine. The Chinese state did not need to invent a new gene-editing statute for the conviction. Under what existing charge did the court actually convict him?
answer: Illegal practice of medicine
choices: Illegal practice of medicine
Endangering public safety by dangerous means
Fraud in scientific research grants
Producing counterfeit pharmaceuticals
context: He and two colleagues, Zhang Renli and Qin Jinzhou, were also banned for life from reproductive medicine. He was released from prison around April 2022. Source: science.org, 'Chinese scientist who produced genetically altered babies sentenced to 3 years in jail'.

question: The volunteer parents in He Jiankui's project signed a consent form that struck bioethicists as a warning sign in itself. It dressed pressure up as paperwork. What did the form threaten a couple with if they tried to withdraw after embryo implantation?
answer: Repayment of all project costs, with fines for late payment
choices: Repayment of all project costs, with fines for late payment
Loss of legal custody of any resulting children
Public disclosure of their HIV-positive status
A ten-year ban from all fertility clinics in China
context: The form also described the study as an 'AIDS vaccine development project' rather than as germline editing. The people who could not consent at all, of course, were Lulu, Nana and Amy -- no future form can fix that. Source: scienceretractions.wordpress.com, 'Why is He Jiankui in real trouble'; PMC, 'Informed Consent for Human Embryo Genome Editing'.

question: The near-universal scientific condemnation of He Jiankui's work was not the slogan 'gene editing is evil'. Keeping the specific objections separate is what lets the field distinguish this case from legitimate therapeutic editing. Which set of four charges did the field actually lay against the experiment?
answer: Untested, medically unnecessary, no real consent, heritable
choices: Untested, medically unnecessary, no real consent, heritable
Illegal in China, illegal in the US, unprofitable, unpublished
Wrong gene, wrong strain of HIV, wrong clinic, wrong country
Off-target cuts, mosaicism, viral contamination, cell death
context: Therapeutic gene editing on consenting adults -- Casgevy for sickle-cell in 2023, CAR-T therapies, Luxturna for inherited blindness -- meets exactly the tests He failed: real disease, real consent, tested first, not heritable. That distinction is why the field could praise those treatments in the same decade it condemned him. Source: theconversation.com, 'Tension as scientist at centre of CRISPR outrage speaks at genome editing summit'.

question: On 15 August 1977 the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State University printed out a narrow burst of radio waves so far above the background noise that when the astronomer Jerry Ehman read the paper printout a few days later, he circled the burst in red pen and wrote a single word beside it. That word became the signal's name. What word did he write?
answer: Wow!
choices: Wow!
Bingo!
Aha!
Voila!
context: Ehman was working on a SETI survey and had gone home for the weekend when the burst came in; the paper was already several days old when he saw it. His marginalium is still on the original printout at the Ohio History Connection. See https://www.bigear.org/wow.htm

question: The characters Jerry Ehman circled on the Big Ear printout were '6EQUJ5'. The string is famous, and it is often misdescribed as a coded message from the sender. What is it actually?
answer: A record of how loud the signal was, one character every 12 seconds as it rose and fell
choices: A record of how loud the signal was, one character every 12 seconds as it rose and fell
A frequency stamp, six numbers reading the tuning of the receiver over the burst
A sky coordinate, giving the right ascension and declination of the source in the printout
A checksum the Big Ear computer produced to certify the burst was not receiver noise
context: Big Ear rated the signal in each 12-second window on a scale where numerals and then letters climb: '1' was the smallest bin above the background, 'U' was near the top. The 'U' in '6EQUJ5' marks a peak about thirty times the background noise. The string carries no content whatsoever. See https://academics.uccs.edu/rtirado/PES_1100/wow.pdf

question: The Wow! signal sat right on 1420 megahertz, a frequency SETI researchers had argued a careful broadcaster would deliberately choose. Why is 1420 MHz the frequency they would pick?
answer: It is the natural radio emission line of neutral hydrogen, the most common atom in the universe
choices: It is the natural radio emission line of neutral hydrogen, the most common atom in the universe
It is the low-noise centre of Earth's atmospheric radio window for ground-based receivers
It is the resonance frequency at which a laboratory maser cavity built by Charles Townes rings
It is the frequency at which the Sun's quiet corona happens to be nearly silent as seen from Earth
context: The 1420 MHz line (21 cm wavelength) is produced by a hyperfine flip in the hydrogen atom. Any species anywhere in the galaxy that studies radio astronomy will know this frequency and will listen there, so it is often called the 'universal calling channel'. That the Wow! sat on it made the coincidence unbearable. See https://www.bigear.org/wow.htm

question: The Wow! signal has never repeated. Ohio State and other observatories, including the Very Large Array in New Mexico, have listened to that patch of sky roughly fifty times since 1977 and heard nothing. In 2017 Antonio Paris published a claim that hydrogen clouds around comets 266P/Christensen and P/2008 Y2 had made the signal. Why did the Ohio State observatory staff reject the claim?
answer: Neither comet was anywhere near the beam's position on 15 August 1977
choices: Neither comet was anywhere near the beam's position on 15 August 1977
Neither comet ever comes closer to the Sun than the orbit of Neptune
The Big Ear beam could not have detected an object as cold as a comet
The Ohio State original data logs had been destroyed and could not be checked
context: The Ohio State observatory staff pointed out that Paris's follow-up observations were taken in 2017 near the modern position of the Wow! source, whereas the comets in question were on very different orbits back in 1977. The bank's rule on this signal is honest: it is UNEXPLAINED. It is neither evidence of aliens nor debunked. See http://naapo.org/WOWCometRebuttal.html

question: In 2007 the astronomer Duncan Lorimer and his undergraduate David Narkevic dug back through 2001 archive tapes from the Parkes telescope in Australia and found a five-millisecond radio blast that briefly outshone almost every other radio object in the sky. Parkes then recorded sixteen more brief bursts, nicknamed 'perytons'. In 2015 a team led by Emily Petroff found where the perytons were coming from. Where?
answer: The observatory's own microwave ovens, leaking a burst when a staff member yanked the door open
choices: The observatory's own microwave ovens, leaking a burst when a staff member yanked the door open
A satellite in geostationary orbit that swept the antenna field at roughly the same time each afternoon
The observatory's electric perimeter fence, arcing whenever a kangaroo touched the wire in summer
A defective magnetron in the telescope's own receiver, misfiring intermittently at 1.4 gigahertz
context: Petroff's team installed a real-time radio-interference monitor at Parkes and caught three perytons in January 2015, each coincident with a signal at 2.3-2.5 GHz, exactly the band used by domestic microwave ovens. Yanking the door open shut the magnetron down mid-cycle, and the shut-down transient leaked out near 1.4 GHz. Feynman's rule earned its keep: check your own kitchen before you announce the universe. See https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-news/microwave-ovens-spark-radio-signals-peryton-05122015/

question: The peryton episode killed the kitchen-burst impostors, but Duncan Lorimer's original 2007 Parkes burst survived the check. It carried a huge DISPERSION MEASURE, far larger than anything the electrons inside our own Milky Way could account for. What did that dispersion measure let the Parkes team argue about the source?
answer: That the burst had come from outside our galaxy, from cosmological distances
choices: That the burst had come from outside our galaxy, from cosmological distances
That the burst had come from a compact object less than a kilometre across
That the burst had been beamed straight at Earth by a rotating source
That the burst had passed through the magnetic field of a nearby neutron star
context: As a radio pulse travels, its lower frequencies drag through the sparse plasma of interstellar space slightly slower than its higher frequencies. Adding up all the electrons crossed gives the 'dispersion measure', which can be turned into a rough distance. Lorimer's burst had a dispersion far higher than any line of sight inside the Milky Way could deliver, so the Parkes team argued the source had to be extragalactic. The perytons, being local, showed no such delay. See https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19106

question: On 28 April 2020, in a single event, a fast radio burst was caught inside our own Milky Way and traced to a known object. That was enough to prove that at least SOME fast radio bursts can be made by a particular type of star. What is the type of star that made FRB 200428?
answer: A magnetar, a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field, catalogued as SGR 1935+2154
choices: A magnetar, a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field, catalogued as SGR 1935+2154
A young pulsar, a rapidly spinning neutron star of the kind Jocelyn Bell Burnell found in 1967
A T Tauri star, a young low-mass star still contracting toward the main sequence
A red dwarf flare star, of the kind that periodically brightens by orders of magnitude
context: SGR 1935+2154 lies about 30,000 light-years away in the Milky Way. Its burst was picked up in the 1.28-1.47 GHz band by the STARE2 array and coincided with an X-ray flare. The result showed magnetars CAN make fast radio bursts. It did not show that magnetars make ALL of them; more than one source population may be out there. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SGR_1935+2154

question: Richard Feynman gave the discipline behind the whole peryton episode its clearest single sentence, in the essay 'Cargo Cult Science' adapted from his 1974 Caltech commencement address. What was the sentence?
answer: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool
choices: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool
For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations
It is our responsibility as scientists to teach how doubt is not to be feared but welcomed
The test of all knowledge is experiment, and experiment is the sole judge of scientific truth
context: All four choices are real Feynman quotes, but only the first is the sentence that opens the 'Cargo Cult' essay. The other three come from the Challenger commission appendix, the Nobel lecture, and 'The Feynman Lectures on Physics' respectively. The Parkes team lived the first sentence out: before pointing at aliens or the universe, check the kitchen. See https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/51/2/CargoCult.htm

question: An unopened instant cold pack from a first-aid kit contains no ice, no batteries, and no refrigerant, yet a firm squeeze plunges it toward zero degrees Celsius in seconds. Inside is a sealed bag of water that bursts over crystals of one specific chemical. Which one?
answer: Ammonium nitrate
choices: Ammonium nitrate
Sodium chloride
Calcium chloride
Sodium bicarbonate
context: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water endothermically, absorbing about 25.7 kilojoules per mole; the dissolving pulls heat out of the surroundings (including your hand) fast enough to drop the pack near 0 C. Calcium chloride is the opposite: dissolving it in water releases heat. Source: Wikipedia, Ice pack.

question: A disposable chemical hand warmer only starts warming after you TEAR the outer plastic wrapper. What tearing the wrapper actually does is nothing exotic: it lets AIR get in, so a specific slow process can run on the powder sealed inside. Which process is it?
answer: Iron powder oxidising to ordinary rust
choices: Iron powder oxidising to ordinary rust
Sodium powder reacting with air moisture
Charcoal powder slowly smouldering to ash
Aluminium powder reacting with the oxygen
context: The pouch contains iron powder plus salt, water, activated charcoal, and vermiculite; when oxygen enters, the iron oxidises to rust and gives off heat (about 1.7 kilocalories per gram of iron) for hours. The mix reaches around 74 C in about twenty minutes. Source: Wikipedia, Hand warmer.

question: A squeezed instant cold pack really does drop toward 0 degrees Celsius in seconds; a common story is that the pack 'creates' cold. What is a physicist's more precise account of what is happening between the pack and your palm?
answer: Heat flows out of your palm into the pack, where dissolving crystals absorb it
choices: Heat flows out of your palm into the pack, where dissolving crystals absorb it
Cold rays radiate outward from the pack's crystals into your skin
A tiny refrigerator cycle inside the pack pumps heat away from your palm
A supercold liquid inside the pack seeps out against your bare skin
context: Cold is not a substance; nothing 'makes' cold. Whenever something feels cold, heat is FLOWING OUT OF YOU into a colder thing (or, as here, into a chemical process that absorbs it). This one reframe unlocks half of chemistry-in-the-kitchen. Source: Wikipedia, Endothermic process.

question: A reusable heat pad sold as a hand-warmer looks like a clear liquid inside a plastic pouch, until you press and release the small metal disc floating inside. Within seconds a wave of change races through the pouch and it becomes HOT to hold. What is releasing the heat?
answer: A liquid solidifying and giving off its stored energy
choices: A liquid solidifying and giving off its stored energy
A salt reacting chemically with the plastic lining
A tiny lithium battery buried in the metal disc
A slow oxidation of iron flecks in the disc
context: The clear liquid is a supersaturated solution of sodium acetate, sitting far below the temperature at which it OUGHT to have crystallised, held there by having no seed to start on. The click creates a nucleation site; the wave you see is crystallisation, which is exothermic. Reset by boiling until every crystal redissolves. Source: Wikipedia, Hand warmer.

question: In 1893 the German chemist Hans Goldschmidt patented a reaction ignited with a stub of magnesium ribbon: dry aluminium powder mixed with iron-oxide powder that, once started, climbs above 2,500 degrees Celsius. Since about 1899 railway crews around the world have used exactly this reaction, working outdoors on the track with no power supply, for what specific job?
answer: Welding one steel rail to the next steel rail
choices: Welding one steel rail to the next steel rail
Hardening rail-ends by localised heat treatment
Cutting through a snapped rail so it can be lifted out
Casting replacement wheel bearings on the spot
context: Aluminium 'wants' oxygen more than iron does, so it simply takes it, releasing enormous heat and depositing molten iron exactly where the small clay crucible is aimed: the rail-end joint. The reaction needs no power supply and no external heat once ignited, which is why the same 1893 chemistry still welds rails outdoors on remote track today. Source: Wikipedia, Hans Goldschmidt; Britannica, Thermit.

question: A sound engineer gets an odd order: a beep of exactly 440 hertz, one pure frequency and nothing else, lasting one thousandth of a second. He says it cannot be done. Why not?
answer: No such sound exists — a tone that starts and stops spreads across frequencies
choices: No such sound exists — a tone that starts and stops spreads across frequencies
No such purity exists — a speaker's cone never holds one frequency steady
No speaker can start and stop its cone cleanly in one millisecond
No microphone can sample a millisecond burst without smearing it
context: Engineers call this the Gabor limit: a signal's duration times its bandwidth, both measured as standard deviations, can never drop below 1/(4*pi). Improve the localization in one and the spread in the other necessarily widens. There is no quantum mechanics anywhere in it — it falls straight out of the Fourier transform, and it governs ocean waves and radio signals just as strictly. Test it tonight: pluck a guitar string, let it ring, and a phone tuner locks onto a note; pluck it and clamp it dead, and the tuner finds nothing, because a click is not a pitch. Source: Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle', Applications > Signal Processing — https://grokipedia.com/page/Uncertainty_principle

question: Munich, 23 July 1923: Werner Heisenberg, twenty-one, is failing his doctoral oral. Wilhelm Wien asks him the resolving power of an interferometer, a telescope, a microscope; he cannot do any of them. Wien tries one last question, with no optics in it at all, and Heisenberg is still lost. What had Wien asked?
answer: How a storage battery works
choices: How a storage battery works
How a telephone carries speech
How a thermometer is calibrated
How a compass needle finds north
context: Arnold Sommerfeld graded him top marks; Wien failed him outright. The compromise left the future Nobel laureate with a III — roughly a C — in physics and for the doctorate overall. Four years later the argument that made his name was built on an imaginary microscope, the very instrument he had fumbled that afternoon. Source: AIP Center for History of Physics, Heisenberg exhibit, 'The Sad Story of Heisenberg's Doctorate' — https://history.aip.org/exhibits/heisenberg/sad-story.html ; APS News, January 1998.  (Legend.)

question: Dennis Gabor, an electrical engineer, spent 1946 stuck on a problem that sounds too simple: describing a siren. Its pitch slides steadily upward, and Fourier analysis — the standard method, which rebuilds any signal out of pure tones — kept failing on it. What was the method's flaw?
answer: It builds from tones that run forever, so it cannot say when a pitch happened
choices: It builds from tones that run forever, so it cannot say when a pitch happened
It handles only tones a human ear can hear, and a siren climbs past them
It assumes the signal repeats exactly, and a siren's sweep never repeats
It requires the loudness to hold steady, and a siren swells and fades
context: Gabor published it as 'Theory of communication. Part 1: The analysis of information' in the Journal of the Institution of Electrical Engineers Part III, vol. 93 no. 26 (1946), pp. 429-441 — importing Heisenberg's trade-off wholesale into radio and sound engineering. His fix was to analyse a signal in short windowed chunks instead of all at once, which is the ancestor of every spectrogram you have ever seen. Source: Wikipedia 'Gabor atom', citing Gabor 1946 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabor_atom ; corroborated by Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle' > Signal Processing.

question: Werner Heisenberg, writing in Copenhagen in March 1927, rested his whole argument on an instrument nobody could build: a microscope that locates a single electron by bouncing gamma rays off it. Short wavelengths would give a sharp position. Heisenberg's paper named the price of that sharpness. What was it?
answer: The photon would kick the electron's momentum to an unknown value
choices: The photon would kick the electron's momentum to an unknown value
The gamma rays would strip the electron from its atom before imaging
The lens would need to be wider than any laboratory to catch the rays
The exposure would last so long the electron had already moved on
context: His own words: 'At the instant of time when the position is determined, that is, at the instant when the photon is scattered by the electron, the electron undergoes a discontinuous change in momentum.' The paper was 'Ueber den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik', March 1927, written at Niels Bohr's institute. Note the constant: Heisenberg estimated the product as roughly Planck's constant h; the sharper h-bar/2 that textbooks print belongs to Earle Kennard's proof, not to the microscope story. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Uncertainty Principle', quoting Heisenberg 1927 pp. 174-175 — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/  (Legend.)

question: Every other substance on Earth freezes if you make it cold enough. Helium does not. At ordinary atmospheric pressure it boils at 4.2 kelvin, and then, chilled all the way down toward absolute zero, it simply stays liquid — you have to squeeze it past about twenty-five atmospheres before it will form a solid at all. Why does helium alone hold out?
answer: Its atoms can never come fully to rest, and that motion beats their feeble attraction
choices: Its atoms can never come fully to rest, and that motion beats their feeble attraction
Its atoms fill their outer shell, and a filled shell leaves no bonds for a lattice
Its atoms turn superfluid as they cool, and a superfluid cannot hold a rigid lattice
Its atoms are all bosons, and bosons crowd into a single state instead of a lattice
context: Helium-4 boils at 4.222 K and needs pressures above about 2.5 MPa — roughly 25 atmospheres — before it will solidify near 1 K. Its van der Waals attraction is simply too weak to overcome the zero-point energy of atoms that are not permitted to be at rest. Below the lambda-point at 2.17 K the liquid instead turns into a superfluid. This is the one entry in the phase tables you can point at and say: that blank space is the uncertainty principle. Source: Grokipedia 'Helium', Physical and Chemical Properties > Phase Transitions and States of Matter — https://grokipedia.com/page/Helium

question: Niels Bohr spent the early months of 1927 on a skiing holiday in Norway; Werner Heisenberg spent them in Copenhagen writing the gamma-ray microscope paper. Bohr came back, read it, and told Heisenberg the microscope argument was misleading. They argued hard and did not agree, and the paper was already submitted. What did Heisenberg do?
answer: He added a last-minute note crediting Bohr and left the argument standing
choices: He added a last-minute note crediting Bohr and left the argument standing
He withdrew the paper and rewrote the whole argument along Bohr's lines
He published it unchanged and answered Bohr in a separate paper that autumn
He cut the microscope out entirely and kept only the mathematical relation
context: Bohr had been working out complementarity on that holiday. Heisenberg's addition is titled 'Nachtrag bei der Korrektur' — Addition in proof — and it grants Bohr's point that what matters is not that the momentum changes but that the change cannot be measured in the same experiment. He did not withdraw the microscope, which is one reason the picture outlived the objection to it. (No primary source supports the popular story that Bohr reduced Heisenberg to tears; the record says only that they discussed intensely and disagreed.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Uncertainty Principle' (Hilgevoord & Uffink) — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/  (Legend.)

question: Niels Bohr's complaint about the gamma-ray microscope was not only philosophical; part of it was a plain mistake in the optics. Ernst Abbe had shown in the 1870s that how finely a microscope can resolve depends on more than the light it uses, and Werner Heisenberg had simply left that other factor out of his 1927 paper — he set the resolution equal to the wavelength and stopped there. What had he ignored?
answer: The width of the lens's opening, which sets the range of angles it gathers
choices: The width of the lens's opening, which sets the range of angles it gathers
The thickness of the lens, which bends edge rays differently from central ones
The brightness of the source, which fixes how many photons form the image
The distance from specimen to lens, which sets the image's magnification
context: Abbe's theory shows that the directions along and across the optical axis behave differently, so the lens's half-angle has to enter the resolution. Put it back in and the position blur is about the wavelength divided by the sine of that half-angle, while the momentum kick goes as Planck's constant over the wavelength times that same sine — the wavelength and the angle cancel and the product comes out around h. Bohr's deeper objection was conceptual, and he later wrote that 'the uncertainty in question is not simply a consequence of a discontinuous change of energy and momentum.' Source: Werner & Farrelly, 'Uncertainty from Heisenberg to Today', arXiv:1904.06139 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06139 ; Bohr quote via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Bohr 1985: 93).

question: The inequality every physics textbook prints under Werner Heisenberg's name was first proved by somebody else. Earle Hesse Kennard published the rigorous version in 1927, deriving it from Erwin Schroedinger's wave mechanics: delta-x times delta-p is at least h-bar over two, where each delta means a standard deviation — a spread. What does Kennard's inequality constrain?
answer: Which quantum states can exist: none holds a sharp position and a sharp momentum
choices: Which quantum states can exist: none holds a sharp position and a sharp momentum
How hard a probe must hit: no photon is gentle enough to leave momentum sharp
How good instruments can get: no detector will ever pin both quantities at once
What a particle secretly holds: both values are sharp but no test reveals them
context: This is the load-bearing distinction in the whole subject. Kennard's relation — and Howard Robertson's 1929 generalization of it to any pair of observables, with Schroedinger's 1930 sharpening on top — are PREPARATION relations: they describe the spreads of the probability distributions belonging to a given quantum state. In the Stanford Encyclopedia's words, they 'do not address simultaneous measurement accuracy or disturbance from the act of measuring itself.' No quantum state of any particle, however gently anyone handles it, has both a sharp position and a sharp momentum. It is a statement about which states exist, not about how carefully you look. Equality holds exactly for Gaussian wave packets, and it is a floor rather than a value: the nth state of a harmonic oscillator sits at h-bar(n + 1/2), so only the ground state touches the bound. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Uncertainty Principle' — https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-uncertainty/ ; Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle' > Kennard Inequality.

question: An electron circling a nucleus is, in nineteenth-century physics, an accelerating charge — and accelerating charges radiate away their energy. Do the arithmetic that way and every atom in your body should collapse in well under a nanosecond. Atoms have been holding open for billions of years instead. What holds the electron out?
answer: A kinetic energy that squeezing the electron into a small space forces on it
choices: A kinetic energy that squeezing the electron into a small space forces on it
A centrifugal push from the orbit that grows stronger as the radius shrinks
A short-range repulsion from the nucleus that outmuscles the electric pull
A radiating-and-reabsorbing balance that keeps the orbit's energy books even
context: Confine an electron closer to the nucleus and its momentum spread must grow, which forces a minimum kinetic energy that no cooling can remove. That zero-point kinetic energy is what balances the attractive Coulomb pull and sets the size of the atom. The bookkeeping is checkable: minimizing h-bar^2/(8m<x^2>) plus (1/2)m*omega^2*<x^2> for a harmonic well returns exactly the true ground-state energy, (1/2)h-bar*omega. The same effect shows up in chemistry — hydrogen's zero-point energy of about 0.27 eV is why its measured dissociation energy is 4.48 eV while the well itself is 4.75 eV deep. The molecule can never sit at the bottom of its own well. Source: Grokipedia 'Zero-point energy', Theoretical Foundations > Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle and Atomic Physics Phenomena — https://grokipedia.com/page/Zero-point_energy

question: Scientific American ran a headline on 8 March 2012: 'One Thing Is Certain: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle Is Not Dead.' Earlier that year, Yuji Hasegawa's group in Vienna had sent neutron spins through an interferometer and broken a limit that had carried Werner Heisenberg's name since 1927 — and the result stood. Aya Furuta, who wrote the piece, explained why nothing had died: two different statements had been sharing that one name, and only one of them fell. Which statement fell?
