answer: The claim that observing something must inevitably disturb what is observed
choices: The claim that observing something must inevitably disturb what is observed
The claim that no particle can hold a sharp position and a sharp momentum at once
The claim that the same limit covers every pair of incompatible quantities
The claim that states with correlated spreads obey a still tighter bound
context: Furuta separated the two statements cleanly: what the Vienna team violated was Heisenberg's 1927 measurement-disturbance claim that 'in observing the world, we inevitably disturb it', while the Kennard-Robertson relation, which describes a state's own fluctuations in position and momentum, 'does not say anything about what happens when a measurement is performed'. The Vienna paper was Erhart, Sponar, Sulyok, Badurek, Ozawa and Hasegawa, 'Experimental demonstration of a universally valid error-disturbance uncertainty relation in spin-measurements', Nature Physics 8, 185-189 (2012), posted as arXiv:1201.1833 on 9 January 2012. Two independent confirmations followed the headline rather than preceding it: Rozema, Darabi, Mahler, Hayat, Soudagar and Steinberg in Toronto used weak measurements on single photons, Physical Review Letters 109, 100404, published 6 September 2012; and Baek, Kaneda, Ozawa and Edamatsu at Tohoku reported flatly that 'Ozawa's relation always holds, whereas Heisenberg's relation fails for all measurement strengths', Scientific Reports 3, 2221 (2013). All three matched Masanao Ozawa's corrected 2003 relation, which carries three terms where the naive version had a single product, so the first term alone can dip below the old bound. Kennard's preparation relation was never in danger and was never tested by any of it. Source: Aya Furuta, Scientific American, 8 March 2012 — https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/heisenbergs-uncertainty-principle-is-not-dead/ ; arXiv:1201.1833 ; arXiv:1208.0034 ; Scientific Reports 3, 2221 (2013).

question: Collider experiments do not report a single number for the rho meson's mass. Plot the energies of what it decays into and you get a broad bump about a hundred and fifty million electron-volts across, and physicists fit that width straight off the data and print it beside the mass. The fuzziness is a measured property of the particle, not a shortcoming of the apparatus. What is that width telling them?
answer: How briefly the particle exists before it decays
choices: How briefly the particle exists before it decays
How fast the particle was moving when it formed
How many different ways the particle can decay
How much energy the collision that made it carried
context: A state that decays with lifetime tau has a spectral width Gamma = h-bar/tau. The rho meson lives about ten to the minus twenty-three seconds, which is exactly why its width comes out around 150 MeV — its mass is a Breit-Wigner bump rather than a number. Be careful with the energy-time version, though: it is not the same kind of statement as position-momentum, because time in quantum mechanics is a parameter rather than an observable, and Pauli's theorem shows no self-adjoint time operator conjugate to a bounded-below Hamiltonian can exist. The usable form is Mandelstam and Tamm's 1945 relation, in which delta-t means the time an observable's expectation value takes to shift by about its own uncertainty — not the duration of a measurement. Source: Grokipedia 'Uncertainty principle', Energy-Time Uncertainty > Time in Quantum Mechanics and > Mandelstam-Tamm Relation — https://grokipedia.com/page/Uncertainty_principle

question: Henrietta Lacks, a tobacco farmer and mother of five, lay unconscious at Johns Hopkins on 8 February 1951, radium about to go in for her cervical cancer. Before it did, Dr. Lawrence Wharton Jr did something her treatment did not require. What did he do?
answer: He cut two dime-sized pieces from her cervix.
choices: He cut two dime-sized pieces from her cervix.
He scraped cells from her cervix with a wooden spatula.
He drew two large vials of blood from her arm.
He took a swab of cells from inside her cheek.
context: One piece was healthy tissue, one was tumour; neither was needed for her treatment, and nobody asked her. George Gey, whose lab received the sample, did not take it himself - the popular retelling that puts him in the room is wrong. She was dead by 4 October 1951, aged 31, with tumours through nearly every organ. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Lacks ; grokipedia.com/page/HeLa

question: Mary Kubicek, George Gey's young lab assistant, had never seen a corpse when she was sent to Henrietta Lacks's autopsy on 4 October 1951. Keeping her eyes away from the dead woman's face, she caught sight of one small detail and nearly fainted. What had she seen?
answer: Her chipped red toenail polish.
choices: Her chipped red toenail polish.
Her plain gold wedding ring.
Her tight hospital wristband.
Her cracked and callused hands.
context: Kubicek later told the writer Rebecca Skloot: 'When I saw those toenails, I nearly fainted. I thought, Oh jeez, she's a real person.' Kubicek was the one who had labelled the culture tubes 'HeLa', two letters from each of her names, to keep the donor anonymous. Source: Johns Hopkins Magazine, 'Immortal Cells, Enduring Issues' (2010), quoting Rebecca Skloot's 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks'.

question: George Gey never patented Henrietta Lacks's cells and never took a penny for them; he mailed vials free to anyone who wrote and asked. Packed in sawdust in cardboard boxes, HeLa reached Texas, Amsterdam, India and Chile in the shirt pockets of airline pilots. What carried one shipment part of the way?
answer: A mule's saddlebag.
choices: A mule's saddlebag.
A fisherman's ice chest.
A beekeeper's crate.
A dogsled's supply pack.
context: Gey shipped the line free for the rest of his life and died without earning anything from it. Later, companies sold HeLa products for decades; the estate's suit against Thermo Fisher Scientific settled in 2023. Source: Cathy Gere, 'Dying and Not Dying: Henrietta Lacks', London Review of Books v32 n11 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Otto_Gey

question: Every human sample George Gey's lab had ever tried to keep alive had died within weeks. For Henrietta Lacks's tumour, his wife Margaret and his assistant Mary Kubicek minced the tissue and fed it a homemade broth, turning the tubes slowly in a roller drum Gey had built himself. What was in the broth?
answer: Chicken plasma, calf embryo extract and umbilical cord serum.
choices: Chicken plasma, calf embryo extract and umbilical cord serum.
Beef bouillon, powdered egg white and distilled rainwater.
Horse serum, evaporated milk and dried brewer's yeast extract.
Sheep blood, boiled potato starch and warm glucose syrup.
context: The roller drum was Gey's own invention, built to keep every cell bathed as the tubes turned. In the tube beside the tumour, Henrietta's own healthy cervical tissue withered and died, exactly as human cells always had. The tumour cells doubled every 20 to 24 hours instead. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Otto_Gey

question: For twenty-five years the public was told that the world's most-used human cells had come from a woman called 'Helen Lane.' In 1976 the journalist Michael Rogers published the first major press report to put Henrietta Lacks's real name to those cells. Where did it appear?
answer: In Rolling Stone.
choices: In Rolling Stone.
In Esquire.
In Harper's.
In The Village Voice.
context: The cover name varied - 'Helen Lane' in most tellings, sometimes 'Helen Larson.' Rogers's 1976 article was the first major press piece to put the real woman's name to the world's most famous cells, twenty-five years after her death; Rebecca Skloot's book followed in 2010. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Lacks

question: In 1954 Jonas Salk's polio vaccine went into a field trial on more than 1.8 million children, and laboratories had to test batch after batch of virus and vaccine first - slow, costly work. In 1953 William Scherer, Jerome Syverton and George Gey showed that a single tube of HeLa could give a plain yes-or-no answer. What made HeLa work as the test?
answer: Poliovirus infects HeLa and visibly destroys it.
choices: Poliovirus infects HeLa and visibly destroys it.
Poliovirus makes HeLa clump into visible strands.
Poliovirus makes HeLa glow under ultraviolet light.
Poliovirus turns the broth around HeLa bright red.
context: Dead cells in the tube meant live virus; healthy cells meant none. Scherer, Syverton and Gey demonstrated poliovirus typing in HeLa in 1953, and the vaccine was licensed on 12 April 1955. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa

question: By 1953 demand for HeLa had swamped George Gey's lab, which mailed out a few tubes at a time. To supply the laboratories testing Jonas Salk's polio vaccine, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis built a mass-production centre that turned out 20,000 tubes - roughly six trillion cells - every single week. Where did the foundation build it?
answer: At the Tuskegee Institute, a college in Alabama.
choices: At the Tuskegee Institute, a college in Alabama.
At the Wistar Institute, a lab in Philadelphia.
At the University of Minnesota, a school in Minneapolis.
At the Rockefeller Institute, a lab in New York.
context: Charles Bynum, the foundation's first Black executive, recommended the site, and Dr. William Scherer shipped the seed culture there in April 1953. Six Black scientists and technicians ran the centre at the start and about 35 staff at its peak, many of them women; they supplied the laboratories that ran the tests on the Salk vaccine. This HeLa factory is a completely different thing from the Tuskegee syphilis study, an unrelated U.S. Public Health Service experiment that withheld treatment from Black men in the same town from 1932 to 1972. Sources: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7484676/ ; Scientific American, 'Hidden Black Scientists Proved the Polio Vaccine Worked'

question: George Gey had spent nineteen years growing Henrietta Lacks's cells and mailing them around the world. In 1970 surgeons opened him up for pancreatic cancer, found it had spread to his lymph nodes, lungs and heart, and closed him again without doing the one thing he had asked of them beforehand. Gey woke from the anaesthetic furious. What had he asked for?
answer: To cut a piece of his tumour for a new cell line.
choices: To cut a piece of his tumour for a new cell line.
To inject HeLa cells into the tumour as a treatment.
To photograph every organ the cancer had reached.
To try an experimental drug first tested in HeLa.
context: He wanted a line called 'GeGe' grown from his own cancer. The surgeons judged that cutting would kill him on the table and took nothing. Gey died on 8 November 1970. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Otto_Gey ; Rebecca Skloot, 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks', ch.22

question: A normal human cell can divide only about fifty times. Each division shortens its telomeres - the protective caps on the ends of its chromosomes - and once the caps are worn away the cell stops for good. HeLa has been dividing since 1951 and has never stopped. How did Henrietta Lacks's tumour cells escape the fifty-division limit?
answer: Viral DNA in the tumour keeps the enzyme telomerase switched on, so fresh caps are built after every division.
choices: Viral DNA in the tumour keeps the enzyme telomerase switched on, so fresh caps are built after every division.
Her radium treatment fused the chromosome ends into closed rings, leaving no caps that could wear away at all.
The tumour cells divide so quickly that the caps have no time to wear down between one division and the next.
The cells pull spare caps off the chromosomes of their dying neighbours each time they are about to divide.
context: A human papillomavirus had spliced its DNA into her tumour; its E6 and E7 proteins disable p53 and Rb, which leaves telomerase permanently on, so the countdown never starts. Switch E6 and E7 back off in a HeLa culture and the telomeres shorten, the cells age, and they stop - which is how the causal link was proven. Human telomerase itself was first caught and characterised in 1989 in extracts of HeLa: the immortal cells were the tool used to find the enzyme that made them immortal. Source: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa (Mechanism of Immortality and Telomerase Expression)

question: In September 1966, at a cell-culture conference in Bedford, Pennsylvania, the geneticist Stanley Gartler faced some seven hundred researchers and told them that eighteen of the world's most-used human cell lines - supposedly from different patients, different organs, different countries - were every one of them Henrietta Lacks's HeLa. A single piece of evidence had caught all eighteen. What was it?
answer: All eighteen carried G6PD-A, an uncommon variant of a human enzyme.
choices: All eighteen carried G6PD-A, an uncommon variant of a human enzyme.
All eighteen carried an extra chromosome 21, the marker of Down syndrome.
All eighteen typed as blood group AB, the rarest of the four human groups.
All eighteen doubled in exactly twenty-four hours in an identical broth.
context: Henrietta Lacks was a Black tobacco farmer from Virginia, and G6PD-A is found almost exclusively in Black Americans - one woman's rare marker turned up in eighteen laboratories at once. Gartler published the finding in 1968 as 'Apparent HeLa Cell Contamination of Human Heteroploid Cell Lines'; scientists called it the HeLa bomb. Walter Nelson-Rees then spent the 1970s using chromosome banding to document roughly 240 misidentified lines - HEp-2, published for years as a laryngeal cancer line, was HeLa. Modern surveys still find 20-36% of cell lines in active use contaminated or misidentified. Labs now check identity by short tandem repeat profiling at 8-21 genetic loci, standardised in 2012, and by a nested PCR that can spot five HeLa cells hiding in a culture. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; Gartler, Nature 217 (1968) ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa

question: For twenty-two years Henrietta Lacks's husband and children knew nothing about her cells. What finally brought a researcher to their door in 1973 was the contamination problem: to tell HeLa apart from the lines it had invaded, Victor McKusick needed the family's genetic markers, so he sent a postdoctoral fellow, Susan Hsu, to draw their blood. Given almost no explanation, what did the family think the blood was for?
answer: To test them for the cancer that had killed her.
choices: To test them for the cancer that had killed her.
To screen them for an inherited blood disease.
To sign them up as donors of a rare blood type.
To give them a free check-up from the hospital.
context: They were not told that the blood was for cell-line identification, and no result ever came back to them. The irony runs deep: the family learned of HeLa at all only because HeLa had contaminated so many other laboratories that researchers needed her relatives' DNA to sort the mess out. Sources: Rebecca Skloot, 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks', ch.23 ; grokipedia.com/page/HeLa

question: One charge is made again and again: that Johns Hopkins broke the law in 1951 by cutting tissue from Henrietta Lacks without asking her. Her family was in fact shut out of every decision and every dollar for decades afterwards. On the narrow question of the law, though, what did an American hospital in 1951 actually have to do about leftover surgical tissue?
answer: Nothing: no American law and no Hopkins rule required asking the patient.
choices: Nothing: no American law and no Hopkins rule required asking the patient.
Nothing in law, though Hopkins' own written rules required the patient's consent.
Get a signed tissue-release form from the patient, as federal law required.
Obey the Nuremberg Code of 1947, which bound American hospitals directly.
context: Taking leftover surgical tissue was routine practice, and nothing then-illegal happened. The Nuremberg Code of 1947 existed but was not binding on American hospitals and had almost no effect on the practice. Both halves of the honest statement hold at once: no crime was committed in 1951, and the family was shut out of every decision and every dollar for decades. The bank reports both and does not resolve them for you. Source: grokipedia.com/page/HeLa (Consent Practices in 1950s Medical Research)

question: On 11 March 2013 a team at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory published HeLa's complete genome - in large part the inherited information of Henrietta Lacks's children and grandchildren - without asking them. The family objected, and by that August the National Institutes of Health had negotiated an agreement with them. What did the agreement give the family?
answer: Two seats on the board that reviews every request for the data.
choices: Two seats on the board that reviews every request for the data.
A share of the fee charged to laboratories that download the data.
The right to have the genome erased from every public database.
A veto over any paper that names Henrietta Lacks as the donor.
context: Announced 7 August 2013: the data went behind controlled access in dbGaP, two Lacks family members joined the working group reviewing every application, and resulting publications must acknowledge Henrietta Lacks. On 1 August 2023 - what would have been her 103rd birthday - the estate settled its unjust-enrichment suit against Thermo Fisher Scientific; terms are confidential and the company admitted no liability. A further suit against Novartis and Viatris followed in August 2024. No court has ever ruled on whether the family owns the cells. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HeLa ; NIH, 'The NIH-Lacks Family Agreement' ; CNN and NPR, 1 August 2023

question: The virologist Harald zur Hausen proved that papillomaviruses cause cervical cancer, cloning two cancer-causing types in 1983 and 1984, and took the 2008 Nobel Prize for it. The Gardasil vaccine, approved in 2006, blocks both of those types. Henrietta Lacks had been dead for more than thirty years before the first of them was cloned. What does Gardasil have to do with the cells taken from her?
answer: The virus in her tumour is one of the two types it blocks.
choices: The virus in her tumour is one of the two types it blocks.
The virus proteins in every dose of it are grown in HeLa.
The safety test for every batch of it is run in HeLa cells.
The tumour that killed her is where the virus was first seen.
context: The two types zur Hausen cloned were HPV-16 in 1983 and HPV-18 in 1984, both out of cervical tumours; the virus in Henrietta Lacks's own tumour was HPV-18. The cells taken from Henrietta Lacks helped build the vaccine against the exact cancer that killed her. The rest of the ledger: HeLa appears in over 110,000 publications and roughly 11,000 patents, by 2009 at a rate of over 300 new papers a month, and it flew in the early American satellite programme to see what weightlessness does to a dividing human cell. One scientist estimated that all the HeLa ever grown would weigh more than 50 million metric tons - from a woman who weighed about a hundred pounds at the end. In 2021 the WHO gave her a posthumous Director-General's award, accepted in Geneva by her 87-year-old son Lawrence. Sources: nobelprize.org, 2008 Medicine press release ; grokipedia.com/page/HeLa ; who.int, 13 October 2021

question: 18 August 1868, total solar eclipse, Guntur in southern India. A French astronomer turns a spectroscope on a bright red loop rising from the Sun's edge and records a brilliant yellow line at 587 nanometres, sitting right beside but plainly not on the familiar sodium lines. It matches no known substance anywhere on Earth. Who was he?
answer: Pierre Janssen
choices: Pierre Janssen
Camille Flammarion
Urbain Le Verrier
Francois Arago
context: Janssen had crossed the Indian Ocean to catch totality. The 'red loop' was a solar prominence -- an arch of glowing gas held up by the Sun's magnetic field. The mystery yellow line became the D3 line of a new element. Source: aps.org 'August 18 and October 20, 1868: Discovery of Helium'.

question: Janssen's second Guntur result mattered as much as the first. Solar eclipses are rare -- barely a minute or two of totality every few years, chased across the globe by ships. Yet his prominence lines glared so brightly through the spectroscope that he saw a way to record them without ever needing another eclipse. What was the shortcut?
answer: Reading them out of the ordinary daytime sky
choices: Reading them out of the ordinary daytime sky
Bouncing sunlight off the full Moon at night
Waiting for the annual dust haze after monsoon
Flying a hydrogen balloon above the weather
context: Norman Lockyer in London worked out the same daylight method independently within weeks. Their letters reached the French Academy within minutes of each other, and the Academy later struck a single medal carrying both their faces. Source: aps.org; britannica.com Lockyer.

question: London, late 1868. The astronomer Norman Lockyer thinks the mystery yellow line in the Sun's spectrum belongs to an element unknown on Earth. He brings in a serious professional chemist to co-sign the naming letter with him -- their coinage will be helium, from the Greek helios, 'the Sun'. Which chemist stood with Lockyer on the name?
answer: Edward Frankland
choices: Edward Frankland
William Crookes
Justus von Liebig
Dmitri Mendeleev
context: Naming an element nobody had ever held struck many chemists as reckless, and for nearly thirty years helium remained a line on a chart and nothing more -- until William Ramsay isolated it from a uranium rock in 1895. Source: sciencemuseum.org.uk 150-years blog; aps.org discovery-of-helium-1868.

question: In 1927 Ira Bowen finally cracked nebulium: the mysterious green lines were forbidden transitions from a familiar element in a state that Earth laboratories cannot produce (too little collision, too much rarefaction). Which familiar element, doubly stripped of electrons, had been posing as 'nebulium' all along?
answer: Oxygen
choices: Oxygen
Carbon
Nitrogen
Hydrogen
context: In extremely thin nebular gas an oxygen atom stripped of two electrons can sit for seconds in a metastable state before it slowly relaxes -- a 'forbidden' transition. Coronium was cracked a decade later: Grotrian and Edlen (around 1939-41) showed the coronal green line came from IRON with thirteen electrons ripped off, at temperatures of millions of degrees. Not new elements, familiar elements under exotic conditions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebulium.

question: 10 July 1908, Leiden. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes finally forces helium -- the last common gas to hold out -- into a liquid at 4.2 kelvin. Three years later, using his new liquid-helium bath, he cools a thread of mercury and its electrical resistance abruptly does something no metal had ever been known to do. What did the mercury do?
answer: Its electrical resistance fell to zero
choices: Its electrical resistance fell to zero
Its electrical resistance climbed to infinity
It emitted a bright yellow light
It fused with the helium into an alloy
context: Kamerlingh Onnes had discovered superconductivity, and won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics for the low-temperature work. Below 2.17 K, liquid helium-4 does its own trick: it becomes a superfluid, with zero viscosity, and creeps up and over the walls of its container. Both effects only became reachable because Onnes had learned how to keep helium liquid. Sources: ethw.org superconductivity 1911; wmi.badw.de on liquid helium.

question: In 1669 in Hamburg, the German alchemist Hennig Brand launched a project that sounds absurd today. He was convinced that a common bodily fluid, if patiently boiled down, would let him transmute base metal into a specific other metal that he could then sell. Which metal was Brand ultimately hunting for?
answer: Gold
choices: Gold
Silver
Copper
Iron
context: The old doctrine of signatures said 'like reveals like': the deep yellow of urine, Brand thought, must hide gold. He was wrong about the goal and stumbled onto something better. Source: Science History Institute, Hennig Brandt and the Discovery of Phosphorus.

question: By the time Hennig Brand had collected around fifty buckets of urine from Hamburg's beer-drinkers and let his stockpile stand for weeks, he was chasing the one prize every serious European alchemist wanted -- the same legendary object Isaac Newton and Robert Boyle both spent years hunting for. What was that prize called?
answer: The philosopher's stone
choices: The philosopher's stone
The alkahest
The elixir of life
A homunculus
context: The philosopher's stone was said to transmute lead into gold and confer long life; every serious alchemist in Europe wanted one. The alkahest was a hypothetical universal solvent; the elixir was for long life alone; the homunculus was a made-in-a-flask miniature person. Beer-drinkers were preferred donors because their contribution was more plentiful. Source: Wikipedia, Hennig Brand.

question: Hennig Brand treated his recipe as a family secret. He sold the method to a Dresden merchant, Johann Daniel Kraft, for 200 thalers, and the German alchemist Johann Kunckel, who had only ever seen samples of the finished substance, worked out his own urine route by about 1678. What finally turned the marvel into public science was one Englishman lodging his own recipe with the Royal Society in 1680. Who?
answer: Robert Boyle
choices: Robert Boyle
Robert Hooke
Christopher Wren
Isaac Newton
context: Boyle worked out his own preparation and, unlike Brand, published it in full. Publication is what turned a fairground marvel into a reproducible experiment; Lavoisier only classified phosphorus as an element more than a century later. Source: Wikipedia, Hennig Brand; encyclopedia.com on Kunckel.

question: At the Harvard College Observatory around 1900, Edward Pickering hired a room of women to measure stars on glass photographic plates, paying Henrietta Swan Leavitt about 30 cents an hour. What was the job title Pickering gave these women?
answer: computer
choices: computer
librarian
secretary
draftsman
context: Long before the machines took the name, a 'computer' was a person who computed. Leavitt joined as a volunteer in 1895 and was formally hired in 1902 at roughly 30 cents an hour -- about $10.50 a week -- measuring star images on glass plates with a magnifying glass at a light table. Source: lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/henrietta-swan-leavitt/

question: Delta Cephei sits about 890 light-years away in the constellation Cepheus and is bright enough to see with the naked eye. A kid with a notebook can watch it brighten and dim against its fixed neighbors on a repeating schedule. About how long is one full cycle of Delta Cephei?
answer: 5.4 days
choices: 5.4 days
90 minutes
48 hours
27 days
context: John Goodricke first noticed Delta Cephei was variable in 1784. It cycles between magnitudes 3.48 and 4.37 every 5.366 days -- the naked-eye prototype for the whole class of Cepheid variable stars. Test it yourself: pick a clear-sky week and log its brightness against the nearby fixed stars each night. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Cephei

question: Henrietta Swan Leavitt never once looked through a telescope. She worked at a light table in Cambridge, Massachusetts, measuring stars on glass plates that had already been exposed on the far side of the world. Where were those plates of the southern sky actually taken?
answer: Arequipa, Peru
choices: Arequipa, Peru
Cape Town, South Africa
Sydney, Australia
Valparaiso, Chile
context: Harvard ran a southern-sky outpost called the Boyden Station in Arequipa, Peru. Plates were exposed there and shipped back to Cambridge, where Leavitt measured star brightness with a magnifying glass. The Magellanic Clouds -- her hunting ground -- are only visible from the southern hemisphere. Source: fords.org/solving-the-unknown-what-astronomer-henrietta-swan-leavitt-accomplished/

question: A VARIABLE STAR is a star whose brightness changes on a schedule you can time. Leavitt hunted them on the Harvard plates and in 1908 published a landmark catalog listing every variable star she had found in the two nearby cloud-like galaxies visible from the southern hemisphere. About how many variable stars did that 1908 catalog list?
context: Her paper was titled '1777 Variables in the Magellanic Clouds' and appeared in the Annals of the Astronomical Observatory of Harvard College. Source: fords.org/solving-the-unknown-what-astronomer-henrietta-swan-leavitt-accomplished/

question: In 1912, working from a sample of 25 Cepheid variables inside the Small Magellanic Cloud, Leavitt plotted each star's brightness against how long it took to complete one bright-dim-bright cycle. The dots fell into a strikingly simple pattern. What did she find?
answer: the longer the cycle, the brighter the star
choices: the longer the cycle, the brighter the star
the shorter the cycle, the brighter the star
brightness swung wildly with no relation to cycle length
every star in the cloud shared the same cycle length
context: This is Leavitt's period-luminosity relation. Time a Cepheid's cycle and you know how bright it truly is; compare that to how bright it looks and you know how far away it is. It became astronomy's first honest yardstick for anything beyond parallax range -- the bottom rung of the cosmic distance ladder still in use today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Swan_Leavitt  (Legend.)

question: Leavitt was scrupulous about what her law did and did not do. She had timed 25 Cepheids and compared them, but she flagged one hard limit in the 1912 circular itself and left that piece of the problem for other astronomers to solve. What was the honest limit she named?
answer: her law gave only relative distances, not absolute ones
choices: her law gave only relative distances, not absolute ones
her sample of 25 Cepheids was too small to trust
the relation held only for Cepheids inside the Milky Way
the same relation would not hold for fainter Cepheids beyond her sample
context: She had no measured distance to any single Cepheid, so she could sort stars by true brightness but could not convert those sorts into miles or light-years. A ruler with no zero mark is still a ruler once someone marks the zero. Ejnar Hertzsprung supplied the first calibration in 1913 using Milky Way Cepheids; Harlow Shapley refined it in 1918. Leavitt named the gap in her own paper rather than paper over it. Source: lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/henrietta-swan-leavitt/

question: On the night of October 5-6, 1923, Edwin Hubble was hunting exploding stars on a photographic plate of the Andromeda Nebula taken with Mount Wilson's 100-inch Hooker telescope. He first marked three dots with the letter N, for nova. Then he checked older plates going back to 1909, saw one of them had been dimming and brightening on a schedule, crossed out the N in red pen -- and wrote what across the plate?
answer: VAR!
choices: VAR!
NOVA
H335H
context: The plate is catalogued H335H and the red 'VAR!' is still visible on it. That single Cepheid, timed against Leavitt's law, put Andromeda far outside the Milky Way -- Andromeda was not a fuzzy patch in our galaxy, it was a whole galaxy of its own. Hubble announced the result in the New York Times on November 23, 1924. Source: obs.carnegiescience.edu/PAST/m31var  (Legend.)

question: In 1925 the Swedish mathematician Gosta Mittag-Leffler mailed a letter to Henrietta Swan Leavitt at Harvard, telling her he intended to nominate her for the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for her period-luminosity relation. The reply he got back from the Harvard College Observatory was one he had not braced for. What did the observatory tell him?
answer: she had died of stomach cancer nearly four years earlier
choices: she had died of stomach cancer nearly four years earlier
she had retired and moved away from Cambridge
she had already declined all prize nominations on principle
she was now the head of the Harvard College Observatory
context: Leavitt died on December 12, 1921, at age 53, and is buried in Cambridge Cemetery beneath a hexagonal monument topped by a globe. The Nobel is not awarded posthumously, so the nomination went nowhere. Harlow Shapley wrote back to Mittag-Leffler suggesting the real credit for interpreting her findings belonged to him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_Swan_Leavitt  (Legend.)

question: The phrase 'herd immunity' began literally in a barnyard. In 1894 the Chief of the US Bureau of Animal Industry wrote about well-fed livestock resisting disease as a group. Which livestock did his article describe?
answer: hogs
choices: hogs
sheep
goats
horses
context: Daniel Elmer Salmon, a veterinary scientist, was writing about hog nutrition and disease resistance; by 1916 the same Bureau was using 'herd immunity' about cattle recovered from brucellosis. It was a farmer's observation before it was ever an equation. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herd_immunity ; vaxopedia.org/2020/02/19/on-the-origins-of-herd-immunity/

question: In 1923 the British bacteriologists W. W. C. Topley and Graham Wilson turned herd immunity from a figure of speech into an experimental fact. In cages of what animal did they deliberately run epidemics to prove that not every individual has to be immune to stop an outbreak?
answer: mice
choices: mice
rabbits
guinea pigs
pigeons
context: Topley and Wilson published in the Journal of Hygiene in 1923: they added susceptible newcomers to a stable cage, watched a fresh wave of infection rise, and watched it fade as immune numbers grew. This was the moment 'herd immunity' was first used in a human-medicine context. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34111938/ ; sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673620319243

question: A. W. Hedrich spent the early 1930s combing through three decades of one American city's monthly measles records. He found the same protective pattern in the human data that Topley and Wilson had produced in cages. Which city's records did Hedrich work through?
answer: Baltimore
choices: Baltimore
Boston
Chicago
Philadelphia
context: Hedrich's 1933 paper analysed Baltimore monthly measles cases from 1900 to 1931 and showed epidemics faded once a large enough fraction of children had already had measles - protection you receive without possessing it. Source: American Journal of Hygiene 1933 (17: 613-636); health.baltimorecity.gov/sites/default/files/The%20Baltimore%20Statement%20on%20Childhood%20Vaccination.pdf

question: Epidemiologists write R-nought for the average number of new infections one case produces in a wholly susceptible crowd. Measles is the textbook hard case for herd immunity because its R-nought is estimated to sit in which range?
answer: about 12 to 18
choices: about 12 to 18
about 2 to 3
about 5 to 6
about 25 to 30
context: A 2017 Lancet Infectious Diseases systematic review put measles R0 in the 12-to-18 range, which is why the classical threshold for measles is 92 to 95 percent immune. Flu, with R0 near 1.3, has a classical threshold near 23 percent. Source: thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(17)30307-9/abstract

question: In 1927 two Scottish researchers proved a threshold theorem: below a certain density of susceptible people, a large epidemic simply cannot take off. The theorem is the mathematical parent of every modern herd-immunity number. Whose theorem is it?
answer: Kermack and McKendrick
choices: Kermack and McKendrick
Ross and Hudson
Reed and Frost
Snow and Farr
context: William Ogilvy Kermack and Anderson Gray McKendrick, working in Edinburgh, published the 1927 paper that also introduced what is now called the SIR (Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered) model. Their threshold theorem is why an epidemic can peak and then die out even when many people never catch it. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02464422

question: The tidy classroom version of the herd-immunity threshold is a single fraction of the population that must be immune to make new outbreaks impossible in a homogeneously mixing crowd. Written in terms of R-nought (the average new infections one case sparks in a fully susceptible crowd), that fraction is:
answer: 1 - 1/R-nought
choices: 1 - 1/R-nought
1/R-nought
R-nought / (R-nought + 1)
the square root of R-nought
context: Plug in: measles at R0 = 15 gives 1 - 1/15 = about 93 percent; flu at R0 = 1.3 gives 1 - 1/1.3 = about 23 percent. One fraction explains why measles is the hard case and flu is not. Source: historyofvaccines.org/vaccines-101/what-do-vaccines-do/how-herd-immunity-works/

question: Take a disease whose R-nought - the average new infections per case in a fully susceptible crowd - equals 2.5. The tidy classroom formula puts its herd-immunity threshold at 60 percent immune. In 2020, Britton and colleagues rebuilt the same disease inside an age-structured population where people mostly mix with their own age group, and the disease-induced threshold in their model came out at about:
answer: 43 percent
choices: 43 percent
18 percent
72 percent
85 percent
context: The classical formula quietly assumes homogeneous mixing - everyone equally likely to meet everyone else. Real people cluster by age, workplace, and neighbourhood; when a model respects that, its threshold falls sharply. The same math also warns the other way: a 95 percent national average can hide a 60 percent local pocket where measles tears through. Source: Britton, Ball, Trapman, Science 2020 (science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abc6810); pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7236739/

question: Left to run itself, an epidemic keeps producing new infections even after transmission has turned over, because cases already in flight keep landing. Modellers call this extra tail 'overshoot'. A 2023 result on the classical SIR model derived the LARGEST overshoot possible - the biggest fraction of the population that can be infected past the turning point. That maximum is approximately:
answer: 30 percent
choices: 30 percent
5 percent
50 percent
70 percent
context: The Royal Society Interface paper (Kreck and Brauner, 2023) fixed the bound at roughly 0.30 of the population, occurring near R-nought = 2.15. The herd-immunity threshold marks the turning point of the curve, not where it stops - which is why 'let it burn to herd immunity' quietly comes with a large added bill. Source: royalsocietypublishing.org/rsif/article/20/209/20230322/90454/Fundamental-bound-on-epidemic-overshoot-in-the-SIR

question: When William Herschel first noticed the strange object of 13 March 1781, he needed to tell whether it was a star or something closer. He had a simple test any kid with a telescope can copy on Jupiter tonight. What did he do?
answer: He cranked up the magnification and watched it swell into a disk
choices: He cranked up the magnification and watched it swell into a disk
He waited for it to twinkle the way stars do at the horizon
He timed how long it took to cross the eyepiece
He held a candle behind a card to compare its colour
context: Stars stay stubborn points however hard you magnify -- they are too far to resolve. Planets and comets show a real disk that grows with the eyepiece. Any kid comparing Jupiter and a bright star through binoculars sees the same effect. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

question: Herschel had reported his 13 March 1781 discovery as a comet, but the Finnish-Swedish astronomer Anders Johan Lexell then computed its orbit -- and the shape of that orbit rewrote the map of the solar system. What did Lexell find?
answer: A nearly circular orbit far beyond Saturn
choices: A nearly circular orbit far beyond Saturn
A tightly stretched orbit diving inside Mercury
A short two-year orbit crossing Mars
A wildly wobbly orbit fitting no known shape
context: Uranus orbits at about 19 AU, roughly twice Saturn's 9.5 AU -- Lexell's near-circular orbit beyond Saturn proved the object was a new planet, not a comet, and roughly doubled the known solar system. It was the first planet added in recorded history; the other five had been known since antiquity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

question: Once Herschel's planet had an orbit, astronomers went back through old star catalogues and found it had been written down as a star at least twenty times without anyone noticing it moved. What entry did John Flamsteed give it in his 1690 catalogue?
answer: 34 Tauri, an ordinary star in the constellation Taurus
choices: 34 Tauri, an ordinary star in the constellation Taurus
78 Ceti, an ordinary star in the constellation Cetus
12 Leonis, an ordinary star in the constellation Leo
56 Orionis, an ordinary star in the constellation Orion
context: Flamsteed's 1690 entry as '34 Tauri' was one of the earliest known pre-Herschel sightings; Pierre Charles Le Monnier logged the same object a dozen times between 1750 and 1769 without noticing it wandered. Evidence in plain sight, filtered out by what people expected to see. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus

question: An arithmetic recipe published by Johann Titius and Johann Bode reproduced the spacing of the known planets and put a slot at about 19.6 astronomical units. Uranus turned up at 19.2 AU, and confidence in the rule sent astronomers hunting for the missing planet another of its slots demanded, in the gap between Mars and Jupiter. Who found something there on 1 January 1801, and what did they call it?
answer: Giuseppe Piazzi found a body he named Ceres
choices: Giuseppe Piazzi found a body he named Ceres
Heinrich Olbers found a body he named Pallas
Karl Harding found a body he named Juno
Franz von Zach found a body he named Astraea
context: Piazzi, working in Palermo, spotted Ceres on New Year's night 1801 -- exactly where the Titius-Bode rule said a planet should be. Olbers found Pallas in the same belt in 1802, Harding found Juno in 1804; dozens more turned up over the next fifty years, and the lot were eventually reclassified as asteroids. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titius%E2%80%93Bode_law

question: The Titius-Bode rule had reproduced the spacing of the known planets, correctly slotted Uranus at about 19 AU, and pointed astronomers at Ceres. The rule puts the next planet out near 39 astronomical units. Where does Neptune actually orbit?
answer: About 30 astronomical units
choices: About 30 astronomical units
About 36 astronomical units
About 42 astronomical units
About 48 astronomical units
context: Neptune orbits at about 30 AU; the Titius-Bode rule wanted a planet at ~39 AU (which is roughly where Pluto and the Kuiper belt sit). A recipe that fits the data you already have, with no mechanism underneath it, is a curve fit and not a law of nature. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titius%E2%80%93Bode_law

question: In 1800, at his home in Slough, William Herschel spread sunlight through a glass prism, slid a blackened-bulb thermometer along the coloured band, then moved it one step further, into a strip where nothing at all could be seen. The reading there was HIGHER than in any visible colour. What kind of light had he just discovered?
answer: infrared
choices: infrared
ultraviolet
microwaves
X-rays
context: Herschel published his results in 1800. He called the new rays 'calorific rays' -- the word 'infrared' (Latin infra, 'below') came in decades later, once physicists had a wavelength picture. Source: Cool Cosmos / IPAC-Caltech.

question: William Herschel did not stumble on invisible light while pondering the nature of the spectrum. He was chasing a very practical problem at his telescope: he needed a coloured-glass filter that would tame the Sun's glare and heat enough to let him do one particular kind of solar work without risking his eye. What was he trying to do more safely?
answer: watch and sketch sunspots through the eyepiece
choices: watch and sketch sunspots through the eyepiece
time the transit of Mercury across the Sun's face
sketch the exact shape of a total solar eclipse
track a bright daytime comet passing close to the Sun
context: Herschel wanted a filter that dimmed the Sun's light without letting through the burning heat. The systematic thermometer-on-a-spectrum experiment was set up to find one; the invisible rays past red were an unlooked-for bonus. Source: Institute of Physics -- Spark.

question: Herschel did not lay a single thermometer along his prism's rainbow. He laid THREE mercury thermometers with blackened bulbs on the table, and placed only one of them in the coloured band at a time. Why did he insist on the other two?
answer: as controls, to catch the room itself drifting warmer
choices: as controls, to catch the room itself drifting warmer
as replicates, to average out reading noise on the middle bulb
as calibration checks, to confirm all three agreed at room temperature
as before/after tests, warmed by breath to check each bulb's response
context: This is why the discovery stands. A rising reading in the beam meant nothing if the whole room was drifting warmer. The two extra thermometers, kept out of the sunlit spectrum, isolated the real effect from any background warming. Source: InterNACHI -- History of Infrared Thermography.

question: The 1800 experiment is one of the very few discoveries in physics a curious ten-year-old can literally reproduce with pocket-money gear on a Saturday afternoon. Which shopping list is the classic recipe for that reproduction?
answer: a prism, a sunny window and three blackened-bulb thermometers
choices: a prism, a sunny window and three blackened-bulb thermometers
a bell jar, a vacuum pump and a burning candle stub
a laser pointer, two mirrors and a smoke machine
a copper coil, a magnet and a hand compass
context: Place the prism in the sunny window, catch the rainbow on a table, run the thermometer bulb from violet to red to just past red, and record. The space past red reads warmest. Source: Cool Cosmos -- Herschel Backyard Experiment.

question: The James Webb Space Telescope is fundamentally an infrared instrument -- its detectors chill to around 40 kelvin, and its MIRI camera to under 7 kelvin, using a tennis-court-sized sunshield and a dedicated cryocooler. Why do infrared telescopes have to be run so brutally cold?
answer: the telescope itself glows in the infrared and would drown the signal
choices: the telescope itself glows in the infrared and would drown the signal
the beryllium mirrors only reflect infrared efficiently below about 50 kelvin
the sunshield only holds its taut shape at cryogenic temperatures
the detectors would lose their gold anti-reflection coating above 100 kelvin
context: Every warm object radiates infrared -- your body, the walls, the telescope tube. To see faint infrared from a distant galaxy, the instrument must be colder than the source, or its own glow swamps what it is trying to see. Herschel's discovery is why the whole 10-billion-dollar architecture of Webb is a giant refrigerator. Source: NASA -- How Does Webb Stay Cold.

question: On 13 November 1886 in a darkened Karlsruhe laboratory, Heinrich Hertz cranked an induction coil until a spark jumped across two brass spheres. Metres away, unconnected to any wire, a plain loop of copper with a tiny gap in it sparked in sympathy. What had he built the first working example of?
answer: A radio
choices: A radio
An X-ray tube
A vacuum diode
A phonograph cartridge
context: A transmitter and a receiver, coupled only by an invisible wave crossing empty air. Maxwell had died in 1879, seven years before Hertz's experiments, and never saw his equations confirmed with hardware. Source: ethw.org Milestones - First Generation and Experimental Proof of Electromagnetic Waves.

question: Hertz then set out to prove his invisible waves behaved in every way like ordinary light. He reflected them off metal mirrors and polarised them with a grid of parallel wires. To REFRACT them - to bend a beam by passing it through a transparent block - Hertz built a large 1.5-metre prism out of what unlikely-looking material?
answer: Pitch
choices: Pitch
Salt crystal
Paraffin wax
Sulphur
context: Pitch (asphalt) is opaque to visible light but transparent to radio waves; Hertz's prism bent the beam by 22 degrees, giving an index of refraction of 1.69 for pitch at those wavelengths. Source: Wikimedia commons file Hertz radio wave experiments - refraction.

question: In 1887 Hertz kept noticing that his receiver's tiny spark jumped MORE readily when ultraviolet light happened to fall on the gap. He wrote the observation up in Annalen der Physik and moved on to other things. Einstein would explain the phenomenon eighteen years later, in a March 1905 paper. What is the effect Hertz stumbled on and never pursued?
answer: The photoelectric effect
choices: The photoelectric effect
The Zeeman effect
The Compton effect
The Doppler effect
context: Ultraviolet light on the gap knocked electrons out of the metal, easing the spark's leap. Einstein's March 1905 paper explained it by proposing that light comes in QUANTA (photons); the Nobel Committee awarded him the 1921 Prize specifically for that paper, not for relativity. Source: aps.org Einstein and the Photoelectric Effect; spark.iop.org Hertz's photoelectric effect.

question: Asked by a student what practical use his beautiful new waves could possibly have, Hertz answered flatly, by his students' later recollection, that they were of no use at all - he had only wanted to prove Maestro Maxwell right. The quote is second-hand, not from any Hertz manuscript. Within seven years, whose attic experiments would prove Hertz spectacularly wrong about that?
answer: Guglielmo Marconi
choices: Guglielmo Marconi
Thomas Edison
Alexander Graham Bell
Nikola Tesla
context: Marconi read Augusto Righi's 1894 memorial article on Hertz's work and began his experiments at Villa Griffone near Bologna in 1895, aged 21. Hertz himself had died of granulomatosis on New Year's Day 1894, aged 36. Source: en.wikipedia.org Augusto Righi.  (Legend.)

question: Hertz was not the only person working on Maxwell's waves in the late 1880s and 1890s. One English physicist demonstrated wireless signalling at the Royal Institution in June 1894 - a year before Marconi's attic work near Bologna - but did not pursue the commercial side of it. Who was he?
answer: Oliver Lodge
choices: Oliver Lodge
William Crookes
John Ambrose Fleming
Silvanus P. Thompson
context: Lodge's Royal Institution lecture on 1 June 1894 memorialised Hertz and demonstrated wireless transmission across a few metres. He also improved the coherer detector Branly had invented. Other contemporaries: Jagadish Chandra Bose in Calcutta, and Nikola Tesla in the United States. Source: en.wikipedia.org History of radio receivers.

question: In December 1872 the Royal Navy refitted HMS Challenger, a wooden steam corvette, at Sheerness for a three-year voyage. Her spars were cut down and 15 of her 17 guns were pulled out. What filled the gun deck when she sailed?
answer: laboratories
choices: laboratories
coal bunkers
extra marines' quarters
casks of fresh water
context: HMS Challenger was a working warship stripped for science; the gun deck was fitted out with chemistry, biology and sounding labs before she left Portsmouth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_expedition

question: HMS Challenger measured the depth of the ocean the crude way. A weighted line was paid out from the deck until it went slack, then hauled back and its length read off. In what unit was every one of those depths recorded in the ship's log?
answer: fathoms
choices: fathoms
leagues
cubits
furlongs
context: A fathom is six feet, the reach of a sailor's outstretched arms; a single deep sounding could take most of a day, hauled by hand or by steam winch. Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01490419.2013.837849

question: Before Challenger sailed, the reigning theory of the deep sea came from Edward Forbes, dredging in the Aegean aboard HMS Beacon in 1843. From what his nets brought up, Forbes made a bold claim about the ocean below about 300 fathoms. What did he claim?
answer: no animals could survive down there
choices: no animals could survive down there
the water was fresh, not salt
a single warm current ran through it northward
the seabed was heated from below by volcanoes
context: This was the azoic hypothesis (Greek a- + zoe, 'without life'), the reigning consensus. Challenger's dredges kept coming back with living animals from thousands of fathoms and finished the idea off. Norwegian zoologist Michael Sars had already dented it before the voyage, pulling 427 species from 450 fathoms off Norway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azoic_hypothesis

question: On 23 March 1875, at Station 225 near the Marianas, HMS Challenger paid out her sounding line and watched it keep going. When the reading came back the crew sounded a second time in the same spot to check it. What did the doubled sounding read?
answer: 4,475 fathoms
choices: 4,475 fathoms
1,200 fathoms
2,340 fathoms
6,900 fathoms
context: 4,475 fathoms is about 8,184 m, the deepest sounding anyone had made; the place still carries the ship's name as the Challenger Deep. Modern multibeam sonar now puts the same spot at about 10,935 m -- a rope can only underestimate a drifting depth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep  (Legend.)

question: In 1868, four years before Challenger sailed, Thomas Huxley pulled the stopper on an old bottle of Atlantic mud dredged in 1857, peered at a translucent gelatinous slime laced with veins, and announced it to the world as a living organism. He named it Bathybius haeckelii, for Ernst Haeckel. What did Huxley claim this slime was?
answer: a primordial protoplasm bridging non-living matter and life
choices: a primordial protoplasm bridging non-living matter and life
the larval stage of the giant squid
a new kind of colonial deep-sea coral
the eggs of an unknown abyssal fish
context: Haeckel had already theorized an Urschleim, a primordial slime out of which life arose; Huxley believed Bathybius was the thing itself, dredged up from the seabed. Source: https://bigthink.com/the-past/primordial-slime-huxley/  (Legend.)

question: The Report on the Scientific Results of the Voyage of H.M.S. Challenger was not finished until 1895, nineteen years after the ship docked and thirteen years after Charles Wyville Thomson died. John Murray took it over and saw it through. Roughly how big was the finished Report?
answer: 50 volumes and over 29,500 pages
choices: 50 volumes and over 29,500 pages
3 volumes and about 900 pages
one folio of about 200 plates
a single 400-page monograph
context: It is still the largest publication ever produced from a single scientific expedition. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_expedition  (Legend.)

question: Aboard HMS Challenger the young ship's chemist John Young Buchanan set out to check Thomas Huxley's celebrated Bathybius haeckelii on fresh samples right out of the dredge. He came away certain it was not an organism at all. What did Buchanan show Bathybius actually was?
answer: a chemical precipitate thrown down in the sample bottle
choices: a chemical precipitate thrown down in the sample bottle
a colony of abyssal bacteria feeding on iron in the mud
shredded protoplasm from surface plankton that had sunk
amoebae released only under the pressure of the deep
context: Buchanan traced it: the alcohol used to preserve the mud met dissolved salts in the seawater and threw down a gelatinous white precipitate -- calcium sulfate -- that looked like protoplasm; fresh samples with no alcohol never produced it. Charles Wyville Thomson sent Huxley a courteous letter with the finding; Huxley published part of it in the journal Nature and formally recanted Bathybius at the 1879 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, publicly killing his own celebrated discovery. Ernst Haeckel, however, refused to give it up and was still defending Bathybius into the 1880s. Source: https://www.realclearscience.com/blog/2022/11/09/the_great_primordial_slime_affair_863783.html  (Legend.)

question: John Murray sorted the sediment hauls into a map of the seabed by what it is MADE of. Across the barren abyss, where any calcareous shells had dissolved before reaching the bottom, the dredges came back full of one particular material -- and, growing on top of it, black lumps from marbles to potato-sized. What was the seabed material in the deepest, most barren stretches?
answer: red clay from volcanic dust
choices: red clay from volcanic dust
white sand from ground coral
black basalt gravel
sheets of frozen methane
context: Murray also mapped globigerina ooze and radiolarian ooze -- carpets of microscopic shells -- across the shallower abyss. The black lumps were nearly pure manganese oxide; Murray and Renard's 1891 Deep-Sea Deposits volume named them manganese nodules, and they are still commercially and scientifically argued over today. Source: https://doi.pangaea.de/10.1594/PANGAEA.849073

question: Challenger's quiet triumph was the thermometer, not the sounding rope. In every ocean the crew crossed they lowered thermometers to the bottom and read the temperature. What global pattern did their deep-water readings first hint at?
answer: cold polar water sinks and creeps along the seabed worldwide
choices: cold polar water sinks and creeps along the seabed worldwide
warm surface water descends in the tropics and rises at the poles
the deep ocean is heated from below by seabed volcanism
the deep ocean sits in still, layered basins that never mix
context: Challenger found the deep water uniformly cold in every ocean, tropics to poles -- the earliest empirical hint of what is now called the global overturning circulation, the conveyor of cold, dense polar water that keeps the abyss cold and moves heat around the planet. Source: https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/hms-challenger-expedition-oceanography-trailblazer

question: The honest weakness of Challenger's weighted rope was that a line drifts, catches and stretches, so every deep reading was one unverifiable number. The answer, when it came in the 1920s, was not more rope but different physics. What replaced the weighted line?
answer: timing the echo of a sound pulse off the seabed
choices: timing the echo of a sound pulse off the seabed
timing a small explosive charge's pressure return
triangulating from surface waves reflected off the seabed
measuring the pull of the seabed on a plumb bob
context: A ship pings the seabed and times the return of the echo; because a rope can only underestimate a drifting depth, the modern Challenger Deep figure of about 10,935 m by multibeam sonar is well below the ship's own 8,184 m rope reading. Source: https://tos.org/oceanography/article/implosion-in-the-challenger-deep-echo-sounding-with-the-shock-wave

question: Robert Hooke, curator of experiments for the Royal Society, sharpened a penknife "as keen as a Razor" and shaved off a sliver thin enough to see light through. Under his microscope it was not solid at all: row upon row of tiny hollow boxes, each walled off from the next. Describing them, he wrote down a word biology has used ever since. What had he sliced?
answer: A shaving of cork
choices: A shaving of cork
A curl of birch bark
A paring of ox horn
A leaf of dried moss
context: Observation XVIII of Micrographia (1665). Hooke laid the slice "on a black object Plate, because it was it self a white body" and cast light onto it through a deep plano-convex glass - the black backing is the trick that made the pale cork readable. His sentence coined the word: the pores, "or cells," were "a great many little Boxes, separated out of one continued long pore, by certain Diaphragms." He knew he was first: "the first microscopical pores I ever saw, and perhaps, that were ever seen." The unit of all life got its name from a bottle-cork - dead bark, with nothing living in it. (Micrographia, Observ. XVIII, primary text.)

question: Robert Hooke had to draw each specimen while it sat under his lens, and one of them nearly beat him. An ant would not hold still - it kept twisting and winding its body - and Hooke complained it was more troublesome to draw than anything else in Micrographia. What did he do to it?
answer: Dosed it with brandy until it dropped
choices: Dosed it with brandy until it dropped
Pinned it through the body to a board
Chilled it on ice from the cellar
Glued its feet down with tree gum
context: Hooke gave the ant "a Gill of Brandy, or Spirit of Wine" - a gill is about a quarter-pint - "which after a while e'en knock'd him down dead drunk, so that he became moveless." It stayed "moveless about an hour," long enough for him to finish the drawing, and then, "upon a sudden, as if it had been awaken out of a drunken sleep, it suddenly reviv'd and ran away." (Micrographia, "Of an Ant or Pismire," Observ. XLIX.)

question: Robert Hooke did not just look at his cork slice - he counted. He tallied the little boxes lying end to end under the lens, multiplied the rate outward, and printed the total in Micrographia: 1,259,712,000 of them. How much cork held that many?
answer: One cubic inch, a lump the size of a sugar cube
choices: One cubic inch, a lump the size of a sugar cube
One whole bottle stopper, about a thumb's length
One square foot of sheet cork, the size of a mat
One cubic foot, a hatbox packed full of the stuff
context: Hooke's own arithmetic: "there were usually about threescore of these small Cells placed end-ways in the eighteenth part of an Inch in length, whence I concluded there must be neer eleven hundred of them... in the length of an Inch, and therefore in a square Inch above a Million, or 1166400. and in a Cubick Inch, above twelve hundred Millions, or 1259712000. a thing almost incredible." Sixty boxes in one-eighteenth of an inch, and he did the rest with a pen. You can run the same move on anything that repeats: count a short measured row, then multiply outward. (Micrographia, Observ. XVIII.)

question: Micrographia, Robert Hooke's 1665 book of microscope drawings, ran to sixty observations and thirty-eight copperplate engravings. The plates readers remembered were the ones printed bigger than the book itself, folded up to three times and opening out to roughly seventeen inches by ten - a creature spread across the whole table. Which two creatures got those giant fold-outs?
answer: The flea and the louse
choices: The flea and the louse
The ant and the bee
The fly and the gnat
The spider and the moth
context: The Royal Society describes the louse plate as unfolding to nearly twice the size of the book; Wikipedia says four times - the sources disagree on the multiple, so trust the drama, not the number. The ant, the fly and the spider are all really in there too; only the flea and the louse got the monster fold-outs. Of the sixty observations, fifty-seven were microscopic and three telescopic. The Royal Society also notes that Hooke drew the flea's recessed antennae with a precision that "could not have been visible to Hooke with the degree of magnification afforded by his microscope" - his eye and hand outran his instrument. (Royal Society blog, "Micrographia online," 2020.)

question: Samuel Pepys, the London naval official whose private diary recorded the plague and the Great Fire, spotted Robert Hooke's Micrographia at the bookbinder's and carried it home on 20 January 1665, "very proud" of it. The next night's entry in his diary calls it "the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life." How had Pepys spent that evening?
answer: Sat up in his chamber reading until two in the morning
choices: Sat up in his chamber reading until two in the morning
Read it aloud to his wife and her maid after supper
Took it to the coffee-house to show it to the company
Sent it out to be rebound in finer calfskin and gilt
context: Pepys, 21 January 1664/65: "Before I went to bed I sat up till two o'clock in my chamber reading of Mr. Hooke's Microscopicall Observations, the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life." He had bespoken it at the bookbinder's on 2 January, before it was even bound: "so pretty that I presently bespoke it." Micrographia sold out fast and is usually called the first science bestseller; it sent Antonie van Leeuwenhoek off to grind his own lenses and made Christopher Cock's microscope business boom. (The Diary of Samuel Pepys, 2 / 20 / 21 January 1664-65.)

question: Robert Hooke's cork slice gave biology a word, but it also did something humbler. Cork had been in daily use for centuries, and one familiar thing about it had never had an explanation - everyone knew cork did it, nobody could say why. Hooke read the answer straight off what his lens showed him and printed it in Micrographia beside the drawing. Which property of cork did he explain?
answer: That it floats and rides high in water
choices: That it floats and rides high in water
That it grips a glass neck so tightly
That it springs back when you squeeze it
That it keeps wine from soaking through
context: Hooke concluded cork's substance is "altogether fill'd with Air, and that that Air is perfectly enclosed in little Boxes or Cells," which makes it "a very small quantity of a solid body, extended into exceeding large dimensions" - hardly any matter at all, spread over a large volume, so it rides high. Worth holding on to: the word that now names the unit of every living thing was coined for a piece of dead bark. (Micrographia, Observ. XVIII.)

question: The first published picture of a microorganism - a growth whose structure no unaided eye can resolve - sits inside Micrographia, and Robert Hooke did not have to leave his house to find the specimen. Under the lens he drew slender transparent stalks, not quite straight, each bending under the weight of a round white knob at its top. What was the blue mould growing on?
answer: The sheepskin covers of a small book
choices: The sheepskin covers of a small book
The whitewashed plaster of a wall
The crust of a loaf gone stale
The rind of a cheese in the larder
context: Observation XX, drawn as Figure 1 of Scheme XII. Hooke's specimen was mould on "the red covers of a small book, which, it seems, were of Sheeps-skin, that being more apt to gather mould, even in a dry and clean room, then other leathers." He drew "small long cylindrical and transparent stalks, not exactly streight, but a little bended with the weight of a round and white knob that grew on the top of each of them." Careful with secondary sources here: Grokipedia labels this Observation XII, but XII is the scheme number - the observation is XX. (Micrographia, Observ. XX; Royal Society print archive RS.5095.)

question: Robert Hooke's compound microscope, built for him by the London instrument maker Christopher Cock, was not a great instrument: about thirty to fifty times magnification, with colour fringes smearing every edge. Hooke admitted in print that a single lens gave a brighter, clearer image than his own multi-lens tube. His real edge over everyone else lay somewhere other than magnifying power. Where did he put his ingenuity?
answer: Into the light: a lamp beamed through a glass globe of brine
choices: Into the light: a lamp beamed through a glass globe of brine
Into the stage: a screw mount that gripped the specimen still
Into the eyepiece: smoked glass ground to kill the colour fringe
Into the mirror: a polished steel dish throwing sun up the tube
context: From the Preface: "I procur'd me a small Pedestal... on the undermost of these I plac'd a pretty large Globe of Glass G, fill'd with exceeding clear Brine... on the upper Arm was placed a small Lamp K," with "a deep plain Convex glass" to steer the beam. He had conceded that "the fewer the Refractions are, the more bright and clear the Object appears" - his own compound tube lost to a single lens - so he built a light he could summon "at any time," and drew at night. His discipline followed: "I never began to make any draught before by many examinations in several lights, and in several positions to those lights, I had discover'd the true form." Try it with any magnifier you own: better lighting usually beats more magnification. (Micrographia, Preface.)

question: Robert Hooke laid a piece of petrified wood beside a piece of ordinary wood under the same lens and found the two built alike inside. From that match he argued the stone had once been a living tree - which set him against the learned view of his day, that such stones had never been alive at all and owed their shapes to something else entirely. What did that view say had made them?
answer: A shaping power latent in the Earth, growing stone into lifelike forms
choices: A shaping power latent in the Earth, growing stone into lifelike forms
A stray influence of the stars, pressing shapes into the rock below
A sporting of Nature, throwing off odd shapes to no purpose at all
A seed of stone, sprouting in the rock as a seed sprouts in soil
context: Observation XVII. Under the same lens the petrified wood's structure matched ordinary wood's, and from that match Hooke argued that fossils are the remains of things that were once alive, against the prevailing view that they were "Stones form'd by some extraordinary Plastick virtue latent in the Earth itself." Micrographia was never only biology: in Observation IX, on the colours in thin plates of Muscovy glass, Hooke argued that light travels as pulses or vibrations in a subtle medium rather than as flying particles - a wave picture of light well over a century before Fresnel formalised one. (Micrographia, Observ. XVII; roberthooke.org.uk, "Fossils"; Grokipedia: Micrographia.)

question: Robert Hooke coined the word "cell" for the little boxes he saw in a shaving of cork. That was Observation XVIII of Micrographia, and the cork was only where it began: Hooke went on cutting - elder pith, fennel, carrots, burdocks, teasels, ferns and reeds - and laid every one of them under the lens. What did he report finding inside those plants?
answer: Cells full of juices, sweating them out by degrees
choices: Cells full of juices, sweating them out by degrees
Walls as dry and bare as the ones in the cork
No cells at all, only long unbroken fibres
Boxes far larger and more regular than the cork's
context: The plant biologist Winfried Peters went back to Observation XVIII in 2024 to correct a line repeated in classrooms - that Hooke only ever saw dead, empty walls. "It is incorrect that Hooke only saw dead cell walls," Peters writes; Hooke had reported "these Cells or Pores fill'd with juices, and by degrees sweating them out." What does stay true is narrower and stranger: the word "cell" was coined for boxes of air in dead bark, and Hooke had no idea he had named the unit every living thing is built from. That took another 173 years - Matthias Schleiden on plants in 1838 and Theodor Schwann on animals in 1839 turned the word into cell theory. Hooke named the brick long before anyone knew there was a building. (Winfried S. Peters, "Will the real Robert Hooke please stand up?", The Plant Cell 36(11):4680, 2024.)

question: Robert Hooke drew the blue mould on a book's leather covers - the slender stalks, the round white knob bending each one over - and beneath the drawing he wrote down his account of where such growth comes from in the first place. What did Hooke conclude?
answer: That mould needs no seed, arising from rotting matter kept moist and warm
choices: That mould needs no seed, arising from rotting matter kept moist and warm
That invisible seeds drift in the air and settle wherever a surface is damp
That the leather's own substance was slowly changing form into a new plant
That the mould had been alive in the sheep's skin before the beast was killed
context: Hooke's words: "Mould and Mushroms require no seminal property, but the former may be produc'd at any time from any kind of putrifying Animal, or Vegetable Substance, as Flesh, &c. kept moist and warm." That is spontaneous generation - the very claim Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flasks would later have to kill, and the drifting-seeds option is far closer to what we now know. The first published picture of a microorganism arrived with the wrong account of where microorganisms come from. That is not a mark against Hooke; it is what the record shows, and it is why a published drawing and a published explanation have to be judged separately. (Micrographia, Observ. XX.)

question: Open almost any textbook and you will read that Robert Hooke named the boxes in his cork "cells" because they reminded him of the bare little rooms monks slept in. In 2024 the plant biologist Winfried Peters searched Hooke's writings for that comparison and reported that no monk, no monastery, and not even the Latin word cellula appears anywhere in them. What comparison did Hooke actually put on the page?
answer: A honeycomb with irregular pores
choices: A honeycomb with irregular pores
A sponge riddled through with holes
A froth of bubbles on new ale
A pomegranate packed with seeds
context: Hooke's actual sentence: the cork was "all perforated and porous, much like a Honey-comb, but that the pores of it were not regular." Peters calls the monastic version "the monastic myth" - and Grokipedia, Britannica and National Geographic all repeat it, which is exactly why a famous story is worth checking against the original text. Micrographia is free to read online; the cork passage is Observation XVIII. Popularity is not evidence. (Winfried S. Peters, "Will the real Robert Hooke please stand up?", The Plant Cell 36(11):4680, 2024; Micrographia, Observ. XVIII.)  (Legend.)

question: In 1945 Ray Owen tested the blood of Wisconsin cattle born as fraternal twins — two eggs, no more alike than ordinary siblings. Genetics said one red-cell type per calf. Owen found two. Where did the second come from?
answer: From its twin, through blood vessels fused in the womb.
choices: From its twin, through blood vessels fused in the womb.
From its twin, through cells taken in with milk after birth.
From its mother, through her blood crossing the placenta.
From its own marrow, through a second line starting late.
context: Owen published it in Science in 1945 — 'Immunogenetic consequences of vascular anastomoses between bovine twins' — reporting red-cell types 'usually identical, contrary to genetic expectation.' The calves' blood vessels had fused across a shared placenta before birth, so each animal grew up a permanent mosaic of two cell populations and never attacked the borrowed half. It also explained the freemartin, the sterile heifer born twinned to a bull calf: she carries her brother's blood-forming cells for life. Tolerance, it turned out, is not inherited — it is learned, and it is learned before birth. Source: Science 102(2651):400 (1945); Royal College of Surgeons of England Bulletin, 'Observations from the farmyard: cattle, chimerism and a Nobel prize.'

question: A ten-year-old is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, a disease that, unlike type 2, has nothing to do with weight or diet. Her own immune system has singled out one population of cells in her body and destroyed them. Which cells did it kill?
answer: The insulin-making beta cells of her pancreas.
choices: The insulin-making beta cells of her pancreas.
The liver cells that store sugar as glycogen.
The gut cells that absorb sugar from food.
The muscle cells that pull sugar from her blood.
context: Type 1 diabetes is the self-or-other checkpoint failing on exactly one cell type — the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. Grokipedia states plainly that, unlike type 2 diabetes, it 'is not linked to lifestyle factors like obesity.' Source: Grokipedia, 'Type 1 diabetes'.

question: In 1948 the Edinburgh cattle researcher Hugh Donald needed a way to tell identical calf twins from fraternal ones, and asked the zoologist Peter Medawar. Medawar proposed skin grafts: identical twins should keep each other's skin, fraternal twins should throw it off within days. At Donald's farm the test proved useless. Why?
answer: Fraternal twins kept each other's grafts as readily as identicals.
choices: Fraternal twins kept each other's grafts as readily as identicals.
Identical twins threw off each other's grafts within a few days.
Every graft on every calf, twin or not, sloughed away.
The grafts healed so slowly that no result could be read.
context: Medawar went to Donald's farm expecting a quick diagnostic and watched it break: the freemartin accepted skin from the bull calf she had shared a womb with, and he accepted hers. The useless test was the evidence — anything present while the immune system is being built gets filed as 'self'. Five years later Medawar turned that failure into the mouse experiment that won him a Nobel Prize. Source: Royal College of Surgeons of England Bulletin, 'Observations from the farmyard: cattle, chimerism and a Nobel prize.'

question: In 1912 the Japanese surgeon Hakaru Hashimoto described four thyroid glands he had cut out of his patients. Each was swollen and turning to fibrous scar, yet he found no infection in them and no cancer. What filled the gland tissue instead?
answer: The patient's own white blood cells, packed in crowds.
choices: The patient's own white blood cells, packed in crowds.
Hardened crystals of iodine, gathered in clumps.
Fat from the neck, pushed in as smooth sheets.
Small cysts of clear fluid, in scattered nests.
context: Hashimoto called it struma lymphomatosa — a goitre full of lymph cells — working from just four surgical cases. He was describing an immune attack on the body's own tissue decades before anyone could demonstrate in a laboratory that such a thing was possible; the disease still carries his name. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmunity'.

question: Type 1 diabetes appears when a child's immune system turns on one of the child's own tissues. Parents hearing the diagnosis almost always search the family tree for someone else who had it. Roughly what share of people diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have no family history of it at all?
answer: About 80 to 90 percent.
choices: About 10 to 20 percent.
About 30 to 40 percent.
About 55 to 65 percent.
About 80 to 90 percent.
context: Roughly 80–90% of people diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have no family history of it. Genes load the dice across autoimmune disease without deciding the outcome: identical-twin concordance is only about 15% for rheumatoid arthritis and 20–25% for multiple sclerosis, and HLA-B27 is carried by 5–8% of the general population while only about 1–5% of carriers ever develop ankylosing spondylitis. Something outside the genome has to pull the trigger. Source: Grokipedia, 'Type 1 diabetes' and 'Autoimmunity'.

question: Paul Ehrlich gave the Croonian Lecture to the Royal Society in 1900 and coined horror autotoxicus — the horror of self-poisoning — for a law he thought the living body obeyed. It would be 'dysteleological in the highest degree,' he wrote — badly designed — for a body to make poisons against itself. The phrase became doctrine, and for fifty years it stalled the study of self-attacking disease. What did Ehrlich claim about antibodies aimed at a body's own tissue?
answer: The body can make them, but safeguards stop them doing harm.
choices: The body can make them, but safeguards stop them doing harm.
The body can make them, but only against dying tissue.
The body clears them out of its blood within hours of making them.
The body cannot make them at all, in health or illness.
