context: In Collected Studies on Immunity (1906) Ehrlich named the safeguards himself: 'the organism possesses certain contrivances by means of which the immunity reaction, so easily produced by all kinds of cells, is prevented from acting against the organism's own elements.' He allowed that self-directed attacks could occur; he held that innate protections would stop them ever becoming pathological. The textbook one-liner — that a body simply cannot make antibodies against itself — is a flattening of what he wrote, and it cost the field decades: when Julius Donath and Karl Landsteiner showed in 1904 that serum from patients with paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria destroyed red cells after being chilled and then warmed, the first human autoantibody ever shown to cause disease was filed away as a curiosity. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmunity' (Croonian Lecture, 1900); Wikipedia, 'Horror autotoxicus' / 'Paul Ehrlich'.

question: Before 1961 the thymus, a soft lump of tissue behind the breastbone, was written off as a leftover organ — a graveyard where worn-out lymph tissue collected. Jacques Miller cut it out of newborn mice and raised them to adulthood. What could those mice no longer do?
answer: Throw off a skin graft, even one from another species.
choices: Throw off a skin graft, even one from another species.
Clot their blood after even the smallest cut.
Put on anything close to a normal adult weight.
Clear ordinary bacteria out of the gut wall.
context: Miller's thymectomised mice also could not make antibodies to ordinary antigens. He published a preliminary communication in The Lancet in 1961 and the full account in Proceedings of the Royal Society B in 1962, and the 'vestigial' organ became the training school of the immune system. Source: Nature, Cell Death & Differentiation, 'The early work on the discovery of the function of the thymus, an interview with Jacques Miller'; Science, 'The function of the thymus and its impact on modern medicine'.

question: In 1953 Rupert Billingham, Leslie Brent and Peter Medawar injected cells from one mouse strain into the embryos and newborn pups of another. Grown up, those mice wore skin grafts from the donor strain indefinitely, where an untreated mouse tears such a graft off within days. A critic could answer that the injections had simply crippled the animals' defences. Which finding in the same paper met that objection?
answer: Skin from a third, unrelated strain was still rejected on schedule.
choices: Skin from a third, unrelated strain was still rejected on schedule.
The treated mice cleared injected bacteria as fast as untreated ones.
Their blood destroyed foreign red cells normally in a test tube.
Their lymph nodes held normal numbers of cells at autopsy.
context: '"Actively acquired tolerance" of foreign cells,' Nature 172:603–606 (1953). The third-strain graft is what makes the result mean something: the mice were not defenceless, they had learned a specific list of what counts as 'me'. Frank Macfarlane Burnet and Frank Fenner had written the prediction in 1949 in The Production of Antibodies — implant foreign cells during embryonic life and the grown animal should mount no antibody response against them — and other people's mice proved it. In Prague, Milan Hašek reached the same conclusion by a stranger route, surgically joining two chick embryos of different strains so their blood mixed; he was left out when Burnet and Medawar shared the 1960 Nobel Prize, though Medawar credited the chicken experiments in his Nobel lecture. Source: Nature 172:603–606 (1953); WEHI history, 'Publication of Burnet's Nobel Prize-Winning Immune Tolerance Theory'; Nature Reviews Immunology, 'Milan Hašek and the discovery of immunological tolerance'.

question: Ernest Witebsky refused to believe his own student. Noel Rose had spent months injecting rabbits with purified thyroid protein, and Witebsky — raised inside Paul Ehrlich's own scientific line — twice sent him back to the bench to run it again more carefully. Each time the result held. Then Witebsky named the single version of the experiment he would accept as proof. What did he demand?
answer: Take the protein from a rabbit and inject it back into that same rabbit.
choices: Take the protein from a rabbit and inject it back into that same rabbit.
Take the whole series through a second species before publishing it.
Show the same damage with no adjuvant added to the protein at all.
Prove the protein came from thyroid tissue and from no other organ.
context: Witebsky's first objection was the reasonable one — the thyroglobulin must have been denatured in purification, so the rabbits were reacting to a mangled protein rather than a real self-protein. Gentler handling gave the same result. So he demanded the version no objection could survive: a protein taken out of an animal's own body and returned to that same body, which then destroyed its own thyroid. Note the record precisely — the published 1956 paper used homologous (other-rabbit) thyroid extract; the same-animal version was the confirmation Witebsky insisted on. He was not an outsider attacking a doctrine but a protégé of one of Ehrlich's own trainees, which is exactly why he fought the result so hard. Source: The Scientist, 'The Father of Autoimmunity: A Profile of Noel Rose'.

question: A child gets over a strep throat, and weeks later a doctor hears a new murmur in her chest: one of her heart valves is scarring over. The bacteria are long gone from her body, and there are none in the valve. What is doing the damage?
answer: Antibodies raised against the bacterium that also stick to heart tissue.
choices: Antibodies raised against the bacterium that also stick to heart tissue.
A toxin left behind by the bacteria that slowly stiffens the valve.
White cells drawn to the valve during the illness that never left.
A clot thrown during the infection that hardened onto the valve.
context: Molecular mimicry: the streptococcus wears an alpha-helical coiled-coil M protein and a group A carbohydrate (N-acetylglucosamine) that structurally resemble cardiac myosin. Antibodies against the carbohydrate bind valve endothelium and switch on VCAM-1; activated T cells then push into the avascular valve and a Th1 response scars it. The murmur of rheumatic carditis is friendly fire. HONEST CAVEAT, and the bank states it plainly: 'Although rheumatic fever has been attributed to molecular mimicry for half a century no antigen has been formally identified.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Autoimmunity' (caveat verbatim); Microbiology Spectrum, 'Molecular Mimicry, Autoimmunity, and Infection: The Cross-Reactive Antigens of Group A Streptococci and their Sequelae'.

question: Every T cell that leaves the thymus has passed an audition inside it: the cell is shown fragments of the body's own proteins, and any cell that grips them too tightly is killed on the spot. But the thymus sits behind the breastbone and never meets the pancreas, the retina or the adrenal gland, so a trainee there should never once see insulin — and a T cell that would attack insulin should stroll out alive. It does not. So how does the thymus stop that cell?
answer: Thymus cells switch on thousands of genes belonging to other organs.
choices: Thymus cells switch on thousands of genes belonging to other organs.
Thymus cells display protein fragments built at random, shape after shape.
Thymus cells show trainees proteins left over from the embryo's tissues.
Thymus cells release a hormone that bars trainees from entering organs.
context: The gene is AIRE, found in 1997 by positional cloning on human chromosome 21 at band 21q22.3. In medullary thymic epithelial cells it forces 'promiscuous gene expression' — thymus cells switch on thousands of tissue-restricted antigens borrowed from organs all over the body, so trainees can be shown insulin, eye protein and adrenal protein, and killed if they react. Roughly 95% of thymocytes never leave the thymus alive; cells with intermediate self-affinity are not killed but diverted into regulatory T cells, the body's own suppression squad. When AIRE breaks — over 150 pathogenic variants are known — the result is APECED, autoimmunity striking several organs at once. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmune regulator' and 'Immune tolerance'.

question: Hospital labs test blood for antinuclear antibodies — antibodies aimed at a cell's own nucleus — and a positive result sounds like proof of autoimmune disease. Yet 20 to 30 percent of perfectly healthy people carry them at low levels, and every healthy body makes self-binding antibodies of the IgM class. In a healthy body, what job do those antibodies do?
answer: They stick to damaged and dying cells and mark them for clearance.
choices: They stick to damaged and dying cells and mark them for clearance.
They soak up loose iron spilled by cells that have burst open.
They plug tears in cell membranes until the cell repairs itself.
They coat newly made cells so the body registers them as its own.
context: A little self-recognition is normal and useful. Healthy people carry natural autoantibodies, mostly germline-encoded IgM, that bind damaged and dying cells and tag them for clean-up; germ-free mice have markedly less of this natural autoreactivity than ordinary mice. The line between health and disease is a threshold of affinity and persistence, not the mere presence of self-recognition. Source: Grokipedia, 'Autoimmunity' (Low-Level Autoimmunity).

question: About 78 percent of Americans living with an autoimmune disease are women, and nobody has explained why. In 2024 Howard Chang's team went after the best clue available: Xist, a long RNA that only females make, which coats one of a female's two X chromosomes to switch it off and drags a crowd of proteins along with it. To find out whether Xist itself was part of the answer, what did they do?
answer: Engineered male mice to make a non-silencing form of Xist.
choices: Engineered male mice to make a non-silencing form of Xist.
Deleted Xist from female mice before they reached puberty.
Transplanted marrow from female mice into male littermates.
Bred female mice carrying only one X chromosome instead of two.
context: The engineered males produced autoantibodies, their T and B cells shifted to resemble wild-type females', and SJL/J males carrying the transgene developed markedly worse disease in a pristane-induced lupus model; human autoimmune patients carry autoantibodies against components of the XIST protein complex. It is the best clue anyone has — it is not the answer. Wikipedia states the puzzle flatly: 'Being female is the single greatest risk factor for developing autoimmune disease than any other genetic or environmental risk factor yet discovered.' Hashimoto's thyroiditis runs roughly 10:1 female, systemic lupus erythematosus 9:1, Graves' disease 7:1 — and no one yet knows why. Source: Cell (2024), 'Xist ribonucleoproteins promote female sex-biased autoimmunity'; Nature Reviews Rheumatology commentary; Wikipedia, 'Autoimmunity'.

question: In 1966 a 27-year-old venereal-disease investigator inside the US Public Health Service, Peter Buxtun, filed a formal written objection to the Tuskegee syphilis study. He was overruled. He argued it in person in Atlanta in 1967. He was overruled again. In 1972 he finally did the one thing that actually closed the study within months. What did he do?
answer: He handed the file to a reporter
choices: He handed the file to a reporter
He resigned in a public protest
He mailed the file to a Senator
He filed a suit against the Service
context: The chain ran Peter Buxtun to AP's Edith Lederer to Jean Heller, whose story broke on July 25, 1972 in more than 100 newspapers. The Service ended the study inside a few months. The chain was employee, then journalist; the institution was never in it. Source: cnn.com/2024/07/16, uclawsf.edu.

question: Harrison Martland was the medical examiner for Essex County, New Jersey, in the 1920s. Radium-dial painters were dying and their employers denied any link to the paint they had been licking to point their brushes. Martland could not X-ray the whole body of a living woman, but he found a way to prove the paint was still inside her using a single exhalation. What did he capture from her breath?
answer: A trace of radon gas
choices: A trace of radon gas
A trace of mercury vapour
A trace of luminescent dust
A trace of vaporised lead
context: Radon is the daughter product of radium decay; it drifts out through the lungs. Detecting it in exhaled breath was direct forensic proof the women's own bodies had become radium sources. Source: environmentalhistory.org.

question: The Radium Girls' bosses controlled the payroll, the medical records, and the courtroom. Their bodies, however, were their own. Martland worked out what to do with the exhumed dead: he laid their bones on unexposed photographic plates for several weeks. When developed, the plates showed a soft image printed into the emulsion. Where had the image come from?
answer: The bones themselves were radioactive
choices: The bones themselves were radioactive
A weak lamp above the storage shelf
The developer bath used on the plates
Bacteria feeding on residues in the bone
context: The dial-painters' bones were so contaminated with radium that they took their own picture - a jaw, a spine, a hand, printed by their own decay. When a company controls the records, the physical evidence in the victim IS the record. Source: environmentalhistory.org, history.com.

question: In 2010 the world learned that the US Public Health Service had, in Guatemala in the late 1940s, deliberately infected hundreds of people with syphilis and gonorrhoea. It was found sixty-two years after it happened. Where, exactly, was the evidence found?
answer: In the personal papers of a dead PHS doctor
choices: In the personal papers of a dead PHS doctor
In a declassified batch of State Department cables
In court exhibits from a settled civil lawsuit
In transcripts of a Congressional subcommittee
context: Susan Reverby, a Wellesley College medical historian, was reading John Cutler's own donated notes in the University of Pittsburgh archives while researching Tuskegee. Perpetrators keep files. Files outlive them. Source: neh.gov, oah.org.

question: Frances Kelsey, the FDA reviewer who kept thalidomide off the US market in 1961, was not braver than her critics and not more famous. She simply kept asking the drug's maker for one specific thing and refused to sign until she got it. She never got it. What was the specific thing she kept demanding?
answer: Adequate animal safety data on the drug
choices: Adequate animal safety data on the drug
A signed sign-off from a foreign regulator
A larger sample of surveyed US patients
The chemist's original synthesis notes
context: The data did not exist because the drug had never been properly tested for pregnancy safety. Thousands of babies in Europe were born with severe birth defects; Kelsey's demand for evidence prevented an American cohort. The test was never courage - it was evidence. Source: fda.gov/about-fda/histories-product-regulation.

question: A small forward-facing tube juts from an airliner's nose and gives the pilot his airspeed, the number he can least afford to lose. Its ancestor was built in 1732 by Henri Pitot, an engineer of the Academie Royale des Sciences, and the first thing he pushed it into was not the sky. What was it?
answer: The current of the Seine, to learn how fast the river ran
choices: The current of the Seine, to learn how fast the river ran
The rush of a Loire mill-race, to learn how fast the water ran
The blast of a Rouen forge bellows, to learn how fast the air ran
The updraught of a Lyon chimney, to learn how fast the smoke ran
context: Henri Pitot (1695-1771) was a French hydraulic engineer, and the Academie he served sat in Paris, on the Seine. His machine was two glass tubes fixed in a wooden triangular-prism frame - one bent to face the current, one straight and side-on - with a movable copper scale for reading the two heights. He published it in the Memoires de l'Academie Royale des Sciences for 1732 as 'Description d'une machine pour mesurer la vitesse des eaux courantes, et le sillage des vaisseaux': a machine for measuring the speed of running water, and the wake of ships. Henry Darcy, from 1856 with Henri Bazin, added the second, side-facing opening that makes the modern pitot-static tube. Source: Grokipedia, 'Pitot tube'.

question: A Boeing 757 stood twenty days at Puerto Plata in the Dominican Republic, and for at least the last two nobody had put the covers back on its pitot tubes, the forward-facing tubes that read a pilot's airspeed. It took off on 6 February 1996; the captain's airspeed read a false 350 knots while it was really doing 220, the autopilot believed it, and all 189 aboard died. What was inside his tube?
answer: A mud dauber wasp's nest, built of mud and grit
choices: A mud dauber wasp's nest, built of mud and grit
A plug of sea salt crusted from the coastal air
A strip of masking tape left on by a cleaner
A wad of straw dropped in by a nesting bird
context: Mud dauber wasps (Sceliphron caementarium) had packed the captain's tube with mud and debris. The autopilot, trusting the false reading, pulled the thrust back to idle and raised the nose, and the crew mistook the stick shaker for a configuration warning. Ice does the same thing: on 1 June 2009 the Thales pitot probes of Air France 447, an Airbus A330 crossing the Intertropical Convergence Zone at 35,000 feet, iced over in cumulonimbus and all three air-data units lost airspeed at 02:10:05 UTC. The autopilot dropped out, the pilots held persistent nose-up inputs, and the aircraft fell in a stall at more than 10,000 feet per minute into the Atlantic; all 228 aboard died and the wreckage lay about 3,900 metres down. The BEA's 2012 final report issued 25 safety recommendations. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Birgenair Flight 301' and 'Air France Flight 447'.

question: Hold a strip of paper to your lower lip and blow across the top of it: the far end rises. Generations of teachers have called this Bernoulli's principle at work, the fast air above being low-pressure air that lifts the paper. Now turn the strip over and blow along its underside instead, with nothing at all moving above it. What does the strip do?
answer: It rises again, just as it did before
choices: It rises again, just as it did before
It swings downward instead of rising
It flutters hard but stays where it is
It curls up at the far end and droops
context: Try it both ways yourself. What lifts the strip is not a comparison between its two sides at all. The air leaving your mouth is at exactly the pressure of the room around it - moving air is not automatically low-pressure air - and 'it is false to make a connection between the flow on the two sides of the paper using Bernoulli's equation since the air above and below are different flow fields.' What does the work is the curving of the jet you blow: the paper bends your jet, and the bent jet pushes back. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle', 'Misunderstandings about the generation of lift'.

question: A glass pipe on a physics bench narrows to a throat and widens again, with slender liquid-filled side tubes tapped into its wall along the way. Water is pumped steadily through, the same amount passing every point, so at the pinch it must hurry. Each side tube reports the pressure at its own spot on the wall. What do they show?
answer: The liquid stands lowest at the throat
choices: The liquid stands lowest at the throat
The liquid stands highest at the throat
The liquid stands level along the whole pipe
The liquid climbs steadily toward the outlet
context: This is a Venturi tube, and it is what a genuine demonstration of Bernoulli's principle looks like: a pressure drop measured directly where the flow is measured to be fastest. Daniel Bernoulli published the principle in Hydrodynamica in 1738 and it has never been in doubt - it lets a Venturi meter read a pipe's flow rate off nothing but that drop, draws petrol into the airstream at a carburettor's throat, drives an aspirator and a scent atomiser, and gives a pilot his airspeed through a pitot tube. Keep this straight: when the schoolbook explanation of a wing fails, the principle is not the part that fails. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle'; Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle'.

question: Holger Babinsky, professor of aerodynamics at Cambridge, asks audiences whether they were taught this argument for how a wing lifts: the air splits at the wing's nose; the upper surface is the longer path; the two halves rejoin at the trailing edge, so the top air hurries; and faster-moving air runs at lower pressure, so the wing is sucked up. About 95% of hands go up, and Babinsky says only a handful know it is wrong. Which of those four steps is the story's invention?
answer: That the two halves rejoin at the trailing edge
choices: That the two halves rejoin at the trailing edge
That the flow divides at the wing's leading edge
That the upper surface is the longer of the two paths
That faster-moving air runs at lower pressure
context: Note which step survived the audit: Bernoulli's. The principle is sound physics; what fails is the equal-transit assumption bolted onto it. Wikipedia's 'Lift (force)' is blunt: 'There is no physical principle that requires equal transit time in all situations and experimental results confirm that for a body generating lift the transit times are not equal.' There is a second, quieter error too: 'No difference in path length is needed, and even when there is a difference, it is typically much too small to explain the observed speed difference.' Babinsky's own verdict on the story 95% of every audience raises a hand to: 'But this is wrong.' Sources: University of Cambridge, 'How wings really work'; Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)'; Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)'.

question: Holger Babinsky mounted an aerofoil in a Cambridge wind tunnel and released pulses of smoke into the airflow, filming what became of them. Each pulse split at the wing's nose, half riding over the humped top and half running along underneath; he published the frames in Physics Education in 2003. Freeze one frame and look at the wing's trailing edge. Where have the two halves of a single pulse got to?
answer: The top half is past the trailing edge; the bottom half is not
choices: The top half is past the trailing edge; the bottom half is not
The bottom half is past the trailing edge; the top half is not
Both halves reach the trailing edge together, side by side
Both halves meet again a little past the trailing edge
context: The smoke over the top arrives early and has already left the wing behind. Babinsky published the physics in 'How do wings work?', Physics Education 38(6), page 497, 2003; the abstract says the popular explanation 'is common, quick, sounds logical and gives the correct answer, yet also introduces misconceptions.' The numbers convict the story too: if the parcels really had to meet, the top air would need to run only about 3-5% faster than the air underneath, yet measurements show it running as much as 50% or more above the freestream speed. David Anderson of Fermilab and Scott Eberhardt of the University of Washington did the arithmetic for a Cessna 172, whose upper surface is only 1.5-2.5% longer than its lower: on the equal-transit story 'a Cessna 172 would have to fly at over 400 mph to generate enough lift.' It cruises at about 110 knots. The historian J. A. D. Ackroyd adds that Babinsky was not the first - 'over the years, photographs and films have consistently shown the same behaviour' - the evidence was there and simply went unbelieved. Sources: Babinsky, Physics Education 38 497 (2003); Ackroyd, Journal of Aeronautical History Paper No. 2015/01; Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)'; Anderson & Eberhardt, 'How Airplanes Fly'.

question: On the schoolbook story an aeroplane could never fly upside down. Rolled onto its back, a wing's humped surface is now the lower one, so the longer path is underneath and the wing ought to be pressed toward the ground. Stunt pilots hold steady inverted flight at every airshow. What keeps the upside-down wing lifting?
answer: The pilot holds the nose up, and the wing's tilt alone makes the lift
choices: The pilot holds the nose up, and the wing's tilt alone makes the lift
The pilot flies faster, and the extra speed alone carries the weight
The engine angles its thrust up, and that push alone holds the plane
The propeller blasts the wing's underside, and that wash alone lifts it
context: The tilt has a name: the angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. 'When a cambered airfoil is upside down, the angle of attack can be adjusted so that the lift force is upward.' The same point kills the shape story outright, since it 'does not explain how flat plates, symmetric airfoils, sailboat sails, or conventional airfoils flying upside down can generate lift.' Thin-aerofoil theory gives a flat plate - no hump at all - a lift coefficient of CL = 2 x pi x alpha, with alpha the angle of attack in radians: a plain plate lifts perfectly well the moment it is tilted. Babinsky on a sail, whose two faces are exactly the same length: 'here the distance on each side is the same but it is slightly curved when it is rigged and so it acts as an aerofoil.' Throw a flat balsa glider across the room and you have tested this yourself. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)'; Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)'; University of Cambridge, 'How wings really work'.

question: A teacher points a hairdryer straight up, rests a ping-pong ball in the jet, and the ball hovers there and will not fall out. Bernoulli, says the teacher: the fast air of the jet is low-pressure air, so the ball sits in a pocket of suction. Measure the plume, though, and its pressure is exactly the room's. What holds the ball in the jet?
answer: Off-centre, the ball meets lopsided flow that shoves it back inward
choices: Off-centre, the ball meets lopsided flow that shoves it back inward
Spinning, the ball drags air around itself and steers itself inward
Clinging, the flow follows the ball's curve and draws it inward
Warmed, the plume thins and the ball slides down into its core
context: 'The air in the plume has the same pressure as the surrounding air. The ball remains in the plume since as it moves away from the center of the plume it experiences an asymmetric air flow which pushes it back toward the center.' A charming demonstration with a wrong caption. A genuine Bernoulli demonstration is a Venturi tube read with a liquid gauge, where the pressure at the throat is measured directly. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle'; Grokipedia, 'Bernoulli's principle', 'Common Demonstrations and Errors'.

question: The photographer Paul Bowen, shooting for Cessna, caught an aeroplane a moment after it had passed low over a flat bank of fog. Where the machine went by, a huge hole now stands open in the grey deck. Aerodynamicists reprint the frame whenever they argue about lift. What punched the hole?
answer: The wing had thrown a whole column of air downward as it passed
choices: The wing had thrown a whole column of air downward as it passed
The engine's hot exhaust had burned a trench through the droplets
The low pressure above the wing had drawn the fog up after it
The propeller's swirl had wound the fog into a rope and flung it
context: 'A huge hole is punched through the fog by the downwash from the airplane that has just flown over it' (Fig. 6, photograph by Paul Bowen, courtesy Cessna Aircraft Co.). By Newton's third law, air pushed down pushes the wing up - and the downward turning 'is not produced solely by the lower surface of the airfoil'; the flow above the wing does much of it. Anderson and Eberhardt estimate that a Cessna 172 at 110 knots, with an average downwash of about 9 knots, must pump 'a whopping 2.5 ton/sec of air' downward to make its 2,300 lb of lift, accelerating essentially all the air within about nine feet above the wing - and they note their own estimate 'may be as much as a factor of two too low.' The same tight downward column shows under a helicopter's rotors, behind a propeller and below a household fan, all of which are rotating wings. 'If a plane were to fly over a very large scale, the scale would register the weight of the plane.' Sources: Anderson & Eberhardt, 'How Airplanes Fly'; Wikipedia, 'Lift (force)'.

question: A pilot eases the nose up and the wing lifts harder; further still, and harder still. Then, near fifteen degrees of tilt, the lift does not merely level off, it collapses, falling by 60 to 80% in an instant while the drag surges. This is the moment pilots call a stall. What has happened to the air flowing over the wing's upper surface?
answer: It has torn away from the surface instead of following it round
choices: It has torn away from the surface instead of following it round
It has slowed to a standstill and settled into a still cushion
It has been squeezed to a higher pressure than the air beneath
It has run faster than sound and thrown a shock wave across it
context: Past the critical angle of attack - roughly fifteen degrees - the boundary layer, the thin sheet of air right against the wing's skin, separates from the upper surface, and with the flow no longer following the wing round the lift collapses, often by 60-80% from its maximum value, while drag surges. Recovery shows hysteresis: the pilot must lower the nose further than the angle at which it broke before the flow will reattach. Leading-edge slats and vortex generators buy back only about five degrees. Source: Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)', 'Boundary Layer, Drag, and Stalling'.

question: Write down the ideal-flow equations for air streaming past a wing and they refuse to give a single answer. They allow an infinity of solutions, each with a different circulation, a different strength of spin running round the wing, and each satisfies the mathematics perfectly. Only one of them describes a real wing in real air. What one physical requirement picks it out?
answer: That the flow must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly, not whip round it
choices: That the flow must leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly, not whip round it
That the flow must close up smoothly behind the wing, leaving no vortex
That the flow's spin must add up to zero on a loop around the wing
That the flow must reach its lowest pressure at the wing's thickest point
context: This is the Kutta condition: 'A body with a sharp trailing edge which is moving through a fluid will create about itself a circulation of sufficient strength to hold the rear stagnation point at the trailing edge.' Mathematically it 'enforces a specific choice among the infinite allowed values of circulation' - and it is why aerofoils are built with sharp trailing edges even though sharp edges are awkward to make. The circulation it fixes IS the lift, by the Kutta-Zhukovskii theorem: L = rho x V x Gamma, with rho the air density, V the flow speed, and Gamma the circulation - the sum, round any imaginary loop enclosing the wing, of the flow's speed along that loop. How anyone knows this is true: in the 1920s British researchers measured airflow velocities all round wind-tunnel aerofoils and then did the laborious hand-summation of the circulation round a loop. Bryant and Williams (results published 1924, a thick cambered aerofoil) got a lift from L = rho V Gamma within 6% of the lift computed from the measured pressures; Tanner (1930, an RAF 30 symmetrical section at 7 degrees incidence) got within 2%. And because a vortex cannot simply end, the trailing vortices behind a wing 'can be traced right back to the airfield at which the wing first generated lift', where the loop is closed by the starting vortex shed the instant the wing first took up lifting incidence. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kutta condition'; Ackroyd, Journal of Aeronautical History Paper No. 2015/01.

question: Two camps argue about a wing. One says lift is a pressure difference: lower pressure pulling from above, higher pressure pushing from below. The other says lift is Newton's third law: the wing turns air downward and the air shoves back. Each calls the other's account a mere by-product. The Euler equations, which govern the flow itself, settle the quarrel. What do they say about which of the two comes first?
answer: Neither is primary; pressure and turned flow produce each other together
choices: Neither is primary; pressure and turned flow produce each other together
Pressure is primary; the turning of the flow is only its visible after-effect
Flow turning is primary; the pressure difference is only its book-keeping
Neither is primary; both follow from the air's friction against the skin
context: 'Changes in velocity induce pressure gradients that, in turn, cause streamline curvature and further alterations in velocity... neither pressure nor velocity can be considered primary; instead, they evolve together in a self-consistent manner throughout the flow field.' The concrete grip: a curved streamline needs a centripetal force to bend it, and the pressure gradient across the streamlines supplies it - sharper curvature over the top is exactly why the pressure there is lower. Babinsky's positive statement of the mechanism: 'What actually causes lift is introducing a shape into the airflow, which curves the streamlines and introduces pressure changes - lower pressure on the upper surface and higher pressure on the lower surface.' Viscous skin friction contributes less than 5% of the total lift, so lift really is a pressure phenomenon, even though viscosity is what sets the circulation up in the first place. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Lift (force)', 'Pressure-Velocity Interactions and Limitations of Simpler Models'; University of Cambridge, 'How wings really work'.

question: Jeremiah Horrocks aimed a telescope at the Sun in November 1639 to catch Venus crossing it. Put your eye to the far end of such a telescope and you are blinded in an instant. Horrocks watched for half an hour and kept his sight. How?
answer: He cast the Sun's image out of the telescope onto paper.
choices: He cast the Sun's image out of the telescope onto paper.
He capped the eyepiece with a disc of smoked glass.
He caught the Sun's reflection in a basin of still water.
He waited for thin cloud to dim the Sun enough to look.
context: Horrocks threw the Sun through the telescope onto a sheet of paper on which he had already drawn a circle, so he could measure Venus against it. He watched from about a quarter past three until sunset at about ten to four, and wrote: 'I then beheld a most agreeable spectacle, the object of my sanguine wishes, a spot of unusual magnitude and of a perfectly circular shape.' You can do exactly this yourself: hold a white card behind binoculars or a small telescope and let the Sun's image fall on it -- and never, ever look through them at the Sun. Source: Wikipedia, '1639 transit of Venus'; tide-and-time.uk, 'Local heroes: Jeremiah Horrocks'.

question: The Greek astronomer Aristarchus of Samos, around 280 BC, wanted to know how much farther away the Sun is than the Moon. He had no instrument but his own eyes, and a plan of pure geometry: wait for one particular moment, then take a single measurement. Which moment did he wait for?
answer: When the Moon showed exactly half lit.
choices: When the Moon showed exactly half lit.
When the Moon slid fully into Earth's shadow.
When the Moon blotted out the Sun entirely.
When the full Moon rose exactly at sunset.
context: At the instant the Moon is exactly half lit, the angle at the Moon between Earth and Sun must be a right angle -- so the angle between Moon and Sun as seen from the ground fixes the whole triangle. Aristarchus measured that angle as 87 degrees. It is really 89.853, and no naked eye can catch a difference that fine, so he put the Sun at 18 to 20 times the Moon's distance instead of about 390. His geometry was sound; his instrument was not. Go out at a half Moon and try to judge how far around the sky the Sun sits from it, and you will feel how brutal the measurement is. (Eratosthenes' famous stick-and-shadow trick, often muddled with this one, sizes the Earth -- it says nothing about the Sun's distance.) Two thousand years later the true distance was still unknown, which is why a black dot creeping across the Sun was worth crossing oceans for. Source: Wikipedia, 'Astronomical unit' (Aristarchus, 87 degrees against 89.853; 18-20 times).

question: Edmond Halley published his method for measuring the Sun's distance in the Philosophical Transactions of 1716. The method was worthless without a transit of Venus, and the next two would not come until 1761 and 1769. What did Halley put in the closing lines of that paper?
answer: A plea to strangers not yet born to make the observation.
choices: A plea to strangers not yet born to make the observation.
A table of the exact hours the 1761 crossing would fall.
A challenge to the Paris Observatory to attempt it first.
A warning that his own arithmetic might hide an error.
context: The paper was 'A new Method of determining the Parallax of the Sun, or his Distance from the Earth' (Philosophical Transactions, 1716); Halley had read an early version to the Royal Society back in 1691, and wrote in Latin on purpose, so astronomers all over Europe could use it. One common English rendering of his closing words: 'I recommend it therefore again and again to those curious astronomers who, when I am dead, will have an opportunity of observing these things.' He died nineteen years before the first of the two transits he had planned. Source: classicalastrologer.com, 'Edmund Halley: Admonition of 1716'; Grokipedia, 'The Transit of Venus'; skyandtelescope.org, 'Transits of Venus in history, 1631-1716'.

question: Edmond Halley's way of measuring the Sun's distance needs two observers on far-apart parts of Earth. Each sees the planet cut a slightly different line across the Sun's face, so each records a slightly different crossing time - and that difference is the whole measurement. Mercury crosses the Sun too, and more often. Why did Halley insist on Venus?
answer: Venus passes far nearer Earth, so its shift is far bigger.
choices: Venus passes far nearer Earth, so its shift is far bigger.
Venus crosses far more slowly, so the timings are easier.
Venus shows a far bigger disc, so its edge is sharper.
Venus rides nearer the Sun's centre, so its line is longer.
context: The difference between the two timings gives what astronomers call the Sun's parallax, and that number is the whole point. Kepler's laws had already fixed the spacing of the solar system perfectly -- Venus at 0.723 of Earth's distance from the Sun, Mars at 1.524, Jupiter at 5.203 -- but in relative units only: nothing anywhere said how many miles one unit was. Measure a single real distance and every other one follows. Halley's arithmetic promised that if observers could time the moments of contact to within two seconds, the Sun's distance would come out good to one part in 500. That promise is what persuaded governments to pay. Source: Grokipedia, 'The Transit of Venus'; Wikipedia, "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"; Ohio State Astronomy 161 notes, 'Venus and the Sun'.

question: Guillaume Le Gentil left Paris in March 1760 for Pondicherry in India, to time the transit of 6 June 1761. The British took the town before he arrived, and on transit morning he was still at sea, unable to fix his position on a rolling deck - and a shipboard timing is worthless. Rather than go home, he stayed in the Indian Ocean for the eight years to the next transit. What survey did he carry out?
answer: He charted the east coast of Madagascar.
choices: He charted the east coast of Madagascar.
He mapped the reefs of the Coromandel coast.
He surveyed the volcanoes of the Java coast.
He measured the tides of the Persian Gulf.
context: Le Gentil sailed from Paris on 26 March 1760, reached Mauritius that July, and was still aboard ship when Venus crossed the Sun on 6 June 1761 under a clear sky. He filled the eight years with work: he charted Madagascar's east coast, went to Manila in 1766, was driven out by a Spanish governor-general who insisted his royal letters were forgeries, and reached Pondicherry -- French again after the 1763 peace -- in March 1768, where he built himself a small observatory on a ruined fort. Source: Wikipedia, 'Guillaume Le Gentil'; armaghplanet.com, 'The unluckiest astronomer in history'.

question: In 1639 the Rudolphine Tables of Johannes Kepler were the finest astronomical tables in Europe, and they promised no transit of Venus before 1761. Jeremiah Horrocks, barely into his twenties, was at Much Hoole in Lancashire with a single telescope, and on 24 November that year - by the Julian calendar England still kept - he was watching the Sun anyway. What had put him there?
answer: He had reworked Kepler's own numbers and found the crossing himself.
choices: He had reworked Kepler's own numbers and found the crossing himself.
He had a letter from a Dutch astronomer predicting the crossing.
He had watched the Sun daily for sunspots and caught it by luck.
He had followed a rival set of tables printed that year in Paris.
context: Kepler's tables had Venus passing just above the Sun that day -- a near miss. Horrocks recomputed them, found the near miss was really a hit, and had under four weeks to prepare. England was still on the Julian calendar; that date was 4 December 1639 on the Gregorian calendar used across the Channel. Only one other human being saw it: his friend William Crabtree at Broughton near Manchester, who got a glimpse through a cloud gap and sketched fast -- and whose rushed estimate of Venus's size beat Horrocks's careful one by an arcsecond. Horrocks's figure for the Sun's distance came out near 60 million miles, about two-thirds of the truth, but ten times larger than the value astronomers had inherited from Ptolemy. He died on 3 January 1641, aged 22; his account 'Venus in sole visa' sat unpublished for 22 years until Hevelius printed it in 1662. Source: Wikipedia, '1639 transit of Venus' and 'Jeremiah Horrocks'; Grokipedia, '1639 transit of Venus'.

question: For the 1761 transit the French astronomer Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche hauled his instruments across a continent to Tobolsk in Siberia. That spring the rivers there flooded worse than anyone could remember. Chappe timed the whole crossing successfully - from a hilltop, with armed Cossacks standing round him. Why did he need the guard?
answer: Peasants blamed that spring's floods on his meddling with the Sun.
choices: Peasants blamed that spring's floods on his meddling with the Sun.
Flood refugees had been looting the town for anything portable.
The governor suspected him of mapping the frontier for France.
A rival Russian party had threatened to seize his instruments.
context: Chappe got the entire 1761 transit despite the hostility. For 1769 he travelled to the mission at San Jose del Cabo in Baja California and again got a clean observation -- and then an epidemic swept the settlement. He caught it while nursing the sick and died on 1 August 1769, aged 47. Only one member of his party survived to carry his notebooks back to Paris. Source: Wikipedia, 'Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche'; IMCCE (Paris Observatory), promenade.imcce.fr.

question: Guillaume Le Gentil had lost the 1761 transit at sea, and had waited eight years in the Indian Ocean for the next one. On the morning of the 1769 transit a cloud covered the Sun over Pondicherry, while Manila - the station he had given up - stayed clear all day. Dysentery and a hurricane delayed him further. He crossed into France in October 1771, after eleven years, six months and thirteen days away. What had French law done with him in the meantime?
answer: It had declared him dead and let his heirs divide his estate.
choices: It had declared him dead and let his heirs divide his estate.
It had seized his estate to repay the crown's outlay on him.
It had granted him a pension against his eventual return.
It had held his estate in trust under a court's appointed man.
context: His seat at the Academy of Sciences had also been filled, and it took lengthy litigation and the intervention of the king to get it back. He later married, had a daughter, and died in Paris on 22 October 1792. His own published verdict on the whole affair: 'That is the fate which often awaits astronomers. I had gone more than ten thousand leagues...' Sources differ on whether the Pondicherry cloud fell on 3 or 4 June 1769, and the often-repeated claim that his wife had remarried is disputed -- the losses above are the ones the records agree on. Source: Wikipedia, 'Guillaume Le Gentil'; armaghplanet.com, 'The unluckiest astronomer in history'; IMCCE, promenade.imcce.fr.

question: James Cook took his ship the Endeavour to Tahiti for the transit of 3 June 1769 and set up his instruments in a fortified camp on the beach at Matavai Bay. On the day, he wrote, 'not a Cloud was to be seen the whole day and the Air was perfectly clear.' Cook, Charles Green and Daniel Solander each timed the exact instants when Venus's edge met the Sun's - and their three sets of times disagreed far more than anyone had expected. What did Cook's journal blame?
answer: A dusky shade clinging round the body of the planet.
choices: A dusky shade clinging round the body of the planet.
A tremor in the sandy ground beneath the telescopes.
A fault in the clock the Royal Society had supplied.
A dispute over which edge marked the first contact.
context: The Royal Society got 4,000 pounds from King George III for the voyage, and Cook built an earthwork-and-palisade camp he called Fort Venus; the headland at Matavai Bay is still called Point Venus today. Cook wrote that the three of them 'differ'd from one another in observeing the times of the Contacts much more than could be expected', and that they 'very distinctly saw an Atmosphere or dusky shade round the body of the Planet which very much disturbed the times of the Contacts.' Astronomers came to call it the black drop. Perfect weather was not enough; the limit was in the light itself. Source: Wikipedia, '1769 transit of Venus observed from Tahiti' (quoting Cook's journal); aaa.org, 'History of the transit of Venus'.

question: The transit campaigns were mounted to measure one distance, and that is not what they are best remembered for. Watching the 1761 crossing from St Petersburg, Mikhail Lomonosov noticed something at the two instants when Venus sat half on and half off the Sun's face - a detail nobody had sailed anywhere to look for, and he read it correctly on the spot. What had Lomonosov become the first human being to detect?
answer: An atmosphere on another planet.
choices: An atmosphere on another planet.
A moon orbiting another planet.
A ring of dust round another planet.
A mountain range on another planet.
context: Lomonosov saw a luminous arc standing around the part of Venus still hanging off the Sun, at entry and again at exit, and read it as sunlight bent through the planet's own air. It is the first detection of an atmosphere on any world beyond Earth -- found by a man who had come to measure a distance and got a planet's weather instead. Source: Wikipedia, 'Transit of Venus'; arXiv:1206.3489, "Lomonosov's discovery of Venus atmosphere in 1761".

question: The black drop defeated Halley's method. As Venus's disc meets the inner edge of the Sun, it seems to stretch a dark thread back to that edge, like a drop refusing to fall, and no two observers agree on the instant it breaks. It smeared the timings by around ten seconds; Halley's arithmetic had needed two. Astronomers argued for a century about the cause, and most of them blamed something belonging to Venus itself. Which observation ruled that out?
answer: Mercury's transits show the same thread, and Mercury has no air.
choices: Mercury's transits show the same thread, and Mercury has no air.
The Moon's edge shows the same thread at a partial eclipse.
The ligament appeared on the Sun's far edge, well away from Venus.
Ships' observers saw it, while mountain observers saw none at all.
context: Friedrich Bessel and Friedrich Argelander made the point with Mercury's transits in 1832: the same dark thread appears, and Mercury has essentially no atmosphere at all. The modern explanation is not the planet -- it is the extreme darkening of the Sun's own disc near its edge, combined with the limited resolving power of the telescope and the shimmer of Earth's air. A method that needed two-second precision was being asked for it by eyes looking through a wobbling atmosphere. Source: Wikipedia, 'Black drop effect'; Grokipedia, 'black drop effect'.

question: Maximilian Hell, a Jesuit astronomer, timed the 1769 transit from Vardo, inside the Arctic Circle. Decades later Carl Littrow, who had inherited Hell's papers at Vienna, went through the original data sheets, found figures scraped out and written over in ink of a slightly different shade, and published the charge that Hell had faked his results. The charge stood for decades. In 1883 Simon Newcomb examined the very same sheets. What did Newcomb discover?
answer: Littrow was colour-blind, and the two inks were one ink.
choices: Littrow was colour-blind, and the two inks were one ink.
The darker ink was added at Vienna years after Hell died.
The ink had faded unevenly where the sheets were kept damp.
Littrow's own hand had made the changes while cataloguing.
context: Newcomb first showed that the smudges had been made with a wet finger while the ink was still fresh -- corrections made on the spot by an observer fixing his own numbers, not a forger's later work. Then he found that Littrow, who had convicted Hell on the evidence of colour, could not distinguish colours. Hell's Vardo data were sound. The lesson generalises: when a charge rests on one man's observation, check the observer. Source: faculty.fairfield.edu/jmac/sj/hell.htm; Wikipedia, 'Maximilian Hell'; Newcomb's 1883 paper "On Hell's alleged falsification of his observations of the transit of Venus in 1769".

question: The transits gave their best answer long after the last one: Johann Encke's 1824 reanalysis of every 1761 and 1769 timing put the Sun at 153.3 million kilometres, against a true 149.6 million - an error of two and a half per cent wrung out of ships, clouds and shaky pendulum clocks. Then in 1961 teams in the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain each got the figure independently, and none of them watched Venus cross anything. How did the three teams get their figure?
answer: They bounced radio pulses off Venus and timed the returning echo.
choices: They bounced radio pulses off Venus and timed the returning echo.
They photographed Venus from opposite poles on the same night.
They timed starlight grazing the Sun's edge during an eclipse.
They weighed the Sun's pull with pendulums at three latitudes.
context: Muhleman and colleagues, using 12.5 cm radar, published 149,598,845 km give or take 250 km; Millstone Hill got 149,597,700 and Jodrell Bank 149,601,000. That is a few hundred kilometres of uncertainty, not metres -- the metre-level figures came later, from tracking spacecraft, and in 2012 the IAU simply defined the astronomical unit as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres. The transits were not wasted, either: Thomas Hornsby's reduction of the 1769 data gave 93,726,900 miles against a true 92,955,000 -- an error of 0.8 per cent, from men timing a black dot by pendulum clock on a Pacific beach. Source: Muhleman et al., Astronomical Journal 67, 191 (1962); IEEE, 'The 1961 JPL Venus radar experiment'; Wikipedia, 'Astronomical unit' and '1769 transit of Venus observed from Tahiti'.

question: A single strand of your own hair is about 70 micrometres across. If you tried to lay your own cells side by side to span its width, how many would fit?
answer: About three to seven
choices: About three to seven
About sixty to eighty
About five hundred
About ten thousand
context: A typical human cell runs 10-30 micrometres. About 500 E. coli bacteria fit across the same hair -- bacteria are roughly a hundred times smaller by volume. Source: Medical News Today, 'How many cells are in the human body?'

question: Ron Sender and Ron Milo's 2016 count put the human body at about 30 trillion cells; Eva Bianconi's 2013 count put it at about 37 trillion. Both counts agree on one surprise -- roughly 84 percent of your cells belong to a single tiny kind that contributes only about 4 percent of your body mass. Which kind?
answer: Red blood cells
choices: Red blood cells
Skin cells shed from the outer layer
Fat cells stored under the skin
Muscle cells in the heart and gut
context: Each red blood cell is about 8 micrometres across and jettisons its nucleus before entering circulation -- which is why it stays small and fast and is thrown away after ~120 days. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: For forty years textbooks and TED talks repeated a startling line: 'you are only 10 percent human -- bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one.' In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo simply redid the arithmetic. What ratio did the fresh count give?
answer: Roughly 1.3 bacteria to 1 human cell
choices: Roughly 1.3 bacteria to 1 human cell
Roughly 100 bacteria to 1 human cell
Roughly 1 bacterium to 10 human cells
Roughly 1,000 bacteria to 1 human cell
context: The 10:1 line traced back to a single 1972 back-of-the-envelope estimate by microbiologist Thomas Luckey and had never been checked. The whole microbiome weighs about 0.2 kg, not the widely repeated 1-2 kg. A myth killed by careful counting -- no new instrument needed. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: In 2022 researchers described a single bacterium growing on sunken red-mangrove leaves in the Guadeloupe archipelago. How big was one cell?
answer: Up to about 2 centimetres long -- visible without a microscope
choices: Up to about 2 centimetres long -- visible without a microscope
Up to about 100 micrometres -- just visible in a hand lens
Up to about 5 micrometres -- typical bacterial size
Up to about 20 metres -- as long as a blue whale
context: Thiomargarita magnifica -- 'magnificent' -- can be picked up with tweezers, roughly 5,000 times larger than a normal bacterium and 50 times larger than the previous record-holder. Source: Natural History Museum (UK), 'World's largest bacteria are visible to the naked eye'.

question: A typical bacterium 5 micrometres long has no trouble feeding its interior. Thiomargarita magnifica is thousands of times bigger and should starve. It does not. What cheat lets the giant get around the surface-area-to-volume trap?
answer: A vast internal vacuole pins its living cytoplasm to the outer skin
choices: A vast internal vacuole pins its living cytoplasm to the outer skin
It uses tiny internal fans to stir its cytoplasm continuously
It grows a second, inner surface to double its intake area
It slows its metabolism to about a hundredth of normal
context: The central vacuole fills 65-80% of the cell, so the living, hungry cytoplasm sits as a thin shell against the outside -- and its DNA is packed into membrane-bound sacs called 'pepins' rather than floating loose. Bacteria are supposed not to have membrane-bound organelles; this one does. Source: Natural History Museum (UK), 2022.

question: The surface-to-volume rule says a cell that grows too big starves in the middle -- yet the single longest cell inside your own body runs from the base of your spine all the way down to your toe. How does one cell get away with being roughly a metre long?
answer: It is a thin thread, so every point is still close to its surface
choices: It is a thin thread, so every point is still close to its surface
It is packed with tiny internal hearts that pump nutrients along it
It survives on stored food and dies after a few weeks
It is actually thousands of small cells fused end to end
context: A motor neuron running from the lumbar spinal cord to the foot is a single cell -- but a wire, not a ball. The surface-to-volume trap punishes SPHERES; stretch the same volume into a thread and the surface stays generous. The rule bends where the shape bends. Source: Interesting Engineering, 'How many cells are in the human body?'

question: In warm broth with all the food it can eat, a single E. coli splits into two roughly every 20 minutes. What is the consequence of that number a first-year microbiology student meets in lab?
answer: One invisible cell becomes a visible colony overnight
choices: One invisible cell becomes a visible colony overnight
The population level stabilises within a few hours
Individual cells grow steadily larger for a day
Only every tenth cell in the flask stays alive
context: 20 minutes is the ideal-broth doubling time; nothing in nature ever gets ideal broth for long, or the biosphere would be one enormous petri dish. Source: Medical News Today, 'How many cells are in the human body?'

question: The three cone types in the human retina are labelled red, green and blue. Microspectrophotometry — measuring a single pigment's response wavelength by wavelength — has now been run on all three. Where does the cone everyone calls the red one actually peak?
answer: In greenish-yellow, just past the green cone's peak
choices: In greenish-yellow, just past the green cone's peak
In deep red, far past the green cone's peak
In orange, roughly midway between green and red
In blue-green, just short of the green cone's peak
context: The measured peaks: S about 420 nm, M about 534 nm, L about 564 nm — and the L and M pigments overlap broadly right through the yellow-green. Wikipedia is blunt: 'while the L cones have been referred to simply as red receptors, microspectrophotometry has shown that their peak sensitivity is in the greenish-yellow region of the spectrum.' Red is not the wavelength the L cone likes best. Red is what you see when L outruns M. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision (checked first); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_cell.

question: A phone screen is built from pixels, and each pixel from a few smaller subpixels — small enough that a magnifying loupe pressed against the glass will pull them apart. Fill the screen with a solid patch of yellow, then put the loupe on it. What is actually sitting under the glass where the yellow looks solid?
answer: Red and green dots firing together, with no yellow dot
choices: Red and green dots firing together, with no yellow dot
Yellow dots packed in between the red and green ones
White dots shining up through a thin yellow filter
Orange and green dots blurring together at this size
context: Wikipedia: 'A single pixel on a color display is made of several subpixels, typically three arranged left-to-right as red, green, and blue (RGB),' and 'the components are readily visible with a small magnifying glass, such as a loupe.' The screen fires red and green so that your three cones receive the same three numbers real yellow light would produce. Two physically different spectra a human cannot tell apart are called METAMERS, and because the eye samples the whole spectrum at only three points they are unavoidable — Grokipedia notes that human vision 'samples the spectrum at only three points, ignoring finer variations that might distinguish the stimuli physically.' Photography, television and printing are all built on that blind spot. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subpixel_rendering; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamerism_(color); grokipedia.com/page/Color_photography.

question: On 17 May 1861, at a Royal Institution lecture in London, James Clerk Maxwell showed the first durable colour photograph ever made. The photographer Thomas Sutton had shot one object three times, through a red, a green and a blue-violet filter; Maxwell then threw the three plates back onto a screen from three magic lanterns, one filter each, stacked on top of each other. What was the object?
answer: A tartan ribbon
choices: A tartan ribbon
A bowl of oranges
A vase of roses
A stained-glass panel
context: Maxwell had predicted the whole trick in a paper read to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in March 1855 — six years before anyone made the picture. The surviving 1861 photograph is held at the Science Museum in London. Sutton patented the world's first single-lens reflex camera that same year: a wooden sliding box with a movable mirror, so a photographer could see exactly what the lens saw. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sutton_(photographer); grokipedia.com/page/James_Clerk_Maxwell; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell. (Grokipedia's separate Color photography page says Royal Society of London; two other sources say Royal Institution, which is used here.)

question: Ewald Hering spent most of his working life arguing with Hermann von Helmholtz about colour, and in the 1870s he landed an objection that needed no laboratory at all — only your imagination. Try to picture each of these four colours. Which one has no human being ever reported seeing?
answer: A reddish green
choices: A reddish green
A greenish blue
A reddish yellow
A bluish red
context: Greenish blue is teal, reddish yellow is orange, bluish red is purple — but a reddish green is nothing at all, and neither is a bluish yellow. Wikipedia puts it exactly: 'In the same way that there cannot exist a "slightly negative" positive number, a single eye cannot perceive a bluish-yellow or a reddish-green.' Three independent sensors predict no such hole, so Hering proposed instead that colour rides on OPPOSING pairs — red set against green, blue against yellow — which makes a reddish green a colour that cancels itself. Sources give the year as 1872, 1878 and 1892, so 'the 1870s' is the safe framing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewald_Hering; webvision.pitt.edu (colour perception).

question: Here is a test you can run right now, while you are reading. Find something a strong solid red — a book cover, a patch of screen — and stare at one point on it, without letting your eyes wander, for a full half-minute. Then look at a blank white wall. A shape floats there. What colour is it?
answer: A green shape
choices: A green shape
A blue shape
A grey shape
A red shape
context: Around 25 to 30 seconds of fixation is the standard figure. Grokipedia describes the mechanism: 'prolonged fixation on a color like red fatigues the red-excitatory channel, leading to rebound excitation in the green-inhibitory counterpart when viewing a white field, resulting in a green afterimage.' The afterimage always arrives as the opponent partner — a green square gives magenta, blue gives yellow. You are watching your own retina's wiring on a blank wall. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opponent_process; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afterimage.

question: Thomas Young stood before the Royal Society in November 1801 with a theory of colour vision and not a scrap of anatomy behind it — nobody would see a cone for generations, so his case rested on reasoning alone. His whole argument turned on rejecting one rival picture of the retina. Which picture did he reject?
answer: A separate nerve for each of the thousands of tints the eye can tell apart
choices: A separate nerve for each of the thousands of tints the eye can tell apart
A separate kind of nerve for each of the seven hues Newton had named in sunlight
A single kind of nerve, reporting each hue by the rate at which it vibrates
A pair of nerves for every hue, one to report it and one to report its opposite
context: Young reasoned his way to three receptors before anyone could see a cone. His Bakerian Lecture 'On the Theory of Light and Colours' was delivered on 12 November 1801 and published the following year, and he argued from impossibility rather than anatomy: as one summary of the paper puts it, 'perception of colour can be coded by three principal colour receptors rather than thousands of colour receptors coding for individual colours.' A separate nerve for every wavelength was not a thing a retina could plausibly carry. Hermann von Helmholtz took the idea up around 1850, which is why it is called the Young-Helmholtz theory. (The famous verbatim Young quote about 'each sensitive point of the retina' could not be checked against the primary text, so it is not quoted here.) Sources: webvision.pitt.edu (colour perception); grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Young_(scientist); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young–Helmholtz_theory.

question: Thomas Sutton shot three filtered plates for James Clerk Maxwell's first colour photograph, outdoors in bright sunlight, one exposure through each filter. Wet collodion plates responded far better to blue light than to red. The blue-filtered plate was finished in about six seconds. How long did the red-filtered plate take?
answer: About eight minutes
choices: About eight minutes
About twenty seconds
About ninety seconds
About forty minutes
context: Grokipedia's figures for that session: roughly 6 seconds for the blue-filtered image, 8 minutes for red, and 12 minutes for green, all in bright sunlight. The red exposure ran about eighty times as long as the blue one, under the same sun and on the same subject. Wikipedia's history of the process explains why: collodion was 'for all practical purposes totally insensitive to red light and only marginally sensitive to green.' The exposure figures are single-sourced to Grokipedia's Sutton page; treat the exact numbers as that source's. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Sutton_(photographer); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_color_photography.

question: Send sunlight through a prism and it fans out into a band running from about 700 nanometres at the red end to about 380 at the violet end. Hold a magenta card up against that band and you can search all day without finding a match — magenta is simply not in there. Why not?
answer: Magenta needs long and short wavelengths together, with the middle silent
choices: Magenta needs long and short wavelengths together, with the middle silent
Magenta lies past violet, where a prism cannot bend light far enough
Magenta needs more light than a prism throws into one narrow band
Magenta is a printing colour, and inks subtract light instead of adding
context: Magenta is a NON-SPECTRAL colour. It appears when long-wave light around 650-700 nm and short-wave light around 450-500 nm fire the L and S cones together while the M cone stays quiet, and the brain 'interpolates the gap between the spectrum's red and violet ends.' The visible spectrum is a straight line that never closes into a loop; magenta is the stitch your brain invents to join the two ends. Browns and pinks are non-spectral too. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision (Hue Detection and Non-Spectral Colors).

question: Wet collodion plates were, for practical purposes, blind to red light — which means the red-filtered plate in Maxwell's 1861 demonstration had no business recording anything at all. It did, the projection worked, and for a hundred years nobody asked how. In November 1961 Ralph M. Evans published the answer in Scientific American. What had got through?
answer: Ultraviolet the red dyes reflected, which the red filter passed
choices: Ultraviolet the red dyes reflected, which the red filter passed
Infrared from the sunlight, which the plate registered as heat
Green light leaking around the edge of the red filter
Blue light bouncing off the bright sky into the lens
context: Ralph M. Evans, 'Maxwell's Color Photograph', Scientific American Vol. 205 No. 5, November 1961: 'many red dyes also reflect ultraviolet light, coincidentally transmitted by Sutton's red filter,' and 'the three images were probably due to ultra-violet, blue-green and blue wavelengths, rather than to red, green and blue.' The founding demonstration of three-colour photography worked by luck — and it took a century before anyone checked the claim instead of repeating it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_color_photography; scientificamerican.com/article/maxwells-color-photograph/.

question: Young and Helmholtz had the retina holding a few kinds of receptor, each answering to its own stretch of the spectrum. Ewald Hering had colour riding on opposing pairs, each hue cancelling its partner. For a century the two accounts were treated as rivals; then it turned out both were right, describing the same wire at different points along it. Where does the opponent stage sit?
answer: In the retina's own ganglion cells, before the signal leaves the eye
choices: In the retina's own ganglion cells, before the signal leaves the eye
In the visual cortex, after the signals cross at the optic chiasm
In the cone pigments themselves, as they bleach and regrow
In the optic nerve, where fibres from the two eyes interleave
context: Wikipedia states it exactly: 'trichromacy arises at the level of the receptors, and opponent processes arise at the level of retinal ganglion cells and beyond.' The retina rewrites three cone signals into three channels before they ever reach the brain — L versus M, S versus L plus M, and a plain light-versus-dark luminance channel. That re-encoding is why an afterimage comes back in the opposite colour. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opponent_process.

question: John Dalton read the first scientific account of colour blindness to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1794, and the case was his own: he saw scarlet as green and pink as blue, and so did his brother. He blamed a blue tint in the fluid of his own eyeball, and asked that his eyes be opened after he died to check it. They were, in 1844 — the fluid was perfectly clear. His preserved eye stayed in a Manchester collection until 1995, when researchers pulled DNA from it. What did the DNA show?
answer: The gene for the green-cone pigment was missing altogether
choices: The gene for the green-cone pigment was missing altogether
The gene for the red-cone pigment carried one faulty letter
The gene for the blue-cone pigment had been copied three times
The gene for the green-cone pigment coded a red-like pigment
context: The paper was 'Extraordinary Facts Relating to the Vision of Colours', read on 31 October 1794 — nine years before Dalton brought atomic theory to the same room. He died on 27 July 1844, and the 1995 DNA work showed deuteranopia: the medium-wave (green) opsin gene gone entirely. The Swiss naturalist Pierre Prevost coined 'daltonisme' in print in 1827, and 'Daltonism' was still standard in English medical writing well into the twentieth century. His hypothesis was wrong and his self-observation was gold — and he is the one who set up the test that killed his own idea. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/John_Dalton; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dalton.

question: Red-green colour blindness turns up in about one man in twelve and about one woman in two hundred. Blue-yellow deficiency is far rarer — under one person in ten thousand — and it strikes men and women at the same rate. The difference is genetic architecture, not pigment chemistry. What makes the red-green case so lopsided between the sexes?
answer: Its two genes sit side by side on the X and trade segments easily
choices: Its two genes sit side by side on the X and trade segments easily
Its two genes sit on chromosome 7, which men copy less faithfully
Its two genes are switched off in one of a woman's two X copies
Its two genes lie next to the sex-determining gene on the Y
context: OPN1LW and OPN1MW — the long-wave and medium-wave opsin genes — sit in a TANDEM ARRAY at Xq28 on the X chromosome, governed by a shared locus control region. Near-identical neighbours swap segments during recombination, so the array scrambles easily, and a man with one X has no spare copy to fall back on. The blue-yellow gene OPN1SW sits on chromosome 7 instead — not sex-linked — which is why that deficiency hits both sexes equally, at under 1 in 10,000. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Color_vision; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_blindness.

question: On 26 February 2015 Caitlin McNeill posted a photograph to Tumblr asking whether a dress was white and gold or blue and black, and within a day the argument had swallowed the internet. Roman Originals settled the object question: the dress is royal blue and black, and no white-and-gold version was ever made. Everyone arguing was looking at exactly the same pixels. What were the two camps' visual systems disagreeing about?
answer: What colour the light falling on the dress had been
choices: What colour the light falling on the dress had been
How many cone types their own retinas carried
How bright their screens were set at the time
Which part of the picture their eyes landed on first
context: Cecilia Bleasdale took the photograph on her iPhone under indoor lighting on the Scottish island of Colonsay; McNeill's caption read 'guys please help me - is this dress white and gold, or blue and black?' Roman Originals confirmed the real colours on 27 February 2015. Lafer-Sousa, Hermann and Conway surveyed about 1,400 people (Current Biology 25(13):R545, 2015): 57 percent saw blue and black, 30 percent white and gold, 11 percent blue and brown, 2 percent something else. The name for what the brain is doing is COLOUR CONSTANCY — subtracting the colour of the light so an object keeps its identity from noon to lamplight. Bevil Conway described the brain as trying to 'discount the chromatic bias of the daylight axis.' When the researchers simulated yellow room lighting, nearly everyone saw blue and black. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/The_dress; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_dress.

question: The mantis shrimp is famous for the richest colour equipment on Earth: twelve to sixteen photoreceptor types against the human three, running from deep ultraviolet out to far red. In 2014 Hanne Thoen and colleagues trained the animals and measured, for the first time, how finely they could tell two wavelengths apart. What did the test find?
answer: They failed below about 25 nanometres apart, where humans manage a few
choices: They failed below about 25 nanometres apart, where humans manage a few
They beat humans by roughly ten times across the whole visible range
They matched humans closely, but only inside the ultraviolet band
They beat humans in the red and fell well behind them in the blue
context: Thoen, How, Chiou and Marshall, 'A different form of color vision in mantis shrimp', Science 343:411 (2014), reported 'a surprisingly poor performance': the animals could not discriminate wavelengths less than about 25 nm apart, where a human with three cones manages 1-4 nm. The authors posed the puzzle themselves: 'Why use 12 color channels when three or four are sufficient for fine color discrimination?' The likely answer is that the shrimp compares photoreceptor outputs directly, like scanning a barcode, instead of running them through opponent channels. More sensors turned out to mean less discrimination — and a decade of popular claims had to be rewritten. Sources: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458639/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantis_shrimp; grokipedia.com/page/Mantis_shrimp.  (Legend.)

question: About 12 percent of women carry the genetic recipe for a fourth cone type — tetrachromacy, four colour channels instead of three — because a shifted copy of one pigment gene rides alongside the usual set. Carrying the extra cone and using it are different things, though: fewer than one carrier in a hundred shows any measurable gain, and only a handful have ever passed stringent testing. In 2010 Gabriele Jordan's team tested one of those who did, logged as cDa29. What could she do that no three-cone eye can?
answer: Tell apart yellows and reds that look identical to everyone else
choices: Tell apart yellows and reds that look identical to everyone else
See a band of ultraviolet beyond the violet end of the spectrum
Pick out colours in light far too dim for anyone else to see
Match a colour from memory weeks after seeing it just once
context: X-inactivation gives a carrier a mosaic retina, so the extra pigment — peaking somewhere around 535-545 nm, between the standard green and red cones — can genuinely be present. Jordan's subject cDa29 discriminated along a fourth dimension in the 546-670 nm range, the stretch running from green-yellow out to deep red (Jordan et al., Journal of Vision 10(8):12, 2010). But Grokipedia notes that 'no new confirmed functional cases have been reported since the early 2010s,' and the finding is still contested — a real claim, not an established one. (Sources disagree on Jordan's institution, so it is left unnamed.) Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Tetrachromacy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrachromacy.

question: On 27 August 2021 the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence did something intelligence products almost never do: it published, on one page, an itemised disagreement among its own agencies about how COVID-19 began. How did the assessment describe the split?
answer: Four elements plus the NIC leaned spillover; one leaned a lab incident; three declined to choose
choices: Four elements plus the NIC leaned spillover; one leaned a lab incident; three declined to choose
Six elements leaned a lab incident; two leaned spillover; the CIA declined to choose
The FBI and CIA jointly concluded a lab incident; five other elements dissented for spillover
The NSA led a majority for spillover from a bat cave; three dissented for a market origin
context: The one element leaning laboratory-related was the FBI, at MODERATE confidence; the four elements plus the National Intelligence Council leaned natural spillover at LOW confidence. Publishing an open, itemised disagreement was the newsworthy thing -- most intelligence products speak as one voice. Source: ODNI unclassified summary (dni.gov / odni.gov).

question: US intelligence assessments grade their conclusions with a published vocabulary -- 'high', 'moderate' and 'low confidence'. What do those words actually MEASURE?
answer: The quality and consistency of the evidence backing the judgement
choices: The quality and consistency of the evidence backing the judgement
How strongly the analyst personally feels about the conclusion
The share of analysts in the agency who voted for the finding
How much money and manpower the agency put into the report
context: 'Low confidence' does not mean 'we do not believe our conclusion' -- it means 'the underlying evidence is thin, inconclusive, or contradictory, and a reasonable person might read it another way'. Reading assessments without this vocabulary is why headlines routinely mangle intelligence findings. Source: ODNI declassified assessment methodology note.

question: For all the disagreement in the 2021 ODNI report about how the pandemic began, every element of the intelligence community concurred on one specific claim about SARS-CoV-2. What did they all agree on?
answer: That the virus was not developed as a biological weapon
choices: That the virus was not developed as a biological weapon
That the virus first jumped to humans at the Huanan Seafood Market
That the virus originated in a bat cave in Yunnan province
That the virus escaped from the Wuhan Institute of Virology
context: All IC elements agreed the virus was not developed as a bioweapon; most also assessed with low confidence that it was probably not genetically engineered, though two elements said the evidence was too thin to judge either way.
