The bioweapon hypothesis was ruled out early; the argument was over natural spillover versus a research-related accident. Source: ODNI unclassified summary (odni.gov).

question: Between 2021 and 2025 several US agencies revisited the question and MOVED. In February 2023 one element that had previously been undecided shifted to lean laboratory-related, at low confidence. Which one?
answer: The Department of Energy
choices: The Department of Energy
The Central Intelligence Agency
The National Security Agency
The Defense Intelligence Agency
context: The Wall Street Journal broke the DOE shift in February 2023. The CIA did not report a lean until January 2025, when it too came in for a research-related origin at LOW confidence, explicitly noting no new intelligence had driven the change. Sources: NPR 2023-02-27; CBS 2025-01-25.

question: On 2 December 2024 the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic released its 520-page final report concluding that COVID-19 most likely emerged from a laboratory in Wuhan. One of its central arguments was a specific biological feature of SARS-CoV-2 that has not been observed in nature in the virus's close cousins. What was the feature?
answer: A furin cleavage site in the spike protein
choices: A furin cleavage site in the spike protein
A double-stranded DNA genome instead of single-stranded RNA
A protein coat modelled on the polio virus's capsid
A missing envelope layer typical of ebolavirus
context: The subcommittee argued that the furin cleavage site -- a short stretch that lets the spike protein be cleaved by a common human enzyme, boosting infectivity -- has not been found in any close bat sarbecovirus. The report also cited the star-like early phylogeny (consistent with a single introduction into humans) and reported illness among Wuhan Institute of Virology researchers in autumn 2019. Source: oversight.house.gov COVID Select final report.

question: The strongest specific piece of evidence for the natural-spillover hypothesis is not a smoking gun but a co-location. On 1 January 2020, hours after the Huanan Seafood Market in Wuhan was closed, Chinese CDC investigators swabbed the stall surfaces. Alongside SARS-CoV-2 RNA they detected DNA from live animals of one particular kind at the wildlife stalls. Which animal?
answer: Raccoon dogs
choices: Raccoon dogs
Palm civets
Pangolins
Dromedary camels
context: Raccoon dogs -- SARS-CoV-2-susceptible mammals known to have been sold live at Huanan -- had their DNA co-located with viral RNA on the wildlife stall surfaces. That is short of proof any of the raccoon dogs were infected, and no infected intermediate host has ever been identified in years of animal sampling (SARS-CoV-1's civets and MERS's camels were pinned down comparatively fast). WHO's SAGO panel in June 2025 still leaned zoonosis on the weight of such evidence, while stating explicitly that a laboratory incident must remain on the table -- the honest scientific answer at this point is that no one yet knows. Sources: Nature Crits-Christoph et al. 2023; SAGO report 2025-06-27.

question: On the night of October 5-6, 1923, Edwin Hubble aimed the 100-inch Hooker telescope at the fuzzy Andromeda 'nebula' and took a 45-minute exposure on a glass plate. Where was that giant telescope perched?
answer: Mount Wilson, in California
choices: Mount Wilson, in California
Kitt Peak, in Arizona
Mauna Kea, in Hawaii
Cerro Tololo, in Chile
context: The 100-inch Hooker was the largest telescope in the world from 1917 until Palomar came online in 1949. Hubble's Andromeda plate is catalogued as H335H -- the 335th plate he had exposed at the Hooker. Source: https://carnegiescience.edu/about/history/archives/plate-archives/m31var  (Legend.)

question: Edwin Hubble first marked three suspected new stars on his 1923 Andromeda plate with the letter N -- for nova. Then he pulled older Mount Wilson plates of the same patch of sky and found that one of the N stars kept getting brighter and dimmer on a regular schedule. What did he do to that mark on the plate?
answer: Crossed out the N and wrote VAR! in red ink
choices: Crossed out the N and wrote VAR! in red ink
Circled it and labelled it Nova I
Erased it and drew a red star
Underlined the N three times in pencil
context: Plate H335H still carries the red-ink annotation. The 'VAR!' star is now catalogued as M31-V1, the first Cepheid variable ever identified beyond the Milky Way -- and one word in red ink multiplied the known size of the universe. Source: https://carnegiescience.edu/about/history/archives/plate-archives/m31var  (Legend.)

question: Hubble ran his single Cepheid through Leavitt's period-luminosity relation and got a distance to Andromeda that shredded every existing map of the cosmos -- about 900,000 light years. The modern averaged figure is roughly how far?
answer: About 2.5 million light years
choices: About 2.5 million light years
About 250,000 light years
About 25 million light years
About 250 million light years
context: The modern number is 2.54 million light years (765 kiloparsecs) -- about 2.8 times Hubble's original 1923 figure. His answer was wrong by nearly a factor of three, but it was already vastly bigger than any then-imagined Milky Way, so the qualitative conclusion held: Andromeda is another galaxy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andromeda_Galaxy

question: Three years before Hubble's Cepheid settled the question, the two leading American astronomers on the size of the universe faced off in a public showdown at the U.S. National Museum in Washington, D.C., on 26 April 1920. Who were the two men on stage?
answer: Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis
choices: Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis
Edwin Hubble and Harlow Shapley
Heber Curtis and Vesto Slipher
George Ellery Hale and Edwin Hubble
context: It became known simply as 'the Great Debate.' Shapley put the Milky Way at roughly 300,000 light years across and argued the spiral nebulae were objects inside it; Curtis put the Milky Way at only about 30,000 light years across and argued the spirals were separate 'island universes.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Debate_(astronomy)  (Legend.)

question: Harlow Shapley's strongest card in the Great Debate was a set of photographic measurements by Adriaan van Maanen, comparing plates of spiral nebulae like the Pinwheel taken years apart. Van Maanen claimed the plates showed the spirals were doing something that would be impossible at any great distance. What did they appear to be doing?
answer: Visibly rotating over a few years
choices: Visibly rotating over a few years
Drifting sideways across the sky
Splitting into pairs of stars
Shrinking as they cooled
context: If a spiral really was turning by measurable arc in a few years, its outer edges would be moving faster than light unless it was near enough to sit inside the Milky Way. The measurements were later shown to be spurious -- an artefact of how van Maanen compared plates. Curtis was right about the spirals; Shapley was right that the Milky Way is very large and the Sun is far from its centre. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Debate_(astronomy)

question: The redshifts that later got plotted against Hubble's distances were not Hubble's own data. A quieter astronomer at Lowell Observatory had begun measuring spiral-nebula spectra back in 1912 -- Andromeda first, approaching at about 300 km per second, and by 1917 twenty-five more, almost all racing away. Who was he?
answer: Vesto Slipher
choices: Vesto Slipher
Milton Humason
Percival Lowell
Heber Curtis
context: Slipher's spectrograph work at Flagstaff was the first hint that the universe was in motion on the largest scale. Hubble and Milton Humason later supplied the distances that turned Slipher's velocities into a straight line on a graph. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesto_Slipher

question: Hubble's partner on the 1929 distance-velocity paper had a resume unlike any other astronomer on Mount Wilson. He had dropped out of school at 14, hauled supplies up the mountain as a mule driver, then worked as the observatory janitor before being hired onto the scientific staff in 1919 -- no high-school diploma, let alone a Ph.D. Who was he?
answer: Milton Humason
choices: Milton Humason
Adriaan van Maanen
Harlow Shapley
Vesto Slipher
context: Humason turned out to be one of the finest observers of his generation. He took the exquisitely long exposures needed to catch the redshifts of faint, distant galaxies -- exactly the data Hubble's distance ladder needed to make its case. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Humason  (Legend.)

question: When Georges Lemaitre pitched an expanding universe to Albert Einstein in person, Einstein delivered a famous French one-liner in reply. By Lemaitre's own recollection, what did Einstein say?
answer: Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable
choices: Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable
Your mathematics is a game, and your universe a fantasy
Your equations betray you; the true cosmos does not move
Your derivation is clever, but your assumptions are heretical
context: In the original French: 'Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable.' Einstein had earlier added his 'cosmological constant' to general relativity precisely to keep the universe static; he later called it his greatest blunder. The exact wording of the Lemaitre exchange is by Lemaitre's later recollection, so it is preserved here as testimony. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Lema%C3%AEtre  (Legend.)

question: Hubble's 1929 slope gave a Hubble constant of about 500 km/s per megaparsec, which implied a universe only about 2 billion years old -- YOUNGER than rocks already dated on Earth. In 1952 Walter Baade announced a fix to a stunned IAU meeting in Rome that roughly doubled every extragalactic distance overnight. What had Baade discovered?
answer: Cepheid variables come in two populations with different luminosities
choices: Cepheid variables come in two populations with different luminosities
Andromeda contains a supermassive black hole distorting the distances
Interstellar dust dims Cepheids by a factor of two
The Milky Way itself is drifting toward Andromeda at 300 km/s
context: Baade had used Mount Wilson during the wartime Los Angeles blackouts to resolve individual stars in Andromeda's core. Hubble had been reading Population II Cepheids against a Population I calibration -- his photography was fine; the standard candle was miscalibrated. Correcting the populations doubled the distance scale, pushed the age of the universe past the age of the Earth, and dissolved the paradox. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Baade  (Legend.)

question: Modern astronomy has TWO good ways to pin down the Hubble constant. The Planck satellite fits the cosmic microwave background and reads 67.4 km/s/Mpc; the SH0ES team's local Cepheid-and-supernova ladder (confirmed by JWST in 2023) reads about 73. The two answers now disagree at more than 5 sigma. Where does the field stand on WHY?
answer: Nobody yet knows -- it may be a hidden systematic, or genuinely new physics
choices: Nobody yet knows -- it may be a hidden systematic, or genuinely new physics
The Planck value is confirmed; the local ladder has a known dust bias
The local ladder is confirmed; Planck missed a foreground galaxy
The two are being averaged into a single accepted value of 70
context: This is the 'Hubble tension' -- one of the sharpest live disagreements in cosmology, and a rung the bank tells honestly rather than papering over. If the tension survives further tests, it points at unknown physics in the early universe (extra radiation, evolving dark energy, or something stranger); if it dies, someone will have found a subtle systematic in one of the two pipelines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_tension

question: In 1991 the comedy Naked Gun 2 1/2 dressed a barroom wall with framed pictures of history's famous disasters, and hung the year-old Hubble Space Telescope among them. Which pair did the gag put Hubble between?
answer: The Hindenburg and the Titanic
choices: The Hindenburg and the Titanic
The Edsel and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge
Chernobyl and the Andrea Doria
The Maginot Line and the Spruce Goose
context: Hubble launched aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on 24 April 1990; on 21 June the project manager announced that it could not be properly focused. America turned it into a joke. Humorist Dave Barry called it the 'Orbiting Space Punch Line,' and Senator Barbara Mikulski -- one of the telescope's strongest defenders in Congress -- called it a 'techno-turkey' with a 'cataract.' On 13 January 1994, after the repair, that same senator stood beside NASA Administrator Dan Goldin, showed the first sharp pictures, and announced: 'The trouble with Hubble is over.' Sources: NASA Science, 'Hubble's Comeback Story'; NASA History, 'Lewis Experts Supported a Critical Repair on Hubble in the 1990s'; NASA Goddard SVS, 'Senator Mikulski Celebrates Hubble Success'; NASA, 'Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report' (Allen Commission, Nov 1990), Executive Summary.

question: Hubble's mirror had been polished a shade too flat around its outer rim -- the flaw opticians call spherical aberration. In 1990, aimed at a single star, both of Hubble's high-resolution cameras returned the same picture. What did that picture of the star show?
answer: A small bright core drowned in a wide halo
choices: A small bright core drowned in a wide halo
A short comet-like tail flaring to one side
A line stretched one way, squeezed the other
A sharp point fringed with red and blue
context: Rim light and centre light never met at one point, so a star arrived not as a point but as a bright spot wrapped in a halo holding most of its light. Both high-resolution cameras -- the Wide Field/Planetary Camera and the Faint Object Camera -- showed the same signature, which is how investigators knew the trouble lay in the mirrors themselves. The other three answers are real optical faults with their own signatures: the comet-tail smear is coma, the stretched line is astigmatism, and the colour fringes are chromatic aberration -- which a mirror cannot produce at all, because reflection does not depend on the colour of the light. That is exactly why Isaac Newton, having concluded that a colour-free lens telescope could not be built, made his telescope out of a mirror. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Executive Summary and Appendix C; Wikipedia, 'Newton's reflector.'

question: Hubble's primary mirror is a 2.4-metre disc of glass under a thin skin of aluminium, and it cost astronomers the sharpest view ever built because its outer edge was too flat. By how much was that edge too flat?
answer: About 2.2 micrometres, roughly 1/450 of a millimetre
choices: About 2.2 micrometres, roughly 1/450 of a millimetre
About 22 micrometres, roughly 1/45 of a millimetre
About 0.22 millimetres, roughly 1/5 of a millimetre
About 2.2 millimetres, roughly 1/450 of a metre
context: About 2,200 nanometres -- 2.2 micrometres, or roughly 1/11,000 of an inch. That was the whole error. The contract asked Hubble to put 70 percent of a star's light inside a circle 0.1 arcsecond in radius; what it delivered was 70 percent inside 0.7 arcsecond, ten times wider. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Hubble Space Telescope'; Physics Today, 'Hubble's blurry years'; NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter V 'The Failure.'

question: NASA's Allen Commission could not lay a hand on Hubble's primary mirror in 1990 -- the 2.4-metre disc was already in orbit. What the Board could read was Perkin-Elmer's own Danbury file: the tests made on the finished glass against its template, the target shape the polishers had been told to work to. How closely did the glass match that template?
answer: It beat the contract tolerance across the whole disc
choices: It beat the contract tolerance across the whole disc
It met the contract tolerance exactly, edge to centre
It beat the contract tolerance at the centre but not the rim
It fell just short of the contract tolerance everywhere
context: The fit was better than 0.014-wave rms at 632.8 nanometres -- in the Board's words, 'better than the contract specification.' The grinding was superb; the shape they had been aiming at was not. That is the distinction this whole story exists to teach: precision means landing in the same spot every time, accuracy means landing in the right spot, and Hubble had one without the other. It went unnoticed partly because no end-to-end test of the assembled telescope was ever made -- checking the finished optics at full accuracy would have needed a large flat mirror plus a spherical one about 15 percent larger, two more mirrors as big as Hubble's own, at roughly the cost of the entire optical telescope assembly. The Board noted that in hindsight 'a much less severe test could have been done to check for a gross' error. NASA formed the investigating board on 2 July 1990 under Lew Allen, director of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory; it found the mirror 'made in the wrong shape, being too much flattened away from the mirror's center,' an error 'ten times larger than the specified tolerance.' Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter IV sections D and E, and Executive Summary.

question: Perkin-Elmer's opticians could not judge Hubble's shape by eye. They read it off a null corrector -- a rig of two small mirrors and a field lens that shows a featureless pattern only when the glass has reached the shape wanted -- and polished until it came out clean. In 1990 the Allen Commission measured the rig. What was wrong with it?
answer: Its field lens sat about a millimetre out of position
choices: Its field lens sat about a millimetre out of position
Its field lens had been ground to the wrong curvature
One of its two mirrors was tilted a fraction of a degree
One of its two mirrors had been polished a shade too flat
context: The reflective null corrector's internal spacings had to be right to 10 micrometres. Its field lens was sitting about 1.3 millimetres too far from the lower mirror -- roughly 130 times the allowed tolerance -- and nobody at Perkin-Elmer ever re-verified the corrector's dimensions after it was first assembled. The rig was a novel design of Perkin-Elmer's own, and one of the things that won them the Hubble contract. In 1990 the Board found that corrector and its interferometer still standing in the test chamber, unused and unchanged since 1982, measured the lens spacing in place, and reported that 'the measured amount, 1.3 mm, accounts in detail for the amount and character of the observed image blurring.' The murder weapon was still on the table. Mismark a ruler and every length you measure with it comes out wrong -- and this was the ruler. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Executive Summary and Chapters IV and VII.

question: Ten small corrective mirrors had to reach out into Hubble's light beams, yet the package holding them had to slide into a bay about the size of a telephone booth. Jim Crocker, the engineer leading the design, was stuck on the mechanism until a hotel room in Germany handed it to him. By his own telling, what did he notice there?
answer: A showerhead on a rod, folded flat to the wall
choices: A showerhead on a rod, folded flat to the wall
A reading lamp on a hinged arm above the bed
A shaving mirror swung out beside the basin
A luggage rack that dropped from the wardrobe
context: This is Crocker's own account of where the idea came from. At a meeting in Germany in late 1990 he noticed that his hotel showerhead rode on a vertical rod and could be clamped at any height and angle -- and the maid had left it folded flat against the wall, taking up almost no space. Fold the mirrors flat, slide them in, then deploy them on arms into the beam. COSTAR (Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement) cost roughly $50 million, was built by Ball Aerospace, and carried ten mirrors about 18 to 24 millimetres across on swing-out arms, feeding corrected light to the Faint Object Camera, the Faint Object Spectrograph and the Goddard High Resolution Spectrograph. To make room for it, the High Speed Photometer -- judged the least important of the four axial instruments -- was pulled out and brought home. Sources: 'Life With Hubble: An insider's view of the world's most famous telescope' (IOP), ch. 3; Georgia Tech AE seminar bio of James Crocker; Wikipedia, 'COSTAR.'  (Legend.)

question: The Allen Commission wanted to know whether Hubble's flaw could have been caught while the mirror was still on the ground. In July 1990 the Board set up one of Perkin-Elmer's own alignment instruments and took a fresh interferogram -- a picture of a mirror's shape written in light and dark fringes -- which showed the aberration plainly. Then they went looking for an older one to compare it with. Where did the matching 1982 interferogram turn up?
answer: In the personal notebook of a Perkin-Elmer employee
choices: In the personal notebook of a Perkin-Elmer employee
In the sealed quality-assurance file at NASA headquarters
In the launch-readiness review submitted to Congress
In the microfilmed test records at the Danbury plant
context: The Board's fresh interferogram was taken on 22 July 1990; the one in the notebook was dated 22 June 1982. The two were virtually identical, both clearly showing spherical aberration. The proof had been sitting in a private notebook for eight years, to the month. The mirror's own timeline explains how there was time for that: rough grinding began in December 1978 at Wilton, Connecticut, polishing was finished at Danbury in April 1981, the final post-coating test was made in February 1982 -- and then the mirror waited eight years for a launch, already the wrong shape, with every test saying it was perfect. Hence the report's central sentence, and the reason this story is taught: 'The most unfortunate aspect of this HST optical system failure, however, is that the data revealing these errors were available from time to time in the fabrication process, but were not recognized and fully investigated at the time.' Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter I, Chapter VI (Figure 6-2), and Executive Summary.

question: Hubble spent three and a half years working with the wrong mirror, but the blur that mirror made had been measured exactly. Sandra Faber, of Hubble's science team, helped develop deconvolution -- arithmetic that starts from a known blur and works back through it -- and observers ran it over pictures already taken. What did the restored pictures show?
answer: One blob came apart into a group of separate stars
choices: One blob came apart into a group of separate stars
One star's halo drew in to a hard, bright ring
One star's halo vanished, its core left as it was
One galaxy came out finer than the mirror could record
context: Richardson-Lucy iterations, and rival methods such as maximum entropy, put photons back where they belonged, and could pull apart what had looked like one blob into individual stars. The Space Telescope Science Institute ran workshops on 'The Restoration of HST Images and Spectra'; the second, on 18-19 November 1993, drew 126 participants and 55 papers -- two weeks before the repair crew launched. Hubble was never useless in the meantime. Roughly 40 percent of the planned observing programmes went ahead with the aberrated telescope, project scientist Robert O'Dell's own figure: about 15 percent of a star's light still landed in a sharp core while the other 85 percent smeared into a halo several arcseconds across, so compact bright objects came through, the spectrographs worked whenever the field was not crowded, and ultraviolet observations were precious because almost nothing else could make them. Blurry-era results include the proplyds -- the dusty disks around newborn stars, picked out in 1992 images of the Orion Nebula -- and SN 1987A's thin tilted ring with debris moving at 6,000 km/s. Hubble also had a second, unrelated problem: crossing the day/night line each 94-minute orbit, the solar arrays' booms expanded and contracted in the temperature swing and shook the telescope. Sources: Physics Today, 'Hubble's blurry years'; Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 'The New and Improved Hubble Space Telescope'; STScI, 'The Restoration of HST Images and Spectra II'; ESA, 'How Hubble got its wings.'

question: By 1993 Hubble's blur had been measured so exactly that opticians could write it down as a number. Nobody could regrind the 2.4-metre primary mirror in orbit, so the fix had to work on the light after it left that mirror. What did the new optics -- Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, and COSTAR, a package of ten small mirrors on swing-out arms -- do to the beam?
answer: They carried the equal and opposite error, cancelling the mirror's
choices: They carried the equal and opposite error, cancelling the mirror's
They cropped the beam down to the mirror's well-shaped centre
They split the beam and recombined it to average the blur away
They steered each colour of the beam to a detector of its own
context: Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 carried relay mirrors with the inverse aberration ground into them, correcting the light before it reached its four CCDs; COSTAR swung its ten small mirrors into the beams of the three older instruments. The telescope's own bad data had specified its own prescription. Servicing Mission 1 flew as STS-61 on Endeavour, launched 2 December 1993 with a crew of seven -- Richard Covey, Ken Bowersox, Kathryn Thornton, Claude Nicollier, Jeffrey Hoffman, Story Musgrave and Thomas Akers -- and two alternating spacewalk pairs made five EVAs totalling 35 hours 28 minutes, a record at the time, installing WFPC2 and COSTAR and fitting new solar arrays, gyroscopes and a computer upgrade. It landed on 13 December 1993. Sources: NASA Science, 'Hubble's Mirror Flaw'; Wikipedia, 'COSTAR' and 'STS-61'; NASA History, '30 Years Ago: STS-61, the First Hubble Servicing Mission.'

question: Inside the null corrector -- two small mirrors and a field lens stacked along one beam -- the spacings had to be right to ten micrometres, and an operator set them by bouncing a laser down onto the rounded, polished end of one of the Invar metering rods. Perkin-Elmer had slipped a small cap over each rod's end to keep it from tipping. The laser came back clean, and the operator wrote down a number that was wrong by more than a millimetre. What had the laser reflected off?
answer: The cap's own metal, bared around its central hole
choices: The cap's own metal, bared around its central hole
The rounded end of a second rod, one place over
The polished underside of the field lens above it
The lower mirror of the corrector, down the beam
context: The top of the field cap was coated with non-reflecting material -- and in the Board's words, 'some of this material had, apparently inadvertently, broken away from a small area around the field cap aperture,' so the operator's laser auto-reflected off that exposed metal instead of the rod end. One wrong reflecting surface, and the field lens ended up 1.3 millimetres out. Invar is a metal that barely expands with temperature, which is why the rods were made of it. The Board rebuilt the setup in 1990 and tried the measurement itself: 'A test performed in 1990 with the equipment showed that it was quite easy, even probable, to make this error with the configuration used.' The mistake was designed in, not merely careless. Note that the popular retelling differs from the official finding: in September 1990 the Baltimore Sun reported strong evidence that a technician had put the flat end of the rod, rather than the finely polished rounded end, into the cap, and quoted board chairman Lew Allen calling the error 'painful and tragic' and saying 'adequate prudence was not taken.' The published report settles on the field-cap reflection. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter VII and Figure 7-5; Baltimore Sun, 'Upside-down rod blamed as cause of Hubble flaw,' 14 Sept 1990.

question: Technicians setting up the null corrector brought the field lens towards the end of rod B and ran out of travel in the positioning screws: the lens would not go where the measurement said it belonged. What did they do next?
answer: Slipped extra spacers in behind the lens
choices: Slipped extra spacers in behind the lens
Reground the rod ends until it seated
Swapped in the spare rod and started over
Logged the shortfall for the designers
context: 'There was no adjustment left in the screws used for this positioning,' the Board found. Rather than ask why the lens would not reach, the technicians made the extra room by inserting spacers between the field lens and the lower mirror mounting plate -- and the adjustment mechanism was then never staked, that is, secured against movement, even though staking was a specified procedure. The apparatus had physically resisted the wrong setting, and the resistance was engineered around. Source: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter VII, p. 7-7.

question: Perkin-Elmer's optical division ran two other correctors at Danbury alongside the reflective one -- an inverse null corrector built to mimic the reflection of a perfect mirror, and a refractive corrector made only of lenses. Both showed something was wrong, one as early as 1982, and the division discounted both results. The Allen Commission asked why. What did it find?
answer: That the division trusted no instrument but the reflective corrector
choices: That the division trusted no instrument but the reflective corrector
That the division blamed the odd readings on chamber vibration
That the division's report of them reached NASA too late to matter
That the division's managers overruled the staff who flagged them
context: The Board was blunt: because Perkin-Elmer had concluded the reflective corrector was the only device accurate enough, they refused to consider any less-accurate independent measurement, and 'such independent data were obtained incidental to other measurements and were rationalized away due to this mindset.' It also found that the Optical Operations Division ran a 'closed-door' environment 'which permitted discrepant data to be discounted without review,' and that some technical staff there 'were deeply concerned at the time that the discrepant optical data might indicate a flaw' but never raised it outside the division -- nobody overruled them, because nobody outside ever heard. Then the Board checked the instruments that had been dismissed: an analysis 'verified that the RvNC was accurate to better than 0.02 wave rms,' and of the inverse corrector the report says it 'was quite accurate enough to detect the gross error, and indeed did so.' The witnesses nobody believed had been telling the truth. The Board also found the failure to press 'particularly surprising since the members were aware of the history of manufacture of other Ritchey-Chretien telescopes, where spherical aberration was known to be a common problem.' Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Executive Summary, Chapter VI, and Chapter IX 'Judgmental Statements' items 2, 4, 7 and 9.

question: NASA had directed Perkin-Elmer to order a spare Hubble primary from a rival firm, Eastman Kodak, and Kodak polished and tested a 2.4-metre mirror of its own. The Allen Commission listed that subcontract among the opportunities NASA let slip. What check did it make available that NASA never ran?
answer: Having Kodak's finished mirror checked against Perkin-Elmer's
choices: Having Kodak's finished mirror checked against Perkin-Elmer's
Having Kodak's opticians re-measure Perkin-Elmer's null corrector
Having Kodak repeat the curvature test on Perkin-Elmer's mirror
Having Kodak's opticians witness Perkin-Elmer's final mirror test
context: Kodak polished its mirror against a refractive and a reflective null corrector of completely different design, matched both templates to better than 0.014-wave rms, and the Board 'has every reason to believe it is the correct hyperboloidal shape.' A correct Hubble mirror existed on Earth the whole time. The two firms were fierce competitors, and the Board wrote that 'NASA did not utilize the opportunity offered by this directed subcontract to validate, and gain confidence in, the P-E approach to the primary mirror manufacture.' Two independent answers existed and were never put side by side -- which is the cheapest test in science and the one nobody ran. Kodak's mirror was never aluminised; it sat in storage at Danbury until the end of 2000 and is now in the collection of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. Sources: NASA Allen Commission report, Chapter IV section D and Chapter IX item 5; Smithsonian NASM object record, 'Mirror, Primary Backup, Hubble Space Telescope.'

question: John Playfair, the Edinburgh mathematician who sailed to Siccar Point with James Hutton in 1788, came to mathematics late. In 1782 he resigned a settled post he had held for nine years so that he could tutor and study. What post did he give up?
answer: Minister of two country parishes in Scotland
choices: Minister of two country parishes in Scotland
Surveyor of harbours for the Royal Navy
Physician at the Edinburgh public infirmary
Engineer at a coal mine in Lanarkshire
context: Playfair was ordained in the Church of Scotland in August 1773 and served the united parishes of Liff and Benvie until he resigned in 1782 to tutor and pursue mathematics. By 1785 he was joint Professor of Mathematics at the University of Edinburgh - the post he held when he stepped into Hutton's boat three years later. Source: Grokipedia, 'John Playfair'; Wikipedia, 'John Playfair'.

question: James Hutton's junction at Siccar Point is a few metres of rock on a Berwickshire cliff. The American Museum of Natural History in New York wanted its visitors to stand in front of it. What did a crew hanging off the cliff do?
answer: They painted it with thick liquid latex and lifted the mould
choices: They painted it with thick liquid latex and lifted the mould
They cut a slab from the cliff with a diamond-toothed saw
They photographed it and printed it life-size on a wall
They quarried matching stone and rebuilt it by hand
context: Research Casting International hung on scaffolding off the cliffs at Siccar Point and painted a large section of the rocks with thick liquid latex to make the mould; the resulting cast of Hutton's Unconformity stands in the Gottesman Hall of Planet Earth at the American Museum of Natural History. In October 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences put Siccar Point first on its list of 100 global geological heritage sites. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point'.

question: In the spring of 1788 James Hutton hired a boat down the Berwickshire coast and landed at Siccar Point. Grey rock layers stand there almost on end; red-brown layers lie flat across their tops. Hutton told the two men with him that the grey rock had a long history before any red sand settled on it. What had it been through?
answer: Laid down flat, hardened, tilted on end, worn down, then drowned
choices: Laid down flat, hardened, tilted on end, worn down, then drowned
Settled from one universal ocean that afterwards drained away
Buckled upright by a great flood that then laid down the sand
Folded upright while still soft, then buried by blowing sand
context: Hutton called what the sea had exposed there 'a beautiful picture of this junction washed bare by the sea.' The grey rock is greywacke: laid down flat on a sea floor, hardened into stone, folded and lifted until it stood on end, worn off to a flat stump, and drowned again before the red sand ever arrived. The two men with him were the mathematician John Playfair and Sir James Hall of Dunglass, from whose family estate the boat had set out. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton' and 'Siccar Point'.

question: Every retelling of the Siccar Point trip quotes John Playfair: 'The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far back into the abyss of time.' It is usually staged as something he gasped while standing on the rock. Where did that sentence actually first appear?
answer: In his account of Hutton's life, printed eight years after Hutton died
choices: In his account of Hutton's life, printed eight years after Hutton died
In a letter Sir James Hall wrote home from Dunglass that same evening
In a footnote Hutton himself added to his own printed paper of 1788
In a speech Playfair gave with Hutton himself sitting there listening
context: The line comes from Playfair's biographical memoir of Hutton, printed in Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, vol. V, pt. III, 1805 - eight years after Hutton's death in 1797. Nobody wrote it down at the outcrop. The full sentence runs: 'The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far back into the abyss of time; and whilst we listened with earnestness and admiration to the philosopher who was now unfolding to us the order and series of these wonderful events, we became sensible how much further reason may sometimes go than imagination may venture to follow.' The 'philosopher' is Hutton himself. Note that some reference sites wrongly place the line in Playfair's 1802 Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory; the 1805 Transactions citation is the one Wikipedia carries in two separate articles. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point' and 'James Hutton'; full text on the Geological Society of London Siccar Point Geosite page.

question: After Siccar Point, James Hutton's party sailed on along the coast and found more of the grey beds standing on end. On the upright surfaces of those beds was something that told Hutton exactly how they had formed, and gave him, he said, 'great satisfaction.' What was on them?
answer: Ripple marks, like the ones on a sandy sea bed
choices: Ripple marks, like the ones on a sandy sea bed
Burrows dug by worms living in the mud
Beds of shells broken and packed together
Trails left by snails crawling over the floor
context: Ripples form on sand under water and are preserved when the sand hardens to stone, so finding them on beds now standing on end proved those beds had been laid down flat under water before anything tilted them - a confirmation Hutton had only supposed until that afternoon. Of the whole day he said: 'we never should have dreamed of meeting with what we now perceived.' Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'.

question: The bottom of the red sandstone lying across the junction at Siccar Point is not clean sand at all. For up to six metres it is a jumble of rounded pebbles and sharp broken chunks cemented together. Geologists call a junction like this an angular unconformity. Where did the chunks come from?
answer: From the grey rock lying directly beneath them
choices: From the grey rock lying directly beneath them
From a coral reef growing on that same sea floor
From lava erupted onto that same stretch of coast
From a desert lying inland from that same coast
context: The basal Devonian conglomerate and breccia - up to about six metres thick - carries rounded pebbles and angular fragments derived from the greywacke directly under it: the worn-down older rock's own wreckage, recycled into the rock that buries it. That is the erosion step proved by the rock itself rather than argued from a diagram, which is why the outcrop settled the question and a drawing could not. An unconformity is defined as a buried surface of erosion or non-deposition representing a significant gap in the record - a real old ground surface you can lay a hand on. Source: Grokipedia, 'Siccar Point' and 'Unconformity'; Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point'.

question: Heat limestone in an open fire and it burns to quicklime, its gas escaping into the air. Sir James Hall, who had sailed with James Hutton to Siccar Point, wanted to know what limestone does when it is cooked deep underground instead, where nothing can escape. He packed limestone into a sealed gun barrel and heated it hard. What came out of the barrel?
answer: A block of crystalline marble
choices: A block of crystalline marble
A cake of powdered quicklime
A lump of clear green glass
A crust of hardened ash
context: Sealing the carbonate of lime kept its gas from escaping, so under pressure it did not burn to quicklime at all - it came out crystalline marble. Between 1798 and 1805 Hall ran more than 500 separate experiments, reaching over 1000 degrees C and pressures equal to a column of seawater 2,720 metres deep. He is described as the first geologist directly to apply the test of laboratory experiment to geological hypotheses; his motto, borrowed from Paracelsus, was that 'Vulcan is a second nature, imitating concisely what the first takes time and circuit to effect.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Sir James Hall, 4th Baronet'; Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Hall, James (1761-1832)'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Hall, Sir James'.

question: James Hutton's Theory of the Earth ran to 2,138 pages, and his friend John Playfair judged that 'the great size of the book, and the obscurity which may justly be objected to many parts of it, have probably prevented it from being received as it deserves.' Hutton died in 1797. What did Playfair spend the next five years doing?
answer: Rewriting Hutton's whole theory as a book of his own
choices: Rewriting Hutton's whole theory as a book of his own
Translating the book into French for the Paris academies
Cutting the book down into a short pamphlet for miners
Hunting the Scottish coast for more of Hutton's junctions
context: Playfair spent almost five years, from Hutton's death in 1797 until 1802, writing Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory of the Earth; Charles Lyell then carried the ideas the rest of the way in Principles of Geology (1830-33). The ideas had also been attacked as dangerous, not merely unreadable - the chemist Richard Kirwan called them atheistic and illogical, which is what pushed Hutton to expand the theory into his 1795 volumes. One historian's verdict on the irony: 'It is ironic that Hutton, the man whose prose style is usually dismissed as unreadable, should have coined one of the most memorable, and indeed lyrical, sentences in all science.' Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'James Hutton'; Keith Stewart Thomson, American Scientist 89(3): 212 (2001).

question: Modern dating gives the grey rock at Siccar Point an age of about 440 million years and the red sandstone lying across it about 375 million - numbers James Hutton had no way to measure, though he was certain the time involved was beyond imagining. That leaves roughly 65 million years missing at a contact you can cover with two fingers. What happened during the missing time?
answer: An ocean closed and Himalayan-sized mountains rose, then wore away
choices: An ocean closed and Himalayan-sized mountains rose, then wore away
A deep sea covered the whole region and never once drained away
A desert basin filled with dune sand and dried out again and again
Ice sheets ground across the region and scraped it flat again
context: The Iapetus Ocean, which had lain between what is now Scotland and what is now England, closed during those missing years, throwing up mountains of Himalayan scale to the north-west. The Devonian sand that buries the greywacke washed south off those very mountains as they wore down - so the younger rock is made of the older range's remains. The lower unit is early Silurian (Llandovery) greywacke at c.440 Ma; the flat-lying unit above is late Devonian sandstone at c.375 Ma. Hutton knew the time was unimaginably vast; he had no method that could give him a number. Source: Wikipedia, 'Siccar Point'; Grokipedia, 'Siccar Point'.

question: Abraham Werner taught that every rock on Earth - granite included - had precipitated chemically out of one universal ocean that once covered the whole planet and then receded. In the summer of 1785 James Hutton went up Glen Tilt in the Scottish Highlands to look at granite in place for the first time. What were the granite veins doing to the layered schist around them?
answer: Cutting clean across its layers and breaking through them
choices: Cutting clean across its layers and breaking through them
Lying in flat sheets neatly between each of its layers
Wrapping around it in smooth rounded lumps of stone
Crumbling to loose sand everywhere along its edges
context: Granite that cuts across the layers it sits among must have arrived molten and been forced in, which makes it younger than the rock it invades - and a chemical sediment settling out of water can never cut across the layer it settled onto. Glen Tilt was Hutton's first geological field trip, taken as a guest of the Duke of Atholl at Forest Lodge; he hauled a 400-pound granite-veined boulder out of the River Tilt and carted it back to Edinburgh. Werner taught his theory, Neptunism, at the Freiberg Mining Academy in Saxony and never published a complete treatise on it - it spread almost entirely through his lectures. He also insisted basalt was a water-laid sediment containing fossils; Hutton answered that basalt never contains fossils and is always insoluble, hard and crystalline, and one of Werner's own star students, Leopold von Buch, defected after fieldwork among the volcanic cones of the Auvergne. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton' and 'Neptunism'; Grokipedia, 'James Hutton' and 'Abraham Gottlob Werner'.

question: James Hutton is remembered for reading rock correctly, but on the Isle of Arran he got it wrong. At Lochranza in 1787 he found tilted rock lying under flat rock for the first time, in an exposure too poor to show what the rock did below the surface he could see. What did he wrongly conclude about the rock down there?
answer: That the two sets ran parallel again further down
choices: That the two sets ran parallel again further down
That the upper set was the older of the two down there
That both sets had settled out of one and the same sea
That an earthquake had cracked the two sets apart below
context: The Lochranza exposure was too limited to show the deeper strata, and Hutton incorrectly decided that the two sets were conformable - running parallel - below the outcrop he could see. Siccar Point mattered precisely because there the sea had already dissected the junction and laid it open, leaving nothing to guess at. He had also found granite veins at Glen Tilt in 1785, another such junction at Jedburgh on the Jed Water later in 1787, and a magma intrusion at Salisbury Crags in Edinburgh now called Hutton's Section. He was hunting on purpose: at Jedburgh he wrote that he 'rejoiced at my good fortune in stumbling upon an object so interesting in the natural history of the earth, and which I had been long looking for in vain.' Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'.

question: Sir James Hall of Dunglass owned the estate the 1788 boat trip set out from, and he had argued with James Hutton for three years before he accepted the theory - then set out to test it by melting rock in a furnace. Hutton disapproved, objecting 'to judge of the great operations of the mineral kingdom from having kindled a fire and looked into the bottom of a little crucible.' What did Hall do about his friend's objection?
answer: He held back every result until Hutton died in 1797
choices: He held back every result until Hutton died in 1797
He published anyway and the two men never spoke again
He rebuilt the experiments at the scale of a hillside
He put his results out under another man's name instead
context: Hall postponed publishing any of his results until after Hutton's death in 1797, then melted whinstone and lava collected from fifteen British and foreign localities and showed that a melt cooled quickly turns to glass while the very same melt cooled slowly turns stony and crystalline - basalt and even ordinary bottle-glass both did it. Hall also drew the Siccar Point outcrop in 1788, and the rock is still much as he sketched it; he ran the first analogue model of rock folding in 1815 and served as President of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. He was fallible too: he attributed the erratic boulders scattered across the Jura to a great sea-flood or 'debacle', following de Saussure and Pallas and against Hutton and Playfair, where we now recognise glaciers. Source: Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Hall, James (1761-1832)'; Wikipedia, 'Sir James Hall, 4th Baronet' and 'Siccar Point'.

question: Nicolas Steno had described junctions where tilted rock lies under flat rock a full century before James Hutton reached Siccar Point, and the naturalist Horace-Benedict de Saussure had found them in the Alps. Hutton was the first man to read one as an enormous stretch of time. What had those earlier observers taken the very same rock for?
answer: Primary formations left by a retreating universal ocean
choices: Primary formations left by a retreating universal ocean
Broken wreckage dumped by one violent worldwide flood
Mountain roots heaved upward by fire beneath the crust
New formations raised by a second, separate creation
context: Steno and de Saussure had both looked at angular unconformities and read them in Neptunist terms, as 'primary formations' left by the universal ocean. Hutton was the first to read one as a quantity of time. The observation was available to anyone standing on the ledge; what changed was the question asked of it - which is why the outcrop is remembered under his name and not theirs. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Hutton'; Grokipedia, 'Unconformity'.

question: James Hutton's 1788 paper ends: 'we find no vestige of a beginning, - no prospect of an end.' He meant that the rocks keep no record of a starting point, not that the Earth never had one - and he had no way to put a number on any of it. In 1956 Clair Patterson finally fixed the age of the Earth at 4.54 billion years. What did Patterson measure to get it?
answer: The lead built up inside a handful of fallen meteorites
choices: The lead built up inside a handful of fallen meteorites
The salt building up in the water of the world's oceans
The thickness of every sedimentary rock layer known
How long a molten ball the size of Earth needs to cool
context: Patterson established the figure in 1956 by lead-lead dating of several meteorites, including the Canyon Diablo meteorite; the accepted age is 4.54 plus or minus 0.05 billion years, on a clock built from radioactive decay that Hutton had no way to imagine. His closing sentence came out of an engine with no starting line - land wears to sediment, sediment is buried and cemented into rock, and the Earth's internal heat lifts that rock back up as new land, which wears down again. Note the honest limit: Hutton's picture of endless identical cycles is not modern geology, which has a definite time of formation and directional change through time. Earlier estimates fell far short - Archbishop James Ussher had put the creation of the world at 4004 BC in his Annales Veteris Testamenti of 1650, and Lord Kelvin's 1862 calculation gave only 20 to 400 million years because he did not know about radioactive heat. Source: Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth', 'James Hutton', 'Ussher chronology'.

question: Seoul National University's Hwang Woo-suk was South Korea's most celebrated scientist. Of all his headline claims, one 2005 result survived every later investigation. What was it?
answer: Snuppy, an Afghan hound - the first cloned dog
choices: Snuppy, an Afghan hound - the first cloned dog
eleven patient-matched embryonic stem-cell lines
a human embryo cloned from an adult skin cell
a paralysed dog walking again after a stem-cell graft
context: Snuppy was born April 24, 2005 at Seoul National University; his name is a portmanteau of SNU and puppy. He was made from ear tissue of a 3-year-old male Afghan hound named Tai, and out of 1,095 implanted embryos across 123 surrogate mothers he was the only survivor. When the fraud investigation was over, Snuppy was the one thing the panel confirmed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snuppy

question: Before the fraud came out, Hwang Woo-suk was such a national hero in South Korea that the state honoured him with something ordinary scientists never get. What?
answer: his own commemorative postage stamp
choices: his own commemorative postage stamp
a statue outside the Blue House
a public holiday in his home province
his face on the 10,000-won banknote
context: He was called the 'Pride of Korea'. The national post office pulled the stamp from sale on January 11, 2006, the day after the Seoul National University panel reported that his stem-cell lines were fabricated. He had also been given a government bodyguard and free first-class Korean Air travel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Woo-suk

question: The 2005 Science paper claimed eleven separate patient-matched stem-cell colonies. Anonymous scientists on a Korean research website called BRIC did something no one at the journal had thought to do, and it broke the story in December 2005. What did they do?
answer: compared the photographs and spotted the same colony printed twice
choices: compared the photographs and spotted the same colony printed twice
ran the DNA sequences and found none matched the patients
grew the cell lines themselves and got different chromosome counts
checked the hospital records and found the patients did not exist
context: On December 5, 2005 an anonymous poster on BRIC laid the images side by side and showed that photos of the supposedly eleven different colonies had been duplicated and Photoshopped. Ordinary readers, on a message board, with nothing but the printed figures - that was the first crack. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/korean-university-will-investigate-cloning-paper

question: When the Seoul National University panel finished its investigation of Hwang Woo-suk, it had to decide whether Snuppy the Afghan hound was also fabricated. It reached its verdict by running a specific check. What did the check show?
answer: Snuppy's DNA matched the donor dog Tai - the cloning was real
choices: Snuppy's DNA matched the donor dog Tai - the cloning was real
Snuppy shared DNA with the other faked embryos
Snuppy was genetically the surrogate mother's own pup
Snuppy's cells could not be sequenced at all
context: Two independent DNA analyses appeared in Nature in 2006. Nuclear microsatellite markers plus mitochondrial DNA confirmed Snuppy was a genuine genetic clone of the ear-tissue donor, an adult male Afghan hound named Tai. Amid the wreckage of the human stem-cell claims, the dog was real. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04686

question: The MBC investigative programme PD Note aired on November 22, 2005 and turned public opinion against Hwang Woo-suk. What did it report about where the eggs for his experiments had come from?
answer: they came from his own junior researchers and from paid donors
choices: they came from his own junior researchers and from paid donors
they came from unclaimed IVF embryos at a Seoul fertility clinic
they came from illegal cross-border shipments out of China
they came from cadavers taken without family consent
context: The 2004 paper had claimed 16 unpaid volunteers. PD Note's reporting - which the public initially rejected, forcing sponsors to pull ads - turned out to be accurate. On November 21 co-author Roh Sung-il admitted he had paid women US$1,400 each; junior female staff, unable to freely refuse, had also donated. The bank names this once because it matters, not to dwell. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Woo-suk

question: The Seoul National University panel reported on January 10, 2006 that all eleven claimed stem-cell lines were fabricated. It also totted up how many human eggs Hwang's team had actually consumed between November 2002 and December 2005. The number stunned even the scientific press. What was it?
answer: at least 2,061 eggs
choices: at least 2,061 eggs
roughly 185 eggs
roughly 427 eggs
at least 12,400 eggs
context: The 2005 paper had reported 185 eggs. The panel's audit put the real figure at over ten times that. It was the scale of the waste - human eggs harvested from paid strangers and coerced juniors - that made the ethical failure inseparable from the scientific one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwang_Woo-suk

question: Hwang Woo-suk claimed he could make patient-matched pluripotent cells by cloning. The problem was real and worth solving. A year after his fraud was exposed, someone else solved it by a completely different route. Who, and how?
answer: Shinya Yamanaka - reprogrammed ordinary adult cells with four genes
choices: Shinya Yamanaka - reprogrammed ordinary adult cells with four genes
Ian Wilmut - refined the Dolly nuclear-transfer technique
James Thomson - isolated cells from unused IVF blastocysts
Jennifer Doudna - edited embryonic cells with CRISPR-Cas9
context: In 2006 the Japanese researcher Shinya Yamanaka showed that four transcription factors delivered into an ordinary adult skin cell could dial it back to a pluripotent state - induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells. He shared the 2012 Nobel for it. The lesson: the real answer to Hwang's question did not need a shortcut, or a lie, or a single human egg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_pluripotent_stem_cell

question: Karl Lashley spent about thirty years training rats to run mazes, then cutting out pieces of their cerebral cortex to find the exact place the maze memory was stored. What did he find where he expected the memory to live?
answer: Nothing -- the memory was never in the piece he removed
choices: Nothing -- the memory was never in the piece he removed
A dense knot of neurons that glowed under stain
A cluster of cells just behind the eyes in every rat
A ring of scar tissue that formed only in trained rats
context: Karl Spencer Lashley (1890-1958) ran this programme from the 1920s to about 1950 at Harvard and elsewhere. He would train the rats, cut, then re-test. The maze memory was never in the piece he removed. He wrote up the search under the title 'In Search of the Engram' in 1950 and admitted, half seriously, that his own evidence had begun to make him wonder whether learning was even possible.

question: From his thirty-year failure to locate the maze memory in any one piece of rat cortex, Karl Lashley proposed two principles about how memory sits in the brain. What are the two principles now called?
answer: Mass action and equipotentiality
choices: Mass action and equipotentiality
Localization of function and cortical modularity
Cerebral dominance and hemispheric specialization
Phrenological faculties and cranial mapping
context: MASS ACTION says impairment scales with the AMOUNT of cortex lost; EQUIPOTENTIALITY says other cortical areas can take over the missing part's role. Together they paint memory as distributed across the cortex rather than filed in one drawer. Lashley did NOT prove memory has no physical trace -- he showed the maze memory is distributed, at least for the tasks he tested.

question: The word Lashley was hunting -- for a physical trace a memory leaves behind in the nervous system -- had actually been coined decades earlier, before any instrument existed that could look for one. Who invented the word 'engram'?
answer: Richard Semon, a German biologist, in his 1904 book Die Mneme
choices: Richard Semon, a German biologist, in his 1904 book Die Mneme
Sigmund Freud, in his 1900 book The Interpretation of Dreams
Ivan Pavlov, in his lectures on conditioning in the 1920s
William James, in his 1890 Principles of Psychology
context: Semon (1859-1918) also named the encoding step (engraphy) and the retrieval step (ecphory), and argued that memory must leave a physical modification in the nervous tissue. He was ignored for most of the twentieth century -- the term 'engram' outlived his other coinages -- and rediscovered in the modern engram-cell literature.

question: In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a rule for how learning changes cell assemblies in the brain. The rule is now usually remembered as a rhyme. Which rhyme?
answer: Cells that fire together, wire together
choices: Cells that fire together, wire together
Use it or lose it
What fires last, lasts
Neurons that misfire, must retire
context: Hebb published the idea in The Organization of Behavior (1949): when two neurons are repeatedly active at the same moment, the synapse between them grows stronger, and groups of cells become 'assemblies' that behave as a unit. It became the theoretical spine of memory research -- and exactly the picture Tonegawa's optogenetic engram experiments would later make testable in a live animal. Eric Kandel won a Nobel in 2000 for showing in the sea slug Aplysia that specific synapses really do strengthen with learning, at single identified connections.

question: In 2012 a team in Susumu Tonegawa's lab at MIT tagged the exact hippocampus neurons that lit up while a mouse learned to fear one box, using a light-sensitive protein called channelrhodopsin. Then they moved the mouse into a completely different, completely safe box. They fired a pulse of blue light down a fibre-optic into the tagged cells. What did the mouse do?
answer: It froze in place, as if the shock were about to come
choices: It froze in place, as if the shock were about to come
It reared up on its hind legs and vocalized
It darted to the far corner and defecated
It groomed itself calmly in place
context: Liu, Ramirez, Pang and colleagues, Nature 484:381, April 2012. The tagged cells were in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. The technique is OPTOGENETICS -- installing a light-operated switch (a light-sensitive channel from a green alga) into chosen neurons so that a pulse of blue light through a fibre-optic turns just those cells on. Reactivating that specific set of cells REPLAYED the fear memory those cells had helped store. Freezing is the standard rodent fear response, but rearing, darting, and defecation are all real defensive/arousal behaviors -- the point is that the tagged cells drove the SPECIFIC learned response.

question: The following year the same MIT lab published a follow-up experiment in Science. This time the mouse froze in a box where nothing bad had EVER happened to it -- yet the fear was real and specific to that box. How had they done it?
answer: They reactivated the tagged cells for that box while shocking the mouse in a different box
choices: They reactivated the tagged cells for that box while shocking the mouse in a different box
They tagged fear cells in the amygdala and reactivated those instead of hippocampus cells
They gave a drug that erased the memory of the shock box so the safe box took its place
They surgically joined two mice so one felt the other's shock through shared blood
context: Ramirez, Liu, Redondo, Tonegawa and colleagues, Science 341:387, July 26, 2013. The mouse first explored a neutral box (box A) and the neurons that lit up were tagged. Then in a second box (box B), the tagged A-cells were reactivated by light AT THE SAME MOMENT the mouse got a foot-shock. Back in box A, unshocked, the mouse froze -- the shock had been welded to the tagged memory of A rather than the memory of B. A false memory, implanted.

question: In August 2005 the open-access journal PLoS Medicine printed an essay by Stanford physician-epidemiologist John Ioannidis whose title read like a charge sheet against the whole scientific literature. What did that title actually say?
answer: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
choices: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
The End of Certainty in Modern Biology
How Statistics Lie in the Medical Age
context: PLoS Medicine 2(8): e124, August 30, 2005. Widely reported as the most-downloaded article in the history of open-access publishing. Ioannidis was at Stanford; the paper is one of the founding documents of the metascience movement. Kuhn's Structure came out in 1962 -- a real book, wrong here.

question: Ioannidis's 2005 essay is only a few pages long and contains no data tables. He worked out a single equation and applied it to what the medical literature already looked like. What quantity did that equation compute for a finding stamped 'significant'?
answer: the positive predictive value of the finding
choices: the positive predictive value of the finding
the Bayes factor comparing the two rival hypotheses
the statistical power of the test that produced the finding
the false discovery rate across the whole journal issue
context: PPV = (1 - beta) * R / (R - beta*R + alpha), where alpha is the false-positive rate and (1 - beta) is the study's power. The whole paper is arithmetic applied to the shape of the existing literature -- no new experiments, no data tables. TEST-IT-YOURSELF: you can work the equation on paper.

question: Ioannidis's model isolates a single quantity that decides how trustworthy a 'p < 0.05' finding is. In his framework, what mostly determines whether that quantity is high or low?
answer: the true-hypothesis ratio, times the study's power
choices: the true-hypothesis ratio, times the study's power
the study's chosen p-value threshold, all on its own
the study's sample size multiplied by its effect size
the number of prior independent replications
context: Ioannidis's core inequality: a research finding is more likely true than false only when (1 - beta) * R > alpha -- power times the true-hypothesis ratio has to beat the false-positive rate. A field testing thousands of long shots at low power will publish mostly noise, no matter how strict the p-value threshold looks.

question: Ioannidis's Corollary 1 predicts what a scientific field will publish if it runs mostly small under-powered trials. What does the corollary say that shelf will be dominated by?
answer: noise that will not replicate
choices: noise that will not replicate
settled truth that other labs will confirm
null results that quietly correct the field
effects too small for journals to print
context: Corollary 1 verbatim: 'The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific field, the less likely the research findings are to be true.' Small samples swing wildly and only the lucky swings clear p < 0.05, so the shelf that survives publication is the shelf of lucky swings.

question: Ioannidis's Box 1 worked example imagines a field testing 100,000 gene polymorphisms for schizophrenia, of which only about 10 are truly linked to the disease. Which of his six numbered corollaries does that hypothetical illustrate?
answer: the greater the number and the lesser the selection of tested relationships, the less likely the findings are to be true
choices: the greater the number and the lesser the selection of tested relationships, the less likely the findings are to be true
the smaller the studies conducted in the field, the less likely the findings are to be true
the greater the flexibility in designs, definitions, outcomes, and analytical modes, the less likely the findings are to be true
the hotter a scientific field, with more scientific teams involved, the less likely the findings are to be true
context: Corollary 3 verbatim. In Box 1, at 60% power and p < 0.05 the post-study probability of any single significant SNP-schizophrenia hit being real is only about 12/10,000 -- and any bias in the pipeline drops it further. Firing 100,000 shots at 10 real targets means most of your 'hits' are noise.

question: Corollary SIX of Ioannidis's list sounds paradoxical until you picture the race. It says the more scientific teams pile into a hot question, the worse the published record on that question gets. What mechanism makes the racing itself manufacture false positives?
answer: the first team to hit p < 0.05 publishes, so racing selects the lucky noisy runs out of the pack
choices: the first team to hit p < 0.05 publishes, so racing selects the lucky noisy runs out of the pack
the labs share equipment and contaminate each other's samples with each hand-off
hot fields recruit dishonest researchers who go on to fabricate data on purpose
peer reviewers cannot keep up with the submission rate and wave more mistakes through
context: Corollary 6: 'The hotter a scientific field (with more scientific teams involved), the less likely the research findings are to be true.' Twenty teams testing the same shaky hypothesis at 5% false-positive rate expect one to hit significance by chance -- and that team goes to print first, while the nulls stay in drawers.

question: David Chavalarias and John Ioannidis ran a text-mining survey of MEDLINE abstracts (JAMA, 2016) counting reported p-values across 1990-2015. Among papers reporting any p-value, what fraction reported at least one that cleared the p < 0.05 line -- a number Ioannidis said was impossible if honest testing were happening?
context: Chavalarias, Wallach, Salem, Ioannidis, JAMA 2016. Ioannidis: 'It's impossible that 96 percent of all the hypotheses being tested would be significant.' What you are seeing is a shelf, filtered -- the null results were strained out before print. The publication-bias mechanism has a name: the file-drawer problem.

question: The Ioannidis paper has been argued with in print. Leah Jager and Jeffrey Leek published a 2014 reanalysis in the journal Biostatistics that estimated the science-wise false-discovery rate at a much smaller figure than the headline claim. What was Jager and Leek's number -- the challenge the bank must not pretend away?
answer: about 14%
choices: about 14%
about 42%
about 71%
about 88%
context: Jager and Leek, Biostatistics 15(1), 2014. Steven Goodman and Sander Greenland separately argued Ioannidis's model rested on plausible-but-chosen assumptions rather than measured ones. Ioannidis replied in the same issue; the argument is live. Feynman's rule applied to the bank's own favorite paper: 'you must not fool yourself.'

question: What Ioannidis's paper is often WRONGLY said to have claimed matters as much as what it said. When critics steelman his argument, which of these does the paper NOT actually claim?
answer: that science is worthless and its published findings should be ignored
choices: that science is worthless and its published findings should be ignored
that small studies chasing small effects are especially vulnerable to false positives
that pre-registration and larger studies would help repair the filter
that financial interests raise the false-positive rate in a field
context: Ioannidis explicitly named the repairs: better-powered evidence (larger studies), low-bias meta-analyses, and upfront pre-registration of studies such as randomized trials. The claim is that the FILTER is weak, not that inquiry is worthless.

question: Ioannidis argued that people misread 'p < 0.05' as a much stronger claim than it actually makes. What does that p-value actually mean, in the strict technical sense?
answer: under a true null, data at least this extreme would appear less than 5% of the time
choices: under a true null, data at least this extreme would appear less than 5% of the time
there is less than a 5% chance that the finding itself is wrong
there is at least a 95% chance the finding will replicate in future studies
the researcher's underlying hypothesis is at least 95% likely to be true
context: The p-value is a statement about the data under the null hypothesis, not about the hypothesis itself. Ioannidis's paper attacks exactly the three misreadings listed here -- readers see 'significant' and hear 'true,' 'unlikely to be wrong,' or 'will replicate.' Feynman's rule for your own favorite paper: 'you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.'

question: Scurvy killed more British sailors than enemy guns. On 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors sick with it and split them into six pairs, each pair to get a different remedy. Before the first dose, what did he do with all twelve?
answer: Put them in one sick berth on one identical diet.
choices: Put them in one sick berth on one identical diet.
Sent them back to their normal watch and rations.
Let each pair eat whatever it could keep down.
Moved each pair to a different part of the ship.
context: In Lind's own words the twelve lay together in 'a proper apartment for the sick in the fore-hold' and had 'one diet in common to all': water-gruel sweetened with sugar in the morning, fresh mutton broth for dinner, light puddings and boiled biscuit with sugar, and barley, raisins, rice, currants, sago and wine for supper. Same room, same food, one thing changed between the pairs. That is the whole idea of a controlled trial, and Lind built its shape roughly two centuries before anyone had the phrase. 20 May is now marked every year as International Clinical Trials Day in honour of this experiment. Sources: Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753), quoted at sportsci.org/news/history/lind/lind_sp.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; jameslindlibrary.org/articles/james-lind-aboard-salisbury/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_trial.

question: In 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, James Lind put twelve sailors sick with scurvy on six remedies, a pair to each. So little fruit was aboard that the citrus pair - two oranges and a lemon a day - ran out after six days. Where did six days leave the two men?
answer: One was fit for duty; the other nursed the rest.
choices: One was fit for duty; the other nursed the rest.
One had improved a little; the other was unchanged.
Both had stopped bleeding; neither could stand yet.
Both could walk the deck; neither could work yet.
context: Lind wrote that 'the most sudden and visible good effects were perceived from the use of the oranges and lemons; one of those who had taken them, being at the end of six days fit for duty.' The second man was 'the best recovered of any in his condition' and Lind put him to work as nurse to the other sick. All twelve had begun the trial the same way - putrid gums, the spots, lassitude and weak knees - and Lind's opening sentence is the founding line of clinical trials: 'On the 20th May, 1747, I took twelve patients in the scurvy on board the Salisbury at sea. Their cases were as similar as I could have them.' Sources: Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753), quoted at hekint.org/2017/01/29/the-mysteries-of-james-lind-and-scurvy/ and renalrounds.substack.com/p/twelve-patients-on-the-salisbury; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind.

question: George Anson sailed in 1740 to raid the Spanish Pacific with about 1,854 men. Four years later he came home rich, having taken the Spanish treasure galleon at a cost of exactly one man killed in the fight. How many of the 1,854 came home aboard his Centurion?
context: Roughly 500 of the squadron's 1,854-1,900 men survived the voyage at all, and 188 came home in the Centurion. Disease - overwhelmingly scurvy - did nearly all the killing, while the richest sea-fight of the age cost one life. Shipowners of the period simply budgeted for a 50% death rate on long voyages; between Columbus's crossing and the mid-1800s scurvy killed more than two million sailors, more than storms, shipwreck, combat and every other disease combined. Anson's losses are what made the Admiralty care, and Lind dedicated his 1753 Treatise of the Scurvy to him. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Anson%27s_voyage_around_the_world; sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/; nzgeo.com/stories/a-scurvy-business/.

question: Aboard HMS Salisbury in 1747, James Lind gave each of six pairs of scurvy patients a different remedy - every one a treatment serious physicians pressed on the fleets. The pair on oranges and lemon recovered; four pairs gained nothing at all; one pair improved slightly. Which remedy gave that slight improvement?
answer: A quart of cider a day.
choices: A quart of cider a day.
A quart of malt wort a day.
A quart of spruce beer a day.
A quart of tamarind water a day.
context: The cider pair improved slightly and no one else did. The seawater, the vinegar and the elixir of vitriol - twenty-five drops of dilute sulphuric acid, taken three times a day - produced nothing, and neither did the sixth pair's electuary: a lump the size of a nutmeg made of garlic, mustard seed, balsam of Peru, dried radish root and gum myrrh, taken three times a day and washed down with barley water acidulated with tamarinds. None of the six was a joke. Every one was a remedy serious physicians of the day pressed on the fleets, which is exactly why a fair comparison was worth running. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; sportsci.org/news/history/lind/lind_sp.html; sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/.

question: Salt beef, hard biscuit, nothing fresh: that was the standing diet on a long passage, and scurvy the standing result. Yet the food was almost impossible to convict, because a crew eating it stays perfectly well for a stretch before the gums begin to bleed. How long is that stretch?
answer: At least a month.
choices: At least a month.
About a week.
Three or four months.
The better part of a year.
context: It takes at least a month of little or no vitamin C before symptoms appear. That delay is why the cause was so hard to trace: the meal that starts the damage and the bleeding gums that announce it are separated by weeks of open ocean, and by then the ship is a thousand miles from the port where the fresh food ran out. Any effect that lags its cause by a month is a punishing thing to spot without a deliberate test - which is what makes Lind's six-pair comparison so much more powerful than shipboard experience. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy.

question: Citrus could cure scurvy, but fresh oranges rot in weeks, so no ship bound for the Indies could carry them. The naval surgeon James Lind's answer was a keepable substitute: citrus juice held in near-boiling water for hours until it cooked down to a sixth of its volume, a syrup he called a 'rob'. What did those hours near boiling do to the vitamin C in the juice?
answer: Destroyed most of it, leaving a syrup that could not cure.
choices: Destroyed most of it, leaving a syrup that could not cure.
Concentrated it sixfold, exactly as Lind had hoped.
Left it intact, but only for a few weeks in cask.
Left it intact, so the rob cured as well as fresh fruit.
context: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid, and heat destroys it - cooking alone can cut the vitamin C in a food by around 60%, and hours near boiling takes far more than that. So Lind's practical recommendation, the one piece of his work built for real ships, was the version of the medicine that did not work. It is a hard, honest lesson about engineering a cure without knowing the mechanism: the man who ran the best test of the century then shipped the broken version of the answer. Sources: jameslindlibrary.org/articles/james-lind-and-scurvy-1747-to-1795/ ('a process that destroyed much of the ascorbic acid, rendering it ineffective'); Jeremy Hugh Baron, 'Sailors' scurvy before and after James Lind - a reassessment', hekint.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/sailors_scurvy-final.pdf; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C.

question: A sailor deep in scurvy has putrid gums, spots up his legs and knees too weak to hold him. The ration the Royal Navy came to issue against the disease was two-thirds of an ounce of lemon juice a day, stirred into the grog - about ten milligrams of vitamin C. What does ten milligrams a day do to a man already that far gone?
answer: Reverses every obvious symptom of the disease.
choices: Reverses every obvious symptom of the disease.
Slows the disease but cannot turn it back.
Protects the healthy but cannot cure the sick.
