Helps only alongside fresh meat and vegetables.
context: Ten milligrams a day is enough to completely reverse all the obvious symptoms of scurvy. The whole catastrophe - fleets emptied, voyages ended, a 50% death rate budgeted in advance, more than two million sailors dead between Columbus's crossing and the mid-1800s - turned on about a spoonful of juice a day. For scale: oranges and lemons carry roughly 53 mg of vitamin C per 100 g of fruit. You can check how fragile the stuff is in a kitchen, since cooking alone can cut a food's vitamin C by around 60%. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind (the Suffolk ration); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C ('All obvious symptoms of scurvy could be completely reversed by supplementation of only 10 mg a day'); sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/.

question: Lind's A Treatise of the Scurvy came out in 1753 and ran to some four hundred pages. The whole book is remembered now for one thing: the twelve men in six pairs aboard the Salisbury. How much of his own book did Lind give that trial?
answer: About five paragraphs, two hundred pages in.
choices: About five paragraphs, two hundred pages in.
The opening chapter and the dedication.
A third of the book, with all the case notes.
Roughly a quarter, spread across the text.
context: The most influential experiment in the history of medicine sits about five paragraphs long, roughly two hundred pages into a four-hundred-page book - and by the third edition in 1772 Lind had added disclaimers that further undercut his own finding. He did not know what he had. A reader in 1753 hunting for the cure would have had to wade two hundred pages to find the five paragraphs that contained it. Source: sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/ (page and paragraph counts are that account's; treat them as approximate).

question: The two men on oranges and lemon were the only clear recovery among Lind's six pairs. Yet when he wrote the trial up in 1753, Lind did not name citrus as the cure for scurvy. What did he argue instead?
answer: That scurvy had several causes at once, so needed several remedies.
choices: That scurvy had several causes at once, so needed several remedies.
That the fruit worked only on scurvy caught in its first weeks.
That the sick berth's warmth, not the fruit, had done the healing.
That the men would have mended in time with no remedy at all.
context: Lind held that scurvy had many causes acting together and therefore needed many remedies, leaning on damp, cold and blocked perspiration: moisture, he wrote, 'concurring with other peculiar circumstances, as a gross diet, cold etc. disposes in a particular manner to the scorbutic corruption.' He treated the fruit as one remedy among several. He was also not the first to suspect citrus - John Woodall, first Surgeon-General of the East India Company, wrote in The Surgeon's Mate (1617) that 'the use of the juyce of Lemmons is a precious medicine and well tried... let it have the chiefe place, for it will deserve it', and Sir Richard Hawkins had called oranges and lemons 'our chief refreshing and the most fruitful remedy' after his 1593 voyage. Lind's contribution was never the idea. It was the test - and he then read his own test wrong. Sources: hekint.org/2017/01/29/the-mysteries-of-james-lind-and-scurvy/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/library-archive/surgeons-mate-john-woodall; Baron, hekint.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/sailors_scurvy-final.pdf.

question: Aboard George Anson's Centurion, a sailor who had taken a wound at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690 watched it break open again more than fifty years after it healed shut. The chaplain Richard Walter wrote that a long-mended broken bone was found 'dissolved, and the fracture seemed as if it had never been consolidated'. Why does scurvy undo a body's oldest repairs?
answer: Scar and bone callus are collagen, which scurvy stops the body rebuilding.
choices: Scar and bone callus are collagen, which scurvy stops the body rebuilding.
Scar and knitted bone are calcium, which scurvy leaches slowly back out.
Scurvy thins the blood until old scars are forced open from beneath.
Damp and cold rot the flesh inward, and old scar tissue gives way first.
context: Collagen is the fibre that stitches a body together, and the body is always tearing old collagen down and building new. Vitamin C is the required cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, the enzymes that convert proline and lysine inside collagen into hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine - and those are what let collagen strands cross-link into a stable triple helix. Without vitamin C the demolition continues and the rebuilding cannot, so scar tissue and bone callus come apart and the body literally comes unstitched. The Boyne case comes from Richard Walter's A Voyage Round the World (1748), the chaplain's own account of Anson's voyage. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Anson%27s_voyage_around_the_world; nzgeo.com/stories/a-scurvy-business/.

question: Lind ran his trial in 1747 and published in 1753; the Navy's Sick and Hurt Board turned down fruit-juice proposals the very next year. The order came at last after Rear Admiral Alan Gardner had lemon juice issued on HMS Suffolk for a twenty-three-week run to Madras, and Gilbert Blane pressed the case from inside that same board. How long after the trial did the Admiralty issue lemon juice to the whole fleet?
answer: Forty-eight years.
choices: Forty-eight years.
Eleven years.
Twenty-two years.
Ninety-one years.
context: The fleet-wide order came in 1795 - forty-eight years after the twelve men in six pairs, and forty-two years after the book. The Suffolk had reached Madras in 1794 with no serious scurvy aboard, and that voyage, not the Treatise, is what moved the Admiralty. Lind himself had seen the problem coming: before the subject could be set right, he wrote, it was necessary to remove 'a great deal of rubbish' from what was already believed. The evidence existed for half a century and did not implement itself. Sources: jameslindlibrary.org/articles/james-lind-and-scurvy-1747-to-1795/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lind; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Blane.

question: By the 1860s the Royal Navy had scurvy beaten with Mediterranean lemon juice. Then the Admiralty switched its supply to lime juice, which carries about a quarter of the scurvy-fighting power - and by 1875 scurvy was back in the fleet, and polar expeditions met it for decades after. What drove the switch?
answer: Limes came from Britain's own colonial plantations.
choices: Limes came from Britain's own colonial plantations.
Limes kept their strength far better in tropical casks.
Limes had tested stronger than lemons in Navy trials.
Limes replaced lemons after Mediterranean crops failed.
context: A solved problem, un-solved by a purchasing decision. Limes carry about 30 mg of vitamin C per 100 g against 53 mg for lemons, and processing takes more still. There is a darkly funny wrinkle: the 1867 Merchant Shipping Act made a daily citrus ration a legal requirement on British ships - and the legally required juice was the one that did not work, which is where the nickname 'limey' comes from. When a laboratory finally analysed the Navy's lime juice in 1918, it found virtually no antiscorbutic power at all, after more than half a century of issue. (A widely repeated claim adds that the juice was pumped through copper piping, which would degrade it further; the chemistry is solid - copper and iron salts do accelerate vitamin C loss - but the piping detail itself is contested, so treat it as an unproven anecdote.) Sources: idlewords.com/2010/03/scott_and_scurvy.htm; psychiatrymargins.com/p/how-the-citrus-cure-for-scurvy-was; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C; thevintagenews.com/2018/08/24/limey/.

question: Joseph Svirbely set out in 1931 to test whether the substance Albert Szent-Gyorgyi had isolated was the thing in the fruit. He fed one group of guinea pigs boiled food, and a matched group the same food with the isolate stirred in; the boiled-food group sickened and died. Why do guinea pigs come down with scurvy when most animals never do?
answer: They carry a broken gene for making their own vitamin C, as we do.
choices: They carry a broken gene for making their own vitamin C, as we do.
They cannot store the vitamin for more than a few days at a time.
They lose the vitamin through the gut faster than they take it in.
They eat a dry grain diet close to a ship's biscuit and salt beef.
context: Guinea pigs, higher primates and most bats all carry a broken, non-functional GULO gene and cannot make their own vitamin C - which is why a guinea pig can stand in for a sailor. Notice the design: two matched groups, one variable, boiling already known to destroy the substance. Svirbely ran Lind's experiment again, in a laboratory, 184 years later. Szent-Gyorgyi had isolated the substance in 1927-28 without knowing what it was, and half-jokingly proposed calling it 'ignose' and then 'godnose' - as in, God knows what it is; the journal editor refused, so it was published as 'hexuronic acid'. After Svirbely's proof it was renamed ascorbic acid, 'the acid that prevents scurvy', and Szent-Gyorgyi took the 1937 Nobel Prize. His supply problem was solved at the dinner table - by one telling of the story, he was served fresh paprika in Szeged, did not want to eat it, carried it to the lab instead and found Hungarian paprika an extraordinarily rich source; he and Ilona Banga then made ascorbic acid from it by the kilogram. Sources: sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/albert-szent-gyorgyi/ (which reports the paprika dinner explicitly as 'one version of the legend'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C; nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1937/szent-gyorgyi/biographical/; profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/wg/.

question: Bell Labs asked Stanford condensed-matter physicist Malcolm Beasley to chair the investigation. His committee's report, released 25-26 September 2002, examined twenty-four separate allegations against Schon. In how many did it find scientific misconduct established?
answer: Sixteen
choices: Sixteen
Two
All twenty-four
None
context: The Beasley report established misconduct in 16 of 24 allegations, including whole datasets reused across unrelated experiments and 'measurements' generated from mathematical functions rather than any real instrument. Of the remaining eight allegations, two had no clear tie to a publication and six were 'troubling' but did not rise to conclusive misconduct. Source: Beasley Committee report, Sept 2002; UCLA-hosted PDF.

question: Schon had put roughly twenty different co-authors' names on the fraudulent papers -- collaborators at Bell Labs and at universities on two continents. When the Beasley committee reached its verdict on those co-authors, what did the report say?
answer: All co-authors were formally cleared of scientific misconduct
choices: All co-authors were formally cleared of scientific misconduct
About half the co-authors were found complicit
Every named co-author was dismissed alongside Schon
Only the most senior co-authors were exonerated
context: The Beasley report explicitly stated that all of Schon's co-authors were completely cleared of scientific misconduct and that no co-author's laboratory practices lay outside accepted norms. This matters: Schon's collaborators trusted samples and figures he produced alone, and were themselves victims of the fabrication. Source: Beasley Committee report, Sept 2002.

question: About two dozen of Schon's papers were withdrawn from Science, Nature, Physical Review, Applied Physics Letters and Advanced Materials. His alma mater -- the University of Konstanz -- then went after his doctorate, though a court in Freiburg reinstated it in 2010. Which court had the final word, and when?
answer: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe, in 2014
choices: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe, in 2014
The Federal Court of Justice (BGH) in Karlsruhe, in 2011
The Federal Administrative Court in Leipzig, in 2013
The Baden-Wurttemberg Higher Administrative Court (VGH Mannheim), in 2012
context: The University of Konstanz revoked Schon's doctorate in 2004, invoking a state law that lets degrees be withdrawn from a recipient later shown 'unworthy'. After a decade of appeals, on 1 October 2014 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe confirmed the revocation as within the university's rights. Source: Bundesverfassungsgericht press release, Oct 2014.

question: On 14 May 1796, in the Gloucestershire village of Berkeley, the country doctor Edward Jenner made two shallow cuts in the arm of James Phipps — the eight-year-old son of his own gardener — and rubbed matter into them. Where had Jenner taken that matter from?
answer: A milkmaid's blistered hand
choices: A cow's diseased udder
A milkmaid's blistered hand
A smallpox patient's ripe pustule
A horse's inflamed heel
context: The donor was Sarah Nelmes, a dairymaid at a farm near Berkeley who had caught cowpox from her master's cows that same May. Jenner's Case XVI names her; Case XVII records the boy: 'I selected a healthy boy, about eight years old... the matter was taken from a sore on the hand of a dairymaid... and it was inserted, on the 14th of May, 1796, into the arm of the boy by means of two superficial incisions.' Source: Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (1798), Cases XVI-XVII (gutenberg.org/files/29414); grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner.

question: Edward Jenner's 1798 pamphlet never names the cow at the bottom of his story, but tradition has called her Blossom ever since. She has not entirely vanished either: part of her still hangs on the library wall at St George's medical school in London. What part?
answer: Her hide
choices: Her horns
Her skull
Her hide
Her bell
context: The hide is at St George's in Tooting; the horns are at Dr Jenner's House museum in Berkeley. Flagged as tradition, not testimony: the NAME Blossom is an attribution attached to the surviving hide long afterwards — Jenner names no cow anywhere in the Inquiry. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Jenner; Jenner, An Inquiry (1798).  (Legend.)

question: On 14 May 1796 Edward Jenner deliberately infected eight-year-old James Phipps, his gardener's son, with cowpox — the mild disease of the dairy herds. Six weeks later the boy was perfectly well, which proved nothing about whether he could now resist smallpox. On 1 July 1796 Jenner came back to him. What did he do to the boy that day?
answer: He scratched matter from a smallpox sore into the boy's arm
choices: He scratched matter from a smallpox sore into the boy's arm
He sent the boy to sleep beside a smallpox patient
He wrapped the boy in blankets from a smallpox sickbed
He walked the boy through a ward full of smallpox cases
context: Jenner's own words: 'In order to ascertain whether the boy... was secure from the contagion of the Small-pox, he was inoculated the 1st of July following with variolous matter... no disease followed.' He deliberately gave a child real smallpox — that was variolation, the standard immunising method of the day, which killed roughly one or two in every hundred who took it against about thirty in a hundred for natural smallpox. Jenner repeated the challenge; over his life Phipps was inoculated with smallpox more than twenty times and never caught it. Sources: Jenner, An Inquiry (1798), Case XVII; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Phipps; grokipedia.com/page/Variolation.

question: James Phipps was the gardener's boy Edward Jenner had experimented on, and Jenner never forgot him. Nor did Jenner ever charge a penny for vaccinating anyone: he treated the poor for free from a rustic hut in his own garden. What did Jenner give Phipps?
answer: The lease of a cottage for his family
choices: A place as his apprentice in medicine
The lease of a cottage for his family
A pension paid from his own practice
A share of his parliamentary award
context: Jenner called the hut at his house, The Chantry, the TEMPLE OF VACCINIA, and vaccinated the poor there free. Phipps got the lease of a cottage in Berkeley, rent-free, for himself, his wife and their two children. He attended Jenner's funeral on 3 February 1823 and died in 1853, buried at St Mary's, Berkeley — the church where he had been baptised. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Phipps.

question: Edward Jenner knew exactly what the old smallpox protection cost, because he had been put through it himself at about eight years old, in Gloucester around 1757. The procedure was the least of it: the six weeks of preparation beforehand wrecked his health for years. What did those six weeks consist of?
answer: Repeated bleeding, purging and near-starvation on a vegetable drink
choices: Repeated cold baths, mercury rubs and a course of hot cupping
Daily blistering plasters, sweating powders and forced bed rest
Six weeks of quarantine at home on beef broth and fortified wine
Repeated bleeding, purging and near-starvation on a vegetable drink
context: 'He was bled until pale, then purged and fasted repeatedly, until he wasted to a skeleton. He was denied solid food in favor of a vegetable drink that was supposed to sweeten the blood; after the inoculation itself — the least traumatic event of the entire experience — he was removed to an "inoculation stable," and, according to an early biographer, "haltered up with others in a terrible state of disease, although none died."' It matters for reading everything he did later: Jenner was not hunting a FIRST method of protection, he was hunting a SAFER one. Sources: Jenner On Trial, ch.2 (bioethicscourse.info/jotsite/jot-chp2.html); EBSCO Research Starters, 'Edward Jenner'.

question: In 1797 Edward Jenner wrote up what he had done to an eight-year-old boy in Berkeley and sent the account to the Royal Society, the most respected scientific body in Britain. The Society did not print it. What did Jenner get back instead?
answer: A warning not to risk his reputation on it
choices: An invitation to demonstrate before the Fellows
A warning not to risk his reputation on it
A referral to the Royal College of Physicians
A demand for a dozen more cases first
context: Jenner 'was given to understand that he should be cautious and prudent, and that he ought not to risk his reputation by presenting anything, which appeared so much at variance with established knowledge.' Not a refutation — a career warning. He paid a printer himself the next year: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (1798), a slim pamphlet of 23 numbered cases with four engraved plates of cowpox sores by William Skelton so that doctors could recognise the real thing, posted to physicians across Britain and Europe at his own expense. Sources: 'Edward Jenner, Benefactor to Mankind', in Artenstein (ed.), Vaccines: A Biography (Springer); grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner.

question: In 1774, with smallpox loose in his Dorset village, the cattle farmer Benjamin Jesty — no medical training at all, and a butcher's son — walked his wife Elizabeth and their two small boys about seven miles to a farm at Chetnole where the cows were diseased. There he scratched matter from those cows into all three of their arms. What did Jesty scratch it in with?
answer: A darning needle
choices: A surgeon's lancet
A butcher's knife
A darning needle
A sharpened quill
context: His neighbours did not applaud. Jesty 'was labelled inhuman, and was "hooted at, reviled and pelted whenever he attended markets in the neighbourhood"' — some genuinely feared his family's 'metamorphosis into horned beasts' for having a cow's disease put into them. It nearly went badly, too: the two boys had mild local reactions, but Elizabeth's arm 'became very inflamed and for a time her condition gave cause for concern', though she recovered fully. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Jesty; grokipedia.com/page/benjamin_jesty.

question: In August 1805 the Original Vaccine Pock Institution in London sent for Benjamin Jesty, a Dorset cattle farmer with no medical training, and sat him before twelve medical officers to answer for the cowpox he had scratched into his own wife and two sons thirty-one years earlier. What happened in front of the officers?
answer: His eldest son Robert took an inoculation of live smallpox
choices: His eldest son Robert took an inoculation of live smallpox
His younger son Benjamin took a fresh scratch of cowpox matter
His wife Elizabeth bared the scar left by the 1774 cut
His wife Elizabeth swore a statement about the 1774 scratching
context: The son took the risk in public, and showed only mild inflammation and no disease. Jesty went home with a signed testimonial affirming the experiment's success over 31 years, a pair of gold-mounted lancets, and a portrait painted by Michael William Sharp, later engraved by William Say. He never got money. Dr George Pearson had put Jesty's 1774 case before a House of Commons committee in 1802 — before Jenner's first award — and the committee granted Jesty nothing; in Pearson's own pamphlet the farmer's name came out as 'Justins'. Parliament paid Jenner £10,000 in 1802 and a further £20,000 in 1807, £30,000 in all. Jesty's gravestone at St Nicholas of Myra, Worth Matravers, Dorset still makes the claim in stone: he was 'particularly noted for having been the first Person (known) that Introduced the Cow Pox by Inoculation, and who from his great strength of mind made the Experiment from the (Cow) on his Wife and two Sons in the Year 1774.' Elizabeth was buried beside him in 1824; both headstones are Grade II listed. THE HONEST ACCOUNTING, stated exactly as the sources state it: Jenner was not the first to put cowpox into a person — Jesty (1774), John Fewster and Peter Plett all preceded him. What Jenner did first was the scientific act: 'he was the first to publish his evidence and distribute vaccine freely, provide information on selection of suitable material, and maintain it by arm-to-arm transfer.' Jesty 'did not publicise his findings made some twenty years earlier in 1774.' Sources: grokipedia.com/page/benjamin_jesty; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Jesty; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine; grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner; Pead, 'Benjamin Jesty: the first vaccinator revealed', The Lancet.

question: Edward Jenner was right that the dairy disease protected people and wrong about where the protection began. He did not think it started in the cow at all: in the Inquiry he traced it to a sore on a different farm animal, and blamed farmhands who dressed that sore and then went to the milking without washing their hands. Which sore did Jenner blame?
answer: A horse's diseased heel
choices: A pig's ulcerated snout
A sheep's rotting hoof
A dog's running ear
A horse's diseased heel
context: Jenner's text: 'There is a disease to which the Horse, from his state of domestication, is frequently subject. The Farriers have termed it the Grease... One of the former having been appointed to apply dressings to the heels of a Horse affected with the Grease, and not paying due attention to cleanliness, incautiously bears his part in milking the Cows, with some particles of the infectious matter adhering to his fingers.' And the kicker: the virus in the vaccine that eventually wiped out smallpox is not cowpox at all. Allan Watt Downie showed in 1939 that it was serologically distinct from cowpox, and it was recognised as its own species, vaccinia; whole-genome sequencing since has found vaccinia's closest relative is HORSEPOX — a smallpox vaccine manufactured by Mulford in 1902 turned out to be 99.7% similar to horsepox. Jenner's horse hunch may have been nearer the mark than his cow. Sources: Jenner, An Inquiry (1798); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine; grokipedia.com/page/Edward_Jenner.

question: Edward Jenner put a promise into the Inquiry that doctors were still repeating decades later, and that his own century proved false. What had Jenner promised in print?
answer: That one course of cowpox protected a person for life
choices: That a vaccinated mother passed her protection to her children
That one course of cowpox protected a person for life
That no vaccinated person could carry smallpox to another
That the matter could pass arm to arm without ever weakening
context: Jenner wrote that 'the person who has been thus affected is for ever after secure from the infection of the Small Pox' — he 'rashly claimed that the protective effect was lifelong. This last proved to be incorrect.' 'Late in the 19th century, it was realized that vaccination did not confer lifelong immunity and that subsequent revaccination was necessary.' The man who found the effect got the duration of his own discovery wrong, inside his own century — and it was testing, not his authority, that settled it. Sources: Jenner, An Inquiry (1798); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox_vaccine; Riedel, 'Edward Jenner and the history of smallpox and vaccination', Proc Bayl Univ Med Cent (PMC1200696).

question: For most of a century, Edward Jenner's Latin cow-word — he had named cowpox Variolae vaccinae, from vacca, a cow — meant that one cowpox procedure and nothing else. Then in 1881, with laboratories across Europe turning out protective inoculations against entirely different diseases, one leading scientist proposed, in Jenner's honour, that the cow-word be stretched to cover them all. The profession took him up on it, which is why a flu shot is called a vaccine today. Who made that proposal?
answer: Louis Pasteur
choices: Louis Pasteur
Robert Koch
Joseph Lister
Paul Ehrlich
context: Pasteur made the proposal in his 1881 'Address on the Germ Theory' (The Lancet 118 (3024), pp. 271-272), and he made it as a tribute: he asked that 'vaccine' and 'vaccination' be extended from Jenner's cowpox procedure to every protective inoculation then being developed. So Jenner's one Latin cow-word, minted for one 1796 result, was generalised forward by a proposal rather than by a result — the name spread across the new products, while the trials and the safety record behind each of them stayed separate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccine, citing Pasteur, 'Address on the Germ Theory', The Lancet 118 (3024), 1881, pp. 271-272.

question: Cholera struck Soho on 31 August 1854, and 127 people were dead within three days. John Snow, a London doctor who had studied cholera for years, walked the district to find the cause. What did he do?
answer: He marked every death as a black bar at the address where it happened.
choices: He marked every death as a black bar at the address where it happened.
He measured how high each street stood above the level of the Thames.
He sampled the air in the worst courts, morning and night.
He counted the dead parish by parish in the weekly returns.
context: The bars were short, and stacked where several had died in one house — and the pile-up sat around a single object: the public water pump on Broad Street. 616 people were dead by the end of the outbreak. Snow had doubted for years that bad air carried cholera, but doubt is not evidence. Plotting each death at the address where it happened, rather than counting by parish or by height above the river, is the move that started epidemiology. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; grokipedia.com/page/John_Snow (Grokipedia checked first).

question: The Broad Street pump stood among the outdoor toilets and leaking waste pits of one of the most crowded quarters in London. During the outbreak Edwin Lankester drew a glass from it and examined the water. What did he find?
answer: It was clear, odourless and pleasant to the taste.
choices: It was clear, odourless and pleasant to the taste.
It was clear but bitter, tasting of chalk and iron.
It was cloudy with white flecks and smelled of the drains.
It was yellowish and oily, with a taste of coal tar.
context: Lankester, inspecting while the outbreak was running, found the water clear, odourless and palatable — and residents widely regarded it as the purest water in the neighbourhood. That is the trap: the killer water looked and tasted better than the safe water, so people carried it home on purpose. Nothing your eyes or tongue can do will tell you a well is poisoned; only the pattern of who fell ill could. Source: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Edwin Lankester's Assessment').

question: A brewery stood in the middle of Broad Street's dying, and not one of its seventy-odd workmen had died of cholera. John Snow called on the owner, Mr Huggins, to ask how his men had escaped it. What did Huggins tell him?
answer: They were allowed a daily ration of beer and drank no water at all.
choices: They were allowed a daily ration of beer and drank no water at all.
They worked all day in the heat rising off the boiling coppers.
They were dosed with brandy and quinine at the start of each shift.
They lodged out beyond the parish and only came in to work.
context: Snow's own words in 1855: 'There is a Brewery in Broad Street, near to the pump, and on perceiving that no brewer's men were registered as having died of cholera, I called on Mr. Huggins... He informed me that there were above seventy workmen employed in the brewery, and that none of them had suffered from cholera, — at least in a severe form, — only two having been indisposed... The men are allowed a certain quantity of malt liquor, and Mr. Huggins believes they do not drink water at all.' A quiet irony: Snow signed the abstinence pledge around 1836 and had been a vegetarian since seventeen, and the cleanest piece of evidence he ever found was seventy men saved by their beer ration. (Beware retellings that say '500 employees' — that figure belongs to the Poland Street workhouse, not the brewery.) Sources: epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_c.html (verbatim Snow 1855); grokipedia.com/page/John_Snow.

question: The workhouse in Poland Street, where the parish housed its poor, was ringed on three sides by houses where people were dying, and 535 people were packed inside it. Five died of cholera. John Snow went looking for what the workhouse had that the streets around it did not. What did he find?
answer: A well of its own, sunk in the yard behind the wards.
choices: A well of its own, sunk in the yard behind the wards.
A rainwater cistern, fed from the roofs of the wards.
A floor of quicklime, laid down at the end of August.
A rule against going out, kept while the cholera lasted.
context: Snow in 1855: 'The Workhouse in Poland Street is more than three-fourths surrounded by houses in which deaths from cholera occurred, yet out of five hundred and thirty-five inmates only five died of cholera, the other deaths which took place being those of persons admitted after they were attacked. The workhouse has a pump-well on the premises, in addition to the supply from the Grand Junction Water Works, and the inmates never sent to Broad Street for water.' Notice the second half of that sentence: Snow refused to count people who arrived already sick as cases the house had produced. Deciding who counts as a case is half of an epidemiologist's work. Source: epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_d.html (verbatim Snow 1855).

question: Late in 1854 Henry Whitehead, a curate at St Luke's in Berwick Street, went door to door through Soho, interviewing 497 of the 896 people who had lived in the stricken streets and writing to those who had moved away — the most thorough inquiry made into the outbreak. Why had he begun it?
answer: He believed in bad air himself and meant to break Snow's water theory.
choices: He believed in bad air himself and meant to break Snow's water theory.
He had been hired by the parish to price the rebuilding of the sewers.
He was collecting names for a memorial to be raised in the churchyard.
He had been sent out by Snow to canvass the streets he could not reach.
context: Whitehead ended up convinced by the evidence he had gone looking to destroy, and became one of Snow's defenders. His door-to-door work is what turned up the outbreak's first case: five-month-old Frances Lewis at 40 Broad Street, daughter of the police constable Thomas Lewis and his wife Sarah. The baby died on 2 September 1854. A hostile investigator who follows his own data wherever it goes is worth more to a theory than ten friendly ones. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Henry Whitehead's Field Inquiry'); choleraandthethames.co.uk/cholera-in-london/cholera-in-soho/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Whitehead_(priest).

question: The outbreak's first case was a five-month-old baby at 40 Broad Street, whose mother, Sarah Lewis, rinsed the soiled nappies into the cesspit — the household waste pit — sunk in front of the house. The Broad Street pump drew its water from a well a short way off. How did the pit's filth reach that well?
answer: The cesspit's brick lining had rotted, and the well stood in loose gravel.
choices: The cesspit's brick lining had rotted, and the well stood in loose gravel.
The cesspit had been sluiced out into the sewer that ran past the well.
The cesspit stood uphill of the well, on ground that sloped sharply.
The cesspit had been emptied into the gutter above the well's shaft.
context: The well was only about eleven feet deep, sunk in loose gravel and sand with no layer of impermeable clay to stop seepage, and the cesspit's brick lining had rotted through. Sources genuinely disagree on how far apart the two stood — Wikipedia gives about three feet, Grokipedia about twenty — so the decayed brickwork and the porous ground are the parts you can rely on. Frances Lewis died on 2 September 1854; the reported dates for when she first fell ill vary across sources, which is why the death date is the one worth remembering. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak.

question: On 2 September 1854 a widow of 59 died of cholera at West End in Hampstead, miles north of Soho, in a district where there was no cholera at all; she had been seized on the Friday evening and was dead by Saturday. What had come to her from Broad Street?
answer: A cart brought her a large bottle of the pump's water each day.
choices: A cart brought her a large bottle of the pump's water each day.
Her son had come up from the street to sit with her that week.
A basket of fruit had been sent up to her from the market there.
Her washing went down to a laundress in the street and came back.
context: Snow: 'A cart went from Broad Street to West End every day, and it was the custom to take out a large bottle of the water from the pump in Broad Street, as she preferred it.' The water went out on Thursday 31 August; she drank it that evening and again on Friday. Then the knockout line — 'A niece, who was on a visit to this lady, also drank of the water; she returned to her residence, in a high and healthy part of Islington, was attacked with cholera, and died also,' and 'There was no cholera at the time, either at West End or in the neighbourhood where the niece died.' Bad air does not travel in a cart. Snow's register calls her the widow of a percussion-cap maker; other accounts name her Susannah Eley, whose sons ran the Eley Brothers works in Broad Street and sent the water out to her. Sources: epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream1_introduction_d9.html (verbatim Snow 1855); choleraandthethames.co.uk/cholera-in-london/cholera-in-soho/.

question: John Snow argued his case to the parish board, and the next day, 8 September 1854, the board had the handle taken off the Broad Street pump. What did Snow write about that removal when he wrote the outbreak up in 1855?
answer: He could not decide whether the well still held the poison by then.
choices: He could not decide whether the well still held the poison by then.
He could not doubt that the removal had cut the outbreak short.
He could not find a single death that had begun after that day.
He could not trust the water again while the cesspit stood beside it.
context: Snow's actual words: 'There is no doubt that the mortality was much diminished... but the attacks had so far diminished before the use of the water was stopped, that it is impossible to decide whether the well still contained the cholera poison in an active state, or whether, from some cause, the water had become free from it.' The reason deaths were already falling is that Soho had emptied — panic set in from 31 August and by 1 September the local streets were largely stripped of inhabitants, so there was hardly anyone left to catch it. Henry Whitehead wrote in 1867 that the outbreak 'had already reached its climax, and had been steadily on the decline for several days before the pump-handle was removed.' The schoolbook version — handle off, epidemic over — is not Snow's claim; he argued against his own best story, which is what a scientist is supposed to do. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak (quoting Snow 1855); grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_e.html (Whitehead 1867).

question: John Snow's 1855 map of the Soho cholera deaths is famous for its black bars, but it also carries a line that most people never notice — and the line, not the bars, is where his argument lives. What does that line enclose?
answer: Every spot that lay nearer to the Broad Street pump than to any other.
choices: Every spot that lay nearer to the Broad Street pump than to any other.
Every spot that lay within two hundred yards of the Broad Street pump.
Every spot that lay above the new sewers driven under the parish.
Every spot that lay lower than thirty feet above the level of the river.
context: Snow plotted every public pump in the district first, then drew the boundary enclosing all the points closer to the Broad Street pump than to any other. Wikipedia describes the method plainly: 'He mapped the individual water pumps and generated cells representing all the points on his map that were closest to each pump.' Mathematicians now call that partition a Voronoi diagram; Snow drew one in 1855, long before it had a name, and the deaths sat inside his line. It is widely reported that the second map measured distance by the nearest road on foot through the alleys rather than in a straight line — treat that refinement as reported rather than nailed down. The exceptions are the best part: only ten deaths fell in houses decidedly nearer some other pump, and in five of those ten 'the families of the deceased persons informed me that they always sent to the pump in Broad Street, as they preferred the water to that of the pumps which were nearer.' People walked past a safe pump because the deadly one tasted better. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak; epi-snow.ph.ucla.edu/Stream2_BSPoutbreak_f.html.

question: In October 1854 the General Board of Health sent three investigators — Edmund Parkes, J. Lea Smith and William Ranger — house to house through Soho. They rejected the pump, holding up the brewery's untouched workmen and the workhouse's five dead as proof that the water could not be the cause. What did their report blame instead?
answer: The new sewers, built too flat and choked with butchers' waste.
choices: The new sewers, built too flat and choked with butchers' waste.
The old graveyards, packed too full and dug over for new burials.
The low ground, lying too near the river to drain or to dry.
The night fogs, hanging too thick over the streets after dark.
context: The three investigators catalogued the sewers driven under the parish between 1851 and 1854 with a fall of only one in 250 — too shallow to carry anything away — choked with waste from the slaughterhouses and the tripe-boilers, and the cesspools overflowing beside them, and they blamed the air rising off all of it. The sting is in what they used against Snow: the two anomalies he had built his case on — the brewery's men who drank beer instead of water, and the workhouse drawing on its own well — read to the Board as houses in the middle of the dying that the pump had spared, and so as proof the pump was innocent. The same facts, read through a different theory, gave the opposite verdict; that is why the argument had to be settled by a test rather than by inspection. Faecal-oral transmission was also close to unmentionable in polite Victorian company. Source: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Official Board of Health Evaluation').

question: In 1855 John Snow published his case: the map, a widow dead miles away, two water companies. The physician Edmund Parkes reviewed the book and named the weakness Snow's critics had all felt. What could Snow not produce?
answer: Any impurity in the pump water itself that his own analysis could show.
choices: Any impurity in the pump water itself that his own analysis could show.
Any record of where each victim had gone in the days before falling ill.
Any animal made ill by a dose of water drawn from the Broad Street pump.
Any case of the cholera passing from one person to another under his eye.
context: Parkes pointed out that Snow's own examination of the pump water had found 'so little impurity... of an organic nature' — no visible filth, no demonstrated sewage, and certainly no microbe. Snow never saw a cholera germ and never claimed to; he inferred a self-multiplying poison that was swallowed and multiplied in the gut. He won on pattern, not on a specimen. The specimen already existed on paper, unread: in that same year, 1854, the Italian anatomist Filippo Pacini examined victims during an outbreak in Florence, saw a comma-shaped organism he called a vibrio in their intestinal contents, and published it. Italian medicine was committed to bad air and ignored him; Robert Koch re-found the same comma bacillus in Egypt and India in 1883-84 and got the credit. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak ('Contemporary Objections from Miasmatists'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Pacini.

question: South London's two water companies ran their pipes down the same streets, sometimes into neighbouring houses. Lambeth had moved its intake upriver to Seething Wells in 1852; Southwark and Vauxhall still drew from the sewage-fouled tidal Thames. Over the first seven weeks of the 1854 epidemic John Snow counted the cholera deaths house by house, and Southwark and Vauxhall's 40,046 houses lost 1,263 people. How much deadlier was cholera in their houses than in Lambeth's?
answer: About eight and a half times as many deaths per house.
choices: About eight and a half times as many deaths per house.
About two and a half times as many deaths per house.
About four and a half times as many deaths per house.
About sixteen and a half times as many deaths per house.
context: Lambeth's 26,107 houses lost 98 people against Southwark and Vauxhall's 1,263. That is 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses against 37 — neighbours on one street, breathing the same air, eating the same food, working the same trades, drinking different rivers and dying at about eight and a half times the rate. Snow called it a grand experiment, and it is as close to a controlled trial as a city ever hands you: the only thing that differed between the two groups was which company's pipe reached the house. Careful with the famous numbers — Snow separately reported that over the first FOUR weeks cholera was 'between thirteen and fourteen times' as fatal in the Southwark and Vauxhall population, and 'nearly eight times as great' over the next three weeks. The '14 times' and the per-house figures cover different periods; name the period, never blend them. Sources: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/cholera-john-snow-and-the-grand-experiment-33494689/; archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section2.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Snow.

question: William Farr, the government's statistician, had built the best case bad air ever had: a real and repeatable link between cholera deaths and how low a district lay above the Thames. In 1866 cholera came back to London's eastern parishes and killed more than 5,000 people. Farr went house to house after it. What did he trace the deaths to?
answer: The reservoir belonging to one of the water companies.
choices: The reservoir belonging to one of the water companies.
The low ground lying nearest the river below the city.
The clothing carried away from the beds of the sick.
The fruit sold cheap in the streets of those parishes.
context: Farr followed the water supply house by house and the trail ran to the Old Ford Reservoir of the East London Water Company. Note what his elevation correlation had been: real, reproducible, and still not the cause — low ground near the river is also where the fouled water was. A correlation can be perfectly solid and still point at the wrong thing, which is exactly why Snow's two-company comparison mattered. Snow never saw the vindication: he had a stroke in his office on 10 June 1858 and died six days later, on 16 June 1858, aged 45 — eight years before the man who had opposed him used his method to shut a reservoir. Sources: ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/farr/farr_eastlondon_a.html (Halliday, 'William Farr: campaigning statistician'); sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/medicine/cholera-victorian-london; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Snow.

question: Joseph Black kept asking a Glasgow question in the late 1750s: when the spring thaw finally comes, why does a snowdrift take days to disappear instead of vanishing in minutes the way a simple warming should predict? Where was the heat going?
answer: Into melting the ice without raising its temperature
choices: Into melting the ice without raising its temperature
Down through the soil and lost to the bedrock
Straight back into the air by reflection
Sideways into the surrounding puddles
context: The heat was pouring in and the thermometer refused to move -- because the incoming energy was busy turning ice into water, not warming anything up. Black had found the biggest missing entry in the heat-books. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Black

question: In December 1761 Joseph Black did the experiment. He put a lump of ice at 0 C into a warm room and clocked how long it took to melt, then took the same weight of water at 0 C and clocked how long IT took to warm all the way up to the temperature the melted ice had reached. Which took longer?
answer: The ice, by many times over
choices: The ice, by many times over
The water, by many times over
The two took almost exactly the same time
The ice took slightly less because ice is thinner
context: The ice sat there absorbing heat with no reading on the thermometer -- Black measured the hidden intake as enough to raise the same water by about 143 F. Heat was going IN with no temperature going up. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Black

question: Black needed a name for the heat that pours into melting ice or boiling water without moving the thermometer -- present but invisible to the instrument. He built the name from a Latin word meaning 'hidden' or 'lying in wait'. What did he call it?
answer: Latent heat
choices: Latent heat
Fixed heat
Silent heat
Dormant heat
context: From the Latin latens, hidden. The name has stuck: latent heat of fusion (ice to water) and latent heat of vaporisation (water to steam) are still the terms every physics student meets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latent_heat

question: Here is Black's discovery you can do at your kitchen stove. Put a thermometer in a pot of vigorously boiling water and crank the burner to maximum. What does the reading do?
answer: Stays stuck at about 100 C
choices: Stays stuck at about 100 C
Climbs steadily as long as you leave the burner on
Drops slightly because the steam takes heat away
Spikes to about 130 C at the surface
context: Every extra joule you push in goes into ripping liquid molecules apart into vapour -- the same latent heat Black had seen in his melting ice, this time hiding in the steam. The thermometer will not move off 100 C until all the water is gone. Source: https://www.tec-science.com/thermodynamics/heat/why-steam-burns-are-more-dangerous-than-water-burns/

question: Black also showed that equal weights of different substances warmed by the same amount take VERY different amounts of heat to get there -- he called this the specific heat. He found the appetite of one common substance to be unusually large -- ounce for ounce it soaked up more heat, for the same rise, than almost anything else Black tested. Which was it?
answer: Water
choices: Water
Iron
Sand
Mercury
context: Water's high specific heat is why the sea moderates coastal climate, why radiators use water, and why your body -- mostly water -- is thermally stable. Black noted that mercury, in contrast, has a very small appetite for heat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Black

question: Joseph Black taught chemistry at Glasgow while a young man named James Watt earned his living as the university's instrument maker; the two became friends. In 1763 Watt was asked to repair a model Newcomen atmospheric engine and saw it was wasting most of its coal on ONE thing per cycle. In May 1765, on a Sunday walk on Glasgow Green, he solved it. What was the engine's ruinous waste?
answer: Reheating the cylinder after chilling it with cold water
choices: Reheating the cylinder after chilling it with cold water
Pumping the same water up and down forever
Blowing steam straight out of the exhaust valve
Turning the flywheel against a slipping belt
context: Newcomen's design shot cold water into the working cylinder every stroke to condense the steam -- then had to reheat the whole cold cylinder from scratch. Watt's answer was the SEPARATE CONDENSER: condense the steam in a chamber next door, keep the working cylinder always hot. It roughly quartered fuel consumption. (Black taught the friendship and lent money; historians treat the design as Watt's own invention.) Source: https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co50928/watts-second-separate-condenser-1765

question: At ordinary kitchen pressure, water boils at 100 C and the steam coming off it is also at 100 C -- exactly the same temperature. And yet a burn from that steam is far worse than a burn from the boiling water it came out of. Applying what Black had shown about the heat hiding in a phase change, why?
answer: The steam condenses on the skin and dumps its latent heat there
choices: The steam condenses on the skin and dumps its latent heat there
The steam clings to the skin longer than water does
Water vapour is chemically more corrosive than liquid water
The steam pushes heat in faster because it is under pressure
context: Water's latent heat of vaporisation is about 2260 J/g -- a huge reservoir. When steam at 100 C touches cooler skin it condenses back into water AT 100 C, unloading all that hidden energy in an instant, roughly five times what the same mass of boiling water would deliver. It is also why sweating cools you: evaporating water carries latent heat OFF your skin the same way. Source: https://www.tec-science.com/thermodynamics/heat/why-steam-burns-are-more-dangerous-than-water-burns/

question: You fizz vinegar and baking soda in a jug. When you tilt the jug over a lit candle -- with no liquid leaving the jug -- the flame goes out. What property of carbon dioxide is at work?
answer: It is denser than ordinary air and displaces the oxygen the flame needs
choices: It is denser than ordinary air and displaces the oxygen the flame needs
It is lighter than ordinary air and rises past the flame in an updraft
It reacts chemically with the candle wax and smothers the wick
It cools the wick below the temperature a flame can sustain
context: CO2 is about 1.5 times as dense as ordinary air, so it flows out of the tilted jug like an invisible liquid and slides down over the candle, pushing the oxygen away. The flame goes out because it is starved, not chilled or chemically attacked. Source: https://sensidyne.com/application/brewery-gas-detection/

question: Edinburgh, 1754. Joseph Black heated a sample of magnesia alba on his balance and reweighed the white residue. What did the balance show, and what did Black conclude?
answer: It weighed less; a definite gas had escaped from the powder
choices: It weighed more; heat had added something from the furnace to the powder
It weighed the same; heating had only rearranged the powder
It weighed less; a definite gas had escaped from the powder
It weighed less; part of the powder had simply burned away into fire and light
context: Black called the escaping gas 'fixed air' because it had been fixed inside the solid. He gave it its own chemical account that had to balance -- before him, air was one substance; after him, a gas was a specific chemical you had to weigh. His 1756 paper 'Experiments Upon Magnesia Alba, Quicklime, and Some Other Alcaline Substances' is the quantitative-chemistry precedent Lavoisier built on. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Experiments-Upon-Magnesia-Alba-Quicklime-and-Some-Other-Alcaline-Substances

question: OSHA and NIOSH list one gas as a leading confined-space killer in old wells, grain silos and the fermentation cellars beneath breweries. Which gas is it, and by what mechanism does it kill the worker who enters?
answer: Carbon dioxide, which is denser than air and pools in the space the worker must stand in, starving him of oxygen
choices: Methane, which forms an explosive atmosphere and detonates when the worker's lamp ignites it
Hydrogen sulfide, which paralyses the sense of smell within seconds so the worker cannot detect the rising dose
Nitrogen, which is vented pure to purge the vats and silently displaces the oxygen a worker needs to breathe
Carbon dioxide, which is denser than air and pools in the space the worker must stand in, starving him of oxygen
context: CO2 is colourless, odourless and heavier than air, so it collects invisibly at the lowest point of a silo, well or cellar until a worker walks into a lungful. It is the same physics that lets you pour it onto a candle in a kitchen; on the scale of a fermentation vat it is a documented killer. Methane and hydrogen sulfide are real confined-space hazards too, by the mechanisms named in the other choices -- but CO2 is the one specifically associated with fermentation. Source: https://www.osha.gov/publications/hib19960605

question: James Prescott Joule hung weights on strings that turned a paddle wheel sealed inside an insulated barrel of water. Each time he let them fall, the water warmed slightly. Run after run, that warming matched one quantity exactly. Which one?
answer: the heaviness of the weights times how far they fell
choices: the heaviness of the weights times how far they fell
the speed of the paddle wheel times how long it spun
the volume of the water times the depth of the barrel
the length of the strings times the number of runs
context: The Science Museum's own label on Joule's surviving apparatus puts it plainly: 'Falling weights turned the paddles to churn water; the churning raised the water's temperature slightly, and Joule found that the temperature rise was in direct proportion to the amount of work done by the falling weights.' Not that heat appeared -- heat appeared IN PROPORTION. Weight multiplied by distance fallen is what physicists call WORK, and the fixed ratio between work put in and heat that comes out is the mechanical equivalent of heat: an exchange rate between two things nobody had thought were the same currency. Source: Science Museum Group Collection, object 1876-492, 'Mechanical equivalent of heat apparatus'.

question: James Prescott Joule's weights were four pounds each. They fell twelve yards at about a foot a second, and he wound them up and dropped them sixteen times over for one single reading. How much warmer was the water when he was done?
answer: about one degree Fahrenheit
choices: about one degree Fahrenheit
about one tenth of a degree Fahrenheit
about fifteen degrees Fahrenheit
about forty degrees Fahrenheit
context: Joule's own words from the 1845 paper: the weights were 'each of four pounds', they 'descended at the slow rate of about one foot per second', the pulleys stood 'twelve yards' high, and 'this operation had been repeated sixteen times'. Sixteen separate winds and drops for one measurement, and the whole reward is a single degree. The first law of thermodynamics rests on a man chasing a fraction of a degree over and over before the room could steal it back. You can chase it yourself: take the temperature of water in a sealed jar, shake it hard for five minutes, and take it again. Source: primary text of Joule 1845, 'On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat' (British Association, Cambridge, June 1845).

question: James Prescott Joule's copper cylinder held a brass wheel with eight arms to churn the water. But a wheel spinning in a smooth can simply carries the water round with it in one lazy body, and water that merely travels never rubs. What did Joule fit inside the cylinder to stop that happening?
answer: a set of fixed vanes bolted to the inner wall
choices: a set of fixed vanes bolted to the inner wall
a second brass wheel geared to turn the other way
a narrower cylinder built to almost touch the arms
a heavy iron plate laid flat across the water
context: Four fixed vanes were bolted to the inside of the copper cylinder, so the eight-armed brass wheel had to shear the water past them instead of swinging it round in one lump. Rubbing is the whole point: friction is where the weights' fall gets ground into heat, and without the vanes most of the fall would simply have gone into spinning the water. Joule later rebuilt the machine with a wrought-iron wheel churning mercury, and again with cast iron grinding on cast iron -- three different substances, one answer. Source: Grokipedia 'James Prescott Joule'; Royal Society commentary, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 373:20140348, 'Heat, work and subtle fluids'.

question: James Prescott Joule knew the warming he was chasing was so faint that almost anything in the room could counterfeit it. So for every run he set a large wooden screen around the apparatus, and mounted the barrel on wood touching at as few points as he could manage. What was the screen shutting out?
answer: the heat coming off his own body
choices: the heat coming off his own body
the warmth of the oil lamp on the bench
the draught coming in under the door
the sunlight falling through the window
context: The experimenter was the contaminant. Joule screened his own body heat away from the apparatus and stood the barrel on wood, touching at as few points as possible, so heat could not conduct out of it either. It is a small detail that carries the whole scientific virtue: the first person a careful investigator suspects is himself. Source: Stephen Curry, 'Joule's Jewel', Reciprocal Space, 3 January 2011, reading Joule's 1850 Philosophical Transactions paper directly.

question: The Science Museum still holds a Joule paddle-wheel apparatus: a copper barrel with a fitted lid, lagged with wood and textile, no bigger than a large kitchen bin. The runs that fixed the exchange rate between work and heat were done in the 1840s. Where did the object in that case come from?
answer: Joule built it himself in Salford in 1876, decades later
choices: Joule built it himself in Salford in 1876, decades later
A London instrument firm made it to his drawings in 1845
His brewery workmen put it together for the 1845 trials
The museum reconstructed it from his papers in the 1930s
context: Object 1876-492 in the Science Museum Group Collection: three parts, copper and copper alloy with wood and textile insulation, roughly 700 by 210 millimetres overall. Joule built this one himself in Salford in 1876, so the piece in the case is his own later build rather than the apparatus that produced the original readings -- a man making his own machine again, by hand, long after the argument was won. Either way the point holds: no accelerator, no observatory, no budget. The first law of thermodynamics came out of a copper bucket a man built in a brewing town, and you can still go and look at the bucket. Source: Science Museum Group Collection, object 1876-492, 'Mechanical equivalent of heat apparatus'.

question: James Prescott Joule never held a university post. From 1837 he ran his family's brewery in Salford, and Manchester's science museum argues that his doubters underrated exactly what that job had given him. What did the brewery give him that the professors did not have?
answer: a trade where a fraction of a degree decides what the beer becomes
choices: a trade where a fraction of a degree decides what the beer becomes
a cellar full of vats big enough to hold any apparatus he built
a workforce of draymen who could be spared to turn a crank
a brewer's income that freed him from chasing a university salary
context: Mash temperature decides what beer you end up with, so Joule already owned habits of temperature measurement that professors simply did not need. The Science and Industry Museum's verdict on his critics is blunt: they 'neglected his experience in the art of brewing and his access to its practical technologies.' The amateur beat the academy because his day job was measuring heat for a living. Source: Science and Industry Museum, Manchester, 'James Joule: from establishment irritant to honoured scientist'; Grokipedia 'James Prescott Joule'.

question: When James Prescott Joule began, nearly every physicist explained heat as caloric - a weightless fluid that soaked into matter and flowed from hot bodies to cold ones. A convinced believer in caloric, watching the paddle wheel warm the water, had a ready explanation for what he was seeing. What was it?
answer: the stirring squeezed out caloric the water was already holding
choices: the stirring squeezed out caloric the water was already holding
the falling weights dragged caloric down the strings into the can
the brass wheel gave up caloric it had soaked up in the workshop
the thermometer's own caloric leaked into the water it touched
context: Caloric was not a stupid idea; it was the live consensus of serious people, and it explained a great deal. Under caloric, heat can be moved from place to place but never made -- so a paddle wheel cannot manufacture warmth, it can only wring out warmth the water was already hiding. What caloric could not survive was the exchange RATE: a fixed amount of falling always bought a fixed amount of heat, and the water never ran out of heat to give. Source: Science and Industry Museum, Manchester, 'James Joule'; Grokipedia 'James Prescott Joule'.

question: James Prescott Joule read a paper on his heat experiments to the Royal Society in London - the most respected scientific body in the world - on 20 June 1844. What did the Society do with it?
answer: refused to publish it, so he settled for the Philosophical Magazine
choices: refused to publish it, so he settled for the Philosophical Magazine
published it in full in its own Philosophical Transactions that year
published it, but only as a short abstract buried in its Proceedings
sent it back for more experiments, then printed it two years later
context: Rejected. He published in the Philosophical Magazine in 1845 instead, and presented the paddle-wheel result to the British Association at Cambridge that June under the title 'On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat'. It was not even his first cold shoulder: in August 1843, at the British Association in Cork, he read an earlier version and was 'met by silence' -- the contemporary Dictionary of National Biography records simply that no notice was taken of it. The most important experiment of the century was a rejected submission. Source: Wikipedia 'James Prescott Joule'; Dictionary of National Biography 1885-1900, 'Joule, James Prescott'.

question: When James Prescott Joule brought his paddle-wheel result to Britain's physicists, they did not begin by disputing his conclusions. They went after the work itself, at one specific point, and the objection kept him out of the leading journals for years. What did his critics say was impossible?
answer: that anyone could read a thermometer to a two-hundredth of a degree
choices: that anyone could read a thermometer to a two-hundredth of a degree
that a barrel of water could be insulated well enough to hold heat
that a brewery cellar could be kept still enough for fine work
that weights on a string could fall at a steady enough speed
context: Joule claimed he could read a thermometer to within one two-hundredth of a degree Fahrenheit. His contemporaries did not believe that was possible for anyone, and Manchester's museum is direct about it: it was the very precision of his measurements that made scientists balk, not his theory. Note that the objection was reasonable -- the Royal Society's own modern commentary judges even a claim of about 0.005 degrees F 'optimistic'. Reasonable, and wrong. That is the shape of most scientific resistance. Source: Science and Industry Museum, Manchester, 'James Joule'; Royal Society commentary, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 373:20140348.

question: James Prescott Joule did not trust James Prescott Joule. Before he would believe his own thermometer, he added one extra procedure to every single trial - forty times over with water, twenty with mercury, ten with cast iron. What was the extra procedure?
answer: he ran the whole experiment through without moving the weights at all
choices: he ran the whole experiment through without moving the weights at all
he read the thermometer twice over and averaged the two readings
he weighed the barrel before and after to check for water leaking out
he had a second man read the thermometer without telling him the first
context: He went through the entire motions of the experiment with the weights and paddle left still, and measured what the thermometer did anyway. That phantom rise -- the room drifting, nothing more -- averaged 0.012975 degrees Fahrenheit, and he subtracted it from every result. This is a CONTROL RUN: do everything except the one thing you are testing, and see what you get regardless. Joule was running a control on himself, because the person he distrusted most was himself. You can run one on any home experiment you ever do. Source: Stephen Curry, 'Joule's Jewel', Reciprocal Space, 3 January 2011, reading Joule's 1850 Philosophical Transactions paper.

question: James Prescott Joule left the 1847 Oxford meeting of the British Association with one convert: a young William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, who had come to hear him sceptically. From about 1852 the two ran a long series of experiments together, and one result still carries both their names. What does the Joule-Thomson effect do?
answer: it cools a gas when the gas is forced to expand through a plug
choices: it cools a gas when the gas is forced to expand through a plug
it warms a wire when an electric current is pushed along it
it cools a liquid when the liquid is allowed to evaporate away
it warms a gas when the gas is squeezed into a smaller space
context: Joule was put on late in the day at Oxford and asked by the chairman to keep it brief, with Michael Faraday and George Gabriel Stokes sitting in the audience. Thomson wrote that at Oxford he learned the dynamical theory of heat from Joule and 'was forced to abandon many statical preconceptions regarding the ultimate causes of apparently statical phenomena.' The porous-plug experiments that followed gave the gas-cooling principle every refrigerator and air conditioner still runs on. The distractors are all real physics: warming a wire with a current is Joule heating, Joule's own earlier discovery. One disputed detail from that day -- Joule remembered a young man at the back standing up to ask penetrating questions; Thomson denied it, insisting he stayed in his seat and asked afterwards. Two eyewitnesses, same five minutes, neither lying. Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson'; Wikipedia 'James Prescott Joule'; Grokipedia 'Joule-Thomson effect'.

question: When the Royal Society did at last publish James Prescott Joule, its committee made him cut his third conclusion out first - the one stating that friction is mechanical power being converted into heat. Joule recorded the loss in his own hand: a third proposition, he wrote, 'suppressed in accordance with the wish of the committee'. The anonymous referee behind that cut admired the measurements but would not follow the leap. Who was he?
answer: Michael Faraday
choices: Michael Faraday
John Herschel
William Whewell
George Airy
context: Joule's full note: 'A third proposition, suppressed in accordance with the wish of the committee ... stated that friction consisted in the conversion of mechanical power into heat.' Faraday's objection was that the inference did not follow from the measurements alone -- that because a given amount of heat always requires the same amount of force, heat is therefore convertible into force and force into heat. The greatest experimentalist of the age was the man holding the door shut. It does not make Faraday a villain; it makes him a working scientist who judged an inference and judged it wrong, which is the ordinary condition of the trade. Source: Royal Society commentary on Joule (1850), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 373:20140348, 'Heat, work and subtle fluids'.

question: James Prescott Joule married Amelia Grimes on 18 August 1847 and took her to the Alps. He had argued in print two years earlier that a waterfall must warm its own water on the way down - he had even put a figure on Niagara - and he and William Thomson had arranged to test the idea on the Cascade de Sallanches in Haute-Savoie, a free fall of 270 metres. How did the attempt turn out?
answer: it proved impractical, and he never got a figure from the waterfall
choices: it proved impractical, and he never got a figure from the waterfall
it matched his prediction closely, and he published the result in 1848
it came out ten times too large, and he blamed the thin mountain air
the spray drove him to a smaller fall nearby, where it finally worked
context: The waterfall beat him. The man who could read a two-hundredth of a degree indoors could not defeat spray and evaporation outdoors, and the attempt 'subsequently proved impractical'. Be careful with the popular version in which he succeeds -- it did not happen. Be careful too with the famous image of the bridegroom striding about with a long thermometer while his bride waits in a carriage: Thomson told that story thirty-five years later, and his own letter home AT THE TIME says only that the two men had a few minutes together and that Joule had raised waterfall experiments BEFORE the marriage. The 1845 paper already contains the idea: 'the temperature of the river Niagra will be raised about one fifth of a degree by its fall of 160 feet.' Always ask whether a great story is contemporaneous or recollected. Source: Wikipedia 'James Prescott Joule'; David Lindley, 'Degrees Kelvin', excerpt at National Academies Press; Joule 1845 primary text.  (Legend.)

question: James Prescott Joule's contemporaries assumed his certainty that force - what we now call energy - can never be annihilated came out of his thermometer readings. Joule said in print that it did not. What did he say the conviction actually rested on?
answer: his belief that the power to destroy belongs to the Creator alone
choices: his belief that the power to destroy belongs to the Creator alone
his belief that nature abhors any kind of waste or loss
his belief that Dalton's atoms could never be broken apart
his belief that the total quantity of caloric must stay fixed
context: Verbatim: 'Believing that the power to destroy belongs to the Creator alone I affirm ... that any theory which, when carried out, demands the annihilation of force, is necessarily erroneous.' He did not reason from the arithmetic to the principle; he held that only God could destroy, so any theory requiring destruction had to be wrong -- and then he spent decades measuring until the world agreed. His headstone in Brooklands Cemetery, Sale, carries both halves of the man: the number 772.55, his 1878 value for the exchange rate after thirty-five years of sharpening it, and beneath it John 9:4 -- 'I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.' Source: Wikipedia 'James Prescott Joule'; Family History Society of Cheshire, Brooklands Cemetery plot B208-9.

question: Charles David Keeling's carbon dioxide graph from Mauna Loa in Hawaii is one of the most reproduced lines in science. It does not climb cleanly. What does the line actually do on its way up?
answer: It saws up and down about six parts per million every year
choices: It saws up and down about six parts per million every year
It jumps in sudden steps of ten parts per million, flat between
It wanders a few parts per million with no repeating pattern
It shot up thirty parts per million in the 1970s, then calmed
context: Keeling switched the Mauna Loa instrument on in March 1958, and the first reading, on 29 March, came out at 313 parts per million. NOAA calls it 'the longest record of direct measurements of CO2 in the atmosphere.' The saw is not a flaw in the instrument and not a rounding artefact -- it is the largest regular feature of the whole record, and it showed up in Keeling's very first year of data. (Grokipedia, 'Keeling Curve'; NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Trends in CO2, gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends.)

question: Charles David Keeling's first Mauna Loa reading, on 29 March 1958, came out at 313 parts per million. Scripps and NOAA still post the Mauna Loa figure free every month, so anyone can pull up what the same mountain reads now. What does it read?
answer: About 429 parts per million
choices: About 429 parts per million
About 316 parts per million
About 358 parts per million
About 690 parts per million
context: The two pages are keelingcurve.ucsd.edu and gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends, both free and both refreshed every month. NOAA's posted Mauna Loa monthly mean for July 2026 was 429.12 ppm, against 427.87 ppm for July 2025 -- and against Keeling's 313 ppm in March 1958. Go and read this month's figure for yourself. That is the whole invitation of the record: a number anyone can look up, taken the same way every month for nearly seventy years. (NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Trends in CO2, retrieved August 2026.)

question: The Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record is often called unbroken. It is not. In early 1964 Charles David Keeling's measurements stopped for about three months, and the gap sits in the graph to this day. What stopped them?
answer: The instrument broke and no money was left for a technician
choices: The instrument broke and no money was left for a technician
A lava flow buried the access road and cut the power line
A storm tore the sampling intake off the tower
The Weather Bureau ordered the observatory closed for a season
context: Congress pruned federal budgets in the mid-1960s and the Weather Bureau stopped paying for research unrelated to forecasting; with nothing left for a full-time technician, the broken analyser sat idle from roughly February to April 1964. Keeling then used the failure itself as the argument for hiring one. As the American Institute of Physics history puts it, 'The hiatus is visible for all time to come in Keeling's graph' -- a budget cut drawn permanently into a scientific record. The lava answer is real, but from a different year: the November 2022 Mauna Loa eruption did bury the access road and cut the power line, and Scripps bridged that gap with a near-identical analyser at the Maunakea Observatories 21 miles north from 14 December 2022, until Mauna Loa itself resumed on solar and battery power on 9 March 2023. (AIP, Spencer Weart, 'Money for Keeling: Monitoring CO2'; Scripps, 'Update on CO2 readings commencing at Maunakea'; NOAA GML.)

question: Charles David Keeling's Mauna Loa record saws up and down by about six parts per million every year. That rhythm is not instrument noise: something real puts carbon dioxide into the air and pulls it back out again on a yearly cycle. What is doing it?
answer: Northern Hemisphere land plants pulling carbon in as they grow, then releasing it as they decay
choices: Northern Hemisphere land plants pulling carbon in as they grow, then releasing it as they decay
The Pacific Ocean taking carbon in as it cools, then giving it back as it warms
Mauna Loa's summit vents pushing gas out hard in some months, weakly in others
Fossil-fuel burning climbing for heating in cold months, easing in warm ones
context: Keeling's own words on watching the sawtooth emerge in his first year of data: 'We were witnessing for the first time nature's withdrawing CO2 from the air for plant growth during summer and returning it each succeeding winter.' The peak comes in MAY and the low in late September or October -- not midwinter and midsummer -- because decay keeps outrunning new growth well into spring, and the drawdown runs on into early autumn. The swing's size tracks how much seasonally green land lies beneath a station: about 15 ppm a year at Utqiagvik (Barrow) in Alaska at 71 degrees north, about 6 ppm at Mauna Loa, and hardly any at all at the South Pole. Tropical rainforests have plants in abundance but almost no temperature seasons, so they barely contribute; the saw is cut mostly by the forests and fields between about 45 and 70 degrees north, and its amplitude there has grown by as much as 50 percent over the record. (Grokipedia, 'Keeling Curve'; Scripps, 'The History of the Keeling Curve' and 'Why are Seasonal CO2 Fluctuations Strongest in Northern Latitudes?')

question: Carbon dioxide made up about three parts in ten thousand of the air Charles David Keeling wanted to weigh, and he needed that share to better than one part per million. He collected air in five-litre flasks and froze the carbon dioxide out of it with liquid nitrogen. How did the instrument he built himself then measure what he had trapped?
answer: By the pressure it pushed against a column of mercury
choices: By the pressure it pushed against a column of mercury
By shining infrared light through it and reading what was absorbed
By weighing the frozen crystals on a fine chemical balance
By dissolving it in a solution and titrating the acid formed
context: The design was a constant-volume mercury manometer fed by a vacuum extraction line and a liquid-nitrogen cold trap; Keeling based it on a prototype described in a journal article from 1916, and got a precision of 0.1 percent -- about 0.3 ppm at the levels he was measuring. Infrared gas analysers are entirely real and became the workhorse of the continuous stations, including Mauna Loa; what Keeling's manometers became was the primary standard those analysers are calibrated against. (Grokipedia, 'Charles David Keeling'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Keeling, Charles David'; History.com, 'When Global Warming Was Revealed by the Keeling Curve'.)

question: Through the 1960s Charles David Keeling's Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record was rising by about 0.7 parts per million a year, a slope so gentle that a decade of it barely showed on a printed page. What has become of that rate of climb since?
answer: It has more than tripled, passing 2.5 parts per million a year
