She rubbed it between her fingers, and it did not fray
context: Her words: 'Unlike ordinary nylon, this fiber was very difficult to break by hand. At that moment I knew we had a most unusual fiber.' Her first instrument was her own two hands - the same test anyone can run on a thread, which is exactly why the moment is so easy to picture. The machines confirmed it afterward. Source: Invention & Technology Magazine, Jim Quinn, 'Stephanie Kwolek, Kevlar' (Winter 2020), inventionandtech.com/content/stephanie-kwolek-kevlar

question: A cloudy liquid almost always means something solid is drifting in it, undissolved. Stephanie Kwolek's batch was cloudy, and the obvious verdict was that she had contaminated it. She settled that at the bench with one simple test, and the result was flat: whatever was scattering the light, it was not floating solids. What was the test?
answer: She pushed the batch through a fine filter, and none was caught
choices: She pushed the batch through a fine filter, and none was caught
She spun the batch in a centrifuge, and nothing settled out
She left the batch standing overnight, and nothing sank down
She shone a lamp through the batch, and saw no glinting specks
context: Kwolek's words: 'The solution that I prepared looked like a dispersion but was totally filterable through a fine pore filter.' Every drop went through, so the cloudiness could not be suspended solids - she had ruled out the dirty-beaker explanation before she ever asked for the batch to be spun. She added that she did not yet understand what she was actually looking at. This one test is the cleanest answer to anyone who says she simply got lucky with a contaminated batch: she tested it. Source: Kwolek 1993 speech, quoted at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: The strength numbers coming off Stephanie Kwolek's new fiber were so far above anything DuPont had ever spun that a scientist hunting a reputation would have run down the hall with them. Kwolek did not. What did she do before she would let herself say she had discovered anything?
answer: Had the strength tests repeated over and over again
choices: Had the strength tests repeated over and over again
Sent a sample to an outside lab for a second opinion
Asked a second chemist to make the polymer again
Checked the machine against a fiber of known strength
context: Her account: 'I had the tests repeated a number of times before I became convinced that I had made a significant discovery.' Tensile strength, elongation and stiffness, run again and again, because the numbers were too good and she suspected herself first. Skepticism of your own result is the first scientific virtue and the hardest to practise - the extraordinary measurement you want to be true is exactly the one to re-run. Source: Invention & Technology Magazine, Jim Quinn, 'Stephanie Kwolek, Kevlar' (Winter 2020), inventionandtech.com/content/stephanie-kwolek-kevlar

question: Stephanie Kwolek and Paul Morgan published a beaker demonstration in 1959 that chemistry teachers still perform today - the Nylon Rope Trick. Two liquids go into a single beaker, no heat anywhere in the process, and a solid nylon strand can be lifted out and reeled off continuously, like thread from a spool. Where in the beaker is the nylon being made?
answer: At the line where the two liquids meet
choices: At the line where the two liquids meet
Throughout the beaker, wherever they have mixed
At the top, where the liquid meets the air
At the bottom, where the beaker is coolest
context: The strand forms at the boundary line where the two liquids meet, and it can be drawn out of the beaker continuously - a rope of nylon at room temperature, with no heat needed. Morgan and Kwolek's 1959 paper 'The Nylon Rope Trick' (Journal of Polymer Science 40(137):299-327) won an American Chemical Society publication award and is still standard in classrooms; Kwolek performed it for schoolchildren herself after retiring in 1986. Worth asking a chemistry teacher to run it: the woman who discovered Kevlar also wrote the demonstration. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek; grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: Nothing solid floated in Stephanie Kwolek's cloudy batch - all of it went through a fine filter - and yet it scattered light like milk. Ordinary polymer solutions stay clear because their molecules are floppy tangles, tumbling every which way past one another. Kwolek's molecules were doing something else in that flask, and that is what was throwing the light back. What were her molecules doing?
answer: Lining up side by side into liquid-crystal patches
choices: Lining up side by side into liquid-crystal patches
Cross-linking into one loose three-dimensional net
Curling into tight coils packed like small springs
Splitting into microscopic droplets of a second liquid
context: This is the whole discovery. Kwolek's para-aramid molecules are stiff rods, not floppy coils, and above a critical concentration rods can no longer tumble freely past one another - they snap into parallel domains, a lyotropic liquid crystal. Those aligned domains scatter light, which is why the batch looked cloudy: the reason it looked wrong is the reason it was strong. Rods already lined up in the beaker come out of the spinneret still lined up, and alignment is strength. The Science History Institute records the team's surprise - 'Though their liquidity was initially a cause of technical concern, to everyone's surprise, these liquid crystalline solutions spun beautifully.' Kwolek's poly-p-benzamide and PPTA solutions were the first liquid crystal polymers ever prepared. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/stephanie-l-kwolek; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: A police vest is twenty to thirty layers of woven Kevlar, and the standard models are rated for handgun rounds - a 9mm, even a .44 Magnum. The word for them is bullet-resistant, not bulletproof, and the gap between those two words is real: a rifle round punches straight through. What has to be added to stop one?
answer: A hard ceramic plate slid into the vest
choices: A hard ceramic plate slid into the vest
A steel mesh sewn between the layers
A thicker stack of the same woven layers
A rubber backing to spread the impact
context: Soft Kevlar vests are rated NIJ Level II or IIIA - handgun rounds, including 9mm full metal jacket and .44 Magnum. Rifle rounds need hard ceramic or UHMWPE plates. A second honest limit: a vest that stops bullets does not reliably stop a knife or a spike, because edged and pointed threats defeat soft armor and need different construction entirely. What the fabric does do is real - the National Institute of Justice credits Kevlar armor with saving more than 3,000 officers' lives, and an officer wearing a vest is about 76% less likely to die of a torso gunshot wound. The first documented life saved by a Kevlar vest was in Seattle in 1975. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Kevlar, citing NIJ Standard-0101.06; grokipedia.com/page/Stephanie_Kwolek

question: Kevlar's molecules lie stretched out and parallel along the fiber, which is why pulling on it is so hard - weight for weight it beats steel about five to one. But a single chain on its own would simply slide past its neighbors, and the fiber would come apart like a handful of loose threads. Something grips neighboring chains together sideways. What holds them?
answer: Hydrogen bonds, each N-H reaching the next C=O
choices: Hydrogen bonds, each N-H reaching the next C=O
Covalent bridges, one carbon welded to the next
Ionic bonds, metal ions bridging chain to chain
Sulfur cross-links, the trick that hardens rubber
context: Each amide's N-H reaches across to the neighboring chain's C=O, building the parallel chains into hydrogen-bonded sheets; pull along the fiber and a colossal number of those bonds have to resist at once (Kevlar 29 modulus about 70.5 GPa, Kevlar 49 about 112 GPa; tensile strength about 2,900-3,000 MPa at a density of 1.44 g/cm3 against steel's 7.8). The honest other side is that this strength runs one way only. Push or bend Kevlar instead of pulling it and it fails by kink bands - the fiber buckles and folds. It is a rope, not a pillar. It does not stretch to save itself either: elongation at break is only 2.4% (Kevlar 49) to 3.6% (Kevlar 29), a nearly straight line to fracture with no warning. And unprotected Kevlar keeps only about 60% of its strength after 1,000 hours of sunlight, because ultraviolet snaps the chains - which is why it is rarely used outdoors uncovered. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Kevlar; 'Compressional behaviour of Kevlar fibres' (1981) and 'Compressive properties of aramid fibres' (1997), ScienceDirect

question: Kevlar reached the market in 1971, six years from beaker to product, and the fiber has since earned several billion dollars. US Patent 3,819,587, 'Wholly Aromatic Carbocyclic Polycarbonamide Fiber,' granted in 1974, names Stephanie Kwolek as its inventor. What became of that patent?
answer: She signed it over to DuPont and earned nothing from it
choices: She signed it over to DuPont and earned nothing from it
She licensed it to DuPont and drew a royalty per pound
She held it jointly with DuPont and shared the profits
She sold it to DuPont and took a single lump payment
context: Kwolek was a DuPont employee, so the patent went to the company: she signed over US Patent 3,819,587, 'Wholly Aromatic Carbocyclic Polycarbonamide Fiber,' granted 1974. The discovery earned DuPont several billion dollars; she never benefited from it financially, and her comment on the six years from beaker to market was 'It turned out to be a great team effort in the end.' She held 17 US patents in all, and had already handed DuPont a second fiber: she worked out the conditions for the meta-aramid released in 1961 as Nomex, the flame-resistant one. Nomex and Kevlar are the same chemistry with one difference - meta linkages put a permanent bend in the chain, so Nomex stays flexible and heat-resistant but never reaches Kevlar's strength. During the week Kwolek died, in June 2014, the one-millionth bullet-resistant vest made with Kevlar was sold. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Kwolek (citing Jeremy Pearce, New York Times obituary, June 21, 2014, and Alyssa Newcomb, Good Morning America, June 20, 2014); invent.org/inductees/stephanie-louise-kwolek; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/stephanie-kwolek

question: In 1809 the French biologist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published 'Philosophie Zoologique' with a famous illustration of giraffes reaching for high leaves. What did he say the picture proved?
answer: each giraffe stretched for high leaves, and its calves inherited the longer neck
choices: each giraffe stretched for high leaves, and its calves inherited the longer neck
each parent shed tiny gemmules from every organ that gathered in the seed to shape the calf
calves were an average blend of the two parents' necks, with the blend fixed at birth
giraffes descend from a much taller ancestor, and their necks have been shrinking
context: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published this in his 'Philosophie Zoologique' (1809). The idea is called the inheritance of acquired characteristics: a trait a parent worked into its own body during life is handed down to its offspring. Distractor B is Charles Darwin's own later heredity guess, pangenesis (1868); distractor C is blending inheritance -- both were seriously held by working scientists of the era and both turned out wrong. Sources: Britannica 'August Weismann'; sciencereader.com on Lamarckian evolution.

question: August Weismann cut the tails off 68 white mice and did the same to their pups, and then their pups, for five generations of 901 offspring. He was checking whether an acquired mutilation could be handed down. What did he find?
answer: zero shortened tails, not one single mouse across all 901 offspring
choices: zero shortened tails, not one single mouse across all 901 offspring
a handful of pups with shortened tails, all clustered in the fifth generation
one litter with kinked tails in the third generation, then none after
no shortened tails, but a steady rise in coat-color anomalies by the fifth generation
context: Weismann's own words: '901 young were produced by five generations of artificially mutilated parents, and yet there was not a single example of a rudimentary tail or of any other abnormality in this organ.' Weismann himself was careful about the scope; he said the result settled the specific claim about inherited MUTILATIONS, and used the outcome to argue his broader germ-plasm theory (published as 'Das Keimplasma' in 1892), which held that body cells cannot write back to the cells that make the next generation. Source: Wikipedia, 'August Weismann'.

question: Before 1900 a blood transfusion was effectively a coin flip. Some patients rallied within the hour, others burned with fever, passed dark urine and died, and no one could say why the same operation did both. In 1900 a young pathologist in his own laboratory set out to solve it. Who was he?
answer: Karl Landsteiner
choices: Karl Landsteiner
Paul Ehrlich
Emil von Behring
Elie Metchnikoff
context: Landsteiner (1868-1943) trained as a physician in Vienna and turned to serology when the clinical mystery of transfusion killings caught his interest. His 1900 note and 1901 paper opened the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Landsteiner

question: When Landsteiner sorted the pattern of clumped and smooth squares from his six-donor grid, the donors did not fall into a random tangle. Their blood sorted cleanly into three categories, and he gave each category a short letter label. Which labels did he choose?
answer: A, B and C
choices: A, B and C
I, II and III
alpha, beta and gamma
plus, minus and neutral
context: Landsteiner's original three-group scheme was A, B and C. The C group was renamed O in 1910 by Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil von Dungern, and that is the name it still carries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: Six donors were enough to reveal three blood groups. They were not enough to reveal a fourth, rarer one. In 1902 two of Landsteiner's students went back to the problem with a far larger set of samples and pulled out the missing group, later named AB. Who were they?
answer: Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli
choices: Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli
Emil Behring and Paul Ehrlich
Robert Koch and Friedrich Loeffler
Jules Bordet and Octave Gengou
context: The lesson buried in the discovery story is a lesson about sample size: rare types show up only when you test enough people. Decastello and Sturli found AB in 1902; Hirszfeld and von Dungern gave it its modern name in 1910. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: The clumping on Landsteiner's plate was not the red cells themselves misbehaving. It was a real, chemical fight between two invisible partners, and Landsteiner realised what the two combatants were. What were they?
answer: sugar antigens attacked by matching antibodies
choices: sugar antigens attacked by matching antibodies
iron atoms attacked by digestive enzymes
cholesterol patches attacked by cell walls
clotting factors attacked by platelets
context: A-type plasma carries anti-B antibodies, B-type carries anti-A, O carries both, AB carries neither. The antibodies grip the mismatched sugar markers on the donor red cells and pull them into visible clumps, which is why an incompatible transfusion can kill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: Emergency rooms keep a small stock of one particular donor blood on hand because, in a crisis with no time to type the patient, it can be given to almost anyone. Which donor blood is that emergency stock?
answer: O-negative red cells
choices: O-negative red cells
AB-positive red cells
A-negative red cells
B-positive red cells
context: O-negative red cells lack A, B and Rh(D) surface markers, so almost no recipient's antibodies bind them. For PLASMA the picture is opposite: AB plasma carries no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so AB is the universal plasma donor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABO_blood_group_system

question: The very first attempt to put one creature's blood into another began in Paris on 15 June 1667. A young physician named Jean-Baptiste Denys transfused a 15-year-old boy with the blood of another creature, and the boy survived. Later Denys tried the same trick on a man named Antoine Mauroy; Mauroy died. Whose blood had Denys been using?
answer: a lamb's
choices: a lamb's
a horse's
a dog's
another man's
context: Denys used lamb's blood on the boy and calf's blood on Mauroy. After the deaths, the Royal Society and French government banned the practice in 1668 and the Vatican condemned it in 1670; human transfusion stayed nearly untouchable for a century and a half. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_transfusion

question: Set a wad of steel wool on one pan of a kitchen balance and level the beam. Then touch a lit match to the wool: it glows orange, spreads, and crumbles into a dark brittle crust. What does the beam do?
answer: It tips down on the burnt side; the crust outweighs the wool.
choices: It tips down on the burnt side; the crust outweighs the wool.
It tips up on the burnt side; the crust weighs less than the wool.
It stays level; burning rearranges matter but never adds any.
It tips down, then rises back level once the crust cools.
context: The burnt side sinks: burnt steel wool weighs MORE than the wool did, which is exactly the result that broke chemistry open in the 1770s. Burn a candle in an open jar instead and mass seems to vanish. Neither one breaks the law of conservation of mass; both show that you cannot keep the books unless you count the gases too -- which is why Antoine Lavoisier did his burning inside sealed vessels. Closed-system version you can run at home: put baking soda and vinegar in a bottle with a balloon stretched over the neck. The balloon inflates, and the whole apparatus weighs exactly what it did before. Sources: RSC Education, 'The combustion of iron wool' (edu.rsc.org/experiments/the-combustion-of-iron-wool/717.article); Grokipedia, Conservation_of_mass.

question: On 1 August 1774 Joseph Priestley focused sunlight through a big burning lens onto red powder scraped from heated mercury, and caught the gas that came off in a jar. He lowered a lit candle into it. What did the candle do?
answer: It blazed up, five or six times brighter than in ordinary air.
choices: It blazed up, five or six times brighter than in ordinary air.
It shrank to a small blue bead and burned on without smoke.
It went out at once, as though it had been smothered.
It burned exactly as it would have in ordinary air.
context: It blazed. A mouse sealed in the same gas lived roughly four times as long as in an equal volume of ordinary air, and Joseph Priestley breathed it himself, reporting a feeling of lightness and ease in his lungs. He called it 'dephlogisticated air' -- air emptied of fire-stuff and therefore hungry for more -- and he never gave the theory up: in 1800, exiled in Northumberland, Pennsylvania, he published 'The doctrine of phlogiston established, and that of the composition of water refuted,' and died a phlogistonist on 6 February 1804. Priestley was not first, either. Carl Wilhelm Scheele, a self-taught Swedish apothecary, had made the same gas around 1771-72 and called it 'fire air,' but published only in 1777. Lavoisier came last of the three: he did not discover this gas -- he weighed it, showed it was a distinct element, and named it. Sources: Grokipedia, Oxygen and Carl_Wilhelm_Scheele; archive.org scan of Priestley (1800).

question: Antoine Lavoisier kept four ounces of mercury simmering in a sealed glass vessel of air for twelve days, until red particles crusted the silver surface and the air inside had shrunk by about a sixth. He lowered a lit taper into what was left of that air. What did the flame do?
answer: It went out instantly, as though plunged into water.
choices: It went out instantly, as though plunged into water.
It flared white, then guttered down and smoked.
It burned steadily, a little dimmer than in open air.
It burned brighter and faster than in open air.
context: In Lavoisier's own words, the leftover air killed the taper 'as if it had been immersed into water,' and animals put into it 'were suffocated in a few seconds.' The sixth that had gone missing was the part of the air that does the burning; what stayed behind is what we now call nitrogen. His numbers for the run: four ounces of mercury and about 50 cubical inches of air, twelve days of simmering, 45 grains of red crust collected, and the air down to 'between 42 and 43 cubical inches; consequently it had lost about 1/6 of its bulk.' (His better-known 'about a fifth' figure for the respirable part of air comes from a different memoir; this twelve-day run never went to completion.) Source: Lavoisier, Elements of Chemistry, trans. Robert Kerr (1790), Part I ch. III -- gutenberg.org/files/30775/30775-h/30775-h.htm.

question: Before Lavoisier, every chemistry student in Europe learned Georg Stahl's phlogiston: a fire-stuff bound up inside anything that will burn. It earned its keep because it explained a trick smelters had used for centuries -- heat a dull grey calx, the powder a roasted metal leaves behind, with charcoal, and bright metal comes back out. What did the theory say the charcoal was doing?
answer: Handing over its own phlogiston to the starved calx.
choices: Handing over its own phlogiston to the starved calx.
Drawing the last phlogiston out of the calx.
Shielding the calx from the phlogiston in the air.
Splitting the calx into two simpler earths.
context: Charcoal was reckoned almost pure phlogiston, so it could restock a calx that had lost its own -- and the theory got the direction right every time, which is why competent men held it for eighty years. It also explained the small pile of ash left when wood burns: the fire-stuff had gone, and only the earthy residue stayed. Georg Ernst Stahl renamed Johann Joachim Becher's 'terra pinguis' (fatty earth) to phlogiston in 1703, from the Greek phlogistos, 'burnable'; he taught at the University of Halle from 1694 to 1716, and his 1723 Fundamenta Chymiae carried the theory across Europe. Source: Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory.

question: In 1630 the French doctor Jean Rey was handed a puzzle: an apothecary named Brun had melted two pounds six ounces of tin in a furnace for six hours, and the powder he poured out weighed seven ounces MORE than the tin had. What did Rey say had added the weight?
answer: Air, thickened by the long heat, had attached itself to it.
choices: Air, thickened by the long heat, had attached itself to it.
Fire-matter from the furnace had soaked into it.
A heavy earth had risen out of the crucible into it.
Water in the metal had been baked to a denser stuff.
context: Rey published it as 'Essays ... on an Enquiry into the Cause Wherefore Tin and Lead Increase in Weight on Calcination' (1630). Brun had repeated the trial with six pounds of lead and gained six ounces. Rey's idea was that air, thickened and made adhesive by the long furnace heat, attached itself to the metal -- substantially the right answer, a hundred and forty-four years before Lavoisier's sealed vessels, and it sank without trace. It was dug up again only during the eighteenth-century arguments over calcination weight. Being right is not enough; you also have to be heard. Sources: Wellcome Collection scan of Rey's 1630 Essays (wellcomecollection.org/works/grnfnfwy); 'The Essays of Jean Rey,' Popular Science Monthly vol. 44 (Dec 1893); revival noted at Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory.

question: Antoine Lavoisier sealed eight ounces of tin inside a glass vessel with about fifteen grains of air, weighed the whole thing, and heated the tin until it crusted over. Weighed again with the seal unbroken, the vessel came out at exactly its old weight -- not a tenth of a grain different. He then broke the seal and weighed the crusted metal by itself. What had happened to the tin, and to the air shut in with it?
answer: The tin gained 3.12 grains; the air lost the same 3.12.
choices: The tin gained 3.12 grains; the air lost the same 3.12.
The tin lost 3.12 grains; the air gained the same 3.12.
Tin and air both lost grains; the glass had taken them up.
Neither had changed; the tin had only changed its colour.
context: The tin came out 3.12 grains heavier, and the air sealed in with it had lost 3.12 grains -- the same figure to the last decimal. The extra weight had come from inside the jar, not from the fire outside it, and the sealed vessel as a whole never changed at all. This is the experiment the memoir is named for: 'Memoir on the calcination of tin in closed vessels and on the cause of the gain in weight which this metal acquires in the operation,' in the Memoires de l'Academie Royale des Sciences for 1774, published 1777. Lavoisier's whole method is in that one run -- weigh everything, before and after, and let nothing escape, on balances sensitive to about a tenth of a grain, what Grokipedia calls his 'scrupulous exactitude.' Robert Boyle had run nearly the same trial in 1673 and drew the opposite conclusion for one procedural reason: he broke the seal BEFORE weighing again, found the calx heavier, and decided that corpuscles of fire had passed through the glass into the metal. Lavoisier's advance was not a new idea but a new order of operations. Sources: Le Moyne 'Classic Chemistry' on Lavoisier's 1774 tin memoir (web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/classicalcs/lavoisier.html); Grokipedia, Antoine_Lavoisier; sethi.org/phlogiston timeline (Boyle).

question: Phlogiston said that a burning body is LOSING something -- fire-stuff streaming out of it -- so a roasted metal ought to come out lighter. Chemists put it on the balance, and the ashy calx came out heavier than the metal every single time. In 1764 the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Chardenon offered a rescue that kept the theory alive another twenty years. What was it?
answer: Phlogiston has negative weight, so losing it adds weight.
choices: Phlogiston has negative weight, so losing it adds weight.
Phlogiston drags off a lighter earth than the one it leaves.
Furnace soot is driven into the metal while it roasts.
The metal's pores shut, trapping water the fire cannot expel.
context: Chardenon proposed in 1764 that phlogiston has levity -- negative weight -- so that a body which loses it must end up heavier. Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau argued the same repulsive-levity idea in his 1772 'Digressions academiques,' where he also confirmed that the weight gain happens across metals generally. Critics answered that negative weight flatly contradicts Newton's gravitation. This is what a theory looks like in its last years: it stops predicting and starts being patched. Source: Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory.

question: In 1777 Antoine Lavoisier proposed a name for the new gas, built out of two Greek words, and it is the name we still use today. He picked it to record something he was convinced the gas did -- a conviction most chemists of the 1780s shared with him. What did he think the gas was?
answer: The substance that makes every acid an acid.
choices: The substance that makes every acid an acid.
The substance that gives every flame its colour.
The substance that makes every metal a metal.
The substance that gives a living body its warmth.
context: He built the name from the Greek oxys, 'sharp' or 'acid,' and genes, 'producer': the acid-maker. Lavoisier proposed 'oxygine' in 1777, and it was formally fixed as 'oxygene' in the 1787 'Methode de nomenclature chimique,' written with Guyton de Morveau, Berthollet and Fourcroy; it entered English as 'oxygen' in 1790. He did not discover the gas -- Carl Wilhelm Scheele made it first, around 1771-72, and Joseph Priestley published first, in 1774-75. What Lavoisier supplied, between 1775 and 1777, was the quantitative evidence that it was a distinct element. Sources: Grokipedia, Oxygen and Antoine_Lavoisier.

question: Richard Kirwan's 'Essay on Phlogiston' (1787) was the strongest defence of the theory anyone had written. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier -- who sat in the laboratory writing down measurements called out during trials, and had already translated Priestley, Black and Cavendish for it -- put the whole of Kirwan's book into French the following year. What did the Paris edition of 1788 carry that Kirwan's original did not?
answer: The French chemists' refutation, running in notes underneath.
choices: The French chemists' refutation, running in notes underneath.
The experiments Kirwan had described but never actually run.
The names of the French chemists Kirwan had quoted uncredited.
Lavoisier's own memoirs on the gases, bound in behind it.
context: The Paris 1788 title page says it outright: 'Essai sur le phlogistique, et sur la constitution des acides ... avec des notes de MM. de Morveau, Lavoisier, de La Place, Monge, Berthollet, & de Fourcroy.' The best case anyone had made for phlogiston was printed in French with the refutation running underneath it, note by note -- the opposition steel-manned and answered on the same page. Marie-Anne added a preface and notes of her own, and Nicholson translated the whole thing back into English. She also engraved the thirteen folding copperplates of apparatus in the 1789 Traite -- the drawings that let chemists across Europe rebuild the sealed vessels and check the results for themselves -- having learned to draw for the purpose under the painter Jacques-Louis David. Sources: Smithsonian Libraries record si.edu/object/siris_sil_335133; Grokipedia, Marie-Anne_Paulze_Lavoisier.

question: Antoine Lavoisier's laboratory was paid for by his other job: he had bought into the Ferme generale, the consortium that collected France's taxes on salt, tobacco and goods entering the cities. On 24 November 1793 the Revolution ordered every surviving tax farmer arrested; Lavoisier was tried with twenty-seven others in a single day on 8 May 1794 and guillotined that afternoon, at fifty. One charge accused him of a fraud he had spent years detecting himself. What was it?
answer: Watering the tax farm's tobacco to inflate its weight.
choices: Watering the tax farm's tobacco to inflate its weight.
Debasing the coin struck for the tax farm's accounts.
Short-weighting the salt sold under the royal monopoly.
Forging the seals on goods entering the city gates.
context: He was condemned as a tax farmer, not as a chemist: the verdict was 'conspiracy against the people of France,' and among the charges was watering tobacco to inflate its weight -- a fraud Lavoisier had personally spent years devising tests to catch. Twenty-eight men were tried that day, including his own father-in-law Jacques Paulze. His widow Marie-Anne was imprisoned for over two months, and the family's instruments and notebooks were inventoried and seized the very next day. In 1796 the French government formally exonerated him and returned the property, declaring the charges false. Lagrange's remark on hearing of the execution -- reported through the astronomer Delambre, and not traceable to a primary source -- was that it took the mob only a moment to remove his head, and a century would not suffice to reproduce it. Sources: Grokipedia, Antoine_Lavoisier and Marie-Anne_Paulze_Lavoisier; MacTutor, Lagrange quotations.

question: Twelve days of simmering mercury in a sealed jar of air had left Antoine Lavoisier with two things: a red crust that had formed on the metal, and a jar of air that had lost several cubic inches of its bulk. He put the crust alone into a fresh vessel and heated it hard. What came off it?
answer: Running mercury, and the very air the jar had lost.
choices: Running mercury, and the very air the jar had lost.
Running mercury, and no trace of any gas at all.
A white ash, and far more air than the jar had lost.
Nothing at all, until charcoal was added to restock it.
context: From 45 grains of red crust Lavoisier recovered '41 1/2 grains of running mercury' and '7 or 8 cubical inches of elastic fluid' -- and 7 to 8 cubical inches is exactly what the air in the jar had lost (50 down to 42 or 43). The mercury came back, the air came back, and the books balanced in both directions. That is the step phlogiston could not match: a fire-substance that escapes when something burns can never be poured back in. Source: Lavoisier, Elements of Chemistry, trans. Robert Kerr (1790), Part I ch. III -- gutenberg.org/files/30775/30775-h/30775-h.htm.

question: Antoine Lavoisier had named the gas oxygen, from the Greek for acid-producer. In 1810 Humphry Davy took apart muriatic acid -- the fuming acid that ate through metals in every laboratory in Europe -- and weighed everything that came out of it. What is muriatic acid made of?
answer: Hydrogen and chlorine.
choices: Hydrogen and chlorine.
Oxygen and chlorine.
Hydrogen and sulphur.
Chlorine and sulphur.
context: Davy found no oxygen in it whatever: hydrogen, and a green gas he named chlorine, a new element. Oxygen is not the acid-maker; hydrogen is. Davy recognised that around 1815, but the argument dragged on -- a dozen oxygen-free acids were known by 1830, and the hydrogen theory of acids was not generally accepted until about 1840. Muriatic acid is what we now call hydrochloric acid. The word 'oxygen' has meant 'acid-former' and been wrong about it for over two hundred years: the man who destroyed one wrong theory carved his own mistake into a word we still say every day. Sources: Grokipedia, Oxygen; chemteam.info/AcidBase/Early-Acid-Base.html.

question: 'Nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed' -- conservation of mass in a single sentence -- is printed under Antoine Lavoisier's name in chemistry textbooks. Where does that sentence come from?
answer: A later French summing-up, found in nothing he wrote.
choices: A later French summing-up, found in nothing he wrote.
The closing sentence of his Traite elementaire de chimie.
The eulogies read over him after the Revolution killed him.
A maxim of the Greek atomists that he liked to repeat.
context: It is a later French paraphrase. 'Rien ne se perd, rien ne se cree, tout se transforme' has not been found in the Traite or in the sourced collections of his quotations -- the most famous sentence Lavoisier ever gets credited with, he never wrote. What he did write, in the 1789 Traite elementaire de chimie (Robert Kerr's 1790 translation), he called an incontestible axiom: 'We may lay it down as an incontestible axiom, that, in all the operations of art and nature, nothing is created; an equal quantity of matter exists both before and after the experiment; the quality and quantity of the elements remain precisely the same; and nothing takes place beyond changes and modifications in the combination of these elements. Upon this principle the whole art of performing chemical experiments depends.' That closing line turns a piece of bookkeeping into the foundation of a craft. If you are going to quote him, quote the axiom. Sources: gutenberg.org/files/30775/30775-h/30775-h.htm; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Antoine_Lavoisier.  (Legend.)

question: In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier printed the first modern table of elements in his Traite elementaire de chimie: thirty-three substances he judged could not be broken down into anything simpler. Two entries stand at the very top of that list, printed ahead of oxygen itself. What are they?
answer: Light, and caloric -- the fluid he believed heat was.
choices: Light, and caloric -- the fluid he believed heat was.
Air, and water -- the survivors of the four elements.
Gold, and mercury -- the metals the alchemists ranked first.
Fixed air, and inflammable air -- the two newly caught gases.
context: Light and caloric -- caloric being the weightless fluid Lavoisier believed heat was made of. Both are classed in his table as imponderable: unweighable. The man whose entire case against phlogiston was that nobody could ever put it on a balance printed two unweighable substances at the head of his own list of elements, and caloric turned out to be just as wrong as phlogiston was. Reformers carry their own ghosts. Sources: Grokipedia, Phlogiston_theory; Lavoisier's table of simple substances, Traite (1789) p.192, transcribed at chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Antoine Lavoisier's law is taught as exact: equal matter before and after, and the books always balance. A student who pushes on it deserves the honest answer, which is that it is very slightly false. Burn one gram of carbon inside a sealed vessel and weigh the whole apparatus again, and the total really has dropped -- by about three ten-billionths of a gram, roughly a hundred-millionth of the mass of one electron for every carbon atom burned. No balance ever built could catch it. Where did that missing mass go?
answer: It left with the heat and light; energy has mass.
choices: It left with the heat and light; energy has mass.
It leaked out; no glass vessel is perfectly tight.
It was destroyed; a few carbon atoms ceased to be.
It left as light alone; heat carries no mass at all.
context: It left with the heat and light. Energy has mass, so a reaction that pours energy out really does end up lighter: burning graphite loses about 3.6 x 10^-10 grams per gram of carbon -- roughly a third of a part per billion, about a hundred-millionth of the mass of one electron per carbon atom. No balance ever built could see it, which is why Lavoisier's law is exactly right for every purpose a chemist has. In nuclear reactions the same effect runs about a thousand times bigger for the same amount of material -- the decay of one mole of carbon-14 loses 0.000168 g -- and in uranium fission it reaches about 0.1 per cent, which is where it finally becomes something you could weigh. Conservation of mass is a superb approximation, not a law of the universe. The equation behind the correction, E = mc^2, has itself been checked to within 0.0004 per cent by measuring the gamma rays given off by silicon-28 and sulphur-32 nuclei (ILL/NIST, 2005). Sources: Chemistry LibreTexts, 'Converting Mass to Energy: Mass Defect and Nuclear Binding Energy'; Grokipedia, Conservation_of_mass.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek never went to university and never worked in a laboratory. The magnifying glasses he first used -- three to five times, no more -- were tools of the shop trade he apprenticed into in Amsterdam in 1648. Which trade was it?
answer: Selling cloth, where a glass counted threads per inch
choices: Grinding spectacles, where a glass checked the curve
Testing coin, where a glass read the mint's stamp
Selling cloth, where a glass counted threads per inch
Engraving seals, where a glass guided the cutting tip
context: Leeuwenhoek apprenticed from 1648 to 1653 under William Davidson, a Scottish cloth merchant in Amsterdam, then opened his own draper's shop in Delft in 1654. The shop glass was called a thread counter -- three to five times magnification, just enough to count threads per inch and check a weave. The man who would open the microbial world met his first lens over a bolt of fabric. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' (Early Life / Transition to Scientific Pursuits); The American Scholar, 'A Kingdom of Little Animals'.

question: In September 1674 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek looked at a drop from Berkelse Mere, the lake outside Delft that turned whitish every midsummer with 'little green clouds.' Under his lens the clouds were green streaks wound like serpents. But it was the other thing in that drop that made his letter famous. What else was in it?
answer: Very many little animals, swimming
choices: Very many little animals, swimming
A fine white mould, spreading fast
Small green seeds, sprouting open
Thin red worms, coiled up tight
context: The green spirals were Spirogyra, a freshwater alga. The letter describes the lake as clear in winter but turning 'whitish, and there are then little green clouds floating in it,' and the streaks inside as 'spirally wound serpent-wise, and orderly arranged.' Then the line that changed biology: 'among these streaks there were besides very many little animalcules.' The first sighting of the microbial world happened at a lake, not in a laboratory. Source: Nick Lane, 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124).

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's readers in London owned no lens like his, so a bare number would have told them nothing. In his 1674 letter he judged his little animals 'above a thousand times smaller' than a creature every one of them had already seen with their own eyes at home. Which creature did he name?
answer: A mite on the rind of a cheese
choices: A gnat on a summer windowpane
A flea on a dog's winter coat
A nit in a child's braided hair
A mite on the rind of a cheese
context: 'I judge that some of these little creatures were above a thousand times smaller than the smallest ones I have ever yet seen, upon the rind of cheese.' Cheese mites were the smallest creature most people in 1674 had ever laid eyes on. He kept doing this all his life -- sizing microbes against a grain of coarse sand, a millet seed, a hair from his own beard -- so a reader who owned no lens could still picture the scale. Source: Nick Lane, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124); Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Counting the Little Animals'.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek never learned Latin, the working language of European science. For fifty years he wrote to the Royal Society in Dutch instead, leaving other men to turn his letters into Latin, English and French. For the things he had found swimming in a drop of lake water he invented no grand term -- he used a homely Dutch word, the kind a Delft draper used for anything small. Which word was it?
answer: Diertjes
choices: Stofjes
Diertjes
Kiempjes
Wormpjes
context: In Dutch he wrote diertjes, dierkens or diertgens -- diminutives of dier, 'animal,' meaning roughly 'little beasties.' 'Animalcule' is the word every textbook puts in his mouth, and he never wrote it: 'animalcule' and 'little animals' are what his English and Latin translators made of him. He was embarrassed enough by his lack of Latin that he hesitated to approach the Royal Society at all; his physician friend Reinier de Graaf forwarded his first letter for him on 28 April 1673. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' and 'Animalcule'; Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'How many letters did Leeuwenhoek write?'

question: By 1683 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek had found his little animals in lake water, rainwater and pepper-water. Then, on 17 September, he wrote to Francis Aston at the Royal Society about a sample from a place nobody had thought to look -- one he carried about with him all day. The drawings sent with that letter are the first pictures of bacteria ever made. Where did the sample come from?
answer: The soft white matter between his own teeth
choices: The wax taken from inside his own ear
The sweat scraped from the crook of his arm
The soft white matter between his own teeth
The grit washed from between his own toes
context: Letter L-135, 17 September 1683, to Francis Aston: he scraped the soft white matter from between his own teeth, mixed it with clean rainwater, and found it swarming with living animalcules. Published in Philosophical Transactions Vol. 14 (1684), pp. 568-574, it is the first documented observation of bacteria, and the drawings that went with it are the first pictures of bacteria ever made. Getting a sample took planning -- 'I am in the habit of rubbing my teeth with salt in the morning, and then rinsing my mouth with water,' he wrote, so he deliberately stopped cleaning for three days to collect enough. For contrast he also sampled an old man who 'had never washed his mouth all his life.' Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston.

question: Robert Hooke's microscope was a tall tube on a stand with several lenses inside. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's was nothing like it: two thin metal plates riveted around a single tiny lens, about 5 cm by 2.5 cm, the specimen skewered on a brass pin and shifted by two fine screws. How did he use it?
answer: He held the plate to his eye and aimed it at a candle flame
choices: He held the plate to his eye and aimed it at a candle flame
He held the plate at arm's length and squinted past the pin
He held the plate to his eye and turned his back to the window
He laid the plate on his knee and bent his eye down to the lens
context: You held the whole instrument in your fist, pressed the plate flat against your eye, and aimed it at a candle flame or a window; a sharp brass pin carried the specimen and two fine screws moved it. ACCURACY RAIL: he did not invent the microscope. Compound instruments had existed in the Netherlands since about 1590 (credited to Zacharias and Hans Janssen, with Hans Lippershey a rival claimant), and Hooke's illustrated Micrographia appeared in 1665, before Leeuwenhoek ground his first lens around 1670. His innovation was a far better SIMPLE (single-lens) microscope plus the screw rig that held and focused the specimen. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' (Lens Grinding and Microscope Design / Operational Techniques); Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Leeuwenhoek's Microscopes'.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's letter of 17 September 1683 told the Royal Society what was living in the film he had scraped from his own teeth, in numbers he could hardly convey. So he reached for a comparison, and it is the line of his still quoted three centuries later -- with the dry addition, 'especially in those who don't ever clean their teeth.' What was the comparison?
answer: More animals in one man's mouth than men in a whole kingdom
choices: More animals in one man's mouth than stars in a clear sky
More animals in one man's mouth than grains in a sack of wheat
More animals in one man's mouth than drops in the Delft canal
More animals in one man's mouth than men in a whole kingdom
context: 'There are more animals living in the scum on the teeth in a man's mouth, than there are men in a whole kingdom' -- and then the dry addition, 'especially in those who don't ever clean their teeth.' A common alternate translation runs: 'there are more living animals in the unclean matter in the teeth in one's mouth than there are men in a whole Kingdom.' Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston; The American Scholar, 'A Kingdom of Little Animals'.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek did not only look at the creatures he found between his teeth -- he went after them. He tried hot coffee on them, and he tried vinegar, to see what would still them: one of the first kill-tests anyone had run on a microbe. When the vinegar result was printed in London it had an effect on readers he can hardly have intended. What did it do to them?
answer: Some were so disgusted they swore off vinegar for good
choices: Some wrote in demanding he test the wine trade next
Some were so disgusted they swore off vinegar for good
Some accused him of killing creatures he had invented
Some began selling vinegar as a guard against plague
context: He attacked his mouth animalcules with vinegar and with hot coffee to see what would still them -- an early kill-test on microbes, and one of the first times anyone tried to do something TO a microbe rather than merely watch it. The published account of the vinegar work had a side effect on readers: some 'were so disgusted at the spectacle, that they vowed they would never use vinegar again.' Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was ninety and dying of pneumonia in Delft in August 1723, fifty years after his first letter to the Royal Society. His friend Johan Hoogvliet was turning the last letters into Latin for him -- Leeuwenhoek 'being already in the throes of death,' Hoogvliet wrote, 'though none the less mindful of his art.' Thirty-six hours before the end, his limbs already going numb, he was still dictating. What was he dictating about?
answer: Sand an East India Company director had brought him, to test for gold
choices: Sand an East India Company director had brought him, to test for gold
A bee's eye dried onto a flake of mica so it would not distort
Blood moving in the tail of a live eel, held still in a glass tube
Tartar from an old man who had never once washed out his mouth
context: His publisher friend Reinier Boitet recorded that 'six-and-thirty hours before his death, when his limbs were already growing numb,' Leeuwenhoek was still dictating -- about sand samples a director of the East India Company had brought him, asking whether they contained gold. For the last two letters he summoned Johan Hoogvliet to translate them into Latin for James Jurin, editor of Philosophical Transactions; Hoogvliet wrote that Leeuwenhoek was 'being already in the throes of death, though none the less mindful of his art.' In that final letter he defended his spermist theory and described the palpitations of his own diaphragm, along with a glass device of his own design he had built to treat them. He died of bronchial pneumonia on 26 August 1723 in his house in the Hippolytusbuurt, aged 90, and was buried in the Oude Kerk; the letter was read aloud at a Royal Society meeting on 21 November 1723, three months after he was in the ground. The condition he described in himself is now called 'Leeuwenhoek's disease' -- respiratory myoclonus, or diaphragmatic flutter: he wrote up his own symptoms so precisely that the illness carries his name. Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Leeuwenhoek's Death' and Letter L-588 of August 1723 to James Jurin.

question: Henry Oldenburg, Secretary of the Royal Society, had been printing Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's letters in Philosophical Transactions within months of receiving them -- a Delft tradesman's observations, welcomed and set in type. Then the letters began claiming there were living creatures in a drop of water too small for any eye to see. Twelve more letters went to London. What did Oldenburg do with them?
answer: He printed three, and none of those touched the creatures
choices: He printed nine, and cut the animalcule passages out of them
He printed all twelve, with a note distancing the Society
He printed three, and none of those touched the creatures
He printed one, and asked Delft for sworn witnesses first
context: Oldenburg had been printing Leeuwenhoek within months of receipt. Once the animalcule claims arrived, he went quiet: of the next twelve letters, only three were published, and not one of those touched the animalcules. An extraordinary claim had stalled at the editor's desk -- not refuted, not answered, just not printed. Source: Nick Lane, 'The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) Concerning little animals', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (PMC4360124).

question: On 11 November 1677 the Royal Society sat and heard the sworn affidavits Antonie van Leeuwenhoek had sent from Delft: men of standing -- a notary, ministers, a lawyer, a physician -- swearing on oath that they had put their own eyes to his lens and seen the little animals. The Fellows heard every one of them out, and were not satisfied. What did they do next?
answer: They ordered Robert Hooke to reproduce the observation himself
choices: They had Henry Oldenburg write to Delft for a fuller account
They sent Nehemiah Grew to Delft to watch Leeuwenhoek at work
They asked Christopher Wren to design a lens of equal power
They ordered Robert Hooke to reproduce the observation himself
context: The Society read the Delft affidavits on 11 November 1677 and went ahead with its own test anyway, ordering Robert Hooke, its Curator of Experiments, to reproduce the observation. Once Hooke succeeded, the affidavits ceased to matter. That is the whole difference between science and testimony: eight men under oath is still eight men saying so, and the Society trusted the repeat instead -- a test run by someone with nothing invested in Leeuwenhoek being right. Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, '1677: To confirm his observations' and 'Hooke's Three Tries'.

question: Robert Hooke, Curator of Experiments, tried in front of the Fellows and failed twice. On 1 November 1677 he examined pump-water in glass pipes: 'There was no discovery made in the liquor... of any such minute animals.' On 8 November he came back with a better mount, better lighting and pepper-water: still 'nothing of Mr. Leeuwenhoek's animals could be seen.' On 15 November he tried once more and saw 'great numbers of exceedingly small animals swimming to and fro,' with Christopher Wren, John Aubrey and Nehemiah Grew watching. What had he changed?
answer: He had let the pepper-water steep nine or ten days
choices: He had ground a finer lens for the third attempt
He had let the pepper-water steep nine or ten days
He had warmed the pepper-water over a small flame
He had drawn his water from a canal instead of a pump
context: Two public failures, then patience. The pepper-water Hooke brought on 8 November had steeped only two or three days; for the third try he let it stand nine or ten, and that alone was the difference between nothing and 'great numbers.' Birch's History of the Royal Society records the verdict after 15 November: 'there was no longer any doubt of Mr. LEEWENHOECK's discovery... there could be no fallacy.' John Hoskyns and Jonas Moore were in the room too. The lesson is sharper than the story: a failed replication is not automatically a refutation -- sometimes it means the protocol was not run long enough. Hooke's first failure also owed something to his instrument and a badly lit room. Source: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Hooke's Three Tries' and 'Hooke finally succeeded in replicating Leeuwenhoek's observations'.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek told the Royal Society in 1676 that his method for seeing the smallest creatures he kept 'for myself alone.' In 1685 he showed Thomas Molyneux his working microscopes, then said he owned another sort 'which no man living had looked through setting aside himself' -- and would not let Molyneux look. For three centuries people assumed a lost lens-making secret. In 2021 Tiemen Cocquyt and a Delft team fired neutrons through two sealed instruments to image the lenses without prising them apart. What was the high-power lens?
answer: A blown glass globule, by a method Robert Hooke had published
choices: A ground biconvex lens, by the method Christiaan Huygens used
A polished rock-crystal bead, by the method Delft jewellers used
A blown glass globule, by a method Robert Hooke had published
A stacked pair of thin lenses, by the method the Janssens used
context: Tiemen Cocquyt of Rijksmuseum Boerhaave with Zhou Zhou, Jeroen Plomp and Lambert van Eijck of TU Delft published the neutron tomography in Science Advances on 14 May 2021. They used neutrons rather than X-rays because 'the metal apertures would hinder x-ray radiation to detect the relatively low electron density of the glass compared to that of the metal (brass); the neutrons interact with the nuclei of atoms (rather than their electrons), yielding a more favorable contrast between the metal and glass.' The medium-power lens was a ground biconvex lens 2.7 mm across; the high-power lens in the 266x Utrecht instrument was a blown glass globule 1.3 mm in every direction with the glass stem still attached -- made by melting the end of a thin glass thread in a flame, a method Robert Hooke himself had published in 1678 as 'exceeding easie to make' and then set aside as too fiddly. The paper's conclusion: 'Van Leeuwenhoek did not need to resort to secret lens-making procedures to achieve superior performance.' The edge was patience, specimen preparation, aperture control and lighting. Source: Cocquyt, Zhou, Plomp & van Eijck, Science Advances 7(20):eabf2402 (PMC8121416); Lens on Leeuwenhoek, 'Secrets'.

question: On 24 February 1988 Richard Lenski filled twelve flasks with identical broth, added E. coli, and set them shaking. They are still running today, past 80,000 generations. What has kept them fed all that time?
answer: A person moves a drop into fresh broth by hand, every morning
choices: A person moves a drop into fresh broth by hand, every morning
A technician refills each flask with fresh broth once a week
A pump trickles in fresh broth and drains off the overflow
A robotic arm swaps the broth in all twelve on a timer
context: Someone carries 0.1 mL out of each 10 mL culture into 9.9 mL of fresh medium, every day, including weekends and holidays. One correction worth carrying: this did not begin in Michigan. Lenski started it at the University of California, Irvine, and moved it to Michigan State University in 1991; it went to Jeffrey Barrick at UT Austin in 2022 and came back to Michigan State in 2025. Sources: Grokipedia, 'E. coli long-term evolution experiment'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Lenski; msutoday.msu.edu/news/2025/11/evolution-under-a-microscope-going-strong-at-msu.

question: Lenski's twelve flasks of E. coli have been kept going since 1988, through moves, sabbaticals and staff changes. The routine that sustains them has failed exactly once, and the cause was neither contamination nor equipment failure. What stopped it?
answer: A COVID-19 lockdown emptied the building for months
choices: A COVID-19 lockdown emptied the building for months
A funding gap cut off the lab's supply money
A blizzard closed the campus for several weeks
A fire in a neighbouring lab forced an evacuation
context: The populations were put into the freezer in early 2020 at roughly 73,000 generations and thawed back into the daily routine that September. Thirty-seven years of unbroken biology, stopped once, and not by anything biological. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli_long-term_evolution_experiment ('frozen early 2020, resumed September 2020'); iflscience.com/the-longest-running-evolution-experiment-has-been-going-for-80000-generations-81930.

question: Lenski's broth is deliberately stingy: 25 milligrams of glucose per litre, poured fresh each morning and kept shaking until the next. What does a day inside one of the flasks look like?
answer: The sugar is gone in about six hours; the rest of the day is famine
choices: The sugar is gone in about six hours; the rest of the day is famine
The sugar is gone in about eighteen hours; the last stretch is famine
The sugar thins all day long; the famine never quite arrives
The sugar is gone within minutes; almost the whole day is famine
context: DM25 carries just 25 milligrams of glucose per litre. The cells clear it out in about six hours, then sit through roughly eighteen hours of starvation before the next morning's transfer. Three quarters of the day is hunger, and that thin ration is what the twelve populations have been adapting to since 1988. The chore of keeping them fed gets handed down: when longtime lab manager Neerja Hajela passed it to graduate student Devin Lake, she marked the handover with a mock knighting, using a baseball bat. Around 1998, on sabbatical in France, Lenski came close to ending the experiment altogether; his wife and colleagues talked him out of it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli_long-term_evolution_experiment; longnow.org/ideas/lenski-long-term-evolution-experiment/; Discover magazine, discovermagazine.com/how-a-30-year-experiment-has-fundamentally-changed-our-view-of-how-40784.

question: Every 500 generations since 1988, someone in Lenski's lab has stirred a sample from each flask into glycerol and dropped it into a minus-eighty-degree freezer. Thirty-seven years of those tubes now fill a rack. Take out the oldest one and let it warm up: what do the 1988 cells inside do?
answer: They start dividing again and rebuild a full population
choices: They start dividing again and rebuild a full population
They stay whole but inert, like a pressed flower in a book
They burst as the ice melts, leaving only their DNA behind
They revive briefly, then die out within a few hours
context: Lenski calls the rack a frozen fossil record, except that these fossils are alive. He describes it as time travel done in a scientifically meaningful way: any descendant can be compared directly against its own ancestor. Samples are archived in 15% glycerol at minus eighty degrees Celsius, roughly every 75 days. Sources: Grokipedia, 'E. coli long-term evolution experiment'; iflscience.com (Lenski quoted); discovermagazine.com/how-a-30-year-experiment-has-fundamentally-changed-our-view-of-how-40784.

question: The E. coli strain Lenski put into his twelve flasks in 1988 took about an hour to double its numbers on the lab's deliberately thin broth. Grow a population of its descendants today on exactly the same broth and time them with a kitchen clock. How long does a doubling take now?
answer: About forty minutes
choices: About forty minutes
About fifty-five minutes
About twenty minutes
About ninety minutes
context: Thirty-odd years of selection on the same stingy ration cut roughly a third off the doubling time, and you can catch that difference with nothing more exotic than a clock. The ration is deliberately meagre: DM25 carries just 25 milligrams of glucose per litre, cleared out in about six hours, followed by roughly eighteen hours of starvation before the next morning's transfer. Sources: discovermagazine.com/how-a-30-year-experiment-has-fundamentally-changed-our-view-of-how-40784; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli_long-term_evolution_experiment; longnow.org/ideas/lenski-long-term-evolution-experiment/.

question: Stephen Jay Gould argued that if you could rewind the tape of life and play it again, the living world would come out looking nothing like ours. Lenski has twelve tapes running side by side: twelve populations from one ancestor, in identical flasks, on identical food. One change appeared independently in all twelve. What was it?
answer: Their cells grew steadily larger
choices: Their cells grew steadily larger
Their cells split into shorter rods
Their cells began sticking to the glass
Their cells grew tougher outer coats
context: Parallel evolution seen not once but a dozen times over. It has a measurable side effect: an evolved population reaches only about half the colony count of the ancestor on the same glucose, because each cell is bigger and eats more. Gould's replaying-the-tape thought experiment is the frame Blount and Lenski explicitly invoke, and the LTEE is the only place anyone has actually had the tape to rewind. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli_long-term_evolution_experiment; the-ltee.org/crib-sheet/; Blount, Borland & Lenski 2008, PNAS, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2430337/.

question: Lenski wants a number for how much better a population is at flask life today than the 1988 ancestor it grew from. Someone thaws a tube of that ancestor. Nothing about the flask, the broth or the shaker has changed since 1988. How does the lab turn the two strains into that number?
answer: It puts both into one flask and compares how fast each multiplies
choices: It puts both into one flask and compares how fast each multiplies
It grows each in its own flask and compares the final cell counts
It times how fast each strain alone clears the sugar from its broth
It reads both genomes and counts up the mutations that differ
context: Relative fitness is the ratio of the two competitors' realized rates of increase, their Malthusian parameters, measured while they share a flask. The gains front-loaded hard: fitness rose 0.108 per 1,000 generations between generations 1,000 and 2,000, but only 0.008 per 1,000 between generations 5,000 and 10,000, a thirteen-fold slowdown. Source: Lenski, 'Dynamics of Adaptation and Diversification: A 10,000-Generation Experiment', ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK232213/.

question: Six of Lenski's twelve populations differ from the other six by one harmless mutation in a sugar-processing gene called araA. It changes nothing about how the cells eat or grow, but without it nobody could tell two of his strains apart once they had been mixed in a flask. What does that one mutation make visible?
answer: Spread on the right plate, one version's colonies grow red and the other's white
choices: Spread on the right plate, one version's colonies grow red and the other's white
Under ultraviolet light one version glows green and the other stays dark
On a plate with an antibiotic added, only one of the versions grows
Spun in a tube, one version settles to the bottom and the other floats
context: The two founding strains are REL606 and REL607, differing by a single point mutation in araA: six populations are Ara-minus and six Ara-plus. On tetrazolium-arabinose plates the Ara-minus colonies come up red and the Ara-plus white, so a competition between two strains is settled by counting red dots and white dots on a dish. Sources: barricklab.org/twiki/bin/view/Lab/ProtocolsAraMarker; the-ltee.org/crib-sheet/; Grokipedia, 'E. coli long-term evolution experiment'.

question: Around generation 31,500 one of Lenski's populations, Ara-3, began eating the citrate that had sat in its broth since 1988, something E. coli is defined as unable to do while oxygen is present. When the team read Ara-3's genome, what had changed?
answer: An existing citrate carrier was copied next to a switch that runs in air
choices: An existing citrate carrier was copied next to a switch that runs in air
A citrate carrier that works in air was picked up from another species
A single letter rewrote a sugar carrier into one that works in air
A virus inserted a citrate carrier that runs in air into the chromosome
context: A 2,933-base-pair tandem duplication of the rnk-citG region put a second copy of the transporter gene citT downstream of the rnk promoter, which is active when oxygen is present. The cell already owned the door; the duplication moved it next to a light switch that was already on. And the meal had been there the whole time: the medium carried about 1,700 micromolar citrate, roughly eleven times the glucose, from the very first flask, put in as a routine ingredient rather than as food. Sources: Blount, Borland & Lenski 2008, PNAS, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2430337/; Blount et al. 2012, Nature 489:513, summarised at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5918244/.

question: A cell that breaks its own DNA-proofreading genes copies its genome carelessly ever after, and that carelessness costs it about one percent of its growth rate. In six of Lenski's twelve populations, cells that had broken those genes took over the flask anyway. Where is the profit?
answer: Such a cell is far likelier to be the one that hits the next winning mutation
choices: Such a cell is far likelier to be the one that hits the next winning mutation
Such a cell shrugs off the daily starvation that kills its careful neighbours
Such a cell can undo a harmful mutation as fast as it makes a new one
Such a cell's sloppy copying also fends off the viruses that hunt bacteria
context: Lenski puts it plainly: 'Although the hypermutators are a small minority, on a per capita basis each of them has a 100-times higher probability than a normal cell of generating the next winner.' And: 'A hypermutator only needs to get lucky once, and then it becomes extremely difficult to displace it... at least so long as the population is far from the fitness peak.' Most of the six wrecked mismatch repair (mutS, mutL); Ara-1 was the odd one out, going through uvrA and mutT instead. Sources: the-ltee.org/what-weve-learned-about-evolution-from-the-ltee-number-5/; Good and Tenaillon et al., 'Divergent Evolution of Mutation Rates and Biases in the LTEE', academic.oup.com/gbe/article/12/9/1591/5898197.

question: Lenski's team could do something no other evolution study can: rerun a population's own history. They thawed samples from thirteen points in Ara-3's frozen past, restarted each one, and screened tens of trillions of cells across thousands of cultures. What did the replays show?
answer: Citrate eating arose again, but only from samples frozen after about generation 20,000
choices: Citrate eating arose again, but only from samples frozen after about generation 20,000
Citrate eating arose again at much the same rate from samples of every age
Citrate eating never arose again, in any culture from any frozen sample
Citrate eating arose again, but only from the earliest samples, frozen before 1990
context: The largest replay screened about 4 x 10^13 cells across 2,800 cultures from thirteen frozen timepoints. Citrate eating re-evolved 4 times in the first replay experiment, 5 in the second and 8 in the third, and every one came from a clone frozen after roughly generation 20,000. Earlier mutations had to be in place first: the door had to be unlocked before it could be opened. Blount's model runs potentiation, then actualization (the first citrate eaters gained only about 1 to 2 percent), then refinement. Sources: Blount, Borland & Lenski 2008, PNAS, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2430337/; Blount et al. 2012, summarised at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5918244/.

question: Every earlier model of Lenski's flasks had to guess at the shape of the far future. By 50,000 generations the twelve populations had produced enough data to fit the real curve of fitness against time. When Wiser, Ribeck and Lenski fitted it in 2013, what was that curve doing?
answer: Still rising, ever more slowly, with no ceiling anywhere in the data
choices: Still rising, ever more slowly, with no ceiling anywhere in the data
Flat since about generation 20,000, pinned against an upper limit
Rising in sudden jumps with long flat stretches in between them
Drifting back down as harmful mutations piled up in every line
context: The trajectory fits a power law, and mean fitness 'appears to increase without bound', overturning the earlier hyperbolic models that had predicted the populations would hit a ceiling. The curve never goes flat; it only climbs more slowly. Sources: Wiser, Ribeck & Lenski 2013, Science 342:1364, pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24231808/; summarised at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._coli_long-term_evolution_experiment.

question: By generation 50,000, six of Lenski's twelve populations had broken their own DNA-repair genes and were mutating about a hundred times faster than their careful cousins. In one of those six, two separate lineages later converged on exactly the same change. What change did both of them make?
answer: Both cut the mutation rate back by about half, not all the way
choices: Both cut the mutation rate back by about half, not all the way
Both restored the broken repair genes to full working order
Both raised the mutation rate higher still, hunting bigger wins
Both shed the damage by swapping DNA with neighbouring cells
context: Trimming the rate cut the fitness cost from roughly 1 percent to about 0.5 percent while keeping some of the evolvability that made hypermutation pay in the first place. Evolution tuned its own mutation rate down in stages rather than reverting all the way. Sources: Lenski, 'What We've Learned about Evolution from the LTEE: Number 5', the-ltee.org/what-weve-learned-about-evolution-from-the-ltee-number-5/; Wielgoss et al. 2013.

question: Cambridge, August 1967. A radio-astronomy PhD student named Jocelyn Bell is hand-scanning about thirty metres of pen-recorder chart paper per day when she notices a quarter-inch of odd ink trace that keeps coming back from the same spot in the sky. She called that flicker of squiggle by which nickname in her notes?
answer: A bit of scruff
choices: A bit of scruff
A slice of static
A jagged smear
A ghost fringe
context: Bell had been carefully marking recurring signals across the daily paper trace. The 'scruff' turned out to be a repeating pulse from a single spot in the constellation Vulpecula. Source: J. Bell Burnell, 'Reflections on the discovery of pulsars' (Annals NY Acad. Sci. 302, 1977); Cambridge Digital Library exhibit.

question: When Jocelyn Bell ran the pen recorder FAST across the suspect region, the smear of ink resolved into a train of pulses. What period and precision did the team pin down?
answer: One pulse every 1.337 seconds, regular to about one part in a million
choices: One pulse every 1.337 seconds, regular to about one part in a million
One pulse every 0.089 seconds, regular to about one part in ten thousand
One pulse every 4.31 seconds, regular to about one part in a hundred thousand
One pulse every 1.62 seconds, regular to about one part in ten million
context: Nothing natural then known kept time that well - no star, no galaxy, no known radio source. The precision itself was the shock. Source: Hewish, Bell et al. 1968, Nature 217, 709; PSR B1919+21 discovery paper.

question: The pulses were so metronomic that the Cambridge team half-jokingly labelled the source LGM-1, for Little Green Men, while they worked to rule out an artificial origin. What piece of evidence FIRST argued against the alien hypothesis?
answer: The pulse rate showed no Doppler shift from a distant planet orbiting a distant sun
choices: The pulse rate showed no Doppler shift from a distant planet orbiting a distant sun
The frequency sat outside the narrow band any known radio transmitter used
The pulses arrived a full second late every winter, ruling out Earth-locked signal
The signal grew weaker as Earth rotated toward it, ruling out an aimed broadcast
context: If aliens on a planet were sending it, the planet's orbital motion around its own star should have shifted the pulse rate up and down through the year. Only the Earth's own orbital motion showed up. Source: Hewish et al. 1968, Nature 217, 709.

question: The alien hypothesis lasted only weeks. What finally killed LGM as an explanation was not a philosophical objection but a second observation Jocelyn Bell made a few weeks later. What did she find that made 'intelligent broadcast' impossible to defend?
answer: A second pulsing source in another constellation, with its own quite different period
choices: A second pulsing source in another constellation, with its own quite different period
A hidden nearby TV transmitter whose stray harmonic matched the original pulse rate
A faulty pre-amplifier in the receiver chain that had been generating the pulses itself
A geostationary satellite passing overhead every day at the same local sidereal time
context: Two unrelated alien civilizations, broadcasting simultaneously on the same frequency at similar precision, was too much to swallow. Bell found a third and fourth soon after. The disproof came from evidence, not embarrassment. Source: Pilkington et al. 1968; Bell Burnell reflections (1977).

question: The receiver that caught the pulses had not been designed to find them. Jocelyn Bell had helped build it herself over two years at Lord's Bridge, west of Cambridge - about 2,048 dipole antennas strung on 120 miles of cable across roughly four acres. What was the instrument built to study?
answer: How quasars twinkle as their radio signal passes through the turbulent solar wind
choices: How quasars twinkle as their radio signal passes through the turbulent solar wind
Radio emissions from Jupiter and the outer planets as they crossed the ecliptic plane
Radar echoes off the Moon and inner planets for precise Solar System distance work
The 21-centimetre hydrogen line from clouds of neutral gas within the Milky Way disk
context: Antony Hewish had designed the array to measure quasar sizes via interplanetary scintillation - the reason it recorded fast fluctuations at all. A slower survey telescope would have averaged the pulses into nothing. The instrument answered a different question than it was built for. Source: Hewish et al. 1968.

question: The neutron star was not a total surprise on paper. In 1934, just two years after James Chadwick first identified the neutron itself, two astronomers proposed that some massive stars would collapse at the end of their lives into an object made almost entirely of neutrons. They also coined the word 'supernova' in the same paper. Who were they?
answer: Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky, working at Mount Wilson and Caltech
choices: Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky, working at Mount Wilson and Caltech
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and Arthur Eddington, in a Royal Society exchange
Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff, in a Berkeley theory paper on collapse
Lev Landau and George Gamow, in a joint note out of Copenhagen
context: Baade and Zwicky's 1934 short papers predicted both supernovae and their neutron-star remnants; almost nobody thought one would ever actually be observed. It took 33 years and a graduate student reading paper. Source: Baade & Zwicky 1934, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 20, 254.

question: The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the pulsar discovery went to Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle; Jocelyn Bell Burnell was omitted. In a 1977 speech Bell Burnell herself gave a stance on the exclusion. Which line is from that speech?
answer: I believe it would demean Nobel Prizes if they were awarded to research students, except in very exceptional cases, and I do not believe this is one of them
choices: I believe it would demean Nobel Prizes if they were awarded to research students, except in very exceptional cases, and I do not believe this is one of them
A doctoral thesis is a training exercise, and training discoveries belong in the first instance to the supervisor who set the problem for the student
The prize honours the design of the telescope and the interpretation of the data, both of which properly belong to my seniors and not to me
Discoveries made inside a large collaboration should be credited to the group leader, and I accept that convention as it stood in Stockholm in 1974
context: That was Bell Burnell in 1977. By 2021 she was noting publicly that being a graduate student AND a woman together had 'demoted' her standing in the discovery's telling - a shift the player can weigh, without the bank ruling on it. Source: Bell Burnell, 'Petit Four' (Annals NY Acad. Sci. 302, 1977).

question: In 2018 Jocelyn Bell Burnell received the $3 million Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics for her role in the pulsar discovery. What did she do with the prize money?
answer: Donated every penny to fund physics PhDs for women, minorities and refugee students, via the Institute of Physics
choices: Donated every penny to fund physics PhDs for women, minorities and refugee students, via the Institute of Physics
Donated it to Cambridge to endow a Hewish Memorial Chair in Radio Astronomy, held in his name in perpetuity
Split it between the Royal Society and the Institute of Physics as unrestricted general research grants
Gave it to the Cambridge observatory to fund a new dedicated pulsar-search receiver at Lord's Bridge
context: Every penny went to the Institute of Physics to set up graduate scholarships for candidates from under-represented backgrounds. It was called the Bell Burnell Graduate Scholarship Fund. Source: Institute of Physics announcement, September 2018; NPR interview 06 Sep 2018.

question: In 1972 a private circle of businessmen and scientists paid an MIT team of seventeen to model humanity's future on a computer. What was the circle called?
answer: the Club of Rome
choices: the Club of Rome
the Royal Society
the Bilderberg Group
the Trilateral Commission
