context: J. J. Thomson bent cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields and measured e/m, arguing the beam was a stream of tiny charged corpuscles. Thirty-one years later his son showed that same corpuscle diffracts like a wave. Both were right; wave-particle duality is why. Source: chemistryworld.com/culture/a-history-of-the-electron-jj-and-gp-thomson/6090.article

question: Green light has a wavelength of about 550 nanometres, and no light microscope can ever resolve anything much finer than about half of that. Speed an electron up to 100 kilovolts and its de Broglie wavelength shrinks to about 3.9 picometres, roughly a hundred thousand times shorter. What does that shrinking wavelength let a modern electron microscope do that no light microscope can?
answer: Photograph individual atoms in a crystal
choices: Photograph individual atoms in a crystal
See straight through solid lead as if it were glass
Read writing on a coin buried under a metre of soil
Freeze the motion of light itself for later playback
context: The rule that resolution is limited to about half a wavelength was known before de Broglie; his formula turned it into an invitation. The wave nature of matter is why we can see the things atoms are made of. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_microscope ; advanced-microscopy.utah.edu/education/electron-micro/

question: In 1925 a young Austrian physicist read de Broglie's thesis, became convinced particles really were waves, and spent that winter writing down the equation that governs the wave itself. The equation he produced the next year is still the backbone of chemistry and solid-state physics. Who was he?
answer: Erwin Schrodinger
choices: Erwin Schrodinger
Werner Heisenberg
Wolfgang Pauli
Max Born
context: Schrodinger's wave mechanics and Heisenberg's matrix mechanics turned out to be the same theory in different dress. de Broglie's single line lambda = h/p is the seed of both. Source: ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/reso/031/01/0063-0082

question: Press a button on a television remote in a dark room and nothing happens that you can see. Hold the same remote up to a phone's selfie camera and press again: the screen shows a bright glow flashing at the remote's front end. Nothing was added to the phone -- it is an ordinary camera, built for ordinary photographs. What is it picking up?
answer: a pulse of infrared light
choices: a pulse of infrared light
a pulse of ultraviolet light
a pulse of radio waves
a pulse of microwaves
context: That is the remote's infrared LED -- the same mechanism as visible light, only a longer wavelength, and a sensor built for visible light registers it anyway because to the sensor there is no difference. Rear cameras more often carry an infrared-blocking filter, which is why the selfie camera works better. Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are one phenomenon at different wavelengths, all moving at the same speed in vacuum -- and that is Maxwell's claim, not a later addition to it. Sources: IOP Spark, 'Invisible Wavelengths'; Sony support, 'Test if your remote control sends an infrared (IR) signal'; Carolina Knowledge Center, 'Detecting IR Light with a Smart Phone'; NASA Imagine the Universe, 'Electromagnetic Spectrum'.

question: At Karlsruhe in 1887 Heinrich Hertz laid two metre-long copper wires on a bench, each capped with a zinc ball thirty centimetres across, and drove them hard with an induction coil. Metres away, joined to nothing -- no wire, no battery -- sat a plain wire loop with a narrow slit cut in it. Hertz watched that slit. What did he see?
answer: a tiny spark jumped across it
choices: a tiny spark jumped across it
a bead of metal formed across it
its cut edges slowly blackened
a compass needle beside it swung
context: A tiny spark, metres away, with nothing whatever connecting the two -- that was the entire result, and it was the first electromagnetic wave anyone had made on purpose. The induction coil was driving a discharge across a gap of about 7.5 mm between the inner ends of the two copper wires; the loop had no source of its own at all. Hertz went on to bounce the waves off metal sheets to build standing waves and read their length off the node spacing: 0.7 to 6 metres, roughly 50-450 MHz. They reflected, refracted and polarised exactly like light. Published as 'Uber elektromagnetische Wellen im Raume', Annalen der Physik, 1888. Source: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations', section 'Experimental Confirmation by Hertz (1880s)'.

question: Michael Faraday made his curved lines of magnetic force visible by scattering iron filings on a card and tapping it, but he could write no equation for them, and the physicists of his day dismissed the picture, holding that a magnet simply reaches across empty space and pulls, instantly, with nothing in between. In two essays read at Cambridge in 1855 and 1856, the young James Clerk Maxwell put numbers on those lines. What did he treat each one as?
answer: a tube of incompressible fluid
choices: a tube of incompressible fluid
a chain of magnets, pole to pole
an orbit traced by one particle
a ridge on a stretched sheet
context: 'On Faraday's Lines of Force', read to the Cambridge Philosophical Society in December 1855 and February 1856. Faraday had almost no mathematics; what he had was a picture. By modelling each line as a tube of incompressible fluid, Maxwell could carry the whole machinery of fluid mechanics across to magnetism -- flow rates, pressures, tube cross-sections -- and so put arithmetic on a drawing its own author could not calculate with. In the same essays he went after the reigning action-at-a-distance theories of Coulomb and Ampere for demanding instantaneous forces with nothing in between. Source: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations' and 'James Clerk Maxwell'.

question: Every physics classroom prints four compact equations under James Clerk Maxwell's name. Open 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field', the paper he read to the Royal Society on 8 December 1864, and you will not find them there. What is actually on those pages?
answer: twenty simultaneous equations in twenty variables
choices: twenty simultaneous equations in twenty variables
eight simultaneous equations in eight variables
twelve simultaneous equations in six variables
three simultaneous equations in twelve variables
context: Twenty, written out component by component; they can be grouped as eight lettered relations, A through H -- law of total currents, magnetic potential, Ampere's circuital law, electromotive force, electric elasticity, Ohm's law, Gauss's law, continuity of charge. The four compact vector equations everyone recites were a later compression by another hand entirely. Maxwell's own summing-up in that paper: 'The agreement of the results seems to show that light and magnetism are affections of the same substance, and that light is an electromagnetic disturbance propagated through the field according to electromagnetic laws.' Sources: IEEE Spectrum, 'The Long Road to Maxwell's Equations'; Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations'; Wikipedia, 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field'.

question: Heinrich Hertz had just managed what nobody had managed before: invisible waves sent across his laboratory and caught at the far side, confirming the prediction of a Scottish physicist nine years dead. His students asked him what the discovery was good for. What is Hertz reported to have told them?
answer: that it was of no use whatsoever
choices: that it was of no use whatsoever
that it was a new kind of telegraph
that it was proof the ether was real
that it was a way to heat at a distance
context: Pressed on what could actually be done with the waves, Hertz is said to have added, 'Nothing, I guess.' Treat the exchange as reported rather than documentary -- it is widely repeated but second-hand. Guglielmo Marconi was sending signals across the Atlantic by 1901, about thirteen years later, and every radio, phone and wifi link since runs on Hertz's useless discovery. Sources: IOP Spark, 'Hertz's useless discovery'; Marconi and 1901 from Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations'.  (Legend.)

question: In January 1862 James Clerk Maxwell printed two figures side by side in the Philosophical Magazine: 310,740 kilometres per second, the speed he had calculated for a ripple in his medium, and 314,858, Fizeau's measured speed of light. Every number feeding that calculation came from one 1856 experiment by Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch in Germany -- an experiment with no lamp, no mirror, no spinning toothed wheel in it. What were those two men measuring?
answer: the charge in a Leyden jar, gauged by force and by current
choices: the charge in a Leyden jar, gauged by force and by current
the spark from a Leyden jar, timed as it leapt an air gap
the pull between two magnets, gauged at fixed distances
the current in a coil, gauged as its iron core withdrew
context: Weber and Kohlrausch were after the ratio between the electrostatic and the electromagnetic unit of charge -- the same charge in a foil-lined glass jar, weighed once by the force it exerts and once by the current it makes. The ratio came out carrying the units of a velocity: 3.107 x 10^8 metres per second. No lamps, no mirrors, no light of any kind. Weber had even labelled the constant 'c' in an 1846 paper with no thought of light, and neither man made much of the coincidence. Maxwell saw what it was, and set the punchline in italics: '...we can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations' and 'Leyden jar'; Wikisource scan of Philosophical Magazine, series 4, vol. 23 ('On Physical Lines of Force', Part III, Prop. XVI).

question: Take the turntable out of a microwave oven so that nothing can spin, lay a flat bar of chocolate across the floor of it, and run the oven until the first patches soften. The melted patches come out in a neat row, roughly six centimetres apart, with firm chocolate between them, and they appear in the same places every time -- the oven's waves are standing still inside the box. The frequency is printed on the oven's back plate. What does that six-centimetre spacing correspond to?
answer: half of one wavelength
choices: half of one wavelength
one full wavelength
two full wavelengths
a quarter of a wavelength
context: Neighbouring hot spots sit half a wavelength apart, so double the six centimetres and multiply by the frequency printed on the oven -- almost always 2450 million cycles per second -- and you get about 3 x 10^8 metres per second. You have just measured the speed of light on a countertop, with an invisible wave made purely by electricity: Maxwell's whole claim, tested in an afternoon with a chocolate bar. A tray of marshmallows works too. Sources: Science Buddies, 'Measuring the Speed of Light with a Microwave Oven'; Open University OpenLearn; University of Georgia Extension, 'Cooking at the Speed of Light'.

question: Richard Feynman told his Caltech students to imagine looking back on the 1860s from ten thousand years in the future. From that distance, he said, one event of that decade would still be judged the most significant thing that happened in the nineteenth century -- James Clerk Maxwell working out the laws of electrodynamics -- and one famous event of the very same decade would 'pale into provincial insignificance' beside it. Which event did he name?
answer: the American Civil War
choices: the American Civil War
the unification of Italy
the opening of the Suez Canal
the freeing of the Russian serfs
context: Verbatim, from The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II, Lecture 1, section 1-6: 'From a long view of the history of mankind -- seen from, say, ten thousand years from now -- there can be little doubt that the most significant event of the 19th century will be judged as Maxwell's discovery of the laws of electrodynamics. The American Civil War will pale into provincial insignificance in comparison with this important scientific event of the same decade.' Einstein made a similar claim at the 1931 centenary of Maxwell's birth, calling the change in the conception of physical reality that Maxwell brought about 'the most profound and the most fruitful that physics has experienced since the time of Newton'. Sources: Wikiquote, Richard Feynman, citing The Feynman Lectures Vol. II ch. 1 (1964); James Clerk Maxwell Foundation, for Einstein's centenary essay.

question: Charge a capacitor and the current runs up the wire and stops dead at the gap between the plates; no charge at all crosses that space. Ampere's law, which ties the magnetic field around a loop to the current threading it, now returns two answers for the same circuit -- stretch an imaginary surface so the wire pierces it and you get a field; stretch it through the gap instead and you get nothing. James Clerk Maxwell's repair was to rule that something else in the apparatus counts as a current too. What?
answer: a changing electric field in the gap
choices: a changing electric field in the gap
a magnetic current between the plates
a charge piling on the plate faces
a slow warming of the air in the gap
context: He named it the displacement current, and in 'On Physical Lines of Force' he pictured it physically, as a 'displacement of the rows of particles' in the ether. Do the arithmetic and the displacement current through the gap comes out exactly equal to the conduction current in the wires: the circuit closes. That one term is also why light exists in the equations at all -- a changing electric field sources a magnetic field, whose change sources an electric field, and the disturbance regenerates itself outward with nothing to wave in. Delete the term and the equations support no self-sustaining oscillation in free space, and sunlight could not cross the vacuum. Source: Grokipedia, 'Displacement current' (the two-surface paradox, the continuity violation, the derivation, and the 'Electromagnetic Waves' section).

question: Oliver Heaviside never sat in a university lecture. Scarlet fever left him partly deaf at nine; he left school at sixteen because his family had no money, worked the Denmark and Newcastle telegraph cables, and quit at twenty-four to do physics alone in his parents' house. Maxwell's twenty equations were written in both fields and potentials -- a potential being a quantity a field is worked out from. Over the summer of 1884 Heaviside cut those twenty down to the four that every textbook now prints, and he said one drastic move was what finally let him do it. Which move?
answer: he threw out the potentials and kept the fields
choices: he threw out the potentials and kept the fields
he threw out the fields and kept the potentials
he threw out the ether and worked in empty space
he threw out the vectors and worked in quaternions
context: His own words: 'I never made any progress until I threw all the potentials overboard.' Heaviside insisted on writing the theory in the measurable fields themselves, and Maxwell's twenty simultaneous equations in twenty variables collapsed into four vector equations over the summer of 1884, published in 1885. He was no dullard for all his missing schooling: he had ranked fifth out of five hundred pupils in 1865, the year before the money ran out. On first getting hold of Maxwell's 1873 Treatise he wrote, 'I saw that it was great, greater and greatest... I was determined to master the book.' Even the name is his: the phrase 'Maxwell's equations' first appears in his 1885 series 'Electromagnetic Induction and its Propagation' in The Electrician, where he wrote 'Maxwell's equations of propagation' -- before that people said 'Maxwell's theory', and Oliver Lodge's 1888 lectures pushed the new phrase into general use. Heaviside died on 3 February 1925 in a Torquay nursing home after a fall, on a civil-list pension of 220 pounds a year, and was buried in an unmarked plot beside his parents in Paignton Cemetery; admirers added his name and 'F.R.S.' to the stone years later. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Oliver Heaviside' and 'History of Maxwell's equations'; IEEE Spectrum, 'The Long Road to Maxwell's Equations'.

question: Behind James Clerk Maxwell's 1861 calculation of how fast a ripple would run through his medium sat a picture he had drawn in full mechanical detail: space packed with spinning molecular vortices lined up along the magnetic lines of force, and between them tiny spherical particles rolling without slipping, like the idle wheels in a gear train, an electric current being those particles on the move. Then, in the same paper, Maxwell wrote about his own gear train. What did he say about it?
answer: that he did not offer it as existing in nature
choices: that he did not offer it as existing in nature
that only the vortices, not the particles, were real
that he had built a brass model to test it
that Faraday had described the same gearing
context: His exact words: the conception of a particle connected to a vortex by perfect rolling contact 'may appear somewhat awkward', and 'I do not bring it forward as a mode of connexion existing in nature, or even as that which I would willingly assent to as an electrical hypothesis.' He built a machine he did not believe in, turned the crank, and the speed of light came out of it. Three years later he threw the vortices away and rebuilt the theory abstractly in 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field'. Note the scope of the doubt: it was this gear-train machinery Maxwell disowned, not the ether itself, which he never doubted was there. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations'; Bruce J. Hunt, 'Maxwell, Measurement, and the Modes of Electromagnetic Theory' (2015), for both verbatim hedges.

question: James Clerk Maxwell worked his electromagnetic equations out over the summer of 1861 at Glenlair, his family's estate in Galloway, with none of his reference books to hand -- he did not have Weber and Kohlrausch's laboratory figures there at all. He carried the result back to London late that year, looked their measurements up, converted them into his own units, and got 310,740 kilometres per second. Three rival optical measurements of the speed of light were then in circulation. How did his figure sit among those three?
answer: they disagreed with each other by more than any did with his
choices: they disagreed with each other by more than any did with his
they agreed with each other more closely than any did with his
they clustered tightly together, and all three sat above his
they fell either side of his, each about equally far off
context: The rival optical values then in circulation were Fizeau's 314,858 km/s, Foucault's 298,000, and roughly 308,000 from stellar aberration. Maxwell's 310,740 landed inside that spread: the measurers of light stood further apart from each other than any of them stood from a figure he had got out of electricity and magnetism alone, with no light in it anywhere. The order of events matters as much as the closeness. He made the equations out at Glenlair before he had any suspicion of the nearness between the two velocities, and said so to William Thomson in his December 1861 letter -- a number that falls out of a theory before its author has looked the measurement up cannot have been fitted to that measurement, which is the whole working difference between a prediction and a curve fit. The modern value is 299,792,458 metres per second, exact by definition. Sources: Grokipedia, 'History of Maxwell's equations', for the rival figures; Wikipedia, 'On Physical Lines of Force'; Instituto de Matematicas, Universidad de Sevilla, 'Maxwell sees the light' (Glenlair, the missing books, the December 1861 letter to Thomson).

question: Maxwell's waves rippled through a luminiferous ether: a real medium filling all of space, which he never doubted was there, because a wave had to be a wave in something. Between April and July 1887 -- the very years Heinrich Hertz was making those waves real on a laboratory bench -- Albert Michelson and Edward Morley floated an interferometer on a sandstone slab in a pool of mercury in a Cleveland basement and turned it slowly, hunting the Earth's motion through that ether. What did they report that November?
answer: a drift too small to detect in any direction
choices: a drift too small to detect in any direction
a drift in the direction astronomers expected
a drift that reversed between April and July
a drift far larger than the Earth's known speed
context: No ether drift showed up at any orientation of the slab. Reported in the American Journal of Science in November 1887. Both men judged the experiment a failure; Hertz himself already doubted the ether was a physical thing. Maxwell had been dead since 5 November 1879, at forty-eight, of abdominal cancer -- he never saw one of his waves made, and never learned that the medium he thought carried them was not there. That is the honest shape of this story: correct equations inside a picture that was later abandoned. Sources: Case Western Reserve Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, 'Michelson-Morley Experiment'; APS News, 'November 1887: Michelson and Morley report their failure'; Grokipedia, 'James Clerk Maxwell' and 'History of Maxwell's equations'.

question: Maxwell wrote to Tait about a 'finite being' at the trapdoor and never used any spookier word for it. Seven years later, in the journal Nature on 9 April 1874, another famous physicist pinned a nickname on it that stuck. Who named it a 'demon' -- meaning the Greek daemon, an agent working behind the scenes?
answer: William Thomson (Lord Kelvin)
choices: William Thomson (Lord Kelvin)
Ludwig Boltzmann
Peter Guthrie Tait
Rudolf Clausius
context: Kelvin's 'Kinetic Theory of the Dissipation of Energy' (Nature, 9 April 1874). Maxwell was deeply religious and disliked the word; Kelvin meant it in the Greek sense of a helpful attendant spirit, not an evil one. Source: Wikipedia -- Maxwell's demon.

question: The trapdoor story is almost always mistold as Maxwell trying to overthrow a great pillar of physics. He was doing the opposite -- teaching a subtle point about what kind of rule that pillar really is. What deeper truth about the second law was Maxwell actually illustrating with his gatekeeper?
answer: that it holds only statistically for bulk gas, not as a ban on any single molecule
choices: that it holds only statistically for bulk gas, not as a ban on any single molecule
that it can be broken outright by a clever enough sorting machine
that it is not a real physical law but a bookkeeping convention
that it applies to heat as a fluid substance stored inside each molecule
context: Maxwell's point: any single molecule is free to move the 'wrong' way; the second law of thermodynamics wins only because there are Avogadro-many of them. The demon was a teaching device, not a proposed perpetual-motion machine. Source: Wikipedia -- Maxwell's demon.

question: In 1929 the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard sharpened Maxwell's puzzle down to a cylinder holding ONE molecule, and argued that the demon's engine could not be free -- one specific step it had to perform must itself carry a thermodynamic price. Which step did Szilard identify as the one that had to cost entropy?
answer: finding out which half of the cylinder the molecule was in
choices: finding out which half of the cylinder the molecule was in
inserting the partition into the middle of the cylinder
letting the trapped molecule push the piston outward
resetting the piston to its starting position
context: Szilard, 'Uber die Entropieverminderung...', Zeitschrift fur Physik 53, 1929. Reducing the gas to a single particle stripped the puzzle to its skeleton: no measurement, no engine. He was the first to link information to entropy in a quantitative way. Source: Wikipedia -- Maxwell's demon.

question: Landauer's limit sat as pure theory for fifty-one years. In 2012 a team in Lyon, Augsburg and Kaiserslautern -- Antoine Berut and colleagues -- finally measured it in a tabletop bit-erasure experiment. What did they actually hold and watch, to confirm the kT ln 2 heat bill for erasing one bit?
answer: a single 2-micrometre silica bead trapped between two laser wells
choices: a single 2-micrometre silica bead trapped between two laser wells
a swarm of hydrogen atoms held in a magnetic bottle
a single trapped calcium ion cooled by a radio-frequency cage
a nitrogen-vacancy centre inside a chilled diamond chip
context: Berut et al., Nature 483, 187-189 (2012). Left-well and right-well encoded the two possible bit values; tilting the trap forced the bead into one well regardless of where it started -- an erasure. The released heat matched Landauer's floor. A 19th-century thought experiment was closed by a measurement in the 21st.

question: The Landauer floor is genuinely fundamental, but the bank's own honest caveat is important. Which statement most accurately describes how today's real computer chips stand next to it?
answer: they dissipate orders of magnitude more heat per bit than the limit demands
choices: they dissipate orders of magnitude more heat per bit than the limit demands
they already run right at the limit, so no further cooling is possible
they run below the limit because transistors are quantum devices
they cheat the limit by using reversible logic in every operation
context: Modern CMOS erases a bit with roughly a million times Landauer's minimum, so the limit is not today's engineering bottleneck -- it is a floor no future chip can pass. In principle a fully REVERSIBLE computer would dodge it, since only bit-destruction pays; no one has built a practical one. Source: Wikipedia -- Landauer's principle.

question: In the summer of 1840 a young German ship's doctor named Julius Robert von Mayer, sailing to Java on a Dutch three-master, bled several sick sailors on deck and got a shock. The venous blood coming out of them -- the blood that had already run through their tissues -- looked wrong to him. In what way?
answer: It was nearly as bright red as arterial blood
choices: It was nearly as bright red as arterial blood
It ran black instead of the usual dark red
It came out watery and thin
It was noticeably cooler than blood back in Europe
context: Venous blood back home was dark because tissues had stripped most of the oxygen out of it on the way. In the tropics the crew's bodies were burning far less oxygen to keep warm, so the returning blood still glowed red. Mayer stood on deck holding a bucket and puzzled about it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: Mayer stared at the bright red venous blood and worked back to why. Very little oxygen had been stripped out of it on the way through the sailors' tissues. What internal process were their bodies running less of in the tropical heat?
answer: Burning food to make their own heat
choices: Burning food to make their own heat
Sweating salt out through the skin
Pumping blood through the lungs
Storing sugar in the liver
context: Less internal fire meant less oxygen consumed, so less oxygen taken out of the venous blood. To Mayer this was a clue that heat, food-energy and work were all the SAME quantity in different forms -- warmth pouring in from outside could stand in for warmth burned from within. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: Mayer put a number on how much mechanical work a given amount of heat is worth -- the mechanical equivalent of heat. Unusually for such a headline result, he did not measure it with an apparatus of his own. Where did his number come from?
answer: Published heat-capacity data for gases
choices: Published heat-capacity data for gases
A paddle wheel he built and stirred water with
Steam-engine coal-burn records from the Ruhr
The temperature rise in bent iron bars
context: Mayer used the difference between the specific heat of air at constant pressure and at constant volume (Cp minus Cv) -- the extra heat needed when a gas is allowed to expand and do work against the atmosphere -- to compute about 365 kilogram-metres per kilocalorie. Because he had never actually done an experiment, the English experimentalists found him easy to dismiss. Source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/mayer-julius-robert

question: In June 1841 Mayer sent his first paper on the conservation of force to Johann Christian Poggendorff, editor of the leading German physics journal Annalen der Physik. What did Poggendorff do with it?
answer: Filed it away without reply and never printed it
choices: Filed it away without reply and never printed it
Sent it back with a page of demolishing corrections
Forwarded it to Helmholtz for a second opinion
Printed a short version, then a retraction three months later
context: The paper was neither published nor returned. Mayer had to work up a second version essentially from memory. Poggendorff's copy of the original turned up in his papers 36 years later, long after the priority fight was over. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer

question: In 1848 two of Mayer's children died in rapid succession, and Joule's supporters in England openly denied that Mayer had gotten there first. On 18 May 1850 Mayer, unable to bear it, jumped from a second-storey window in Heilbronn. The fall did not kill him, but it did leave him with a lifelong injury. Where did the years that followed take him?
answer: Into a series of asylum confinements
choices: Into a series of asylum confinements
Into voluntary exile in Paris and London
Into a monastery in the Black Forest
Into private practice as an army surgeon
context: Mayer spent the early 1850s in and out of the asylums at Goppingen, Kennenburg and Winnenthal; his own circle described him as a broken man when he emerged. He did not die in the fall or the asylum -- he lived on to 1878. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_von_Mayer  (Legend.)

question: In 1862, more than twenty years after that Java voyage, the Irish physicist John Tyndall stood up at London's Royal Institution to lecture on the discovery of energy. He had prepared a punchline. After crediting his ideas to 'a man of whom you have scarcely ever heard,' whom did he name?
answer: A German physician named Mayer
choices: A German physician named Mayer
A Prussian steam engineer named Krupp
A Danish civil servant named Colding
An Alsatian brewer named Reiss
context: Tyndall had rediscovered Mayer's buried 1842 paper while preparing his own lectures on heat and made rescuing Mayer a personal cause. The Royal Society finally handed Mayer its Copley Medal -- its highest honour -- in 1871; Joule had received the same medal only the year before. Even Joule eventually conceded the IDEA to Mayer while keeping the experimental proof. Source: https://skullsinthestars.com/2023/07/31/john-tyndall-rescues-julius-mayer-1862/

question: Barbara McClintock published her jumping-gene mechanism in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 1950. She had traced the speckled patches on maize kernels to TWO pieces of chromosome working together. What did she name them?
answer: Dissociation and Activator
choices: Dissociation and Activator
Sender and Receiver
Silencer and Enhancer
Cassette and Trigger
context: Ds (Dissociation) lands inside a pigment gene and shuts it off; Ac (Activator) can pop Ds back out partway through kernel development, and every cell descended from THAT one cell restarts the pigment. The colour patch is that family made visible. Source: Ac/Ds transposable controlling elements, Wikipedia.

question: For half a century before McClintock, the triumph of genetics had been mapping genes as units fixed in a fixed order along the chromosome -- and mapping meant nailing down their positions. What was heretical about McClintock's 1950 claim?
answer: Some of those units get up and move
choices: Some of those units get up and move
The chromosome itself was chemically misidentified
Mapping distances were pure statistical luck
Every unit was really two units fused together
context: Fixed-order mapping was the crown jewel of Morgan's fly-room and every classroom since. McClintock did not reject it -- she added an exception the model could not accommodate. Source: PMC 3528533, 'Barbara McClintock and the discovery of jumping genes'.

question: Barbara McClintock presented her Ac/Ds evidence at the 1951 Cold Spring Harbor Symposium to a room that included George Beadle and Salvador Luria. According to attendees, what reception did her talk actually meet?
answer: Puzzlement rather than argument
choices: Puzzlement rather than argument
Immediate applause and unanimous acceptance
An organised campaign to have her fired
A demand that she rerun the crosses at scale
context: By the mid-1950s she had stopped giving talks on controlling elements and largely stopped publishing on them. Not shunned; simply not followed. Source: MCB140 lecture notes (Berkeley) on McClintock.

question: Confirmation that genes really can move arrived not from corn but from a bacterium, when 'insertion sequences' were spotted jumping around chromosomes in 1968. Which bacterium?
answer: Escherichia coli
choices: Escherichia coli
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Bacillus subtilis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
context: Through the 1970s transposons were cloned and sequenced across many species, McClintock's picture was vindicated, and in 1983 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to her ALONE -- still the only unshared prize a woman has held in that category. Source: PMC 3528533.

question: The story goes that Barbara McClintock was a shunned, unemployed genius rediscovered by a Nobel committee in 1983. Historian Nathaniel Comfort's archival work 'The Tangled Field' (2001) shows a different picture: she held major professional offices even during her supposed wilderness years. Which of these did she actually hold in the 1940s?
answer: President of the Genetics Society of America
choices: President of the Genetics Society of America
Director of the Carnegie Department of Genetics
Editor-in-chief of the journal Genetics
President of the American Society of Naturalists
context: She took the GSA presidency in 1945 -- its first woman president -- and had been elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1944, only its third woman. What her colleagues resisted was her CLAIM about jumping genes, not her STANDING as a geneticist. A more useful lesson than martyrdom. Source: Comfort, 'The Tangled Field'; Wikipedia, 'Barbara McClintock'.

question: Once transposons were accepted, geneticists could total up how much of the human chromosome complement they and their broken remains account for. Roughly what fraction of the human genome is transposon-derived DNA?
answer: About half
choices: About half
About one percent
About five percent
Essentially all of it
context: Roughly 40-80% of many plant genomes too. Whether those elements are cellular machinery, cellular garbage or cellular parasites is the honest next question. Source: Current Biology, 'C-value paradox, junk DNA and ENCODE'.

question: In April 1980, two Nature papers appeared back-to-back giving transposons an unflattering new reading -- the opposite of McClintock's own controller interpretation. Leslie Orgel and Francis Crick published one; W. Ford Doolittle and Carmen Sapienza published the companion. What did the two 1980 papers argue transposons mostly are?
answer: Freeloaders replicating themselves at the cell's expense
choices: Freeloaders replicating themselves at the cell's expense
Relics of ancient viruses reawakened by stress
The primary drivers of new species forming
Sequences inherited only through the mother
context: Orgel and Crick titled theirs 'Selfish DNA: the ultimate parasite'; Doolittle and Sapienza's companion piece ran in the same issue. McClintock had read her elements as controllers doing something useful for the plant; the 1980 papers said no, they are propagating at the host's expense. The honest modern answer is that BOTH happen, and telling which is which in any given case is unfinished work. Source: Nature 288, 645 (1980), 'Selfish DNA'.

question: The Academy could not just declare a fraction of the planet - somebody had to measure it. From 1792 to 1798 two astronomers triangulated a long slice of the Paris meridian to nail the number down. Between which two coastal cities did their survey run?
answer: Dunkirk and Barcelona
choices: Dunkirk and Barcelona
Calais and Cadiz
Le Havre and Lisbon
Ostend and Marseille
context: Jean-Baptiste Delambre took Dunkirk south to Rodez; Pierre Mechain took Rodez through the Pyrenees to Barcelona. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement_of_Delambre_and_Mechain.

question: The two astronomers had to work through the French Revolution, hauling brass instruments up bell towers on hills nobody could explain. Suspicious villagers kept accusing them of one crime in particular and having them arrested. Of what were they accused?
answer: spying for the royalists
choices: spying for the royalists
practising forbidden witchcraft
hiding smuggled gold in the instrument cases
trespassing on private church land
context: Locals could not imagine a peaceful reason for strangers with polished brass and telescopes on their roofs; both men were detained more than once during the survey. Source: frieze.com/article/walking-dunkirk-barcelona-measure-curvature-earth.

question: The survey's key sighting instrument was a graduated brass ring built in 1784. Its cleverness was that stacking the same angle around the ring shrank the random error of any single sighting to a level no earlier instrument had reached. What was it called?
answer: Borda's repeating circle
choices: Borda's repeating circle
Ramsden's zenith sector
Cassini's meridian quadrant
Ramsden's theodolite
context: Designed by Jean-Charles de Borda and built by Etienne Lenoir in 1784. Its trick was to observe the same angle again and again around the ring; stacking N sightings divided the reading error by roughly N. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement_of_Delambre_and_Mechain.

question: Before choosing the meridian, the 1791 commission also considered a rival definition already in use around Europe: take the length of a pendulum that ticks once per second and call THAT the metre. The commission threw the idea out. What was the deciding objection?
answer: its length depends on local gravity and would differ from town to town
choices: its length depends on local gravity and would differ from town to town
wooden pendulums swell and shrink with the weather
no clock in France was accurate enough to time the ticks
the Church claimed pendulums as its own liturgical property
context: Jean Richer had discovered the gravity-with-latitude effect on his 1671-1673 Cayenne expedition. Talleyrand had proposed the pendulum standard in 1790; the commission - Borda, Lagrange, Laplace, Legendre, Lavoisier - rejected it in March 1791. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_metre.

question: Pierre Mechain measured the latitude of Barcelona from TWO different stations - the Mont-Jouy fortress and a rented inn. The two figures should have agreed to a whisker; they disagreed by about three arcseconds, roughly a hundred metres on the ground, and he could not explain it. What did he do with the second set?
answer: concealed it and altered his notebooks to shrink the gap
choices: concealed it and altered his notebooks to shrink the gap
blamed the Spanish military and demanded a new site
burned the papers and wrote a public confession
handed both sets to Delambre to arbitrate
context: The concealment tormented him for the rest of his life. He avoided returning to Paris to meet Delambre and produced almost no work for two years, and refused to share his raw data. Source: mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Mechain.

question: Modern analysis has largely vindicated Pierre Mechain: his Barcelona latitudes were being thrown off by a real geodetic effect nobody in 1795 had budgeted for. Roughly 95% of the missing length of the legal metre traces to this same effect, and it would not be properly modelled until the late 1800s. What is the effect called?
answer: deflection of the vertical
choices: deflection of the vertical
atmospheric refraction bias
sidereal parallax drift
polar wobble correction
context: Massive nearby terrain pulls a plumb line sideways, so 'straight down' does not point at the Earth's centre and a latitude taken by star sightings is genuinely thrown off. About 95% of the residual error in the legal metre traces to this unaccounted tilt. Mechain had stumbled on a real geodetic effect that would not be properly modelled for another century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement_of_Delambre_and_Mechain.

question: Kungalv, Sweden, Christmas 1938. Lise Meitner is on holiday when her nephew Otto Frisch arrives with a baffling letter from Berlin. They argue it out in the snowy woods, Frisch on skis, Meitner at sixty on foot. What did the two do when it came to arithmetic?
answer: Sat on a tree trunk and calculated on scraps of paper
choices: Sat on a tree trunk and calculated on scraps of paper
Turned back and telephoned Niels Bohr in Copenhagen
Waited until Frisch reached Bohr's institute
Posted the problem back to Otto Hahn in Berlin
context: Frisch's own memoir: 'we both sat down on a tree trunk... and started to calculate on scraps of paper.' Meitner was spending Christmas with the von Bahr family and had asked Frisch to come; there was nowhere else to go. She was a refugee sharing bench space in Manne Siegbahn's Stockholm institute, with no funding and no research group of her own; she called it her exile from physics. The physics of the atomic age got worked out sitting on a log. Source: Wikipedia 'Lise Meitner', quoting O. R. Frisch, What Little I Remember.

question: Lise Meitner is buried in St James's churchyard at Bramley, in Hampshire. The words on her gravestone were chosen by Otto Frisch, the nephew who had argued nuclear physics with her in the snow. They call her a physicist who never lost one particular thing. Which?
answer: Her humanity
choices: Her humanity
Her curiosity
Her nerve
Her country
context: The full inscription: 'Lise Meitner: a physicist who never lost her humanity.' She had lost her country, her laboratory, her name on papers she helped write, and the prize. The man who knew her best thought this was the thing worth carving. Source: De Gruyter Conversations, 'Lise Meitner: A physicist who never lost her humanity'; Atomic Heritage Foundation profile. (Grokipedia's Meitner page instead claims a Bible verse; that is unsupported elsewhere.)

question: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann had spent four years in Berlin firing neutrons at uranium and sorting the products by chemistry alone. In December 1938 they hit something that made no sense: the 'radium' they had been collecting refused to behave like radium. Hahn wrote to Lise Meitner on 19 December naming the element it was acting like instead, one far too light to be a chip off uranium. Which element?
answer: Barium
choices: Barium
Lanthanum
Cerium
Strontium
context: Hahn to Meitner: 'more and more we come to the frightful conclusion: our Ra-isotopes do not behave like Ra but like Ba.' He could not explain it, and asked whether she could suggest some fantastic explanation. They had been partners on the uranium problem since 1907. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'; APS News, 'December 1938: Discovery of Nuclear Fission'.

question: By July 1938 Lise Meitner had lived in Berlin for thirty-one years, and the Nazi regime had forbidden her to leave Germany legally. She boarded a train for the Dutch border with two small suitcases and no exit visa, and the Dutch physicist Dirk Coster rode with her to see her across. Otto Hahn gave her one thing to take with her. What?
answer: A diamond ring from his mother, to sell if she ran short
choices: A diamond ring from his mother, to sell if she ran short
A letter of introduction to Niels Bohr in Copenhagen
A packet of banknotes sewn into the lining of a case
The key to an account he had opened for her in Zurich
context: Hahn and Paul Rosbaud packed the two suitcases; Coster travelled down from the Netherlands to ride the train out with her; they crossed on 13 July 1938 at the lightly used Bad Nieuweschans station and were not stopped. She was fifty-nine, and the ring was Hahn's inheritance from his own mother. Source: Wikipedia 'Lise Meitner'; Sime, 'Lise Meitner's escape from Germany', American Journal of Physics.

question: The British contingent heading for Los Alamos invited Lise Meitner to join the bomb project. Her nephew Otto Frisch was already going, and the physics they meant to use was the physics she had worked out. She was a refugee with no laboratory, no funding and no permanent post, so the offer was everything she lacked. What did she answer?
answer: That she would have nothing to do with a bomb
choices: That she would have nothing to do with a bomb
That she would go only if the bomb were never used
That she would send the bomb team her calculations only
That she would wait to see what Germany built first
context: Her recorded reply: 'I will have nothing to do with a bomb!' She never worked on a nuclear weapon for any country. Grokipedia and the Atomic Heritage Foundation date the invitation to 1943, the US National Park Service to 1942; the refusal itself is not in dispute. Source: Ruth Lewin Sime, 'Lise Meitner: A Life in Physics' (1996), p. 305, quoted by the National Park Service and the Atomic Heritage Foundation.

question: Lise Meitner, out in the snow at Kungalv at Christmas 1938, recalled the empirical formula for the mass of a nucleus and added up the two fragments Otto Hahn's chemistry had produced. Together they came out lighter than the uranium nucleus they had come from, by about one-fifth the mass of a single proton. Otto Frisch put that missing sliver through E=mc-squared. Set against burning, how much energy per atom was it?
answer: About a hundred million times as much
choices: About a hundred million times as much
About a hundred thousand times as much
About a thousand times as much
About a million times as much
context: One-fifth of a proton mass works out to roughly 200 million electron-volts, 200 MeV, for every single atom that splits; a chemical reaction such as burning releases a few electron-volts per atom. That factor is the whole difference between a bonfire and a reactor, and it came off a scrap of paper. Source: Wikipedia 'Lise Meitner' (Frisch's account); Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission'.

question: Otto Hahn's letter of 19 December 1938 asked Lise Meitner to make sense of a light element his chemistry kept catching where only radium should have been, and hinted that she might suggest some fantastic explanation. She wrote back on 21 December. Nothing in the physics of 1938 allowed a heavy nucleus to come apart like that. What position did she take in the reply?
answer: She told him she doubted it but would not rule it out yet
choices: She told him she doubted it but would not rule it out yet
She told him the light element had to be contamination
She told him she had been expecting exactly this for years
She told him to publish nothing until she saw the raw data
context: Her exact words: 'At the moment the assumption of such a thoroughgoing breakup seems very difficult to me, but in nuclear physics we have experienced so many surprises, that one cannot unconditionally say: It is impossible.' She did not yet believe it. She refused to declare it impossible. That single sentence is what an open mind looks like in practice. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: Back at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen in January 1939, Otto Frisch had to write up a nuclear process nobody had a name for: a uranium nucleus coming apart into two pieces. He asked a colleague from another science what their own field called it, and borrowed their word. Which field did 'nuclear fission' come from?
answer: From biology: it is what a living cell does when it divides in two
choices: From biology: it is what a living cell does when it divides in two
From geology: it is what a crystal does when it cleaves in two
From engineering: it is what a loaded cable does when it parts in two
From metallurgy: it is what a hot billet does when it shears in two
context: Frisch asked what biologists call it when a living cell splits in two, was told 'binary fission', and borrowed the word. Sources disagree about the colleague: Wikipedia's fission-discovery page calls William A. Arnold a biologist, its nuclear-fission page calls him a physicist. The borrowing from biology is not in dispute. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'; Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission'.

question: A team at GSI Darmstadt led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Munzenberg fired iron-58 at bismuth-209 on 29 August 1982 and made a single atom of element 109. They proposed a name ten years later, and IUPAC approved meitnerium on 30 August 1997. Among all the named elements, meitnerium holds one distinction. Which?
answer: The only element named for a real woman and no one else
choices: The only element named for a real woman and no one else
The only element named for a person who held no doctorate
The only element named for a person who never saw it exist
The only element named for a person honoured while alive
context: Curium honours Pierre and Marie Curie together, which is why meitnerium stands alone as the one element named specifically after a woman who is not a figure out of myth. The whole basis for the honour was a handful of single atoms, made fifteen years before the name was approved. Source: Grokipedia 'Meitnerium'; Wikipedia 'Meitnerium'.

question: Niels Bohr pictured a heavy nucleus as a droplet of liquid: like a water drop, it is pulled into a ball by a kind of surface tension. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch imagined a captured neutron setting such a drop wobbling until it stretched out into a dumbbell. At that stretched moment, what finally pinches the drop in two?
answer: The protons' electric repulsion overpowers the surface tension
choices: The protons' electric repulsion overpowers the surface tension
The surface tension gathers each end into a ball of its own
The wobble itself builds until the stretched neck shakes apart
The thinned neck sheds an alpha particle and parts there
context: A uranium nucleus is crowded with protons, every one of them pushing on all the others. Stretching the drop pushes the two ends further apart, which loosens surface tension's grip while the electrical push between the halves keeps working; past a certain elongation the repulsion wins and the drop ruptures. The two positively charged fragments then hurl each other apart, and that is where the energy goes. Source: Grokipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: If Lise Meitner was right, each splitting nucleus would hurl its two halves apart with about 200 million electron-volts between them. The trouble was that a lump of uranium spits alpha particles constantly, and Otto Frisch had one Geiger counter and one day, 13 January 1939. What did he do to the counter so the answer could not be mistaken?
answer: Raised its trigger threshold until alpha particles were too weak to register
choices: Raised its trigger threshold until alpha particles were too weak to register
Put a foil in front of it thick enough to stop the alpha particles dead
Ran it for hours and subtracted the average alpha background afterwards
Packed it in paraffin so that slow neutrons would show up in the count
context: He set the threshold above anything an alpha could produce, so a fission fragment would give a pulse enormously bigger than any background. He switched it on and the giant pulses were there, exactly as predicted. A prediction that says 'you will see something far larger than this instrument has ever shown' is about as testable as physics gets. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann mailed their uranium paper to Die Naturwissenschaften on 22 December 1938. Where they had expected radium, actinium and thorium, their separations kept coming out barium and its chemical neighbours, elements a little over half uranium's weight. What did the published paper do about explaining the result?
answer: It gave the chemistry and said they could not bring themselves to believe it
choices: It gave the chemistry and said they could not bring themselves to believe it
It gave the chemistry and announced that the uranium nucleus had broken in two
It gave the chemistry and blamed a contaminant somewhere in the apparatus
It gave the chemistry and appealed in print for a physicist to explain it
context: Their own sentence: 'As chemists... we should substitute the symbols Ba, La, Ce for Ra, Ac, Th. As "nuclear chemists" fairly close to physics we cannot yet bring ourselves to take this step which contradicts all previous experience in physics.' They had the fact and refused to claim the explanation, and they printed the refusal rather than hide it. Published 6 January 1939. Source: Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences left the 1944 Chemistry prize unawarded, and did not settle it until November 1945, three months after the war ended. It was to go for the discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei, worked out by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin and Lise Meitner in Stockholm. What did the Academy's narrow majority decide?
answer: To give it to Otto Hahn alone, for discovering fission
choices: To give it to Otto Hahn alone, for discovering fission
To give it to Lise Meitner alone, for explaining fission
To give it jointly to Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann
To give it jointly to Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner
context: Hahn collected it in Stockholm on 10 December 1945, 'for his discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei'. Neither Meitner nor Strassmann was included. Get the date right: the 1944 prize was decided in November 1945. Grokipedia's fission page gives 16 November 1944, which contradicts its own Meitner page and the archival study. Source: Crawford, Sime & Walker, 'A Nobel Tale of Postwar Injustice', Physics Today 50(9), Sept 1997; NobelPrize.org.

question: Enrico Fermi announced in 1934 that neutron-bombarded uranium had made brand-new elements heavier than uranium itself. That same year the German chemist Ida Noddack published an objection: the products, she wrote, need not be uranium's neighbours at all, because the nucleus might break up into several large fragments. Fermi brushed the suggestion aside. What did Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann do about Fermi's new elements over the four years that followed?
answer: They published seven papers of their own hunting the same new elements
choices: They published seven papers of their own hunting the same new elements
They left uranium alone for four years and stayed with older work
They wrote to Ida Noddack and worked the fragment idea up with her
They set the chemistry aside to hunt for the missing energy first
context: Hahn, Meitner and Strassmann themselves published seven papers between 1935 and 1938 on transuranic elements that were not there, and the Joliot-Curies in Paris reported the same. Noddack had the idea four years early, with no mechanism and no energy calculation to go with it, so nobody took it up. Being right is not enough to move a field; the mechanism and the numbers are what Meitner and Frisch supplied four years later. Source: Wikipedia 'Nuclear fission'; Wikipedia 'Discovery of nuclear fission'.

question: The Nobel committees' files stay sealed for fifty years. When Elisabeth Crawford, Ruth Lewin Sime and Mark Walker read the file on the 1944 Chemistry prize and published it in 1997, they found no considered judgement against Lise Meitner at all. Evaluators could not handle a discovery straddling chemistry and physics; the committees knew little theoretical physics; wartime Sweden was cut off. One cause was uglier: the published record they were reading had itself been bent against her. What had bent it?
answer: Nazi rules had forced her name off the German papers she helped produce
choices: Nazi rules had forced her name off the German papers she helped produce
Wartime censors had held the Berlin journals back until after the war
Her Stockholm host had published her Swedish results under his own name
The Nature letters she wrote with Otto Frisch had been printed unsigned
context: Crawford, Sime and Walker found four causes, none of them a weighed rejection of her work: the evaluators' inability to handle a cross-disciplinary discovery, the committees' thin competence in theoretical physics, Sweden's wartime isolation, and nobody allowing for the fact that Nazi persecution had distorted the published record itself. The failure belongs to the Academy's committees, not to Hahn. Source: Crawford, Sime & Walker, 'A Nobel Tale of Postwar Injustice', Physics Today 50(9), Sept 1997.

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar in Brno, needed to know exactly which plant fathered every pea he grew - and a pea blossom is quite capable of pollinating itself. So he pried each young bud open with fine forceps. What did he do before brushing on his chosen pollen?
answer: Cut out its anthers before they could shed
choices: Cut out its anthers before they could shed
Snipped its petals off so no bee would land
Brushed its own pollen away with a feather
Tied the young bud shut until he was ready
context: He then bagged the blossom so no insect could interfere. Every cross in the whole eight-year run, 1856-1863, was made by hand this way, in the vegetable garden of St Thomas's Abbey - roughly 28,000 plants, seven either/or traits, one at a time. The pea's habit of fertilising itself inside the closed flower is exactly why its lines breed true, and exactly why Mendel had to open every single blossom himself. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Hybridization Methods and Observations; Methodological Innovations).

question: Gregor Mendel crossed a pea line whose seeds were always round with a line whose seeds were always wrinkled - two parents, each utterly reliable. He grew the whole hybrid generation and opened the pods. What was inside?
answer: Every seed round, and not one wrinkled anywhere
choices: Every seed round, and not one wrinkled anywhere
Every seed faintly dimpled, halfway between them
Round seeds and wrinkled seeds in equal numbers
Round seeds in some pods, wrinkled in others
context: The wrinkled form was not weakened and not averaged away. It was simply gone - and Mendel could only find out what had become of it by letting these hybrids pollinate themselves and counting the generation after, seed by seed. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Quantitative Data; Hybridization Methods and Observations).

question: Gregor Mendel bred mice before he ever touched a pea - grey crossed with white, in his own room at St Thomas's Abbey, to watch how coat colour passed from parent to young. The story goes that the mice had to go. What ended them?
answer: His bishop objected to a monk breeding animals that mate
choices: His bishop objected to a monk breeding animals that mate
His abbot claimed the room back for the abbey library
The town council feared mice loose in the granaries
His physician judged the cages a risk to his health
context: Mendel switched to plants, and is said to have remarked, with some amusement, that the objection had overlooked the fact that plants have sex lives too. The tale reaches us through later tellings rather than Mendel's own papers, so treat it as a good story with a plausible core - the mouse work itself is well attested. Sources: Asimov Press, 'Origins of the Lab Mouse'; PNAS 119 (2022), 'Behavioral genetics and genomics: Mendel's peas, mice, and bees'.  (Legend.)

question: Gregor Mendel's round-by-wrinkled hybrids had all grown round seeds; the wrinkled form had vanished, and nothing told him whether it was gone for good. He let those hybrids pollinate themselves and counted the whole next generation, 7,324 seeds, one at a time. How did that harvest come out?
answer: 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled - near three to one
choices: 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled - near three to one
7,324 round to none wrinkled - the form was gone
3,662 round to 3,662 wrinkled - a dead even split
6,591 round to 733 wrinkled - near nine to one
context: Never exactly three to one: seed shape came out at 2.96, the seed interior at 3.01 (6,022 yellow to 2,001 green), stem height at 2.84 (787 tall to 277 dwarf), and the remaining four traits between 2.82 and 3.15. Mendel got a law out of numbers that never landed clean by counting until the wobble stopped mattering. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Quantitative Data); remaining four traits per OpenStax Biology 2e, ch.12.

question: Gregor Mendel taught physics and natural history to over 300 boys at the Brunn Realschule for thirteen years - and for all thirteen he was only a substitute. He had even gone to Vienna to study physics under Christian Doppler. What kept him off the permanent staff?
answer: He twice failed the teaching-certificate examination
choices: He twice failed the teaching-certificate examination
His abbey forbade him any salaried post outside it
He refused the loyalty oath the state demanded
His weather station for Moravia ate half his week
context: He flunked the oral portion in 1850, then failed again in 1856 after two years at the University of Vienna under Doppler in physics and Franz Unger in botany. The man who founded the study of heredity was never certified to teach school science. He did also run the abbey's official weather station for Moravia, log sunspots, and keep the abbey's bees - the peas were the side project of a man with no spare time. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (University of Vienna; Daily Life and Responsibilities).

question: Gregor Mendel spent eight years counting peas to test a doctrine of inheritance that every naturalist of his day simply assumed. Nobody thought it needed checking. His tallies broke it. Which doctrine was it?
answer: Blending: the parents' traits mix like paints and cannot be unmixed
choices: Blending: the parents' traits mix like paints and cannot be unmixed
Pangenesis: every organ sheds tiny particles that gather in the seed
Use-inheritance: traits a parent strengthens in life pass to its young
Preformation: a whole miniature lies folded in the seed already
context: Under blending inheritance, a wrinkled form crossed into a round-seeded line should have been thinned away for good. Instead it vanished for one whole generation and came back undiluted - heredity travels in units that can hide without being watered down. The other three were real rival doctrines held by serious people: pangenesis was Darwin's own proposal, use-inheritance was Lamarck's, and preformation had ruled the previous century. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Factors Hindering Immediate Recognition; Foundational Role in Genetics).

question: Before Gregor Mendel crossed a single flower, he spent two years, 1856 and 1857, on 34 varieties of pea - planting them, leaving them alone, and watching what came up. Only 22 varieties went forward into the experiment proper. What was he checking?
answer: Whether each gave identical offspring, generation after generation
choices: Whether each gave identical offspring, generation after generation
Whether each could ripen inside the short Moravian summer
Whether each flowered early enough to be crossed with the rest
Whether each threw enough seed to be counted in thousands
context: Those 22 bred true: left to pollinate themselves, they gave back the same form year after year, which is the only thing that makes a hybrid's behaviour readable at all. The screening came first and the experiment came second - two of Mendel's eight years went into testing his own materials before he tested a single idea. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Rationale for Pea Plants).

question: For thirty-four years Gregor Mendel's pea paper sat unread in the proceedings of a small Brno society. Then, within a few months of 1900, three botanists - Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak - each dug that paper out. What had happened to all three?
answer: Each had hit the same ratios himself, in a different plant
choices: Each had hit the same ratios himself, in a different plant
Each had been handed a copy by a teacher who knew Mendel
Each was combing old journals for forgotten Austrian science
Each had been sent the paper by the abbey after Mendel died
context: De Vries found the ratios in evening primrose and published in French in June 1900 without citing Mendel, then amended his German report to acknowledge Mendel's priority; Correns had them in four-o'clocks and credited Mendel outright in April 1900; von Tschermak was working on peas and published in July. Three plants, three laboratories, one forgotten friar - sixteen years dead. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Key Rediscoverers in 1900).

question: Gregor Mendel also ran the cross with two traits at once, using peas that differed in both seed shape and seed colour. Out of 556 seeds he counted 315 round-and-yellow, 108 round-and-green, 101 wrinkled-and-yellow and 32 wrinkled-and-green. What did that four-way split show him?
answer: Shape and colour are dealt out independently of each other
choices: Shape and colour are dealt out independently of each other
Shape and colour travel together, inherited as one package
Colour comes from the pollen parent and shape from the other
Each trait halves the other's chance of showing at all
context: That is the 9:3:3:1 pattern - two independent near-three-to-one splits multiplied together. The two middle classes are easy to swap: 101 is the wrinkled-yellow class and 108 the round-green one, per Mendel's own tabulation. Independence does not hold for every pair of traits in nature; ones riding close together on the same chromosome are handed down as a set, which nobody would understand until long after Mendel died. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (dihybrid tabulation, N=556).

question: On New Year's Eve 1866 Gregor Mendel posted his pea paper to Carl Naegeli, the most eminent botanist he could reach. Naegeli's private verdict, four words in the margin, was 'only empirical and not rational'. Ten letters passed between them over seven years and he never once engaged with the counts - but he did give Mendel one piece of advice. What was it?
answer: Run the whole experiment again in hawkweed, his own speciality
choices: Run the whole experiment again in hawkweed, his own speciality
Run the whole experiment again in beans, an easier flower to open
Rewrite the paper for a Vienna journal with a far wider reach
Hand his seed to a professional breeder who could check it
context: Naegeli did write back, two months later: 'It seems to me that the experiments with Pisum, far from being finished, are only a beginning.' Then he steered Mendel into Hieracium, the genus Naegeli had made his own. It cost Mendel four years and very nearly his eyesight, and it produced nothing. Sources: The Scientist, 'The Mendel-Naegeli Letters, circa 1866-73'; grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel.

question: Gregor Mendel's 1866 pea paper does not stop at the counts. Having set out which trait masks which, and how often the hidden one comes back, he tells his readers what he thinks actually passes from parent to offspring. What did Mendel say it was?
answer: Differing elements inside the cell
choices: Differing elements inside the cell
Genes strung along the chromosomes
Gemmules shed by every organ
Pangens gathered in the cell
context: Mendel wrote in German of differirende Zellelemente - differing cell elements - and of Merkmale, traits. He could not have written 'gene': Wilhelm Johannsen coined it in 1909, and William Bateson coined 'genetics' in 1905, both more than twenty years after Mendel's death. He never saw a chromosome identified as the carrier, and never wrote a word about DNA. Two of his own words did survive intact into that vocabulary assembled long after he was dead: 'dominant' and 'recessive' are his. Sources: Hereditas (2023), 'Mendel's terminology and notation reveal his understanding of genetics'; genome.gov, '1909: The Word Gene Coined'; historyofinformation.com, 'William Bateson Coins the Term Genetics'.

question: From 1869 Gregor Mendel worked not on peas but on hawkweed, a daisy whose flower head is a crowd of florets so tiny that he dissected them under a plain hand lens, often in poor light, until 'a peculiar fatigue and exhaustion of the eyes' set in. Past 5,000 florets later he had no clean ratios at all - and he blamed his own clumsy hands. What had really defeated him?
answer: Much hawkweed seed forms with no fertilisation at all, so nothing is shuffled
choices: Much hawkweed seed forms with no fertilisation at all, so nothing is shuffled
Hawkweed traits all ride on one chromosome, so nothing ever separates
His hawkweed stocks had never been screened, so none of them bred true
Hawkweed hybrids are sterile, so the second generation never arrived
context: The trick is apomixis: many Hieracium build a seed with no meiosis and no fertilisation, so the offspring are clones of the mother and nothing is ever dealt out afresh. In H. piloselloides and H. aurantiacum only about 2.0% and 2.4% of seeds formed sexually. Mendel read his clone-like offspring as his own botched handiwork and blamed his hands for a plant that had simply skipped sex. His verdict, July 1870: 'the hybrids of Hieracium show a behaviour exactly opposite to those of Pisum.' He had the right law and the wrong organism, and no way in 1870 to tell which. Sources: PMC5121183, 'Seeds of doubt: Mendel's choice of Hieracium to study inheritance'; J. Exp. Botany 62(5):1699, 'Apomixis in hawkweed: Mendel's experimental nemesis'.

question: In 1936 the statistician R. A. Fisher checked Gregor Mendel's tables with chi-square tests, the standard measure of how far a set of counts strays from the theory it is meant to fit. Fisher's complaint was not that Mendel's counts missed. It was that they hugged theory too tightly - the joint odds of fits that good ran near one in twenty thousand. Fisher stopped short of accusing Mendel. What did he offer instead?
answer: That an assistant who knew what was expected had deceived him
choices: That an assistant who knew what was expected had deceived him
That the Brunn printers had tidied the tables before setting them
That the rediscoverers of 1900 had recopied the figures wrongly
That peas themselves ripen too unevenly ever to be counted well
context: Fisher's own words were blunt - the data 'have been falsified so as to give a closer fit to expectations than would have been likely to occur by chance' - but he added that 'it remains a possibility among others that Mendel was deceived by some assistant who knew too well what was expected.' And the laws stood. Modern replications of Mendel's crosses reproduce his patterns, and a 2020 Monte Carlo fact-check of his two-trait data found the goodness-of-fit well inside what honest experiment can produce: differential seed viability, pollen-tube competition and aggregated replicates can all tighten a ratio with nobody's thumb on the scale. Science audited its own founder in public, and the finding survived the audit. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Gregor_Mendel (Mendelian Paradox; Defenses Based on Empirical Rigor), citing Fisher 1936, Annals of Science 1:115-137; Franklin et al., 'Ending the Mendel-Fisher Controversy'.

question: Gregor Mendel counted wrinkled peas for years without ever learning what wrinkles them. In 1990 researchers found the recessive form of his seed-shape factor: a piece of DNA had jumped into the middle of a gene and killed it, and that gene's job had been to lock loose sugar away as starch. Why does a broken copy leave the ripe seed wrinkled?
answer: The unpacked sugar pulls in water, and the swollen seed collapses on drying
choices: The unpacked sugar pulls in water, and the swollen seed collapses on drying
The unused sugar hardens the seed coat, which then cracks into deep ridges
The seed runs short of food, shrivels early and never fills out its pod
The jumped DNA also breaks the gene that smooths the growing seed coat
context: The gene is starch-branching enzyme SBEI, broken by a transposon-like insertion of about 0.8 kb (Bhattacharyya, Smith et al., Cell 60, 1990). With the enzyme dead the seed makes far less starch, leaves nearly twice as much sucrose sitting in the cell, draws in extra water as it grows fat, then collapses into wrinkles as it dries - answered 124 years after Mendel counted them. The last of his seven traits was pinned to DNA only in 2025: a roughly 100,000-base deletion upstream of the chlorophyll-synthase gene ChlG makes yellow pods, an Ogre retrotransposon in a MYB gene plus a premature stop in a CLE peptide gene make constricted pods, and a five-base deletion moves the flowers to the tip of the plant. Every one turned out to be a single locus, exactly as the counting had said. Sources: Cell 60 (1990); Nature (2025), 'Genomic and genetic insights into Mendel's pea genes'.

question: Seven years before Mendeleev, in 1862, Beguyer de Chancourtois arranged the known elements so that chemical cousins fell together. Then the journal printed his paper without its diagram, and nobody could follow the argument. What had the missing diagram shown?
answer: The elements wound in a spiral round a cylinder
choices: The elements wound in a spiral round a cylinder
The elements stacked in a staircase of eight steps
The elements linked in rings of three by family
The elements plotted as a rising and falling curve
context: Beguyer de Chancourtois called his 1862 arrangement the 'telluric screw': the elements wound round a cylinder in order of atomic weight, so that ones with similar properties came out above one another. The paper went to print without its diagram, so nobody could follow the argument, and the work sank. The rival schemes of those years were all real and clever - Johann Doebereiner's 1817 'triads', John Newlands' 1865 'law of octaves', Lothar Meyer's 1870 atomic-volume curve - and every one of them sorted the elements. Not one of them bet on a hole. Mendeleev did: conclusion 6 of his 1869 paper reads, 'One can predict the discovery of many new elements, for example analogues of Si and Al with atomic weights of 65-75.' He was too ill to present that paper himself - his colleague Nikolai Menshutkin read it to the Russian Chemical Society in St Petersburg on 6 March 1869 (22 February, Old Style). Sources: Grokipedia 'Dmitri Mendeleev'; Mendeleev 1869, English translation in Carmen Giunta's Classic Chemistry archive; Chemistry World, 'Ordering the elements'.

question: Gallium, the metal Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran teased out of zinc ore in 1875, is soft and silvery, much like aluminium, and sits solid on the shelf. Close a bare hand around a lump and hold it a minute or two, and it does what no other common metal does. What happens to the lump?
answer: It melts into a silvery puddle at body heat
choices: It melts into a silvery puddle at body heat
It tarnishes to a dull black crust in seconds
It grows cold enough to numb the fingers
It crumbles into brittle grey flakes
context: Gallium melts at 29.8 degrees C. That was on the shopping list: in 1871 Mendeleev specified for the square under aluminium an atomic weight of about 68, an oxide of formula E2O3, a chloride ECl3, salts more basic than aluminium's, and a notably LOW melting point. Gallium's atomic weight is 69.72 and its oxide is Ga2O3. Boisbaudran announced it on 27 August 1875, having caught two violet lines at about 417.2 and 403.1 nanometres in the spark spectrum of sphalerite from the Pierrefitte mine in the Hautes-Pyrenees, and named it after Gallia, the Latin name for France. Sources: Grokipedia "Mendeleev's predicted elements"; Wikipedia 'Gallium'; Grokipedia 'Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran'.

question: Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran built his own spectroscopes, published 246 papers between 1866 and 1911, and found three elements - the first of them dropping straight into one of Mendeleev's empty squares. He worked in a laboratory on the second floor of his family's house in western France, paid for out of the family business. What was that business?
answer: Distilling brandy for the export trade
choices: Distilling brandy for the export trade
Smelting zinc and lead from mountain ore
Grinding optical glass for instrument makers
Milling flour for the towns along the river
context: The laboratory sat on the second floor of the family house on Rue de Lusignan in the town of Cognac, and cognac paid for it. Boisbaudran never held an academic post of any kind. A rumour later went round that he had quietly named gallium after himself - 'le coq' is French for 'the rooster', and the Latin for rooster is gallus - and he denied the conjecture in print in an 1877 article. Treat that one as a story, not a fact. Sources: Grokipedia 'Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran'; Wikipedia 'Gallium'.

question: Mendeleev's table had squares with nothing in them, and he needed to call those squares something before anyone found their tenants. He did not improvise: every empty square got its name by the same rule. What was the rule?
answer: Name it for the element directly above, plus a counting word
choices: Name it for the element directly above, plus a counting word
Name it for the atomic weight its tenant was expected to have
Name it for the mineral its tenant was expected to hide in
Name it for a planet, taken in order outward from the Sun
context: The counting words were Sanskrit: eka- ('one'), dvi- ('two'), tri- ('three'), attached to the element sitting directly above the hole. 'Eka-aluminium' therefore meant simply 'one row below aluminium', and 'eka-silicon' meant 'one row below silicon'. Mendeleev knew Otto von Boehtlingk, the Sanskrit scholar at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, and the neutral, numerical naming had a diplomatic advantage: it favoured no living language and staked no national claim on an element nobody had yet found. Source: Grokipedia "Mendeleev's predicted elements".

question: The most-repeated story about the periodic table has it arriving in a dream - Mendeleev falling asleep exhausted, seeing the whole arrangement complete, waking and writing it out. His own notebooks describe a different method entirely. How did Mendeleev actually work the arrangement out?
answer: He shuffled element cards, like a game of patience
choices: He shuffled element cards, like a game of patience
He built a wooden model with rows that slid on rails
He sorted them by the colours of their burning salts
He read the pattern off a graph of atomic volumes
context: The record shows years of sorting element cards 'in a way similar to playing a game of patience' - solitaire - not a vision. The dream story, with its night of drinking and card-playing, is not supported by the evidence; nor is the related claim that Mendeleev set Russian vodka at 40% alcohol, a figure that comes from 18th-century tax law and predates his thesis on alcohol and water. One of the wrong answers is a real chemist's real method: the graph of atomic volumes is Lothar Meyer's 1870 curve, a rival system to Mendeleev's table rather than a way of building it.
