context: Miller himself was a careful and honest observer; his apparatus was simply not thermally isolated. The Miller episode is a useful reminder that a positive signal can be as much an artefact as a null one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment.

question: Milutin Milankovic married Kristina Topuzovic on 14 June 1914 and took her to his home village of Dalj. Two weeks later Franz Ferdinand was shot in Sarajevo, and Austro-Hungarian police arrested the 35-year-old engineer. What made him worth arresting?
answer: He held a commission in the Serbian army reserve
choices: He had signed a petition against Austrian rule
He was carrying survey maps of the Danube frontier
He held a commission in the Serbian army reserve
He taught at Belgrade's university, in the enemy capital
context: Milankovic held a reserve commission in the Royal Serbian Army, which turned a professor on his honeymoon into an enemy officer the moment Austria-Hungary moved against Serbia. He never got back to Belgrade: roughly six weeks under house arrest, then a train to the internment camp at Nezsider in Hungary, today Neusiedl am See in Austria. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; Smithsonian Magazine, 'This World War I Prisoner of War Solved the Mystery of the Ice Ages', 26 August 2024.

question: Milankovic was held overnight after his arrest. He opened the luggage he still had with him: inside were his printed papers and his notes on what he called the cosmic problem. By his own memoir, what did he do with the rest of that night?
answer: He started writing, and stopped long past midnight
choices: He read one paper over and over until the light failed
He started writing, and stopped long past midnight
He hid the notes where the guards would not find them
He wrote to his old Vienna professor asking for help
context: His memoirs, word for word: 'In the suitcase I had my printed works and my notes on the cosmic problem, there was clean paper too and I started writing. It was far past midnight when I stopped.' Smithsonian describes the container as a briefcase holding a few scientific papers and some of his notes. Flagged as testimony because the only witness to that night is Milankovic himself, writing years later. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic', quoting the memoirs; Smithsonian Magazine, 26 August 2024.  (Legend.)

question: Milankovic walked out of the internment camp at Nezsider on Christmas Eve 1914, but not into freedom: he was moved to Budapest, barred from leaving the city and ordered to report to the police every week. Kalman Szily, who ran the library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, heard which prisoner had come to town. What did Szily do?
answer: Gave him a desk in the library and left him to work
choices: Found him paid work cataloguing the library's maps
Set him to translating papers for the Academy's journal
Had the library's clerks copy his notes for the Academy
Gave him a desk in the library and left him to work
context: Szily 'eagerly accepted Milankovic and enabled him to work undisturbed in the Academy's library and the Central Meteorological Institute' -- for the remaining four years of the war. The release itself was arranged by his old Vienna professor Emanuel Czuber, pressed by Milankovic's wife Kristina and his uncle Vasa. Kristina, an amateur opera singer, crossed a war to join him, and their only child Vasilije was born in Budapest on 25 December 1915 -- in the city his father was forbidden to leave. Milankovic on those years: 'I was her prisoner of war, and in her my four-year longing for freedom would have drained my core, if I had not found refuge in scientific work.' Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; European Geosciences Union portrait; Grokipedia; Smithsonian Magazine, 26 August 2024.

question: Milankovic spent the rest of the war at a desk in Budapest, doing the same calculation over and over: a hundred days of it for one set of tables, and no calculating machine in the room. Every line was worked by hand with a pen, and every finished line gave him one number. A number for what?
answer: The sunlight arriving at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
choices: The sunlight arriving at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
The hours of daylight at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
The height of the noon Sun at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
The snow left unmelted at one latitude of Earth in one ancient season
context: The quantity has a name: insolation, the sunlight arriving on a patch of Earth. Those hundred days produced a graph of solar radiation at 55, 60 and 65 degrees north reaching back about 600,000 years, computed line by line without a machine. The same problem filled roughly 27 years and four works: 'Theorie mathematique des phenomenes thermiques produits par la radiation solaire' (1920), the curve printed by Wladimir Koppen and Alfred Wegener in 1924, 'Mathematische Klimalehre' (1930), and the 1941 Canon. A laptop now redoes the whole calculation in a fraction of a second. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; Grokipedia; European Geosciences Union portrait.

question: Milankovic was not the first to blame the ice ages on Earth's orbit. Fifty years earlier a Scot named James Croll had published that idea in the Philosophical Magazine, bylined 'James Croll, Anderson's University' in Glasgow. Croll had been a wheelwright and a tea merchant, had taught himself physics and astronomy, and corresponded with Charles Darwin. What was his post at Anderson's University?
answer: The janitor, who swept and locked up
choices: The porter, who carried and fetched
The clerk, who shelved the journals
The janitor, who swept and locked up
The technician, who mended the instruments
context: James Croll (1821-1890) worked as a wheelwright, a tea merchant, a temperance-hotel manager and an insurance agent before becoming janitor at Anderson's University in 1859 -- and then taught himself physics and astronomy out of the library he was employed to keep. His orbital ice-age theory ran in the Philosophical Magazine in 1864. By the end of the century it was discredited, partly because estimates of how fast Niagara Falls was cutting back its gorge did not fit his chronology. Some scholars now argue the cycles should be called Croll-Milankovitch cycles. Source: Wikipedia, 'James Croll'.

question: Milankovic sent the manuscript of his life's work, the 626-page 'Canon of Insolation and the Ice-Age Problem', to a Belgrade printing house on 2 April 1941. Four days later, on Hitler's order to destroy the city from the air, German bombers levelled the printing house. What became of the book?
answer: The printed sheets survived in the warehouse and it appeared that year
choices: A set of proofs reached Vienna and was printed there after the war
The printed sheets survived in the warehouse and it appeared that year
He rewrote it from his surviving notes and published it in 1948
Only the first hundred pages survived, issued later as a pamphlet
context: 'The manuscript was submitted to print on 2 April 1941 -- four days before the attack of Nazi Germany and its allies on the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In the bombing of Belgrade on 6 April 1941, the printing house where his work was being printed was destroyed; however, almost all of the printed sheet paper remained undamaged in the printing warehouse.' The raid was German, not Allied: the Luftwaffe's Operation Retribution, first bombs at 06:30 on a Sunday morning, after Hitler ordered that Belgrade be destroyed from the air by continual day and night attack. The National Library of Serbia burned to the ground in the same raid. The 626-page 'Kanon der Erdbestrahlung und seine Anwendung auf das Eiszeitenproblem' was published that same year by the Royal Serbian Academy. (Grokipedia's article calls it Allied bombing; for 6 April 1941 that is wrong.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'; EGU portrait; RFE/RL, 'Operation Punishment: The Nazi Bombing Of Belgrade 80 Years Ago'.

question: Milankovic's tables held one quantity over and over: the sunlight arriving at 65 degrees north, season by season, epoch by epoch. Buried in those columns was the one condition that lets an ice sheet thicken year after year until it covers a continent. Putting a number on that condition is what turned an old hunch into a theory anyone could test. By his arithmetic, which condition is it?
answer: A summer too cool to melt off the winter's snow
choices: A spring thaw that comes weeks late in the year
A summer too cool to melt off the winter's snow
A first autumn snow that falls weeks early
A winter cold enough to bury the ground in snow
context: James Croll had argued in the 1860s that glacials begin when winters are long and cold -- more snow, more ice. Milankovic turned the argument around: what matters is not winter but summer. Snow that survives one weak summer reflects sunlight back to space and helps keep the next summer cool, so the ice compounds; melting is the lever, not snowfall, which is why he computed summer sunlight at 65 degrees north. He did not invent the idea: Joseph John Murphy proposed in 1869 that ice ages need a long, cool summer and a short, mild winter, and Milankovic adopted it. His own contribution was to make it calculable -- an actual sunlight number for a given latitude in a given epoch -- which is what turned a hunch into something testable. Sources: CliMA/Caltech, 'Sunlight and the pace of ice ages', 4 August 2026; Encyclopedia of the Environment, 'Astronomical theories of climate'.

question: On 15 May 1941, a month after the raid, two German officers knocked at Milankovic's house in occupied Belgrade. They were geology students in uniform, and they brought greetings from Professor Wolfgang Soergel of Freiburg. Milankovic sent something back to Soergel with them, into the country whose bombers had flattened his printer. What did he put in their hands?
answer: The only complete printed copy of his Canon
choices: The only complete printed copy of his Canon
The hand-drawn plates of his insolation curves
His wartime notebooks from the Budapest library
The manuscript pages he had kept from the printer
context: Wikipedia records it plainly: the two officers 'brought greetings from Professor Wolfgang Soergel of Freiburg. Milankovic gave them the only complete printed copy of the Canon to send to Soergel, to make certain that his work would be preserved.' The man whose printer had just been bombed handed his only finished book to two soldiers of the army that bombed it -- because they were geology students, and they would keep it safe. Flagged as testimony: the scene comes down from the Milankovic side rather than from an independent record. Source: Wikipedia, 'Milutin Milankovic'.  (Legend.)

question: Milutin Milankovic died in December 1958, and the Belgian climatologist Andre Berger has recounted that a geologist called his ice-age theory rubbish just a year before that. Eighteen years later J. D. Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton tested it in Science, in a paper titled 'Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages'. Checking a curve of ancient sunlight meant finding somewhere the climate of the past 450,000 years had left a readable record. Where did they read it?
answer: In the mud collecting on the floor of the deep ocean
choices: In the moraines left by the four Alpine glaciations
In the mud collecting on the floor of the deep ocean
In the gorge Niagara Falls has cut back since the ice
In the ice sheet standing over the middle of Greenland
context: Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton read three indices of global climate over the past 450,000 years out of Southern Hemisphere ocean-floor sediments. The record gave 'three discrete spectral peaks at periods of 23,000, 42,000, and approximately 100,000 years', holding about 10, 25 and 50 percent of the climatic variance, and the three authors concluded that 'changes in the earth's orbital geometry are the fundamental cause of the succession of Quaternary ice ages'. Milankovic had died on 12 December 1958 -- eighteen years, almost to the day, before the paper appeared. His own answer to obscurity: 'As many scientific discoveries, far greater than mine, had remained unrecognized for years, I knew that, if my work was to become a real contribution to science, it would find its way without any help, recommendation or praise.' Sources: Science, 10 December 1976, vol. 194 no. 4270, pp. 1121-1132, DOI 10.1126/science.194.4270.1121; Smithsonian Magazine, 26 August 2024.

question: The 1976 cores vindicated Milankovic and left one hole nobody has filled. One of his three wobbles gives by far the feeblest push: it alters the sunlight Earth receives by less than a fifth of a watt per square metre, a small fraction of what the other two swing. Yet for the last million years the ice ages have marched to that feeble wobble's roughly 100,000-year beat, and why the weakest push moves the most ice is still unsolved. The cores held one more clue: before about a million years ago the ice ages kept a different, shorter rhythm. Which rhythm?
answer: About 41,000 years, the beat of the axis tipping
choices: About 26,000 years, the beat of the axis wheeling
About 41,000 years, the beat of the axis tipping
About 23,000 years, the beat of the seasons drifting
About 19,000 years, the beat of the orbit swiveling
context: The switch is called the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, roughly 1.25 to 0.7 million years ago: before it, the ice ages followed the 41,000-year tipping of Earth's axis between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees; after it, the ~100,000-year beat took over, and nobody has explained either the switch or why the feeblest forcing dominates. The numbers that make it bite: eccentricity moves the global annual mean by under 0.2 watts per square metre, precession swings midsummer sunlight at 65 degrees north by 3 to 5, obliquity by roughly 0.5 to 1 in high-latitude annual means. Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton flagged the puzzle in their own 1976 abstract -- explaining the eccentricity correlation 'probably requires an assumption of nonlinearity'. The most recent major attempt, Stephen Barker and colleagues in Science on 28 February 2025, still says the 100,000-year problem 'remains unresolved'. One prediction from the 1941 Canon has not expired: this warm interglacial holds, and the next glacial advance begins in roughly 50,000 years. Sources: Grokipedia, '100,000-year problem'; Science 1976 and 2025.

question: In December 1952 a 22-year-old graduate student in Chicago sealed methane, ammonia, hydrogen and boiling water into a loop of glass and shot a spark through it for a whole week to imitate lightning over a young ocean. What was his name?
answer: Stanley Miller
choices: Stanley Miller
Linus Pauling
James Watson
Carl Sagan
context: Miller was working under Harold Urey at the University of Chicago. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Miller ; nasonline.org (Miller memoir).

question: Long before Stanley Miller ever built his apparatus, Charles Darwin had guessed in an 1871 letter to Joseph Hooker that life's first chemistry might have happened in a certain kind of place, 'with all sorts of ammonia and phosphoric salts, light, heat, electricity.' What did Darwin call the setting?
answer: a warm little pond
choices: a warm little pond
a deep sea trench
a lightning-struck peak
a fresh volcanic crater
context: Darwin never published on the origin of life; the phrase survives only because Hooker kept the letter. Source: darwinproject.ac.uk letter DCP-LETT-7471.

question: Miller's supervisor was a chemistry Nobel laureate, and he had actually pushed his student toward a safer project about meteorites. Which famous chemist was the supervisor Miller had to talk into the origin-of-life experiment?
answer: Harold Urey
choices: Harold Urey
Glenn Seaborg
Fritz Haber
Otto Hahn
context: Urey won the 1934 Nobel for discovering deuterium. When the paper was ready he refused co-authorship, fearing his name would drown out Miller's. Source: nasonline.org memoir; wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Urey.

question: Two guesses from the 1920s framed everything Miller was testing: a Russian biochemist proposed in 1924 that organics could pile up in a warm reducing ocean, and a British biologist arrived at the same idea in 1929. The joint proposal became known by a homely nickname. What was that nickname?
answer: the primordial soup
choices: the primordial soup
the vital ferment
the ozone cradle
the ether broth
context: Alexander Oparin (1924) and J. B. S. Haldane (1929) never met but converged on the same picture. Source: britannica.com/science/Oparin-Haldane-theory.

question: Miller could name the chemistry that had done the work. The spark broke the sealed gases into two small reactive molecules, which then combined with more ammonia to give amino acids. Which pair of intermediates was doing the building?
answer: hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde
choices: hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde
carbon monoxide and nitric oxide
acetylene and ethylene
urea and glucose
context: The pathway is called Strecker synthesis after Adolph Strecker's 1850 amino-acid recipe; Miller had rediscovered it running on lightning. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Urey_experiment.

question: The Miller-Urey poster picture is sunny; the accounting is honest. Of the carbon that started as methane in the flask, about ten to fifteen percent ended up in organic molecules, and only about two percent became amino acids. Where did the rest of the carbon go?
answer: into an intractable brown tar
choices: into an intractable brown tar
back out as pure methane
into microscopic diamonds
into liquid oxygen
context: The tar coated the inside of the glass; no sugars and no nucleotides ever appeared. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Urey_experiment.

question: The assumption under Miller's whole design was that early Earth's air was strongly reducing, packed with methane and ammonia. Geochemists reading Archean rocks now think the young air was something quite different, and when the flask is rerun with that atmosphere the amino-acid yield drops by orders of magnitude. What is the atmosphere the rocks now suggest?
answer: mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen
choices: mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen
mostly oxygen and helium
mostly ozone and chlorine
pure water vapor
context: The chemistry Miller demonstrated is real; the recipe he used may just not match the young planet. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18204914 (Cleaves et al. 2008).

question: In every Miller-Urey rerun -- warm ponds, alkaline vents, iron-sulfur mineral surfaces, clay templates -- the amino acids come out fifty-fifty left-handed and right-handed. Life on Earth then does something the chemistry does not. What does living protein use?
answer: only the left-handed forms
choices: only the left-handed forms
only the right-handed forms
a fifty-fifty mix
a random mix per organism
context: This still-open puzzle is called the homochirality problem. Meteorite amino acids show a small left-hand excess, and autocatalytic amplification is one candidate mechanism; no one yet knows how nature picked a hand. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2012.12850.

question: Every B cell owes its letter to a small lymph pouch tucked near a chicken's tail, named for the 16th-century anatomist Fabricius. Anatomists call it the bursa of Fabricius. Mammals have no bursa at all - so in a human, B cells finish maturing not in a pouch but inside which tissue?
answer: bone marrow
choices: bone marrow
the thymus
the spleen
the tonsils
context: The letter survived the organ: the 'B' still stands for bursa but human B cells mature in the marrow of long bones. T cells still mature in the thymus. The naming accident is the reason immunology owes chicken farms a footnote. Source: sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/bursa-of-fabricius ; fortislife.com/resources/antibody-resources/b-is-for-bursa

question: In 1955 at Ohio State, poultry graduate student Bruce Glick had been removing the bursa of Fabricius from young chicks and finding nothing at all. Then fellow graduate student Timothy Chang borrowed some of the birds for a routine classroom demonstration - and the birds made no antibody and most of them died. Which pathogen was Chang trying to demonstrate the antibody response against?
answer: Salmonella
choices: Salmonella
rabies virus
anthrax
polio virus
context: The failed class demo WAS the experiment. Chang immunised the borrowed chicks with Salmonella O antigen; the bursectomised birds could not raise antibodies and died, and Glick, checking his notes, realised the intact-bursa chicks were the survivors. A teaching lab uncovered a whole lineage of the immune system. Source: popsci.com/chickens-bursa-immune-award/ ; academic.oup.com/cei/article/145/1/1/6458731

question: Jacques Miller went on to a distinction so specific it is almost eerie. Historians of medicine describe him as the last living scientist to have discovered the function of what?
answer: a human organ
choices: a human organ
a mammalian hormone
a childhood disease
a vitamin
context: The great organ hunts - liver, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, thyroid - were finished by the mid-20th century. The thymus was the last one left with 'unknown' next to its function line, and Miller settled it in 1961. There is no organ left in the human body whose function is still up for discovery. Source: thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(11)61565-1/fulltext

question: Miller's mouse discovery predicted that a human born without a thymus should be catastrophically vulnerable to infection - and specifically short of T cells. That prediction has a real, tragic natural experiment: a syndrome in which some infants really are born with little or no thymus. What is the syndrome called?
answer: DiGeorge syndrome
choices: DiGeorge syndrome
Down syndrome
Marfan syndrome
Turner syndrome
context: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome causes facial anomalies, heart defects and, in about 1 percent of cases, complete athymia - no thymus, no T cells, and no protection until a thymus transplant is arranged. It is the human confirmation of Miller's mouse. Source: msdmanuals.com/home/immune-disorders/immunodeficiency-disorders/digeorge-syndrome ; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8249278/

question: At the University of Chicago's Ryerson Physical Laboratory in 1909, Robert Millikan sprayed a fine mist of oil between two charged horizontal metal plates and held a single droplet suspended between them. What did he adjust to make one specific droplet hang perfectly still?
answer: The voltage on the plates
choices: The voltage on the plates
The temperature of the chamber
The tilt of the plates
The pressure of the surrounding air
context: The upward electric pull on the charged droplet grew or shrank with the voltage across the plates; at the right setting the pull exactly balanced the droplet's weight and it hung motionless. Millikan then read off that voltage to work out the charge the drop was carrying. Source: Wikipedia, Oil drop experiment.

question: Millikan and Harvey Fletcher deliberately chose oil for their suspended droplets instead of the water that J.J. Thomson and H.A. Wilson had used a few years earlier. Why did water fail?
answer: The drops evaporated as they were watched, changing mass mid-measurement
choices: The drops evaporated as they were watched, changing mass mid-measurement
The drops carried too little charge to respond to any manageable voltage
The drops froze solid in the cool laboratory air within a few seconds
The drops broke apart into finer droplets whenever the field was turned on
context: Oil has an extremely low vapor pressure, so a droplet held in view for minutes barely shrinks. Source: Wikipedia, Oil drop experiment.

question: Millikan measured the charge on hundreds of individual oil droplets. What did the numbers look like when he wrote them all down?
answer: Every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of one base amount
choices: Every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of one base amount
The charges spread smoothly across every value with no gaps
Half the drops carried the same charge and half carried none
The charges doubled from drop to drop in a geometric sequence
context: That pattern -- one, two, three, seven times a single lump, never one-and-a-half -- is what showed electric charge is quantized. The base lump is the charge on one electron. Source: Wikipedia, Oil drop experiment.

question: Millikan's published value for the electron's charge sat about 0.6 percent below what modern measurements give. Feynman traced the offset to one specific input Millikan had gotten slightly wrong. What was it?
answer: The viscosity of air
choices: The viscosity of air
The mass of the electron
The density of the oil
The strength of Earth's gravity
context: The formula turning a drop's fall speed into its size uses the air's viscosity; a slightly wrong tabulated value fed straight into the answer. Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science,' Caltech commencement 1974.

question: In his 1974 Caltech commencement address 'Cargo Cult Science,' Richard Feynman plotted later measurements of the electron's charge over the decades after Millikan. What did the numbers do?
answer: Crept upward from Millikan's value in small steps until they settled near the modern answer
choices: Crept upward from Millikan's value in small steps until they settled near the modern answer
Jumped immediately to the modern answer within a year of Millikan
Swung wildly above and below Millikan with no trend at all
Stayed exactly at Millikan's value for fifty years, then corrected in a single 1959 paper
context: Feynman's point was psychological, not arithmetic -- an experimenter who got a number much higher than Millikan's went hunting for what was wrong with his own apparatus, and stopped hunting once the number sat near Millikan's. The next rung names the rule that fixes this.

question: To keep the Millikan effect from steering their own answers, modern particle-physics collaborations now use a discipline called BLIND ANALYSIS. What do they actually do to the data?
answer: Hide the signal region or add a secret offset until the analysis method is frozen, then unblind
choices: Hide the signal region or add a secret offset until the analysis method is frozen, then unblind
Run the entire experiment twice and average the two answers together
Have the theorists compute the expected answer first and use it as a check on every cut
Rotate lab shifts each night so no single person sees more than a few hours of data
context: Common tricks include a hidden numerical shift added to every measurement, a scrambled sample, or a covered 'signal box.' Once the selection cuts and the analysis code are locked in, the collaboration unblinds -- and whatever comes out is what gets published. Source: Klein & Roodman, Blind Analysis in Nuclear and Particle Physics, Ann. Rev. Nucl. Part. Sci. 55.

question: For years after 1910 a serious physicist ran his own drop experiments -- often on silver particles instead of oil -- and kept publishing that Millikan was wrong: that charge was NOT quantized and that fractional 'subelectrons' below the electron were real. Who was he?
answer: Felix Ehrenhaft
choices: Felix Ehrenhaft
Arnold Sommerfeld
Ralph Fowler
Erwin Schrodinger
context: Ehrenhaft, at the University of Vienna, never conceded. Einstein wrote in 1940 that he did not believe Ehrenhaft's numbers but that nobody had a clear explanation for what Ehrenhaft was actually seeing. Millikan's view won because everyone else's drops kept giving the same lump. Source: Wikipedia, Felix Ehrenhaft.

question: Millikan's OTHER Nobel-cited work was an experiment on the photoelectric effect that ran from 1912 to 1915 -- and that Millikan himself launched with a specific expectation about Einstein's 1905 light-quantum equation. What was he trying to do?
answer: Disprove it -- and instead confirmed it in fine detail, pinning Planck's constant to under a percent
choices: Disprove it -- and instead confirmed it in fine detail, pinning Planck's constant to under a percent
Confirm it -- exactly the clean vindication of Einstein he had expected from the start
Extend it to X-rays -- and found Einstein's equation broke down completely in that range
Replace it -- with a rival classical-wave formula of his own that the community adopted
context: Millikan long thought the light-quantum interpretation had no proper theoretical foundation; as late as 1916 he was still calling the interpretation unfounded even as his own data confirmed the equation. His 1923 Nobel citation covered both the elementary charge and the photoelectric effect. Source: Nobel Prize 1923; Millikan 1916 review.

question: Harvey Fletcher, Millikan's graduate student, later wrote a memoir published only after his death that told what happened when it came time to publish the key 1913 oil-drop paper. What did he say Millikan did?
answer: Took sole authorship of the main paper, invoking a Chicago rule that a thesis had to be single-authored
choices: Took sole authorship of the main paper, invoking a Chicago rule that a thesis had to be single-authored
Listed Fletcher as first author of the main paper and put himself second, as Fletcher had done the bench work
Removed his own name from the main paper entirely so his graduate student could have full credit
Split the byline exactly evenly with Fletcher on every paper the two of them ever published together
context: Fletcher's memoir 'My Work with Millikan on the Oil-Drop Experiment' appeared in Physics Today in June 1982, after Fletcher had died -- he had asked that it be held. Source: Physics Today, 1982.

question: In 1930 the chemist Thomas Midgley Jr. wanted to prove Freon's safety to a meeting of the American Chemical Society. What did he do on the spot?
answer: He inhaled a lungful of it and exhaled it onto a candle, snuffing the flame.
choices: He inhaled a lungful of it and exhaled it onto a candle, snuffing the flame.
He sealed himself in a chamber flooded with the vapor for ten minutes.
He poured a beaker of the liquid across a lit Bunsen burner.
He drank a full glass of the liquid in front of the audience.
context: Freon (dichlorofluoromethane, a CFC) really was non-toxic and non-flammable at ordinary exposures -- exactly the properties that let it drift intact into the stratosphere fifty years later and cause the problem Molina and Rowland would predict in 1974. Sources: Chemistry World 'Life-changing chemistry'; Smithsonian Magazine 'One Man Invented Two of the Deadliest Substances of the 20th Century'.  (Legend.)

question: In 1974 Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland at UC Irvine published in Nature a paper about chlorofluorocarbons -- the refrigerants everyone thought were harmless because nothing on Earth reacts with them. The two chemists asked a different question: if nothing reacts with a CFC, where does it eventually end up? Their calculation said the CFC drifts intact all the way to the stratosphere, where at last something DOES break it and free a chlorine atom. What breaks it?
answer: ultraviolet light from the Sun
choices: ultraviolet light from the Sun
cosmic rays from deep space
lightning inside stratospheric clouds
collisions with high-energy oxygen atoms
context: Above roughly 20 km altitude the atmosphere lets through the short-wavelength UV that lower down is filtered by the ozone itself. That UV finally breaks the C-Cl bond in an intact CFC molecule and liberates a chlorine atom into the stratosphere. Molina and Rowland won a share of the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this line of reasoning. Sources: Wikipedia 'Mario Molina' and 'Ozone depletion'.

question: How did the chair of DuPont's board publicly respond to the 1974 Molina-Rowland ozone-depletion theory?
answer: outright ridicule as a science fiction tale and utter nonsense
choices: outright ridicule as a science fiction tale and utter nonsense
a call for a decade of confirming atmospheric measurements first
a pledge of voluntary CFC production cuts pending further study
a commissioning of DuPont scientists to test the calculation themselves
context: The direct quotation is preserved on the Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion' article and in the contemporary press: 'a science fiction tale ... a load of rubbish ... utter nonsense.' It is the classic case of an industry chairman ridiculing a calculation that turned out to be right, and it is also why Molina and Rowland's later vindication became one of the founding stories of atmospheric chemistry. Source: Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion' (direct quotation).

question: The Molina-Rowland calculation had a twist that made a tiny amount of chlorine devastating. A chlorine atom is a CATALYST -- it is not used up in the reaction, so it comes out the other side of each destruction ready to strike again. Roughly how many ozone molecules does a single chlorine atom destroy before some other reaction finally removes it from the cycle?
answer: around 100,000
choices: around 100
around 10,000
around 100,000
context: The number 100,000 is stated exactly on Wikipedia's Ozone depletion article and traces back to standard atmospheric-chemistry reviews. It is why a few million tonnes of a supposedly inert refrigerant could plausibly matter to a planet-sized shield -- the multiplier is the whole story. Source: Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion'.

question: Molina and Rowland were not starting from nothing. Four years earlier, in 1970, another atmospheric chemist had already shown that a different family of gases could catalytically eat ozone in exactly the same way -- and in 1995 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded jointly to all three men. Who was the earlier chemist, and what family of gases did he implicate?
answer: Paul Crutzen, nitrogen oxides from nitrous oxide
choices: Paul Crutzen, nitrogen oxides from nitrous oxide
James Lovelock, bromine compounds from sea spray
Sydney Chapman, atomic oxygen from oxygen photolysis
Gordon Dobson, sulfur oxides from volcanic eruptions
context: Crutzen's 1970 work on the NOx catalytic cycle gave Molina and Rowland the template they applied to chlorine four years later. The 1995 Nobel in Chemistry went jointly to Crutzen, Molina and Rowland 'for their work in atmospheric chemistry, particularly concerning the formation and decomposition of ozone.' The other three names in the distractors are real atmospheric scientists -- Lovelock actually invented the electron-capture detector that measured CFCs in the air; Chapman worked out the classical gas-phase ozone cycle; Dobson invented the ground-based spectrophotometer used at Halley. Sources: Wikipedia 'Paul J. Crutzen' and 'Mario Molina'.

question: For years the ground-based Dobson spectrophotometer at Halley Station on the Antarctic coast, running since the 1950s, had been showing October ozone falling. In 1985 three British Antarctic Survey scientists -- Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin -- published the numbers in Nature. What size collapse did their paper report over Antarctica in austral spring?
answer: up to 70 percent of the ozone column
choices: up to 30 percent of the ozone column
up to 50 percent of the ozone column
up to 70 percent of the ozone column
up to 95 percent of the ozone column
context: The paper -- 'Large losses of total ozone in Antarctica reveal seasonal ClOx/NOx interaction', Nature vol. 315 issue 6016 p. 207 -- was the moment the abstract 1974 prediction became a measured emergency, and it came from a hand-calibrated ground instrument the satellite community had almost forgotten. Shanklin's specific contribution was calibrating the Dobson instrument itself. Sources: Wikipedia 'Jonathan Shanklin' and 'Ozone depletion'.

question: In 1987, two years after the Halley Bay paper, 43 nations signed the Montreal Protocol to freeze and then halve CFC production. What distinction does that treaty still hold, alone among all UN environmental treaties?
answer: It is the only one every UN member state has ratified.
choices: It is the only one every UN member state has ratified.
It is the only one with a binding global carbon-price mechanism.
It is the only one to have set legally binding species-recovery targets.
It is the only one requiring signatories to submit annual satellite verification.
context: The Montreal Protocol is the only UN environmental treaty ever ratified by every member state -- and the enforcement mechanism turned out to be the measurement itself: atmospheric chlorine peaked in the late 1990s and has been falling since. The 2023 UN scientific assessment projects a return to 1980 ozone values by around 2040 globally, 2045 over the Arctic, and 2066 over Antarctica. Source: Wikipedia 'Ozone depletion'.

question: The story that circulated for years was that NASA's TOMS satellite had spotted the Antarctic ozone hole first but its computer had 'thrown the data away.' The 1993 NASA reference publication that reprocessed the archive tells a different and more instructive story. What did NASA's algorithm actually do with ozone column readings below 180 Dobson units?
answer: It flagged them as suspected sensor error for later human review.
choices: It deleted them permanently as digital noise.
It flagged them as suspected sensor error for later human review.
It auto-corrected them upward to match a physical model.
It overwrote them with monthly averages from surrounding grid cells.
context: The NASA team had checked the very low TOMS values against other data, which showed around 300 Dobson units, and reasonably assumed the sensor was malfunctioning. The British Halley ground data was not available to them. After Farman et al. 1985 the entire TOMS archive was reprocessed (Version 6, released November 1990) and confirmed the hole had been sitting in the data all along. The real lesson is sharper than the myth: a filter that encodes what you expect to be normal can hide the abnormal. Sources: robjhyndman.com 'The ozone hole and the anomaly detector' (citing Fleig et al. 1986 GRL and NASA Reference Publication 1323, 1993).

question: Molina and Rowland's 1974 calculation predicted gradual global thinning through gas-phase chemistry. It did NOT predict a sudden gaping hole every September over one continent -- which surprised them too. In 1986 Susan Solomon proposed the explanation: the destruction over Antarctica was not happening in gas at all. Where was the chlorine chemistry actually taking place?
answer: on the surfaces of ice crystals in polar stratospheric clouds
choices: on the surfaces of ice crystals in polar stratospheric clouds
inside supercooled droplets of liquid nitric acid
on the underside of the Antarctic ice sheet itself
in the plumes of erupting Antarctic volcanoes
context: The winter polar vortex chills the Antarctic stratosphere to around or below -80 C, cold enough to form clouds that almost never form anywhere else. On the ice surfaces of those clouds, harmless chlorine reservoir compounds are converted into active chlorine that then waits, storing up, until the September sun returns. Then the destruction happens all at once. Solomon, about 30 years old at the time, was the sole leader of the 1986 and 1987 National Ozone Expedition to McMurdo and the only woman on the team; her group measured chlorine oxide roughly 100 times higher than expected. Sources: Wikipedia 'Susan Solomon' and 'Ozone depletion'.

question: The Solomon hypothesis needed a decisive test done inside the vortex itself. In August and September 1987 James Anderson's team flew instruments out of Punta Arenas, Chile aboard NASA's ER-2 -- the civilian version of the U-2 spy plane -- crossing directly into and out of the Antarctic polar vortex. What did their 'smoking gun' plot show as the aircraft crossed the vortex edge?
answer: chlorine monoxide climbing exactly where and when ozone crashed
choices: chlorine monoxide climbing exactly where and when ozone crashed
nitric oxide and ozone rising and falling together in step
carbon dioxide climbing steadily on both sides of the vortex
methane concentrations doubling inside the vortex core
context: The ClO-versus-ozone anti-correlation from the Airborne Antarctic Ozone Experiment (AAOE) is the plot people mean when they say a single graph ended a scientific debate. Anderson himself: 'That anti-correlation between ClO and ozone was a dramatic clue to what was happening.' Rival explanations that serious atmospheric scientists had proposed -- a natural dynamical cycle lifting ozone-poor air, solar-cycle nitrogen oxides, volcanic emissions -- were all tested and rejected against this measurement. Sources: NOAA CSL 'AAOE overview'; Smithsonian Magazine 'The Ozone Problem is Back'.

question: In 1913 a young Oxford physicist named Henry Moseley set one pure metal after another inside an evacuated tube, bombarded each sample with a beam, and photographed the sharp lines the sample threw back onto a strip of film. What was he firing at the metals?
answer: A beam of electrons
choices: A beam of electrons
A beam of neutrons
A beam of visible light
A jet of hot mercury vapour
context: Electrons knocked deep-shell electrons out of the target atoms; when outer electrons fell in to fill the holes, each element emitted its own characteristic X-rays. Moseley diffracted those X-rays off a crystal and let them expose photographic film, using Bragg's law to read off the wavelength. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moseley

question: Moseley's staircase gave every element a whole-number label that rose by exactly one from element to element. In a paper of 1914 he identified that whole number with a physical count inside the atom itself. What was he counting?
answer: The positive charges in the nucleus
choices: The positive charges in the nucleus
The layers of electrons around the atom
The neutrons inside the nucleus
The isotopes of the element known so far
context: Ernest Rutherford's 1911 experiment had already shown the atom has a small, dense, positively charged core (its nucleus). Moseley measured how much charge sits in that core for each element. The Dutch amateur van den Broek had guessed as much in 1911; Moseley supplied the proof. The particle carrying one unit of that charge (the proton) was not named by Rutherford's group until 1920. Source: chemteam.info/AtomicStructure/AtNum-Moseley.html

question: Dmitri Mendeleev had put tellurium in front of iodine and cobalt in front of nickel on chemical grounds even though the weighing scale disagreed in each pair; he blamed the atomic weights on sloppy laboratory work. Moseley's X-ray staircase showed the chemistry was right, but for a reason Mendeleev had never guessed. What is that reason?
answer: Tellurium and cobalt each carry fewer nuclear charges than their heavier neighbour
choices: Tellurium and cobalt each carry fewer nuclear charges than their heavier neighbour
Tellurium and cobalt each hold an extra outer electron shell
Tellurium and cobalt each occupy two boxes on the table at once
Tellurium and cobalt are each really mixtures of two undiscovered elements
context: The extra weight comes from neutrons (isotopes), not from more protons. Mendeleev had the elements in the right order for the right chemical reason and the wrong stated reason. After Moseley, the table stopped being ordered by mass and started being ordered by nuclear charge, an idea we now call the atomic number. Source: ck12.org/flexi/physical-science/Mendeleevs-Periodic-Table

question: Because Moseley's staircase forbade any missing step between whole numbers, he could point straight at the gaps in the sequence and predict that certain elements had to exist somewhere and nothing else could be squeezed between them. Which set of holes did he name?
answer: Elements 43, 61, 72 and 75
choices: Elements 43, 61, 72 and 75
Elements 3, 11, 19 and 37
Elements 84, 86, 88 and 92
Elements 2, 10, 18 and 36
context: The four holes were filled later as technetium (43), promethium (61), hafnium (72) and rhenium (75). Moseley also settled a running argument by proving that the rare-earth (lanthanide) row must contain exactly fifteen members, no more and no less. The table stopped being a matter of judgement and became a matter of counting. Source: nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/02/henry-moseley-and-periodic-table-elements

question: Henry Moseley had done about two years of work on the X-ray staircase when he volunteered for the British Army in 1914. He was killed by a Turkish sniper on 10 August 1915 at Gallipoli, aged 27. Robert Millikan called his loss one of the heaviest costs of the war to science. Which rule kept his name off the Nobel roll that his living rivals collected?
answer: The Nobel Prize is never awarded posthumously
choices: The Nobel Prize is never awarded posthumously
The Nobel Prize was suspended for the whole of the First World War
British officers were barred from Swedish scientific honours
Only work published after 1915 was eligible for the physics prize
context: The physics prize for 1917 went to Charles Barkla, who had done earlier X-ray work. Rutherford summed up Moseley's discovery by saying the X-ray wavelength changes could be explained by supposing the charge on the nucleus increases from one element to the next by exactly one unit. Source: aps.org/apsnews/2012/08/henry-moseley-killed-action-1915

question: In 1903 a respected physicist at the University of Nancy in France announced a new kind of radiation. He named the discovery for the first letter of his hometown. Which physicist was he?
answer: Prosper-Rene Blondlot
choices: Prosper-Rene Blondlot
Antoine Henri Becquerel
Paul Ulrich Villard
Gabriel Jean Lippmann
context: Blondlot named the rays N-rays (N for Nancy) in the spring of 1903 while trying to polarize X-rays. Becquerel had discovered radioactivity in 1896, Villard discovered gamma rays in 1900, and Lippmann won the 1908 Nobel for colour photography -- so a kid in that decade would meet all four as respected French physicists.

question: The 'detector' for the new rays announced in Nancy in 1903 was a small spark and a strip of phosphorescent paint, whose brightness a seated observer had to judge by eye. What made this reading method the fatal weakness of the entire N-ray program?
answer: The observer knew when the apparatus was supposedly 'on'.
choices: The observer knew when the apparatus was supposedly 'on'.
The phosphor decayed after only a few minutes of use.
The spark could not be photographed on the plates of the day.
The apparatus lost calibration whenever the room warmed up.
context: Nobody was ever blinded to the setup: the observer knew which trials were the 'on' trials, the effect sat at the very threshold of detection, and expectation itself became the instrument. All three distractors are real worries for a dim optical detector, but the fatal one is that the human doing the seeing knew what he was supposed to see, and when.

question: N-rays became a full-blown scientific field between 1903 and 1906. About how many papers on N-rays were published in the scientific press before the whole subject collapsed?
answer: about 300
choices: about 300
about 30
about 3,000
about 30,000
context: Roughly 300 papers by about 120 scientists, with 26 papers from Blondlot himself. The scale is the whole point of the story: this was not one crank -- it was normal, credentialed physics running for three years without a hitch.

question: In 1904 the American physicist Robert W. Wood travelled to the Nancy laboratory to see the N-ray demonstration for himself. During the demonstration, in the dark, Wood palmed one small piece of the apparatus into his pocket. Which piece did he remove?
answer: the aluminium prism from the spectroscope
choices: the aluminium prism from the spectroscope
the phosphorescent thread from the detector
the electrical filament from the discharge tube
the copper collimator from the front of the apparatus
context: The prism was the piece that supposedly separated the incoming N-rays into their spectrum -- without it there could be no reading at all. The demonstrator went on calmly reading off exactly the same spectrum after Wood pocketed it. All four distractors are real parts of the sort of dim optical rig Wood was looking at, but the prism was the load-bearing one.

question: During the same Nancy visit, Robert W. Wood ran a second quiet test on the N-ray apparatus. He was told that a steel file was one of the objects emitting the rays, so he substituted something on the sly to see if the demonstrator noticed. What did Wood swap for the steel file?
answer: a plain piece of wood
choices: a plain piece of wood
a heavy bar of lead
a small slab of copper
a length of glass rod
context: Green wood, in Blondlot's own catalogue, did NOT emit N-rays. When Wood substituted wood for the file, the readings kept coming anyway -- which no consistent N-ray theory could allow. Lead, copper and glass are real materials Wood might plausibly have grabbed, but wood was the specific test-case, and it was the substance N-rays were said NOT to emit.

question: In December 1904, three months AFTER Wood's letter had appeared, the French Academy of Sciences still voted Blondlot the Prix Leconte and its 50,000 francs. The Academy was not willing to abandon its own; it kept the prize but rewrote the citation. For what did it now honour him?
answer: the totality of his work
choices: the totality of his work
his measurement of the speed of radio waves
his long service to the University of Nancy
his defence of French science against attack
context: The rewording was a bureaucratic finesse -- the prize was announced, but the citation quietly dropped the N-rays and pointed backward at Blondlot's career. All three distractors are things Blondlot had genuinely done or could plausibly have been cited for; the specific replacement wording is the whole point of this rung.

question: Half a century after the N-rays evaporated, Irving Langmuir gave a colloquium naming the whole family of failures they belonged to -- from N-rays through mitogenetic rays to the Davis-Barnes effect. The talk was given on 18 December 1953 at General Electric's Knolls laboratory. What name did Langmuir give to the pattern?
answer: pathological science
choices: pathological science
cargo cult science
the tyranny of expectation
the observer effect
context: Langmuir called it 'the science of things that aren't so.' The Knolls talk survived only on a microgroove disk transcript and was finally published in Physics Today in October 1989 (edited by Robert Hall). 'Cargo cult science' is Feynman's later, related name for a slightly different failure mode -- both belong on any bookshelf about self-deception in the lab.

question: In 1971 a Bell Labs chemist named Denis Rousseau ended a decade-long scare about a supposed new form of water -- polywater, said to freeze at -40 C and boil at 150 C -- by comparing its infrared spectrum with a fluid he collected from his own body. What was the fluid?
answer: his sweat, collected after a handball game
choices: his sweat, collected after a handball game
his saliva, taken after breakfast in the lab
his blood plasma, drawn during a routine physical
his tears, produced during a wind test on the roof
context: The two spectra matched: polywater was ordinary water contaminated with the ionic soup of a sweaty athlete. First reported by Nikolai Fedyakin in Kostroma in 1961 and pushed by Boris Derjaguin, polywater fits every one of Langmuir's symptoms -- the effect never grew when the apparatus was scaled up, and every failed replication met a fresh excuse.

question: On 23 March 1989 two electrochemists in Utah, Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons, announced they had achieved nuclear fusion in a small tabletop cell of heavy water. Physicists worldwide were furious not only because the excess heat would not replicate but because of HOW the Utah pair had gone public. What had they done first?
answer: They called a press conference before submitting any paper for peer review.
choices: They called a press conference before submitting any paper for peer review.
They briefed the Department of Energy under embargo before releasing details.
They published in Nature the same week as the press conference.
They posted the full apparatus schematic on a scientific preprint server.
context: The press conference of 23 March 1989 was called under pressure from University of Utah administrators eager to secure priority against a competing group. Laboratories worldwide were unable to reproduce the excess heat; mainstream physics rejects the claim -- said flatly and without the word 'fraud'. Publication-by-press-conference is now a warning in every science-methods textbook.

question: Athens, 430 BC. As the plague emptied the city, the historian Thucydides watched who was willing to sit with the dying and nurse them without fear, and he wrote down one thing those people had in common. What was it?
answer: They had already been through the disease and recovered
choices: They had already been through the disease and recovered
They had been given a physician's protective mixture
They came from families the priests judged favoured
They had grown up in the villages outside the city
context: Thucydides' own words, in the Crawley translation: "Yet it was with those who had recovered from the disease that the sick and the dying found most compassion. These knew what it was from experience, and had now no fear for themselves; for the same man was never attacked twice - never at least fatally." This is the first written record of immunity in any language, and the man who wrote it was a general and a historian, not a physician - and he had caught the plague himself and survived it. Sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 2 ch. 51 (Crawley translation), MIT Internet Classics Archive - http://classics.mit.edu/Thucydides/pelopwar.2.second.html ; Grokipedia, 'Plague of Athens' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Plague_of_Athens

question: The Faroe Islands, 1846. Measles landed at Thorshavn in April and ran through nearly the whole population: about 6,000 of the 7,782 islanders fell ill within half a year. Peter Ludvig Panum, the young Dane sent out to study the epidemic, went looking for the people it had passed over. Who were they?
answer: The old people who had gone through measles in their youth
choices: The old people who had gone through measles in their youth
The people who had come through smallpox or scarlet fever
The families that had scrubbed their homes clean of filth
The households that kept fires burning against the bad air
context: Panum's own sentence: "In this connection it is quite remarkable, however, that of the many aged people still living on the Faroes who had had measles in 1781, not one, as far as I could find out by careful inquiry, was attacked the second time. I myself saw ninety-eight such old people, who were exempt because they had had the disease in their youth." Measles had last visited the islands in 1781 - a gap Panum states as "sixty-five years" - so almost everybody under sixty-five was meeting it for the first time. One traveller brought it back: a Faroese man who had visited someone ill with measles in Copenhagen, felt perfectly well through the nine-day crossing, and broke out about a week after landing. Source: P. L. Panum, 'Observations Made During the Epidemic of Measles on the Faroe Islands in the Year 1846' (English translation, Delta Omega archive) - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf

question: At a Faroe Islands farmhouse in 1846, the Danish investigator Peter Ludvig Panum found the churchwarden's daughter just recovered from measles, while the other nine in the house felt well and hoped they had escaped. He asked when her rash had appeared, called for the almanac, and drew a black line under one later date. What was he predicting?
answer: That measles would strike the rest of the house that day
choices: That measles would strike the rest of the house that day
That their daughter would stop being infectious that day
That the family could safely rejoin the village that day
That the last of her rash would have faded by that day
context: Panum had pinned the gap between catching measles and the rash at about a fortnight: "thirteen to fourteen days intervene between the reception of the contagion and the eruption of the exanthem," and "the latent stage of measles of about fourteen days was so conspicuously constant, that many laymen had already made this observation." The isolated villages were his laboratory - in a city nobody could ever say a patient had been exposed once, on one known day. In his own words on what followed: "In Fuglefjord, on Osteroe, on account of my observations, I acquired the reputation of being able to prophesy." A falsifiable prediction, written on a calendar, in front of witnesses - which is the whole method in miniature, and something you can still do yourself with a household outbreak and a wall calendar. Source: Panum 1847 treatise (English translation) - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf

question: The Athenian historian Thucydides recorded that survivors of the plague of 430 BC were congratulated by everyone around them, and that in the elation of the moment the survivors themselves half-entertained a hope he calls vain in the same breath. What did they hope?
answer: That they would never fall ill of anything again
choices: That they would never fall ill of anything again
That the plague would leave the city before winter
That their children would be born proof against it
That the gods had marked them out for something
context: The sentence runs straight on from his immunity observation: survivors "not only received the congratulations of others, but themselves also, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were for the future safe from any disease whatsoever." In one breath Thucydides records the correct fact - you are not struck twice by THIS disease - and the wrong inference drawn from it. It is the first written case of over-reading a true finding, and it is 2,400 years old. Source: Thucydides, Book 2 ch. 51 (Crawley translation) - http://classics.mit.edu/Thucydides/pelopwar.2.second.html

question: The Faroe Islands, 1846. Peter Ludvig Panum, the Danish investigator sent out to study the measles epidemic sweeping the islands, kept meeting elderly islanders the disease had left alone - and each of them had been through the islands' previous epidemic, back in 1781. Two explanations fitted: great age itself protects, or having had measles long ago protects. Panum found his test among the old islanders who had never been through 1781. What happened to them?
answer: Every one of them caught measles
choices: Every one of them caught measles
Most of them escaped it as well
About half of them caught it
They caught it, but only mildly
context: Panum's own sentence is what turns an anecdote into a measurement: "a high age by no means lessened the susceptibility to measles, since, as far as I know, all the old people who had not gone through with measles in earlier life were attacked when they were exposed to infection; whereas certain young persons, although constantly exposed, were exempt." He found the same thing village by village: "there were, however, several houses and small villages that had not been invaded in 1781 and in these the older folk were attacked just as the others." Age did nothing. Having had the disease did everything. Panum was twenty-five, had qualified only the year before, and his title page reads "Candidate in Medicine and Surgery"; he stayed almost five months and personally treated about 1,000 of the roughly 6,000 cases. Source: Panum 1847 treatise (English translation) - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf

question: The first time a germ gets into you, your body needs four to seven days to put any antibody into the blood - protein built to lock on to that one germ - and what it makes grips only loosely. The second time that same germ arrives, antibody is out in one to three days and it grips hard. How much of it does the body make that second time, compared with the first?
answer: A hundred to a thousand times as much
choices: A hundred to a thousand times as much
A thousand to ten thousand times as much
Ten to a hundred times as much
Two to ten times as much
context: A primary response is dominated by low-affinity IgM and peaks at seven to ten days - which is roughly how long you feel ill. A secondary response has a lag of only one to three days, switches straight to high-affinity IgG, and reaches antibody titres 100- to 1,000-fold higher. That is why you never notice the second attack: the fight is finished before the symptoms would have started. Source: Grokipedia, 'Immune system' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Immune_system

question: Years after you have beaten an infection, some of your plasma cells are still turning out antibody - the protein that locks on to one particular germ and marks it for destruction - at up to ten thousand molecules a second. The plasma cells thrown up during the illness itself lived only three to five days. How do these ones keep going for decades?
answer: They moved into survival niches in the bone marrow and never left
choices: They moved into survival niches in the bone marrow and never left
Scraps of the germ held in the lymph nodes keep prodding them along
Memory cells restock them every time any other infection comes by
They divide over and over, each one replacing itself before it dies
context: These are long-lived plasma cells. They park in survival niches in the bone marrow and the gut lining, are "capable of persisting for decades," and each one secretes up to 10,000 immunoglobulin molecules per cell per second - supported by an enormously expanded rough endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's protein assembly line. Nothing keeps prodding them: immunological memory is maintained without any further antigen, on the cytokines IL-7 and IL-15 and the survival factors BAFF and APRIL. Memory B cells retreat the same way, into niches in the bone marrow and spleen; their estimated lifespan runs beyond 50 years, and antigen-specific memory B cells are still detectable more than 50 years after smallpox vaccination. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Plasma cell' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Plasma_cell ; Grokipedia, 'Immunological memory' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Immunological_memory

question: In 2008 a research team tracked down 32 people who had lived through the 1918 influenza pandemic as small children and were by then aged 91 to 101, drew their blood, and grew antibody-making cells from eight of them. Ninety years after that flu, what were those cells still turning out?
answer: Antibody that saved mice from a lethal dose of the 1918 virus
choices: Antibody that saved mice from a lethal dose of the 1918 virus
Antibody that left mice dying of the 1918 virus just as fast
Antibody that stuck to the 1918 virus without disabling it
Antibody that matched the flus of the 1950s but not the 1918 one
context: Every one of the 32 donors still had serum that neutralised the 1918 virus, and 94 per cent were still serologically reactive to the 1918 hemagglutinin; they had been two to twelve years old when it swept the world. The team cultured B cells from eight donors, made monoclonal antibodies from three, and those antibodies protected mice against a lethal dose of the reconstructed 1918 virus. James Crowe: "The B cells have been waiting for at least 60 years - if not 90 years - for that flu to come around again. That's amazing, because it's the longest memory anyone's ever demonstrated." Sources: Yu X et al., Nature 455:532 (2008) - https://www.nature.com/articles/nature07231 ; CIDRAP report carrying the Crowe quote - https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/h1n1-2009-pandemic-influenza/researchers-find-long-lived-immunity-1918-pandemic-virus

question: One bout of measles protects almost everyone for life. Influenza comes back and finds you again the following winter. The difference is not that your immune system treats the two differently - it is in the viruses themselves. What is it about measles?
answer: It barely mutates, so decades later it still looks the same
choices: It barely mutates, so decades later it still looks the same
It is far larger, so the immune system sees more of it at once
It lingers in the nerves and keeps the memory topped up
It infects mostly children, whose memory forms most strongly
context: Measles virus has a mutation rate of about 9 x 10^-5 per nucleotide per replication cycle - remarkably low for an RNA virus - "minimizing antigenic variation and facilitating durable, lifelong immunity after primary infection." A pathogen that cannot change its coat cannot escape your memory of it. That is the mechanism underneath the Faroese finding, and it is also why measles is the clean case and influenza is not: flu redesigns its surface every year, so last year's memory meets a stranger. Source: Grokipedia, 'Measles' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Measles

question: The mRNA and subunit COVID-19 vaccines showed the immune system a single piece of SARS-CoV-2: the spike protein studding its surface. Someone who caught the virus met the whole of it. When new variants arrived carrying a heavily altered spike, that difference mattered - the recovered still carried T-cell memory aimed at a piece of the virus those shots never contained. Which piece was it?
answer: The nucleocapsid, the protein coat wound around the virus's genes
choices: The nucleocapsid, the protein coat wound around the virus's genes
The membrane protein, the most abundant protein in the virus's shell
The envelope protein, the tiny channel set into that same shell
The copying enzyme the virus assembles once it is inside a cell
context: Grokipedia's summary of what natural infection adds: "The immune response to natural infection typically encompasses the full antigenic repertoire of the pathogen, fostering broader cross-reactivity than subunit or mRNA vaccines, which may focus on spike proteins or select epitopes. For instance, in SARS-CoV-2, natural infection induces T-cell responses targeting conserved nucleocapsid proteins absent in some vaccines, correlating with reduced severe outcomes upon variant exposure." The nucleocapsid is the protein wound around the virus's RNA inside the shell - it is not out on the surface where antibody pressure drives change, so it shifts far less between variants than the spike does. There is a second difference alongside breadth: route. A germ you actually caught arrived through nose, throat or gut, so the defences are built where it lands - mucosal IgA at the doorway, plus circulating IgG and CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell memory, with memory T cells settling in lymphoid and mucosal tissue. The garrison is posted at the door the bug uses. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Herd immunity' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Herd_immunity ; Grokipedia, 'Immunological memory' - https://grokipedia.com/page/Immunological_memory

question: The lifelong immunity the Faroese won in 1846 was not free: of the roughly 6,100 islanders who caught measles, about 170 died. The dying fell very unevenly. Among children aged one to nine, measles killed about three in every thousand. Among babies under a year old it killed a far larger share. What share of those babies died?
answer: Nearly three in ten
choices: Nearly three in ten
About six in ten
About one in ten
About one in thirty
context: The editor's table appended to Panum's treatise gives the accounting: population 7,864, attacked 6,100, deaths 170, case-fatality 2.8 per cent overall - but 28.6 per cent among infants under one year, 16.3 per cent among those over eighty, and only 0.3 per cent among children aged one to nine. Panum's own contemporaneous count was "a total of 255 persons died, of whom at least 102 died of measles or its sequelae." Both halves of this ladder are true at once: the immunity was real, measured, and lifelong, and more than a hundred islanders paid for it with their lives. A bank that told you only one half would be lying to you. Sources: Panum 1847 treatise and its editorial appendix - https://s3.amazonaws.com/aspphwebassets/delta-omega/archives/PanumFaroeIslands.pdf ; Wikipedia, 'Measles' - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measles

question: Through 2021 California and New York tracked COVID-19 case rates in four groups: vaccinated with no previous infection, unvaccinated with a previous infection, both, and neither. The CDC published the comparison in its own weekly report in January 2022. Before the Delta variant took over that June, case rates were lower among the vaccinated-only group than among those who had survived an earlier infection. What did the same tracking show by early October?
answer: The order had reversed: previous infection now had the lower rate
choices: The order had reversed: previous infection now had the lower rate
The two groups had converged on almost identical rates
The gap had widened further in favour of the vaccinated-only group
Both groups' rates had risen above the never-exposed group's
context: The CDC's own summary sentence, verbatim from MMWR 71(4), mm7104e1: "Before Delta became the predominant variant in June, case rates were higher among persons who survived a previous infection than persons who were vaccinated alone. By early October, persons who survived a previous infection had lower case rates than persons who were vaccinated alone." The numbers, both directions, compared with people who were neither vaccinated nor previously infected. Week of 30 May 2021: case rates 19.9-fold (CA) and 18.4-fold (NY) lower among the vaccinated with no previous infection, versus 7.2-fold and 9.9-fold lower among the unvaccinated with a previous infection. Week of 3 October 2021: 6.2-fold and 4.5-fold lower for the vaccinated with no previous infection, versus 29.0-fold and 14.7-fold lower for the unvaccinated with a previous infection. For hospitalisation, 3-16 October: 19.8-fold versus 55.3-fold lower. That protection follows from surviving an infection had been ordinary textbook immunology since Panum - yet a great deal of 2020-21 public messaging proceeded as though prior infection could not be counted at all, while the agencies' own data was reporting this. The bank reports the measurement; it does not tell you what to do about it. Sources: CDC MMWR 71(4), mm7104e1 - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9351527/ ; https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/pdfs/mm7104e1-H.pdf

question: In 2023 the Lancet published a systematic review pooling 65 studies from 19 countries on how much protection a previous COVID-19 infection left behind. Forty weeks after infection, protection against simply catching the virus again had fallen to about a third. Over those same forty weeks, where did protection against severe disease stand?
answer: About ninety per cent
choices: About ninety per cent
About ninety-nine per cent
About seventy per cent
About fifty per cent
context: The COVID-19 Forecasting Team's pooled figures at 40 weeks: protection against severe disease 90.2 per cent (95% CI 69.7-97.5) for pre-omicron variants and 88.9 per cent (84.7-90.9) for omicron BA.1; protection against re-infection itself 36.1 per cent (24.4-51.3) and against symptomatic disease 37.7 per cent (22.8-54.1). That is the honest shape of the thing, and it is worth learning as a shape: protection against being infected again erodes, protection against being badly hurt holds. Neither half is the whole story, and quoting only one of them - in either direction - is how a real measurement gets turned into a slogan. Source: COVID-19 Forecasting Team, 'Past SARS-CoV-2 infection protection against re-infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis,' The Lancet, 16 February 2023 - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9998097/

question: Measles leaves behind lifelong immunity to itself. Michael Mina and colleagues asked what else it leaves behind. Using a technique that tests one drop of blood against thousands of pathogens at once, they measured 77 unvaccinated children before they caught measles and again two months after. What had measles done to the antibodies those children already carried against everything else?
answer: It had wiped out between a tenth and three-quarters of them
choices: It had wiped out between a tenth and three-quarters of them
It had roughly doubled three-quarters of them
It had left nine in ten of them exactly as they were
It had strengthened the viral ones and erased the rest
context: The VirScan result, verbatim: "Measles caused elimination of 11 to 73% of the antibody repertoire across individuals... these immune system effects were not observed in infants vaccinated against MMR... but were confirmed in measles-infected macaques." The epidemiology matches the laboratory: an earlier study by the same group found that measles-induced immune suppression "extend[s] over 2 to 3 years," with non-measles infectious-disease mortality tracking measles incidence at exactly that lag, in both the pre-vaccine and post-vaccine eras. Measles buys its lifelong immunity to itself by burning the library of everything else you had learned - and the deaths it causes that way, years later, never carry its name. Sources: Mina MJ, Kula T et al., Science 366(6465):599-606 (2019) - https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672891/ ; Mina MJ et al., Science 348(6235):694-9 (2015) - https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25954009/

question: Charles Darwin opens On the Origin of Species not with wild animals but with pigeons: the fantail, with forty tail feathers where a normal bird has twelve; the pouter, inflating a huge crop; the tumbler, its beak almost a finch's. Where did the breeds come from?
answer: All from one wild species, the rock pigeon
choices: All from one wild species, the rock pigeon
Each breed from a different wild species
From three wild species, crossed by breeders
From wild doves caught across Asia and tamed
context: Darwin, Origin ch.1: 'I am fully convinced that the common opinion of naturalists is correct, namely, that all have descended from the rock-pigeon (Columba livia), including under this term several geographical races or sub-species.' The whole zoo -- fantail, pouter, tumbler, carrier, barb, runt, turbit, Jacobin -- was pulled out of one wild bird inside a few human centuries. His punchline: show a score of them to an ornithologist as wild birds and 'they would certainly, I think, be ranked by him as well-defined species.' Source: Darwin, On the Origin of Species ch.1, https://talkorigins.org/faqs/origin/chapter1.html

question: Charles Darwin knew no reader would take his word that selection could reshape a creature, so he went after evidence he could put in front of them: domestic pigeons. How did he get it?
answer: He bred every breed he could buy and joined two London pigeon clubs
choices: He bred every breed he could buy and joined two London pigeon clubs
He wrote to breeders across Britain and printed all their replies
He bought preserved skins from dealers and measured every one
He sent his sons to the bird shows to copy out the judges' rules
context: In his own words, Origin ch.1: 'Believing that it is always best to study some special group, I have, after deliberation, taken up domestic pigeons. I have kept every breed which I could purchase or obtain... I have associated with several eminent fanciers, and have been permitted to join two of the London Pigeon Clubs.' Secondary accounts date the start of the hobby to March 1855 (lower confidence than the quotes). Years later, when the publisher John Murray sent the manuscript to his reader Whitwell Elwin, Elwin advised Darwin to scrap the theory book and write one about pigeons instead -- 'Every body is interested in pigeons.' Darwin declined; he had only the last chapter left to write. Sources: https://talkorigins.org/faqs/origin/chapter1.html ; https://darwin200.christs.cam.ac.uk/pigeons ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_Species

question: Charles Darwin wanted a number his readers could not argue with, so he chose the animal he called the slowest breeder known: the elephant. He worked out on paper what a single pair would leave behind if every calf lived and bred at its natural rate. After five hundred years, how many elephants?
answer: About fifteen million
choices: About fifteen million
About fifteen thousand
About three thousand
About four hundred
context: Darwin, Origin ch.3: 'The elephant is reckoned to be the slowest breeder of all known animals... at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair.' He picked the slowest breeder precisely so no reader could dismiss the result as a trick of fast-breeding vermin. He also gave the pressure an image: 'The face of Nature may be compared to a yielding surface, with ten thousand sharp wedges packed close together and driven inwards by incessant blows.' Source: https://talkorigins.org/faqs/origin/chapter3.html

question: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck taught that what a body gains or loses in its own lifetime passes to its young. August Weismann tested that with scissors: he cut the tails off 68 white mice, then off their young, for five generations, and 901 young were born. What did the young mice show?
answer: Not one was born with a short or missing tail
choices: Not one was born with a short or missing tail
Tails were about a third shorter by the fifth
Roughly one in twenty was born without a tail
Tails grew normally, then dropped off in weeks
context: Weismann reported that among the 901 young 'there was not a single example of a rudimentary tail or of any other abnormality in this organ.' Lamarck's second law had held that 'all the acquisitions or losses wrought by nature on individuals... through the influence of the predominant use or permanent disuse of any organ... are preserved by reproduction to the new individuals which arise' -- and Lamarck's own illustration was a giraffe stretching for high leaves. Darwin's half-cousin Francis Galton ran a cousin experiment between 1869 and 1871, transfusing blood between rabbit breeds to see whether traits travelled in it. Nothing did. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamarckism ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangenesis

question: Charles Darwin had kept his mechanism unpublished for twenty years when a manuscript reached him from Alfred Russel Wallace, collecting specimens in the Malay Archipelago, setting out the same mechanism Wallace had reached alone. Darwin's friends arranged a hearing at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. What did the Society hear that night?
answer: Both men's papers, read out one after the other
choices: Both men's papers, read out one after the other
Darwin's paper only, with Wallace's held till winter
Wallace's paper only, at Darwin's own insistence
A joint summary written for them by Charles Lyell
context: The theory went public that evening -- five months before the book. On the Origin of Species followed on 24 November 1859, published in London by John Murray in a first printing of 1,250 copies that sold out on the day of release. Wallace had reached the same mechanism independently, from population pressure he watched at work in the Malay Archipelago. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Natural_selection
