choices: Attested statements from clergymen and lawyers
A sworn affidavit from the Vermont state coroner
The tamping iron itself, sent to Boston to be weighed
A second surgeon's countersignature on the report
context: Harlow's own opening remarks in 1868: the case 'was received by the Metropolitan Doctors with several grains of caution, insomuch that MANY UTTERLY REFUSED TO BELIEVE THAT THE MAN HAD RISEN, UNTIL THEY HAD THRUST THEIR FINGERS INTO THE HOLE OF HIS HEAD, and even then they required of the Country Doctor attested statements, FROM CLERGYMEN AND LAWYERS, before they could or would believe — many eminent surgeons regarding such an occurrence as a physiological impossibility.' The doubt was finally settled by evidence, not authority: Henry Jacob Bigelow, Professor of Surgery at Harvard, wrote to Harlow, paid Gage's expenses to come to Boston, kept him under observation for eight or nine weeks while many medical men examined him, and published the case with illustrations in July 1850. Source: Harlow 1868 and its footnote.

question: Phineas Gage had a long inscription cut along his tamping iron before he handed it to the museum of Harvard's medical school in January 1850. The inscription gets the date of the accident wrong by a day and spells his own first name 'Phinehas'. What does it claim about the injury?
answer: That he had fully recovered from it
choices: That he had fully recovered from it
That it killed two other men beside him
That no doctor had expected him to live
That it cost him the sight of both eyes
context: The inscription reads: 'This is the bar that was shot through the head of Mr. Phinehas P Gage at Cavendish Vermont Sept 14, 1848. He fully recovered from the injury & deposited this bar in the Museum of the Medical College of Harvard University.' Three errors in one object: the accident was 13 September, not the 14th; his name was Phineas; and 'fully recovered' is the very claim the case is now famous for disputing. The iron is catalogue number 03106, mounted in brass and wood. Source: Warren Anatomical Museum object record, Harvard Countway Library.

question: The portrait that made Phineas Gage famous — 'fitful, irreverent', 'capricious and vacillating', a foreman his own contractors would not take back — comes from one paper John Harlow read aloud to the Massachusetts Medical Society in 1868. His 1848 report had deliberately held the personality material back for 'a future communication', and twenty years went by before he delivered it. What had become of Gage by the day Harlow finally read it out?
answer: He had been dead in California for eight years
choices: He had been dead in California for eight years
He had been driving coaches in Chile for six years
He had been living under Harlow's roof for two years
He had been back at work in New England for four years
context: The vivid portrait everyone quotes describes Harlow's re-examination of April 1849 — a short observation window, written down two decades later, published eight years after the patient it describes was in his grave. Harlow's own summing-up was far more careful than the retellings: physically 'the recovery was quite complete during the four years immediately succeeding the injury,' while mentally it 'certainly was only partial, his intellectual faculties being decidedly impaired, but not totally lost; NOTHING LIKE DEMENTIA, but they were enfeebled in their manifestations, his mental operations being perfect in kind, but not in degree or quantity.' And the famous phrase 'no longer Gage' is reported speech, not Harlow's verdict — he attributes it to Gage's friends and acquaintances. Sources: Harlow 1848; Harlow 1868.

question: For a short time Phineas Gage put himself and his iron on show for money — the one grain of truth behind the sideshow version of his story. Henry Bigelow, the Harvard surgeon who had examined him, wrote that Gage was 'quite disposed to do anything of that sort to turn an honest penny'. Where does Harlow's account place him?
answer: At Barnum's American Museum in New York
choices: At Barnum's American Museum in New York
At Barnum's travelling circus and menagerie
At the Boston Museum on Tremont Street
At Peale's old museum in Philadelphia
context: Malcolm Macmillan, who spent years checking the retellings against the documents, is emphatic about the distinction: 'Harlow tells us that Phineas was an attraction at BARNUM'S AMERICAN MUSEUM in New York City (NOT Barnum's later circus!)' — Barnum's circus did not exist until 1871. Gage tried it briefly and gave it up. A surviving broadside shows him lecturing and exhibiting himself alone in Concord, New Hampshire, with doctors' testimonial letters he seems to have solicited himself. Bigelow's remark comes from an 1868 letter held by the Warren Museum. Sources: Macmillan, University of Akron Phineas Gage pages.

question: For about thirty years Jack and Beverly Wilgus owned a daguerreotype — an early photograph on a silvered plate — of a scarred, well-dressed young man holding a metal pole, and called it 'The Whaler': they took the pole for part of a harpoon and made up a whale to explain the closed eye. They posted it online in 2008, and a stranger commented that it might be Phineas Gage. How did the Wilguses settle it?
answer: They matched the writing on the pole to Harvard's tamping iron
choices: They matched the writing on the pole to Harvard's tamping iron
They matched the pole's length to Harvard's catalogue entry
They matched the closed eye to Harlow's note on the drooping lid
They traced the plate's earlier owners back to Gage's family
context: In their own words: 'we thought the pole he held was part of a harpoon.' The Flickr commenter was Michael Spurlock, who wrote '...maybe you found a photo of Phineas Gage? If so, it would be the only one known.' They tested the guess two ways — matching the lettering legible on the pole in the image to the inscription on the real tamping iron at Harvard, and matching the forehead scars to the plaster life mask Bigelow had made of Gage's head in 1849. It is the only known photograph of him. They donated it to the Warren Anatomical Museum in June 2016. Sources: Jack and Beverly Wilgus, brightbytes.com/phineasgage; Wilgus & Wilgus, Journal of the History of the Neurosciences 18:340-345 (2009).

question: Years after a tamping iron blew through the front of Phineas Gage's brain, he was in Chile driving a six-horse Concord coach on the Valparaíso–Santiago run: 110 miles, thirteen hours, a four in the morning start. Malcolm Macmillan and Matthew Lena rebuilt the driver's day from an 1860 advertisement for the line — the horses fed, groomed and harnessed before dawn, the luggage loaded, the passengers kept comfortable for thirteen hours. What else fell to the driver at each departure?
answer: Taking every passenger's fare and giving the change
choices: Taking every passenger's fare and giving the change
Fetching the locked mail satchel from the post office
Lighting the coach lamps for the ride out of the city
Rousing each passenger from his lodging before dawn
context: Passengers paid $10 and were allowed fifty pounds of luggage; the coach was built by Abbot-Downing of Concord, New Hampshire; Gage drove back to Valparaíso twenty-four hours after arriving. Handling the money is the part that matters: arithmetic, memory and the management of strangers, done daily for years by a man whom modern scientific articles routinely describe as a lying, insulting, violent wreck. A witness backs the record up: around 1860 Prof. J. W. Hamilton of Columbus, Ohio wrote down that Dr Henry Trevitt of Valparaíso 'KNEW GAGE WELL; that he lived in Chili, where he was engaged in stage driving; and that he was IN THE ENJOYMENT OF GOOD HEALTH, WITH NO IMPAIRMENT WHATEVER OF HIS MENTAL FACULTIES.' Macmillan's argument is that this punishing daily routine supplied informally what modern brain-injury rehabilitation supplies formally — the structured-environment programmes pioneered by the Soviet neuropsychologist Aleksandr Luria with wounded Red Army soldiers. His closing line: 'If Phineas was "No longer Gage" for some time after the accident HE FINALLY CAME CLOSE ENOUGH TO BEING GAGE AGAIN.' Even the date he left New England is unsettled: Harlow puts it in August 1852, but Dominic Hall of Harvard's Countway Library found an envelope apparently written by Gage and dated August 1854, asking that his tamping iron be handed to a Mr B. R. Sweatland. Sources: Macmillan & Lena, University of Akron Phineas Gage pages; Macmillan & Lena, Neuropsychological Rehabilitation 20:641-658 (2010); Harlow 1868.

question: In 2022 a team read every scientific journal article published between 1994 and 2020 that described Phineas Gage — twenty-five papers, written by working neuroscientists. Twenty-three reported that his personality changed, thirteen described him lying, insulting people and turning violent, and only four mentioned that he later worked in a livery stable and drove coaches in Chile for years. Twenty-four of the twenty-five laid the change entirely at the door of the brain damage. What did the twenty-fifth paper raise instead?
answer: That the disfigurement and the shunning had changed him
choices: That the disfigurement and the shunning had changed him
That the infection in the wound had spread the damage
That the years of exhibiting himself had coarsened him
That the drink of his later years had done the rest
context: Sixteen per cent mentioned his later employment and recovery; only one paper in twenty-five considered any alternative explanation for the reported change, such as disfigurement or social exclusion. The same review noted that Bigelow's contemporary assessment — after examining Gage in Boston in 1849-50 he called him 'quite recovered in faculties of body and mind', with only 'inconsiderable disturbance' — is routinely left out of modern articles. Macmillan's point about the popular version is blunter still: the drunken, brawling, unemployable drifter of the retellings appears in Harlow, in Bigelow, and in no other period document at all. Sources: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 16:734174 (2022), 'Neuroscience Education Begins With Good Science'; Macmillan, University of Akron Phineas Gage pages.

question: In 1994 Hanna Damasio's team announced where the iron had wrecked Phineas Gage's brain: they measured his skull, mapped it onto a computer model built from a different, cadaver skull deformed to fit, and concluded the damage was bilateral — both frontal lobes. In 2004 Peter Ratiu and Ion-Florin Talos put Gage's actual skull through a thin-slice CT scanner and rebuilt the path themselves. What did their reconstruction show?
answer: The left frontal lobe, with the ventricles and vessels spared
choices: The left frontal lobe, with the ventricles and vessels spared
The left frontal lobe, with the lateral ventricle laid open
The left frontal lobe, with the left temporal lobe behind it
The left frontal lobe, with the right one struck as well
context: Ratiu and Talos found the injury on the left side only, sparing the ventricles and the major blood vessels inside the skull — siding with Harlow's original reading against the 1994 model. They also concluded the skull hinged open as the iron passed through and the muscles of the face pulled it closed again. A third pass in 2012 (John Van Horn and colleagues) warped brain scans from 110 healthy men into a model of Gage's cranial vault and produced the strangest number of all: the iron crossed only about 3.97% of his cortical grey matter but destroyed roughly 10.7% of his white matter — the wiring, not the tissue, was the larger loss. And here is why the argument has no end: no autopsy was ever performed. Harlow wrote in 1868, 'It is regretted that an autopsy could not have been had.' Nobody has ever seen Gage's brain; every claim about which lobes were hit is inferred from the shape of a skull. Sources: H. Damasio et al., Science 264:1102-1105 (1994); Ratiu & Talos, NEJM 351:e21 (2004); Van Horn et al., PLoS ONE 7(5):e37454 (2012); Harlow 1868.

question: In a basement laboratory beneath the chemistry building at King's College London, Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling aimed a beam of X-rays at a bundle of damp DNA fibres less than a millimetre thick, and left the film in the dark to catch whatever scattered off it. Gosling ran the camera under Franklin's protocols. How long did that single exposure last?
answer: About sixty-two hours
choices: About forty minutes
About seven hours
About sixty-two hours
About eleven days
context: About sixty-two hours - two and a half days of X-rays for one photograph. The run began on 2 May 1952 and Gosling developed the plate on 6 May. He operated the camera under Franklin's protocols, which is why both names belong on the picture. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51; grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin; UKRI archive, 'From the archive: Rosalind Franklin's famous photo 51'.

question: A sharp X-ray picture of DNA needs a sample so pure that every fibre can be drawn out pointing the same way. Franklin and Gosling used DNA from a batch the Swiss chemist Rudolf Signer had handed out to researchers at a 1950 conference. What had Signer extracted it from?
answer: The thymus gland of a calf
choices: The sperm cells of a herring
The thymus gland of a calf
The root tips of a pea seedling
The liver tissue of a sheep
context: The DNA in the most famous photograph in biology came out of a cow: highly oriented fibres of sodium deoxyribonucleate from calf thymus. Signer's sample was exceptionally pure, and Maurice Wilkins found it could be drawn out into uniform fibres - which is what made sharp diffraction pictures possible at all. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51; NLM Profiles in Science, 'The DNA Riddle: King's College, London, 1951-1953'.

question: The most famous photograph in the history of biology has one of the least poetic names in science: Photo 51. It is not a code name, and it is not a nickname the newspapers invented. Where does the number come from?
answer: It was the fifty-first DNA picture in Franklin's numbered series at King's
choices: It was the fifty-first frame on the roll of film loaded in the camera
It was the fifty-first exposure attempted before a usable image appeared
It was the fifty-first DNA picture in Franklin's numbered series at King's
It was the fifty-first item logged in the King's College equipment ledger
context: It is a filing number. Photo 51 was simply the fifty-first photograph in Franklin's numbered series of DNA diffraction images taken at King's - the plainest possible name for an image that settled the shape of the molecule of life. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51.

question: At King's College London, Raymond Gosling ran the camera on a bundle of damp DNA fibres under Rosalind Franklin's protocols, then developed the plate in the darkroom. Only one molecular shape, and essentially no other, throws X-rays into the pattern that came up on that film - which is why a single photograph could settle the shape of the molecule of life. What was on the film?
answer: A dark cross of blobs running corner to corner
choices: A dark cross of blobs running corner to corner
A tight bullseye of rings circling the centre
A ladder of straight bars across the middle
A pair of dark arcs above and below the centre
context: A dark cross of blobs running corner to corner - the X that made the picture famous. A helix, and essentially nothing else, throws scattered X-rays into that crossed pattern of layer lines, which is why one photograph could settle the shape of the molecule of life. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51; UKRI archive, 'From the archive: Rosalind Franklin's famous photo 51'.

question: Rosalind Franklin's first research job had nothing to do with living things: from 1942 she X-rayed coal for the British Coal Utilisation Research Association, mapping the pores hidden inside it and pushing gases in to measure them. The narrow necks between the pores act as molecular sieves, and heating the coal squeezes those necks tighter. Which gas kept getting in the longest, until above about 1000 degrees C even it was shut out?
answer: Helium
choices: Argon
Methane
Helium
Nitrogen
context: Helium - the smallest atom there is, and heat coal past about 1000 degrees C and the constrictions close even on that. Franklin found the tightest necks of all in coals of 89 to 93 per cent carbon, and measurements like these let her predict how a given coal would behave in a furnace or a gas-mask filter. She published nineteen papers on coal and carbon, took her Cambridge PhD in 1945 with a thesis on solid organic colloids, and her split between graphitizing and non-graphitizing carbons still underpins carbon-fibre and nuclear-graphite work. She had written to her father in the summer of 1940, aged nineteen or twenty: 'Science and everyday life cannot and should not be separated. Science, for me, gives a partial explanation of life. In so far as it goes, it is based on fact, experience, and experiment.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin; quoteinvestigator.com/2021/09/12/science-everyday/, tracing the letter to Ellis Franklin quoted in Brenda Maddox, 'Rosalind Franklin: The Dark Lady of DNA' (2002).

question: DNA turns out to have two forms. The dry, crystalline A form appears when the air around the fibre is fairly dry; the wet B form, the shape DNA takes inside a living cell and the one Photo 51 shows, only holds together when the air stays above about 92 per cent humidity. Rosalind Franklin built a sealed chamber to hold her fibres in the wet form for days at a stretch. How did she moisten the air inside it?
answer: She bubbled hydrogen gas through salt solutions
choices: She pumped steam in from a heated glass flask
She bubbled hydrogen gas through salt solutions
She lined the chamber with damp blotting paper
She stood a dish of seawater beside the fibre
context: She bubbled hydrogen through salt solutions to set the humidity precisely. The dry A form appears at roughly 75% relative humidity; the biologically real B form needs about 92% or higher, and that is where Photo 51 was taken. Two more tricks did the rest: she filled the camera itself with hydrogen gas so stray air molecules would not scatter the beam and fog the picture, and drew her fibre bundles under a millimetre thick. Earlier pictures by William Astbury in the 1930s and by Wilkins around 1950 mixed the A and B forms in one fibre and blurred both. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin; grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51; NLM Profiles in Science; UKRI archive blog.

question: Photo 51 carries more than a shape. The spacings between the blobs give the size of the molecule, a full turn every 34 angstroms and a step every 3.4, but the brightness of the spots carries something else: it says where in the molecule the heavy phosphate-and-sugar chains are sitting. Where did those intensities put them?
answer: On the outside of the molecule, with the bases turned inward
choices: In the core of the molecule, with the bases turned outward
On the outside of the molecule, with the bases turned inward
In the core of the molecule, held together by magnesium ions
Along one edge of a flat ribbon, with the bases on the other
context: Backbone outside, bases turned in. The spacings gave a 3.4 angstrom rise between bases, a 34 angstrom pitch for one full turn - therefore about ten bases per turn - and an overall diameter near 20 angstroms; the intensity distribution put the phosphate-sugar backbone on the outer surface. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51; grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin.

question: In March 1953 Rosalind Franklin left King's for Birkbeck College, a move she described as going from a palace to a slum, and pointed her camera at tobacco mosaic virus, a rod-shaped virus whose protein subunits wind in a helix around a hollow central channel. Her pictures were the finest X-ray work then existing on any virus, and they did something nobody had managed: they located the virus's RNA. Where in the rod does it lie?
answer: Embedded in the protein coat, out from the axis
choices: Lying loose inside the hollow central channel
Coated over the outer surface of the whole rod
Knotted into a tight ball at one end of the rod
Embedded in the protein coat, out from the axis
context: Not down the middle: the RNA spiral lies embedded about 40 angstroms out from the rod's axis, threaded into the protein itself. Franklin published seventeen papers on virus structure in five years at Birkbeck, and had begun on poliovirus - keeping live virus in the lab - when she died. Aaron Klug, John Finch, Kenneth Holmes and Donald Caspar carried the work on; Klug took the 1982 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for what grew out of it. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin; A. Klug, 'The tobacco mosaic virus particle: structure and assembly'; nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1982/.

question: At a departmental talk at King's College London in November 1951, Rosalind Franklin laid out her DNA results in front of a visiting James Watson, who took no notes. Watson went back to Cambridge, and he and Francis Crick built a three-chain model out of what he half-remembered, with the water content wrong by a large factor. They invited the King's group over to admire it, and Franklin demolished it where she stood. What did Lawrence Bragg, the director of Watson and Crick's own laboratory, do about it?
answer: He banned the pair from working on DNA at all
choices: He ordered them to rebuild it with more chains
He banned the pair from working on DNA at all
He sent them to King's to apologise in person
He wrote to Nature withdrawing the model
context: Bragg barred them from DNA - the two men who would share the 1962 Nobel for it were, in 1951, ordered off the problem entirely. Franklin's own notes for that talk survive in the Churchill College Archives at Cambridge: 'Either the structure is a big helix or a smaller helix consisting of several chains.' She was reading the data; they were guessing at a model. Source: NLM Profiles in Science, 'The DNA Riddle: King's College, London, 1951-1953'.

question: By January 1953 Rosalind Franklin was preparing to leave King's, and under the laboratory's rules she had handed the DNA work and materials over to Maurice Wilkins; Raymond Gosling had been reassigned to him as well. On 30 January James Watson came down from Cambridge to visit the King's laboratory. What did Wilkins do that day?
answer: He showed Watson the photograph, without telling Franklin
choices: He showed Watson the photograph after asking Franklin
He let Watson copy Franklin's exposure notebooks instead
He showed Watson the photograph, without telling Franklin
He refused Watson the photograph and argued the numbers
context: He showed Watson Photo 51, without Franklin's knowledge or consent. Wilkins had legitimate institutional access - Gosling had been reassigned to him and Franklin had handed the materials over under the lab's rules - but nobody asked her before her photograph went outside the building. That is the precise shape of the grievance: not theft of a photograph, but the unconsented showing of it to a competitor. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51, sections 'Sharing and Access by Maurice Wilkins' and 'Allegations of Unauthorized Use'.

question: James Watson's 1968 memoir The Double Helix calls Rosalind Franklin 'Rosy' from beginning to end, a nickname she disliked and one nobody used to her face, while every man in the book gets his surname. The portrait it draws of her is where most of the modern bitterness about the discovery comes from, and it arrived ten years after she died. What did Watson himself do about that portrait in the same book?
answer: He conceded in an epilogue that it had been unjust
choices: He defended it in a preface as strictly accurate
He blamed it on Crick's recollection in a footnote
He struck her name out of the later printings
He conceded in an epilogue that it had been unjust
context: He took it back, in the same volume. Watson's epilogue: 'Since my initial impressions of her, both scientific and personal (as recorded in the early pages of this book), were often wrong, I want to say something here about her achievements.' He added that 'Rosalind's exemplary courage and integrity were apparent to all when, knowing she was mortally ill, she did not complain but continued working on a high level until a few weeks before her death.' Worth knowing too: Franklin and Francis Crick became genuine friends afterwards. She convalesced at the Cricks' Cambridge home after her cancer operations and sent Crick her draft papers for comment, and she never accused either man of anything. Source: Watson, 'The Double Helix' (1968), epilogue; nautil.us, 'Crick and Watson Did Not Steal Franklin's Data'; Rosalind Franklin Institute.

question: Photo 51's cross is built of blobs marching outward along each arm, and the most sophisticated thing in the whole picture is one that is not there: on each arm, the fourth blob is missing. A gap like that is not a flaw in the plate or a slip in the developing. It is the photograph telling you how the molecule's two strands sit in relation to each other. What does the missing blob say?
answer: The two strands sit offset along the axis by three-eighths of a turn
choices: The two strands sit exactly level with each other, rung against rung
The two strands sit offset along the axis by three-eighths of a turn
The two strands twist a full half-turn out of step with each other
The two strands swap places with one another once every full turn
context: A missing layer-line reflection means the two strands are not lined up with each other - they are staggered along the axis by about three-eighths of the helical pitch. The photograph does not merely say 'helix'; read carefully, it says 'two strands, offset'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Photo_51; UKRI archive blog, 'one missing blob revealing that DNA strands run offset from each other'.

question: It is repeated everywhere that the Nobel committee snubbed Rosalind Franklin. The 1962 Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins for the molecular structure of nucleic acids, and her name is not on it. The reason it is not on it, though, is arithmetic rather than malice, and the arithmetic is written into the Nobel Foundation's own statutes. One of them caps a shared prize at three people. What does the other one forbid?
answer: Awarding a prize to anyone who has already died
choices: Awarding a prize to anyone who has won one before
Awarding a prize for work published ten years earlier
Awarding a prize to anyone who has already died
Awarding a prize to an institution, not a person
context: A Nobel is not awarded posthumously (before 1974 the sole exception covered someone nominated while still alive). Rosalind Franklin died of ovarian cancer at her London home on 16 April 1958, aged thirty-seven - four years before the 1962 prize. She was not passed over by the committee; she was never in the running, because she was dead. The statutes' other line, verbatim: 'In no case may a prize amount be divided between more than three persons.' The story that the committee snubbed her is false, and the bank corrects it rather than repeating it. Source: nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1962/summary/; nobelprize.org/frequently-asked-questions/; grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin.  (Legend.)

question: Photo 51 was not the only thing that crossed from King's College London to Cambridge in early 1953. A Medical Research Council progress report carrying Rosalind Franklin's measurements reached Francis Crick, who was building DNA models at the Cavendish with James Watson, by way of Max Perutz. Crick's eye stopped on three dry words in it: 'face-centred monoclinic', crystallographers' shorthand for the symmetry of a crystal's repeating unit. He had met that symmetry before in horse haemoglobin, and saw at once what it forced on the molecule. What did those three words tell Crick about the chains inside DNA?
answer: The two chains run in opposite directions to each other
choices: The two chains run in opposite directions to each other
The two chains carry identical sequences of bases
The two chains are mirror images, one of them left-handed
The two chains are joined end to end into a single loop
context: They run in opposite directions - one chain up, one chain down, an arrangement chemists call antiparallel. 'Face-centred monoclinic' names the C2 space group, and C2 symmetry means the molecule carries a two-fold axis lying across it: turn the whole thing end over end and it looks the same, which can only be true if the two chains point opposite ways. Crick recognised the symmetry at a glance because he had met it in horse haemoglobin. Photo 51 gave Watson and Crick the shape of the molecule; Franklin's progress report, reaching Crick through Max Perutz in early 1953, gave them the way the two chains face - a second channel out of King's that mattered as much as the photograph. Source: NLM Profiles in Science, 'The DNA Riddle: King's College, London, 1951-1953'; grokipedia.com/page/Rosalind_Franklin.

question: Watson and Crick's April 1953 paper ends with one sentence about the King's laboratory: they had been 'stimulated by a knowledge of the general nature of the unpublished experimental results and ideas' of the researchers there. An earlier draft had said considerably more. It called Rosalind Franklin's work 'very beautiful experimental work' and admitted to 'much unpublished experimental material'. Neither phrase survived into print, and Watson and Crick agreed to drop them both. Who asked them to?
answer: Maurice Wilkins
choices: Lawrence Bragg
Rosalind Franklin
Maurice Wilkins
Max Perutz
context: Wilkins asked for both phrases to come out, and Watson and Crick agreed. The published sentence thanks 'Dr. M. H. F. Wilkins, Dr. R. E. Franklin and their co-workers at King's College, London' - historian Lynne Elkin's objection is that 'general' is doing enormous work there, since they had her photograph and her specific measurements. Three papers ran back to back in Nature on 25 April 1953: Watson and Crick first, Wilkins, Stokes and Wilson second, Franklin and Gosling's 'Molecular Configuration in Sodium Thymonucleate' third - so generations of readers assumed hers merely confirmed the model, when she had written it before seeing theirs. In 2023 Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, working from two overlooked 1953 documents in her Churchill College archive, argued she should be seen not as a victim but as 'an equal member of a quartet who solved the double helix'. Source: Exploratorium, Cold Spring Harbor origins archive; nature.com/articles/171740a0; Cobb & Comfort, Nature 616:657 (2023).

question: On 18 December 1912, Charles Dawson and the British Museum's Arthur Smith Woodward stood before the Geological Society of London and unveiled bones from a gravel pit that they said belonged to a very early human ancestor. Arthur Smith Woodward soon wrote a short book giving the creature what nickname?
answer: The earliest Englishman
choices: The earliest Englishman
The Sussex chimp
Man of the Downs
The London ape
context: That the largest early human skull had turned up in a British field was part of the appeal. Germany had Neanderthals, France had Cro-Magnon - Britain now had its own missing link, or so it thought. Source: livescience.com/56327-piltdown-man-hoax

question: Piltdown's find slotted neatly into the leading theory of the day about which feature of the human body had evolved first. Which feature did that theory put ahead of the others?
answer: A modern-sized brain
choices: A modern-sized brain
An upright walking posture
A grasping opposable thumb
Small, flat, human-style teeth
context: A creature with a large braincase but a still-ape-like jaw was exactly what a brain-first hypothesis predicted. The counter-view - that walking upright came first and the big brain last - had to wait for evidence Piltdown would keep suppressing. Source: nationalgeographic.com/history/article/taung-child-human-ancestor

question: Raymond Dart published his description of the Taung Child, a small-bodied upright ancestor from South Africa, in Nature on 7 February 1925. How did the British scientific establishment mostly react?
answer: They dismissed it as a young ape and kept teaching the Sussex specimen instead
choices: They dismissed it as a young ape and kept teaching the Sussex specimen instead
They accepted it immediately as vindication of an African origin
They demanded the fossil be shipped to the British Museum for safekeeping
They quietly withdrew the Sussex specimen from their textbooks that year
context: Dart's find had a small brain and an upright body - the exact opposite of what Piltdown predicted. Search for human origins stayed pointed at Europe for another twenty years. Arthur Keith, one of the loudest doubters, only admitted in 1947 that 'Prof. Dart was right and I was wrong'. Source: nationalgeographic.com/history/article/taung-child-human-ancestor

question: Not everyone was fooled. As early as 1913, the Edinburgh anatomist David Waterston looked at the two Sussex bones and said something that ought to have ended the story. What did he say?
answer: The cranium and the jaw simply did not belong together
choices: The cranium and the jaw simply did not belong together
The bones were less than a century old
The gravel pit had been salted with fake tools
The signature on the field notes had been forged
context: In the 1920s the German anatomist Franz Weidenreich went further and said the jaw was an orangutan's. British prestige swallowed both dissents whole. Being right on the anatomy was not enough. Source: nhm.ac.uk/our-science/services/library/collections/piltdown-man

question: In 1949 the British Museum's Kenneth Oakley applied a chemistry test that would eventually undo Piltdown. His method used fluorine absorbed from groundwater. What kind of dating does the fluorine test give you?
answer: Relative - whether two bones from a site share an age
choices: Relative - whether two bones from a site share an age
Absolute - the age of a bone in years since it was buried
Environmental - the water chemistry of the burial site
Dietary - what the animal ate in its last months alive
context: Bones lying together in the same wet gravel soak up fluorine at roughly the same rate. Oakley used it to compare the Piltdown pieces against the animal bones supposedly buried with them - and the human-sized cranium and the ape-shaped jaw came back with very different values. Source: britannica.com/biography/Kenneth-Page-Oakley

question: In 1953 Oakley returned to Piltdown with Joseph Weiner of Oxford and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark. This time they added a nitrogen test that measures how much protein is left in a bone. What did the jaw give them?
answer: The protein levels of a modern bone
choices: The protein levels of a modern bone
The same reading as the mammoth teeth beside it
No reading - the jaw was too mineralised to measure
A protein signature matching Neanderthal bones from France
context: Old bones lose their protein slowly; the Piltdown jaw still held roughly a modern amount. Two different chemical clocks were now both saying the same thing: this bone did not belong in that pit. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Oakley

question: Under a microscope the 1953 team looked at the chewing surfaces of the Piltdown molars. Instead of ordinary wear from a lifetime of chewing, what did they see?
answer: Scratches running in directions no chewing motion would ever make
choices: Scratches running in directions no chewing motion would ever make
A perfect polish left by centuries in acidic soil
Symmetrical grooves matching a modern dental crown
Tiny embedded grains of Nile River sand
context: Somebody had FILED the teeth flat, then stained the whole assembly with iron salts and potassium dichromate so it would match the rusty gravel. It was the microscope that saw the file marks the naked eye had missed for forty years. Source: historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/piltdown-man

question: The 1953 verdict is the load-bearing fact everyone should get right. What were the Piltdown pieces actually made of?
answer: A human braincase joined to the jaw of an orangutan
choices: A human braincase joined to the jaw of an orangutan
A gorilla braincase joined to a chimpanzee jaw
Two matching pieces of a single early Neanderthal
A carved and cured lump of freshwater bog oak
context: The braincase was a human skull only a few centuries old; the jaw was from an orangutan, most likely from Borneo. A 2016 micro-CT study by Isabelle De Groote showed the emptied tooth sockets had been packed with Piltdown gravel and repaired with dental putty. Source: royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/3/8/160328

question: In 2016 Isabelle De Groote and colleagues published a DNA study in Royal Society Open Science. They compared the canine tooth from the 1912 site with a molar from a second site nearby. What did the DNA show?
answer: Both teeth came from the same orangutan, from southwest Sarawak in Borneo
choices: Both teeth came from the same orangutan, from southwest Sarawak in Borneo
The teeth came from two unrelated orangutans a century apart
One tooth was a modern zoo specimen, the other genuinely ancient
Both teeth were carved from mammoth ivory, not tooth at all
context: One forger, one specimen, two dig sites - which points hard at the only man who was present at every find. Charles Dawson turns out to have a documented history of at least 38 other faked antiquities. Source: nhm.ac.uk/discover/news/2016/august/piltdown-man-charles-dawson-likely-fraudster

question: There is one strong circumstantial fact about the Piltdown finds themselves that any detective would notice. The bones and tools appeared steadily from 1912 through 1915, and then the digging suddenly went dry. What happened in August 1916?
answer: Charles Dawson himself died and was buried
choices: Charles Dawson himself died and was buried
The British Museum sealed the Piltdown pit
Arthur Smith Woodward retired from field work
The First World War closed the site to civilians
context: No Dawson, no more Piltdown. A bizarre bone implement from 1914, shaped nothing like a real tool, had already been nicknamed 'the cricket bat' - the digs were getting silly, and then they stopped. Source: nhm.ac.uk/our-science/services/library/collections/piltdown-man

question: The lesson of Piltdown is not that fossil hoaxes stopped - it is that they now get caught faster. In October 1999, National Geographic unveiled 'Archaeoraptor', supposedly a missing link between dinosaurs and birds from China. How was it exposed within months?
answer: CT scanning showed it was several fossils glued together
choices: CT scanning showed it was several fossils glued together
Carbon dating showed the rock was actually modern plaster
A whistle-blower posted photographs of the forger at work
A microscope showed the feathers were modern chicken down
context: Xu Xing of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology in Beijing found the matching counter-slab that carried the real dinosaur tail; Timothy Rowe's CT scans showed the whole specimen was assembled from pieces of at least two different animals. Piltdown took forty years, Archaeoraptor took a few months. Source: royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/3/8/160328

question: Step outside on a winter night and find Orion. Two of its brightest stars sit at opposite extremes: Betelgeuse, at the hunter's shoulder, is about 3,800 K, while Rigel, at his foot, is about 12,100 K — more than three times hotter. Your naked eye can tell which is which, with no instrument at all. What colour does Rigel show?
answer: Blue-white
choices: Blue-white
Orange-red
Deep yellow
Dull crimson
context: Rigel is blue-white, spectral type B8 Ia, effective temperature around 12,100 K. Betelgeuse is the orange-red one, type M1-M2 Ia-ab at 3,779 +/- 38 K. Hotter means bluer, so a star's colour is a thermometer you can read from your own back yard — and both stars sit in the same constellation on the same evening, so go outside and check the claim yourself tonight. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigel; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betelgeuse.

question: Physicists studying glowing objects needed a perfect absorber: an object that takes in every ray of every wavelength that reaches it. In 1859 Gustav Kirchhoff described how to build one, and laboratories have copied his design ever since. What is it?
answer: A closed opaque box with one small hole
choices: A closed opaque box with one small hole
A hollow sphere with a soot-lined inner wall
A thick slab of lampblack behind a glass plate
A deep cone lined with black velvet
context: Light that gets in through the little hole rattles around inside, losing a bit at every bounce, and essentially never finds its way back out — so the hole absorbs everything, and therefore emits the pure universal glow. Physicists call the device a hohlraum, or cavity radiator, and the aperture has to be much smaller than the cavity. The blackest thing in the laboratory is a hole. Source: Grokipedia 'Planck's law' (Kirchhoff 1859: cavity radiation from a small hole in an otherwise closed box, multiple internal reflections mimicking perfect absorption).

question: Heat an iron poker and its glow marches through the colours — dull red, then orange, then white. In 1893 Wilhelm Wien reduced that whole progression to one line of arithmetic, simple enough to point at a star and read off its temperature. What does Wien's displacement law say the brightest wavelength does?
answer: Falls to half every time the temperature doubles
choices: Falls to half every time the temperature doubles
Falls to a quarter every time the temperature doubles
Falls to a sixteenth every time the temperature doubles
Falls by a fixed number of micrometres per degree
context: Wien's displacement law: lambda_max x T = b, with b about 2898 micrometre-kelvin. He got it from thermodynamics alone, no new physics required. Double the temperature and the brightest wavelength is cut in half, which is exactly why the poker slides from red toward blue-white as the forge heats it. Source: Grokipedia 'Planck's law' ('In 1893, Wilhelm Wien derived a displacement law from thermodynamic considerations... lambda_max T = b'; 'b approx 2898 micro-m.K').

question: In 1879 Josef Stefan combed through other people's measurements of heated bodies and found a rule hiding in the numbers: the total power radiated by a blackbody — an object that absorbs every ray landing on it — climbs with its absolute temperature raised to a fixed power. Ludwig Boltzmann derived the same rule from theory in 1884. Double a star's absolute temperature, and how much more energy does it pour out each second?
answer: Sixteen times as much
choices: Twice as much
Four times as much
Eight times as much
Sixteen times as much
context: The power is the FOURTH power of temperature, so doubling T multiplies the output by 2^4 = 16. Stefan spotted the pattern in 1879 in data he had not taken himself; Boltzmann derived it from thermodynamics in 1884, which is why it is now the Stefan-Boltzmann law. It is also why a hot blue star outshines a cool red one so brutally. Source: Grokipedia 'Planck's law' (Stefan 1879 T^4 dependence, Boltzmann's 1884 derivation).

question: Take three of Gustav Kirchhoff's cavity radiators — one built of iron, one of clay, one of charcoal — and heat all three to the same temperature until their apertures glow. Kirchhoff proved in 1859, from thermodynamics alone and without touching an experiment, what those three glows must do. What is his result?
answer: The holes glow identically, though their bare surfaces do not
choices: The holes glow identically, though their bare surfaces do not
The holes match in brightness, though their colours differ
The holes match in colour, though their brightness differs
The holes match at long waves, though they differ in the visible
context: Kirchhoff argued that the ratio of a body's emitting power to its absorbing power is a universal function of wavelength and temperature alone — independent of what the body is made of and independent of its shape. A cavity is where that argument bites hardest: whatever the walls are made of, the little hole absorbs everything that enters, so it must emit the pure universal glow, set by temperature and nothing else. Bare surfaces are a different story — polished iron emits far less than charcoal at the same temperature, which is exactly why the laboratory standard is a hole and not a slab. That universality is what turned one curve into THE open problem of nineteenth-century physics: find it once and you have found it for every glowing thing in the universe. Sources: Grokipedia 'Planck's law'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirchhoff's_law_of_thermal_radiation.

question: Take classical physics at its word and apply it to the light rattling around inside a furnace, as Lord Rayleigh did in 1900 and James Jeans refined in 1905, and it predicts something that should have stopped physics dead: open the door and the light pouring out should carry unlimited energy, ever more of it at ever shorter wavelengths. The whole disaster follows from one innocent-looking rule about how a hot body's energy gets shared out. What was the rule?
answer: Every vibration gets exactly the same average share
choices: Every vibration gets exactly the same average share
Every vibration gets a share proportional to its frequency
Every vibration gets a share proportional to its amplitude
Every vibration gets a share proportional to the volume
context: This is the equipartition theorem: classical thermodynamics hands every vibration mode in the cavity the same average energy, kT. Because there is no ceiling on how many short-wavelength modes a cavity can hold, the predicted energy density climbs as nu^2 T with no limit — B_nu(T) runs to infinity as nu does. The name everyone now uses for the absurdity, 'ultraviolet catastrophe', was attached to it much later, by Paul Ehrenfest. Sources: Grokipedia 'Planck's law' (Rayleigh 1900, Jeans 1905); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet_catastrophe.

question: Max Planck's new radiation formula contained a constant nobody had ever needed before, and he had no instrument that could measure it directly. So he fitted it to Otto Lummer and Ernst Pringsheim's cavity data — a fundamental number of nature, squeezed out of a laboratory oven in 1900 by curve-fitting. Since the 2019 redefinition of the SI units that constant has been fixed at an exact value. How close was Planck's first, oven-fitted figure?
answer: Within about one percent
choices: Within about one percent
Within about thirty percent
Within a factor of two
Within a factor of ten
context: Planck got 6.55 x 10^-27 erg.s, that is 6.55 x 10^-34 J.s; the value frozen into the SI in 2019 is exactly 6.62607015 x 10^-34 J.s. He got more than that out of the oven, too: from the same fit he extracted Boltzmann's constant, Avogadro's number and the charge on the electron, all within about 3 percent — and his electron charge beat J. J. Thomson's own direct electrical measurements, which scattered as high as 2.186 x 10^-19 C. Sources: Grokipedia 'Max Planck' and 'Planck's law'; scielo.br/j/rbef/a/XMkjKHvTWdsTF9k5HF6Vzwv.

question: On Sunday 7 October 1900 Heinrich Rubens and his wife came to dinner at Max Planck's house in Berlin. Over the meal Rubens described measurements he had just finished at a wavelength of 51 micrometres, far out in the infrared, roughly a hundred times longer than visible light. Then the guests went home. What did Planck do before the night was out?
answer: Worked out a new formula and mailed it to Rubens on a postcard
choices: Worked out a new formula and mailed it to Rubens on a postcard
Wrote to Wilhelm Wien warning him that his law was in trouble
Repeated Rubens's arithmetic to look for a mistake in it
Sent word to Otto Lummer asking for his oven data as well
context: Rubens had the postcard in his hands the next day, and a few days later reported back that the formula seemed to fit all of his measurements. Planck presented it publicly on 19 October 1900. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rubens (dinner of 7 October 1900, the 51 micrometre data, the postcard, Rubens's confirmation); corroborated by handwiki.org/wiki/Biography:Heinrich_Rubens and jqi.umd.edu/news/planck-and-birth-quantum-mechanics — note that the JQI piece misnames him 'Hermann'; he was Heinrich.

question: Nobody could study the far-infrared end of a hot body's glow without some way to pull one narrow band of very long waves out of the broad mess a lamp throws off. Heinrich Rubens found a way using nothing but crystals, and named the surviving light Reststrahlen — 'residual rays'. By 1898 it had him working at about 60 micrometres, a hundred times the wavelength of visible light. What did his apparatus do to the beam?
answer: Bounced it off several crystals in succession
choices: Bounced it off several crystals in succession
Spread it with a crystal prism and cut the far edge
Passed it through a stack of crystal plates
Cooled a crystal until only one band survived
context: A crystal reflects most strongly at exactly the wavelengths it absorbs most strongly. So every reflection throws away more of the unwanted light and leaves the beam purer; after several bounces in a row, only a narrow far-infrared band is left. That instrument is the whole reason Rubens could see where nobody else could — and it is what let him carry Max Planck numbers no theory had ever been tested against. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rubens.

question: Textbooks say Max Planck invented the quantum to slay the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' — classical physics' prediction of unlimited energy at short wavelengths. Historians say otherwise: Planck never accepted the energy-sharing rule that prediction rested on, so he ignored it, and the phrase itself was coined by Paul Ehrenfest in 1911, eleven years too late to have driven anything. What actually cornered Planck came from the opposite end of the spectrum, in Heinrich Rubens and Ferdinand Kurlbaum's long-wavelength measurements. Holding the wavelength fixed and raising the temperature, what did they find the radiated energy doing?
answer: Climbing in a straight line with the temperature
choices: Climbing in a straight line with the temperature
Climbing as the square of the temperature
Climbing as the fourth power of the temperature
Climbing steeply at first, then flattening off
context: The law Planck was actually trying to justify was Wien's 1896 distribution — an exponential fall-off that fitted the SHORT-wavelength data beautifully. Rubens and Kurlbaum showed it failed at LONG wavelengths, where the energy simply rose in proportion to temperature. That is the opposite end of the spectrum from the ultraviolet, and one historian's verdict on the famous catastrophe is blunt: it 'played no part at all in the earliest phase of quantum theory'. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Rubens; physicsworld.com/a/max-planck-the-reluctant-revolutionary/; Grokipedia 'Planck's law'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet_catastrophe (Ehrenfest, 1911, Annalen der Physik).

question: Max Planck wrote to the American physicist Robert Williams Wood in 1931, thirty-one years after the December 1900 paper that started quantum theory, and set down the plainest account of it anyone ever got from him: how he had come to the idea, and what he made of his own move. In that letter Planck gave the move a name, and the name has stuck to it ever since. What did he call it?
answer: An act of desperation
choices: An act of desperation
A leap in the dark
A purely formal assumption
A surrender to the numbers
context: Verbatim: 'Briefly, what I did can be described simply as an act of desperation. By nature I am peaceful and opposed to uncertain adventures. However, I had already struggled unsuccessfully for six years with the problem of the equilibrium between radiation and matter without reaching any successful result.' A theoretical interpretation, he added, 'had to be found at any cost, no matter how high.' The letter is dated 7 October 1931; the dinner at which Rubens handed him the data was 7 October 1900. Sources: institucional.us.es/blogimus/en/2018/12/lord-kelvins-second-little-cloud-ii/ (verbatim, dated); provenance via en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Max_Planck (Archive for the History of Quantum Physics, as quoted in Kuhn, 'Black-Body Theory and the Quantum Discontinuity', 1978).

question: Max Planck's radiation formula of 1900 required energy to come in whole packets, sized by a new constant of nature. For most of the decade that followed, Planck poured his effort into a single project, which he later called 'unavailing attempts' that 'caused me much trouble'; only around 1908 did he abandon it. What had all that effort gone into?
answer: Trying to fit the packets back inside classical physics
choices: Trying to fit the packets back inside classical physics
Trying to derive the new constant from the ether's properties
Trying to rebuild Boltzmann's statistics without probability
Trying to stretch the formula to cover the new X-rays
context: In Planck's own words: 'My unavailing attempts to somehow reintegrate the action quantum into classical theory extended over several years and caused me much trouble.' Between 1901 and 1906 he published nothing at all on blackbody radiation or quantum theory, and only around 1908, largely persuaded by the Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz, did he accept that the quantum of action was real and irreducible. The man who started quantum theory spent most of a decade trying to undo it, and it was Einstein, not Planck, who first took the packets seriously as real things. In 1913 Planck, Walther Nernst, Heinrich Rubens and Emil Warburg nominated Einstein to the Prussian Academy and excused his light-quantum hypothesis as an occasional miss by a man willing to take risks; that 'miss' won Einstein the Nobel Prize eight years later. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck; physicsworld.com/a/max-planck-the-reluctant-revolutionary/.

question: In January 1990 John Mather stood up at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society and put up the first nine minutes of data from a new satellite instrument: a blackbody curve matched so exactly that the error bars would not show on the plot. The room rose and applauded. What was glowing?
answer: The faint microwave glow filling the entire sky
choices: The faint microwave glow filling the entire sky
The outer atmosphere of the Sun, seen from orbit
The satellite's own helium-cooled reference cavity
The ring of dust around the centre of the Milky Way
context: The instrument was FIRAS aboard COBE, and the object was the cosmic microwave background at about 2.725 K. Final analysis put the deviations from a perfect blackbody below 50 parts per million of the peak intensity — the most perfect blackbody spectrum ever measured, and it happens to be the whole sky. A formula that Max Planck fitted to a Berlin laboratory oven in 1900 turned out to describe the leftover heat of the universe itself. Sources: nobelprize.org 2006 Physics popular information (Mather's 1990 AAS chart and the standing ovation); lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/cobe/firas_overview.html; ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Sept05/Gawiser2/Gawiser2.html.

question: Every school poster of the states of matter shows the same three: solid, liquid, gas. Yet a lightning bolt is none of them, the glow inside a neon sign is none of them, and the Sun itself is none of them. What is the fourth state of matter they all share?
answer: Plasma
choices: Plasma
Vapour
Mist
Foam
context: Lightning, neon signs, fluorescent tubes, the hottest part of a candle flame, the Sun and the aurora are all plasmas -- ionised matter with free electrons and positive ions. It is by far the most common state of ordinary matter in the visible universe, and it is the one most children never meet at school. Source: iter.org, 'Plasma: a strange state of matter'.

question: A hot gas and a plasma look similar in a glass tube, but a plasma does two things a gas cannot. Hold a magnet near a neon sign's discharge and it visibly bends; wire the tube into a circuit and current flows through it. What has changed inside the gas to give it these new powers?
answer: Its atoms have been torn into free electrons and positive ions
choices: Its atoms have been torn into free electrons and positive ions
Its atoms have been packed close enough to touch
Its atoms have been cooled into their ground state
Its atoms have been fused into heavier elements
context: Ionisation is what promotes a gas to a plasma. The free charges make it conduct electricity, and because the particles all carry charge they respond collectively to electric and magnetic fields -- a gas cannot do either. Source: iter.org, 'Plasma: a strange state of matter'.

question: On 22 August 1879, in Sheffield, a British chemist showed the British Association a set of evacuated glass tubes that glowed strangely when he ran high voltage through them. He argued the stuff inside was so different from gas that it deserved to be called a fourth state of matter, and titled his lecture 'On Radiant Matter'. Who was he?
answer: William Crookes
choices: William Crookes
Michael Faraday
J. J. Thomson
Humphry Davy
context: Crookes was already famous for discovering thallium and inventing the Crookes radiometer. His mechanism was wrong -- he thought the glow was a stream of charged molecules, and Thomson later showed the rays were electrons -- but his intuition of a distinct fourth state stuck. Source: sheffieldhistory.co.uk on the 1879 Sheffield lecture.

question: In 1928 at General Electric, an American chemist studying ionised gas in vacuum tubes wrote a paper called 'Oscillations in Ionized Gases' and coined the word we now use for the fourth state. His colleague Harold Mott-Smith later said he chose it because the way the ionised gas seemed to carry electrons along reminded him of the way blood carries corpuscles. Who was he?
answer: Irving Langmuir
choices: Irving Langmuir
Enrico Fermi
Robert Millikan
Percy Bridgman
context: The paper appeared in PNAS 14:627 (1928). Langmuir borrowed the name from biology: blood plasma is the pale fluid carrying red and white cells, and he thought his ionised gas played the same role for its electrons. Langmuir won the 1932 Nobel in Chemistry for his surface-chemistry work. Sources: pnas.org 14:627; iter.org 'Why plasma?'.

question: It is often said that '99% of the universe is plasma'. That claim needs one careful word to be true. Which qualifier makes it right?
answer: 99% of the universe's ordinary matter is plasma
choices: 99% of the universe's ordinary matter is plasma
99% of the universe's total mass-energy is plasma
99% of the universe's dark matter is plasma
99% of the universe's total volume is plasma
context: Dark matter and dark energy together make up about 95% of the universe's mass-energy in the standard model, and neither is plasma. Of what is left -- ordinary baryonic matter, the stuff of stars and gas clouds -- well over 99% is in the plasma state. Precision matters: the popular slogan drops the qualifier and quietly becomes false. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Dark matter'.

question: In 1929 Lowell Observatory hired a 23-year-old Kansas farm boy to photograph the same patch of sky twice, then flick between the two plates in a blink comparator looking for the single dot that had shifted. On 18 February 1930 he caught it. What was his name?
answer: Clyde Tombaugh
choices: Clyde Tombaugh
Milton Humason
Vesto Slipher
Andrew Douglass
context: Tombaugh (1906-1997) was hired straight off the family farm on the strength of his own hand-ground telescopes. The official announcement was made on 13 March 1930, the anniversary of Percival Lowell's birth and of Herschel's discovery of Uranus. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: Once Lowell Observatory had confirmed the new world beyond Neptune in March 1930, they needed a name for it. The winning suggestion came over breakfast one morning from an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, and her grandfather passed it to an astronomer friend. What did she call it?
answer: Pluto
choices: Pluto
Persephone
Minerva
Cronus
context: Venetia Burney, then aged 11, suggested the name at breakfast; her grandfather passed it to the astronomer Herbert Hall Turner, who cabled it to Lowell. The name won a unanimous vote and Disney later borrowed it for a puppy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: Pluto's demotion story had actually played out once before. On 1 January 1801 Giuseppe Piazzi in Palermo found a body between Mars and Jupiter that was called the eighth planet for decades. Then dozens more of the same kind turned up in the same region, and by the 1850s astronomers had reclassified the lot. What did they choose to call this new class of body?
answer: Asteroids
choices: Asteroids
Moonlets
Nebulae
Comets
context: William Herschel coined 'asteroid' (star-like) for these small bodies in 1802; the label caught on as the belt filled up. Ceres, Pallas, Juno and Vesta were called planets for about fifty years before the reclassification. The same argument was waiting for Pluto. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: Clyde Tombaugh had been hired to hunt Percival Lowell's 'Planet X', predicted from apparent wobbles in the orbit of Uranus. Pluto turned up close to a position Lowell had predicted -- but there is a problem with calling it a success. What is the problem?
answer: Pluto is far too small to tug Uranus, at about a five-hundredth of Earth's mass
choices: Pluto is far too small to tug Uranus, at about a five-hundredth of Earth's mass
Pluto turned up on the wrong side of its own orbit that year
Pluto had actually been catalogued as a star fifty years earlier
Pluto's orbit crosses Uranus's, which Lowell's model forbade
context: Lowell had predicted a body of several Earth masses to explain the apparent perturbations. Pluto is roughly 0.002 Earth masses -- so the discovery near Lowell's position was a coincidence, a right answer for a wrong reason. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: For sixty years astronomers argued a hidden body must be tugging Uranus's orbit. In 1989 Voyager 2 flew past Neptune and made the whole Planet X problem simply vanish. What was the finding that killed it?
answer: Neptune weighed about 0.5 per cent less than assumed, and the wobbles evaporated
choices: Neptune weighed about 0.5 per cent less than assumed, and the wobbles evaporated
Neptune had a large dark companion whose pull explained the Uranus data
Neptune's orbit was slightly tilted the wrong way for the old model
Neptune carried a strong magnetic field able to nudge Uranus off course
context: With Neptune's revised mass, the apparent perturbations of Uranus's orbit that had motivated the entire Planet X search vanished into the ordinary error bars. Lowell's prediction had been chasing a ghost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: In 2005 a Caltech team led by Mike Brown, with Chad Trujillo and David Rabinowitz, found a world beyond Pluto and first announced it as bigger. Later measurements sharpened the comparison. How does the body -- now called Eris -- actually compare with Pluto?
answer: Very slightly smaller in diameter, but about 27 per cent more massive
choices: Very slightly smaller in diameter, but about 27 per cent more massive
About twice Pluto's diameter and about twice its mass
Nearly identical in size and mass, and probably a twin
Considerably smaller in every way -- the announcement was a measurement error
context: Eris's diameter is about 2326 km against Pluto's 2377 km, but Eris's mass -- pinned down from the orbit of its moon Dysnomia -- is roughly 27 per cent greater. Denser, and stranger. Its discovery is what forced the IAU to finally define the word 'planet'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eris_(dwarf_planet)

question: On 24 August 2006 the International Astronomical Union, meeting in Prague, adopted a three-part definition of the word 'planet'. To count, a body must orbit the Sun and be round under its own gravity -- Pluto passes both. It fails the third test. What is that third requirement?
answer: It must have cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other bodies
choices: It must have cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other bodies
It must be more massive than the largest asteroid
It must lie inside the orbit of Neptune
It must have at least one moon of its own
context: Pluto shares the Kuiper belt with thousands of comparable bodies -- Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Sedna, Quaoar and many more -- and therefore fails the clearing test. Alan Stern and other planetary scientists still argue for a geophysical definition that would restore Pluto and add Ceres, Charon and Eris to the roster. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: On 14 July 2015 NASA's New Horizons probe flew past what many people had written off as a dead ice ball. It found water-ice mountains kilometres high and a vast heart-shaped nitrogen-ice plain called Sputnik Planitia, divided into polygonal cells and carrying essentially no impact craters. What does the empty crater count tell us about that plain?
answer: Something is actively resurfacing the plain right now
choices: Something is actively resurfacing the plain right now
Meteors have avoided this hemisphere for billions of years
The plain is younger than the solar system and captured intact
Pluto's atmosphere is thick enough to burn incoming rocks
context: Craters accumulate over time; a smooth surface means it is being renewed. Sputnik Planitia's polygons are convection cells in a several-kilometre-thick layer of solid nitrogen, slowly turning over. What powers that convection on so cold and small a world remains an open question -- no one yet knows what keeps a world this small and this cold geologically alive. The ladder ends where the science does. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto

question: 1808, Paris. A young French army engineer glances out from his home in the rue d'Enfer at the setting Sun reflected in the windows of the Luxembourg Palace, holding to his eye a crystal of Iceland spar -- which normally shows every scene DOUBLED. As he rotates the crystal, one of the two Suns fades to nothing. Plain reflection off a window had done something to the light that no theory expected. Who was he?
answer: Etienne-Louis Malus
choices: Etienne-Louis Malus
Augustin-Jean Fresnel
Jean-Baptiste Biot
Francois Arago
context: Malus, a Newtonian corpuscularist, coined the word 'polarization' to describe the effect -- he pictured the light particles as having sides or 'poles' that the reflection had lined up. He died just four years later, at 36, worn out by fever from Napoleon's Egyptian campaign. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etienne-Louis_Malus ; polarization.com/history/history.html.

question: Iceland spar, a transparent calcite crystal, does something startling in ordinary daylight: lay a piece over a line of printed text and every letter appears TWICE, side by side. Rotate the crystal and the pair swings around each other. What is actually happening to the light INSIDE the crystal?
answer: It splits into two rays that travel through the crystal at different angles
choices: It splits into two rays that travel through the crystal at different angles
It slows almost to a stop and is re-emitted from every atom in turn
It bends into a spiral around the crystal's long axis
It changes colour depending on which crystal face it enters
context: Calcite is birefringent -- it has two refractive indices, one for each direction the light wave can wobble in. Incoming light with mixed wobble-directions is split into two rays that bend by different amounts and emerge as two images. That is why Malus's crystal showed two Suns -- and why he could kill one of them by rotating the crystal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_spar.

question: Before 1929 a polarizing filter meant a bulky calcite prism on a lab bench. A Harvard undergraduate changed everything -- he aligned microscopic herapathite crystals in a plastic sheet, patented the trick while still a student, and in 1938 replaced it with a cheaper stretched iodine-stained polyvinyl-alcohol film. His H-sheet still sits in every pair of polarized sunglasses and the front of every LCD screen. Who was he?
answer: Edwin Land
choices: Edwin Land
David Brewster
William Nicol
George Airy
context: Land left Harvard without a degree to found what became the Polaroid Corporation in 1937. Herapathite (iodoquinine sulphate) had been known to physicists as a spectacular polarizer since the 1850s but was too fragile to use in bulk -- Land's insight was to freeze millions of tiny crystals into a plastic film. The instant camera came later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaroid_(polarizer) ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_H._Land.

question: Stare steadily at a bright uniformly-lit white patch on an LCD screen -- or at a clear patch of blue sky 90 degrees away from the Sun -- and a faint yellowish bowtie shape shimmers at the centre of your vision. It rotates when you tilt your head, fades within seconds as the retina adapts, then reappears when you blink. The Austrian mineralogist who first reported it in 1844 gave his name to it. What is this effect called?
answer: Haidinger's brush
choices: Haidinger's brush
Purkinje's tree
Fraunhofer's fringe
Fresnel's shadow
context: The bowtie is caused by yellow pigment molecules in the macula that happen to lie in a radial pattern around the fovea -- they preferentially absorb the wobble-direction perpendicular to their alignment, so a uniformly polarized field paints a faint absorption cross on the retina. Most people go a lifetime without being told to look for it. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2010.15252 ; Current Biology 2020 doi 10.1016/j.cub.2020.12.017.

question: On a heavily overcast day, when the Sun is completely hidden behind cloud, a honeybee can still fly a straight bee-line home. In 1949 Karl von Frisch pinned down exactly what cue she is using -- a cue no human eye can see unaided -- and it helped win him the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. What is the bee reading off the sky itself?
answer: The direction the sky's scattered daylight is wobbling in
choices: The direction the sky's scattered daylight is wobbling in
The infrared warmth glowing up from the ground below
The Earth's magnetic field lines running north to south
The scent trail left in the air by earlier foragers
context: Sunlight scattered by air molecules at right angles to the Sun comes out strongly polarized in a great band across the sky -- and a bee's compound eye has UV-sensitive receptors arranged like a compass to read that pattern. Von Frisch shared the Nobel with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen for founding modern ethology. He is also the man who cracked the honeybee waggle dance. Source: nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/frisch/biographical/.

question: Icelandic sagas mention a 'solarsteinn' -- a sunstone that Viking navigators supposedly used to find the Sun through fog. Calcite would physically do the job: planetarium tests show a sailor with one could pin a hidden Sun to within a few degrees. Two hundred years of Norse archaeology have opened thousands of Viking ships and graves. What has that archaeology so far produced by way of a sunstone?
answer: Not a single specimen has surfaced despite two centuries of Norse archaeology
choices: Not a single specimen has surfaced despite two centuries of Norse archaeology
Only a handful of ambiguous calcite fragments, all from post-Viking contexts
Two well-attested finds, both from ship burials at Oseberg and Gokstad
Several sunstones, all recovered from Birka's navigator graves
context: The only crystal actually recovered NEXT to navigation gear came from an English warship sunk off Alderney in 1592 -- five centuries after the Viking age. It is calcite; it does polarize; it sits in the same wreck as its ship's compasses. But it is Elizabethan, not Norse. The Norse archaeology gives us not a single sunstone. Plausible and testable, not proven -- the bank refuses to pretend otherwise. Source: livescience.com/27696-viking-sunstone-shipwreck.html ; science.org/content/article/scienceshot-sunstone-unearthed-shipwreck.  (Legend.)

question: Every LCD pixel in your laptop or phone is a thin sandwich of layers only a few microns thick. Between the backlight and your eye, what is doing the actual work of switching that pixel from bright to dark?
answer: Two crossed polarizing filters with a twistable liquid crystal between them
choices: Two crossed polarizing filters with a twistable liquid crystal between them
Three coloured LEDs -- red, green and blue -- under a fine diffuser
A row of tiny incandescent filaments behind a coloured mask
A phosphor coating excited by a scanning electron beam behind it
context: Try this: tilt a pair of polarized sunglasses in front of a bright laptop screen -- at one angle the whole screen blacks out completely, because the LCD's own light is already polarized and the sunglasses can kill it. Inside the pixel, with no voltage the liquid crystal molecules form a 90-degree helical twist that rotates the wobble-direction of the incoming light so it can pass the second (perpendicular) filter -- the pixel is bright. Apply a voltage and the molecules straighten, the rotation is lost, and the second filter blocks the light -- the pixel is dark. Source: spie.org/samples/TT100.pdf ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid-crystal_display.

question: Cut a model of a bridge or a dam out of clear plastic and place it between two polarizing filters. Squeeze or bend the model, and rainbow fringes blaze out along particular curves running through it. From David Brewster's 1816 discovery down to the 1930s, this was the working way engineers hunted for weak points in a design -- before a computer could calculate them. What do those bright fringes MAP inside the plastic?
answer: The lines of greatest internal stress carrying the load through the material
choices: The lines of greatest internal stress carrying the load through the material
Small cracks that are already forming quietly under the applied load
Warm and cool patches from friction heating during the squeeze
Impurities and tiny air bubbles trapped inside the casting
context: Under load, transparent plastics become birefringent in proportion to the local stress -- so the two wobble-directions of a light wave now travel through them at different speeds, get out of step, and interfere to produce coloured fringes when the analyser filter recombines them. The technique is called photoelasticity and it was the workhorse of stress analysis for gear teeth, gun turrets, dams and bridges through the 1930s. Source: sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/photoelastic-stress-analysis.

question: On 31 May 1881 every sheep at Pouilly-le-Fort, vaccinated and unvaccinated alike, was injected with a lethal dose of live anthrax. On 2 June the crowd walked into the paddock and looked. What did they see?
answer: the unvaccinated flock dead, the vaccinated flock grazing
choices: the unvaccinated flock dead, the vaccinated flock grazing
the two flocks looking about equally sick
no visible difference between the flocks
the vaccinated flock dying, the unvaccinated flock well
context: The result on 2 June was as clean as science ever gets in public: complete kill in the untreated animals, complete survival in the treated ones. It made Pasteur famous overnight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur

question: Two years before Pouilly-le-Fort, Pasteur stumbled on the principle that made the anthrax vaccine possible at all. In 1879 an assistant went off on holiday without giving fresh chicken-cholera cultures to the birds; on his return he used the old, air-exposed cultures anyway. What did those stale doses do?
answer: left the chickens healthy and later immune
choices: left the chickens healthy and later immune
killed the chickens within a day
spoiled the cultures beyond use
gave the chickens a new disease
context: Pasteur named the weakened form 'attenuated' and realised that air-exposed cultures lost virulence in a graded, useful way. The chicken-cholera holiday accident is the seed of every live-attenuated vaccine that followed. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/d42859-020-00008-5

question: In public Pasteur told the world he had used his own oxygen-attenuated live anthrax vaccine at Pouilly-le-Fort. A century later the historian Gerald Geison opened Pasteur's laboratory notebooks and found that the doses given to those sheep had actually been prepared by his assistant Charles Chamberland, using a chemical method borrowed from Pasteur's rival Toussaint. Which chemical did Chamberland use?
answer: potassium dichromate
choices: potassium dichromate
phenol
mercuric chloride
iodine tincture
context: Geison's 1995 book The Private Science of Louis Pasteur showed the trial result was genuine but the story of how Pasteur got there was not. The bank tells both: a real vaccine worked at Pouilly-le-Fort, and Pasteur misreported the recipe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur

question: In May 1968 the Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich published a paperback called 'The Population Bomb'. It sold over two million copies and ran through twenty reprints in three years, and its opening lines announced that a battle had already been lost. What did those opening lines say would happen during the 1970s?
answer: Hundreds of millions of people would starve to death
choices: Hundreds of millions of people would starve to death
Whole nations would collapse into wars over water
A new plague would sweep the crowded cities
The world's fisheries would be emptied to the last catch
context: Ehrlich's opening lines were: 'The battle to feed all of humanity is over. In the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now.' Later printings quietly changed '1970s' to '1970s and 1980s'. Published by Ballantine Books with the Sierra Club, the book went through twenty reprints by 1971. Ehrlich was a serious biologist writing about a real trend -- world population was climbing fast. What his forecast could not see was that food production was about to climb faster still. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'The Population Bomb'.

question: In 'The Population Bomb' Paul Ehrlich wrote that he had yet to meet anyone who thought India would be self-sufficient in food by 1971. India's wheat harvest was 12.3 million tonnes in 1965; by 1970 it was 20 million, and by 1985 past 50 million. Something had reached India in 1965, three years before the book, that Ehrlich's arithmetic never allowed for. What was it?
answer: Sacks of Mexican seed bred to grow short
choices: Sacks of Mexican seed bred to grow short
Shiploads of American surplus grain
Wagonloads of imported nitrogen fertiliser
Crates of diesel pumps for irrigation wells
context: The seed came from Norman Borlaug's wheat program in Mexico. In 1965 -- three years before 'The Population Bomb' was printed -- he shipped 250 tons of semi-dwarf wheat seed to India and 350 tons to Pakistan, working with the Indian scientist M. S. Swaminathan; India took 18,000 tons more in 1966. India's wheat went from 12.3 million tonnes in 1965 to 20 million in 1970 and past 50 million by 1985, and Pakistan's from 4.6 to 8.4 million tonnes over those same five years. Why short?
