Tall wheat given heavy fertiliser 'lodges' -- it falls flat under the weight of its own grain -- so fertiliser alone runs into a ceiling, while a short, stiff-stemmed plant can carry a heavy head and answer the fertiliser instead of collapsing. Ehrlich had also written that he could not see how India could possibly feed two hundred million more people by 1980; the 1971 edition of the book dropped the India passage after India's food situation improved. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Norman Borlaug'; Wikipedia, 'The Population Bomb'.

question: Julian Simon and Paul Ehrlich signed a wager on 29 September 1980, to be settled ten years later to the day. Ehrlich and his colleagues chose the materials: chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten, $200 of each. If the same quantities cost more in 1990 after inflation, Simon would pay; if less, Ehrlich would. All five came in cheaper. What arrived in Simon's post that October?
answer: A cheque for $576.07 and no letter at all
choices: A cheque for $576.07 and no letter at all
A cheque for $312.85 and a note of congratulation
A cheque for $848.43 and a demand for a rematch
A cheque for $164.62 and a long letter of protest
context: In real terms the $1,000 basket had fallen 57.6%, to roughly $424 -- tin and tungsten each down more than 60%, copper about 24%. Ehrlich mailed the difference, with a sheet of metal prices and no letter. Simon had started it by printing an open challenge in Social Science Quarterly, staking $10,000 that the cost of non-government-controlled raw materials would not rise in the long run and inviting anyone to name any material and any date more than a year away; he cut his own stake to $1,000 to make it easier to accept. He then offered a rematch on any five commodities over any span of five years or more. Ehrlich declined, and in May 1995 he and the Stanford climatologist Stephen Schneider proposed instead a $10,000 bet on fifteen 'indicators of material change' for 1994-2004, including atmospheric carbon dioxide, cropland per person, ocean fisheries and human sperm counts. Simon refused those as indirect measures of human welfare and insisted on prices and living standards. No second bet was ever made; Simon died on 8 February 1998. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Simon-Ehrlich wager'.

question: Richard Feynman gave the Caltech commencement address in 1974 and called it 'Cargo Cult Science'. He told the graduating class that one rule stands as the first principle of doing science honestly. Which rule did Feynman name?
answer: That you must not fool yourself about your own work
choices: That you must publish the data that disagrees with you
That you must not fool yourself about your own work
That you must credit everyone who paid for the work
That you must repeat a rival's result before your own
context: The full passage: 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself -- and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you've not fooled yourself, it's easy not to fool other scientists.' A forecast with a date on it is that principle made checkable: anyone with a calendar can grade it, in public, including the person who made it. A forecast with no date cannot be wrong -- and a claim that cannot be wrong is not yet science. Source: Richard P. Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science', Caltech commencement address 1974, published in Engineering & Science.

question: In 1945 Norman Borlaug was breeding wheat in Mexico and began running his program in two places at once: the Yaqui Valley in Sonora, warm and near sea level, and highland plots near Toluca about 8,500 feet up, roughly 700 miles and ten degrees of latitude apart. His colleagues told him it would not work. What did the two-site program buy him?
answer: Two wheat generations a year instead of one
choices: Two wheat generations a year instead of one
One season's results from two climates at once
A crop that ripened a month earlier in the field
Seed hardened against the rusts that plagued Sonora
context: Borlaug called it shuttle breeding, and it halved the time needed to produce a new variety. The second half of his trick was a shorter plant: from 1953 he crossed the Japanese semi-dwarf wheat Norin 10 -- already crossed with Brevor 14 in the United States by Orville Vogel -- into tall Mexican wheats. Tall wheat given heavy fertiliser 'lodges': it falls flat under the weight of its own grain. Short, stiff-stemmed wheat could carry a heavy head and answer fertiliser instead of collapsing. In 1970 the Nobel Committee gave Borlaug its Peace Prize -- not for a treaty, for wheat. Estimates commonly credit his varieties with sparing up to a billion people from starvation; world cereal production rose more than 250% between 1950 and 1984 while cropland grew only about 21%. Source: Grokipedia, 'Norman Borlaug'.

question: On 12 December 2007 the BBC ran the headline "Arctic summers ice-free 'by 2013'", reporting Wieslaw Maslowski of the Naval Postgraduate School, who told the reporter Jonathan Amos that his 2013 projection might even be 'too conservative'. Further down the same article another scientist was quoted on that same date -- Mark Serreze of the US National Snow and Ice Data Center. What did Serreze tell the reporter?
answer: That Maslowski was a little aggressive; his own date was 2030
choices: That Maslowski was far too cautious; his own date was 2010
That Maslowski was roughly right; his own date was 2014
That Maslowski was a little aggressive; his own date was 2030
That Maslowski was decades out; his own date was 2100
context: Serreze's full sentence: 'I think Wieslaw is probably a little aggressive in his projections, simply because the luck of the draw means natural variability can kick in to give you a few years in which the ice loss is a little less than you've had in previous years. But Wieslaw is a smart guy and it would not surprise me if his projections came out.' His own number that day was 2030. The caveat was printed at the time, in the same article as the headline -- it is the line almost nobody quotes. Also in that article was Peter Wadhams of Cambridge, who had used Royal Navy submarine sonar to measure ice thickness: 'The ice is thinning faster than it is shrinking... In the end, it will just melt away quite suddenly. It might not be as early as 2013 but it will be soon, much earlier than 2040.' Two years later, at Copenhagen on 14 December 2009, Al Gore said some models suggested 'a 75% chance that the entire north polar ice cap, during some of the summer months, could be completely ice-free within the next five to seven years'; Maslowski told the Times of London the next day that it was unclear how that figure was arrived at and that he would never estimate a likelihood so exactly. The scientist publicly corrected the politician quoting him. Sources: BBC News, 12 December 2007; PolitiFact, 2 March 2021.

question: The ice-free-Arctic deadlines that researchers named in the 2000s came and went with summer sea ice still in place. But the satellites that graded those deadlines have measured Arctic sea ice every summer since 1979, and on 16 September 2012 they recorded the lowest September extent in the whole record: 3.41 million square kilometres. How does that low compare with the average September minimum of 1979 to 2000?
answer: About half of it
choices: About half of it
About four-fifths of it
About nine-tenths of it
About the same as it
context: The 1979-2000 average September minimum was 6.70 million square kilometres, so 2012 came in 49% below it -- and 18% below the previous record, set in 2007. That summer the Arctic lost 11.83 million square kilometres between its March maximum and its September minimum, the largest melt in the satellite record, helped along by a huge storm over the central Arctic in early August. The record holds both halves at once: the 2025 minimum was 4.60 million square kilometres on 10 September, tied for tenth lowest, and the nineteen summers from 2007 to 2025 are the nineteen lowest September extents ever measured -- while the National Snow and Ice Data Center also notes no significant trend in the September minimums within those nineteen years. A blown deadline is not a refuted trend, and a stalled trend is not a restored one. Sources: NSIDC, 'Arctic sea ice extent settles at record seasonal minimum', 18 September 2012; NSIDC, '2025 Arctic sea ice minimum squeezes into the ten lowest minimums'.

question: Three researchers -- Paul Kench, Murray Ford and Susan Owen -- measured every one of the 101 islands of the Pacific nation Tuvalu across the years 1971 to 2014, a stretch in which local sea level at Tuvalu rose about 3.9 millimetres a year, roughly twice the global average. What had happened to the country's total land area over those decades?
answer: It had grown by about 3%
choices: It had grown by about 3%
It had grown by about 15%
It had shrunk by about 3%
It had shrunk by about 15%
context: Tuvalu gained 73.5 hectares, or 2.9%. Eight of its nine atolls gained land; 73 islands grew, 28 shrank, and exactly one vanished -- a 0.08-hectare speck on the rim of Nukufetau. One tiny island, Tapuaelani, more than doubled, growing 113%. Virginie Duvat's global survey of 709 atoll islands across 30 atolls found 73.1% stable, 15.5% larger and 11.4% smaller, with no atoll losing area overall and every island above 10 hectares stable or expanding. The mechanism is dull and physical: coral rubble, broken shell and sand pile onto the island from the reef faster than the sea climbs. There is a dated prophecy in this story too. In September 1988 a news-agency dispatch reported that a gradual rise in average sea level was threatening to cover the Maldives -- 1,196 small islands in the Indian Ocean -- completely within the next thirty years; the dispatch quoted the country's environmental affairs director, Hussein Shihab, saying that a rise of 20 to 30 centimetres over the next 20 to 40 years could be catastrophic for islands standing barely a metre above the sea. The thirty years ran out in 2018, and all 1,196 islands were still there. (That 1988 wire copy survives only as quoted by later writers, so treat its exact wording as reported rather than verified.) Now the honest other half, which matters just as much. Land AREA is not the same as a place people can live, and the Maldives is not acting relaxed: more than 80% of its roughly 1,190 islands stand less than a metre above the sea, the lowest terrain of any country on Earth, and beside the capital, Male, Maldivians have pumped seabed sand onto a submerged reef to build an entirely artificial island, Hulhumale -- about 4 square kilometres, raised to roughly 2 metres, ringed by walls about 3 metres high, and already home to more than 50,000 people. You can hold both facts at once: the islands are not drowning on schedule, and the Maldivians are still building walls. Sources: Kench, Ford & Owen, Nature Communications 9:605 (2018); Duvat, WIREs Climate Change 10:e557 (2019); September 1988 Agence France-Presse dispatch as quoted in later reporting; NASA Earth Observatory, 'Preparing for Rising Seas in the Maldives'; Global Center on Adaptation, 'Hulhumale, Maldives'.

question: On 28 April 1975 Newsweek ran a story by its science writer Peter Gwynne called 'The Cooling World', warning of ominous signs that the Earth's weather patterns had begun to change and of a possible 20% drop in world food production within a decade. Thirty-nine years later, in 2014, Gwynne himself published a piece about that article. What did he say in it?
answer: That he had been over-enthusiastic, and had not made today's scientists wrong
choices: That he had been over-enthusiastic, and had not made today's scientists wrong
That he stood by the story, and that the warming case had been oversold
That his editors had added the food claim, and had never told him
That the cooling was delayed by soot, and would arrive after all
context: Gwynne titled it 'My 1975 Cooling World Story Doesn't Make Today's Climate Scientists Wrong'. He wrote: 'In retrospect, I was over-enthusiastic in parts of my Newsweek article,' admitting he had 'suggested a connection between the purported global cooling and increases in tornado activity that was unjustified by climate science' and had 'also predicted a forthcoming impact of global cooling on the world's food production that had scant research to back it.' He noted the piece had reportedly become the most-cited article in Newsweek's history -- cited, he complained, mostly by people using it to argue the opposite of what he now believed. Time had run 'Another Ice Age?' on 24 June 1974, and Newsweek issued its own correction in 2006, saying the story had been 'so spectacularly wrong about the near-term future'. The best witness against a story is often the person who wrote it. Sources: Peter Gwynne, Inside Science / American Institute of Physics, 21 May 2014; Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Global cooling'.

question: 'Scientists in the 1970s predicted an ice age' is itself a claim with a date on it, so Thomas Peterson, William Connolley and John Fleck went and graded it. They found every peer-reviewed paper published between 1965 and 1979 that made a prediction about global temperature -- 71 of them -- and counted which way each one pointed, publishing the tally in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society in 2008. How did the 71 papers divide?
answer: 44 predicted warming and 7 predicted cooling
choices: 44 predicted warming and 7 predicted cooling
7 predicted warming and 44 predicted cooling
31 predicted warming and 30 predicted cooling
12 predicted warming and 39 predicted cooling
context: The remaining 20 papers were neutral. The authors called it 'The Myth of the 1970s Global Cooling Scientific Consensus' (BAMS 89(9), 1325-1337). The magazines were louder than the literature -- which is why this rung cuts against a talking point that flatters the sceptical side, and belongs in this ladder for exactly that reason. Worth reading too is the 1975 US National Academy of Sciences report often cited as the scare in official dress: 'Understanding Climatic Change: A Program for Action' recorded that temperature 'increased from the 1880s until about 1940 and has been decreasing thereafter', then said 'we do not have a good quantitative understanding of our climate machine' and that therefore 'it does not seem possible to predict climate'. It declined to forecast. Admitting you cannot yet predict is a scientific result too. Sources: Peterson, Connolley & Fleck 2008, doi:10.1175/2008BAMS2370.1 (counts via two independent secondary reports; the AMS full text blocked direct fetch); Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Global cooling'.

question: Julian Simon won his decade, but a decade is one sample. Economists later went back over metal prices and graded every non-overlapping ten-year window between 1910 and 2007 -- 98 of them -- asking who would have won each one. If Simon and Paul Ehrlich had signed the same wager in a window drawn at random from that century, what would the count say?
answer: Ehrlich would have won most of the windows
choices: Ehrlich would have won most of the windows
Simon would have won nearly all of the windows
The two would have split the windows evenly
Most windows would have been too close to score
context: Kiel and colleagues, in 'Luck or skill? An examination of the Ehrlich-Simon bet', found Ehrlich's side -- rising metal prices -- would have won about 61% of the 98 windows. So Simon's decade was a good decade for his thesis, not a proof of it. Then the argument turns again: analyses using 'time prices' -- how many hours of work it takes to buy the metal, rather than dollars -- flip the result, giving Simon roughly 70% of the windows. The bet was one data point, and one data point is not a law. What it did settle was one specific claim, on terms its loser chose, on a date fixed in advance. That is still more than most arguments ever manage. Source: Grokipedia, 'Simon-Ehrlich wager', summarising Kiel et al. and the time-price re-analyses.

question: Climate models are graded partly by their 'climate sensitivity' -- how much the planet warms if you double the carbon dioxide in the air. The IPCC's sixth assessment put the likely range at 2.5 to 4 degrees Celsius. On 4 May 2022 five scientists who all accept human-caused warming -- Zeke Hausfather, Kate Marvel, Gavin Schmidt, John Nielsen-Gammon and Mark Zelinka -- published a comment in Nature about the more than 50 models in the CMIP6 collection. What were they warning their own field about?
answer: That about a fifth of the models run hot, and averaging them all biases the answer upward
choices: That about a fifth of the models run hot, and averaging them all biases the answer upward
That most of the models share one cloud scheme, so their close agreement proves little
That the models were tuned to the twentieth century, so the range cannot be tested
That the models omit ocean heat uptake, so the low end of the range is too low
context: The comment was titled 'Climate simulations: recognize the hot model problem' (Nature 605, 26-29). Roughly a fifth of the CMIP6 models warm more than 5 degrees Celsius for a doubling of CO2 -- above the IPCC AR6 assessed likely range -- and those same runs do a poor job of reproducing past temperatures and the last ice age. The authors' own sentence: 'The problem is not that these high sensitivity models exist, but rather that the preponderance of them in the CMIP6 ensemble biases the mean and uncertainty range upwards.' This is the sharpest published criticism of climate models, and it comes from inside the field, in Nature, from people who accept that humans are warming the planet. Their message to their colleagues: stop treating every model output as equally credible. Sources: Hausfather, Marvel, Schmidt, Nielsen-Gammon & Zelinka, Nature, 4 May 2022, doi:10.1038/d41586-022-01192-2; the authors' companion guest post at Carbon Brief.

question: In 1796 the Paris anatomist Georges Cuvier compared the jaws and teeth of Indian elephants, African elephants, Siberian mammoths and the American 'Ohio animal' at the National Institute. What did that comparison establish?
answer: Some kinds of animal are simply gone from the world.
choices: Some kinds of animal are simply gone from the world.
The mastodon is an African elephant deformed by cold.
Mammoths and modern elephants are all one species.
The Siberian mammoth is the parent of today's Indian elephant.
context: Cuvier compared jaws, teeth and skulls and argued they were four different species; he later named the Ohio animal the mastodon. Before this, the standing assumption was that nothing could be lost from creation. Source: Biodiversity Heritage Library, 'Proving Extinction: Cuvier and the Elephantimorpha'.

question: The same year, 1796, Georges Cuvier examined a huge skeleton shipped from the bank of the Lujan River in Argentina to a museum in Madrid. From the skull alone he identified it as a beast nobody had ever seen alive. What kind of animal did he say it was?
answer: A ground-dwelling giant sloth (Megatherium)
choices: A ground-dwelling giant sloth (Megatherium)
A woolly rhinoceros that crossed the Atlantic
A South American cousin of the sabre-toothed cat
A hoofed relative of the modern hippopotamus
context: Cuvier's name Megatherium means 'great beast'. He was reading the animal's whole shape from its skull - the reasoning method he called the correlation of parts. Source: recentlyextinctspecies.com, Megatherium americanum.

question: In 1800, Cuvier was sent a drawing - not a specimen, only a drawing - of a strange fossil from Bavaria. Working from the sketch alone he correctly identified it as a member of a whole group of animals nobody had ever suspected existed. What did he say it was?
answer: A small flying reptile (later named Pterodactylus)
choices: A small flying reptile (later named Pterodactylus)
A saltwater bird ancestral to modern penguins
A juvenile long-necked freshwater crocodile
A bat-winged mammal from the age of horses
context: Eight years later Cuvier examined the Maastricht 'monster' skull - looted from Dutch quarries by French troops - and declared it a giant marine lizard, the first known mosasaur. Both calls were made using his correlation-of-parts rule: every bone implies the whole animal. Source: Biodiversity Heritage Library, 'Fact or Fiction? Discovering the Mosasaur'.

question: Cuvier's first reaction to Mary Anning's 1823 plesiosaur was that the neck was so absurdly long the specimen must be a forgery - bones from different animals glued together. William Buckland and William Conybeare sent him further evidence. What did Cuvier then do?
answer: Examined the evidence and publicly withdrew his forgery charge
choices: Examined the evidence and publicly withdrew his forgery charge
Never replied, and went to his grave calling Anning a fraud
Denounced Anning by name at a public lecture in Paris
Bought the specimen himself and hid it in his private cabinet
context: Buckland and Conybeare sent engravings, anatomical detail, and Mary Morland's careful sketch of Anning's own drawings. Cuvier accepted the specimen and reversed his position. The honest version of the story is better than the popular 'Cuvier never took it back.' Source: paleonerdish.wordpress.com, 'On the bicentenary of Mary Anning's Plesiosaurus'.

question: Mary Anning noticed that the stony conical lumps often lying in the belly area of her ichthyosaurs - people had been calling them 'bezoar stones' - were not what they seemed. She worked out what they really were, and William Buckland gave them a Greek name in 1829. What were they, and what did he call them?
answer: Fossilised dung, which Buckland named coprolites
choices: Fossilised dung, which Buckland named coprolites
Kidney stones, which Buckland named ichthyoliths
Ballast pebbles, which Buckland named gastroliths
Egg cases, which Buckland named ovoliths
context: Anning had noticed the lumps were packed full of fossil fish scales and small bones - what was inside a coprolite told you who had eaten whom, and she had read a Jurassic food chain out of fossil poop. 'Coprolite' is Greek for dung-stone. Buckland presented the finding to the Geological Society of London in 1829. Source: Biodiversity Heritage Library, 'Uncovering the Truth about Fossil Feces'.

question: In 1928 Frederick Griffith injected mice with a mixture: live pneumococci of a harmless strain, plus deadly ones he had already killed with heat. The mice died, so Griffith cultured their heart blood to find what had killed them. What grew?
answer: Living bacteria of the very type he had killed
choices: Living bacteria of a third type he had never used
Living bacteria of the very type he had killed
Only the harmless strain, in enormous numbers
No bacteria at all, the blood being sterile
context: The colonies came up smooth and glistening, and typing showed them to be the same type as the heat-killed strain; reinjected into fresh mice, they killed those too. Dead cells had permanently taught living ones. Griffith could name no substance and never claimed one - only that something had moved. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Griffith's_experiment (Results and Interpretation; Key Observations).

question: Pneumococcus comes in two forms. The deadly one wears a coat of sugar called a capsule; the harmless one has lost it. A hundred thousand capsuled cells kill a mouse, while uncapsuled ones cannot infect at any dose. What does the capsule do?
answer: It keeps white blood cells from swallowing the bacteria
choices: It keeps white blood cells from swallowing the bacteria
It releases a poison that bursts the blood vessels
It glues the bacteria to the lining of the lung
It hides the bacteria inside the mouse's own cells
context: The capsule blocks phagocytosis: the mouse's macrophages and neutrophils cannot get a grip, so as few as 100,000 capsuled cells multiply unchecked and kill. Rough strains have lost the capsule to spontaneous mutation and are eaten on arrival, which is why they cannot start an infection at any dose. One sugar coat is the entire difference between deadly and harmless. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Griffith's_experiment (Bacterial Pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae).

question: In 1952 Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase let phages, viruses that infect bacteria, settle onto E. coli and inject their contents. To see what had gone in, they had to strip the clinging virus shells off the bacteria without harming them. What did they use?
answer: A Waring kitchen blender, in sixty-second bursts
choices: A Raytheon sonic oscillator, in ten-minute runs
A Potter-Elvehjem homogeniser, ground by hand
A Waring kitchen blender, in sixty-second bursts
A French pressure cell, the culture forced through
context: A semimicro Waring blendor at 10,000 r.p.m., in 60-second bursts, cooled in ice water between runs, and then a spin in the centrifuge. The most famous experiment in genetics ran on an appliance you can buy in a shop - worth remembering whenever a result seems to depend on equipment you could never own. Source: A. D. Hershey and Martha Chase, 'Independent Functions of Viral Protein and Nucleic Acid in Growth of Bacteriophage', Journal of General Physiology 36:39-56 (1952).

question: Frederick Griffith's strangest mice were the ones given live harmless pneumococci together with heat-killed deadly ones. Those mice died, and he cultured bacteria out of their blood. He grew those bacteria on in fresh broth, batch after batch, with nothing dead anywhere near them. What did the descendants do?
answer: They stayed capsuled and deadly, generation after generation
choices: They stayed capsuled and deadly, generation after generation
They lost the capsule after a few transfers and turned harmless
They kept the capsule but could no longer kill a mouse
They grew weaker with every batch until the culture died out
context: No reversion: the transformed line kept its capsule and its lethality indefinitely in culture. That is what made the result enormous. A passing infection or a smear of leftover chemical would have faded within a few divisions; this was inherited, so something out of the dead cells had been added to the living ones' own instructions. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Griffith's_experiment (Discovery of Transformation).

question: Frederick Griffith belonged to no genetics laboratory. He was a medical officer for Britain's Ministry of Health, and his daily work was to grow pneumococci from pneumonia patients and record which type each one carried, case after case. What turned on getting a patient's type right?
answer: One type's antiserum did nothing against a different type
choices: One type's antiserum did nothing against a different type
Each type called for a different dose of the same antiserum
Only one of the types could spread from patient to family
One type killed within days while the others took weeks
context: Serum therapy was type-specific: an antiserum raised against one pneumococcal type did nothing for a patient carrying another, so the whole business of vaccines and antisera turned on knowing which type a patient had. That is what set Griffith mixing strains - he had found patients carrying more than one type at once, and he wanted to know whether one type could turn into another inside a patient. His 1928 paper was titled 'The Significance of Pneumococcal Types' (Journal of Hygiene). He was not hunting the gene and never claimed to have found one. The largest question in biology was opened by a public-health officer checking whether his categories held still. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Griffith's_experiment (Griffith's Objectives and Hypothesis); grokipedia.com/page/Frederick_Griffith.

question: The 1952 phage experiment is remembered as Alfred Hershey's. Martha Chase grew the labelled viruses, ran the machine that shook them loose, and counted the radioactivity in every fraction, at Cold Spring Harbor. What was Chase's standing in that laboratory?
answer: A research assistant of twenty-four, one year out of college
choices: A postdoctoral fellow visiting from Columbia University
A research assistant of twenty-four, one year out of college
A doctoral student three years into a thesis on viruses
A physician retraining in genetics after wartime service
context: Martha Chase took her bachelor's degree from the College of Wooster in 1950 and worked as Hershey's research assistant at Cold Spring Harbor from 1950 to 1953, much of it in the laboratory's Animal House. The 1969 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Hershey, shared with Max Delbruck and Salvador Luria; Chase was never recognised in her lifetime. In 2020 the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses named a whole family of bacterial viruses Chaseviridae after her. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Martha_Chase; grokipedia.com/page/Hershey-Chase_experiment.

question: Frederick Griffith's mice had shown in 1928 that something in heat-killed bacteria could permanently remake living ones, and other laboratories soon reproduced it without a mouse at all. Griffith himself never learned what that something was. What stopped him?
answer: A German bomb struck his London flat during a night air raid
choices: A pneumonia caught from the strain he had spent his life culturing
A Ministry order closed his laboratory and dispersed his cultures
A German bomb struck his London flat during a night air raid
A stroke left him unable to work through his last three years
context: Griffith was killed in his flat alongside his longtime colleague, the bacteriologist William M. Scott, during a Luftwaffe raid in April 1941; the two were given a joint obituary. (Sources differ on whether it was the night of the 16th or the 17th - the year and the circumstance are firm, the exact day is not.) The answer to his question was published three years later. The replications he did live to see: Martin Dawson and Richard Sia transformed pneumococci in a test tube in 1931, and James Alloway in 1932 did it with sterile, cell-free extracts, proving the agent was a soluble substance and not a surviving cell. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Frederick_Griffith (Later Research and Death); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Griffith; grokipedia.com/page/Griffith's_experiment (Immediate Scientific Implications).

question: At the Rockefeller Institute, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty set out to get Griffith's transforming principle in pure form. They grew deadly pneumococci in beef-heart broth in seventy-five-litre batches, killed them with heat, pulled the protein out with chloroform and precipitated what was left with alcohol. How much purified material did seventy-five litres give?
answer: Ten to twenty-five milligrams, a fibrous wisp
choices: Ten to twenty-five milligrams, a fibrous wisp
Two to three hundred milligrams, a pill's worth
One to two grams, about a quarter-teaspoon
Twenty to forty grams, about a small jarful
context: Ten to twenty-five milligrams out of seventy-five litres, deproteinized by the chloroform method of Sevag. The fibrous material was over 90 per cent pure: no detectable protein, lipid or polysaccharide, a single sharp boundary in the ultracentrifuge, and a nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio of 1.58 to 1.75 against the 1.67 expected of pure DNA. And it was ferocious - as little as 0.01 to 0.1 micrograms per millilitre still transformed, active at dilutions of roughly one part in 100,000,000. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Avery-MacLeod-McCarty_experiment (Extract Preparation; Transformation Assays).

question: To follow a virus's DNA and its protein coat separately, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase grew one batch of phage with one radioactive element and a second batch with another, so that each batch had only one of its two parts marked. The trick worked because of a difference in what the two molecules are built from. Which difference?
answer: DNA has phosphorus and no sulfur; protein has sulfur and no phosphorus
choices: DNA has sulfur and no nitrogen; protein has nitrogen and no sulfur
DNA has iron and no phosphorus; protein has phosphorus and no iron
DNA has nitrogen and no carbon; protein has carbon and no nitrogen
DNA has phosphorus and no sulfur; protein has sulfur and no phosphorus
context: Phosphorus-32 marked the DNA only; sulfur-35 marked the coat only. Grow the phage in E. coli fed one isotope or the other, and every particle carries a label in exactly one of its two halves. The whole experiment rests on one chemical fact - and it is a habit worth copying: before building an apparatus, look for the difference that already exists. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hershey-Chase_experiment (Isotope Labeling Methods).

question: By the early 1940s Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty had an extract that turned harmless pneumococci permanently deadly, and no way to say which molecule in it was doing the work. How did the three of them settle which molecule it was?
answer: Destroyed one candidate molecule at a time and saw which loss stopped it
choices: Split the extract in a spinning tube and tested each layer for the power
Destroyed one candidate molecule at a time and saw which loss stopped it
Heated the extract in steps and found the point where the power failed
Diluted the extract further and further until the power finally failed
context: Trypsin and chymotrypsin, which chew up protein: the transforming power survived intact. Ribonuclease, which destroys RNA: survived. Deoxyribonuclease: the power vanished completely, a loss of more than 99 per cent. Destroy each suspect in turn and see which destruction stops the effect - a test you can run on anything with more than one possible cause. Published in 1944 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine, under a title that mentions no gene at all: 'Studies on the Chemical Nature of the Substance Inducing Transformation of Pneumococcal Types: Induction of Transformation by a Desoxyribonucleic Acid Fraction Isolated from Pneumococcus Type III.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/Avery-MacLeod-McCarty_experiment (Biochemical Characterization).

question: In May 1943, a year before publishing, Oswald Avery wrote a long letter to his younger brother Roy, a bacteriologist and physician at Vanderbilt, laying out everything he had, down to the vanishing dose that still worked. 'Sounds like a virus,' Avery wrote, and added four more words. Which four?
answer: may be a gene
choices: may be a poison
may be a capsule
may be a gene
may be an enzyme
context: The full line: 'Sounds like a virus - may be a gene. But with mechanisms I am not now concerned.' He also wrote, 'We have isolated highly purified substance of which as little as 0.02 of a microgram is active in inducing transformation,' and 'Who could have guessed it?' Then he policed his own excitement: 'It's lots of fun to blow bubbles - but it's wiser to prick them yourself before someone else tries to,' and 'It's hazardous to go off half cocked - and embarrassing to have to retract later.' None of that reached the published paper. Source: Letter, Oswald T. Avery to Roy Avery, 26 May 1943, NLM Profiles in Science (collections.nlm.nih.gov, Oswald T. Avery Papers).

question: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase were not finished when their blender run was counted: it showed only where the two radioactive labels sat minutes after the phage, viruses that infect bacteria, had settled on their E. coli. It said nothing about what was passed on. So the pair waited for the infected bacteria to burst and release a fresh crop of phage, then counted the parents' phosphorus and sulfur in that new generation. How much of each label did the offspring carry?
answer: Thirty per cent or more of the parents' phosphorus, under one per cent of their sulfur
choices: About a third of the parents' phosphorus and about a third of their sulfur
Thirty per cent or more of the parents' sulfur, under one per cent of their phosphorus
Thirty per cent or more of the parents' phosphorus, under one per cent of their sulfur
Under one per cent of the parents' phosphorus and under one per cent of their sulfur
context: From the paper's own summary: phage grown inside bacteria infected by sulfur-35 parents carried less than 1 per cent of the parental radioactivity, while phage from phosphorus-32 parents carried 30 per cent or more of the parental phosphorus. The first run had been messier than the story usually told - it freed 75 per cent of the phage sulfur but also 15 per cent of the phosphorus - which is why this second count mattered. What gets passed down is what counts. Source: Hershey & Chase, J. Gen. Physiol. 36:39-56 (1952), Summary items 4 and 6.

question: Phoebus Levene worked out what DNA is built from - four blocks, A, G, C and T - and in 1909 he published his picture of how those four run along the chain. It went into the textbooks and stood for thirty years, shaping which molecule biologists thought could carry heredity. What was Levene's picture?
answer: The four in one fixed repeating unit, one of each, down the chain
choices: The four in an order that differed from one species to the next
The four in one fixed repeating unit, one of each, down the chain
The four in long runs of one kind, then long runs of the next
The four in proportions that differed from one species to the next
context: This is Levene's tetranucleotide hypothesis: one A, one G, one C, one T, over and over - a molecule far too monotonous to spell out a living thing, which is exactly why serious people looked to protein instead, built as it is from twenty different amino acids. It was a reasonable inference from the evidence of 1909, and it was wrong. Erwin Chargaff, one of the few who took Avery's 1944 result seriously (he called it epochal), reorganised his whole Columbia laboratory that year to measure DNA's base composition, and by 1949 had the rules that destroyed the tetranucleotide picture: A equals T, and G equals C. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Hershey-Chase_experiment (Debate on Genetic Material); grokipedia.com/page/Erwin_Chargaff.

question: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty published in 1944, and their paper named a deoxyribonucleic acid fraction as the substance that turned harmless pneumococci permanently deadly. Alfred Mirsky, a respected colleague at the same institute, refused the conclusion and went on refusing it into the early 1950s, and his objection was good science rather than stubbornness. What did he argue?
answer: A trace of protein left in the preparation could be the real agent
choices: The DNA-destroying enzyme was simply killing the bacteria outright
A trace of protein left in the preparation could be the real agent
The harmless strain was turning deadly on its own, with no agent
The result held for pneumococcus alone and said nothing of genes
context: Mirsky held that the agent was 'a protein associated with nucleic acids', and pressed the case both inside the Rockefeller and in public; at the 1946 Cold Spring Harbor meeting H. Bentley Glass recalled the room still asking whether 'some protein does not remain in the preparation.' That is a fair demand - a purification is only as good as what it leaves behind - and it is part of why the 1944 paper landed almost silently: fewer than 50 citations in 1945 and 239 in the whole decade to 1954. Avery himself framed the result cautiously, as a chemical phenomenon in pneumococcus rather than a claim about heredity in general, and retired in 1948 without ever promoting it. He was nominated 38 times for a Nobel Prize between 1932 and 1957 and never received one; the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal in 1945. Sources: profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/cc/feature/after; grokipedia.com/page/Avery-MacLeod-McCarty_experiment (Contemporary Responses); grokipedia.com/page/Oswald_Avery.

question: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase's 1952 blender experiment is usually told as the day DNA was proved to be the genetic material, once and for all. In the paper itself, their counts had followed two radioactive labels through a single round of infection; about a fifth of the phage coat protein may or may not have entered the bacteria, and blending never shook all of it loose. How did the two authors word their closing claim?
answer: The protein probably has no function; the DNA has some function
choices: The DNA is the genetic material of this virus, beyond any doubt
Neither the protein nor the DNA can yet be given any function
The protein probably has no function; the DNA has some function
Both the DNA and the protein appear to be needed for growth
context: Verbatim from the paper: 'This protein probably has no function in the growth of intracellular phage. The DNA has some function. Further chemical inferences should not be drawn from the experiments presented.' They added that 'the chemical identification of the genetic part must wait.' What they did claim was subtler and better: 'Our experiments show clearly that a physical separation of the phage T2 into genetic and non-genetic parts is possible' - they had split a living thing into the part that carries the instructions and the part that merely delivers them. The textbook line that the blender settled it once and for all is exactly what the two authors refused to say. Source: Hershey & Chase, J. Gen. Physiol. 36:39-56 (1952), Discussion and Summary items 6 and 8.

question: Why was 'an infectious agent with no genes' heresy in 1982? It broke the central rule of molecular biology that Francis Crick had put on paper decades earlier. What rule is that?
answer: Genetic information flows in one direction: DNA to RNA to protein
choices: Genetic information flows in one direction: DNA to RNA to protein
Every disease-causing agent must be either a virus or a bacterium
Proteins can only be assembled inside a living cell, never in a test tube
Every enzyme catalyzes exactly one specific chemical reaction
context: This is Crick's 'central dogma.' A protein was supposed to be an END product, never a self-copying cause. Every known infectious thing -- virus, bacterium, fungus, parasite -- carried nucleic-acid instructions of its own.

question: The prion protein exists as a coiled, alpha-helical form (PrP-C) in every healthy brain, and Prusiner showed a dangerous version of the same protein exists too. What does the dangerous version DO to healthy PrP-C molecules on contact?
answer: Templates them into the same misfold -- a shape, not a code, is what gets copied
choices: Templates them into the same misfold -- a shape, not a code, is what gets copied
Binds and unfolds them, releasing free copies of the same molecule into solution
Splices small RNA fragments into their genes to reprogram them
Wraps them in a protective envelope so they can enter neighbouring cells
context: The two forms are named PrP-C (cellular, healthy alpha-helix) and PrP-Sc (scrapie, beta-sheet). The dangerous form is the SAME amino-acid sequence refolded into flat beta sheets; on contact it induces its neighbour into the same misfold. PrP-Sc resists proteases -- the enzymes that normally chew proteins up -- and piles up as plaque in the brain.

question: Well before Prusiner's 1982 paper, an American doctor had already won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that kuru was infectious and worked out how it spread among the Fore people. Who was he?
answer: Carleton Gajdusek
choices: Carleton Gajdusek
Baruch Blumberg
Joshua Lederberg
Peyton Rous
context: Gajdusek spent years in the Papua New Guinea highlands and traced kuru to the Fore practice of eating deceased relatives at funerals (mostly women and children handled the bodies). He called the agent a 'slow virus'; Prusiner would later show it was a prion. Blumberg (hepatitis B), Lederberg (bacterial genetics), and Rous (tumour viruses) are also real Nobel medicine laureates.

question: The steel-manned scientific objection to Prusiner's protein-only hypothesis had a name in the 1980s -- an alternative infectious agent that skeptical virologists said was really hiding in the preparations. What was the alternative?
answer: A 'virino' -- a tiny nucleic acid wrapped in host protein, too small or too shielded to detect
choices: A 'virino' -- a tiny nucleic acid wrapped in host protein, too small or too shielded to detect
A 'megavirus' -- a giant virus bigger than the smallest bacteria and easy to miss in the assays
A 'prophage' -- a bacterial virus integrated into the neuron's own DNA and passed down at cell division
A 'symbiont mycoplasma' -- a tiny wall-less bacterium living inside neurons and shed on cell death
context: The virino was the honest skeptical move: if you cannot find nucleic acid, maybe your detection is not sensitive enough. That is exactly the right challenge; it simply turned out to be wrong. Nobel laureate David Baltimore was a long-time public doubter.

question: David Baltimore -- a Nobel laureate himself and a former public doubter of the prion hypothesis -- told reporters on the day of Prusiner's 1997 Nobel that this was one of 'the mythological stories of science.' What pattern did he say it exemplified?
answer: Scientists who kept their own faith through years of opprobrium and were finally discovered to be right
choices: Scientists who kept their own faith through years of opprobrium and were finally discovered to be right
Heretics whose lucky guess was later given rigor by others who supplied the missing mechanism
Discoveries so counter-intuitive that a single decisive experiment finally forced the whole field to consensus
Fields that had to wait a full generation for the old opponents to retire or die off before change came
context: Baltimore's exact words to the press: 'These are the mythological stories of science -- people who have really kept their own faith for so many years and lived through a period of opprobrium and finally are discovered to be right.' A serious scientist who had objected honestly, then followed the evidence. Prusiner took the 1997 Nobel alone -- rare in the Physiology or Medicine category. The three distractor patterns are all real named narratives in the history and philosophy of science, but none is what Baltimore said that day.

question: It is tempting to say 'prion diseases have nothing to do with the host's DNA,' but prion research has turned up several counter-examples. Which case is the direct one -- a mutation in the host's own gene giving you the disease with no outside prion needed at all?
answer: Inherited mutations in the host's own PrP gene cause fatal familial insomnia and some forms of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
choices: Inherited mutations in the host's own PrP gene cause fatal familial insomnia and some forms of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Codon 129 polymorphisms in the PrP gene strongly modify a person's susceptibility to variant CJD after exposure
Different prion strains show different incubation times and brain-lesion patterns, suggesting the misfold itself carries heritable strain information
In sporadic CJD, a rare stochastic misfold in a normal PrP-C molecule slips past the cell's quality control
context: The infectious AGENT carries no gene of its own, which is what shocked biology. But the misfolding target is a normal host protein coded by a normal host gene (PRNP) -- and if that gene is mutated in the germline, the wrong fold can arise on its own without any outside seed. The three distractors are all real live findings in prion research: codon 129 M/M vs V/V polymorphism does modify vCJD susceptibility (Collinge et al.); prion strains do carry heritable conformational information (Weissmann/Collinge work); sporadic CJD is thought to arise from rare stochastic misfolds. Only inherited PRNP mutation is a direct Mendelian cause without any outside prion needed.

question: In one live research frontier, injected extracts from Alzheimer's or Parkinson's brains have been shown in mouse models to seed and spread misfolded protein aggregates through the brain in a pattern that looks a lot like prion templating. Which two proteins are the leading candidates for this prion-like spread in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's specifically?
answer: Tau (Alzheimer's) and alpha-synuclein (Parkinson's)
choices: Tau (Alzheimer's) and alpha-synuclein (Parkinson's)
Amyloid-beta (Alzheimer's) and dopamine (Parkinson's)
TDP-43 (Alzheimer's) and huntingtin (Parkinson's)
SOD1 (Alzheimer's) and myelin basic protein (Parkinson's)
context: Misfolded tau tangles in Alzheimer's and misfolded alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in Parkinson's both spread through the brain in ways that resemble prion templating in animal studies -- but 'resembles' is not 'proven in patients.' The bank flags such live questions as live and does not pretend they are settled. The distractors mix real neurodegeneration proteins with wrong pairings: dopamine is a neurotransmitter, not a spreading misfold; TDP-43 is the ALS/FTD protein, huntingtin is the Huntington's-disease protein; SOD1 is another ALS protein, myelin basic protein is a target in multiple sclerosis.

question: A father shoves an empty park swing as hard as he can, over and over, and the seat never climbs far. Beside him a small girl gives her sister's swing nothing but light taps, and soon the sister is level with the top bar. What is the girl doing that he is not?
answer: Spacing her taps to the swing's own natural interval
choices: Spacing her taps to the swing's own natural interval
Pushing at the top of each arc, not at the bottom
Following the seat with her hands the whole way
Pushing the seat sideways as well as straight forward
context: Every object has favourite frequencies, and only pushes that arrive in step with one of them add up. Wikipedia puts it exactly: pushing 'in time with the natural interval of the swing (its resonant frequency) makes the swing go higher and higher (maximum amplitude), while attempts to push the swing at a faster or slower tempo produce smaller arcs.' The variable that decides the outcome is not force. It is timing. Source: Wikipedia, 'Resonance'.

question: A singer stands across the room from a wine glass she has never seen before, meaning to crack it with her voice alone. What does she need to learn from the glass before she takes a breath?
answer: The note it rings when a fingernail flicks the rim
choices: The note it rings when a fingernail flicks the rim
The time its ring takes to fade away to nothing
The depth of the wine standing in the bowl
The thickness of the wall where the bowl is thinnest
context: Loudness by itself will not do it: the rim has to flex a shade further on every pass until the glass exceeds its own strength, and that only builds if her note is the one the glass already answers to. Try this at the dinner table: flick a wine glass rim with a fingernail, and the note you hear is that frequency. Scientific American: 'If a person sings the same tone as that ringing note... the sound of her voice will vibrate the air molecules around the glass at its resonant frequency, causing the glass to start vibrating as well.' Whether it actually breaks also depends on microscopic defects already present in the glass. Wikipedia adds the sober note: 'The classic example of this is breaking a wine glass with sound at the precise resonant frequency of the glass, although this is difficult in practice.' Sources: Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: An Opera Singer Can Shatter Glass'; Wikipedia, 'Resonance'.

question: In April 1831 seventy-four men of the 60th Rifle Corps marched home to barracks across the Broughton suspension bridge near Manchester. The deck began to bounce under their boots, and one corner of it dropped some sixteen feet, spilling about forty of them into the River Irwell. What standing order did the British Army issue afterwards, and still gives today?
answer: Break step when crossing a bridge.
choices: Break step when crossing a bridge.
Cross a bridge only in single file.
Halt and send one man over a bridge first.
Cross a bridge at a run, never at a walk.
context: Nobody died. The Irwell was only about two feet deep at that point, so the fall that should have been a massacre produced twenty injured men, six of them severely, with broken arms and legs and head contusions. Contemporary newspapers warned that the same danger applied to other suspension bridges, naming the Menai Bridge in particular. The order outlived the bridge: soldiers are still told to break step on a bridge today. Source: Wikipedia, 'Broughton Suspension Bridge'.

question: On 18 May 2005 MythBusters set out to settle an old claim: can a singer break a wine glass with nothing but his voice? Rock vocal coach Jaime Vendera hit about 105 decibels, almost as loud as a jackhammer, and a glass on the table burst. Columbia mechanical engineer Jeffrey Kysar summed up how hard the feat really is in one line. What was it?
answer: It's possible, but you have to be both good and lucky.
choices: It's possible, but you have to be both good and lucky.
It's possible, but you have to be both bold and tireless.
It's possible, but you have to be both calm and precise.
It's possible, but you have to be both fit and fearless.
context: Kysar's verdict on the feat, in full: 'It's possible, but you have to be both good and lucky.' The luck was literal. Scientific American reports that Vendera 'tried 12 wine glasses before stumbling on the lucky one that splintered at the blast of his mighty pipes.' Only the finest leaded crystal is 'dainty and resonant enough to break at volumes that some people can produce without amplification -- upward of 100 decibels.' The episode was 'Breaking Glass', and Scientific American calls that 2005 test the first video proof of the unaided feat -- everything before it was sound driven through a speaker. Sources: Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: An Opera Singer Can Shatter Glass'; Wikipedia, 'MythBusters (2005 season)'.

question: Seventy-four men of the 60th Rifle Corps were marching back to barracks across the Broughton suspension bridge near Manchester on 12 April 1831 when they felt the deck start to move under their boots in time with their footsteps. What did some of them do next?
answer: They found it funny, whistled a marching tune and played along.
choices: They found it funny, whistled a marching tune and played along.
They broke ranks and hurried for the far bank in a loose crowd.
They halted where they stood and waited for the deck to settle.
They spread out down the deck and cut their pace by half.
context: Wikipedia records it plainly: 'finding the vibration amusing, some of them started to whistle a marching tune, and to "humour it by the manner in which they stepped".' They were deliberately feeding the oscillation -- driving the deck harder at exactly the interval it wanted, for the pleasure of feeling it move. Lieutenant Percy Slingsby Fitzgerald was in command of the column. Source: Wikipedia, 'Broughton Suspension Bridge'.

question: The Broughton suspension bridge near Manchester came down under a column of soldiers in 1831 with a sound witnesses compared to an irregular discharge of firearms, one corner dropping some sixteen feet into the river. The span was 144 feet, built five years earlier by John Fitzgerald. Investigators traced the collapse to a single part of the structure. Which part let go?
answer: A badly forged bolt where a stay-chain met its ground anchor.
choices: A badly forged bolt where a stay-chain met its ground anchor.
The deck planking beneath the marching column of soldiers.
A main suspension chain, stretched past what it could carry.
The masonry pier carrying the deck at the Salford end.
context: The intuitive verdict -- their combined weight overloaded it -- does not survive the arithmetic: seventy-four men on a 144-foot span is a modest static load. The anchor attachment relied on a single bolt where it should have had two, and when that bolt failed an iron column carrying the suspension chains toppled towards the deck and dislodged a large stone from its pier. Rhythm supplied the driving; the bolt was the weak link. About forty soldiers were thrown into the water or against the chains. Source: Wikipedia, 'Broughton Suspension Bridge'.

question: On 16 April 1850 a French battalion was crossing the Basse-Chaine suspension bridge over the Maine at Angers when the deck folded into the river beneath them. Two hundred and twenty-six of the 483 soldiers on it died. What did the official inquiry blame for the failure?
answer: The men's cadence, plus corroded cable anchors in a storm.
choices: The men's cadence, plus corroded cable anchors in a storm.
The men's cadence, plus a deck built for far lighter traffic.
The men's cadence, plus a wind gust matching the deck's own sway.
The men's cadence, plus a snapped bolt at the ground anchor.
context: The inquiry attributed the collapse to 'dynamic load due to the storm and the soldiers, particularly as they seem to have been somewhat in step, combined with corrosion of the anchors for the main cables.' The corrosion had crept in because the cable wire strands had separated from their cement surrounds, letting water reach the metal. 'Marching resonance destroyed the bridge' is the storybook version of a messier finding, and the messier finding is the honest one. The sharpest detail of all: the soldiers had already been ordered to break step and to space themselves farther apart than normal, yet on a swaying deck in a thunderstorm they apparently 'involuntarily march[ed] with the same cadence, causing resonance.' The upstream anchoring cable let go in its concrete mooring with a sound witnesses compared to 'a badly done volley from a firing squad.' The bridge, designed by Joseph Chaley and Bordillon and built 1836-39, had a 335-foot span. France abandoned suspension bridges until 1870, and later designs went to stiffened decks -- the Brooklyn Bridge being the exemplar. Source: Wikipedia, 'Angers Bridge'.

question: London's Millennium Bridge opened on 10 June 2000, and about ninety thousand people crossed it that day, up to two thousand on the deck at once. They were strolling, not marching. The whole span began swinging sideways, by as much as seventy millimetres, and it was shut two days later. What was driving the sway?
answer: The crowd's own footfalls, each walker adjusting his stride to the deck.
choices: The crowd's own footfalls, each walker adjusting his stride to the deck.
The crowd's sheer weight bowing so slender a deck from side to side.
Wind funnelled along the Thames, gusting at the deck's own frequency.
Tension left uneven in the steel cables when the span was assembled.
context: Engineers call it synchronous lateral excitation. A slight sideways movement of the deck prompts walkers to adjust their gait to match the bridge's oscillation frequency, and a second layer of pedestrian-pedestrian synchronisation piles on top, 'where individuals unconsciously align their stepping patterns' -- a positive feedback loop in which the crowd becomes the driver of its own bridge. It only kicks in past a critical crowd size (166 in the worked example) and only inside a vulnerable lateral band of about 0.5 to 1.1 hertz. It had been seen before: the Toda Park Bridge in Japan in the 1990s, the Auckland Harbour Bridge at 0.67 hertz in a 1975 demonstration, and Birmingham's NEC Link bridge at 0.7 hertz. Londoners christened it the Wobbly Bridge. The cure was damping, not stiffness: Arup fitted 37 viscous fluid dampers and 52 tuned mass dampers, taking the damping from about 0.5% to 20% of critical, for 5 million pounds between May 2001 and January 2002. It reopened on 22 February 2002 and has been stable ever since. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Millennium Bridge, London' and 'Synchronous lateral excitation'.

question: Taipei 101 hangs a 660-tonne steel sphere, five and a half metres across, from its ninety-second floor down to its eighty-eighth, where visitors walk around it on a viewing deck. When Typhoon Soudelor struck on 8 August 2015 the sphere swung a full metre, the largest movement ever recorded for it, and the tower's own sway is cut by up to forty per cent. How does a hanging weight steady a skyscraper?
answer: It swings against the tower's motion, arriving just as the tower leaves.
choices: It swings against the tower's motion, arriving just as the tower leaves.
It swings with the tower's motion, adding weight to each lean it makes.
It swings on a far longer cycle than the tower, so the two never meet.
It swings freely, spending the wind's energy on its cables, not the frame.
context: This is a tuned mass damper, and the trick is deliberate mistiming. Near the troublesome frequency the damper mass runs '180 degrees out of phase' with the main mass, 'maximizing the damping effect by maximizing the amplitude of x2 - x1' -- every swing of the sphere pulls against the building's motion and bleeds the energy away. In Wikipedia's worked example a damper mass equal to 10% of the structure cuts the peak response 'from 9 units down to 5.5 units.' The deeper principle: what makes resonance dangerous is precision plus low damping, not force. The quality factor Q measures how underdamped a thing is -- about 0.5 for a door closer, about 1,000 for a tuning fork, about 100 billion for a laser -- and a system that leaks its energy away fast cannot build a big amplitude no matter how hard you drive it. Taipei's sphere is 41 circular steel plates, each 125 mm thick, welded together; it cost about US$4 million, and it is popular enough that Sanrio created an official mascot for it called 'Damper Baby'. Two extra 6-tonne dampers sit at the tip of the spire. Boston's John Hancock Tower (1976) was the first building retrofitted with a tuned mass damper after completion. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Taipei 101', 'Tuned mass damper', 'Resonance'.

question: The usual explanation of the microwave oven runs like this: 2.45 gigahertz was picked because it is the natural frequency of the water molecule, so the waves set the water ringing and leave the plate cold. It is a textbook staple, and it is wrong. So how does the oven actually heat the food?
answer: The waves tug every lopsided molecule back and forth, across a wide band of frequencies.
choices: The waves tug every lopsided molecule back and forth, across a wide band of frequencies.
The waves knock electrons loose from the food's atoms, across a wide band of frequencies.
The waves drive dissolved salt ions through the food, and only salty patches get hot.
The waves warm the oven's metal walls, and the hot walls radiate into the food.
context: Wikipedia states it flatly: 'It is a common misconception that microwave ovens heat food at a special resonance of water molecules in the food.' The real mechanism is dielectric heating -- 'all polar molecules participate, and dielectric heating for each molecule can happen over a wide range of frequencies.' A polar molecule is one whose electric charge sits lopsidedly, so a passing field can grab it and twist it; the oven's field reverses billions of times a second, and the endless twisting is the warming. Nor was 2.45 gigahertz chosen for any physics: the selection came from 'regulatory and cost constraints', specifically that 2.45 gigahertz is set aside for this kind of equipment worldwide while 915 megahertz is reserved in only some countries. The lesson is worth keeping: not everything called resonance is resonance. Source: Wikipedia, 'Microwave oven'.  (Legend.)

question: The Sun's core sits at 15 million kelvin — yet the average particle there carries only 1 keV, while two protons need roughly 500 keV before their electric repulsion lets them meet. Hundreds of times too feeble, and the Sun burns anyway. What are the protons doing?
answer: Passing through the barrier instead of over it
choices: Passing through the barrier instead of over it
Riding the rare fast tail that clears the barrier
Being crushed over the barrier by sheer density
Shedding their charge so the barrier vanishes
context: kT at 15 million K works out to roughly 1.3 keV; two protons need on the order of 500 keV to shove past their mutual electric repulsion. The particles are hundreds of times too feeble to climb that wall — so they do not climb it. A quantum particle is described by a wave, and a wave does not stop dead at a barrier: it decays inside it, and if the barrier is thin enough a little of it comes out the far side. That is a real, calculable probability of finding the proton on the other side. Every ray of sunlight you have ever stood in got out through a leak in a wall. SOURCE: Grokipedia 'Coulomb barrier' (grokipedia.com/page/Coulomb_barrier) and 'Quantum tunnelling' (grokipedia.com/page/Quantum_tunnelling) — pp Coulomb barrier ~0.5 MeV vs average proton energy ~1 keV, core ~15 million K, density ~150 g/cm3; core temperature corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_core (15,000,000 K).

question: Photographs of individual atoms sitting on a surface are real pictures, not drawings. The instrument that takes them holds a sharp metal needle about half a nanometre above the sample — a gap a few atoms wide — and scans it across. What does it measure to build the picture?
answer: The electrons crossing the empty gap
choices: The electrons crossing the empty gap
The light the surface gives off
The force the surface exerts on it
The heat flowing up into the needle
context: It is called a scanning tunnelling microscope. The tip rides 4 to 7 angstroms (0.4–0.7 nm) above the surface and never touches it; the signal is a sub-nanoampere trickle of electrons tunnelling across the vacuum, under a bias of a fraction of one volt. Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer got the first one working at IBM's Zurich Research Laboratory in March 1981, and in 1983 used it to resolve the 7x7 reconstruction of a silicon (111) surface in real space — individual atoms, in a picture. They took the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for it, sharing the year with Ernst Ruska of electron-microscope fame. SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanning_tunneling_microscope (tip–sample separation 4–7 angstroms, sub-nanoampere current, bias of fractions of 1 V); Grokipedia 'Scanning tunneling microscope' (grokipedia.com/page/Scanning_tunneling_microscope) — first prototype March 1981 at IBM Zurich, Si(111) 7x7 resolved in the 1983 Physical Review Letters paper, 1986 Nobel shared with Ruska.

question: A USB stick keeps your files for years with no power and no moving parts. Inside every cell sits a 'floating gate' — a scrap of conductor with no wire running to it — and a bit is stored by parking electrons on it. How do they get there?
answer: A strong field drives them through the insulator
choices: A strong field drives them through the insulator
A burst of heat boils them over the insulator
A magnetic pulse drags them around the insulator
A gap in the insulator lets them slip inside
context: The mechanism has a name: Fowler–Nordheim tunnelling. There is no gap and no door — a strong electric field drives electrons straight across a thin oxide layer onto the floating gate, where they are stranded, and the trapped charge shifts the transistor's threshold voltage, which is how the cell reads back as a 1 or a 0. Your holiday photos are held in place by particles that were forced through a wall and cannot get back out. SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling (flash memory relies on tunnelling through floating-gate oxide layers); ScienceDirect Topics, 'Fowler–Nordheim Tunneling' (sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/fowler-nordheim-tunneling); techtarget.com/searchstorage/definition/flash-memory — field drives electrons through the oxide into the floating gate, trapped by surrounding oxide; charge state sets the threshold voltage.

question: Harold Lyons at the US National Bureau of Standards switched on the first atomic clock in 1948. It counted neither a pendulum nor a quartz crystal but a motion inside one kind of molecule, a motion that repeats about 24 billion times every second. What was flipping back and forth?
answer: A nitrogen atom passing through its plane of three hydrogens
choices: A nitrogen atom passing through its plane of three hydrogens
A hydrogen atom swinging around the end of a carbon chain
An oxygen atom rocking between its two hydrogen partners
A carbon atom sliding along inside a cage of six hydrogens
context: The molecule is ammonia. Its nitrogen atom sits to one side of a triangle of three hydrogens and tunnels straight through that plane and back — the measured inversion frequency is 23.8 GHz, about 24 billion round trips a second. Lyons built the ammonia absorption clock in 1948 and demonstrated it publicly in early 1949. And ammonia has a second claim: the very first thing anyone ever explained with tunnelling was not a star or a nucleus but a smell. In 1927 Friedrich Hund solved the Schrodinger equation for a double-well potential and realised it accounted for ammonia's inversion spectrum — a year before the famous alpha-decay papers. SOURCE: Chemistry LibreTexts, 'The Ammonia Inversion and the Maser'; 'Tunneling Quantum Dynamics in Ammonia' (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8348077/) — measured inversion transition ~23.8 GHz. Clock: ETHW 'Milestones:First Atomic Clock, 1948' (ethw.org/Milestones:First_Atomic_Clock,_1948). Hund: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling and Grokipedia 'Quantum tunnelling'.

question: On 9 and 10 November 1989 Don Eigler and Erhard Schweizer sat at a scanning tunnelling microscope in a California laboratory and used its needle to pick up 35 xenon atoms one at a time, setting each down exactly where they wanted it on chilled nickel. Nobody had ever placed single atoms before. What did they make?
answer: The letters I, B and M, five nanometres tall
choices: The letters I, B and M, five nanometres tall
A ring of 35 atoms, five nanometres across
A single straight line of 35 spaced atoms
A tiny copy of the nickel pattern beneath
context: The laboratory was IBM's Almaden Research Center, and Eigler and Schweizer spelled out their employer's name in 35 xenon atoms, the letters five nanometres tall. It was the first time anyone had put single atoms exactly where they wanted them; the image ran in Nature in 1990 and in newspapers around the world. The tool that placed them was the same one that photographs them — a needle reading a current of electrons crossing an empty gap. SOURCE: Chemical & Engineering News, '30 years of moving atoms: How scanning probe microscopes revolutionized nanoscience' (cen.acs.org/analytical-chemistry/imaging/30-years-moving-atoms-scanning/97/i44) — 9–10 November 1989, Donald M. Eigler and Erhard K. Schweizer, 35 xenon atoms, 5 nm tall letters, cold nickel surface, IBM Almaden. Primary paper: Eigler and Schweizer, 'Positioning single atoms with a scanning tunnelling microscope', Nature 344, 524 (1990).

question: Tunnelling — a particle crossing a barrier it has not the energy to climb — is not a yes-or-no affair: quantum mechanics hands you a number, a real probability of getting through. That number falls away exponentially with three quantities at once, and an exponential never reaches zero, so nothing is ever forbidden outright. Which three quantities?
answer: The barrier's height and width, and the particle's mass
choices: The barrier's height and width, and the particle's mass
The barrier's height and width, and the particle's charge
The barrier's height and width, and the particle's speed
The barrier's height and width, and the particle's spin
context: Barrier height, barrier width, and the mass of the moving particle — and mass is the term that quietly separates the quantum world from yours. Nothing in the physics forbids a cricket ball from tunnelling through a wall; that triple exponential simply crushes the ball's odds so far below anything measurable that it will not be seen in the lifetime of the universe. There is no line in the equations where the rule switches off and the everyday world begins. It is a smooth, savage falloff, and mass is the term that does the killing — which is exactly why the effect is decisive for an electron or a proton and utterly invisible for anything you can hold. SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling ('Tunnelling probability decreases exponentially with barrier height, width, and particle mass'); Grokipedia 'Quantum tunnelling' (grokipedia.com/page/Quantum_tunnelling), which states the same exponential dependence on barrier height, width and particle mass.

question: In the summer of 1928 a 24-year-old visitor was working at Göttingen as Max Born's guest. The puzzle in front of him had been open since 1911: an alpha particle sits inside a radioactive nucleus behind an electric barrier far taller than the energy the alpha carries, and yet uranium decays. He solved it that summer. Who was he?
answer: George Gamow
choices: George Gamow
Friedrich Hund
Edward Condon
Fritz Houtermans
context: George Gamow, born 4 March 1904 in Odessa, was twenty-four and a summer visitor at Gottingen when he worked out that the alpha particle escapes by tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier. He was not alone: Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon published 'Wave Mechanics and Radioactive Disintegration' in Nature that same year (vol. 122, p. 439, 1928), arguing that radioactive decay follows from the ordinary laws of quantum mechanics with no special hypothesis added; Leonid Mandelstam and Mikhail Leontovich hit on tunnelling independently in 1928 as well; and J. Robert Oppenheimer's two 1928 papers on field emission were the same physics under a different name. Nobody even called it tunnelling yet — the German Tunneleffekt appears with Walter Schottky in 1931, and the English 'tunnel effect' entered use in 1932 via Yakov Frenkel's textbook. SOURCE: Grokipedia 'George Gamow' (grokipedia.com/page/George_Gamow) — born 4 March 1904 in Odessa, age 24 at Gottingen under Max Born in summer 1928. Nature 122, 439 (1928), Gurney and Condon (nature.com/articles/122439a0). Mandelstam/Leontovich, Oppenheimer, and the naming dates: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling.

question: In August 1957, at a small Tokyo firm called Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo — soon to rename itself Sony — Leo Esaki and Yuriko Kurose built a heavily doped germanium junction and turned up the voltage. Every textbook says current rises with voltage. Theirs did something else, and that made their device the first product ever built on tunnelling. What did the current do?
answer: It fell steadily as the voltage rose
choices: It fell steadily as the voltage rose
It froze at one value however high the voltage
It stopped dead and then flowed backwards
It oscillated at one fixed frequency
context: Push harder, get less: that backwards behaviour is called negative resistance, and it was electrons tunnelling straight through the junction instead of climbing over it. The tunnel diode became the first commercial device built on the effect. Esaki took a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics for it, alongside Ivar Giaever for tunnelling in superconductors (1960) and Brian Josephson for predicting that paired electrons could tunnel across an insulating gap (1962) — three men, three walls. The story is not over: the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis 'for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit', for Berkeley experiments in 1984–85 showing that a whole superconducting circuit, not just a single particle, can tunnel from one state to another. Clarke on hearing the news: 'To put it mildly, it was the surprise of my life.' SOURCE: Semiconductor History Museum of Japan, 'D1 Invention of tunnel diode' (shmj.or.jp/innovation50/english/detail_D01E.htm) — August 1957, Esaki and Kurose at Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, now Sony. 1973 Nobel: nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/esaki/facts/ and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling. 2025 Nobel and Clarke quote: Physics World, 'John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis win the 2025 Nobel Prize for Physics'.

question: Arthur Eddington told the British Association in 1920 that the stars run on hydrogen turning into helium, resting the whole claim on Francis Aston's measurement that a helium atom weighs about one part in 120 less than four hydrogen atoms. Physicists objected that stellar interiors were nowhere near hot enough for nuclei to force past their electric repulsion — and their arithmetic was correct. How did Eddington answer them in print?
answer: He told his critic to go and find a hotter place
choices: He told his critic to go and find a hotter place
He proposed a new force that cancelled the repulsion
He withdrew the claim and published a correction
He argued the stars must be far younger than thought
context: The exact sentence: 'We do not argue with the critic who urges that the stars are not hot enough for this process; we tell him to go and find a hotter place.' ACCURACY NOTE: the wording is documented, but the citation that can be confirmed is Eddington's book The Internal Constitution of the Stars (1926); his 1920 Cardiff address carries the same title, which is very likely why the line is so often dated to 1920. The CLAIM is firmly 1920 — delivered 24 August 1920 at the British Association in Cardiff and printed in Nature a week later (vol. 106, p. 14). And here is the wonder: Eddington was right for a reason that did not exist yet. Tunnelling was not worked out until 1927–28, seven or eight years after he made the claim. In 1929 Robert d'Escourt Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans picked up Gamow's brand-new result and applied it to stars, showing that light nuclei could indeed fuse at the modest temperatures Eddington had calculated rather than the impossible ones his critics demanded. He won the argument before anyone knew why he should. SOURCE: en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Arthur_Stanley_Eddington (exact wording, cited to The Internal Constitution of the Stars, 1926); Bernard Schutz, 'Eddington in Cardiff 100 years ago today' (bfschutz.com) — address 24 August 1920, Nature vol. 106, p. 14, Aston mass deficit about 1 part in 120; Atkinson and Houtermans 1929: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_d%27Escourt_Atkinson.

question: A scanning tunnelling microscope resolves height differences of about a hundredth of a nanometre — a small fraction of one atom's width — using a hand-ground needle inside a building full of vibration. Nothing about the needle is that precise; the precision is in the current. Widen the gap by 0.1 nanometre. What happens to the tunnelling current?
answer: It divides by ten
choices: It divides by ten
It divides by two
It divides by three
It divides by a hundred
context: A whole order of magnitude for every extra angstrom. That brutal exponential is what turns a crude metal point into an instrument with a depth resolution of about 0.01 nm — ten picometres, roughly a tenth the width of an atom — and a lateral resolution better than 0.1 nm. The needle is not precise; the physics is. Because the current is so violently sensitive to distance, essentially all of it flows from the single atom at the very end of the tip that happens to be closest to the surface. SOURCE: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanning_tunneling_microscope — current is 'exponentially dependent on the separation of the sample and the tip, typically reducing by an order of magnitude when the separation is increased by 1 A (0.1 nm)'; depth resolution '0.01 nm (10 pm)'; lateral resolution better than 0.1 nm.

question: By its 65-nanometre chips Intel had thinned the silicon-dioxide insulator under each transistor gate to 1.2 nanometres — five atomic layers — and electrons were tunnelling straight through it and leaking away, wasting power and heating the chip.
