question: A psychology journal happily prints a study that finds a striking effect but rejects one that finds nothing. Repeat that across thousands of studies and the published literature looks stronger than the real evidence. In 1979 Robert Rosenthal gave this leak a name -- what did he call it?
answer: The file drawer problem
choices: The file drawer problem
The publication paradox
The peer-review gap
The null-effect blackout
context: Rosenthal named it in Psychological Bulletin (1979) and proposed a 'fail-safe N' -- a rough count of how many unpublished null studies would be needed to erase a meta-analysis's apparent effect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publication_bias

question: J. B. Rhine's Duke laboratory ran ESP card-guessing trials through the 1930s and reported some subjects with astonishing streaks. Martin Gardner argued Rhine had discovered nothing. What was Gardner's central charge?
answer: Rhine repeated the tests but did not report the failures
choices: Rhine repeated the tests but did not report the failures
Rhine's shuffling was too regular to count as random
Rhine's assistants had marked the backs of the cards
Rhine had used the wrong statistical formula to score hits
context: Gardner: Rhine tried to replicate his own work and produced only failures he never reported. His star subject Hubert Pearce could not score above chance when anyone but Rhine was watching. If you test enough people at guessing 25 shuffled cards, chance alone will produce some subjects with astonishing streaks -- report only those streaks and hide the failures, and you have discovered nothing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Banks_Rhine

question: 'Steve Jobs, Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg all dropped out of college and got rich -- so dropping out helps you get rich.' The reasoning is broken. Which of these four adjacent statistical leaks is doing the damage here?
answer: The losing cases are missing from the sample entirely
choices: The losing cases are missing from the sample entirely
Extreme cases drift back toward the average next time
The target was drawn around the shots after the fact
People count the hits and forget the misses
context: This is survivorship bias, the same shape as Wald's diagram: the sample is only the winners, so the millions of dropouts who stayed poor never appear and the pattern is an illusion. The other three name real, adjacent leaks worth learning to tell apart -- regression to the mean, the Texas sharpshooter fallacy, and confirmation bias. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias

question: A drug trial reports a positive effect only on left-handed women over sixty. The obvious worry: the researchers hunted through the data until they found a subgroup that worked. Modern journals demand a discipline called preregistration to block exactly this move. What does preregistration actually require?
answer: Committing publicly to your analysis plan before you see the data
choices: Committing publicly to your analysis plan before you see the data
Hiding which patients got the drug from the doctors running the trial
Assigning patients to treatment or placebo by coin flip
Sending the finished manuscript to two independent expert reviewers
context: Preregistration locks the analysis in advance, so a null result cannot quietly disappear into the file drawer and a subgroup 'finding' cannot be quietly invented. The other three choices are real, distinct disciplines -- blinding, randomization, peer review -- worth telling apart. It is the same rule Wald was reaching for: decide what counts BEFORE you see who survived. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preregistration_(science)

question: SV40 turned up in 1960 in the rhesus monkey kidney cells used to grow polio vaccine, and 80 to 100 per cent of captive adult rhesus macaques carry antibodies to it. What was the virus doing in the macaques?
answer: Living in their kidneys for life, causing no disease
choices: Living in their kidneys for life, causing no disease
Living in their gut for a season, then clearing away
Scarring their kidneys into a slow, lasting decline
Raising tumours in the lining of their chests
context: SV40's natural host is the rhesus macaque. In a normal monkey it settles into the kidney epithelium as a chronic, silent infection with no described disease -- which is exactly why nobody went looking for it in the vaccine substrate. Seroprevalence in macaque breeding colonies passes 75 per cent by two to three years of age. Sources: IARC Monographs Vol. 104, Simian Virus 40 (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK294242); PMC3122853.

question: Bernice Eddy, a virologist at America's National Institutes of Health, injected extracts of the rhesus monkey kidney cells that polio vaccine was grown in into 154 newborn hamsters. Over the next three and a half to nine months, what appeared in the animals?
answer: Tumours, in 109 of the 154
choices: Tumours, in 109 of the 154
Paralysis, in 109 of the 154
Kidney failure, in 40 of the 154
Nothing at all, in any of the 154
context: Eddy BE, Borman GS, Berkeley WH, Young RD, 'Tumors induced in hamsters by injection of rhesus monkey kidney cell extracts', Proc Soc Exp Biol Med 1961;107:191-197 (PMID 13725644). About 70 per cent of the injected animals grew subcutaneous tumours over three and a half to nine months. She had injected the vaccine's own substrate rather than a purified virus -- which is exactly what her critics would fasten on. Sources: Europe PMC PMID 13725644; IARC Monographs Vol. 104 (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK294242).

question: The Salk polio vaccine was made safe by a single step: the poliovirus in it was soaked in formaldehyde until it was dead, and the soak was timed and measured against poliovirus. SV40 was riding in the same fluid, and it is tougher. What fraction of the SV40 particles came through the formaldehyde alive?
answer: About one in 10,000
choices: About one in 10,000
About one in ten
About one in a thousand
About one in a million
context: The one-in-10,000 figure rests on the account of virologist Leonard Norkin and should be read as his estimate; the qualitative point is independently reported -- conditions sufficient to inactivate poliovirus were insufficient to completely inactivate SV40. The safety step was real and it worked. It simply was not aimed at this. Sources: norkinvirology.wordpress.com/2014/07/24/sv40-contaminated-polio-vaccines-and-human-cancer; PMC153983 (Clin Microbiol Rev, 'Simian Virus 40 Infection of Humans').  (Legend.)

question: In November 1960 Ben Sweet and Maurice Hilleman published the new monkey virus under the title 'The vacuolating virus, S.V.40', and their own paper did not soften what they had found. Where did they report the virus had already got to?
answer: Into all three types of Sabin's live polio vaccine
choices: Into all three types of Sabin's live polio vaccine
Into the chick-embryo cultures used for measles work
Into the human cell lines kept for testing vaccines
Into the mouse colonies housed in the same building
context: Sweet BH & Hilleman MR, Proc Soc Exp Biol Med 1960;105:420-427 (PMID 13774265). They described the agent as a common and essentially ubiquitous contaminant of rhesus monkey kidney cultures, reported it in all three types of Sabin's live poliovirus vaccine and in numerous respiratory-virus seed lines already used in human volunteer inoculations, and speculated in print about the possible long-term effects of introducing such a virus into the human population. Sources: Europe PMC PMID 13774265; PMC4675525.

question: In October 1960 Bernice Eddy told a cancer conference in New York what the monkey-kidney material used to make polio vaccine had done to her hamsters. Her superior, Joseph Smadel, had already reviewed the same data. What did Smadel do after the conference?
answer: Forbade her to speak on it in public without clearing her words first
choices: Forbade her to speak on it in public without clearing her words first
Ordered the hamster work repeated in three outside laboratories
Took the data to the licensing board and had suspect lots withheld
Resigned his post rather than approve another season of vaccine
context: Smadel reviewed Eddy's data and dismissed her finding of a tumour-inducing virus in early Salk lots; after the October 1960 conference he required her to clear any public remarks with him first. The honest other half: Maurice Hilleman alleged that her experiments were poorly controlled, and the dispute cut both ways -- which is why the control she published in 1962 matters so much. This account comes from virologist Leonard Norkin's history rather than from a primary document. Sources: norkinvirology.wordpress.com/2014/07/24/sv40-contaminated-polio-vaccines-and-human-cancer; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_Eddy.

question: Between 1955 and 1963 about 98 million Americans, most of them children, were given the inactivated polio vaccine, and it is the assumed main route of human SV40 exposure in the United States. When Shah and Nathanson went back over it in 1976, what share of that vaccine did they estimate had carried live SV40?
answer: 10 to 30 per cent of it
choices: 10 to 30 per cent of it
Under 1 per cent of it
About 60 per cent of it
Nearly all of it
context: On that arithmetic an estimated 10 to 30 million Americans were actually exposed. The Institute of Medicine's 2002 review used the same figures: 'IPV administered between 1955 and 1963 to about 98 million children and adults is assumed to be the primary source of human exposure to SV40 in the United States'; 'Shah and Nathanson (1976) estimated that 10% to 30% of IPV contained live SV40.' Source: IOM, Immunization Safety Review: SV40 Contamination of Polio Vaccine and Cancer (2002), ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK221118.

question: From 1961 American rules required every lot of polio vaccine to test negative for SV40 before release, and other countries were assumed clear after 1962. In 2005 Cutrone and colleagues tested stored vaccine samples from 13 countries. What did they find?
answer: One eastern European maker's oral vaccine carried live SV40 to 1978
choices: One eastern European maker's oral vaccine carried live SV40 to 1978
Every sample made after 1962 was free of live SV40 everywhere
Only vaccine made before the 1955 licence carried live SV40
American-made vaccine carried live SV40 until about 1970
context: Cutrone R, Lednicky J, Dunn G, Rizzo P, Bocchetta M, Chumakov K, Minor P, Carbone M, 'Some oral poliovirus vaccines were contaminated with infectious SV40 after 1961', Cancer Res 2005;65:10273. The contaminated oral vaccine was produced from the early 1960s until approximately 1978, because that manufacturer's heat-inactivation step did not completely inactivate SV40. The American fix was forward-looking only: already-approved lots were not recalled, and potentially contaminated vaccine from those earlier lots may have been used until early 1963. Sources: aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/65/22/10273; IARC Vol. 104 (NBK294242); IOM 2002 (NBK221112).

question: SV40 makes a protein called large T antigen, and in a hamster that one protein is enough to turn a healthy cell cancerous. A cell is held in check by two brakes: p53, which orders a damaged cell to stop or to die, and Rb, which holds back the machinery of division. What does large T antigen do to them?
answer: Clamps onto both of them at once, holding each out of action
choices: Clamps onto both of them at once, holding each out of action
Clamps onto p53 alone, and leaves Rb working normally
Cuts the genes for both of them out of the cell's own DNA
Copies itself into the gene for Rb and silences it there
context: Large T antigen binds p53 through a region at its C-terminal end, and binds Rb and its relatives p107 and p130 through a short motif spelled LxCxE at residues 103 to 107. Holding Rb pries loose the E2F transcription factors that push a cell into dividing; holding p53 blocks the cell's own order to stop or to die. One viral protein, both brakes, released at once -- and no mutation of the cell's own genes required. Sources: PMC153983 (Clin Microbiol Rev, 'Simian Virus 40 Infection of Humans'); EMBO J 2001;20:295, 'Structural basis for the inactivation of retinoblastoma tumor suppressor by SV40 large T antigen'.

question: Bernice Eddy's hamster tumours proved something in the monkey-kidney extract caused cancer, but not what, and Maurice Hilleman alleged her experiments were poorly controlled. In 1962 she pulled virus back out of the tumours and injected it into fresh newborn hamsters, and tumours grew again. What did she do to one batch of that virus so that no tumours grew at all?
answer: Mixed it with rabbit antiserum raised against SV40 before injecting
choices: Mixed it with rabbit antiserum raised against SV40 before injecting
Heated it to sixty degrees for half an hour before injecting
Passed it through a filter fine enough to hold back bacteria
Diluted it a thousandfold in sterile saline before injecting
context: Eddy BE, Borman GS, Grubbs GE, Young RD, 'Identification of the oncogenic substance in rhesus monkey kidney cell culture as simian virus 40', Virology 1962;17:65-75 (PMID 13889129). Block the antibody's target and you block the cancer: the tumours were this virus's doing and not something else in the soup. It is also the answer to the 'poorly controlled' charge -- she supplied the control herself. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13889129.

question: Reports that SV40 DNA sits inside human mesotheliomas kept appearing, so in 2004 Lopez-Rios and his colleagues ran 71 frozen mesotheliomas through PCR. Their first primer sets found SV40 in 56 to 62 per cent of the tumours, matching the earlier positive studies exactly. Then they looked hard at the primers themselves. What had those primers been reading?
answer: SV40 sequence that also sits inside ordinary laboratory plasmids
choices: SV40 sequence that also sits inside ordinary laboratory plasmids
BK virus sequence, a human cousin of SV40 living in the same tissue
Human DNA that happens to spell the same short stretch of letters
Adenovirus sequence left behind in the tumours by an old infection
context: Primers designed to avoid that stretch gave only 4 faint positives out of 71 (6 per cent). All 71 tumours were negative for T-antigen transcripts by RT-PCR and none carried T-antigen-positive tumour cells on immunohistochemistry. The loop is exact: large T antigen is now a routine laboratory reagent for immortalising cells, and SV40's promoter and regulatory sequences are built into an enormous number of ordinary expression plasmids -- the tool made from the virus contaminated the test for the virus. Cross-reaction with the human polyomaviruses BK and JC is a real confounder too, but for antibody tests rather than for this study's primers. Lopez-Rios F, Illei PB, Rusch V, Ladanyi M, The Lancet 2004 (PMID 15451223).

question: A group of 1,073 people given SV40-contaminated polio vaccine as newborns between 1961 and 1963 were followed for 35 years. Cancer deaths overall came to 4 against 3.16 expected -- nothing at all. One cancer alone broke the pattern, with 2 deaths against 0.05 expected. Which cancer was it?
answer: Testicular cancer
choices: Testicular cancer
Brain cancer
Bone cancer
Chest-lining cancer
context: Two testicular-cancer deaths against 0.05 expected gives P = 0.002. The authors called their results 'for the most part, consistent with other negative epidemiologic investigations' while noting that 'further study of testicular cancer may be warranted'. The larger negative stands beside it: Strickler and colleagues (JAMA 1998), using US SEER registry data with more than 30 years of follow-up, found no significant excess of ependymomas and other brain cancers, osteosarcomas or mesotheliomas among the exposed -- osteosarcoma relative risk 0.87 (95% CI 0.71-1.06). The Institute of Medicine's 2002 review put the position in two sentences that point different ways: 'the evidence is inadequate to accept or reject a causal relationship between SV40-containing polio vaccines and cancer', and 'the biological evidence is moderate that SV40 exposure could lead to cancer in humans under natural conditions'. In 2013 IARC placed SV40 in Group 3 -- not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans. The exposure is not in dispute; the consequence is not settled. Sources: Br J Cancer (PMC2375249); JAMA 1998 (PMID 9605895); IOM 2002 (NBK221118); IARC Monographs Vol. 104 (NBK294242).

question: Leo Szilard read Rutherford's 'moonshine' verdict in The Times the next morning in London and went walking. By his own later account, the idea struck him while he was standing at a crossing waiting for a light to change. Which London street corner did Szilard name as the setting?
answer: Southampton Row at Russell Square
choices: Southampton Row at Russell Square
Baker Street at Marylebone Road
Fleet Street at Ludgate Hill
Oxford Street at Marble Arch
context: Szilard told the story decades later; Richard Rhodes's 'The Making of the Atomic Bomb' (1986) is the standard secondary source. He realised that if a nucleus struck by ONE neutron could throw off TWO, the reaction would feed itself. Twenty-four hours after Rutherford's dismissal.  (Legend.)

question: Szilard's 1934 patent needed a real substance that would spit out more neutrons than it swallowed - and no one knew of one. Szilard tried candidates himself at St Bartholomew's Hospital and at Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory in 1934 and 1935. Which pair of elements did he actually test and eliminate?
answer: Beryllium and indium
choices: Beryllium and indium
Uranium and thorium
Radium and polonium
Cadmium and boron
context: Neither worked; Szilard concluded indium was incapable of chain-reacting. The idea then sat idle until the 1939 fission papers gave him a candidate he had not thought of - uranium. Source: dannen.com Szilard chronology.

question: At 3:25 pm on 2 December 1942, under the west stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, Enrico Fermi's team slowly pulled the last long rod out of a lattice of graphite and uranium until the neutron counter stopped falling and started climbing on its own. What material was that final rod made of?
answer: Cadmium
choices: Cadmium
Beryllium
Tungsten
Lead
context: Chicago Pile-1: about 400 tons of graphite and 50 tons of uranium; the first self-sustaining chain reaction ran for 28 minutes. Cadmium was chosen because its nuclei absorb neutrons very effectively, so pulling the rods out lets the multiplication factor rise past 1 - the definition of 'critical' Szilard had coined eight years earlier. Source: aps.org first self-sustained chain reaction.

question: The balloon Zenith rose from Paris on 15 April 1875 with three men - Sivel, Croce-Spinelli and Tissandier - past roughly 8,000 m on a scientific climb. What happened up there?
answer: Two of the three suffocated at altitude; only Tissandier came down alive
choices: Two of the three suffocated at altitude; only Tissandier came down alive
All three came back safe but were struck deaf for life by pressure change
The basket broke free and the men parachuted down from the upper air
A lightning strike lit the envelope and forced an emergency descent
context: Sivel and Croce-Spinelli died of hypoxia (oxygen starvation) at altitudes we now know push into mountaineering's 'death zone'. The men had carried oxygen bags but not nearly enough for the climb they attempted. Tissandier survived but was left partly deaf. Source: Beauchamp, 'Martyrs made in the sky', Notes & Records of the Royal Society 74 (2020).

question: After the 1875 Zenith deaths French upper-air science drew a hard lesson from the tragedy. Instead of sending scientists higher and higher into the thin air themselves, they changed the whole approach. What did they change to?
answer: Small unmanned balloons carrying self-recording thermometers up on their own
choices: Small unmanned balloons carrying self-recording thermometers up on their own
Tall observation towers built in the Alps to reach the same altitudes on foot
Kites tethered to the ground carrying a wire back down to the recording gear
Artillery shells with instruments that recorded during the shell's arcing flight
context: Send the instrument, not the man. From 1898 Leon Teisserenc de Bort ran the first sustained programme of unmanned soundings, at his private observatory in Trappes near Versailles - eventually more than 200 flights. Source: UCAR SciEd, 'The History of Atmospheric Discovery'.

question: Leon Teisserenc de Bort ran many of his upper-air balloon launches AT NIGHT on purpose. Why did he insist on the night flights?
answer: So no critic could argue that sunlight had warmed the thermometer and skewed the reading
choices: So no critic could argue that sunlight had warmed the thermometer and skewed the reading
So the balloons would be invisible from the ground and not draw hostile military attention
So he could track the balloons visually against the stars with a fixed transit telescope
So the colder night air let the hydrogen envelopes carry more instrument payload aloft
context: This is a control - a deliberate step to kill an objection before anyone could raise it. Teisserenc de Bort knew that a bright thermometer reading in the upper air would be waved away as 'the sun warmed the instrument'. By running many launches at night, he removed the objection from the argument. Source: Wikipedia; hogback.atmos.colostate.edu, 'Discovery of the Stratosphere'.

question: For centuries physicists had assumed one obvious thing about the upper air: keep going up and it just keeps getting colder. Above roughly 11 km over France, Teisserenc de Bort's thermometers reported something no one expected. What did they report?
answer: The temperature simply stopped falling and stayed nearly flat as the balloons climbed higher
choices: The temperature simply stopped falling and stayed nearly flat as the balloons climbed higher
The temperature dropped abruptly by about 40 degrees in a narrow band a few hundred metres thick
The temperature fluctuated wildly by 20 degrees within each single balloon flight
The temperature fell TWICE as fast as at lower altitudes, then went off the thermometer's scale
context: Teisserenc de Bort announced the finding to the French Academy of Sciences on 28 April 1902, and later coined the name STRATOSPHERE for the calm upper deck and TROPOSPHERE for the churning lower one. Source: Ebsco, 'Stratosphere and Troposphere Are Discovered'; Britannica, 'Leon Teisserenc de Bort'.

question: A finding as strange as an atmosphere that stops cooling would normally be dismissed as instrument error - one man's thermometers behaving oddly. What convinced other scientists in 1902 to take Teisserenc de Bort's isothermal layer seriously?
answer: Richard Assmann in Berlin reported the same layer, from his own separate balloon programme
choices: Richard Assmann in Berlin reported the same layer, from his own separate balloon programme
The Paris Observatory verified it by measuring air temperature from a Himalayan expedition
The French Academy re-flew Teisserenc de Bort's exact balloons under a supervising committee
The King of Belgium personally funded a repeat programme run by a Jesuit meteorological order
context: Assmann announced the same isothermal layer to the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 1 May 1902, three days after Teisserenc de Bort - independently, from a separate programme. Independent confirmation, not the authority of any one man. Source: AMS abstract 269395; Wikipedia, 'Richard Assmann'.

question: The tropopause - the boundary Teisserenc de Bort found where the air stops cooling - is not a shelf at one fixed altitude around the whole Earth. Where does it sit at the equator, and where at the poles?
answer: About 17 km up over the equator, but only about 8 km up over the poles
choices: About 17 km up over the equator, but only about 8 km up over the poles
About 8 km up over the equator, but climbing to about 17 km over the poles
About 12 km up worldwide, varying by less than one kilometre with latitude
About 25 km up over the equator, but pressed all the way down to the ground at the poles
context: Vigorous tropical convection lifts the boundary; cold polar air lets it sag. This is why 'the stratosphere begins at 11 km' is a French average, not a planetary constant. Source: code7700.com, 'Tropopause'; NOAA JetStream.

question: There are two official 'edges of space' in use today, and they disagree by about 20 km. The world sporting body FAI uses 100 km - the famous Karman line. The United States has always awarded astronaut wings at 50 miles, about 80.5 km. How did that disagreement come about?
answer: Von Karman's own aerodynamic estimate was closer to 84 km; the FAI rounded up to 100 km for a tidy figure
choices: Von Karman's own aerodynamic estimate was closer to 84 km; the FAI rounded up to 100 km for a tidy figure
The FAI adopted 100 km from a UN treaty on outer-space liability, ratified in 1967
The US Air Force's 80 km figure was chosen to match the ceiling of the X-15 rocket plane
Von Karman himself proposed both numbers and let each nation choose which one to adopt
context: Nobody discovered where space starts. Two committees defined it, differently, and neither number matches Karman's original calculation. When someone in the news claims a rocket 'reached space', ask which line they used. Source: McDowell, 'The edge of space: Revisiting the Karman Line', Acta Astronautica (2018), arXiv/planet4589.

question: The stratosphere - the calm deck above Teisserenc de Bort's boundary - is upside down compared to the air below it: WARM at the top, cold at the bottom. Why does that inversion exist, and why does it mean airliners get such a smooth ride once they climb into it?
answer: Ozone up there absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and heats the air where it sits; warm-over-cold refuses to overturn, so the layer barely mixes
choices: Ozone up there absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and heats the air where it sits; warm-over-cold refuses to overturn, so the layer barely mixes
The atmosphere thins so much that molecules almost never collide, so heat cannot travel downward at all through the layer
The Earth's magnetic field traps solar-wind particles at that height and heats the layer by direct particle bombardment from above
The stratosphere is dominated by dry descending polar air that only sinks and never rises anywhere on Earth
context: Because the stratosphere does not convect, anything injected into it - volcanic sulfate from Pinatubo, CFCs, aircraft soot - lingers for years and drifts sideways instead of rinsing out. That non-mixing is exactly what makes it calm to fly in and what makes it globally consequential when it is polluted. Source: NOAA JetStream, 'Layers of the Atmosphere'; Lumen 'Layers of the Atmosphere'.

question: In 1957 the West German pharmaceutical firm Chemie Gruenenthal put a new sedative on the market as Contergan, and advertised it as so safe that a person could not overdose on it. Doctors handed it out for anxiety, insomnia and one particular complaint of pregnancy that no other drug was helping. Which complaint?
answer: morning sickness
choices: morning sickness
back pain
heartburn
swollen ankles
context: Gruenenthal marketed Contergan aggressively to expectant mothers on the strength of the 'cannot overdose' claim, which was based on rodent studies that never tested for effects on a developing fetus. The active ingredient was thalidomide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide_scandal.

question: In November 1961 the German paediatrician Widukind Lenz and the Australian obstetrician William McBride independently linked thalidomide to a wave of babies born with severe congenital malformations. One specific medical term came out of the crisis and into common use to describe the injury pattern. Which term?
answer: phocomelia
choices: phocomelia
spina bifida
hydrocephalus
clubfoot
context: Phocomelia (from Greek phoke, seal + melos, limb) describes limbs shortened or absent, sometimes leaving hands or feet attached close to the trunk. Between 10,000 and 12,000 children were affected worldwide, with about 40 percent dying at or shortly after birth; Germany was hardest hit. The other three conditions are unrelated birth defects with their own causes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide_scandal.

question: Only ONE of thalidomide's two mirror-image forms - the (S) form - was responsible for the birth defects, and this was because it fit like a key into one particular human protein and jammed the cellular machinery that a fetus uses to build limbs. The (R) form did not fit that lock. Which protein is the (S) form binding?
answer: cereblon
choices: cereblon
haemoglobin
insulin
actin
context: Handa's group in Japan identified cereblon as the target in 2010, almost fifty years after the disaster. Cereblon is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, a molecular machine that tags other proteins for destruction; thalidomide misdirects that tagging, taking out proteins the developing limb needs. Haemoglobin carries oxygen, insulin regulates blood sugar, actin builds muscle filaments - all correct answers to different questions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: The injury pattern was strikingly specific to a narrow developmental window: only fetuses exposed between roughly day 20 and day 36 after conception were affected, and different days within that fortnight hit different body parts. That is because the drug interfered with one particular building process only under way during those two weeks. Which process?
answer: the formation of the limb buds
choices: the formation of the limb buds
the closing of the neural tube
the descent of the kidneys
the fusion of the palate
context: Between days 20 and 36 the limb buds emerge and pattern themselves head-to-tail and thumb-to-little-finger; (S)-thalidomide's binding to cereblon disrupts that pattern. Day 24 exposure hit arms; day 28 hit legs. The neural tube closes earlier, the kidneys migrate later, the palate fuses later still. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: A common moral drawn from the thalidomide story is 'if only they had sold the good (R) hand of the molecule alone, none of this would have happened.' That moral is wrong, and getting it wrong hides the real chemistry. Thalidomide's chiral centre (its single carbon with four different groups around it) carries an ACIDIC hydrogen, which lets the molecule do something inside the body that defeats the whole scheme. What does it do?
answer: the (R) form spontaneously inverts into (S) inside the body
choices: the (R) form spontaneously inverts into (S) inside the body
the (R) form is oxidized by a liver enzyme into (S)
both forms break down to a common toxic metabolite
both forms are metabolized to an achiral intermediate
context: Give a patient pure (R)-thalidomide and the body manufactures (S) anyway - the acidic proton at the chiral centre falls off and re-adds from the other face at random. This spontaneous inversion is called racemization; it happens without any enzyme and is why the tidy 'sell one enantiomer' fix could never have saved thalidomide. Modern chirally-pure medicines have to be checked case by case for in-vivo inversion; it is not the general rule for chiral drugs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: The United States was largely spared from the thalidomide disaster, and not by luck. A brand-new FDA medical officer, on her very first assignment in August 1960, refused Richardson-Merrell's application again and again over inadequate safety data - including the absence of any evidence about whether the drug crossed the placenta - while the company complained about her over her head. President Kennedy honoured her in 1962. Who was she?
answer: Frances Oldham Kelsey
choices: Frances Oldham Kelsey
Rosalind Franklin
Barbara McClintock
Gertrude Elion
context: Kelsey delayed the Kevadon application through more than a year of 60-day rebuffs. Richardson-Merrell had, in the meantime, distributed about 2.5 million tablets in the US as 'investigational' samples; confirmed US birth-defect cases came to about 17. Kennedy gave her the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service in August 1962. Rosalind Franklin was Photo 51; McClintock the corn geneticist; Elion the drug designer who made azathioprine and acyclovir. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Oldham_Kelsey.

question: The direct legislative consequence of the thalidomide scandal in the United States came the very next year. Congress passed the Kefauver-Harris Amendment to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which required drug makers to report adverse events to the FDA and, for the first time in American history, to prove ONE thing about a new medicine that had never been legally required before, on top of ordinary safety. What did the amendment newly require?
answer: proof that the drug actually works for its claimed use
choices: proof that the drug actually works for its claimed use
proof that the drug's active ingredient is chemically pure
proof that the drug does not cross the placenta
proof that informed consent was obtained in the clinical trials
context: Before 1962 a company only had to show a new drug was not obviously toxic; it did not have to show it worked at all. That is why so many outright useless remedies had been on shelves for decades. The Kefauver-Harris Amendment made EFFICACY - proof the drug does what it says - a legal prerequisite for approval, and it applied retroactively, so hundreds of grandfathered drugs were pulled from the market when they failed to demonstrate any real effect. Chemical purity was already covered under earlier FDA rules, placental transfer testing was Kelsey's specific concern but never became a general legal requirement, and formal informed-consent rules for trials came later (post-Helsinki, and the 1979 Belmont Report). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kefauver%E2%80%93Harris_Amendment.

question: The strangest coda to the thalidomide story is that the same molecule, better understood, has come back into medicine. It is now prescribed under strict pregnancy-prevention programmes for a painful complication of leprosy called erythema nodosum leprosum, and since 2006 the FDA has also approved it as a treatment for one particular blood cancer, given together with dexamethasone. Which cancer?
answer: multiple myeloma
choices: multiple myeloma
Hodgkin's lymphoma
chronic leukaemia
acute leukaemia
context: Thalidomide (with dexamethasone) received FDA approval for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma in 2006. The same cereblon-binding action that once wrecked limb-building in fetuses turns out, in adult multiple-myeloma cells, to degrade proteins those cells depend on to survive. Hodgkin's uses combination chemotherapy; chronic and acute leukaemias have their own targeted regimens (imatinib, ATRA, chemotherapy). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide.

question: A clay band no thicker than a finger cuts through the pink limestone above Gubbio, Italy. Walter Alvarez wanted to know how long it took to settle, so his father Luis Alvarez, a Nobel-winning physicist, offered to time it. What did Luis propose measuring in the clay?
answer: a metal that space dust sprinkles down steadily
choices: a metal that space dust sprinkles down steadily
a gas that seeps out of buried rock steadily
a shell layer that dead plankton leave steadily
a salt crust that drying seawater leaves steadily
context: The metal was iridium, which drifts down in cosmic dust at a slow, fairly steady trickle -- so the amount buried in a layer should say how long the layer took to form. Luis Alvarez had won the 1968 Nobel Prize for the liquid hydrogen bubble chamber and had flown observation missions over Hiroshima and Nagasaki to measure blast yields; here he was offering a physicist's clock for a geologist's problem, with no thought of what killed anything. Walter was at Gubbio in the mid-1970s working on paleomagnetic reversals, and had noticed that the limestone below the 1-2 cm clay band is crammed with the chalky shells of planktonic foraminifera while the limestone above holds almost none. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Alvarez research origins; iridium anomaly discovery); Grokipedia, 'Luis Walter Alvarez'.

question: Right above the thin clay that ends the Cretaceous, in Colorado and Utah, fern spores swamp the fossil pollen record -- as much as ninety percent of everything preserved. What landscape does that spike record?
answer: bare ground being colonised from scratch
choices: cool bog thickening into a bed of peat
bare ground being colonised from scratch
old forest closing into deep, wet shade
coastal swamp drowning under a rising sea
context: Charles Orth and colleagues reported the 'fern spike' in 1981, and it has since been documented at over 100 sites: ferns are the pioneers that move first onto scorched, emptied ground, and their spores briefly drown out everything else in the pollen record. The same 1981 study carried a second, quieter blow. Orth's iridium spike sat in rocks laid down in FRESH water, which destroyed the standing objection that seawater chemistry had somehow concentrated the metal at sea-floor boundaries. Source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (1981, Orth et al.); Grokipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Paleontological correlations).

question: Walter Alvarez sampled the Gubbio clay in 1977 and sent it to two Berkeley nuclear chemists, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel. Iridium drifts steadily down in cosmic dust, so slow settling should leave the clay a little richer in it than the limestone around it, fast settling a little poorer. What did their count come back as?
answer: about thirty times the iridium in the limestone beside it
choices: about the same iridium as in the limestone beside it
about half the iridium in the limestone beside it
about thirty times the iridium in the limestone beside it
about a thousandth of the iridium in the limestone beside it
context: The Gubbio clay ran roughly 3-9 parts per billion of iridium (peak about 9.1 ppb) against about 0.3 ppb in the limestone on either side. The answer was wrong in the most interesting possible way: no rate of settling produces that. The team then went to the chalk cliffs of Stevns Klint in Denmark and found the same spike about 160 times background, up to 29 ppb. Asaro and Michel measured it by neutron activation analysis -- dissolve away the carbonate, irradiate the residue so iridium-191 becomes radioactive iridium-192, then count its gamma emissions -- good down to about 0.001 ppb. Source: Grokipedia, 'Iridium anomaly' (discovery; initial reports); Grokipedia, 'Walter Alvarez' (neutron activation analysis).

question: Earth's crust holds almost no iridium -- a few hundredths of a part per billion -- while the meteorites left over from the same building material run about five hundred parts per billion. What happened to Earth's share while the young planet was still molten?
answer: it sank with the iron that was forming the core
choices: it boiled off with the gases that made the first air
it stayed behind in crystals deep in the mantle
it left with the rock flung out to form the Moon
it sank with the iron that was forming the core
context: Iridium is a siderophile -- an 'iron-lover'. When the young molten Earth separated and its iron sank to build the core, the iridium dissolved in that iron and went down with it, leaving the crust stripped to about 0.02-0.05 parts per billion. Asteroids never differentiated that way, so they kept theirs: carbonaceous chondrite meteorites run about 500 ppb. That single fact is what turns a chemistry reading into a detective's fingerprint. Any iridium spike sitting at Earth's surface is a visitor from outside. Source: Grokipedia, 'Iridium anomaly' (siderophile behaviour, planetary differentiation, CI chondrite abundance).

question: The 1980 paper by Luis Alvarez, Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel did more than report an oddity: it turned the oddity into a number anyone could check. All the iridium spread through boundary clays around the world came to roughly fifty thousand tonnes, and from that mass alone the four of them calculated one thing. What did fifty thousand tonnes of iridium tell them?
answer: the width of the body that fell, about ten kilometres
choices: the width of the body that fell, about ten kilometres
the depth of the sea it fell into, about four kilometres
the time the clay took to settle, about ten thousand years
the age of the boundary itself, about sixty-six million years
context: That number is what made the hypothesis dangerous to its own authors: a body roughly 10 km across leaves a crater of matching age 150-200 km wide, so such a crater had to exist somewhere on Earth and had to be findable. 'Extraterrestrial cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction' ran in Science on 6 June 1980 (vol. 208, pp. 1095-1108). A rival got there first and almost nobody remembers: the Dutch paleontologist Jan Smit, working the boundary at Caravaca in Spain, published the same conclusion independently with Jan Hertogen in Nature on 22 May 1980, two weeks earlier. The boundary's age, 66.04 million years, was measured much later and by other means. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Publication and early reception); Smit & Hertogen, Nature 285:198-200, 22 May 1980.

question: Iridium is chemistry, and chemists could argue over how a chemical gets concentrated. Harder to argue with were the quartz grains in the boundary clay: inside single crystals run several sets of dead-straight glassy lamellae, crossing one another, each a few hundred nanometres wide. Stamping them in takes shock pressure far past anything volcanoes or mountain-building supply, and geologists were not guessing what such grains look like -- they had man-made ones to compare against. Where did the reference grains come from?
answer: quartz dug out from under a buried nuclear test
choices: quartz melted in a furnace and cooled in seconds
quartz dug out from under a buried nuclear test
quartz squeezed between the tips of two diamonds
quartz fired from a gas gun into a steel plate
context: The lamellae are planar deformation features, and it takes shock above roughly 5-10 gigapascals to make them at all. The 1962 Sedan test at the Nevada Test Site -- 104 kilotons, buried -- drove pressures above 30 gigapascals and produced quartz with multiple crossing sets of planar deformation features, which became the calibration standard; the Soviet 140-kiloton Chagan test of 1965 did the same. Slow tectonic squeezing leaves a single, broader, curved set instead, and explosive volcanism generally cannot reach the pressure at all. The boundary grains matched the bomb-crater grains. When Bruce Bohor's team found shocked quartz in boundary claystone in Montana in 1984, it swayed skeptics partly for a sociological reason: Bohor's people were geologists using geologists' methods, so it did not read as outsiders lecturing the field. Source: Grokipedia, 'Shocked quartz' (planar deformation features; Sedan 1962; Chagan 1965); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (1984, Bohor).

question: The Alvarez paper had ordered up a crater of exactly the right age, and for a decade nobody produced one. The crater had in fact already been mapped: in 1978 Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo, flying magnetic surveys for the Mexican oil company Pemex, found a buried semicircle about 180 kilometres across under the Yucatan. Penfield wrote to Walter Alvarez in 1980 and got no reply. What finally put his buried structure in front of the impact scientists in 1990?
answer: a newspaper reporter told a geologist about it
choices: a satellite image of the Yucatan reached the journals
a graduate student dug out his 1981 conference talk
a newspaper reporter told a geologist about it
a new oil well cut straight through its melt rock
context: Carlos Byars of the Houston Chronicle mentioned Penfield's buried structure to the geologist Alan Hildebrand in 1990. Hildebrand and Penfield then tracked down surviving Pemex drill cores that had sat in storage in New Orleans for decades -- others had burned in a warehouse fire -- found shocked quartz and impact melt in them, and matched the chemistry to boundary tektites from Haiti; Hildebrand and William Boynton published the identification in 1991. Penfield had done everything right: Pemex held the survey data as proprietary so he could not publish it, and when he and Camargo presented the structure to the Society of Exploration Geophysicists in 1981 -- explicitly proposing it as the Alvarez crater -- the conference was under-attended and the report attracted little notice. Argon-argon dating of the crater's melt rock later gave 66.04 +/- 0.05 million years, landing exactly on the boundary. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chicxulub crater' (Initial Discovery; 1990 Critical Connection); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (1978, 1980, 1981, 1990-91); Grokipedia, 'Chicxulub crater' (Ar-Ar age).

question: Chicxulub's damage owed as much to the ground it hit as to the asteroid. Beneath the Yucatan lay three to five kilometres of limestone, and under that a bed of gypsum and anhydrite -- sulfur-rich rock left behind where ancient seas dried out -- some three hundred to eight hundred metres thick. When drillers cored the crater's peak ring in 2016, the gypsum was the surprise: in the shattered rock there was almost none of it left. Where had it gone?
answer: vaporised outright and flung into the high atmosphere
choices: dissolved away by the seawater that poured back in
pushed far downwards as the crater floor rebounded
melted and refrozen into the glass sheets below
vaporised outright and flung into the high atmosphere
context: The gypsum went up as sulfate aerosol, injected into the stratosphere, where it blocks sunlight far more effectively than dust. This is the asteroid's geological bad luck: had the same rock struck sulfate-poor crystalline bedrock, the chemistry of the aftermath would have been far less lethal. The near-complete absence of gypsum in the peak-ring cores is the physical evidence that it was vaporised rather than merely buried or melted. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chicxulub crater' (Pre-Impact Target Rocks); Wikipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (2016 cores, near-complete absence of gypsum).

question: In 2016 Expedition 364 drilled 1,334 metres below the seabed into the ring of hills at the centre of the buried Chicxulub crater, thirty kilometres off the Yucatan coast, and recovered 829 metres of core. The rock in that peak ring was granite -- continental basement that normally sits some ten kilometres down -- and it had been hoisted to the surface within minutes of the impact. What lets a mountain's worth of granite move like a fluid for those few minutes?
answer: shaking briefly cancels the friction inside the rock
choices: shaking briefly cancels the friction inside the rock
heat from the impact melts it into a thick liquid
pressure turns its quartz into a slippery glass
water boiling in its cracks floats the grains apart
context: The mechanism is called acoustic fluidization: seismic shaking temporarily cancels the internal friction that holds broken rock rigid, so for a few minutes a mountain's worth of granite behaves like a fluid, rises about 10 km, and slumps into a ring. Borehole M0077A reached 1,334.7 m below the sea floor with over 99 percent core recovery. Directly above the peak ring the cores held the largest known graded sand layer on Earth -- a megatsunami deposit dropped within hours as the ocean poured back into the hole; modelling puts rim waves near the crater above 1.5 km high, with run-ups of 100-300 m recorded onshore in Texas and Alabama. Source: Grokipedia, 'Peak ring' (Expedition 364; acoustic fluidization); Wikipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (granite peak ring; graded sand layer).

question: Before the iridium, the leading explanation of the great extinction was astronomical but not an impact: in 1971 Dale Russell and Wallace Tucker proposed that a nearby star had exploded, and as late as 1979 Russell judged a supernova the only viable candidate. It made its own checkable promise -- an exploding star forges short-lived isotopes such as plutonium-244 and iron-60, and those would still be sitting in the boundary clay today. What did the search of the clay turn up?
answer: none of those isotopes, at any boundary site
choices: iron-60, in amounts far above the prediction
none of those isotopes, at any boundary site
both isotopes, but only in deep-sea cores
plutonium-244 alone, and only in Denmark
context: No excess plutonium-244 or iron-60 has been detected at the boundary, and modelled iridium yields from a supernova at 10-20 parsecs fall orders of magnitude short of the 10-100 nanograms per square centimetre actually measured. The supernova idea died the honourable way -- on a test it had proposed for itself. Notice what the impact hypothesis then survived that it did not choose: the same spike, at the same stratigraphic level, is now confirmed at over 350 sections worldwide, from Hell Creek in Montana to China's Nanxiong Basin to Seymour Island in Antarctica. The boundary clay carries other independent markers too: nickel-rich spinels, glass spherules, soot from global fires, and an osmium ratio far off the crustal value. In 2024, ruthenium isotopes identified the impactor as a carbonaceous asteroid formed beyond Jupiter's orbit. Source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event research' (Russell & Tucker 1971; Russell 1979); Grokipedia, 'Iridium anomaly' (no short-lived radionuclides; global confirmations; 2024 ruthenium result).

question: The Chicxulub impact never had the field to itself. In west-central India the Deccan Traps were erupting one to two million cubic kilometres of lava across the same stretch of time, and Gerta Keller and others have argued for decades that the volcanoes, not the asteroid, did the main killing; her team's uranium-lead dates put the biggest pulses within about 250,000 years of the boundary. At Berkeley, Mark Richards and Paul Renne put forward a third position -- with Walter Alvarez himself on the team. What do they argue?
answer: the impact's shaking set off the largest Deccan eruptions
choices: the impact's dust smothered the eruptions for a century
the impact and the eruptions had a single deeper cause
the impact's shaking set off the largest Deccan eruptions
the eruptions weakened the crust the asteroid then struck
context: Richards, Renne and colleagues (2015) argue that seismic shaking from the impact -- felt 13,000 km away -- triggered the largest phase of Deccan eruptions 50,000 to 100,000 years later, and that the continuing volcanism is why marine ecosystems took so long to recover. Walter Alvarez is an active member of the team arguing that his own asteroid had an accomplice. The rival case is real science, not crankery: the geologist Dewey McLean proposed volcanism as the killer in 1978, two years before the Alvarez paper, and Keller calculates 7-9 degrees C of ocean warming during the biggest pulse. In 2010 Science published a review by 41 authors coming down firmly for the impact and ruling out massive volcanism -- and dozens of other scientists challenged its methods and its conclusions. The dispute is bitter enough to have earned a nickname, the 'dinosaur wars'. The argument has narrowed a great deal. It has not closed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alvarez hypothesis' (Alternative theories; Richards et al. 2015 GSA Bulletin; Schulte et al., Science 327:1214-1218, 5 March 2010); Grokipedia, 'Deccan Traps'; Grokipedia, 'Gerta Keller'.

question: There is one reaction in nature that spends matter entirely: bring an electron together with its opposite-charge twin, and both particles vanish -- no ash, no fragments, only light. Which kind of light photons carry the energy away?
answer: gamma rays
choices: gamma rays
radio waves
visible light
microwaves
context: Electron + positron annihilation produces two gamma-ray photons, each about 511 keV -- the tightest E = m c-squared demonstration nature offers. Source: home.cern/science/physics/antimatter.

question: In 1928 a young British physicist wrote an equation for the electron that had a second solution he could not delete: it required a partner particle with the OPPOSITE electric charge -- an antimatter twin that no experiment had ever seen. Who was he?
answer: Paul Dirac
choices: Paul Dirac
Niels Bohr
Max Planck
Erwin Schrodinger
context: Dirac was 25; the positron he predicted was found four years later. Source: ebsco.com/research-starters/physics/dirac-equation.

question: On 2 August 1932 Carl Anderson at Caltech was photographing tracks in a cloud chamber and caught one particle curving the wrong way in a magnetic field -- the first sighting of Dirac's predicted positive electron. Which natural source produced the particle that made the track?
answer: cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere
choices: cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere
the Sun's ultraviolet light
a lightning strike nearby
the Earth's magnetic field
context: Anderson didn't know Dirac's paper when he saw the track; he named the particle the positron. He shared the 1936 Nobel. Source: spark.iop.org/andersons-accident.

question: The Big Bang should have made matter and antimatter in equal amounts that would annihilate into pure light, leaving no atoms at all. Yet you exist. Roughly what fraction of the original particles survived to build every atom in every star and person?
answer: about 1 in a billion
choices: about 1 in a billion
about 1 in a thousand
about half
none -- new matter appeared later
context: That one-in-a-billion excess is every atom in every star, planet and person; the photons from all that annihilation are still around as the cosmic microwave background. Source: home.cern/science/physics/matter-antimatter-asymmetry-problem.

question: In September 2023 the ALPHA-g team at CERN reported the result of a decades-long project: for the first time they released atoms of antihydrogen (an antiproton with an orbiting positron) inside a vertical magnetic bottle and watched which way they went. What did the antihydrogen do?
answer: fell downward like ordinary matter
choices: fell downward like ordinary matter
floated upward
hovered motionless
shot out horizontally
context: Antimatter's acceleration matched ordinary matter's within about 20 percent, closing off the antigravity escape route from the asymmetry problem. Source: nature.com/articles/d41586-023-03043-0.

question: Telescopes have searched the sky for annihilation borders -- glowing seams where matter and antimatter galaxies would grind against each other -- and cosmic-ray detectors have hunted for antihelium nuclei drifting in from far away. What have the searches found?
answer: no evidence of antimatter regions at all
choices: no evidence of antimatter regions at all
large antimatter clouds near the galactic center
one antimatter galaxy in Virgo
annihilation borders around every quasar
context: If the universe held equal amounts of matter and antimatter divided into regions, we would see gamma-ray borders; the sky is silent. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0211260.

question: Every symmetry test so far -- gravity in ALPHA-g, the light spectrum of antihydrogen matching hydrogen's to extraordinary precision, mass measurements of the antiproton -- says antimatter is a nearly perfect mirror of matter. What does that growing pile of matched measurements do to the puzzle of why any matter survived at all?
answer: makes it harder to explain, not easier
choices: makes it harder to explain, not easier
solves it via leptogenesis
proves the universe is symmetric after all
removes the need for Sakharov's conditions
context: The tinier the differences experiments find, the harder it is to build up even a one-in-a-billion excess. No one yet knows the answer. Source: home.cern/alpha-experiment.

question: In 1660 Robert Boyle hung a ticking pocket watch by a thread inside the glass receiver of his new air pump, and then began drawing the air out. What did the watch do as the receiver emptied?
answer: Its ticking faded to nothing
choices: Its ticking faded to nothing
It stopped running and had to be rewound
It sped up as the pressure dropped
It kept ticking as loudly as before
context: This was Experiment 27 of 'New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air, and its Effects'. The ticking returned the instant Boyle let air back in. He built the pump with the young Robert Hooke; it was the first controlled test that sound needs a medium. Source: Royal Society blog, https://royalsociety.org/blog/2024/11/making-waves/

question: When you hear a friend shout across a room, sound crosses the space between you. What is actually carrying the shout from their mouth to your ear?
answer: Patches of air squeeze and release, each pushing on the next
choices: Patches of air squeeze and release, each pushing on the next
Tiny sound particles stream out and drift into the ear
The room's walls flex outward and carry the message
Invisible waves in the ether pass across the space
context: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave: each layer of gas shoves its neighbour and springs back. That is why an empty jar goes silent (no neighbours to shove) and a rubber ball can bounce fine in a vacuum but a bell cannot ring. Source: Royal Society blog, https://royalsociety.org/blog/2024/11/making-waves/

question: Athanasius Kircher and Otto von Guericke both reported hearing bells ring inside pumped-down jars, and both had genuinely leaky pumps. But a second, hidden flaw would have fooled them even with a perfect vacuum. What was it?
answer: Their bells were bolted to the vessel, so vibration walked out through the metal
choices: Their bells were bolted to the vessel, so vibration walked out through the metal
The glass jars amplified any faint sound like a lens focuses light
Their bells were tuned too high for the human ear to catch
Their ears grew more sensitive as the jar was pumped down
context: Solid contact between the ringing body and the vessel routes sound through the walls of the container. Kircher was defeated by his own apparatus, not his reasoning; the demo only works when the source is suspended clear of the vessel and the pump seals well. Source: Museo Galileo biography, https://catalogue.museogalileo.it/biography/AthanasiusKircher.html

question: Even after his watch went silent in the receiver in 1660, Robert Boyle refused to declare the case closed. He had two honest reasons for holding back a verdict. Which pair kept him cautious?
answer: His pump still leaked, and the suspending thread might be carrying the ticking itself
choices: His pump still leaked, and the suspending thread might be carrying the ticking itself
His watch was faulty, and Hooke had not verified the setup
Kircher outranked him, and the Royal Society had not yet met
The glass distorted the sound, and no one else had a similar jar
context: Boyle wrote up the demonstration as suggestive, not decisive, and named the leak and the thread as the two loopholes. The whole story is a lesson in the Feynman rule about fooling yourself first. Source: Journal of Applied Physiology overview, https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/japplphysiol.00759.2004

question: The question of whether sound can travel through a vacuum stayed genuinely open for roughly 45 years after Boyle's 1660 demonstration. Around 1705 Francis Hauksbee finally closed it at the Royal Society. What let him settle a debate his predecessors could not?
answer: A far tighter air pump that reached a much better vacuum
choices: A far tighter air pump that reached a much better vacuum
A louder bell rung by a spring-loaded hammer
A larger glass jar that muffled outside noise
A new mathematical proof that vacuums must be silent
context: Better apparatus, not better argument, ended the debate. Hauksbee's improved double-barrelled pump reached low enough pressure that even a suspended bell went nearly silent, and he then reported that condensed (compressed) air made the same bell sound louder still. Source: Royal Society Philosophical Transactions, https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rstl/article/26/321/367/110425/II-An-account-of-an-experiment-shewing-that-actual

question: In 2003 a team led by Andrew Fabian used a 53-hour Chandra X-ray observation of the hot gas filling the Perseus galaxy cluster and found real pressure waves rippling through it, driven by the central supermassive black hole. What pitch did those waves turn out to carry?
answer: A B-flat about 57 octaves below middle C
choices: A B-flat about 57 octaves below middle C
A C-sharp near the low end of a piano keyboard
A pure tone matching a low human whisper
A pitch matching the natural note of the cluster's brightest star
context: A grand piano covers about seven octaves, so the Perseus note sits more than fifty octaves below the lowest key any piano can play, and over a million billion times deeper than the human ear can hear. The vacuum of space really is silent, but the hot cluster gas is a medium, and sound obeys the rule of a medium there too. Source: Chandra press release, https://chandra.harvard.edu/press/03_releases/press_090903.html

question: Seroprevalence surveys during 2020 lined up COVID-19's per-infection death rate against a single characteristic of the person infected: it was near zero at one end and several percent at the other. Which characteristic showed that steep gradient?
answer: age
choices: age
blood type
handedness
eye colour
context: O'Driscoll and colleagues, in Nature in early 2021, found the lowest infection fatality rate in children aged 5-9 and a log-linear rise above age 30. That is the fact the whole ladder rests on: schools were closed for the age group least at risk from the disease schools were closed for. Source: O'Driscoll et al., Nature (2021).

question: In September 2022 the United States published results from an assessment that had been measuring nine-year-olds since the early 1970s. For the first time in the entire history of that test, one subject's score went down. Which subject?
answer: mathematics
choices: mathematics
science
civics
geography
context: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) long-term trend found nine-year-olds' maths scores had fallen 7 points from 2020 to 2022 - the first-ever mathematics decline in the assessment's roughly 50-year history. Reading fell 5 points, the largest reading drop since 1990. Source: NAGB press release, 1 September 2022.

question: Bastian Betthauser and colleagues published a meta-analysis in Nature Human Behaviour on 30 January 2023 that pooled 42 pandemic learning-loss studies from 15 countries into one headline estimate. When they broke that pooled deficit down by school subject, which subject had taken the bigger hit?
answer: mathematics
choices: mathematics
reading
science
history
context: A meta-analysis is a study that pools many earlier studies to give one combined estimate on a common scale. Betthauser and colleagues screened their 42 studies from a much larger pool using inclusion rules fixed before the analysis began, and reported that pandemic-era deficits were larger in mathematics than in reading. Source: Betthauser, Bach-Mortensen and Engzell, Nature Human Behaviour, 30 January 2023.

question: The Betthauser meta-analysis reported its headline as a Cohen's d of -0.14. Cohen's d is expressed in standard deviations, a unit that lets different tests be put on one scale. Since typical schoolchildren gain about 0.4 standard deviations of achievement in a normal school year, roughly what fraction of a school year's learning does -0.14 represent?
answer: about a third
choices: about a third
about a tenth
about a full year
about two full years
context: Roughly 35% of a normal school year (0.14 / 0.4). The 95% confidence interval on the estimate ran from -0.17 to -0.10, so the honest range is roughly a quarter to two-fifths of a year - not the 'lost generation' rhetoric of the headlines, but not small either. Source: Betthauser et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023); University of Oxford SPI summary.

question: The Betthauser meta-analysis broke its overall d = -0.14 pandemic learning-loss estimate down several ways and reported the deficit was NOT spread evenly across children. Which cut showed the LARGEST deficit?
answer: children from low-income homes
choices: children from low-income homes
children in mathematics rather than reading
children in the pandemic's later months rather than its early months
children in countries with the longest school closures
context: Deficits WERE larger in mathematics than in reading, so that cut is a real finding - but the largest cut Betthauser and colleagues reported was by socio-economic background. The pandemic-learning-loss deficit also arose EARLY and then held steady rather than growing across later months, so the 'later months' cut is not where the largest loss sits. The gap the closures were often said to protect against was the one they widened most. Source: Betthauser et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023).

question: Per Engzell and colleagues (PNAS, April 2021) measured about 350,000 primary pupils in one country across an eight-week school closure and found a learning loss roughly the size of the closure itself. They picked that country as a best-case test: high broadband, equitable schools, a short closure. Which country?
answer: the Netherlands
choices: the Netherlands
South Korea
Finland
Singapore
context: The Dutch primary system re-tested pupils on national exams before and after the eight-week 2020 closure, giving something rare in pandemic research: a genuine before/after measurement on the same test in the same country. Even so, pupils lost about a fifth of a normal school year, with losses up to 55% larger among children from less-educated homes. Source: Engzell, Frey and Verhagen, PNAS (2021).

question: One European country kept its primary schools open through the whole pandemic. In a study of 97,073 grade-1-to-3 pupils, its published reading assessments showed no measurable decline compared with pre-pandemic scores. Which country?
answer: Sweden
choices: Sweden
France
Germany
Italy
context: Sweden was a rich, well-schooled European country running a school policy nearly opposite to most of its neighbours through the pandemic. The paper also noted very low rates of severe COVID-19 in Swedish preschoolers and primary pupils across the same period. Source: Hallin et al., 'No learning loss in Sweden during the pandemic' (2022).

question: A WHO scientific brief released on 2 March 2022 attached a single headline estimate to the pandemic's mental-health toll - a 25% rise in global prevalence of anxiety and depression in the pandemic's first year - and named the two groups on whom it fell disproportionately hardest. Which two groups?
answer: young people and women
choices: young people and women
the elderly and men
healthcare workers and teachers
urban residents and children under five
context: The brief also warned that mental-health services expanded far more slowly than need. The bank cites the WHO's own headline figure and its own named groups; a critical reader should note the wide uncertainty in a global first-year prevalence estimate and the difficulty of disentangling closures from disease and disruption. Source: WHO scientific brief, 2 March 2022.

question: The Betthauser meta-analysis reported the SHAPE of the pandemic learning deficit as well as its size, and the shape matters for what closures cost. Which of these best describes what the deficit did over time?
answer: appeared early and then held steady
choices: appeared early and then held steady
grew steadily each pandemic month
vanished within one school year
reversed once schools reopened
context: Children hit a step down and then resumed the normal rate of learning from a lower baseline, rather than falling further behind each week. That shape is consistent with the Dutch finding that loss scaled roughly with time out of school. It also means catch-up is possible in principle but not automatic; nothing in the data shows the deficit closing on its own. Source: Betthauser et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023).

question: A pandemic-era meta-analysis of school outcomes cannot by itself separate one thing from another: it measures the pandemic, not policy in isolation, because illness, fear and family disruption were all in the mix. Which of these real-world comparisons does the CLEANEST causal work of separating school policy from the pandemic itself?
answer: Sweden's open primary schools vs its neighbours' closed ones
choices: Sweden's open primary schools vs its neighbours' closed ones
US states that reopened in autumn 2020 vs states that stayed remote
Nordic countries vs Mediterranean countries generally
private schools vs public schools within the US
context: Sweden kept its primary schools open through the entire pandemic while nearby countries closed theirs, giving a long, consistent policy contrast between culturally similar rich European nations. US-state reopening dates shifted mid-pandemic and were confounded with local politics; Nordic-vs-Mediterranean comparisons drag in enormous cultural, demographic and health-system differences; private-vs-public schooling within the US selects heavily on family background. Sweden's flat primary-reading line, set against the closed-school deficits measured across 15 countries in the Betthauser meta-analysis, is what lets a careful reader attribute the international loss largely to time out of school rather than to the virus itself. Source: Betthauser et al. (2023); Hallin et al. (2022).

question: On 2 December 2022, weeks after buying the social-media company, Elon Musk began handing its internal emails and Slack messages to outside journalists -- Matt Taibbi first, then Bari Weiss and Michael Shellenberger. The disclosures became known by one collective name. What was it?
answer: The Twitter Files
choices: The Twitter Files
The Panama Papers
The Pentagon Papers
The Facebook Files
context: Musk let the journalists publish what they found on the platform itself, forcing the story into the same feeds whose posts the internal tools had been shaping. The Facebook Files (a 2021 Wall Street Journal series) and the earlier Panama and Pentagon papers were all real disclosures -- knowing WHICH is the point.

question: One name Weiss's thread singled out was a Stanford professor whose account had been placed on a 'Trends Blacklist' after he argued that COVID lockdowns would harm children. The professor was not banned. His follower count stayed exactly the same -- he simply became quietly harder to find. Who was he?
answer: Jay Bhattacharya
choices: Jay Bhattacharya
Scott Atlas
John Ioannidis
Vinay Prasad
context: Bhattacharya had co-authored the Great Barrington Declaration in October 2020. The three distractors -- Atlas, Ioannidis and Prasad -- were all real Stanford or Stanford-adjacent COVID commentators, so knowing which one Weiss actually named is the point.

question: An internal message quoted in Weiss's thread, from one of the company's own engineers, described the machinery in a single sentence. He said the company controlled visibility and amplification 'quite a bit' -- and closed with what admission about ordinary users?
answer: They do not know how much we do
choices: They do not know how much we do
They can appeal any decision
They can buy their way to the top
They set their own reach limits
context: Verbatim: 'We control visibility quite a bit. And we control the amplification of your content quite a bit. And normal people do not know how much we do.' That admission is what turned 'shadow-banning is a conspiracy theory' into 'shadow-banning is a workflow'.

question: On 5 May 2022 the attorneys general of two U.S. states filed the lawsuit that would eventually produce most of the White House emails through pre-trial discovery. The suit began under the name of one state's attorney general and was met in court by the federal government. Which two states brought the case?
answer: Missouri and Louisiana
choices: Missouri and Louisiana
Texas and Florida
Ohio and Kentucky
Arizona and Georgia
context: The case ran first as Missouri v. Biden and later as Murthy v. Missouri when it reached the Supreme Court. In discovery, emails from White House digital-strategy director Rob Flaherty pressing Facebook and Twitter for takedowns first became public.

question: In 1963 a Rhode Island commission sent bookstores warning letters listing 'objectionable' titles -- no arrests, no statute, just letters on official stationery. In Bantam Books v. Sullivan the Supreme Court still struck the practice down as unconstitutional censorship. The First Amendment has a specific one-word name for this kind of unlegislated pressure a government puts on a private party. What is it?
answer: Jawboning
choices: Jawboning
Filibustering
Redlining
Gerrymandering
context: Bantam Books is the 1963 precedent the 2022-24 social-media cases turned on: a government need not pass a statute to violate the First Amendment -- an official threat is enough. The word 'jawboning' names exactly that pressure.

question: On 4 July 2023 Federal District Judge Terry A. Doughty issued a sweeping preliminary injunction against most of the Biden administration in Missouri v. Biden. His ruling called the case, in one striking phrase, arguably the most massive attack against WHAT in United States history?
answer: Free speech
choices: Free speech
Public health
Election integrity
Presidential authority
context: Doughty also wrote that the government 'seems to have assumed a role similar to an Orwellian Ministry of Truth'. These are the district court's own words -- attribute them to the ruling, not to the bank. The injunction blocked most of the administration from contacting social-media platforms about constitutionally protected speech.

question: On 26 June 2024 the Supreme Court decided Murthy v. Missouri 6-3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett's majority did NOT rule on whether the government had censored anyone. The Court disposed of the case on a threshold doctrine -- and Justice Alito, joined by Thomas and Gorsuch, dissented, calling the record a coordinated campaign. On which threshold doctrine did the majority decide the case?
answer: Standing
choices: Standing
Sovereign immunity
Mootness
Res judicata
context: Article III standing requires a plaintiff to show a concrete injury the court can redress. Barrett's opinion held the plaintiffs could not tie particular takedowns to particular government demands, so the courts had no injury to remedy -- the underlying record was not disputed, the case simply never reached the merits. Alito warned the ruling would 'be seen by some as giving the Government a green light to use heavy-handed tactics to skew the presentation of views'.

question: Thomas Young, a London physician lecturing at the Royal Institution, let a sunbeam in through a small hole and then split the thin beam with a slip of card less than a millimeter wide. He looked at what landed on the far side. What did he see?
answer: Alternating bands of light and darkness
choices: Alternating bands of light and darkness
A single bright stripe with crisp edges
Two beams bending back toward the card
A perfect circle of light with a dark rim
context: Two pieces of light overlapping to make DARKNESS is the one thing a stream of particles cannot do, and that is why the card-split sunbeam mattered. Young had stated the rule himself in 1802: the general law 'may be very easily deduced from the interference of two coincident undulations, which either cooperate, or destroy each other.' ACCURACY NOTE: what Young is documented as doing is this card-split beam plus a water ripple tank (a candle under a glass tank, viewed in a mirror tilted overhead). Wikipedia says flatly that 'it is not clear which experiments Young performed and which ones he described as thought experiments' -- the pristine 'double slit' of the textbooks is partly later tidying-up. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%27s_interference_experiment; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Young_(scientist)

question: Augustin-Jean Fresnel was a government road engineer building an imperial highway toward Italy when Napoleon escaped from Elba in 1815. Fresnel called the return 'an attack on civilization', quit his post to join the royalist resistance, and the highway corps suspended him. How did he spend the suspension?
answer: Running optical experiments at his mother's house
choices: Running optical experiments at his mother's house
Drilling with royalist volunteers near his old post
Surveying a valley road for a private client
Reading law in Paris until his reinstatement
context: The man who overturned Newton's optics was not a professor. Fresnel served in the Corps des Ponts et Chaussees and had been posted to Nyons in the Drome; the suspension sent him home to Mathieu, where he worked on light. Three years later he beat the Academy of Sciences at its own game. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin-Jean_Fresnel

question: Augustin-Jean Fresnel had designed a lighthouse lens built from rings of separate glass prisms, and the commission that would pay for it wanted proof. On 20 August 1822 he assembled a rotating eight-panel apparatus in the middle of Paris and lit it for observers standing 32 km outside the city. Where did he mount it?
answer: On the top of the Arc de Triomphe
choices: On the top of the Arc de Triomphe
On the north tower of Notre-Dame
On the great dome of the Pantheon
On the roof of the Louvre palace
context: A claim anyone can check beats a claim you must take on trust. Fresnel did not argue the commission into the stepped lens -- on 20 August 1822 he mounted a rotating eight-panel apparatus on the Arc de Triomphe and had it judged by observers standing 32 km outside Paris, with their own eyes. The first lens went into a lighthouse the following year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel_lens

question: Thomas Young told his 1803 audience that his experiments 'may be repeated with great ease, whenever the sun shines, and without any other apparatus than is at hand to every one.' He was right: you can watch light interfere using nothing but your hand and a lamp. What do you do?
answer: Look through the gap between two almost-touching fingers
choices: Look through the gap between two almost-touching fingers
Look past the edge of one fingertip held close to the eye
Look through a fist closed loosely to leave a pinhole
Look through your fingers spread wide across the lamp
context: Hold two fingers close to one eye with a gap of about a millimeter between them and look at a bright window or lamp -- NEVER at the sun. Dark lines appear in the gap, running parallel to your fingers: those are diffraction fringes, light canceling light. No apparatus, no laboratory, no permission needed -- exactly the claim Young made to his audience in 1803, and you can settle it yourself in about ten seconds. Source: physicslens.com/single-slit-diffraction-using-fingers/

question: Simeon Denis Poisson judged the Paris Academy's 1819 prize with a Newtonian's certainty that light is a stream of particles. To finish off Fresnel's rival wave theory, he worked through Fresnel's own equations hunting for a consequence absurd enough to discredit them -- and found one he thought was self-evident nonsense. What did Fresnel's mathematics demand?
