answer: A small round disc must show a bright spot in the center of its shadow
choices: A small round disc must show a bright spot in the center of its shadow
A straight razor's edge must cast a shadow with no boundary at all
A candle seen through a pinhole must appear as two separate flames
A beam crossing a second beam must be pushed sideways out of its line
context: Poisson meant it as a reductio ad absurdum -- a knockout blow, not a discovery. Fresnel's mathematics said the middle of the shadow would be 'illuminated as brightly as the exterior', as if the disc were not there at all. Physics World renders Poisson's reaction as: 'Obvious nonsense!' Arago tested it, the spot was sitting exactly where Poisson had said it could not be, and Fresnel won the prize. The spot has carried Poisson's name ever since -- named for the man who invented it to destroy the theory it went on to prove. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel%27s_physical_optics; physicsworld.com/a/the-spot-in-the-shadow/

question: Thomas Young published his work on interference in 1802 and 1803, and from January 1803 an anonymous writer in the Edinburgh Review -- Henry Brougham, one of the journal's founders -- savaged it as 'destitute of every species of merit'. What did the attacks do to Young's optics?
answer: His publisher dropped the lectures and Young turned to medicine
choices: His publisher dropped the lectures and Young turned to medicine
The Royal Society refused to print his next Bakerian lecture
The Royal Institution canceled the rest of his lecture course
Young answered in print and the Review dropped the campaign
context: Brougham attacked anonymously, and the smear worked: the publisher who had agreed to print Young's Royal Institution lectures backed out, Young redirected himself toward medicine and later the Rosetta Stone, and the wave theory was 'generally ignored for more than a decade' until Fresnel and Arago revived it. English loyalty to Newton was part of the hostility. Young was no lightweight -- he had learned eleven languages by the age of fourteen, became physician to St George's Hospital in 1811, and by 1814 had worked through 86 demotic words of the Rosetta Stone, groundwork Champollion later built on. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%27s_interference_experiment; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Young_(scientist)

question: The word 'diffraction' was coined by neither Young nor Fresnel. Francesco Maria Grimaldi published it in 1665, after showing that light through a small hole spreads wider than straight lines allow, with colored fringes along the edges of shadows. He had the effect and the name a century and a half early. What did Grimaldi take light to be?
answer: A very fine fluid, undulating like ripples in water
choices: A very fine fluid, undulating like ripples in water
A stream of hard particles, as Isaac Newton later argued
A pressure wave running through the air, like sound
A flow of heat, the same substance that warms a room
context: Grimaldi's 'Physico-Mathesis de Lumine, Coloribus, et Iride' (1665) gave the effect its name and showed it plainly -- but he read light as a substance, a fine fluid, with color arising from undulations inside it. Seeing an effect is not the same as having the theory that makes the effect mean something. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Maria_Grimaldi

question: Fresnel's wave mathematics puts a bright spot in the dead center of a round disc's shadow, and the roundness is doing real work: one geometrical property of the disc's circular rim is why the light grazing the edge piles up at that single point instead of canceling. What property?
answer: Every point on the rim lies the same distance from the shadow's center
choices: Every point on the rim lies the same distance from the shadow's center
Every point on the rim aims its light straight at the shadow's center
Every point on the rim bends its grazing light by the same fixed angle
Every point on the rim has a twin directly opposite across the center
context: Because every point on the circumference is the same distance from the center of the shadow, light passing close by the edge all the way around travels exactly the same distance and arrives IN PHASE -- crest lining up with crest -- so it adds instead of canceling. That is also why the edge has to be smooth: rough corrugations on the rim smear the spot away, and they should stay under about 10% of the width of the neighboring Fresnel zone (roughly 77 micrometers for a 4 mm disc in the standard setup) or the contributions stop arriving together. You can see the spot for yourself: aim a laser pointer at a small ball bearing and a bright dot appears dead center in the ball's shadow. Physicists have since produced the same bright dot using beams of electrons and of neutral deuterium molecules. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arago_spot; web.physics.ucsb.edu/~lecturedemonstrations/Composer/Pages/84.12.html; Reisinger et al., 'Poisson's spot with molecules', Phys. Rev. A 79, 053823 (2009)

question: A century before the Paris Academy's 1819 prize for explaining diffraction, the bright point at the center of a small ball's shadow had already been seen and printed. Joseph-Nicolas Delisle reported it in 1715 and Giacomo Filippo Maraldi in 1723, both describing bright and dark rings around it. The reports sat in the journals for a hundred years and started no argument at all. Why not?
answer: Neither man had a theory of light that the bright point could test
choices: Neither man had a theory of light that the bright point could test
Both men blamed a flaw in the glass of their own telescope lenses
Newton's particle theory already explained it, so no one was startled
Maraldi's measurements contradicted Delisle's, and both were set aside
context: Arago himself pointed out the priority afterwards. This is the honest footnote to the whole story: an observation can be correct, published, and repeated, and still count for nothing for a century, because nobody yet has a framework that makes it a test of anything. Data alone does not decide; data plus a theory that could have come out wrong does. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arago_spot; grokipedia.com/page/Arago_spot

question: Fresnel's waves explained polarization only if light wobbles sideways to its direction of travel -- a transverse wave, shaking side to side as it moves forward. That put a hard demand on the ether, the invisible medium then believed to fill all of space and carry light. What did the ether have to be?
answer: As rigid as a solid, though the planets sailed through it untouched
choices: As rigid as a solid, though the planets sailed through it untouched
As thin as the finest gas, yet far stiffer close to the Sun
Two fluids intermingled, one carrying light and one carrying heat
Electrically charged throughout, though matter felt no force from it
context: Transverse waves cannot travel through an ordinary fluid -- they need a medium that resists being sheared sideways -- so the ether had to be stiff like a solid AND completely unobstructive to the planets at the same time. Nearly everyone found the picture repellent, and they were right to: the ether was abandoned about seventy years later. The predictions were still correct. A correct theory can ride for decades on a mental image that turns out to be wrong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin-Jean_Fresnel

question: Fresnel's waves won so completely that light looked settled for most of a century -- until Albert Einstein's 1905 paper on the photoelectric effect, in which light falling on a metal knocks electrons out of it. On the wave picture the whole story was brightness: pour more light in, and each electron should come flying out with more energy. The experiments said otherwise. What did an electron's energy actually track?
answer: The color of the light alone, from deep red through to violet
choices: The color of the light alone, from deep red through to violet
The time the light had been shining on the metal beforehand
The temperature of the metal rather than anything about the light
The angle at which the beam struck the metal's polished surface
context: Color is frequency, and Einstein's 1905 argument was that light arrives in discrete packets of energy E = h x nu, proportional to frequency. Brightness turned out to set only how MANY electrons came out, not how hard each one was kicked: below a threshold color no amount of brightness helps, and above it even a dim light works instantly. Particles came back into the story and the argument Fresnel seemed to have closed reopened. That is the honest ending: the wave victory was real and earned, and it was not the last word. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers; grokipedia.com/page/History_of_quantum_mechanics

question: Fresnel's practical monument was the stepped lens. In July 1823 the first one was lit at the Cordouan lighthouse, replacing twelve big polished parabolic reflectors that had lit that tower since 1791. Fresnel's argument against those reflectors was blunt. What was wrong with them?
answer: Their mirrors never got half the light out of the tower
choices: Their mirrors never got half the light out of the tower
Their twelve frames were too heavy for the tower to turn
Their polished faces dulled within weeks in the salt air
Their beam spread so wide it faded within a few miles
context: A lens bends light where the light crosses its surface; the thick body of glass behind that surface is dead weight. Fresnel kept the surface and threw the bulk away -- his 1820 prototype panel was a square 55 cm on a side built from 97 separate polygonal prisms. The Cordouan lens was visible more than 32 km out to sea. The same idea now sits in overhead projectors, car headlamps and traffic lights. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresnel_lens; cordouan.culture.gouv.fr/en/cordouans-first-lens

question: A radiocarbon lab will cheerfully date a mammoth tusk from Siberian permafrost. Send it a Tyrannosaurus bone from a 66-million-year-old bed and nobody will open the box. The bone is genuine. Why will no lab radiocarbon-date a dinosaur?
answer: Its carbon-14 ran out long ago, leaving none to count.
choices: Dinosaurs never took carbon-14 into their bones.
Its carbon-14 ran out long ago, leaving none to count.
Deep burial sped its carbon-14 decay past reading.
No counter can separate its carbon from the rock.
context: Carbon-14 halves away every 5,730 years, and radiocarbon runs out of signal at roughly 50,000 to 60,000 years, where so little is left that it sinks toward the detection limit. A 66-million-year-old bone sits about 11,500 half-lives past that wall, so there is nothing left to count -- which is a statement about the clock, not a hint that the bone is fake. The mammoth is well inside the window; the dinosaur is not remotely close. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: A wooden bowl, a linen shirt and a deer-bone needle come out of the same dry cave, and a lab can radiocarbon-date all three. In each one, the carbon-14 still left inside measures the time since one particular moment. Which moment?
answer: When the tree, flax and deer died.
choices: When a craftsman shaped each object.
When the tree, flax and deer sprouted.
When the tree, flax and deer died.
When each object was buried in the cave.
context: A living plant keeps swapping carbon with the air and animals keep eating the plants, so everything alive carries roughly the same carbon-14 fraction as the atmosphere. Only when the organism dies does that exchange stop, and the carbon-14 begins to run down with nothing replacing it. A radiocarbon age is therefore the time since the sample ceased exchanging carbon with its environment -- which is why the beam of a house can date centuries older than the house. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: Carbon-14 decays away steadily, so every atom of it in the air should have vanished long ago. Yet the air you are breathing right now holds a fresh supply, remade high overhead as fast as it drains away. Which atom up there becomes carbon-14, and how?
answer: Nitrogen-14, when a neutron knocks a proton out of it.
choices: Oxygen-16, when ultraviolet sunlight splits it apart.
Argon-40, when a cosmic ray shatters it into pieces.
Carbon-12, when it absorbs two extra neutrons.
Nitrogen-14, when a neutron knocks a proton out of it.
context: The reaction is 14N + n -> 14C + p: a cosmic-ray neutron strikes a nitrogen-14 nucleus, which takes in the neutron and throws out a proton, so nitrogen becomes carbon. The loop closes at the far end -- when that carbon-14 finally decays it emits an electron and an antineutrino and turns straight back into nitrogen-14. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: Willard Libby could put a date on any scrap of once-living carbon, but he had no way to make anyone believe the number. His answer became the centrepiece of his 1960 Nobel lecture: a plot of his laboratory's results against ages already established by completely separate evidence. What did he run through his counters to build it?
answer: Egyptian tomb timber and rings from a felled sequoia.
choices: Bank notes and newsprint printed with their own years.
Egyptian tomb timber and rings from a felled sequoia.
Deep-sea mud and lake clay with their layers counted.
Whale bone and driftwood taken from dated shipwrecks.
context: Libby called the plot the 'Curve of Knowns'. Timber from the tomb of the pharaoh Zoser came back at about 2800 BCE +/- 250, against the Egyptologists' settled 2625 +/- 75; the tree rings came from the 'Centennial Stump', a giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) from California's Sierra Nevada. Even the paper title was the argument -- Libby and James Arnold, 'Age Determinations by Radiocarbon Content: Checks with Samples of Known Age', Science, December 1949. A clock earns trust by first retelling a story you already know. The first dedicated radiocarbon laboratory opened at the University of Chicago in 1949; the Nobel Prize in Chemistry followed in 1960. Sources: Pearson et al., 'Dendrochronology and Radiocarbon Dating', Radiocarbon (Cambridge University Press); Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating'.

question: Every living thing on Earth is faintly radioactive: carbon-14 is decaying inside it right now. Willard Libby built his whole method on counting those decays, so his laboratory burned each sample down to pure carbon and sat it in front of a counter. Take one gram of modern carbon, a pinch the size of a pencil lead. How fast does it tick?
answer: About fourteen times a minute.
choices: About fourteen times a second.
About fourteen times a minute.
About fourteen thousand times a minute.
About fourteen million times a minute.
context: Roughly 14 disintegrations per minute per gram of modern carbon (13.5 dpm/g in later measurements) -- about one decay every four seconds in a pinch of carbon the size of a pencil lead. An anti-coincidence circuit rings a second detector around the first: anything that trips both at once arrived from outside and is thrown away, leaving only the whisper from the sample itself. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: The oldest bristlecone pines alive are about 4,000 years old -- nowhere near enough to calibrate radiocarbon back toward the last ice age. Yet the oak-and-pine chronology assembled at Hohenheim in central Europe now runs 12,460 years, every single ring pinned to its own calendar year, with no living tree anywhere near that age. How was the sequence pushed back that far?
answer: Overlapping ring patterns chained dead logs onto living trees.
choices: Radiocarbon dates on each log fixed its place in the sequence.
Growth-rate formulas restored the rings each log had lost.
Overlapping ring patterns chained dead logs onto living trees.
Peat layers buried above each log were counted down to it.
context: Crossdating is the trick. A run of fat and thin rings is a barcode that wet decades and droughts stamp on every tree in a region, so a dead log's pattern can be locked onto the overlapping years of a younger log, and that one onto a living tree -- no radiocarbon involved at any step, which is exactly what keeps the calibration from being circular. Hohenheim's oak and pine sequence reaches 12,460 years (Friedrich et al. 2004); bristlecone pine (Pinus longaeva) chronologies from California's White Mountains run past 8,800 years. Measure the carbon-14 in each calendar-dated ring and you have built the calibration curve. The modern curve, IntCal20, spans 55,000 years, its most precise stretch -- about the last 13,900 years -- resting directly on tree rings, with lake varves, uranium-thorium-dated corals and speleothems carrying it deeper. Sharpest of all are the solar spikes: a storm in AD 774-775 punched about 12 per mil of extra carbon-14 into the air in one or two years, visible in tree rings on every continent, and a second spike hit in 993. In 2021 Kuitems, Dee and colleagues found the 993 ring in Norse-cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, counted 28 rings out to the bark, and got a felling year of AD 1021 -- three separate trees agreeing. Sources: Pearson et al., 'Dendrochronology and Radiocarbon Dating', Radiocarbon (Cambridge UP); Grokipedia, 'Dendrochronology'; Kuitems et al., Nature (2021).

question: In 1977 teams at the University of Rochester and McMaster University demonstrated a new way of doing radiocarbon, and it changed what a museum is willing to sacrifice: a date that once ate a lump of pure carbon can now be had from one flax seed, a single thread pulled from a robe, or a fleck of charcoal weighing under a milligram. What do the new machines do that the old counters could not?
answer: They count individual carbon-14 atoms inside an accelerator.
choices: They run each sample for months to gather far more decays.
They concentrate the carbon-14 chemically before counting.
They chill the counters to near absolute zero to kill background.
They count individual carbon-14 atoms inside an accelerator.
context: Beta counting waits for atoms to decay, and with a half-life of 5,730 years almost none of them oblige while you watch. Accelerator mass spectrometry ignores decay altogether: it accelerates the sample's ions and sorts them by mass, so the carbon-14 atoms are counted one at a time. That drops the sample needed from tens of grams to under a milligram, which is why a single seed, a thread or a scraping of pigment can now carry a date. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating' and 'Radiocarbon dating'.

question: To date a rock by uranium turning into lead, you must know how much lead the rock started with -- and usually you cannot. So geologists reach past the whole rock for one tough little crystal, zircon, which survives erosion, burial and even re-melting. What does a growing zircon crystal do that makes it such an honest clock?
answer: It takes uranium into its lattice but shuts lead out.
choices: It takes in uranium and lead in a fixed, known ratio.
It takes uranium into its lattice but shuts lead out.
It takes in only lead-204, never lead made by decay.
It takes in uranium and vents lead each time it reheats.
context: It is a size-and-charge mismatch. In zircon (ZrSiO4) a uranium-4+ ion of radius 1.05 angstrom can slip into a zirconium-4+ site of 0.87 angstrom, but lead-2+ is shut out: too big at 1.32 angstrom and carrying the wrong charge. A fresh zircon therefore starts with essentially no lead at all, so every lead atom found inside it had to be manufactured there by decay. The crystal starts its own clock at zero, and holds it up to a closure temperature near 900 C. Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Importance of zircon in uranium-lead dating'; Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating'.

question: Every radiocarbon laboratory on Earth knows Willard Libby's original figure for the half-life of carbon-14 -- the time for half of any amount of it to decay away -- was wrong. He measured 5,568 years; the accepted value is 5,730. Raw ages are still calculated today with the wrong number, then corrected against a calibration curve built from calendar-dated tree rings. Why not simply switch to the right figure?
answer: Because a date published in 1955 must still mean the same as one published now.
choices: Because switching would change every date by well over a thousand years.
Because the counters in every laboratory were built around his number.
Because a date published in 1955 must still mean the same as one published now.
Because the older figure gives ages that agree better with tree rings.
context: The Libby half-life of 5,568 +/- 30 years is retained by convention -- the constant 8033 in the age formula is simply 5568/ln2 -- rather than silently rewriting every age published before the correction. The genuine correction, which is larger than the half-life error anyway, is made openly at the calibration step. Radiocarbon dates are calibrated, not apologised for; the true Cambridge half-life is 5,730 +/- 40 years. The method also names its own blind spots. The Hallstatt plateau, roughly 800 to 400 BCE, is a flat stretch of the curve where a single date can be ambiguous by up to 400 calendar years, which genuinely muddles Iron Age chronology; and the marine reservoir effect makes ocean shells date about 400 years too old worldwide, because upwelling water carries carbon that has been out of contact with the air for centuries -- in hard-water lakes the offset can reach 2,000 to 2,700 years. Source: Grokipedia, 'Radiocarbon dating' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Radiocarbon_dating).

question: The Jack Hills of Western Australia have given up the oldest dated piece of this planet, and it is not a rock: a zircon grain a couple of hundred micrometres across -- about two hairs' width -- picked out of a conglomerate at Erawondoo Hill and dated in 2001 to 4,404 million years, older than any rock that survives anywhere. Locked in the same grain is a second reading, the ratio of its oxygen isotopes (the same element in two slightly different weights), which records the magma the crystal grew in. What did that ratio say about the infant Earth?
answer: That the magma had already met liquid water near the surface.
choices: That the crust was still a worldwide ocean of molten rock.
That the magma had already met liquid water near the surface.
That the magma had been re-melted by a giant impact.
That the magma rose from far deeper than any magma today.
context: The grain's delta-18O of 8.5 to 9.5 per mil is heavier than mantle magma, the signature of rock that had been weathered by liquid water before being melted -- evidence for water at Earth's surface 4.4 billion years ago, within roughly 150 million years of the planet forming. Hadean grains older than 4.0 billion years make up as much as 12% of the Jack Hills zircon population. The site is now treated like a monument: Erawondoo Hill joined Australia's National Heritage List on 30 June 2020, and on 28 October 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences named 'the Archean Zircons of Erawondoo Hill' one of the First 100 Geological Heritage Sites in the world. Source: Grokipedia, 'Jack Hills' (https://grokipedia.com/page/Jack_Hills).

question: The obvious objection to deep time is that a rock spends aeons under crushing pressure and searing heat, with chemistry going on around it the whole while -- surely that must speed a decay clock up or slow it down. Laboratories have pushed decay rates from -255 C to 1350 C, to pressures near 2,000 atmospheres, and into magnetic fields of 8.3 tesla, and measured no change at all. What is the physical reason the rate is so hard to touch?
answer: Decay happens in the nucleus, while heat and chemistry move electrons.
choices: The crystal lattice around each atom shields it from outside conditions.
Heating speeds decay while pressure slows it, and the two cancel out.
Decay happens in the nucleus, while heat and chemistry move electrons.
Each atom's own internal heat drives its decay, and never changes.
context: The nucleus is about one hundred-thousandth the width of the atom around it, and heat, pressure and chemical bonding all act on the electron cloud far outside it. Marie Curie and Heike Kamerlingh Onnes made the point as early as 1913, chilling a radium sample to 20 kelvin and finding its decay constant unchanged to within 0.1 percent. Sources: Goodwin et al., 'Absence of low-temperature dependence of the decay of 7Be and 198Au in metallic hosts', arXiv:0805.0024; G. T. Emery, 'Perturbation of Nuclear Decay Rates', Annual Review of Nuclear Science 22 (1972) 165.

question: From the mid-1950s to 1963 the United States and the Soviet Union set off hundreds of nuclear tests in the open air, and the carbon-14 in the atmosphere climbed to roughly double its natural level before the test-ban treaty let it drain away again. Every child alive then breathed that spike, and tooth enamel is laid down in childhood and never afterwards replaced. Kirsty Spalding, Jonas Frisen and colleagues at the Karolinska Institute measured the carbon-14 in the enamel of 22 people. What did the enamel give them?
answer: The calendar year each person was born in.
choices: The dose of fallout each had breathed as a child.
The hemisphere each of them had grown up in.
The main food of each one's childhood diet.
The calendar year each person was born in.
context: Atmospheric carbon-14 peaked in 1963-65 at nearly 100 percent above normal, then drained into the ocean and biosphere after the 1963 test ban; levels are now back near pre-nuclear values. That steep, precisely dated slope is the 'bomb pulse', and because it falls fast it dates recent things far more sharply than ordinary radiocarbon can. Spalding, Frisen and colleagues published the enamel result in Nature in 2005, recovering birth years to within 1.6 years. The same trick catches poachers: Kevin Uno, Thure Cerling and colleagues (PNAS, 2016) radiocarbon-dated tusks from 14 ivory seizures made between 2002 and 2014, pinning each elephant's death to about a year -- most of the ivory proved to be under three years old, recent killing rather than old stockpile. One seizure was the exception: a large fraction was over 30 years old, matching markings showing it had come out of a government stockpile. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Bomb pulse'; Spalding et al., Nature 437, 333 (2005); Cerling, Uno et al., PNAS (2016).

question: Chemistry and environment shift the decay rate of uranium in a rock by perhaps one part in ten million, which is why no geologist loses sleep over it. Then physicists at the GSI storage ring in Darmstadt took rhenium-187 -- whose ordinary neutral atoms halve in 42 billion years, three times the age of the universe -- and stripped every last electron off them before letting them decay. What happened to its half-life?
answer: It fell from 42 billion years to about 33 years.
choices: It fell from 42 billion years to about 33 million.
It fell from 42 billion years to about 33 years.
It rose from 42 billion years to about 400 billion.
It held at about 42 billion years, unchanged.
context: Fully ionized rhenium-187 nuclei at GSI decayed with a half-life of 32.9 +/- 2.0 years -- more than nine orders of magnitude faster than the neutral atom. In beta decay the emitted electron normally has to shove out past the crowd already surrounding the nucleus; strip the atom bare and it can drop straight into an empty orbital instead, a channel called bound-state beta decay, and it matters for how rhenium behaves inside stars. There is a smaller, honest cousin worth saying out loud: electron capture uses one of the atom's own electrons, so chemistry really can nudge it. Beryllium-7 sealed inside a carbon-60 cage has a half-life of 52.68 +/- 0.05 days against 53.12 +/- 0.05 days in beryllium metal, about 0.8 percent faster. Real, measured, tiny -- and irrelevant to uranium-lead, where environmental effects on alpha decay are estimated at one part in ten million or less. A rule you can state the exceptions to is stronger than one you cannot. Sources: Bosch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. (1996), OSTI 404092; UC Riverside Physics FAQ, 'How to Change Nuclear Decay Rates'.

question: The weak spot in dating a rock is the starting line. To turn a count of the daughter isotope -- the new element the decay produces -- into an age, you must assume how much of it was already sitting there when the rock formed, and an assumption is not a measurement. So geologists stopped assuming: they take several different minerals out of the same rock and plot each one's strontium against its rubidium. What does that plot hand them that a single sample never could?
answer: A line whose intercept gives the start and whose slope gives the age.
choices: A curve whose lowest point gives the start and whose steepness gives the age.
A line whose intercept gives the start and whose slope gives the age.
A cluster whose centre gives the start and whose spread gives the age.
A band whose lower edge gives the start and whose width gives the age.
context: This is the isochron. Plot strontium-87/strontium-86 against rubidium-87/strontium-86 for several minerals from one rock: if the rock stayed a closed system the points fall on a straight line whose slope is e^(lambda*t) - 1, which gives the age, while the y-intercept is the initial strontium-87/strontium-86 the rock was born with -- measured, not assumed. And the method polices itself: scatter off the line is the warning that the sample was disturbed. Zircon runs the same audit a different way. Wetherill's concordia diagram (1956) plots lead-206/uranium-238 against lead-207/uranium-235; a grain that stayed sealed lands on the concordia curve, while a grain that leaked lead falls below it along a straight discordia line whose upper intercept still recovers the crystallization age and whose lower intercept dates the disturbance. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating'; Wikipedia, 'Isochron dating'.

question: Lucy, the Australopithecus afarensis skeleton dug out of Hadar in Ethiopia, is famously about 3.18 million years old -- and nobody has ever dated Lucy. Her bones carry no usable clock at all. The number comes from somewhere else in the landscape around her. From where?
answer: Volcanic ash layers above and below her, argon-dated.
choices: Charcoal from the layer she lay in, radiocarbon-dated.
Volcanic ash layers above and below her, argon-dated.
Zircon grains in the sandstone around her, uranium-lead dated.
Minerals from the rock beneath her, rubidium-strontium dated.
context: Lucy is bracketed rather than dated: argon-argon ages on the volcanic ash layers that sandwich her set a maximum and a minimum, with the older ash lying about 18 metres beneath the fossil, and Lucy has to fall between them -- roughly 3.18 million years. Radiocarbon could not have touched her: it runs out near 50,000 years, and 3.18 million is far past its wall. The precise work followed Derek York's improved technique, applied by Aronson and Walter in 1992. Geochronologists also publish their own worst cases, which is how the traps got named: submarine basalts from eruptions witnessed in historical time have yielded potassium-argon ages as old as 22 million years, because argon trapped under water pressure never escaped the lava. Excess argon, inherited older zircon cores and entrained foreign crystals are the known routes to a wrong number -- which is exactly why step-heating and cross-method checks exist. On the Alder Creek Rhyolite, argon-argon on sanidine gives 1.1850 +/- 0.0016 million years while chemical-abrasion uranium-lead on zircon gives 1.1978 +/- 0.0046 million; when two independent methods disagree badly, that disagreement is itself the signal. Sources: Institute of Human Origins, 'About the Fossil Lucy'; Becoming Human, 'Geology and Dating'; Grokipedia, 'Radiometric dating'.

question: In September 1894 C. T. R. Wilson spent a few weeks as a relief observer at the observatory atop Ben Nevis. When the sun broke through, it threw his own shadow onto the cloud below, ringed with colour. What did Wilson decide to do about what he had seen?
answer: Make the effect happen in a jar in his laboratory
choices: Make the effect happen in a jar in his laboratory
Return each summer to photograph it from the summit
Hunt other Scottish peaks for the same coloured rings
Work out how high the cloud must sit to show it
context: Wilson opened his 1927 Nobel Lecture with that fortnight on the summit, in his own words: the coronas and glories "greatly excited my interest and made me wish to imitate them in the laboratory." He was chasing weather, not particles. CERN's own build manual is blunt about it: he "wanted to study cloud formation and optical phenomena in moist air. He discovered soon, that by accident he had invented a particle detector." Sources: C. T. R. Wilson, Nobel Lecture 1927; J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, p.2.

question: Muons come from the upper atmosphere, made about 15 kilometres up, and physicists once hauled detectors up mountains to study them. Sitting where you are right now, about how often does one pass through the palm of your hand?
answer: About once a second
choices: About once a second
About once an hour
About once a week
About once a year
context: CERN states it flatly: "On average, 1 muon passes through the palm of your hand every second with an energy of typically 1 GeV to 1 TeV." At sea level muons are about 70% of all charged cosmic particles arriving, roughly one per square centimetre per minute, and there are 1.3 times more anti-muons than muons. They have been crossing you your whole life; a box of cold air is all it takes to see them. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, pp.11 and 14.

question: Physics in the 1890s held that a cloud cannot form without dust: water vapour needs specks of dirt to condense on. C. T. R. Wilson, trying to make clouds on a laboratory bench, filtered his air until it was scrupulously dust-free, and in 1895 found that if he expanded it hard enough it clouded over anyway. Something else was seeding the droplets. What was it?
answer: Ions, molecules left carrying an electric charge
choices: Ions, molecules left carrying an electric charge
Salt grains too fine for any filter to catch
Scratches in the glass wall of the chamber
Cold spots where the air chilled the fastest
context: Droplets appeared only above a critical expansion ratio of about 1.25, corresponding to roughly fourfold supersaturation, and what they were growing on was electric charge. A meteorologist trying to explain rain had just found that ions make clouds, and with that, without meaning to, the first instrument that could show where an invisible particle had been. Source: Grokipedia, 'Cloud chamber' (History: invention and early concept).

question: By the 1930s C. T. R. Wilson's chamber was the fastest route in physics to a new particle. Wilson himself worked on into his late eighties and published his last paper in 1956, at the age of 87. What was that final paper about?
answer: The electricity inside thunderclouds
choices: The electricity inside thunderclouds
The tracks left by cosmic-ray particles
The rings of colour around a mountain shadow
A faster way to expand a chamber's air
context: The paper was 'A Theory of Thundercloud Electricity', 1956. Wilson was born on 14 February 1869 at Glencorse, Midlothian, the son of a sheep farmer, John, who died when Charles was four; he died on 15 November 1959, aged 90. He spent his whole working life on the weather. The particle detector that carried physics for forty years was the side effect. Source: Wikipedia, 'C. T. R. Wilson'.

question: CERN publishes a manual for building a working particle detector at home. The parts: a clear plastic box about the size of a fish tank, a strip of felt fixed inside it, a black metal plate for the floor, dry ice, and one very bright torch. The felt has to be soaked, and that liquid is what supplies the vapour. What is it?
answer: Isopropyl alcohol, over 90 per cent pure
choices: Isopropyl alcohol, over 90 per cent pure
Distilled water, warmed to blood heat
Liquid paraffin, thinned with white spirit
Glycerine, mixed half and half with water
context: CERN's shopping list in full: a clear box roughly 20 x 30 x 15 cm, 5 mm felt, a 5 mm black anodised aluminium plate (black so the white tracks show against it), dry ice at -78 C, isopropanol over 90% purity, and one tightly bundled bright torch. Safety, in CERN's own plain words: dry ice, "touching it directly will cause burns... only use in well ventilated rooms", and "dry ice in airtight containers will build up high pressure"; the alcohol, "never drink it, handle with gloves and goggles." Leather gloves for the ice, nitrile for the isopropanol. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, pp.3-5.

question: People say a cloud chamber lets you see a particle. C. T. R. Wilson never claimed that; he wrote only that the cloud condensed along the tracks. A charged particle tears electrons off the molecules it passes, leaving a line of charged molecules called ions, and vapour then grows droplets on that line until they are big enough for your eye to catch. By the time you see the thread, how long has the particle been gone?
answer: About a tenth of a second
choices: About a tenth of a second
About a millionth of a second
About ten full seconds
About a full minute
context: Roughly 100 ion pairs per centimetre for a fast minimum-ionising particle, thousands per centimetre for an alpha. The droplets grow to 1-10 micrometres across in about 100 milliseconds and last a few seconds. So the fog in the photograph is thousands of times fatter than the particle that made it, and it arrives a tenth of a second after the particle has already left the box. You are looking at a wake, not a thing, which is the more interesting claim. Source: Grokipedia, 'Cloud chamber' (Physics of supersaturation and ionization; Expansion and track formation).

question: In CERN's home cloud chamber the alcohol-soaked felt sits at the warm top of the box while the dry ice sits under the floor. After about five minutes a supersaturated layer, holding more vapour than it normally could, forms roughly a centimetre thick just above the plate, down at the bottom, which is where every track appears. Why does the vapour gather down there rather than rising to the top?
answer: Isopropanol vapour is heavier than air, so it sinks
choices: Isopropanol vapour is heavier than air, so it sinks
The cold floor drags the vapour down by convection
The felt drips liquid alcohol onto the plate below
Evaporation drives the vapour away from the warm top
context: Alcohol evaporates off the warm felt, sinks because isopropanol vapour is denser than air, and gets chilled hard on the way down by dry ice at -78 C. That builds the thin supersaturated layer hugging the black plate, which is why every track you see runs along the floor. CERN: "The tracks look a little like spider's threads going along the chamber floor." Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, pp.6-7.

question: You are watching threads cross the floor of a home cloud chamber. Most are thin and straight, muons made high in the atmosphere and passing through your kitchen. Then one thread turns a sharp corner in mid-flight and carries on. What has just happened inside your box?
answer: A muon decayed into an electron and two neutrinos
choices: A muon decayed into an electron and two neutrinos
A muon glanced off the nucleus of an air atom
A muon crossed from the cold layer into warmer air
A muon knocked an electron loose from an atom
context: CERN's key to reading your own fog: a thin straight thread is a muon or anti-muon from the upper atmosphere; a thick straight stub about 5 cm long is an alpha particle from radon-222 in the room air; a curly wandering line is a slow electron; a Y-fork is a muon knocking an electron off an atom; and a sudden kink is a muon transforming in mid-flight into an electron plus two neutrinos. Particle decay, in your kitchen, for the price of a bag of dry ice. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, p.8 ('What can you see?').

question: In 1925 Patrick Blackett filled a cloud chamber with nitrogen and fired alpha particles from polonium into it, exposing plates for several weeks to catch the rare frame where one struck a nucleus head-on. Ernest Rutherford had claimed such a strike was possible; Blackett's fog is what showed it happening. What do those plates record, for the first time in a photograph?
answer: Nitrogen turning into oxygen as a proton flies out
choices: Nitrogen turning into oxygen as a proton flies out
A nitrogen nucleus splitting cleanly into two halves
An alpha particle bouncing off a nitrogen nucleus
An electron being flung out of a nitrogen nucleus
context: N-14 + He-4 goes to O-17 + H-1. An alpha particle from polonium strikes a nitrogen nucleus, sticks to it, and knocks a proton out, leaving oxygen behind. Rutherford had claimed the reaction; Blackett's weeks of patient exposure are what turned the claim into a picture of one element becoming another. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Patrick Blackett' (Broader contributions to nuclear physics); Grokipedia, 'Cloud chamber'.

question: Carl Anderson kept photographing tracks that were positive but far too light to be protons. There was a catch: a photograph cannot tell you which way a thing was moving, so each track might be an ordinary electron travelling upward or an unknown light positive particle travelling down. Anderson settled it by adding one piece of hardware to his chamber. What did he add?
answer: A slab of lead laid across the chamber
choices: A slab of lead laid across the chamber
A second camera facing the opposite wall
A shutter timed to a single millisecond
Two counters, one above and one below
context: Six millimetres of lead. A particle crossing it loses energy, so its curve tightens on the far side, and the tighter half has to be the later half. A piece of metal is how you read the direction of time out of a still picture. On the evening of 2 August 1932 the frame came out: something entering from below at 63 million electron-volts, losing 40 MeV in the lead, leaving at 23 MeV. Anderson's logbook that night was deadpan: "Track 75. Thru Pb showing energy change or double ejection". He did not coin the name 'positron' either; he allowed it at the suggestion of the Physical Review editor. Sources: Per Carlson, 'Carl Anderson's 1932 upward going positron', PoS(ICRC2023)337; Science Museum Group Collection; Wikipedia, 'Positron'.

question: Carl Anderson developed a frame from his Caltech chamber on the evening of 2 August 1932 and found a track that should not exist: too faint for a proton, yet curving the wrong way through his magnet's field for an electron. Antimatter was not his first thought. He assumed instead that something mundane had gone wrong in his laboratory. What did he suspect?
answer: Students had reconnected the wires to his magnet
choices: Students had reconnected the wires to his magnet
The film had gone into his camera backwards
A scratch on the plate had faked the faint track
Someone had logged the field strength wrongly
context: Anderson told Luis Alvarez in 1934 that his first assumption was that students had reconnected the wires to the magnet and reversed its polarity; he checked the photographs taken just before and just after, nobody could have touched it, and only then did he believe the track. His boss Robert Millikan, the Nobel laureate everyone at Caltech called the Chief, pushed the safe reading: "...he repeatedly pointed out that cosmic ray particles travel downward, and not upward, except in extremely rare instances, and that these particles must be protons." Anderson admitted, "In the spirit of scientific conservatism, I tended at first toward the former interpretation." He had not read Dirac's antiparticle prediction at all. He had the Nobel Prize in 1936, at 31, sharing it with Victor Hess. Sources: Luis Alvarez interview by Charles Weiner, AIP 1967, and C. D. Anderson in 'The Discovery of Antimatter' (Weiss ed., 1999) p.29, both quoted in Per Carlson, PoS(ICRC2023)337; Grokipedia, 'Carl David Anderson'.

question: In 1936 Carl Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer hauled a cloud chamber to the summit of Pikes Peak, 4,300 metres up, with a slab of platinum set across it. The particle they caught, about 207 times an electron's mass, they named the mesotron, and physics spent eleven years taking it for the nuclear glue Hideki Yukawa had predicted in 1935. The clue had been on those first plates all along. What were the mesotron's tracks doing at the platinum?
answer: Punching through a centimetre of platinum almost undeflected
choices: Punching through a centimetre of platinum almost undeflected
Stopping dead inside the first millimetre of the platinum
Curling into tight spirals before ever reaching the platinum
Bursting into showers of secondary tracks below the platinum
context: Anderson and Neddermeyer's 1936 plates show the tracks punching through a centimetre of platinum almost undeflected. By the mid-1940s experiments had confirmed what that meant: muons barely interact with nuclei at all, so this could not be the glue holding a nucleus together. The mesotron was the muon, the same particle whose thread you can watch cross a kitchen table. Yukawa's real particle, the pion, turned up in 1947. For eleven years physics had the right measurement and the wrong identification, and nothing but further tests fixed it. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Carl David Anderson' (Identification of the muon); Grokipedia, 'Muon' (Discovery); Anderson and Neddermeyer, Physical Review 50(4), 263-271 (1936).

question: George Rochester and Clifford Butler ran a cloud chamber at Manchester for 1,500 hours, hunting cosmic rays, and took about 5,000 photographs. Two of them carried the prize: a pair of tracks that begin out in the middle of the gas and splay into a V, with nothing whatever leading in to the point where they meet. Why does the chamber show the fork but nothing arriving at it?
answer: Because the parent was electrically neutral and left no ions
choices: Because the parent was electrically neutral and left no ions
Because the parent arrived above the thin sensitive layer
Because the parent was moving too fast to ionise the gas
Because the parent's own track had already faded away
context: Two frames, out of five thousand, after 1,500 hours of running. A cloud chamber only draws what ionises the gas, so an electrically neutral particle crosses it invisibly and announces itself only when it decays in flight into charged pieces. That V was the decay: a neutral particle about a thousand times an electron's mass with a lifetime near 10^-10 seconds, the kaon, the first of the 'strange' particles. In 1949 the Manchester group carried their chamber up to the Pic du Midi observatory in the Pyrenees to catch more of them. Sources: Grokipedia, 'V particle' (Initial detection in cosmic rays); Grokipedia, 'Kaon'; Physics World, 'George Rochester'.

question: A muon is made about 15 kilometres up and lives, on average, 2.2 microseconds before it decays. Even at nearly the speed of light the trip down to the ground takes about 50 microseconds, more than twenty muon lifetimes, so almost none of them should ever reach your kitchen floor. A home cloud chamber shows them arriving in floods. Why do so many of them get here?
answer: At their own speed, their internal clock runs slow
choices: At their own speed, their internal clock runs slow
Decay is random, so out of vast numbers a few survive
Each decay makes a fresh muon that carries on down
Most are anti-muons, which take longer to decay
context: Special relativity, happening on a kitchen table. The 2.2-microsecond lifetime is measured on the muon's own clock, and at close to light speed that clock runs slow compared with yours, so the journey that costs the muon a fraction of its life costs the ground below far longer. Random survival cannot rescue the arithmetic: twenty lifetimes would leave a billionth of them, not floods. Every thin straight thread in a home chamber is a piece of evidence for Einstein that you collected yourself, with a fish tank, some dry ice and a torch. Source: J. Woithe, CERN S'Cool LAB DIY Cloud Chamber manual v7, 'Test of special relativity', p.11.

question: Before the 1880s polio struck children one at a time, never in waves. Then epidemics began: Sweden in 1887, Vermont in 1894, Norway in 1905. Epidemiologists comparing those first-struck places found one thing they shared. What was it?
answer: Unusually clean drinking water and sewers
choices: Unusually clean drinking water and sewers
Unusually crowded schools and shared classrooms
Unusually large dairy herds and raw-milk trade
Unusually damp and mosquito-rich summers
context: This is mainstream epidemiology, not a fringe claim. Sweden reported the first recognized outbreak in 1887; Vermont's 1894 epidemic counted 132 cases; Norway followed in 1905, and summer epidemics swept Europe by the 1920s. In poorer regions poliovirus stayed endemic and mostly harmless. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Polio; Neal Nathanson and John R. Martin, 'The Epidemiology of Poliomyelitis: Enigmas Surrounding Its Appearance, Epidemicity, and Disappearance', American Journal of Epidemiology, December 1979, 110(6):672-692.

question: Vienna, 1908: Karl Landsteiner and Erwin Popper ground up the spinal cord of a nine-year-old boy killed by polio and injected the emulsion into two rhesus monkeys. Both were paralysed, their cords damaged just as the boy's had been. One preparation step made the result decisive. Which step?
answer: Passing it through a bacteria-proof filter
choices: Passing it through a bacteria-proof filter
Boiling it until every bacterium was dead
Letting it settle and skimming the clear top
Mixing it with a recovered patient's blood
context: They used a Chamberland L3 porcelain candle filter, built to hold back every known bacterium, and injected what came through into the monkeys' brains and spinal fluid. One monkey died on the seventeenth day; the second was so ill it was put down on the twenty-fourth. Both showed destruction concentrated in the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, the same lesion as in the human cases. Whatever caused polio was smaller than any bacterium, could be passed on, and hunted nerve tissue. The work was done in 1908 and published the following year as 'Ubertragung der Poliomyelitis acuta auf Affen'. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Landsteiner; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erwin_Popper.

question: In 1928 two Harvard hygiene professors, Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw, built a sealed metal tank that breathed for children whose chest muscles polio had paralysed. On 12 October it reached a dying eight-year-old girl at Boston Children's Hospital, and she came round inside a minute. The pumps driving air in and out were cannibalised from a pair of ordinary domestic appliances. Which?
answer: Two vacuum cleaners
choices: Two vacuum cleaners
Two kitchen refrigerators
Two hair dryers
Two electric fans
context: An electric motor drove air pumps taken from two vacuum cleaners, and the girl's recovery within less than a minute made the machine famous. An adult iron lung cost about $2,000 in 1930, roughly $39,000 in today's money. In 1959, 1,200 Americans were living in tank respirators; by 2004, 39. Paul Alexander of Dallas entered one at six and lived in it for 72 years, until his death on 11 March 2024. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_lung.

question: Rockford, Illinois declared an emergency on 14 August 1945: 382 polio cases and 36 deaths in the county that season, most of them children. The city banned swimming, opened its schools six weeks late, and had a B-25 bomber fog the whole town with DDT. What did Rockford think the DDT would kill?
answer: Houseflies breeding in rubbish and sewage
choices: Houseflies breeding in rubbish and sewage
Mosquitoes breeding in standing summer water
Fleas living on the town's rats and cats
Ticks carried in on dogs from nearby farms
context: The guess was wrong but it was not stupid. Polio arrived in a sharp summer and early-autumn wave, often inside a two-or-three-month window, and outbreaks tracked poor sewage disposal, swimming pools and food handling - exactly the signature of an insect-borne disease. San Antonio did the same thing in 1946: a Universal newsreel, 'City Gets D.D.T. Treatment', shows special vehicles laying a DDT smoke-screen over the streets. The epidemics came anyway. Sources: 1440wrok.com/rockfords-polio-epidemic-of-1945/; unwritten-record.blogs.archives.gov (Universal News, 1946); grokipedia.com/page/Polio.

question: Alcohol hand gel destroys flu and cold viruses in seconds, which is why dispensers hang on hospital walls. Against poliovirus the same gel does almost nothing, and only soap and water will do. What is it about the poliovirus particle that defeats the gel?
answer: It has no fatty envelope for alcohol to dissolve
choices: It has no fatty envelope for alcohol to dissolve
It has no surface proteins for alcohol to clot
It has a sugar coat alcohol cannot soak through
It has a DNA core alcohol cannot break apart
context: Alcohol works by dissolving the greasy membrane that influenza and coronaviruses wrap themselves in. Poliovirus has no such wrapping: it is a bare particle about 30 nanometres across, a twenty-sided protein shell built from 60 copies each of four proteins around a single strand of RNA, and it shrugs off acid and detergents alike. That is why it survives the stomach, and why the sink beats the dispenser. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polio.

question: In five American polio epidemics between 1907 and 1912, most reported cases were children aged one to five. By the 1950s the average age of a child catching the disease had climbed to six. Neal Nathanson and John Martin argued in 1979 that this delay in a child's first meeting with poliovirus is what turned a common infection into an epidemic crippler: the delay let a child outgrow a protection infants have and older children do not. Which protection?
answer: Antibodies handed on by his mother, which fade within months
choices: Antibodies handed on by his mother, which fade within months
Antibodies made by his own gut bacteria, which fade within months
A gut lining too thick for the virus to cross in the first years
A body temperature too high for the virus to survive in infancy
context: Maternal antibodies have a half-life of roughly a month once breastfeeding ends. Meet poliovirus while they are still circulating and the infection is usually silent and leaves lifelong immunity; meet it afterwards and the odds of paralysis rise. Nathanson and Martin put it bluntly: epidemic polio appeared 'paradoxically' because of improvements in sanitation and personal hygiene. Sources: American Journal of Epidemiology, December 1979, 110(6):672-692; Nathanson and Kew, Am J Epidemiol 2010;172(11):1213; ourworldindata.org/polio.

question: When the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began in 1988, wild poliovirus was paralysing an estimated 350,000 children a year across more than 125 countries. Wild type 2 was last seen in 1999 and wild type 3 in 2012, and in 2024 wild poliovirus was still circulating in Pakistan and Afghanistan. How many wild poliovirus cases were confirmed worldwide that year?
context: Seventy-four in Pakistan, twenty-five in Afghanistan. This stretch matters because the case definition did not change again across it, so the fall cannot be a bookkeeping effect - which is precisely why the 1988-to-now record answers 'did paralysis fall?' differently from the 1955-to-1957 record, and why the two must be argued separately. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polio.

question: Before laboratories could type the virus in a patient's sample, a summer illness with fever, headache and a stiff neck went onto the books as polio on the doctor's judgement alone. Herman Kleinman, epidemiologist for the Minnesota Department of Health, reported that much of what his state had recorded as non-paralytic polio in 1956, and a staggering outbreak the year after that, had been caused by other viruses entirely. Which two?
answer: Coxsackie B-5, then ECHO 9
choices: Coxsackie B-5, then ECHO 9
Coxsackie A-9, then ECHO 30
ECHO 6, then Coxsackie B-3
ECHO 11, then Coxsackie A-16
context: Kleinman's words in the record: 'In 1956 in much of our so-called nonparalytic polio, the etiology turned out to be Coxsackie B-5 virus, and in 1957 a staggering outbreak turned out to be Echo 9 virus.' Both are enteroviruses, cousins of poliovirus, and both can cause the same aseptic meningitis. Better laboratories did not cure those children; they moved them out of one column and into another. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings before the House Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, 87th Congress 2d Session, on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed p. 98.

question: Bernard Greenberg headed biostatistics at the University of North Carolina's School of Public Health and had chaired the American Public Health Association's own committee on evaluation and standards. In 1960 he told a panel of Illinois physicians, in a text later entered into the record of a 1962 House hearing, that health departments had changed how a paralytic polio case got onto the books in 1955. Until then the World Health Organization definition asked only for paralysis found on two medical examinations. What did the 1955 criteria add?
answer: Paralysis still present on re-examination about sixty days after onset
choices: Paralysis still present on re-examination about sixty days after onset
Paralysis affecting at least two separate muscle groups on both sides
Paralysis confirmed by a laboratory test isolating the poliovirus
Paralysis reported to the state within forty-eight hours of diagnosis
context: Until 1955 the definition asked for paralysis found on two examinations at least twenty-four hours apart; the new criteria asked for paralysis still present on re-examination about sixty days after onset. Greenberg's line: 'This change in definition meant that in 1955 we started reporting a new disease, namely, paralytic poliomyelitis with a longer lasting paralysis.' He was not arguing that the vaccine was worthless - two paragraphs on he wrote, 'Without doubt, the increasing trend has been reduced to some extent by the Salk vaccine,' and 'If there were no other vaccine, complete vaccination of all susceptible persons in the population with Salk vaccine would be justifiable.' His actual position was that the live Sabin-type vaccine should be adopted faster. Note the provenance: Greenberg never appeared as a witness. Clinton R. Miller of the National Health Federation, an opponent of the bill, asked that the reprinted 1960 panel discussion be inserted into the record. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed pp. 90, 96-97.

question: Herman Kleinman, epidemiologist for the Minnesota Department of Health, was the one man on the 1960 panel who had committed himself in print that the Salk vaccine worked: his 1957 paper with Leonard Schuman put two doses at 83 per cent protective against paralytic polio. Of the vaccine he told the room, 'I am not against it.' Kleinman then turned to Bernard Greenberg's argument that part of the post-1955 fall in paralytic polio was a change in what got counted. Which position did he take?
answer: He backed it: only unmistakable paralysis was now being reported
choices: He backed it: only unmistakable paralysis was now being reported
He rejected it: Minnesota's own criteria had never been changed
He allowed it for Minnesota alone: other states had not changed
He set it aside: the 1954 field trial had already settled it
context: Kleinman's words: 'It is no wonder then that the average doctor does not want to make a diagnosis of polio in the absence of frank lower motor neuron flaccid paralysis. As a result, the only polio that's being reported today are cases with frank paralysis.' He also called the new duration requirement 'absolutely silly'. That the counting changed is therefore not a claim only critics make; it is agreed across the argument. What remains contested is how much of the fall it explains. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed pp. 90, 97-98.

question: From 1910 doctors kept noticing the same pattern: a child whose tonsils came out during a polio season was more likely to be paralysed a week or two later. It sounded like the sort of coincidence frightened parents invent. In the 1940s the Harvard Infantile Paralysis Commission worked through more than two thousand case histories and found the operation really did raise the risk of the brainstem form of the disease, and in 1998 Matthias Gromeier and Eckard Wimmer found the mechanism. What does an injury to tissue do that helps poliovirus paralyse?
answer: It opens nerve pathways the virus can travel inward along
choices: It opens nerve pathways the virus can travel inward along
It leaves raw nerve endings where the virus can multiply
It strips the mucus that normally traps the virus in the throat
It floods the wound with white cells the virus prefers to infect
context: The effect is now accepted and has a name: provocation polio. Injured tissue - from certain operations and certain injections - gives poliovirus easy access to the nerve channels that lead to the spinal cord and brainstem. Anxiety peaked in 1950, when clinical evidence suggested tonsillectomy could treble the risk; the American Journal of Public Health ran an editorial on it in August 1954, and a 1957 paper cited nineteen studies reporting the association. A folk observation that sounded like superstition turned out to be a real biological effect - a reminder that 'that sounds like nonsense' is not a test. Sources: cam.ac.uk research feature, 'Polio provocation'; AJPH 1954;44(8):1065-1067.

question: Herbert Ratner, health commissioner of Oak Park, Illinois, chaired the 1960 panel where Bernard Greenberg made his case about how individual polio cases were counted. Ratner pointed to a second definition that had also moved. Before the Salk vaccine, he said, the National Foundation called it an epidemic when a community reported 20 or more polio cases per 100,000 people in a year, and on that count American communities had epidemics every year. After the vaccine arrived, what became of that threshold?
answer: It was raised to 35 cases per 100,000 in a year
choices: It was raised to 35 cases per 100,000 in a year
It was raised to 50 cases per 100,000 in a year
It was rewritten as 20 paralytic cases per 100,000
It was rewritten as 20 polio deaths per 100,000
context: Ratner's own gloss in the record: the higher rate produced 'not a real, but a semantic elimination of epidemics'. Clinton Miller then put the question to the House committee directly: 'Is a polio epidemic 20 cases per 100,000 or is it 35 cases per 100,000? Who decides upon what evidence what constitutes an epidemic?' Note the attribution: this threshold point is Ratner's, not Greenberg's - retellings routinely credit it to the wrong man, and the primary record does not support them. Source: Intensive Immunization Programs, Hearings on H.R. 10541, May 1962 (govinfo CHRG-87hhrg84426), printed pp. 82, 94 fn.2, 111.

question: Forrest Maready's 2018 book The Moth in the Iron Lung sets out one author's hypothesis: that the pesticide era, DDT and the lead arsenate sprayed on American orchards before it, shaped the curve of paralysis the world called polio. Researchers who reject the hypothesis do not answer it with credentials. They point to a single piece of evidence as the reason a poison cannot be the cause of the paralysis, at most something that alters the risk. Which?
answer: Landsteiner and Popper injecting monkeys in 1908 with fluid from a dead boy's spinal cord
choices: Landsteiner and Popper injecting monkeys in 1908 with fluid from a dead boy's spinal cord
John Enders and his Boston team growing poliovirus in human tissue in the late 1940s
Herman Kleinman typing the other viruses behind Minnesota's polio counts in 1956
Harvard's Infantile Paralysis Commission reviewing two thousand case histories in the 1940s
context: This is how a hypothesis gets answered: not by ruling the author out of bounds, but by naming the evidence it has to get past. Landsteiner and Popper demonstrated a transmissible, sub-bacterial agent that produced the exact lesion of polio, decades before DDT existed. A toxin therefore cannot replace the virus as the cause; the most it could do is change who the virus paralyses - which is a real question, and an open one. Maready's book is one named author's argument, neither established nor suppressed. Sources: openlibrary.org (Maready, The Moth in the Iron Lung, 2018); grokipedia.com/page/Karl_Landsteiner.  (Legend.)

question: The picture almost everyone carries of polio is a hospital ward lined with iron lungs, and America's worst year seems to back it: 1952 reported 57,628 cases, of whom 3,145 died and 21,269 were left with paralysis. But a reported case was already a visibly sick child, and the great majority of people who met the virus never became one. Of all poliovirus infections, what share ended in any paralysis at all?
answer: About one in two hundred
choices: About one in two hundred
About one in two thousand
About one in fifty
About one in twenty
context: Roughly 70 to 75 per cent of poliovirus infections produced no symptoms at all, about 25 per cent a brief flu-like illness, and about 0.5 per cent - one in two hundred - acute flaccid paralysis, of which 5 to 10 per cent died of respiratory failure. Of paralytic cases about 79 per cent were spinal, 19 per cent bulbospinal and 2 per cent bulbar; the bulbar form, which takes out swallowing and breathing, is the one that filled the iron lungs, and it is the smallest slice. The photograph is true of a real ward and false as a picture of the disease - and 21,269 paralysed children in a single year is a real number too. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Polio; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_poliomyelitis.

question: In Lind's 1747 trial aboard HMS Salisbury, one pair of scorbutic sailors got cider, another got vinegar, another seawater, another elixir of vitriol, another a garlic paste, and one pair got two of a certain fruit and one of another every day. Within about six days that pair was fit for duty. What were they given?
answer: Two oranges and a lemon
choices: Two apples and a pear
Two oranges and a lemon
Two limes and a fig
Two peaches and a plum
context: Within six days one of the citrus pair was fit for duty and the other had nearly recovered; none of the other five remedies moved the disease. Source: https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/2021/february/finding-cure-scurvy

question: Lind's own book on scurvy did not draw the clean modern conclusion. He still believed scurvy came from blocked perspiration, and the citrus 'rob' he later recommended to keep aboard ship was prepared in a way that undid the very thing that had worked. What did he do to the juice?
answer: He boiled the juice down
choices: He mixed it with rum
He boiled the juice down
He filtered it through cloth
He sweetened it heavily with sugar
context: Lind boiled the juice down to about a tenth of its volume to make a keepable syrup he called a 'rob' -- but heat destroys vitamin C, so the very step meant to preserve the cure ruined it. Lind himself never gave up his blocked-perspiration theory. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/the-age-of-scurvy/

question: Lind's 1747 trial did not become Royal Navy policy. Fleet-wide daily citrus juice for every sailor did not arrive until 1795 -- forty-eight years later, and after Lind's death -- when a Scottish physician on the Sick and Wounded Board pushed it through the Admiralty. Who was he?
answer: Gilbert Blane
choices: Thomas Trotter
Gilbert Blane
James Cook
Edward Jenner
context: Gilbert Blane, as Commissioner of the Sick and Wounded Board and drawing on Rodney's support, persuaded the Admiralty in 1795 to issue three-quarters of an ounce of lemon juice daily to every sailor -- and by 1797 scurvy had all but vanished from the fleet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Blane

question: In 1830s Paris the physician Pierre Charles Alexandre Louis took what he called the 'numerical method' -- simply counting who lived and who died -- and applied it to the most respected treatment of the day, one used since Galen. What treatment did his 1835 book find did not work for pneumonia?
answer: Bleeding the patient with lancets and leeches
choices: Bleeding the patient with lancets and leeches
Blistering the chest with heated cups
Purging with mercury and calomel
Applying poultices of hot linseed
context: Louis's 1835 book on bloodletting for pneumonia used the numerical method -- just count outcomes across matched cases -- to argue the 2,000-year-old treatment did not help. He is a founder of modern clinical epidemiology. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Charles_Alexandre_Louis

question: A trial can still fail even when the two groups look matched on paper. A kind physician, seeing each patient, will steer the sicker ones away from the promising drug and toward familiar care -- and the drug will look better than it is. Which enrollment method blocks this leak?
answer: Assign each patient to a group by chance
choices: Alternate patients by admission order
Let each patient choose their own arm
Match on age and sex before assigning
Assign each patient to a group by chance
context: Selection bias is the reason 'matched groups' are not enough. Alternation is guessable, patient choice reintroduces the sicker/healthier tilt, and matching only balances what you thought to measure. Random assignment -- ideally with the sequence hidden from the enrolling doctor -- is what stops the leak. Source: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/why-the-1948-mrc-trial-of-streptomycin-used-treatment-allocation-based-on-random-numbers/

question: One afternoon at Rothamsted Experimental Station in the 1920s, the algologist Muriel Bristol told her colleagues she could taste whether the milk had gone into the cup before the tea or after. A young statistician did not laugh; he laid out eight cups on the spot, four made each way, in a random order. Who?
answer: Ronald Fisher
choices: Karl Pearson
Ronald Fisher
William Gosset
Egon Pearson
context: Muriel Bristol's tea claim at Rothamsted in the 1920s prompted Ronald Fisher to design an eight-cup test in random order. He later made the design the opening illustration of The Design of Experiments in 1935. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea

question: Fisher's eight-cup design gave Muriel Bristol four cups poured milk-first and four poured tea-first in random order, and asked her to sort them. What are the odds of picking all four milk-first cups correctly by pure luck?
answer: 1 in 70
choices: 1 in 8
1 in 24
1 in 70
context: There are exactly 70 ways to choose 4 cups from 8, so a lucky guesser has a 1-in-70 chance of getting all four right. Witnesses (including Fisher's daughter Joan Fisher Box) reported Bristol did in fact get all eight cups right, though Fisher's book presents the design without stating the outcome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_tasting_tea  (Legend.)

question: In 1948 the Medical Research Council published in the British Medical Journal the first properly randomized clinical trial in medicine: streptomycin versus bed rest alone for pulmonary tuberculosis, with patients allocated by random numbers in sealed envelopes. Which statistician designed the trial?
answer: Austin Bradford Hill
choices: Marc Daniels
Austin Bradford Hill
Philip d'Arcy Hart
Richard Doll
context: Austin Bradford Hill of the MRC Statistical Research Unit designed the 1948 streptomycin trial for pulmonary TB; allocation used random numbers in a set of sealed envelopes, one per hospital, hidden from the doctors enrolling patients. Source: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/medical-research-council-1948b/

question: Bradford Hill sealed the MRC streptomycin allocations in numbered envelopes at each hospital. This safeguard, called allocation concealment, is aimed at one particular person's judgement in the enrollment chain. Whose?
answer: The enrolling doctor deciding whom to admit next
choices: The patient deciding whether to consent
The ward matron assigning beds
The referring GP choosing which hospital to send the patient to
The enrolling doctor deciding whom to admit next
context: Allocation concealment protects against the enrolling doctor gaming the sequence -- if they can guess which arm the next envelope holds, they can quietly wait for a sicker or healthier patient before enrolling, and the whole trial rots. It is a separate safeguard from double-blinding, which hides which arm a patient is in AFTER enrolment. Source: https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/why-the-1948-mrc-trial-of-streptomycin-used-treatment-allocation-based-on-random-numbers/

question: Through the whole of 2020, while most of the Western world shut its classrooms, one European country let children under sixteen go on attending school right through the spring wave, with no closures and no masks. Which country?
answer: Sweden
choices: Sweden
Denmark
Norway
Finland
context: Sweden's Public Health Agency, under state epidemiologist Anders Tegnell, chose recommendations over mandates for children in compulsory school (ages 1-15); upper-secondary schools (age 16+) did go remote from 18 March 2020. Its Nordic neighbours -- Denmark, Norway and Finland -- all closed their schools that spring. Source: The Local, March 2021.

question: Jonas Ludvigsson and colleagues, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in January 2021, followed about 1.95 million Swedish children aged 1 to 16 who attended class through the whole spring 2020 wave. Out of those children, how many died of COVID-19?
answer: Not one
choices: Not one
Fifteen
Ninety-two
About three hundred
context: The NEJM letter (online 6 January 2021) reported 15 admissions to intensive care with COVID-19 or the related inflammatory syndrome across the whole cohort -- four of them children with a serious pre-existing condition such as cancer or chronic kidney disease -- and zero deaths in the 1-16 age group. Source: NEJM, Ludvigsson et al., 6 Jan 2021.

question: The loudest worry about keeping the classrooms open was the danger to the teachers. Ludvigsson's Swedish study compared the severe-COVID rate of the country's schoolteachers to the average across other occupations (excluding health-care workers). Where did the teachers land?
answer: Below the average, at a relative risk of about 0.43
choices: Below the average, at a relative risk of about 0.43
About the same, close to 1.0
Somewhat above the average, near 1.5
Roughly triple the average, near 3.0
context: The reported relative risk for schoolteachers was 0.43 (95% CI 0.28-0.68) after excluding health-care workers -- meaningfully LOWER than the workforce average, not higher. Preschool teachers came in at 1.10 (0.49-2.49), essentially the same as average. Source: NEJM, Ludvigsson et al., 6 Jan 2021.

question: Anders Tegnell, state epidemiologist at Sweden's Public Health Agency, built the whole pandemic response around one core method choice that set his country apart from almost every other Western government. What was it?
answer: Recommendations rather than enforced mandates
choices: Recommendations rather than enforced mandates
A single hard national lockdown at the first case
A universal mask order in all public spaces
A border closure to all non-citizens
context: Tegnell bet on sustained voluntary compliance -- stay home when symptomatic, avoid crowded indoor gatherings, keep distance from the over-70s -- rather than police-enforced orders. Later (2023) he said the decision NOT to close schools was the one he remained most pleased with. Source: Grokipedia; Irish Times, April 2023.

question: For 2020 alone, Sweden's excess deaths were WORSE than Denmark's, Norway's and Finland's -- and the country's own Corona Commission, in its first report on 15 December 2020, said plainly why. Where did that year's excess deaths concentrate?
answer: In the country's nursing and care homes
choices: In the country's nursing and care homes
Among primary-school teachers
Among healthy adults under forty
Among tourists returning from ski holidays
context: The Corona Commission report of 15 December 2020 named hospital discharge policies that did not require testing, lack of PPE, and staffing and organizational problems as drivers; the government and the Public Health Agency both admitted the attempt to shield the elderly had failed. The school decision was vindicated by measurement; the care-home decision was not. Source: The Local, Oct 2021; PMC PMC8436291.

question: After the spring 2020 wave, researchers ran the standard primary-school reading assessments on the Swedish pupils who had sat in class straight through the pandemic -- the fair test of whether keeping the classrooms open had cost the children something academically. What did the assessments show?
answer: No measurable learning loss on the reading tests
choices: No measurable learning loss on the reading tests
A drop of roughly one grade level, comparable to closure countries
A drop of nearly two grade levels, worse than closure countries
A small gain, credited to shrinking class sizes
context: Analyses of Swedish primary-school reading assessments spanning the pandemic period found no measurable learning loss in the pupils who kept attending school, while countries that closed classrooms recorded documented drops in reading and math attainment (the OECD/World Bank literature converged on roughly a third to half a year lost per closure period). The test the closures were meant to protect the children from -- the risk to their learning -- came back clean for the country that refused to run it. Source: PMC PMC9162440.

question: Wilhelm Ostwald, one of Germany's most celebrated chemists, travelled from Berlin to see the room in Paris where radium had been found. The Curies were away, so he looked around the empty place alone and wrote down his verdict. What did he say it resembled?
answer: A cross between a stable and a potato-cellar
choices: A cross between a stable and a potato-cellar
A workshop no better than a village blacksmith's
A glasshouse someone had emptied of its plants
A schoolroom with the desks pushed to the walls
context: Ostwald wrote: 'It was a cross between a stable and a potato-cellar, and, if I had not seen the worktable with the chemical apparatus, I would have thought it a practical joke.' The room was an abandoned wooden shed in the courtyard of the Ecole superieure de physique et de chimie industrielles, off the rue Lhomond - a former dissecting room for a medical school, with a leaking glass roof, a bituminous floor, worn pine tables and a cast-iron stove that barely worked. Summers turned it into a hothouse; winters dropped it below freezing. Marie Curie's own verdict on the same building: 'it was in this miserable old shed that we passed the best and happiest years of our life.'
