Both the shed and its adjoining workshop were demolished between the two world wars. (Ostwald quoted in R. Reid, 'Marie Curie', 1974, p. 95, via todayinsci.com; shed described by the Musee Curie, lamethodecurie.fr/en/article14.html; Marie Curie's line from 'Pierre Curie', 1923.)

question: In July 1898 the Curies announced a new element pulled out of pitchblende, and Marie Sklodowska Curie claimed the right to name it. Historians call her choice plausibly the first element name ever meant as a protest. What did she name it after?
answer: A homeland the empires had wiped off the map
choices: A homeland the empires had wiped off the map
An uprising the empires had put down in blood
A university the empires had shut by decree
A chemist the empires had driven into exile
context: Marie Sklodowska-Curie was born in Warsaw. When she named the element, Poland had been partitioned among Russia, Prussia/Germany and Austria-Hungary and appeared on no map of Europe as a country at all - so she put her erased homeland into the periodic table instead. Radium followed five months later, announced on 26 December 1898, its name taken from the Latin for ray. In the course of the same work the Curies coined the word 'radioactivity' itself. (Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'; polonium's naming at wordorigins.org and Smithsonian, 'Six Secrets of Polonium'.)

question: Marie Curie's 1923 memoir of Pierre describes one of the joys of the shed: going back into the workroom after dark, with no lamp lit and no work to do. What did she describe seeing?
answer: Faintly luminous silhouettes of bottles and capsules on the shelves
choices: Faintly luminous silhouettes of bottles and capsules on the shelves
The red glow of the iron stove sliding across Pierre's blackboard
Moonlight through the leaking glass roof lying on the pine tables
The courtyard lamps outside picking out the cracks in the walls
context: Her words: 'One of our joys was to go into our workroom at night; we then perceived on all sides the feebly luminous silhouettes of the bottles or capsules containing our products. It was really a lovely sight and one always new to us.' The passage is universally quoted with a closing line - the glowing tubes 'looked like faint, fairy lights'. She carried tubes of radium in her pockets and kept them in her desk drawers. Neither of them knew what the light was doing to them: Marie Curie died on 4 July 1934, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia - her bone marrow had stopped making blood cells - attributed to decades of exposure in the shed and to her wartime X-ray work. (Marie Curie, 'Pierre Curie', Macmillan, 1923; the autobiographical notes first ran in The Delineator, Jan-Mar 1922.)  (Legend.)

question: In April 1898 Marie Curie put a current meter to every uranium-bearing material she could get. Pure uranium metal read 24 on her scale; pitchblende ore from Joachimsthal read 67, and pitchblende from Johanngeorgenstadt read 83. What did she publish as the likely explanation?
answer: That the ore might hold an element far more active than uranium
choices: That the ore might hold an element far more active than uranium
That pitchblende holds far more uranium than assayers had thought
That thorium in the ore was supplying the extra activity
That the rock around the uranium was concentrating its rays
context: Her printed table, in units of 10^-12 amperes: uranium 24; pitchblende from Johanngeorgenstadt 83; pitchblende from Joachimsthal and Pribram 67; natural chalcolite 52. Pitchblende is mostly other rock with uranium only part of it, so pure uranium metal should have been the ceiling - and instead the ores ran two to three and a half times hotter than the metal inside them. Her paper called that fact 'most remarkable' and printed the conclusion that it 'suggests that these minerals may contain an element much more active than uranium'. Thorium is a real wrong answer rather than a silly one: the same paper is titled 'Rays emitted by compounds of uranium and of thorium', and she reported thorium compounds active in it. The excess in pitchblende turned out to be two elements nobody had yet named. The scientific virtue in this rung is what she did NOT do - blame the instrument, quietly round the number down, or set the odd sample aside. She went looking instead. (Marie Sklodowska Curie, Comptes Rendus 126, 1898; English translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/ea/curieann.html.)

question: Marie Curie boiled pitchblende in open cauldrons out in the courtyard beside her wooden shed off the rue Lhomond in Paris, sometimes for a whole day at a stretch. Her own account of the work names the one piece of equipment that left her 'broken with fatigue at the day's end'. What was it?
answer: An iron rod nearly as tall as she was
choices: An iron rod nearly as tall as she was
An iron mortar as wide as her two hands
A stoneware basin the length of her arm
A pair of iron tongs half her own height
context: 'Sometimes I had to spend a whole day mixing a boiling mass with a heavy iron rod nearly as large as myself. I would be broken with fatigue at the day's end.' She also noted there 'was no question of obtaining the needed proper apparatus in common use by chemists'. The boiling was done outdoors because the shed had no fume hoods: 'There were no hoods to carry away the poisonous gases thrown off in our chemical treatments, so that it was necessary to carry them on outside in the court, but when the weather was unfavorable we went on with them inside, leaving the windows open.' HONEST CAVEAT, from the American Institute of Physics' own historians: the heroic 'she did it all alone, by hand, in a shed' story is partly Marie Curie's own emphasis and served a fundraising purpose. The gross first-stage treatment of the first tonne of pitchblende was done at a factory, the Central Chemical Products Company; the Curies were reasonably well funded by the standards of French science; and Andre-Louis Debierne worked alongside them. The boiling cauldrons and the iron rod are real. Total solitude is not. (AIP exhibit, 'Marie Curie and Her Legend', history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/romleg_text.htm; ventilation quote via the Musee Curie, lamethodecurie.fr/en/article14.html.)

question: Marie Curie spent about four years boiling, filtering and purifying sackfuls of Joachimsthal pitchblende in her Paris shed. By 1902 she had roughly a tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride to show for it — less than a pinch of salt. All that labour existed to pin down one number about radium. Which one?
answer: The weight of a single atom of radium
choices: The weight of a single atom of radium
The heat that one gram of radium gives off
The temperature at which radium melts
The density of a lump of radium metal
context: She got her number: 225, fixed in 1902 from just 0.09 g of radium chloride and, she judged, good to within one unit. That figure is radium's relative atomic mass - how heavy one of its atoms is set against the lightest atom, hydrogen - and it is what tells a chemist where a new element belongs in the periodic table. She refined it to 226.45 in 1907 using 0.4 g of very pure salt; the modern accepted value is 226. Her earlier attempts on dirtier samples had given 138, then 146, then 174 - the number walking towards the truth as the salt got cleaner, which is exactly why the purifying had to be finished before the measuring meant anything. ACCURACY NOTE: the sources genuinely disagree on how much ore went in - Wikipedia says a tonne of pitchblende, the Musee Curie says thirteen tons, the American Institute of Physics says several tons - so only the yield, a tenth of a gram, is stated here as precise. (Musee Curie, 'Radium's atomic weight', lamethodecurie.fr/en/article27.html; 'Closing in on radium', EDP Sciences; history.aip.org/exhibits/curie/romleg_text.htm.)

question: Marie Curie handled radium salts bare-handed for years and kept tubes of it in her desk drawers. Her laboratory notebooks now sit in lead-lined boxes at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. What does the library require of a reader who asks to consult one?
answer: Put on protective clothing and sign a waiver of liability
choices: Put on protective clothing and sign a waiver of liability
Read the pages through glass in a sealed viewing cabinet
Handle them with cotton gloves and a full face shield
Work from photographs, since the originals never open
context: You sign a liability waiver to read a chemistry notebook. The contaminant is radium-226, whose half-life - the time for half of a sample to decay away - is about 1,600 years. She has been dead more than ninety years, and roughly four percent of it has gone; the pages will still be hot when everyone reading this is a footnote. Her furniture and even her cookbooks are contaminated too, because she carried tubes of radium in her pockets and desk drawers. (Christian Science Monitor, 'Marie Curie: Why her papers are still radioactive'; Wikipedia, 'Marie Curie'.)

question: Pitchblende was expensive, and the Curies had no money for tonnes of it. In 1898 the Austrian government agreed to ship them 100 kg from the Joachimsthal mine at no charge, and it was exactly the material they wanted. What was in the sacks?
answer: Residue left over after the uranium had been extracted
choices: Residue left over after the uranium had been extracted
Tailings from the mine's older silver workings
Sweepings from the floor of the ore-crushing house
Low-grade rock rejected before the ore was sorted
context: In the Curies' own words: 'we received from the Austrian government a shipment, at no charge, of 100 kg of a residue from the processing of Joachimsthal pitchblende.' The uranium - the part worth money - had already been pulled out and sold. The radium stayed behind in the discards, which is why the mine's waste was better raw material than fresh ore would have been, and why the Austrians were happy to give it away. Joachimsthal is now Jachymov, in the Czech Republic. The same paper reports the barium-bearing fraction they precipitated was already 'sixty times stronger than that of metallic uranium'. (P. Curie, Mme P. Curie and G. Bemont, Comptes Rendus 127, 1898; translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/curiesra.html.)

question: Henri Becquerel carried a tube of radium in his waistcoat pocket and it burned a sore into his side. Pierre Curie decided a chance accident was not evidence, and in 1901 he set out to produce the same injury deliberately and record how it developed. How did he do it?
answer: He bound a radium salt against his own forearm for ten hours
choices: He bound a radium salt against his own forearm for ten hours
He strapped a radium tube to a rabbit's shaved flank for a day
He sewed a radium tube into a coat and wore it for a fortnight
He fixed a radium tube inside a glove and wore it while working
context: Ten hours against his own arm, then a day-by-day chart of the wound as it reddened, blistered and scabbed like a burn; a grey scar was still there after about fifty-two days. Those two injuries - Becquerel's accident and Pierre Curie's deliberate copy of it - are where radiotherapy comes from. The reasoning is brutally simple: a thing that destroys healthy skin on purpose can be aimed at a tumour instead. (Reviewed in 'Pioneers of nuclear medicine, Madame Curie', PubMed 16868638; RSC Education, 'Radium - a key element in early cancer treatment'.)

question: Chalcolite is a natural uranium mineral, and Marie Curie measured a crystal of it running at more than twice the activity of pure uranium metal. In 1898 she ran a single experiment that settled whether the extra activity belonged to the mineral itself or to something else riding along inside the crystal. What did she do?
answer: She built the same mineral from pure laboratory chemicals and measured it
choices: She built the same mineral from pure laboratory chemicals and measured it
She compared crystals of it collected from four different mines
She measured a copper phosphate mineral holding no uranium at all
She dissolved the crystal and measured each separated fraction in turn
context: She 'prepared chalcolite from pure reagents according to the procedure of Debray' - a counterfeit mineral with the identical chemical formula, assembled from clean chemicals so that nothing from the mine could be riding along in it. On her scale, plain uranium metal read 24, the natural chalcolite read 52, and her artificial copy read 9. Same formula, one-sixth the activity. So the extra was an impurity hiding in the real rock, not the compound. That is a control experiment in its purest form, run by someone who did not yet have a name for the thing she was chasing - and it is the move you can copy at any kitchen table: build the version WITHOUT the suspected ingredient and see what changes. (Marie Sklodowska Curie, Comptes Rendus 126, 1898.)

question: By December 1898 the Curies had concentrated a barium-bearing fraction of the pitchblende residue until it was sixty times more active than uranium. High activity alone proves nothing, though: a perfectly ordinary substance carrying an unknown contaminant would look the same. They sent a sample to the Paris chemist Eugène Demarçay. What did he find that let them announce a new element?
answer: A line in its light matching no known element
choices: A line in its light matching no known element
A crystal shape matching no known element
A melting point matching no known element
A flame colour matching no known element
context: The December 1898 paper puts it in one sentence: 'M. Demarcay has found in the spectrum a line which does not appear to belong to any known element.' Heat any element and the light it gives off carries a fixed pattern of bright lines - a barcode unique to that element. One unfamiliar line on a photographic plate is what turned 'an anomaly in our ore' into 'a new element'. Same paper: 'we propose to give the name radium.' The third author on it, Gustave Bemont, is almost always forgotten. (Curie, Curie & Bemont, Comptes Rendus 127, 1898; translation at web.lemoyne.edu/~giunta/curiesra.html.)

question: In 1903 members of the Paris Academy of Sciences sent Stockholm their nominations for the physics prize: Henri Becquerel and Pierre Curie, for the work on radioactivity. Marie Curie's name was not on the list. The Swedish mathematician Gösta Mittag-Leffler got word to Pierre unofficially. What did Pierre do?
answer: He wrote asking to be considered jointly with Marie Curie
choices: He wrote asking to be considered jointly with Marie Curie
He refused the prize outright unless her name was added
He asked the Academy to withdraw his own name in her favour
He said nothing and split the prize money with her later
context: His letter of 6 August 1903: 'I would very much like to be considered jointly with Mrs. Curie for our work on radioactive bodies', adding that 'her initial research led to the discovery of new elements, and she played a major role in it.' The committee could act on it only because Professor Charles Bouchard of the Paris Faculty of Medicine had already nominated her independently - a request from a nominee is not itself a nomination. The prize was split: half to Becquerel for discovering spontaneous radioactivity, half to the two Curies jointly. Neither Curie attended the ceremony on 10 December 1903, pleading teaching duties and Marie's health. In 1911 she took the Chemistry Prize alone, and remains the only person holding Nobels in two different sciences. (Association Curie et Joliot-Curie, 'The 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics'; nobelprize.org.)

question: Radium sits directly below barium in the periodic table, and the two behave almost identically in the chemist's hands — no filter and no ordinary chemical trick will part them. Marie Curie found one small difference between radium chloride and barium chloride and applied it over and over, several thousand times across four years, until she had a pure salt. What was the difference she used?
answer: Radium chloride is slightly less soluble in water than barium chloride
choices: Radium chloride is slightly less soluble in water than barium chloride
Radium chloride is slightly denser as a solid than barium chloride
Radium chloride melts at a slightly lower heat than barium chloride
Radium chloride is slightly more stable in air than barium chloride
context: Dissolve the mixed chlorides, then let the solution cool so crystals form. Because radium chloride is a shade less willing to stay dissolved, the crystals that drop out first are slightly richer in radium and the liquid left behind is slightly poorer. Pour off the liquid, redissolve the crystals, do it again. That is fractional crystallisation, and she ran it several thousand times. The entire four years - the cauldrons, the iron rod, the ruined hands - is ONE small difference in solubility, applied over and over until a difference too small to see became a pure salt. (Musee Curie, 'Radium's atomic weight', lamethodecurie.fr/en/article27.html; Indian Academy of Sciences, 'Discovery of Radium'.)

question: In March 1903 Pierre Curie and Albert Laborde published a measurement nobody could account for: a radium salt sitting on a bench gives off heat, roughly 100 calories per gram every hour, and goes on giving it off month after month. Where is that heat coming from?
answer: The atoms themselves are coming apart, one element turning into another
choices: The atoms themselves are coming apart, one element turning into another
The salt is burning slowly in the air, a chemical reaction too faint to see
The salt soaked up light beforehand and is giving it back as warmth
The atoms are drawing in energy from the ether that fills all space
context: The three wrong choices were not silly - they were the live hypotheses of serious physicists in 1903: a slow chemical reaction, phosphorescence re-emitting stored light, and the atom absorbing energy out of the luminiferous ether. People reached for them because the alternative broke conservation of energy as it was then understood: heat pouring out forever with nothing going in. Two facts killed all three. The output was orders of magnitude beyond anything chemistry can supply, and the rate did not change with temperature, pressure or light - which is exactly how chemical reactions and phosphorescence DO change. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy supplied the real answer with their transmutation theory: the atoms themselves are coming apart, and one element is turning into another. (P. Curie & A. Laborde, Comptes Rendus, March 1903; contemporary framing in 'A New Source of Heat: Radium', Popular Science Monthly vol. 63, May 1903.)

question: In late April 1955, five children in California came down with paralytic polio about a week after their polio shots. One thing the five had in common told doctors this was not coincidence. What was it?
answer: All five were paralysed in the vaccinated arm.
choices: All five had been vaccinated at one clinic.
All five had a brother or sister with polio.
All five were paralysed in the vaccinated arm.
All five fell ill on exactly the same day.
context: Idaho State University's polio history records the detail that turned suspicion into evidence: 'It was found that all five of the California children became paralyzed in the left arm, which had received the vaccine.' Wikipedia's Polio vaccine article gives the same tell for the wider wave - the Surgeon General's reports described paralysis 'starting in the limb the vaccine was injected into.' A vaccine holding only killed virus cannot paralyse the limb it went into. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio_vaccine; sites.google.com/isu.edu/polioinidaho/home/the-cutter-incident-1955.

question: Five companies won the federal licence to make Salk's polio vaccine in 1955. The one whose lots paralysed children was a family firm in Berkeley, California, with little experience of growing virus in bulk. What had Cutter Laboratories mainly made before polio?
answer: Vaccines and medicines for animals.
choices: Vaccines and medicines for animals.
Blood plasma for army hospitals.
Insulin for diabetic patients.
Antibiotics for surgical wards.
context: Cutter Laboratories was a family-owned Berkeley firm best known for veterinary vaccines and general pharmaceuticals, with limited prior experience of large-scale virology compared with competitors such as Eli Lilly - an inexperience that, per Grokipedia, 'evaded detection during pre-licensing inspections by NIH's Division of Biologics Standards.' Its 1955 sales were $11,482,000. It stayed in business, bought Hollister-Stier in 1958, and was itself bought by Bayer AG in 1974. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories.

question: On 24 April 1955 a doctor in Pocatello, Idaho reported that Susan Pierce, a seven-year-old vaccinated days earlier, had fever and paralysis; she died three days after her symptoms began. What did the officials running the local vaccination programme first say about her case?
answer: She must have caught polio before her shot.
choices: She must have been given a double dose.
She must have had a different illness.
She must have missed her second injection.
She must have caught polio before her shot.
context: Susan Pierce was the first reported death of the outbreak: fever and paralysis within days of her injection, then death from fulminating bulbar polio three days after symptoms appeared. Local vaccine administrators first dismissed the case as an infection she had already been carrying. Within days the Surgeon General was receiving the same kind of report from several states. Sources: history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems; sites.google.com/isu.edu/polioinidaho/home/the-cutter-incident-1955.

question: Idaho counted fourteen more polio cases than usual in the week after its vaccination drive began, and a thirty-three-year-old mother of two vaccinated children was among the paralysed. The outbreak was reaching people who had never had the shot. How were they catching polio?
answer: The vaccinated children were shedding live virus.
choices: A wild epidemic had reached Idaho that spring.
The vaccinated children were shedding live virus.
Spilled vaccine had got into the town water supply.
Doctors were carrying the virus from house to house.
context: Wikipedia states the outcome plainly: 'The exposures led to an epidemic of polio in the families and communities of the affected children.' Children given Cutter's vaccine excreted live poliovirus and infected people who had never been vaccinated - a preventive shot starting an outbreak. Idaho alone reported fourteen extra cases that week, and the thirty-three-year-old mother caught polio from her own vaccinated children. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories; history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems.

question: By early May 1955 Cutter's vaccine had been withdrawn, and no other company's product had been tied to a single case of paralysis. Surgeon General Leonard Scheele acted anyway on 8 May. What did he order?
answer: Every polio vaccination in the country stopped.
choices: Every polio vaccination in the country stopped.
Cutter's Berkeley plant closed by federal marshals.
All unused doses returned to the five makers.
Vaccination restricted to children over seven.
context: Scheele halted Cutter's vaccine on 27 April 1955 and suspended the entire national polio vaccination programme on 8 May until a cause could be determined; vaccination resumed in the autumn under a new testing regime. Sources split on which date to call 'the' suspension: Grokipedia gives 27 April for the immediate nationwide halt of Cutter's product and 8 May for Scheele's announced suspension, while history.com gives 8 May for the halt of all vaccinations. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories; history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems.

question: Surgeon General Leonard Scheele sent William Tripp and Karl Habel of the NIH to Cutter's plant in Berkeley to question the workers and go through the production records. What did their inspection conclude?
answer: Nothing was wrong with Cutter's production methods.
choices: Cutter had skipped a required safety test.
Cutter's monkey kidney cultures were contaminated.
Nothing was wrong with Cutter's production methods.
Cutter's records had been altered after the recall.
context: Wikipedia's sentence is verbatim: 'After a thorough investigation, they found nothing wrong with Cutter's production methods.' The flaw was real but invisible to an inspection of practice. A congressional hearing that June went on to blame the NIH's own Laboratory of Biologics Control for lack of scrutiny rather than the company. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories (citing Breakthrough: The Saga of Jonas Salk, Trident Press, 1966, pp. 313-315).

question: Cutter made its vaccine the standard way: poliovirus grown on monkey kidney cultures, then held in formaldehyde for about two weeks to kill every particle. In some lots live Type 1 virus survived into the bottles anyway. Investigators argued over how. What had gone wrong?
answer: Clumped cell debris shielded virus from the formaldehyde.
choices: A poliovirus strain had grown resistant to formaldehyde.
Clumped cell debris shielded virus from the formaldehyde.
The monkey kidney cultures carried a second, unknown virus.
The formaldehyde had been neutralised days too early.
context: Grokipedia states the failure mode: 'formaldehyde penetration could be impeded by viral aggregates or tissue remnants.' Cell debris left behind by inadequate filtration wrapped poliovirus particles and kept the formaldehyde off them, so live Type 1 virus survived into the finished product; history.com puts it as proteins in the vaccine clumping together. Paul Offit traced the key manufacturing flaw to a change in the method of filtration - and found it at more than one company. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories; gavi.org/vaccineswork/book-club/review-cutter-incident-paul-offit; history.com/articles/salk-polio-vaccine-shortages-problems.

question: Before a lot of 1955 polio vaccine could be sold, the maker had to test it for surviving live virus and report the result. After the first paralysis reports, investigators pulled Cutter's own paperwork for the lots that had paralysed the children. What did it show?
answer: The lots had passed every test the licence required.
choices: The lots had been shipped before testing finished.
The lots had been tested for strength but not safety.
The lots had come from an unlicensed second plant.
The lots had passed every test the licence required.
context: Wikipedia puts it in one clause: 'some lots of the Cutter vaccine - despite passing required safety tests - contained live polio virus in what was supposed to be an inactivated-virus vaccine.' Cutter's release testing was simply less sensitive than its competitors': other makers looked for residual live virus by inoculating animals, while Cutter relied on protein-nitrogen assays and monkey-kidney tissue-culture tests that could not detect a low viral load. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories; grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine.

question: All five licensed makers, not only Cutter, had trouble killing every virus particle in 1955; only Cutter's lots produced an outbreak. Federal controls were imposed and American children were vaccinated again from that autumn, which made the next few years a test of whether a killed-virus vaccine worked at all. What happened to polio in the United States between 1953 and 1957?
answer: Cases fell from about 35,000 to under 6,000.
choices: Cases fell from about 35,000 to under 6,000.
Cases fell from about 35,000 to about 25,000.
Cases held steady at about 35,000 a year.
Cases rose from about 35,000 to over 50,000.
context: Grokipedia's judgement of the incident is that it 'exposed manufacturing inconsistencies rather than flaws in the trial design or vaccine formulation itself.' Eli Lilly, Parke-Davis, Wyeth and Pitman-Moore all found complete inactivation difficult, and three of them were sued and settled out of court; only Cutter's lots caused paralysis. U.S. polio cases fell from roughly 35,000 in 1953 to under 6,000 by 1957. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories; grokipedia.com/page/Polio; grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk.

question: In 1954, a year before the licence, Bernice Eddy of the NIH's Laboratory of Biologics Control tested the manufacturers' polio vaccines in eighteen monkeys, and three of Cutter's six batches failed. Eddy sent her superiors a report with one piece of evidence attached. What did she attach?
answer: Photographs of the paralysed animals.
choices: Statements signed by her laboratory staff.
Photographs of the paralysed animals.
Slides of spinal cord from her monkeys.
Samples of vaccine from the bad batches.
context: Wikipedia: 'in 1954, staff member Bernice Eddy had reported to her superiors that some inoculated monkeys had become paralyzed and provided photographs. William Sebrell, the director of NIH, rejected the report.' Her immediate superior, William Workman, head of the Laboratory of Biologics Control, invalidated her findings, removed her from polio research and reassigned her to flu vaccine. The problem never reached the licensing advisory committee. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories (citing Edward Shorter, The Health Century, Doubleday 1987, pp. 68-70); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_Eddy; grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine.

question: Nathanson and Langmuir's 1963 study counted the Cutter cases in two separate groups. Among the vaccinated children themselves: 40,000 with fever, headache and aching muscles but no paralysis, 56 paralysed, 5 dead. The second group was the brothers, sisters, parents and neighbours who caught polio from those children. What did that second count come to?
answer: 113 paralysed and 5 dead.
choices: 14 paralysed and 1 dead.
113 paralysed and 5 dead.
41 paralysed and 5 dead.
300 paralysed and 12 dead.
context: On this narrower per-group accounting the bystanders were about two-thirds of all the paralysis - 113 of 169 - so more of the permanently crippled were people who never received the vaccine than were vaccinated children. Keep it separate from the headline figure usually quoted (roughly 120,000 defective doses, over 200,000 children vaccinated in five states, about 40,000 ill, about 200 paralytic cases with over 160 permanent, 10 deaths), which counts vaccinees and contacts together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories, citing Nathanson N. & Langmuir A.D., Am. J. Hyg. 1963;78:29-60, and Offit P.A., N Engl J Med 2005;352:1411-1412.

question: A congressional hearing in June 1955 put the blame not on Cutter but on the NIH laboratory that was supposed to be watching it; the NIH director resigned, and so did the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Later that year that laboratory was rebuilt as the Division of Biologics Standards. What power did the new division have?
answer: To test and release each lot before sale.
choices: To retest any lot after complaints arrived.
To test and release each lot before sale.
To license only firms with virus experience.
To publish each maker's own test results.
context: The Division of Biologics Standards held explicit authority over facility inspections, pre-licensing approval, and lot-by-lot federal potency and safety testing, replacing the earlier reliance on manufacturers' self-certification: no vaccine could be distributed until the DBS had verified it carried no live virus. The DBS ran until 1972, when its functions moved to the FDA's Bureau of Biologics. The officials who went: Secretary Oveta Culp Hobby, and NIH director William H. Sebrell Jr. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Cutter_Laboratories; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories (citing Edward Shorter, The Health Century, 1987).

question: Anne Gottsdanker took Cutter vaccine in her right thigh and was paralysed ten days later; at the trial in Oakland the lawyer Melvin Belli showed the jury that her lot had contained live virulent Type 1 poliovirus. In January 1958, after two days of deliberation, the jury voted ten to two that Cutter had not been negligent - that the company had made its vaccine as the industry and the federal licence required. What did the jury do next?
answer: It ordered Cutter to pay the families anyway.
choices: It cleared Cutter and awarded the families nothing.
It sent the case back to be tried a second time.
It divided the blame between Cutter and the NIH.
It ordered Cutter to pay the families anyway.
context: The same jury voted eleven to one that Cutter had broken an implied warranty - the law's presumption that a thing sold is fit for what it is sold for - and protested that the warranty law as the judge had spelled it out was 'extremely harsh.' The awards were $131,500 to the Gottsdankers and $15,800 to the Phippses, $147,300 in all. The California Court of Appeal affirmed on 12 July 1960, extending to vaccines and drugs the 'food exception' that lets a buyer sue a maker he never bought from directly: a company could be liable for harm with no negligence proved, even having made the product to industry standards under a federal licence. Paul Offit calls it liability without fault. Sources: TIME, 'Medicine: Cutter in Court', 27 January 1958; Gottsdanker v. Cutter Laboratories, 182 Cal.App.2d 602 (1960); discovery.org/a/2272/.

question: Jonas Salk's safety standard was straight-line inactivation: if formaldehyde killed poliovirus at a steady rate, a maker could calculate the moment when none was left rather than hunt for survivors. Salk told the Cutter court, 'I can produce safe vaccine with no live virus every time.' The Nobel laureate Wendell Stanley then testified for the other side. What did Stanley tell the court?
answer: That he had often seen the curve depart from that theory.
choices: That formaldehyde had never killed poliovirus reliably.
That Cutter had grown the wrong strain of poliovirus.
That he had often seen the curve depart from that theory.
That the 1954 field trial had been too small to judge.
context: TIME reported the exchange from the 1957-58 trial. Salk: 'I can produce safe vaccine with no live virus every time.' Wendell M. Stanley, from the stand: 'I have seen many times where the curve does not follow that theory.' Straight-line inactivation let a manufacturer calculate an endpoint instead of measuring it - which is exactly what failed when clumped debris kept formaldehyde off some virus particles. Sources: TIME, 'Medicine: Cutter in Court', 27 January 1958; gavi.org/vaccineswork/book-club/review-cutter-incident-paul-offit.

question: The fullest account of the Cutter incident - the warning that was shelved, the lots that passed their tests, the liability without fault - is a 2005 Yale University Press book, The Cutter Incident, by Paul Offit. What else is Offit known for in the vaccine world?
answer: He co-invented a rotavirus vaccine and advised the CDC.
choices: He argued the vaccine-injury cases in the federal courts.
He co-invented a rotavirus vaccine and advised the CDC.
He ran the NIH laboratory that licensed the 1955 vaccine.
He directed the March of Dimes fundraising campaigns.
context: Paul Offit directs the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, co-invented the RotaTeq rotavirus vaccine, sat on the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices from 1998 to 2003, co-edits Plotkin's Vaccines and holds the Albert B. Sabin Gold Medal - the most prominent public defender of vaccination in America. He also wrote the companion paper 'The Cutter incident, 50 years later' (N Engl J Med 2005;352:1411-1412). Offit was born in Baltimore in 1951; his family's pediatrician delayed his own polio vaccine because of Cutter, and at five, recovering from clubfoot surgery, he spent months in a ward beside polio patients in iron lungs. The 1955 record is not hidden: it was assembled and published by the movement's leading advocate. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Paul_Offit; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutter_Laboratories.

question: On 6 April 1938 at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory in New Jersey, Jack Rebok opened the valve on a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas and nothing came out. The valve worked fine. Roy Plunkett made one check before writing the cylinder off. What did it show?
answer: He weighed it: it was still as heavy as a full one.
choices: He weighed it: it was still as heavy as a full one.
He soaped the valve seat: no bubbles rose at all.
He warmed it in a bath: a thin trickle of gas came.
He tilted it slowly: nothing shifted or sloshed.
context: Plunkett's own account, via the Science History Institute: when he and Rebok prepared the cylinder for use, none of the gas came out - yet the cylinder weighed the same as before. The scale is the hero of this story: an anomaly is only an anomaly if somebody measured. Plunkett's first thought was not triumph. Asked in a 1986 oral history what his reaction had been, he said: 'Well, we have to start over now.' He tested the batch anyway instead of throwing it out. Source: Science History Institute, 'Roy J. Plunkett'; Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'.

question: The slipperiest solid ever measured was found by a man who was not looking for a solid at all. Roy Plunkett was 27, two years out of an Ohio State doctorate, and DuPont had set him one assignment; tetrafluoroethylene was only the raw material for it. What was the assignment?
answer: A non-toxic replacement refrigerant.
choices: A non-toxic replacement refrigerant.
A non-flammable dry-cleaning solvent.
A non-corrosive hydraulic fluid.
A non-toxic fumigant for grain stores.
context: Plunkett had no business recognising a polymer: his 1936 Ohio State doctorate was titled 'The Mechanism of Carbohydrate Oxidation.' His college roommate at Manchester College, Paul Flory, would win the 1974 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for exactly this field - the physical chemistry of polymers. The specific target DuPont set him was the compound CF2Cl-CF2H, chosen because Frigidaire already held the patent on Freon-114 and DuPont wanted a way around it; tetrafluoroethylene was only the feedstock. Source: Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett'; Science History Institute, 'Roy J. Plunkett'.

question: In the spring of 1938 Roy Plunkett and Jack Rebok had made about a hundred pounds of tetrafluoroethylene at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory, and they did not simply stand the cylinders on a shelf. Every one was packed in dry ice. Why the cold?
answer: Warm, the gas would explode and burst the cylinder.
choices: Warm, the gas would explode and burst the cylinder.
Warm, the gas would leak past the valve packing.
Warm, the gas would corrode the steel from inside.
Warm, the gas would slowly turn poisonous to breathe.
context: Roughly 100 pounds of tetrafluoroethylene went into pressure cylinders packed in dry ice, specifically so the gas would not explode or rupture its container; one RSC account puts a single cylinder's contents at about 1 kg. Tetrafluoroethylene is documented as liable to explode when exposed to heat, light or contaminants. Both men already knew this gas was touchy before anything went wrong - which is what makes what they did next remarkable. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'; RSC Education, 'The discovery of Teflon'.

question: In April 1938 a DuPont cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene refused to empty and still weighed full, so Roy Plunkett and Jack Rebok took a saw to its steel shell - a deliberate decision, with that gas's habit of exploding well known to both of them. What did they find inside?
answer: A white waxy powder packed on the bottom and lower walls.
choices: A white waxy powder packed on the bottom and lower walls.
A clear oily liquid pooled in the bottom of the shell.
A grey metallic crust grown over the inside of the steel.
A dry brown scale ringing the throat of the valve.
context: Plunkett's own account: 'When he opened the valve - to let the TFE gas flow under its own pressure from the cylinder - nothing happened... we decided to cut open the cylinder. When we did, we found more of the powder packed onto the bottom and lower sides of the cylinder.' Another account has the first shake sending a whitish powder down onto the lab bench. The gas had polymerised itself into PTFE with nobody adding anything. Source: Plunkett's account via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_J._Plunkett; Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene'.

question: Roy Plunkett's laboratory powder did not walk into kitchens by itself. In France in the early 1950s an engineer named Marc Gregoire was coating something of his own with it, and his wife Colette watched him do it and told him to put the same coating on her frying pan. What had Gregoire been coating?
answer: His aluminium fishing tackle, to stop the line tangling.
choices: His aluminium fishing tackle, to stop the line tangling.
His bicycle chain, to stop the links from seizing.
His ski bases, to make them run faster on wet snow.
His garden shears, to stop sap gumming the blades.
context: Gregoire's French patent was granted in 1954 and he founded Tefal near Paris in 1956. The US FDA cleared PTFE for food contact in 1960, and Marion Trozzolo sold the first American-made version, the Happy Pan, from 1961 - twenty-three years after the cylinder was opened. Source: Grokipedia, 'Non-stick surface'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-stick_surface; Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'.

question: Aqua regia dissolves gold; poured on PTFE it does nothing at all. The molecule is only a plain chain of carbon atoms, but every carbon is sheathed in fluorine. What is it about that sheath that leaves an attacking chemical nowhere to start?
answer: Fluorine holds carbon in the strongest single bond carbon forms.
choices: Fluorine holds carbon in the strongest single bond carbon forms.
Fluorine gives the whole chain a charge that repels acids.
Fluorine packs the chains too tightly for acid to seep in.
Fluorine caps the chain ends so no reaction can spread.
context: The carbon-fluorine bond has a dissociation energy of about 485 kJ/mol - the strongest single bond carbon forms in organic chemistry, against roughly 413 for carbon-hydrogen and 348 for carbon-carbon. The consequences, in numbers: a coefficient of friction of 0.05-0.10, the lowest of any solid material; surface free energy of only about 18-20 mN/m, where untreated cotton is 40-50; water beading at a contact angle near 110 degrees; continuous service to 260 degrees C. Aqua regia and chlorosulfonic acid do nothing to it; the only things that attack it are molten alkali metals and certain fluorinating agents. Source: Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon-fluorine_bond.

question: PTFE's inertness came with a bill attached. Heated, it never really flows - its melt viscosity is around 10^11 pascal-seconds, so it barely moves at all. How do factories shape the loose powder into gaskets and sheet?
answer: They press the powder in a mould and fire it, the way you fire a ceramic.
choices: They press the powder in a mould and fire it, the way you fire a ceramic.
They dissolve the powder in solvent and cast it, the way you cast varnish.
They soften the powder in steam and roll it, the way you roll rubber.
They compress the powder cold and bond the layers, the way you press plywood.
context: The process is called sintering: the powder is compacted in a mould and held at 360-380 degrees C, fusing without ever melting, exactly the way a ceramic is fired. Because its melt viscosity is on the order of 10^11 Pa.s, PTFE cannot be injection-moulded like an ordinary plastic. Its inertness was itself the first engineering problem it created. Source: Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene'; Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett'.

question: Open almost any account of Teflon's discovery and you meet the same photograph: three men in shirtsleeves bent over a cylinder, cutting it open, Roy Plunkett among them. It is captioned as 6 April 1938. The caption is wrong. Why?
answer: The picture was staged in 1966, with the three men posing.
choices: The picture was staged in 1966, with the three men posing.
The man holding the saw is Plunkett's supervisor, not Plunkett.
The picture shows a second cylinder, opened some weeks later.
The picture was taken in 1938 but at a different DuPont plant.
context: No photograph of the actual 6 April 1938 moment exists. The famous image was staged in 1966, with Plunkett, Robert McHarness and Jack Rebok posing over a cylinder. Plunkett went on to the John Scott Medal in 1951, the Plastics Hall of Fame in 1973 and the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1985; he died on 12 May 1994, aged 83. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Long, Strange History of Teflon'; Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett'.

question: PTFE's first real job was not a frying pan. In 1942 DuPont offered the still-secret material to a government plant at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where it went into gaskets and valve seals along more than four hundred miles of steel piping - and held until the site closed in 1985. What was destroying the ordinary seals?
answer: Uranium hexafluoride, the gas the plant pushed through the pipes.
choices: Uranium hexafluoride, the gas the plant pushed through the pipes.
Nitric acid, the bath used to strip and replate the pipes.
Molten sodium, the coolant circulating in the plant's loops.
Chlorine gas, the by-product vented from the plating shop.
context: The plant was K-25, the gaseous diffusion facility; its converter shells and pipes were nickel-plated steel, and uranium hexafluoride was chewing through the gaskets and valve seals meant to contain it. In the words of one account, DuPont came saying 'we have this unique family of materials, we think it would make a good corrosion resistant gasket.' PTFE sealed that piping from 1942 until the facility closed in 1985. The material stayed a war secret: patent applied for 1 July 1939 and granted 4 February 1941 as U.S. Patent 2,230,654, 'Tetrafluoroethylene Polymers'; DuPont registered the name TEFLON only in 1945, and the first commercial sales came in 1946 - eight years after the cylinder was cut open. Source: Smithsonian Magazine; American Chemical Society, 'Uranium isotopes' landmark; Grokipedia, 'Tetrafluoroethylene'.

question: At 3M in 1953 Patsy Sherman and Samuel Smith were chasing a rubber that jet fuel could not dissolve. An assistant knocked a bottle of Sherman's experimental fluorochemical latex off the bench, splashing it across the assistant's new white canvas tennis shoes. Sherman watched that shoe over the following days. What had the splash done to it?
answer: The splashed patch stayed clean while the rest of the shoe grew dirty.
choices: The splashed patch stayed clean while the rest of the shoe grew dirty.
The splashed patch turned glassy while the rest of the shoe stayed rough.
The splashed patch went brittle while the rest of the shoe stayed soft.
The splashed patch faded grey while the rest of the shoe stayed white.
context: Sherman said the treated canvas shed liquid 'like water off a duck's back.' She and Smith spent about three years turning the ruined shoe into a product: Scotchgard, launched in 1956 and sold first to textile mills rather than shoppers. They ended up holding 13 joint patents in fluorochemical polymers. Sherman was the first woman named to 3M's Carlton Society, in 1974, and was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2001. Her line: 'Girls should follow their dreams. They can do anything anybody else can do.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy_Sherman; Grokipedia, 'Scotchgard'; invent.org, 'Patsy Sherman and Samuel Smith'.

question: By 1969 Bob Gore had spent months trying to stretch heated PTFE rods by about ten per cent, and they kept snapping. One October night he changed a single thing about how he pulled, and the rod stretched roughly eight hundred per cent, opening into a solid that is about seventy per cent air. What did he change?
answer: He yanked the rod fast instead of drawing it slowly.
choices: He yanked the rod fast instead of drawing it slowly.
He chilled the rod first instead of heating it through.
He pulled in short repeated tugs instead of one long draw.
He twisted the rod as he pulled instead of pulling straight.
context: The result is expanded PTFE, or ePTFE: microporous, about 70 per cent air, and the basis of Gore-Tex fabric, vascular grafts and Elixir guitar strings. The trick was the speed of the pull - the opposite of what patience would tell you to do. Source: Science History Institute, 'Robert W. Gore'; invent.org, 'Robert W. Gore'.

question: Roy Plunkett's cylinder at DuPont in 1938 had nothing poured into it, yet the tetrafluoroethylene inside turned itself into a solid polymer - against everything polymer science of the day predicted. Chemists have argued about what set the reaction off ever since. Which is the prime suspect?
answer: The iron of the cylinder wall itself.
choices: The iron of the cylinder wall itself.
The pressure of the compressed gas alone.
Heat left from the pump that filled it.
The jolt of the cylinder being moved.
context: Grokipedia records the white solid as forming 'due to spontaneous polymerization, likely initiated by trace impurities or the iron surface of the container.' Tetrafluoroethylene is separately documented as liable to explosive polymerization when exposed to heat, light or contaminants. An RSC piece notes that even now 'no one seems to have a clear explanation' of the exact trigger - the honest answer is that the leading suspect is the cylinder's own iron acting as a catalyst under pressure, and that it has never been proven. Grokipedia's note on the period is that the reaction ran against the predictions of polymer science of the day. Source: Grokipedia, 'Roy J. Plunkett' and 'Tetrafluoroethylene'; RSC Education, 'The discovery of Teflon'.

question: PFOA, a processing chemical used in making PTFE since 1951, turned up in the blood of the men who worked in the fluorochemical plants. Researchers followed a group of them who had retired and taken in none of it since, drawing blood to measure what was left. How long did a man need to shed just half of the PFOA he already carried?
answer: About four years.
choices: About four years.
About four days.
About four weeks.
About four decades.
context: The same carbon-fluorine bonds that make PTFE untouchable are why the PFAS family does not break down in a river or a bloodstream either. In retired fluorochemical production workers the measured mean serum elimination half-life was about 3.8 years for PFOA and about 5.4 years for PFOS - years, not days, for the body to clear half of what it holds. PFOA was the processing surfactant used in making PTFE from 1951; US manufacturers phased it out by the end of 2015 under the EPA's PFOA Stewardship Program. Purified PTFE itself is a large molecule the body does not absorb, and has been FDA-cleared for food contact since 1960: the persistence problem is the small processing chemicals, not the finished pan. Source: Olsen et al., serum elimination half-life study, PMC1964923; Grokipedia, 'Polytetrafluoroethylene' and 'Non-stick surface'.

question: Until 2019 the kilogram was defined by a single actual physical thing - one small cylinder sitting in a vault outside Paris that every scale in the world ultimately answered to. What was that cylinder made of?
answer: platinum-iridium alloy
choices: platinum-iridium alloy
polished tungsten carbide
sintered ceramic and gold
solid quartz crystal
context: The International Prototype of the Kilogram (nicknamed Le Grand K), a cylinder about the size of a plum, was 90% platinum and 10% iridium - chosen for hardness and chemical stability. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Prototype_of_the_Kilogram.

question: The cylinder that defined the kilogram was locked in a safe at the BIPM in Sevres under three nested glass bell jars. Opening the safe required something no single BIPM official could carry alone. What was that requirement?
answer: three separate keys, held by three different custodians
choices: three separate keys, held by three different custodians
a written order signed by the French Minister of Science
an escort of French national police officers
a matching key issued to the visiting national laboratory
context: All three custodians had to be physically present. The cylinder was compared to its official copies only three times in about 130 years. Source: smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/redefine-kilogram.

question: Over about a century the Paris prototype and its official copies quietly drifted apart by roughly 50 micrograms - about the mass of a fingerprint. Yet nobody could say WHICH object had actually changed. Why not?
answer: the prototype could not itself be weighed - it WAS one kilogram by definition
choices: the prototype could not itself be weighed - it WAS one kilogram by definition
the copies were kept in labs that no longer trusted each other's balances
the drift was below what any balance of that era could resolve
the older comparison records had been lost in the two world wars
context: By law and convention, Le Grand K WAS the kilogram; it could only be compared to something else. If it and the copies disagreed, the copies were 'wrong.' The direction of the drift is genuinely unresolved. Source: chemistryworld.com/news/game-over-for-the-original-kilogram.

question: The kilogram was the last hold-out. The second had already escaped the astronomers and been redefined in 1967 in terms of an atom - a specific number of oscillations of one particular atom's radiation. Which atom was chosen?
answer: caesium-133
choices: caesium-133
hydrogen-1
krypton-86
strontium-87
context: One SI second = 9,192,631,770 periods of the transition between the two hyperfine levels of caesium-133's ground state. Krypton-86 was the atomic standard for the metre (1960-1983). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second.

question: In 1983 the CGPM redefined the metre in terms of a constant of nature, and this move had a surprising side effect: one quantity that had, until then, been an experimental result was suddenly fixed by fiat and could no longer, in principle, be measured. Which quantity STOPPED being a measurement and BECAME a definition?
answer: the speed of light in vacuum
choices: the speed of light in vacuum
the wavelength of the sodium D-line
the length of the equatorial degree
the local strength of Earth's gravity
context: The 1983 definition: one metre = the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Every improvement in measurement now refines the METRE, not c. This is the trick of every constant-anchored definition: fix a number of nature and let the unit float to it. Source: bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/17-1983/resolution-1.

question: A completely independent challenger to the electromagnetic route came at the problem from the opposite end - it tried to COUNT the atoms in a single object. To do that, the International Avogadro Project grew and polished a small sphere of almost perfectly pure silicon-28, roughly 94 mm across and often called the roundest object ever manufactured. Why did they insist on the pure silicon-28 isotope in particular?
answer: so nearly every atom in the sphere had the same mass, simplifying the count
choices: so nearly every atom in the sphere had the same mass, simplifying the count
so the sphere would not slowly release radiation into the lab
so the polishing lasers would not scatter off other isotopes
so the crystal would grow in a perfect body-centred cubic pattern
context: The spheres are about 99.9995% silicon-28. Surface deviations were below about 50 nanometres - if scaled up to Earth-size, the tallest mountain to deepest trench would be only a few metres. Source: nist.gov/si-redefinition/kilogram/kilogram-silicon-spheres.

question: The 2019 redefinition was blocked for years even after the Kibble balance was producing perfectly usable numbers for the Planck constant. What further evidence did the CGPM demand before it would accept a new value of h and rewrite the kilogram around it?
answer: independent confirmation by the silicon-sphere atom-count to the required precision
choices: independent confirmation by the silicon-sphere atom-count to the required precision
a fresh 'periodic verification' of Le Grand K against its official copies
adoption of the Kibble balance by at least three national metrology institutes
reduction of the balance's uncertainty below one part in a billion
context: Two routes with entirely different error sources landing on the same Planck value is a stronger check than any single number: if two independent methods agree, unknown systematic errors are unlikely to be moving them together. Only when the Kibble and Avogadro projects converged did the CGPM lock in h. Source: physicsworld.com/a/new-definition-of-the-kilogram-comes-into-force.

question: On 20 May 2019 - World Metrology Day - the redefinition took effect. The SI fixed one number at an exact value with no error bar, and the kilogram was then written in terms of it. Which constant was pinned at exactly 6.62607015e-34 joule-seconds?
answer: the Planck constant
choices: the Planck constant
the Boltzmann constant
the elementary charge
the Avogadro constant
context: Boltzmann's k, the elementary charge e, and Avogadro's N were also fixed at exact numbers on the same day, but the KILOGRAM keys off the Planck constant via the Kibble route. Those constants stopped being measurements and became definitions. Source: physicsworld.com/a/new-definition-of-the-kilogram-comes-into-force.

question: What does the 2019 redefinition BUY you in practice - the thing you could not do while the kilogram was defined by a French cylinder?
answer: a properly equipped lab anywhere on Earth or Mars can realise a kilogram from scratch
choices: a properly equipped lab anywhere on Earth or Mars can realise a kilogram from scratch
the world's national kilogram copies could finally be replaced with fresh, undrifted platinum-iridium cylinders
the BIPM could ship certified 1 kg wafers of silicon-28 to any national lab on demand
atomic clocks became accurate enough to detect Le Grand K's drift in real time
context: The point of a natural-constant definition: no shipping, no borrowing, no French artifact. Give a lab a Kibble balance, the defined value of h, and the SI second, and it can build a kilogram out of physics. Source: nist.gov/si-redefinition/kilogram.

question: In early-1600s Padua, Santorio Santorio spent about thirty years living in a large hanging chair he had built, meticulously weighing every meal, drink, and excretion. The books never balanced -- his intake was much heavier than what came out. Where did Santorio conclude the missing weight had gone?
answer: Out through his skin and breath as an invisible loss
choices: Out through his skin and breath as an invisible loss
Into the growth of his own bones and muscles
Down into the wooden chair itself as absorbed sweat
Up into the air only when he laughed or shouted
context: Ars de statica medicina (1614) names the loss perspiratio insensibilis -- insensible perspiration. A kid with a bathroom scale can watch the same gap open overnight. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorio_Santorio

question: In 1929 in Eberswalde, Germany, Werner Forssmann was a 25-year-old surgical trainee who had been forbidden to try what he was about to try. He picked up a thin rubber tube used for draining urine and passed it 65 cm up a vein in his own arm, aiming for one specific place. Where did he stop?
answer: Inside the right side of his own heart
choices: Inside the right side of his own heart
In a vein at the back of his own throat
In the artery running to his own liver
Just above his own collarbone
context: Before that day, textbooks warned that any catheter reaching the heart chambers would trigger fatal spasm. Forssmann needed to prove otherwise, so he chose himself as the patient. Source: http://scihi.org/werner-forssmann-cardiac-catheterization/

question: With the catheter still inside his own heart, Werner Forssmann needed a documentary record before anyone could dismiss what he had done. What did the trainee do next?
answer: Walked to the radiology department to have himself X-rayed
choices: Walked to the radiology department to have himself X-rayed
Photographed his own chest through a shaving mirror
Sent his nurse to fetch a chaplain as an eyewitness
Waited for a colleague to trace the tube on his skin in ink
context: The chest film, catheter tip clearly inside the heart, ran with his write-up in Klinische Wochenschrift in November 1929. His boss fired him and cardiology closed to him; he moved to urology. Source: https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(18)30548-2/fulltext

question: Cuba, summer 1900. Jesse Lazear of the US Army's Yellow Fever Commission wanted to know whether the mosquito really carried yellow fever from patient to patient. Rather than wait, he let mosquitoes that had bitten yellow-fever patients bite him. What happened to Lazear?
answer: He caught yellow fever and died within weeks
choices: He caught yellow fever and died within weeks
He caught it and recovered in a fortnight
He never caught it and lived to publish his data
He caught malaria instead and pulled through
context: Lazear died on 25 September 1900, aged 34. The commission was later so shaken by his death that Walter Reed drew up written contracts, in Spanish and English, promising volunteers $100 in gold and $100 more if they took ill -- among the first written informed-consent forms in medical research. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_William_Lazear

question: In 1892 in Munich, the eminent hygienist Max von Pettenkofer set out to prove, in front of witnesses, that a mere germ could not by itself cause cholera. He was about to swallow a flask of billions of live Vibrio cholerae bacteria, and he took one deliberate precaution first. What did he do just before drinking?
answer: Drank baking soda to neutralise his stomach acid
choices: Drank baking soda to neutralise his stomach acid
Fasted for three days to empty his gut of food
Warmed the flask to blood temperature in his armpit
Injected himself with a mild sedative to slow digestion
context: Pettenkofer suffered only diarrhoea and announced that he had been vindicated. He had not. Robert Koch had isolated the cholera vibrio in 1884; Pettenkofer's mild illness was a sample of one, and the drinker is the person least able to judge his own result. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Joseph_von_Pettenkofer

question: The catheter Werner Forssmann wanted was locked away and his supervisor had forbidden the stunt. He talked the surgical nurse Gerda Ditzen into fetching the instruments -- but she would only agree if he tried it on her, not himself, and she lay down and let him strap her arm to the table. What did Forssmann do next?
answer: He slipped away and threaded the tube up his own arm instead
choices: He slipped away and threaded the tube up his own arm instead
He performed the catheterisation on Ditzen as she had asked
He untied her and confessed the plan to his supervisor
He waited until she dozed off, then began the puncture on her wrist
context: Ditzen only realised she had been tricked when she caught sight of him at a mirror, tube already in his vein; she then followed him to the X-ray room and helped push the catheter the rest of the way. Source: https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(18)30548-2/fulltext

question: Twenty-seven years after Werner Forssmann was fired for the tube-in-his-own-heart stunt, a New York pair -- Andre Cournand and Dickinson Richards -- had turned it into cardiac catheterisation, the standard way to measure pressure inside a living heart. What did the Nobel Committee do about that in 1956?
answer: Awarded the prize jointly to Forssmann, Cournand, and Richards
choices: Awarded the prize jointly to Forssmann, Cournand, and Richards
Awarded it to Cournand and Richards, passing Forssmann over
Awarded it to Forssmann alone as the original discoverer
Awarded it to the Eberswalde hospital where the first film was taken
context: Forssmann, then a small-town urologist, said he felt like the village priest who had suddenly been made a bishop. Every modern procedure that threads a wire into a blocked coronary artery -- angioplasty, stenting, ablation -- descends from his 1929 self-experiment. Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Werner-Forssmann

question: A modern doctor who wanted to run Pettenkofer's or Forssmann's experiment on themselves today could not simply do it. The rules changed after cases like these. What must a researcher who wants to experiment on their own body now get first?
answer: Written approval from an outside ethics committee
choices: Written approval from an outside ethics committee
A signed waiver from their own medical insurer
A second doctor to run the same test on themselves
A patent on the technique they intend to try
context: Research authorities now treat an experiment on the researcher's own body as human-subject research needing outside review -- for exactly Feynman's reason: 'you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.' Source: https://hekint.org/2026/08/31/self-experimentation/

question: The paper that announced the shape of DNA — a note in the journal Nature dated 25 April 1953, barely more than a page long — carried exactly one picture. What was that single picture?
answer: a hand drawing of the helix made by Odile Crick, an artist
choices: a hand drawing of the helix made by Odile Crick, an artist
an X-ray photograph of DNA fibres taken by Rosalind Franklin
a chart of the four base amounts measured by Erwin Chargaff
a sketch of a single base pair drawn by Jerry Donohue
context: Odile Crick was Francis Crick's wife and a professional artist. In March or April 1953 she drew the two ribbons and their connecting rungs to her husband's spoken instructions — the first picture ever made of the double helix, and it has been called the most famous scientific drawing of the twentieth century. The paper itself ran under two pages, with that one illustration and no data at all. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odile_Crick; royalsociety.org/blog/2018/04/history-of-the-double-helix/; embryo.asu.edu (Watson and Crick, 1953).

question: James Watson and Francis Crick cracked the structure of DNA at Cambridge without running an experiment of their own: the X-ray measurements came from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London. What did the pair spend their days doing instead?
answer: clamping metal parts into a model of the molecule
choices: clamping metal parts into a model of the molecule
hunting the literature for a matching molecule
deriving the shape by algebra from published angles
queuing for time on Cambridge's EDSAC computer
context: The parts came out of the Cambridge metal shop: cut plates for the bases, rods and clamps for the backbone. Watson gradually accumulated the list of pieces and assembled them while Crick advised. Every number came from somebody else — the X-ray measurements from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London, the base ratios from Erwin Chargaff at Columbia, the chemistry advice from Jerry Donohue. Building a model out of other people's measurements is how a great deal of theoretical work gets done — and it is also why who was owed what credit for DNA has been argued over ever since. Sources: scientificamerican.com/blog/the-curious-wavefunction/the-structure-of-dna-61-years-later-how-they-did-it/; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/francis-crick-rosalind-franklin-james-watson-and-maurice-wilkins/

question: James Watson's memoir The Double Helix tells a story Francis Crick himself never remembered: on the lunchtime in 1953 when their model finally came together, Crick walked into the Eagle, a pub near the Cavendish Laboratory, and announced to the whole room what the two of them had just found. By the legend, what did he say they had found?
answer: the secret of life
choices: the secret of life
the shape of the gene
the key to inheritance
the plan of the cell
context: The line survives only in Watson's telling. Crick said he had no memory of saying it, and nobody else recorded it at the time. Repeat a story often enough and it becomes part of the furniture — a good reminder that a famous quotation and a documented one are not the same thing. Source: scalar.fas.harvard.edu/the-river-divides-into-thousands-of-branches (chapter 7).  (Legend.)

question: Before 1950 most biochemists wrote DNA off as too dull to carry heredity: a monotonous repeat of the four bases in equal amounts. Erwin Chargaff at Columbia broke DNA apart, spread the bases out on paper and measured each by the ultraviolet light it swallowed. Calf thymus gave him about 30% adenine. What else did his numbers show, species after species?
answer: adenine matched thymine, and guanine matched cytosine
choices: adenine matched thymine, and guanine matched cytosine
adenine matched guanine, and thymine matched cytosine
every species gave the amounts calf thymus gave
each base rose and fell with the animal's size
context: Chargaff hydrolysed DNA, separated the bases by paper chromatography and measured them by absorbance at 260 nanometres. Calf thymus came out near 30% adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine and 20% cytosine, and the A-with-T, G-with-C match held sample after sample. That killed the 'tetranucleotide' idea that DNA was a boring repeating unit — and the match only makes sense if A sits opposite T and G opposite C the whole way down the ladder. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Chargaff%27s_rules

question: Watson and Crick's note in Nature of 25 April 1953 ran barely more than a page and closed with one deadpan sentence now among the most quoted in science. Having described how the bases pair off across the ladder, they wrote that it had 'not escaped our notice' that this specific pairing 'immediately suggests' something. What did they say it suggested?
answer: a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material
choices: a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material
a possible chemical basis for the mutation of genes
a possible route from a gene to a finished protein
a possible reason for the variety of living species
context: The sentence in full: 'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.' — J. D. Watson and F. H. C. Crick, 'Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids', Nature 171, 25 April 1953. It is the punchline of the whole structure: because each strand spells out the complete instructions for building the other, the shape itself answers how a cell copies its genes. Source: annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/printit.html (annotated full text).

question: Watson and Crick's ladder holds every rung to the same width — a large base always facing a small one — and each rung is clasped shut by hydrogen bonds, weak links where two atoms share a hydrogen between them. Weak is deliberate: these are the links that must let go when the strands part. How many hydrogen bonds hold a G-C rung, and how many an A-T rung?
answer: three across a G-C rung, and two across an A-T rung
choices: three across a G-C rung, and two across an A-T rung
two across a G-C rung, and three across an A-T rung
four across a G-C rung, and three across an A-T rung
two across a G-C rung, and two across an A-T rung
context: Two hydrogen bonds hold an A-T rung; three hold a G-C rung. G-C-rich DNA does melt at a higher temperature — for a short strand in standard salt, Tm = 69.3 + 0.41(%GC) − 650/length, so the melting point climbs about 0.41 degrees Celsius for every extra percent of G and C, and anyone designing PCR primers uses that every working day. The textbook then adds one step too many and credits the extra bond for the extra heat. When Yakovchuk, Protozanova and Frank-Kamenetskii measured the two forces separately in 2006, that G-C effect turned out to come from how neighbouring bases stack face to face rather than from the third hydrogen bond — the counting is right, the explanation usually hung on it is not. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix; Yakovchuk, Protozanova & Frank-Kamenetskii, Nucleic Acids Research 34(2):564-574, 2006.

question: The double helix solved one problem and created another it could not touch. A human cell nucleus measures about six thousandths of a millimetre across, and the DNA inside it, pulled out straight, would run about two metres — the textbook comparison is packing 40 kilometres of very fine thread into a tennis ball. What does the cell do to fit it in?
answer: winds it in short lengths around millions of protein spools
choices: winds it in short lengths around millions of protein spools
folds it flat into sheets stacked like the pages of a book
cuts it into pieces stored in separate walled compartments
twists it into one tight rope coiled from corner to corner
context: Roughly 147 base pairs wind about 1.65 left-handed turns around each spool — a core of eight histone proteins, two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 — touching the protein every 10 base pairs and bending to a radius of about 4.2 nanometres. There are millions of these spools in a single nucleus. Alberts' Molecular Biology of the Cell states the problem as 'geometrically equivalent to packing 40 km (24 miles) of extremely fine thread into a tennis ball!' Sources: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK26834/; grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix

question: Watson and Crick's structure implied how a cell copies its genes, but implying is not proving. In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen-15 until every DNA molecule was weighted, then switched them to ordinary nitrogen-14 and spun the DNA in a density gradient — a tube in which molecules settle out by weight. After exactly one generation, what did the tube show?
answer: one band, sitting exactly half-way between heavy and light
choices: one band, sitting exactly half-way between heavy and light
two bands, one heavy and one light, in equal amounts
one band, still sitting where the heavy DNA had been
a smear spread evenly along the whole length of the tube
context: A single band at exactly intermediate density means every molecule was half old and half new — one original strand paired with one freshly built one, precisely as the structure demanded. After two generations the tube showed half intermediate and half light, which is what you get if those hybrid molecules split again. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix (Meselson-Stahl section).

question: Linus Pauling submitted his own structure for DNA on 31 December 1952, and it appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that February — weeks before Watson and Crick published. Pauling had just solved the alpha-helix of proteins, and he would win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry the next year. What had he proposed?
answer: three chains wound together with the phosphates at the core
choices: three chains wound together with the phosphates at the core
two chains wound together with the sugars at the core
one chain folded back on itself into a flat pleated sheet
four chains braided around a core of trapped water
context: Pauling and Corey's 'A Proposed Structure For The Nucleic Acids' ran in PNAS 39(2):84-97: three chains around a central axis, the phosphate groups crammed inside and the bases sticking outward like the spokes of a bicycle wheel — exactly inside-out from the truth. Watson and Crick had built the same wrong idea themselves on 28 November 1951 and watched it collapse within days, when colleagues from King's College pointed out they had badly miscounted how much water the molecule carries. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Linus_Pauling; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.39.2.84; royalsociety.org/blog/2018/04/history-of-the-double-helix/

question: For weeks James Watson pushed cut-out cardboard shapes of the four bases around his desk at the Cavendish, trying to fit them into a ladder of constant width, and nothing came out even. Jerry Donohue, a chemist who shared his office and had trained under Linus Pauling, looked at the cardboard and told him the textbook pictures he had copied were guessing. What had Watson drawn wrong?
answer: hydrogen atoms drawn on the wrong side of each base
choices: hydrogen atoms drawn on the wrong side of each base
one extra ring on two of the four base shapes
the angle at which each base joins its sugar
the gap he left between one base and the next
context: Watson had copied guanine and thymine in their rare 'enol' forms; Donohue told him those molecules strongly prefer the 'keto' forms, which puts a few hydrogen atoms somewhere else entirely. Watson had also been trying to pair like with like — adenine with adenine, guanine with guanine — which can never give a ladder of one width. He recut his cardboard shapes, and A-T and G-C fell out on Saturday 28 February 1953. The paper thanks him in a single line: 'We are much indebted to Dr. Jerry Donohue for constant advice and criticism, especially on interatomic distances.' Sources: scientificamerican.com/blog/the-curious-wavefunction/the-structure-of-dna-61-years-later-how-they-did-it/; annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/printit.html

question: Linus Pauling's DNA model of early 1953 packed three phosphate backbones into the core of the molecule, where their negative charges sat close enough to shove the whole structure apart. Pauling saw the problem and wrote in a fix — and it was that fix, more than the three chains, that Watson and Crick attacked in print weeks later. What was Pauling's fix?
answer: he left a hydrogen attached to every phosphate group
choices: he left a hydrogen attached to every phosphate group
he threaded magnesium ions between the three backbones
he angled every phosphate away from its neighbours
he packed a sleeve of water between the chains
context: A phosphate group carries its negative charge because it lets go of an acidic hydrogen into the water. Pauling drew those hydrogens still attached — which quietly meant that deoxyribonucleic acid, in his model, was not an acid at all. James Watson's verdict was that without ionized phosphates 'the chains would immediately fly apart', and he noted the sting: the correct chemistry was printed in Pauling's own textbook, General Chemistry. Watson and Crick put the objection in print, politely and lethally: 'We believe that the material which gives the X-ray diagrams is the salt, not the free acid. Without the acidic hydrogen atoms it is not clear what forces would hold the structure together, especially as the negatively charged phosphates near the axis will repel each other.' Pauling took it like a scientist — on 27 March 1953 he wrote that he was looking forward 'to finding out what the decision will be as to which is incorrect'. Sources: scarc.library.oregonstate.edu/coll/pauling/dna/narrative/page24.html; annex.exploratorium.edu/origins/coldspring/printit.html; paulingblog.wordpress.com

question: Every textbook picture of DNA gives the credit for holding the two strands together to the hydrogen bonds reaching across each rung. In 2006 Yakovchuk, Protozanova and Frank-Kamenetskii measured DNA molecules built with deliberate nicks and gaps, which let them weigh two different contributions separately — and the textbook picture had the strongest force wrong. What supplies roughly 70% of the molecule's stability?
