answer: the flat faces of neighbouring bases pressing together
choices: the flat faces of neighbouring bases pressing together
the salt ions the negative backbone pulls in from the water
the twist of the helix squeezing every rung inward
the sugars locking to one another along each backbone
context: Base stacking — flat faces pressed together by van der Waals attraction and by the hydrophobic effect of hiding those faces from water — accounts for roughly 70% of the free energy holding a duplex together. You can watch it happen: stacked bases shade one another, so double-stranded DNA swallows LESS ultraviolet at 260 nanometres than the same DNA taken apart. Heat a sample while watching that absorbance and it jumps as the helix melts — the hyperchromic effect, and the standard way melting temperatures are measured to this day. Sources: Yakovchuk, Protozanova & Frank-Kamenetskii, Nucleic Acids Research 34(2):564-574, 2006 (academic.oup.com/nar/article/34/2/564/2401647); grokipedia.com/page/Nucleic_acid_double_helix

question: A red laser pointer and one hair pulled from your own head are enough to do real optics on a bedroom wall tonight. Tape the hair upright across the beam — never aiming it near anyone's eyes — and let the light land on the wall a few paces away. What does that wall show?
answer: A row of bright spots split by dark gaps
choices: A row of bright spots split by dark gaps
A single crisp shadow with clean sharp edges
A soft red glow that fades evenly outward
A bright ring circling one dark centre spot
context: Babinet's principle: the diffraction pattern from an opaque body is identical to that from a hole of the same size and shape, apart from the forward beam. So a hair paints the same stripes a slit of its width would. The classroom demo uses a wire about 0.1 mm thick; a human hair is roughly 0.05-0.1 mm, the same scale. And it is measurable: bright-fringe spacing follows beta = lambda x L / d (wavelength times distance to the wall, divided by the separation), so with the pointer's wavelength and a pace-count to the wall, a ruler across the stripes lets you work back to the thickness of your own hair. Safety, per the standard protocols: avoid direct eye exposure, use a low-power pointer, block the beam past the wall. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Babinet's principle'; Grokipedia, 'Diffraction' and 'Double-slit experiment' (Standard Experimental Apparatus).

question: Around 1801 Thomas Young sent sunlight through a pinhole to make one clean beam, then split that beam in two so the halves overlapped further on. Bright and dark bands appeared on a distant screen, and their spacing gave him wavelengths close to modern values. What split the beam?
answer: A thin card held edgewise in the beam
choices: A thin card held edgewise in the beam
A pair of slits cut through blackened foil
A sewing needle stood upright in the beam
A fine wire of drawn gold stretched across it
context: Almost everyone pictures two slits. Young used a card about one-thirtieth of an inch wide, held edge-on in the sunbeam so its two sides acted as the pair of coherent sources. Careful with the dating: the November 1801 Bakerian Lecture was 'On the theory of light and colours' (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 92, 12-48), while the card experiment and the wavelength calculations appear in 'Experiments and calculations relative to physical optics', the 1803 Bakerian Lecture (Phil. Trans. 94, 1-16), and Physics World notes Young published no full account until his 1807 Lectures on Natural Philosophy. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment' (Origins in Classical Optics); Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (reference list); Grokipedia, 'Thomas Young (scientist)'.

question: In 1909 G. I. Taylor, a 23-year-old research student at the Cavendish under J. J. Thomson, set a sewing needle in front of a gas flame and choked the light with stack after stack of smoked glass, until his dimmest source was about as bright as a candle burning a mile away. To register any pattern at all on his photographic plate at that setting, how long did Taylor leave it exposed?
answer: Three months
choices: Three months
Three hours
Three days
Three weeks
context: Each smoked screen absorbed a large fraction of the light and the screens could be stacked, so Taylor could push the attenuation as far as he liked. At his feeblest setting there was, on average, roughly one photon at a time inside the apparatus. Published as G. I. Taylor, 'Interference fringes with feeble light', Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 15, 114-115 (1909). Sources: Wikipedia, 'G. I. Taylor'; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (candle quote and citation); Skulls in the Stars, 'Taylor sees the (feeble) light (1909)'.

question: In 1989 Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi filmed their detector while electrons arrived one at a time, each landing as a single bright dot. Their published photographs freeze the picture at 10 electrons, then 200, then 6,000, then 40,000, then 140,000. What did the plate look like at 10 electrons?
answer: A few scattered dots in no pattern
choices: A few scattered dots in no pattern
A few dots along one narrow band
A few faint stripes already crossing it
A few dots crowded at the centre
context: Random speckle at 10, unmistakable stripes at 140,000 — the pattern is not in any single electron, it is in the statistics of many. Tonomura, Endo, Matsuda, Kawasaki and Ezawa, 'Demonstration of single-electron buildup of an interference pattern', Am. J. Phys. 57, 117-120 (1989). In May 2002 Robert Crease asked Physics World's readers to name the most beautiful experiment in physics; more than 200 replied, with nominations ranging from Schroedinger's cat to the 1945 Trinity test, and this won — the only entry in the top ten with no scientist's name attached to it. Sources: Am. J. Phys. 57, 117 (1989) figure series; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (reporting Crease, September 2002).

question: To make electrons interfere, Gottfried Möllenstedt and Heinrich Düker at Tübingen in the mid-1950s strung a conducting thread across the beam to bend its two halves back together. No wire they could buy would do, so Möllenstedt made the thread himself, from a natural fibre coated in gold. What did he use for the fibre?
answer: Threads pulled from spiders' webs
choices: Threads pulled from spiders' webs
Threads unwound from silkworm cocoons
Hairs pulled from a horse's tail
Fibres teased from a cotton boll
context: The gold-coated fibre is the electron biprism, and it is what made electron interference practical. Physics World reports that Möllenstedt made the wires by coating fibres from spiders' webs with gold — 'indeed, it is said that he kept spiders in the laboratory for this purpose', a detail told as tradition rather than documented record. One of his Tübingen students, Claus Jönsson, would take the next step. Source: Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment'.  (Legend.)

question: G. I. Taylor shot five photographs of his fringe pattern — the alternating bright and dark bands — at wildly different light levels, the first at full brightness in minutes, the last from a source no stronger than a candle burning a mile away. Writing the result up for the Cambridge Philosophical Society, what did Taylor report about the plates made with the starved light?
answer: Their fringes had come out every bit as sharp as before
choices: Their fringes had come out every bit as sharp as before
Their fringes had shifted measurably closer together
Their fringes had faded into an even grey glow
Their fringes had inverted, bright bands turning dark
context: Taylor's own words: 'In no case was there any diminution in the sharpness of the pattern although the plates did not all reach the standard blackness of the first photograph.' Starving the light did nothing to the stripes. The sentence this result eventually led to is Dirac's, in The Principles of Quantum Mechanics (4th edn, p. 9): 'each photon then interferes only with itself.' Not particles of light jostling one another — one particle, doing it alone. Sources: Skulls in the Stars, 'Taylor sees the (feeble) light (1909)', quoting Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 15, 114; Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (Dirac quote and citation).

question: In the early 1970s three physicists in Bologna — Pier Giorgio Merli, GianFranco Missiroli and Giulio Pozzi — became the first to record electrons arriving one at a time and slowly piling up into interference fringes, using a Siemens electron microscope. To catch individual electrons landing they needed a detector far more sensitive than they owned, and they borrowed one. Where did their image intensifier come from?
answer: An anatomy institute in Milan
choices: An anatomy institute in Milan
A television studio in Rome
A military observatory in Turin
An astronomy institute in Bologna
context: The rig was a Siemens Elmiskop 101 and the intensifier was on loan from an anatomy institute in Milan. Their film 'Electron Interference' won the physics-category award at the International Festival on Scientific Cinematography in Brussels in 1976; the paper is Am. J. Phys. 44, 306-7 (1976), submitted May 1974 — fifteen years ahead of the famous Hitachi run, and still barely known. Merli's own account of how it happened: the first single-electron double-slit experiment 'was actually a by-product of research into the practical applications of electron interferometry.' Source: Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (letters from John Steeds and from Merli, Pozzi and Missiroli, May 2003).

question: Akira Tonomura's 1989 Hitachi run sent electrons through so sparsely — fewer than a thousand a second, never two inside the machine at once — that the interference pattern took more than twenty minutes to assemble itself dot by dot. A working laboratory is full of ordinary nuisances, and one of them could have ruined the picture before it finished. What would have wiped the pattern out?
answer: The apparatus drifting a fraction of a fringe's width
choices: The apparatus drifting a fraction of a fringe's width
The detector missing one electron in every hundred
The electrons arriving slower than one per second
The beam voltage rising by a few extra volts
context: Fringe spacing in the Hitachi rig was of order 900 angstroms, so a drift of a fraction of that over twenty minutes would have smeared every stripe into grey. Detection efficiency was almost 100% with error under 1%, using a fluorescent film plus a photon-counting image acquisition system adapted from Hamamatsu Photonics. The sparse beam was deliberate: physicists including Sin-Itiro Tomonaga had objected that fringes might come from electrons interacting on the way through, and Tonomura ran it 'from beginning to end with constant and extremely low electron intensities... so there was no chance of finding two or more electrons in the apparatus at the same time.' Sources: Tonomura's letter in Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment' (May 2003); fringe spacing from the matter-wave review arXiv:1211.3493.

question: Richard Feynman told readers of his Lectures on Physics that this experiment “contains the only mystery” in all of quantum mechanics — then warned them off it in the next breath: “you should not try to set up this experiment. This experiment has never been done in just this way... We are doing a thought experiment.” Feynman began giving those lectures in 1961, and Physics World notes it is not clear he ever learned that in that same year someone had run the thing for real — electrons, two slits, fringes on the far side. Who had already done it?
answer: Claus Jönsson, a physicist at Tübingen
choices: Claus Jönsson, a physicist at Tübingen
Gottfried Möllenstedt, a physicist at Tübingen
Lester Germer, a physicist at Bell Laboratories
Ernst Ruska, a physicist at Berlin
context: Jönsson, one of Möllenstedt's Tübingen students, ran the first actual electron double slit in 1961 with 40 keV electrons (de Broglie wavelength about 0.006 nm) — and did not stop at two, getting interference from up to five slits (Zeitschrift fuer Physik 161, 454-474). Because it was published in German it stayed obscure until the American Journal of Physics reprinted it in English thirteen years later, in 1974. Editors Anthony French and Edwin Taylor called it a 'great experiment' but noted there are 'few professional rewards' for doing 'real, pedagogically clean fundamental experiments', and admitted: 'Few such recent presentations acknowledge that the two-slit electron interference experiment has now been done.' Full quote of Feynman's larger claim, Lectures ch. 37-1 / Vol. III ch. 1-1 (1963): 'a phenomenon which is impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery.' Sources: Physics World, 'The double-slit experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment'; Feynman Lectures on Physics, ch. 37.

question: In 1999 Markus Arndt, Anton Zeilinger and their Vienna colleagues sent whole C60 buckyballs — sixty carbon atoms locked in a closed cage, 720 atomic mass units apiece — through a grating whose openings were 50 nanometres wide, and interference fringes appeared. What condition were the buckyballs themselves in as they flew through?
answer: Glowing at about 900 kelvin, fresh out of an oven
choices: Glowing at about 900 kelvin, fresh out of an oven
Chilled to about 3 kelvin in a jet of cold helium
Cooled to about 77 kelvin by a nitrogen-cooled nozzle
Held at about 300 kelvin, no warmer than the room
context: They made the beam by sublimating fullerene powder in an oven at about 900 K, so every molecule came through glowing hot and shuddering in 174 vibrational degrees of freedom — and it interfered anyway. Most probable velocity about 220 m/s; matter wavelength about 2.5 picometres, roughly 350-400 times smaller than the molecule itself, which is about a nanometre across. Molecules were counted by laser ionization. Arndt and colleagues: 'all these observations support the view that each carbon-60 molecule interferes with itself only.' Nature 401, 680-682 (1999). Sources: Physics World, 'Wave-particle duality seen in carbon-60 molecules'; Univ. Vienna QuantumNano, 'The Origin: C60 Diffraction'; review arXiv:1211.3493.

question: In 2019 Yaakov Fein, Stefan Gerlich, Markus Arndt and their Vienna colleagues built a two-metre-long interferometer and sent single tailored molecules through it — more than two thousand atoms apiece, over forty thousand protons, neutrons and electrons bound into one object, each staying in superposition, spread across both paths at once, for over seven milliseconds. Every moving object also has a matter wavelength, the wave-scale that governs how it interferes. How big was the matter wavelength of these molecules?
answer: About a thousandth of one hydrogen atom's width
choices: About a thousandth of one hydrogen atom's width
About the width of one whole hydrogen atom
About a thousand hydrogen atoms laid across
About the width of the whole molecule itself
context: The molecules were functionalized oligoporphyrins beyond 25,000 daltons; the largest single one was C707H260F908N16S53Zn4. Fein's own comment: 'Our experiments show that quantum mechanics, with all its weirdness, is also amazingly robust, and I'm optimistic that future experiments will test it on an even more massive scale.' Fein et al., 'Quantum superposition of molecules beyond 25 kDa', Nature Physics 15, 1242-1245 (2019). Sources: Nature Physics 15, 1242 (2019); phys.org, '2000 atoms in two places at once: A new record in quantum superposition'.

question: The story usually told is that G. I. Taylor's marathon 1909 exposure proved a single photon interferes with itself. Taylor's plates are real and his measurement was honest, but physicists today will not let that conclusion rest on them, because of what his light source was: a gas flame turned down behind smoked glass. What is the problem with a source like that?
answer: A dimmed flame emits its photons in random clumps
choices: A dimmed flame emits its photons in random clumps
A dimmed flame emits its photons in twinned pairs
A dimmed flame emits its photons in a strict even drumbeat
A dimmed flame emits its photons in one continuous stream
context: Attenuated thermal light keeps photon-number statistics that allow coincidences, so two photons could still overlap in the apparatus; by modern standards Taylor's conditions were not sufficient to demonstrate genuine single-photon interference. Safe phrasing for his run is 'on average roughly one photon at a time'. The airtight version came in 1986, when Philippe Grangier, Gerard Roger and Alain Aspect used heralded single photons — each one announced by the detection of its twin — in an interferometer equivalent to a double slit, with interference visibility close to 100%. Checking your own strongest claim hardest is the point, not a footnote. Sources: Wikipedia, 'G. I. Taylor' (explicit caveat); Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment' (Single-Particle Interference).

question: Put a detector at the slits that reveals which one the particle took, and the fringes disappear. For decades the standard explanation was Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: pinning down the position necessarily kicks the particle's momentum, and the kick smears the stripes away. In 1998 Gerhard Rempe's group, with Simon Dürr and Thomas Nonn, built an atom interferometer — a rig that splits an atom's path in two and folds it back together — in which the size of that kick could be measured directly. What did the measurement show?
answer: The kick was far too small to wash the pattern out
choices: The kick was far too small to wash the pattern out
The kick was exactly the size the textbooks predicted
The kick grew larger as the two paths were separated
The kick reversed direction depending on the path taken
context: From the abstract of Dürr, Nonn and Rempe, Nature 395, 33 (1998): 'we report a which-way experiment in an atom interferometer in which the back action of path detection on the atom's momentum is too small to explain the disappearance of the interference pattern. We attribute it instead to correlations between the which-way detector and the atomic motion, rather than to the uncertainty principle.' In one sentence: the detector did not shove the atom hard enough to blur the stripes — the stripes died because the path became knowable. Berthold-Georg Englert's 1996 duality relation makes it exact: V squared plus K squared is at most 1, where V is fringe visibility and K is path distinguishability. Perfect path knowledge forces the fringes to zero; partial knowledge gives partial fringes. The relation is derived without invoking uncertainty at all — it is about information, not about kicks. Nothing here involves anyone looking, and no mind collapses anything. Sources: Nature 395, 33-37 (1998); Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment' (Which-Way and Delayed-Choice Experiments).

question: In 2000 Yoon-Ho Kim's team made entangled pairs of photons — pairs whose measurement outcomes stay linked — and sent one of each pair through a two-path apparatus onto a screen, arranging that the partner photon's path information could be either preserved or destroyed, the choice falling eight nanoseconds after its twin had already landed. Destroy the information and the fringes are there; preserve it and they are gone. Headlines called it the future rewriting the past. What does the screen's own raw record show?
answer: A smooth blur, with fringes only after the data are sorted
choices: A smooth blur, with fringes only after the data are sorted
Sharp fringes that fade away across the eight-nanosecond delay
Sharp fringes that appear the moment the partner is destroyed
A smooth blur that sharpens into fringes all by itself
context: This is the rung that kills the myth. Kim's setup used entangled pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion and gave coincidence-counted interference with 95% visibility when path information was erased, and none when it was path-marked, despite the 8 ns delay. But as the sources put it, no information travels backward in time: the overall data show no interference until conditioned on the eraser outcome, reflecting the experimenter's choice of analysis rather than any alteration of past events. The signal-photon screen never shows stripes. The stripes appear only when you take hits already recorded and sort them by which detector the partner landed in. Nothing in the past was changed; a subset was selected. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Quantum eraser experiment'; Grokipedia, 'Double-slit experiment'.

question: Archbishop James Ussher's chronology of 1650 fixed the beginning of the world with startling exactness: the evening before 23 October, 4004 BC. Ussher was no crank but a serious scholar, and his tool was arithmetic. What was he adding up?
answer: The generations and reign-lengths listed in scripture.
choices: The generations and reign-lengths listed in scripture.
The sediment layers stacked in Ireland's sea cliffs.
The years between the oldest eclipses ever written down.
The coins struck by a long succession of kingdoms.
context: Ussher was not guessing at the far end of his chain. He pinned it to a date secular historians already accepted -- the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk in 562 BC, reached through 2 Kings 25:27 -- and counted backwards from there, even cross-checking the autumn equinox against Kepler's Rudolphine Tables of 1627. He measured nothing; he counted, carefully, on the evidence he had. Sources: Grokipedia and Wikipedia, 'Ussher chronology'.

question: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon wanted a number from an experiment, not a text. At his foundry he had iron globes cast, pulled them white-hot from the furnace, and stood over them with a watch. What was Buffon timing?
answer: How long a globe took to cool enough to hold bare-handed.
choices: How long a globe took to cool enough to hold bare-handed.
How long a globe went on glowing before its colour died.
How long a globe kept a wax seal beside it from melting.
How long a globe took to boil away a small dish of water.
context: Buffon repeated the trial with globes of different sizes, and with glass and stone, to find how cooling time scales with size, then scaled up to a globe the size of the Earth. In Les Epoques de la Nature (1778) he published the answer: 74,832 years. Wrong by a factor of tens of thousands -- but it was the first age of the Earth that came out of an experiment instead of a document. Sources: American Institute of Physics, 'Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707-1788)'; Grokipedia, 'Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon'.

question: In 1948 a graduate student at the University of Chicago, Clair Patterson, was handed the problem of measuring the age of the Earth. His supervisor Harrison Brown sent him off with a promise: 'It will be duck soup, Patterson.' How long did the job actually take?
answer: Seven years.
choices: Seven years.
Eleven months.
Two years.
Nineteen years.
context: The obstacle was never the clock; it was the dirt. Lead was already in the beakers, the distilled water, the reagents, the dust and the air -- Patterson found it in his own hair. Before he could weigh the atoms he had to build a room clean enough to weigh them in, one of the first clean rooms in the world: filtered air, acid-washed apparatus, chemicals he re-distilled himself, visitors made to change their clothes. The contamination turned out to be real pollution. He later measured a 200- to 300-fold rise of lead in polar ice since the 1700s, traced it to tetraethyl lead in petrol, and spent the rest of his career fighting the lead industry until leaded petrol was driven out of American cars. Sources: Caltech Magazine, 'Duck Soup and Lead'; Wikipedia, 'Clair Cameron Patterson'.

question: In 1899 the Irish geologist John Joly built a clock out of the saltiness of the sea. He measured how much sodium the world's rivers carry down each year, assumed the ocean began with none, and divided its whole load by that yearly rate. Out came 80 to 90 million years -- close to the 98 million Kelvin preferred. What does sodium do that Joly's clock never allowed for?
answer: It leaves the sea again; it does not just pile up.
choices: It leaves the sea again; it does not just pile up.
It poured into the sea far faster in ages past.
It rises chiefly from sea-floor vents, not rivers.
It sits in deep water that no ship had sampled.
context: Salt does not simply accumulate. Sodium leaves seawater again, so the sum Joly did -- how much sits in the ocean, against how fast it arrives -- gives the average time a sodium ion stays in the sea before something removes it. Oceanographers call that a residence time, and that is what Joly measured, beautifully, by accident. It is not the age of anything. Two clocks built on completely different principles, Kelvin's cooling rock and Joly's salt, now agreed on tens of millions of years, and both were out by a factor of about fifty. Sources: Wikipedia, 'John Joly'; Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day - John Joly'; Grokipedia, 'Geochronology'.

question: William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, treated the age of the Earth as a physics problem: assume the planet began as a molten ball, then run the equations of heat backwards to find how long the cooling has gone on. The calculation needed one measured fact about the real Earth to start from -- something miners had known for years. What did Kelvin build his 1862 estimate on?
answer: Temperature climbs about one degree for every fifty feet down.
choices: Temperature climbs about one degree for every fifty feet down.
Deep rock carries heat away about twice as fast as surface rock.
Rock pressure roughly doubles every thousand feet of depth.
Water pumped from the deepest shafts comes up steadily warm.
context: Kelvin's 1862 paper states it exactly: 'there is, on the whole, about 1 degree Fahr. of elevation of temperature per 50 British feet' of depth. From that single gradient, plus Fourier's heat equation and a molten start, he concluded that the Earth's consolidation 'cannot have taken place less than 20,000,000 years ago... nor more than 400,000,000 years ago'. The whole age of the planet hung on how much warmer a mine shaft gets as you climb down it. Source: Lord Kelvin, 'On the Secular Cooling of the Earth' (1862), full text at zapatopi.net/kelvin/papers/.

question: Natural selection needed time in enormous quantities, and the first edition of Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) handed his critics a number to shoot at: 300 million years, Darwin reckoned, just to wear away the Weald valley in Kent. Then Lord Kelvin's far shorter ceiling for the Earth gained authority. What became of the Weald figure in later editions?
answer: Darwin halved it, then dropped the estimate altogether.
choices: Darwin halved it, then dropped the estimate altogether.
Darwin doubled it and defended it in a new closing chapter.
Darwin kept it and printed Kelvin's objection beside it.
Darwin replaced it with a range holding both men's figures.
context: Darwin said out loud what the conflict felt like: 'Thomson's views of the recent age of the world have been for some time one of my sorest troubles', and, thinking of the long ages natural selection needed, 'then comes Sir W. Thomson, like an odious spectre.' The best physics of the age was in open conflict with the best field evidence, and neither side was being dishonest. Sources: Darwin Correspondence Project, 'How old is the earth?'; Scientific American, 'When Lord Kelvin Nearly Killed Darwin's Theory'.

question: In 1896 Henri Becquerel left uranium salts sitting on a wrapped photographic plate and later found the plate fogged, with no sunlight involved. Radioactivity had been found, and it knocked out one of the two assumptions holding up Kelvin's calculation. Which assumption did it break?
answer: That the Earth only loses heat and makes none of its own.
choices: That the Earth only loses heat and makes none of its own.
That the Earth began as a molten ball rather than a cold one.
That heat crosses solid rock at a steady, measurable rate.
That the Sun has burned at roughly its present strength.
context: The consequence for Kelvin's model was direct: the Earth is not simply spending an inheritance of heat from a fixed start -- it makes heat, on the order of 20 terawatts of radiogenic heating, most of it in the crust. Becquerel's fogged plate is also about as close as a great discovery gets to being kid-repeatable in spirit: a wrapped plate, a mineral, and the patience to look at what came out. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Absolute dating' and 'Lord Kelvin'; Wikipedia, 'Age of the Earth'.

question: By the 1890s Kelvin's short Earth rested on physics no geologist could match, and his arithmetic was in fact flawless. Then in 1895 John Perry, an engineer who had once been Kelvin's own assistant, showed in Nature that changing a single assumption about the deep Earth let the very same cooling equations allow two to three billion years. What did Perry assume that Kelvin had not?
answer: That the interior stirs and circulates as it cools.
choices: That the interior stirs and circulates as it cools.
That the interior began far hotter than Kelvin allowed.
That the interior is layered, each shell holding heat in.
That the core keeps making heat as it slowly crystallizes.
context: Perry's assumption has a name: convection -- deep rock creeping and turning over like a pot on a stove, carrying its heat bodily upward instead of passing it from atom to atom through rock that never moves. Perry tried the polite route first: three weeks before going public he sent Kelvin his own solution for a cooling sphere whose conductivity changes with depth, and Kelvin brushed him off. Only then did Perry publish in Nature -- and he still opened by deferring to 'Lord Kelvin's letter'. He revered the man he was refuting. Note the date: 1895, before radioactivity was known to exist. The popular line that radioactivity proved Kelvin wrong is only half true, and the smaller half; Grokipedia's assessment is that Kelvin's 'primary shortfall stemmed not from ignorance of radioactivity... but from Kelvin's assumption of a rigid, homogeneous Earth conducting heat solely by diffusion, neglecting mantle convection.' Sources: John Perry, 'On the Age of the Earth', Nature 51 (1895); England, Molnar & Richter, GSA Today 17(1), 2007; Grokipedia, 'Lord Kelvin'.

question: Science's best-loved rescue story: Ernest Rutherford, lecturing at the Royal Institution in 1904, spots Lord Kelvin in the audience and saves himself by declaring that Kelvin had capped the Earth's age only 'provided no new source was discovered' -- radium being that source. The old man, Rutherford said, then beamed at him. Kelvin did write such a caveat in 1862: his limit held 'unless sources now unknown to us are prepared in the great storehouse of creation'. Which of Kelvin's calculations does that caveat close?
answer: His estimate of how long the Sun could keep shining.
choices: His estimate of how long the Sun could keep shining.
His estimate of how long the Earth had been cooling.
His estimate of how long the Moon could hold its heat.
His estimate of how long the sea had been salting up.
context: The caveat closes 'On the Age of the Sun's Heat' (Macmillan's Magazine, March 1862), where Kelvin warned that the inhabitants of the Earth cannot expect light and heat for many million years longer 'unless sources now unknown to us are prepared in the great storehouse of creation.' Rutherford had borrowed a prophecy from the wrong calculation. The scene itself is no sturdier. It survives only in A. S. Eve's 1939 biography of Rutherford, page 107 -- printed thirty-five years after the lecture and two years after Rutherford's death -- where Eve records that Rutherford 'used to tell humorous stories about this lecture long afterwards', and the passage carries no quotation marks at all: it is Eve's recollection of Rutherford's much-repeated retelling. Kelvin, for his part, published no retraction of his age-of-the-Earth work before his death in 1907, conceding only privately to J. J. Thomson that radioactivity made some of his assumptions unworkable -- which makes the beaming-old-boy ending the least reliable part of the tale. Enjoy the story; do not cite it as evidence. Sources: Lord Kelvin, 'On the Age of the Sun's Heat' (1862); A. S. Eve, 'Rutherford' (1939), p.107; Paul Braterman, 'Kelvin, Rutherford, and the Age of the Earth: I, The Myth'.  (Legend.)

question: By 1907 the physicists' Earth was still a young one, and geologists had no way to answer it with a number of their own. That February Bertram Boltwood published ages for minerals gathered around the world, running from 410 million years up to 2.2 billion for one crystal out of Ceylon -- the first figures with the right count of zeros. What had Boltwood measured inside the minerals?
answer: How much lead had piled up against the uranium still left.
choices: How much lead had piled up against the uranium still left.
How much helium had leaked out through the crystal's cracks.
How much heat the mineral still gave off as it lay there.
How far the crystal's colour had faded from the outside in.
context: Boltwood's figures ran about 20 percent high, but the order of magnitude ended the short timescale for good -- the Ceylon thorianite alone gave fifty times Kelvin's entire allowance. Arthur Holmes then spent a career pushing the number up: a Norwegian rock at about 370 million years in 1911, at least 1.6 billion in his 1913 book The Age of the Earth, and an upper limit of 3.0 billion by the 1927 edition. He argued for a billions-of-years Earth for four decades before anyone could prove it. Sources: American Physical Society, 'February 1907: Bertram Boltwood Estimates Earth is at Least 2.2 Billion Years Old'; Grokipedia, 'Arthur Holmes'; Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day - Arthur Holmes'.

question: Clair Patterson's 1956 paper settled the age of the Earth, and its title names what he actually dated: 'Age of meteorites and the earth'. Reading the planet's age off rocks that fell out of the sky sounds like the wrong plan entirely. What made a meteorite a better clock than a rock picked up on Earth?
answer: It is a leftover of the event that built the planets, unchanged.
choices: It is a leftover of the event that built the planets, unchanged.
It formed long before the planets did, far out beyond the Sun.
It cooled in vacuum, so no water has ever touched its minerals.
It broke off a planet whose own age astronomers can measure.
context: Earth's own original surface has been recycled away by its restless interior. The oldest intact rock yet found is the Acasta Gneiss of northwest Canada, about 4.02 billion years old, and the oldest Earth material of any kind is a scatter of zircon grains from the Jack Hills of Western Australia at about 4.4 billion -- loose crystals whose parent rocks are gone. Patterson's key sample was troilite, an iron sulfide from the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite that holds lead but almost no uranium, so its lead has barely shifted since the solar system formed: the starting position of the hands. Five meteorites plotted on one straight line, and the slope of that line was the age -- 4.55 +/- 0.07 billion years. One more sample made it the age of the EARTH: ocean-floor sediment, taken to stand for the bulk planet, fell right on the same line. That line is now called the geochron. Today's accepted value, 4.54 +/- 0.05 billion years, still sits inside Patterson's error bars. He is said to have driven to his mother's house in Iowa after the 1953 measurement and asked her to take him to hospital, convinced he was having a heart attack -- a widely retold story rather than a documented one. Sources: C. C. Patterson, 'Age of meteorites and the earth', Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta 10:230 (1956); Wikipedia, 'Lead-lead dating' and 'Age of the Earth'; University of Chicago Magazine, 'Immeasurable'.

question: John Perry's 1895 answer to Kelvin was that the deep Earth stirs and circulates rather than sitting still, which would allow the planet to be far older than Kelvin's physics permitted. Perry was right, and it changed nothing: the paper was forgotten. A 2007 re-assessment in GSA Today argues that the age question was not even the biggest thing lost with it. What else did the neglect of Perry's paper cost?
answer: Decades of the continental-drift debate, argued with no mechanism.
choices: Decades of the continental-drift debate, argued with no mechanism.
A century of underrating how much heat the crust makes by itself.
An early route to dating the ocean floor, long before the drills.
A warning that the mine-shaft heat gradient varies from place to place.
context: England, Molnar and Richter put it plainly: a powerful argument in favour of a mobile Earth interior 'was overlooked during the first few decades of debate about continental drift.' Perry had handed geology a moving mantle in 1895 and nobody picked it up. The shape of the whole story sits in one line: Ussher counted generations in a text, Buffon counted minutes on a cooling iron ball, Kelvin counted degrees per fifty feet of mine shaft, John Joly counted grains of salt delivered to the sea, and Boltwood and Patterson counted atoms. Every estimate was honest for the evidence its author had, and every one fell to a better instrument rather than to a better argument. Source: England, Molnar & Richter, 'John Perry's neglected critique of Kelvin's age for the Earth: A missed opportunity in geodynamics', GSA Today 17(1), 2007.

question: In 2012 Harvard social psychologist Amy Cuddy stepped onto a TED stage and told the audience to hold a particular two-minute posture before their next job interview. Her talk became one of the two most-watched TED talks ever. What was the physical stance she asked people to hold?
answer: Feet apart, hands on hips, chest open
choices: Feet apart, hands on hips, chest open
Arms crossed, chin tucked, eyes down
Both hands raised over head, palms flat
One knee on the floor, head bowed low
context: Cuddy called it the 'Wonder Woman' pose. By 2017 the talk was near 47 million views; today it is over 75 million. Source: TED (ted.com); Cuddy TEDGlobal 2012.

question: Behind Amy Cuddy's TED talk sat a single 2010 study in Psychological Science by Dana Carney, Cuddy, and Andy Yap. How many people were in that original power-pose experiment?
answer: 42 undergraduates
choices: 42 undergraduates
420 undergraduates
4,200 undergraduates
42,000 undergraduates
context: One study, 42 people, one lab, one afternoon -- and a TED sensation. Small samples let random noise look like a real effect. Source: Carney, Cuddy, Yap, Psychological Science 2010.

question: The 2010 power-pose paper did not just claim posing felt good. It claimed two minutes in the pose changed the chemistry of the body. What was the specific biological pair the paper reported?
answer: Testosterone went up and cortisol went down
choices: Testosterone went up and cortisol went down
Adrenaline went up and dopamine went down
Insulin went up and glucagon went down
Melatonin went up and serotonin went down
context: And risk-taking gambles went up. The claim was hormonal, not just psychological -- which made the later failure to replicate the hormones a serious matter. Source: Carney et al. 2010.

question: In 2015 Eva Ranehill and colleagues at Zurich ran the power-pose experiment again in Psychological Science with a much larger sample. Their results split the original claim clean in half. Which half of Cuddy's story SURVIVED the retest?
answer: The self-reported feeling of power
choices: The self-reported feeling of power
The rise in salivary testosterone levels
The fall in salivary cortisol levels
The rise in monetary risk-taking behaviour
context: The hormones and the risk-taking did not survive. This is why it matters to say 'power posing does not do X', not 'power posing does nothing'. Source: Ranehill et al., Psychological Science 2015.

question: In September 2016 something rare happened: the ORIGINAL 2010 power-pose paper's first author posted a public statement on her UC Berkeley Haas faculty page walking away from the finding. Who was that first author?
answer: Dana Carney
choices: Dana Carney
Amy Cuddy
Andy Yap
Eva Ranehill
context: Her statement said 'I do not believe that "power pose" effects are real', and listed the analytic choices in her own data that had produced them. Amy Cuddy still defends a milder version of the claim. Source: Carney, faculty page 2016; KPBS 2016.

question: In Roy Baumeister's famous 1998 experiment on willpower, participants sat in a room warm with the smell of freshly baked chocolate-chip cookies. Half were told to eat only the radishes in a bowl instead. Then EVERYONE was given an unsolvable puzzle. What happened to the radish-eaters?
answer: They gave up on the puzzle sooner
choices: They gave up on the puzzle sooner
They kept working on the puzzle longer
They refused to try the puzzle at all
They solved a modified version faster
context: Baumeister concluded willpower was like a fuel tank you could run dry -- he called it 'ego depletion'. The idea would govern self-help and academic psychology for fifteen years. Source: Baumeister et al., JPSP 1998.

question: By 2010 the willpower-as-fuel-tank idea looked bulletproof. A meta-analysis pooled 198 separate tests of ego depletion and put the effect at a solid d of about 0.6, declaring it extremely unlikely to be absent. Then something reversed the verdict. What was it?
answer: A 23-lab preregistered replication found essentially no effect
choices: A 23-lab preregistered replication found essentially no effect
A single new study in one lab found a much bigger effect
The original author confessed to having faked the 1998 data
A statistical error was found in the 1998 paper's coding
context: The 2016 Registered Replication Report coordinated by Hagger and colleagues ran one preregistered protocol on 2,141 participants across 23 labs; combined effect d = 0.04 (95% CI -0.07 to 0.15). Source: Hagger et al., Perspectives on Psychological Science 2016.

question: The alarm on ego depletion was actually printed BEFORE the 23-lab replication ran. In 2014, Carter and McCullough reanalysed the 2010 meta-analysis by correcting for a well-known statistical distortion -- and the effect shrank to something you could no longer tell from zero. What was the distortion they corrected for?
answer: Publication bias
choices: Publication bias
Randomisation failure
Regression to the mean
Instrument miscalibration
context: Once you account for studies that get filed in a drawer when they don't work, the big pooled effect (d ~ 0.6) collapsed to around d = 0.2 or lower. The signal was in the publishing, not the biology. Source: Carter & McCullough, Frontiers in Psychology 2014.

question: In 1996 John Bargh, Mark Chen, and Lara Burrows had NYU students unscramble sentences seeded with words like Florida, bingo, and wrinkle. Researchers with hidden stopwatches then timed them walking down the corridor. What did the paper report those primed students did?
answer: Walked more slowly to the elevator
choices: Walked more slowly to the elevator
Walked more quickly to the elevator
Refused to walk out of the lab entirely
Turned back before reaching the elevator
context: It became one of the most-cited results in social psychology, and starred in Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. Source: Bargh, Chen & Burrows, JPSP 1996.

question: In 2012 Stephane Doyen and colleagues, publishing in PLOS ONE, redid the elderly-priming walk experiment with one important change to the measurement. When they made that change, what did they find?
answer: No difference in walking speed between the groups
choices: No difference in walking speed between the groups
A much bigger walking-speed difference than Bargh had
The primed group walked FASTER, not slower, to the door
Only the female participants slowed down after priming
context: They swapped the human stopwatch for infrared beams that timed the 120 walkers with no observer bias. The Bargh effect vanished. Source: Doyen et al., PLOS ONE 2012.

question: Doyen and colleagues then ran a second, diabolical experiment. They TOLD ten different experimenters, in advance, which condition each subject was in -- so half of the experimenters expected a slow walk and half did not. The infrared beams still saw no priming effect. But something happened on the HUMAN stopwatches. What?
answer: The slow walk appeared only when experimenters expected slowness
choices: The slow walk appeared only when experimenters expected slowness
The slow walk appeared only when experimenters expected quickness
Both stopwatches and beams now showed the priming effect equally
The stopwatches showed the primed subjects walking faster, not slower
context: The Bargh effect was living in the experimenter's thumb, not in the participants' feet. This is why every good behavioural test today is blinded -- neither subject nor tester knows the condition. Source: Doyen et al., PLOS ONE 2012.

question: In late September 2012 an unusual open letter went out to the leading researchers in social priming. It warned of 'a train wreck looming' and urged them to organise their own replication ring before others did it for them. Which psychologist wrote and sent that letter?
answer: Daniel Kahneman
choices: Daniel Kahneman
Roy Baumeister
Elizabeth Loftus
Steven Pinker
context: Kahneman had praised priming studies in his own bestseller Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011). The letter went to leading priming researchers directly and became one of the founding documents of psychology's replication reform. Source: Kahneman open letter, 26 September 2012.

question: After the power-pose, ego-depletion, and elderly-priming walk results collapsed on retest, investigators combed the original labs' data, code, and records for signs of misconduct. What did those audits conclude about the original researchers -- Cuddy, Baumeister, and Bargh?
answer: No fraud was found in any of the three
choices: No fraud was found in any of the three
Deliberate data fabrication in every one
Paid subjects producing the desired result
Students blocked from publishing replications
context: Cuddy, Baumeister and Bargh are real scientists who were not shown to have faked anything. Small samples, flexible analysis, and an audience that wanted the story were enough. Robust effects survive (the Stroop effect, the spacing effect, semantic priming). Fragile ones dissolve on retest. Source: BPS Psychologist, decade retrospective.

question: In October 1990 the biologist Paul Ehrlich, who had spent twenty-two years warning that mass starvation was coming, mailed the economist Julian Simon a cheque. What did the cheque settle?
answer: a public wager
choices: a public wager
a libel suit
an unpaid book royalty
a research grant repayment
context: The two men had agreed a ten-year bet in September 1980 about the price of natural resources. Ehrlich lost, paid on time and in full. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: Paul Ehrlich and Julian Simon formalised their public wager in September 1980. One of the two men insisted the other pick the raw materials and the time span, so no one could later say the terms were rigged. Which man insisted?
answer: Simon, offering Ehrlich free choice
choices: Simon, offering Ehrlich free choice
Ehrlich, offering Simon free choice
both men, in a joint agreement
a neutral referee they had chosen
context: Simon's move was what turned a public quarrel into a real test rather than a stunt: the loser could not later say the terms were rigged. Ehrlich then picked five metals and a decade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: The Ehrlich-Simon contract was formalised on 29 September 1980, with $200 staked on each of five metals for a total of $1,000 -- payoff ten years later. Which five metals did Ehrlich pick?
answer: copper, chromium, nickel, tin, tungsten
choices: copper, chromium, nickel, tin, tungsten
iron, aluminium, zinc, silver, cobalt
gold, platinum, palladium, silver, rhodium
lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, graphite
context: These were core industrial metals in 1980. Ehrlich and his colleagues, including the physicist John Harte and the biologist John Holdren, made the selection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: The ten-year clock on the wager ran out in September 1990. Where did the five metals -- chosen by Ehrlich, priced in real terms -- end up compared with 1980?
answer: all five cost less
choices: all five cost less
three of five rose, two fell
four of five rose sharply
all five had roughly held their value
context: A clean sweep. Chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten each cost less in real, inflation-adjusted terms in 1990 than they had at the signing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon-Ehrlich_wager.

question: In The Ultimate Resource (1981), Simon spelled out why he thought Ehrlich would lose. In his account, what is a rising price of a metal?
answer: a signal that pays people to find substitutes and use less
choices: a signal that pays people to find substitutes and use less
a countdown to the exhaustion of the reserve
proof that population has outrun capacity
an accident of foreign-exchange movements
context: Simon's core mechanism. That is why he called the human mind 'the ultimate resource' -- more people, more problem-solvers, and each price rise pays someone to answer it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ultimate_Resource.

question: Ehrlich did not concede intellectual defeat when he paid up. He told the New York Times in December 1990 that 'the bet doesn't mean anything' and told the BBC how, exactly?
answer: it had been an excellent bet that his side happened to lose
choices: it had been an excellent bet that his side happened to lose
the metals had been secretly manipulated by traders
Simon had used inflation numbers rigged in his favour
he had never agreed to the bet in the first place
context: Documented at the time. Ehrlich's paid graciously, but held the failed forecast harmless. The wager settled the price question and left the deeper argument untouched -- for him. Source: spiked-online.com/2015/09/29/the-simon-ehrlich-wager-25-years-on/.

question: Hammer a copper coin and it flattens into a disc. Hammer a lump of rock salt and it shatters into pieces with flat, angled faces. Both start as neat stacks of particles. Copper bends; salt breaks. Why?
answer: The bond in a metal points in no particular direction; the bond in salt does
choices: The bond in a metal points in no particular direction; the bond in salt does
The copper is much warmer than the salt at the moment you hit it
The salt is much more crystalline than the copper is
The copper is much denser than the salt and absorbs the blow
context: In a metal the outer electrons form a shared, non-directional glue, so layers of ion cores can slide and re-bond. In an ionic crystal the bonds link specific positive and negative neighbours, so once layers slip the wrong charges meet. Source: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Chemical_Bonding/Fundamentals_of_Chemical_Bonding/Metallic_Bonding

question: In 1900 Paul Drude wrote down the first simple picture of a metal, meant to explain in one stroke why copper conducts electricity, bends without breaking, and shines. What did he say the outermost electrons of the atoms actually do?
answer: Form a shared sea roaming the whole block, with the positive ion cores sitting in it
choices: Form a shared sea roaming the whole block, with the positive ion cores sitting in it
Orbit the nearest three neighbours in a fixed triangular pattern
Hop between just two atoms at a time as ordinary covalent bonds
Sit locked in place until heat knocks them briefly loose to carry current
context: This is the electron-sea model of metallic bonding. Drude's 1900 picture is classical -- quantum band theory has replaced it underneath -- but the sea image still explains conduction, malleability, thermal flow, and shine together. Source: https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physical-science/metallic-bond/describe-the-electron-sea-model-of-metallic-bonding./

question: A layer of a metal can slide over the next layer and simply re-bond in its new position, so the block changes shape without breaking. Slide one layer of a rock-salt crystal by one atomic spacing, though, and something disastrous happens along the new plane. What?
answer: Like charges suddenly face like charges, and the layers repel and split
choices: Like charges suddenly face like charges, and the layers repel and split
The salt melts at the sliding surface from friction alone
The heavier atoms cluster on one side and the crystal tips over
The salt turns clear where the layer slid, opaque where it did not
context: Ionic crystals cleave along flat planes exactly because slipping brings like charges into contact. It is the SAME hammer blow and the SAME kind of orderly stack -- one mechanism, opposite outcomes. Source: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Supplemental_Modules_(Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry)/Chemical_Bonding/Fundamentals_of_Chemical_Bonding/Metallic_Bonding

question: Leave a metal spoon in a bowl of hot soup for a minute and the handle scalds your fingers; leave a wooden spoon and the handle barely warms. What inside the metal makes heat move down the handle so much faster than through wood?
answer: The same free electrons that carry current also carry heat, quickly, all through the metal
choices: The same free electrons that carry current also carry heat, quickly, all through the metal
The metal is denser, so heat has more matter to conduct through per second
The metal's atoms are lighter and vibrate faster from the hot end onwards
The metal absorbs the soup's steam and warms from the outside in
context: The Wiedemann-Franz law, from 1853, gave the empirical clue: metals' thermal and electrical conductivities are locked together in a fixed ratio at a given temperature. Drude's 1900 free-electron picture explained why -- one carrier does both jobs. Test it at supper. Source: https://www.tutorchase.com/answers/igcse/chemistry/what-causes-metals-to-be-lustrous

question: A polished silver spoon is nearly a perfect mirror; a piece of dry chalk cut to the same shape is dull. What single fact about a metal is responsible for its mirror-like shine?
answer: Its free electrons respond to the light's electric field and re-radiate almost all of it back out
choices: Its free electrons respond to the light's electric field and re-radiate almost all of it back out
Its surface atoms are packed so tightly that no visible light can pass any gap
It emits a faint visible glow of its own at ordinary room temperature
Its polish makes the surface atomically smooth, so every ray reflects at one angle
context: Because a typical metal's plasma frequency lies in the ultraviolet, visible light drives the electron sea faster than it can lag, so almost all visible light is reflected. Distractor 4 is the popular wrong answer: many well-polished non-metals are dull because they lack the free-electron response, not because they are rough. Source: https://www.webexhibits.org/causesofcolor/9.html

question: Pure copper is softer than bronze; pure iron is softer than steel. What does adding tin (for bronze) or carbon (for steel) actually do inside the crystal to make the alloy harder than either pure metal alone?
answer: The differently sized atoms jam the slip planes so the layers can no longer glide easily
choices: The differently sized atoms jam the slip planes so the layers can no longer glide easily
They fill the empty gaps between atoms and make the metal denser
They react chemically to grow tiny hard grains that pin the surface
They neutralise the shared electron sea in patches, stiffening the block
context: Solid-solution strengthening: solute atoms of the wrong size warp the lattice around them and block dislocation motion, the microscopic slip that lets pure metals bend. Bronze was humanity's first engineered material of this kind. Source: https://www.nuclear-power.com/nuclear-engineering/metals-what-are-metals/metalworking/solid-solution-strengthening-alloying/

question: Gold is so malleable that a skilled beater can hammer it into leaf less than 100 nanometres thick -- so thin that some visible light passes straight through the sheet. Reflected gold still looks gold. What colour is the light after it has passed through the leaf?
answer: Bluish-green
choices: Bluish-green
Deep red
Bright orange
Pure white
context: Reflected and transmitted light see the electron sea differently. Gold reflects the yellow-red end strongly; the wavelengths it does NOT reflect leak through, giving transmitted light a striking bluish-green tint. You can see it in gilded stained-glass work and museum leaf demonstrations. Source: https://www.webexhibits.org/causesofcolor/9.html

question: Robert Liston, operating in Edinburgh and London, could take a leg off above the knee in twenty-five to thirty seconds, on a patient wide awake and held down by strong assistants. Before 1846 speed was the surgeon's chief virtue. Why did it matter so much?
answer: Patients often died of the shock of the pain itself
choices: Patients often died of the shock of the pain itself
Assistants could hold a struggling man only briefly
A wound held open longer was likelier to fester
Bleeding could not be stopped once a vessel opened
context: Surgical shock was the killer. Many patients died not of the wound but of the pain and blood loss, sometimes within hours, so every second the knife spent in the body counted against them. Restraint was the other half of the arrangement: several strong assistants, or straps and iron frames. Liston's speed was not showmanship. Source: Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome (section: 'Early Methods of Pain Relief').

question: Massachusetts General Hospital opened its domed operating theatre in Boston in 1821, lit by a skylight so surgeons could see. In 1823 the trustees accepted a gift and stood it in the theatre as an 'appropriate ornament.' It is there still, after eight thousand operations. What is it?
answer: The mummified body of an Egyptian stonemason
choices: The mummified body of an Egyptian stonemason
A marble bust of the physician Hippocrates
An anatomical skeleton in a glass case
An oil portrait of the hospital's founders
context: His name is Padihershef, a stonemason from Thebes who died around 600 BCE. He was uncrated in 1824 and has stood in the room ever since, including on the morning of 16 October 1846; the hospital calls him its oldest patient. The theatre itself was designed by Charles Bulfinch and built of Chelmsford granite cut by state penitentiary inmates. It served as the hospital's main operating room until 1867, became a National Historic Landmark in 1965, and is still used for teaching. Source: Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome (sections: 'Curated Displays in the Dome', 'The Bulfinch Building Amphitheater').

question: Edward Gilbert Abbott, twenty-one, lay on the table in a Boston operating theatre on 16 October 1846 while John Collins Warren cut into his neck. Abbott had breathed a vapour from a glass globe, and he did not cry out. The hospital record sets down what he said he felt. What was it?
answer: Like the spot being scraped with a blunt tool
choices: Like the spot being scraped with a blunt tool
Nothing at all, from first cut to last stitch
A dull warmth spreading down from his jaw
A far-off ache belonging to somebody else
context: The hospital's own wording is 'a sensation like that of scraping the part with a blunt instrument.' The versions usually retold -- 'as if my neck had been scratched with a hoe' -- are later paraphrases of that line, not Abbott's words. Abbott had been admitted on 25 September 1846; he was born 2 September 1825 and died in 1855 of tuberculosis, unrelated to the surgery. Source: 'Ether Day Revisited: The Surgical Records of Edward Gilbert Abbott', Annals of Surgery Open (2022) -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10431558/

question: The device William Morton held to his patient's face in the Boston theatre was almost comically plain: a glass globe the size of a quart jar with an ether-soaked sponge inside, a narrow tube, a mouthpiece. It worked. Morton was back at his bench that night, and had a modified version by the next morning. What had the first design got wrong?
answer: The patient breathed his own exhaled air back in
choices: The patient breathed his own exhaled air back in
The ether leaked out around the mouthpiece
The glass fogged over and hid the ether level
The sponge dried out before the cutting ended
context: Morton fitted one-way inhale and exhale valves on 17 October 1846, the day after the demonstration. The glass was the other clever part of the design: you could watch the ether level drop and judge the dose by eye. Source: Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome (section: "Morton's Ether Inhaler").

question: At nine at night on 30 September 1846 Eben Frost walked into William Morton's Boston office with a toothache and let the dentist try something. He breathed ether; the tooth came out; he felt nothing. Sixteen days later Morton stood in the Massachusetts General Hospital operating theatre with the city's senior surgeons watching. What had brought that invitation?
answer: A paragraph in the next morning's Boston Daily Journal
choices: A paragraph in the next morning's Boston Daily Journal
A paper read to the Boston Society for Medical Improvement
A private demonstration for the hospital's trustees
A circular posted to every physician in the city
context: A reporter named Albert G. Tenney happened to be in the room that night. The Boston Daily Journal told its readers the next morning that the tooth had come out 'without giving him the slightest pain.' It was that newspaper paragraph, not a medical paper, that opened the hospital's doors to a dentist sixteen days later. Source: Countway Library, 'The Operation on Eben Frost' -- https://collections.countway.harvard.edu/onview/exhibits/show/introduction/morton-and-jackson/eben-frost-operation

question: In 1800 a twenty-one-year-old English chemist, Humphry Davy, published his experiments on nitrous oxide, which had relieved his own toothache. Printed in that book is a sentence saying the gas 'appears capable of destroying physical pain' and might 'be used with advantage during surgical operations.' Nobody acted on it for forty-four years, while surgeons went on cutting into patients who were wide awake. What did nitrous oxide and ether become in those years instead?
answer: Party entertainments for gentry and students
choices: Party entertainments for gentry and students
Industrial solvents for cleaning machinery
Preservatives for anatomical specimens
Veterinary drugs for quieting horses
context: Nitrous oxide fuelled 'laughing gas parties' among the British upper classes; ether fuelled 'ether frolics' among American medical students. Crawford Long got the whole idea from joining in -- he inhaled ether and nitrous recreationally with fellow students at the University of Pennsylvania in 1838-39, and noticed bruises he could not remember getting. For forty-four years the cure for surgical agony was a party trick. Sources: Humphry Davy, Researches, Chemical and Philosophical (1800), quoted in 'Nitrous oxide: are you having a laugh?', RSC Education -- https://edu.rsc.org/feature/nitrous-oxide-are-you-having-a-laugh/2020202.article ; Grokipedia, 'Crawford Long' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Crawford_Long

question: Horace Wells, a Connecticut dentist who had once shared a Boston practice with William Morton, went to a travelling showman's laughing-gas exhibition in December 1844 and was so struck that he had his own tooth pulled under nitrous oxide the following evening, to test the idea on himself. Weeks later he arranged a public demonstration in Boston. It went badly. What happened in front of that audience?
answer: The dose ran short, the patient cried out, and the room jeered
choices: The dose ran short, the patient cried out, and the room jeered
The gas bag split, the patient slept an hour, and the room panicked
The patient lost his nerve, refused the gas, and walked out
The tooth broke in the socket, blood ran, and the room emptied
context: The showman was Gardner Quincy Colton; Wells's own extraction was on 11 December 1844. The public attempt came in late January 1845, and Wells left disheartened. The right idea can fail its first public test. Where it happened is contested: popular accounts place it at Massachusetts General Hospital on 20 January 1845, but R. P. Haridas found no primary evidence it was ever held in that amphitheatre and argues for a public hall on Washington Street at the end of the month. Sources: Grokipedia, 'William T. G. Morton' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/William_T._G._Morton ; R. P. Haridas, 'Horace Wells' Demonstration of Nitrous Oxide in Boston', Anesthesiology.

question: Crawford Long, a country doctor in Jefferson, Georgia, soaked a towel in sulphuric ether, held it over James Venable's face and cut a tumour out of the young man's neck on 30 March 1842 -- four and a half years before anyone did such a thing in public. His ledger for the day charges two dollars for 'ether and excising tumour.' Long then kept it out of print for seven years. What was he afraid of?
answer: That critics would call the painlessness imagination or mesmerism
choices: That critics would call the painlessness imagination or mesmerism
That a rival doctor in Georgia would take the credit for it
That the state medical society would strip him of his licence
That Venable's family would sue him for experimenting
context: He also wanted more cases first, and a country practice did not supply many: between 1842 and 1845 he used ether in only about twelve to fifteen operations, including a toe amputation on 3 July 1842 and his own wife's childbirth on 27 December 1845. He finally published in December 1849, in the Southern Medical and Surgical Journal. Because 30 March is Long's date, the United States observes National Doctors' Day on 30 March, proclaimed nationally by President George H. W. Bush in 1990. Source: Grokipedia, 'Crawford Long' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Crawford_Long

question: Eleven days after the Boston demonstration William Morton filed for a patent on the vapour, and to keep the secret he sold it under a name of his own invention -- 'Letheon,' after Lethe, the mythological river of forgetfulness. US Patent 4,848 was granted on 12 November 1846 and never named the substance inside. Within a year the patent was worth nothing. What had defeated it?
answer: Anyone who opened a bottle could smell it was ordinary ether
choices: Anyone who opened a bottle could smell it was ordinary ether
A Paris chemist published the formula in a journal within weeks
The Patent Office struck it out as a monopoly on a medicine
Congress bought the method out and put it in the public domain
context: Ether was not new. Valerius Cordus mixed alcohol and sulphuric acid in 1540 and called the result 'sweet oil of vitriol.' The patent was unenforceable by 1847, and Morton spent the rest of his life chasing money for it: he asked Congress for $100,000 in December 1846, bills for up to $200,000 died in committee, and the French Academy of Sciences split its 5,000-franc Montyon Prize of 1850 down the middle between Morton and his rival Charles T. Jackson. He died of a stroke in a New York hotel room on 15 July 1868, aged 48, in poverty. Physicians had objected on ethical grounds too: in 1850 the new American Medical Association protested his 'unwarrantable assumption' of exclusive discovery. Sources: Grokipedia, 'William T. G. Morton' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/William_T._G._Morton ; Grokipedia, 'Ether Dome' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/Ether_Dome

question: John Collins Warren turned to a sceptical Boston crowd on 16 October 1846 and said, by every retelling, 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug.' The line survives only as a remark witnesses recalled afterwards; no document from the day records it. Warren's own journal, written that evening, is the primary record. How does that entry begin?
answer: Did an interesting operation at the Hospital this morning
choices: Did an interesting operation at the Hospital this morning
Saw a great triumph over pain at the Hospital this morning
Performed a bold experiment at the Hospital this morning
Removed a tumour from the neck at the Hospital this morning
context: Warren's journal entry for that evening reads: 'Did an interesting operation at the Hospital this morning while the Patient was under the influence of Dr. Morton's preparation to prevent pain.' The surgeon who had just watched the end of surgical agony called it interesting. The 'no humbug' line is a reported remark, not a documented quotation; even Wikipedia flags its origin as questionable. The journal is the primary record of the day, and it names the drug plainly: 'the Substance employed was Sulphuric Ether.' A story can be true in spirit and still have no source -- worth checking before repeating. Sources: Massachusetts Historical Society, 'Ether Day, 16 October 1846: the Conquest of Pain' (Object of the Month, October 2016), reproducing Warren's journal entry -- https://www.masshist.org/object-of-the-month/october-2016 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Gilbert_Abbott  (Legend.)

question: Boston's Public Garden holds a forty-foot granite and marble monument, the garden's oldest statue, raised in 1868 to the conquest of surgical pain: a Good Samaritan lifting an unconscious man. Four men had claims on that discovery: one had done it first and stayed silent, one had failed in public, one had only suggested it, one had shown it to the world. How did the builders handle the question of whose name to carve?
answer: They carved no man's name anywhere on the stone
choices: They carved no man's name anywhere on the stone
They carved all four claimants' names in a row
They carved Morton's name alone, above the rest
They carved Long's name, the first to use ether
context: The priority quarrel was never settled, so the inscription commemorates a discovery and no discoverer: 'To commemorate the discovery that the inhaling of ether causes insensibility to pain; first proved to the world at the Bullfinch Building in the Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, October, A.D. MDCCCXLVI.' The claimant who only suggested it was the Boston chemist Charles T. Jackson, who had taught Morton and told him to use pure sulphuric ether; he staked his priority in a sealed letter to the French Academy of Sciences dated 13 November 1846, but he never once gave ether to a patient or demonstrated it publicly -- an idea without a trial. Oliver Wendell Holmes, who had proposed the word 'anaesthesia' to Morton in a letter of 21 November 1846, is said to have joked that the monument honoured neither Morton nor Jackson but 'either.' Sources: Grokipedia, 'William T. G. Morton' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/William_T._G._Morton ; https://theclio.com/entry/48248

question: The story told for over a century is that John Collins Warren removed a tumour from Edward Gilbert Abbott's neck under ether that October morning. In 2022 surgeons published a re-reading of the surviving Massachusetts General Hospital records. Abbott had a congenital malformation of the blood vessels under his left jaw; Warren cut in, found 'a congeries of large veins & small arteries,' and passed a ligature -- a tie -- around the mass. He was discharged on 7 December 1846. What do the records say about the mass on the day Abbott left?
answer: It was the same size as when he came in
choices: It was the same size as when he came in
It had shrunk to roughly half its old size
It had gone, leaving only a healed scar
It had grown, and a second operation was set
context: The operative index entry reads 'Ligature of Erectile Tumor,' and the discharge note says the mass was 'of same size as on Entrance.' The anaesthesia was incomplete as well: Abbott 'did not shrink nor cry out' at the first incision, but 'during the insulation of the veins he began to move his limbs and utter extraordinary expressions.' The paper's authors argue the inscription in the operating theatre would be more honest if it read 'an influential experiment in producing insensibility to pain during a surgical operation.' What that morning proved was the anaesthetic, not the surgery -- and saying so out loud is what going back to the records is for. Source: 'Ether Day Revisited: The Surgical Records of Edward Gilbert Abbott', Annals of Surgery Open (2022) -- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10431558/

question: Anaesthetists take patients under and bring them back thousands of times a day, at a risk of about one death per hundred thousand operations. A 2024 review in Frontiers in Pharmacology still calls the mechanism 'elusive': nobody can yet say how these drugs switch off a person. One thing, though, is solid -- a single property of the drug molecule predicts its anaesthetic strength so closely that the pattern has its own name. Which property?
answer: How readily the molecule dissolves in fat
choices: How readily the molecule dissolves in fat
How readily the molecule dissolves in water
How tightly the molecule grips its receptor
How quickly the molecule breaks down in the liver
context: An anaesthetic's potency tracks how well it dissolves in fat so closely that the pattern has its own name, the Meyer-Overton rule. Much of the middle of the story has since been traced: propofol grips the GABA-A receptor and holds a chloride channel open so neurons will not fire, inhaled agents blunt the excitatory NMDA receptor, scans show the traffic between the thalamus, the brain's relay hub, and the cortex going quiet, and the EEG collapses from fast beta waves into slow delta and then into burst suppression. What is missing is the bridge from those molecules to the disappearance of the person: the review's own words are that 'a comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying the induction of unconsciousness by general anesthetics remains elusive.' Nearly two centuries after the Ether Dome, nobody has it, and the bank will not pretend otherwise. Meanwhile the unexplained thing works: anaesthesia-related death runs at roughly 0.5 to 1 per 100,000 operations in high-income countries, lower than the risk of a car journey, while unintended awareness under anaesthesia still occurs in about 1 to 2 cases per 1,000. Sources: Frontiers in Pharmacology (2024), 'Recent advances in neural mechanism of general anesthesia induced unconsciousness' -- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2024.1360864/full ; Grokipedia, 'General anaesthesia' -- https://grokipedia.com/page/General_anaesthesia

question: Ether reached the operating theatre in the 1840s, and surgeons, freed from the screaming patient and the stopwatch, began to cut longer and deeper than they ever had. Of the patients who lived through the operation itself, what happened over the following twenty years to the share who died in the days afterwards?
answer: It rose, and went on rising
choices: It rose, and went on rising
It fell by roughly half
It stayed about where it was
It dropped, then climbed back
context: The era's word for it was 'hospitalism': wound infection killing patients who had survived the knife. Surgeons operated on far more people as well as for longer, still wearing the same coat from one patient to the next, on a table that was not cleaned between operations -- because painless surgery arrived roughly twenty years before germ theory reached the operating room. The freedom came first and the cleanliness came second. Joseph Lister's own figures show the scale of the correction: his operative mortality was 45.7 per cent in 1864-66, and fell to 15 per cent in 1867-69 after he began treating instruments and dressings with carbolic acid. Conquering pain was only half the problem, and the wrong half came first. Sources: Encyclopedia.com, 'Joseph Lister, 1st Baron Lister' -- https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/medicine/medicine-biographies/joseph-lister-1st-baron-lister ; Science Museum, "Lister's antisepsis system" -- https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/medicine/listers-antisepsis-system

question: In 1979 Harvard psychologist Robert Rosenthal, writing in Psychological Bulletin, gave a memorable name to the thing that eats scientific evidence: the studies that found nothing, were never written up, and simply vanish. What did he call it?
answer: The file drawer problem
choices: The file drawer problem
The dark matter problem
The hidden bench problem
The lost letter problem
context: Rosenthal worried that journals were filling with the 5% of studies that showed effects, while the other 95% sat unread. The name stuck. Source: Rosenthal, Psychological Bulletin 86(3), 1979.

question: In 2008 Erick Turner and colleagues, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, compared the published record for antidepressant trials against the FDA's own registry, which had 74 trials on 12,564 patients logged BEFORE anyone saw the results. What split did they find between the two?
answer: 51% positive in the registry, 94% positive on the shelf
choices: 51% positive in the registry, 94% positive on the shelf
94% positive in the registry, 51% positive on the shelf
60% positive in the registry, 60% positive on the shelf
80% positive in the registry, 80% positive on the shelf
context: The registry could not hide -- every trial had been logged before the outcome was known. The published shelf could, and did. Source: Turner et al., NEJM 2008.

question: Turner's 2008 study looked at what happened to the 36 antidepressant trials the FDA had judged negative or questionable. Some vanished from the literature entirely. Others were published in a curious way. What did those OTHER trials do?
answer: Written up as though they had come out positive
choices: Written up as though they had come out positive
Retracted before they could reach typesetting
Combined into a single meta-analysis paper
Republished only in non-English translation
context: Of the 36 FDA-negative trials, 22 were never published at all and 11 more were spun as positive. Only 3 were published matching what the FDA had seen. Source: Turner et al., NEJM 2008.

question: The size of the distortion Turner measured mattered because a doctor writing a prescription reads the published literature, not the FDA registry. By how much did selective publication INFLATE the apparent effect of the antidepressants overall?
answer: About 32%
choices: About 32%
About 3%
About 300%
Not at all
context: And by as much as 69% for individual drugs. This is how an entire profession can be sincerely misled by a filtered shelf without one fabricated number. Source: Turner et al., NEJM 2008.

question: A 1998 review by Andrew Vickers looked at controlled trials of medical treatments published in several countries and asked a diagnostic question: how often did the tested treatment come out INEFFECTIVE? In two of the countries the answer was: never, not once, in any published trial. Which two countries?
