answer: China and Russia
choices: China and Russia
France and Germany
Britain and Sweden
Brazil and Argentina
context: Japan hit 89%, Taiwan 95%. A 100% success rate is a publishing policy, not a scientific finding. Source: Vickers et al., Control and Clinical Trials 1998.

question: It is easy to imagine editors and reviewers doing the filtering. But in 2014 Annie Franco and colleagues, writing in Science, tracked 221 government-funded social-science studies from grant to fate, and located the censorship in a different place. Where does most of the null-result vanishing actually happen?
answer: The authors themselves never write up their null results
choices: The authors themselves never write up their null results
The peer reviewers reject null results at final review
The editors quietly kill null results before review
The funders demand null results be withheld from press
context: Strong results were 60 percentage points more likely to be written up at all, and 40 points more likely to be published. Correctly expecting rejection, most researchers spare themselves the effort. The censorship is largely self-administered. Source: Franco, Malhotra, Simonovits, Science 345:1502, 2014.

question: During the swine-flu scare, governments stockpiled billions of dollars of the antiviral oseltamivir (Tamiflu) on the strength of published trial summaries. Cochrane reviewers led by Tom Jefferson spent years demanding the unpublished full clinical study reports from the maker, Roche. When the full data finally arrived in 2014, what had the drug's actual benefit shrunk to?
answer: Roughly a day less of symptoms, with no drop in hospitalisation
choices: Roughly a day less of symptoms, with no drop in hospitalisation
Roughly a week less of symptoms and a large drop in deaths
Roughly two weeks less of symptoms and a full cure most times
No measurable benefit whatsoever in any age group
context: The claim that had justified the stockpiles -- fewer complications, fewer hospital admissions -- did not survive contact with the full trial data. Britain alone had spent around 500 million pounds. Source: Cochrane 2014; CEBM Oxford.

question: In September 2004 the world's major medical journals announced a repair for the file-drawer problem that has actually worked. From then on, a clinical trial had to do ONE specific thing beforehand, or the journals would refuse to publish its results. What was that thing?
answer: Register publicly in a trial registry in advance
choices: Register publicly in a trial registry in advance
Post its full raw dataset in advance
Publish its statistical analysis plan in advance
Recruit an independent auditor team in advance
context: The ICMJE policy took effect on 1 July 2005. You cannot quietly bin a study you were required to announce. Source: ICMJE editorial, September 2004; DeAngelis et al., NEJM.

question: The recognition skill the file-drawer story teaches a careful reader is a short question you can put to any bold claim in the news. When somebody says 'study after study shows X', what is the question that actually matters?
answer: Not how many showed X, but how many were run
choices: Not how many showed X, but how many were run
Not how many showed X, but which authors ran them
Not how many showed X, but which country funded them
Not how many showed X, but which journals printed them
context: The shelf reports what worked. The drawer holds what didn't. Registries, when honoured, let you count both. Source: Rosenthal 1979; ICMJE 2004.

question: The file drawer is one of several publication-bias detection tools statisticians talk about. Which of these is the ORIGINAL 1979 file-drawer idea, as Rosenthal proposed it -- not a related later technique?
answer: Estimating how many hidden nulls would erase an effect
choices: Estimating how many hidden nulls would erase an effect
Testing whether a scatter of studies is asymmetric on a plot
Adding imputed missing studies to rebalance a meta-analysis
Ranking studies by their published p-values on a curve
context: Rosenthal's original 'fail-safe number' asked how many drawer-hidden nulls it would take to nullify a published finding. Funnel plots, trim-and-fill, and p-curve came later. Source: Rosenthal 1979.

question: In 1892 a Russian botanist, Dmitri Ivanovsky, pressed sap from mosaic-diseased tobacco through a porcelain filter with pores too fine for any known bacterium to pass. He brushed the filtered juice onto healthy tobacco leaves. What did it do?
answer: Gave the plants the same mosaic disease as the originals
choices: Nothing - the filter had cleaned the sap completely
Killed the leaves faster than the raw sap ever had
Gave the plants the same mosaic disease as the originals
Cured leaves that already had the mosaic disease
context: Ivanovsky reported to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences on 12 February 1892 that tobacco sap remained infectious even after passing through a Chamberland porcelain candle - the first hint that a disease agent could be smaller than any known bacterium. Source: https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/dmitri-ivanovsky/

question: Ivanovsky's 1892 filter experiment did not, by itself, invent the idea of a virus. Ivanovsky himself never claimed a new kind of agent - he offered two mundane guesses for what had come through. Which pair of guesses did he actually make?
answer: A chemical toxin, or a bacterium small enough to slip the pores
choices: A brand-new category of agent, or a very small fungal spore
A chemical toxin, or a bacterium small enough to slip the pores
A plant enzyme leaking through, or an inorganic mineral trace
A bacterial spore, or a magnetic disturbance in the plant's vessels
context: Ivanovsky ran the experiment but did not make the conceptual leap. He assumed either that a bacterial toxin had come through with the sap or that the pores had leaked a very small bacterium. The idea of a genuinely new category was not his. Source: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/medicine/medicine-biographies/dmitri-iosifovich-ivanovsky

question: The new category was supplied six years later by the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck. He repeated Ivanovsky's filtration in 1898, but then did one more thing: he passed the filtered juice through healthy plant after healthy plant in series. What conclusion did that serial-passage result push him to that Ivanovsky had not reached?
answer: That the agent was replicating inside the plant, not a fixed dose of poison
choices: That the agent could infect a plant at all, rather than only irritate its leaves
That the agent was replicating inside the plant, not a fixed dose of poison
That the agent could survive being dried and stored on a shelf for later use
That the agent was carried on the outside of the researcher's tools between plants
context: A fixed dose of toxin would dilute out across successive passages; Beijerinck's agent did not. He concluded it must be replicating inside the living plant, and coined contagium vivum fluidum - a contagious living fluid - to name a new category of agent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contagium_vivum_fluidum

question: In 1935, the American biochemist Wendell Stanley pushed the strangeness further. He purified tobacco mosaic virus from tons of diseased plants and, at the end, held up something that stunned biologists: a bottle of dry, needle-like crystals that could sit on a shelf indefinitely like table salt. What happened when he redissolved those crystals and brushed the solution onto healthy tobacco leaves?
answer: The solution infected them just as vigorously as the raw sap had
choices: The solution was inert - crystallising had killed the infectivity
The solution was toxic but no longer produced the mosaic pattern
The solution infected them just as vigorously as the raw sap had
The solution worked only if a small amount of raw sap was added
context: Stanley published the crystallisation of TMV in Science in 1935 and won the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. An object that behaves like a chemical compound in a jar and like a living pathogen in a leaf broke the tidy line between chemistry and life. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1946/stanley/facts/

question: In 1992 a British public-health officer, Timothy Rowbotham, was hunting the source of a pneumonia outbreak and pulled water from a cooling tower in Bradford. Inside amoebae from that water he found something that took up the Gram stain like a bacterium, and he filed it away in his freezer as an unidentified bug he called Bradfordcoccus. In 2003 a Marseille lab finally put it under an electron microscope and identified it. What did it turn out to be?
answer: A virus - but one so big it had been mistaken for a bacterium
choices: A new strain of Legionella bacterium, the classic cooling-tower bug
A tiny parasitic protozoan living inside the amoeba's cytoplasm
A virus - but one so big it had been mistaken for a bacterium
A prion, a misfolded protein with no genome and no reproduction
context: The Bradford microbe was named mimivirus (microbe-mimicking virus) - about 750 nm across, with a genome of roughly 1.18 million base pairs and about a thousand genes, including protein-building genes viruses were not supposed to have. It had been misfiled for eleven years because it was too big to be a virus. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1081867

question: Viruses are not a rare curiosity. Count the individual particles across the whole planet - in oceans, in soil, in every living thing - and virus particles outnumber every other biological entity on Earth. In the surface ocean alone, one class of virus is doing something enormous to microbial life every single day. What are marine bacteriophages doing to the ocean's bacteria daily?
answer: Killing 10 to 40 percent of them every day by bursting their host cells open
choices: Injecting them with useful genes fast enough to double bacterial populations every few days
Herding them into thin surface films where ultraviolet kills up to 50 percent daily
Killing 10 to 40 percent of them every day by bursting their host cells open
Fusing about 5 percent of them per day into large multicellular colonies
context: Marine bacteriophages lyse (burst) their host cells to release new virus particles, and estimates of the daily kill rate for ocean bacteria run from roughly 10 percent up to 40 percent depending on water and season. The biggest predator on the planet is one you cannot see. Source: https://asm.org/articles/2023/june/marine-viruses-submerged-players-of-climate-chang

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek never attended a university and never learned Latin, yet he ground glass lenses better than any scholar's in Europe. He did not take up lens-grinding to study nature. He took it up for the sake of his trade. What was he trying to look at more closely?
answer: The threads woven into cloth
choices: The threads woven into cloth
The grain in polished timber
The gems set into gold rings
The ink on a printed page
context: Leeuwenhoek apprenticed in the drapery trade in Amsterdam at about sixteen, then went home to Delft and ran his own linen shop. Cloth was judged by its thread, and the magnifying glasses of the day reached only about 20x, so he learned to grind better ones. Every report he later sent to London was written in plain Dutch, because he had no Latin. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek'; Robert Gaynes, 'Antony van Leeuwenhoek, Pioneer of the Microscopic World', Emerging Infectious Diseases 32(6), CDC, 2026.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft tradesman with no scientific training, built instruments reaching about 275 times magnification when Robert Hooke's best microscopes managed 40 or 50, and never told anyone how. What was the working part of a Leeuwenhoek microscope?
answer: One glass bead clamped between two metal plates
choices: One glass bead clamped between two metal plates
Three lenses stacked inside a sliding leather tube
A lens and a mirror set facing in a brass box
Two lenses fixed either side of a water chamber
context: He ground over 500 lenses and built at least 25 microscopes; only about nine survive. The bead did all the work - the plates simply held the specimen at its focus, and the whole device was pressed against the eye. Gaynes notes that some may have reached 500 times. Leeuwenhoek kept the lens-making method to himself for life. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek'; Gaynes, Emerging Infectious Diseases 32(6), CDC, 2026; George Dunea, 'Van Leeuwenhoek's discovery of animalcules', Hektoen International, 2018.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek had just watched swarms of living creatures moving in the film he scraped from between his own teeth. To make the Royal Society in London feel how many there were, he set the number against something any reader could picture. What did he say the creatures in one man's mouth outnumbered?
answer: The people in a whole kingdom
choices: The people in a whole kingdom
The ships in the Dutch fleet
The bricks in the Delft walls
The stars on a clear night
context: In his letter of 17 September 1683 he asked whether there are more animals living in the scum on the teeth in a man's mouth than there are men in a whole kingdom - especially in those who never clean their teeth. Gaynes calls this letter the first known description of bacteria. Of the fastest sort Leeuwenhoek wrote that they shot through the water like a pike does; a second kind, far more numerous, spun round like a top. The English wording follows the standard translation from his Dutch. Sources: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston; Dunea, Hektoen International, 2018; Gaynes, EID 32(6), 2026.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek rubbed his teeth with salt every morning, rinsed them with water, and worked at them after meals with a toothpick and a cloth. Then he held them up to a magnifying mirror and found them dirtier than he had assumed. Before taking the tooth scraping he described in his 1683 letter, he did one thing on purpose to set up the test. What did he do?
answer: He left his mouth uncleaned for three days
choices: He left his mouth uncleaned for three days
He scraped the same tooth on three mornings
He took the scraping before he had eaten
He fasted from all food and drink for a day
context: He also built a comparison group, which is what makes the letter an experiment rather than an anecdote: the same letter reports samples from two women who cleaned their mouths daily, a child of about eight, an old man of sober habits, and an old man who had never washed his mouth in his life - in whom he found an unbelievably great company of living animalcules, swimming more nimbly than any he had ever seen. Sources: Lens on Leeuwenhoek, Letter L-135 of 1683-09-17 to Francis Aston; University of California Museum of Paleontology, 'Antony van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723)'.

question: Ann O'Hara and Fergus Shanahan argued in 2006 that the bacteria of the large intestine amount to an organ in its own right, and counted a hundred billion to a trillion of them in every gram of its contents. Most people picture what leaves the body at the toilet as leftover food. What share of its weight did the two put down to bacteria?
answer: About 60 per cent
choices: About 60 per cent
About 10 per cent
About 35 per cent
About 85 per cent
context: O'Hara and Shanahan put bacterial concentration in the large intestine at 10^11-10^12 per gram of colonic content, 'which contributes to 60% of faecal mass'. Most of what you flush is not food you failed to digest; it is the organ's own population, shed and replaced. Source: O'Hara AM & Shanahan F, 'The gut flora as a forgotten organ', EMBO Reports 2006;7(7):688-693.

question: Textbooks, lectures and review papers all carried the same figure: the bacteria in your body outnumber your own cells ten to one. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo chased every citation of it back through the literature in 2016, and found that every trail ended at the same source. What was that source?
answer: A sentence of rough arithmetic in a 1972 paper
choices: A sentence of rough arithmetic in a 1972 paper
A tally of gut samples in a 1930s survey
A count of bowel contents in a 1950s autopsy series
A rule of thumb in a 1965 bacteriology textbook
context: Thomas Luckey's 'Introduction to intestinal microecology' (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 1972;25:1292-4) assumed 10^11 bacteria per gram of gut content and about a litre - roughly a kilogram - of alimentary tract, giving 10^14. Sender et al. describe a derivation that 'only consists of a sentence-long' calculation. The first public challenge came 42 years later: Judah Rosner of the US National Institutes of Health published a letter in Microbe in 2014 titled 'Ten Times More Microbial Cells than Body Cells in Humans?' - the question mark is his. Sender and his colleagues are not against estimating; they call such back-of-the-envelope Fermi problems 'effective sanity checks'. The sin was never re-checking the guess. Sources: Sender R, Fuchs S, Milo R, PLoS Biology 14(8):e1002533, 2016; Luckey T, Am J Clin Nutr 1972;25:1292-4.

question: Every textbook gave the same figure: ten bacterial cells in your body for each human one. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo of the Weizmann Institute did the count organ by organ in 2016 for a reference adult of 70 kilograms and published a replacement, carrying an uncertainty of about 25 per cent, that they said the literature should adopt. How many bacterial cells did they find for each human cell?
answer: About 1.3
choices: About 1.3
About 0.4
About 3.5
About 20
context: Their figures: about 3.8x10^13 bacterial cells against about 3.0x10^13 human cells in the 70 kg reference man, giving 'B/H = 1.3, with an uncertainty of 25%'. In print: 'This B/H value of about 1:1 ... should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature.' The honest headline is about as many of them as of you - not that you are mostly bacteria. By weight they are almost nothing: roughly 0.2 kg wet, about 0.3 per cent of body weight. The ratio is not one fixed number either; across a reference woman, a four-week-old, a one-year-old, a 66-year-old and a 140 kg adult it runs from 1.3 to 2.3, and they refused to give a newborn figure at all, saying it is 'yet to be charted in high resolution'. Their closing line: correcting the number 'does not take away from the biological importance of the microbiota'. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, recounting the cells of the human body in 2016, had to tally the human side of the ledger too - and it is not what a biology diagram suggests. Of roughly 30 trillion human cells in a 70-kilogram adult, about 26 trillion carry no nucleus and no DNA at all. Which cells make up almost all of those 26 trillion?
answer: Red blood cells
choices: Red blood cells
Blood platelets
Outer skin cells
Lens fibre cells
context: Red blood cells alone are about 84 per cent of the total cell count; platelets, also without nuclei, add a few per cent more. Only about 3 trillion of your cells - roughly a tenth - are anything other than blood. Weighing instead of counting flips the picture completely: fat cells and muscle cells are 75 per cent of total cell mass but only about 0.2 per cent of cell number. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016 (Table 3 note 2; 'Mass-Centered Approach as Sanity Check for Cell Count').

question: Thomas Luckey's 1972 estimate of how many bacteria a human body carries was one line of arithmetic: assume a hundred billion bacteria in every gram of gut content, multiply by about a kilogram of gut, and out comes a hundred trillion. When Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo went back over it in 2016, the error was not in the multiplication but in where Luckey had assumed the bacteria were. Which stretch of the gut holds almost none of them?
answer: The stomach and the upper small intestine
choices: The stomach and the upper small intestine
The lower small intestine and the appendix
The ascending colon and the transverse colon
The descending colon and the rectum
context: Bacteria do not fill the alimentary canal. Stomach acid and the fast flow of food hold the stomach and the upper two-thirds of the small intestine to about 10^3-10^4 bacteria per millilitre - essentially nothing. Nearly all of them live in the colon, which 'exceeds all other organs by at least two orders of magnitude', and MRI measurements put the colon's real content at about 0.4 litre, not the assumed litre. A quiet irony sits inside that: the mouth, where the hidden half was first seen, is one of the emptiest places in the body - Sender et al. put the whole mouth at less than 1 per cent of the colon's bacterial number. Leeuwenhoek found a kingdom's worth of creatures in the crumbs of the real thing. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016.

question: Mitochondria, the power units inside your cells, are taken by biologists to be descendants of free-living bacteria that were swallowed whole and kept, generation after generation. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo add one line to the discussion of their 2016 recount of the body's cells, setting those captured bacteria against the roughly 38 trillion bacteria living in the gut. How do the two populations compare?
answer: Several times more mitochondria than gut bacteria
choices: Several times more mitochondria than gut bacteria
Several times more gut bacteria than mitochondria
About ten times more gut bacteria than mitochondria
About equal numbers of mitochondria and gut bacteria
context: Most cell types carry hundreds of mitochondria or more - red blood cells, having none, are the exception - so the descendants of ancient captured bacteria inside your own cells probably outnumber the free-living ones in your gut several fold. Sender et al. flag it in a single sentence of their discussion, citing Robin ED & Wong R, J Cell Physiol 1988;136:507-13. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016, Discussion.

question: A germ-free mouse is delivered into a sterile isolator and reared on sterilised food and air so that it never meets a microbe in its life. It grows up visibly wrong. In one strain the caecum - the pouch where small and large intestine meet - swells until it reaches a fifth of the animal's whole body weight. Suppose that mouse is then given an ordinary gut community. What happens to the swollen caecum?
answer: It shrinks back to normal size within a few weeks
choices: It shrinks back to normal size within a few weeks
It keeps swelling until the animal can no longer walk
It stays swollen for the whole of the animal's life
It shrinks by about half and then stops improving
context: The swelling has a known cause: mucopolysaccharides in gut mucus that bacteria would normally break down stay intact and hold water. In germ-free B6J mice cecal weight can represent up to 20 per cent of total body weight, about 5-10 per cent in NMRI and BALB/c strains; colonisation with intestinal bacteria 'normalizes the cecal size to the size observed in colonized animals within a few weeks'. That reversal is why germ-free animals are the field's causal tool: take the microbes away and something breaks, put them back and it mends - which is a test, not a correlation. Germ-free rodents also have smaller Peyer's patches, fewer intraepithelial lymphocytes and lower serum immunoglobulin, need more calories to hold their weight, and must be given supplementary B and K vitamins, the ones their missing bacteria would have made. Sources: 'The Genetic Background Is Shaping Cecal Enlargement in the Absence of Intestinal Microbiota', Nutrients 2023;15(3):636; O'Hara AM & Shanahan F, EMBO Reports 2006;7(7):688-693; Wikipedia, 'Germ-free animal'.

question: Rochellys Diaz Heijtz and colleagues reported in 2011 that germ-free mice - reared in sterile isolators so that they never acquire gut bacteria - grow up more active and less anxious than mice with a normal gut microbiota, with altered expression of synaptic genes in the brain regions governing movement and anxiety. The team then colonised germ-free mice with an ordinary gut community to see whether the behaviour could be shifted back. Which mice, if any, ended up behaving like normally raised ones?
answer: Those colonised early in life
choices: Those colonised early in life
Those colonised as adults
All of them, whatever their age
None of them, at any age
context: Colonising germ-free mice early in life normalised the pattern; colonising adults did not. There is a developmental window, and once it closes the microbes arrive too late. The mouse evidence is real and specific - increased motor activity, reduced anxiety-like behaviour, and reduced PSD-95 and synaptophysin in the striatum. What it does not license is the leap to human mood, and researchers in the field draw that line themselves: a 2024 review of germ-free models in neuropsychiatric research by Delgado-Ocana and Cuesta urges 'extreme caution when interpreting experimental results as they may be influenced by the bias imposed by the germ-free condition', notes that the artificial rearing of these animals 'raises some questions about the direct generalizability of findings from germ-free studies to real-life contexts', and concludes there is 'no one model that fits all'. There is no germ-free human to compare against, so in people no one yet knows. Sources: Diaz Heijtz R et al., PNAS 2011;108(7):3047-3052; Delgado-Ocana S & Cuesta S, 'From microbes to mind: germ-free models in neuropsychiatric research', 2024.

question: Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, whose 2016 recount replaced the famous ten-to-one figure, never claimed the old number was simply a lie. They point out in their discussion that it comes back almost exactly under one change in what you agree to count - and they say plainly that this is a question of definition rather than of measurement. Which change brings ten to one back?
answer: Counting only the human cells that carry a nucleus
choices: Counting only the human cells that carry a nucleus
Counting each mitochondrion as a bacterium of its own
Counting the bacteria of the skin and lungs as well
Counting the viruses of the gut alongside its bacteria
context: From the paper: 'if one chooses to compare the number of bacteria in the human body (3.8x10^13) to the number of nucleated human cells (about 0.3x10^13), the ratio will be about 10:1. This is because the dominant population of non-nucleated red blood cells is not included in the calculation.' The authors then turn the scepticism on themselves: whether cells without a nucleus should be included 'seems to be a question of definition. We view red blood cells as bona fide cells, as their name suggests. But it is also plausible to choose not to include them as some may think of them as bags full of hemoglobin.' A scientist naming which of his own assumptions could be argued with is the method in one paragraph. Source: Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biology 2016, Discussion.

question: In 1953, a year before the mass field trial, Jonas Salk was already putting his killed-virus polio vaccine into arms, one at a time. Who got those first 1953 injections?
answer: He injected himself, his own wife and their three sons
choices: He injected himself, his own wife and their three sons
He injected prisoners who volunteered at a federal prison
He injected Thomas Francis and his students at Michigan
He injected volunteers found for him by the March of Dimes
context: Salk inoculated himself, his wife and their three sons in 1953 as a demonstration of confidence, a full year before he asked any other family to volunteer a child for the field trial. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk.  (Legend.)

question: On 12 April 1955, under television spotlights in Ann Arbor, Thomas Francis Jr. read his verdict on the polio vaccine to over 500 scientists. How did the University of Michigan's press release, embargoed to 10:20 a.m., open?
answer: 'The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.'
choices: 'The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.'
'The results are encouraging. Further study is needed.'
'The vaccine protects. Its duration remains unknown.'
'The trial is complete. Licensing should now proceed.'
context: The release, headed 'FOR RELEASE AT 10:20 E.S.T.', opened: 'ANN ARBOR: The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.' Francis read the result in Rackham Auditorium 'at a meeting of over 500 scientists and physicians and before the penetrating eyes of cameras and powerful spotlights'. It was ten years to the day since Franklin Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945 -- and it was Roosevelt's own charity, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, that had paid for the trial. Sources: University of Michigan press release of 12 April 1955, sph.umich.edu/polio; theconversation.com/lessons-from-how-the-polio-vaccine-went-from-the-lab-to-the-public-that-americans-can-learn-from-today-145604.  (Legend.)

question: In 1954 more than 1.8 million American schoolchildren enrolled as 'Polio Pioneers'. In the strictest districts only half of them were getting Salk's vaccine, and no child, parent or doctor was told which half. So the other children were injected too. What was in their syringe?
answer: Culture fluid made to the vaccine's recipe, minus the virus
choices: Culture fluid made to the vaccine's recipe, minus the virus
Sterile salt water drawn from an unmarked glass bottle
A dose of the flu vaccine Francis had helped develop
A live poliovirus weakened by growth in monkey kidney cells
context: It was Mixture 199, a synthetic tissue-culture medium carrying antibiotics, formalin, red colouring and a buffer -- the vaccine's own formula with the poliovirus left out, so the needle, the sting and the look of the syringe were identical. A dummy treatment like this is called a placebo, and keeping everyone ignorant of who got which is called blinding. Each child in the course got three injections, and on the third a Polio Pioneers button and a March of Dimes membership card. Sources: vaxopedia.org/2024/08/11/the-1954-poliomyelitis-vaccine-field-trial/; sph.umich.edu/polio; americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_1937859.

question: Thomas Francis Jr. of Michigan -- the epidemiologist in whose department Jonas Salk had trained -- agreed to evaluate the vaccine only on his own terms. Besides a matching group of children getting a dummy shot, he demanded one thing of the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, the charity paying for the whole trial. What was it?
answer: That it keep its hands off the evaluation entirely
choices: That it keep its hands off the evaluation entirely
That it publish every objection Salk had raised
That it double the number of children enrolled
That it pay for a second trial in Canada and Finland
context: Francis's stated conditions were that 'an equal or larger number of children were injected with an inert solution and followed in the same manner', plus a policy of non-interference by the National Foundation. The Foundation had put $7,500,000 of March of Dimes money into the trial, raised from contributions by over 80 million Americans -- which is precisely why Francis wanted the people who raised it kept away from the evaluation of it. Francis had founded Michigan's Department of Epidemiology in 1941, Salk did his postgraduate training under him there, and the two co-authored influenza-vaccine papers through the 1940s. Sources: polioplace.org/people/thomas-francis-jr-md; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114166; sph.umich.edu/polio.

question: Thomas Francis Jr.'s design meant that in the strictest districts, half the enrolled children would get a dummy shot in the middle of a polio season. Jonas Salk fought the design hard, and not over credit -- he lost the argument, and Francis did not budge. What was Salk's objection?
answer: That the paralysed dummy-shot children would be paralysed at his own hands
choices: That the paralysed dummy-shot children would be paralysed at his own hands
That parents would pull their children out once they heard of the dummy shot
That the donors had given their dimes for vaccine, not for a dummy shot
That one polio season was too short to prove the vaccine held up
context: Salk wrote that the design was enough 'to make the humanitarian shudder [and] Hippocrates turn over in his grave', and that 'I would feel that every child who [gets] a placebo and becomes paralyzed will do so at my hands.' He was not alone: the National Foundation's research director Harry Weaver and its scientific director Joseph Bell both left over the control-group design before Francis was brought in, while Basil O'Connor's foundation held that it had 'a mandate from its volunteers and donors to proceed'. Sources: Oshinsky, Polio: An American Story, quoted at blog.rootsofprogress.org/polio-and-the-controversy-over-randomized-clinical-trials; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114166.

question: Thomas Francis Jr.'s design -- a random draw, a dummy shot for half the children, and nobody told who got what -- did not reach everywhere. Of 211 study areas across 44 states, 127 areas in 33 states refused to give any child a dummy injection and ran a different comparison instead. What did those districts do?
answer: Vaccinated the second grade and simply watched the first and third
choices: Vaccinated the second grade and simply watched the first and third
Vaccinated half of each grade and compared the two halves later
Vaccinated whole schools and compared them with the schools nearby
Vaccinated willing children and compared them with last year's figures
context: This was the 'observed control' design. 84 test areas in 11 states ran the randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled version; 127 test areas in 33 states ran observed controls -- 749,236 children in the placebo-controlled areas and 1,080,680 in the observed-control areas, 1,829,916 children in all, among whom 1,013 cases of polio were reported. The observed arm's own figures showed what it cost: 221,998 vaccinated second-graders at 17.1 paralytic cases per 100,000 against 725,173 first- and third-graders at 45.5. Sources: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114166; sph.umich.edu/polio; randomservices.org/random/data/Polio.html.

question: About 400 reporters were packed into Ann Arbor on 12 April 1955, waiting for one percentage they could put in a headline. Thomas Francis Jr.'s report ran over 113 pages and refused to give them one, because averaging everything into a single figure would have hidden something the data plainly showed. How did the report break the result down instead?
answer: By poliovirus type, since the three types came out very differently
choices: By poliovirus type, since the three types came out very differently
By state, since polio rates varied enormously across the 44 states
By age, since younger children fared differently from older ones
By calendar month, since the trial ran across a whole polio season
context: Francis reported roughly 60-70% protection against Type I poliovirus, over 90% against Types II and III, and about 94% against bulbar polio; the finer strain figures are given as Type III 100%, Type II 92%, Type I 68%. The report also noted that 'in no area did Type II virus prevail. There was, however, prevalence in certain areas of Types I and III' -- so the single rounded headline number reporters wanted would have hidden the fact that the vaccine did worst against one of the two types actually circulating. Francis further reported that where good antibody responses were obtained 'the effect was maintained with but moderate decline after five months.' The university had set out four teletype machines and ten tables, and the Ann Arbor News lent the Associated Press its darkroom; the moment Francis finished, reporters grabbed the report and ran for the telephones. Sources: acsh.org/news/2016/02/23/62-years-ago-today-first-mass-trials-of-the-salk-polio-vaccine; vaxopedia.org/2024/08/11/the-1954-poliomyelitis-vaccine-field-trial/; sph.umich.edu/polio; aadl.org/features/polio.

question: In the districts where a random draw decided which children got Salk's vaccine and which got a dummy shot, paralytic polio struck the dummy-shot children at 57.1 cases per 100,000. Those same districts also held 338,778 children who never took part at all, because their parents had refused to let them be injected -- children with exactly the protection the dummy-shot children had, which is none. What rate did the refused children come in at?
answer: 35.7 per 100,000 -- well below the dummy-shot children's rate
choices: 35.7 per 100,000 -- well below the dummy-shot children's rate
57.4 per 100,000 -- almost exactly the dummy-shot children's rate
81.2 per 100,000 -- well above the dummy-shot children's rate
16.9 per 100,000 -- roughly the rate among the vaccinated children
context: The full Francis Report table for the randomised districts: 200,745 vaccinated children, 33 paralytic cases, 16.4 per 100,000; 201,229 placebo children, 115 cases, 57.1 per 100,000 -- two groups matched to within 484 children out of four hundred thousand, which is what randomisation buys you. And 338,778 not-inoculated children, 121 cases, 35.7 per 100,000. Francis's own report said out loud that the two kinds of family were not alike: 'Marked sociological differences were noted by the U-M's Survey Research Center among the participating and non-participating children in the study. For example, there was a higher proportion of children participating who had been vaccinated against small-pox, diphtheria, and whooping cough than among the non-participants.' Sources: randomservices.org/random/data/Polio.html; sph.umich.edu/polio.

question: On the evening of 12 April 1955, hours after the result was announced, Edward R. Murrow put Jonas Salk on CBS's See It Now and asked him something nobody had put to him in public: who owned the patent on the vaccine? What did Salk say?
answer: That the people owned it -- there was no patent; could you patent the sun?
choices: That the people owned it -- there was no patent; could you patent the sun?
That the March of Dimes owned it, having paid for every dose of it
That the University of Pittsburgh held it on the country's behalf
That he had signed it over to the National Foundation for one dollar
context: Verbatim: Murrow asked, 'Who owns the patent on this vaccine?' Salk answered, 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk; retroreport.org/transcript/transcript-could-you-patent-the-sun/; libquotes.com/jonas-salk/quote/lbj2w7e.  (Legend.)

question: The 1954 polio vaccine field trial threw up a result that looks backwards. In the districts where a random draw decided who got Salk's vaccine and who got a dummy shot, the children whose parents had refused to enrol them at all came down with paralytic polio LESS often than the children who took the dummy shot -- and both groups had exactly the same protection, which is none. The difference lay in who volunteered: the better-educated and better-off families were the likeliest to sign their children up. Why did that make their children the higher-risk group?
answer: Cleaner plumbing meant less early exposure and so less natural immunity
choices: Cleaner plumbing meant less early exposure and so less natural immunity
Bigger houses meant more brothers and sisters sharing the same rooms
Better food meant a stronger fever response to any infection at all
More travelling meant more contact with children from other towns
context: This is the whole case against the observed-control design in one number. Volunteering families were not a random slice of the country, and the bias ran the opposite way to intuition: better sanitation delayed a child's first meeting with poliovirus past infancy, when infection is far likelier to paralyse, so the most comfortable families had the most vulnerable children. A design that compares volunteers with non-volunteers is therefore comparing unlike groups -- which is exactly why the observed-control districts' controls (45.5 per 100,000) sat well below the randomised districts' placebo children (57.1), diluting the measured benefit. Only the random draw makes the two groups alike in everything except the injection. Sources: blog.rootsofprogress.org/polio-and-the-controversy-over-randomized-clinical-trials; randomservices.org/random/data/Polio.html.

question: 'Could you patent the sun?' is one of the most quoted lines in the history of science -- Jonas Salk's answer to Edward R. Murrow when Murrow asked who owned the patent on the polio vaccine. The line is true, and it is also not the whole story: the National Foundation's lawyers had already looked into patenting the vaccine before Murrow ever asked. What had they found?
answer: That it could not be patented anyway -- killing virus with formalin was old work
choices: That it could not be patented anyway -- killing virus with formalin was old work
That defending a patent would have cost more than the vaccine could ever earn
That the rights belonged to Salk personally and not to the Foundation at all
That a patent would have broken the terms of the March of Dimes appeal
context: Foundation lawyers concluded that the key techniques, such as viral inactivation with formaldehyde, built on too much prior scientific knowledge to clear the novelty bar. Salk's refusal was ethical conviction and legal reality at the same time -- which makes the story better, not worse, and is the sort of detail a good record keeps and a good soundbite loses. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk; Jane S. Smith's archival finding as reported at slate.com/technology/2014/04/the-real-reasons-jonas-salk-didnt-patent-the-polio-vaccine.html.

question: A field trial tests the vaccine exactly as it was made for the trial; it cannot tell anyone what a different factory will turn out next month. Thirteen days after the Ann Arbor announcement, vaccinated children in Idaho and California began turning up paralysed, and about 120,000 doses from Cutter Laboratories were the cause. Over 250 children caught polio, more than 200 of them paralytic, at least ten died, and the national vaccination programme was suspended on 27 April 1955. What had gone wrong in those doses?
answer: The formalin had not killed all the virus, so live poliovirus went out
choices: The formalin had not killed all the virus, so live poliovirus went out
The doses had been stored too warm and had lost their potency in transit
The children had been given the three shots far too close together
The lots had been made with a poliovirus strain the trial never used
context: The first victim had a name: Susan Pierce, aged seven, of Pocatello, Idaho, paralysed in the same arm the needle went into, dead of fulminating bulbar polio three days after her symptoms began. Over 100 further cases appeared among family and contacts. Nothing in the Francis Report was wrong -- the trial had answered the question it was built to answer, honestly and at enormous scale. It simply could not answer a different question about a different production line, and no trial can. Albert Sabin, who had opposed the killed vaccine all along, told a Congressional subcommittee that the Salk vaccine should be suspended until a safer version could be made. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Jonas_Salk; grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine; sites.google.com/isu.edu/polioinidaho/home/the-cutter-incident-1955; sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/jonas-salk-and-albert-bruce-sabin/.

question: The lifting gas in a party balloon, the glow in an old diner sign, the atmosphere sealed inside a hot filament light bulb - three well-known everyday objects use three different elements from a single column of the periodic table. For sixty years the whole column was taught to combine with nothing at all. What was the column called?
answer: the inert gases
choices: the inert gases
the alkali metals
the halogens
the transition metals
context: The balloon is helium, the sign is neon, and old-style incandescent bulbs were filled with argon to stop the tungsten filament burning up. The column was called 'inert' - meaning refusing to react at all - and every high-school textbook printed before 1962 said so. After Bartlett they were quietly renamed 'noble' instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas.

question: The full-outer-shell idea predicts a hard number you can look up in a table: for one particular element, more energy is needed to pull off its outermost electron than for ANY other element on the whole periodic table. Which element holds that record?
answer: helium
choices: helium
fluorine
hydrogen
iron
context: Helium's first ionization energy is about 2372 kJ/mol - the highest of any element - because its two electrons sit as close as any electrons ever do to a two-proton nucleus, both filling the tightest shell there is. Fluorine is high but not the highest; hydrogen has only one electron and it is easier to pull off; iron is a metal and gives up electrons cheaply. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionization_energy.

question: Working alone in his laboratory at the University of British Columbia on the evening of 23 March 1962, Neil Bartlett broke the seal between a flask of red platinum hexafluoride gas and a flask of a colourless noble gas. An orange-yellow solid precipitated immediately - the first chemical compound anyone had ever made from a noble gas. Which noble gas was in the second flask?
answer: xenon
choices: xenon
helium
neon
argon
context: Bartlett had already shown that PtF6 was strong enough to ionise an element with a comparable ionisation energy. Among the noble gases that pointed at xenon rather than the tighter helium, neon or argon - and the flask experiment confirmed it in seconds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Bartlett_(chemist).

question: Bartlett did not pick his target by trial and error. He had noticed that xenon's outermost-electron energy sat almost exactly on top of one particular everyday MOLECULE's - about 1170 versus 1175 kilojoules per mole - and he had already ionised that molecule with platinum hexafluoride, so he reasoned the same reagent should also grab an electron from xenon. Which molecule matched xenon's number?
answer: molecular oxygen (O2)
choices: molecular oxygen (O2)
molecular nitrogen (N2)
molecular hydrogen (H2)
carbon monoxide (CO)
context: The near-identity of the two ionization energies is the physicist's insight that made the chemist's reaction plausible on paper before he ran it. The other three sit much further away: N2 at 1503 kJ/mol, CO at 1352, H2 at 1488. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Bartlett_(chemist).

question: The sharpest twist in the whole story concerns one Nobel-winning chemist: back in 1933 he PREDICTED in print that heavier noble gases should form fluorides such as KrF6 and XeF6, but in 1961, one year before Bartlett's flask experiment, he published a paper saying xenon was 'completely unreactive chemically'. The same man on both sides of the question. Who was he?
answer: Linus Pauling
choices: Linus Pauling
Fritz Haber
Glenn Seaborg
Dmitri Mendeleev
context: Pauling's 1933 prediction was based on his own theory of the chemical bond; his 1961 retraction was based on how firmly the 'inert' consensus had settled in the decades between - a warning about how even a founder can drift with a paradigm. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas_compound.

question: Bartlett wrote his 1962 product down as the neat formula Xe[PtF6], and every popular retelling still uses that formula. But later analysis showed the orange-yellow solid was NOT the pure salt he described. The bank is honest about the correction. What did the more careful analysis actually find?
answer: the solid was a mixture of two salts, not a single pure compound
choices: the solid was a mixture of two salts, not a single pure compound
the yellow colour came from an oxide of platinum; there was no xenon in it
the true product was krypton hexafluoride; the xenon flask had been contaminated
the reaction only ran at liquid-nitrogen temperature, never at room temperature
context: At room temperature the primary product reacts with more PtF6 to give a mixture containing [XeF]+[PtF6]- and [PtF5]-. The DISCOVERY - that a noble gas would react at all - stood on its own; the formula did not. Source: Graham et al., 'Neil Bartlett and the First Noble-Gas Compound', Structural Chemistry 21 (2010).

question: A rival pre-1962 explanation said noble gases refused to react because their atoms were the wrong SIZE or wrong WEIGHT to bond at all - not because of any full-shell electron arithmetic. The discovery killed that story cleanly. Which noble gases actually formed the first compounds?
answer: the heaviest ones (xenon, krypton, radon)
choices: the heaviest ones (xenon, krypton, radon)
the very lightest one (helium)
the middle of the column (argon and neon)
only the artificial one (oganesson)
context: The old 'too small or too heavy to bond' story predicted the biggest atoms should be the LEAST reactive; instead they were the first to yield, because their outer electrons sit farthest from the nucleus and are easiest to persuade off. The full-shell / ionisation-energy explanation gets the direction right; the size story got it exactly backwards. Oganesson (element 118) is real but too short-lived for real chemistry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_gas.

question: Lord Kelvin, the most respected physicist of the Victorian age, calculated in 1862 that the Sun could shine for at most a few tens of millions of years. He then told Charles Darwin and the geologists that their slow Earth was impossible. What power source did Kelvin assume was keeping the Sun hot?
answer: the Sun slowly shrinking under its own gravity
choices: the Sun slowly shrinking under its own gravity
the Sun burning like an enormous coal fire
meteors constantly falling into the Sun
the Sun powered by an unknown chemical fuel
context: This is the Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism: as a ball of gas contracts, gravitational potential energy turns into heat. Kelvin's math was correct for the physics of his day. What he could not know is that the atom hides an energy source Victorian physics had never imagined. Radioactivity, found by Henri Becquerel in 1896, was the first hint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_Earth

question: In 1920 Francis Aston used his new mass spectrograph to weigh atoms one kind at a time and found a strange result: four hydrogen nuclei weigh very slightly MORE than the single helium nucleus they could combine to make. About how much heavier are the four hydrogens?
answer: about 0.7 percent heavier
choices: about 0.7 percent heavier
about 7 percent heavier
about 25 percent heavier
about 70 percent heavier
context: A tiny sliver, but Aston saw its meaning at once. He wrote that 'if hydrogen is transformed into helium a certain quantity of mass must be annihilated in the process' and called out its 'cosmical importance.' That missing 0.7 percent, multiplied by c^2, is the fuel of every star. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_nuclear_fusion

question: Arthur Eddington took Aston's tiny mass defect and, at the British Association meeting in Cardiff on 24 August 1920, proposed a bold answer to what makes stars shine. In his presidential address 'The Internal Constitution of the Stars,' what did Eddington propose was powering the Sun?
answer: hydrogen nuclei joining together to make helium
choices: hydrogen nuclei joining together to make helium
helium nuclei splitting apart into hydrogen
heavy elements at the core slowly decaying
the Sun's rotation being braked by its magnetic field
context: Eddington was proposing what we now call hydrogen fusion, more than a decade before anyone worked out the reactions. His only clue was Aston's 0.7 percent of missing mass. Source: https://bfschutz.com/2020/08/24/eddington-in-cardiff-100-years-ago-today-the-first-proposal-that-stars-are-powered-by-fusion/  (Legend.)

question: Critics told Eddington that the Sun's interior, calculated at 'only' millions of degrees, was too cold for hydrogen nuclei to overcome their electric repulsion and merge. In his 1920 Cardiff address, how did Eddington answer them?
answer: he told them to go and find a hotter place
choices: he told them to go and find a hotter place
he admitted the calculation was probably wrong
he proposed the Sun ran on gravity instead
he said the missing heat came from radioactivity
context: The full line: 'The helium which we handle must have been put together at some time and some place. We do not argue with the critic who urges that the stars are not hot enough for this process; we tell him to go and find a hotter place.' Quantum tunneling, still ten years away, would prove him right. Source: The Observatory, October 1920  (Legend.)

question: The Sun's core sits at about 15.7 million kelvin and has been shining for about 4.6 billion years. To keep up its power output of roughly 3.85 x 10^26 watts, how much of its own matter does the Sun turn into pure energy every single second?
answer: about four million tonnes
choices: about four million tonnes
about four thousand tonnes
about four billion tonnes
about four trillion tonnes
context: Every second, roughly the mass of a small mountain vanishes from the Sun as energy (E = m c^2). It has been doing this since the Earth was young and will keep it up for billions of years more, because the Sun is a very large mountain. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun

question: In 1925 a Harvard graduate student named Cecilia Payne measured the Sun's composition from its spectrum in her PhD thesis. Her senior colleague Henry Norris Russell pressed her to call the result 'almost certainly not real,' then quietly confirmed it himself four years later. What did she find the Sun is mostly made of, by mass?
answer: hydrogen and helium
choices: hydrogen and helium
iron and silicon
carbon and oxygen
sodium and calcium
context: By mass, roughly 74 percent hydrogen and 24 percent helium. A Sun full of hydrogen is exactly what the fusion story needs. Payne-Gaposchkin was later called 'undoubtedly the most eminent woman astronomer of all time.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Payne-Gaposchkin  (Legend.)

question: The path to carbon inside a star has a nasty problem. Two helium-4 nuclei can stick together to make beryllium-8, but beryllium-8 is fantastically unstable: it falls apart into two heliums again in roughly what amount of time?
answer: about a ten-thousandth of a trillionth of a second
choices: about a ten-thousandth of a trillionth of a second
about a millionth of a second
about a thousandth of a second
about a full second
context: The measured half-life is about 8.19 x 10^-17 seconds. A third helium nucleus must arrive inside that vanishing window, or beryllium-8 splits back and no carbon is made. This is the triple-alpha bottleneck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium-8  (Legend.)

question: In 1953 Fred Hoyle stared at the triple-alpha bottleneck and made one of the strangest successful predictions in the history of physics. He argued that carbon-12 MUST have a specific, unknown excited state near 7.68 MeV, and pressed William Fowler's Caltech nuclear lab to look for it. What reason did Hoyle give for insisting the state had to be there?
answer: carbon exists in huge abundance and we are made of it
choices: carbon exists in huge abundance and we are made of it
the beryllium-8 measurement demanded a matching state
quantum mechanics forbade any other stable resonance
the Sun's spectrum showed a carbon line at that energy
context: Hoyle's argument was blunt: carbon is plainly here in vast quantity, so the nuclear physics must permit its formation. If the resonance did not exist, we would not exist to look for it. This kind of reasoning is often called anthropic. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-alpha_process  (Legend.)

question: Hoyle's prediction of a specific carbon-12 excited state was startling, but within months it was tested. At Caltech, Ward Whaling used an old Van de Graaff particle accelerator and found the resonance almost exactly where Hoyle had said it would be, near 7.65 MeV. What is this excited state of carbon-12 now called?
answer: the Hoyle state
choices: the Hoyle state
the Fowler state
the Whaling state
the Bethe state
context: The predicted level was near 7.68 MeV; the measured level came in near 7.65 MeV. Every carbon atom in your body slipped through this narrow doorway inside a dying star. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-alpha_process  (Legend.)

question: To test whether the Sun's core really did what the fusion theory said, Raymond Davis Jr wanted to catch the ghostly particles it should be producing. Starting in 1970 he ran a bizarre-looking experiment for over twenty years, nearly a mile underground in the Homestake gold mine in South Dakota. What sat inside his tank?
answer: 100,000 gallons of ordinary dry-cleaning fluid
choices: 100,000 gallons of ordinary dry-cleaning fluid
100,000 gallons of ultra-purified drinking water
a block of solid lead the size of a small car
a chamber of extremely cold liquid helium
context: The fluid was perchloroethylene, filling a 380 cubic metre tank 1,478 metres down. Neutrinos from the Sun's core very rarely turn a chlorine atom into an argon atom, and Davis literally counted the argon atoms one by one. He shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestake_experiment  (Legend.)

question: For about thirty-five years, Davis's dry-cleaning-fluid tank kept catching only around a THIRD of the solar neutrinos that John Bahcall's carefully checked model of the Sun said it should. Either the Sun's model was wrong or the detector was, and neither team could find a mistake. In 2001 the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, using 1,000 tonnes of heavy water deep in a Canadian nickel mine, finally cracked it. What did SNO show?
answer: neutrinos change from one type to another as they fly
choices: neutrinos change from one type to another as they fly
the Sun's core is a little cooler than the model assumed
chlorine detectors miss most of the neutrinos that hit them
the Sun makes far fewer neutrinos than fusion predicts
context: Neutrinos come in three flavours (electron, muon, tau). Davis's tank could only see the electron flavour; SNO's heavy water could see all three, and the total matched Bahcall's prediction exactly. The 'missing' two-thirds had turned into the other flavours in flight. That change is only possible if neutrinos have mass. Kajita (Super-Kamiokande) and McDonald (SNO) shared the 2015 Nobel Prize. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudbury_Neutrino_Observatory  (Legend.)

question: The 1957 B2FH paper by Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle mapped where every chemical element in the periodic table comes from. Fusion inside stars builds elements up to iron. On 17 August 2017, LIGO and Virgo caught event GW170817 and astronomers watched in real time where the heaviest elements are forged. What kind of event was it?
answer: the merger of two neutron stars
choices: the merger of two neutron stars
the core collapse of a single blue supergiant
a nova on the surface of an old white dwarf
a giant flare from a young magnetic star
context: The kilonova AT 2017gfo, seen 11 hours after the gravitational-wave signal, is estimated to have forged about 16,000 Earth masses of heavy elements, including roughly 10 Earth masses of gold and platinum alone. B2FH predicted this half a century earlier. Fowler received half the 1983 Nobel; Hoyle, controversially, was left out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GW170817; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B2FH_paper  (Legend.)

question: In October 2020 three epidemiologists -- Martin Kulldorff of Harvard, Sunetra Gupta of Oxford and Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford -- signed a one-page open letter arguing that shielding the old and the sick hard was a better COVID response than locking everyone down. What name did their letter give this approach?
answer: Focused protection
choices: Focused protection
Zero COVID
Herd immunity
Ring vaccination
context: The distinction matters: focused protection called for HARDER shielding of nursing homes and the immunocompromised than generic lockdowns actually achieved, not for ignoring the virus. Critics often conflated it with 'let it rip'. The letter is named for the small Massachusetts town where the three met and signed.

question: The three doctors were called 'fringe' -- a word that mattered because their credentials were the opposite. One held a chair in medicine at Harvard, another a chair in theoretical epidemiology at Oxford, and the third was a Stanford professor of health policy. Within about two weeks, how many medical and public-health scientists had co-signed the declaration?
answer: More than ten thousand
choices: More than ten thousand
About one hundred
About five hundred
About one thousand
context: By 16 October 2020 the count was over 10,000 medical and public-health scientists, tens of thousands of practitioner signatures, and hundreds of thousands of citizen signatures. Whatever they were, they were not three.

question: Days after the letter was released, Francis Collins -- then the director of the NIH -- wrote a private email about it to Anthony Fauci and Eric Green. He described the three authors as 'fringe epidemiologists' and asked for a very specific kind of response to their letter. What did he ask for?
answer: A quick devastating takedown
choices: A quick devastating takedown
A blue-ribbon expert panel
A formal peer review
A congressional hearing
context: Collins's line, verbatim: 'There needs to be a quick and devastating published take down of its premises.' The emails came out later through a Freedom of Information Act request filed by the American Institute for Economic Research.

question: The John Snow Memorandum -- the scientific reply to the declaration published in The Lancet on 14 October 2020 -- made two central objections to 'focused protection'. Alongside the argument that shielding the vulnerable was not achievable in practice, what was the SECOND main objection the memorandum raised?
answer: Uncontrolled spread would overwhelm hospitals
choices: Uncontrolled spread would overwhelm hospitals
Long COVID would disable a working-age generation
New variants would evade any acquired immunity
Vaccines were only weeks away and would end the epidemic
context: The John Snow Memorandum's two-pronged case was practical infeasibility of shielding plus health-system overload from uncontrolled transmission. Kulldorff, Gupta and Bhattacharya answered that generic lockdowns had ALSO failed to protect the vulnerable -- roughly 40 percent of early U.S. COVID deaths were traced to nursing homes anyway -- but the hospital-overwhelm concern was a genuine one, and one that being called 'fringe' did nothing to address.

question: The declaration's authors argued that one particular category of closure had the flimsiest risk case AND the deepest measured cost. Sweden under state epidemiologist Anders Tegnell kept these facilities open through 2020 as the real-world counterfactual. Which closure did the authors condemn most sharply?
answer: Schools
choices: Schools
Indoor dining
Gyms and fitness centres
Houses of worship
context: Sweden kept most primary and lower-secondary schools open across 2020-21 and became the standing counterfactual. Measured learning loss and mental-health harm from U.S. and U.K. school closures now runs to multiple years in disadvantaged cohorts. Indoor dining, gyms and worship services were all closed in various jurisdictions, but the declaration's authors flagged schools as the sharpest case.

question: On 25 March 2025 the U.S. Senate confirmed one of the three 'fringe epidemiologists' as Director of the National Institutes of Health -- the same post Francis Collins had held when he wrote the 'devastating takedown' email in 2020. Which of the three took the job?
answer: Jay Bhattacharya
choices: Jay Bhattacharya
Martin Kulldorff
Sunetra Gupta
Marty Makary
context: The vote was 53-47, on party lines. Bhattacharya took office on 1 April 2025. Marty Makary, the Johns Hopkins surgeon, was confirmed to lead the FDA the same week. Whatever else it was, it was not vindication of the declaration as a whole -- but the man they had called fringe now ran the agency.

question: In a 2024 interview Francis Collins admitted he had never seen the evidence behind one specific COVID number that CDC guidance had enforced for two years. Which rule was it?
answer: Six-foot social distancing
choices: Six-foot social distancing
The 14-day quarantine after exposure
The five-day post-symptom isolation window
The three-foot classroom-cohort rule
context: In deposition and interviews Collins said he had never seen any evidence supporting the six-foot figure. In the same period he acknowledged that ignoring lockdown side-effects had been 'really unfortunate' and that calling Kulldorff, Bhattacharya and Gupta 'fringe' had been a mistake.

question: Textbooks for decades reported that the end-Permian killed '96% of marine species' -- a figure from an older genus-level statistical extrapolation. Careful species-level work has since revised the number DOWN. It is still by far the worst extinction in the record, but what is the current estimate for marine species lost?
answer: About 81%
choices: About 81%
About 96%
About 55%
About 41%
context: The 96% number came from a genus-level 'reverse rarefaction' estimate; direct species counts now put the marine loss around 81%. The number changed because the METHOD improved, not because the crisis shrank -- it remains uniquely severe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian-Triassic_extinction_event.

question: The murder weapon for the end-Permian is written in the rock of one country: one of the largest volcanic outpourings in Earth history erupted across exactly this interval and buried an area the size of a continent -- originally up to about 7 million square kilometers -- in flood basalt. Which volcanic province is the prime suspect?
answer: The Siberian Traps
choices: The Siberian Traps
The Deccan Traps
The Ontong Java Plateau
The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province
context: The Deccan Traps in India erupted at the end-Cretaceous, alongside the Chicxulub impact. Ontong Java is a mid-Cretaceous oceanic province. CAMP is the End-Triassic trigger. Only the Siberian Traps match the end-Permian date. Source: simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Traps.

question: The Siberian eruptions buried a continent in basalt, but the basalt itself did not do most of the killing. The rising magma pushed sills up THROUGH the Tunguska sedimentary basin, and what those sills roasted on the way up mattered far more than what poured out on top. Which buried Tunguska rock, when cooked by the intruding sills, released the CO2 pulse that drove global warming and ocean anoxia?
answer: Permian coal beds
choices: Permian coal beds
Evaporite (salt) beds
Organic-rich marine shales
Dolomite reef limestones
context: Field studies find charred coal fragments in the sills themselves -- direct evidence the intrusions burned through Tunguska coals. Evaporites and organic shales are also present in the basin and contributed halogens and hydrocarbons, but the measured coal-combustion signature is the biggest carbon source. CO2 rose toward ~2,500 ppm; temperatures climbed ~8 C. Source: pubs.geoscienceworld.org/gsa/geology/article/48/10/986.

question: For decades the end-Permian pulse could only be placed 'sometime late in the Permian'. Then a sharper radiometric clock was applied to microscopic crystals harvested from volcanic ash beds at Meishan, China, squeezing the main extinction pulse to roughly 60,000 years -- a geological instant. Which method delivered that precision?
answer: Uranium-lead dating of zircons
choices: Uranium-lead dating of zircons
Carbon-14 dating of fossil shells
Potassium-argon dating of feldspar
Optically stimulated luminescence of quartz
context: U-Pb via CA-ID-TIMS on zircons gives precision at the tens-of-thousands-of-years level even at 252 Ma. Carbon-14 dies at ~50,000 years old -- useless in deep time. K-Ar and OSL cannot approach this precision at this age. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian-Triassic_extinction_event.

question: In the earliest Triassic bone beds of South Africa's Karoo Basin, one stubby tusked survivor is so common it can make up as much as 90% of all recovered land vertebrate fossils -- a whole planet apparently running on a single herbivore lineage. Which genus is that disaster-taxon?
answer: Lystrosaurus
choices: Lystrosaurus
Dimetrodon
Cynognathus
Thrinaxodon
context: Dimetrodon is early Permian and long gone by 252 Ma. Cynognathus and Thrinaxodon are later Triassic cynodonts. Lystrosaurus's runaway abundance is the pattern signature of a disaster taxon: empty niches, few competitors, one lineage inheriting the earth. Full land faunas took about 30 million years to rebuild. Source: nature.com/articles/s41467-020-15243-7.

question: Even with the Siberian trigger identified and the main pulse timed to 60,000 years, the end-Permian remains genuinely unsettled at the research frontier -- several open disputes are all live in the peer-reviewed literature. Of the following, which is currently THE headline open dispute in the review papers?
answer: Ranking the several kill mechanisms by damage done
choices: Ranking the several kill mechanisms by damage done
Ranking intruded sills against surface lavas for the killing
Ordering the terrestrial pulse and the marine pulse in time
Setting full recovery closer to 5 million or 30 million years
context: The candidates -- extreme warming, ocean deoxygenation, ocean acidification, and ozone damage from volcanic halogens -- are all real, all measurable in the rock, and all argued over as to which killed the most species and in what order. The sills-vs-lavas, land-vs-sea timing, and recovery-length questions are also live in the literature but generate less contention. Source: academic.oup.com/nsr/article/11/1/nwad273.

question: For decades a respectable rival explanation held that the green flash was not in the sky at all -- it was on the back of the observer's own eye. Which everyday visual effect were those scientists appealing to?
answer: The complementary-colour ghost the eye sees after staring at a bright red patch
choices: The complementary-colour ghost the eye sees after staring at a bright red patch
The persistence-of-vision blur that makes a spinning ember look like a solid ring
The Purkinje shift that makes reds fade to grey first as the light dims at dusk
The Troxler fading that erases a steady patch held in peripheral vision
context: A retina that has stared at a red Sun has bleached most of its red-sensitive photopigment, so a following white or dark scene reads as the complementary colour -- cyan or green. It is the same opponent-process effect that makes a red square leave a green ghost image on a white wall. The hypothesis was reasonable; it just happened to be wrong, and only the photograph could show that.

question: Dispersion behind the flash happens at every clear sunset -- air bends short wavelengths a hair more than long ones, so the green image of the Sun sets a fraction of a second after the red image. Yet the effect is rare and needs a very specific horizon. What atmospheric condition almost always has to be present for a watcher to actually catch it?
answer: A temperature inversion or mirage layer over the horizon
choices: A temperature inversion or mirage layer over the horizon
A high cirrus deck adding extra prismatic dispersion to the sunlight
A very dry stratosphere that stops scattering the shortest wavelengths
A viewer at high altitude looking down through less air than at sea level
context: The pure refractive green rim is only a few arcseconds thick and normally too thin to see. Warm air over cool water (or cool air over warm land) sets up a density gradient that behaves like a slow lens, stretching the last bit of the disc vertically until the green edge is thick enough to register. That is why a stable sea horizon, or a high desert horizon, is where amateurs actually catch it. And why 'blue flashes' are rarer still: violet and blue are bent even MORE than green, but they are scattered away by air along the long horizon path (Rayleigh scattering), so almost nothing at that end of the spectrum reaches the eye. Safety note: the flash is only safe to look for at the very last instant, when the disc is essentially gone -- do not stare at the Sun to catch it.

question: Two satellite instruments -- NOAA's AVHRR since 1981 and NASA's MODIS since 1999 -- have been counting how much leaf every patch of ground carries. A 2016 paper led by Zaichun Zhu, published in Nature Climate Change, added up 35 years of the counts and reported something the models had not been forecasting. What had happened to Earth's plant cover?
answer: between a quarter and a half of the vegetated land had greened significantly
choices: between a quarter and a half of the vegetated land had greened significantly
the total leaf area had stayed within one percent of its 1982 value
the tropics had greened but the temperate zone had lost half its leaves
leaf area had shrunk by about a fifth as drought spread on every continent
context: The satellites were not looking for good news; they were counting leaves. NASA's own release put the extra leaf area at roughly twice the area of the continental United States. Source: Zhu et al., Nature Climate Change (2016); NASA Goddard release.

question: The Zhu paper ran the satellite counts through ten global ecosystem models to sort out WHY the planet was greening. The models converged on one dominant driver -- roughly 70 percent of the trend -- with three smaller runners-up. Which driver did they hand the 70 percent to?
answer: fertilisation by richer atmospheric carbon dioxide
choices: fertilisation by richer atmospheric carbon dioxide
extra nitrogen falling out of polluted air
longer growing seasons from a warmer climate
abandonment and regrowth of old farmland
context: The full split reported was 70% CO2, 9% nitrogen deposition, 8% climate change, 4% land cover. Co-author Ranga Myneni of Boston University stated the 70% figure publicly. The percentages are MODEL output, not a direct measurement. Source: Zhu et al., Nature Climate Change (2016).

question: A 2019 paper in Nature Sustainability, led by Chi Chen, used the finer-resolution MODIS record to ask WHERE the new green was. The answer was politically awkward for the CO2-only story. Two countries alone accounted for about a third of the new leaf area, mostly through tree-planting and intensive cropping. Which pair?
answer: China and India
choices: China and India
Brazil and Indonesia
the United States and Canada
Russia and Kazakhstan
context: China's greening was mostly forests (42%) and croplands (32%); India's was mostly croplands (82%). Those two countries hold only about 9% of Earth's vegetated land. So a large chunk of the greening is land MANAGEMENT, not the CO2 fertilisation the 2016 paper had highlighted. Source: Chen et al., Nature Sustainability (2019).

question: Instead of trusting models, another line of research just grows real crops or forests at raised CO2 in the open air. FACE experiments -- Free-Air CO2 Enrichment -- ring an outdoor plot with vertical pipes that release CO2 all season. When the Oak Ridge sweetgum FACE ran for eleven years, what happened to the early growth boost?
answer: it faded as soil nitrogen ran short and could not keep up
choices: it faded as soil nitrogen ran short and could not keep up
it accelerated, because the trees learned to use the extra CO2 better
it flipped to a loss, because the trees started shedding leaves early
it held perfectly steady across all eleven growing seasons
context: The Oak Ridge result is the textbook caution against extrapolating sealed-greenhouse gains to real forests: without extra nutrients, the CO2 boost hits a nutrient ceiling. It is exactly the kind of check a modelled 70% share needs. Source: Norby et al., PNAS (2010).

question: A 2014 Nature paper led by Samuel Myers put wheat, rice, peas and soybeans through open-air CO2 enrichment and measured what came out at harvest. The plants grew more grain and more leaf, as expected. What went DOWN in the grain relative to plants grown at ambient CO2?
answer: the concentrations of zinc, iron and protein
choices: the concentrations of zinc, iron and protein
the concentrations of vitamin C and beta-carotene
the concentrations of calcium and vitamin D
the concentrations of omega-3 fats and folate
context: Bigger crops do not automatically mean more nutrition per bite -- a real cost of CO2 fertilisation in C3 grains and legumes, and the reason 'more leaf = pure good news' is a cartoon the bank refuses in both directions. Source: Myers et al., Nature (2014).

question: Every day in ordinary operating theatres, one medical professional performs a routine procedure that switches a person's inner experience off and then back on within minutes -- and no one can point to the specific physical thing being switched. Which professional does that switching?
answer: an anaesthetist
choices: an anaesthetist
a radiologist
a paramedic
a dentist
context: General anaesthesia is the most repeated, most routine consciousness experiment on the planet, and neither the drug companies nor the neuroscientists can tell you what it is doing to the felt world. Source: iep.utm.edu/hard-problem-of-conciousness.

question: In 1974 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel wrote a Philosophical Review essay meant to make the shape of the mystery visible. He picked one particular animal and argued you could learn every detail of how it sensed the world and still not know what sensing that way is LIKE from the inside. Which animal did he pick?
answer: a bat
choices: a bat
an octopus
a honeybee
a mantis shrimp
context: The essay was 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' -- the animal chosen because echolocation is fully describable in physics, so any leftover is the leftover. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Is_It_Like_to_Be_a_Bat%3F.

question: In 1998, neuroscientist Christof Koch bet philosopher David Chalmers a case of fine wine that within a set number of years, science would pin down the specific neural signature of consciousness. When the clock ran out at the 2023 ASSC meeting, who paid whom?
answer: Koch paid Chalmers
choices: Koch paid Chalmers
Chalmers paid Koch
the bet was called a draw
the wager was voided
context: The philosopher won; the neuroscientist handed over a case of Portuguese wine on stage and then immediately proposed a rematch on another 25-year clock. Source: scientificamerican.com/article/a-25-year-old-bet-about-consciousness-has-finally-been-settled.

question: In the seventeenth century, Rene Descartes had his own answer for where the mind and the body meet inside the head. He pointed to one specific small structure and named it as the spot where thought and matter touch. Which structure did Descartes name?
answer: the pineal gland
choices: the pineal gland
the hippocampus
the corpus callosum
the medulla
context: Descartes picked it partly because it sits on the midline and does not come in a left-right pair; modern neuroscience has moved on, but the puzzle of where subjective experience 'happens' has not. Source: iep.utm.edu/hard-problem-of-conciousness.
