question: Two rival theories make DIFFERENT and testable brain predictions. Giulio Tononi's Integrated Information Theory says consciousness tracks how much a system's information is welded into one irreducible whole. Which part of the brain does IIT predict is the physical seat of consciousness?
answer: the hot zone in the back of the cortex
choices: the hot zone in the back of the cortex
the cerebellum at the base of the skull
the brainstem
the hypothalamus
context: The 'hot zone' spans temporal, parietal and occipital areas. IIT sits opposite Global Neuronal Workspace, which pushes the burden forward. Source: scholarpedia.org/article/Integrated_information_theory.

question: The COGITATE adversarial collaboration made rival consciousness camps pre-register their theory's predictions before any scanning began, then tested more than 250 participants using three brain-imaging methods together. Which three methods did COGITATE combine?
answer: fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG
choices: fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG
PET, ultrasound and scalp EEG
CT, X-ray and near-infrared spectroscopy
fNIRS, DTI and single-cell recording
context: The intracranial EEG data came from epilepsy patients who already had electrodes placed inside their brains for clinical reasons -- the only ethical way to record neurons directly. Source: arc-cogitate.com/project.

question: The COGITATE result appeared in Nature on 30 April 2025 and refused to crown a winner. Each camp had sealed three predictions in advance. How did the two theories score on those sealed predictions?
answer: IIT 2 of 3 passed, GNWT 0 of 3 passed
choices: IIT 2 of 3 passed, GNWT 0 of 3 passed
IIT 3 of 3 passed, GNWT 0 of 3 passed
IIT 0 of 3 passed, GNWT 3 of 3 passed
IIT 1 of 3 passed, GNWT 2 of 3 passed
context: The paper's honest headline was that neither theory survived intact -- IIT scored better on the sealed predictions but neither camp got a clean sweep, and both have been forced to refine their claims. Source: psy.ox.ac.uk/news/a-landmark-experiment-published-in-nature.

question: On 15 September 2023, 124 researchers -- including Bernard Baars, Daniel Dennett and Joseph LeDoux -- posted an open letter on PsyArXiv arguing that Integrated Information Theory should be labelled something specific until it makes sharper testable predictions. What label did the letter demand?
answer: pseudoscience
choices: pseudoscience
unfalsifiable
religion
philosophy
context: Christof Koch and Anil Seth answered in print defending IIT; this is a live public fight about where the border of science actually runs. Source: nature.com/articles/d41586-023-02971-1.

question: Live rival theories at the frontier include Higher-Order Thought accounts, predictive-processing accounts, and one radical proposal by mathematical physicist Roger Penrose and anaesthesiologist Stuart Hameroff that places the seat of consciousness in quantum-scale collapses inside a specific cell part. Which cell part?
answer: microtubules inside neurons
choices: microtubules inside neurons
the myelin sheath
ribosomes
the synaptic cleft
context: Their theory is called Orchestrated Objective Reduction, or 'Orch-OR'; most consciousness scientists reject it, but it is a serious, real, published rival, not a joke. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_information_theory (rivals section).

question: On 23 December 1954 in Boston, Joseph Murray took a healthy kidney from Ronald Herrick and sewed it into Ronald's dying identical twin brother Richard. Earlier attempts on other pairs had failed within days. What was the first sign, right there in the operating room, that this one was going to work?
answer: The transplanted kidney began making urine on the table
choices: The transplanted kidney began making urine on the table
Richard's own kidneys started working again beside it
Ronald's blood pressure held steady after the cut
The ward telephone rang with the wire service asking for the outcome
context: The organ pinked up, filled with blood and produced urine before the surgeons had closed. Murray later said the next day the patient was hungry with a sparkle in his eye. Source: https://www.harvardmagazine.com/alumni-profiles/harvard-joseph-murray-transplantation

question: Joseph Murray served three years on a WWII Army burn ward at Valley Forge General Hospital, where surgeons routinely covered burns with skin taken from other people. What happened to a graft cut from someone else once it was stitched onto a burned soldier?
answer: It took hold, looked healthy for weeks, then was attacked and died
choices: It took hold, looked healthy for weeks, then was attacked and died
It knitted in cleanly and lasted the whole recovery
It never bled properly and greyed within hours
It slowly took on the patient's own skin colour
context: Grafts between identical twins on the same ward, by contrast, were kept for good. That difference told Murray the barrier was immunological -- the recipient's body could tell whose tissue was whose. Source: https://www.harvardmagazine.com/alumni-profiles/harvard-joseph-murray-transplantation

question: The 1954 operation forced Joseph Murray's team to cut a healthy organ out of a healthy man who did not need surgery. Before Ronald Herrick agreed to give up a kidney for his dying twin, the team met with him again and again. On one point they deliberately refused to help him. What did they refuse to do?
answer: Tell Ronald whether they thought he should go ahead
choices: Tell Ronald whether they thought he should go ahead
Bring the family priest into any of the meetings
Speak to Ronald without a lawyer present in the room
Give Ronald a written estimate of his own odds of dying
context: The team laid out the risks in full and even consulted clergy of several denominations and legal counsel, but stayed neutral on the decision itself -- the choice to give up a kidney had to be Ronald's alone. Source: https://collections.countway.harvard.edu/onview/exhibits/show/reconstructing-lives/transplantation/herrick-twins

question: Richard Herrick, the world's first lasting transplant recipient, lived about eight more years after the 1954 operation, married one of his nurses, and fathered two children. When he died in March 1963, what killed him?
answer: Heart failure
choices: Heart failure
Rejection of the transplanted kidney
Pneumonia caught from his brother
A stroke during a second operation
context: The transplanted kidney was still working at his death; some sources also note the underlying nephritis returning in it, but the immediate cause was cardiac. His donor brother Ronald lived to 79. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Herrick

question: In 1964 Peter Higgs sent a short theory paper to Physics Letters, edited at CERN. They rejected it. He added one paragraph and resubmitted to Physical Review Letters, which printed it. What did the extra paragraph point out?
answer: his idea implied a brand-new massive particle
choices: his idea implied a brand-new massive particle
his equations reproduced the orbit of Mercury
his mechanism replaced Einstein's theory of gravity
the maths could build a much better transistor
context: That paragraph is why we now say 'the Higgs boson'. Physical Review Letters accepted the second version. The other 1964 papers by Englert-Brout and by Guralnik-Hagen-Kibble had the mechanism but not the explicit prediction of a new particle -- Higgs's rejection-driven addendum put a target on the wall for the next forty-eight years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Higgs.

question: It was not just Peter Higgs. Three groups published the same mass-giving mechanism in a burst of a few months in 1964, working independently. Which pair published first, in August, months before Higgs?
answer: Francois Englert and Robert Brout
choices: Francois Englert and Robert Brout
Gerald Guralnik and Tom Kibble
Steven Weinberg and Abdus Salam
Sheldon Glashow and Julian Schwinger
context: The proper name is the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism. Six people published it in 1964: Englert and Brout in Brussels in August; Higgs in Edinburgh in October; Guralnik, Hagen and Kibble in November. The 2013 Nobel went to Englert and Higgs; Brout had died in 2011 and Nobels are not awarded posthumously. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: It is often said that the Higgs field 'gives things their mass'. That is true for fundamental particles like electrons and quarks -- but if you weigh a proton, only about one percent of the number comes from the Higgs. Where does the other 99 percent of a proton's mass come from?
answer: the churning quark and gluon binding energy inside it
choices: the churning quark and gluon binding energy inside it
the total electric charge of its constituent quarks
the gravitational self-attraction of the proton itself
the sea of neutrinos passing constantly through it
context: A proton is three quarks and a boiling sea of gluons bound by the strong force. Einstein's E = mc squared runs both directions: the tremendous binding energy of that churn shows up as mass. So most of your body weight is not the Higgs -- it is quantum chromodynamics doing its work inside every proton and neutron you are made of. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: The 4 July 2012 CERN announcement was staged by two experiments the lab had deliberately kept apart, so that neither team could see the other's data before the reveal. Both saw the same bump at about 125 GeV. What are the two detectors called?
answer: ATLAS and CMS
choices: ATLAS and CMS
LHCb and ALICE
COMPASS and NA62
DELPHI and OPAL
context: ATLAS (A Toroidal LHC Apparatus) and CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) are separate collaborations of thousands of physicists, sitting on opposite sides of the 27-km ring. Independent analyses of independent detectors seeing the same particle within days of each other -- that is what discovery looks like when the community insists on replication. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: Peter Higgs was 83 years old and sitting in the CERN seminar room on 4 July 2012 when ATLAS and CMS presented their results -- forty-eight years after his 1964 paper. Asked for a reaction on camera, what did he say?
answer: 'really an incredible thing that it's happened in my lifetime'
choices: 'really an incredible thing that it's happened in my lifetime'
'this is the beginning of a new physics'
'I told you so, and it took you long enough'
'the goddamn particle turned out to exist after all'
context: Higgs, born 1929, was visibly emotional -- he wiped his eyes during the presentation. He shared the 2013 Nobel with Francois Englert; Robert Brout, the third author of the earliest 1964 paper, had died in 2011 and Nobels are not awarded posthumously. Higgs himself died in April 2024. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Higgs.

question: The Higgs boson is often called 'the God particle' in popular writing, and Peter Higgs himself hated the phrase. Where did the nickname actually come from?
answer: the title of Leon Lederman's 1993 popular-science book
choices: the title of Leon Lederman's 1993 popular-science book
a Time magazine cover from the week of the 2013 Nobel
Peter Higgs's own religious upbringing in Newcastle
the Latin motto over the main entrance to CERN
context: Lederman, a Nobel-winning physicist himself, said he had wanted to call it 'the goddamn particle' because it was so hard to find; his publisher pushed the tamer title. Higgs, an atheist, objected because the phrase muddled people about what the mechanism actually claims. It claims something about how W and Z bosons get their mass, not about the origins of the universe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Higgs.

question: The Higgs mass sits at about 125 GeV, but a naive quantum calculation says it should be dragged up near the Planck scale, a trillion trillion times higher. This gap is called the hierarchy problem, and for decades physicists had a favourite proposed fix -- a whole family of predicted partner particles the LHC then went hunting. Which framework predicted those partners?
answer: supersymmetry
choices: supersymmetry
loop quantum gravity
string landscape inflation
Kaluza-Klein extra dimensions
context: Supersymmetry pairs every known particle with a heavier partner whose quantum contributions would cancel the runaway drag on the Higgs mass. It was the leading candidate for decades and a major reason the LHC was built. As of the current runs the partner particles have not shown up in the expected energy range, and the hierarchy problem is more open, not less. As the bank says: no one yet knows. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson.

question: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson were not out hunting for the beginning of the universe when they found the hiss. At Bell Labs in 1964 they were pointing the 20-foot horn antenna at the sky for a much more ordinary reason. What were they actually trying to do?
answer: calibrate the horn for radio astronomy
choices: calibrate the horn for radio astronomy
test a new design for a passenger radar system
search for signals from alien civilizations
map the Milky Way's spiral arms
context: The horn had been built in 1959 for Project Echo, NASA's passive communications satellite program. Penzias and Wilson wanted a quiet instrument for radio astronomy, and the mysterious hiss was a stubborn nuisance they were trying to make go away. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmdel_Horn_Antenna

question: After Penzias and Wilson evicted the pigeons from inside the Holmdel horn and scrubbed out the droppings, they climbed back down, powered the antenna up, and listened again. What happened to the hiss?
answer: it stayed exactly as loud as before
choices: it stayed exactly as loud as before
it dropped by roughly half
it vanished within a few hours
it grew louder for several days and then faded
context: That is the whole point of the story: the noise was not coming from the birds. Whatever the source was, it was arriving through the sky itself, not from anything nesting in the metal. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_cosmic_microwave_background_radiation  (Legend.)

question: Penzias and Wilson refused to shrug off their unexplained hiss. They ruled out New York City's radio racket to the north, military radar, and even the possibility that fallout from a 1962 high-altitude nuclear test was glowing in the upper atmosphere. Suspicious that the metal joints of the horn itself might be leaking noise, what did they do to the antenna's riveted aluminum seams?
answer: they taped over the seams
choices: they taped over the seams
they welded the seams shut
they repainted the seams with copper
they replaced the rivets with brass bolts
context: Nothing they tried made the hiss go away. What refused to leave was an excess antenna temperature of about 3.5 K, and it was the same in every direction they aimed the horn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_cosmic_microwave_background_radiation

question: About forty miles from Holmdel, at Princeton, Robert Dicke's group -- with James Peebles, Peter Roll, and David Wilkinson -- was already building an antenna to hunt for the leftover heat of a hot early universe. When Dicke hung up the phone after Penzias described the excess noise at Bell Labs, what did he turn and say to his team?
answer: 'Boys, we've been scooped.'
choices: 'Boys, we've been scooped.'
'Gentlemen, our instrument is obsolete.'
'We were right, and now we must prove it.'
'Then we shall build a bigger one.'
context: The radio astronomer Bernard Burke had heard about the Princeton work and told Penzias to call Dicke. That phone call connected two groups who had spent months chasing the same signal from opposite ends. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background  (Legend.)

question: The Holmdel discovery was not the first time the prediction had been written down. Working from George Gamow's hot-start cosmology, two physicists had already estimated in 1948 that the early universe should have left behind a faint glow of about 5 K -- and no one built the instrument to look. Who were they?
answer: Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman
choices: Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman
Fred Hoyle and Thomas Gold
Hans Bethe and Edward Teller
Robert Dicke and James Peebles
context: Alpher and Herman's estimate sat in the physics literature for sixteen years before Penzias and Wilson stumbled into the signal. Their number -- about 5 K -- turned out to be startlingly close to what the horn measured. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Asher_Alpher

question: An unrecognized clue about the leftover glow had actually been sitting on a spectrograph plate since 1940-41. Andrew McKellar, working from absorption lines W. S. Adams had recorded, noticed that a particular kind of interstellar molecule was gently excited, as if it were being warmed by something only a few degrees above absolute zero. What molecule was doing the noticing?
answer: cyanogen (CN)
choices: cyanogen (CN)
molecular hydrogen (H2)
hydroxyl (OH) radicals
carbon monoxide (CO)
context: McKellar's estimate for the exciting temperature was about 2.3 K -- eerily close to the modern value. No one at the time connected that gently warm interstellar cyanogen to a leftover glow from the beginning of the universe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_cosmic_microwave_background_radiation

question: The hiss that filled Penzias and Wilson's horn is light that was released when the early universe finally cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms and the primordial fog cleared. Roughly how long after the beginning did that happen?
answer: about 380,000 years
choices: about 380,000 years
about 3 seconds
about 30 million years
about 1 billion years
context: At that moment the universe was around 3,000 K -- a fierce visible glare. Expansion has stretched that glare all the way down into microwaves, with a present-day temperature COBE measured at 2.72548 K. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background

question: COBE, launched in November 1989, was built to look at the leftover glow with instruments no ground-based horn could match. Its FIRAS instrument produced the most perfect blackbody spectrum ever measured, and its DMR instrument found something new: faint temperature ripples across the sky, roughly one part in 100,000. What are those ripples understood to be?
answer: the seeds that grew into galaxies, stars, and eventually us
choices: the seeds that grew into galaxies, stars, and eventually us
the imprint of gravitational waves from cosmic inflation
the shadows of primordial black holes forming
the boundaries between separate bubble universes
context: Where the sky was very slightly warmer, matter was very slightly denser -- and gravity pulled those denser patches into the first structures. John Mather and George Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for the COBE blackbody and anisotropy results. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_Background_Explorer

question: In May 1996 the New York University physicist Alan Sokal published a paper in the cultural-studies journal Social Text arguing something a physicist would never actually argue - and three weeks later he announced in Lingua Franca that he had done it deliberately, as a test. What was the paper's central claim?
answer: that physical reality is a social and linguistic construct
choices: that physical reality is a social and linguistic construct
that Einstein's relativity theory has been quietly falsified
that string theory is not falsifiable and so is not physics
that the Copenhagen interpretation is the true theory of mind
context: The paper was titled 'Transgressing the Boundaries: Towards a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity.' Sokal salted it with real physicists' terms used wrongly, plus claims a first-year physics student would refuse. The test was narrow and stated: would a journal print flattering nonsense if the jargon and the politics were agreeable? Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokal_affair

question: After the Sokal hoax broke, defenders of Social Text pointed out one thing about how the journal worked in 1996 - a detail the headlines mostly ignored, but the bank insists on. What was it?
answer: Social Text did not operate peer review and never sent the paper to a physicist
choices: Social Text did not operate peer review and never sent the paper to a physicist
Sokal had submitted the paper under a false name to hide his politics
the editors had asked Sokal to revise it heavily before publication
a physicist reviewer had approved the paper without spotting the errors
context: The editors accepted the paper on Sokal's NYU credentials and its ideological fit with a special 'Science Wars' issue. What the hoax actually demonstrated, then, was a failure of editorial judgement, not a failure of peer review - and Sokal's own stated claim was that narrower one. Getting the target right is part of getting the lesson right. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokal_affair

question: Between 2017 and 2018 three writers - Peter Boghossian, James Lindsay, and Helen Pluckrose - fixed the Sokal-era objection by sending fabricated papers to journals that DID run peer review. They submitted twenty. How many made it through to publication or acceptance before the project was exposed?
answer: four published and three more accepted
choices: four published and three more accepted
one published and one more accepted
twelve published and six more accepted
all twenty published outright
context: Six were rejected outright and the remaining seven were still under review when the exposure came. The trio called it 'Sokal squared.' They aimed at fields they termed 'grievance studies' where they thought only certain conclusions were welcome. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: One of the four published grievance-studies hoaxes appeared in the journal Gender, Place & Culture under the pseudonym Helen Wilson. Its subject was described by a peer reviewer as 'incredibly innovative, rich in analysis, and extremely well-written and organized.' What was the paper actually about?
answer: rape culture and queer performativity in Portland dog parks
choices: rape culture and queer performativity in Portland dog parks
colonial legacies in the layout of Parisian arrondissements
toxic masculinity in the boardrooms of Silicon Valley
gendered patterns of household electricity consumption
context: The full title was 'Human reactions to rape culture and queer performativity at urban dog parks in Portland, Oregon.' The reviewer's phrase 'incredibly innovative' is the one the bank quotes - because it is documented, not caricatured. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: Another accepted grievance-studies paper, submitted to the social-work journal Affilia, was accepted as an original contribution to feminist theory. It was not original at all. What was it really?
answer: a passage of Hitler's Mein Kampf rewritten in feminist-theory language
choices: a passage of Hitler's Mein Kampf rewritten in feminist-theory language
a Marxist manifesto essay with the nouns swapped for gender terms
a chapter of Ayn Rand paraphrased into critical-theory prose
a chatbot's answer to a prompt about intersectional ethics
context: The passage was picked precisely because a competent reviewer should have recognised the source rhetoric. Affilia accepted it. The three authors published the manuscript record with each paper so the audit trail was public. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: The grievance-studies project was not brought down by a reviewer spotting the content of the papers. It ended in October 2018 when someone at Gender, Place & Culture asked a much simpler question about the dog-park paper's author. What was the question?
answer: was Helen Wilson a documented real person
choices: was Helen Wilson a documented real person
was Helen Wilson affiliated with an ethics board
was Helen Wilson listed in the copyright registry
was Helen Wilson current on the article-processing fee
context: She was not. The Wall Street Journal broke the story on October 2, 2018. The dinner-test payoff of the whole affair is exactly this: the hoax survived peer review and died the moment someone requested proof that the author existed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grievance_studies_affair

question: A methodological objection the bank refuses to duck: a hoax with no control group tells you what gatekeeping caught, not whether the field's ideas are true. What happened in 2014 that shows the same trick works in technical journals?
answer: Springer and IEEE withdrew over 120 computer-generated SCIgen papers
choices: Springer and IEEE withdrew over 120 computer-generated SCIgen papers
Nature retracted every paper from the Duke genomics group
a Chinese paper-mill was caught forging 400 peer-review reports
the Bogdanov brothers had their physics dissertations annulled
context: SCIgen is a random paper generator built at MIT using a context-free grammar; Cyril Labbe of Grenoble catalogued its output across more than 30 peer-reviewed conference proceedings from 2008 to 2013. The lesson: a hoax measures what a review system catches. It cannot, by itself, tell you whether the underlying field is right or wrong. The bank reports the finding and the objection and lets the reader weigh them. Source: https://retractionwatch.com/2014/02/24/springer-ieee-withdrawing-more-than-120-nonsense-papers/

question: The most-argued-over graph in climate science was audited not by a rival climatologist but by two men from outside the field entirely. In April 2003 Stephen McIntyre, working from Toronto, asked Michael Mann for the numbers behind the curve and was sent a spreadsheet; Ross McKitrick, at the University of Guelph, worked through the statistics with him. What did the two men do for a living?
answer: A minerals-exploration consultant and an economics professor
choices: A minerals-exploration consultant and an economics professor
A petroleum geologist and an applied mathematics professor
A television weather forecaster and a statistics professor
A software engineer and an experimental physics professor
context: Stephen McIntyre was a Canadian minerals-exploration and mining consultant whose working life was spent on the statistics of drilling data; Ross McKitrick was an economics professor at the University of Guelph. Neither was a climatologist. McIntyre downloaded the published 1999 data, then asked Mann directly for the 1998 dataset in April 2003, and found he could not reproduce the published result from the published description. That failure, not any opinion about the weather, is what set the whole audit going. Source: Wikipedia, 'Stephen McIntyre'; Wikipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Michael Mann built the temperature reconstruction that made him famous at the University of Massachusetts Amherst between 1996 and 1998, working with Raymond Bradley there and Malcolm Hughes in Arizona. Nature published it in April 1998, and within three years it was a political emblem. What was Mann's position at the university while he was building it?
answer: A postdoctoral fellow funded by the Department of Energy
choices: A postdoctoral fellow funded by the Department of Energy
A tenured professor in the department of atmospheric science
A visiting scientist on loan from a national laboratory
The director of the university's climate research centre
context: Mann held a US Department of Energy postdoctoral fellowship at UMass Amherst from 1996 to 1998, and the paper known as MBH98 came out of it: Mann, Bradley and Hughes, Nature, 23 April 1998, a Northern Hemisphere reconstruction reaching back to AD 1400. A follow-up in Geophysical Research Letters in March 1999 pushed it back to AD 1000. A long gentle decline ending in a sharp 20th-century rise looked like a hockey stick lying on its side, which is where the nickname came from. Source: Wikipedia, 'Michael E. Mann'; Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: In January 2001 government delegates in Shanghai approved a report by the IPCC, the UN climate panel, and at the televised launch its co-chair Sir John Houghton spoke in front of a poster-sized blow-up of the Mann, Bradley and Hughes Northern Hemisphere curve. It also went into the Summary for Policymakers, the short document officials and journalists actually read. What claim did that Summary attach to it?
answer: That the 1990s was likely the warmest decade of the past thousand years
choices: That the 1990s was likely the warmest decade of the past thousand years
That human emissions had caused all of the warming measured since 1850
That the Medieval Warm Period had never happened anywhere outside Europe
That sea level would rise by a full metre before the end of this century
context: The wording was that it was 'likely that, in the Northern Hemisphere, the 1990s was the warmest decade and 1998 the warmest year' of the past thousand years. The 1999 paper itself had described the millennium as a long slow cooling of roughly 0.02 degrees C per century, interrupted by the modern rise. Once a research figure is a backdrop at a televised launch it stops being easy to revise, which is the whole trouble this ladder is about. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)', quoting the IPCC Third Assessment Report Summary for Policymakers; Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: Nobody owns a thermometer from AD 1400, so the Mann, Bradley and Hughes curve was stitched from things that grew or froze while the weather happened: 112 indicators in all, among them tree-ring widths, ice-core isotopes, coral growth bands and written records of glaciers advancing and retreating. But the network is not the same size at every date. Roughly how many of those 112 series still run as far back as AD 1400, the oldest year the 1998 paper reached?
answer: About 22
choices: About 22
About 46
About 75
About 103
context: Roughly 24 series still run at AD 1820 and about 22 at AD 1400. The oldest end of the graph, the stretch people argued about most loudly, rests on the fewest records, and that is a structural fact about every long reconstruction rather than a fault of this one. The network also included maximum latewood density, borehole temperatures and a few early instrument series. Source: Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)', section 'Mann, Bradley, and Hughes (1998-1999) Methodology'.

question: McIntyre and McKitrick's February 2005 paper in Geophysical Research Letters named the exact step it disputed. Before MBH98 combined its North American tree-ring records, it ran them through principal-component analysis, a routine step that boils many wobbly series down to a few summary patterns. Everything, the two men argued, turned on which stretch of years that step was measured against. Which stretch had MBH98 centred it on?
answer: 1902 to 1980, the window with thermometer records
choices: 1902 to 1980, the window with thermometer records
1400 to 1980, the whole length of the reconstruction
1000 to 1400, the stretch before the network thins
1961 to 1990, the standard meteorological baseline
context: 'Hockey sticks, principal components, and spurious significance' was received on 14 October 2004, accepted 17 January 2005 and published 12 February 2005 in Geophysical Research Letters. Centring on the 1902-1980 calibration window rather than on the full 1400-1980 record means every series is measured against its own 20th-century average, which pushes series that behave unusually in the 20th century toward the front of the queue. Their earlier 2003 paper in Energy & Environment had already argued the shape was 'primarily an artefact of poor data handling and use of obsolete proxy records'. Source: McIntyre & McKitrick 2005, GRL 32(3), doi:10.1029/2004GL021750; Grokipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: The US National Research Council put twelve people on the argument over the Mann, Bradley and Hughes curve, chaired by the Texas A&M climatologist Gerald North, and they reported on 22 June 2006. On the disputed statistics the panel sided with the critics: the convention McIntyre and McKitrick had attacked in the tree-ring step 'tends to bias the shape of the reconstructions', it wrote, and was 'not recommended'. Then it took up a separate question, whether that bias had actually changed the curve. What did the panel conclude?
answer: Reconstructions run without that step came out much the same
choices: Reconstructions run without that step came out much the same
Reconstructions run without that step lost the modern rise entirely
Reconstructions run without that step showed a warmer medieval peak
Reconstructions run without that step could not be produced at all
context: The panel's sentence, in full: 'As part of their statistical methods, Mann et al. used a type of principal component analysis that tends to bias the shape of the reconstructions... In practice, this method, though not recommended, does not appear to unduly influence reconstructions of hemispheric mean temperature; reconstructions performed without using principal component analysis are qualitatively similar to the original curves presented by Mann et al.' Both halves are the finding. The critics were right that the step was biased; the referee judged the bias did not drive the answer. Source: National Research Council (2006), 'Surface Temperature Reconstructions for the Last 2,000 Years', ch. 11.

question: The US National Research Council panel that reported in June 2006 handed the critics a second point, about one kind of tree in the network. A strip-bark bristlecone pine is an ancient tree whose trunk is mostly dead, with a single surviving ribbon of living bark still laying down a ring each year; such samples 'should be avoided' for temperature reconstructions, the panel wrote. It then named something besides warmth that may be fattening their recent rings. What was it?
answer: Nitrogen from human sources settling out of the air
choices: Nitrogen from human sources settling out of the air
Desert dust settling on the slopes and feeding the soil
Deeper winter snowpack lasting later into the spring
Less competition as neighbouring old trees died back
context: The panel's tree-ring chapter says: 'While "strip-bark" samples should be avoided for temperature reconstructions, attention should also be paid to the confounding effects of anthropogenic nitrogen deposition.' Extra carbon dioxide in the air is a candidate for the same effect. The worry is simple and testable: if a ring gets fatter because the tree is being fertilised rather than because the summer was warm, then reading ring width as a thermometer reads the wrong thing. Source: National Research Council (2006), 'Surface Temperature Reconstructions for the Last 2,000 Years', ch. 4 'Tree Rings'.

question: On 16 November 1999 Phil Jones, director of the Climatic Research Unit at the University of East Anglia, wrote to Michael Mann and two colleagues about a cover graphic for a World Meteorological Organization report: he had used 'Mike's Nature trick... to hide the decline'. Ten years later the email was published and the sentence went round the world. Among scientists a trick is simply a technique, the way a mathematician calls a clever substitution a trick, but the picture on that cover was not quite what it looked like. What did the graphic do?
answer: Swapped measured temperatures in for the post-1960 tree-ring values
choices: Swapped measured temperatures in for the post-1960 tree-ring values
Stopped all three plotted curves at 1960 and left the century blank
Dropped the two reconstructions that disagreed, showing only Mann's
Stretched the scale until the last forty years filled half the cover
context: The full sentence, typo and all: 'I've just completed Mike's Nature trick of adding in the real temps to each series for the last 20 years (ie from 1981 onwards) amd from 1961 for Keith's to hide the decline.' The graphic was the cover of the WMO Statement on the Status of the Global Climate in 1999, showing three reconstructions as smoothed anomalies from the 1961-1990 normal. The decline was in Keith Briffa's tree-ring values, which had begun falling after 1960 while thermometers rose. Splicing the measured temperatures on gave the reader one smooth continuous line, with nothing to show that a proxy had failed, and the caption said nothing about it. Source: FactCheck.org, 'Climategate'; WMO-No. 913 cover and caption.

question: Eight separate inquiries examined the emails taken from the Climatic Research Unit at the University of East Anglia, among them a House of Commons committee, two Pennsylvania State University panels and the National Science Foundation's inspector general, and not one of them found fraud or scientific misconduct. The Muir Russell review, reporting on 7 July 2010, wrote that the scientists' 'rigour and honesty as scientists are not in doubt'. The same report then judged the 1999 WMO cover graphic itself. What did it say about that figure?
answer: It was misleading, though splicing data is not improper in itself
choices: It was misleading, though splicing data is not improper in itself
It was sound, and the complaints about it rested on a misreading
It was improper, because reconstructions must never be spliced at all
It was outside the review's remit, so no judgement was offered on it
context: Muir Russell wrote both sentences and softened neither: 'The figure supplied for the WMO Report was misleading in not describing that one of the series was truncated post 1960 for the figure, and in not being clear on the fact that proxy and instrumental data were spliced together. We do not find that it is misleading to curtail reconstructions at some point per se, or to splice data.' The doing was allowed; the not-saying was not. Several of the same reports also criticised the unit sharply for poor data archiving and for resisting requests to share. Source: Independent Climate Change E-mail Review (Muir Russell), 7 July 2010, findings 13 and 23; Wikipedia, 'Climatic Research Unit email controversy'.

question: In July 2006 a US congressional committee released a review of the statistics behind the temperature reconstruction, led by the statistician Edward Wegman, and it backed McIntyre's case. Part of the review, a study of who co-authors papers with whom in the field, was later republished in a statistics journal, and in May 2011 that journal retracted the paper; George Mason University reprimanded Wegman for research misconduct. What had been found in it?
answer: Passages copied word for word from textbooks and Wikipedia
choices: Passages copied word for word from textbooks and Wikipedia
Co-authorship links invented to make the network look tighter
Funding from an energy company that was never once disclosed
Calculations nobody at the journal could reproduce from the data
context: The Wegman Report, by Edward Wegman, Yasmin Said and David Scott, was announced on 14 July 2006, three weeks after the National Research Council reported. Its social-network section was published in Computational Statistics & Data Analysis and retracted in May 2011 for plagiarism. Auditing cuts in every direction: the people checking other people's work are checkable too, and the same standard that caught a sloppy statistical step also caught a copied paragraph. Source: Nature 473, 419 (2011), 'Copy and paste'; Retraction Watch; Wikipedia, 'Hockey stick graph (global temperature)'.

question: In 2008 Michael Mann and his colleagues published a fresh reconstruction in PNAS, built from 1,209 proxy series, and reported that it still worked back to about AD 1000 with every tree-ring record dropped from the network. Near the end the paper carried one line the 1998 paper never had. What did that line say?
answer: That the data and the Matlab source code sat at a public web address
choices: That the data and the Matlab source code sat at a public web address
That the raw proxy series had been deposited in the PNAS archive itself
That the authors would send data and code to any reader who asked
That the code would be released once the follow-up paper appeared
context: The 2008 PNAS paper carried a line the 1998 paper never had: 'All data used in this study and Matlab source codes for implementing the algorithms described, as well as additional supporting information are available at www.meteo.psu.edu/~mann/supplements/MultiproxyMeans07'. That is what the whole fight settled: not a knockout argument but an address anyone could type in. The same paper reported a skilful reconstruction back to about AD 1000 with tree-ring data left out of the network entirely. The 2006 panel had put the remedy in one dry sentence: 'Improving access to data used in publications would also increase confidence in the results.' By 2017 the PAGES 2k Consortium was posting 692 records from 648 locations openly for anyone to download and check. Source: Mann et al. (2008), PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.0805721105; NRC (2006) Summary; PAGES2k Consortium (2017), Scientific Data 4:170088.

question: On 1 October 1990 the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health began the Human Genome Project: an effort to read the complete DNA of a human being, letter by letter. The published plan allowed fifteen years and three billion dollars. How did the finished project measure against that plan?
answer: It came in two years early, at about $2.7 billion
choices: It came in two years early, at about $2.7 billion
It came in on schedule, at about $5.4 billion
It came in six years late, at about $3.2 billion
It came in nine years late, at about $8.1 billion
context: Thirteen years instead of fifteen, and roughly $2.7 billion instead of three. James Watson, co-discoverer of the double helix, was the first director of the NIH genome centre. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: The consortium running the Human Genome Project could have announced its finished human reference sequence on any day in the spring of 2003. Its leaders argued over the date, because they wanted the day itself to carry a message, and settled on 14 April. Which discovery was turning fifty that spring?
answer: Watson and Crick's description of the DNA double helix
choices: Watson and Crick's description of the DNA double helix
Beadle and Tatum's one gene, one enzyme rule
Avery and MacLeod's proof that genes are made of DNA
Meselson and Stahl's demonstration of DNA copying
context: Watson and Crick described the double helix in 1953, and the consortium timed 14 April 2003 to land on the fiftieth anniversary. The sequence they called finished covered about 92% of the genome and 99% of the gene-rich euchromatic portion, with fewer than 400 gaps and roughly one wrong letter in every 10,000. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: In May 1998 J. Craig Venter announced Celera Genomics, a private company that would sequence the human genome itself and beat the public consortium to the finish. The consortium had been at it since October 1990 on a plan of fifteen years and three billion dollars. Venter named his own deadline and his own price the same day. What did he promise?
answer: Three years and about $300 million
choices: Three years and about $300 million
Two years and about $150 million
Four years and about $900 million
Six years and about $1.8 billion
context: Venter founded Celera on 9 May 1998 with PerkinElmer and ran the sequencing on roughly 300 ABI PRISM 3700 machines at once. The public project he was racing had been running since October 1990 on a plan of fifteen years and three billion dollars, so Venter was promising the same result in a fifth of the time for a tenth of the money. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project; genengnews.com, 'From Sequencing to Sailing: Three Decades of Adventure with Craig Venter'

question: Celera's human genome was not one person's DNA. Craig Venter's company built it from five anonymous donors, three women and two men, who described themselves as African, American, Hispanic, Chinese and Caucasian. What did Venter reveal about those five after he left Celera in 2002?
answer: One of the five donors had been Venter himself
choices: One of the five donors had been Venter himself
None of the five donors had signed a consent form
All five of the donors had been Celera employees
Two of the five donors had withdrawn beforehand
context: After leaving the company in 2002, Venter revealed that his own DNA was one of the five strands blended into Celera's composite human genome. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Venter; dnalc.cshl.edu/view/15364-DNA-donors-for-sequencing-at-Celera-Craig-Venter.html

question: In 1998 J. Craig Venter's new company, Celera Genomics, packed one building with about 300 ABI PRISM 3700 sequencing machines and promised a finished human genome years before the public consortium could reach one. The machines alone could not deliver that; the speed depended on how Celera chose to attack three billion letters of DNA. Which approach did Celera take?
answer: Broke the whole genome into random fragments and had computers reassemble them
choices: Broke the whole genome into random fragments and had computers reassemble them
Read only the messenger RNA in cells and worked backwards to the DNA
Cloned each chromosome into bacteria and read the pieces in fixed order
Sorted the chromosomes one at a time and read each from end to end
context: This was whole-genome shotgun sequencing: blast the genome apart, sequence every fragment at once on those 300 machines, then let supercomputers hunt for the overlaps that put the puzzle back together. The public consortium had gone the other way, mapping each chromosome first, cutting it into known, ordered pieces, and reading those one at a time. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: Before the human sequence came in, biologists were confident they already knew roughly how many protein-coding genes a human must carry. The working figure was 100,000 or more, and some published estimates ran to 120,000, on the reasoning that a complicated animal needs a great many genes. When the counting was finally done, how many protein-coding genes did a human turn out to have?
answer: About 20,000
choices: About 20,000
About 55,000
About 140,000
About 400,000
context: The 2000-2001 drafts said 26,000-40,000; by 2005 it had fallen to 20,000-25,000; the finished 2022 sequence annotates 19,969 protein-coding genes. That is about what Caenorhabditis elegans carries - a soil roundworm one millimetre long whose whole body is 959 cells - and fewer than rice is annotated with (roughly 32,000-35,600, though plant counts are inflated by whole-genome duplication and annotation methods differ between species, so that comparison is loose). The count is always of protein-coding genes; counting RNA genes gives a larger number. Complexity is not gene count. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project; genome.gov roundworm education kit

question: In March 1997 an advertisement in the Buffalo News recruited twenty volunteers, ten men and ten women, to give blood at Roswell Park in Buffalo, New York. Their DNA would become the human reference genome, and their consent form promised that no more than 10% of the final sequence would come from any one of them. How much of the published 2001 draft came from a single donor?
answer: About 70 to 75 percent, from one anonymous man
choices: About 70 to 75 percent, from one anonymous man
About 40 to 45 percent, from one anonymous man
About 30 to 35 percent, from one anonymous man
About 20 to 25 percent, from one anonymous woman
context: The consortium promised each volunteer that no more than 10% of the final sequence would be his or hers, then drew roughly three-quarters of the published draft from one man. He is known to this day only by the code RP11, and most of the reference genome the world has used ever since is his. Source: statnews.com, 9 July 2024; undark.org, 9 July 2024

question: A human cell carries about 3.2 billion base pairs of DNA, and it is tempting to assume that a more elaborate creature needs more of it. The evolutionary biologist T. Ryan Gregory tests that assumption with something anyone can pick up at a market: the common onion, Allium cepa. How much DNA does an onion carry?
answer: About 16 billion base pairs, five times the human figure
choices: About 16 billion base pairs, five times the human figure
About 6 billion base pairs, twice the human figure
About 32 billion base pairs, ten times the human figure
About 130 billion base pairs, forty times the human figure
context: Gregory named this the onion test in 2007 and puts it as a question to anyone who insists nearly every stretch of non-coding DNA is essential: 'Can I explain why an onion needs about five times more non-coding DNA for this function than a human?' And the onion is no freak case - different Allium species carry more than fourfold different amounts of DNA from one another. Source: journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1004351 ('The Case for Junk DNA', Palazzo & Gregory 2014); grokipedia.com/page/Junk_DNA

question: In May 2000, in a bar at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, the bioinformatician Ewan Birney opened a betting pool on how many protein-coding genes a human would turn out to have. More than 460 researchers put money in over the next three years. Lee Rowen of Seattle won the pool in 2003 with her guess of 25,947. Where did her winning number sit among all those bets?
answer: It was the lowest bet in the pool, and it was still too high
choices: It was the lowest bet in the pool, and it was still too high
It was the lowest bet in the pool, and it was slightly too low
It sat near the middle of the field, and it was slightly too high
It sat near the middle of the field, and it was still too low
context: Rowen, of the Institute for Systems Biology, placed the lowest bet in the pool - and the true count still came in under it. The highest wager was above 200,000 genes, and John Quackenbush staked his on 118,253; when Hugues Roest-Crollius entered 27,000, Birney remembered thinking, 'This guy's mad! There can't be 27,000.' Rowen took $600 of the $1,200 pot and an autographed copy of James Watson's The Double Helix; Paul Dear and Olivier Jaillon split the rest. The pool, called GeneSweep, charged $1 to enter in 2000, $5 in 2001 and $20 in 2002 as more sequence came in. Science reported the result on 30 May 2003 under the headline 'A Low Number Wins the GeneSweep Pool.' Source: genome.gov/virtual-exhibits/GeneSweep; science.org/doi/10.1126/science.300.5625.1484b

question: A gene is first copied into a working transcript, a messenger RNA, which the cell then reads to build a protein. Beadle and Tatum's mould experiments had made the pairing textbook doctrine: one gene, one protein. Post-project analyses of human transcripts caught most human genes breaking that rule outright. What did those analyses catch a single human gene doing with its transcript?
answer: Cutting its transcript apart and rejoining the pieces in different combinations
choices: Cutting its transcript apart and rejoining the pieces in different combinations
Stitching its transcript onto a neighbouring gene's transcript to make hybrids
Slipping the cell's reading frame partway along its transcript by one letter
Reading its transcript straight through into several proteins in a row
context: The mechanism is called alternative splicing: one gene's transcript is cut into pieces and those pieces are joined back together in different combinations, so a single stretch of DNA yields many different proteins. Post-project analyses found that over 90% of human genes built from more than one coding block produce such variants, which retired the one gene, one protein rule that Beadle and Tatum's Neurospora work had made textbook doctrine. It is a large part of the answer to 'so few genes'. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: When the Human Genome Project announced in April 2003 that the human genome was complete, the newspapers took the word literally. It was not true. Roughly 8% of it, some 200 million bases, had defeated every sequencing machine then built and was simply left out of the sequence called finished. Which parts were missing?
answer: The long repeated stretches at the centromeres and telomeres
choices: The long repeated stretches at the centromeres and telomeres
The stretches that vary most from one person to the next
The regions packed most densely with protein-coding genes
The mitochondrial DNA that sits outside the cell nucleus
context: Identical repeats are what break an assembly: a computer hunting for overlapping fragments cannot tell one copy from another. The Telomere-to-Telomere consortium - over 100 researchers using PacBio HiFi and Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads on the CHM13 cell line - closed the last gaps on 31 March 2022, producing a gapless 3,054,815,472-base sequence with nearly 200 million bases nobody had ever seen. The Y chromosome, about 60% repetitive, held out until 2023. Source: science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abj6987; grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: On 5 September 2012 the ENCODE consortium, more than 440 researchers across 32 laboratories, published about thirty coordinated papers at once and declared at least 80% of the human genome functional. Newspapers announced the death of junk DNA. Dan Graur and five colleagues fired back in print the next year. What was their objection?
answer: ENCODE counted molecular activity, not the jobs natural selection maintains
choices: ENCODE counted molecular activity, not the jobs natural selection maintains
ENCODE counted activity in cancer cell lines, not in healthy human tissue
ENCODE counted stretches twice, not once, wherever its datasets overlapped
ENCODE counted a sampled slice of the genome, not the whole three billion
context: Graur and five colleagues published in Genome Biology and Evolution in 2013 under the title 'On the Immortality of Television Sets: Function in the Human Genome According to the Evolution-Free Gospel of ENCODE.' Their line: claiming DNA stays functional without selection is like claiming 'a television set left on and unattended will still be in working condition after a million years.' ENCODE later clarified that by functional it had meant biochemical function specifically - observable molecular activity, not evolutionary selection or any proven job - and its 2013-2014 follow-ups adopted a tiered definition. Source: academic.oup.com/gbe/article/5/3/578/583411; nature.com/articles/nature11247

question: Biologists have argued for half a century over how much of the human genome is doing a job at all, since only a sliver of it spells out protein. One way to get a number instead of an argument: line the human genome up beside other mammals' and hunt for the stretches that have stayed nearly unchanged for tens of millions of years while the DNA around them drifted freely. If a stretch has not been allowed to drift, something is holding it in place. A 2014 study did this, and a 2023 analysis compared 240 mammal species. What share of the human genome came out held that way?
answer: Roughly 8 to 11 percent of it
choices: Roughly 8 to 11 percent of it
Roughly 2 to 3 percent of it
Roughly 30 to 35 percent of it
Roughly 60 to 65 percent of it
context: What the studies measured is called purifying selection: mutations that land in a stretch the animal needs get weeded out, while junk drifts freely. The 2014 PLOS Genetics study put the human figure at 8.2%, with a 95% confidence interval of 7.1 to 9.2%; the 2023 comparison of 240 mammal genomes put it at 10.7%, about 332 million bases. Plenty of genuinely functional regulatory DNA exists beyond the protein-coding stretches. How much of the remainder does any job at all, no one yet knows. Source: journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgen.1004351; grokipedia.com/page/Junk_DNA

question: Tony Blair, joining the White House by satellite in June 2000, called the draft human genome 'a revolution in medical science whose implications far surpass even the discovery of antibiotics.' Sequencing one person's genome, which cost hundreds of millions of dollars for the first draft, now runs to roughly $600. What has that flood of cheap sequence delivered for the diseases caused by a fault in a single gene?
answer: Gene-therapy cures for fewer than one percent of them
choices: Gene-therapy cures for fewer than one percent of them
Gene-therapy cures for roughly a quarter of them
Gene-therapy cures for roughly two thirds of them
Gene-therapy cures for almost every one of them
context: The cost collapse is real: about $300 million for the first draft, under $1,500 by late 2015, roughly $600 by 2023. The medicine has arrived unevenly. Fewer than 1% of known single-gene (Mendelian) disorders have a gene-therapy cure, and the early SCID trials around 2000 restored immunity to several children only to give them T-cell leukaemia when the inserted virus landed in an oncogene, halting those protocols by 2003. For common diseases, genomics has produced risk statistics rather than cures. Source: genome.gov/about-genomics/fact-sheets/Sequencing-Human-Genome-cost; grokipedia.com/page/Human_Genome_Project

question: In January 1912 the French surgeon Alexis Carrel snipped a fragment from the heart of a chick embryo, dropped it in a flask at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, and started feeding it every day. New York papers began reporting the culture's birthday every January. Roughly how long did the Rockefeller lab keep the culture going before quietly ending it?
answer: About thirty-four years
choices: About seven years
About fifteen years
About thirty-four years
About sixty years
context: The Rockefeller Institute maintained Carrel's strain 725 from January 1912 until 1946, roughly thirty-four years, on daily feedings of chick embryo extract. Source: https://www.gothamcenter.org/blog/alessandro-fabbri-the-rockefeller-institute-amp-the-immortal-chicken-heart

question: Alexis Carrel presented his ever-fed chicken heart culture as more than a curiosity; it was, he said, the proof of a very large biological claim. What was the claim the newspapers repeated at every reported birthday?
answer: That cells given enough good food never age at all
choices: That cells given enough good food never age at all
That heart tissue can be moved between different animals
That French surgery was ahead of American surgery
That the chick embryo is the ancestor of every warm-blooded animal
context: Carrel used the culture to promote the view that cellular aging was not intrinsic, only a failure of nutrition and cleanliness. His stature (he had won the 1912 Nobel Prize for vascular surgery) gave the claim decades of authority. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Carrel

question: In 1961, at the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead published a paper in Experimental Cell Research on normal human fibroblasts kept in culture. Their finding was the exact opposite of Carrel's teaching. What did their human cells do?
answer: Divided roughly forty to sixty times, then stopped dividing
choices: Kept dividing indefinitely, faster than the chick heart
Divided roughly forty to sixty times, then stopped dividing
Turned into a different cell type after about a year
Died completely within a few weeks in every flask
context: Hayflick and Moorhead reported that normal human diploid cells go through about 40 to 60 population doublings and then enter a state biologists later named replicative senescence: still alive, still respiring, no longer copying themselves. Source: https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/serial-cultivation-human-diploid-cells-lab-1958-1961-leonard-hayflick-and-paul-s-moorhead

question: The senior cell biologists said Hayflick and Moorhead must have been sloppy: bad medium, dirty glassware, waste piling up. To answer that, the pair built one flask no external excuse could survive: male fibroblasts already at their fortieth doubling and young female fibroblasts at only their fifteenth, sharing every drop of medium. Twenty doublings later, only female cells were left. What did that flask prove?
answer: That the counter was inside each cell, not in the shared medium
choices: That female cells outcompete male cells for glucose
That the counter was inside each cell, not in the shared medium
That fibroblasts secrete a poison that kills older neighbors
That cells need a second cell type nearby to keep dividing
context: Because the young and old cells shared everything in the flask, any external explanation (bad food, waste build-up, glass contamination) would have killed both populations together. Instead, each cell type stopped at its own scheduled doubling number. The clock had to be intrinsic. Source: https://gerontology.fandom.com/wiki/Hayflick_limit

question: So how had Alexis Carrel's Rockefeller flask apparently kept the same chicken heart cells alive for decades, when nobody else could ever reproduce the result? Leonard Hayflick pointed at Carrel's daily feed, which was made by mashing whole chick embryos. What was his ordinary, unglamorous explanation?
answer: The mash carried in fresh living cells that quietly replaced the old ones
choices: The mash carried in fresh living cells that quietly replaced the old ones
The mash contained an unknown hormone that reset the cells' age
Carrel had secretly restarted the culture from a new embryo every year
The chick heart tissue had accidentally become a cancer cell line
context: Hayflick argued that Carrel's chick embryo extract was almost certainly not sterile of cells: each daily feeding smuggled fresh living cells into the flask, so the culture was continuously restocked rather than endlessly self-renewing. The honest historical position is 'never replicated, most likely contaminated,' not 'proven fraud.' Source: https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/7644467B52FB7B4005F25283536B4667/S0025727300040126a.pdf/div-class-title-dr-carrelandapos-s-immortal-cells-a-href-fn01-ref-type-fn-a-div.pdf

question: If the counter is inside the cell, where inside the cell is it? In 1971 the Russian biologist Alexei Olovnikov worked it out from the mechanics of how DNA gets copied. He predicted that the counter had to sit at a specific place on every chromosome, and had to shrink a little every time the chromosome was copied. Which place did he predict?
answer: At the very ends of the chromosome
choices: At the centromere, the pinched middle of the chromosome
At the very ends of the chromosome
At the origins where copying begins
At the nuclear membrane where chromosomes anchor
context: Olovnikov reasoned that the machinery that copies DNA cannot fully copy a linear template all the way to its tip, so a little of each end is lost per division. Sooner or later the end erodes into essential territory and the cell stops dividing. He called the idea marginotomy in 1971; the physical structures he predicted are now called telomeres. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S0006297923110032

question: Olovnikov's prediction demanded a rebuilder: some enzyme, somewhere, must be able to add fresh DNA back onto a chromosome tip, or germ cells and single-celled organisms would run down too. In 1984 a graduate student in Elizabeth Blackburn's Berkeley laboratory found exactly such an enzyme in the pond ciliate Tetrahymena, and named it telomerase. Who ran the experiment that isolated it?
answer: Carol Greider
choices: Barbara McClintock
Rosalind Franklin
Carol Greider
Lynn Margulis
context: Greider, then a first-year graduate student, ran the assays that identified telomerase in Tetrahymena thermophila in Blackburn's lab; she and Blackburn published the discovery in Cell in 1985. Greider, Blackburn and Jack Szostak shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for telomeres and telomerase. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/onc201015

question: Almost every cancer cell in the human body has broken past the Hayflick limit; it will divide forever if fed. HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951, have been dividing in labs worldwide for seventy years. What trick have these cancer cells done to their own biology to make that possible?
answer: Switched telomerase back on so the chromosome tips get rebuilt
choices: Duplicated all of their chromosomes so there is always a spare
Switched telomerase back on so the chromosome tips get rebuilt
Stopped copying their DNA and started copying only RNA
Turned off their nucleus and split by budding instead
context: In healthy adult somatic tissue telomerase is largely silent, which is why the Hayflick limit exists. Roughly 85-90 percent of human cancers reactivate telomerase so that the chromosome tips are constantly rebuilt; the same mechanism that keeps HeLa cells growing for a lifetime is the mechanism the cell was supposed to keep switched off. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10522-006-9043-9

question: A kid recovers from measles and never gets it again -- her immune system kept two long-lived cell populations behind, the same two a vaccine is designed to train without the illness. What are those two populations called?
answer: Memory B cells and memory T cells
choices: Memory B cells and memory T cells
Naive B cells and naive T cells
Plasmablasts and neutrophils
Regulatory T cells and NK cells
context: This is ordinary textbook immunology, uncontroversial since the mid-twentieth century. Memory B cells rapidly re-secrete antibody on a second encounter; memory T cells recognize protein fragments displayed on infected cells and kill them. Vaccines exist because they can train these two populations without exposing you to the pathogen. Source: Cell/Immunity review S1074-7613(21)00037-6.

question: The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation's COVID-19 Forecasting Team pooled 65 studies from 19 countries and asked how much protection a past infection still offered against SEVERE disease -- ending up in hospital or worse -- at 40 weeks out, even against Omicron BA.1. Their pooled answer, published in The Lancet in February 2023, was:
answer: About 88.9%
choices: About 88.9%
About 40%
About 15%
Essentially zero
context: The meta-analysis reported protection against severe disease of about 88.9% (84.7-90.9) at 40 weeks for Omicron BA.1, and above 78% for all earlier variants. The T-cell arm of adaptive immunity holds up well against severe outcomes even as new variants appear. Source: The Lancet, IHME COVID-19 Forecasting Team, 16 Feb 2023.

question: The same Lancet meta-analysis asked a very different question: at 40 weeks out, how much did a past infection still protect against simply CATCHING Omicron BA.1 again? Their pooled figure was:
answer: About 29%
choices: About 29%
About 55%
About 78%
About 99%
context: Protection against reinfection at 40 weeks fell to about 29.0% for Omicron BA.1, though about 78.2% for ancestral, Alpha and Delta variants. Both results -- strong protection against severe disease AND weak protection against reinfection -- were true at the same time; headlines in both directions reported only one. Source: The Lancet, IHME COVID-19 Forecasting Team, 16 Feb 2023.

question: In an MMWR bulletin dated 28 January 2022, Tomas Leon and colleagues at the CDC compared COVID case rates in California and New York from May to November 2021 across four groups. On the specific comparison of unvaccinated-with-prior-infection versus vaccinated-without-prior-infection during the Delta-dominant weeks that autumn, what did the bulletin report?
answer: Prior infection produced LOWER case rates than vaccination alone
choices: Prior infection produced LOWER case rates than vaccination alone
Vaccination alone produced lower case rates than prior infection
The two groups had essentially identical case rates
Neither group's rate was low enough to distinguish from the unvaccinated-no-prior baseline
context: In the Delta-dominant week of 3 Oct 2021, unvaccinated persons with prior infection had case rates 29.0-fold lower (California) and 14.7-fold lower (New York) than unvaccinated persons without prior infection -- lower than the vaccinated-only cohort in the same weeks. The study covered 1,108,600 incident cases. The hybrid group (vaccinated AND prior infection) was lowest of all. Source: MMWR 71(4), 28 Jan 2022.

question: Through 2021 and into 2022 -- while the CDC's own bulletin was reporting that a documented prior infection outperformed vaccination alone during the Delta weeks -- most jurisdictions running vaccine mandates gave that same documented prior infection a very specific weight toward the requirement. What weight?
answer: None; it counted as zero
choices: None; it counted as zero
Half; it counted as one dose
A full course; it counted as complete
More than a full course; it counted as booster-equivalent
context: Prior-infection status was almost universally excluded from mandate compliance in the United States and most of Western Europe through this period, despite the MMWR and Lancet measurements. The policy set aside a measured immune status that its own agencies were publishing. Source: MMWR 71(4), 28 Jan 2022.

question: In August 1947, a United States military tribunal sitting in Nuremberg finished the trial of twenty-three doctors and officials who had run medical experiments on prisoners. The tribunal's verdict opened with ten principles that would go on to found modern research ethics. What was the first principle?
answer: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential
choices: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential
The experiment must be conducted only in a licensed hospital
The experiment must always use the smallest possible sample
The subject must first exhaust all approved treatments
context: The Nuremberg Code, delivered on 19 August 1947, was the direct response to what the tribunal had just heard about the concentration-camp experiments. Its first sentence is the doctrine that a medical intervention requires the free, informed consent of the person receiving it -- not a public-health preference, but the first line of the founding document of research ethics. Source: Nuremberg Code, 1947.

question: Sit on a table edge tonight with one leg hanging loose, tap the tendon just below the kneecap, and the leg kicks before you could decide anything. The whole loop takes about eighteen thousandths of a second because the signal never reaches the part of you that could stop it. Where does the signal actually turn around?
answer: The spinal cord
choices: The spinal cord
The base of the brain
The knee joint itself
The thigh muscle
context: The tap fires a sensory fibre that runs into the cord and comes right back out to the muscle; the brain is out of the loop for the kick itself. StatPearls, Physiology, Deep Tendon Reflexes.

question: The knee-jerk is famous for having about the shortest wiring in the human body. The sensory fibre from the thigh enters the spinal cord at the L2 to L4 level and reaches its motor partner almost instantly. How many synapses sit between the fibre coming in and the motor neuron going out?
answer: One
choices: One
Three
Six
Twelve
context: This is the classic MONOSYNAPTIC arc; the withdrawal reflex, by contrast, is polysynaptic (multiple interneurons in the middle) and takes noticeably longer. StatPearls, Physiology, Deep Tendon Reflexes.

question: The Cambridge physiologist Charles Sherrington noticed something elegant hiding inside the knee-jerk. In the same instant the cord tells the thigh muscle to contract, it silences a different muscle so the two are not fighting. Which muscle does the cord silence at the moment the thigh muscle fires?
answer: The hamstring at the back of the thigh
choices: The hamstring at the back of the thigh
The calf muscle at the back of the shin
The gluteus at the top of the hip
The abdominal wall at the front of the belly
context: Muscles can only pull, never push, so a smooth kick needs the puller ON and the opposite puller OFF. Sherrington called this reciprocal innervation and shared the 1932 Nobel for this whole family of discoveries. Oregon State Anatomy 2e.

question: A patient's knee-jerk is barely visible. The doctor asks him to hook his fingers together and pull hard while she taps again; the leg now kicks briskly. Erno Jendrassik discovered this trick in the 19th century. What does its success show about the brain's relationship to a reflex it cannot command?
answer: The brain cannot cause the kick but can turn its volume up
choices: The brain cannot cause the kick but can turn its volume up
The brain fires the kick directly along a second pathway
The brain overrides the spinal cord to abort the kick
The brain replaces the sensor signal with a stronger one
context: The finger-pull reduces the brainstem's normal damping of the reflex arc, so more motor units fire. It is the loop's volume knob, not its switch. Wikipedia, Jendrassik maneuver.

question: Try this tonight. Flip a fair coin ten times and count the heads; then imagine doing the same with a thousand flips. Which of these outcomes is fairly common in the short run but essentially never seen in the long one?
answer: Landing 80 percent heads or more
choices: Landing 80 percent heads or more
Landing exactly half heads
Landing at least one tail
Landing more heads than tails
context: In ten flips, roughly one run in eighteen lands eight or more heads by pure chance; in a thousand flips, 800 or more heads essentially never happens. That is the whole law of small numbers in one demonstration -- small samples do not merely carry more error, they manufacture extremes at both ends. Elementary binomial probability; illustrated in Kahneman, 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' Ch. 10.

question: In 1971 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman handed a questionnaire to professional psychologists at their own conference and found the experts reasoning about a twenty-person study the way a gambler reasons about a streak. What witty diagnosis did they put in the title of the paper they published in Psychological Bulletin?
answer: Belief in the Law of Small Numbers
choices: Belief in the Law of Small Numbers
Judgment under Uncertainty
Prospect Theory
The Framing of Decisions
context: Tversky & Kahneman, 'Belief in the Law of Small Numbers,' Psychological Bulletin 76(2), 105-110, 1971. The other three titles are real Tversky-Kahneman papers on other topics, which makes the recognition an actual test of the paper's provenance.

question: Tversky and Kahneman put this puzzle to their colleagues. A town has two hospitals. About 45 babies are born each day in the larger one and about 15 in the smaller one. Over a year, in which hospital would MORE days be recorded on which over 60 percent of that day's babies were boys?
answer: The smaller hospital
choices: The smaller hospital
The larger hospital
About the same in each
Cannot be determined without more data
context: 56 percent of the responding psychologists answered 'about the same'. The correct answer is the smaller hospital, and it is not close: with only 15 births in a day the daily proportion of boys wanders much further from 50 percent than it does with 45. Tversky & Kahneman 1971, Psychological Bulletin.

question: Howard Wainer and Harris Zwerling mapped kidney-cancer rates across the roughly 3,141 US counties. The counties with the LOWEST rates were rural and mostly in the Midwest, South and West -- and so were the counties with the HIGHEST rates. What actually produces that puzzling map?
answer: The extreme counties simply have very few people in them
choices: The extreme counties simply have very few people in them
Regression to the mean pulled the extreme counties back in
Simpson's paradox reversed the direction inside each county
Selection bias dropped the middle counties from the survey
context: Rural life cannot cause and prevent the same cancer. Rural counties simply have small populations, and small samples yield extreme results in both directions more often than large samples. The three distractors are real statistical ideas, and none is what is happening here. Kahneman, 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' Ch. 10, citing Wainer & Zwerling.

question: Wainer and Zwerling then looked at 1,662 Pennsylvania schools. The best-performing fifty were heavily made up of small schools, and school reformers rushed to fund small schools on that basis. Where else on the same list were small schools showing up in unusual numbers?
answer: Among the worst-performing fifty schools
choices: Among the worst-performing fifty schools
Among the schools that had recently expanded
Among the schools with the most experienced staff
Among the schools in the wealthiest districts
context: Small schools were over-represented in the bottom fifty by a factor of six. Small schools are not better on average; they are simply more variable, and the reformers had ranked them by an unstable measure and read that instability as merit. Wainer & Zwerling, 'Evidence That Smaller Schools Do Not Improve Student Achievement'.

question: The small-schools ranking then became a policy programme, and one American donor invested very heavily in creating small schools -- sometimes by breaking large schools into smaller units -- on the strength of exactly the statistical mirage Wainer and Zwerling had described. Which donor was it?
answer: The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
choices: The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
The Ford Foundation
The Rockefeller Foundation
The Carnegie Corporation of New York
context: Kahneman names the Gates Foundation in 'Thinking, Fast and Slow' Ch. 10 as the funder that acted on the small-schools ranking. The other three foundations are real education funders which makes the recognition specific rather than generic.

question: In 1962 Jacob Cohen surveyed the studies published in a leading psychology journal and reported a median statistical power of about 0.46 for a medium effect. Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer repeated the exercise across 1960 to 1987 and found the figure had moved -- but which direction had it moved?
answer: It had dropped, to about 0.37
choices: It had dropped, to about 0.37
It had risen, to about 0.60
It had held roughly steady at 0.46
It had risen sharply, to about 0.80
context: Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer 1989, 'Do Studies of Statistical Power Have an Effect on the Power of Studies?' Twenty-four years after Cohen's diagnosis, more than half of real medium effects were still being missed by underpowered studies -- and the field had not corrected.

question: Katherine Button, John Ioannidis and colleagues estimated the median statistical power of neuroscience studies at somewhere between 8 percent and 31 percent. In a field that underpowered, why does the average published effect end up systematically LARGER than the true underlying effect?
answer: Only results that chance pushed too far clear significance
choices: Only results that chance pushed too far clear significance
Reviewers prefer studies whose effects match prior findings
Authors round their reported effects up before submission
Journals publish only the largest study of each hypothesis
context: This is called the winner's curse.
