When power is low the only findings that reach the significance bar are the ones a lucky sample happened to inflate, so the published record is a filtered gallery of over-estimates. Button et al., 'Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience', Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2013.

question: The world's first compulsory sterilization law was passed in 1907 -- not by a dictatorship, but by a US state legislature. Which state?
answer: Indiana
choices: Indiana
Georgia
Vermont
Nevada
context: Governor J. Frank Hanly signed the law on April 12, 1907, letting superintendents of state prisons and asylums sterilize inmates judged criminal, insane, or 'imbecilic.' More than thirty US states and about a dozen foreign countries later followed. Sources: Indiana Historical Bureau, in.gov/history/state-historical-markers; uvm.edu/~lkaelber/eugenics/.

question: By the 1930s about thirty US states had eugenic sterilization laws. Roughly how many Americans were sterilized under those laws across the decades they ran?
context: About two-thirds of those sterilized were women. Historians give a range rather than a precise total because state records varied in quality and completeness. Sweden's parallel welfare-state program sterilized a similar number -- about 62,000 -- from 1934 to 1976. Sources: The Conversation on forced-sterilization policies; uvm.edu/~lkaelber/eugenics/.

question: One US state ran by far the largest sterilization program of any -- about 20,000 procedures between 1909 and 1979, roughly a third of the country's total -- at a time when it was one of the most modern and scientifically advanced states in the union. Which state?
answer: California
choices: California
Illinois
New York
Massachusetts
context: California's program, authorized in 1909, sterilized patients in state hospitals for the 'feebleminded' and 'insane.' California was the third US state to pass such a law, after Indiana and Washington. Sources: Wikipedia, Eugenics in California; Foundation for Economic Education.

question: North Carolina's Eugenics Board sterilized about 7,600 people between 1929 and 1974. Compared with its pre-1945 work, what did the Board do after the Second World War?
answer: It did more of its work after 1945 than before
choices: It did most of its work before 1945 and tapered off sharply after
It did roughly the same amount of work in each period
It did more of its work after 1945 than before
It did about a quarter of its work after 1945
context: This is the fact that breaks the comfortable story that Nazi revelations ended American eugenics. North Carolina's Board reviewed cases on IQ scores and social histories for nearly three more decades after the war. Source: NPR, 2013 coverage of NC compensation program.

question: One US state's eugenics board outlasted every other -- it ordered its last forced sterilization in 1981 and was not abolished until 1983. Which state?
answer: Oregon
choices: Oregon
Alabama
Utah
Kansas
context: Oregon's State Board of Eugenics, created in 1917, was later renamed the Board of Social Protection. Then-Senator John Kitzhaber -- a physician who later became governor -- helped write the 1983 repeal. Sources: Arizona State Embryo Project; Oregon Encyclopedia.

question: The formal state apologies for eugenic sterilization did not begin until 2002 -- roughly 25 years after the last programs wound down. Which US state was the first to issue such an apology?
answer: Virginia
choices: Virginia
North Carolina
Washington
Indiana
context: Governor Mark Warner apologized in May 2002; Oregon Governor John Kitzhaber followed the same year, and California's Gray Davis apologized in 2003. In 2013 North Carolina became the first state to actually pay living victims -- a $10 million fund. Sources: UPI, May 2002; WUNC 2014.

question: Three economists - Jonas Herby of Copenhagen, Lars Jonung of Lund and Steve Hanke of Johns Hopkins - decided to ask one narrow, checkable question about the mandated lockdowns of spring 2020. What was the question?
answer: by how much did they reduce COVID-19 deaths
choices: by how much did they reduce COVID-19 deaths
how much did they cost taxpayers
how did they affect mental health
how well were the rules obeyed
context: The narrow, quantitative framing is what made the whole project auditable; every one of the other three questions is a real research question but they measured only the first. Their paper is explicit that this is the BENEFIT side of a cost-benefit question - the other side was not their subject. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: A meta-analysis takes many earlier studies and combines them into one estimate on a common scale. Herby, Jonung and Hanke began by identifying 19,646 candidate papers that might address their question and screened them through three levels down to a shortlist that qualified. How many studies made the shortlist?
context: Of those 32, estimates from 22 could be converted to a common standardised effect size and entered the pooled result. The wide funnel and narrow spout is exactly the shape a serious systematic review looks like: thousands screened, dozens read, a handful used. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Herby, Jonung and Hanke's most important design rule was to exclude every study whose comparison came from a computer model - Imperial College's Report 9 among them. What design did the surviving studies share?
answer: difference-in-differences
choices: difference-in-differences
randomised control trial
regression discontinuity
propensity score matching
context: Difference-in-differences compares the change in one group before and after a policy against the change in a comparison group that never got the policy, so any common time-trend drops out and only the policy effect remains. That single rule excluded every study whose counterfactual was a model output - Imperial College's Report 9 among them. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: The Herby-Jonung-Hanke meta-analysis was published in Public Choice on 28 November 2024. Their headline finding, from studies using the Oxford stringency index, was that the average European and American lockdown of spring 2020 reduced COVID-19 mortality by roughly how much?
context: Their second, upper-bound estimate - built from nine specific interventions such as school closures and business closures - came out at 10.6%. Both numbers are on the low end of what supporters of mandates argued in 2020; both are far from zero. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice, vol. 203 (2025), pp. 337-367.

question: Herby, Jonung and Hanke translated their 3.2% figure into people: roughly 6,000 avoided COVID-19 deaths across Europe and 4,000 across the United States by 30 June 2020. To give a reader a scale for those figures they set them against another recurring annual cause of death the reader already knows. Which one?
answer: seasonal influenza
choices: seasonal influenza
road traffic accidents
lung cancer
heart disease
context: Ordinary-year influenza kills roughly 72,000 people in Europe and 38,000 in the United States, so the estimated benefit of the average spring-2020 lockdown was of a similar magnitude to about a month of one bad flu season. The bank cites the comparison because that is what the authors used, and because a number without a scale is not information. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: The 2024 Public Choice paper was not Herby, Jonung and Hanke's first pass at their question. Their January 2022 Johns Hopkins working paper, on very similar data, had reported an average mortality reduction of 0.2%. Between the two papers their own headline number moved. In which direction?
answer: upward by more than an order of magnitude
choices: upward by more than an order of magnitude
upward within statistical noise
downward to almost zero
downward into negative territory
context: 3.2 / 0.2 = 16, so more than an order of magnitude - and in the direction of admitting more benefit from the very policies the authors had publicly criticised. The revision is the best rung in this ladder: same three authors, same question, refined method, published under their own names in a peer-reviewed journal. That is what self-correction looks like when nobody made anyone do it. Source: Herby-Hanke Johns Hopkins working paper (Jan 2022); Herby-Jonung-Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: The best-known estimate on the OTHER side of the lockdown-benefits debate was published in Nature in June 2020 by Seth Flaxman and colleagues at Imperial College. Using a Bayesian model across 11 European countries, they reported an estimate of averted deaths attributable to non-pharmaceutical interventions through early May 2020. Roughly how many averted deaths?
answer: 3.1 million
choices: 3.1 million
6 million
1.3 million
context: The Flaxman paper's central estimate was 3.1 million averted deaths across 11 European countries (95% credible interval 2.8-3.5 million). The Herby-Jonung-Hanke number for Europe was in the thousands. The bank keys BOTH; a ladder that hides the strongest opposing estimate has argued instead of taught. Source: Flaxman et al., Nature (2020).

question: Herby, Jonung and Hanke's own reading of their 3.2% figure is not that nothing worked in spring 2020. They argue that something OTHER than the mandates did much of the mitigation work in that period. What?
answer: voluntary behaviour change
choices: voluntary behaviour change
warmer spring weather
prior natural immunity
faster hospital care
context: Their point is that when a virus becomes visible and dangerous, people change what they do - stop shaking hands, stop crowded indoors, watch the sick - before and after any order tells them to; that voluntary shift shows up in every dataset. It is why open-school, light-restriction Sweden's death curve did not diverge wildly from its neighbours'. The finding is 'the mandate added less than you were told', not 'the virus was mild'. Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: Herby, Jonung and Hanke are careful about the LIMITS of what their meta-analysis says. They wrote explicitly that it measures only one side of a two-sided question. Which side?
answer: the benefit side only
choices: the benefit side only
the cost side only
both benefit and cost
the compliance side only
context: The costs - lost schooling, mental-health harm, business collapse, deferred cancer diagnoses, elderly people dying alone - were left for other researchers to measure. The paper's honest self-limitation is what lets it function as evidence rather than advocacy: 'this is what we measured, this is what we did not, and here is a number a reader can now check.' Source: Herby, Jonung and Hanke, Public Choice (2024).

question: About 40 miles off the Sunda Strait on 27 August 1883, Captain Sampson of the British ship Norham Castle heard the volcano explode and wrote a single blunt line in his log about the state of his crew. What did he report?
answer: the eardrums of over half the men aboard had been shattered clean by the noise
choices: the eardrums of over half the men aboard had been shattered clean by the noise
the men on watch had been thrown flat to the deck and could not stand for an hour
the helmsman had gone momentarily blind from the flash over the water
the cook and half the galley crew had been scalded by kettles thrown from the stove
context: Captain Sampson's log line, quoted in the contemporary Royal Society report: 'So violent are the explosions that the ear-drums of over half my crew have been shattered.' The Norham Castle was about 64 km (40 miles) from Krakatoa. Source: classicfm.com summary of Royal Society of London's 1888 report on the Krakatoa eruption.

question: The '172 decibel' figure often quoted for the 1883 eruption was not measured with a microphone; microphones capable of that recording did not exist in 1883. What instrument, sitting at a Batavia gasworks about 160 km away, actually recorded the value the number is calculated from?
answer: a barometer, which registered a pressure spike of more than 2.5 inches of mercury
choices: a barometer, which registered a pressure spike of more than 2.5 inches of mercury
a seismograph, which registered ground displacement of more than 2.5 centimetres
a thermograph, which registered a spike of more than 2.5 degrees above ambient
an anemometer, which registered a wind gust of more than 2.5 times the daily average
context: The Batavia (now Jakarta) gasworks gauge spiked by more than 2.5 inches of mercury (about 8.5 kilopascals). Converting that pressure amplitude into a sound-pressure level at that distance gives roughly 172 dB. The '172 dB' number is therefore inferred from a pressure record, not measured as sound. Source: Nautilus, 'The Sound So Loud That It Circled the Earth Four Times.'

question: A viral internet figure gives the 1883 eruption as '310 decibels.' A physicist will say that number cannot be right in principle, because in ordinary air at sea level a sound wave tops out near 194 dB. Why does the ceiling sit right there?
answer: at that amplitude the low-pressure half of the wave has already been pulled down to a vacuum
choices: at that amplitude the low-pressure half of the wave has already been pulled down to a vacuum
at that amplitude the wave breaks up the oxygen molecules and stops carrying any pressure at all
at that amplitude the wave heats the air enough to change the speed of sound and cancel itself
at that amplitude the wave saturates the human eardrum, which is what sets the top of the scale
context: A sound wave in air swings symmetrically around atmospheric pressure. The compression half can climb indefinitely, but the rarefaction half has a hard floor at zero pressure (a vacuum). At about 194 dB at sea level the rarefaction has reached that floor. Anything more energetic is no longer a sound wave; it is a blast wave, an asymmetric pressure jump moving faster than sound. The '310 dB' figure has no measurement behind it and could not describe a sound wave in sea-level air. Source: ScienceABC, 'What's the Loudest Sound Possible on Earth?'

question: Past a few thousand kilometres from Krakatoa the wave dropped below the roughly 20 Hz floor of human hearing and stopped being audible sound. What did barographs quietly record it doing next?
answer: passing seven times as it travelled back and forth around the planet
choices: passing seven times as it travelled back and forth around the planet
reflecting off the base of the stratosphere and fading within a few hours
splitting into two waves that never rejoined and reached each pole separately
dying out at the first major mountain range it met and going no further
context: Beyond a few thousand kilometres the pressure disturbance dropped below the roughly 20 Hz threshold of human hearing and continued as infrasound. Weather-station barographs on several continents registered the pulse passing seven times over about five days as it circled the Earth (three and a half round trips). The same worldwide infrasound listening idea is what the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation now uses to catch clandestine nuclear tests. Sources: Nautilus, 'The Sound So Loud That It Circled the Earth Four Times'; historyfacts.com.

question: On 7 September 2019, months before COVID, the BBC convened a private international body that would meet weekly through the pandemic. It brought Reuters, the Associated Press, Agence France-Presse, the Washington Post and the New York Times to the same table as Google, YouTube, Facebook, Microsoft and Twitter. What did the BBC call it?
answer: The Trusted News Initiative
choices: The Trusted News Initiative
The Global Disinformation Index
The Election Integrity Partnership
The Stanford Internet Observatory
context: The alliance grew out of a June 2019 summit chaired by then-BBC director-general Tony Hall and was directed by BBC executive Jessica Cecil. The other three named bodies are real adjacent organisations working in the same space, which is why they belong in the recognition set. Sources: Wikipedia 'Trusted News Initiative'; Reuters Institute biography of Jessica Cecil.

question: What made the Trusted News Initiative distinctive from the moment it launched was who was seated at the same table. Alongside the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and the Washington Post, which OTHER kind of organisation was also a founding partner?
answer: The technology platforms that distributed the news
choices: The technology platforms that distributed the news
The national broadcast regulators in each member country
The universities that trained the members' journalists
The professional associations that certified those journalists
context: Google, YouTube, Facebook, Microsoft and Twitter joined the news outlets as founding partners -- the publishers and their distribution channels agreeing together about what would spread. That is the fact that makes the alliance recognisable as a piece of machinery rather than an ordinary press body. Sources: Wikipedia 'Trusted News Initiative'; Influence Watch entry for TNI.

question: On 27 March 2020, the Trusted News Initiative's members formally extended the alliance's remit to a new subject. Which subject?
answer: COVID-19 information
choices: COVID-19 information
Anti-vaccine content on childhood immunisation
Climate change reporting
Deepfake video detection
context: The TNI had been founded in September 2019 to coordinate against election disinformation. The 27 March 2020 announcement pulled COVID-19 into the alliance's scope, and in July 2020 a second extension anticipated the US presidential election. Sources: Wikipedia 'Trusted News Initiative'; EBU announcement, July 2020.

question: In January 2023 Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Children's Health Defense sued the Associated Press, the BBC, Reuters and the Washington Post over the Trusted News Initiative. The suit's key recognition move was to file the case not under free-speech law but under a DIFFERENT area of law. Which one?
answer: Antitrust law, under Section 1 of the Sherman Act
choices: Antitrust law, under Section 1 of the Sherman Act
Consumer protection law, under the Lanham Act
Broadcast law, under the Communications Act
Election law, under the Federal Election Campaign Act
context: The theory is that competitors had agreed among themselves to suppress rival publishers -- a boycott. That is a filed claim, not a proven finding. In July 2025 the US Department of Justice Antitrust Division filed a 22-page Statement of Interest supporting the plaintiffs, arguing that antitrust law does play a part in protecting viewpoint competition in news markets. Sources: Bloomberg Law; Politico Pro, July 2025.

question: The American version of the same story lasted three weeks in the open. On 27 April 2022, testifying to a House appropriations subcommittee, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas announced a new internal working group inside his department, with Nina Jankowicz as its executive director. What did he call it?
answer: The Disinformation Governance Board
choices: The Disinformation Governance Board
The Countering Foreign Influence Task Force
The Election Integrity Steering Committee
The Public Information Protection Office
context: The board had no enforcement authority -- it was an internal coordinating working group inside DHS -- but its name, remit and choice of director drew immediate objection across the political spectrum. Sources: CBS News, May 2022; Wikipedia 'Nina Jankowicz'.

question: The Disinformation Governance Board was paused on 18 May 2022 after Nina Jankowicz resigned in the backlash, and it was formally terminated on 24 August 2022. What ordinary piece of machinery inside the department recommended that Alejandro Mayorkas shut it down?
answer: The Homeland Security Advisory Council
choices: The Homeland Security Advisory Council
The DHS Office of Inspector General
The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency
context: The Council, co-chaired for this review by former DHS Secretary Michael Chertoff and former Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, unanimously recommended dissolution. This is the honest end of the sub-strand: the machinery was stopped in public, by ordinary argument, in under four months -- and the ordinary body that stopped it is worth knowing by name. Sources: CNN, August 2022; First Amendment Encyclopedia (MTSU).

question: In late-1800s Berlin, Paul Ehrlich kept seeing something under his microscope: a lab dye soaked into one kind of cell and left its neighbour untouched. He reasoned that a chemical that picks one cell out of a smear might pick out an invader inside the body. What did Ehrlich name the imagined drug?
answer: A magic bullet -- Zauberkugel in his German
choices: A magic bullet -- Zauberkugel in his German
An antitoxin -- like the diphtheria serum
A vaccine -- like Jenner's smallpox jab
An antiseptic -- like Lister's carbolic
context: Ehrlich called the goal a Zauberkugel -- 'magic bullet' -- and coined the word chemotherapy for the systematic chemical hunt that would try to find one. Source: https://centennial.rucares.org/index.php?page=Chemotherapy

question: Ehrlich's method was slow and boring: pick a family of arsenic drugs, make and number them one at a time, test each on an infected rabbit. He needed a name for this systematic drug hunt that no one had needed before. What word did Ehrlich coin for it?
answer: Chemotherapy
choices: Chemotherapy
Serotherapy
Immunotherapy
Phototherapy
context: Chemotherapy first meant the systematic hunt for antibacterial drugs -- one chemical after another until one hits the invader but not the patient. The word only later broadened to cancer drugs. The rival 1900s -therapy words were real too: serotherapy (antitoxin serums), immunotherapy (immune-system approaches), and Finsen's Nobel-winning phototherapy. Source: https://centennial.rucares.org/index.php?page=Chemotherapy

question: Compound 606, the arsenic drug that would be sold as Salvarsan and cure syphilis for decades, was almost thrown away. It had been made in 1907 and set aside on the shelf as a failure. What rescued it?
answer: Sahachiro Hata retested it two years later at Ehrlich's insistence
choices: Sahachiro Hata retested it two years later at Ehrlich's insistence
Alfred Bertheim spilled it onto a rabbit that was infected anyway
Emil von Behring re-synthesised it and got the credit for the cure
Fritz Schaudinn injected himself with it and reported he had been cured
context: Ehrlich's Japanese bacteriologist Sahachiro Hata reran the test with more care and better records; the drug that had been called useless turned out to be the first real chemical cure. A 'negative result' can be a badly run test. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsphenamine

question: In late December 1932 at Bayer in Germany, Gerhard Domagk ran the same brute-force screen on industrial dyes. He gave one group of mice a red dye called Prontosil and then hit both that group and an untreated control group with a dose of streptococcus known to kill mice reliably. When he opened the cages on Christmas Eve, what did he find?
answer: Every treated mouse alive; every untreated mouse dead
choices: Every treated mouse alive; every untreated mouse dead
Roughly half of each group survived, no clear difference
Every mouse in both groups dead by the second day
Only the untreated mice alive; the dye had killed the treated ones
context: Twelve mice given Prontosil all survived; fourteen untreated mice all died. Domagk began the run on 20 December 1932 and read it out on 24 December. Prontosil went on to save many lives from childbed fever, wound infections, and pneumonia -- years before penicillin was available in quantity. Source: https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/gerhard-domagk/

question: Prontosil had one strange property the bank refuses to skip. Chemists at the Pasteur Institute in 1935-36 discovered it when they compared how the drug behaved in glassware and in a live animal. What did the red dye do in a test tube?
answer: Nothing -- it killed no bacteria at all in glassware
choices: Nothing -- it killed no bacteria at all in glassware
It killed streptococcus even faster than in the body
It turned the water pink but left the bacteria growing
It refused to dissolve in anything except living blood
context: Prontosil worked only inside a body. Jacques and Therese Trefouel and their team showed the animal splits the dye, releasing a smaller, colourless half -- sulfanilamide, a molecule already known and unpatentable -- which is the real antibiotic. If Domagk had screened in glassware, as was cheaper and standard, he would have thrown the winner away. Source: https://www.chm.bris.ac.uk/motm/sulfanilamide/sulfanilh.html

question: Gerhard Domagk was awarded the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the Prontosil work. He would not collect the medal until 1947. What kept him from accepting it in 1939?
answer: The Gestapo arrested him and forced him to sign a refusal
choices: The Gestapo arrested him and forced him to sign a refusal
He himself judged the discovery too small for the honour
The Second World War had closed the Swedish border
The Nobel Committee had asked him to test the drug for another year
context: Hitler had forbidden any German to accept a Nobel Prize after the 1936 Peace Prize went to the concentration-camp prisoner Carl von Ossietzky. Domagk received his medal in 1947, though the prize money had by then been forfeit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_controversies

question: The Ghirardi-Rimini-Weber theory of 1986 and the Diosi-Penrose gravity-driven proposal are not interpretations. They add a real, mass-dependent breakdown of superposition to the equations, so they PREDICT something the others do not. What does that mean for their status today?
answer: some of their parameter ranges have already been ruled out by experiment
choices: some of their parameter ranges have already been ruled out by experiment
they were confirmed together by the 2015 loophole-free Bell tests in Delft
they were shown mathematically equivalent to many-worlds by a 2003 proof
they were withdrawn by their own authors after the 2020 underground results
context: Because objective-collapse theories predict a real, spontaneous breakdown of superposition, they leave a signature: a tiny radiation from charged particles as their wave functions collapse. Underground low-background searches published in 2020-2021 ruled out the simplest parameter-free version of the Diosi-Penrose gravity-driven collapse; matter-wave interference with heavier and heavier molecules continues to squeeze GRW-type parameters. A question that sounded like pure metaphysics turned into an experimental programme with a budget. Source: Quanta, 'Physics Experiments Spell Doom for Quantum Collapse Theory' (2022).

question: In the garden at Passy in 1784, a Parisian doctor named Charles d'Eslon secretly treated one tree, then had a blindfolded boy led out to embrace tree after tree until he found it. At which tree did the boy actually collapse in a swoon?
answer: At the fourth tree, none of which had been touched
choices: At the treated tree, on his first try
At the fourth tree, none of which had been touched
At the second tree, which had been treated
At no tree at all, and the test was called off
context: In the Passy orchard trial, d'Eslon magnetized one tree and had a boy said to be sensitive to the force blindfolded and led to embrace trees one by one. The boy collapsed at the fourth tree, which had not been touched at all -- the belief did the work, not the fluid. Source: https://www.fibonaccimd.com/post/mesmer-frankin-mesmerism-placebos

question: The Vienna-born doctor whose theory the 1784 test was checking, Franz Mesmer, ran a Paris salon around an oak tub called a baquet, from which iron rods jutted for patients to grip as music played and they fell into fits. What did he say the tub moved through them?
answer: An invisible fluid he called animal magnetism
choices: The four humours of ancient Greek medicine
An invisible fluid he called animal magnetism
Nervous energy passed from one patient to the next
Blood, warmed and thinned by the tub
context: Mesmer taught that an invisible universal fluid he called animal magnetism flowed between all bodies; illness came when it dammed up. The word 'animal' meant living, not beasts -- from Latin anima, breath or soul -- to mark it off from ordinary iron magnets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Mesmer

question: In the spring of 1784, King Louis XVI, tired of the mesmerist craze sweeping his court, appointed a commission to test the doctrine. The most famous member was the seventy-eight-year-old American ambassador, hobbled by gout and a bladder stone, whose Passy house and garden hosted most of the trials. Who was he?
answer: Benjamin Franklin
choices: Thomas Jefferson
Benjamin Franklin
John Adams
John Jay
context: Franklin, then 78 and America's minister to France, was too weak from gout and a bladder stone to travel from Passy into Paris, so the commissioners held many of the trials at his own house and orchard. He is the reason the joint royal commissions are usually called the Franklin Commission. Source: https://benjaminfranklinhouse.org/benjamin-franklin-and-the-glass-armonica/

question: Mesmer himself refused to have anything to do with the commissioners, and they took up the offer of his best-known Paris disciple, the court physician Charles d'Eslon, and tested the doctrine on d'Eslon's own patients instead. That switch actually strengthened the test. Why?
answer: The subjects were already believers, so a null result could not be blamed on stacked patients
choices: The subjects were already believers, so a null result could not be blamed on stacked patients
D'Eslon was known to be a fraud, so the trial would expose the trick
D'Eslon owned a baquet larger than Mesmer's, so more patients could be tested at once
The court paid d'Eslon well, so his cooperation cost the commissioners nothing
context: Because Mesmer cut off contact and d'Eslon offered his practice, the commissioners tested the doctrine on a believer's own patients -- people convinced the force was real. If the tests failed even there, no one could say the subjects had been picked to fail. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_Animal_Magnetism

question: Music in Mesmer's crisis rooms came from an unearthly-toned instrument, spun by a foot pedal, whose eerie voice Franklin recognized on sight. Why did Franklin know it so well?
answer: He had invented that very instrument, the glass armonica
choices: He had commissioned Mozart to write pieces for it
He had invented that very instrument, the glass armonica
He had shipped one to Paris as a gift for Queen Marie Antoinette
He had heard it years earlier at a court in Vienna
context: Franklin invented the glass armonica in 1761, and its world premiere came in 1762; it became so popular that Mozart wrote for it, and Mesmer used its unearthly sound to help bring on the convulsive crises his patients treated as their cure. Source: https://benjaminfranklinhouse.org/benjamin-franklin-and-the-glass-armonica/

question: In August 1784 the commission's public report, printed in some 20,000 copies, concluded that Mesmer's invisible fluid did not exist. But the report was careful about the patients themselves: it said their crises were real and worth explaining, and traced them to a single cause. Which cause did it name?
answer: The imagination of the patients themselves
choices: Fraud, deliberately staged by the mesmerists
A subtle drug added to the water in the baquet
A form of contagious hysteria unique to women
The imagination of the patients themselves
context: The August 1784 Rapport blamed the crises on imagination and imitation, not fraud or a hidden drug. This is the passage most historians treat as the first scientific description of what modern medicine calls the placebo effect. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_Animal_Magnetism

question: A small silvery ingot placed on a warm human palm turns into a puddle in about a minute; its melting point is 29.76 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature. Which metal is it?
answer: Gallium
choices: Gallium
Caesium
Indium
Tin
context: Gallium (element 31) melts at 29.76 C. Caesium melts even lower (28.5 C) but reacts violently with skin moisture and cannot be safely held; indium melts at 156 C, tin at 232 C. Source: Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: A small chunk of frozen gallium is dropped into a beaker of the same metal in liquid form. What actually happens, the outcome that makes gallium unusual among metals?
answer: It floats on the surface
choices: It floats on the surface
It sinks straight to the bottom
It dissolves back into the liquid within seconds
It shatters into brittle silver crumbs
context: Gallium expands as it freezes, like water, so the solid is less dense than the liquid and floats. Only a handful of substances behave this way (bismuth and antimony are two other metals that do). Source: Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: Gallium melts on a warm palm at 29.76 degrees Celsius. What is the astonishing thing about the OTHER end of gallium's liquid range, the temperature at which it finally boils?
answer: It boils above 2,200 degrees Celsius, an enormous liquid range
choices: It boils above 2,200 degrees Celsius, an enormous liquid range
It boils at just above 100 degrees Celsius, like water
It boils around 357 degrees Celsius, the same as mercury
It skips liquid boiling and sublimates directly to a vapour
context: Almost nothing else stays liquid across so vast a span (roughly 2,000 degrees). This is why sealed quartz thermometers filled with gallium can read the interior of a furnace or a molten-metal bath, up to about 1,500 C, where a mercury thermometer would have boiled away centuries ago. Source: Wikipedia, Gallium; RSC Periodic Table.

question: In August 1875 the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran was examining zinc ore from the Pyrenees. Within an hour he was sure he had found a new element, which he later named gallium. What was the specific evidence that convinced him on the spot?
answer: Two violet lines in his spectroscope
choices: Two violet lines in his spectroscope
A grey powder left behind after roasting the ore
A magnet lifting silvery grains out of the ore
A vivid crimson flame in his Bunsen burner
context: Every element gives a unique fingerprint of coloured lines when its atoms are excited. Lecoq had built one of the best spectroscopes in France; the two violet lines belonged to no known element. He then isolated the metal itself by electrolysis. Source: Wikipedia, Gallium; Linda Hall Library biography of Lecoq de Boisbaudran.

question: Just after Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated gallium in 1875 he measured its density on a small sample and got about 4.7 grams per cubic centimetre. Dmitri Mendeleev's 1871 periodic table had predicted about 5.9 for the missing 'eka-aluminium' that gallium had just filled. Mendeleev promptly wrote Lecoq a letter with a single confident claim. What did the letter tell him to do?
answer: Repurify the sample and measure again, because his metal was still contaminated
choices: Repurify the sample and measure again, because his metal was still contaminated
Reassign the discovery to a different gap in the table, one under boron instead
Publish a full retraction, because the low density proved it was not a new element
Cool the metal in an ice bath before weighing, because the reading was distorted by heat
context: Lecoq did exactly that; the repurified metal measured 5.904 grams per cubic centimetre, almost exactly Mendeleev's number. A table on a sheet of paper had corrected the man holding the actual metal, one of the sharpest vindications of a scientific prediction on record. Source: Slate, 'Gallium: It Proved That Mendeleev Wasn't a Crackpot' (2010); Wikipedia, Mendeleev's predicted elements.

question: In a materials lab a technician leaves a single droplet of liquid gallium on the edge of a heavy aluminium workbench overnight. The next morning the bench edge crumbles when he grips it, though nothing has burned and no visible pool of metal has formed. At the atomic scale, what has the gallium actually done to the aluminium?
answer: Seeped along the grain boundaries and destroyed the cohesion between the aluminium crystals
choices: Seeped along the grain boundaries and destroyed the cohesion between the aluminium crystals
Melted the aluminium into a soft gallium-aluminium alloy across the whole bench
Oxidised the surface layer, so the outer skin flaked away and exposed weaker metal beneath
Lowered the surface tension of the protective oxide, letting cracks propagate freely
context: Metallurgists call what just happened liquid metal embrittlement. Gallium atoms are small and mobile enough to diffuse into the microscopic seams between aluminium's crystal grains; once the grains no longer stick to each other, the bulk metal loses its strength while looking almost unchanged. Hydrogen embrittlement is a real cousin (hydrogen atoms doing something similar in steels). Source: PMC11901249 (2025 EBSD study of Al after Ga embrittlement); Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: Gallium is famous for melting on a warm palm at 29.76 degrees Celsius. But another soft silvery metal, caesium, melts at an even lower 28.5 degrees Celsius, and yet it is caesium, never gallium, that no chemist would ever demonstrate as a palm-puddle party trick. What is the specific reason caesium cannot be held on bare skin?
answer: It reacts violently with the moisture on human skin
choices: It reacts violently with the moisture on human skin
It stains the skin a bright indelible yellow for months
It is one of the rarest metals on Earth and too costly to waste
Its liquid is opaque black and hides the melting moment entirely
context: Caesium is an alkali metal, one row below rubidium; even trace water on skin sets off a vigorous exothermic reaction that would burn the hand. Rubidium (melts at 39 C) has the same problem. Gallium, by contrast, is a post-transition metal that shrugs off skin moisture, which is why it, and not caesium, became the classic melts-in-your-hand demonstration. Source: Wikipedia, Caesium; Wikipedia, Gallium.

question: In our solar system Mercury races and Neptune crawls -- outer planets orbit slower because gravity weakens with distance. Around 1970 Vera Rubin and Kent Ford asked Andromeda the same question: how fast do stars and gas orbit at different distances from its centre? What did the outer ones do?
answer: orbited just as fast as the inner ones
choices: orbited just as fast as the inner ones
spiralled slowly inward toward the centre
orbited far slower, matching the Neptune pattern
drifted outward and escaped the galaxy
context: Rubin and Ford's 1970 paper 'Rotation of the Andromeda Nebula from a Spectroscopic Survey of Emission Regions' (Astrophysical Journal 159:379) plotted a rotation curve that stayed FLAT out to the visible edge. In a solar-system Kepler pattern the outer objects fall off. Andromeda's outskirts behaved like outer horses on a carousel keeping pace with the inner ones -- a hint that unseen mass was tugging them along. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Rubin ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_rotation_curve

question: In 1965 Vera Rubin became the first woman granted official observing time at the Palomar Observatory. She arrived at the dome and found there was no women's restroom -- only a men's-room door with a stick-figure man on it. What did Rubin do?
answer: cut a paper skirt and taped it onto the stick figure
choices: cut a paper skirt and taped it onto the stick figure
insisted the observatory build a new restroom that night
held her observing run out in the parking lot
shared the men's restroom without saying a word
context: Rubin told the story herself; it is one of the more-told anecdotes in twentieth-century American astronomy. She got her observations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Rubin

question: Rubin's collaborator Kent Ford built the key instrument for their Andromeda work -- a spectrograph that let them record faint outer gas clouds in about a tenth the exposure time an unaided photographic plate needed. What kind of spectrograph was Ford's?
answer: an image-tube spectrograph
choices: an image-tube spectrograph
an echelle spectrograph
a prism spectrograph
a grating spectrograph
context: Ford's image tube was an early image intensifier -- a vacuum device that amplified the trickle of photons from faint targets before they hit the recording medium. Echelle, prism, and grating spectrographs are all standard designs, but none of them boost dim signals; Ford's intensifier is what turned nights-long exposures into feasible ones, which is why Rubin and Ford could survey dozens of spirals and see the flat-curve pattern repeat almost every time. Source: https://carnegiescience.edu/vera-rubin-opening-doors-dark-matter-and-women-stem

question: In 1933 an astronomer measured how fast individual galaxies were flying around inside the Coma Cluster, applied the virial theorem, and found the cluster needed vastly more mass than its light could account for -- otherwise it would fly apart. He named the missing stuff dark matter. Who was he?
answer: Fritz Zwicky
choices: Fritz Zwicky
Jan Oort
Edwin Hubble
Harlow Shapley
context: Zwicky's paper 'Die Rotverschiebung von extragalaktischen Nebeln' appeared in Helvetica Physica Acta 6:110-127; he called the missing stuff 'dunkle Materie'. His headline factor -- roughly 400 times the visible mass -- relied on an era estimate of the Hubble constant that was much too large; modern Coma numbers put the mass-to-light ratio far lower (around 30 solar units, up to a few hundred by some estimates), so the true missing-mass factor is smaller than his figure -- but the missing-mass problem itself is real. Jan Oort had hinted at unseen mass in the Milky Way disk in 1932. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Zwicky ; https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Biviano/Biviano3_3.html

question: Fritz Zwicky's 1933 dark-matter claim sat mostly unused for about forty years -- not disproven, not embraced, largely ignored. In the 1970s a new line of observation forced astronomers to take the missing-mass idea seriously again. What kind of measurement revived it?
answer: flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies
choices: flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies
the cosmic microwave background power spectrum
distant supernova brightness measurements
pulsar timing across the Milky Way
context: Rubin and Ford on Andromeda, and Morton Roberts, Albert Bosma, and Ken Freeman working the same problem on other spirals, all found outer stars and gas keeping pace with inner ones -- the same missing-mass signature Zwicky had seen in a whole cluster forty years earlier. Zwicky was a difficult, brilliant outsider whose ideas were often dismissed in his lifetime; he was famous for calling people he disliked 'spherical bastards -- bastards no matter which way you look at them'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Zwicky ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter

question: The Bullet Cluster (2006) is two galaxy clusters caught in the act of colliding. X-ray images show that most of the ordinary matter -- the hot gas -- got shocked and stripped and left glowing in the middle of the crash. Gravitational lensing of galaxies behind the collision shows where most of the MASS went. What did the lensing reveal?
answer: most of the mass had sailed straight through with the galaxies
choices: most of the mass had sailed straight through with the galaxies
most of the mass had collapsed into a single black hole at the centre
the mass and the hot gas were still in exactly the same place
the mass had scattered evenly across the whole sky
context: Clowe et al. 2006 published the result as 'A Direct Empirical Proof of the Existence of Dark Matter' -- an eight-sigma offset between the visible mass (the X-ray gas) and the gravitational mass (the lensing). The 'bullet' subcluster smashed through the main cluster at roughly 4,500 km/s, more than one percent of the speed of light, creating a bow-shock visible in X-rays (Markevitch 2007, ApJ 661:L131). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_Cluster

question: In 1937 Fritz Zwicky predicted an effect general relativity implied but no one had yet confirmed on a galactic scale: a massive galaxy sitting in front of a more distant one should act as a lens. In 1979 Walsh, Carswell, and Weymann aimed the Kitt Peak 2.1-metre telescope at the quasar Q0957+561 and caught the first confirmed example. What did they see?
answer: two images of the same quasar
choices: two images of the same quasar
a ring of light around the foreground galaxy
the foreground galaxy suddenly glowing brighter
the quasar flickering on and off
context: Q0957+561 became known as the Twin Quasar -- the first confirmed gravitational lens. A complete Einstein ring (choice B) is a real later result, seen when the alignment is perfect; here the alignment was slightly off, splitting the quasar's image in two. Today lensing is one of the sharpest tools for weighing dark matter -- it does not care whether the mass is luminous; it just weighs what is there. That is exactly how the Bullet Cluster's mass was mapped. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Quasar ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Zwicky

question: The serious rival to dark matter is Modified Newtonian Dynamics, or MOND, proposed by Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom in 1983. MOND tweaks gravity below a tiny acceleration and fits individual spiral-galaxy rotation curves impressively well WITHOUT invoking any invisible matter. Where does MOND struggle worst, giving most physicists a big reason to keep favouring a dark-matter particle?
answer: galaxy clusters, including the Bullet Cluster
choices: galaxy clusters, including the Bullet Cluster
dwarf spheroidal satellite galaxies
wide binary star pairs
the cosmic microwave background power spectrum
context: MOND's tuning acceleration a0 is about 1.2 x 10^-10 metres per second squared -- roughly the acceleration you feel from a car speeding up by one metre per second every 260 years. Dwarf spheroidals, wide binaries, and the CMB power spectrum are all regimes where MOND has been argued about in the literature -- but rich clusters are the toughest case: a residual mass discrepancy remains even after MOND is applied, and the Bullet Cluster's clean separation of visible and gravitational mass is very hard for a pure gravity-modification story to reproduce. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modified_Newtonian_dynamics

question: For decades physicists have hunted the leading dark-matter particle candidate -- WIMPs, weakly interacting massive particles -- with giant vats of ultra-pure liquid xenon buried deep underground to shield out cosmic rays. LUX (2013), XENON1T, and LZ (LUX-ZEPLIN, 2023) have each been more sensitive than the last. What have these underground WIMP hunts found?
answer: no confirmed detection
choices: no confirmed detection
a single confirmed WIMP
a steady confirmed signal
the axion instead
context: LUX (370 kg of xenon), XENON1T (3.5 tonnes), and LZ (multi-tonne) have each pushed the exclusion limits tighter without a confirmed hit. The remaining live particle candidates include axions -- very light particles independently proposed in 1978 by Frank Wilczek and Steven Weinberg -- and sterile neutrinos; both are still being searched for, neither confirmed. The bank says clearly: no one yet knows what dark matter is. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weakly_interacting_massive_particle ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter

question: Ordinary neutrinos were once a serious dark-matter candidate: they have a little mass, there are lots of them, and they barely interact with anything. But cosmologists ruled them out as the BULK of dark matter. What is wrong with neutrinos for the job?
answer: they move too close to light-speed for galaxy-scale structure to form
choices: they move too close to light-speed for galaxy-scale structure to form
they carry the wrong electric charge to bind gravitationally
they decay far too quickly to accumulate in halos
they are far too heavy to have escaped particle detectors
context: In cosmology talk, neutrinos are 'hot dark matter' -- they were still moving relativistically when structure began forming, so they would have streamed out of small clumps and smeared out the fine structure we actually see galaxies condensing from. The dark matter that fits the observed universe is 'cold': slow-moving, clumping easily. Vera Rubin herself did not treat any of this as settled -- she liked to say the ratio of dark to light matter in a spiral galaxy 'is about a factor of 10 -- that's probably a good number for the ratio of our ignorance to knowledge.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter

question: In the winter of 1869, working in Felix Hoppe-Seyler's laboratory in a converted kitchen of Tuebingen Castle, the young Swiss physician Friedrich Miescher needed a fresh supply of white blood cells for his chemistry. Where did he get them from every morning?
answer: Off used surgical dressings from the town clinic
choices: Off used surgical dressings from the town clinic
From salmon sperm shipped in from the Rhine fisheries
From calves' thymus glands ordered from the abattoir
From blood drawn by lancet from the medical students
context: Miescher soaked the pus off the bandages, washed out the leucocytes, and by the end of the year had precipitated a strange substance out of their nuclei he named 'nuclein' -- what we now call DNA. The stuff of genes was first scooped off used surgical dressings. Source: Dahm 2005 (Human Genetics); Univ. Tuebingen MUT exhibit.

question: When Friedrich Miescher's 1869 nuclein extract was tested, two chemical features made clear it was not a protein: it was rich in phosphorus, and it shrugged off the digestive enzyme pepsin. What was the third clue?
answer: It contained no sulfur at all
choices: It contained no sulfur at all
It dissolved cleanly in pure alcohol
It turned bright green under iodine
It crystallized instantly on cooling
context: Two amino acids that proteins depend on -- cysteine and methionine -- carry sulfur, so any protein sample contains some. Miescher's nuclein contained none, which was chemically decisive. Source: Dahm 2008 (Current Biology).

question: When Miescher submitted his 1869 paper on the strange phosphorus-rich substance from cell nuclei, his supervisor Felix Hoppe-Seyler was not impressed enough to trust it. What did Hoppe-Seyler do before letting the manuscript be published in 1871?
answer: Made his own students repeat the entire extraction themselves
choices: Made his own students repeat the entire extraction themselves
Sent a sealed sample to Louis Pasteur in Paris for arbitration
Presented the finding to the Prussian Academy under his own name
Struck Miescher's name from the byline and published it as his own
context: Replication before publication -- a supervisor's skepticism doing exactly the job skepticism is meant to do. The 1871 issue eventually carried Miescher's paper, a confirming paper by a second student, and an article by Hoppe-Seyler backing the finding. Source: Univ. Tuebingen MUT exhibit; Dahm 2005.

question: In May 1952, Erwin Chargaff met two young researchers at Cambridge and told them face-to-face what his lab had measured about DNA base ratios. He thought little of them. What did he later write about that encounter with James Watson and Francis Crick?
answer: That he had never met two men who knew so little and aspired to so much
choices: That he had never met two men who knew so little and aspired to so much
That they had already worked out the double helix on the blackboard in front of him
That they had grasped the base-pairing hint on the spot and thanked him warmly
That he shook their hands and told them the Nobel Prize was theirs to lose
context: Chargaff spent the rest of his life resenting the model that Watson and Crick built out of his numbers. His memoir Heraclitean Fire (1978) is the sourced record of the quote. Source: Chargaff, Heraclitean Fire (1978); CSHL DNA Learning Center.

question: Friedrich Miescher, in 1892, floated a strikingly prescient idea about nuclein and heredity -- comparing it to how a 24 to 30 letter alphabet can express every word of every language. How did the idea reach the wider scientific world in his lifetime?
answer: It did not -- he confided it only to his uncle Wilhelm His and never argued it publicly
choices: It did not -- he confided it only to his uncle Wilhelm His and never argued it publicly
He announced it in a triumphant address to the Basel Academy of Sciences
He convinced Charles Darwin by mail and Darwin cited him in a late edition
He founded a research institute in Basel to prove the alphabet analogy
context: The 1892 letter to Wilhelm His speculated that the stereochemistry of asymmetric carbon atoms could encode hereditary richness -- an idea almost a century early. But Miescher published nothing of the sort, and for decades nuclein was written off as a mere phosphorus store. Source: Dahm 2008; Portin 2020.

question: For decades after 1871, most biologists who thought about nuclein at all dismissed it as chemically important but functionally dull. Which of these best captures the working guess about what nuclein did inside the cell nucleus?
answer: It was a phosphorus storage compound the cell drew on when needed
choices: It was a phosphorus storage compound the cell drew on when needed
It was a scaffolding fiber that held the chromosomes in shape
It was a signalling molecule the cell released to trigger division
It was an energy currency the nucleus burned during mitosis
context: The phosphorus-storage guess is the reason serious biologists could look straight at DNA and see nothing important. It took Avery in 1944 and Chargaff in 1950 to force the field to look again. Source: Dahm 2005; Portin 2014.

question: By 1900 electrical factories were insulating their wires with a natural varnish that had to be collected by hand, and demand was outrunning supply. Leo Baekeland set out to make a synthetic substitute for it, and in 1907 he ended up with Bakelite instead. Which natural varnish had he been chasing?
answer: Shellac, secreted by an Indian insect
choices: Shellac, secreted by an Indian insect
Beeswax, rendered from honeycomb
Gum arabic, tapped from acacia trees
Linseed oil, pressed from flax seed
context: The lac insect coats twigs across India with a resin that is scraped off, washed and dried into flakes - the wiring of the electrical age depended on insects. Baekeland's replacement, cooked under heat and pressure in a riveted steel vessel he called the Bakelizer, was sold as 'the material of a thousand uses'; its first mass-produced items included billiard balls, which replaced scarce ivory. The Bakelizer was made an ACS National Historic Chemical Landmark on 9 November 1993 and now sits in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. (Source: Grokipedia 'Bakelite', sections Invention, Commercialization, Cultural and Historical Significance.)

question: Measure the molecular weight of rubber, starch or cellulose and the answer came back in the tens of thousands, far past anything a chemist could draw on paper. Before 1920 almost nobody took that reading at face value. What did chemists say rubber really was?
answer: A clump of small molecules clinging together
choices: A clump of small molecules clinging together
A crowd of tiny crystals too small to see
A jelly of small molecules trapped in water
A stack of flat sheets sliding over one another
context: This was colloid, or association, theory, and it was the ruling view: the huge measured weights were an illusion produced by ordinary small molecules stuck together by weak physical forces rather than by chemical bonds. Emil Fischer, who had mapped the sugars, and Heinrich Wieland both held it. It was not a stupid idea - nobody had ever seen a molecule with thousands of links - but it was wrong, and it took thirty years to dislodge. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Origins of the Macromolecular Hypothesis.)

question: Cut a strip from a plastic grocery bag, grip both ends and pull slowly. A thin waist forms somewhere along the strip and turns cloudy white - engineers call it a neck. Keep pulling at the same steady rate. What does the neck do next?
answer: It lengthens, swallowing the unstretched strip
choices: It lengthens, swallowing the unstretched strip
It tears through, leaving two ragged ends
It springs back and a new neck forms elsewhere
It crumbles into a brittle white powder
context: The neck refuses to be the weak point: it stops thinning and eats its way along the strip instead, so a whole strip can be drawn out to several times its length without parting. This is cold drawing, and it is how a synthetic fibre is made. In April 1930 Julian Hill, working in Wallace Carothers's DuPont laboratory, used a high-vacuum 'molecular still' to push a polyester to a molecular weight of about 12,000, drew filaments out of the hot melt like taffy, and found that stretching them cold turned them tough and elastic, with properties approaching silk. Stretching, not chemistry, made the fibre. (Sources: Wikipedia 'Necking (engineering)'; Grokipedia 'Wallace Carothers', section Development of Polyesters.)

question: Long molecules were not a human invention; living things had been building them for a billion years before any chemist made one on purpose. The most abundant of them all on Earth is one substance that makes up roughly a third of all the plant matter there is. Which substance is it?
answer: Cellulose
choices: Cellulose
Starch
Lignin
Pectin
context: Cellulose is a chain of glucose units and about 33% of all plant biomass, which makes it the most abundant organic polymer - repeating-unit molecule - on the planet. You are built of chains too: collagen is a chain of amino acids wound into a triple helix, which is what gives tendon and skin their tensile strength, and DNA is a chain of nucleotides. After his Nobel, Hermann Staudinger extended his macromolecular argument straight into biology, to proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. The fight over rubber decided how we read life's molecules too. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Polymer', section Natural Polymers; Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Extensions to Biological Macromolecules.)

question: In 1920 Hermann Staudinger published a paper, 'Über Polymerisation', that set almost every senior chemist in Germany against him. What did he claim rubber's molecules are?
answer: Single molecules thousands of units long, joined by ordinary bonds
choices: Single molecules thousands of units long, joined by ordinary bonds
Ring molecules threaded through one another like woven chain mail
Sheet molecules one atom thick, stacked in parallel flat layers
Star molecules with short arms radiating from one central core
context: The claim was simple and enormous: the same valence rules that hold a small organic molecule together will hold a chain of ten thousand units. In 1922 Staudinger coined a word for them, 'Makromolekül' - macromolecule. He needed a new word because 'polymer' was already taken: Jöns Jacob Berzelius had coined it in 1833 from the Greek poly, many, and meros, parts, but he used it for compounds that share an empirical formula while their molecular weights differ by whole multiples. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Origins of the Macromolecular Hypothesis; Grokipedia 'Polymer', section Etymology.)

question: By 1927 Hermann Staudinger had spent seven years fighting the leaders of German chemistry over what rubber is made of, and he was losing. That year Heinrich Wieland, who won the 1927 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, wrote to him privately and urged him to drop the idea. No organic molecule can weigh more than about 5,000, Wieland told him; anything heavier would be as unstable as one particular famous structure. Which structure did Wieland name?
answer: The Tower of Babel
choices: The Tower of Babel
The Colossus of Rhodes
The walls of Jericho
The wings of Icarus
context: Grokipedia gives the 1927 letter as: 'organic molecules with a molecular weight higher than 5000 do not exist; they would be as unstable as the Tower of Babel.' The line circulates in several English wordings, so that is the sourced version rather than one to reshape. The fight had career teeth: Richard Willstätter, himself a Nobel laureate, is reported to have blocked Staudinger's academic appointments over the disagreement, deepening his isolation in post-war Germany. Carl Freudenberg started out against the hypothesis and later converted. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Debate with the Scientific Establishment.)

question: Charles Goodyear vulcanised rubber with sulfur in 1839; Alexander Parkes patented mouldable Parkesine in 1862; celluloid and rayon were both in the shops well before 1900. Chemists still hand Leo Baekeland's 1907 Bakelite the title of the first true plastic. What sets Bakelite apart from those four materials?
answer: It started from small manufactured chemicals
choices: It started from small manufactured chemicals
It started from a single ingredient, not a blend
It started from a liquid rather than a powder
It started from cheaper materials than the others
context: Vulcanised rubber, Parkesine, celluloid and rayon are all modified natural polymers - rubber and cellulose, treated with sulfur, nitric acid or solvents. Bakelite began from phenol and formaldehyde, two small chemicals made in a works, reacted under heat and pressure into a material with no natural parent at all. Baekeland filed on 13 July 1907 and was granted U.S. Patent 942,699 on 7 December 1909; he had funded the work with money from Velox photographic paper, which he sold to Eastman Kodak in 1899, and he eventually held over 400 Bakelite-related patents. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Polymer', section Historical Development; Grokipedia 'Bakelite', sections Invention, Key Patents.)

question: Hermann Staudinger answered the colloid chemists at the bench rather than in print. If rubber really were a loose clump of small molecules stuck together, then attacking the chemistry that held the clump together should have left nothing but low-weight waxes. So in 1922, with Jakob Fritschi, he chemically modified natural rubber - and the product came out with nearly the same elasticity, solubility and thickness in solution as before, and counting its chain ends put its weight above 100,000. What had the two of them done to the rubber?
answer: Added hydrogen to it, saturating every double bond
choices: Added hydrogen to it, saturating every double bond
Added sulfur to it, the way Goodyear vulcanised tyres
Added chlorine to it, making a rubber chloride
Added nitric acid to it, nitrating the rubber
context: Hydrogenation kills rubber's carbon-carbon double bonds, the very bonds association theory leaned on - yet the 'hydro-rubber' still behaved like rubber and still weighed over 100,000 daltons. Staudinger's other tool was thickness: a solution's intrinsic viscosity rises in step with chain length, and the telling result was that viscosity did not change when he chemically dressed a polymer in new side groups. It dropped only when bonds were actually cut. A clump would have fallen apart; a chain just wore a new coat. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', section Key Experiments and Evidence.)

question: What finally ended the argument came from outside it. At Uppsala, Theodor Svedberg built a machine that could do what no chemist had managed: measure the weight of a single dissolved molecule directly. In 1926 he and Robin Fåhraeus turned it on haemoglobin and got about 67,000 daltons for one uniform molecule - more than thirteen times the ceiling Heinrich Wieland had declared impossible. How did Svedberg's machine weigh a molecule?
answer: It spun the solution until molecules settled out by weight
choices: It spun the solution until molecules settled out by weight
It fired X-rays through the solution and read the pattern
It pushed the solution through a membrane and read the pressure
It burned the solution and weighed the gases given off
context: Svedberg's ultracentrifuge - a 1924 prototype built with H. Rinde reaching about 7,000 g, refined by 1926 to roughly 100,000 g at 42,000 rpm - drove molecules down through the solution at a rate set by their mass, so the sedimentation itself was the measurement. He took the 1926 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. Two other instruments from outside the quarrel pointed the same way: Herman Mark's X-ray work on stretched fibres, and membrane osmometry, which confirmed the high molecular weights independently. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Ultracentrifuge', section Invention and Early Advances; Wikipedia 'Hermann Staudinger'.)

question: Pull a strip of plastic bag slowly and a thin white neck forms, and then refuses to break. Instead of tearing there, the neck travels along the strip until the whole strip is thin. Everywhere else in engineering a thinned spot is the weak spot: a steel bar that necks snaps there within seconds. What makes the thinned plastic stronger than the plastic around it?
answer: Its tangled chains rotate into parallel alignment
choices: Its tangled chains rotate into parallel alignment
Its chains snap and re-form into shorter pieces
The stretching squeezes out trapped air pockets
The friction of stretching anneals the thin spot
context: In a ductile polymer, molecular orientation is a hardening mechanism that dominates at large strains: as the chains line up, the necked material carries more load than the tangled material beside it, so the neck stabilises and travels along the strip instead of tearing through. That is why drawing a fibre makes it strong, and why the effect is easiest to see in polyethylene - the plastic of a grocery bag. (Source: Wikipedia 'Necking (engineering)'.)

question: In 1965 Stephanie Kwolek, hunting a lighter tyre cord at DuPont because the company feared coming petrol shortages, dissolved a newly made polymer and got a solution that was wrong in every way: cloudy, opalescent, and as thin as water, where a spinnable solution should be clear and syrupy. The technician refused to run it through the spinneret, afraid it would clog the machine. Kwolek insisted, Charles Smullen spun it, and the fibre tested about five times as strong as steel for its weight. Why had the solution looked so wrong?
answer: Its stiff rod-like chains had already lined up in the liquid
choices: Its stiff rod-like chains had already lined up in the liquid
Lumps of undissolved polymer were still floating in it
Air beaten in during mixing had filled it with bubbles
The solvent had begun to freeze into very fine crystals
context: Kevlar is poly-para-phenylene terephthalamide: benzene rings joined straight through by amide bonds, which makes each chain a rigid rod instead of a floppy string. Rods in solution stack themselves into parallel domains - a liquid crystal - and that ordering is what scattered the light. The molecules had aligned before spinning, so the fibre came off the spinneret already ordered, over 90% crystalline. At 1.44 g per cubic centimetre against steel's 7.8, it carries the same load for a fifth of the weight, and it has no melting point at all: it decomposes at 427-482 degrees C. Kwolek said she never expected to get the properties she did the first time she spun it. She held 17 U.S. patents, retired in 1986, and in retirement toured schools doing the 'nylon rope trick'. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Stephanie Kwolek'; Grokipedia 'Kevlar'.)

question: In 1927 Hermann Staudinger and Johannes Hengstenberg fired X-rays at crystalline polyoxymethylene to find its unit cell - the small repeating box whose copies, stacked in three directions, build the whole crystal. The box came out tiny: four to six -CH2O- units, no more. Yet viscosity measurements and end-group counting said the chains in that same solid ran well over a hundred units long. What did Staudinger read off that mismatch?
answer: The molecules run on through cell after cell
choices: The molecules run on through cell after cell
The unit cell is a fragment of a far larger one
The crystal holds only the shortest chains present
The viscosity had over-counted the chain length
context: A self-contained clump has to fit inside the box it sits in; a chain does not - it threads through many cells, which is exactly what the X-rays showed. This is the argument at its cleanest: two independent measurements, crystal geometry from diffraction and chain length from viscosity and end-groups, that cannot both be true unless the molecule is longer than its own crystal cell. Staudinger took the 1953 Nobel Prize in Chemistry at 72, thirty-three years after the 1920 paper. He had founded the journal Die Makromolekulare Chemie in 1939 and, in January 1940, the Freiburg Institute for Macromolecular Chemistry, the first institution in Europe devoted only to polymer science; Allied bombing destroyed it on 27 November 1944 and it was rebuilt after the war. (Source: Grokipedia 'Hermann Staudinger', sections Key Experiments and Evidence, Nobel Prize and Vindication.)

question: Wallace Carothers's team at DuPont found that making a long chain is an arithmetic problem before it is a chemical one. Average chain length is 1/(1-p), where p is the fraction of reacting groups that have actually reacted: to average 100 units you need p = 0.99, and to average 1,000 you need 0.999. Nylon 6,6 is condensed from two different monomers - the small units a chain is built from - adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, and one spare molecule of either caps a growing chain and stops it dead, so the two had to be present in exactly equal numbers. How did the chemists guarantee that one-to-one ratio?
answer: They crystallised the two together into a single salt first
choices: They crystallised the two together into a single salt first
They weighed each one out on an analytical balance
They titrated the mixture to neutrality before heating
They distilled the mixture until the ratio came right
context: Weighing is not good enough at 99.9%: a trace of moisture or a slightly impure batch throws the count off, and every stray monomer is a dead end. Crystallising adipic acid with hexamethylenediamine gives 'nylon salt', one compound holding exactly one of each, so the ratio is enforced by chemistry rather than by the balance. Nylon 6,6 was first made on 28 February 1935 and melts at 255-265 degrees C, high enough to survive a hot wash, which the earlier polyester was not. DuPont had recruited Carothers from Harvard in 1928, through Charles M. A. Stine, to do pure research with no products required, in a lab the chemists nicknamed 'Purity Hall'; Carothers hired Paul Flory in 1934 to work out the statistics of chain lengths, and Flory won the 1974 Nobel Prize. Carothers was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1936 and died by suicide on 29 April 1937, aged 41, after years of depression; the two key nylon patents were granted posthumously in 1938. (Sources: Grokipedia 'Wallace Carothers', sections Development of Polyesters, Exploration of Polyamides, Key Patents; Grokipedia 'Nylon', section Key Monomers and Polymerization Reactions.)

question: In 1963, in a cookery class at Magamba Secondary School in Tanzania, a 13-year-old named Erasto Mpemba was making ice-cream. The freezer was filling up, so to save space he put his mix in while it was still HOT -- and his froze BEFORE the classmates' cooled mix. What did his teacher tell him?
answer: That he must have confused himself
choices: That he must have confused himself
That he had discovered a new effect
That he should redo the experiment tomorrow
That he had accidentally spilled another boy's mix
context: Mpemba was ridiculed by his teacher and classmates, and he kept asking anyway. The right lesson from this rung is the shape of the reception a real observation can get from the people around it. Sources: PBS NOVA 'The ice cream that changed physics'; Skeptical Inquirer 'The Rise and Fall of the Mpemba Effect'.

question: When the physicist Denis Osborne of University College Dar es Salaam visited the school, Erasto Mpemba asked him the ice-cream question. Osborne was openly sceptical. Instead of dismissing the boy, what did he actually do?
answer: He went back to his laboratory and tested it
choices: He went back to his laboratory and tested it
He wrote to Nature reporting Mpemba's claim
He asked the school to repeat the observation
He looked up the earlier work of Francis Bacon
context: Osborne's controlled experiments back at the university appeared to confirm something, and in 1969 he and Mpemba jointly published 'Cool?' in Physics Education, with Mpemba credited as first author. Osborne wrote 'no question should be ridiculed'. Aristotle, Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes had all reported something similar in earlier centuries -- and been forgotten. Sources: Chemistry World; Physics Education 4, 172 (1969).

question: Sixty years after Mpemba, physicists still argue about whether hot water reliably freezes faster than cold. In 2016 Henry Burridge and Paul Linden at Cambridge ran the most tightly controlled experiments to date, published in Nature Scientific Reports. What did they find?
answer: No evidence of any reproducible effect at all
choices: No evidence of any reproducible effect at all
Reproducible speed-ups only in salt-water samples
A clear effect once dissolved gases were removed
A larger effect than any earlier study had reported
context: Burridge and Linden defined freezing as cooling to zero degrees Celsius and found no consistent effect; other laboratories continue to report one, and the argument is not settled. Live candidate mechanisms include evaporation reducing the mass, dissolved gases, convection currents, differences in supercooling, and frost layers acting as insulation. This is a MYSTERY-mode rung: the honest answer to what is really going on is still 'no one yet knows'. Try it at home with two ice-cube trays -- if you see nothing, that is a real result. Sources: Nature Scientific Reports 6, 37665 (2016); Quanta Magazine, June 2022.

question: Cosmic rays smashing into the top of the atmosphere spray a rain of one particular particle down onto the ground -- roughly one is passing through every square centimetre of the reader's hand every minute, and their behaviour makes them the everyday classroom proof of Einstein's special relativity. Which particle is this?
answer: the muon
choices: the muon
the neutron
the neutrino
the positron
context: The muon is a heavier sibling of the electron, born about 15 km up. About one passes through every square centimetre of the ground each minute. Neutrinos also arrive but almost never interact; neutrons and positrons do not survive the trip through the atmosphere in anything like these numbers. Source: Wikipedia -- Experimental testing of time dilation; CERN HST 2000.

question: A muon is created about 15 kilometres above the ground and races downward at 99.5% of the speed of light. Its short mean lifetime says it should only travel about 660 metres before decaying into lighter particles. Yet what actually happens to muons over that 15-kilometre plunge?
answer: they arrive at the ground in huge numbers
choices: they arrive at the ground in huge numbers
they all decay long before hitting the ground
they slow down and drift as cosmic dust
they merge with air molecules to form nitrogen
context: About one muon strikes every square centimetre of ground per minute -- a handful are going through the reader's hand every second. The mismatch between 660 metres and 15 kilometres is exactly what makes them a walking experiment in relativity. Source: CERN HST 2000 -- muon calc.

question: Frisch and Smith clocked about 563 muons per hour on top of Mount Washington. Classical physics -- with no relativity at all -- said that only about 27 an hour should still be around when they reached sea level. How many did they actually count in Cambridge, Massachusetts?
answer: about 412 per hour
choices: about 412 per hour
about 30 per hour
essentially zero
about 4000 per hour
context: Frisch and Smith, Am. J. Phys. 31, 342 (1963). Twenty-seven predicted, four hundred and twelve arrived. The muons' internal clocks were running slow -- as measured from the ground -- by a factor of about nine. Source: Wikipedia -- Experimental testing of time dilation.

question: The Mount Washington experiment is the famous version of the muon time-dilation test, but it was not the first. Twenty-three years earlier, two other physicists had already compared muon counts between a high-altitude station and a valley, and found the fast ones outliving the slow ones. Which pair got there first, in 1940?
answer: Bruno Rossi and D. B. Hall, in Colorado
choices: Bruno Rossi and D. B. Hall, in Colorado
Robert Millikan and Carl Anderson, over Pasadena
Enrico Fermi and Emilio Segre, above Rome
Arthur Compton and Robert Oppenheimer, in Chicago
context: Rossi and Hall, 1940, compared Echo Lake, Colorado (3240 m) with Denver (1616 m). It was crude, but the direction of the effect was unmistakable. Frisch and Smith made the sharp quantitative check the textbook remembers. Source: arXiv:physics/0008012 -- Interpretations of time dilation experiments.

question: There is a mind-bender inside the muon story. From the GROUND'S seat, the muon's own clock is running slow, so it lives long enough to cross 15 kilometres. From the MUON'S own seat, though, nothing about its clock has slowed at all -- yet it still reaches the ground. What has changed instead, from the muon's point of view?
answer: the 15 kilometres of atmosphere is squashed to a few hundred metres
choices: the 15 kilometres of atmosphere is squashed to a few hundred metres
gravity is much weaker at that speed and pulls it less
the atmosphere becomes transparent to the muon's mass
the Earth is spinning fast enough to meet the muon halfway
context: Time dilation and length contraction are the same fact seen from two seats. From the ground, muon clocks slow; from the muon, our distances shrink. Neither observer sees both effects at once, but both agree on the final outcome: it arrives. Source: Open Book -- 'Consider the Muon's PoV'.

question: The Nuremberg Code opens with a single sentence -- so plain and so absolute that it has been quoted in every research-ethics document written since. It sets the bedrock of the whole Code. What are the exact opening words of Point 1?
answer: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.
choices: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.
First, do no harm -- above all else, spare the patient injury.
The interests of the subject must prevail over those of science.
Every adult has a right to decide what shall be done with his body.
context: The line is the whole Code in one breath: no matter what the science is worth, the person deciding for their own body has to actually decide, and no one else may decide for them.
