Every research-ethics framework since -- Helsinki, Belmont, the Common Rule -- traces this principle back to Point 1. Source: https://research.unc.edu/human-research-ethics/resources/ccm3_019064/

question: Point 5 of the Nuremberg Code forbids any experiment where death or disabling injury is expected. But the point has one deliberate exception written directly into it -- a hole the judges carved out on purpose. Who does the exception protect?
answer: the researcher who serves as his own test subject
choices: the researcher who serves as his own test subject
the terminally ill patient with no other treatment
the volunteer soldier under military orders
the prisoner offered a reduced sentence
context: The exact wording: 'except, perhaps, in those experiments where the experimental physicians also serve as subjects.' The judges wrote a special hole for the scientist who runs the risk on himself -- the same virtue this bank celebrates in Barry Marshall drinking his H. pylori beaker and the Wright brothers testing their own wing tables. Source: https://research.unc.edu/human-research-ethics/resources/ccm3_019064/

question: The Nuremberg Code was drafted by the tribunal itself, but the medical substance came from two American doctors called as expert witnesses. One of them wrote a memorandum to prosecutor Telford Taylor in April 1947 whose six ethics principles reappeared -- word for word in some cases -- as part of the judges' final ten. Who was that doctor?
answer: Leo Alexander
choices: Leo Alexander
Henry Beecher
Ludwig Guttmann
William Osler
context: Alexander's April 15, 1947 memorandum, 'Ethical and non-ethical experimentation on human beings,' laid out six principles that ended up structurally inside the Code. The other expert witness, physiologist Andrew Ivy of the University of Illinois, was endorsed by the American Medical Association and contributed further principles. Authorship of the Code is genuinely shared between Alexander and Ivy. Source: https://www.pedneur.com/article/S0887-8994(21)00242-3/fulltext

question: In America, the Nuremberg Code was met with something like disdain. The medical historian Jay Katz later summarized the profession's attitude at the time: the Code, American doctors seemed to feel, was written for the sort of people they were not. How did Katz characterize the American view?
answer: 'a code for barbarians and not for civilized' investigators
choices: 'a code for barbarians and not for civilized' investigators
'a set of rules for defeated Germans, not free men'
'the price of victory, to be paid and put away'
'a curious document, drafted by lawyers for lawyers'
context: Katz's phrase is a scholarly characterization -- not a contemporaneous quote from a named physician -- of how American medicine actually behaved. It read the Code as a rule for Nazis, not for itself. The next twenty-five years of American research proved him right. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5719679/

question: The Nuremberg Code came out in August 1947. American medicine kept running research programs that violated its principles for decades afterward. Historians point to one pair above the rest as the sharpest measure of how little the Code changed U.S. medical practice. Which pair?
answer: the Tuskegee study and the Guatemala experiments
choices: the Tuskegee study and the Guatemala experiments
the Willowbrook hepatitis studies and the Fernald oatmeal study
the Human Radiation Experiments and the CIA's MKUltra program
the Holmesburg Prison trials and the Stateville malaria studies
context: The Tuskegee syphilis study ran for 25 more years after the Code was published in 1947. The Guatemala experiments (1946-1948) -- in which U.S. physician John Cutler infected roughly 1,300 Guatemalans through prostitutes and open sores -- were being conducted during the trial itself. The Code was moral force, not law; American medicine treated it as somebody else's problem. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala_syphilis_experiments

question: The Nuremberg Code, for all its moral weight, had one glaring weakness that explains why it was so easily ignored: it was not itself binding on anyone. Its force came only when its principles were rewritten into three later documents that were binding. Which sequence carried the Code into enforceable form?
answer: Helsinki 1964, National Research Act 1974, Belmont Report 1979
choices: Helsinki 1964, National Research Act 1974, Belmont Report 1979
Hippocratic Oath, AMA Code of Ethics, WHO Charter of 1948
Geneva Conventions 1949, UNESCO 1954, ILO covenant 1966
FDA amendments 1962, NIH policy 1966, Common Rule 1991
context: The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) put the Code into medical-society law. The U.S. National Research Act (1974), passed after Tuskegee was exposed, created Institutional Review Boards. The Belmont Report (1979) codified respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as the framework for federally funded human research. The Code alone was moral force; these three made it law. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199711133372006

question: Point 1 of the Nuremberg Code doesn't stop at 'consent.' It requires that the subject's decision be free of 'any ulterior form of constraint,' and it names four specific pressures the subject must be shielded from. What four does the Code list?
answer: force, fraud, deceit, and duress
choices: force, fraud, deceit, and duress
coercion, pressure, threat, and reward
money, family, position, and duty
authority, custom, ignorance, and shame
context: The full clause: 'without the intervention of any element of force, fraud, deceit, duress, over-reaching, or other ulterior form of constraint or coercion.' The four alliterative words are the most-quoted phrase in the whole Code because they map directly onto how consent gets broken in real research settings -- and Point 1 says the duty to prevent all four cannot be delegated. Source: https://research.unc.edu/human-research-ethics/resources/ccm3_019064/

question: Albert Einstein was 26 in 1905, with no laboratory and no university post, when Annalen der Physik received four papers from him in a little over six months. His day job in Bern rated him 'technical expert, third class'. What did that job have him doing?
answer: Examining patent applications for new inventions
choices: Examining patent applications for new inventions
Certifying weights and measures for shopkeepers
Drafting timetables for the federal railways
Testing telegraph gear for the postal service
context: The Swiss Patent Office in Bern. Einstein started there on 23 June 1902 at 3,500 francs a year, ranked 'technical expert, third class' (provisional), and stayed until October 1909. He divided his own day into three parts: 'eight hours work in the Patent Office, eight hours Allotria [fun] connected with scientific work, and eight hours of sleep.' The middle eight hours produced the four papers, which Annalen der Physik received on 18 March, 11 May, 30 June and 27 September 1905. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers; einstein-website.de/en/patent-office/

question: Albert Einstein wrote the 1905 papers at home, in a rented second-floor flat at Kramgasse 49 in Bern. He was not alone in those rooms. Who was living there with him?
answer: His wife Mileva Maric and their baby son Hans Albert
choices: His wife Mileva Maric and their baby son Hans Albert
His mother Pauline and his younger sister Maja
His schoolfriend Marcel Grossmann and Grossmann's wife
Two fellow clerks who rented the rooms with him
context: Einstein, Mileva Maric and their son Hans Albert lived at Kramgasse 49 from 1903 to 1905 — so the four papers were written in a second-floor flat with a baby in it, not in any laboratory. The flat is now the Einstein House museum: you can walk in and stand in the room. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_House

question: Albert Einstein's Nobel Prize citation, for the prize of 1921, never names relativity. Committee member Carl Wilhelm Oseen had engineered the wording so the Academy could honour the most famous physicist alive without endorsing a theory many of its members still doubted. Which of his results did the citation name instead?
answer: His work on the photoelectric effect
choices: His work on the photoelectric effect
His work on the dimensions of molecules
His work on the motion of suspended particles
His work on the specific heats of solids
context: The citation in full: 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.' Relativity is not named anywhere in it — Einstein never won a Nobel Prize for relativity, special or general. The prize was late as well: no physics prize was awarded for 1921 at all, and in September 1922 the Academy voted to hand Einstein the held-over 1921 prize and Niels Bohr the 1922 one. Einstein missed the ceremony on 10 December 1922; he was travelling in Japan, and the German minister Rudolf Nadolny read his speech at the Stockholm banquet. When he finally gave his Nobel lecture, at Gothenburg on 11 July 1923, he titled it 'Fundamental Ideas and Problems of the Theory of Relativity' — and lectured on the theory the prize had refused to name. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics; arxiv.org/abs/2112.13519; nobelprize.org

question: Robert Brown, a Scottish botanist, watched specks shaken out of pollen grains under his microscope in 1827. In water left to settle they jerked and wandered and never once stopped, and for nearly eighty years nobody could say why. Einstein's May 1905 paper named the culprit. What was shoving the specks about?
answer: Water molecules, battering them from every side
choices: Water molecules, battering them from every side
Faint currents from uneven warmth in the water
Electric charge gathering on the glass slide
A trace of life left in the pollen grains
context: Classical hydrodynamics said a particle in a fluid at rest should sit still, so Brown's endless jitter had been an embarrassment for nearly eighty years. Einstein's answer: a speck small enough gets struck unevenly by the molecules of the liquid from one moment to the next, and staggers under the imbalance. Anyone with a microscope can watch the same motion today. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Four of Albert Einstein's 1905 papers went to the journal Annalen der Physik. A fifth piece of work went that same year to the University of Zurich instead. What did he send Zurich?
answer: His doctoral dissertation, on the size of molecules
choices: His doctoral dissertation, on the size of molecules
His application for a lecturing post in physics
A textbook on electrodynamics for schoolteachers
A review of Hendrik Lorentz's work, at Planck's request
context: 'A New Determination of Molecular Dimensions', approved by Zurich in July 1905. Einstein had no doctorate at all when the first papers went out: the March and May papers were posted by a man nobody could yet call 'Doctor', who had no professorship either. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: In December 1901 Albert Einstein, still months away from his patent office job, put a small advertisement in a Bern newspaper: private lessons in mathematics and physics, three francs an hour. Maurice Solovine, a Romanian philosophy student, answered it and came round. The first lesson ran nearly two hours. What happened to the three francs an hour?
answer: No money changed hands, and the lesson became an argument
choices: No money changed hands, and the lesson became an argument
Solovine paid the first hour, then never paid again
Solovine paid in books, which Einstein read and returned
Einstein raised the fee once the lessons ran long
context: No fee was ever paid: the two argued instead, and the lesson turned into a friendship that outlasted the papers. Solovine, Einstein and Conrad Habicht turned those arguments into a three-man club they named the Akademie Olympia, mocking the real academies that had no place for them; Einstein's joke title for himself was 'Albert Ritter von Steissbein' — Albert, Knight of the Tailbone. Over cheap suppers and three- and four-hour arguments they read Hume's Treatise of Human Nature, Spinoza's Ethics, Mill's System of Logic, Poincare's Science and Hypothesis, Karl Pearson's Grammar of Science, Ernst Mach's Science of Mechanics — and Cervantes' Don Quixote. Mach's attack on absolute space runs straight into the June 1905 relativity paper. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Olympia_Academy

question: When Albert Einstein published on the jiggling of suspended particles in 1905, two of the most respected scientists in Europe still refused to grant that atoms were real: one dismissed them as unnecessary hypotheses about things nobody can observe, the other insisted everything was really transformations of energy, with no invisible particles needed. Who were the two holdouts?
answer: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald
choices: Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald
Hendrik Lorentz and Henri Poincare
Max Planck and Paul Drude
Ludwig Boltzmann and Jean Perrin
context: Mach the positivist would not admit unobservable things into physics at all; Ostwald the 'energeticist' wanted a physics of energy transformations with no particles in it. Neither man was a crank — they were two of the leading minds of the age, and whether atoms existed was still a live argument in 1905. Jean Perrin's patient measurements of suspended particles in 1908-09 matched Einstein's prediction and ended the argument; Perrin took the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for that work. Consensus did not settle this one. A measurement did. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Michele Besso, a Swiss-Italian mechanical engineer, is the only person Albert Einstein thanks in his June 1905 relativity paper. The two ate lunch together at the Bern patent office and argued physics on the walk home. Einstein had urged the director to take Besso on, and the office hired him in January 1904. What position did it give him?
answer: A rank above Einstein himself
choices: A rank above Einstein himself
A rank below Einstein himself
A post in a different section
A temporary post with no rank
context: The office took Besso on as technical expert, SECOND class — one rank above the man who had recommended him — and he stayed above Einstein for more than two years: Einstein was still third class until his promotion on 1 April 1906. The paper's entire acknowledgement is its last sentence: 'In conclusion I wish to say that in working at the problem here dealt with I have had the loyal assistance of my friend and colleague M. Besso, and that I am indebted to him for several valuable suggestions.' Einstein later told his biographer Carl Seelig: 'I could not have found a better sounding-board in the whole of Europe.' The paper itself has no bibliography and cites no publication whatsoever; only five other scientists are named anywhere in it — Newton, Maxwell, Hertz, Doppler and Lorentz. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Michele_Besso; einstein-website.de/en/patent-office/; fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/specrel/www/

question: The last of Albert Einstein's four 1905 papers runs three pages, about 1,500 words, the shortest of them by far. Its title does not announce a result. It asks a question. Which question?
answer: Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?
choices: Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?
Is the Speed of Light the Same for Every Observer?
Can the Motion of the Molecules in a Liquid Be Counted?
Does Light Travel as Waves or as Separate Grains?
context: 'Ist die Tragheit eines Korpers von seinem Energieinhalt abhangig?', received by Annalen der Physik on 27 September 1905 — three pages, volume 18, pages 639-641. Inertia is a body's resistance to being shoved: how hard you have to push to change its motion, which is what we usually call its mass. For contrast, the June relativity paper ran 31 pages. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annus_mirabilis_papers; grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Arguing that atoms exist persuades nobody who has decided they are a convenient fiction. Albert Einstein's May 1905 paper did something better: it gave a formula tying how far a suspended speck wanders in a given time to the temperature, the thickness of the liquid and the size of the speck. Anyone with a microscope, a thermometer and patience could now measure a quantity that had only ever been guessed at. Which one?
answer: Avogadro's number, the count of molecules in a mole
choices: Avogadro's number, the count of molecules in a mole
The mean free path, a molecule's flight between hits
Molecular diameter, the width of one water molecule
Atomic mass, the weight of a single hydrogen atom
context: Einstein predicted the mean square displacement <x^2> = 2Dt, with D = kT / (6 pi eta r): temperature T, the fluid's viscosity eta, the particle's radius r. Track a speck's wandering under a microscope, measure the fluid's thickness, and the number of molecules in a mole falls out — without anybody ever seeing an atom. (A mole is just a chemist's counting unit: a fixed number of molecules, the way a dozen is a fixed number of eggs.) Jean Perrin did exactly this in 1908-09 and got about 6.0 x 10^23; his 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics was for confirming the patent clerk's arithmetic. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Albert Einstein's fourth 1905 paper runs three pages, and in it he first ties a body's mass to its energy content. The English translation is online, so anyone can open the paper and find the relation on the page. Which letters does he use there for energy and for the speed of light?
answer: L for energy and V for the speed of light
choices: L for energy and V for the speed of light
E for energy and c for the speed of light
L for energy and c for the speed of light
E for energy and V for the speed of light
context: Einstein's own words in the paper: 'The mass of a body is a measure of its energy-content; if the energy changes by L, the mass changes in the same sense by L / 9 x 10^20, the energy being measured in ergs, and the mass in grammes.' No E, no m, no c anywhere. That 9 x 10^20 is the speed of light in centimetres per second, squared. The famous shorthand came later — so when a book says the 1905 paper 'derived E = mc^2', that is a modernizing gloss, not what is on the page. Check it yourself: the English translation is online. Source: fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/E_mc2/www/

question: Albert Einstein's mass-and-energy paper of September 1905 does not end in triumph. Its final sentence hands the idea to the experimenters: it is 'not impossible', he writes, that the theory 'may be successfully put to the test', using bodies whose energy content varies to a high degree. What did he tell them to try it on?
answer: Salts of radium
choices: Salts of radium
Ores of uranium
Foils of polonium
Crystals of thorium
context: The closing line in full: 'It is not impossible that with bodies whose energy-content is variable to a high degree (e.g. with radium salts) the theory may be successfully put to the test.' Einstein had no laboratory of his own; what he could do was state exactly what a test would look like and hand it to the people who did. That is the shape of the whole paper — a question for a title, three pages of argument, and a proposed experiment for a last line. Source (English translation): fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/E_mc2/www/

question: In June 1905 Albert Einstein, a 26-year-old patent examiner with no university post, mailed a paper rewriting space and time to Annalen der Physik, the leading physics journal in Germany. Which physicist there passed 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies' for printing?
answer: Max Planck
choices: Max Planck
Wilhelm Wien
Philipp Lenard
Arnold Sommerfeld
context: Annalen der Physik had no formal peer review in 1905. Its editors, Max Planck and Paul Drude, simply read what came in and decided. Nobody refereed special relativity; Planck read it and printed it. Worth sitting with: the most heavily tested theory in physics entered the world through no review process at all, and has been checked ever since by everyone who could get at it. Peer review is a filter, not a truth-detector — the test is what settles things. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Annus_mirabilis_papers

question: Albert Einstein wrote to his friend Conrad Habicht in May 1905, opening the letter 'you frozen whale, you smoked, dried, canned piece of soul'. He promised four papers and rated them: exactly one he called 'very revolutionary', the other three he described flatly. Which of the four did he call revolutionary?
answer: The one on radiation and the energy properties of light
choices: The one on radiation and the energy properties of light
The one on the electrodynamics of moving bodies
The one on particles suspended in a still liquid
The one on the inertia of a body and its energy content
context: Einstein's own ranking: 'The first deals with radiation and the energy properties of light and is very revolutionary.' Relativity he described flatly, as 'an electrodynamics of moving bodies which employs a modification of the theory of space and time.' History remembers relativity; Einstein in May 1905 thought the light-quantum paper was the dangerous one — and he was right about how it would land. It was dismissed for years as incompatible with the wave theory of light and cited almost not at all until the 1910s. The Nobel citation, when it finally came, named the photoelectric effect. Sources: Isaacson, 'Einstein: His Life and Universe', ch.6; ecologicallyoriented.wordpress.com/2014/05/24/einstein-to-habicht-1905/

question: In 1848 an English collector near Manchester netted the first recorded coal-black specimen of a common speckled-grey moth. Half a century later almost the whole local population was black. Who was that first collector, whose name is fixed to the specimen?
answer: R. S. Edleston
choices: R. S. Edleston
Alfred Russel Wallace
Henry Walter Bates
E. B. Ford
context: R. S. Edleston caught the first live carbonaria peppered moth near Manchester in 1848 and reported it in 1864, by which time it was already the commoner form in his garden. Before industrialisation the black form was roughly 0.01% of the population. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: The pale, lichen-speckled form of the peppered moth vanished from Manchester in fifty years because two things were killing the camouflage: coal soot was blackening tree bark, and one particular pollutant was killing the pale lichens on that bark. Which pollutant?
answer: sulphur dioxide
choices: sulphur dioxide
carbon monoxide
methane
nitrous oxide
context: Sulphur dioxide, a major coal-smoke pollutant, killed the crustose lichens that gave clean bark its pale mottled look; combined with soot deposition on the bark, this destroyed the camouflage of the pale (typica) form and unmasked it to hunting birds. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: In the 1950s a British lepidopterist wanted to prove that birds were doing the killing. He marked, released and re-caught peppered moths in two woods with opposite bark colours: sooty Birmingham and unpolluted Dorset. The survival advantage flipped between the two woods, exactly as camouflage predicted. Who ran the experiment?
answer: Bernard Kettlewell
choices: Bernard Kettlewell
E. B. Ford
Cyril Clarke
Philip Sheppard
context: Bernard Kettlewell's 1953-1956 mark-release-recapture work found birds took about 75% of light moths in polluted Birmingham and about 86% of dark moths in unpolluted Dorset. The mirrored result made bird predation the leading explanation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: In 1924 a British geneticist did the arithmetic on Manchester's peppered moths. He showed that going from about 2% black in 1848 to about 95% black in 1895 could not be luck: the dark form must have carried roughly 50% greater fitness than the pale form. Who did the calculation?
answer: J. B. S. Haldane
choices: J. B. S. Haldane
R. A. Fisher
Sewall Wright
Julian Huxley
context: Haldane's 1924 paper on the mathematics of selection used the peppered moth as a worked example, ruling out genetic drift and pinning a large selective advantage on the dark form long before Kettlewell went into the woods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: In 2002 a popular book called Of Moths and Men, by the journalist Judith Hooper, pushed real methodological criticisms of Bernard Kettlewell's peppered-moth work into a much stronger charge. Textbooks wobbled and creationists cheered. When biologists actually examined the accusation, what did they conclude?
answer: that the fraud charge was without merit
choices: that the fraud charge was without merit
that the raw data had been destroyed
that Kettlewell had confessed
that the Royal Society had already retracted him
context: Scientists including Michael Majerus and Bruce Grant went back through the record and rejected the fraud accusation while agreeing that the underlying methodological criticisms about release-in-daylight and placement on trunks were legitimate and worth answering with better experiments. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: A British geneticist answered the public accusation against Kettlewell by refusing to argue at all. Instead he spent seven summers, from 2001 to 2007, releasing nearly five thousand moths onto natural resting positions in his own garden and personally watching birds take them. He died before he could publish; colleagues brought the paper out in 2012. Who was he?
answer: Michael Majerus
choices: Michael Majerus
Laurence Cook
Paul Brakefield
James Mallet
context: Majerus (1954-2009) ran the largest predation experiment ever attempted on the species and confirmed that nine bird species differentially took the more-visible form. His colleagues analysed the data and published in Biology Letters in February 2012, closing the case. Source: https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsbl/article/8/4/609/49215

question: In 1956 the British Parliament passed the Clean Air Act after the Great Smog of London. Over the following decades moth surveyors watched a large-scale experiment run in reverse: at surveyed sites the black form fell from over 90% back toward under 5%. In 2003 the definitive long-term survey of that decline appeared. Who published it?
answer: Laurence Cook
choices: Laurence Cook
Bernard Kettlewell
Bruce Grant
Cyril Clarke
context: As soot cleared and lichens regrew, pale bark returned and pale moths regained their camouflage. Kettlewell reported the early turn in 1956, Bruce Grant tracked the decline in 1996, and Laurence Cook of the University of Manchester published the definitive long-term survey in 2003. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peppered_moth_evolution

question: In 2016 a team led by Ilik Saccheri traced what makes a peppered moth black down to a specific piece of DNA: a roughly 22,000-base sequence sitting inside the first intron of a wing-patterning gene, statistically dated to around 1819 -- one moth generation before R. S. Edleston's 1848 catch. Which wing-patterning gene did the insertion land in?
answer: cortex
choices: cortex
doublesex
optix
engrailed
context: The carbonaria allele is a large class-II DNA transposon inserted into the first intron of cortex, a gene that regulates wing scale development across butterflies and moths. The estimated 1819 origin sits about one moth generation before R. S. Edleston's 1848 specimen, so the variant was already in the population, at low frequency, when the soot arrived. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17951

question: A modern smartphone is a slab you hold in one hand. Yet by rough count, what share of the periodic table's stable elements are physically present, in trace amounts or more, inside it?
answer: About two thirds of the stable elements
choices: About one in twenty of the stable elements
About one in ten of the stable elements
About one third of the stable elements
About two thirds of the stable elements
context: Element-audits of modern smartphones (Compound Interest 2014; various teardowns) put the tally at roughly sixty elements, close to two-thirds of the ~80 stable elements on the periodic table. Every one of those elements is doing a specific engineering job that no cheaper element would do as well. Source: https://www.compoundchem.com/2014/02/19/the-chemical-elements-of-a-smartphone/

question: The face of a phone is a sheet of glass you can also tap on. For the screen to sense your finger, a signal has to travel across the whole face without you ever seeing the wiring - and it has to do it cheaply enough to put on billions of phones. Which conductor is coated as an invisible film across the glass to make that work?
answer: A layer of indium tin oxide
choices: A film of aluminium sputtered onto the glass
A grid of very fine copper wires
A layer of indium tin oxide
A coating of graphite ink
context: Indium tin oxide (ITO), roughly 90 percent In2O3 and 10 percent SnO2 by weight, is one of very few materials that conducts electricity while staying optically clear, which is why almost every touchscreen uses it. Copper and silver conduct better but are opaque, so a copper screen would be a mirror; aluminium films are used elsewhere in phones but block light too. Indium is a soft, silvery metal recovered mostly as a by-product of refining zinc. Source: https://www.chemistryworld.com/podcasts/indium-tin-oxide-ito/3008984.article

question: Two of the loudest, tiniest jobs in a phone are the earpiece speaker and the vibration motor. Both have to move air, or move mass, using a magnet only a few millimetres across, so the magnet has to be exceptionally strong for its size. Which family of permanent magnets does that job?
answer: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets
choices: Ceramic ferrite magnets
Neodymium-iron-boron magnets
Samarium-cobalt magnets
Ordinary steel bar magnets
context: NdFeB magnets are the strongest permanent magnets known, which is why a phone can be a few millimetres thick and still move enough air to be heard. Samarium-cobalt magnets are a real alternative, but weaker and much pricier; ferrite and steel magnets do not come close. Source: https://www.stanfordmagnets.com/use-of-ndfeb-magnets-in-mobile-phones.html

question: A permanent magnet loses strength as it warms up, and a phone in your pocket during a game can get uncomfortably hot. Manufacturers add a small amount of a heavy rare-earth element to the neodymium-iron-boron mixture specifically to keep the magnet from weakening in the heat. Which element does that heat-hardening job?
answer: Dysprosium
choices: Dysprosium
Holmium
Erbium
Thulium
context: Dysprosium (and, secondarily, terbium) is added to NdFeB magnets to raise the temperature at which the magnet gives up its field, which lets speakers and motors survive above 200 degrees Celsius during manufacture and shrug off ordinary use. Holmium, erbium and thulium are all heavy lanthanides sitting next to dysprosium on the periodic table, but none of them does the phone-magnet job. Dysprosium is one of the priciest and most supply-constrained elements in the phone. Source: https://www.arnoldmagnetics.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Important-Role-of-Dysprosium-in-Modern-Permanent-Magnets-150906.pdf

question: The bright reds in a phone display are surprisingly hard to get. Ordinary paints and dyes emit a smear of wavelengths, which looks muddy on a small screen. Screens instead sit a special phosphor in front of a white or blue backlight so it re-emits a pure, narrow-band red near 611 nanometres. Which element's ions do that red job?
answer: Europium
choices: Terbium
Cerium
Europium
Gadolinium
context: Europium(III) doped into an yttrium-oxide or related host emits a sharp red line near 611 nm - it is the reason on-screen reds look like reds and not orangey mud. Terbium(III) does the analogous green job near 545 nm. These narrow lines are a quantum-mechanical trick of the rare-earth f-electrons. Source: https://www.snexplores.org/article/rare-earth-elements-electrons-properties-technology

question: A phone's main board is dotted with small components that store electrical charge for a moment and hand it back on demand. Space is the constraint - hundreds of them need to fit. One family of capacitor packs a huge amount of charge into a tiny volume by growing an extremely thin oxide layer (as little as 20 nanometres) on a metal powder. Which metal's oxide is used?
answer: Tantalum, in a tantalum-pentoxide capacitor
choices: Aluminium, in an aluminium electrolytic capacitor
Titanium, in a titanate ceramic capacitor
Silicon, in a thin-film silicon-oxide capacitor
Tantalum, in a tantalum-pentoxide capacitor
context: Tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5) grown on tantalum powder makes a dielectric only 20-400 nm thick, which is why a tantalum capacitor stores more charge per unit volume than the alternatives. Aluminium electrolytics can store more charge per dollar but need a much larger case, so they lose the space race inside a phone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalum_capacitor

question: Silicon is a superb material for computing, but it is a poor light emitter and mediocre at the very high frequencies a modern phone uses to talk to a cell tower. The element that fills those two gaps - in the phone's LEDs and its radio-frequency chips - was famously predicted in 1871 by Dmitri Mendeleev, who called it eka-aluminium and gave its density and melting point before anyone had seen the metal. Which element is it?
answer: Gallium
choices: Germanium
Gallium
Scandium
Indium
context: Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated gallium from a zinc ore in 1875 and its properties matched Mendeleev's 1871 eka-aluminium prediction almost exactly - the first triumph of the periodic table as a predictive tool. Today gallium arsenide handles the Wi-Fi and cellular radio-frequency chips, and gallium nitride the blue LEDs. Germanium was Mendeleev's eka-silicon (found 1886) and scandium his eka-boron (found 1879). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendeleev%27s_predicted_elements

question: Point a small telescope at Venus for a few months and it runs through the same shape-cycle as the Moon: thin crescent, half, fat gibbous, almost full, and back to crescent. Roughly how long does one complete cycle take?
answer: about 584 days
choices: about 584 days
about 88 days
about 29 days
about 4 years
context: The 584-day synodic period is Venus's Earth-observed cycle from new phase back to new phase; 88 days is Mercury's year around the Sun, 29 days is the Moon's own phase cycle, and 4 years is nothing in particular. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phases_of_Venus

question: Venus does not just change shape - it also swells and shrinks enormously through the telescope. Near full it is a small bright dot about 10 arcseconds across, and at its widest and closest to Earth it swells to about 65 arcseconds, roughly six times wider. Which phase of Venus therefore shines brightest in our night sky?
answer: the thin crescent
choices: the thin crescent
the fat gibbous
the exact half
the almost-full disc
context: The near-Earth Venus is a thin crescent - between us and the Sun, catching sunlight only along a sliver of its edge - yet its sheer apparent size wins. The near-full disc is on the far side of the Sun and much dimmer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phases_of_Venus

question: In Ptolemy's arrangement Venus was carried on an epicycle whose centre stayed fixed on a line between the Earth and the Sun - Venus was always jammed between us and the Sun. Through a telescope, what shapes could such a Ptolemaic Venus ever show?
answer: only crescent phases
choices: only crescent phases
only gibbous and full phases
an exact half, always
any phase, just like the Moon
context: Venus's lit face always points toward the Sun. In Ptolemy's system Venus sits between us and the Sun, so we see mostly its unlit night side with a thin lit edge - always a crescent. Galileo saw a fat gibbous Venus through his telescope, and a gibbous Venus is fatal to that geometry. Source: thonyc.wordpress.com/2014/06/09/the-phases-of-venus-and-heliocentricity-a-rough-guide

question: To stake priority before he was ready to publish, Galileo mailed Johannes Kepler a jumbled string of letters: 'Haec immatura a me iam frustra leguntur o y'. Unscrambled it read 'Cynthiae figuras aemulatur Mater Amorum' - 'the Mother of Love copies the shapes of Cynthia'. The 'Mother of Love' was Venus in Roman poetry. What was Cynthia?
answer: the Moon
choices: the Moon
the Sun
Mercury
Sirius
context: Cynthia was a poetic name for Diana, the Roman moon goddess, so the unscrambled boast reads: 'Venus copies the phases of the Moon.' The anagram let Galileo timestamp the discovery without giving it away, in case a rival beat him to publication. Source: eaae-astronomy.org/images/workshops/galileoandthephasesofvenus.pdf

question: Galileo formally announced the phases of Venus in a letter of 30 December 1610 to a mathematician in Rome. The recipient's identity mattered: he was in his seventies, had co-designed the Gregorian calendar, and was the most respected astronomer in the Catholic world. His Jesuit colleagues would soon confirm the phases with their own telescopes. Who was he?
answer: Christoph Clavius
choices: Christoph Clavius
Johannes Kepler
Simon Marius
Christoph Scheiner
context: Clavius, chief mathematician of the Collegio Romano, was the astronomer whose endorsement could shield or sink a claim inside the Church. Kepler was in Prague; Marius was a rival telescopic astronomer in Germany; Scheiner was another Jesuit who later clashed with Galileo over sunspots. Source: thonyc.wordpress.com/2014/06/09/the-phases-of-venus-and-heliocentricity-a-rough-guide

question: Popular retellings often say the phases of Venus proved that the Earth orbits the Sun. That is too strong. Tycho Brahe had proposed a compromise cosmos in which the Earth stayed fixed at the centre, the Sun circled the Earth, and all the OTHER planets circled the Sun. Through Galileo's telescope, what would a Tychonic Venus have looked like?
answer: exactly the same phase cycle as the Copernican Venus
choices: exactly the same phase cycle as the Copernican Venus
only crescent phases, exactly as Ptolemy had it
no phases at all - a steady bright disc all year
phases running backwards, gibbous shrinking to crescent
context: In both the Copernican and the Tychonic systems Venus orbits the Sun, so from Earth its lit face sweeps through the same cycle either way. The phases killed Ptolemy and left Tycho's compromise standing for another century - until Newton's gravity and Bradley's stellar aberration finally closed the case for a moving Earth. Source: thonyc.wordpress.com/2014/06/09/the-phases-of-venus-and-heliocentricity-a-rough-guide

question: You can check the geometry yourself without any telescope. Venus is only ever seen close to sunrise or sunset, as the 'morning star' or the 'evening star' - never high overhead at midnight. That is because Venus never wanders more than a specific maximum angle away from the Sun in our sky. What is that maximum angle, roughly?
answer: about 47 degrees
choices: about 47 degrees
about 28 degrees
about 65 degrees
about 80 degrees
context: Venus's orbit sits inside Earth's, so from our viewpoint it can never appear far from the Sun; its greatest elongation is about 47 degrees. Mercury, closer to the Sun still, is limited to about 28 degrees - which is why it is even harder to spot. The 47-degree cap is itself the observation that pins Venus's orbit inside Earth's. Source: earthsky.org/astronomy-essentials/greatest-elongation-definition-venus-mercury/

question: On 27 May 1931 a Swiss physicist and his assistant lifted off from Augsburg under a hydrogen balloon and climbed higher than any humans ever had -- the first people to enter the stratosphere. Who rode the gondola up to 15,781 m?
answer: Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer
choices: Auguste Piccard and Paul Kipfer
Wiley Post and Harold Gatty
Charles Lindbergh and Anne Morrow
Otto Lilienthal and Gustave Whitehead
context: First manned flight into the stratosphere. Post and Gatty had just circled the globe the same summer; Lindbergh flew the Atlantic in 1927; Lilienthal was a 19th-century glider pioneer. Sources: history.com/articles/auguste-piccard-balloon-stratosphere; balloon.hu/new/2015/05/27.

question: The 1931 stratosphere flight faced a killer no balloonist had solved: outside pressure fell below a tenth of sea-level, and a person exposed to it would black out and die. Auguste Piccard's answer -- the invention that made the flight possible, and that you now sit inside every time you fly -- was what?
answer: a spherical pressurized aluminium capsule
choices: a spherical pressurized aluminium capsule
a rubber suit fed by an air pump
a heated oxygen tent over the basket
bottled-oxygen masks for the crew
context: Piccard's gondola held sea-level pressure inside while outside pressure fell away -- the direct ancestor of every airliner cabin. Source: amusingplanet.com/2022/06/auguste-piccard-man-who-flew-to.html.

question: After the stratosphere flight, Auguste Piccard turned his own idea upside down. A balloon, he said, is really a heavy cabin hung under a light fluid rising through a heavier one -- so invert it and you get a heavy steel cabin hung under a tank of a lighter-than-water liquid sinking through the sea. He built the first one and it launched a whole class of deep-sea craft. What is that class called?
answer: bathyscaphes
choices: bathyscaphes
bathyspheres
submarines
diving bells
context: Bathyscaphe is Piccard's own coinage from Greek bathys (deep) + skaphos (ship). The bathysphere was Beebe and Barton's earlier cable-lowered ball; a submarine is powered horizontal; a diving bell is open at the bottom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathyscaphe.

question: On Trieste's descent to Challenger Deep, at about 9,000 m, something on the craft failed with a bang that shook the entire vessel. Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh talked it over inside the pressure sphere and pushed on to the bottom anyway. What had actually broken?
answer: an outer Plexiglas pane on the entry tunnel
choices: an outer Plexiglas pane on the entry tunnel
the main viewport of the crew sphere
an electromagnet on the ballast hopper
the acoustic telephone to the surface ship
context: Their steel crew sphere was intact; the crack was on the flooded entry trunk they had climbed down through, so they were never in the same water as the crack. Source: sea-technology.com/60th-anniversary-of-deepest-ocean-dive.

question: Piccard and Walsh reported seeing a flatfish on the bottom of Challenger Deep -- a claim biologists still doubt. Paul Yancey and colleagues (PNAS 2014) argue that bony fish hit a physiological ceiling near 8,200 m, because ONE small molecule that keeps their proteins from being crushed can only be packed so densely into their cells. Which molecule?
answer: TMAO
choices: TMAO
myoglobin
haemoglobin
chlorophyll
context: TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) stabilises folded proteins against pressure; fish need more of it the deeper they go, and near 8,200 m their cells would become isosmotic with seawater, past which they cannot easily go. What Piccard and Walsh actually saw remains argued about. Source: pnas.org/doi/pdf/10.1073/pnas.1322003111.

question: Trieste reached the bottom of Challenger Deep in 1960 -- and then, remarkably, the deepest place on Earth was left completely alone by crewed craft. How long was the gap before a human being went back down to it?
answer: 52 years, until 2012
choices: 52 years, until 2012
12 years, until 1972
24 years, until 1984
38 years, until 1998
context: James Cameron dived Deepsea Challenger solo on 26 March 2012; Victor Vescovo's Limiting Factor (2019) was the first submersible built to make the trip REPEATABLE. A record is not a capability. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/613583.

question: Every crewed deep-sea submersible ever built -- Trieste, Alvin, Deepsea Challenger, Limiting Factor -- puts its people inside a sphere. It is not tradition; the sphere is the ONE shape that answers uniform outside pressure with a single kind of internal stress that steel and titanium handle well. What single kind of stress?
answer: pure compression
choices: pure compression
pure tension
torsion
shear
context: Any other shape develops bending stresses under uniform pressure, and bending is the failure mode both metals lose to first. A sphere loads the wall in compression alone. Source: engineering.org.cn/sscae/EN/10.15302/J-SSCAE-2019.06.018.

question: Placebo researchers have measured a strange dose-response: the fake works better the more it looks like a real treatment. Two dummy pills relieve pain better than one, and a capsule beats a tablet of the same fake. Which fake beats them all?
answer: An injection of salt water
choices: A pill that has been coloured bright red
A pill labelled with the name of an expensive brand
An injection of salt water
A drop of sugar water on the tongue
context: Placebo strength scales with the impressiveness of the ritual: injections outperform capsules, capsules outperform tablets, two dummy pills outperform one, and larger pills outperform smaller ones. Nothing at all, dressed up more, works more. Source: https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/306437

question: You give a hundred people with sore knees a new drug and eighty of them say the knee feels better. That number by itself does not prove the drug works, and everyone who runs trials knows why. What is the missing comparison?
answer: How many would have felt better without the drug
choices: How many kept taking their other medicines
How many would have felt better without the drug
How many knew they were getting the new drug
How many were on their worst day when tested
context: Because most people improve on their own -- illnesses come and go, and bad days are followed by better ones -- the honest question is never 'did the patients get better?' but 'did they get better than the ones who got the fake?'. That is why control arms exist. The other three choices are also real trial-design worries (co-intervention, blinding, regression to the mean) but only the control arm answers the missing comparison. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM200105243442106

question: In 1959 the Seattle cardiologist Leonard Cobb tested a popular chest operation for the crushing pain of angina, in which a surgeon tied off an artery running behind the breastbone. He compared the real operation to a sham in which he only cut the skin. What did the sham do?
answer: It relieved angina about as well as the real surgery
choices: It did nothing, and confirmed that the real surgery worked
It relieved angina about as well as the real surgery
It caused more chest pain than doing nothing at all
It caused fatal complications and ended the trial early
context: Cobb's 1959 paper 'An Evaluation of Internal-Mammary-Artery Ligation by a Double-Blind Technic' in the New England Journal of Medicine compared the real ligation of the internal mammary artery to a sham in which only the skin was cut. The two arms did equally well; the operation, then widely used, was abandoned. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM195905282602204

question: It happened again in living memory. In the New England Journal of Medicine in July 2002, the Houston surgeon Bruce Moseley published a trial of arthroscopic knee surgery for osteoarthritis, in which one arm of patients were wheeled in, given anaesthesia, and awoke with real incisions but nothing done inside. How did that placebo arm do?
answer: About the same as the real surgery
choices: Much worse than the real surgery
Slightly worse than the real surgery
Slightly better than the real surgery
About the same as the real surgery
context: Moseley's 11 July 2002 NEJM trial randomized patients with knee osteoarthritis to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or sham surgery (skin incisions only). At no point did either real-surgery arm report less pain or better function than the placebo arm. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259

question: In 2001 Asbjorn Hrobjartsson and Peter Gotzsche published a big NEJM review of trials that compared placebo to no treatment at all. Where did placebos reliably move the needle?
answer: On subjective reports, above all pain
choices: On subjective reports, above all pain
On measurable disease
On both, in equal measure
On almost nothing at all
context: Hrobjartsson and Gotzsche 2001, 'Is the Placebo Powerless?' in NEJM, reviewed trials with a no-treatment arm and found placebos reliably moved subjective outcomes (especially pain) but did not meaningfully change objective disease measures. Placebos mostly change how you feel, not what the disease is doing. Source: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM200105243442106

question: Henry Beecher's 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo' fixed a headline number in the medical imagination -- 'about a third of patients respond to placebo' -- that gets quoted to this day. When Kienle and Kiene reanalysed Beecher's fifteen trials in 1997, what did they find really explained most of that response?
answer: Patients simply getting better on their own
choices: Deliberate cheating by the original researchers
Publication bias in which studies made it into print
Patients simply getting better on their own
The colour of the placebo tablets used at the time
context: Kienle and Kiene's 1997 reanalysis of Beecher's fifteen trials in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology found no evidence of a real placebo effect in the underlying data. Most of the improvement Beecher had counted as placebo response was just the natural course of illness -- people getting better anyway. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9449934/

question: In a 2010 PLOS ONE trial run by Ted Kaptchuk at Harvard, patients with irritable bowel syndrome were handed pills in a bottle labelled 'placebo' and told openly that the pills were inert. Small trial, subjective outcomes, three weeks. What did that open placebo arm do?
answer: Significantly better than no-treatment controls
choices: Significantly better than no-treatment controls
About the same as no-treatment controls
Significantly worse than no-treatment controls
The same as a fully-blinded placebo arm
context: Kaptchuk et al., PLOS ONE 2010: 80 IBS patients, three-week trial, one arm given pills openly labelled as inert sugar pills, one arm given no treatment with matched provider interactions. The open-label placebo arm improved significantly more. Caveat: small study, subjective outcomes, short follow-up. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0015591

question: On 19 September 2019, months before anyone had heard of COVID-19, the World Health Organization published a free PDF -- still downloadable now -- that a parent can open at a kitchen table. The 88-page document was on:
answer: non-pharmaceutical measures for pandemic influenza
choices: non-pharmaceutical measures for pandemic influenza
coronavirus outbreak response in the Western Pacific
vaccine stockpiling for future respiratory pandemics
hospital surge capacity in low-income countries
context: 'Non-pharmaceutical public health measures for mitigating the risk and impact of epidemic and pandemic influenza', WHO Global Influenza Programme, 19 September 2019, ISBN 9789241516839. NPIs are what you have BEFORE a vaccine exists. Source: WHO publication page.

question: The summary table of the WHO's September 2019 pandemic-influenza guidance had four severity columns and one striking category column. Its header reads, word for word:
answer: Not recommended in any circumstances
choices: Not recommended in any circumstances
Recommended only in wealthy nations
Reserved for research use only
Under active scientific review now
context: The category column ran alongside the severity grid (Any, Moderate, High, Extraordinary) and gathered measures the evidence review had concluded should not be used at ANY severity. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, summary of recommendations.

question: On school measures, the WHO's 2019 pandemic-influenza guidance did not put coordinated proactive school closures in its not-recommended column. Its actual written language on them was that they:
answer: are suggested during a severe epidemic or pandemic, with adverse effects considered and duration limited
choices: are suggested during a severe epidemic or pandemic, with adverse effects considered and duration limited
are recommended at any pandemic level to slow community spread as early as possible
are recommended only after two weeks of confirmed in-school transmission has been documented
are recommended for primary schools and specifically advised against for secondary schools
context: School closures were conditionally recommended at severe-and-above pandemic levels, with an explicit written caveat about community harm and duration. The 2020 US school closures ran vastly longer than the document's caveat contemplated, but the guidance itself did contemplate them. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, social measures section.

question: The WHO's 2019 pandemic-influenza guidance refused to recommend quarantining exposed but well people. The two written reasons it gave for the refusal were:
answer: no obvious rationale for the measure, and considerable difficulties in implementing it
choices: no obvious rationale for the measure, and considerable difficulties in implementing it
evidence from the 2009 H1N1 review showed no measurable slowing of transmission
modelling suggested contact tracing alone would substitute effectively for it
household transmission would still occur inside the quarantined home anyway
context: The evidence and practicality argument sits in the text; it is not a values statement. Note the document does not appeal to 'freedom' -- it appeals to evidence and to feasibility, which is what a public-health document should. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, contact management section.

question: The WHO's 2019 pandemic-influenza guidance refused to recommend screening arriving travellers at borders. What did it say the fatal problem with airport screening was?
answer: it cannot see infected people who are still pre-symptomatic
choices: it cannot see infected people who are still pre-symptomatic
symptomatic travellers can hide fevers by taking paracetamol before landing
the incubation window for influenza can exceed 14 days in some cases
screening sensitivity drops below 50% when local prevalence is low
context: The document phrased it as a 'lack of sensitivity' of symptom-based screening 'in identifying infected but asymptomatic (i.e. pre-symptomatic) travellers'. A hunting tool that cannot see the thing it hunts does not catch it -- an argument grade-schoolers can follow. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, travel measures section.

question: On workplace closures, the WHO's 2019 pandemic-influenza guidance used the phrase:
answer: a last step only considered in extraordinarily severe epidemics and pandemics
choices: a last step only considered in extraordinarily severe epidemics and pandemics
recommended only where the community weekly attack rate exceeds five percent
suggested during moderate or above pandemics, with the closure kept under fourteen days
recommended only for high-risk industries and only during the pandemic peak
context: 'Extraordinarily severe' was the top of the document's four-level severity ladder; 'last step' was in the guidance's own language. Broad 2020 workplace closures did not observe that threshold. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, social measures section.

question: Under GRADE, the 2019 WHO pandemic-influenza guidance rated the quality of evidence behind nearly every recommendation as:
answer: very low
choices: very low
low
moderate
high
context: GRADE ratings run very low, low, moderate, high; nearly every line in this document was rated at the bottom. That is what makes the 2019 document important -- it is a public document being modest about itself. 'We are following the science' does not describe what a document rated 'very low' throughout can say. Source: WHO 2019 NPI guidance, GRADE evidence-profile tables.

question: In autumn 2018, France scheduled a rise in the carbon portion of the fuel tax that fell hardest on diesel. Starting 17 November, protesters filled roundabouts across the country wearing the same identifying garment. Why THAT garment?
answer: French drivers are required by law to keep one in every vehicle.
choices: French drivers are required by law to keep one in every vehicle.
The Elysee Palace staff had worn them during a recent strike.
It matched the color of the ruling party's campaign posters.
Truckers' unions had adopted it as their formal uniform in 2015.
context: The high-visibility yellow safety vest ('gilet jaune') has been mandatory in French cars since 2008. Because every driver already owned one, it worked as a leaderless, instant symbol - anyone could join by pulling one out of the glovebox. Source: International Budget Partnership, France: The Yellow Vests.

question: The gilets jaunes protests spread from mid-November 2018 into weeks of clashes. On 10 December 2018 President Emmanuel Macron went on national television and did what to the scheduled 2019 fuel-tax increase?
answer: Cancelled it outright for the coming year
choices: Cancelled it outright for the coming year
Doubled it and earmarked the extra for pensions
Tied it to a national referendum in 2020
Handed the decision to the European Parliament
context: Prime Minister Edouard Philippe first suspended the hike on 5 December; five days later Macron scrapped it altogether for 2019 and announced a 100-euro rise in the minimum wage. Nothing about the physics of CO2 changed that month; the politics did. Source: NPR, 10 December 2018.

question: Washington State's Initiative 732 in 2016 would have imposed a carbon tax starting at $15 per tonne and cut the sales tax from 6.5% to 5.5% - a revenue-neutral swap. It lost 59% to 41%. Which coalition helped defeat it?
answer: The state Democratic Party, the Sierra Club and labour groups
choices: The state Democratic Party, the Sierra Club and labour groups
Chevron, ExxonMobil and the American Petroleum Institute
The Cascade Policy Institute and Washington Farm Bureau
The Federalist Society and the National Rifle Association
context: They objected not to taxing carbon but to giving the money back to taxpayers via a sales-tax cut instead of spending it on their preferred programs. The fight was over who got the revenue. Source: Ballotpedia, Washington Initiative 732 (2016).

question: For the 2022 World Economic Forum in Davos, the Dutch consultancy CE Delft was commissioned to count aircraft movements at the airports serving the resort during the meeting week. What did they report?
answer: About 1,040 private-jet flights in and out of the airports
choices: About 1,040 private-jet flights in and out of the airports
About 40 chartered flights in and out of the airports
About 12,000 helicopter movements in and out of Zurich
About 300 commercial airliner arrivals into Zurich alone
context: 38% of those flights were under 500 km. The report was commissioned by Greenpeace International; the researchers attributed about half the flights to the meeting itself. The bank reports the count and the method and adds no adjective. Source: Greenpeace / CE Delft, January 2023.

question: In 2021 the psychotherapist Caroline Hickman and colleagues published a survey of 10,000 people aged 16 to 25 across ten countries, in The Lancet Planetary Health. What fraction reported being 'very or extremely worried' about climate change?
answer: About 59%
choices: About 59%
About 8%
About 22%
About 91%
context: 1,000 respondents per country in Australia, Brazil, Finland, France, India, Nigeria, Philippines, Portugal, the UK and USA. 75% agreed the future is frightening. The bank treats this neither as proof the danger is fake nor as proof it is real - it is a measured effect of HOW the danger is communicated to children. Source: The Lancet Planetary Health, December 2021.

question: Two mainstream economists - Nicholas Stern (2006) and William Nordhaus - work in the same tradition and reach carbon-tax numbers that differ by more than an order of magnitude, roughly $5 per tonne versus $85+ per tonne. What single modelling choice, applied over centuries, opens that gap?
answer: The discount rate they apply to harms falling on future generations
choices: The discount rate they apply to harms falling on future generations
Which damage function best fits observed 20th-century impacts
How to weight low-probability, high-severity catastrophic tails
Whether to price methane and nitrous oxide alongside CO2
context: Stern uses a near-zero discount rate (~0.1%/year); Nordhaus uses ~1.5%/year. Damage functions and fat-tail weighting are real live disputes too, but it is the discount rate that drives the order-of-magnitude gap here. The fight about carbon taxes is over ethics and economics, not the infrared physics. Source: PNAS, 'Agreeing to disagree on climate policy'.

question: In 2007 Boston Globe columnist Ellen Goodman wrote that 'global warming deniers are now on a par with Holocaust deniers.' The label 'denier' spread through mainstream commentary against people who accept the greenhouse effect but dispute sensitivity or policy. The Associated Press later updated its stylebook - how?
answer: Advised its writers to avoid the label, and to avoid 'skeptic' as well
choices: Advised its writers to avoid the label, and to avoid 'skeptic' as well
Made 'denier' the required term for anyone questioning any climate claim
Kept 'denier' but told writers to flag the Holocaust link in a footnote
Replaced 'denier' with 'contrarian' as the AP's preferred neutral term
context: The AP asked reporters to avoid 'denier' (Holocaust connotation) and also 'skeptic' (which the AP said belongs to honest inquiry), suggesting 'doubter' instead. A word that makes a person unaskable is not an argument. Source: National Association of Scholars, 'AP Denies the Denier Label'.

question: In a single year running from 1976 into 1977, India performed 8.3 million sterilisations, most of them without the patient's consent. The year before, the figure had been 2.7 million. Under which crisis of government did the surge happen?
answer: Indira Gandhi's Emergency
choices: Indira Gandhi's Emergency
the Bengal famine relief
the Partition of Bengal
the Sino-Indian border war
context: The Emergency ran from June 1975 to March 1977; Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and ruled by decree. The Hindi word for sterilisation, 'nasbandi', became its lasting name in Indian memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: In September 1976 Indira Gandhi's son took personal charge of the population campaign, and the sterilisation numbers exploded. Who was he?
answer: Sanjay Gandhi
choices: Sanjay Gandhi
Rajiv Gandhi
Morarji Desai
Jayaprakash Narayan
context: Sanjay Gandhi ran the drive as an unofficial parallel government. Rajiv was his elder brother, who kept out of politics until Sanjay's death in 1980. Desai and Narayan were the opposition figures who beat Congress in 1977. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: In 1968 the American biologist Paul Ehrlich published The Population Bomb. On the subject of India, what did the book actually recommend?
answer: compulsory sterilisation of men with three or more children
choices: compulsory sterilisation of men with three or more children
voluntary contraception funded by the World Bank
raising the legal marriage age to twenty-five
importing American grain to buy the crisis time
context: Ehrlich went further -- he proposed the United States supply helicopters and surgical instruments to speed the vasectomy programme. The recommendation is in his book; the bank names it, and names it as recommendation, not as cause. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Population_Bomb.

question: In the Emergency's population drive, Sanjay Gandhi's team did not just lean on doctors. Which other government workers were handed sterilisation numbers they had to produce, on pain of losing pay or their job?
answer: teachers and clerks
choices: teachers and clerks
railway engineers
customs inspectors
postal sorters
context: Targets were passed down the civil service until schoolteachers were nudging parents into vasectomies and clerks were bringing in relatives. Attach a career to a number and the number is what you get -- honestly or otherwise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: On 18 October 1976 in Muzaffarnagar, Uttar Pradesh, police detained seventeen people to be sterilised. A crowd surrounded the station demanding their release. How did the day end?
answer: police opened fire and about thirty people died
choices: police opened fire and about thirty people died
the crowd freed the detainees and dispersed
the seventeen were quietly released overnight
a magistrate cancelled the operations by court order
context: One of the sharpest recorded incidents of the campaign. Muzaffarnagar became a byword for what a quota costs when it meets a village that says no. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: The Emergency ended not by proclamation but by ballot. In the March 1977 general election, Congress lost and Indira Gandhi lost her own seat in Rae Bareli. What single Hindi word did the winning opposition slogans hammer?
answer: nasbandi
choices: nasbandi
swaraj
satyagraha
ahimsa
context: 'Nasbandi' means sterilisation. The other three are famous words from earlier Indian politics -- swaraj (self-rule), satyagraha (truth-force), ahimsa (non-violence) -- Gandhi-era slogans, not 1977 slogans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India).

question: Song Jian, a Chinese engineer, had trained on the mathematics that steers a missile to a target. In March 1980 he ran China's population through the same class of equations at a meeting in Chengdu. What figure did his group give as China's 'ideal' long-term population?
answer: about 700 million
choices: about 700 million
about 1.5 billion
about 300 million
about 2.4 billion
context: Song and his team put the ideal at 650 to 700 million, roughly two-thirds of the then-population of one billion. To reach it required a one-child rule maintained for decades. He had encountered the cybernetic population theory of the Club of Rome at a control-engineering conference in Helsinki in 1978. Source: socsci.uci.edu 2010-09-23.

question: Scholars including Wang Feng and Daniel Goodkind have challenged the strong story that Song Jian's equations caused the one-child policy. What do they show instead?
answer: Party leaders had already decided on one-child restrictions before 1980
choices: Party leaders had already decided on one-child restrictions before 1980
Song's equations were sound but rested on a bad fertility estimate
the policy was pushed from below by provincial cadres, not Beijing
the policy was copied wholesale from India's 1976 Emergency campaign
context: Goodkind's phrase: Song's team functioned 'more like expert witnesses for a government already determined to prosecute'. The equations may have supplied authority rather than the decision, and that is its own lesson about the misuse of scientific prestige. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-child_policy.

question: The arithmetic of the one-child rule came back in an unplanned form. China's sex ratio at birth rose from about 108 boys per 100 girls in 1981 to about 117 per 100 by 2000. Roughly how many more men than women did that leave in those cohorts?
answer: 32 to 36 million
choices: 32 to 36 million
3 to 4 million
300 to 400 million
under a million
context: The planners modelled births as a number. They did not model the preference, family by family, for a son to carry the name -- a preference that under a one-child rule crossed the modern ultrasound and became this gap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-child_policy.

question: Two Bell Labs physicists, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, spent the autumn of 1947 pressing tiny gold contacts onto a purified crystal. On 23 December they demonstrated a small device that amplified a voice signal about a hundred times - the machine that would replace the vacuum tube in almost everything electronic. What crystal did they use?
answer: high-purity germanium
choices: high-purity germanium
single-crystal silicon
gallium arsenide
natural quartz
context: Silicon took over the industry within a decade, but the FIRST working transistor was point-contact germanium. Brattain's lab notebook for 16 December 1947 records the amplification; the 23 December demonstration played speech through the device so the audience could hear it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor.

question: Writing in Scientific American in February 2001, Max Tegmark and John Archibald Wheeler estimated that roughly thirty percent of United States gross national product rested on inventions that quantum mechanics had made possible. Of these four pairs of quantum-based devices, which pair did the two authors single out as carrying most of that share?
answer: semiconductors and lasers
choices: semiconductors and lasers
MRI scanners and atomic clocks
CCD image sensors and photovoltaic cells
flash memory and superconducting magnets
context: Tegmark & Wheeler, '100 Years of Quantum Mysteries', Scientific American 284:2 (Feb 2001), pp. 68-75. All four listed pairs are genuine quantum-based technologies - MRI relies on nuclear spin, CCDs on the photoelectric effect, flash memory on quantum tunneling through an oxide - but the 2001 article specifically named semiconductors and lasers as the load-bearing pair inside that ~30 percent number. The wonder is that quantum theory sits inside your phone, your ceiling bulb and your barcode scanner all at once.

question: On 9 October 1962 at General Electric's lab near Syracuse, New York, Nick Holonyak passed current through a small diode grown from an alloy of gallium arsenide and gallium phosphide, and it emitted light a human eye could see - the first visible LED. What colour did it glow?
answer: red
choices: red
green
blue
yellow
context: The alloy GaAs0.6P0.4 has a band gap that emits in the red. Green LEDs followed within a few years; blue took three more decades. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Holonyak.

question: John Bardeen shared the 1956 Nobel in Physics for co-inventing the transistor. Fifteen years later he shared a SECOND Nobel in Physics, with Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer, making him the only person ever to win the physics prize twice. What was that second prize for?
answer: the theory of superconductivity
choices: the theory of superconductivity
the design of the atomic clock
the discovery of the neutrino
the invention of holography
context: The 1972 prize citation reads 'for their jointly developed theory of superconductivity, usually called the BCS-theory'. It explains why the electrons in certain cooled metals pair up and glide through the lattice with zero resistance - itself a purely quantum result. Source: nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1972.

question: Bardeen and Brattain's original 1947 point-contact device was fragile and hard to manufacture. A third colleague on the project soon designed a sandwich-of-doped-crystal version that was rugged, mass-producible, and became the shape of essentially every transistor since - the design that made modern electronics buildable. Who was he?
answer: William Shockley
choices: William Shockley
Jack Kilby
Robert Noyce
Charles Townes
context: Shockley's bipolar JUNCTION transistor (1948) replaced the finicky point-contact geometry with three doped layers pressed together. He shared the 1956 Nobel in Physics with Bardeen and Brattain 'for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect'. Kilby (at Texas Instruments) and Noyce (at Fairchild) would come later, for the integrated circuit; Townes for the maser. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor.

question: White LED bulbs took thirty years longer to arrive than red ones because the industry could not make one particular colour of diode efficiently. Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura finally cracked it with gallium nitride crystals and shared the 2014 Nobel in Physics for it. Which colour was the missing piece?
answer: blue
choices: blue
green
yellow
infrared
context: The Nobel citation reads 'for the invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes which has enabled bright and energy-saving white light sources'. Every white bulb in the house is a blue LED coated with a yellow phosphor (cerium-doped YAG) - the blue light pumps the phosphor and the eye adds the two into white. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode.

question: On 16 May 1960, working alone at Hughes Research Laboratories in Malibu, Theodore Maiman fired the first working laser at a small rod pumped by a photographic flash lamp. His paper was rejected twice by Samuel Goudsmit at Physical Review Letters and finally published in Nature. What was the rod made of?
answer: synthetic ruby
choices: synthetic ruby
neodymium-doped YAG crystal
titanium-doped sapphire
neodymium-doped glass
context: Charles Townes and Arthur Schawlow had assumed a gas medium would come first; Maiman used a small cylinder of chromium-doped aluminium oxide - synthetic ruby - pumped by a spiral flashtube. Nd:YAG, Ti:sapphire and Nd:glass are all now-standard solid-state laser media, but each came later. The Nature paper 'Stimulated Optical Radiation in Ruby' appeared on 6 August 1960. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Maiman.

question: Different LED colours come from different crystals with different sizes of the electronic energy-gap that quantum mechanics opens up inside every solid. Whichever crystal you choose, one electron does one specific thing inside the diode when a current flows, and that fixes the colour of the bulb. What does the electron do?
answer: falls from a higher band to a lower one and releases one photon
choices: falls from a higher band to a lower one and releases one photon
collides with another electron and both heat the crystal
spins in place and the magnetism of the spin glows
orbits the nucleus faster and radiates infrared
context: Electron energy = photon energy: E = h*nu, so a wider gap makes a higher-energy (bluer) photon. That is why an LED's colour is fixed by its material, not by voltage - and why blue took gallium nitride rather than a tweak to a red LED. This is a purely quantum result; classically an electron would radiate a smear of colours. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_gap.

question: You can measure the wavelength of a cheap laser pointer on your kitchen table by shining it at a shallow angle at one everyday object; a row of bright spots then appears on the wall, and their angles let you solve for the wavelength. Which object?
answer: a CD or DVD
choices: a CD or DVD
a bathroom mirror
a sheet of aluminium foil
a printed newspaper page
context: CD track pitch is 1.6 micrometres; DVD 0.74 micrometres - both close enough to red-laser wavelengths (~650 nm) that the tracks act as a diffraction grating, and d*sin(theta) = m*lambda solves for lambda from the measured spot angles. A mirror gives a single reflection; foil scatters; newsprint is too irregular. Test-it-yourself is the deepest goal of the bank: don't take the wavelength on the packet on trust, measure it. Reference: American Journal of Physics 65(9), 1997.

question: Transistors, LEDs and lasers are settled quantum tech running the world. Of these four much-hyped near-term quantum technologies, only one has yet to beat a classical machine on a problem people actually want solved. Which one, and what is the specific open obstacle?
answer: a general-purpose quantum computer, blocked on error correction
choices: a general-purpose quantum computer, blocked on error correction
a quantum-key-distribution network, blocked on repeater range
a quantum gravity sensor, blocked on vibration isolation
a topological qubit device, blocked on Majorana confirmation
context: All four are genuine near-term quantum-tech programs with their own real bottlenecks - QKD does work over short fibre links and is limited by the lack of practical quantum repeaters; atom-interferometer gravity sensors work in the lab and are limited by isolating the atoms from vibration; the topological-qubit route is stalled on confirming Majorana zero modes. But the specific answer to the stem is the general-purpose quantum computer: narrow 'quantum-advantage' demonstrations exist on contrived sampling tasks, yet a fault-tolerant machine that solves a wanted problem faster than a classical one does not - the qubits decohere too fast and the error-correction overhead is huge. Reference: Preskill, 'Quantum Computing in the NISQ era', arXiv:1801.00862.

question: For roughly thirty years after 1898, glowing radium was sold as a health boost. Wristwatch dials flickered on the nightstand, Doramad toothpaste and Tho-Radia face cream carried the label, and one popular stoneware crock stood in kitchens across America. The buyer filled the crock with water at bedtime, let a lining of radium ore 'charge' it overnight, and drank the water in the morning. What was the crock called?
answer: The Revigator
choices: The Revigator
The Halcyon
The Cordial Jar
The Lourdes Font
context: The Revigator was patented in 1912 and sold in the thousands through the 1920s and 30s. Adverts promised the treated water would prevent arthritis, senility and flatulence, delivering 'the lost element of original freshness, radioactivity'. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium_ore_Revigator

question: The most notorious radium tonic was Radithor, small bottles of distilled water spiked with a measured dose of radium. Its maker was so confident he offered $1,000 to anyone who could prove a bottle contained less radium than the label claimed. Who was that maker, a Harvard dropout who styled himself a doctor?
answer: William J. A. Bailey
choices: William J. A. Bailey
Elisha Perkins
John Brinkley
Charles Aycock
context: Bailey grew rich on Radithor before his flagship customer's death forced the Federal Trade Commission to shut him down in December 1931. He was never a physician. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radithor

question: The Pittsburgh industrialist and US amateur golf champion Eben Byers hurt his arm in 1927, his doctor recommended Radithor, and Byers found it made him feel wonderful. He drank about 1,400 small bottles of the stuff over the next three years. In 1932 the Wall Street Journal ran his obituary under a very specific headline. What did the headline say the radium water had done?
answer: It worked fine until his jaw came off
choices: It worked fine until his jaw came off
It gave him a wonderful glow
It cured his ailments but ruined his stomach
It saved his life then broke his heart
