context: By the end most of Byers' upper and lower jaw had been surgically removed, and holes were forming in his skull. He died in March 1932 with about 36 micrograms of radium distributed through his bones; ten micrograms is a fatal quantity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eben_Byers

question: Radium is chemically almost indistinguishable from one common element the body needs every day, so once swallowed it gets sorted like that element and filed into the same tissue. That is the mechanism that turned the tonics from harmless fads into slow-acting poisons: because radium-226 has a half-life of about 1,600 years, whatever is filed keeps firing alpha particles for the rest of the person's life. Which everyday element does the body mistake radium for?
answer: Calcium
choices: Calcium
Iron
Iodine
Sodium
context: Group 2 metals share two loosely held outer electrons and are chemically similar. Once radium follows calcium into the skeleton, roughly 70 to 95 percent of an ingested dose ends up filed into bone. That is why radium tonics did their damage inside people, not on the way through. Source: sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/radium

question: From 1917 the US Radium Corporation in Orange, New Jersey hired hundreds of young women to paint luminous numbers on watch and instrument dials with a radium paint called Undark. Male chemists in the same building were quietly issued lead aprons and tongs, but the supervisor taught the women a jaunty little routine, three quick actions repeated dial after dial, to keep their brushes fine-pointed. What was that routine called?
answer: Lip, dip, paint
choices: Lip, dip, paint
Trim, dab, stroke
Kiss, fill, brush
Wet, coat, mark
context: The women, who ingested a little of the paint dozens of times a day, were told the material was safe; the men handling it in bulk downstairs were protected. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium_Girls

question: When the dial painters began sickening in the early 1920s, the US Radium Corporation kept its own consulting experts busy producing reassuring reports, and several of the first deaths were officially blamed on causes that had nothing to do with the paint. Which pair of diagnoses did company-friendly doctors pin on the women before the real cause was finally admitted?
answer: Syphilis and phosphorus poisoning
choices: Syphilis and phosphorus poisoning
Tuberculosis and childhood rickets
Diphtheria and typhoid fever
Lead poisoning and mercury poisoning
context: The 'phosphorus poisoning' label came from a real occupational disease of the day (matchstick workers developed 'phossy jaw' from white phosphorus); the syphilis label was especially cruel because it also destroyed the women's reputations. In 1924 the pathologist Harrison Martland and the dentist Theodor Blum finally identified the disease as radium poisoning and named it 'radium jaw'. Source: environmentalhistory.org/people/radiumgirls

question: One of the sick women in Orange, New Jersey refused to accept the company diagnosis. She recruited four of her old workmates and sued the US Radium Corporation in 1927. Newspapers dubbed the plaintiffs 'the five women doomed to die'; the case settled in 1928 and helped force the recognition of workplace radiation as a hazard. Who was the woman who brought the suit?
answer: Grace Fryer
choices: Grace Fryer
Alice Hamilton
Frances Kelsey
Rachel Carson
context: The chemist who had invented the Undark paint, Sabin von Sochocky, died of radium-induced aplastic anaemia in November 1928, having sawed off the poisoned tip of his own finger in an attempt to save himself. His autopsy helped confirm Fryer's case. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Fryer

question: The honest twist the story cannot skip is that radium really does kill cells, which is why the same property that made it lethal in a tonic is put to careful use in a modern cancer drug. On 15 May 2013 the FDA approved an alpha-emitting radium compound, given as monthly injections, for one specific job. What kind of cancer is radium-223 (Xofigo) licensed to treat?
answer: Prostate cancer that has spread to bone
choices: Prostate cancer that has spread to bone
Skin melanoma on the face and neck
Leukaemia in the bone marrow of children
Brain tumours behind the eye
context: Radium-223 follows calcium into bone exactly like the old radium-226 did, but its half-life is only about eleven days, so it delivers a concentrated alpha dose to the tumours in the skeleton and is largely gone before it can do wider harm. The ALSYMPCA trial showed a 3.6-month survival benefit. Source: ecancer.org/en/news/4085-fda-approves-radium-223-dichloride-for-bone-metastases-from-castration-resistant-prostate-cancer

question: At the United States Radium Corporation in Orange, New Jersey, young women hired to paint glowing numbers on watch dials were trained in a three-word routine they were told would keep the brush sharp before every stroke. What were the three words?
answer: lip, dip, paint
choices: lip, dip, paint
wet, twist, stroke
clean, load, dot
point, dip, wipe
context: The routine put a little of the paint into the mouth on every stroke. Source: Wikipedia, 'Radium Girls.'

question: The paint sold to the New Jersey and Illinois dial factories was so novelty-bright that many of the young painters, laughing, used the leftover from the workday to decorate themselves before a night out. What did they mainly do with it?
answer: painted their fingernails and teeth so they would glow in the dark
choices: painted their fingernails and teeth so they would glow in the dark
used it to write love letters that only showed under lamplight
streaked it into their hair for photographs
poured it into perfume bottles as a party favor
context: Some also painted their eyelids. The brand name was Undark. Source: Wikipedia, 'Undark.'

question: The glow itself was a real, teachable mechanism the factory sold under the brand name Undark: the radium was mixed with a second ingredient that did the actual shining. What was the second ingredient?
answer: zinc sulfide
choices: zinc sulfide
phosphorus white
sodium borate
magnesium oxide
context: Alpha particles from the radium hit zinc sulfide crystals and excited them into giving off a faint blue-green light -- radioluminescence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Undark.'

question: In the same years the dial painters were falling ill, radium was being sold across America as a HEALTH TONIC. A wealthy Pittsburgh industrialist and former amateur golf champion, on a doctor's advice for an arm injury, drank about three bottles of the tonic Radithor a day for two years -- and died in 1932, so radioactive that undertakers used a lead-lined coffin. Who was he?
answer: Eben Byers
choices: Eben Byers
William Bailey
Frederick Flinn
Charles Norris
context: Byers's upper and lower jaw had to be surgically removed before his death on March 31, 1932. William Bailey was Radithor's promoter and profited even after Byers died; Frederick Flinn was the industrial hygienist US Radium hired to publicly deny any radium harm to the dial painters; Charles Norris was New York City's chief medical examiner. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eben Byers.'

question: Dr Harrison Martland, the Essex County medical examiner, needed proof he could show a jury that radium was still inside the dial painters years after they left the factory. He used the women themselves as the instrument. Which pair of measurements did he actually take?
answer: gamma rays from their living bodies plus radon gas from their exhaled breath
choices: gamma rays from their living bodies plus radon gas from their exhaled breath
urine samples analyzed for radium salts plus blood samples cultured for infection
spinal-fluid samples plus a controlled dose of iodine tracer
hair samples plus the temperature of their fingertips
context: He also laid bone samples from victims on unexposed dental X-ray film in the dark: the bones fogged the film by themselves. Source: Wikipedia, 'Harrison Stanford Martland'; Rowland, 'The National Bureau of Standards and the Radium Dial Painters.'

question: In Ottawa, Illinois, the Radium Dial Company kept lip-pointing going long after the New Jersey settlement. On February 10, 1938, dial painter Catherine Wolfe Donohue -- too weak to sit up in court, and later giving the continuation of her testimony from her bed at home -- produced a small box and set it on the table as physical evidence. What was in the box?
answer: fragments of her own jawbone that had come loose from her mouth
choices: fragments of her own jawbone that had come loose from her mouth
the last unopened jar of Undark paint from her workstation
a signed 1925 memo warning managers not to lip-point
a lead-lined necklace her doctor had made for her to wear
context: An Illinois Industrial Commission arbitrator ruled for Donohue on April 5, 1938; she died on July 27, 1938. Source: NPR Illinois, 'The Radium Girls: An Illinois Tragedy'; Northwestern University finding aid for Donohue, Catherine Wolfe.

question: Turn your back to a low evening Sun, set a garden hose to a fine mist, and spray it in front of you: a bow appears, and it is a piece of a circle. That circle has a centre, and the centre is a spot you can put your finger on. Where is it?
answer: At the shadow of your own head, out on the grass
choices: At the shadow of your own head, out on the grass
At the thickest part of the mist, just past the hose
At the point in the sky directly overhead
At the spot where the Sun's light first meets the water
context: That centre has a name: the antisolar point, the direction exactly opposite the Sun, and from where you stand it is marked by the shadow of your own head. Every rainbow anyone has ever seen was aimed personally at that spot. Source: Grokipedia, 'Antisolar point' ('from a person's perspective the antisolar point is the location of the shadow of their head on the ground'); corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow, which notes that in photographs the shadow of the photographer's head marks the centre of the rainbow circle.

question: It is a cloudless July noon, the Sun almost overhead, and the hose mist throws no bow at all. At six that evening the first spray throws one instantly. A rainbow is a slice of a full ring of returning light. Where was that ring at noon?
answer: Below the ground: the whole ring lay under your feet
choices: Below the ground: the whole ring lay under your feet
Directly overhead: the ring rode high above the mist
Behind you: the ring had swung to the Sun's side
Inside the mist: the ring was there but far too faint
context: The ring's centre is driven downward as the Sun climbs, and the arc reaches about 42 degrees up from that centre. So once the Sun stands more than 42 degrees above the horizon, the whole ring has sunk below the ground and no amount of spraying will raise one -- at a July noon you are standing on top of your rainbow. TEST IT: try the hose at midday, then again an hour before sunset. Source: Atmospheric Optics, atoptics.co.uk/blog/low-and-high-rainbows/ ('If the sun is higher than 42 degrees you won't see a rainbow at all'); corroborated at livescience.com/30235-rainbows-formation-explainer.html.

question: Hold a photograph of a rainbow over an Icelandic glacier beside one from a Hawaiian waterfall, then beside a snapshot of your own garden sprinkler: fat cold rain, thundering spray, fine mist. Measure how far each arc stands out from the centre of its own circle. What decides that figure?
answer: Every drop returns its light on a cone of one fixed width
choices: Every drop returns its light on a cone of one fixed width
Every drop returns a wider cone the bigger it happens to be
Every watcher stands about the same distance from the water
Every human eye takes in about the same width of sky
context: Every drop that sends red light to your eye lies on a cone about 42 degrees wide around the antisolar line; violet arrives from about 40 degrees. Drop size does not enter into it, which is why a bow in an Icelandic squall and a bow in your sprinkler are twins. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' -- the primary bow subtends 'an angular radius of approximately 42 degrees from the observer's shadow, with longer wavelengths (red) on the outer edge and shorter wavelengths (violet) on the inner edge'; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow.

question: Two friends stand shoulder to shoulder in the same sprinkler mist, each seeing a bow. One of them walks steadily out through the spray. Which water is building the arc she sees now?
answer: A different set of drops at every step she takes
choices: A different set of drops at every step she takes
The same drops that built it before she started walking
The drops falling closest around her as she walks
The drops that are building her friend's bow as well
context: A rainbow is a direction, not an object sitting at a place, which is why nobody has ever reached one: step sideways and the arc is rebuilt out of entirely new water. Two people standing shoulder to shoulder never see exactly the same rainbow -- their bows are assembled from completely different drops. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow (two observers 'never see exactly the same rainbow'); Atmospheric Optics, atoptics.co.uk/blog/opod-primary-rainbow/, adds that the bow 'forms a cone rather than a fixed location in space'.

question: At Cumberland Falls in Kentucky, on nights near the full Moon, a pale arch stands in the spray. To the eye it is a ghost -- grey-white, barely a tint in it. Put a camera on a tripod and hold the shutter open, and the same arch comes out with its reds and greens plainly there. Why does the camera get colour the eye cannot?
answer: The eye's colour-sensing cone cells never wake in moonlight
choices: The eye's colour-sensing cone cells never wake in moonlight
The eye's pupil cannot open wide enough to take moonlight in
The eye's lens scatters such faint light before it registers
The eye's signals reach the brain too weak to read as colour
context: TEST IT AT NIGHT: a moonbow wants a full or nearly-full Moon lower than about 42 degrees, a properly dark sky, and spray or rain opposite it -- so two to three hours after sunset or before sunrise. Cumberland Falls, Victoria Falls and Yosemite Falls throw them reliably, and in Costa Rican cloud forest they appear almost every full moon from December through February. Aristotle already described one in the Meteorology around 350 BC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonbow; corroborated at Grokipedia, 'moon rainbow'.

question: Every drop in a rain shower splits sunlight into a full spectrum, exactly the way a glass prism does. Yet each of those drops sends your eye just one colour; the rest of its spectrum misses your eye entirely. So when your eye runs across the bow from one edge of the band to the other, what is it actually reading?
answer: A map of how high each drop sits: high ones give red, low ones violet
choices: A map of how high each drop sits: high ones give red, low ones violet
A map of how big each drop is: big ones give red, small ones violet
A map of how far off each drop is: near ones give red, far ones violet
A map of how fast each drop falls: slow ones give red, quick ones violet
context: A single raindrop hands you exactly one colour and flings the rest of the spectrum it made past your head, to land in front of you or behind you. The band of colour you see is therefore a map of drop height, not a spectrum from any one drop: the drops high in the arc are doing the red, the low ones the blue and violet. Source: sciencefocus.com, 'Why do millions of raindrops only make one rainbow'; corroborated at asu.edu/courses/phs208/patternsbb/PiN/rdg/rainbow/rainbow3.shtml.

question: Send a whole sheet of parallel sunlight into one raindrop. Each ray enters at a different height on the drop, bends, reflects off the curved back, and bends again on the way out -- and the rays leave spread across a wide fan of angles. If the light comes back out smeared over all those angles, why do you see a sharp bright band rather than a general glow?
answer: At one angle the rays from many entry heights pile up together
choices: At one angle the rays from many entry heights pile up together
At one angle the drop reflects nearly all the light instead of passing it
At one angle the light spends longest inside, gaining strength
At one angle the drop bends the light twice as far as at any other
context: The bend angle has a minimum near 138 degrees for red (140 for violet), and rays entering at many different heights all crowd into that minimum -- which is exactly what makes a bright arc instead of a smear. Do the subtraction: 180 minus 138 gives the familiar 42 degrees. That crowded ray is still called the Descartes ray. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' and 'Alexander's band' ('minimum deviations around 138 degrees for red and 140 degrees for violet, corresponding to the observed 42 degrees and 40 degrees angular radii from the antisolar point'); corroborated at reed.edu/math-stats/wieting/essays/Rainbow.pdf.

question: Walk a lawn on a clear, dewy morning with a low Sun behind you and a bow can appear lying in the grass rather than standing in the air -- a dewbow, built in the beads of water on the blades. The returning light still comes back on the same cone it always does; the flat ground simply slices through that cone. What curve does the slice draw across the grass?
answer: A hyperbola, opening wider the farther out it runs
choices: A hyperbola, opening wider the farther out it runs
A circle, closed neatly around the watcher's feet
A parabola, the curve of a ball thrown flat and low
A spiral, winding tighter toward the far hedge
context: A dewbow is a rainbow cone cut open where you can walk on it. Atmospheric Optics puts it exactly: 'The path on the grass of the dew forming the bow is a hyperbola or ellipse formed by the intersection of the rainbow cone with the ground. However the bow seen by your eyes at the tip of cone, is always circular.' Its apex sits at the lower end of your own shadow, and an ellipse rather than a hyperbola turns up when the geometry allows. Source: atoptics.co.uk/rainbows/dewbow.htm; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewbow and glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/dewbow/.

question: After a heavy shower a second, fainter bow sometimes stands about nine degrees outside the bright one, and its colours run the other way round -- red on the inside edge this time. It is a broader, softer band as well, which is part of why it is so easy to miss. What did the light that built that outer bow do differently?
answer: It reflected off the drop's back wall twice before it escaped
choices: It reflected off the drop's back wall twice before it escaped
It bounced off the bright bow itself, throwing back a mirror image
It passed straight on through a second raindrop behind the first
It entered through the drop's shaded side instead of the sunlit side
context: Two reflections inside the drop instead of one puts the secondary bow near 51 degrees, about nine degrees outside the primary, and flips the colour order so red faces inward. It carries only about 43 per cent of the primary's total brightness, spread over a band roughly 1.8 times wider -- which is why most people go a lifetime without noticing it. TEST IT: at the next double bow, check the colour order on the outer arc. Source: Atmospheric Optics, atoptics.co.uk/blog/secondary-rainbow/ ('Rays escaping after two reflections make a secondary bow with a radius of 51 degrees... it is broader, 1.8 times the width of the primary bow, and its colours are reversed'); corroborated at Grokipedia, 'Rainbow'.

question: Theodoric of Freiberg, a Dominican friar, shut himself in a darkened room some time between 1304 and 1311 with a single sunbeam and a water-filled glass sphere, and patiently traced where each ray came back out. He wrote the results up as De iride. In his model, what was that sphere standing in for?
answer: A single raindrop, blown up until he could follow rays through it
choices: A single raindrop, blown up until he could follow rays through it
A whole rain cloud, treated as one body reflecting the Sun
A patch of falling mist, its countless drops averaged into one
A curved sheet of water, of the sort a waterfall throws up
context: Everyone before Theodoric had reasoned about the rainbow by reasoning about clouds. Treating one water-filled globe as a single magnified raindrop let him trace the ray paths that build the primary bow and the secondary, and the colour reversal that follows. Kamal al-Din al-Farisi reached the same result independently in Persia within about two years, publishing it in Kitab Tanqih al-Manazir -- 'The Revision of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics'. Two men, two continents, no contact, the same glass sphere. TEST IT: a round glass of water on a sunny windowsill throws the same colours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodoric_of_Freiberg; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_optics; Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' (De iride, written between 1304 and 1310).

question: Alexander of Aphrodisias ran the Peripatetic school in Athens -- Aristotle's own school -- somewhere between AD 198 and 209, and while writing a commentary on Aristotle's Meteorology he set down something about double rainbows that nobody had recorded before. It concerns the strip of sky lying between the two arcs, and it is still called Alexander's band. What did he notice there?
answer: That strip of sky is darker than the sky on either side of the pair
choices: That strip of sky is darker than the sky on either side of the pair
That strip of sky shows a third arc, colourless and very faint
That strip of sky carries the two bows' colours in weak reverse
That strip of sky flickers as the falling drops cross through it
context: The gap is dark because the primary bow throws its light everywhere at angles LESS than about 42 degrees from the antisolar direction, while the secondary throws its light outward at angles GREATER than about 51 degrees. Nothing at all is aimed into the strip between them -- and the sky inside the primary is correspondingly brighter than the rest. TEST IT: on the next good double bow, compare the sky just inside the bright arc against the strip between the two. Source: Grokipedia, 'Alexander's band'; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander%27s_band, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_of_Aphrodisias ('a date between 198 and 209'), and atoptics.co.uk/blog/secondary-rainbow/ for the brightness contrast.

question: Sit at an airliner window at ten thousand metres with a low Sun behind you and a rainbow can appear whole -- a closed ring, complete all the way round, the way it never is from the ground. The bottom of that ring is built from drops lying below the level of the aircraft, and those only come into play once the Sun is low enough behind you. How low does the Sun have to sit?
answer: Under about three degrees up, all but touching the horizon
choices: Under about three degrees up, all but touching the horizon
Under about fifteen degrees up, a fist held at arm's length
Under about thirty degrees up, a third of the way up the sky
Under about forty degrees up, not quite halfway up the sky
context: From an aeroplane the drops below your horizon suddenly come into play and the bow closes into a full circle -- on the ground it is the earth, not the physics, that cuts every rainbow in half. Grokipedia adds the number: at a typical cruising altitude of 10,000 metres the antisolar point clears the local horizon once the Sun drops below about 3 degrees of altitude. Window seat, low Sun, opposite side of the aircraft from the Sun. Source: Grokipedia, 'Rainbow' and 'Antisolar point'; corroborated at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow (full circles visible from aircraft).

question: Just inside the violet edge of a bright rainbow you can sometimes catch two or three extra fringes -- faint pink, purple and green bands crowded close together. They are called supernumerary bows, and here is the trouble with them: trace rays through a drop as carefully as you like and the ray picture predicts nothing there at all. Thomas Young offered the explanation in 1804, and George Airy had to invent a whole new mathematical function in 1838 to get their spacing right. What are those fringes made of?
answer: Light that took two slightly different paths inside one drop, then combined
choices: Light that took two slightly different paths inside one drop, then combined
Light bent a second time by the flattened underside of a falling drop
Light from a much higher layer of drops, arriving a little behind the rest
Light thrown back down off the underside of the cloud above the shower
context: Young's 1804 answer was interference: two routes through the same drop arrive slightly out of step, reinforcing in some directions and cancelling in others. George Airy made it quantitative in 1838 in 'On the intensity of light in the neighbourhood of a caustic' (Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, vol. 6, pp. 379-403), inventing the function that now carries his name. Best part: the fringe spacing reports the DROP SIZE. You need drops about 1 mm across or smaller, and the smaller the drops, the broader and paler the bands -- so you can read the rain off the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernumerary_rainbow; Airy (1838), ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1838TCaPS...6..379A; droplet range from Grokipedia, 'Rainbow'.

question: Physics textbooks like to say that Rene Descartes found the rainbow's angle in 1637 by tracing some ten thousand rays through a raindrop by hand. Frank Barmore went hunting for that number in 1983 and found that textbook writers had simply copied it from one another, with no such labour behind it. What Descartes actually did needed nothing like ten thousand rays. How did he pin the angle down?
answer: He stepped across the drop in tenths, then refined the strip near the edge
choices: He assumed one ray through the drop's centre and scaled the rest from it
He stepped across the drop in tenths, then refined the strip near the edge
He worked backwards from the bow's angle as he measured it in the sky
He derived the angle from the geometry and checked it against a few rays
context: Barmore's 1983 paper 'Descartes, the Rainbow and the Mythical 10 000 Calculations' traced the ten-thousand story to a line in Taylor's physics textbook and, further back, to a nineteenth-century claim by Grau. What Descartes did in 1637 was work through the deviation for entry points from 0.0 to 1.0 across the drop in steps of 0.1, see where the angle stopped changing, then go back and refine the interval between 0.80 and 0.90 -- using seven-figure trigonometric tables. A few dozen careful calculations, not thousands of brute-force ones; he found the answer by knowing where to look. His apparatus was 'a perfectly round and transparent glass ball filled with water' -- a raindrop you could hold. Source: F. Barmore, 'Descartes, the Rainbow and the Mythical 10 000 Calculations' (1983), opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=MO-1983-ThB3; method detail from Wieting, 'The Cartesian Rainbow', Reed College (2006).  (Legend.)

question: In 2021 Anne Scheel, Mitchell Schijen and Daniel Lakens compared two literatures in psychology: 152 standard papers, and 71 studies where the journal had said yes to the study before anyone knew how it would come out. About 96% of the standard papers reported the hypothesis they had tested was confirmed. Roughly what share of the second group did?
answer: About 44%
choices: About 12%
About 44%
About 76%
About 92%
context: Scheel, Schijen and Lakens (2021), 'An Excess of Positive Results,' Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 4(2). 146 of 152 standard papers (~96%) reported a confirming result; 31 of 71 Registered Reports (~44%) did. IMPORTANT: this is a correlation between two different literatures, not a controlled experiment -- the authors themselves caution against a simple causal reading. The 52-point gap is still large enough to make you look twice at anything that comes back positive in the ordinary literature. Source: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/25152459211007467

question: Richard Feynman's 1974 Caltech commencement address, later published as 'Cargo Cult Science,' ended with a single instruction that has become the motto of the whole reform movement. What did he tell the graduates was the first principle?
answer: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool
choices: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool
The first principle is to trust the peer review of your colleagues
The first principle is that a p-value below 0.05 is a discovery
The first principle is that authority in a field is a good guide to truth
context: Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science,' Caltech commencement address, 1974. The line reads in full: 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself -- and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you've not fooled yourself, it's easy not to fool other scientists.' This is why preregistration, Registered Reports, and adversarial collaboration exist: they are devices for not letting yourself off the hook. Source: https://calteches.library.caltech.edu/3043/

question: In the mid-1920s the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi stood at the Aerological Observatory at Tateno, launched hydrogen balloons, and tracked them with a theodolite. High above him he found something nobody had known was there -- a persistent narrow band of extremely fast wind just below the top of the weather layer. What would that river in the sky later be called?
answer: the jet stream
choices: the jet stream
the polar vortex
the Hadley cell
the Ferrel cell
context: Oishi's winter profile at Tateno is the first documented observation of the persistent upper westerlies. The polar vortex is a circumpolar low; the Hadley and Ferrel cells are meridional overturning cells, not bands of fast wind. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi; aos.wisc.edu/~aos610/HW2_Lewis_BAMS_Ooishi.pdf.

question: Wasaburo Oishi published his balloon data honestly and thoroughly -- nineteen aerological reports totalling 1,246 pages between 1926 and 1944. Almost nobody outside Japan read a word of them, because he made one particular choice about the language they were printed in. In what language did Oishi publish?
answer: Esperanto
choices: Esperanto
Latin
German
French
context: Oishi was a devoted Esperantist and president of the Japanese Esperanto Institute; the very first report was titled Raporto de Aerologia Observatorio de Tateno. He picked Esperanto hoping to reach a wide foreign audience; the effect was the opposite. Source: smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/as-next-may-unbelievablebuttrue-180968355.

question: In late 1944 American B-29 crews arrived over Japan planning to bomb from 30,000 ft. At that altitude they suddenly found themselves flying inside winds of 200-300 mph -- Oishi's river, unknown to them. Under full throttle some aircraft made almost no ground speed at all and bombs missed by miles. General Curtis LeMay's response was to change ONE thing about how the B-29s flew. What did he change?
answer: he lowered their bombing altitude to about 25,000 ft
choices: he lowered their bombing altitude to about 25,000 ft
he grounded the daylight raids in favour of night bombing
he ordered new heavier propellers fitted to every airframe
he pulled the fleet back to India and cancelled the campaign
context: LeMay moved the B-29s to roughly 24,500-27,000 ft, out of the jet's core, and later to low-altitude firebombing entirely. Source: historyofwar.org/articles/weapons_B-29_combat.html.

question: Japan tried to turn Oishi's wind into a weapon. Beginning 3 November 1944, its army launched roughly nine thousand paper hydrogen balloons -- fusen bakudan, or fu-go -- carrying incendiaries into the current, hoping the jet would sweep them across the Pacific to burn North America. The plan hinged on a wind-speed calculation, and the calculation was wrong. About how long did the crossing actually take?
answer: about three or four days
choices: about three or four days
about ten hours
about two weeks
about six weeks
context: The fu-go crossings took roughly 72-96 hours rather than the shorter time the plan assumed; only a few hundred of the ~9,300 launched ever reached North America. Six civilians killed near Bly, Oregon on 5 May 1945 were the only WWII enemy-action deaths in the contiguous US. Sources: ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/japanese-balloon-bombs-fu-go/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu-Go_balloon_bomb.

question: The jet stream screams in winter and slackens in summer. It lives where a horizontal temperature difference meets the top of the weather layer, and one particular temperature difference is much sharper in winter than in summer -- that is the engine driving the wind. Which difference?
answer: between equatorial and polar air
choices: between equatorial and polar air
between day-side and night-side air
between land and ocean surfaces
between wet and dry air masses
context: By the thermal-wind relationship, a sharp horizontal temperature gradient at the tropopause forces a fast westerly wind above it; the equator-to-pole gradient is steepest in winter. It is why an eastbound New York to London flight is routinely about an hour shorter than the westbound return -- something a kid can check on any departures board. Source: britannica.com/science/climate-meteorology/Upper-level-winds.

question: In 1831 Michael Faraday mounted a copper disc on a brass axle so that its edge passed between the poles of a permanent magnet, then turned the crank by hand. What historic first did the apparatus achieve?
answer: It turned steady muscle power into a steady electric current.
choices: It turned steady muscle power into a steady electric current.
It split water into hydrogen and oxygen without any chemical bath.
It sent a coded message down a wire from one room to another.
It boiled a beaker of water without any flame under it.
context: The device, later called the Faraday disc or homopolar generator, is the ancestor of every dynamo and every alternator on the planet. Feed a current back INTO the same disc and it spins itself -- the first hint that motor and generator are one machine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homopolar_generator .

question: A common intuition after Faraday's disc is that if you held a bar magnet still, right next to a coil of wire, the coil should give a steady current. Faraday's experiments killed the intuition. What did he actually find?
answer: The coil gives a current only while the field is CHANGING, never while it sits still.
choices: The coil gives a current only while the field is CHANGING, never while it sits still.
The coil gives a current the whole time the magnet is present, moving or not.
The coil gives a current only when the magnet is touching the wire directly.
The coil gives a current only when the magnet is aligned with the Earth's field.
context: A magnet at rest, even a strong one, produces no current in a nearby coil. Move it, spin it, or switch it off and the coil sees a pulse. This is Faraday's law: it is the RATE of change of flux that drives induction. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faraday%27s_law_of_induction .

question: At the Vienna World Exposition of 1873, Belgian inventor Zenobe Gramme's business partner Hippolyte Fontaine ran a copper cable from one Gramme dynamo to a second Gramme dynamo about five hundred metres away, meaning to demonstrate long-distance transmission. What UNEXPECTED thing did the second machine do?
answer: Its shaft started spinning under its own power.
choices: Its shaft started spinning under its own power.
Its coils caught fire and had to be doused with water.
Its output voltage climbed to twice what the first was producing.
Its galvanometer needle swung around and stayed at zero.
context: Nobody had meant to demonstrate that the machine was reversible, but there it was: pour current in, get rotation out. A dynamo run backwards is a motor. The Vienna accident is the moment industrial electric motors were born. Source: bie-paris.org Zenobe Gramme's electrifying discovery at Expo 1873 Vienna .

question: Pedal a bicycle whose front hub is a small dynamo powering a headlamp, and something honest happens the moment the lamp lights up: the pedals get harder to push. Which physical law is doing the bookkeeping?
answer: The induced current always opposes the change that produced it.
choices: The induced current always opposes the change that produced it.
The induced current always adds to the change that produced it.
The induced current is proportional to the square of the wheel's speed.
The induced current only flows when the wheel is spinning downhill.
context: This is Lenz's rule, and it is really conservation of energy in disguise. The electricity in the lamp had to come from somewhere; the extra push your legs feel is exactly that energy leaving your body and going into the bulb. Source: spark.iop.org electromagnetic-braking-copper-pipe .

question: An electric car coasting down a long hill does not turn its friction brakes on -- it flips a switch that puts its drive motor into a different mode. What does the motor do now, and where does the energy go?
answer: It acts as a generator; the current it makes refills the battery.
choices: It acts as a generator; the current it makes refills the battery.
It acts as a heater; the energy is dumped through a radiator.
It acts as a flywheel; the energy is stored as its own spin.
It acts as a transformer; the energy is stepped down to a lower voltage.
context: Regenerative braking is Faraday's principle sold as a feature: the shaft is being spun by the car's own momentum, so induction pushes current back INTO the battery instead of drawing it out. The kinetic energy that would have become brake-pad heat becomes usable charge instead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regenerative_braking .

question: Take a small, strong neodymium magnet and hold it at the top of a length of thick copper pipe held vertically. Let it go. Copper is not magnetic. What actually happens as the magnet falls through the pipe?
answer: It sinks slowly, as if falling through honey.
choices: It sinks slowly, as if falling through honey.
It falls at normal free-fall speed, exactly as a pebble would.
It sticks to the inner wall of the pipe halfway down.
It shoots out the bottom faster than free-fall.
context: The moving magnet changes the magnetic field inside the pipe wall, and that changing field drives circulating eddy currents in the copper. Those currents make their own magnetic field, oriented to push back on the magnet by Lenz's rule -- a three-second home demonstration of conservation of energy. Source: phys420.phas.ubc.ca p420_2018 lalond72 .

question: A transformer is Faraday's iron ring wearing a third face: two coils sharing one iron core, one voltage in and a different voltage out. There is one thing a transformer flatly cannot do. What is it?
answer: Transform direct current.
choices: Transform direct current.
Pass power between two coils that share no direct wire connection.
Work with an iron core instead of an air core.
Have more turns on the output coil than the input coil.
context: Induction needs a CHANGING flux, and a steady DC current produces a steady field with no change at all. That is why the domestic grid was built AC in the first place: only AC can be stepped up to high voltage for cheap long-distance transmission and stepped back down for your house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer .

question: Textbooks like to say a motor and a generator are 'the same machine run backwards.' A working engineer will nod, then add a caveat. What is the honest caveat about a REAL motor and a REAL generator?
answer: Each is wound, geared, and cooled for one job; reversibility is a schoolbook ideal.
choices: Each is wound, geared, and cooled for one job; reversibility is a schoolbook ideal.
The two use entirely different physical principles once you look inside the case.
Only Faraday's original disc was ever truly reversible; every later design broke it.
Reversibility fails because energy conservation is only approximate at large scale.
context: In principle the physics is symmetric; in practice a car's drive motor and a hydro plant's generator are built for opposite duty cycles, cooling loads, and torque profiles. 'Run it backwards' is true as a law and engineered around as a product. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_generator .

question: Alexander Glenny, at the Wellcome Physiological Research Laboratory in London in 1926, wanted a purer diphtheria vaccine, not a new idea. He used potassium aluminium sulphate to precipitate the toxoid, injected the precipitate into guinea pigs, and compared them with animals given plain toxoid. What did Glenny find?
answer: The precipitate produced a far stronger antibody response
choices: The precipitate produced a far stronger antibody response
The precipitate produced a far weaker antibody response
The precipitate produced a far quicker antibody response
The precipitate produced a far narrower antibody response
context: Glenny was chasing purity and caught the adjuvant effect instead: an ingredient that teaches the immune system nothing itself, but makes it pay far more attention to what it is taught. Aluminium salts have sat in vaccines ever since 1926, which is why aluminium is the ingredient in the childhood schedule that gets argued about most. Sources: 'Mechanism of Immunopotentiation and Safety of Aluminum Adjuvants', PMC3541479; 'Advances in aluminum hydroxide-based adjuvant research and its mechanism', PMC4514166.

question: In 1986 the American childhood vaccine schedule was eleven doses - seven injections and four given by mouth - protecting against seven diseases. Now count today's schedule by exactly the same rule: every dose from birth through age eighteen, with the annual influenza shot included. How many doses is that?
answer: About 50 to 54 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
choices: About 20 to 24 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
About 50 to 54 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
About 70 to 74 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
About 95 to 99 doses, against 16 to 18 diseases
context: The counting rule is most of the argument. Change it - count injections only, stop at age two, leave influenza out - and the same schedule yields a different headline, which is how one campaign gets '11 to 70+' and another gets a modest rise. Neither side disputes that the schedule expanded; they dispute what the expansion means. The Institute of Medicine, counting its own way in 2013, said the under-six schedule 'is timed to protect children from 14 pathogens' and that children 'may receive as many as 24 immunizations by their second birthday and may receive up to five injections during a single doctor's visit.' The 1980s starting point is corroborated independently by the archived CDC schedules: in 1983, 'Eleven doses of four vaccines protected kids against seven vaccine-preventable diseases.' Sources: STAT News, 'How we know kids don't get too many vaccines too soon' (24 June 2025); IOM, The Childhood Immunization Schedule and Safety, Report Brief (January 2013); vaxopedia.org archive of historical CDC schedules.

question: The National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986 ordered a national early-warning system for vaccine side effects, and VAERS opened on 1 November 1990. Arguments about its numbers never stop, and they usually skip the question of how a report gets into it in the first place. Who may file a VAERS report?
answer: Anyone at all, a patient or a parent included
choices: Anyone at all, a patient or a parent included
Anyone who was present, a parent or a nurse included
Anyone in health care, a nurse or a pharmacist included
Anyone required by law, a doctor or a maker included
context: In the CDC's own description, 'VAERS is a passive surveillance system, meaning it relies on people sending in reports of their experiences after vaccination.' Reports come from 'patients, family members, healthcare providers and vaccine manufacturers', and only providers and manufacturers are legally required to report certain events - nobody else is obliged to file anything. The open door is deliberate: a net meant to catch surprises cannot have a gatekeeper deciding in advance what counts as a surprise. It also means a VAERS entry is an account, not a verified injury. VAERS was built by merging the CDC's 1976 MSAEFI system with an FDA system. Source: CDC, 'About the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS)'.

question: Aluminium is the vaccine ingredient parents ask about most. An American baby in 1986 received about 1.5 mg of it across the first six months of life; today those same six months bring about 4.4 mg. Set beside that the aluminium a formula-fed baby swallows over the very same six months. How much is that?
answer: About 38 mg
choices: About 1 mg
About 12 mg
About 38 mg
About 120 mg
context: By age two the vaccine total is about 6 mg. The 38 mg swallowed figure is offered by the source 'for scale', and scale is all it is: it compares amounts, not routes into the body, and it settles nothing by itself - which is exactly why researchers went and measured vaccine aluminium directly rather than resting on the comparison. Three separate counts of the same schedule are now on the table - doses, antigens and milligrams of aluminium - and each answers a different question. Source: STAT News, 'How we know kids don't get too many vaccines too soon' (24 June 2025); cumulative ~4.4 mg by six months also stated at grokipedia.com/page/Vaccination_schedule.

question: VAERS took roughly 30,000 to 50,000 reports in a typical year before the pandemic; by 31 December 2021 it held over 717,000 reports tied to COVID-19 vaccines. Writers on both sides of the argument quoted totals like those as the risk of being vaccinated. The CDC's own page warns that no risk figure can be got out of VAERS at all, and points to a number the system never collects. Which number?
answer: How many people received the vaccine in the first place
choices: How many people received the vaccine in the first place
How often that reaction strikes people who were never vaccinated
How many separate reports describe the very same patient
How many doctors saw such a case and filed nothing at all
context: A rate is a fraction. VAERS collects the top of it and never sees the bottom: in the CDC's words, 'It is usually not possible to use VAERS data to calculate how often an adverse event occurs in a population', because 'The number of people receiving a vaccine is usually not available.' A system with a numerator and no denominator can raise a flag; it cannot measure a rate. The CDC adds that 'VAERS data alone cannot determine if the vaccine caused the reported adverse event.' Both sides of the vaccine argument have published rates computed straight out of VAERS totals; the people who run the system say that arithmetic cannot be done. The 2021 pile of reports has at least three causes tangled together - the sheer number of doses given, expanded mandatory reporting under Emergency Use Authorization, and publicity, since the CDC notes that 'The number of reports submitted to VAERS can change in response to media attention and public awareness' - and no count alone can pull them apart. Source: CDC, 'About the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS)', Strengths and limitations.

question: The dose count has climbed steeply since the 1980s, and the worry attached to it is the load on a small immune system. So count the load itself - antigens, the distinct molecules an immune system learns to recognise. One whole-cell whooping-cough shot from the 1980s carried over 3,200 of them. Today's entire childhood schedule, every dose added together, carries how many?
answer: About 165 antigens in total
choices: About 165 antigens in total
About 1,250 antigens in total
About 4,100 antigens in total
About 27,000 antigens in total
context: Roughly a 95 percent cut in antigen exposure across the same decades in which the dose count roughly quintupled. Both numbers are true; they are answers to different questions, and each side of the argument quotes the one that suits it. 'Whole-cell' meant the entire killed bacterium went into the vial - thousands of distinct molecules in a single shot - where modern purified vaccines carry a short list of chosen ones. For scale in the other direction, Paul Offit and colleagues calculated that an infant could in theory respond to 10,000 vaccines at once while using under one percent of circulating B-cells, and infants meet an estimated 2,000 to 6,000 unique antigens every day from bacteria, viruses and food. Sources: STAT News (24 June 2025); grokipedia.com/page/Vaccination_schedule.

question: The FDA licensed RotaShield, the first rotavirus vaccine, on 31 August 1998. By 16 July 1999 VAERS held fifteen reports of intussusception - a length of an infant's bowel telescoping into itself - in vaccinated babies, and 87 percent of those cases had followed the very first dose. Fifteen reports, nationwide. What happened next?
answer: The CDC urged suspension in days; the maker withdrew it that October
choices: The CDC urged suspension in days; the maker withdrew it that October
The CDC urged a label warning; the maker sold it for four more years
The CDC urged use after six months only; the maker narrowed the label
The CDC urged wider reporting; the maker paid for a follow-up study
context: The CDC called for immediate suspension on 16 July 1999; ACIP voted on 22 October 1999 to drop the recommendation, and the manufacturer withdrew the product that month - under fifteen months from licensure to withdrawal, on fifteen reports. This is the strongest case for a system that cannot measure anything: it was built to notice, and it noticed. What it could not supply was the size of the risk. Once controlled studies were run they found roughly a 37-fold increase in the three to seven days after the first dose, amounting to 'The excess risk of approximately 1 intussusception case in 10 000 Rotashield recipients.' VAERS produced the hypothesis; epidemiology produced the number. A quieter case ran the same way: eight to ten VAERS reports of vaccine-associated paralytic polio fed the 1997 decision to move the American schedule off routine oral polio vaccine. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Vaccine_Adverse_Event_Reporting_System; 'Intussusception and Rotavirus Vaccination - Balancing Risk Against Benefit', PMC5715718; CDC MMWR 48(43).

question: The Institute of Medicine's 2013 report on the American childhood immunization schedule is quoted by both sides of the argument, because it made two findings. The first was blunt: the committee found 'no evidence that the schedule is unsafe.' The second named a gap in the research literature. What gap?
answer: The number, timing, order and ages of doses had never been studied together
choices: The number, timing, order and ages of doses had never been studied together
The individual vaccines had never been compared against an inert placebo
The children studied had never been followed past their fifth birthday
The safety studies had never included children outside managed-care plans
context: Verbatim: 'Key elements of the entire schedule - the number, frequency, timing, order, and age at administration of vaccines - have not been systematically examined in research studies.' And: 'No studies have compared the differences in health outcomes that some stakeholders questioned between entirely unimmunized populations of children and fully immunized children.' Both halves belong in the same sentence, and the precise wording matters: 'no randomised trial of the whole schedule exists' is TRUE, while 'the schedule is unstudied' is FALSE - large observational comparisons exist and the same committee reviewed them, concluding it 'uncovered no evidence of major safety concerns associated with adherence to the childhood immunization schedule.' The committee also noted its report 'is unique in that it is the first to attempt to examine the entire childhood immunization schedule as it exists today.' Sources: IOM, The Childhood Immunization Schedule and Safety, Report Brief (January 2013), pp.2-4; Summary chapter, NCBI NBK206938.

question: A Danish team followed 1,224,176 children born between 1997 and 2018, matching 50 chronic disorders against how much vaccine aluminium each child had received by age two, and found no raised risk of autoimmune, allergic or neurodevelopmental disease. But this was no trial - nobody randomised anything. So where did the differences in aluminium between these children come from?
answer: Denmark kept switching brands, so the total depended on birth year
choices: Denmark kept switching brands, so the total depended on birth year
Denmark split supply between regions, so the total depended on address
Denmark paused doses one winter, so the total depended on start age
Denmark offered a lighter schedule, so the total depended on parents
context: Aluminium content per dose 'ranged from 0.125 to 1.00 mg', and procurement kept changing - pneumococcal vaccine added in 2007, supply substitutions, newer formulations - so a child's total depended on the year it happened to be born, for reasons having nothing to do with that child. The authors call it 'a natural quasi-experimental framework'. Adjusted hazard ratios per extra 1 mg by age two: 0.98 (95% CI 0.94-1.02) for any autoimmune disorder, 0.99 (0.98-1.01) for any atopic or allergic disorder, 0.93 (0.90-0.97) for any neurodevelopmental disorder. Lead author Anders Hviid: 'Our results are reassuring. By analyzing data from more than one million Danish children, we found absolutely no indication that the very small amount of aluminum used in the childhood vaccination program increases the risk of 50 different health outcomes during childhood.' The authors keep their own limits in view - 'small relative effects, particularly for some rarer disorders, could not be statistically excluded', individual medical records were not reviewed, and follow-up ran to a median age of five - and the design has a hard ceiling: only 15,237 of those children (1.2%) received no aluminium-adsorbed vaccine at all, so this is a study of more aluminium versus less, not of vaccinated versus unvaccinated. A CDC-funded study in the Vaccine Safety Datalink pulled the other way on one outcome: Daley and colleagues, 326,991 children, found aluminium 'positively associated with persistent asthma' (adjusted hazard ratio 1.19 per 1 mg in children without eczema) and wrote that 'additional investigation of this hypothesis appears warranted.' Reviewing that paper, Paul Offit noted the association vanished when the analysis was restricted to fully immunised children, was absent among breastfed children, showed no dose-response, and left dietary aluminium unaccounted for. Neither the Danish null nor the American positive is the end of the story, and that is what an open question looks like. Sources: Andersson NW, Svalgaard IB, Hoffmann SS, Hviid A, Annals of Internal Medicine, 15 July 2025, doi:10.7326/ANNALS-25-00997; Statens Serum Institut news release (July 2025); Daley MF et al., Acad Pediatr 2023; CHOP Vaccine Update.

question: Ross Lazarus and Michael Klompas of Harvard Pilgrim built an automated detector to find out how much VAERS was missing, and their 2011 final report to the federal AHRQ carries the sentence quoted in nearly every argument about the system: 'fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported.' Where does that 'fewer than 1%' figure come from?
answer: From studies published earlier, cited as the reason for the work
choices: From studies published earlier, cited as the reason for the work
From the team's own detector, run across 1.4 million doses
From a CDC estimate the team was contracted to test and confirm
From a match of VAERS entries against the clinics' own records
context: The famous line is background - prior literature summarised to justify the grant, not a measurement the project produced. What the project itself measured was something else entirely, reported on the same page: 'Preliminary data were collected from June 2006 through October 2009 on 715,000 patients, and 1.4 million doses (of 45 different vaccines) were given to 376,452 individuals. Of these doses, 35,570 possible reactions (2.6 percent of vaccinations) were identified.' The full background passage: 'Adverse events from drugs and vaccines are common, but underreported. Although 25% of ambulatory patients experience an adverse drug event, less than 0.3% of all adverse drug events and 1-13% of serious events are reported to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Likewise, fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported.' Checking the provenance of a number you like is the same move as checking one you dislike, and this is a number the schedule's critics like. Two further things sit in the same report. First, Aim 3 - a head-to-head test of the new detector against VAERS and the Vaccine Safety Datalink - never happened: 'there was never an opportunity to perform system performance assessments because the necessary CDC contacts were no longer available and the CDC consultants responsible for receiving data were no longer responsive to our multiple requests to proceed with testing and evaluation.' The report attributes that to 'restructuring at CDC and consequent delays in terms of decision making' and asserts nothing beyond it. Second, 'fewer than 1%' is not a universal constant: measured against active surveillance, VAERS captured 68-72% of vaccine-associated paralytic polio cases and 47% of intussusception after rotavirus vaccine, but only 13% of anaphylaxis after influenza vaccine and 12% of Guillain-Barre after one seasonal flu vaccine. 'No uniform underreporting factor exists across all events.' Sources: Lazarus R, Klompas M, 'Electronic Support for Public Health - Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (ESP:VAERS)', AHRQ Grant Final Report R18 HS 017045 (2011), p.6; grokipedia.com/page/Vaccine_Adverse_Event_Reporting_System.

question: Randomise children, vaccinate one group and leave the other unvaccinated, follow both for years - that is the study that would settle the childhood-schedule question, and the 2013 Institute of Medicine committee refused to endorse it as unethical. The obvious fallback is to compare the children America already has: some on the standard schedule, some on an alternative one. The committee named, in plain words, the flaw that sinks that comparison too. What flaw?
answer: The two groups of children may differ in more ways than the schedule
choices: The two groups of children may differ in more ways than the schedule
The two groups of children may be too young for the illnesses at issue
The two groups' doctors may record the same illness under different names
The two groups' vaccines may vary in strength from batch to batch
context: Verbatim: 'children who are immunized with alternative vaccination schedules may differ in meaningful ways from children who adhere to the schedule, and these differences could make it difficult to tease out health differences that are attributable to the immunization schedule.' That is the healthy-user problem - when people sort themselves into the groups, whatever made them choose travels with them into the results - and the committee stated it by hand. It named a second wall on the same page: 'Fewer than 1 percent of Americans refuse all immunizations. Enrolling sufficient numbers of unvaccinated children and matching them with vaccinated children of the same age, gender, ethnicity, and geographic location - a necessary step to rule out chance findings - would be prohibitively difficult and time-consuming.' On the randomised trial the committee was explicit: 'The committee does not endorse conducting a new randomized controlled clinical trial that would compare the health outcomes of unvaccinated children with their fully immunized peers. Although this is the strongest study design type, ethical concerns prohibit this study, as unvaccinated individuals and communities intentionally would be left vulnerable to morbidity and mortality.' Note where the refusal rests: on ethics, not on power - the committee concedes the design is the strongest there is. What it recommended instead was the Vaccine Safety Datalink, a CDC collaboration with nine managed-care organisations then covering 'more than 9 million children and adults - roughly 3 percent of the U.S. population', which it called 'the best available system for studying the childhood immunization schedule'. The VSD has 13 member sites today and runs rapid-cycle analyses in near-real time: active surveillance, which goes and looks, rather than waiting to be told. Sources: IOM Report Brief (January 2013), p.3; CDC, 'About the Vaccine Safety Datalink'.

question: RotaTeq, the rotavirus vaccine built to replace the withdrawn RotaShield, was licensed only after a trial in 68,038 infants across more than 500 sites in 11 countries, with intussusception - a length of an infant's bowel telescoping into itself - as the primary safety endpoint. That trial found no raised risk. After the vaccine went into routine use, Yih and colleagues searched the FDA's Mini-Sentinel records. How much extra intussusception did they find in the week after a first dose?
answer: About 1.1 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
choices: About 0.1 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
About 1.1 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
About 4 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
About 11 extra cases per 100,000 first doses
context: Yih and colleagues estimated 1.1 excess intussusception cases per 100,000 first doses of RotaTeq in the seven-day window (95% CI 0.3 to 2.7) and 1.5 per 100,000 in the 21-day window (95% CI 0.2 to 3.2). Set that against RotaShield, whose excess risk worked out at 'approximately 1 intussusception case in 10 000 Rotashield recipients' - roughly ten times larger. RotaTeq's trial had been built for this exact question, and its sister vaccine Rotarix was trialled at similar size: the two 'each underwent large clinical trials of approximately 60 000-70 000 infants specifically to assess the risk of intussusception.' Neither trial found an increased risk - and a risk near one in a hundred thousand is precisely what a trial of 68,000 cannot see. This is the cleanest demonstration anywhere that 'the trial found nothing' and 'there is nothing to find' are two different statements. The mirror statement matters just as much: 'a real risk was found' and 'the vaccine should be withdrawn' are also two different statements. RotaTeq stayed on the schedule, because one in a hundred thousand is a different decision from one in ten thousand. The same split showed in 2010-11, when VAERS data mining flagged febrile seizures in children aged six to 23 months after influenza vaccine and the Vaccine Safety Datalink confirmed roughly 2 extra seizures per 10,000 vaccinations: the response was revised guidance on fever medicines and changed labels, not withdrawal. So three sentences that sound alike are not alike - 'no randomised trial of the whole schedule exists', 'it has been investigated and nothing was found', and 'therefore it is dangerous' - and treating any one of them as another is the error, whoever commits it. Sources: Yih WK et al., 'Intussusception Risk after Rotavirus Vaccination in U.S. Infants', N Engl J Med 2014; 'Evaluating the safety of a rotavirus vaccine: the REST of the story', PMC2602609; PMC5715718; grokipedia.com/page/Vaccine_Adverse_Event_Reporting_System.

question: Ian Donald, professor of midwifery at Glasgow, knew a little radar from his RAF years. On 21 July 1955 he took two cars to the Babcock & Wilcox boiler works at Renfrew, where an ultrasonic tester hunted cracks inside steel. He had loaded both boots at his hospital. What was in them?
answer: fibroids and ovarian cysts cut from his patients
choices: fibroids and ovarian cysts cut from his patients
placentas saved from his own delivery room
jars of specimens from the pathology museum
blood and fluid drained from his own wards
context: The source puts it plainly: 'He took with him two cars, the boots of which were loaded up with a collection of lumps such as fibroids and ovarian cysts which had recently been removed from patients in his Department.' Donald had arrived in Glasgow in autumn 1954 with, in his own words, 'a rudimentary knowledge of radar from my days in the RAF' - he served as an RAF medical officer from 1942 to 1946, was mentioned in dispatches after pulling airmen out of a burning bomber, and was awarded the MBE. His question was as plain as he could make it: 'All I wanted to know, quite simply, was whether these various masses differed in their ultrasonic echo characteristics.' The rail worth remembering: Ian Donald did not invent ultrasound. He made the diagnostic application work, on borrowed industrial hardware, alongside the engineer Tom Brown and the clinician John MacVicar. Source: ob-ultrasound.net, Joseph Woo, 'A short History of the development of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology', Part 1 (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/history1.html); Wikipedia 'Ian Donald'.

question: At the Babcock & Wilcox boiler works at Renfrew, Ian Donald ran the ultrasonic tester over the specimens he had carried out from his hospital. To read the traces he needed a comparison - ordinary healthy tissue, run on the same machine that same afternoon, which is what scientists call a control. The company kindly supplied one. What was it?
answer: a large lump of steak
choices: a large lump of steak
a slab of raw liver
a boiled ham hock
a whole plucked chicken
context: Joseph Woo's history records it with a Scottish deadpan: the tests were run '...on a large lump of steak which the company had kindly provided as control material. (No one had the appetite for the steak afterwards!)' Flagged as legend here because the detail survives in the telling rather than in a laboratory notebook. The idea underneath it is dead serious and is one of the oldest tools in experimental science: you cannot know what an odd reading MEANS until you have run the same test on something you already agree is normal. Try it yourself the next time you measure anything - measure something known first. Source: ob-ultrasound.net, Joseph Woo, Part 1 (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/history1.html).

question: Tom Brown, a 23-year-old engineer at the Glasgow instrument firm Kelvin & Hughes, heard a piece of gossip late in 1956 about a professor at the Western Infirmary. It was odd enough that he looked the man up in the hospital directory and telephoned him out of the blue; within a year the two had built the first contact scanner. What was the professor said to be doing?
answer: using a flaw detector to detect flaws in women
choices: using a flaw detector to detect flaws in women
photographing unborn babies with old radar gear
listening to hearts through a submarine hydrophone
hunting tumours with a converted welding rig
context: Joseph Woo's wording: 'Quite by accident, Tom Brown had heard the strange tale of a professor who was attempting to use a metal flaw detector to detect flaws in women. He telephoned Professor Donald and suggested a meeting.' Flagged as legend because accounts differ on how the rumour reached him - Wikipedia has Brown coming across Donald while installing equipment at the Western Infirmary and then looking him up in the hospital directory - though both agree on the phone call. Brown, born 10 April 1933, had just been promoted to research and development engineer in 1956 and had already worked on an automatic flaw detector for industrial products. By late 1957 he and Donald had the first contact B-mode compound scanner in clinical use, its transducer running at 2.5 MHz, and Kelvin & Hughes patented the design that year with Brown named as inventor. Sources: ob-ultrasound.net Part 1; Wikipedia 'Tom Brown (engineer)'.

question: The working heart of an ultrasound probe is a crystal, and the trick it performs was found in a Paris laboratory in 1880 by two brothers still working as laboratory assistants - Jacques Curie, 24, and his younger brother Pierre, 21. They clamped crystals of quartz, topaz, cane sugar and Rochelle salt and squeezed. What appeared when they squeezed?
answer: a voltage across the crystal's faces
choices: a voltage across the crystal's faces
a flash of light inside the crystal
a rise in the crystal's temperature
a faint ringing note from the crystal
context: This is the direct piezoelectric effect: 'The first demonstration of the direct piezoelectric effect was in 1880 by the brothers Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie.' Quartz and Rochelle salt gave the strongest response; the brothers were then working under Charles Friedel at the Faculty of Sciences in Paris. A year later Gabriel Lippmann deduced the converse effect - feed a voltage in and the crystal deforms - mathematically, from fundamental thermodynamic principles, and the Curies immediately confirmed it in the laboratory. Those two halves are exactly the two jobs a probe does: the converse effect lets it speak, the direct effect lets it listen, and one crystal does both. A connective footnote: the sensitive piezoelectric quartz electrometer the brothers built for this crystal work is the very instrument Marie Curie later used to measure the radioactivity of pitchblende and isolate polonium and radium. Modern probes are not quartz but PZT, lead zirconate titanate, a ceramic developed around 1952 at the Tokyo Institute of Technology. Sources: Wikipedia 'Piezoelectricity', 'Jacques Curie', 'Pierre Curie', 'Lead zirconate titanate'.

question: Every ultrasound scan begins the same way: cold gel squeezed onto the skin and smeared flat under the probe. It is not there for the patient's comfort, and without it the screen shows almost nothing at all. What is the gel actually doing?
answer: shutting out the air, which bounces the whole beam back
choices: shutting out the air, which bounces the whole beam back
cooling the crystal, which heats up as it pulses
carrying the electric pulse from the probe into the skin
damping the probe so its own ringing dies away
context: Wikipedia's 'Medical ultrasound' states it directly: 'a water-based gel is placed between the patient's skin and the probe to facilitate ultrasound transmission into the body. This is because air causes total reflection of ultrasound; impeding the transmission of ultrasound into the body.' The mismatch behind it is brutal - acoustic impedance about 429 for air against roughly 1.6 million for soft tissue, which sends essentially the whole beam (about 99.9%) straight back off the first film of air it meets. StatPearls gives the working rule the same way: 'ultrasound waves cannot travel through the air, [so] probes must contact patients' skin through a coupling medium.' You can notice the same physics yourself: duck your head under the bathwater while someone talks above the surface and their voice all but vanishes, because sound crossing between water and air is thrown back at the boundary. Sources: Wikipedia 'Medical ultrasound'; StatPearls 'Ultrasound Physics', NCBI Bookshelf NBK570593; impedance values from OpenStax College Physics 2e 17.7.

question: An ultrasound machine carries no ruler - only a very fast clock. It fires a pulse into the body and times whatever comes back, and sound crosses soft tissue at roughly 1,540 metres per second. Work it out: an echo arrives 100 microseconds after the pulse left the probe, having made the trip down and back. How deep is the structure that threw it?
answer: about 7.7 cm
choices: about 7.7 cm
about 15.4 cm
about 3.9 cm
about 1.5 cm
context: 1,540 m/s multiplied by 100 microseconds is 0.154 m of travel; the echo went down AND back, so the reflector sits 7.7 cm below the probe. (15.4 cm is the trap - it is the round trip, not the depth.) Wikipedia's 'Medical ultrasound' states the principle bluntly: the scanner must determine 'how long it took the echo to be received from when the sound was transmitted. (Time and distance are equivalent.)' Delay fixes where the dot goes on the screen; the strength of the echo fixes how bright it is. Now the honest catch: 1,540 m/s is only an AVERAGE for soft tissue. Fat carries sound at about 1,450 m/s and muscle at about 1,590, so the machine's single assumed speed is itself a source of artefacts, and structures can be drawn slightly off their true depth. Sources: Wikipedia 'Medical ultrasound'; OpenStax College Physics 2e, section 17.7 'Ultrasound'.

question: In 1914 the U.S. Revenue Cutter Miami steamed out to the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, into the ice lanes that had killed the Titanic two years earlier, carrying Reginald Fessenden and his new underwater oscillator. On that trip he sounded the depth of the sea below and caught the echo of an iceberg two miles off. The same oscillator did a third job that day. What was it?
answer: tapped out Morse code through the water itself
choices: tapped out Morse code through the water itself
listened for a submarine running beneath the hull
measured the sea's temperature from its echoes
spoke by voice to a diver below the ship
context: Fessenden's 1914 demonstration covered depth sounding, underwater communications by Morse code and echo ranging, 'detecting an iceberg at a 2-mile (3.2 km) range' - in a year when radio was young and radar did not exist. Sending a coded message through the water itself was the third strand of that demonstration; the record credits it without saying who, if anyone, was listening at the far end, and without claiming it as a first - so this rung does not claim one either. The point for this ladder is the ORDER of events: sound-ranging was a sea technology first, and medicine borrowed it decades later. Lewis Fry Richardson, a Quaker meteorologist who pioneered numerical weather forecasting and served the First World War as a conscientious objector in the Friends' Ambulance Unit, had patented iceberg detection by acoustic echolocation in air in April 1912, within weeks of the sinking, and filed a second patent for the same trick in water a month after that. Paul Langevin then built the first transducer that really worked, a submarine detector running at 150 kHz between 1915 and 1918, made from thin quartz crystals glued between two steel plates. Sources: Wikipedia 'Sonar'; Wikipedia 'Lewis Fry Richardson'; ob-ultrasound.net Part 1.

question: A woman came to Ian Donald's department in Glasgow already given up for lost: X-ray and clinical examination together had put her down as an inoperable stomach cancer. Donald ran his ultrasound over her abdomen and the echoes flatly contradicted the diagnosis. Surgery proved the echoes right, and Donald wrote afterwards that 'there could be no turning back.' What had the machine found?
answer: a huge ovarian cyst filling her whole abdomen
choices: a huge ovarian cyst filling her whole abdomen
a swollen liver, enlarged but not cancerous
a knot of scar tissue from an older operation
a mass of fibroids pressing on her stomach
context: The laparotomy confirmed a pseudomucinous cyst filling the entire abdomen - large, and removable. This is the case Ian Donald himself treated as the turning point: a woman told she would die, opened up instead and cured, because a borrowed industrial instrument disagreed with an X-ray. Donald's own account of what kept the work moving afterwards is worth keeping: 'As soon as we got rid of the backroom attitude and brought our apparatus fully into the Department with an inexhaustible supply of living patients with fascinating clinical problems, we were able to get ahead really fast.' The proof was published as Donald I, MacVicar J, Brown TG, 'Investigation of abdominal masses by pulsed ultrasound', The Lancet, 7 June 1958, 1(7032):1188-95. Sources: Wikipedia 'Ian Donald'; ob-ultrasound.net, Ian Donald biography (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/iandonaldbio.html); PubMed PMID 13550965.

question: Ultrasound reached the human head before it reached the belly. From the 1940s the Vienna physician Karl Dussik, working with his physicist brother Friedrich, sat patients with the upper part of the head immersed in a water bath and published pictures by a method he called hyperphonography, reading them as the brain's fluid-filled ventricles. His 1947 pictures were the first ultrasound images anyone had published. How did his machine work?
answer: the sound was sent through the head to a receiver on the far side
choices: the sound was sent through the head to a receiver on the far side
the sound was pulsed in and the echoes coming back were timed
the sound was made to resonate the skull and the ringing measured
two beams were crossed inside the head and the interference read
context: Dussik, born in Vienna on 9 January 1908, presented his first paper in 1941 and, with his younger brother Friedrich (a radio and mathematical physicist with a 1938 Vienna PhD) and the physicist L. Wyt, published the first ultrasound images in 1947. The method: 'a through-transmission technique with two transducers placed on either side of the head... Coupling was obtained by immersing the upper part of the patient's head and both transducers in a water bath.' He called it hyperphonography. Dating note: ob-ultrasound gives 1941 for the paper and 1947 for the images, while BMUS dates the first published work on medical ultrasonics to 1942, so 'the 1940s' is the honest span. Dussik was a serious pioneer, not a fraud - a test published years later showed that the pattern he had been reading came from somewhere other than the ventricles. Sources: ob-ultrasound.net, Karl Theodore Dussik biography (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/dussikbio.html); BMUS 'History of Ultrasound'.

question: John Wild, an English surgeon at Minnesota's Medico Technological Research Institute, began by borrowing a US Navy radar training device and pointing it at tissue instead of at the sky. With the engineer John Reid he published in Science in 1952, and by 1956 their instrument had examined 117 breast cases at better than 90% accuracy. What had Wild and Reid found that made the machine diagnostic?
answer: cancerous tissue echoes more strongly than healthy tissue
choices: cancerous tissue echoes more strongly than healthy tissue
cancerous tissue carries sound faster than healthy tissue
cancerous tissue shifts the pitch of the echo as it grows
cancerous tissue swallows the beam almost completely
context: In the sources' own words, Wild and Reid found that 'malignant tissue was more echogenic than benign tissue' - malignant meaning cancerous, benign meaning harmless. Their landmark paper was 'Application of Echo-Ranging Techniques to the Determination of Structure of Biological Tissues', Science, 1952; Reid called it 'the first publication... on intensity-modulated cross-section ultrasound imaging.' By May 1953 they had real-time 15 MHz breast images. Their route - REFLECTION, listening for what comes back - is the road that won, and Ian Donald attended a lecture by Wild in 1954. On the same road, Douglass Howry at the University of Colorado built the first 2-D compound scanner in 1951 with engineers William Roderic Bliss and Gerald Posakony, mounting the transducer around the rim of a large metal tank of water; his 1957 Pan-scanner seated patients in modified dental chairs, and the AMA gave the work a Certificate of Merit in 1958. Source: ob-ultrasound.net Part 1 (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/history1.html).
