question: Every boundary inside the body throws some of the beam back, and those returning echoes are the entire picture - no echo, no image. What decides how much returns is the jump in acoustic impedance, a tissue's density multiplied by its sound speed. Take the commonest boundary of all, fat against muscle: 925 against 1,075 kg per cubic metre, and 1,450 against 1,590 m/s. How much of the sound striking that boundary comes back?
answer: about 1.4 per cent
choices: about 1.4 per cent
about 7.2 per cent
about 26 per cent
about 64 per cent
context: OpenStax works the case out: the intensity reflection coefficient is a = (Z2 - Z1)^2 / (Z1 + Z2)^2, and for ultrasound crossing from fat into muscle a = 0.014 - 'only 1.4% of the incident intensity is reflected, with the remaining being transmitted.' An entire ultrasound image is assembled out of that 1.4%. The mirror image is why gel exists: air's impedance is about 429 against roughly 1.6 million for tissue, which throws essentially the whole beam back. Accuracy note, because the textbook version is routinely overstated: put the published bone impedance (5.7 to 7.8 million) into the same formula and a muscle/bone boundary reflects roughly 29-41% - a lot, but NOT 'almost everything'. Bone blanks out the picture mainly by ABSORBING the beam, whereas air really does reflect nearly all of it. Source: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, section 17.7 'Ultrasound'; Z = rho x c corroborated by Wikipedia 'Acoustic impedance'.

question: Karl Dussik published pictures of the living human head from the 1940s, and for a decade the field read them as maps of the brain's fluid-filled ventricles - the most promising images anyone had. In 1952 W. Guettner and colleagues at the Siemens laboratories in Erlangen published the paper that ended them. The pattern everyone had been reading was real enough; it simply came from something other than the brain. From what?
answer: the varying thickness of the skull bone
choices: the varying thickness of the skull bone
the standing waves in the water bath
the folds of the scalp and its hair
the pulsing of the arteries in the neck
context: The paper: Guttner W., Fielder G. and Patzold J. (1952), 'Uber Ultraschallabbildungen Am Menschlichen Schadel' (On ultrasound images of the human skull), Acustica 2:148-156, out of the Siemens Laboratories at Erlangen. They showed that 'reflections within the skull and attenuation patterns produced by the skull were contributing to the attenuation pattern which Dussik had originally thought represented changes in acoustic transmissions through the cerebral ventricles.' In plain terms: a decade of pictures of the brain were pictures of bone. The honest reading is not that Dussik was foolish - it is that a promising method can produce beautiful, consistent, entirely artefactual results for years until somebody tests the assumption underneath it. The skull absorbs and reflects so strongly that sending sound straight through the head could never have worked. (Spelling note: this source prints 'Fielder'; other accounts write 'Fiedler'.) Source: ob-ultrasound.net, Karl Theodore Dussik biography (https://www.ob-ultrasound.net/dussikbio.html).

question: An ultrasound operator can drive a probe anywhere from about 1 to 18 megahertz and picks the setting for each job. Higher frequency means finer detail: you can never make out anything much smaller than one wavelength, and at 7 MHz the wavelength in tissue is only about 0.22 mm. Yet nobody scans a liver at 7 MHz - that job is done at 3 to 5 MHz, and the detail is given up on purpose. What goes wrong at 7 MHz?
answer: a 7 MHz beam is swallowed by tissue long before it gets there
choices: a 7 MHz beam is swallowed by tissue long before it gets there
a 7 MHz beam is scattered into noise by any flowing blood
a 7 MHz beam warms the tissue more than is thought safe
a 7 MHz beam fills the picture with grainy speckle noise
context: Acoustic absorption costs roughly 0.5 dB per centimetre of depth per megahertz, so a 5 MHz wave loses about 5 dB in the first centimetre and another 5 in the next; push the frequency up and the beam dies nearer the surface. Wikipedia states the trade directly: 'The attenuation of the sound wave is increased at higher frequencies, so penetration of deeper tissues necessitates a lower frequency (3-5 MHz).' OpenStax gives the other side: 'we will never observe details significantly smaller than the wavelength,' and at 7 MHz you 'can effectively scan to a depth of about 500 lambda' - around 11 cm. Resolution and reach are traded against each other in every single scan. The other honest limit: unlike a CT, image quality depends heavily on the hand holding the probe. What ultrasound has in exchange is exactly why it is the tool used on the unborn - nothing ionising ever enters the room, and randomised trials that followed children to ages 8 and 9 found no significant differences in developmental outcomes from ultrasound exposure. Sources: Wikipedia 'Medical ultrasound'; StatPearls 'Ultrasound Physics' NBK570593; OpenStax College Physics 2e 17.7; Wikipedia 'Obstetric ultrasonography'.

question: At 09:20 on 15 February 2013 a rock about 18 metres across came apart in the air over Chelyabinsk, Russia, releasing 400 to 500 kilotons -- some thirty Hiroshima bombs -- about 30 kilometres up. Nobody was killed, but 1,491 people needed treatment. What injured almost all of them?
answer: Glass from windows blown in by the shock wave
choices: Glass from windows blown in by the shock wave
Burns from the heat of the fireball above
Masonry falling from walls and chimneys
The blast wind knocking people off their feet
context: Fifty-two people needed hospital care and 311 of the injured were children -- the blast came shortly after the school day began. The shock wave damaged more than 7,200 buildings across six cities and shattered windows over an ellipse roughly 90 km long and 40 km wide along the ground track, and it partly collapsed the roof of the Traktor Ice Arena. Direct damage came to about 1 billion rubles, around 33 million dollars. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'.

question: Most of the Chelyabinsk rock never reached the ground: of some 9,000 tonnes, only four to six tonnes landed at all. The largest surviving piece punched a seven-metre hole in the ice of Lake Chebarkul. Divers raised it on 16 October 2013 and put it on a scale. What happened?
answer: It broke the scale and split into three pieces
choices: It broke the scale and split into three pieces
It read 654 kilograms and was carted off intact
It weighed a tenth of what the hole suggested
It turned out to be iron rather than stone
context: It read 654 kilograms before the scale gave way; the largest of the three resulting pieces weighs 540 kg. About a thousand fragments totalling over 1,000 kg were recovered in all. Every one of them is a splinter: Chelyabinsk was an airburst, and the body that came in had already been destroyed tens of kilometres up. Laboratory work classified the meteorite as an LL5 ordinary chondrite at shock stage S4, carrying shock-melt veins and high-pressure jadeite formed above 1700 degrees C -- scars from a collision on its parent body roughly 100 million years ago. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor' and 'Chelyabinsk meteorite'; Grokipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'.

question: Nearly 1,500 people at Chelyabinsk were cut by window glass, and almost every one of them was standing at a window when the shock wave arrived and blew it in. They were not being careless. What had brought the whole town to its windows first?
answer: The flash reached them at once, and the bang took over two minutes
choices: The flash reached them at once, and the bang took over two minutes
A small first burst drew a crowd, and a bigger one came later
The fireball took a full minute to cross the sky, and they watched
A glowing trail hung overhead for minutes after the fireball passed
context: Depending on distance, the shock wave took between 2 minutes 23 seconds and 2 minutes 57 seconds to arrive. The fireball itself was visible for roughly 30 seconds and could be made out 100 km away; twenty people afterwards reported ultraviolet burns like sunburn. You can measure the same gap yourself in the next thunderstorm: count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, then divide by three for the rough distance in kilometres. Light outran sound over Chelyabinsk, and that gap is exactly why people were hurt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; The Planetary Society, 'What was the Chelyabinsk meteor event?'.

question: By 2013 several telescope surveys were sweeping the sky for asteroids on Earth-crossing paths and had catalogued thousands of them. Not one saw the 18-metre rock that came apart over Chelyabinsk: there was no warning at all, not even minutes. Why was every asteroid-hunting telescope on Earth blind to it?
answer: It came in from the direction of the Sun, lost in the glare
choices: It came in from the direction of the Sun, lost in the glare
It sat inside the Earth's own shadow on its final approach
It was moving too fast for a telescope to hold and track
It approached over the South Pole, where no survey looks
context: Its radiant -- the direction it came from -- lay close to the Sun, so it approached out of the daylight glare, where no ground-based survey can look. About sixteen hours later the tracked 30-metre asteroid 2012 DA14 passed 27,700 km above Earth, inside the ring of geosynchronous satellites. The two objects were completely unrelated, on different orbits from different populations, and the odds of such a same-day coincidence are put near one in a hundred million. The one they were watching missed; the one nobody saw hit. Source: Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; NASA JPL, 'Additional Details on the Large Feb. 15 Fireball over Russia'.

question: On 30 June 1908 something burst high over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia, flattening the forest below. For several nights afterwards, people in Sweden and Scotland photographed each other at midnight without flashbulbs, and in Britain people read outdoors by natural light as late as 2 July. What was lighting the northern nights?
answer: About a million tonnes of fine dust, high above the clouds
choices: About a million tonnes of fine dust, high above the clouds
An unusually strong aurora, spreading south from the Arctic
The tail of a comet, passing between Earth and the Sun
Smoke from Siberian forest fires, drifting west over Europe
context: The dust was flung into the stratosphere and mesosphere -- the calm layers above our weather -- and polarisation measurements made at observatories of the day confirmed the glowing material was high, not low. Those bright nights were the first sign anywhere outside Siberia that something enormous had happened, and for years nobody in Europe connected the two. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tunguska event'; Grokipedia, 'Tunguska event'.

question: No observatory had been watching when the Chelyabinsk rock arrived, so there were none of the tracking data astronomers normally work from. Even so, within a week two astronomers at the University of Antioquia in Medellin, Colombia had published the object's speed, its path through the air, and the orbit it had followed around the Sun before it ever met Earth. What did Jorge Zuluaga and Ignacio Ferrin reconstruct all that from?
answer: Dashboard-camera video that Russian drivers keep running for insurance
choices: Dashboard-camera video that Russian drivers keep running for insurance
Seismic traces from Russian earthquake-monitoring stations nearby
Images from a weather satellite that passed overhead at the time
Radar echoes recorded by a Russian military tracking station
context: They used one camera in Revolution Square in Chelyabinsk, videos from the nearby town of Korkino, and the position of the hole punched in the ice of Lake Chebarkul, and they posted the result on 21 February 2013 -- six days after the event. The reconstructed orbit was an Apollo-type Earth-crossing path with a period near 2.1 years, from the Flora family in the inner asteroid belt, and it closely resembles the orbit of a known asteroid, 86039 (1999 NC43), raising the possibility that the two were once one body. Source: Zuluaga and Ferrin, arXiv:1302.5377; Borovicka et al., Nature 503, 235-237.

question: Chelyabinsk's energy was pinned down twice over, by two completely unrelated kinds of instrument. One was a worldwide array listening for infrasound -- sound pitched far below anything a human ear can hear -- which had been built and deployed for an entirely different job. Twenty of its forty-two stations caught the airburst, one of them in Antarctica, some 15,000 kilometres away. What had that network been built to listen for?
answer: Nuclear tests carried out in secret
choices: Nuclear tests carried out in secret
Earthquakes far out under the ocean
Volcanic eruptions in remote places
Storms gathering over the open sea
context: It was the largest signal the CTBTO's monitoring network had ever recorded, until the Hunga Tonga eruption of 2022. The waves reached stations by paths running from 500 km to 87,000 km, meaning the sound travelled more than twice around the planet before the last detection. The infrasound alone, using period-versus-yield scaling and independent of every other method, gave about 460 kilotons; the estimate combining light curves, satellite sensors and seismic ground-roll gave 500 plus or minus 100 kilotons. Two utterly different instruments, one answer -- that agreement is what turns a number into a measurement. Source: Le Pichon et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2013; Brown et al., Nature 503, 238-241.

question: Dashcam clips are shaky, uncalibrated, and pointed wherever the driver happened to be going -- useless for astronomy, on the face of it. To turn the Chelyabinsk videos into a real trajectory, scientists needed the fireball's exact direction at every instant, as seen from each camera's own viewpoint. So they travelled to the precise spots where the clips had been filmed. What did they do there?
answer: Photographed the night sky from the same spot and overlaid the stars
choices: Photographed the night sky from the same spot and overlaid the stars
Measured the height of every building that appeared in the frame
Re-filmed the whole scene with a surveyed and calibrated camera
Recorded the time showing on each camera's internal clock
context: Superimposing a night starfield on the daytime footage fixed the fireball's true position on the sky, frame by frame. They also measured the directions of the daytime shadows the fireball's light swung across the ground, a second and independent geometric handle on where that light had been. Ordinary consumer cameras, with the stars as a ruler. On the ground, Olga Popova's Russian Academy of Sciences team did the other half on foot: within a month they visited 50 villages, interviewed residents and photographed broken windows to build the damage map the energy estimate leaned on. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chelyabinsk meteor'; Scientific American, 'Chelyabinsk Eyewitnesses Help Scientists Resolve Meteor Mysteries'; Popova et al., Science 342, 1069-1073.

question: The Chelyabinsk body was about 18 metres across and weighed some 9,000 tonnes. It entered the air over Russia at 19 kilometres a second, and 45 kilometres up -- with almost the whole atmosphere still below it -- it began to break apart, then broke again some eleven more times over the next fifteen kilometres. What was tearing it up that high?
answer: The air piling up ahead of it pushed harder than the rock could hold
choices: The air piling up ahead of it pushed harder than the rock could hold
The heat of entry melted it steadily through from the outside in
The cold of the upper air cracked it the way ice cracks glass
Water frozen inside it boiled and blew the rock apart from within
context: Measured from the break-up altitudes, the body's bulk strength was only about 1 megapascal; Peter Brown's team called it 'a heavily fractured single stone'. The first major break came at 45 km, where the pressure of the onrushing air reached about 0.7 MPa, and roughly eleven more fragmentation events between 40 and 30 km, at 1 to 5 MPa, released most of the mass. A body that comes apart like that dumps nearly all its energy into a small volume of air in a fraction of a second. That is an explosion in the sky rather than an impact in the ground, and it is why such events usually leave nothing to dig up. Source: Brown et al., Nature 503, 238-241; Physics Today, 'Chelyabinsk: Portrait of an asteroid airburst'.

question: Not every arriving rock comes apart overhead. On 12 February 1947, in eastern Russia, a body came down and left more than 200 craters -- the largest 26 metres across and 6 metres deep -- from which over 23 tonnes were later recovered. Barringer Crater in Arizona was gouged out by a body of similarly modest size. What did those two have that Chelyabinsk did not?
answer: They were made of solid iron rather than stone
choices: They were made of solid iron rather than stone
They came in far more slowly than Chelyabinsk
They entered on a much steeper, near-vertical path
They were made of ice rather than solid rock
context: The 1947 fall was Sikhote-Alin, in eastern Russia, and the 23 tonnes recovered from its crater field were metal. Small stony asteroids preferentially burst before reaching the ground; small iron ones survive the passage and excavate real holes. Composition, not just size, decides whether you get a crater or an explosion in the sky. Source: Physics Today, 'Chelyabinsk: Portrait of an asteroid airburst'; Grokipedia, 'Tunguska event'.

question: Leonid Kulik reached the centre of the 1908 Siberian blast site in April 1927 -- a boat journey up the Podkamennaya Tunguska from Vanavara, then days on foot and by reindeer through swampy taiga with Evenki guides. He had come to find an iron meteorite lying in its crater. There was no crater and no meteorite. But over a zone about eight kilometres across at the very centre, he found the thing he is remembered for. What was there?
answer: Trees still standing upright, scorched and stripped of every branch
choices: Trees still standing upright, scorched and stripped of every branch
Ground fused into a sheet of glass for kilometres in every direction
A ring of water-filled pits around a low mound of broken rock
Forest floor buried under a metre of fine grey ash and cinders
context: Kulik called it the telegraph-pole forest. Farther out the trunks lay flat in a vast radial pattern pointing away from the centre, about 2,150 square kilometres of taiga in a butterfly-shaped scar with a 70-kilometre wingspan. A blast directly overhead pushes straight down on the trees beneath it and strips their branches without toppling them; only farther out does the wave arrive slanting enough to knock trunks over. The absence Kulik came home with was itself the evidence. He led four expeditions across the 1920s and 1930s and never found the object; he volunteered for the militia in the Second World War, German troops captured him, and he died of typhus in a prisoner-of-war camp on 24 April 1942, aged 58. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tunguska event' and 'Leonid Kulik'; Linda Hall Library, 'Leonid Kulik -- Scientist of the Day'; NASA, '115 Years Ago: The Tunguska Asteroid Impact Event'.

question: In 1965 Willard Libby -- the Nobel laureate who invented radiocarbon dating -- published a proposal in Nature, with Clyde Cowan and C. R. Atluri, that the 1908 Tunguska blast had been a lump of antimatter annihilating in the air. It was a wild idea, and they did the thing that makes a wild idea testable: they said what it must have left behind, then went and looked. Annihilation should have raised the amount of carbon-14 in the air that year by about seven per cent. Where did they go looking for that spike?
answer: In the yearly growth rings of living trees
choices: In the yearly growth rings of living trees
In ice cores drilled from the Greenland sheet
In peat cut from the bogs around the blast site
In museum air samples sealed before 1908
context: They measured tree rings including those of a 300-year-old Douglas fir in Tucson, and found only about 1 per cent for 1909; careful measurements on a tree nearer the blast showed no rise at all. The hypothesis died by the test its own authors had designed. A second wrong idea got the same treatment: in 1973 the physicists A. A. Jackson IV and Michael P. Ryan Jr. proposed in Nature that a tiny primordial black hole had punched through the Earth and out again, which predicted an exit shock wave over the North Atlantic -- and in 1974 Beasley and Tinsley replied that the microbarographs had recorded no such wave. Source: Cowan, Atluri and Libby, Nature 206, 861-865; Nature 208, 772 and Nature 212, 1226; Jackson and Ryan, Nature 245, 88-89; Beasley and Tinsley, Nature 250, 555.

question: Tunguska has been worked on for well over a century. Seismographs at Irkutsk, a thousand kilometres away, logged it at about magnitude 5.0; ordinary weather barographs -- pressure recorders -- in Germany, Britain, Croatia and Washington, D.C. traced its pressure wave twice around the globe; and about 2,150 square kilometres of flattened forest have been mapped on the ground and from the air. Where does the energy figure stand today?
answer: Published estimates still range from about 3 to 50 megatons
choices: Published estimates still range from about 3 to 50 megatons
Published estimates have converged on 10 megatons since 1960
Published estimates have narrowed to between 12 and 14 megatons
Published estimates agree on 30 megatons from the forest area
context: Recent calculations give 3 to 5 megatons, a 2019 paper argues for 20 to 30, and the figure most often quoted in the middle is 10 to 15. There is no settled number. Nor is there a settled object: no fragment of the impactor has ever been confirmed, only microscopic magnetite and silicate spherules and iridium anomalies in peat layers dated to 1908, and whether it was a stony asteroid or a comet is still argued -- a 2001 study by Paolo Farinella and colleagues put the odds near 83 per cent asteroidal against 17 per cent cometary, which is a good bet rather than a settled answer. The largest impact event in recorded history, and no one yet knows how big it was or what it was made of. Note also that the famous '80 million trees' is a preliminary guess, not a count: it came from multiplying tree density by an area overestimated fourfold. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tunguska event'; Grokipedia, 'Tunguska event'.

question: A physics teacher pours liquid nitrogen over a small black ceramic tile on the desk, sets a rare-earth magnet just above it, lets go -- and the magnet does not fall. It hangs in the air over the tile, held in place. What kind of material has she just cooled?
answer: a superconductor
choices: a superconductor
a lightning rod
an electromagnet
a solar cell
context: This is the classic classroom demonstration of the Meissner effect: a superconductor cooled below its critical temperature expels magnetic field and locks a magnet in place above it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissner_effect

question: Once that same black tile is cold enough, an electric current inside it behaves in a way no ordinary copper wire ever manages -- no heating, no fading, no waste of any kind, no matter how long it runs. What value does the tile's electrical resistance take?
answer: exactly zero ohms
choices: exactly zero ohms
roughly one ohm
about one milliohm
close to copper's
context: The defining property of a superconductor below its critical temperature: current runs with no resistance at all -- a hard cliff, not a slope. Onnes phrased it 'practically zero'; the modern measurement is zero within any experimental limit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity

question: Leiden, the Netherlands, 1911. A physicist has just become the first person on Earth able to make helium cold enough to be a liquid, at about 4.2 K. He dips a solid mercury wire in it and finds the wire's resistance not merely small but gone. Whose name is on that notebook entry?
answer: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes
choices: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes
Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen
Antoine Henri Becquerel
Pieter Zeeman
context: Onnes had liquefied helium in 1908, giving Leiden the world's coldest laboratory. His 8 April 1911 notebook entry reads 'Kwik nagenoeg nul' -- 'Mercury practically zero'. He won the 1913 Nobel Prize. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heike_Kamerlingh_Onnes and Physics Today Sep 2010.

question: At IBM's Zurich research lab in Ruschlikon in 1986, two scientists tested a brittle ceramic of exactly the sort metal physicists had written off -- a lanthanum-barium-copper oxide -- and found it superconducted at 35 K. They shared the Nobel Prize just one year later, the shortest gap between discovery and Nobel in physics history. Which pair?
answer: Georg Bednorz and Alex Muller
choices: Georg Bednorz and Alex Muller
John Bardeen and Leon Cooper
Brian Josephson and Alexei Abrikosov
Werner Heisenberg and Max Born
context: Bednorz and Muller's paper in Zeitschrift fuer Physik B (June 1986) opened the cuprate era; the 1987 Nobel followed within about nineteen months. Sources: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1987/press-release/ and https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2023/03/bednorz-muller-high-temperature-superconductivity

question: Within months of that IBM breakthrough, Maw-Kuen Wu at Alabama and Ching-Wu 'Paul' Chu at Houston swapped one element into the recipe and pushed the critical temperature to about 93 K. That jump crossed a practical line -- the coolant needed was suddenly something a working lab could pour out of a Dewar flask. Which cheap coolant?
answer: liquid nitrogen
choices: liquid nitrogen
liquid helium
liquid hydrogen
liquid neon
context: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K and costs less per litre than milk; before YBCO, working superconductors needed scarce liquid helium at 4 K. Source: https://ethw.org/First-Hand:Discovery_of_Superconductivity_at_93_K_in_YBCO

question: Almost forty years after Bednorz and Muller opened the copper-oxide era, physicists have proposed and argued through dozens of pairing models for those ceramics. What is the current status of the theory of how they superconduct?
answer: No accepted mechanism yet exists
choices: No accepted mechanism yet exists
BCS phonon pairing was confirmed
String theory settled it in 1998
Bose-Einstein condensation explains it
context: The tiny or inverted oxygen isotope effect argues against a purely phonon mechanism; the pseudogap and stripe phases remain openly debated. The materials sit inside working MRI magnets and power grids while the microscopic theory is unsolved. Source: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0953-8984/13/29/202

question: On 22 July 2023 two Korean chemists, Sukbae Lee and Ji-Hoon Kim, posted arXiv preprints claiming a copper-doped lead apatite superconducted at room temperature and ordinary pressure; a video of a fragment tilting up off a magnet went around the world. About three weeks later, a Max Planck group in Stuttgart had grown clean single crystals of the compound by floating-zone growth. What did those pristine samples turn out to be?
answer: transparent purple insulators
choices: transparent purple insulators
genuine but weak superconductors
high-Tc superconductors above 200 K
ordinary metallic conductors
context: The Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research reported the pure crystals as transparent purple insulators with resistance in the millions of ohms. The apparent resistance drop in the original mixed samples came from a copper sulfide (Cu2S) impurity whose 385 K structural transition mimicked a superconducting drop; the partial lift came from ferromagnetic contamination. Science did not merely debate the claim -- it made the stuff. Sources: https://physicsworld.com/a/room-temperature-superconductor-lk-99-fails-replication-tests/ and https://www.sciencealert.com/lk-99-is-no-radical-superconductor-after-all-scientists-confirm

question: In 2019 Mikhail Eremets's group at the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz confirmed superconductivity in lanthanum decahydride (LaH10) at 250 K -- only 23 K short of the freezing point of water. Reporters called it a room-temperature superconductor. Why is that reporting misleading?
answer: It only worked near 170 GPa in a diamond anvil cell
choices: It only worked near 170 GPa in a diamond anvil cell
The measurement was later retracted
The Meissner effect was never seen
The temperature was in Celsius, not Kelvin
context: 170 gigapascals is roughly seven times the pressure at the centre of Earth's core; the sample sits between two diamond tips smaller than a pinhead. Hydride superconductivity is real and its temperature is genuinely remarkable, but it is not 'room-temperature' in any practical sense until the pressure comes down by orders of magnitude. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1201-8

question: The University of Rochester physicist Ranga Dias published two room-temperature-superconductor claims in Nature -- October 2020 and March 2023. Both were withdrawn (the second on 7 November 2023, at the request of eight of his own eleven co-authors) and a 2024 Rochester investigation found he had fabricated data. Which lone theorist first flagged that his published curves looked too smooth to be real measurements, and was brushed off for over a year?
answer: Jorge Hirsch
choices: Jorge Hirsch
Brian Josephson
Steven Weinberg
Frank Wilczek
context: Hirsch, a condensed-matter theorist at UC San Diego, campaigned for the raw data for nearly thirteen months and pointed out that some of Dias's data resembled a smooth polynomial curve -- impossible for noisy lab measurements -- and looked suspiciously similar to figures from a 2009 paper on europium. The co-authors' letter accompanying the 2023 retraction said the paper 'does not accurately reflect the provenance of the investigated materials'. Sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00716-2 and https://physics.aps.org/articles/v16/40

question: In the 1920s the Viennese biologist Paul Kammerer said he had proved a serious open claim - that acquired traits can be inherited. His evidence was a change he said had appeared on male midwife toads and passed to their offspring. What did he say had appeared?
answer: dark, rough breeding pads on the fingers
choices: dark, rough breeding pads on the fingers
extra webbing between the hind toes
bright warning patches along the back
hardened claws for gripping wet rocks
context: Kammerer forced the toads to breed in water rather than on land, and reported that the males developed 'nuptial pads' - the dark, rasp-like grip patches other frogs use to hold a mate. If real, that would have been Lamarckism: environment writing itself into the germ line. It was a serious claim in a live debate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kammerer

question: In 1926 the American herpetologist G. K. Noble travelled to Vienna and put the last surviving midwife-toad specimen under a microscope. He reported his finding in Nature. What had Paul Kammerer's dark nuptial pads actually been made of?
answer: India ink injected under the skin
choices: India ink injected under the skin
a natural pigment triggered by tank temperature
a shellac coating brushed on before display
silver nitrate deposits from fixative chemicals
context: The microscope showed the pigment sitting where no living pigment sits. Noble's Nature paper was the ink. Kammerer blamed a lab assistant, then died by suicide six weeks later. The first move in every case that follows is the same one Noble made: someone looks at the physical thing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kammerer

question: In March 1974 the dermatologist William Summerlin at Memorial Sloan-Kettering presented white laboratory mice bearing dark skin grafts he said had been accepted from unrelated donors without immunosuppression - a transplant breakthrough if real. A lab assistant did one specific thing that ended it. What?
answer: wiped a dark patch with alcohol and the colour lifted off
choices: wiped a dark patch with alcohol and the colour lifted off
checked the genotype and found the graft was the mouse's own skin
photographed the mice weekly and found the patches had shifted
traced the shipping records and found no donor mice had arrived
context: Summerlin had coloured the mice with a felt-tip pen. The five-person Sloan-Kettering committee led by C. Chester Stock found his conduct incompatible with science, and 'painting the mice' entered the language of research fraud. A cotton swab did what no committee had done. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Summerlin

question: The American psychologist Leon Kamin read across the British psychologist Cyril Burt's published twin-IQ studies in the early 1970s and noticed something about the correlation coefficients across the sequence of papers. What did the numbers do?
answer: they stayed identical to three decimal places as new twins were added
choices: they stayed identical to three decimal places as new twins were added
they climbed steadily upward as the sample size grew
they alternated exactly between two fixed values across papers
they matched the correlations of an unrelated German study
context: Adding fresh subjects to a real sample perturbs correlation coefficients in the fourth or fifth decimal at minimum; identity at three places across added waves is arithmetically impossible. The tell was not a beaker or a swab this time - it was a column of numbers added up by hand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Burt

question: In 1976 the journalist Oliver Gillie of the Sunday Times went hunting for two people named on Cyril Burt's twin-IQ papers as his research assistants - Margaret Howard and J. Conway. What did he find when he looked?
answer: no trace of them at University College or anywhere else
choices: no trace of them at University College or anywhere else
both had died before the studies they were credited with
both worked at a rival lab and denied any involvement
both had signed statements accusing Burt of fabrication
context: Gillie could not put Howard or Conway on any staff list, student register or address between 1914 and 1976. Names on paper are cheap; names attached to human beings are checkable. That is what Gillie checked. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Burt

question: In 1979 the psychologist Leslie Hearnshaw finished the authorised biography of Cyril Burt he had been commissioned by the family to write - a book everyone had expected to defend him. What did Hearnshaw conclude about Burt's post-war twin-IQ data?
answer: that they were unreliable or invented
choices: that they were unreliable or invented
that they were sound and the critics had misread them
that they were lost in wartime and could not be judged
that they had been faked by his assistants without his knowledge
context: Hearnshaw had full access to Burt's papers and diaries and started as a sympathetic biographer. His verdict was the tell that mattered most: the man's own defender, reading the man's own files, concluded the post-war numbers could not be trusted. Robert Joynson (1989) and Ronald Fletcher (1991) later argued the case was overstated, and independent twin studies by others have since found broadly similar heritability figures - so whether Burt's own papers were faked remains genuinely disputed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Burt

question: From 2007 the biostatisticians Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes at MD Anderson tried to reproduce Duke University's much-praised genomic predictors of which chemotherapy would work for a given cancer patient. They rebuilt the whole analysis from the raw files. What did they find in the data?
answer: gene lists shifted by one row and patient samples mislabelled
choices: gene lists shifted by one row and patient samples mislabelled
batches of missing patients silently dropped from the training set
predictor genes hand-picked to hit a pre-set clinical target
the same tumour sample entered twice under different codes
context: Duke had already opened clinical trials assigning cancer patients to treatments based on the predictor. Baggerly and Coombes did not catch a lie - they found errors, in public writing, over three years. The trials were suspended in 2010 and eleven papers were eventually retracted. Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/deception-at-duke-fraud-in-cancer-care/

question: The Duke genomic-predictor mess had been argued about for three years when the final push came in July 2010 - not from a statistician, but from a small trade paper called The Cancer Letter. What had its editor Paul Goldberg discovered about the lead researcher, Anil Potti?
answer: he had claimed on grant applications a Rhodes Scholarship he never held
choices: he had claimed on grant applications a Rhodes Scholarship he never held
he had a second job at a private cancer clinic he had not disclosed
he had failed his oncology board certification twice under a former name
he had co-founded a company selling the very predictors he was validating
context: The Rhodes Trust had no record of him. Duke suspended Potti within days; he lost a $729,000 American Cancer Society grant and resigned in November 2010. The through-line of this ladder: an ink stain, an alcohol swab, a column of correlations added up by hand, an analysis rebuilt from raw files, a scholarship register checked. Not one authority announcing the truth. Every one somebody checking a physical thing. Source: https://cancerletter.com/the-cancer-letter/20100716_1/

question: William Gilbert, physician to Queen Elizabeth I, wanted to explain why ship compasses point the way they do. In 1600 he took a chunk of lodestone and carved it into a shape he could walk a tiny compass across. What shape did he carve it into?
answer: A sphere
choices: A sphere
A flat disk
A long bar
A horseshoe
context: He called the little globe a terrella, Latin for 'little Earth'. On its surface a tiny compass did exactly what a ship's compass does at sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrella.

question: London compass-maker Robert Norman balanced a magnetised needle on a pivot in 1581. On deck a ship's compass hides this, because it is set to swing horizontally. Freed from that constraint in Norman's workshop, what did the needle do?
answer: Dipped its north end toward the floor
choices: Dipped its north end toward the floor
Spun in slow full circles
Pointed exactly at the Pole Star
Vibrated in time with the tide
context: Norman wrote it up in The Newe Attractive. Gilbert then reproduced the dip on his terrella and showed the angle grows the closer you get to the poles: a bench model that predicted a real shipboard measurement. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dip.

question: Rubbed amber picks up scraps of straw for a moment and then quits; lodestone pulls only iron, but pulls forever and points. Everyone before William Gilbert had lumped these together as one force. He split them, and coined a brand-new Latin name for the amber-and-straw kind. What word did he coin?
answer: Electricus
choices: Electricus
Magneticus
Sideralis
Attractivus
context: Gilbert built the word from the Greek elektron, meaning amber. It took another 220 years, until Oersted's needle jumped near a current-carrying wire in 1820, for the two forces to be joined back together. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gilbert_(physician).

question: One piece of sailor lore William Gilbert dismantled in De Magnete was the claim that a common kitchen ingredient, if rubbed on a compass, would destroy its power. Gilbert put the ingredient on his own needle and watched it work perfectly. What was the ingredient?
answer: Garlic
choices: Garlic
Vinegar
Salt
Honey
context: The claim went back to ancient natural histories and was still repeated in Gilbert's day. He treated it the modern way: he tested it, and it failed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Magnete.

question: Three centuries after Gilbert, the Norwegian physicist Kristian Birkeland built a second terrella. He put a magnetised sphere inside a vacuum chamber, painted its surface so it would glow, and fired something at it. Rings of light appeared around its poles. What did he fire at the sphere?
answer: A beam of electrons
choices: A beam of electrons
A jet of steam
A stream of iron filings
A beam of visible sunlight
context: Cathode rays, in the vocabulary of the day. The glowing rings looked like the aurora, and that was Birkeland's point: he thought he was watching his model do what the sky does. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristian_Birkeland.

question: Kristian Birkeland argued the aurora was caused by charged particles from the Sun, funnelled onto the polar sky. The leading British geophysicist Sydney Chapman led an objection that seemed to sink the whole idea for fifty years. What was the objection?
answer: Currents cannot cross the vacuum of space
choices: Currents cannot cross the vacuum of space
The Sun is too cold to shed electrons
The aurora comes from below, not above
Magnetised needles show no polar dip
context: The consensus of the day held vacuum as an insulator, so no solar circuit could reach the sky. Birkeland died in Tokyo on 15 June 1917 without an answer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristian_Birkeland.

question: Kristian Birkeland died in 1917 with his aurora theory still called crank science. In 1967 a US Navy satellite flew straight through the auroral zone carrying instruments to sample the region directly, and settled the argument in his favour. What did the satellite detect?
answer: Electric currents aligned with Earth's field
choices: Electric currents aligned with Earth's field
A ring of iron dust circling Earth
Micro-lightning between clouds and space
A layer of ozone glowing pale green
context: They are now called Birkeland currents. The auroral glow is the visible bottom end of a circuit reaching most of the way to the Sun. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristian_Birkeland.

question: Volcanic rock freezes a copy of Earth's magnetic field into itself as it cools, and stacked lava flows are Earth's own tape recording of its field. That recording shows the field has fully swapped north and south many times. How long ago was the most recent full flip?
answer: About 780,000 years ago
choices: About 780,000 years ago
About 12,000 years ago
About 65 million years ago
About 4,500 years ago
context: The event is called the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal. When the next flip will come cannot yet be predicted: reversals look statistically random on geological timescales and the underlying mechanism is not settled. The magnetic north pole is moving fast enough to notice, though: since 1970 its drift has sped up from about 9 km per year to over 50 km per year, heading from the Canadian Arctic toward Siberia. That drift, and the aurora, are the two pieces of the story you can watch personally. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomagnetic_reversal ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_magnetic_pole.

question: In 1913 at Marseilles, Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson measured the Sun's spectrum against a glowing body at about 5,500 K. The curves matched everywhere except in the ultraviolet: below 310 nm the sunlight was not there. Something was eating that band. What had the two physicists just detected?
answer: an invisible gas high in the atmosphere
choices: an invisible gas high in the atmosphere
a defect ground into their glass prism
sunspot activity dimming the Sun
the boundary of Earth's magnetic field
context: The shape of the missing-light spectrum would soon be matched to the lab absorption fingerprint of a single chemical -- ozone. Fabry and Buisson had detected an invisible gas overhead by the light it removed. Source: tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.3137/ao.460101.

question: The ozone shield stops the wavelengths of sunlight that would sterilise the surface -- so you might guess it must be a huge, thick blanket. It is not. Gather every ozone molecule above your head and squeeze it down to sea-level pressure -- it forms a surprisingly thin film. About how thick would that squeezed film be?
answer: about three millimetres
choices: about three millimetres
about three centimetres
about thirty centimetres
about three metres
context: Fabry and Buisson calculated this figure in 1913. The Dobson unit later baked it in: 100 DU is exactly 1 mm of pure ozone at sea-level pressure, and the global average column is about 300 DU. Sources: tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.3137/ao.460101; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobson_unit.

question: The Oxford meteorologist Gordon Dobson built the ground instrument that measures the whole overhead column of ozone by comparing two ultraviolet wavelengths in ordinary daylight. Between 1928 and 1958 he did the thing that actually mattered -- what did Dobson build besides the instrument itself?
answer: a permanent worldwide network of matching stations
choices: a permanent worldwide network of matching stations
a set of matching detectors flown on high-altitude balloons
a chemical library of stratospheric samples returned by rocket
a theoretical model of ozone photochemistry from first principles
context: Dobson placed spectrophotometers at Arosa, Table Mountain (California), Helwan (Egypt), Kodaikanal (India), Christchurch (NZ) and many more; the network -- not any single instrument -- is his monument. One of its stations at Halley Bay was installed for the International Geophysical Year of 1957. Source: collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co54435.

question: Twice a day, the Bay of Fundy in eastern Canada rises and falls by as much as 16 metres -- five storeys of water -- on a timetable printed weeks in advance. What clock schedules that rise and fall?
answer: The gravity of the passing Moon
choices: The gravity of the passing Moon
The prevailing winds off the Atlantic
The current of the great Gulf Stream
The rotation of Earth on its axis alone
context: The Bay of Fundy holds the world's largest tidal range: on a flood tide roughly 160 billion tonnes of seawater flow in -- more than four times the combined flow of every freshwater river on Earth in the same six hours. The Moon does the scheduling; the Bay's funnel shape and 12.5-hour natural sloshing period do the amplifying. Sources: bayoffundy.com/about/highest-tides ; noaa.gov/ocean/fundy-max

question: On a beach beside the Bay of Fundy, a tourist watches the water pull far out at dawn and rush back by midday. If they camped for a full lunar day and watched carefully, how many complete high tides would the sea deliver?
answer: Two, roughly twelve hours apart
choices: Two, roughly twelve hours apart
One, at the same time each morning
Four, one every six hours
Six, roughly one every four hours
context: Most coasts see two high tides in a lunar day (about 24 hours and 50 minutes long, because the Moon has moved on in its orbit) with a low in between. The two highs come from a tidal bulge on the near side of Earth AND a matching one on the far side -- and the far-side bulge is one of the finest puzzles in classical physics, one that even Galileo got wrong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide

question: Galileo Galilei's 1632 Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems named the tides as his STRONGEST proof of the Copernican view. He explicitly mocked Kepler's suggestion that the Moon pulled the seas as occult superstition. What did Galileo claim actually causes high and low tides?
answer: Water sloshing in its basin as the Earth spins and orbits
choices: Water sloshing in its basin as the Earth spins and orbits
Water flung outward by the Earth's daily spin toward the equator
Water rocked back and forth by the Earth's yearly orbit around the Sun
Water expanded by the Sun's heat as the Earth turns beneath it
context: Galileo's mistake is the loudest in his career: he had watched water slosh in the barges of Venice and generalised the picture to the whole ocean. Kepler, whom Galileo mocked, had already correctly guessed the Moon was doing the pulling. This is why the ladder is here at all -- a scientific hero being publicly wrong about his best evidence is the sharpest reminder that even the greatest names are checked by the TEST, not their reputation. Sources: pbs.org/wgbh/nova/galileo/mistake.html ; intellectualmathematics.com/blog/galileos-theory-of-tides

question: The tide has a second high on the FAR side of Earth at the same moment as the near one, and a once-popular textbook explanation blamed centrifugal force from Earth-Moon rotation. That explanation is wrong. What actually creates the far-side bulge?
answer: The Moon pulls the solid Earth harder than the far water, so the far water is left behind
choices: The Moon pulls the solid Earth harder than the far water, so the far water is left behind
The Moon's pull curves around the planet and reaches the far side directly
The Sun's pull on the far side matches and reinforces the Moon's near-side pull
Water compressed by the near-side bulge is squeezed out and rises opposite it
context: Tides come from a GRADIENT, not a force. The Moon's gravity weakens with distance, so the water on the near side is pulled toward the Moon more than the solid Earth, and the solid Earth is pulled more than the far water. Subtract Earth's motion, and the near water bulges toward the Moon while the far water bulges away from it. Centrifugal accounts confuse the rotating reference frame with the underlying cause -- the two bulges are BOTH the Moon's gravity, seen as a difference. Sources: wtamu.edu/~cbaird/sq/2012/12/14 ; askanastronomer.org (near-far bulge explainer)

question: Tide tables give the biggest tides each month a name that puzzles English speakers: SPRING tides. What does 'spring' actually mean in this term?
answer: The verb, meaning to leap or spring up
choices: The verb, meaning to leap or spring up
The season, when the Sun's angle steepens
A fresh-water spring opening under the seabed
A coiled spring, matching the shape of the wave crest
context: Spring tides happen TWICE a month, all year round, whenever the Sun and Moon are aligned. The word is the ordinary English verb -- to spring up, to leap -- not the season. Neap tides, at right angles, get their name from an Old English word for scanty or nipped. Source: cosmicave.org/course/astronomy-of-planets/mod3/newtons-explanation-of-tides

question: Earth's rotation drags its tidal bulge slightly ahead of the Moon, and the bulge's own gravity tugs the Moon forward in its orbit -- so the Moon is spiralling outward about 3.8 centimetres every year, and Earth's day is lengthening about 1.7 milliseconds per century. That number is a direct measurement, not a model. What tool makes the measurement possible?
answer: Laser pulses bounced off Apollo retroreflectors still on the Moon
choices: Laser pulses bounced off Apollo retroreflectors still on the Moon
Radio signals timed across the Moon's shadow during eclipses
Optical parallax of the Moon against distant background stars
Gravity measured by tide gauges around the world's coasts
context: Apollo 11, 14, and 15 crews left corner-cube retroreflectors on the lunar surface; astronomers on Earth fire laser pulses at them and time the round trip to millimetre precision. Five decades of Lunar Laser Ranging give the recession as 3.83 cm per year, uncertainty about 0.09 mm. Every Moon-landing skeptic is met with the same clean answer: the mirrors are still on the Moon and still bouncing back light. It is a running scientific test, not an argument from authority. Sources: eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/SEhelp/ApolloLaser.html ; eos.org/features/seeing-the-light

question: A patient finishes strong antibiotics for a chest infection and days later comes down with a raging colon infection from Clostridioides difficile. The bug had been living in the gut all along in small numbers. What did the antibiotics do that let it take over?
answer: Emptied out the neighbours that had kept it in check
choices: Emptied out the neighbours that had kept it in check
Weakened the immune cells that attacked C. diff directly
Damaged the colon lining and gave the bacteria an opening
Made the gut too acidic for the other resident bacteria
context: C. diff is caused by a VACANCY, not by an arrival. The commonest trigger for the infection is the treatment for a different infection. This is the mechanism that makes the disease so hard to break with more antibiotics.

question: In November 1958 the Denver surgeon Ben Eiseman had four critically ill patients whose colon linings were sloughing off from pseudomembranous enterocolitis. Nothing conventional was working, and they were going to die. He and his colleagues published the case in the journal Surgery. What did they give the four patients?
answer: Enemas made from a healthy donor's stool
choices: Enemas made from a healthy donor's stool
Massive intravenous doses of penicillin
Radiation aimed at the inflamed section of colon
A blood transfusion from a recovered patient
context: All four recovered rapidly. The paper appeared as 'Fecal enema as an adjunct in the treatment of pseudomembranous enterocolitis' in Surgery, 1958. The idea then sat almost unused for fifty years, not because it failed but because of disgust.

question: In Amsterdam, Els van Nood and colleagues ran the trial that finally settled whether donor faeces could beat the best available antibiotic for recurrent C. diff. They compared vancomycin against a single infusion of donor stool threaded through a nasal tube down past the stomach. Where did the tube's tip actually release the donor material?
answer: Into the duodenum, the first bend of the small intestine
choices: Into the duodenum, the first bend of the small intestine
Into the caecum, the pouch where the large intestine begins
Into the ileum, the last stretch before the large intestine
Into the jejunum, the middle third of the small intestine
context: The nasoduodenal infusion put the new community upstream so it could seed the whole gut. About 81 per cent of the infusion patients were cured by a single treatment. The paper appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine on 31 January 2013.

question: In December 2022 the FDA licensed the first stool-derived product ever approved as an actual drug in the United States: a rectally-administered treatment for recurrent C. diff called Rebyota. Four months later, in April 2023, a second product followed. It came in a form most patients would find enormously easier to accept. What form did the second approval take?
answer: An oral capsule of purified bacterial spores
choices: An oral capsule of purified bacterial spores
A chewable tablet of freeze-dried whole stool
An intravenous drip of filtered bacterial extract
A nasal spray of live cultured bacteria
context: The product is called Vowst; the FDA licensed it on 26 April 2023 as the first oral fecal microbiota therapy. The whole journey from repulsive folk cure to prescribable medicine ran through one randomised trial.

question: Faecal transplants cure recurrent C. diff in over 80 per cent of patients on the first try, and the successful trials sent researchers rushing to try FMT for obesity, autism, inflammatory bowel disease and depression. Those follow-on results have been far less clear. Beyond mixed results, what does the science still not know about how FMT works?
answer: Which specific microbes in the donor stool are doing the healing
choices: Which specific microbes in the donor stool are doing the healing
Whether the donor's own gut community remains intact afterward
How long the transplanted community continues to protect the recipient
Whether children respond to FMT differently than adults do
context: The purified-spore products like Vowst are partly an attempt to answer this: strip the mixture down to specific spores and see which are enough. Donor screening also genuinely matters, because transmitted organisms have caused serious harm in FMT recipients.

question: The closest known bat-coronavirus relative of SARS-CoV-2 is a virus called RaTG13, whose genome matches SARS-CoV-2 across about 96 percent of its length. Along that match there is one puzzling gap: RaTG13 does not have the piece of code that lets furin cut the spike at all. How LONG is the piece of RNA present in SARS-CoV-2 at this spot and missing in RaTG13?
answer: 12 nucleotides, coding four amino acids
choices: 12 nucleotides, coding four amino acids
24 nucleotides, coding eight amino acids
36 nucleotides, coding twelve amino acids
60 nucleotides, coding twenty amino acids
context: It is the only insertion larger than three nucleotides separating the two genomes. Twelve letters, one small insert, and a huge difference in how the virus behaves in a human airway. Sources: Insertion-and-Deletion Mutations between SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, and RaTG13 (PMC 2022); Frontiers in Virology 2022.

question: A furin cleavage site is not by itself an engineering smoking gun -- several wild coronaviruses carry one in their spike. So what is the specific anomaly about SARS-CoV-2's site?
answer: It is absent from every one of the virus's own nearest wild cousins
choices: It is absent from every one of the virus's own nearest wild cousins
It sits inside a different subunit of the spike than any other coronavirus's does
It uses a run of four arginines rather than the usual two
It is the longest polybasic insert of any known virus
context: The sarbecovirus subgroup contains SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2 and hundreds of bat viruses. Sampling in Yunnan, Laos and elsewhere has turned up more than two hundred sarbecoviruses; RaTG13, the Laotian BANAL-52, BANAL-103 and BANAL-236, and the pangolin coronaviruses all lack the site. Other coronaviruses outside the sarbecovirus group (HKU1, MERS-CoV) do carry S1/S2 cleavage motifs -- the oddity is local absence in the nearest known relatives, not universal presence. Sources: Temmam et al. 2022 (Nature); Chan and Zhan 2022 (Molecular Biology and Evolution).

question: Thomas Peacock and colleagues at Imperial College tested what the twelve-letter insert actually DOES. They built a version of SARS-CoV-2 with the insert deleted and set up ferrets in adjacent cages, one infected and one clean, and watched. What did the stripped-down virus do?
answer: It shed much less virus and barely reached the clean ferrets in the next cage
choices: It shed much less virus and barely reached the clean ferrets in the next cage
It shed just as much virus but stopped reaching the clean ferrets by air
It reached the clean ferrets normally but no longer produced serious disease
It grew fine in the nose but not deeper in the lung tissue
context: The Peacock 2021 study (Nature Microbiology) showed that the small insert is a large part of what made SARS-CoV-2 spread the way it did. It changes tissue tropism toward the upper airway and boosts airborne shedding without changing receptor binding. Sources: Peacock et al. 2021.

question: Genetic code is redundant: the amino acid arginine can be written using six different three-letter codons. In bat sarbecoviruses and in SARS-CoV-2's own genome, one of those six codons is chosen for only about five percent of arginines. Right inside SARS-CoV-2's furin cleavage site, the TWO arginines side by side are BOTH spelled with that same rare codon, back to back. Which codon is it?
answer: CGG
choices: CGG
AGA
CGU
AGG
context: It is the only CGG-CGG doublet anywhere in the SARS-CoV-2 genome. CGG is common in human-codon-optimized laboratory expression constructs and rare in bat coronaviruses. The oddity is suggestive, not proof; natural CGG runs do occur in mammalian viruses. Sources: Sirotkin and Sirotkin 2021 (ACS Med Chem Lett); Dilucca et al. 2020 (Virology Journal).

question: In March 2018, more than a year before COVID, a grant proposal called DEFUSE landed at the Pentagon's DARPA research agency. It was written by EcoHealth Alliance together with Ralph Baric's coronavirus lab at the University of North Carolina and the Wuhan Institute of Virology. DARPA declined to fund it and the document sat unread by the public until it leaked in 2021. What did DEFUSE propose to do?
answer: Add human-adapted cleavage sites to bat coronavirus spikes and test the result in the lab
choices: Add human-adapted cleavage sites to bat coronavirus spikes and test the result in the lab
Vaccinate wild bat colonies across Yunnan to break the sarbecovirus transmission chain
Screen human blood banks across southern China for prior sarbecovirus exposure
Sequence field samples only, with no laboratory work on any live coronavirus at all
context: DARPA rejected the proposal on biosafety grounds, so this specific experiment was PROPOSED, not funded. The document surfaced via a leak in September 2021, three years after submission. DEFUSE also proposed assembling synthetic viruses in six genome segments and screening for spikes adapted to human receptors. Sources: The Intercept September 2021; US Right To Know DEFUSE archive.

question: RaTG13, the bat virus the world now compares SARS-CoV-2 against, did not come from a routine field survey. It came from bat guano that a Wuhan Institute team collected in 2013 inside a mineshaft in Mojiang, Yunnan, where the year before six miners had gone in to clean out the droppings. What happened to those six MINERS in 2012?
answer: All six developed severe pneumonia and three of them died
choices: All six developed severe pneumonia and three of them died
All six recovered within a week and returned to work
None of the six ever showed symptoms; only their families fell ill
The six were quarantined but never sequenced or reported
context: The illness was documented in a 2013 Chinese Master's thesis that identified a SARS-like coronavirus from horseshoe bats as the likely cause. The full RaTG13 genome sat unpublished for years and was only deposited in GenBank on January 27, 2020, weeks after SARS-CoV-2 was sequenced. Sources: Rahalkar and Bahulikar 2020 (Frontiers in Public Health); Wikipedia RaTG13 entry.

question: When SARS-CoV-2 is grown in Vero E6, the most common laboratory cell line for coronavirus work, multiple published studies have watched what happens to the twelve-letter insert across successive passages. What have they actually seen?
answer: It is repeatedly LOST through in-frame deletions and point mutations
choices: It is repeatedly LOST through in-frame deletions and point mutations
It is repeatedly LENGTHENED by an extra polybasic stretch each passage
It is faithfully copied at first, then tandemly duplicated by the tenth passage
It migrates from the S1/S2 boundary down into the S2 subunit
context: Davidson et al. 2020 (Genome Medicine) and later work on Calu-3 cells both showed the site disappears when the virus is grown in cells missing the TMPRSS2 protease. That is why no published coronavirus passaging experiment has ever produced a furin site DE NOVO in a virus that lacked one to begin with -- which is the single strongest natural-origin objection to a lab-leak account of the twelve letters. The counter-example is loud, and it is why the anomaly stays unresolved rather than settled either way. Sources: Davidson et al. 2020; Frutos et al. 2023 (Journal of Virology).

question: Five years on, review papers by researchers on BOTH sides of the origin debate -- Harrison and Sachs 2022, Frutos et al. 2023 -- reach the same one-line description of where these twelve letters came from. What do they say?
answer: An unexplained anomaly whose origin no one has yet demonstrated
choices: An unexplained anomaly whose origin no one has yet demonstrated
A recombination remnant from a bat coronavirus already deposited in GenBank
A relic from a much older ancestral coronavirus that the other sarbecoviruses lost
A convergent adaptation that appeared independently in an unsampled wild lineage
context: The insert has no known match in the closest wild relatives, no coronavirus passaging experiment has generated one, and the genome carries no recognisable engineering scars. Serious researchers on both sides now call the origin of these twelve letters an open question. The Discovery Pattern for a real MYSTERY: the bank says so out loud rather than pretending it is closed. Sources: Harrison and Sachs 2022; Frutos et al. 2023 (Journal of Virology); Chan and Zhan 2022.

question: Bologna, November 1780. A skinned frog's leg lies on Luigi Galvani's dissecting bench, held by a brass hook. A running electrostatic machine crackles nearby, touching nothing. An assistant's steel scalpel brushes the hook. What did Galvani see?
answer: The dead muscle twitched
choices: The dead muscle twitched
A spark leapt to the blade
The hook turned magnetic
The flesh gave off a glow
context: Galvani began systematic experiments on 6 November 1780 and kept at them for more than ten years before publishing anything. He soon found he did not need the machine at all: skinned legs hung from an iron railing by brass hooks kicked the instant hook met rail - no storm, no spark, no apparatus. Hooks of wood, glass or resin gave nothing at all; only conductors moved the dead legs. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Initial Observations and Experiments; Frog Leg Preparations and Electrical Stimulation); date corroborated Backyard Brains, 'The Galvani/Volta Experiment'.

question: London, 18 January 1803. George Forster has been hanged that morning for drowning his wife and baby daughter. His body goes straight to Giovanni Aldini, Luigi Galvani's nephew, who wires it to a voltaic battery before an audience and touches the current to its face. What did the watching room see?
answer: Its jaw quivered and one eye opened
choices: Its jaw quivered and one eye opened
Its lips moved as if forming a word
Its chest rose in one long breath
Its head turned slowly to one side
context: The Newgate Calendar's own words: 'On the first application of the process to the face, the jaws of the deceased criminal began to quiver, and the adjoining muscles were horribly contorted, and one eye was actually opened. In the subsequent part of the process the right hand was raised and clenched, and the legs and thighs were set in motion.' Forster had drowned his wife Jane and their infant daughter Louisa in the Paddington Canal on 5 December 1802. Aldini's aim was medical, not monstrous - he was arguing that galvanism might revive the drowned and the suffocated, which is why he wanted a hanged man. Source: The Newgate Calendar, 'George Foster'; Grokipedia, George Forster (murderer).

question: Luigi Galvani spent ten years making dead frogs' legs kick on his bench in Bologna. He was certain the effect was genuine electricity, and in 1791 he published his account of where it came from - an account Alessandro Volta would spend the next decade attacking. Where did Galvani say the electricity was stored?
answer: In the animal's own body
choices: In the animal's own body
In the metals touching it
In the air around the bench
In the warmth of fresh flesh
context: Galvani called it 'animal electricity' and compared the animal to a Leyden jar, the charge-holding apparatus of his day: the nerve as the inner conductor, the muscle as the outer. His own 1791 words: 'a kind of circuit of a delicate nerve fluid is made from the nerves to the muscles when the phenomenon of contractions is produced, similar to the electric circuit which is completed in a Leyden jar.' The treatise was 'De viribus electricitatis in motu musculari commentarius', published through the Bologna Academy of Sciences. Source: Whipple Museum, University of Cambridge, quoting Galvani 1791; Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani.

question: Alessandro Volta wanted a demonstration that needed no frog, no dissection and no instrument - only his own body. He pressed a strip of zinc and a strip of silver together and laid them on his own tongue. What did Volta report sensing?
answer: A sharp, sour, acid taste
choices: A sharp, sour, acid taste
A sudden sweetness at the tip
A cold numbness spreading back
A prickling, like tiny pins
context: He was not the first to try it. In 1752 Johann Georg Sulzer laid lead and silver foil together on his tongue, felt the same acid tingle - and blamed vibration. Volta read it correctly as a current, one he could feel with his own body and no animal anywhere in the circuit. Two different metals plus something wet is the whole recipe; on the tongue, you are the wet part. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Volta's Criticisms and Alternative Explanation); Grokipedia, Galvanism (Early Observations - Sulzer 1752).

question: Volta's letter describing his column was read in London in the spring of 1800, and William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle had one built within days. In May they used it to do something nobody had ever managed before. What did they do with the current?
answer: They pulled water apart into two gases
choices: They pulled water apart into two gases
They pulled a metal out of a lump of ash
They drove a compass needle right around
They kept a frog's leg twitching for hours
context: Inflammable gas - hydrogen - bubbled off the negative wire, and breathable gas - oxygen - off the positive. Johann Wilhelm Ritter repeated the run, caught both gases and measured them: two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen. An argument about a frog's leg had, within weeks, opened a whole new chemistry. Source: Grokipedia, Electrolysis of water (Early Observations and Fundamental Discoveries).

question: Alessandro Volta read Luigi Galvani's 1791 treatise, privately praised it, and within weeks was attacking it in public letters; the first is dated 3 April 1792. Volta did not argue the twitch away - he went to the bench, changed one detail of Galvani's own setup, and the leg lay dead still. What had Volta changed?
answer: He had made both contacts the same metal
choices: He had made both contacts the same metal
He had warmed both contacts in his hand
He had shortened the wire between contacts
He had left the leg to rest a full day
context: Volta's answer was that the electricity came from the contact of two different metals, and that the frog was merely 'a sensitive detector, analogous to an electroscope.' He backed it two ways: the twitch died when both contacts on the frog were the same metal, and wet paper or leather worked perfectly well in the tissue's place. One myth worth dropping here - the taunt that rivals mocked Galvani as 'the frog's dancing master' appears nowhere in the record. Historians Marco Piccolino and Nicholas Wade traced it to nineteenth-century writers; the two men stayed personally civil, and it was their followers who got vicious. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Volta's Criticisms and Alternative Explanation); Grokipedia, Alessandro Volta; Piccolino & Wade, 'The Frog's Dancing Master'.

question: In 1797 Napoleon's new Cisalpine Republic demanded an oath of allegiance from every professor in Bologna. Luigi Galvani, who had spent ten years making dead frogs' legs kick on his bench and was still defending them against Alessandro Volta, would not swear it. What did the republic take from him?
answer: His chair, his salary, his pension and his house
choices: His chair, his salary, his pension and his house
His laboratory, his instruments and his notes
His passport and his freedom to leave Bologna
A year in prison and a fine he could not pay
context: Refusing the oath cost Galvani everything at once. He moved in with his brother Giacomo and died there on 4 December 1798, aged 61, with the quarrel still unsettled - he did not live to see the pile built or the argument resolved. The two men's endings invert the story: Alessandro Volta took a gold medal from Napoleon in Paris in 1801, the Legion of Honour in 1805, and was made a Count in 1810, and in 1881 an international congress named the volt after him. Source: Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Circumstances of Death); Grokipedia, Alessandro Volta (Retirement and Honors).

question: A nerve cell at rest holds its inside at about seventy thousandths of a volt negative. When it fires, the inside overshoots to forty or fifty thousandths positive - a swing of roughly a hundred thousandths of a volt, over in an instant. Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley worked the mechanism out on the giant nerve fibre of a squid and took the 1963 Nobel Prize for it. What moves to flip the voltage?
answer: Sodium rushes in, potassium rushes out
choices: Sodium rushes in, potassium rushes out
Calcium rushes in, sodium rushes out
Chloride rushes in, calcium rushes out
Electrons rush in, protons rush out
context: That flip has a name: the action potential. It is not electrons running along a wire - it is charged atoms crossing a membrane. Hodgkin and Huxley made the first intracellular recordings in 1939 and published the full mathematical model in 1952; the squid's nerve fibre was chosen because it is fat enough to push a wire inside. Your own nerves are doing exactly this right now, reading this line. Source: 'The Long Journey from Animal Electricity to the Discovery of Ion Channels', PMC11202063; Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani.

question: Alessandro Volta had spent eight years arguing that Galvani's frogs proved nothing about animals. On 20 March 1800 he wrote to Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society, describing a column of alternating zinc and silver discs, every pair parted by cardboard soaked in brine; about forty pairs threw sparks and delivered a shock. The words 'pile' and 'battery' came later, from other people. What did Volta himself ask that it be called?
answer: An artificial electric organ
choices: An artificial electric organ
A perpetual contact machine
A self-renewing electrometer
A permanent Leyden apparatus
context: The name was not a whim: Volta had deliberately copied the stacked, layered structure of a living creature's electric organ, and told Banks so - 'I have constructed it, in its form... to the natural electric organ of the torpedo or electric eel... I would wish to give the name of artificial electric organ.' The man who insisted electricity was not animal named his battery after an animal. His paper's title was a straight rebuttal of Galvani: 'On the Electricity Excited by the Mere Contact of Conducting Substances of Different Kinds.' And you can rebuild the thing in a kitchen, because all it ever needed was two different metals and something wet: copper and aluminium discs with raw potato slices between them, five cells for roughly 2 to 2.5 volts. Every lemon battery a kid has ever built is this letter, rebuilt. Source: Volta's 20 March 1800 letter to Banks, quoted in Trends in Neurosciences, 'The artificial electric organ'; Grokipedia, Voltaic pile; Backyard Brains.

question: On 6 October 1807 Humphry Davy wired up the largest battery in Britain - about a hundred six-inch pairs of plates and another hundred and fifty four-inch - and drove its current into molten potash at the Royal Institution. Shining globules pushed up through the crust and caught fire as they met the air: metallic potassium, a metal nobody on Earth had ever seen. His cousin and assistant Edmund Davy wrote down what Davy did in that moment. What did he do?
answer: He bounded about the room in delight
choices: He bounded about the room in delight
He wrote the result down before speaking
He at once ran the whole thing again
He sat down and had to be given water
context: Edmund Davy's account: when Davy 'saw the minute globules of potassium burst through the crust of potash, and take fire as they entered the atmosphere, he could not contain his joy - he actually bounded about the room in ecstatic delight; some little time was required for him to compose himself to continue the experiment.' Seven years earlier no instrument on Earth could have done it. Source: Edmund Davy, quoted in J. Davy (ed.), 'Memoirs of the Life of Sir Humphry Davy', Collected Works 1839-40, Vol 1 p.109; Grokipedia, Potassium.

question: Alessandro Volta's whole case rested on the metals - brass hook, iron railing, steel blade. In 1794 Luigi Galvani answered him with a preparation that had no metal in it anywhere: nothing in the circuit but one frog and a second frog. The muscle contracted all the same, and Galvani published the result without putting his name on it. What had he laid against the muscle?
answer: A second frog's cut nerve
choices: A second frog's cut nerve
A second frog's fresh blood
A second frog's stripped skin
A second frog's bared bone
context: Galvani touched the cut end of one frog's sciatic nerve directly onto another frog's muscle, and the muscle contracted - no brass, no iron, no scalpel, nothing but animal against animal. He published it anonymously in 1794 as 'Dell'uso e dell'attivita dell'arco conduttore nella contrazione dei muscoli' (sources give slightly different wordings of the title). Source: Britannica, Luigi Galvani; Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Galvani's Responses and Further Experiments); PMC11202063.

question: Lightning cracking down a rod, electrodes bolted at the neck, the creature sitting up on the slab - that is the version of Frankenstein almost everyone carries in their head. Mary Shelley's novel describes none of it: her text lets Victor Frankenstein discover a 'principle of life', then refuses to say what the method was. The lightning and the electrodes came from somewhere else. Who put them there?
answer: James Whale, filming the novel in 1931
choices: James Whale, filming the novel in 1931
Mary Shelley, revising the novel in 1831
Giovanni Aldini, wiring a corpse in 1803
Percy Shelley, prefacing the novel in 1818
context: Galvanism does touch the book, but never in the story itself. It appears in Shelley's own 1831 introduction, recalling the ghost-story talk at the Villa Diodati in 1816: 'Perhaps a corpse would be re-animated; galvanism had given token of such things.' Even there, no lightning and no electrodes - those are Whale's, from his 1931 film. What is real is the galvanic fever of the age: Aldini had been wiring corpses in London in 1803, thirteen years before that evening at the Villa Diodati. When a scene everybody 'knows' turns out to trace back to a movie, that is worth checking before repeating - including the ones you are sure about. Source: Wikipedia, Frankenstein (animation method left deliberately ambiguous; 1831 introduction quote; electricity attributed to James Whale's 1931 adaptation).

question: Giovanni Aldini, Luigi Galvani's nephew, wired the hanged body of George Forster to a voltaic pile in London on 18 January 1803 and sent current through it in front of a room of official witnesses who watched the corpse's limbs move. One of them was Mr Pass, beadle of the Surgeons' Company - a minor company officer, there in an official capacity. The Newgate Calendar's report of the day ends with a claim about Mr Pass that has been retold as fact ever since. What does it say happened to him?
answer: He died of fright soon after reaching home
choices: He died of fright soon after reaching home
He fainted and had to be carried out
He fled the room before it was over
He never entered a dissecting room again
context: The Newgate Calendar's full line names him: 'Mr Pass, the beadle of the Surgeons' Company, who was officially present during this experiment, was so alarmed that he died of fright soon after his return home.' Two centuries of retelling rest on that one sentence - no inquest, no second witness, no other account.
