The same reports cannot even agree on where Aldini worked on the body: the Newgate Calendar says only 'a house not far distant', while most modern retellings place it confidently at the Royal College of Surgeons. If the room itself is in doubt, the frightened beadle deserves the same doubt. Repetition is not evidence - a vivid detail everybody repeats is exactly the kind worth chasing back to its single source. Source: The Newgate Calendar, 'George Foster'; Grokipedia, George Forster (murderer); McGill Office for Science and Society.  (Legend.)

question: Emil du Bois-Reymond would not settle the old quarrel on anybody's authority, so he built his own instruments: a galvanometer he wound himself with twenty-four thousand turns of wire, and electrodes made to cancel the metal-contact effect Alessandro Volta had exposed. In 1847 he dipped his fingers into bowls of salt water wired to that galvanometer, and the needle swung - the first time anyone had caught a living human's own electricity. What had he just done to make it move?
answer: He tensed the muscles of his own arm
choices: He tensed the muscles of his own arm
He held his breath for a full minute
He pricked his fingertip with a pin
He stared hard into a bright lamp
context: He contracted his own arm and the needle answered. He put it in the largest terms he could find, claiming he had realised 'the hundred-year-old dream of the physicist and physiologist: the identity of the nervous principle with electricity.' He had already detected the action current in frog muscle in 1843, and in 1848 he published two volumes of measurements, 'Untersuchungen ueber thierische Elektricitaet'. Those measurements settled the old dispute in the most awkward way possible - both men were right, each about a different thing. Volta had explained the frog-leg experiment correctly: the two metals really were making that current. And Galvani was right about the bigger thing: animals really do generate electricity of their own, as your own arm is doing now. Source: Grokipedia, Emil du Bois-Reymond (Foundations of Experimental Electrophysiology; Instrumentation Innovations and Methodological Advances); Grokipedia, Luigi Galvani (Long-Term Resolution in Favor of Galvani's Core Insight).

question: The federal Right to Try Act, signed on May 30, 2018, is unusual in Washington: it does not carry any legislator's name. Its formal title instead carries four names -- Trickett Wendler, Frank Mongiello, Matthew Bellina, and Jordan McLinn. Who were those four?
answer: Patients or family of patients with terminal illnesses
choices: Patients or family of patients with terminal illnesses
Retired FDA commissioners who backed the bill
Physicians who first prescribed under state laws
Attorneys who wrote the model legislation
context: Three had ALS (Wendler, Mongiello, Bellina); Jordan McLinn was a boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy who lobbied Congress in person. Naming a federal statute after its patients rather than its sponsors was the whole point. Public Law 115-176. Source: congress.gov/115/plaws/publ176.

question: Before Congress ever took Right to Try up, the Goldwater Institute drafted a model bill and shopped it around the states. One state passed it first, on May 17, 2014, and by the time Washington acted in 2018 forty other states had followed. Which state moved first?
answer: Colorado
choices: Colorado
Texas
Arizona
Florida
context: Alaska became the 41st state to enact a Right to Try law before the federal Act. It is a case where the states moved first and Washington caught up rather than led. Source: goldwaterinstitute.org releases; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-to-try_law.

question: Right to Try only opens the door to certain investigational drugs -- specifically, those that have already cleared one particular hurdle in FDA testing but not the whole approval process. Which hurdle must the drug have passed?
answer: Phase I safety testing
choices: Phase I safety testing
Preclinical animal testing
Phase III efficacy trials
Post-marketing surveillance
context: The premise is narrow: a dying patient with no clinical trial option should be able to try a drug already shown reasonably safe in humans, without waiting for the full efficacy proof most patients never had time for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-to-try_law.

question: A common objection to Right to Try is that the law only clears a legal path -- three specific parties in the medical chain can still say no, and often do, so a dying patient with the statute on their side may still walk away empty-handed. Which three?
answer: The drug company, the insurer, and the prescribing doctor
choices: The drug company, the insurer, and the prescribing doctor
The FDA commissioner, the state medical board, and the hospital
The patient's employer, the pharmacy benefit manager, and Medicare
The clinical trial sponsor, the review board, and the patent holder
context: Right to Try is a permission, not a mandate: the manufacturer need not supply, the insurer need not pay, the doctor need not prescribe. Supporters answer that a permission is exactly what a dying patient needs, and that the FDA's older 'expanded access' pathway required the agency's leave rather than the patient's. Source: hklaw.com, 'Right to Try Law Enacted by Congress'.

question: The reason the FDA requires proof of a drug's EFFECTIVENESS, not just its safety, comes from a specific law passed in the immediate wake of the thalidomide near-miss. President Kennedy signed it on October 10, 1962. What is that law?
answer: The Kefauver-Harris Amendment
choices: The Kefauver-Harris Amendment
The Pure Food and Drug Act
The Hatch-Waxman Act
The Prescription Drug User Fee Act
context: Before 1962 a manufacturer only had to show a drug was safe. Afterward it also had to prove the drug worked -- generally through two randomized controlled trials significant at the 0.05 level. That efficacy requirement is the rule Peltzman would later measure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kefauver-Harris_Amendment.

question: In 1973 the economist Sam Peltzman published the first serious cost-benefit study of the 1962 drug amendments, in the Journal of Political Economy. Using pre-1962 data to build a counterfactual, he compared it to the years after and made one striking finding. What did the amendments approximately do?
answer: Cut in half the rate of new drug introductions per year
choices: Cut in half the rate of new drug introductions per year
Doubled the average price of a newly approved drug
Tripled the average length of a Phase III trial
Reduced generic-drug competition by about half
context: Peltzman's finding: the rules cut the flow of new medicines roughly in half, without a matching gain in drug quality. Medicines that were never developed have no patients to interview -- the unseen graveyard the bank keeps in view. Source: journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/260107.

question: On October 11, 1988, in the middle of the AIDS crisis, roughly fifteen hundred activists staged a nine-hour die-in that shut down the headquarters of one federal agency, complete with cardboard tombstones reading 'I died for the sins of ___'. Which agency did the tombstones name?
answer: The FDA
choices: The FDA
The CDC
The NIH
The Department of Health and Human Services
context: The Rockville, Maryland demonstration was ACT UP's first national action; 176 people were arrested. The point was blunt: patients wanted drugs already in trials and the wait was killing them. Source: washingtonpost.com, '1,000 Swarm FDA's Rockville Office'.

question: The mature version of the Right-to-Try argument does not pretend caution's column is empty. It insists on counting both columns. The standing example of caution genuinely saving lives is a Canadian-born pharmacologist who joined the FDA in 1960 and, over the following two years, kept sending back one thalidomide application because the evidence was thin. President Kennedy gave her the President's Award on August 7, 1962. Who was she?
answer: Frances Oldham Kelsey
choices: Frances Oldham Kelsey
Barbara McClintock
Rosalind Franklin
Marie Maynard Daly
context: Thalidomide disfigured at least 4,000 children in Europe (phocomelia); Kelsey's stubborn demand for evidence spared American children from that toll. Her demand was not 'ban it' -- it was 'show me the data'. That is the very rigor Right to Try's advocates say is missing on the other side of the ledger. The distractor scientists (McClintock, Franklin, Daly) are real contemporaries in different fields. Source: fda.gov, 'Frances Oldham Kelsey: Medical Reviewer'.

question: Elisabeth Bik is a Dutch-trained microbiologist who spends her evenings reading published biology papers with an unusually careful eye. What began her hunt for problems in the scientific literature back in 2013?
answer: She discovered one of her own papers had been plagiarised
choices: She discovered one of her own papers had been plagiarised
A journal editor asked her to review a batch of images
She won a grant to build software for spotting fraud
A colleague was fired and asked her to clear his name
context: Bik went looking for other cases like her own and quickly discovered a much larger pattern. She left a full-time science job at Stanford to work on integrity full-time. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Bik

question: In 2016 Elisabeth Bik and her co-authors Arturo Casadevall and Ferric Fang published in the journal mBio the results of hand-screening 20,621 published biomedical papers. Roughly what fraction of them contained inappropriately duplicated images?
answer: About one in twenty-five
choices: About one in twenty-five
About one in two hundred
About one in a thousand
About one in ten thousand
context: That number - 4 percent of the biomedical literature - shocked editors who had assumed peer review was catching this sort of thing. The paper had to be posted as a preprint on bioRxiv first; several journals were reluctant to touch it. Source: retractionwatch.com/2016/04/19/one-in-25-papers-contains-inappropriately-duplicated-images-screen-finds

question: The trick Bik exploits is that a picture of a western blot or a microscope field carries something a table of numbers does not. What is that extra thing?
answer: A unique random speckle pattern - a kind of visual fingerprint
choices: A unique random speckle pattern - a kind of visual fingerprint
A digital timestamp burned into every pixel by the camera
A machine-generated barcode in the lower right corner
A recorded audio note from the technician who took it
context: Rotate that pattern, mirror it, stretch it, drop it into another figure - the speckles still line up. Fabrication that would be invisible in a spreadsheet is visible in a picture, to a patient eye reading printed pages. Source: arxiv.org/pdf/2102.01874

question: Two sites now carry much of the post-publication checking. One, launched in late 2012 by neuroscientist Brandon Stell and two colleagues, lets anyone comment on any published paper by DOI. The other, a blog founded in August 2010 by journalist Ivan Oransky and editor Adam Marcus, tracks retractions across all of science. Which pair are they?
answer: PubPeer and Retraction Watch
choices: PubPeer and Retraction Watch
PubMed Commons and F1000Research
Publons and Faculty Opinions
For Better Science and Neuroskeptic
context: PubMed Commons and F1000Research both hosted post-publication commentary; Publons tracked peer reviews and Faculty Opinions (formerly F1000Prime) ran expert recommendations; For Better Science and Neuroskeptic are individual watchdog blogs. Neither PubPeer nor Retraction Watch is a journal, a university, or a government - both are largely volunteer. Source: retractionwatch.com/2015/08/31/pubpeer-founders-reveal-themselves-create-foundation

question: In 2021 Vanderbilt neuroscientist Matthew Schrag was hired to look into a struggling Alzheimer's drug. His investigation led him to a much bigger target - a landmark 2006 Nature paper by Sylvain Lesne that had been cited about 2,300 times. What did that famous paper claim?
answer: That a specific amyloid oligomer, Ab*56, directly caused memory loss in mice
choices: That a specific amyloid oligomer, Ab*56, directly caused memory loss in mice
That vitamin B12 injections halted memory decline in early Alzheimer's
That gut bacteria seeded protein plaques inside the brain
That sleep alone cleared the brain of Alzheimer's-related waste
context: Ab*56 became one of the most cited candidate molecules in Alzheimer's research. Investigative journalist Charles Piller laid out Schrag's evidence of image splicing and duplication in Science on 21 July 2022; Nature retracted the paper in June 2024. Source: science.org/content/article/researchers-plan-retract-landmark-alzheimers-paper-containing-doctored-images

question: The STAP-cell papers were retracted on 2 July 2014, only six months after publication. Two independent checks converged on the same verdict at the same time. What were they?
answer: Labs worldwide could not reproduce it, and readers on PubPeer found reused images
choices: Labs worldwide could not reproduce it, and readers on PubPeer found reused images
A rival RIKEN team replicated it once, and an internal audit cleared the figures
A senior collaborator confessed at a press conference, and Nature ran its own peer-review inquiry
A whistleblower emailed the journal, and a mass-spectrometry team spotted contamination
context: Failed replication and duplicated images pointing at the same answer from two different directions. Genetic testing later showed the 'STAP cells' were ordinary embryonic stem cells. Source: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519803

question: US Air Force Captain Chuck Yeager was thrown from a horse in the California desert two nights before the most important flight of his life. He did not report the accident: a civilian doctor in Rosamond taped him up quietly, because the Air Force would have grounded him. What had the fall done to him?
answer: It broke two ribs under his right arm.
choices: It broke two ribs under his right arm.
It cracked his right collarbone in two.
It tore a ligament in his right knee.
It broke two bones in his right wrist.
context: A civilian doctor in Rosamond taped the ribs; the flight surgeon was never told, because reporting them would have cost Yeager the flight. Two days later he flew the Bell X-1 past the speed of sound with them still taped. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Yeager  (Legend.)

question: The Bell X-1's rocket drank its whole fuel load in minutes — far too little to also climb from the desert floor to the thin air where a speed record had to be set. So on 14 October 1947 the engineers gave Chuck Yeager his altitude another way. How did the X-1 get up there?
answer: A B-29 bomber carried it up in its bomb bay.
choices: A B-29 bomber carried it up in its bomb bay.
A C-54 transport towed it up on a cable.
A pair of jets in its wing roots lifted it off.
A booster rocket lifted it, then fell away.
context: The B-29 carried the X-1 in its bomb bay and dropped it at 20,000 feet; Yeager lit the rocket and climbed away, reaching Mach 1.06 at about 43,000 feet. Good sources differ slightly on the exact figures — the Smithsonian gives 42,000 feet, Wikipedia 45,000 feet at Mach 1.05 — which is itself worth noticing. He had painted the name Glamorous Glennis on the orange fuselage, after his wife. Source: airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/breaking-sound-barrier; grokipedia.com/page/Bell_X-1

question: Chuck Yeager lowered himself into the X-1's cockpit injured and hiding it. Sealing the rocket plane's side hatch meant bracing the hatch in place and driving a heavy locking lever home with his right arm, and his injury made that impossible. He told nobody but the project engineer, Jack Ridley. What did Ridley bring him?
answer: A sawn-off length of broom handle
choices: A sawn-off length of broom handle
A leather strap from a parachute harness
A long wrench from the ground crew
A padded brace to wear over the ribs
context: Ridley quietly sawed the handle off a broom in the hangar. Yeager slipped it through the hatch fitting and used it as a lever to force the lock home, sealing himself in — and the flight surgeon was never told. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ridley_(pilot)  (Legend.)

question: In 1947 nobody had ever flown faster than sound, so the Bell engineers shaping the X-1 had no flight data to work from. But people had been sending things past the speed of sound for two hundred years, and those things were already known to fly steadily while doing it. So the engineers copied one. What did they model the X-1's fuselage on?
answer: A Browning .50-caliber machine gun round
choices: A Browning .50-caliber machine gun round
A Hispano 20 mm aircraft cannon shell
A Lee-Enfield .303-caliber rifle bullet
A Bofors 40 mm anti-aircraft gun shell
context: Bell's designers called it 'a bullet with wings.' Nobody had flown supersonic, but people had been shooting supersonic for two centuries, so the engineers copied the one supersonic shape they trusted. The wings were made extremely thin, and a four-chamber Reaction Motors XLR-11 rocket gave 6,000 pounds of thrust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_X-1

question: In 1935 the British aerodynamicist W. F. Hilton stood in the National Physical Laboratory, walking a newspaper reporter through his high-speed research. The reporter shortened one of Hilton's sentences into two words that have misled people ever since: 'the sound barrier.' What had Hilton been calling a barrier?
answer: The steep climb of a wing's resistance near the speed of sound
choices: The steep climb of a wing's resistance near the speed of sound
A wall of packed air standing in the sky at the speed of sound
A gap in his data that the wind tunnel could not reach into
A ceiling on engine power that no known fuel could beat
context: Hilton's actual sentence was: 'See how the resistance of a wing shoots up like a barrier against higher speed, as we approach the speed of sound.' He was pointing at a curve on a graph. The papers printed 'sound barrier,' and the public heard a wall hanging in the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_barrier  (Legend.)

question: The word 'barrier' was a bad picture, but the danger under it was real: in the last years of the Second World War, pilots diving from high altitude toward the speed of sound were killed by their own aircraft. Supermarine Spitfire pilots met one of the strangest of these effects when they moved the stick sideways to roll out of a dive. What did the aeroplane do instead?
answer: It rolled the opposite way, because the wings themselves twisted.
choices: It rolled the opposite way, because the wings themselves twisted.
It pitched nose-down hard, because the tail lost its lift.
It yawed sideways, because the rudder stalled in thin air.
It shook itself apart, because the wing skin tore away.
context: Engineers call it control reversal. The Spitfire's wings were torsionally soft, so at high speed deflecting an aileron twisted the whole wing the opposite way — and the wing won. Other fighters had other transonic killers: the P-38 Lightning suffered Mach tuck above about Mach 0.65, the nose pitching down while the elevator lost its grip, and it killed test pilot Ralph Virden in 1941. Thirteen months before Yeager's flight, on 27 September 1946, Geoffrey de Havilland Jr was killed when his DH 108 broke up at roughly Mach 0.9. The wall was imaginary; the danger was not. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_barrier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_tuck

question: A fighter crosses the coast at 30,000 feet, pushes past Mach 1 as it does, holds Mach 1.5 for ten minutes, and slows back below the speed of sound far inland. A boy standing 120 miles from the coast, directly under the flight path, hears a sharp crack. Where was the jet when it made the sound that reached him?
answer: Almost overhead, just short of the boy
choices: Almost overhead, just short of the boy
Back at the coast, where it went supersonic
Deep inland, at the end of the fast run
Halfway between the coast and the boy
context: The boom is not a doorway punched once. The shock cone trails behind the aircraft for the entire time it stays supersonic, dragging a 'boom carpet' along the ground; each person hears their own boom as the cone sweeps over them, far from wherever Mach 1 was crossed. The carpet runs about one mile wide for every 1,000 feet of altitude — roughly thirty miles across from 30,000 feet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_boom

question: In 1964 the United States government wanted to know whether Americans would tolerate supersonic airliners overhead, so it ran the test on a real city. From February to July, military jets deliberately boomed Oklahoma City about eight times a day — 1,253 booms in six months. Residents lodged 9,594 complaints of damage to their buildings and filed 4,629 formal claims. How many claims did the government pay?
answer: 229 of them, for about $13,000 in all
choices: 229 of them, for about $13,000 in all
1,180 of them, for about $70,000 in all
2,400 of them, for about $300,000 in all
3,900 of them, for about $900,000 in all
context: Operation Bongo II ran from 3 February to 30 July 1964, flown by F-104s and B-58 Hustlers, with the overpressure deliberately stepped up partway through. 229 of 4,629 claims were paid, $12,845.32 in total — a 94% rejection rate. About a quarter of residents surveyed said they simply could not accept the booms. They brought a class action, and the government lost on appeal on 8 March 1969. In 1973 the FAA banned civil supersonic flight over US land, and that rule still stands — a rule about annoyance rather than damage: controlled studies found single booms below about 16 pounds per square foot did no significant harm to well-maintained buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_sonic_boom_tests; grokipedia.com/page/Sonic_boom

question: In 1887, sixty years before any aircraft could approach the speed of sound, Ernst Mach and the photographer Peter Salcher photographed the cone of piled-up air trailing from a rifle bullet in mid-flight. The bullet crossed the picture in well under a thousandth of a second. How did they stop it dead on the plate?
answer: They lit it with an electric spark too brief to blur
choices: They lit it with an electric spark too brief to blur
They geared the shutter to a slotted disc spun fast
They left the plate open and let the bullet draw itself
They tripped a row of cameras with wires as it flew
context: Working at Charles-Ferdinand University in Prague, Mach and Salcher fired a bullet from a Werndl carbine and used a spark both to make the light and to freeze the motion. Their paper deduced and then experimentally confirmed a shock wave of conical shape with the projectile at its apex — the same cone a supersonic jet drags today. Mach did not name the Mach number: the Swiss aeronautical engineer Jakob Ackeret proposed naming the speed ratio after him in 1929, more than four decades later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Mach; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_number

question: On the X-1's eighth powered flight the pitch control simply died. At Mach 0.94 — a hair under the speed of sound — Chuck Yeager pulled and pushed the stick and the aeroplane ignored him, and no amount of extra rocket thrust would have given him back control. The project engineer, Jack Ridley, worked out an answer that almost every supersonic fighter since has carried. What did Ridley change?
answer: He made the entire horizontal tail pivot as one piece
choices: He made the entire horizontal tail pivot as one piece
He swept the wings sharply back to delay the trouble
He thinned the tail surfaces to slice the fast air
He moved the tail back and up, clear of the wing's wake
context: A shock wave was standing on the tailplane's hinge line, so deflecting the elevator behind it did nothing at all — worse, on a conventional tail the rearward-moving shock pushes the elevator down and steals the pilot's authority. Ridley's answer was to stop using the elevator for pitch and pivot the whole horizontal stabiliser: the all-moving tail, or stabilator. The crew flew it two flights later. Stabilators are now almost universal on military combat aircraft — 1947 engineering a kid can point at on any fighter overhead. Swept wings were a serious rival line of work at the time; the X-1 deliberately went without them because too little was yet known about them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ridley_(pilot); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stabilator

question: Stand under Concorde's route and you do not hear one bang — you hear two, about three tenths of a second apart, and then nothing. A pressure gauge on the ground draws the shape of the event: pressure jumps suddenly, falls smoothly to below normal, then jumps suddenly back. Each jump is a shock wave arriving, and each takes only a few thousandths of a second, which is why the sound cracks instead of rumbling. Where do the two jumps come from?
answer: One shock from the nose and one from the tail
choices: One shock from the nose and one from the tail
One shock from each wing, a moment apart
One shock from the nose and its echo off the ground
One shock from the engines and one from the nose
context: Engineers call the trace an N-wave, after the letter it draws: a jump at the nose, a smooth fall through the body to below-ambient pressure, a jump back at the tail. The positive and negative halves integrate to zero net impulse. A cruising supersonic aircraft lays down roughly 0.5 to 2 pounds per square foot on the ground, heard at about 105 to 120 decibels. NASA's X-59, unveiled on 12 January 2024, carries a needle nose more than 38 feet long precisely so its shocks never merge into a single N-wave — the aim is a 'sonic thump' rather than a boom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_boom; grokipedia.com/page/Sonic_boom

question: Ernst Mach's spark photographs caught the cone of piled-up air a flying bullet drags with it, and a supersonic jet drags the same cone today. Every such photograph shows the cone closing to a sharp angle at the nose — an angle a protractor can read straight off the print. As an object flies faster and faster beyond Mach 1, what does that angle do?
answer: It narrows and sweeps further back
choices: It narrows and sweeps further back
It widens toward a nearly flat plane
It holds one angle at any speed
It narrows, then opens out again
context: The rule is sin(half-angle) = the speed of sound divided by the object's speed, which is 1 divided by the Mach number. At Mach 3 that gives about 19 degrees; just above Mach 1 the angle opens toward 90 degrees, and the shock is 'hardly a cone at all, but closer to a slightly concave plane.' Measure the angle on a photograph and you have measured the speed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_boom; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mach_number

question: The crack of a bullwhip is a real sonic boom — a scrap of leather beating the speed of sound in a back garden, and the oldest supersonic thing most people have ever stood next to. In 2002 the mathematicians Alain Goriely and Tyler McMillen worked out the shape of a cracking whip: the tip can end up moving more than thirty times faster than the handle did at the start, though the arm makes just one unhurried swing. Where does all that extra speed come from?
answer: A loop speeding up as it runs into the whip's thin end
choices: A loop speeding up as it runs into the whip's thin end
The leather stretching and snapping back like a bowstring
The plaited strands unwinding and whirling the tip around
The wrist adding a second, faster flick mid-stroke
context: Because a whip tapers, a travelling loop must speed up as it runs toward the thin end — the same energy carried by less and less leather. Goriely and McMillen found the tip can reach more than thirty times the handle's starting speed, and it is moving at roughly twice the speed of sound by the moment the loop goes supersonic. Scientific American reported the result as the crack coming from a loop travelling along the whip, gaining speed until it reaches the speed of sound. Humans were sending things past Mach 1 long before aircraft — in 1740 the British mathematician Benjamin Robins used a ballistic pendulum to measure musket balls travelling above Mach 1.5. Source: Goriely & McMillen, 'Shape of a Cracking Whip,' Physical Review Letters 88, 244301 (2002); Scientific American, 'True Cause of Whip's Crack Uncovered,' 28 May 2002

question: In 1886, three years before the war of the currents broke out in earnest, an engineer named William Stanley wired up the small town of Great Barrington, Massachusetts, using the still-new invention that DC could not use. What piece of equipment made his demonstration work?
answer: A transformer that stepped voltage up for the wires and back down for the lamps.
choices: A transformer that stepped voltage up for the wires and back down for the lamps.
A vacuum tube that amplified the current at each customer's meter.
A rotary switch that briefly cut power to every home in turn.
A carbon-arc regulator that held every lamp at the same brightness.
context: Stanley's Great Barrington demonstration proved AC distribution in a real town two years before Tesla's motor patent even issued. The transformer -- an iron ring with two coils, right out of Faraday -- was the piece of hardware DC had no answer for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_currents .

question: The physics argument for alternating current over direct current came down to one equation. To send the same amount of power a hundred miles on modest copper with the least heating loss in the wire, what do you want at the sending end?
answer: The voltage pushed as high as possible, so the current in the wire is small.
choices: The voltage pushed as high as possible, so the current in the wire is small.
The current pushed as high as possible, so the voltage in the wire is small.
The voltage matched exactly to the resistance of the wire between the stations.
The voltage kept low enough that no insulation is needed on the poles.
context: Power equals voltage times current, so for a fixed power a higher voltage means a smaller current -- and because heating loss in the wire goes as current SQUARED times resistance (I-squared-R), collapsing the current collapses the loss. A transformer takes AC from a modest generator voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for transmission and steps it back down at your neighbourhood -- the reason your street wire is AC. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power_transmission .

question: Nikola Tesla's US patent 381,968, granted in May 1888, fed out-of-step alternating currents into separate stator coils. What did those coils create between them that dragged the rotor around?
answer: A magnetic field that itself walked around the inside of the stator.
choices: A magnetic field that itself walked around the inside of the stator.
A pair of carbon brushes arcing continuously on a spinning commutator.
A ring of liquid mercury completing the circuit as the rotor turned.
A spring-loaded centrifugal governor holding the shaft at fixed speed.
context: This is the rotating-field induction motor. Because nothing physical has to slide against the rotor, there is nothing to wear out -- no brushes and no sparking whatsoever. Westinghouse licensed the patents from Tesla in July 1888, giving AC the one thing DC still had over it. Source: patents.google.com/patent/US381968A .

question: The war of the currents did not end with a duel or a court verdict; it ended with a bid. In 1893 Westinghouse and Tesla underbid Edison's team for the contract to light a single event, and on opening night President Cleveland threw one switch and lit about a hundred thousand incandescent lamps at once. What was the event?
answer: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
choices: The World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
The dedication of the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbour.
The Paris Exposition Universelle at the base of the new Eiffel Tower.
The inauguration of the transcontinental railroad at Promontory Summit.
context: About twenty-seven million people saw the White City glow on AC power over the six months of the fair. That contract -- and the spectacle -- won Westinghouse the Niagara Falls hydroelectric commission, which on 15 November 1896 began sending power about twenty miles to Buffalo. Source: teslauniverse.com 1893 tesla lights worlds fair .

question: In 1834 the American naturalist Richard Harlan studied a huge fossil vertebra — a single bone out of a backbone — dug up in Ouachita Parish, Louisiana. Working from that one bone, he named the creature Basilosaurus, 'king lizard'. What kind of animal was it?
answer: A whale
choices: A whale
A sea cow
A giant seal
A sea turtle
context: Harlan compared the vertebra to the fossil sea reptiles Plesiosaurus and Mosasaurus, took the animal for a giant marine reptile, and wrote that it 'could not have been less than from eighty to one hundred feet' long. He had a whale. Under the rules of zoological naming the earliest published name has priority, so the largest whale of its age is stuck being called 'king lizard' forever. Basilosaurus cetoides is today the official state fossil of both Alabama and Mississippi, and Alabama law forbids carrying one out of the state without the governor's written permission. — Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Basilosaurus cetoides'.

question: Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell dug a skull out of fifty-million-year-old rock west of Islamabad, in northern Pakistan, and named it Pakicetus. It is the earliest animal that scientists count as a whale, and its size is the first surprise. How big was it?
answer: About the size of a wolf
choices: About the size of a wolf
About the size of a horse
About the size of a bison
About the size of a rat
context: Pakicetus attocki was one to two metres long. Its sister species Ichthyolestes pinfoldi was smaller still: Hans Thewissen's 2001 Nature paper describes them as 'the fox-sized Ichthyolestes pinfoldi, and the wolf-sized Pakicetus attocki'. The earliest whales were not whale-sized, and telling them apart from any other small mammal of the period took real evidence rather than a glance. — Thewissen, Williams, Roe & Hussain, Nature 413:277-281 (2001); Wikipedia, 'Pakicetus'.

question: A fossil skeleton lay on the bench with no skin, no hair and no soft parts left. Richard Owen, Britain's leading anatomist, used it to overturn Richard Harlan's ruling that the huge Louisiana animal Basilosaurus was a giant sea reptile. Owen pointed to one feature and wrote that it was 'unknown in fishes and reptiles'. What was it?
answer: Molars carried on two roots each
choices: Molars carried on two roots each
Ribs curving in one unbroken arc
Neck bones locked into a single block
Finger bones sealed inside a flipper
context: Reptile teeth are simple single-rooted pegs, shed and replaced over and over through life; mammal cheek teeth are complex and anchored on more than one root. Owen proposed renaming the animal Zeuglodon cetoides — 'yoke tooth, whale-like' — and lost. Under the rules of zoological nomenclature Harlan's earlier name has priority, so the correct anatomy won and the correct name did not. — Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Basilosaurus cetoides'.

question: In July 1845 the showman Albert Koch charged New Yorkers twenty-five cents to view a 114-foot 'sea serpent' he called Hydrarchos. The anatomist Jeffries Wyman needed one visit to call it a fraud; Koch sold it to King Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia anyway. What was the monster actually made of?
answer: Bones from several Basilosaurus skeletons, padded with fossil shells
choices: Bones from several Basilosaurus skeletons, padded with fossil shells
Bones from one Basilosaurus skeleton, stretched with plaster spacers
Bones from three mosasaur skeletons, topped with a wooden skull
Bones from a mastodon skeleton, fitted with carved wooden ribs
context: Koch had assembled at least five or six different Basilosaurus individuals and padded the run of vertebrae out with ammonite shells to reach 114 feet. Wyman saw two things at once: the animal was a mammal, not a serpent, and the bones came from animals of different ages and sizes. Careful anatomy beat showmanship in a single visit — and the fake is why 'sea serpent' sat in the public mind as a live identification for these bones at all. — National Geographic, 'The Phrenology of a Monster'; Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus'.

question: In 1981 Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell described a fifty-million-year-old skull from rock west of Islamabad in northern Pakistan, named it Pakicetus, and declared it the oldest whale known. Nothing about the skull's outward shape looked remotely whale-like. One feature carried the entire claim, and it is still the founding mark of the whale group. What was it?
answer: A dense thickened lip of bone wrapped round the ear capsule
choices: A dense thickened lip of bone wrapped round the ear capsule
A bony plate that sealed the nostrils shut underwater
An oil-filled chamber hollowed out inside the snout
A ring of bone bracing the eye socket against pressure
context: The feature is the involucrum: a dense, thickened inner lip on the bony capsule that houses the ear, sitting on an auditory bulla formed from the ectotympanic bone alone. It isolates vibration so that sound can be located underwater, where an ordinary land ear is useless. When Gingerich and Russell described Pakicetus in 1981, the involucrum was found in whales and in nothing else then known, living or fossil — which is why one bump of bone could settle an argument the rest of the skeleton could not. — Wikipedia, 'Pakicetus'; National Geographic, 'Science Word of the Day: Involucrum'.

question: Ambulocetus natans came out of the Kala Chitta Hills of Punjab, Pakistan in 1992: three metres of early whale, a quarter of a tonne. No one has ever watched one hunt, yet Hans Thewissen could read its hunting style off the skull alone. Which feature of the skull did he read?
answer: Its eyes sat high on the skull, aimed upward
choices: Its eyes sat high on the skull, aimed upward
Its jaw hinge slid forward, giving a huge gape
Its snout flattened out into a broad shovel
Its cheekbones flared into heavy bony shields
context: Large eyes set near the top of the head and looking upward are the eyes of an ambush predator lying just under the surface, watching the world above the waterline — the same arrangement a crocodile uses. Thewissen read Ambulocetus as a hunter that seized prey at the water's edge and held on while it struggled. The name Ambulocetus natans means 'the walking, swimming whale': the animal still carried four working legs, and its hind feet were enormous, probably longer than its twenty-nine-centimetre thigh bone, one toe alone running seventeen centimetres; feet that size suggest it swam like a river otter, with alternating beats of the back legs rather than a tail stroke. Holotype H-GSP 18507, described in 1994 by Hans Thewissen, Sayed Taseer Hussain and Mohammad Arif; about 48 to 47 million years old. — Wikipedia, 'Ambulocetus'; Grokipedia, 'Ambulocetus'.

question: Fossil hunters had spent decades arguing over the whale family tree from bones alone. In 1999 the molecular biologists Nikaido, Rooney and Okada came at it from a completely different direction: jumping genes — stretches of DNA that insert themselves into a genome, are effectively never cut back out, and so mark shared ancestry like a stamp that cannot be forged. Which living animals did their result put closest to whales?
answer: Hippos
choices: Hippos
Seals
Manatees
Otters
context: The method reads SINE and LINE insertions: mobile elements that land at a particular site in a genome and are, in practice, never removed. Two species carrying the same insertion at the same site is very hard to explain except by shared ancestry, which is why the technique is so hard to argue with. Seals, manatees and otters all went back to the water too, but each on its own separate line; the animal the insertions pointed to was the hippopotamus. That confirmed a case Graur and Higgins had already made from other molecular data in 1994 — that whales do not sit beside the even-toed hoofed mammals, the group of deer, pigs, camels and cattle, but INSIDE it. The fossil specialists had a different candidate entirely, and did not believe a word of it. — Nikaido, Rooney & Okada, PNAS 96:10261-10266 (1999); Graur & Higgins, Molecular Biology and Evolution 11:357-364 (1994).

question: Pakicetus, the oldest animal that scientists count as a whale, was known for twenty years from its skull alone. The restoration drawn from that skull put it on the cover of Science: a sleek, crocodile-shaped hunter half-submerged in a river, chasing fish. In 2001 Hans Thewissen's team dug up the rest of the skeleton. What did the bones show?
answer: A long-legged land runner with four full working legs
choices: A long-legged land runner with four full working legs
A seal-shaped swimmer with paddle-like hind limbs
A squat river wader with broadly webbed feet
A heavy-bodied digger with spade-like front claws
context: Thewissen and colleagues wrote that the pakicetids were land mammals, 'no more amphibious than a tapir.' The first reconstruction had been an honest guess from a skull alone, and the guess was wrong — printed on a journal cover, then corrected by the same field that printed it. The bones did carry one aquatic signal, but not the one anyone had drawn: the limb bones are osteosclerotic, abnormally dense. Dense bone is ballast. It lets an animal sink and walk along a riverbed instead of bobbing on the surface, and heavy bones, not flippers, are the first aquatic signal in the whole sequence. — Thewissen, Williams, Roe & Hussain, Nature 413:277-281 (2001); Wikipedia, 'Pakicetus'.

question: In 1990 Philip Gingerich, B. Holly Smith and Elwyn Simons reported in Science a Basilosaurus isis from the Egyptian desert: sixteen metres of animal, with its hind limbs still joined together in place — and each one just thirty-five centimetres long. What did that thirty-five-centimetre leg contain?
answer: A knee, an ankle of fused bones, and three toes
choices: A knee, an ankle of fused bones, and three toes
A thigh bone, a knee, and a shin fused into one rod
A hip socket, a thigh bone, and three flat paddle bones
A knee, a shin, and a single splint of a toe
context: A complete leg in miniature — knee joint, tarsal bones fused in the ankle, three digits — hanging off an animal sixteen metres long. The specimen came from Wadi al-Hitan in Egypt, 'the Valley of the Whales', about 150 km southwest of Cairo: roughly 1,500 marine vertebrate skeletons in rock 40 to 41 million years old, including hundreds of Basilosaurus isis and over 500 of the smaller whale Dorudon atrox. UNESCO listed it in 2005. Its fossils were the first archaeocetes ever found with hind legs, feet and toes at all. — Gingerich, Smith & Simons, Science 249:154-157 (1990); Wikipedia, 'Wadi El Hitan'.

question: The Indohyus fossils spent decades in storage. The Indian geologist A. Ranga Rao had collected them in Kashmir and named the animal after Indira Gandhi; after his death his widow, Dr Friedlinde Obergfell, handed the rocks to Hans Thewissen. In Thewissen's laboratory the fossil finally gave up the feature that makes this small deer-like plant-eater the closest known relative of whales. How did that feature come to light?
answer: A technician accidentally broke one of the skulls open
choices: A technician accidentally broke one of the skulls open
A CT scanner imaged the skulls inside their rock
An acid bath dissolved the rock away from the skulls
A student matched the skulls to an old monograph
context: The break laid the middle ear bare, and there was the dense thickened bony margin that had been the founding mark of whales alone. Thewissen and colleagues published Indohyus in Nature in 2007, establishing the Eocene raoellids of south Asia as the sister group of whales. Indohyus resembles whales, and no other even-toed hoofed mammal, in four things at once: ear structure, premolar shape, limb-bone density, and the oxygen-isotope signature locked into its teeth — a chemical record saying it spent much of its life in water. Its limb bones were thickened as ballast so it could sink and walk on a riverbed rather than swim. A slip of the hand found the whales' closest relative. — Thewissen, Cooper, Clementz, Bajpai & Tiwari, Nature 450:1190-1194 (2007); Wikipedia, 'Indohyus'.

question: By 2000 two methods had produced two answers and neither side would yield. Molecular biologists reading DNA placed whales inside the even-toed hoofed mammals. Fossil specialists, following an idea Leigh Van Valen published in 1966, backed the mesonychians — an extinct order of hoofed carnivores whose odd triangular teeth matched those of the earliest whales. In 2001, in the same month, Hans Thewissen's team in Nature and Philip Gingerich's team in Science published early whale ankle bones from Pakistan. Both carried the same astragalus — the bone that takes the body's weight at the top of the foot — and its shape ended the argument. What was that shape?
answer: An astragalus grooved like a pulley at both ends
choices: An astragalus grooved like a pulley at both ends
An astragalus grooved at one end only, flat at the other
An astragalus with a ball-shaped head riding in a socket
An astragalus with a smooth, ungrooved upper face
context: That double groove has a name: double-trochleated. In even-toed hoofed mammals — deer, pigs, camels, cattle — the astragalus is grooved like a pulley at BOTH ends, front and back, and it is found in that group and in no other mammal alive or extinct. Thewissen's pakicetid skeletons (Nature 413:277-281) and Gingerich's Artiocetus clavis and Rodhocetus balochistanensis, from 47-million-year-old Balochistan rock (Science 293:2239-2242), both carried it. The molecular biologists had been right; the mesonychian hypothesis was finished. Two methods that could easily have contradicted each other — one reading living DNA, one reading 47-million-year-old bone — were forced to the same answer. There is a sharper twist still: Gingerich's own 1990 Basilosaurus paper had read those fossil feet as 'consistent with derivation from mesonychid Condylarthra'. The man who found the feet was wrong about what they meant, and he is the one who published the bones that proved it. — Gingerich et al., Science 293:2239-2242 (2001); Thewissen et al., Nature 413:277-281 (2001).

question: The hind legs of a sixteen-metre Basilosaurus isis were thirty-five centimetres long — no use whatever for walking. Biologists call such a structure vestigial, meaning it has lost its ancestral job; most people hear the word as 'useless leftover'. In their 1990 Science paper Philip Gingerich, B. Holly Smith and Elwyn Simons argued these legs still did real work, and named the job. What job did they propose?
answer: Guiding the two animals into position during mating
choices: Guiding the two animals into position during mating
Steering the body through tight underwater turns
Bracing the animal against the sea floor to rest
Anchoring a calf against the flank while it nursed
context: The 1990 abstract's own closing sentence reads: 'Hind limbs of Basilosaurus are interpreted as copulatory guides.' That is the part of the word vestigial most people miss. Vestigial means a structure has lost its ANCESTRAL job — walking — not that it does nothing at all. A sixteen-metre whale could no more walk on a thirty-five-centimetre leg than you could walk on a matchstick, and the leg was still not idle. — Gingerich, Smith & Simons, 'Hind Limbs of Eocene Basilosaurus: Evidence of Feet in Whales', Science 249:154-157 (1990).

question: In 1942 at Eastman Kodak in Rochester, New York, Harry Coover's team wanted a clear plastic they could mould by the thousand instead of grinding each one from glass. The cyanoacrylate they mixed welded itself to the moulds and the glassware, so they dropped it. What had the team been trying to mould?
answer: Gun sights for fighter planes
choices: Gun sights for fighter planes
Windows for bomber cockpits
Lenses for submarine periscopes
Viewing plates for aerial cameras
context: Kodak gave up and went on making gun sight lenses out of ground glass by the tens of thousands. Coover remembered the 1942 reject in Popular Science (February 1989): 'I was working with some acrylate monomers that showed promise... But everything they touched stuck to everything else. It was a severe pain.' The compound he threw away was cyanoacrylate - superglue - and this was the first of two times it would be thrown away. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Harry_Coover; popsci.com, 'How a shot at making better gunsights became Super Glue instead'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Coover.

question: Art Fry, a chemical engineer at 3M, sang in a church choir in St. Paul, Minnesota, and set his places in the hymnal beforehand so he could turn straight to each hymn. Every service the same thing went wrong, and he stood up to sing with the book open at the wrong page. What kept happening?
answer: His paper slips slid out of the book
choices: His paper slips slid out of the book
His pencil ticks rubbed off the page edges
The choir changed the hymn order late
The hymnal's damp pages stuck together
context: Fry had already sat through a seminar given by his 3M colleague Spencer Silver, who had an adhesive nobody wanted. In the choir stall he put the two halves together: 'I was thinking "I wish I had a bookmark that would stick to the paper but that couldn't pull it apart".' He then saw the key point - that the density of Silver's adhesive controls how hard it grips, so it could be tuned to hold paper and let go again. Sources split on the year: 1973 (The Chemical Engineer, MNopedia) or 1974 (Wikipedia, invent.org, Grokipedia). Fry worked the idea up under 3M's 'permitted bootlegging' policy, which let employees spend company time on self-directed projects.

question: 3M put the Post-it Note on sale across the United States in April 1980 in a canary yellow the pads have kept ever since. What settled that colour?
answer: The scrap paper stacked in the lab next door
choices: The scrap paper stacked in the lab next door
The shade a 3M designer judged most eye-catching
The one dye that survived contact with the adhesive
The colour the product's own sales team voted for
context: The lab beside the Post-it team happened to have canary yellow scrap paper on hand, so that is what the notes were made from. Nobody chose it for the product. The Post-it Note went national on 6 April 1980, reached Canada and Europe in 1981, and won 3M's Outstanding New Product award that year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_note.

question: On 15 January 1959 Harry Coover took Kodak's new adhesive, Eastman 910, onto the American TV panel show 'I've Got a Secret', hosted by Garry Moore, where the panel had to guess what a guest was hiding. Coover put a single drop of it between a metal bar and a cable. What happened next on live television?
answer: The host was hoisted off the studio floor hanging from it
choices: The host was hoisted off the studio floor hanging from it
The panel hauled at the bar in turn and could not part it
A stagehand hung the show's painted scenery from the joint
The bar took the weight of a barrel winched over the stage
context: One drop of Eastman 910 between the bar and the cable held Garry Moore's whole weight clear of the studio floor. Moore's line on air: 'Dr. Coover's secret is the only thing between my 150 pounds and that wire, will be one drop of glue.' Coover had filed his adhesive patent in 1954, and Kodak had put the product on sale in 1958 as the industrial 'Eastman 910', later licensed to Loctite and rebranded Super Glue. Sources cite different patent numbers for that 1954 filing, so the number is not worth quoting. Sources: cbsnews.com, 'Almanac: Super Glue'; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/harry-coover.

question: In 1951, nine years after Kodak had thrown the sticky cyanoacrylate out, the chemist Fred Joyner was working with the same compounds at the company's Kingsport, Tennessee plant on heat-resistant polymers for jet canopies. He loaded a sample into an instrument for one routine measurement, and it cost Kodak the instrument for good. What did Joyner wreck?
answer: A refractometer, its glass prisms welded together
choices: A refractometer, its glass prisms welded together
A viscometer, its narrow capillary plugged solid
A calorimeter, its sample chamber sealed over
A balance, its weighing pan cemented to the beam
context: Joyner was measuring how much the compound bends light, and to do it he spread ethyl cyanoacrylate in a thin layer between the prisms. The accident was identical to 1942; what had changed was the specification Coover was holding. This time he read the ruined instrument as a result rather than a mess: an adhesive that needs no heat, no clamping, no solvent and no drying time. There was no single eureka - the same compound had to be rejected twice before anyone accepted it. Naming note: Grokipedia and several trade retellings name Fred Joyner; the Wikipedia and Lemelson-MIT accounts describe the refractometer incident without naming the chemist. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ethyl_cyanoacrylate; popsci.com; lemelson.mit.edu/resources/harry-coover.

question: In 1968, at 3M's central research laboratories in Maplewood, Minnesota, Spencer Silver added more of a reactant than the recipe called for, and the result astonished him. His assignment, before he changed anything, had been plain: a pressure-sensitive adhesive stronger than anything on 3M's shelf. What was that stronger adhesive for?
answer: Holding panels together in aircraft construction
choices: Holding panels together in aircraft construction
Splicing lengths of photographic film in a lab
Fixing reflective road signs to metal posts
Bonding soles onto shoes on a factory line
context: Silver's own account, given to the Financial Times in 2010: 'I added more than the recommended amount of the chemical reactant that causes the molecules to polymerise. The result was quite astonishing.' The target had been a stronger pressure-sensitive adhesive for aircraft construction; what came out of the flask was the mirror image of Coover's compound, and it sat unused inside 3M for years. Sources: thechemicalengineer.com, 'Spencer Silver and Arthur Fry: in search of an application'; adhesivesmag.com obituary of Spencer Silver; grokipedia.com/page/Spencer_Silver.

question: Superglue is not drying when it sets: nothing evaporates out of it. A drop goes from liquid to hard solid in seconds as its molecules snap together into long chains. Something it meets on the way out of the tube starts that chain reaction. What is it?
answer: The trace of water sitting on almost every surface
choices: The trace of water sitting on almost every surface
The oxygen the liquid meets as the tube is opened
The warmth of the hand or bench it is squeezed onto
The pressure of the two surfaces pressed together
context: Coover put it plainly: 'all surfaces have at least a monomolecular layer of water on them. It's actually the water, or any weak base, that is the catalyst causing the polymerization.' Hydroxide ions from that trace moisture attack the molecule's carbon-carbon double bond and set off an anionic chain-growth polymerisation that zips the monomers into long solid chains. Compare the four glues a person would guess instead, each with a genuinely different mechanism: epoxy (a two-part chemical cure), hot-melt (cooling), rubber cement (solvent evaporating) and white PVA school glue (water evaporating). Skin is the worst thing you can touch, because fingers carry both moisture and amino acids and both start the reaction; acetone frees bonded skin because it breaks the polymer chains down. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanoacrylate; University of Bristol, Molecule of the Month, July 2009; popsci.com (quoting Coover).

question: Peel a Post-it Note off a page and the page comes away undamaged; press the note somewhere else and it grips again, and it will do that dozens of times over. What is on the back of the note?
answer: A sparse layer of tough spheres touching the page at points
choices: A sparse layer of tough spheres touching the page at points
A soft film that stays half-set and grips the page lightly
A strong adhesive diluted down to a fraction of its grip
A mesh of fine fibres holding a strong adhesive off the page
context: Ordinary glue cannot do both jobs: it grips the paper fibres and tears them on the way off, or else it quits after a single use. What is on the back of the note is acrylate copolymer microspheres, roughly 1 to 250 microns across with most between 5 and 150. They will not dissolve in solvent (they only disperse and swell), will not melt or flow when heated, and spring back to round after being squashed. Coated on paper they form what their inventor Spencer Silver called a 'sparse monolayer', so the sheet touches the page only at scattered points - he compared it to sticking to a bunch of marbles. The geometry is the mechanism, not a thinner film of ordinary glue. Silver's patent US 3,691,140, filed 9 March 1970 and granted 12 September 1972, describes 'infusible, solvent-dispersible, solvent-insoluble, inherently tacky, elastomeric copolymer microspheres' and puts the film's tensile strength at 'less than about 10 psi' - a measured, deliberate weakness. Sources: patents.google.com/patent/US3691140A/en; C&EN, 'Sticky Notes'; thechemicalengineer.com.

question: A crime lab seals a stolen laptop in a glass chamber, warms a few drops of superglue inside it until the glue fumes, and shuts the door. When the chamber is opened, fingerprints nobody could see on the plastic are plainly there. What did the fumes do to the prints?
answer: Grew a hard white polymer along every ridge of the print
choices: Grew a hard white polymer along every ridge of the print
Etched the bare plastic everywhere the finger had not touched
Stained the sweat left in the print a deep permanent blue
Baked a faint brown shadow of each print into the plastic
context: The vapour reacts with the invisible sweat residue a finger leaves behind, and white polymer grows along the ridges until the print stands out to the naked eye - that is how latent prints are developed in fuming chambers. The same chemistry has an ugly side: squeezed onto cotton, wool or fibreglass, superglue sets off a fast exothermic reaction violent enough to cause burns and to give off irritating white smoke, which is why it should never be tested on a cotton glove. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanoacrylate.

question: Harry Coover said that 'all surfaces have at least a monomolecular layer of water on them' - a film one molecule thick - and that this water is what sets his glue off. There is water vapour in the air as well. By that account a tube of superglue ought to set solid on the shop shelf, and it does not. What else is in the tube?
answer: An acid, which holds the reaction back until the glue meets a surface
choices: An acid, which holds the reaction back until the glue meets a surface
A solvent, which evaporates the instant the glue leaves the nozzle
A drying agent, which soaks up whatever water reaches the liquid
An inert gas, which fills the space above the liquid as it empties
context: Weak acids slow the polymerisation and strong acids stop it dead, so the monomer sits unreacted in the tube until it meets a moist surface; stabilisers used include sulphur dioxide, hydroquinone and organic sulfonic acid. TEST IT YOURSELF, and expect the opposite of common sense: a thin smear bonds better than a fat blob. The reaction is started at the surfaces, so a thick bead never polymerises all the way through - more glue makes a weaker joint. Sources: University of Bristol, Molecule of the Month, July 2009; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanoacrylate; grokipedia.com/page/Cyanoacrylate.

question: By 1977 3M had the adhesive, the paper and the idea. It test-marketed the pads in four American cities under the name 'Press 'n Peel', on ordinary stationery shelves alongside the notebooks and the envelopes. Sales were negligible. What was going wrong?
answer: A shopper in the aisle could not work out what a pad was for
choices: A shopper in the aisle could not work out what a pad was for
The pads cost several times what a pad of plain paper cost
The adhesive lost its grip after a few weeks on a warm shelf
Shops shelved the pads too low for most shoppers to notice
context: The product had to be used to be understood, and nothing about a pad sitting in a stationery aisle explained it. The four test cities are usually reported as Richmond VA, Denver CO, Tampa FL and Tulsa OK, though the city names come from secondary retellings and are less firmly sourced than the four-city test itself. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Post-it_note; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_note; invent.org, 'The Invention of the Post-it Note'.

question: By the late 1970s 3M's sticky-backed notepads had flopped in a four-city test launch, and two of the company's own men, Geoff Nicholson and his boss Joe Ramey, refused to let them die. They picked one city - Boise, Idaho - and saturated it, and what came back beat anything 3M had ever recorded. What did the two men do in Boise?
answer: Handed free sample pads straight to secretaries and office managers
choices: Handed free sample pads straight to secretaries and office managers
Paid every stationery shop in the city to stack the pads by the till
Ran a week of radio spots with a comedian demonstrating them
Put a free printed pad inside every newspaper delivered in the city
context: Roughly 90% of the people who were handed a sample pad said they would buy it - more than double the best rate any 3M product had ever recorded. The stunt is remembered as the 'Boise Blitz': stop selling it, start giving it away, and let people discover the use by using it. Sources give the year as 1978 (Wikipedia, MNopedia) or 1979 (Grokipedia and several business retellings), so the date is not worth anchoring on. The renamed Post-it Note launched nationally on 6 April 1980. Art Fry's own explanation of why it then spread so fast is itself a mechanism: customers stuck the notes onto documents they sent to other people, so every note advertised itself to its recipient. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_note; grokipedia.com/page/Post-it_note; mnhs.org/mnopedia; invent.org.

question: Water is a feeble chemical trigger; most liquid resins sit in an open dish and ignore it. Cyanoacrylate does not - the film of water on a benchtop sets it polymerising, molecules snapping into long chains, within seconds. The reason is the molecule's build: a cyano group and an ester sit crowded onto the same carbon, right beside the carbon-carbon double bond. What does that pairing do?
answer: They strip the double bond of electrons and leave it open to attack
choices: They strip the double bond of electrons and leave it open to attack
They twist the double bond out of shape so it snaps open on contact
They hold one hydrogen so loosely that plain water snatches it away
They lock the molecule into a strained ring that water prises open
context: The cyano group and the ester between them pull electron density off the carbon-carbon double bond, leaving it wide open to attack, and they also spread the negative charge on the growing chain across the whole molecule so it is stable enough to keep going. That double handicap is why even the feeble hydroxide ion in plain water is a good enough initiator, and why skin - which offers both moisture and amino acids - is the worst thing you can touch. Source: University of Bristol, Molecule of the Month, July 2009.

question: Kodak threw Coover's cyanoacrylate out in 1942. At 3M, Spencer Silver spent five or six years pitching his own odd adhesive at one internal seminar after another, and he had a phrase of his own for what it was. What did he call it?
answer: A solution waiting for a problem to solve
choices: A solution waiting for a problem to solve
A glue that never found anything to hold
An experiment that got clean away from me
A mistake I have never stopped defending
context: Silver also admitted: 'I'd spun my wheels a long time trying to find a product I could put my adhesive on.' Neither compound was ever a chemical failure. The cyanoacrylate was worthless only against a specification that demanded an optically clear, non-sticky gun sight, and the microspheres were a failure only against a specification that demanded maximum bond strength for aircraft. Both men were eventually honoured for the compound each had once been unable to give away: Coover accumulated over 460 patents and received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation from President Obama in 2010; Silver earned 37 patents at 3M and entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame the same year. Sources: adhesivesmag.com obituary of Spencer Silver; popsci.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Coover.

question: In 2014 Elizabeth Holmes's blood-testing company Theranos was worth about $9 billion on paper, built on the promise that its refrigerator-sized Edison box could run hundreds of tests from one finger-prick drop. Investigators later found the Edison ran only about a dozen of those tests. What actually ran the rest?
answer: modified commercial analysers made by Siemens
choices: modified commercial analysers made by Siemens
a network of Theranos boxes placed in Walgreens stores
a prototype microfluidic chip developed at Stanford
a mass spectrometer built in-house by Theranos engineers
context: The 'revolutionary' box in the lab was largely a prop; behind the scenes the company was buying and quietly modifying standard clinical analysers from Siemens. Source: Grokipedia -- Theranos; John Carreyrou, Bad Blood.

question: Forbes valued Elizabeth Holmes's blood-testing company Theranos at about $9 billion in 2014, making her the youngest self-made female billionaire on paper. Two years later, after John Carreyrou's Wall Street Journal expose and the federal lab findings, Forbes revised her personal net worth to what figure?
answer: zero dollars
choices: zero dollars
about one billion dollars
about five hundred million dollars
about fifty million dollars
context: Forbes had put Holmes's personal paper wealth at about $4.5 billion in 2014. In 2016, once the Edison story had broken, the magazine cut her estimated net worth all the way to zero. Source: Britannica -- Elizabeth Holmes; Forbes 2016 revision.

question: One finger-prick drop is only about 50 to 100 microlitres of blood. A routine glucose test alone uses roughly 15 microlitres of sample against 1,500 microlitres of reagent. Split that single drop across the hundreds of assays Theranos advertised, and what breaks first?
answer: each aliquot falls below the chemistry's detection threshold
choices: each aliquot falls below the chemistry's detection threshold
the sample clots before it can reach the reagent chamber
the reagent volume overwhelms and destroys the analyser's optics
the finger wound bleeds so slowly that oxygen ruins the sample
context: The pitch broke analytical chemistry before it broke the law: divide 80 microlitres 200 ways and each test has less than half a microlitre of blood to work with -- well below the sensitivity of standard immunoassays. Source: C&EN, 'Blood tests at your fingertips', 2017.

question: To make a finger-prick sample big enough for a machine designed for a full venous draw, Theranos technicians topped the tiny volume up with fluid. Why was this a disaster for tightly-ranged results like potassium?
answer: dilution drags the measured substance toward the instrument's noise floor and multiplies error
choices: dilution drags the measured substance toward the instrument's noise floor and multiplies error
the added fluid dissolves the red blood cells and destroys any signal
the potassium in the diluent overwhelms whatever came from the patient
salt in the diluent binds potassium and removes it from the sample entirely
context: A small pipetting error on a small sample is a huge percentage error after dilution. For an analyte with a narrow healthy range, that noise can push a normal patient into an alarm zone -- or hide a real crisis. Source: Kallidil Kalidasan, 'How good was Theranos' product?'.

question: In February 2015, federal inspectors would later find, an Edison assay for a hormone that governs testosterone levels was checked against the company's own internal accuracy standard, day after day. What did the check show about how often that assay failed to meet the standard?
answer: about 87% of the time
choices: about 87% of the time
about 12% of the time
about 3% of the time
about 1% of the time
context: Inspectors also documented that 29% of Edison quality-control checks in October 2014 already fell outside Theranos's own acceptable range. The internal numbers were catastrophic long before the public exposure. Source: MedCityNews, March 2016; CMS inspection report.

question: In May 2016, forced to reckon with what its Edison boxes had actually produced, Theranos took an extraordinary step for a clinical laboratory. What did it do to the results already sitting in patient files?
answer: voided or corrected tens of thousands of results covering roughly two years
choices: voided or corrected tens of thousands of results covering roughly two years
asked doctors to keep the results and simply add a caution note
reran every voided sample on the same Edison devices for confirmation
sealed the results and offered patients a discount on a future test
context: The voided tests included calcium, estrogen and testosterone. At least one Phoenix physician had already sent a patient to the emergency room on a bad number. Source: TechCrunch, 'Theranos voids two years of Edison tests', 18 May 2016.

question: On 25 January 2016 the federal lab regulator CMS finished inspecting Theranos's Newark, California laboratory and sent the company a letter about its hematology practices, including prothrombin-time tests used to dose the blood-thinner warfarin. What did the letter formally conclude?
answer: the practices posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety
choices: the practices posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety
the practices required a routine follow-up visit within twelve months
the practices met standards but the paperwork was incomplete
the practices could continue under a temporary research exemption
context: 'Immediate jeopardy' is the most serious finding in the CMS toolkit; Walgreens ordered that no blood drawn in its stores be sent to the Newark lab until the issues were resolved. Source: CMS letter dated 25 January 2016.

question: The Theranos criminal case ended in San Jose in January 2022. Elizabeth Holmes was sentenced that November to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison. Whom did the jury decide she had defrauded?
answer: investors, but not the patients tested at Walgreens
choices: investors, but not the patients tested at Walgreens
patients tested at Walgreens, but not investors
both investors and patients on every count charged
neither investors nor patients -- the case was thrown out
context: The jury convicted Holmes on four counts of wire fraud on investors (wire transfers over $140 million) and acquitted on the counts of defrauding patients. Sunny Balwani, tried separately, was convicted on all twelve counts against him and sentenced to about 13 years. Source: US Attorney NDCA, U.S. v. Elizabeth Holmes.

question: In 1897 J.J. Thomson had a ray streaming off a metal plate inside a glass tube, and nobody knew what it was. He measured how far a magnet bent the ray, then fitted a plate of different metal and measured again, then changed the gas in the tube and measured again. What did the swaps do to his number?
answer: The very same number every time
choices: The very same number every time
A different number for each metal
A different number for each gas
Larger numbers for heavier metals
context: Thomson made the point twice in his 1897 paper: 'the value of m/e is independent of the nature of the gas,' and, of two tubes built with different cathode metals, 'the values of m/e were, however, the same in the two tubes.' A ray that was somehow a property of the metal it came from should have changed when the metal changed. It did not. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' Philosophical Magazine 1897 (primary text, https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html); corroborated at https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson

question: On 30 April 1897 J.J. Thomson told a Royal Institution audience what his cathode-ray measurements had turned up, and the room did not buy it. Forty years later, in his memoirs, Thomson set down what one distinguished physicist who had been there admitted to him. What had the man thought?
answer: That Thomson had been pulling their legs
choices: That Thomson had been pulling their legs
That Thomson had misread his own instruments
That Thomson had rushed into print too soon
That Thomson had borrowed a German result
context: Thomson wrote it down in Recollections and Reflections (1936): 'I was even told long afterwards by a distinguished physicist who had been present at my lecture at the Royal Institution that he thought I had been "pulling their legs."' The talk was a Friday Evening Discourse, the Royal Institution's showpiece slot. The disbelief was not stupidity: he was asking a room of professionals to accept, on one set of deflection measurements, that something existed underneath the atom. Source: J.J. Thomson, Recollections and Reflections (G. Bell and Sons, London, 1936), quoted at https://www.chemteam.info/AtomicStructure/Disc-of-Electron-Intro.html and https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2000/10/discovery-of-the-electron ; date from https://ethw.org/Thomson_Reveals_Electron  (Legend.)

question: J.J. Thomson's 1897 measurement gave a ratio of mass to charge for his cathode-ray particle - how much matter each unit of charge was dragging along - and he set that beside the same ratio measured for the hydrogen ion. Hydrogen was the lightest thing known, and the atom was taken to be the floor of the world. Against that floor, what did Thomson's paper claim for his particle's mass?
answer: About a thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom
choices: About a thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom
About a thousand times heavier than a hydrogen atom
Just about the mass of a hydrogen atom itself
About ten times lighter than a hydrogen atom
context: Thomson's paper spells out the comparison: his value of 10^-7 'is very small compared with the value 10^-4, which is the smallest value of this quantity previously known, and which is the value for the hydrogen ion in electrolysis.' Two cautions. Direction: the MASS-to-charge ratio was about a thousand times lower, so the charge-to-mass ratio was about a thousand times higher, and the two are easy to invert. Number: 'about a thousand' is Thomson's own 1897 claim - the familiar 1,836 comes from later and far more precise measurement, not from the announcement. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' 1897 (https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson

question: Ernest Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering wrecked J.J. Thomson's 1904 model of the atom. When Thomson died in 1940, his ashes were laid in the nave of Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton - a few steps from Rutherford's grave. What had the two men been to each other?
answer: Rutherford trained under Thomson, then took over his chair at the Cavendish
choices: Rutherford trained under Thomson, then took over his chair at the Cavendish
Rutherford taught Thomson, then handed over his chair at the Cavendish
Rutherford trained under Marie Curie, then took over her chair in Paris
Rutherford ran Manchester, then lured Thomson away from the Cavendish
context: Rutherford had arrived at Thomson's Cavendish Laboratory in 1895 as its first foreign research scholar, worked under him, produced the experiment that wrecked his atom, and then succeeded him in the Cavendish chair in 1919. So the 1904 atom was taken apart by the professor's own research student - and the two men now lie a few steps apart in the nave of Westminster Abbey. Thomson's Nobel lecture in 1906 had been titled 'Carriers of Negative Electricity.' Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson (sections 'Death and Memorials' and 'Nobel Prize in Physics'); https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/sir-joseph-john-thomson/

question: Around 1878 Alfred Marshall Mayer pushed magnetised needles through corks, floated them in a dish of water and held a magnet above the dish. Up to six corks, they shoved one another apart and settled into a single evenly spaced ring. Then Mayer floated a seventh - and J.J. Thomson would later borrow the result as his picture of the inside of an atom. Where did the seventh cork settle?
answer: Inside the ring, near the middle of the dish
choices: Inside the ring, near the middle of the dish
In the ring, which spread to make room for it
Outside the ring, in a loose second circle
Off the water, pushed clean over the dish rim
context: That is the whole seed of the shell idea, done with corks and a dish of water, and you can repeat it. Mutual repulsion plus a pull toward the centre does not produce one ever-larger ring; past a certain count the surplus is driven inward and a second, inner group forms. Thomson used Mayer's floating magnets as the physical analogy for how corpuscles would arrange themselves inside an atom, and hoped each new ring would correspond to a period of the periodic table. Source: 'A. M. Mayer's experiments with floating magnets and their use in the atomic theories of matter,' Annals of Science 33(1) - https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00033797600200141 ; https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-70626-7_9 ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model

question: Bending cathode rays with a magnet was easy; physicists had done it for years. Bending them with an electric field was the test that would show the rays carried charge - and every attempt had failed, which was the standard objection to the idea that the rays were charged particles at all. J.J. Thomson got the electric bend in 1897 without raising the voltage others had used. What had been defeating everybody, himself included?
answer: Gas left in the tube was conducting and screening the field out
choices: Gas left in the tube was conducting and screening the field out
The glass walls were soaking up the field before it reached the rays
The rays were moving too fast for a field to act on them at all
The cathode metal held a charge that cancelled the applied field
context: Thomson names the objection in his own paper - 'An objection very generally urged against the view that the cathode rays are negatively electrified particles, is that hitherto no deflexion of the rays has been observed under a small electrostatic force' - and then answers it by pumping harder, down toward roughly 0.001 torr with improved mercury pumps: 'It was only when the vacuum was a good one that the deflexion took place.' The obstacle had been the apparatus, not the world. Worth carrying around: a null result can be a fact about your equipment. Source: J.J.
