Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' 1897 (https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html); vacuum figure from https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson

question: The word 'electron' is older than the electron. When J.J. Thomson measured his cathode-ray particle in 1897 he refused the word outright, called the thing a corpuscle, and held out until 1914. George Johnstone Stoney had put 'electron' into print back in 1891 without ever having seen such a particle; he had worked the quantity out in 1874 from measurements in a quite different corner of physics. Which measurements gave Stoney his number?
answer: Electrolysis - weighing the metal a current lays down
choices: Electrolysis - weighing the metal a current lays down
Spectroscopy - measuring the light a hot gas gives off
Calorimetry - measuring the heat a current produces
Electrostatics - measuring the pull between charged spheres
context: Stoney reasoned from the laws of electrolysis that electric charge comes in a fixed smallest lump, and in 1874 he calculated its size; his first name for it was the 'electrine,' and in 1891 he settled on 'electron.' So the name was coined for a unit of charge years before anyone caught the object that carries it. Thomson relented only by 1914, using 'electron' in his book The Atomic Theory. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Electron ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-Johnstone-Stoney

question: In the 1920s George Paget Thomson - son of J.J. Thomson - sent a beam of electrons through a thin crystal and caught them on a photographic plate behind it. Clinton Davisson was running a similar test in America. In 1937 the two men shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for what those plates showed. What had the electrons done in crossing the crystal?
answer: Spread and interfered, the way light waves do
choices: Spread and interfered, the way light waves do
Passed through unbent, as if the crystal were empty
Scattered at random, an even fog on the plate
Bent all one way, as a magnet would bend them
context: The 1937 citation reads 'for their experimental discovery of the diffraction of electrons by crystals' - the electron behaving as a wave. Here is the family joke buried in it: J.J. Thomson had taken the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics for work showing that the electron behaves as a particle. Father and son, roughly thirty years apart and in the same household, won the same prize for opposite-sounding answers about the same object, and neither prize was ever judged a mistake. That is wave-particle duality. An electron is not a tiny ball that occasionally misbehaves; it is something our two everyday pictures each capture half of. Source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1937/thomson/facts/ ; https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson

question: Around 1913 J.J. Thomson sent positive rays of neon through crossed electric and magnetic fields and let them fall on a photographic plate. Neon was a clean, unreactive, chemically pure element, yet its measured atomic weight came out at an awkward 20.2 that nobody could explain. What did the developed plate show?
answer: Two separate patches, at masses 20 and 22
choices: Two separate patches, at masses 20 and 22
One patch, sitting exactly at mass 20.2
A smear spread evenly from mass 19 to 21
A patch at mass 20, drifting as the tube warmed
context: Thomson's 'parabola method' made each mass-to-charge ratio trace its own curve across the plate, so two patches meant two different weights of neon atom: mass 20 and mass 22. Atoms of one element coming in different weights are what we now call isotopes, and this was the first evidence of them in a stable, non-radioactive element. It also cleared up the awkward 20.2 - that figure is the average of a mixture, not a property of a single kind of atom. Thomson's assistant on the work, Francis Aston, built the technique into mass spectrometry and took the 1922 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson ; https://grokipedia.com/page/james_j_thomson (section 'Work on Positive Rays and Isotopes', citing Thomson's 1913 Bakerian Lecture 'Rays of Positive Electricity')

question: J.J. Thomson's whole evidence in 1897 came to this: he had measured how far a beam of cathode rays bent in a magnetic field, and how far it bent in an electric one. From those two deflections he wrote in the paper that 'we have in the cathode rays matter in a new state' - and then went much further, making a claim not about cathode rays but about every substance in the world. What did Thomson claim?
answer: That all matter is built from one and the same kind of stuff
choices: That all matter is built from one and the same kind of stuff
That every element is a different knot tied in the ether
That the elements are still being manufactured inside stars
That the periodic table hides many elements yet to be found
context: His words: all matter 'is of one and the same kind; this matter being the substance from which all the chemical elements are built up.' Notice the size of the leap - two deflection measurements in one laboratory, and a claim about everything that exists. He turned out to be right, which is exactly why the caution of his critics was reasonable rather than foolish: nothing in the measurement itself guaranteed the conclusion. Kelvin's vortex atom, one of the wrong answers here, was a serious rival idea in which atoms were knots in the ether. Source: J.J. Thomson, 'Cathode Rays,' 1897 (https://web.lemoyne.edu/giunta/thomson1897.html)

question: J.J. Thomson's 1904 atom is remembered as a shape, but he did not build it to be a shape. In a Royal Institution lecture the next year he worked out where corpuscles - his name for electrons - would sit and circulate inside a sphere of positive charge: one at the centre, two at opposite ends of a diameter, three in an equilateral triangle, and rings of them further out. The arithmetic was aimed at a puzzle that had baffled his contemporaries for decades. What was Thomson trying to explain with the rings?
answer: Why the elements repeat their properties in regular periods
choices: Why the elements repeat their properties in regular periods
Why a heated element gives off its own pattern of bright lines
Why some heavy elements break down and throw off radiation
Why gases combine in simple whole-number ratios by volume
context: Thomson proposed that rings fill up and close, that the outermost ring fixes an element's combining power, and that a closed outer arrangement gives you the unreactive elements. Right or wrong, that is a picture with arithmetic attached - which is what makes a picture killable. Note also what the schoolbook cartoon loses: Thomson never wrote the words 'plum pudding,' and his 1904 paper describes 'a number of corpuscles moving about in a sphere of uniform positive electrification.' Moving. Its title investigates their 'stability and periods of oscillation.' Two papers argue the textbook version is a fabrication: Hon and Goldstein (Annalen der Physik, 2013) and Renstrom and Bomark (arXiv:2212.08572), who call it 'a mere caricature with almost no trace of Thomson's work.' Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model ; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786440409463107 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08572

question: By 1906 nobody knew how many corpuscles - J.J. Thomson's own name for electrons - an atom contained, and Thomson's own working figure was about a thousand of them per atom. That year he checked the count three independent ways: how light spreads passing through a gas, how X-rays scatter, and how beta rays are absorbed. All three landed in the same place. Where did they land?
answer: About 1 for hydrogen and about 25 for an air molecule
choices: About 1 for hydrogen and about 25 for an air molecule
About 3 for hydrogen and about 50 for an air molecule
About 70 for hydrogen and about 900 for an air molecule
About 1,000 for hydrogen and about 28,000 for an air molecule
context: The rule the three methods pointed to was that the number of corpuscles is of the order of the atomic weight - about 25 per air molecule, against a molecular weight of 28. Thomson had been wrong by a factor of a thousand, and he was the man who proved it, in a paper of his own titled 'On the Number of Corpuscles in an Atom.' Three unrelated methods agreeing is also the strongest kind of evidence there is: a mistake in one would not survive in the other two. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model (section 'Electron Estimation in 1906', citing Thomson, 'LXX. On the number of corpuscles in an atom', Phil. Mag. 1906)

question: J.J. Thomson published the arithmetic of his own atom's downfall. In a 1910 paper on the scattering of fast electrified particles he worked out what his design predicted for an alpha particle - a heavy, fast, positively charged one - crossing gold foil about four hundred atoms deep. Positive charge smeared smoothly through an atom cannot shove hard, so the alpha would take thousands of feeble random nudges, and random nudges pile up into a bell curve centred on zero. The measurement then came back with about one alpha in twenty thousand bending past ninety degrees. What was the largest bend Thomson's own paper had allowed?
answer: About two degrees
choices: About two degrees
About twelve degrees
About forty degrees
About eighty degrees
context: Thicker foil gave about one in eight thousand coming back the way it came. On a bell curve, ninety degrees was not an unlikely outcome; it was off the bottom of the graph, and no amount of tinkering with the smeared-out positive charge could reach it. That is the point of the whole story: the plum pudding died because it had been made specific enough to be killed. A model that predicts nothing cannot be wrong, which is exactly what makes it useless. Being refuted by your own published prediction is a compliment to the model, not an insult. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model (sections 'Multiple Scattering Integration in 1910' and 'Geiger-Marsden Experiments', citing Thomson, 'On the Scattering of Rapidly Moving Electrified Particles,' 1910)

question: The atom died; the mathematics did not. Building the 1904 model forced J.J. Thomson to ask where N equal charges will settle on a sphere so that their mutual repulsion energy is as small as it can be - a question mathematicians now call the Thomson problem, and one Steven Smale thought important enough to put on his 1998 list of eighteen problems for the twenty-first century. For how many values of N has anyone actually proved the answer, and which are they?
answer: Five of them - N = 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12
choices: Five of them - N = 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12
Five of them - N = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6
Six of them - N = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 20
Three of them - N = 2, 3 and 4 only
context: The five proved cases are the ones you would draw by instinct: an antipodal pair, a triangle, a tetrahedron, an octahedron and an icosahedron. Everything else - including N = 5 - is computer search and conjecture. Smale listed it seventh of his eighteen problems for the twenty-first century. A model can be flatly wrong about the world and still leave behind a question nobody has answered 120 years later. Source: https://phys.org/news/2016-07-chip-smale-7th-unsolved-problem.html ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Plum_pudding_model (section 'The Thomson Problem'); https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ThomsonProblem.html

question: Neil Shubin's team had flown into the Canadian Arctic five summers running and come back with nothing that mattered. In the 2004 field season, at a quarry on southern Ellesmere Island, someone chipping at the rock face looked up. Something was sticking out of the cliff. What was it?
answer: the tip of a flat, pointy snout
choices: the tip of a flat, pointy snout
a row of scales the size of coins
the curve of a jaw lined with teeth
a knot of small bones from a fin
context: Site NV2K17 had first been spotted by team member Jason Downs back in 2000; the 2004 season pulled three partial skeletons out of it, from about four to nine feet long. Accounts of who saw the snout first differ: the UCMP Berkeley newsletter credits Steve Gatesy of Brown University, noticing 'the tip of a flat, pointy snout peering out' of the face, while Shubin's own telling in Nature is first-person -- 'I looked over at a wall; there was a Tiktaalik snout looking out of the cliff at me.' Arctic field seasons ran from 1999 at roughly $100,000 each. Sources: UCMP Berkeley, 'Tiktaalik comes to UCMP' (Sept 2005); Nature News, 'The fish that crawled out of the water' (5 Apr 2006).

question: Neil Shubin's team dug Tiktaalik out of bare tundra on southern Ellesmere Island, more than 700 miles north of the Arctic Circle, with firearms kept close for polar bears. But continents move. Where on the globe did that ground sit when Tiktaalik was alive?
answer: about 30 degrees north, the subtropical belt
choices: about 30 degrees north, the subtropical belt
about 10 degrees north, deep in the tropics
about 60 degrees north, the cool northern belt
about 30 degrees south, the southern subtropics
context: In the Late Devonian that patch of Ellesmere sat near 30 degrees north, in a greenhouse world with atmospheric CO2 estimated near 1000 ppm -- warm, humid, low-lying country of shallow ponds and floodplains vegetated with primitive lycopods. Tiktaalik's neighbours in the same rock include the porolepiform fish Laccognathus embryi. The beds are fine-grained siltstone of the Fram Formation, late Frasnian, about 375 million years old; the team helicoptered in, camped on open tundra, and flew the fossils out in plaster jackets. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik' (Habitat and Environment).

question: Neil Shubin and Ted Daeschler knew the age of rock they needed; what they did not know was where to look for it. In Shubin's office in the late 1990s a geological argument started, and to settle it he pulled out the thing that would end up choosing their dig site. What was it?
answer: a first-year college geology textbook
choices: a first-year college geology textbook
a Canadian oil company's drilling survey
a nineteenth-century Arctic expedition's journal
a museum catalogue of Devonian fish fossils
context: Shubin: 'Everything changed one day in my office, back in the late '90s, when we had a geological debate. And to settle the debate, I pulled out a college geology textbook.' Its map of North America showed three belts of Devonian freshwater rock: Pennsylvania, which Shubin and Ted Daeschler had already worked; east Greenland, which Jenny Clack had already worked; and a strip across the Canadian Arctic that no paleontologist had ever searched for early tetrapods -- those Arctic rocks had been described only in oil-and-gas literature. Sources: iBiology, 'Finding Tiktaalik, the Fossil Link Between Fish and Land Animals' (Neil Shubin lecture); Harvard Gazette (2009); Nature News (5 Apr 2006).

question: The animal Neil Shubin's team had pulled out of the Ellesmere Island rock needed a name, and the team chose not to invent one themselves. They asked, were offered several names, and took one of them. Whom did they ask?
answer: the Nunavut council of Inuit elders
choices: the Nunavut council of Inuit elders
the anonymous donors who funded the digs
the editors who published the description
the schoolchildren of the nearest settlement
context: The team put the naming to the Nunavut Council of Elders (Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit Katimajiit), who offered names; 'Tiktaalik' was chosen -- an Inuktitut word for a large freshwater fish seen in the shallows. The gloss varies by source: the 2006 Nature description reads 'large freshwater fish', Grokipedia gives 'large shallow-water fish'. The species name roseae honours an anonymous benefactor of Devonian paleontology, so the donors did get a name after all -- just the second half of it. Sources: Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins, Nature 440 (2006); Wikipedia and Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik'.

question: Lobe-finned fish are already common in rocks about 385 million years old, and animals with four limbs turn up by about 365, so Neil Shubin's team knew the age band they wanted. Age alone would not do: two more things had to be true of a patch of rock before it was worth flying to it. What were they?
answer: laid down by fresh river water, and bare at the surface
choices: laid down by fresh river water, and bare at the surface
laid down in deep sea mud, and never folded since
laid down by desert wind, and rich in plants
laid down as reef limestone, and easy to split
context: Shubin's own framing of the window: 'we want something between 390 and 365 million years old. That's of a time period known as the Late Devonian.' Freshwater river sediment mattered because that is the setting where the transition happened; surface exposure mattered because a person has to be able to walk on the rock and see it. Shubin on the whole approach: 'We designed this expedition with the goal of finding this exact fossil. And we used the tools of evolution and geology as discovery tools to make a prediction about where to look. And the prediction was confirmed.' Sources: iBiology, Neil Shubin lecture; HHMI BioInteractive, 'It's a Fishapod'.

question: Ted Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins described the Ellesmere fossil in Nature in 2006. Its skull is flat and crocodile-shaped, about 20 cm long, with the eyes set on top of the head instead of at the sides and spiracles opening just behind them. But the feature the specialists called decisive is one that every living fish lacks. Which is it?
answer: a neck
choices: a neck
a tongue
an eyelid
a voice box
context: In a fish, a chain of bony plates bolts the shoulder girdle to the back of the skull, so head and body turn as one unit. In Tiktaalik those plates are gone and the pectoral girdle is fully detached -- the earliest known fish that could turn its head without turning its body. Ted Daeschler: 'The head of these animals was becoming more solidly constructed and, at the same time, more mobile with respect to the body.' The team's own nickname for the animal was the 'fishapod'. Per Ahlberg's 2006 verdict: 'Tiktaalik substantially narrows the gap in the fossil record of the fish-tetrapod transition.' Sources: Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins, Nature 440:757-763 (2006); Nature News (5 Apr 2006); Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik'.

question: In a fish, the hyomandibula is a strut that braces the jaw against the braincase and drives the pump that pushes water over the gills. In Tiktaalik that bone is drastically shrunk, which Jason Downs read as an animal already leaning less on its gills. In you, that same bone is still there, doing a different job. Where is it?
answer: in your middle ear, one of three tiny bones
choices: in your middle ear, one of three tiny bones
in your throat, the bone under your tongue
in your skull, the spike behind your jaw hinge
in your neck, the topmost bone of your spine
context: The bone is the stapes, smallest of the three bones of the human middle ear -- a fish's gill-pump strut, repurposed to carry sound. Jason Downs: 'The bony part of Tiktaalik's hyomandibula is greatly reduced from the primitive condition,' so these animals were 'already beginning to rely less on gill respiration.' Source: UChicago News, 'Fishapod reveals origins of head and neck structures of first land animals' (2008), reporting Downs, Daeschler, Jenkins & Shubin, 'The cranial endoskeleton of Tiktaalik roseae', Nature.

question: In January 2010 Grzegorz Niedzwiedzki, Piotr Szrek and Per Ahlberg published trackways from a quarry at Zachelmie in Poland's Holy Cross Mountains, where something walking on four legs had pressed its prints into rock about 395 million years old. Ahlberg, who had worked on the origin of land animals for 25 years, called it the biggest discovery he had ever been involved in. Neil Shubin's team had predicted the age and the setting of Tiktaalik's rock and found the animal there. What does that make Tiktaalik?
answer: a late cousin of animals that already walked
choices: a late cousin of animals that already walked
a direct ancestor of animals that later walked
a walker's descendant that had gone back to water
a true four-legged animal rather than a fish
context: The Zachelmie prints are roughly 18 million years older than the oldest known bones of any four-limbed animal, and 10 to 20 million years older than Tiktaalik itself: something with feet was already walking before Tiktaalik lived. The prediction still worked -- rock of the predicted age and setting held the predicted kind of animal -- but the word 'ancestor' did not. Tiktaalik is a late-surviving member of the transitional group, a cousin of the first walkers rather than their forefather. Per Ahlberg: 'I've been working on the origin of tetrapods for about 25 years, and this is the biggest discovery I have ever been involved in.' Jenny Clack: 'It's going to change all our ideas about why tetrapods emerged from the water.' Some isolated prints clearly show toes and ankles; the widest track is 26 cm across, implying an animal over 2.5 m long, while one trackmaker was only 40-50 cm. Sources: Niedzwiedzki, Szrek, Narkiewicz, Narkiewicz & Ahlberg, Nature 463:43-48 (7 Jan 2010); National Geographic (Ed Yong).

question: Twenty years after the best Tiktaalik specimen came out of the Arctic quarry, Thomas Stewart and colleagues ran that block through a micro-CT scanner and read out vertebrae and back ribs still buried inside it. Stewart said Tiktaalik was probably not walking on land, but was 'definitely doing something new'. What did the buried bones show it could do?
answer: prop itself up and push off with its hind fin
choices: prop itself up and push off with its hind fin
arch its back and lift its head clear of the water
flex its ribs and pump air down into its lungs
stiffen its trunk and swim in fast bursts
context: Micro-CT of the holotype NUFV 108 exposed sacral ribs 'expanded and ventrally curved', almost certainly tied by ligament to the expanded iliac blade of the pelvis -- a spine-to-hip linkage before limbs existed. The paper's conclusion: 'the origin of novel rib types preceded major alterations to trunk vertebrae, and linkage between pelvic fins and axial column preceded the origin of limbs.' Tom Stewart: 'This creature has so many traits -- large pair of hind appendages, large pelvis, and connection between the pelvis and axial skeleton -- that were key to the origin of walking.' Sources: Stewart, Lemberg, Hillan, Magallanes, Daeschler & Shubin, PNAS 121(15) (9 April 2024), 'The axial skeleton of Tiktaalik roseae'; Phys.org (Apr 2024).

question: Tiktaalik's front appendage holds a stout humerus, a radius and an ulna of about the same length, and a scatter of small irregular wrist bones, with an elbow that bends through roughly ninety degrees. What Neil Shubin's team still had to settle was how far toward a hand it had actually gone. What does its far tip carry?
answer: lepidotrichia, the segmented rays of an ordinary fish fin
choices: lepidotrichia, the segmented rays of an ordinary fish fin
phalanges, the jointed finger bones of a land animal
metacarpals, the long palm bones that spread a hand
ceratotrichia, the unsegmented rods of a shark's fin
context: Not a limb: a fin with a limb inside it. The humerus carries a broad deltopectoral crest and a spirally twisted shaft; the wrist bones include a radiale and an ulnare; preserved fins reach about 30 cm. John Maisey's reframe of the whole story in 2006: 'Tetrapods did not so much conquer the land, as escape from the water.' Sources: Shubin, Daeschler & Jenkins, 'The pectoral fin of Tiktaalik roseae and the origin of the tetrapod limb', Nature 440 (2006); Nature News (5 Apr 2006); Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik'.

question: The Zachelmie trackways in Poland - prints in rock about 395 million years old, older than Tiktaalik - did not settle the matter quietly. In 2015 Spencer Lucas argued that the marks were not footprints at all, and in 2019 Per Ahlberg published a hard rebuttal, pointing to how closely they match the anatomy of tetrapod feet. What had Lucas argued the marks really were?
answer: traces left by fish feeding and fish nesting
choices: traces left by fish feeding and fish nesting
cracks opened in drying mud and later filled
burrows dug by worms through soft sediment
scours cut by cobbles rolled in a storm
context: Ahlberg's 2019 reply was blunt: 'There is no way these could be formed by a natural process,' citing the marks' anatomical consistency with tetrapod feet. Neil Shubin, cautious even though the tracks had displaced his own animal: 'The skeletal anatomy, let alone evolutionary relationships, of a trackmaker is hard to interpret from a track' -- noting that Tiktaalik's own skeleton pressed into sand at different angles could leave prints like these. Later reanalysis also moved the setting from a marginal-marine tidal flat to ephemeral non-marine lakes. The argument is still live, which is the point. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Zachelmie trackways'; 'Non-marine palaeoenvironment associated to the earliest tetrapod tracks' (PMC5773519); National Geographic (Ed Yong).

question: One block from the 2004 Arctic season that produced Tiktaalik - collected days before Tiktaalik itself - sat in storage for about fifteen years before anyone looked inside it. A CT scan in 2020 found an articulated fin in the rock, and in 2022 Thomas Stewart, Neil Shubin and colleagues named the animal Qikiqtania wakei: about 75 cm long against Tiktaalik's nine feet, with a boomerang-shaped upper arm bone. What did that arm bone say the animal's line had done?
answer: gone back to paddling in open water
choices: gone back to paddling in open water
started walking short stretches on land
taken to burrowing in the riverbed mud
kept propping itself up in the shallows
context: Holotype NUFV 137. Its humerus is smooth and boomerang-shaped, missing the muscle ridges and processes that let Tiktaalik prop itself up; Shubin: 'it doesn't have the elements that would support it pushing up on land.' Qikiqtania's ancestors could already prop -- this line went back to the water. The group was experimenting in both directions, not marching toward land. Sources: Stewart, Lemberg, Daly, Daeschler & Shubin, Nature (2022), 'A new elpistostegalian from the Late Devonian of the Canadian Arctic'; UChicago News; Wikipedia, 'Qikiqtania'.

question: Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock, and after a single day each one is about 38 millionths of a second out of step with clocks on the ground -- a gap no human sense could ever notice. But your phone finds you by turning those clock readings into distances at the speed of light. Left uncorrected, how far wrong would your position be after one day?
answer: About 11 kilometres
choices: About 11 kilometres
About 11 metres
About 11 centimetres
About 11 millimetres
context: A GPS receiver converts clock time into distance at the speed of light, so a timing error of one nanosecond is about 30 centimetres of position error, and one microsecond is about 300 metres. The daily discrepancy is 38,640 nanoseconds; multiply that by 30 centimetres and you get roughly 11.6 kilometres, which is where the published figure of about 11.4 km per day comes from. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Error analysis for the Global Positioning System'; GIM International, 'GPS: Position, Time and Distance'; GNSS Metrics, 'Clock Error and Its Effect on Positioning'.

question: In 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating won $8,000 from the US Office of Naval Research to test whether moving clocks really keep different time. Nearly all of it -- $7,600 -- went on a single purchase. What did that money buy?
answer: Eight round-the-world airline tickets, two seats per flight
choices: Eight round-the-world airline tickets, two seats per flight
Eight caesium beam tubes to keep the clocks running
Eight weeks of priority time on the Naval Observatory's clocks
Eight days of chartered jet flying over the Atlantic
context: The published account records $7,600 of the $8,000 grant spent on eight round-the-world plane tickets, 'including two seats on each flight for Mr. Clock.' The four HP 5061A caesium-beam clocks were suitcase-sized and too delicate for the cargo hold, so they rode in the cabin as ticketed passengers on regularly scheduled commercial airliners. Eastward around the world first, then a week sitting side by side, then westward; the flights were completed on 7 October 1971, with the reference clocks left behind at the US Naval Observatory. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hafele-Keating experiment'.

question: A GPS satellite does two things at once that Einstein said would each change its clock's rate, and the two pull opposite ways: it orbits 20,200 kilometres up, where gravity is weaker, and it travels at about 3.9 kilometres per second. Nobody could build a navigation system without knowing which of the two came out on top. Which wins, and what does it do to the clock?
answer: The height effect wins, and the clock runs fast
choices: The height effect wins, and the clock runs fast
The speed effect wins, and the clock runs slow
The height effect wins, and the clock runs slow
The speed effect wins, and the clock runs fast
context: Weaker gravity at 20,200 kilometres altitude makes the satellite clock GAIN about 45.8 microseconds a day. Its orbital speed of roughly 3.87 km/s makes it LOSE about 7.2 microseconds a day (7,214 nanoseconds). Gravity wins, and the net is a gain of about 38.6 microseconds a day -- which is why the common line that 'time dilation makes GPS clocks run slow' is exactly backwards. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Error analysis for the Global Positioning System'; Grokipedia, same article.

question: Gravitational time dilation has a rule simple enough to aim at your own body: two clocks at different heights differ in rate by the fraction gh/c-squared -- gravity times height, divided by the speed of light squared -- so your head has kept different time from your feet all your life. In 2010 a NIST team measured it, raising one aluminium-ion clock 33 centimetres above another. Over a 79-year lifetime, how far apart do the two clocks drift?
answer: About 90 billionths of a second
choices: About 90 billionths of a second
About 90 millionths of a second
About 90 thousandths of a second
About 90 trillionths of a second
context: NIST's 2010 experiment is the calibration anchor: two aluminium-ion optical clocks raised about 33 centimetres (roughly one foot) apart in height differ by about 90 billionths of a second over a 79-year lifetime. Run the arithmetic yourself -- g = 9.8 m/s-squared, h = your own height, c-squared = 9 x 10^16 -- and the answer comes out in the hundreds of nanoseconds for an adult standing up. The same team also caught velocity time dilation at walking-to-cycling speeds of a few metres per second. Sources: Chou, Hume, Rosenband & Wineland, 'Optical Clocks and Relativity', Science, 24 September 2010; NIST/ScienceDaily release; Grokipedia, 'Gravitational time dilation'.

question: On 23 June 1977 the US Navy launched NTS-2, carrying the first caesium atomic clock ever put into orbit -- the prototype for the whole GPS system. Relativity predicted that clock would tick at a different rate up there. But, as the physicist Neil Ashby later put it, 'there were some who doubted that relativistic effects were real'. So what did the engineers build into the satellite's clock system?
answer: A correction circuit that could be switched on only after launch
choices: A correction circuit that could be switched on only after launch
A second, deliberately uncorrected clock running alongside as a control
A radio link that let the ground rewrite the clock's rate at will
A backup clock tuned to the old, pre-relativity frequency
context: Because some engineers doubted relativity was real, a frequency synthesizer was built into the NTS-2 clock system and left switched OFF at launch -- to be turned on afterwards only if the orbiting clock's rate really did match general relativity's prediction. They built an off switch for Einstein. NTS-2 launched on 23 June 1977 with the first caesium clock ever placed in orbit, and they ran it uncorrected for about twenty days before deciding. Sources: Neil Ashby, 'Relativity in the Global Positioning System', Living Reviews in Relativity 6 (2003) 1; leapsecond.com reprint; Gunter's Space Page; eoPortal TIMATION.

question: Gamma rays from iron-57 had to climb 22 metres up a tower shaft in Harvard's Jefferson Physical Laboratory before Robert Pound and Glen Rebka could read them at the top. Every gamma ray scattered on the way up is one the detector never counts, and losing too many would have buried the faint shift the two men were hunting. So what did the gamma rays make that climb through?
answer: A Mylar bag filled with helium gas
choices: A Mylar bag filled with helium gas
A steel pipe pumped down to vacuum
A plastic tube flushed with nitrogen
A brass tube filled with argon gas
context: The gamma rays travelled up the tower inside a Mylar bag filled with helium, put there to cut the scattering that would otherwise have eaten the beam over 22 metres. The shift Pound and Rebka were reading was a few parts in a million billion, produced by gravity alone: ten days of data gave a fractional frequency shift of magnitude 2.56 +/- 0.25 parts in 10^15, first published in Physical Review Letters 3, 439 on 1 November 1959. A definitive run in April 1960 agreed with general relativity to about 10 per cent, and Pound's laboratory reached the 1 per cent level in 1964 with Snider. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'; Pound & Rebka, Phys. Rev. Lett. 3, 439 (1959); Grokipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'.

question: Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew their caesium clocks all the way around the world eastward, rested them for a week, then flew them all the way around westward, while identical clocks stayed behind at the US Naval Observatory. When the westbound clocks were carried back in and read against the ones that had never moved, what did they show?
answer: They read about 273 nanoseconds ahead of the stay-at-home clocks
choices: They read about 273 nanoseconds ahead of the stay-at-home clocks
They read about 273 nanoseconds behind the stay-at-home clocks
They read about 59 nanoseconds ahead of the stay-at-home clocks
They read about 59 nanoseconds behind the stay-at-home clocks
context: Westward the prediction was +275 +/- 21 nanoseconds and the measurement +273 +/- 7 -- agreement to 0.09 sigma, the clean result of the pair. Eastward was the messier one, and honesty requires saying so: predicted -40 +/- 23, measured -59 +/- 10, agreeing to about 0.76 sigma. Close, not perfect. Four HP 5061A caesium-beam clocks made both trips on scheduled commercial airliners; the results appeared in Science on 14 July 1972. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hafele-Keating experiment'.

question: Carroll Alley's University of Maryland team set out to pin the flying-clock result down far tighter than Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating had managed. Between September 1975 and January 1976 they flew five fifteen-hour loops over Chesapeake Bay at about ten kilometres up, carrying a sealed box holding three caesium and three rubidium clocks, and tightened the agreement to about one percent. What let them compare the flying clocks against the ground clocks continuously, in real time?
answer: A pulsed laser link beamed between the aircraft and the ground
choices: A pulsed laser link beamed between the aircraft and the ground
A shortwave radio link relayed through a chain of ground stations
A television broadcast carrier used as a shared timing reference
A trailing wire antenna towed behind the aircraft on each pass
context: The pulsed laser link gave a live comparison between the airborne clocks and identical clocks on the ground, while radar tracked the aircraft precisely enough that the velocity effect could be separated out from the gravitational one. That separation is the whole trick: the two effects pull opposite ways, so you cannot check either unless you can tell them apart. Sources: C. O. Alley, 'Proper Time Experiments in Gravitational Fields with Atomic Clocks, Aircraft, and Laser Light Pulses'; Ben Crowell, lightandmatter.com, 'Historical photos and information about the Hafele-Keating and Alley experiments'.

question: Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew the same clocks in the same kind of aircraft at the same altitudes twice -- eastward around the world, then westward -- and the velocity part of their prediction did not simply repeat itself. It changed sign between the two flights, which is why the direction of travel mattered at all. What made flying west flip it?
answer: The plane's speed partly cancelled the spin of the ground beneath it
choices: The plane's speed partly cancelled the spin of the ground beneath it
The plane flew a longer path against the prevailing jet stream
The plane's speed was measured against the air, not against the ground
The plane's route bent nearer the poles, where the ground moves slower
context: The reference clocks at the Naval Observatory are themselves being carried eastward by the Earth's rotation at hundreds of metres per second. An eastbound plane adds to that motion, moves faster in the non-rotating frame, and loses more to velocity than the ground clock does. A westbound plane subtracts from it, moves more slowly than the ground, and therefore loses less -- so its velocity term comes out positive. Predicted components: eastward gravitational +144 +/- 14 ns and kinematic -184 +/- 18; westward gravitational +179 +/- 18 and kinematic +96 +/- 10. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hafele-Keating experiment'.

question: In 1959 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka set out to catch gravity's effect on time inside a single building: a drop of about 22 metres down a tower in Harvard's Jefferson Physical Laboratory, using gamma rays from iron-57 and Rudolf Mossbauer's newly discovered recoilless emission. The shift they were hunting was a few parts in a million billion -- far too small to read off any dial. So they beat it by imposing a second, opposite shift they could control exactly, and sweeping it until the two cancelled. What produced that opposing shift?
answer: A vibrating loudspeaker coil that moved the gamma-ray source
choices: A vibrating loudspeaker coil that moved the gamma-ray source
A spinning rotor that swung the source through a tight circle
A magnetic field tuning the iron-57 nuclei's energy levels
A heater shifting the source's temperature by a few degrees
context: A vibrating speaker coil imposed a continuously varying Doppler shift on the gamma-ray source, sweeping the absorption curve until the Doppler shift exactly cancelled the gravitational one -- they cancelled gravity with sound. The gamma rays travelled up the tower inside a Mylar bag filled with helium to cut scattering. Ten days of data gave a fractional frequency shift of magnitude 2.56 +/- 0.25 parts in 10^15. First published in Physical Review Letters 3, 439 on 1 November 1959; a definitive run in April 1960 agreed to about 10 per cent, and Pound's laboratory reached the 1 per cent level in 1964 with Snider. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'; Pound & Rebka, Phys. Rev. Lett. 3, 439 (1959); Grokipedia, 'Pound-Rebka experiment'.

question: In 2022 a JILA team in Boulder chilled about a hundred thousand strontium atoms into a single cloud one millimetre tall -- a pencil-point's width -- and watched the atoms at the top of that cloud run faster than the atoms at the bottom, gravity's stretch of time resolved inside one sample. Reading a gap that faint took ninety hours of averaging, and it took holding one fragile thing steady for a record 37 seconds at a stretch. What had to survive those 37 seconds?
answer: Quantum coherence, the atoms all holding one rhythm
choices: Quantum coherence, the atoms all holding one rhythm
Entanglement, one shared quantum state across the cloud
The laser lock, its colour pinned to a reference cavity
The magnetic shield, its field steady around the trap
context: The JILA/NIST strontium lattice clock resolved the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample -- the top of the cloud running faster than the bottom -- with a fractional frequency uncertainty of 7.6 x 10^-21, a tenfold improvement on prior work, built from 90 hours of averaging. What the whole measurement rested on was the atoms' quantum coherence, held for a record 37 seconds: for that long the sample stayed in step with itself, which is what let so faint a gradient be read across one millimetre. Jun Ye on what it opens up: 'This a completely new ballgame, a new regime where quantum mechanics in curved space-time can be explored.' Sources: Bothwell, Kennedy, Aeppli, Kedar, Robinson, Oelker, Staron & Ye, 'Resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample', Nature, 16 February 2022 (arXiv:2109.12238); NIST news release; phys.org.

question: Your blood plasma is about one-fifth antibody by protein weight, and every one of those molecules was pumped out by a plasma cell — a B cell that has quit everything else and become a full-time factory. How many finished antibody molecules does one plasma cell release per second?
answer: About 2,000
choices: About 20
About 200
About 2,000
About 20,000
context: Alberts's Molecular Biology of the Cell calls it 'the astonishing rate of about 2000 molecules per second'. The same chapter notes that antibodies make up roughly 20% of the total protein in blood plasma by weight, and that a single B cell carries about 100,000 antigen receptors in its membrane. Source: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 'B Cells and Antibodies', NCBI Bookshelf (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK26884/).

question: Susumu Tonegawa's 1976 work was not done at a university. The Basel Institute for Immunology, opened in 1970, was built and paid for by the drug company F. Hoffmann-La Roche — reportedly about $24 million a year. What did Roche do about the direction of the research it was funding?
answer: Left the direction of the science alone
choices: Set yearly targets and reviewed each project
Claimed first rights to anything sellable
Left the direction of the science alone
Read and approved papers before publication
context: Roche established the institute in 1969 and it opened on 1 October 1970 with Niels K. Jerne as founding director. It trained over 500 scientists and produced three Nobel laureates — Jerne and Georges Kohler in 1984, Tonegawa in 1987 — before closing in 2001. Source: Wikipedia, 'Basel Institute for Immunology'.

question: In the summer of 1940 Linus Pauling sent the Journal of the American Chemical Society his answer to the puzzle of the blood: how does the body build an antibody shaped to grip an invader it has never met? In Pauling's theory, what gave each antibody its shape?
answer: The invader itself, with the chain moulding around it like clay on a coin
choices: A separate inherited gene, one for every shape the body can make
The invader itself, with the chain moulding around it like clay on a coin
A receptor already on the cell, knocked loose by the invader's touch
Copying errors piling up in the gene as the cell divides again and again
context: The Oregon State archive describes Pauling's antibody as a chain whose loose end moulds to the antigen 'like wet clay pushed against a coin', then folds back on itself 'like pancakes'. Pauling opened the paper by asking 'What is the simplest structure which can be suggested . . . for a molecule with the properties observed for antibodies?' — and elsewhere described his method as asking for 'the most simple, general and intellectually satisfying picture of the world'. The archive's verdict: 'It was only later that it was proven completely wrong.' Pauling did not invent the template idea — Friedrich Breinl and Felix Haurowitz proposed it in 1930 — he made it famous. Source: Oregon State University Libraries SCARC, Linus Pauling 'Proteins' narrative, page 17; Wikipedia, 'Felix Haurowitz'.

question: Renato Dulbecco talked Susumu Tonegawa into leaving the Salk Institute in 1971 for a brand-new immunology institute in Basel, where five years later Tonegawa settled immunology's oldest argument. He had finished his PhD three years before that move, at UC San Diego under Masaki Hayashi. What was the thesis on?
answer: Genetic transcription in a virus that infects bacteria
choices: Genetic transcription in a virus that infects bacteria
Antibody production in rabbits injected with foreign protein
Chromosome behaviour in the fruit fly Drosophila
Protein folding in the haemoglobin of sickle-cell blood
context: Tonegawa took his PhD in 1968 at UC San Diego under Masaki Hayashi, on 'Genetic transcription of phage lambda' — a bacteriophage, a virus that infects bacteria — then did a postdoc with Renato Dulbecco at the Salk Institute; Dulbecco urged the move to Basel in 1971. Until then he had never worked on the immune system at all: the man who answered immunology's biggest question was a molecular biologist by training, not an immunologist. He was the sole recipient of the 1987 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and shared that year's Lasker Award with Leroy Hood and Philip Leder. Source: Wikipedia, 'Susumu Tonegawa'; Wikipedia, 'Leroy Hood'.

question: By 1957 immunologists were arguing hard about where an antibody's shape comes from, and nobody had ever watched a single immune cell on its own. In 1958 Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg managed it: they isolated cells one at a time and tested each for antibody. What did each cell turn out to produce?
answer: One antibody, the same one every time
choices: Several antibodies, one for each invader met
One antibody, the same one every time
No antibody until an invader touched it
A different antibody after each division
context: Nossal G, Lederberg J, 'Antibody production by single cells', Nature 1958;181(4620):1419-1420 — the first direct experimental evidence for clonal selection, the idea that the invader does not instruct a cell what to make but merely picks out the cells that already fit. Source: PubMed PMID 13552693; Wikipedia, 'Clonal selection'.

question: In 1965 William Dreyer and J. Claude Bennett published a paper in PNAS whose own title called antibody formation a paradox. Dreyer, working with Leroy Hood at Caltech, had been staring at antibody protein sequences that no accepted account of how a gene makes a protein could explain, and the fix the two men offered was dismissed for a decade. What did they propose?
answer: That two separate genes, one constant and one variable, make one chain
choices: That one gene is read twice over, in two different reading frames
That two finished protein chains are stitched together after translation
That two separate genes, one constant and one variable, make one chain
That one gene is read off both its strands, giving two different halves
context: Dreyer WJ, Bennett JC, 'The molecular basis of antibody formation: a paradox', PNAS 1965;54(3):864-869 — the 'two genes, one polypeptide' hypothesis. Leroy Hood, working with Dreyer at Caltech, sequenced immunoglobulin amino acids that supported the idea and helped fuel the 1970s debate over how immune diversity is generated. The proposal broke the 'one gene, one polypeptide' rule and was widely dismissed until Tonegawa's 1976 experiment. Source: PubMed PMID 4160200; Wikipedia, 'Leroy Hood'.

question: Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 theory had each lymphocyte fix its receptor shape blindly, before any invader turns up. Burnet saw the danger at once: among millions of blind guesses, some are bound to fit molecules of your own body. So his theory carried a fourth rule, one that predicted immune tolerance and autoimmune disease years before either was demonstrated. What did the fourth rule say becomes of a lymphocyte whose shape fits you?
answer: It is destroyed early, before it is ever put to work
choices: It is stripped of its receptors and released anyway
It is destroyed early, before it is ever put to work
It is held back in the marrow and never allowed to divide
It is bathed in your own molecules until it stops answering
context: Burnet's postulate reads that lymphocytes 'bearing receptors for self molecules ... are destroyed at an early stage'. He published 'A modification of Jerne's theory of antibody production using the concept of clonal selection' in the Australian Journal of Science in 1957 — commentators suggest he chose an Australian journal to publish fast and win priority over David Talmage, who had stated the same logic that year — and expanded it into a 1959 book. Burnet shared the 1960 Nobel Prize with Peter Medawar for acquired immunological tolerance, and said of it: 'My part in the discovery of acquired immunological tolerance was a very minor one - it was the formulation of an hypothesis that called for experiment.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Clonal selection'; Wikipedia, 'Frank Macfarlane Burnet'.

question: Before a developing lymphocyte can assemble an antibody gene out of separate pieces, the RAG proteins have to cut its chromosome open. A child who inherits two completely dead copies of RAG1 has no adaptive immunity at all. But some children inherit a RAG1 that works feebly rather than not at all — blunt scissors instead of no scissors. What do doctors find in these children?
answer: An immune system that attacks their own tissue
choices: A normal immune system that arrives years late
Defence against bacteria but none against viruses
Antibodies that protect the gut but nowhere else
An immune system that attacks their own tissue
context: Complete loss of RAG1 or RAG2 function produces severe combined immunodeficiency. Partial (hypomorphic) RAG variants produce Omenn syndrome and combined immunodeficiency with granuloma and/or autoimmunity (CID-G/A); milder variants show up as antibody deficiency, idiopathic CD4+ T lymphopenia and vasculitis. Source: Wikipedia, 'RAG1'; Wikipedia, 'Recombination-activating gene'.

question: In 1976 Nobumichi Hozumi and Susumu Tonegawa cut DNA from mouse embryo cells, and from a tumour cell that pumps out antibody, with the same restriction enzyme — one that chops DNA wherever an exact sequence appears — then fished in both with the same radioactive probe made from the antibody's own message. In the embryo the probe lit two bands far apart: one holding the DNA for the antibody's fixed tail, one holding the DNA for its gripping tip. Every textbook then taught that every cell in an animal carries the same genome. What did the probe light up in the tumour lane?
answer: One band, smaller than either embryo band, carrying both pieces
choices: One band, larger than the two embryo bands put together
One band, smaller than either embryo band, carrying both pieces
Two bands again, both smaller than the embryo pair, one piece each
Two bands again, in exactly the places of the embryo pair
context: The BALB/c embryo DNA gave two hybridising components, of molecular weight 6.0 million and 3.9 million; the MOPC 321 plasmacytoma DNA gave a single 2.4 million component that hybridised with both the V and the C probe — smaller, because the DNA lying between the two pieces had been cut out. The paper's closing sentence: 'The Vk and Ck genes, which are some distance away from each other in the embryo cells, are joined to form a contiguous polynucleotide stretch during differentiation of lymphocytes.' The dogma it destroyed: that every cell in your body carries an identical, unaltered copy of your genome. Source: Hozumi N, Tonegawa S, 'Evidence for somatic rearrangement of immunoglobulin genes coding for variable and constant regions', PNAS 1976;73(10):3628-3632 (PMID 824647).

question: In December 1989 David Schatz, Marjorie Oettinger and David Baltimore reported a gene they called RAG-1: put it into ordinary connective-tissue cells, which never rearrange anything, and those cells would begin joining antibody gene pieces — rarely, but unmistakably. The next year the team found a second gene sitting immediately beside RAG-1, named it RAG-2, and put both into the cells together. What did that do to the rearrangement rate?
answer: Roughly a thousandfold
choices: Roughly double
Roughly tenfold
Roughly a hundredfold
Roughly a thousandfold
context: Schatz DG, Oettinger MA, Baltimore D, 'The V(D)J recombination activating gene, RAG-1', Cell 1989;59(6):1035-1048 (22 December 1989), then 'RAG-1 and RAG-2, adjacent genes that synergistically activate V(D)J recombination', Science 1990;248(4962):1517-1523: cotransfection of RAG-1 with RAG-2 increased recombination frequency 1000-fold. Source: PubMed PMID 2598259 and PMID 2360047; Wikipedia, 'Recombination-activating gene'.

question: A developing B cell builds its antibody gene by splicing together short pieces called gene segments, picked from a stock it inherited. Two neighbouring cells can pick exactly the same segments and still end up with different antibodies, because an enzyme called terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, or TdT, gets at the raw ends before they are sewn together. What is TdT doing there?
answer: Adding DNA letters that no gene anywhere specifies
choices: Trimming a few letters off each end before joining
Copying letters across from the other chromosome
Adding DNA letters that no gene anywhere specifies
Reopening a folded end at an off-centre point
context: TdT is a template-independent DNA polymerase: it adds non-templated N nucleotides — up to about 20, with a G/C preference — to the coding ends, producing what Wikipedia calls 'a paratope that is highly variable, even when the same gene segments are recombined'. Mice without TdT show a roughly ten-fold drop in T-cell receptor diversity. It is switched on only briefly in immature cells, so mature lymphoid cells are always TdT-negative, and TdT-positive cells in a blood sample point to acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Source: Wikipedia, 'V(D)J recombination'; Wikipedia, 'Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase'; Janeway's Immunobiology, NCBI Bookshelf.

question: About a week after an infection, a temporary structure called a germinal centre organises itself inside your lymph node. In its dark zone, B cells divide furiously while deliberately introducing mutations — copying errors — into the very gene that codes their own antibody; in its light zone the daughters compete for scarce scraps of the invader, and the poorest grippers are killed off. Set that deliberate scrambling against the ordinary mutation rate elsewhere in the same cell's genome. How much faster is it?
answer: Roughly a million times faster
choices: Roughly ten times faster
Roughly a thousand times faster
Roughly a million times faster
Roughly a billion times faster
context: Somatic hypermutation runs at least 100,000 to 1,000,000 times the normal genomic rate, giving one or two mutations per complementarity-determining region per cell generation, concentrated in the gripping surfaces and following hotspot motifs. Dark-zone cells cycle in as little as five hours; the whole germinal centre lasts about three weeks. The same machinery, aimed badly, has been strongly implicated in B-cell lymphomas. The enzyme responsible is activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), which converts cytosine to uracil; Tasuku Honjo's group showed AID is required for both hypermutation and antibody class switching (Muramatsu et al., Cell 2000;102(5):553-563). Source: Wikipedia, 'Somatic hypermutation'; Wikipedia, 'Affinity maturation'; Wikipedia, 'Germinal center'.

question: In every developing lymphocyte the RAG proteins deliberately break the cell's own chromosome in two places and rejoin the cut ends. Biologists traced where such a machine could have come from, and the sequence pointed to an ancient family of genes — one intact ancestral pair, RAG1 and RAG2 side by side, survives in the Chinese lancelet, a small fish-shaped sea animal alive right now. What was RAG's ancestor doing before vertebrates put it to work building antibodies?
answer: Jumping: cutting itself out of a genome and dropping in elsewhere
choices: Jumping: cutting itself out of a genome and dropping in elsewhere
Mending: sealing up chromosome breaks left behind by radiation
Unknotting: nicking tangled chromosomes so they can pull apart
Invading: threading a virus's DNA into its host's chromosome
context: Active Transib transposons carrying both RAG1 and RAG2, dubbed 'ProtoRAG', have been found in the Chinese lancelet Branchiostoma belcheri — a living animal, not a fossil. On core sequence homology, RAG1 is believed to have evolved from a transposase of the Transib superfamily: a jumping gene that invaded an ancestral vertebrate genome and was domesticated into the machine that now builds your antibodies. This is a well-supported inference from sequence and from a living example, not a directly observed event. Source: Wikipedia, 'Recombination-activating gene'.

question: Lampreys and hagfish are jawless fish whose line split from ours before jaws existed. They carry no antibodies and not one RAG gene, yet they do have lymphocytes, and each one displays a receptor assembled from a completely different set of interchangeable protein parts, shuffled by different enzymes entirely. Biologists have counted what that system can generate. How does its range compare with your own?
answer: Around as many as your own antibody system makes
choices: Around a thousandth as many as your own system makes
Around a tenth as many as your own system makes
Around as many as your own antibody system makes
Around ten times as many as your own system makes
context: Jawless vertebrates assemble variable lymphocyte receptors from leucine-rich-repeat cassettes by serial gene conversion driven by the cytidine deaminases CDA1 and CDA2. Wikipedia: the VLR system 'can produce roughly the same number of potential receptors that the Ig-based system found in jawed vertebrates can.' Six VLR classes are known in lampreys and three in hagfish; VLRA/VLRB were identified by Guo and colleagues in 2009, VLRC+ cells by Hirano's team in 2013. Nature solved the same problem twice, with different parts. Source: Wikipedia, 'Variable lymphocyte receptor'.

question: Florentine well-diggers in the 1600s hit a stubborn limit: no suction pump they built could lift water higher than about 10 metres, and nobody could explain the wall. Which everyday object hits the exact same invisible ceiling for the exact same reason?
answer: A drinking straw
choices: A steam kettle
A garden hose
A drinking straw
A pair of bellows
context: You have never sucked anything through a straw in your life. You lower the pressure inside your mouth and the surrounding atmosphere pushes the liquid up the straw -- which is why a straw taller than about 10 metres can never work no matter how hard you pull. Source: Wikipedia 'Barometer' (siphon and suction-pump limit ~10 m; atmospheric-push mechanism).

question: In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube about a metre long with mercury, sealed the top with his thumb, and upended it into a dish. What did the mercury do next?
answer: It fell partway and stopped, leaving an empty space above it
choices: It drained out completely and left the whole tube empty
It stayed pinned to the sealed top by suction from above
It boiled at the sealed top and turned the tube to vapour
It fell partway and stopped, leaving an empty space above it
context: That empty space above the mercury was the first sustained man-made vacuum in history. The column landed at about 76 cm (roughly 30 inches) every time -- the birth of the barometer. Source: Wikipedia 'Evangelista Torricelli' (1643 experiment, ~76 cm / 30 in column, Torricellian vacuum).

question: Torricelli's mercury column stood at about 76 cm. If he had run the exact same experiment with a tube of water instead of mercury, roughly how tall a column would the water stand in?
answer: About 10.3 metres
choices: About 76 centimetres
About 10.3 metres
About 1 metre
About 30 metres
context: Mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water. The same weight of air balances a short column of the heavy stuff or a tall column of the light stuff -- and 0.76 m x 13.6 lands right at about 10.3 m, exactly the height where the Florentine pumps had already stalled. Source: Wikipedia 'Barometer' (mercury ~14x denser than water; ~80 cm of mercury vs ~10.5 m of water).

question: In a letter dated 11 June 1644 to Michelangelo Ricci, Torricelli proposed a picture of the world that would explain everything the mercury tube did. What was the image he used?
answer: We live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air
choices: The heavens push down on the Earth like a great vault
We live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air
The Earth breathes in and out and drives the tides of pumps
Nature draws water upward as a mother lifts her child
context: The Italian is 'Noi viviamo sommersi nel fondo d'un pelago d'aria.' The claim: the air itself has weight, and that weight -- pressing on the dish -- is what holds the mercury up. It reframed the whole puzzle. Source: Wikipedia 'Evangelista Torricelli' (11 June 1644 letter to Ricci, verbatim Italian quote).  (Legend.)

question: Blaise Pascal realised the two rival theories -- 'nature abhors a vacuum' versus 'the air has weight' -- would give different answers to one specific question. What question did he propose to settle it?
answer: Does the mercury column read lower at the top of a mountain?
choices: Does the mercury column read the same in daylight as at night?
Does a longer glass tube hold a taller mercury column inside it?
Does the mercury column change when the tube is tilted sideways?
Does the mercury column read lower at the top of a mountain?
context: If air really has weight, then higher up -- with less air overhead -- there must be less weight pressing the mercury up, so the column must fall. Horror vacui had no reason to care about altitude at all. Pascal had turned a metaphysical fight into a hike. Source: Wikipedia 'Blaise Pascal' (altitude-prediction argument for the Puy de Dome test).

question: On 19 September 1648 Pascal's brother-in-law Florin Perier carried a mercury barometer up the Puy de Dome (summit 1,465 m) in central France, because Pascal himself was too ill to climb. Perier left a second identical barometer at the monastery at the foot of the mountain, watched all day by Father Chastin. What was the point of Father Chastin sitting there all day?
answer: To rule out the weather quietly shifting during the climb
choices: To time the exact moment Perier reached the summit
To pray for Pascal's recovery while the climb was underway
To rule out the weather quietly shifting during the climb
To catch the barometer if the mercury spilled during the day
context: This is a control experiment in 1648. If the base column ALSO drifted during the day, any drop at the summit could not honestly be blamed on altitude. Chastin's job -- watching a barometer that was supposed to do nothing -- was the whole reason the result could be trusted. Source: Wikipedia 'Blaise Pascal' (Father Chastin control barometer at the base monastery).  (Legend.)

question: The Puy de Dome drop was surprisingly large for a climb of only about 1,465 m -- because atmospheric pressure does not fall in a straight line with height. Roughly what fraction of all the air in the atmosphere lies below the shoulder of Mount Everest (about 5.6 km up)?
answer: About half of the total
choices: About one tenth of it
About half of the total
About four fifths of it
Almost all of the air
context: Pressure roughly halves every 5.5 km (about ln(2) times the ~8.5 km scale height), so about half the atmosphere's entire mass sits below 5.6 km. Climb the first mountain and you have already left half the air below you. Source: Wikipedia 'Scale height' (Earth scale height ~8.5 km, halving distance ~5.5 km); NOAA JetStream Air Pressure page (half the atmosphere's mass below ~18,000 ft / 5.6 km).

question: The barometer sensor in a modern smartphone (iPhone 6 onward, most Android flagships) is sensitive enough that ordinary daily activity will nudge the pressure reading in real time. Of these four things you could do with your phone in the next minute, which one will move the reading the MOST?
answer: Riding an elevator up a few floors
choices: Walking briskly around the block
Spinning in a slow circle for one minute
Riding an elevator up a few floors
Setting it flat on a windowsill for a minute
context: The sensor is answering to altitude -- exactly what Pascal predicted -- not to motion. A few floors up is enough vertical distance to shift the pressure by a hair, and the sensor reports it. Walking around at ground level, spinning in place, or sitting on a sill barely changes the number at all. Try it: read the barometer app, take the elevator up ten floors, read it again. Source: method-restatement of the Puy de Dome protocol from Wikipedia 'Blaise Pascal' applied to smartphone MEMS barometer sensors (iPhone 6 onward, most Android flagships); Wikipedia 'Barometer' (atmospheric-pressure-with-altitude mechanism).

question: The same Julian Huxley who named transhumanism in 1957 also held a second, longer-running office across those same decades. From 1959 to 1962 he served as president of which organisation?
answer: the British Eugenics Society
choices: the British Eugenics Society
the Royal Society of London
the British Humanist Association
the Zoological Society of London
context: Huxley was vice-president of the British Eugenics Society from 1937 to 1944 and its president from 1959 to 1962. He also delivered the Galton memorial lecture in 1936 and 1962. Source: Aeon, 'Julian S. Huxley, the man who put eugenics into UNESCO'.

question: After Huxley, the movement organised itself with dates. In 1998 the philosophers Nick Bostrom and David Pearce co-founded a body they called the World Transhumanist Association. Under what shorter name does that same organisation operate today, after a 2008 rebrand?
answer: Humanity+
choices: Humanity+
the Extropy Institute
the Long Now Foundation
the Machine Intelligence Research Institute
context: Max More had already written the Principles of Extropy in 1990 and co-founded the Extropy Institute in 1992; Bostrom and Pearce's WTA was the academic wing, renamed Humanity+ in 2008. Source: Wikipedia, 'Humanity+'.

question: The inventor Ray Kurzweil is the movement's most-graded prophet: in a 2005 book he put two dates on the future -- human-level machine intelligence by 2029, and full human-machine merger by 2045 -- and in 2024 he reaffirmed both. What was the book?
answer: The Singularity Is Near
choices: The Singularity Is Near
The Age of Spiritual Machines
Superintelligence
The Fourth Age
context: Kurzweil's 2024 follow-up, The Singularity Is Nearer, reaffirmed 2029 and 2045. Nick Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014) is a related but distinct book by a different author. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Singularity Is Near'; 'The Singularity Is Nearer'.

question: Kurzweil defends his timeline with what he calls the Law of Accelerating Returns. Which observation does that law actually rest on -- the argument the bank must state at full strength before any objection lands?
answer: Computing power has grown exponentially across five separate underlying technologies, not just one chip.
choices: Computing power has grown exponentially across five separate underlying technologies, not just one chip.
Every decade of computing has produced a machine ten times cheaper than the one before it.
Every published prediction of AI capability has been beaten by the machines within twenty years.
Human brains have doubled in effective processing power every generation since Homo sapiens emerged.
context: The five paradigms Kurzweil names run from electromechanical calculators through relays, vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits -- the point being that Moore's Law is a specific case of a longer pattern. Source: Wikipedia, 'Accelerating change'.

question: In 2011 the Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and the researcher Mark Greaves wrote a MIT Technology Review essay titled 'The Singularity Isn't Near'. Their central objection carried a name. What did they call the effect that would drag Kurzweil's timeline?
answer: the complexity brake
choices: the complexity brake
the diminishing-return wall
the S-curve trap
the intelligence plateau
context: Allen and Greaves argued that as our models of intelligence get finer, the task of adding the next layer gets harder, not easier -- so raw processor gains do not translate into thinking machines on schedule. Source: Paul Allen, 'The Singularity Isn't Near', MIT Technology Review, 12 October 2011.

question: Kurzweil's 2029 and 2045 dates are, unusually for prophecy, gradable -- someone will be alive to check them. Which cognitive scientist, weighing in on the Singularity in 2008, wrote the flatly graded sentence 'There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity'?
answer: Steven Pinker
choices: Steven Pinker
Douglas Hofstadter
Daniel Dennett
Noam Chomsky
context: The sentence appeared in an IEEE Spectrum survey of Singularity views in June 2008. Dennett and Hofstadter have both written skeptically on AI but are not the author of this line. Source: IEEE Spectrum, 'Tech Luminaries Address Singularity' (2008).

question: In a September 2004 Foreign Policy special report, the political scientist Francis Fukuyama argued the transhumanist programme deserved a specific title. What did he call it?
answer: the world's most dangerous idea
choices: the world's most dangerous idea
the last utopian temptation
the second age of eugenics
the great human enclosure
context: Fukuyama, author of The End of History, expanded the argument in Our Posthuman Future (2002). The bank presents the charge with his name attached rather than in the bank's own voice. Source: Francis Fukuyama, 'Transhumanism', Foreign Policy, September/October 2004.

question: Before Coolidge's ductile tungsten wire ended the argument in 1911, several other metals were commercially shipped as bulb filaments and lost. One of them was so precious that when a bulb burned out the customer could return the spent lamp for a partial rebate on the metal inside. Which metal was that?
answer: Osmium
choices: Osmium
Platinum
Tantalum
Iridium
context: Osmium lamps sold from about 1898 to 1905 - the metal was rare enough that the burnt-out bulbs came back for credit. Platinum was tried and shelved as too expensive to burn; tantalum lamps went on sale in 1902 but the filaments deformed and shortened in use; Edison's own carbon and carbonized bamboo had lit the first commercial bulbs. Every one was somebody's product before tungsten won.

question: You pour milk into a mug of coffee and stir once. The white ribbon breaks into curls, and inside those curls are smaller curls, and inside those, smaller still. Where in physics does that everyday swirling belong -- one of the great unsolved problems, sitting on your kitchen table?
answer: turbulence
choices: turbulence
combustion
friction
buoyancy
context: Turbulence is arguably the most famous open problem of classical physics; the Feynman Lectures call it 'the last great unsolved problem'. Every candidate on this list is a real branch of fluid or thermal physics -- friction is real, buoyancy is real, combustion is real -- but only turbulence remains without a closed theory. Source: Feynman Lectures Vol. 1 Ch. 3.

question: You crack a garden tap open only a hair and the water slides out as a glassy column you can see straight through. Open the tap all the way and the same water bursts into a foamy, chaotic gush. An engineer would call that first, glassy regime by what name?
answer: laminar flow
choices: laminar flow
plug flow
Couette flow
Stokes flow
context: Laminar flow (from the Latin 'lamina', a thin plate) is the smooth regime that fills the pipe with parallel layers before turbulence sets in. All four options name real regimes in fluid mechanics: plug flow is the idealisation where a fluid moves as a single block with no velocity gradient across the pipe; Couette flow is shear-driven flow between two moving surfaces; Stokes flow is the extreme low-Reynolds regime where viscosity dominates so completely that time reverses cleanly. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laminar_flow

question: Manchester, 1883. An engineer runs a thin thread of coloured dye down the centre of water flowing through a long glass pipe. At low speed the dye holds a single straight line all the way through; past a threshold speed it bursts apart and fills the pipe. Whose classic experiment is that?
answer: Osborne Reynolds
choices: Osborne Reynolds
James Clerk Maxwell
William Thomson
George Gabriel Stokes
context: Reynolds published this as 'An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous, and of the law of resistance in parallel channels' (Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc., 1883). The dimensionless number that predicts the transition -- ratio of inertial to viscous forces -- now carries his name; for pipe flow it crosses over at about 2000-2300. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynolds_number

question: In 1941 the Soviet mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov made Richardson's cascade quantitative. His central prediction -- confirmed in atmosphere, oceans, and wind tunnels ever since -- was that in the inertial range the energy per unit wavenumber follows a specific power law. Which power law?
answer: k to the minus five-thirds
choices: k to the minus five-thirds
k to the minus one
k squared
k to the fourth
context: E(k) proportional to k^(-5/3), where k is the wavenumber. The exponent -5/3 has been measured in atmospheric turbulence, oceanic microstructure, wind-tunnel jets and grid turbulence, and it remains one of the most-cited pieces of turbulence theory. Sources: Kolmogorov (1941) Doklady Akad. Nauk SSSR 30, 301, and https://www.bohrium.com/en/sciencepedia/feynman/keyword/kolmogorov_five_thirds_law

question: In wind-tunnel and atmospheric turbulence, roughly 4 percent of acceleration measurements come in more than 2.5 standard deviations above the mean -- far more extreme events than Kolmogorov's 1941 theory predicts. What is this well-known correction to the classical picture called?
answer: intermittency
choices: intermittency
anomalous scaling
non-Gaussianity
anisotropy corrections
context: Intermittency: turbulence is not uniformly noisy but punctuated by rare, violent bursts of vorticity, so the higher-order statistics are dominated by the tails. The She-Leveque (1994) scaling gives one phenomenological correction to Kolmogorov's exponents, but no first-principles derivation exists. Anomalous scaling and non-Gaussianity are related consequences of intermittency; anisotropy corrections address a different failure of the 1941 theory (directional biases from boundaries and shear). Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.04893

question: Claude-Louis Navier wrote them down in 1822; George Gabriel Stokes finished the job in 1845. The equations governing viscous fluid flow have been used every day for almost two centuries, but one basic mathematical question about them, in three dimensions, has never been answered. Which question?
answer: whether smooth solutions always stay smooth
choices: whether smooth solutions always stay smooth
whether solutions are unique for turbulent initial data
whether energy dissipates anomalously as viscosity vanishes
whether all invariant measures are ergodic
context: The Navier-Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem: given a smooth initial velocity field in three dimensions, does the solution remain smooth for all time, or can it develop a singularity in finite time? No one knows. The other three are also genuinely open questions in mathematical fluid dynamics: uniqueness for rough turbulent initial data, the Onsager conjecture on anomalous energy dissipation in the vanishing-viscosity limit, and ergodicity of invariant measures for the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations. Engineers simulate turbulent flow every day -- 'unsolved' means the pure-math regularity question is open, not that the equations are useless. Source: https://www.claymath.org/millennium/navier-stokes-equation/

question: Because no one can solve the Navier-Stokes equations at high Reynolds number, one very expensive consequence hits every weather forecast: skilful deterministic predictions run out at roughly what horizon, past which one simulation's storm and another's have drifted completely apart?
answer: about two weeks
choices: about two weeks
about ten hours
about three months
about one year
context: Edward Lorenz's butterfly effect: tiny errors in the initial state grow exponentially until the forecast is no better than climatology. The two-week figure was crystallised in the 1960s by Jule Charney and collaborators; recent work with better models pushes it modestly further, but not by much. Source: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.363.6429.801

question: Every physics textbook of a certain era explained lift with the 'equal transit time' story -- but smoke-tunnel photographs show the air flowing over the top of a wing actually arrives well AHEAD of the air below, not just even with it. NASA specifically warns against that old story. What does the wing REALLY do to hold the plane up?
answer: it turns a large mass of air downward each second
choices: it turns a large mass of air downward each second
the curved top speeds air up so Bernoulli lifts it
the angled bottom acts as a wedge splitting the flow
the low-pressure zone above the wing sucks it up
context: A wing deflects a large mass of air downward each second; by Newton's third law the air pushes the wing upward. The pressure distribution and the downward turning are two views of the same fact, and the sharp trailing edge (Kutta condition) fixes the circulation that ties them together. The equal-transit story is a genuine misconception NASA specifically flags; 'Bernoulli alone', the wedge picture, and the pure-suction picture are the other popular half-truths. Source: https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/airplane/wrong1.html

question: From 1932 to 1972 the United States Public Health Service enrolled 600 poor black men in Macon County, Alabama in what was quietly a study of what untreated syphilis does to the human body over decades. The 399 men who already had the disease were never told they had syphilis. What were they told they were being treated for?
answer: bad blood
choices: bad blood
low fever
night rickets
tired veins
context: 'Bad blood' was a vague folk term in the rural South that could mean anemia, general weakness, or an unnamed infection -- exactly the ambiguity the study wanted. Source: CDC, 'About the Untreated Syphilis Study at Tuskegee.'

question: The Public Health Service did not think of Tuskegee as inventing something new. It thought of itself as continuing an earlier European observational cohort of untreated syphilis, whose long follow-up had been published in 1929 by the original doctor's successor. Whose cohort was Tuskegee framed as extending?
answer: Caesar Boeck's, in Oslo
choices: Caesar Boeck's, in Oslo
Alfred Fournier's, in Paris
Philippe Ricord's, in Paris
Hermann Zeissl's, in Vienna
context: Boeck ran an observational cohort of roughly 2,000 untreated syphilis patients from 1891 to 1910; his successor Edvin Bruusgaard published the follow-up in 1929, and the PHS explicitly framed Tuskegee as its American extension.
