question: In November 1940, Japanese aircraft dropped a strange mix of wheat, cotton scraps, and sand on the Chinese coastal city of Ningbo -- material prepared by the unit at Pingfang. What was hidden in the drop?
answer: Fleas infected with bubonic plague
choices: Fleas infected with bubonic plague
Ceramic bombs of anthrax spores
Drums of cholera-tainted water
Capsules of mustard gas
context: The wheat and cotton were carriers for the insects. An outbreak of plague followed in Ningbo in November and December 1940 that killed more than one hundred civilians. Source: Wikipedia, Ningbo plague attack.

question: In 1947, American officers at Camp Detrick in Maryland interrogated Shiro Ishii's scientists and compiled a classified summary of what they learned. What did the American occupation give the Japanese biological-warfare scientists in exchange for their data?
answer: Immunity from war-crimes prosecution
choices: Immunity from war-crimes prosecution
Postwar research posts at Camp Detrick
Positions in the American zone civil administration
Amnesty from the Tokyo tribunal alone
context: The deal was authorized by General Douglas MacArthur as head of the American occupation, with payments drawn from a secret Army fund. The classified summary is known as the Fell Report, after Norbert Fell of Camp Detrick. Source: Asia-Pacific Journal, Christopher Reed on Payoffs and Amnesty.

question: The Tokyo war-crimes tribunal (the IMTFE, 1946-1948) tried Japan's wartime leaders for many crimes. What did that tribunal do about the biological-warfare program at Pingfang?
answer: It left the program out of the trial entirely
choices: It left the program out of the trial entirely
It convicted Ishii but not his subordinates
It sentenced eight biological-warfare officers to death
It tried the officers separately at Yokohama
context: The exclusion was directed by the American occupation command; it was part of the same bargain that granted the scientists immunity. Japan had signed the 1925 Geneva Protocol banning biological and chemical weapons before the program began. Source: Wikipedia, Unit 731.

question: The Soviets tried twelve Japanese biological-warfare personnel at Khabarovsk in December 1949, with sentences of 2 to 25 years in labor camps. For decades, Western commentators dismissed the whole proceeding as Communist propaganda. How do historians today weigh the Khabarovsk confessions against that dismissal?
answer: Its Stalin-era format has real flaws, but captured Japanese documents and the epidemics themselves independently confirm the substance of what was confessed
choices: Its Stalin-era format has real flaws, but captured Japanese documents and the epidemics themselves independently confirm the substance of what was confessed
Cold War timing shaped the early skepticism, but the confessions have never been corroborated by any independent source outside Soviet custody
Captured Kwantung Army records flatly contradict the Khabarovsk testimony on the plague attacks, so the confessions are treated as extracted fabrications
The Stalinist format so contaminated the record that mainstream historians now set the Khabarovsk material aside entirely
context: Khabarovsk lacked cross-examination and used Stalin-era confessions -- real reasons for caution. But it was the only Allied trial devoted entirely to Japan's bacteriological program, and independent documents and the epidemics themselves corroborate its core. Source: Journal of the History of Medicine, on the West's dismissal of Khabarovsk.

question: Chew a stick of spearmint gum, then bite into a caraway-seed roll. The molecule doing the smelling in each is called carvone, and the two versions share the same formula and the same connectivity between atoms. Yet a five-year-old can tell them apart with one sniff. What is the actual difference between the two carvones?
answer: They are mirror images of each other
choices: They are mirror images of each other
They are packed at different densities
They vibrate at different frequencies
One is a heavier isotope of the other
context: Spearmint is (R)-carvone; caraway is (S)-carvone. Same formula, same connectivity, opposite hands - like a left and right glove. Source: Friedman & Miller, 'Odor Incongruity and Chirality', Science 1971 (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.172.3987.1044).

question: Spearmint carvone and caraway carvone are chemically identical in every measurable way except that they twist polarised light in opposite directions. Given the two molecules are essentially the same, why on Earth can the nose tell them apart at all?
answer: Smell receptors are themselves chiral, so only one shape fits
choices: Smell receptors are themselves chiral, so only one shape fits
The nose senses polarised light directly
Only one of them dissolves in nasal mucus
Nerve cells count how many atoms are present
context: Smell receptors are built from proteins, and proteins are chiral. The binding pocket is a right glove - only a right hand fits. Source: Chiralpedia, 'The Chemistry of Taste and Smell' (https://chiralpedia.com/blog/the-chemistry-of-taste-and-smell-how-chirality-affects-senses/).

question: For most of the 1800s chemists drew a carbon atom's four bonds flat on the page, as Kekule had. In September 1874 a 22-year-old graduate student published a short pamphlet that sent those four bonds off the page into three dimensions - and explained at a stroke why Pasteur's mirror-image crystals had existed. Who wrote that pamphlet?
answer: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff
choices: Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff
Emil Fischer
Johannes Wislicenus
Adolf von Baeyer
context: Van 't Hoff's Utrecht pamphlet, Sept 1874. Joseph Le Bel in Paris published the same 3-D idea independently two months later. Source: 150 Years of the Tetrahedral Carbon (Wiley, 2024) (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/chir.70022).

question: Two months after van 't Hoff's pamphlet appeared in Utrecht, a French chemist published the same tetrahedral-carbon idea independently, from a slightly different starting point, in Paris. Every textbook now pairs his name with van 't Hoff's. Who was the French co-discoverer?
answer: Joseph Le Bel
choices: Joseph Le Bel
Marcellin Berthelot
Charles Wurtz
Henri Moissan
context: Le Bel's paper appeared in the Bulletin de la Societe Chimique in November 1874, two months after van 't Hoff. Pasteur had physically sorted mirror-image tartrate crystals back in 1848 but had no explanation for WHY. Source: 150 Years of the Tetrahedral Carbon (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/chir.70022).

question: Van 't Hoff won the very first Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1901. Almost every school textbook implies the prize was for the tetrahedral carbon paper. But read the Nobel citation itself and it names two completely different achievements: chemical kinetics and osmotic pressure. What honour did the tetrahedron paper itself actually receive at the top of its own field?
answer: The Royal Society's Davy Medal in 1893
choices: The Royal Society's Davy Medal in 1893
The Copley Medal in 1874
The Helmholtz Medal of the Prussian Academy in 1898
The Faraday Lectureship of the Chemical Society in 1889
context: The 1901 Nobel citation was for 'the laws of chemical dynamics and osmotic pressure' - kinetics and solutions, not stereochemistry. The tetrahedron paper had already been honoured with the Davy Medal in 1893. Sources: NobelPrize.org 1901 summary; van 't Hoff biographical entry, Wikipedia.

question: Nikolai Vavilov spent his life crossing more than sixty countries on about 115 expeditions to bring one specific kind of thing home to Leningrad by the hundreds of thousands. What was he collecting?
answer: seeds
choices: seeds
beetles
orchids
meteorites
context: Vavilov brought back roughly 380,000 seeds, grains, roots, tubers and fruits by the early 1930s, building the largest crop-diversity collection on Earth. His stated reason was singular. Source: Science History Institute; Crop Trust.

question: Nikolai Vavilov did not cross continents for adventure. When he was asked why he was collecting crop varieties on such a scale, the reason he gave was:
answer: to end famine in Russia
choices: to end famine in Russia
to catalogue every plant on Earth
to prove Charles Darwin correct on inheritance
to prepare crops for interplanetary agriculture
context: Vavilov lived through the 1891-92 Volga famine as a boy; the stated purpose of the Leningrad collection was practical -- new crop varieties for Soviet fields. It is why he pushed on when Stalin later stopped his travel. Source: Crop Trust; Cornell exhibits.

question: The centres-of-origin idea had a hard practical payoff for a country trying to end famine -- which is why Vavilov kept collecting even after his passport was stopped. The wild and primitive landraces still living in those centres carry something that improved commercial varieties often lack:
answer: disease resistance
choices: disease resistance
drought tolerance
higher protein content
frost hardiness
context: Modern crop breeding tends to select for yield and uniformity and to breed OUT the awkward wild traits -- so the centres are a library of answers to future plant diseases. Norman Borlaug used Vavilov-style landrace collections to build his Green Revolution wheats, whose stem-rust resistance came straight from wild relatives. Source: PMC review.

question: In late 1933 Stalin's Central Committee moved to end Nikolai Vavilov's foreign expeditions. What single administrative step actually shut the collecting down?
answer: his passport was revoked
choices: his passport was revoked
the Party revoked his hard-currency travel funds
a Central Committee decree required Politburo approval for every trip
his chief patron Bukharin was arrested and could no longer protect him
context: The 1916 expedition to Iran had begun the collecting; by 1933 the Party's line under Lysenko no longer wanted a globe-trotting geneticist. Vavilov lost the passport, not (yet) the institute. Source: Nautilus, 'The Botanist Who Defied Stalin'.

question: The tragedy has a painful hinge that stops it becoming a morality play. Before Vavilov and Trofim Lysenko became enemies, Vavilov was Lysenko's INSTITUTIONAL SUPERIOR and had briefly done what?
answer: encouraged Lysenko's vernalization research
choices: encouraged Lysenko's vernalization research
written the pamphlet that made Lysenko famous
arranged Lysenko's first meeting with Stalin
co-authored a textbook with Lysenko in the 1920s
context: Vavilov valued vernalization's 'possible simplification of breeding work' and only withdrew his support when the method failed. That earlier goodwill is what makes the later denunciation so bitter. Source: Wikipedia on Trofim Lysenko.

question: On 6 August 1940, in western Ukraine near Chernivtsi, Nikolai Vavilov was arrested in the field on a seed-collecting trip. Who took him?
answer: the NKVD
choices: the NKVD
the Wehrmacht
the local militia
his own institute staff
context: The People's Commissariat of Internal Affairs -- Beria's secret police. He was taken to Moscow's Lubyanka prison, and over roughly 11 months was interrogated on 400 separate occasions. Charges: sabotage of Soviet agriculture and spying for Britain. Source: Nautilus; Wikipedia.

question: After being sentenced to death in July 1941 and later commuted to twenty years, Vavilov was transferred to Saratov Prison No. 1. What did the man who had built the world's largest seed collection do there, in his cell?
answer: lectured his fellow prisoners on plants and genetics
choices: lectured his fellow prisoners on plants and genetics
kept a hidden diary later smuggled abroad
traded seeds with the prison warden's kitchen garden
wrote weekly appeals to Stalin himself
context: Cornell's Vavilov exhibit records over 100 hours of prison lectures on plants and genetics -- the scientist teaching to the last. Source: Cornell exhibits, 'Cultivating Silence'.

question: The man who had crossed sixty countries and collected 380,000 seeds so that Russia would never starve again died in a Soviet prison on 26 January 1943. What killed him?
answer: starvation
choices: starvation
a firing squad
an infectious outbreak
beating by interrogators
context: The prison medical record lists pneumonia, dystrophy and oedema -- widely and honestly read, that is death from starvation and the conditions that accompany it. Vavilov was 55. His argument -- a library of seeds against famine -- outlived him. Source: Wikipedia; Science History Institute.

question: Less than two months after Vavilov died of starvation in prison for opposing Lysenkoism, on 22 March 1943 the Soviet state honoured Trofim Lysenko with:
answer: a Stalin Prize of the first degree
choices: a Stalin Prize of the first degree
the presidency of Moscow State University
a Hero of Socialist Labour star of gold
an Order of Lenin for wartime civilian service
context: Cited officially for 'the scientific development and introduction into agriculture of a method of planting potatoes with the tops of food tubers'. The timeline is the story: prison starvation for the geneticist in January, Stalin Prize for the anti-geneticist in March. Source: Wikipedia on Lysenko.

question: Through the 872-day siege of Leningrad, the staff of Vavilov's institute chose to starve rather than eat the collection they had been left to guard; nine died at their posts. What did they find on the desk of the botanist Dmitri Ivanov after he was found dead?
answer: several thousand packs of rice
choices: several thousand packs of rice
the last unpublished chapter of Vavilov's book
an unsent letter to the Kremlin
a wireless radio and a Comintern codebook
context: Ivanov -- the institute's rice specialist -- was found starved at his desk surrounded by rice he had refused to eat. Alexander Stchukin, the peanut specialist, likewise died at his writing table in January 1942. Source: Amusing Planet essay drawing on VIR historical records.

question: Vavilov's argument outlived him twice over. In 1955, twelve years after his death, the Military Collegium of the USSR Supreme Court did the first thing:
answer: vacated his sentence and rehabilitated him
choices: vacated his sentence and rehabilitated him
ruled his conviction final and unappealable
commuted his original death sentence posthumously to time served
transferred jurisdiction to a civilian court for a retrial
context: Rehabilitation came under Khrushchev's de-Stalinization; the institute became the N. I. Vavilov All-Russian Scientific Research Institute of Plant Genetic Resources (VIR). And the idea itself lives in the Svalbard Global Seed Vault (2008), inside an Arctic mountain -- Vavilov's library, in permafrost. Source: Wikipedia; Cornell.

question: In a European anatomy lesson of the 1530s the professor never touched the body. He sat in a raised chair reading aloud in Latin from a text thirteen centuries old, while an assistant called the ostensor pointed at whichever part the words named. Who held the knife?
answer: A junior barber-surgeon hired for the day
choices: The ostensor, once his pointing was done
A junior barber-surgeon hired for the day
The senior medical student of the year
The city executioner who supplied the body
context: The physician owned the text; the surgeon owned the knife. The manual being read was usually Mondino de' Liuzzi's Anathomia of 1316, printed in 1478 and reprinted in over forty editions. Andreas Vesalius broke the arrangement by climbing down off the chair and cutting the body himself - he had been handed Padua's chair of surgery and anatomy at 23, the day after taking his degree in December 1537. The frontispiece of his own book makes the argument in a picture: Vesalius stands at the table with his hand inside the opened abdomen, and the barber-surgeons are shoved underneath it, quarrelling, their razors idle. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Anatomical_theatre and /Medieval_medicine_of_Western_Europe (via search snippets); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius; pelviperineology.org, 'The frontispiece of Vesalius' Fabrica'.

question: In Basel in 1543 Andreas Vesalius dissected an executed man in public, mounted the bones and gave them to the university. That skeleton still stands in the city's anatomical museum, the oldest such preparation anywhere. What had the man been executed for?
answer: Knifing his wife when she uncovered the second marriage
choices: Looting a church while garrisoned in the city
Forging silver coin in a cellar beneath his shop
Knifing his wife when she uncovered the second marriage
Poisoning the abbot of the house he entered as a monk
context: The man was Jakob Karrer von Gebweiler, a bigamist. Book I, chapter 39 of the Fabrica is where Vesalius set out in print, for the first time anywhere, the whole process of cleaning and mounting a skeleton - so the thing in Basel is his own written instructions carried out, and it is still there to go and look at, which is the point: a claim you can walk up to and check. Sources: historyofinformation.com, 'The Oldest Surviving Articulated Human Skeleton'; executedtoday.com, 12 May 1543 entry.

question: Galen of Pergamon wrote the anatomy Europe trusted for fourteen hundred years, and he was no fraud: he dissected constantly and wrote up what he saw. Yet when Andreas Vesalius checked those descriptions against the bodies on his own table at Padua, error after error turned up. Where had Galen's insides come from?
answer: Barbary macaques, pigs and dogs cut open in turn
choices: Skeletons lifted from Roman tombs after dark
Barbary macaques, pigs and dogs cut open in turn
Bodies unwrapped from Egyptian mummy cases
Gladiators' wounds glimpsed while patching them up
context: Roman law and custom barred the dissection of human bodies, so Galen worked on animals, favouring the Barbary macaque for its resemblance to us. He even recorded some ape-human differences in the face muscles and the vertebrae: the failure was extrapolating across species, not inventing. And Vesalius never treated him as a fraud - he edited the anatomical sections of Galen for the Giunta family's Latin edition, and historians call him a neo-Galenist who applied Galen's own observational method honestly. The method was Galen's; the corrections were that method used without flinching. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Galen (via search snippet); historymedjournal.com, 'The evolution of Vesalius's perspective on Galen's anatomy'; library.uab.edu on the Giunta edition.

question: Run a finger down the middle of your chest and the breastbone feels like one solid strip. The anatomy books Vesalius was raised on gave that bone seven separate pieces. Counting on an adult human skeleton at Padua, what did he find?
answer: Three pieces, the last of a row fused in childhood
choices: Seven pieces, exactly as the books had it
Five pieces, joined down the line by cartilage
Three pieces, the last of a row fused in childhood
One piece, a single plate with no divisions at all
context: The three are the manubrium at the top, the long body, and the small xiphoid process at the bottom; a child has more, and they knit together as you grow. Seven was a real count - of a chest that was not human. Try it on yourself: press down from the notch at the base of your throat and feel for the small ridge where the manubrium meets the body, roughly level with your second rib. That join is one of Vesalius's corrections, on you. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius; biologyinsights.com, 'Andreas Vesalius's discoveries that changed anatomy'.

question: Galen's physiology ran on spirits: vital spirit rose from the heart and was refined into the animal spirit of thought inside a rete mirabile, a wonderful net of finely woven vessels at the base of the brain. Vesalius opened human head after human head and never found the net. He was not calling Galen a liar, though, because the net is real. Which animals carry one?
answer: Sheep and cattle, cooling the blood on its way to the brain
choices: Sheep and cattle, cooling the blood on its way to the brain
Frogs and newts, feeding the brain while they lie under ice
Snakes and lizards, warming the head after a cold night
Moles and shrews, holding oxygen for the brain underground
context: In cats and in hoofed animals - sheep, pigs, cattle - the rete mirabile is a genuine mesh of vessels that makes up for underdeveloped internal carotid arteries and helps cool the blood heading for the brain. Galen saw a real structure; he saw it in the wrong species. And Vesalius was not even first to say so: Berengario da Carpi had already published that despite many attempts he could not detect the net in a human, so the looking-for-yourself method was spreading before the Fabrica made it famous. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Rete_mirabile (via search snippet); PMC6381050, 'Berengario da Carpi and the Renaissance of Brain Anatomy'.

question: Every household in Europe knew that a man carries one rib fewer than a woman. Andreas Vesalius had opened bodies of both sexes at Padua, and Book I, chapter 19 of the Fabrica prints his count: twelve pairs in men, twelve in women, the odd person at eleven or thirteen. What did he do with the belief itself?
answer: He named Genesis in the text and called the belief plainly absurd
choices: He printed the bare count and left the old belief unmentioned
He named Genesis in the text and called the belief plainly absurd
He set the count beside the belief and left the reader to judge
He asked the theology faculty at Louvain to rule on the point
context: Vesalius wrote in Book I, chapter 19: 'It is commonly believed that men lack a rib on one side, and that men have one rib fewer than women. This is plainly absurd, even if Moses did say in the second chapter of Genesis...' He recorded the same twelve pairs in both sexes and noted genuine individual variation of eleven or thirteen. His move was anatomical rather than theological: the belief was a claim about what a count would show, and a count is something anybody can make. Sources: Fabrica Bk I ch.19 quoted at mistakinghistories.uk; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius.

question: The fourteen muscle-men in Andreas Vesalius's Fabrica are drawn with the skin off, and they do not stand in a void: each is posed in an Italian countryside of hills, farm buildings and Roman ruins. For 360 years readers took the scenery for decoration. In 1903 a scholar finally looked properly at the set. What had everyone missed?
answer: The backgrounds join into continuous stretches of country
choices: The ruins are Paduan buildings that still stand today
The shadows in every plate fall at the very same hour
The backgrounds join into continuous stretches of country
The artist's signature is hidden in the masonry of one
context: Set the plates side by side - reversing some, because of the way a woodblock prints - and the landscapes run on from one to the next. Precision worth having: scholars count TWO panoramas, not one long strip. A six-plate series shows the Euganean Hills between Padua and Venice; an eight-plate series shows country near Padua with the ruins of old Roman baths. The popular version, all fourteen in a single continuous landscape, overstates it. In London in 1545 the surgeon Thomas Geminus copper-engraved forty of the plates without permission and stripped the backgrounds out as superfluous - he had no idea what he was cutting up. Sources: clinicalanatomy.com/mtd/665, 'The landscape panorama of Vesalius' muscle men'; nyamcenterforhistory.org on Geminus; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Humani_Corporis_Fabrica_Libri_Septem.

question: As the story is told, outside the walls of Louvain in 1536 the young Andreas Vesalius came on the body of an executed criminal chained to a roadside gibbet, the flesh gone and the bones still hanging together by their ligaments. He carried off the arms and legs at once, came back after curfew to break the chain and take the trunk, and boiled the bones in secret. Then he built his first skeleton - and lied about where it came from. What did he claim?
answer: That he had brought the skeleton with him from Paris
choices: That a physician in Cologne had left it to him by will
That the town had made him a gift of the bones
That he had bought it from a dealer in Venice
That he had brought the skeleton with him from Paris
context: LEGEND FLAG. The core is well attested - Vesalius took bones from the Louvain gibbet and assembled a skeleton, and Fabrica Book I chapter 39 gives his own method for preparing one. The night climb, the broken chain and the lie come from later biographical retellings and vary between them, so hold those details as the story told about him rather than the record. Bodies were the bottleneck of the whole enterprise: from 1539 Marcantonio Contarini, a judge of the Paduan criminal court, supplied the bodies of executed criminals and would even delay an execution to suit the anatomist, which Vesalius confirmed himself in 1546. Sources: encyclopedia.com, 'Vesalius'; libapps.libraries.uc.edu, 'The Illustrated Human' biography; Standring, 'A brief history of topographical anatomy'.

question: In Galen's heart, blood seeped from the right chamber into the left through passages in the thick muscular wall between them - the step the whole system rested on. Vesalius cut that wall apart on his own table at Padua. What did he set down in the 1555 second edition of his anatomy, the Fabrica?
answer: That he could not see how any blood at all gets through it
choices: That he found no passages except in the newly dead
That he could force a bristle through only in young bodies
That he could not see how any blood at all gets through it
That he traced them lower in the wall than Galen had put them
context: Translators render the line differently - one version runs 'I have not seen even the most obscure passages by which the septum of the ventricles is pervious' - and the 1543 first edition already doubted the pores before 1555 stated the denial plainly, so take the sense rather than one exact wording. Publishing that a textbook's promised structure is simply NOT THERE is one of the hardest results an observer can report, and it left a hole where Galenic physiology needed a mechanism. William Harvey, who studied at the same university, published his account of the circulation in 1628; historians treat Vesalius's vascular work as clearing the ground for it, not as anticipating it. Sources: hekint.org, 'The revolution of Andreas Vesalius'; PMC4462973, Vesalius 500 years (cardiovascular); Garrison translation note, faculty.wcas.northwestern.edu.

question: Vesalius's Fabrica was printed from pear-wood blocks cut by hand, and nobody threw the blocks away. They stayed with his Basel printer until 1568, passed to the Froben family, and were carted from one city to the next for three centuries after that. They could still take ink when a last folio of the plates was pulled from them. Then one night ended the run. What happened?
answer: A bombing raid set fire to the library holding them
choices: A bombing raid set fire to the library holding them
A stove fire in the press room took them mid-printing
A river flood filled the cellar and pulped them past use
A gang of looters burned them through a hard winter
context: On the night of 30 March 1944 a raid burned the University of Munich library where the blocks were stored, and they were destroyed. That made the 1934 printing - Icones Anatomicae, produced by the New York Academy of Medicine with the Bremer Press and the University of Munich - the last impressions ever taken from the original blocks. Four hundred years of survival, ended in one night. Sources: PubMed 28038492, 'The Andreas Vesalius woodblocks: a four hundred year journey from creation to destruction'; codex99.com/anatomy/45.

question: Jacobus Sylvius had taught the young Vesalius anatomy in Paris. In 1551 he published a book titled a refutation of the slanders of a certain madman, punning his former student's name into Vaesanus, with twenty-eight point-by-point rebuttals and Galen hailed as the sole parent of anatomy. Against the corrections made at the table, what did Sylvius argue?
answer: That the human body itself had changed since Galen's day
choices: That copyists had slipped the errors in over the centuries
That Vesalius had cut up criminals rather than sound men
That the pupil's own knife had spoiled the parts he cut
That the human body itself had changed since Galen's day
context: Sylvius also denounced 'that insolent and ignorant slanderer who has treasonably attacked his teachers'. Notice the shape of his defence: he did not claim Vesalius had measured badly. He claimed that if the corpse disagrees with the book, the corpse must have changed. The book was the fixed point and the evidence was the thing that had to bend - which is exactly the move a claim makes when it will not be tested. Anyone could open a body and check; nobody could check the ancients' Rome. Sources: encyclopedia.com on Jacques Dubois (Jacobus Sylvius); Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'Andreas Vesalius'; clinicalanatomy.com/mtd/727.

question: The frontispiece of Andreas Vesalius's Fabrica - the picture facing the title page of the book that broke Galen's fourteen-hundred-year hold on anatomy - shows the dissection itself: over a hundred spectators packed into three tiers, and Vesalius at the table with his hand inside the opened body. The body is a woman's, hanged at Padua, rope marks still on her neck, and a magistrate ordered this dissection. What was he having checked?
answer: Whether the pregnancy she pleaded to escape the rope was real
choices: Whether the pregnancy she pleaded to escape the rope was real
Whether the hangman had botched the drop and killed her slowly
Whether the poison she was convicted of using was in her still
Whether the woman hanged was the woman named in the sentence
context: The woman had been executed at Padua after falsely claiming to be pregnant to escape her sentence, and the magistrate ordered the autopsy to test the claim. So the picture announcing the new anatomy shows a body opened to settle a question of fact, which is the argument of the whole book drawn in one scene. The rest of the plate argues the same way: Vesalius is down off the professor's raised chair with his own hand in the body, and the barber-surgeons are pushed underneath the table with their razors idle. Chained down in the crush are a live dog and a live monkey; scholars who read the plate take those for the animals the old anatomy was actually built on, though nothing in the picture labels them. Sources: pelviperineology.org, 'The frontispiece of Vesalius' Fabrica'; grokipedia.com/page/Galen (via search snippet); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius.

question: On a cold morning your arms suddenly show goosebumps. Under the skin, tiny smooth muscles called arrector pili have contracted and yanked each hair upright. In a furry mammal, what is this reflex actually FOR?
answer: Trapping a layer of warm air and puffing the animal up bigger
choices: Trapping a layer of warm air and puffing the animal up bigger
Cooling the animal by lifting the coat off the skin
Signalling to nearby predators that the animal is diseased
Draining excess sweat outward along the hair shafts
context: You kept the muscles and the sympathetic wiring on skin that no longer has a coat, so it doesn't warm you and it doesn't scare anyone. That is exactly what 'vestigial' means. Source: Wikipedia (Vestigial response); Biology Insights (Arrector Pili Muscle).

question: Around week five or six of pregnancy, a human embryo grows a striking feature that is longer at that moment than the leg buds beside it -- and then normally disappears again by about week eight. What has it grown, and what does it leave behind?
answer: A tail, which is reabsorbed leaving the fused coccyx
choices: A tail, which is reabsorbed leaving the fused coccyx
A gill slit, which fuses to form the eustachian tube
A yolk stalk, which resorbs leaving the umbilical ring
A pineal stalk, which retracts leaving the pituitary stem
context: Most of the tail vertebrae are cleared by programmed cell death (apoptosis) and the remaining segments fuse into the coccyx. In rare cases the tail persists to birth. Source: Jacob et al. 2014; Science Alert.

question: A surgeon removing the small tailbone at the base of a patient's spine finds it is not a loose useless nub: strong sheets of muscle and ligament are anchored to it and have to be carefully cut free. What are those attached tissues doing for the patient?
answer: Forming the pelvic floor that supports the bladder and bowel
choices: Forming the pelvic floor that supports the bladder and bowel
Pumping venous blood back up the spinal column to the heart
Storing marrow that makes the body's red blood cells
Sensing balance signals feeding into the inner ear
context: 'Vestigial' means a structure has lost its ANCESTRAL job (being a tail), not that it has no job today. Whale pelvic bones anchor reproductive muscles, and python 'spurs' are used in mating -- all vestigial, none useless. Source: Wikipedia (Vestigial structure).

question: In 1893 the German anatomist Robert Wiedersheim published The Structure of Man with a long roster of human organs he called wholly or partly functionless. Over the following century, honest biology quietly did what with that roster?
answer: Shrank it as most of the organs turned out to have jobs
choices: Shrank it as most of the organs turned out to have jobs
Grew it as more and more useless organs were catalogued
Threw it out because Wiedersheim was a discredited fraud
Left it exactly as Wiedersheim wrote it into the 21st century
context: The spleen was dismissed as vestigial into the 1950s and is now known to filter blood and mount immune responses. Wiedersheim's original list ran to about 86 organs; later editions grew to about 180 -- and most got quietly crossed out as anatomy caught up. Source: Wikipedia (Wiedersheim); Encyclopedia (Vestigiality).

question: The strongest evidence AGAINST the old 'useless leftover' reading of the appendix comes not from anatomy but from a family tree. When Heather Smith's team mapped the appendix across the mammal phylogeny, what did they find that a truly useless organ would never do?
answer: It has evolved independently at least thirty separate times in mammals
choices: It has evolved independently at least thirty separate times in mammals
It appears only in placental mammals with a diet of tough leafy plants
It shrinks in exact proportion to the length of the small intestine
It is genetically identical in every mammal species that carries one
context: Nobody re-invents a useless organ thirty-odd times. Smith's group also found the appendix has been lost only a handful of times. That is the fingerprint of an adaptive structure, not a leftover. Source: Smith et al. 2013 (C. R. Palevol); Smith et al. 2017.

question: You can check for a small vestigial trait in your own arm right now. Press your thumb to your pinky and lift your palm; if you have it, a thin cord stands up in the middle of your forearm. About one person in seven is missing it, and grip strength is the same either way. What is the tendon?
answer: The palmaris longus
choices: The palmaris longus
The flexor carpi radialis
The brachioradialis muscle
The abductor pollicis brevis
context: Because it does nothing critical, surgeons harvest palmaris longus for tendon grafts. It is one of the cleanest at-home checks for a vestigial structure. Source: Britannica; Everything Lowercase.

question: The cleanest textbook cases of vestigial structures are not human at all. In dark limestone caves in Mexico, the fish Astyanax mexicanus starts developing normal eye primordia as an embryo -- lens, retina, the works -- and then the eye is dismantled before the fish hatches. Which mechanism did NIH researchers pin the collapse on?
answer: The lens undergoes massive apoptosis and skin grows over the shrunken eye
choices: The lens undergoes massive apoptosis and skin grows over the shrunken eye
The eye stops growing while the rest of the skull enlarges around it
Pigment cells fail to migrate to the eye, leaving it non-functional
The optic nerve fails to connect and the eye is reabsorbed as sightless tissue
context: The embryo runs the ancestral eye-building program and then dismantles it -- exactly what evolution predicts when eyes stop being selected for in permanent darkness. Ostriches and emus tell the same story with reduced wing bones and a shrunken keel. Source: NIH News 2018; UMD News 2018.

question: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin flew Vostok 1 around the Earth once, a flight lasting 108 minutes. When he came back down, something was true of the landing that the Soviet Union hid for the next ten years. What was it?
answer: he was not inside the spacecraft when it hit the ground
choices: he was not inside the spacecraft when it hit the ground
he touched down thousands of kilometres off target
he splashed into the Pacific rather than on Soviet soil
he landed hours later than the schedule had promised
context: At about 7 km altitude Gagarin was ejected from the descent module and came down under his own parachute; the empty capsule landed on its own chute nearby. This was the DESIGNED landing mode -- Soviet engineers had never developed a soft-landing system a person could survive inside -- but it was concealed because the Federation Aeronautique Internationale, the body that certified aviation and space records, required the pilot to land with the craft. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://www.amusingplanet.com/2021/04/why-soviet-union-lied-about-yuri.html

question: The American Mercury capsule that carried Alan Shepard and later John Glenn came home a very different way from Vostok 1. Mercury splashed into the Atlantic Ocean and was fished out of the water by a Navy recovery ship. How did the Vostok 1 capsule itself come home?
answer: under its own parachute onto dry Soviet land
choices: under its own parachute onto dry Soviet land
on retro-rockets braking to a hover just above the ground
on a set of shock-absorbing landing skids like an aircraft
on inflated airbags that cushioned a hard bounce
context: Vostok's descent module carried its own parachute and floated down separately from Gagarin, hitting Soviet farmland fairly hard -- the reason engineers had planned pilot ejection at 7 km in the first place. Mercury's blunt cone splashed at sea for a Navy pickup; the American programme ran soft-water landings for years before switching to land landings with the Space Shuttle. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury

question: Before Vostok 1 flew, doctors and engineers were not sure a human mind would function normally in weightlessness. So the cockpit's flight controls were LOCKED for the whole flight. A three-digit code that would unlock them was sealed in an envelope aboard the cabin. Which single system flew the spacecraft instead?
answer: the automatic programme with ground command
choices: the automatic programme with ground command
a purely mechanical clockwork timer
a live radio link to a chase plane
an onboard analogue computer set by dial
context: Vostok 1 was flown entirely by its onboard automatic sequencer with backup commands from ground stations, exactly because the medical staff would not commit to Gagarin thinking clearly in orbit. The sealed envelope was a fallback: if he found himself needing to steer, he could open it, read the code (most often reported as 1-2-5), and unlock manual attitude control. Engineers reportedly told him the digits ahead of time anyway. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://spacedaily.com/t-for-the-first-space-flight-in-1961-soviet-engineers-locked-gagarins-manual-controls-behind-a-code-sealed-in-an-envelope-on-the-cabin-wall-because-they-were-not-sure-a-human-mind-would-function-in-orbit/

question: Vostok's spherical descent module always fell the right way up so its heat shield faced the incoming plasma, without any attitude sensors or thrusters keeping it pointed. What one design choice made a sphere passively self-righting in the airflow?
answer: the centre of mass was offset toward the heavy shield end
choices: the centre of mass was offset toward the heavy shield end
a spinning internal flywheel kept it pointed by gyroscopic force
a sacrificial nose cap ablated asymmetrically to nudge it around
a small tail fin trailed behind and dragged the shield forward
context: A sphere with the heavy end biased forward is passively self-righting: any tumble makes the aerodynamic torque swing the heavy end back into the airflow. That let the capsule reenter without a single thruster or attitude sensor. The price was a steep ballistic reentry -- concentrated deceleration on the pilot's chest -- but no attitude-control hardware to build or debug. Russian pilots nicknamed the capsule the sharik, 'little ball'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_(spacecraft)

question: After Vostok 1's retro-rocket fired, the equipment module was supposed to break cleanly away from the descent capsule. It did not -- the two pieces stayed connected and tumbled violently across half an orbit before finally coming apart. What had held them together?
answer: a bundle of wires that the main separation charge did not sever
choices: a bundle of wires that the main separation charge did not sever
a jammed docking latch that Gagarin punched open by hand
a frozen fuel line that snapped once the tanks warmed up
a stuck explosive bolt that a backup charge finally fired
context: The main separation mechanism fired but a cable bundle did not sever; the two modules stayed connected and the whole thing tumbled violently. Only as they hit the upper atmosphere over roughly Egypt did the wires finally burn through, letting the capsule right itself and reenter properly. The tumble did not injure Gagarin, but it was a real near-miss on the first crewed flight. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1 ; https://www.astronautix.com/v/vostok1.html

question: Berlin, 22 February 1828. Friedrich Wöhler writes to his old teacher Jöns Jacob Berzelius — writing again before Berzelius has answered his last two letters, because he cannot wait. What did Wöhler boast he could make?
answer: Urea, the main solid in urine — with no kidney of man or dog
choices: Urea, the main solid in urine — with no kidney of man or dog
Silk, the thread of fine cloth — with no worm of moth or spider
Lactose, the sugar of milk — with no udder of cow or goat
Gelatin, the jelly of bone — with no hide of ox or calf
context: Wöhler's words, from the manuscript held at the Center for History of Science, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences: 'I cannot, so to say, hold my chemical water and must tell you that I can make urea without the help of a kidney or even an animal, neither man nor dog. Ammonium cyanate is urea.' Translations differ — the Science History Institute renders the boast '...without needing a kidney, whether of man or dog.' He was writing from Berlin, where he lectured to industrial apprentices at the Gewerbeschule, a technical school, on about 400 thalers a year; he held a medical degree from Heidelberg and never practised medicine. Berzelius, his old teacher, was in Stockholm. Source: Yale Chem 125 (J. M. McBride) translation of the letter of 22 February 1828, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu; Wikipedia, 'Friedrich Wöhler'.

question: Friedrich Wöhler's 1828 urea experiment did not begin with a plan to overturn anything. Writing to Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Wöhler named the small, ordinary thing that had set it off — something four years old, dating from his student year in Berzelius's own Stockholm laboratory. What was it?
answer: A note in his own laboratory notebook, which he happened to reread
choices: A note in his own laboratory notebook, which he happened to reread
A jar of the old crystals, still sitting at the back of a cupboard
A remark of Berzelius's that he had copied onto a lecture card
A drawing of those crystals that he had pinned above his desk
context: Wöhler to Berzelius, 22 February 1828: 'Perhaps you still remember the experiment I carried out in that fortunate time when I was working with you, in which I found that whenever one tries to react cyanic acid with ammonia a crystalline substance appears which is inert, behaving neither like cyanate nor like ammonia. On leafing through my notebook this struck me again.' He had spent 1823-24 in Berzelius's Stockholm laboratory. A man rereading his own four-year-old lab note is what set the whole thing off — which is an argument for keeping a notebook. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 22 February 1828 letter, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Jöns Jacob Berzelius — Europe's most influential chemist, and the man who had argued since 1810 that living things run on a 'vital force' — sat down in Stockholm on 7 March 1828 to answer Wöhler's news that he had made urea in a dish. How did Berzelius open his reply?
answer: With a joke: short supply could be topped up from the chamber pot
choices: With a joke: short supply could be topped up from the chamber pot
With a warning: the claim would be torn apart unless he repeated it
With a demand: he wanted the crystals sent to Stockholm at once
With a correction: he had made a salt, and not an animal substance
context: Berzelius, Stockholm, 7 March 1828: 'When one has begun his immortality with urine, there is every reason to end the trip to paradise in the same way... Aluminum and artificial urea, certainly two very different matters, following one another so closely, will, my Lord, be braided as jewels into your crown of laurels, and should the quantity of the artificial not suffice, one could easily make up the difference with a little from the chamber pot.' (The aluminium: Wöhler had isolated the first pure metallic aluminium on 22 October 1827.) Worth checking yourself — Grokipedia's 'Wöhler synthesis' article states that Berzelius 'initially responded with skepticism.' The letter itself does not support that. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 7 March 1828 letter, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Friedrich Wöhler scraped his urea out of one evaporating dish in 1828. Urea is now the most-produced synthetic organic compound on Earth — output passed 184 million tonnes in 2022 — and not a tonne of it is made his way: since 1922 the factories have all run the Bosch-Meiser process. What does that process start from?
answer: Ammonia and carbon dioxide
choices: Ammonia and carbon dioxide
Ammonia and limestone
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and carbon monoxide
context: The Bosch-Meiser process, patented in 1922, joins ammonia and carbon dioxide by way of ammonium carbamate, and it has supplied the world ever since — past 184 million tonnes in 2022, near 200 million tonnes in 2024. More than 90% of that goes out as nitrogen-release fertilizer, spread on fields to feed crops; the rest is scattered across many smaller uses. Wöhler's cyanate route survives only in the textbooks. Urea is still the main nitrogen-carrying substance in mammal urine, and it still melts at 132.4 C whether it came from a kidney, an evaporating dish, or a steel reactor. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Urea'; Grokipedia, 'Wöhler synthesis' (§Applications in Modern Synthesis).

question: Friedrich Wöhler combined cyanic acid with ammonia in 1828 and got white crystals. He had a guess about what they might be before he tested them at all, and he printed that guess in his paper. What did Wöhler expect the crystals to be?
answer: An organic substance, perhaps like the salt-forming bases of plants
choices: An organic substance, perhaps like the salt-forming bases of plants
An inorganic salt, perhaps like the cyanates of lead and of silver
A vegetable acid, perhaps like the oxalic acid of the sorrel plant
An explosive salt, perhaps like the fulminates Liebig was studying
context: From the 1828 paper: 'I imagined that in the union of cyanic acid and ammonia there might be formed an organic substance, perhaps even a substance analogous to the vegetable salt-forming bases' — a plant alkaloid, in later language. He already knew from 1824 that the white crystals were not ammonium cyanate; the open question was what they were. One detail the textbooks get wrong: the standard telling has him mixing silver cyanate with ammonium chloride. Wöhler names two preparations and says the workhorse was the other one — 'By the latter method' (lead cyanate with ammonia solution) 'I have prepared a not insignificant amount of it for use in this investigation.' Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of Wöhler, 'On the Artificial Formation of Urea', Annalen der Physik und Chemie 88, 253-256, 1828.

question: Wöhler's crystals refused to behave like a cyanate — no ammonia given off with caustic potash, no fizzing with acids, no lead or silver salts. Then nitric acid threw down brilliant flakes that, purified again and again, tested sharply acidic, and Wöhler thought for a moment he had found a new acid of his own. What killed that idea?
answer: Neutralized with bases, the flakes gave plain nitrates and the old crystals back
choices: Neutralized with bases, the flakes gave plain nitrates and the old crystals back
Left to dry on the bench, the flakes went off with a crack, as fulminates do
Repeated with fresh crystals, the flakes could not be got a second time
Sent to Berzelius in Stockholm, the flakes were named an acid already known
context: From the paper: the nitric acid 'formed a precipitate of brilliant crystal flakes. After purification by repeated recrystallization, these crystals displayed a decidedly acidic character, and I was already inclined to consider them as a specific acid, when I found that they gave nitrate salts on neutralization with bases from which the crystalline material could be recovered.' A wrong guess, tested and dropped inside a single paragraph — that is what the method looks like from the inside. The failed cyanate tests are his words too: with caustic potash or lime the substance 'evolved no trace of ammonia', with acids it showed none of the ready decomposition of cyanate salts, 'and it even failed to give lead and silver salts as true cyanate salts do'. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 1828 paper.

question: Friedrich Wöhler suspected the crystals in his dish were urea — a substance chemists had been isolating and naming since the 1770s. Suspecting was not proving, and no one in 1828 could see a molecule. What did Wöhler do to settle it?
answer: Isolated pure urea from urine and ran both through the same tests
choices: Isolated pure urea from urine and ran both through the same tests
Burned a sample and compared the elemental analysis with urea's
Grew bigger crystals and measured the angles between their faces
Sent a sample to Berzelius in Stockholm for a second opinion
context: From the paper: 'This similarity in behavior to urea led me to conduct analogous experiments with fully pure urea isolated from urine, with the completely unambiguous result that urea and this crystalline substance... are fully identical substances.' Many summaries — Grokipedia's among them — say he clinched it with an elemental analysis. His own letter says the opposite: 'I recently performed a small experiment... which I quickly completed and which, thank God, did not require a single analysis.' For composition he leaned on William Prout's published 1817 analysis of urea from urine and compared it with the calculated figures for ammonium cyanate. The identification rested on matched chemical behaviour, side by side. Urea had first been crystallized from human urine by Hilaire Rouelle in 1773; Fourcroy and Vauquelin gave it its name in 1799. Sources: Yale Chem 125 translations of the 1828 paper and letter; Wikipedia, 'Urea'.

question: Friedrich Wöhler started from a solution he took to be ammonium cyanate, evaporated it, and what crystallized out was urea — the same stuff a kidney makes. Chemists later worked out exactly what that change amounted to. Which was it?
answer: The atoms already there were rearranged; none was added or taken away
choices: The atoms already there were rearranged; none was added or taken away
One molecule of water joined on, as it does in most ammonium salts
Ammonia was driven off, and its nitrogen was taken up by the carbon
Two salt molecules joined into one, doubling the count of atoms
context: Ammonium cyanate NH4OCN and urea (NH2)2CO carry the same atoms in the same numbers — CH4N2O either way. Not a construction, a rearrangement. Wöhler had guessed as much in the letter, before there was a word for it: 'I supposed it possible that in combining cyanic acid with ammonia the elements might have come together in a different way, albeit in the same proportion.' Berzelius introduced the term isomerism for the phenomenon around 1830, from the Greek isos, 'equal', and meros, 'part'. One caveat about Wöhler's own printed page: in his 1828 notation he had to add an atom of water, 'as all ammonium salts contain water', so his formulas do not read as the clean modern pair — the anhydrous statement came later. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Wöhler synthesis'; Wikipedia, 'Isomer'; Yale Chem 125 translations of the 1828 paper and letter.

question: Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who taught that a 'vital force' inside living matter keeps it running, wrote back to Wöhler on 7 March 1828: 'It is a truly important and beautiful discovery that the doctor has made, and it gives me indescribable delight to hear of it.' He then named the one thing in it he thought most enlightening for future theory. What was it?
answer: That the salt nature vanished when acid and ammonia combined
choices: That the salt nature vanished when acid and ammonia combined
That a substance of the animal body was built from mineral stuff
That a vital force was no longer needed for living chemistry
That cyanic acid had shown a power nobody suspected in it
context: Berzelius, 7 March 1828: 'But now enough raillery... It is a truly important and beautiful discovery that the doctor has made, and it gives me indescribable delight to hear of it. It is a unique situation that the salt nature so entirely disappears when the acid and ammonia combine, one that will certainly be most enlightening for future theory.' The founder of the vital-force doctrine was delighted — about salts. He does not mention vitalism at all, in this letter or in reply to the news. Source: Yale Chem 125 translation of the 7 March 1828 letter, chem125-oyc.webspace.yale.edu.

question: Friedrich Wöhler's paper 'On the Artificial Formation of Urea' fills four pages of Poggendorff's Annalen for 1828 — Article V of that issue, and the whole of what he published on the discovery. Everything turns on how he closes it. What does the paper's final paragraph do?
answer: Declines to draw the conclusions that so naturally suggest themselves
choices: Declines to draw the conclusions that so naturally suggest themselves
Declares the doctrine of the vital force finished, and names Berzelius
Calls on chemists to make a living cell from mineral matter next
Claims priority over Liebig for this whole line of chemical work
context: The closing paragraph in full: 'I refrain from all the considerations which so naturally suggest themselves from this fact, especially in respect to the composition ratios of organic substances and in respect to similar elemental and quantitative compositions among compounds with very different properties, as may be supposed, among others, of fulminic acid and cyanic acid.' He steers the reader toward isomerism, not toward philosophy. What he did claim in print is exact and modest: the result is 'a noteworthy result in as much as it provides an example of the artificial production of an organic, indeed a so-called animal, substance from inorganic substances.' An example — not the end of vitalism, not the founding of organic chemistry. Sources: Yale Chem 125 translation of Wöhler, 'Ueber künstliche Bildung des Harnstoffs', Annalen der Physik und Chemie 88, 253-256, 1828; original scan at archive.org/details/ueberknstliche1221828whle.

question: Peter Ramberg, a historian of chemistry, traced the crusading version of this story — Wöhler trying again and again to synthesize something that would refute vitalism until 'one afternoon the miracle happened' — to a popular history of chemistry published in 1931. Wöhler's own paper had been in print since 1828 for anyone to check. Ramberg's 2000 study counted the organic-chemistry textbooks that still handed students the crusading version. What share was that?
answer: Roughly nine in ten of them
choices: Roughly nine in ten of them
Roughly six in ten of them
Roughly three in ten of them
Roughly one in ten of them
context: Ramberg named it the 'Wöhler Myth' (Ambix 47, 2000). Wikipedia's summary of him: the 1931 popular history, 'ignoring all pretense of historical accuracy, turned Wöhler into a crusader who made attempt after attempt to synthesize a natural product that would refute vitalism and lift the veil of ignorance, until "one afternoon the miracle happened".' The author of that 1931 book is not named in the sources used here, so no name is claimed for it. You can watch the myth still running, in one sitting: Wikipedia's 'Organic chemistry' article says of 1828 that 'the event is now generally accepted as indeed disproving the doctrine of vitalism', while Wikipedia's own 'Vitalism' article says 'contemporary accounts do not support the common belief that vitalism died when Wöhler made urea.' Same encyclopedia, opposite claims — go read both. And the calendar agrees with the second one: Hermann Kolbe made acetic acid from inorganic starting materials in 1845, Marcellin Berthelot repeated the feat for many compounds through the 1850s, and only by about 1931 had biologists almost unanimously given vitalism up. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Vitalism', 'Wöhler synthesis', 'Organic chemistry'; Grokipedia, 'Wöhler synthesis' (§Criticisms and Reassessments).

question: Wöhler got urea out of a dish of salts. A mammal makes it too, and for a century nobody could say how. In 1932 Hans Krebs and his medical student Kurt Henseleit traced the route — six enzymes across four linked reactions, mostly in the liver — the first metabolic cycle anyone had ever mapped, five years before the citric-acid cycle. Two later researchers comparing that cycle with Wöhler's dish pointed to the one feature that gives the living version its almost vitalistic look. Which?
answer: Its steps are split between the mitochondria and the cell fluid
choices: Its steps are split between the mitochondria and the cell fluid
Its enzymes are torn down and rebuilt before every single pass
Its reactions run only inside a cell that is still alive and whole
Its products pass straight into the kidney and never the blood
context: Krebs and Henseleit's ornithine cycle, 1932, was the first metabolic cycle ever discovered. It runs mostly in the liver across six enzymes, with one reaction inside the mitochondria and three out in the cytosol, the fluid filling the cell. Kinne-Saffran and Kinne argue that the cycle's apparently vitalistic character 'is caused by the compartmentalization of the various enzymatic reactions in mitochondria and cytosol, respectively' — the mystery is architecture, not a special force. Chemistry and biology are continuous; that does not make them identical. A closing note on the man: Wöhler pulled the first pure metallic aluminium out of its chloride in 1827 and isolated beryllium and yttrium in 1828, and in 1857 fragments of the Kaba meteorite, which fell on a Hungarian town on 15 April that year, were sent to him. He analysed the stone for two straight years. It became one of the first meteorites in which organic material was detected — 2% carbon by weight. The man who made an 'animal substance' out of salts went on to find organic matter in a rock from space. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Urea cycle'; E. Kinne-Saffran & R. K. H. Kinne, 'Vitalism and Synthesis of Urea: From Friedrich Wöhler to Hans A. Krebs', Am. J. Nephrol. 19(2):290-294, 1999; Wikipedia, 'Kaba meteorite', 'Friedrich Wöhler', 'Beryllium'.

question: The Wakefield paper's careful hedge -- that it did not prove a link -- was drowned out by something else that broke into the news the same day. What amplified the story into a national panic in Britain?
answer: a press conference where Wakefield urged parents to switch to three single vaccines
choices: a press conference where Wakefield urged parents to switch to three single vaccines
a Cabinet Office briefing to health ministers, leaked to reporters that afternoon
a mass mailing of the paper to every general practitioner in Britain
a BBC Panorama investigation broadcast the same evening
context: The Royal Free's own PR film described the twelve-child work as a breakthrough. Wakefield's spoken recommendation went far beyond his printed paper. Source: Vaccinating Britain, NCBI Bookshelf; contemporaneous BBC news coverage.

question: The scientific reply to a twelve-child case series was not a ruling from a committee but a much bigger test. A Danish cohort published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2002 by Kreesten Madsen followed every eligible child born in Denmark from 1991 to 1998. Roughly how many children was that?
answer: about half a million
choices: about half a million
about eighty thousand
about two hundred thousand
about fifty thousand
context: The exact number was 537,303, followed for more than two million child-years. The study found no association between MMR and autism. Source: Madsen et al., NEJM 347:1477 (7 November 2002).

question: The Sunday Times reporter Brian Deer began digging into Andrew Wakefield's finances in 2003. Deer found that from February 1996 -- two years BEFORE the 1998 Lancet paper appeared -- Wakefield had already been paid 150 pounds an hour by a party preparing legal action over MMR. Who was paying him, and where did the money come from?
answer: Richard Barr, a UK solicitor building a lawsuit funded by the Legal Aid Board
choices: Richard Barr, a UK solicitor building a lawsuit funded by the Legal Aid Board
the American law firm Kirkland and Ellis, funded by a US class action
a UK parents' group that had pooled donations for a private prosecution
a rival British firm of solicitors funded by their own MMR claimant panel
context: The Legal Aid Board granted Barr 55,000 pounds in August 1996 to fund the clinical work. By 2006 Deer had documented 435,643 pounds paid to Wakefield through the litigation, none of it disclosed to The Lancet or its readers. Source: briandeer.com, Sunday Times exposure files.

question: Andrew Wakefield had a second undisclosed interest that would have raised alarms at any journal. Alongside the litigation work he had filed a patent, in the years before his 1998 paper. What was the patent for?
answer: a rival single measles vaccine and a related 'transfer factor' product
choices: a rival single measles vaccine and a related 'transfer factor' product
a laboratory test for detecting measles virus in gut biopsy tissue
a dietary supplement to be sold to parents of autistic children
an autism screening questionnaire for use in general practice
context: If parents dropped the combined shot for three separate single vaccines -- which Wakefield had recommended at the press conference -- the market for exactly the kind of product he had patented would open up. Source: Left Brain Right Brain, 'Andrew Wakefield's vaccine patent', 2010.

question: In January 2011 the British Medical Journal published Brian Deer's line-by-line comparison of the twelve children in the 1998 Lancet paper with their actual medical records. What did the comparison show, prompting BMJ editor Fiona Godlee to call the paper 'an elaborate fraud'?
answer: five of the twelve children had developmental problems documented before their MMR shot
choices: five of the twelve children had developmental problems documented before their MMR shot
the histopathology grading of bowel biopsies had been altered to non-specific colitis
the reported time gap between MMR and symptoms had been shortened in eight of the twelve
the paper called the twelve consecutively referred when several were recruited through solicitors
context: Ten of Wakefield's twelve co-authors had already retracted the paper's interpretation in March 2004; The Lancet fully retracted the paper on 2 February 2010; the GMC struck Wakefield off the medical register on 24 May 2010. Source: BMJ, Brian Deer, 'How the case against MMR was fixed', January 2011.

question: The senior clinician on the 1998 paper, paediatric gastroenterologist John Walker-Smith, was struck off the medical register alongside Andrew Wakefield. The bank refuses to skip what happened next. In March 2012 Mr Justice Mitting in the High Court considered Walker-Smith's appeal. What did the judge do?
answer: quashed the GMC's findings against him and restored his name to the register
choices: quashed the GMC's findings against him and restored his name to the register
upheld the GMC's erasure and doubled the ban to a lifetime bar from medicine
sent the case back to the GMC for a second full hearing on the same charges
declined to hear the appeal on procedural grounds and left the erasure in force
context: Wakefield did not successfully appeal; Walker-Smith did. A disciplinary tribunal is not a laboratory, and can be wrong in either direction -- which is exactly why the load-bearing refutation of the MMR-autism claim is the counted evidence, not the erasure of a name. Source: Walker-Smith v General Medical Council [2012] EWHC 503 (Admin).

question: The 1998 paper had never survived a real test, but it did not need to in order to do real damage. Between the press conference and 2004, MMR uptake in England fell sharply. From about 91.8% in 1996 it dropped to what low, followed by outbreaks in Yorkshire, Surrey, London and Cheshire?
answer: about 80% in 2003-04
choices: about 80% in 2003-04
about 88% in 2003-04
about 73% in 2003-04
about 65% in 2003-04
context: The precise low was 79.9% in 2003-04. That drop opened the door for measles to return. In no year between 1995 and 2001 had measles cases in England and Wales exceeded 177; from 2006 large outbreaks resumed, children were hospitalised, and some died. A claim that had never survived a test was paid for by people who never made it. Source: UK Parliament SN/SG/2581, 'Measles and MMR statistics', 2009.

question: On Greenland's southwest coast the roofless stone walls of Hvalsey Church still stand, granite a metre and a half thick. Around it archaeologists have mapped some 500 Norse farm ruins from the four centuries the settlers held on. What did those farms keep?
answer: Cattle and sheep
choices: Cattle and sheep
Reindeer and musk oxen
Pigs and hunting hounds
Ponies and milk mares
context: European livestock farms in Greenland. The Eastern Settlement alone left roughly 500 groups of Norse farm ruins and 16 church ruins; the economy ran on sheep and cattle, with goats, plus some seal hunting, and the colony may have peaked at a few thousand people. Hvalsey Church - about 16 by 8 metres, holding 30 to 35 people, built in the Anglo-Norwegian style and thought to date to the early 1300s - is the best-preserved Norse ruin in Greenland. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hvalsey_Church; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Settlement

question: Hendrick Avercamp, working in the Dutch town of Kampen from about 1608, was the first Northern Netherlandish painter to build a whole career on a single subject, and climate historians now read his pictures as a record of the weather he lived in. What did he paint?
answer: Crowds of skaters on frozen canals
choices: Crowds of skaters on frozen canals
Fishing boats caught in winter gales
Villages buried under deep snowdrifts
Harvest fields flattened by hailstorms
context: Avercamp made winter 'ice scenes' his primary genre from about 1608, the first Northern Netherlandish artist to specialise in them systematically. Dutch winters in his lifetime averaged nearly 2 degrees C colder than modern norms, and those crowded frozen canals are among the Little Ice Age's most direct human records: a whole society out walking on ice that no longer forms. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Hendrick_Avercamp; grokipedia.com/page/Winter_Landscape_with_Skaters

question: Mount Tambora erupted in Indonesia in April 1815 and threw up so much sulfur that the next summer failed across the northern world - snow fell at Albany, New York on 6 June 1816. At Lake Geneva the cold rain kept an English house party shut indoors, where they set each other a ghost-story challenge. What came out of it?
answer: Frankenstein and The Vampyre
choices: Frankenstein and The Vampyre
Dracula and The Raven
Wuthering Heights and Lamia
Faust and The Ancient Mariner
context: 'Eighteen hundred and froze to death', New Englanders called 1816. Tambora was a VEI 7 eruption that ejected at least 37 cubic km of rock; global temperatures fell 0.4 to 0.7 degrees C, frost struck in nearly every month across upland New England and New York, and Europe suffered its worst famine of the century. A second invention traces to the same year: with oats short and horses starving, the German inventor Karl Drais built the draisine, ancestor of the bicycle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer

question: The Thames at London froze right across in twenty-four winters between 1400 and 1831. In the Great Frost of 1683-84 the ice held for two months and reached eleven inches thick; John Evelyn watched coaches ply from Westminster to the Temple, and bull-baiting, horse races and puppet plays set up out on the river. A man named Croom took five pounds a day out there. What was he selling?
answer: Cards printed with the buyer's name and date
choices: Cards printed with the buyer's name and date
Roast ox carved off a fire built on the ice
Iron skates strapped onto the crowd's boots
Sledge rides along the length of the river
context: Croom hauled a printing press out onto the frozen Thames and sold souvenir cards carrying the customer's own name and the date, taking five pounds a day. Evelyn's diary catalogues the rest: 'sleds, sliding with skeetes, a bull-baiting, horse and coach races, puppet plays and interludes, cooks, tipling and other lewd places, so that it seemed to be a bacchanalian triumph.' The 1683-84 freeze sits inside the Maunder Minimum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs

question: Above Chamonix in the French Alps the Glacier des Bois pushed downhill through the 1600s until two hamlets, Le Chatelard and Bonanay, ceased to exist. On 29 May 1644 the Bishop of Geneva, Charles-Auguste de Sales, climbed the valley at the head of about 300 people. What had they come to do?
answer: Bless the ice and drive the spirits out of it
choices: Bless the ice and drive the spirits out of it
Say a mass over the hamlet buried beneath it
Plant a cross at the line the ice had reached
Carry the village church's relics down to safety
context: Villagers had already marched on the glacier in 1643, the year it destroyed Le Chatelard; two Chamonix residents alarmed the bishop, and his 1644 procession went up to bless the ice and drive out what locals took to be evil spirits living inside it. The glacier reached its maximum in the 1640s. Alpine glaciers hit their largest Holocene extent between about 1400 and 1850 - in Switzerland the Allalingletscher advanced far enough to dam the river Saaser Vispa and pond up the lake of Mattmark. Sources: chamonix.net, history of Chamonix glaciers; grokipedia.com/page/Little_Ice_Age

question: Norse Greenland kept its farms, its churches and its bishop's seat for roughly four centuries, and then the written record simply stops. The last surviving document from the settlements is dated September 1408, and it survives only because Icelanders carried the news home and set it down there. What does that final record describe?
answer: A wedding at Hvalsey Church
choices: A wedding at Hvalsey Church
A burial at Gardar cathedral
A cargo of tusks bound for Norway
A plea for grain sent to the king
context: On 14 or 16 September 1408 the Icelanders Thorsteinn Olafsson and Sigridur Bjornsdottir married at Hvalsey Church; two priests, Eindridi Andresson and Pall Halvardsson, had read the banns on three consecutive Sundays. Letters written back in Iceland - by a priest at Gardar and by several Icelandic witnesses - are why we know. The wedding party sailed home in 1410 on the last known voyage between Iceland and Norse Greenland, and after that there is silence. The date 1412, often quoted as the colony's last record, is not supported by the surviving documents. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hvalsey_Church; nunatsiaq.com, 'A wedding at Hvalsey Church'

question: On 8 June 1783 a fissure called Laki tore open in southern Iceland and erupted for eight months, releasing some 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and 8 million tonnes of fluorine. In Hampshire the naturalist Gilbert White wrote that the sun at noon 'looked as blank as a clouded moon'. In Iceland the fluorine came down over the pastures where the sheep and cattle grazed. What did it do to them?
answer: It rotted their teeth and their bones
choices: It rotted their teeth and their bones
It blistered their mouths and tongues
It blinded them within a few weeks
It choked their lungs with ash and grit
context: Icelanders call the aftermath Modhuhardhindin, the 'Mist Hardships'. Fluorine poisoning rotted the animals' teeth and bones: 80% of the sheep died - 190,500 head - along with half the cattle and half the horses, and at least a fifth of Iceland's people died in the famine that followed. Benjamin Franklin noted that the haze over Europe was 'of a permanent nature; it was dry, and the rays of the sun seemed to have little effect towards dissipating it.' White logged 28 days of continuous frost that winter; an estimated 23,000 people died in Britain, and in North America the Mississippi froze at New Orleans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: Carbon and nitrogen taken up from food stay locked in a person's bones, so a chemist can read a long-dead diet straight out of a skeleton. Run that test on Greenland's first Norse settlers and about four-fifths of the diet comes back as farm food - beef, mutton, barley. Run it on Greenlanders who died in the 1300s and the reading has swung right over. What were they living on by then?
answer: Seal
choices: Seal
Cod
Reindeer
Whale
context: Carbon and nitrogen isotope work on Norse Greenlander skeletons shows the first settlers eating roughly 80% agricultural and 20% marine food; by the 14th century 50 to 80% of the diet came from the sea, chiefly seal. Read it both ways at once, because both are true: these were people adapting cleverly to their coast, and people eating seal because the cattle-and-barley life was failing. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Settlement; grokipedia.com/page/Norse_settlements_in_Greenland

question: Walrus ivory was medieval Europe's luxury material - chess pieces, crozier heads, reliquary panels - and a carved tusk tells you nothing about where its animal was killed. Researchers ran ancient DNA on seven twelfth-century tusks recovered at Kyiv. Five of the seven traced back to a single hunting ground. Which?
answer: Western Greenland
choices: Western Greenland
Northern Russia
Arctic Norway
Eastern Svalbard
context: Five of the seven Kyiv specimens could be genetically assigned to a western Greenland origin, and were carved in the style typical of Greenlandic exports - a medieval trade route recovered from the DNA inside the tusk. The Norse held a near-monopoly on Europe's walrus ivory and hunted deep into the High Arctic, especially the North Water Polynya, and appear to have overharvested the herds. Sources: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6111184; grokipedia.com/page/Walrus_ivory

question: Every big eruption salts the polar snow with sulfur, which freezes in as a sulfate layer, and those layers are dependable enough that ice-core teams check their annual-layer counting against the 1815 Tambora horizon to better than two years. But a sulfate layer is anonymous - the chemistry looks much the same whichever mountain blew. What else in the ice can be matched to one particular eruption?
answer: The ash shards
choices: The ash shards
The gas bubbles
The chlorine salts
The mercury traces
context: Volcanic ash - tephra - carries a chemical fingerprint characteristic of the volcano that erupted it, so a single shard in the ice can be matched to a mountain; the sulfate spike alone cannot. The highly conductive 1783 Laki sulfate horizon is a standard dating tie-point across Greenland cores from many locations, and Tambora's 1815 layer is the most prominent marker in West Antarctic cores. Sources: Annals of Glaciology, 'Laki and Tambora eruptions as revealed in Greenland ice cores from 11 locations'; geoinfo.nmt.edu ice-core research

question: In 2012 a team of geologists went after the year the Little Ice Age began, with no thermometers to ask. On Baffin Island the ice caps are shrinking back off ground they had covered for centuries, and the team gathered about 150 samples from the newly bared margins, radiocarbon-dating each one for a 'kill date' - the year the advancing ice buried it. What were the samples?
answer: Plants still rooted where they grew
choices: Plants still rooted where they grew
Lichen still gripping the bare rock
Caribou bone still lying where it fell
Beetle shells still packed in the silt
context: Miller et al., 'Abrupt onset of the Little Ice Age triggered by volcanism and sustained by sea-ice/ocean feedbacks', Geophysical Research Letters, January 2012. About 150 radiocarbon-dated dead plants, collected with their roots still intact from beneath receding Baffin Island ice-cap margins, had been killed and buried where they grew - so each one dates the ice's arrival on that spot. The kill dates cluster at 1275-1300, with a second intensification at 1430-1455; the team argued that an unusual 50-year run of four massive tropical eruptions started the cold, with sea-ice and ocean feedbacks sustaining it. The largest of those, the 1257 'mystery eruption', was tracked down in 2013 to Samalas volcano on Lombok, Indonesia. Sources: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2011GL050168; pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1307520110

question: From about 1645 to 1715, with the telescope newly in hand and astronomers watching the Sun systematically, almost no sunspots were recorded - fewer than fifty logged in the 28 years to 1699, where a modern span of that length records forty or fifty thousand. The Little Ice Age's cruellest winters fall inside that blank window, so the Sun has long been the obvious suspect. Reconstructions put the drop in the Sun's total output over that stretch at how much?
answer: About 0.24 percent
choices: About 0.24 percent
About 0.75 percent
About 1.2 percent
About 2.4 percent
context: About 0.24% - roughly 0.82 watts per square metre averaged over Earth's surface, enough for perhaps 0.1 to 0.3 degrees C of global cooling, against a Little Ice Age cooling of about 0.5 to 1 degree C. So the tidy solar story does not hold: the cooling began BEFORE the solar minimum, and the primary cause is believed to be volcanic activity. The Sun is part of this story, not the story - and one neat explanation should not be swapped for another.
