The gap itself was dug out of the old logbooks by Gustav Sporer, who published in 1887 and 1889; Edward Walter Maunder wrote it up in 1890 and 1894; it then lay forgotten for most of a century until John A. Eddy revived it in a 1976 Science paper and gave it the name we use. Annie Russell Maunder did the sunspot-latitude research and received no public credit, women being barred from that recognition at the time. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maunder_Minimum; swsc-journal.org, Space Weather and Space Climate 2017

question: Was the medieval warm spell a world event or a North Atlantic one? Greenland ice cores and Sargasso Sea sediments both point to conditions about a degree C warmer around AD 1000, and Norse farms on Greenland fit that picture. In 2019 the PAGES 2k consortium tested the global claim, lining up proxy records - tree rings, corals, ice layers, lake mud, the stand-ins scientists use where thermometers never existed - region by region across two thousand years. What did they find about the timing of the warm and cold peaks?
answer: They land at different times in different regions
choices: They land at different times in different regions
They land in the same decades all over the world
They show up in the Northern Hemisphere only
They disappear once tree-ring records are dropped
context: PAGES 2k, 'No evidence for globally coherent warm and cold periods over the preindustrial Common Era', Nature 2019: the coldest century of the last millennium differs by region - the 15th in the central and eastern Pacific, the 17th in northwestern Europe and southeastern North America, the mid-19th elsewhere. The one exception to the patchwork is the 20th century, when warming shows up almost everywhere. The dispute is genuinely live, so hold it open: Grokipedia's Medieval Warm Period page reads multi-site tree-ring, ice-core and marine-sediment records as showing overlapping peak warmth around 950-1100 CE in both hemispheres - 'broad hemispheric coherence rather than isolated regional anomalies'. The IPCC's Third Assessment (2001) held that the evidence 'does not support globally synchronous periods of anomalous cold or warmth'. This bank does not claim the medieval period was globally warmer than today. What is not in dispute: the North Atlantic evidence for medieval warmth is strong - Hubert Lamb made that case in 1965 - and the climate swung hard, repeatedly, long before any smokestack. Sources: nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1401-2; grokipedia.com/page/Medieval_Warm_Period

question: The end of Norse Greenland is usually told as a clean climate parable: the world cooled, the farms failed, the colony died. The cooling was real, and it hurt. But historians who study the abandonment put a different pressure first, and say so flatly - not climate alone. Which pressure do they name as dominant?
answer: Economics: land opening at home, buyers falling away
choices: Economics: land opening at home, buyers falling away
Disease: plague brought in on the supply ships
Conflict: Thule Inuit hunters pressing down the coast
Isolation: Norway losing the ships that sailed there
context: More farmland was becoming available back in Scandinavia, and European demand for Greenland's exports was falling away - the walrus-ivory monopoly broke around 1200, when elephant ivory began arriving from Africa. Add overgrazing that eroded thin Arctic turf, walrus herds hunted out, and a diet swinging from beef to seal. Cooling was one genuine pressure among several, and the discipline runs both ways: a hard climate swing is not the whole explanation, and the cold did bite. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Warm_Period; science.org, 'Why did Greenland's Vikings disappear?'

question: You are handed a card and told: the triple 2, 4, 6 fits a hidden rule. Test any triple you like; you will be told only yes or no. You try 8-10-12 (yes), 20-22-24 (yes), 100-102-104 (yes). Confident, you announce: 'the rule is add two each time.' You are told: wrong. What was the rule?
answer: Any three numbers in increasing order
choices: Any three numbers in increasing order
Any three even numbers
Any three numbers that add to a multiple of six
Any three numbers where the middle one is the average
context: This is Peter Wason's 1960 2-4-6 task. Every triple you tested returned yes, because every triple you tested was ascending -- but so is 1-2-3 and 5-9-11, which you never tried. A string of yeses from tests that could never fail teaches you nothing. Source: P.C. Wason, 'On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1960.

question: Back in the 2-4-6 game, you now want to play well. All four triples below are legal to try. Which is the STRONGEST next test of your candidate rule 'add two each time'?
context: The winning move is a triple you EXPECT to be rejected. If 6-4-2 comes back 'no', direction matters. If it comes back 'yes', your rule is dead. The other three are all ascending sequences that 'add two each time' predicts a 'yes' for -- yeses that could never have been noes, and therefore teach nothing. This is the shape of a strong test. Source: Wason 1960; Nickerson, 'Confirmation Bias' review.

question: Peter Wason (1924-2003), a cognitive psychologist at University College London, gave the 2-4-6 task a title that names the trap it exposes. What was the 1960 paper called?
answer: On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task
choices: On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task
Reasoning and the survival of the fittest guess
The illusion of adding two: a study in inductive error
Why humans cannot count: an experimental note
context: The failure Wason named -- collecting only tests that could confirm your idea -- is the phenomenon he later called 'confirmation bias', the term he coined. Both his 2-4-6 task and his four-card task are still classic labs. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Cathcart_Wason.

question: Wason's second famous puzzle -- the four-card selection task, 1966 -- put four cards on a table: 3, 8, blue, red. Each has a number on one face and a colour on the other. The rule: 'if a card shows an even number on one face, its opposite face is blue'. Which two cards must you turn over to test the rule?
answer: The 8 and the red card
choices: The 8 and the red card
The 8 and the blue card
The 3 and the blue card
Only the 8 card
context: The 8 checks whether an even number really is backed by blue. The red card is the ONLY other card that can break the rule -- if you flip it and find an even number, the rule is dead. Wason reported that fewer than one subject in ten picked correctly. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wason_selection_task.

question: Almost every subject wants to turn over the blue card. Why is flipping the blue card the classic wrong move?
answer: Whatever is on its back, the rule survives
choices: Whatever is on its back, the rule survives
It voids the experiment if flipped out of order
It matches two cards at once and is redundant
It always shows the number that started the rule
context: If the back of the blue card is even, the rule holds. If it is odd, the rule still holds -- the rule says only that even implies blue, not that blue implies even. The blue card is the confirmation trap: turning it can only add yeses, and yeses are exactly what the 2-4-6 game already showed you cannot trust. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wason_selection_task.

question: Wason's abstract card task defeats roughly 90% of adult subjects. Griggs and Cox (1982) dressed the SAME logic as Florida drinking-age enforcement -- cards read 'drinking beer', 'drinking coke', '16 years old', '25 years old', with the rule 'if a person is drinking beer, the person must be over 19'. What happened to the success rate?
answer: It rose to about 74% -- roughly ten times the abstract score
choices: It rose to about 74% -- roughly ten times the abstract score
It stayed near 10%, because logic is logic
It fell close to zero, because the drinking rule was unfamiliar
It rose to exactly 100% in every published replication
context: The Florida rule is 'if P then Q', tested by checking P and not-Q -- the same conditional as the abstract card task. But 'catch the underage drinker' is a scene humans have circuits for; 'catch the even-backed non-blue' is not. Same logic, different context, ten times the accuracy. Source: Griggs & Cox, 'The elusive thematic-materials effect', Memory & Cognition 10(5), 1982.

question: The 2-4-6 game and the card task both point at the same rule about what a strong scientific test looks like. What separates a strong test from a worthless one?
answer: A strong test could have come out against the hypothesis; a worthless test could not
choices: A strong test could have come out against the hypothesis; a worthless test could not
A strong test uses larger numbers than a worthless test
A strong test involves at least three subjects; a worthless test involves one
A strong test always includes a control group; a worthless test never does
context: 'Add two each time', 'even numbers ascending', and 'first two average to the third' are all consistent with 2-4-6 -- and each was announced by real Wason subjects. Their tests all came back yes and taught them nothing, because the tests could not come back no. A prediction that fits every result is not a prediction. Source: Wason 1960; Nickerson review.

question: The home version of Wason's lesson is one sentence. Before you argue for an idea in the world, what should you write down?
answer: An observation, named in advance, that would make you drop the idea
choices: An observation, named in advance, that would make you drop the idea
The three closest experts who already agree with you
A list of previous cases where the idea worked
A friendly opponent's name to check the argument later
context: This is Wason's puzzle, aimed at yourself. If you cannot name an observation that would kill your idea -- a triple you EXPECT the world to answer 'no' to -- you are playing 2-4-6 alone, collecting yeses that could never have been noes. That habit is the difference between a scientist and a fan. Source: Wason 1960; Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', 1963.

question: Here is a five-minute test you can run tonight. In one glass, drop an ice cube into water. In a second glass, chill olive oil in the fridge until a lump of it turns solid, then set that lump into liquid olive oil. Which way does each solid go?
answer: The ice floats and the solid oil sinks.
choices: The ice floats and the solid oil sinks.
The ice sinks and the solid oil floats.
Both the ice and the solid oil float.
Both the ice and the solid oil sink.
context: Almost every substance packs tighter when it solidifies, so its own solid sinks in it. As a fat melts its volume rises and its density therefore falls, which leaves solid fat crystals near 1.0 g/cm3 denser than the roughly 0.9 g/cm3 oil around them. Water is one of a small handful of substances that go the other way. Fair warning before you try it: olive oil begins solidifying somewhere around 37-50 F and thickens gradually into slush rather than forming a clean cube, so watch which way the solid parts drift instead of expecting a tidy sinking block. Sources: btsa.com, 'Physical properties of oils and fats'; centrafoods.com on solidified olive oil.

question: Wood floats high in the water, a cork rides almost clear of it, and a beach ball barely dips in at all. Ice floats far lower than any of them. Roughly how much of a floating ice cube stands above the waterline?
answer: About a tenth of it.
choices: About a tenth of it.
About a third of it.
About half of it.
About three quarters of it.
context: Ice Ih measures 0.9167-0.9168 g/cm3 at 0 C against liquid water's roughly 1.00 g/cm3 -- about 8.3 percent less dense -- so a cube settles until only about a tenth of it clears the surface, and an iceberg does the same thing at ship-killing scale. Keep two numbers apart when you retell this: 8.3 percent is the DENSITY drop, while the VOLUME increase on freezing is about 9 percent. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice; grokipedia.com/page/Ice_crystal.

question: In ice, every water molecule locks onto exactly four neighbours -- never three, never five. Nothing outside the molecule imposes that count; a single molecule's own make-up fixes it. What about one water molecule sets the number at four?
answer: It has two hydrogens on one side and two unshared electron pairs on the other.
choices: It has two hydrogens on one side and two unshared electron pairs on the other.
It has four unshared electron pairs on its oxygen, one aimed at each neighbour.
It has two hydrogens, each one able to hold two neighbours at once.
It has a bent frame with four open faces, one turned to each neighbour.
context: A hydrogen bond needs a donor and an acceptor. Water brings exactly two of each: two hydrogens it can offer, and two lone pairs -- unshared pairs of electrons -- on the oxygen that can receive. Four is the whole budget. A single hydrogen can donate only one such bond, and it takes a full PAIR of electrons to accept one, which is why the other counts do not work. The tetrahedral cage is not a design choice; it is arithmetic on a single molecule. In ice Ih those four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, with neighbouring oxygens about 2.75 angstroms apart. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water ('a maximum of four hydrogen bonds'); grokipedia.com/page/Hydrogen_bond; grokipedia.com/page/Ice_crystal.

question: Cool almost any liquid and its molecules stop jostling and settle into a tighter arrangement, so the solid comes out denser than the liquid was. Water's freeze does the opposite: the locked framework takes up more room than the moving liquid did. Its oxygen atoms sit a fixed distance apart in one repeating pattern. What pattern?
answer: Six-sided rings, with an oxygen at every corner.
choices: Six-sided rings, with an oxygen at every corner.
Cubes packed corner to corner, as in table salt.
Long parallel chains, like a bundle of threads.
Flat stacked sheets, like the layers in graphite.
context: Ice Ih is a hexagonal crystal: the oxygens sit at the vertices of open six-membered rings about 2.75 angstroms apart (lattice parameters a = 4.52 A, c = 7.36 A near 0 C; space group P6-3/mmc, a wurtzite-like oxygen lattice). That rigid cage holds the molecules further apart than the jostling liquid does. One cage, two famous consequences -- the float, and the six arms on every snowflake, which inherit the lattice's six-fold rotational axis. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Ice_crystal; grokipedia.com/page/Snowflake; Kenneth Libbrecht, 'Snow Crystals', arxiv.org/pdf/1910.06389.

question: Water's surface behaves like a stretched skin -- rain pulls itself into beads, and a drop hangs from a tap before it lets go. Measured, that pull is about 72 millinewtons per metre, well above the 20 to 40 of ordinary organic liquids like alcohol and cooking oil. Exactly one liquid you might actually meet beats water, and by nearly seven times. Which?
answer: Mercury.
choices: Mercury.
Glycerine.
Liquid nitrogen.
Molten candle wax.
context: Mercury reaches about 485 mN/m, held together by strong metallic bonding between its atoms. Water's own 71.99 mN/m at 25 C is the outlier among ordinary molecular liquids, and the cause is the same hydrogen-bond network that floats ice: organic liquids get only weak van der Waals attraction and land at 20-40 mN/m. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water; grokipedia.com/page/Surface_tension.

question: People often say water is the only substance on Earth whose solid floats on its own liquid. It is not the only one -- it is one of a small handful, and the others are metals and semiconductors rather than anything in a kitchen. Which of these also expands as it freezes, so its solid floats on its own melt?
answer: Gallium.
choices: Gallium.
Lead.
Mercury.
Zinc.
context: Silicon, germanium, gallium, bismuth, antimony and plutonium all expand when they freeze. Gallium is the cleanest number: solid 5.904 g/cm3 against liquid about 6.095, roughly 3.1 percent expansion. Silicon runs from 2.57 g/cm3 as a liquid to 2.33 as a solid -- but only at 1414 C, so nobody watches it in a glass. Say 'one of very few', never 'the only one'; a claim that overclaims teaches you to overclaim. Sources: van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/1588 (Physics Van, Illinois); completeera.com on liquids denser than their own solids.

question: By February a northern lake carries a lid of ice thick enough to walk on, and underneath it the water is still liquid and the lake is still alive. Now suppose ice were the ordinary sort of solid, heavier than its own liquid. What would that lake do each winter instead?
answer: Fill from the bottom up and freeze solid, with nothing left alive in it.
choices: Fill from the bottom up and freeze solid, with nothing left alive in it.
Grow its lid downward twice as fast, with fish still wintering below it.
Stay ice-free all winter as sinking ice melted at depth, with its fish fine.
Freeze through in a single night, killing every living thing before dawn.
context: Floating ice 'prevents bottom-up freezing of the bodies of water', creating a sheltered environment for the life underneath. Wikipedia's counterfactual is blunt: if water were most dense at its freezing point, winter cooling at the surface would drive convective mixing all the way down and 'all life in it would be killed'. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water.

question: A runner finishing in August is drenched, and the sweat sitting on her skin has cooled her almost not at all -- it cools only as it leaves. Evaporating a single litre of sweat carries roughly 580 kilocalories off the body. What is that energy spent on?
answer: Snapping the hydrogen bonds that tie each molecule to its neighbours.
choices: Snapping the hydrogen bonds that tie each molecule to its neighbours.
Breaking the oxygen-hydrogen bonds inside each escaping molecule.
Heating the sweat the rest of the way up to its boiling point.
Pushing the surrounding air aside as the new vapour expands.
context: Water's heat of vaporisation is 40.65 kJ/mol, or 2257 kJ/kg at the normal boiling point: a molecule cannot leave the liquid until its hydrogen bonds to the neighbours are broken, and that bill is paid in heat taken from your skin. The bonds inside each molecule are untouched -- the vapour is still water. Thermodynamic measurement at body conditions puts the latent heat near 2,430 J/g at 30 C and 2,415 J/g at 37 C. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water; Ashworth et al., 'Sweat evaporation in humans: A molecular and thermodynamic perspective', Experimental Physiology.

question: In January 1611 Johannes Kepler, imperial astronomer in Prague and badly behind on his salary, could not afford a New Year's gift for his patron. Snowflakes settling on his coat gave him one: a small book asking a question nobody had thought to ask -- why is every flake six-cornered? Three centuries before anyone could see the lattice, Kepler had to guess. What did he propose?
answer: The hexagon is one of the few shapes that tiles a surface with no gaps.
choices: The hexagon is one of the few shapes that tiles a surface with no gaps.
Six is the smallest number of arms a falling crystal can balance on.
Cold air currents spin the falling droplets into six-armed pinwheels.
Each flake grows on a speck of dust that has six flat faces to build on.
context: Kepler's book was 'Strena Seu De Nive Sexangula' -- 'A New Year's Gift, On the Six-Cornered Snowflake' -- and the question inside it was genuinely new. His packing guess reached for the right KIND of answer with three centuries too little equipment: the real one had to wait for X-ray crystallography to show the hexagonal ice lattice. The Charles Bridge walk and the phrase 'all with six corners and feathered radii' come from the traditional telling of the episode, so treat those details as story rather than record. Sources: keplersdiscovery.com; Kepler, 'The Six-Cornered Snowflake', Oxford University Press; softbites.org.  (Legend.)

question: A hard freeze runs through the night, and at the thaw a homeowner finds a burst pipe inside a wall. Plumbers give the same advice ahead of every freezing night: leave one tap open at a trickle. Why does that trickle save the pipe?
answer: It gives the water squeezed between the ice and the tap an escape.
choices: It gives the water squeezed between the ice and the tap an escape.
It keeps the water moving fast enough that it cannot freeze at all.
It draws warmer water up from the main into the cold stretch of pipe.
It bleeds air out of the line so the pipe cannot pressurise at all.
context: Freezing pipes fail hydraulically, not by ice shoving the pipe wall. The growing ice plug blocks the pipe; the liquid trapped between that plug and a closed tap then keeps getting squeezed as more ice forms, and pressure climbs from about 35 psi to over 4,000 psi until the pipe lets go -- typically in the unfrozen stretch downstream. An open trickle gives that trapped water somewhere to go. Sources: jlconline.com, 'Understanding how water pipes freeze' (Journal of Light Construction); randrmagonline.com on water dynamics in frozen-pipe damage.

question: A cooling liquid ought to keep getting denser right down to the moment it freezes. Water quits early: it reaches its maximum density at one temperature and then, over the last stretch before it turns to ice, gets lighter again. Where is that peak?
answer: About 4 C.
choices: About 4 C.
About 1 C.
About 12 C.
About 25 C.
context: Liquid water is densest at 3.98 C -- Grokipedia gives the modern refinement as 3.98 plus or minus 0.0005 C at 1 atm. That anomaly is what makes the winter lid possible: as a pond cools past that point the coldest water is no longer the heaviest, so it stops sinking, stays on the surface, and freezes there. It also writes the lake's whole calendar. In autumn the chilled surface keeps sinking until the entire column sits at that temperature and goes uniform, and for a few days a moderate wind can then stir the lake top to bottom -- the 'fall turnover' that carries oxygen down to the deep water and lifts nutrients off the sediment. All winter the lake then runs upside down: near-freezing water on top, densest water resting on the bottom. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water; grokipedia.com/page/maximum_density; iisd.org/ela on lake stratification and turnover.

question: Two very different bonds are at work in a glass of water. One is the covalent O-H bond inside a single molecule, holding its own hydrogens on. The other is the hydrogen bond reaching from one molecule to the next -- the link that floats ice, lifts water's boiling point, and keeps the oceans liquid. Which of the two is stronger, and by roughly how much?
answer: The covalent bond, by about twenty times.
choices: The covalent bond, by about twenty times.
The hydrogen bond, by about twenty times.
The covalent bond, by about twice.
The hydrogen bond, by about twice.
context: A hydrogen bond in liquid water is worth about 23 kJ/mol; the covalent O-H bond inside the molecule runs about 492 kJ/mol -- roughly 21 times stronger. The bond that makes the planet habitable is the WEAK one, about a twentieth the strength of the bond holding the molecule itself together, and it does the job only because every molecule makes four of them at once and they work as a network. Sources: Martin Chaplin, 'Water's Hydrogen Bond Strength', arxiv.org/pdf/0706.1355; water.lsbu.ac.uk on water hydrogen bonding.

question: Water's three chemical cousins in the same column of the periodic table -- hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen selenide, hydrogen telluride -- boil colder and colder as their molecules get lighter, an orderly line any chemistry class can draw. Water is the lightest of the four, so the line predicts a boiling point far below zero. It boils at 99.98 C instead. By roughly how much are hydrogen bonds lifting it above the prediction?
answer: About 180 degrees.
choices: About 180 degrees.
About 120 degrees.
About 250 degrees.
About 300 degrees.
context: Extending the trend puts water's 'expected' boiling point far below zero, but the exact figure depends on how you draw the line: the University of Calgary textbook says about -80 C, other extrapolations reach -100 C, and extending the H2Te-H2Se line down to period 2 gives -130 C. Nobody has measured it -- treat the prediction as an estimate and the gap as roughly 180 degrees. The three cousins have no hydrogen bonding at all; they are held together only by London dispersion forces, which strengthen with molecular size, which is exactly why their boiling points rise down the group in the ordinary way while water's leaps out of line. Without that lift there would be no liquid water anywhere on Earth's surface. Sources: chem-textbook.ucalgary.ca on hydrogen bonding; docbrown.info; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Properties_of_water.

question: Ice is slippery, and physicists are still arguing about why nearly two centuries on. James Thomson proposed in the 1850s that the pressure of a skater's blade melts the ice beneath it; Frank Bowden's group in the 1930s answered that heat from the sliding does the melting. Michael Faraday had gone first, in 1842, and his answer needed no skater at all: he said something was already sitting on the ice before anything touched it. What did he say was there?
answer: A liquid-like film, present even well below freezing.
choices: A liquid-like film, present even well below freezing.
A skin of brine, kept liquid by dissolved salt.
A cushion of air, trapped in the surface as it froze.
A fur of fine crystals, shed by the ice as it dries.
context: Faraday's 1842 idea was surface premelting: a disordered, liquid-like layer sitting on ice even when the whole block is below 0 C, needing neither a skater's weight nor any sliding. The argument he opened has never closed. Luis MacDowell's 2023 simulations concluded that 'All three controversial hypotheses operate simultaneously to one or the other degree', and in 2025 a Saarland University group put forward a fourth candidate -- amorphization, in which sliding smashes the surface crystal into a disordered layer. Achraf Atila, one of its authors: 'either the slipperiness of ice is coming from a combination of all of them or a few of them, or there is something else that we don't know yet.' An argument 180 years old and still running is not a failure of science; it is what an honest open question looks like. Sources: Quanta Magazine, 'Why is ice slippery? A new hypothesis slides into the chat', 8 Dec 2025; Nature Reviews Chemistry, 'Surface premelting of water ice'; physicstoday.aip.org.

question: The James Webb Space Telescope's main mirror is 6.5 metres across -- wider than any rocket's payload bay. On 25 December 2021 there was only one way to get it into space. How did Webb fly?
answer: folded up, with the outer wings hinged back
choices: folded up, with the outer wings hinged back
in three launches, to be bolted together in orbit
wrapped around the outside of the rocket in strips
as loose panels for the crew to assemble on site
context: Webb launched aboard an Ariane 5 from French Guiana on Christmas Day 2021 with three of the mirror's outer segments folded back like the wings of a hinged panel. Once clear of Earth it spent about two weeks unfolding on the way to its destination. Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/fact-sheet/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope

question: The Hubble Space Telescope orbits about 540 km up and has been visited five times by astronauts, who fixed its blurred mirror in 1993 and swapped out worn parts on later flights. The James Webb Space Telescope was designed on a very different assumption. What assumption?
answer: no one would ever be able to service it
choices: no one would ever be able to service it
it would be brought home for repair every ten years
it would be replaced by a twin already on order
it would fix itself with onboard maintenance robots
context: Webb sits about 1.5 million km from Earth at the Sun-Earth L2 point, roughly four times as far as the Moon and far beyond the reach of any current crewed vehicle. Every mechanism on the observatory had to work without a possible repair mission. Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope

question: Engineers going through Webb's deployment sequence step by step counted, with grim precision, the number of steps that had no backup, no redundancy, and no possible rescue if any one of them failed. What number did they arrive at?
answer: 344 single-point failures
choices: 344 single-point failures
12 single-point failures
about 1,800 single-point failures
roughly 40 single-point failures
context: The famous count -- 344 -- included latch releases, motor drives, spring hinges, cable spools, and the tensioning cords on the sunshield. About 80 percent of the 344 were tied to the deployment sequence; roughly 140 release mechanisms and 400 pulleys supported the sunshield alone. Every one of the 344 worked. Sources: https://interestingengineering.com/science/james-webb-has-344-single-point-failures-here-are-the-5-most-critical-elements ; https://keeptrack.space/deep-dive/jwst

question: Webb was built to study the faint light of the earliest galaxies, stretched by the expanding universe into the infrared band. That imposed a demand which shaped the entire observatory. Why did the telescope itself have to be kept extraordinarily cold?
answer: a warm telescope glows in the same infrared band it is trying to observe
choices: a warm telescope glows in the same infrared band it is trying to observe
a warm mirror coating would slowly tarnish and lose its gold shine
a warm beryllium mirror would expand and lose its precise figure
a warm instrument bay would overheat and shut down for safety
context: Anything warm radiates in the infrared. A room-temperature telescope trying to observe the infrared is like a floodlit stadium trying to observe candles -- the observatory's own emission is brighter than the signal. Webb has to be actively kept cold, which is why the sunshield, the L2 orbit and even MIRI's mechanical refrigerator all exist. Source: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/

question: Webb's sunshield is kite-shaped, roughly the size of a tennis court, and built from five separate layers of Kapton foil each thinner than a human hair, held apart with empty space between them. It is not thick insulation. How do those five layers get rid of the Sun's heat?
answer: each layer catches some warmth and re-radiates it out the side
choices: each layer catches some warmth and re-radiates it out the side
the whole sandwich mirrors nearly all sunlight back at the Sun
the layers store warmth in the day and dump it during eclipses
a coolant pumped between the layers carries the warmth off to vent
context: Each Kapton layer, coated with aluminum and doped silicon, catches some incoming warmth and radiates it away edgewise rather than passing it to the layer behind. The temperature falls in five steps, from about 110 degrees C on the sun-facing side to roughly minus 233 to minus 235 degrees C on the telescope side -- a drop of over 300 degrees across five sheets of foil in space. Sources: https://jwst.gsfc.nasa.gov/content/observatory/sunshield.html ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.04869

question: Once Webb was unfolded, engineers had to teach its mirror hexagons to act as one. They pointed the telescope at a single bright reference star -- HD 84406, in Ursa Major -- and looked at what came back. What did the very first alignment image show?
answer: eighteen separate images of the same star, one per segment
choices: eighteen separate images of the same star, one per segment
one perfectly focused star, sharper than expected
a total blank -- the sensor had not been powered on
a smear of light with no distinct star at all
context: Every mis-tilted segment reflected HD 84406 to a different spot on the detector, so the first mosaic showed eighteen ghost images of the same star scattered across the field. Over about three months tiny actuators moved each segment in fine steps of roughly 8 to 10 nanometres each until all eighteen images stacked into one crisp point. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HD_84406 ; https://www.universetoday.com/articles/heres-exactly-how-engineers-are-aligning-jwsts-segmented-mirrors

question: Webb was designed with no possibility of servicing, but 'no repairs' is not the same as 'no damage'. Between 22 and 24 May 2022, before the first science images were even released, one of the mirror segments took a permanent hit. What hit it?
answer: a micrometeoroid larger than any pre-launch model predicted
choices: a micrometeoroid larger than any pre-launch model predicted
a stray fragment shed by the launcher's upper stage
a solar flare that briefly overheated the gold coating
a piece of orbital debris from a Russian satellite test
context: The particle struck segment C3 and left a local deformation Webb's actuators could reduce but never fully cancel; the segment's wavefront error jumped from about 56 to 258 nanometres RMS. There is no repair mission and there never will be, so the dent is part of the telescope for life. Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/webb-telescopes-giant-mirror-struck-by-micrometeoroid/

question: On January 30, 2023 Cochrane published an update by Tom Jefferson and colleagues, 'Physical interventions to interrupt or reduce the spread of respiratory viruses'. It pooled 78 studies and about 610,000 people. What phrase did the authors' conclusions use for wearing a mask in the community, next to not wearing one, for influenza-like and COVID-like illness?
answer: Probably makes little or no difference
choices: Probably makes little or no difference
Cuts the illness roughly in half
Clearly helps adults but not children
Works only alongside a vaccine
context: 'Probably makes little or no difference' is verbatim from the authors' conclusions. It is a claim about the pooled trials, not about fabric physics. Source: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36715243, factcheck.org.

question: The same 2023 Jefferson-and-colleagues Cochrane review asked a second question: when hospital workers do routine care, are they better protected by a fitted N95 respirator than by a plain surgical mask? Pooling the trials that had put the two head to head, what did the authors report?
answer: No clear differences between the two
choices: No clear differences between the two
A large advantage for the N95 group
A clear win for the surgical-mask arm
Not one trial had ever compared them
context: 'No clear differences' is verbatim from the review. That is a claim about the pooled trials in routine care, and different from a bench filter test - bench tests DO show an N95 stops more particles. Source: cidrap.umn.edu, factcheck.org.

question: Every trial pooled in that 2023 Cochrane mask review had the same design bone. Researchers randomised which villages, wards, or households got the free masks and were asked to wear them; they then counted infections in each arm. Given that shape, what were those trials actually a test of?
answer: A recommendation to a population
choices: A recommendation to a population
The particle filtration of the cloth
One individual's own personal risk
How long the virus survives on fabric
context: The trials tested the intervention (asking people to mask) rather than the article (a mask on a face) - which is exactly what a mandate is. Adherence to the mask-wearing was often poor across the trials, and the authors said so in the paper. DANMASK-19 (Bundgaard 2020) and the Bangladesh trial (Abaluck 2022) both used this shape. Source: sciencebasedmedicine.org.

question: Within weeks of publication, headlines were reading the January 2023 Cochrane update as saying 'masks don't work'. On March 10, 2023 the journal's Editor-in-Chief, Karla Soares-Weiser, released a public statement. How did she describe that headline reading?
answer: Inaccurate and misleading
choices: Inaccurate and misleading
A fair summary of the paper
Supported by the plain-language text
A minority view within the field
context: Soares-Weiser also wrote the plain-language summary 'was open to misinterpretation, for which we apologize' and 'we take responsibility for not making the wording clearer'. Source: cochrane.org statement, March 10, 2023.

question: The biggest single trial the 2023 Cochrane review could draw on was the Bangladesh mask trial (Abaluck et al., Science 2022) - a cluster-randomised study in 600 villages and 342,183 adults. Free masks and promotion tripled how many people masked up. Compared with the control villages, by how much did symptomatic COVID seroprevalence fall in the intervention villages?
answer: About 9.5 percent
choices: About 9.5 percent
About 50 percent
About 75 percent
It did not fall at all
context: A real, modest, honestly reported effect - tripling mask usage across 600 villages moved symptomatic seroprevalence by roughly 9.5%. For contrast, the Danish DANMASK-19 trial (Bundgaard et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2020) recruited 6,024 adults and found 1.8% of the mask arm vs 2.1% of the control arm tested positive after a month - a difference too small to call. Two honest trials, two different scales; a careful scientist reports both. Source: science.org, acpjournals.org.

question: Christmas 1891, a Berlin clinic: a girl is dying of diphtheria, a disease killing 50,000 German children a year. In the story medicine still tells, she is injected with something from a ram and a horse made immune to it, and lives. Which part of those animals held the protection?
answer: The clear serum that separates from their blood
choices: The clear serum that separates from their blood
The red marrow that fills their long bones
The soft tissue of their swollen lymph glands
The thin fluid drawn from around their spines
context: Emil von Behring's diphtheria antitoxin was not a drug at all: it was blood serum from an immunised animal, carrying something that animal's own body had manufactured. Before it, diphtheria killed 30 to 50 of every 100 children it struck; standardised serum therapy cut that to 1 to 5 by the early 1900s, and German paediatricians called Behring 'Saviour of the Children'. In 1901 the very first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to him 'for his work on serum therapy, especially its application against diphtheria'. The bedside details of that Christmas case have since been questioned by historians. Source: nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1901/behring/article/ and /facts/.  (Legend.)

question: At the Pasteur Institute in 1923 the veterinarian Gaston Ramon wanted his horses to make more protective serum against diphtheria. He found that stirring plain, dead, non-medical material into the injection made their antibody response far bigger, and he worked through whatever came to hand. What did he stir in?
answer: Tapioca, potato starch and bread crumbs
choices: Powdered glass, chalk and fine sand
Beeswax, lanolin and pressed olive oil
Tapioca, potato starch and bread crumbs
Charcoal, saltpetre and quicklime
context: Ramon's junk worked, and it opened the field of adjuvants: substances that carry no protection of their own but make the immune system take the injected shape seriously. Three years later Alexander Glenny found the same effect with aluminium salts, which are still in vaccines today. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Immunologic_adjuvant.

question: Kitasato Shibasaburo first grew the tetanus bacillus in pure culture, in 1889, and that technique opened the way to the next step: in December 1890 he and Emil von Behring published together the paper that founded serum therapy. When the first Nobel Prize in Medicine was given for that work in 1901, it went to Behring alone. How did Japan mark Kitasato in 2024?
answer: It put his portrait on a redesigned banknote
choices: It made his birthday a public holiday
It issued a set of commemorative postage stamps
It renamed its national medical university for him
It put his portrait on a redesigned banknote
context: The Bank of Japan's redesigned 1,000-yen note, carrying Kitasato's face, entered circulation on 3 July 2024 - 123 years after the prize he was left off. Kitasato's deep-agar hydrogen tube was what made pure tetanus culture possible at all; the 1890 paper was 'Ueber das Zustandekommen der Diphtherie-Immunitaet und der Tetanus-Immunitaet bei Thieren', Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift, 4 December 1890. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Kitasato_Shibasaburo.

question: The Christmas 1891 diphtheria case is immunology's founding bedside story, told for a century as Emil von Behring's triumph. Archive work has complicated it: Behring's laboratory did not have enough of the serum for a human dose, and Ernst von Bergmann, who ran the clinic, had banned its use - so someone went around him. In 1997 archivists found a photograph with a claim scrawled across all four margins, dating the first treated child to 22 December 1891 and taking the credit. Whose handwriting was it?
answer: Erich Wernicke, an assistant in Behring's laboratory
choices: Paul Ehrlich, a chemist measuring the serum's strength
Heinrich Geissler, a physician on Bergmann's ward
Erich Wernicke, an assistant in Behring's laboratory
Kitasato Shibasaburo, Behring's co-author on the serum
context: Wernicke immunised the rams and horses and harvested the serum himself. Christina Oedingen and Joseph Staerk of the Behring Archive found the inscribed photograph in 1997; Wernicke had written across its margins that on 22 December 1891 the first child was treated with serum he had produced, and was cured. The likeliest reconstruction is that Wernicke and Heinrich Geissler, one of Bergmann's house physicians, treated the child around the prohibition. The bank tells the traditional Christmas story AND its honest correction. Source: Don K. Nakayama, 'The Christmas Miracle of Emil von Behring', The American Surgeon (2023), doi:10.1177/00031348221129515.  (Legend.)

question: In 1897 Paul Ehrlich, working out how to measure diphtheria serum, drew the immune system as nobody had before: living cells studded with side-chains, molecular arms each shaped so one particular poison locks in like a key. The antitoxin itself, though - the protection carried in the serum - was known to float free in the blood, attached to no cell at all. What did Ehrlich's picture say put it there?
answer: The cell overproduced its side-chains and the surplus broke off
choices: The cell overproduced its side-chains and the surplus broke off
The cell moulded fresh copies around the poison and released those
Dying cells dissolved and their surfaces drifted loose in the blood
The liver built new ones from fragments it filtered out of the blood
context: Ehrlich's side-chain theory was wrong in its details and right in its essential picture. He also made immunity measurable, defining one antitoxin unit as the amount of serum that neutralises 100 lethal doses of toxin in guinea pigs - a number you could stamp on a vial, which is what finally made Behring's serum reliable in the clinic. Behring and Ehrlich then ran large-scale production out of a laboratory under a railway arch in Berlin. Ehrlich shared the 1908 Nobel Prize with Elie Metchnikoff, whose rival cellular theory came from pushing rose thorns into transparent starfish larvae at Messina in 1882. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Paul_Ehrlich.

question: A week after a vaccination your blood holds hundreds of thousands of cells all making exactly the right antibody for a germ your body had never met. The vaccine itself was only a shape: a killed germ, or one harmless piece of one. Frank Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 paper explained where that army came from. What does that injected shape actually do?
answer: It finds the few cells that already fit it and drives them to divide
choices: It orders the bone marrow to build fresh cells to that germ's shape
It folds a new antibody around itself, like clay pressed into a mould
It is copied into a cell's DNA and read back there as a blueprint
It finds the few cells that already fit it and drives them to divide
context: This is clonal selection - Frank Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 paper and, independently, David Talmage the same year - and it is the fact textbooks most often state backwards. Nothing is taught and nothing new is built: you already carry a lymphocyte for almost any shape before you ever meet it. The matching cell is rare, roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 1,000,000, and one activated lymphocyte makes over 1,000 daughters within days. The 'mould' answer was the seriously held rival, proposed by Fritz Breinl and Felix Haurowitz in 1930 and backed by Linus Pauling in 1940; its supporting experiments could not be reproduced, and in 1958 Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg showed in microdroplets that a single cell makes only ONE kind of antibody. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Clonal_selection.

question: A human body carries something like twenty thousand genes and makes hundreds of millions of different antibody shapes - arithmetic that does not work. In 1976 Susumu Tonegawa and Nobumichi Hozumi, at the Basel Institute for Immunology, went at it directly: they took DNA from mouse embryos and DNA from grown antibody-making cells and probed each with two markers, one for the variable end of an antibody gene and one for the constant end. In embryo DNA the two markers landed on two separate fragments. In the antibody-making cell, both landed on one. What had happened inside that cell?
answer: It had cut its own DNA apart and joined the pieces together
choices: It had folded its chromosome so the two stretches lay touching
It had copied the two stretches and stacked the copies end to end
It had cut its own DNA apart and joined the pieces together
A virus had spliced its own genes in between the two stretches
context: Every developing B cell physically cuts up and reshuffles the DNA it inherited from you - roughly 40 to 50 V segments, 25 D segments and 6 J segments recombined at random, with extra letters jammed into the joins by an enzyme called TdT - which can theoretically yield over a trillion different receptor shapes, while a rule called allelic exclusion makes sure each single cell ends up expressing exactly one. Your body invents receptors for germs that do not exist yet. Tonegawa took the 1987 Nobel alone 'for his discovery of the genetic principle for generation of antibody diversity'. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Susumu_Tonegawa; nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1987/tonegawa/facts/.

question: Alexander Glenny found in 1926 that diphtheria toxoid - the toxin, chemically disarmed - provoked a far bigger antibody response in guinea pigs when precipitated onto aluminium salts than when injected pure. Aluminium went into human vaccines in 1932 and stayed the only such booster, or adjuvant, licensed in the United States for the rest of the century. Glenny explained it as a depot: the aluminium pins the antigen at the injection site and lets it seep out slowly. Then one guinea-pig experiment made the depot story very hard to hold. What did that experiment show?
answer: Cutting away the injected ear two hours later changed nothing
choices: A pump seeping pure antigen for weeks produced no response at all
Aluminium salts injected with no antigen raised the same antibodies
The antigen had drained out of the injection site within ten minutes
Cutting away the injected ear two hours later changed nothing
context: Removing the injection site within four days did block the response in one guinea-pig experiment - but removing the injected ear just two hours after injection changed neither the size nor the duration of the response, so slow leakage from a depot cannot be the whole story. The rival NLRP3-inflammasome explanation is no cleaner: NLRP3-deficient mice have shown marked suppression of antibody production, partial suppression, and no effect at all, in different studies. A century after Glenny, nobody can say cleanly why aluminium works - and the bank says so rather than pretending. Modern alum still raises seroconversion 2- to 10-fold over antigen alone. Source: 'Mechanism of Immunopotentiation and Safety of Aluminum Adjuvants', pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3541479/.

question: Maurice Hilleman, working on influenza at the Walter Reed Army Institute, was first to demonstrate and name the two ways flu rewrites itself: antigenic DRIFT, a steady drip of single-letter mutations in the surface proteins, which is why the flu shot is annual; and antigenic SHIFT, an abrupt swap of whole gene segments producing a subtype nobody's memory has ever seen, which is what makes a pandemic. Measles does neither to any useful degree, so one childhood dose holds. The memory machinery is identical for both viruses; only the target differs. What lets influenza drift so fast?
answer: Its copying enzyme has no proofreading step, so its mistakes stand
choices: Its copying enzyme has no proofreading step, so its mistakes stand
It replicates in cells whose repair enzymes cannot reach its genome
It carries a gene whose whole job is scrambling its surface coat
It copies itself several hundred times faster than measles does
context: Influenza's RNA polymerase errs at roughly 10^-6 to 10^-4 substitutions per nucleotide per replication, and the errors concentrate in five hypervariable antigenic sites on the head of the hemagglutinin protein - exactly the part your memory cells learned. Measles mutates at a comparable raw rate, about 9 x 10^-5, but is far more stable where it counts, minimising antigenic variation, so the coat your memory learned still matches decades later. In 1957 Hilleman spotted the new H2N2 subtype in reports out of Hong Kong, predicted it would reach the United States by early September, and drove 40 million doses out before the season peaked. He developed more than 40 vaccines - more than any other single scientist - and took the National Medal of Science in 1988. Sources: grokipedia.com/page/Maurice_Hilleman; grokipedia.com/page/Antigenic_drift; grokipedia.com/page/Measles.

question: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine is a killed virus injected into the arm; Albert Sabin's is a live weakened virus swallowed on a sugar cube. Three doses of Salk's leave a child 99 to 100 per cent safe from paralysis - a number that makes the two vaccines look interchangeable. They are not. What is still true of a child who has had all three of Salk's doses?
answer: The child can still carry the virus and pass it to other people
choices: The child needs a fresh dose every ten years to stay protected
The child can still carry the virus and pass it to other people
The child is covered against only one of the three types of poliovirus
The child is left unprotected until months after the final dose
context: Protection from disease and blocking transmission are two different things, and the mechanism tells you which one you bought. The injected vaccine fills the bloodstream with a circulating antibody, immunoglobulin G, which intercepts poliovirus before it can travel to the nervous system - but poliovirus is swallowed, and it multiplies for weeks in the lining of the gut long before it ever reaches the blood. Grokipedia's polio-vaccine page states it flatly: the injected vaccine 'generates limited intestinal mucosal immunity, as it does not stimulate significant secretory IgA responses in the gut, allowing vaccinated individuals to potentially shed and transmit virus upon exposure despite protection from paralysis... This mechanism prioritizes individual protection over interruption of fecal-oral transmission chains.' The oral vaccine, replicating in the gut, does raise that secretory IgA and does interrupt the chain. Neither is simply the better one; each buys something different, and the immunology says exactly what. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Polio_vaccine.

question: The strongest thing the OTHER side says about a heretical claim is usually the good part. Wegener's continental drift was rejected for about fifty years for one specific reason -- not because his opponents were foolish, but because his idea had a missing piece. Which of these live-at-the-time scientific objections was the load-bearing one?
answer: He offered no MECHANISM for how continents could move
choices: He offered no MECHANISM for how continents could move
His matching fossils could be explained by ancient land bridges
His matching paleoclimates could be explained by shifting poles on a fixed Earth
His fit of the continental coastlines was too loose to be exact
context: All three distractors were real objections geologists raised, and each had a serious defender: sunken land bridges (to explain the fossil matches), true polar wander (to explain the paleoclimates), and the loose coastline fit. But the objection that STAYED alive for fifty years was the mechanism problem -- geologists could not see how solid continental rock could plow through denser oceanic rock. It stayed unsolved until seafloor spreading was measured in the 1960s. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'When Continental Drift Was Considered Pseudoscience.'

question: A decisive scientific test is one that could have FAILED. In 1980, the father-and-son team of Luis and Walter Alvarez, with chemists Frank Asaro and Helen Michel, proposed an asteroid ended the dinosaurs. Their evidence sat in a thin clay layer at Gubbio in Italy -- and it was ONE specific element, rare in Earth's crust and comparatively common in meteorites, that they found there in enormous excess. Which element?
answer: Iridium
choices: Iridium
Radium
Selenium
Cadmium
context: Concentration was measured at roughly hundreds of times normal crustal levels, worldwide, in exactly the one clay layer at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary -- exactly the signature an impact would leave and nothing else could easily fake. Source: Berkeley Lab, 'Alvarez Theory on Dinosaur Die-Out Upheld' (2010).

question: N-rays were a supposed new radiation announced in 1903 by French physicist Prosper-Rene Blondlot; more than a hundred confirming papers appeared before American physicist R.W. Wood visited the lab and killed the claim with a single quiet act. What did Wood do?
answer: Slipped an essential prism out of the apparatus
choices: Slipped an essential prism out of the apparatus
Demanded Blondlot repeat every measurement in Paris
Photographed the setup for a rival scientific journal
Bribed a lab assistant to switch off the detector
context: The prism was an aluminium element central to Blondlot's optical setup. Wood pocketed it during a demonstration; the assistant kept 'reading' N-rays as if nothing had changed. The readings were an illusion of expectation, and the field collapsed. Source: Lindau Nobel Blog, 'Cold Fusion, Polywater & N-Rays.'

question: Delays in these vindication cases were rarely wickedness -- more often it was authority. On 11 January 1935 at the Royal Astronomical Society in London, Britain's most senior astrophysicist stood up after Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's talk and methodically tore down the young Indian's calculation that a heavy enough white dwarf must keep collapsing. Which one-line dismissal did Arthur Eddington deliver?
answer: A law of nature must prevent this absurd stellar behaviour
choices: A law of nature must prevent this absurd stellar behaviour
The equations are elegant but the physics is not yet ripe
Any theory that predicts infinity has already refuted itself
General relativity cannot be trusted in such extreme regimes
context: Eddington's actual line was 'There must be a law of nature to prevent a star from behaving in such an absurd way.' The other three were also plausible objections of the era -- doubts about extending general relativity into new regimes, distaste for theories that produce infinities, and calls to wait for firmer physics -- but they were not what he said. Chandrasekhar's mass limit -- about 1.44 solar masses -- was eventually accepted and shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics. The delay was Eddington's authority, not his malice: he genuinely believed all stars must end as white dwarfs. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chandrasekhar-Eddington dispute.'

question: Drip molten glass into cold water and it freezes into a glass tadpole: a fat round head with a long thin tail. Put the head on an anvil and swing a hammer at it — nothing. Now take the thin tail between two fingers and snap it. What happens?
answer: The whole drop bursts into fine powder in an instant.
choices: The whole drop bursts into fine powder in an instant.
The tail breaks off and the head is left unharmed.
The head splits into two clean curved halves.
Fine cracks spread over the head but it holds.
context: This is a Prince Rupert's drop, and the two ends of one object behave in opposite ways. Purdue's Srinivasan Chandrasekar, on the 2017 result: 'The head can withstand hammering, and on the other hand, the tail can be broken with just the slightest finger pressure, and within a few microseconds the entire thing shatters.' You can watch it tonight — SmarterEveryDay filmed the disintegration at 130,000 frames per second (2013), and in a 2016 follow-up fired a bullet at the head: the bullet shattered and the drop survived. Sources: Purdue University News, 'Research solves centuries-old riddle of Prince Rupert's drops' (10 May 2017); Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: Lightning strikes a sandy beach and pours its heat into the ground in a few thousandths of a second. Days later someone digs at the strike point. What do they pull out?
answer: A rough branching tube of glass, hollow inside.
choices: A rough branching tube of glass, hollow inside.
A shallow bowl of black fused sand, glassy on top.
A cluster of pea-sized glass beads welded together.
A flat plate of green glass a few inches across.
context: These are fulgurites: the bolt fuses the sand along the channel it takes underground, so the tube is a cast of the strike itself, branches and all. Nature makes glass in other ways too. Obsidian is silica-rich lava (65–80% SiO2) quenched too fast to crystallise; it breaks along smooth curved surfaces, which is why Stone Age knappers used it for their sharpest blades. Tektites are meteorite-impact glass — the Australasian field dates to roughly 0.8 million years ago, and some pieces were shaped into flanged buttons by re-entry at over 11 km/s. Source: Grokipedia, 'Glass' §Natural Occurrence.

question: In March 1661 King Charles II sent the brand-new Royal Society a parcel of five little glass bubbles, delivered by Sir Paul Neile. Two days later the Society's assistant reported back to the meeting. What had he done?
answer: Made his own drops from scratch and got the effect.
choices: Made his own drops from scratch and got the effect.
Broke all five open and found every one of them hollow.
Weighed and measured each one, then read out the figures.
Reported them a glassmaker's trick, not worth study.
context: Thomas Birch's History of the Royal Society (1756) records the king's gift, delivered via Sir Paul Neile on 4 March 1660/1, as 'five little glass bubbles, two with liquor in them, and the other three solid.' The Society's amanuensis — its writing assistant — successfully reproduced them on 6 March 1661, two days after they arrived. That is the whole method in miniature: not 'take the king's word for it' but 'make one yourself and see.' Two of the five really were hollow with liquid in them, which is why a hollow drop is a fair guess — but a Prince Rupert's drop itself is solid glass throughout. Sir Robert Moray delivered the Society's full experimental report on 14 August 1661. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, The Collation, '"Whose least part crackt, the whole does fly": early views on Prince Rupert's Drops'.

question: Guides at medieval cathedrals often point up at the windows and say the panes are thicker at the bottom because glass is a very slow liquid that has crept downward over six hundred years. The panes really are uneven — but they were uneven the day they were cut. What made them so?
answer: Each was cut from a big disc spun flat while still soft.
choices: Each was cut from a big disc spun flat while still soft.
Each was cut from a blown cylinder slit and unrolled flat.
Each was poured onto an iron table and rolled to size.
Each was ground down from a thick slab by hand.
context: This is the crown process: a blown hollow globe was reheated and spun until centrifugal force flung it out into a flat disc up to five or six feet across — thick at the centre around the pontil mark (the 'bullseye') and thinnest at the rim. Every pane cut from that disc was uneven. As for why the thick edge usually ends up at the bottom, John Mauro's explanation is human, not physical: 'Given non-uniform glass, it is only natural to orient the thicker part of the glass at the bottom, since it gives the appearance of being more stable.' A glazier's choice. Edgar Zanotto calculated that medieval glass would have to be held near 414 °C for centuries to flow measurably. And the Corning Museum of Glass answers it flatly: 'There are many glass objects thousands of years older than those windows that show no sign of flow.' Sources: ceramics.org, 'Glass viscosity calculations definitively debunk the myth of observable flow in medieval windows'; Corning Museum of Glass FAQ; Zanotto, Am. J. Phys. 66, 392 (1998).

question: Steve Jobs gave Corning's chief executive roughly six months to put a scratch-proof glass screen on the first iPhone. Bringing a new glass to market normally took the company close to two years, and it had never made a phone screen at all. Corning made the June 2007 date anyway. What did it reach for?
answer: A windshield glass carmakers had refused to buy.
choices: A windshield glass carmakers had refused to buy.
A cookware glass its kitchen brand had retired.
A television glass its own plants had wound down.
A telescope glass an observatory had turned down.
context: The glass was Chemcor, developed in 1962 under an internal programme called 'Project Muscle' and aimed at car windshields. Carmakers would not pay a premium over cheap laminated glass; Chemcor windshields reached little more than the 1970-model-year AMC Javelin and AMX, and by 1971 Corning had shelved it — where it sat for about forty years. What put Jobs on the phone: months before the June 2007 launch he pulled the prototype from his pocket and found its plastic screen scratched by his own keys — 'I don't know if it were my keys or what, but it scratched... we need glass.' Told it was not feasible, he answered that it would ship in June and it would be glass, then called Corning's chief executive, Wendell Weeks. Corning had no capacity and its board wanted a second supplier named; Jobs, in a private meeting: 'Do you know what your problem is? You're afraid' — arguing Weeks was protecting his own reputation and 'keeping your people from greatness.' Weeks's reply: 'You're right. I'm afraid. And I'll go fix that.' Corning converted its Harrodsburg, Kentucky plant, built in the 1950s for Cold War products, to make it. Corning's Gorilla division VP John Bayne notes the normal cycle is close to two years of R&D. Accounts differ on the exact interval between the scratched pocket and the call — Fast Company says the call came about six months before launch. Sources: Fast Company (2017); Fortune (23 Oct 2025); Grokipedia, 'Gorilla Glass'.

question: A Prince Rupert's drop is molten glass dripped into cold water: a glass tadpole whose round head is about the size of a marble. The Hydraulic Press Channel set one head between the hardened steel plates of a hydraulic press, camera running at 380,000 frames a second, and squeezed. What did the film show?
answer: The head pressed dents into the steel before it failed.
choices: The head pressed dents into the steel before it failed.
The head powdered the moment the plates first touched it.
The head crumbled slowly as the plates closed in.
The head shot out sideways from between the plates.
context: The Hydraulic Press Channel filmed the crush at 380,000 frames per second: the drop held out to roughly 20 tons of press force, denting the steel platens first, and then burst into large fragments rather than powdering — a different failure mode from the famous tail trick. The laboratory strength measurement used plates of tungsten carbide, the stuff of drill tips: individual samples held between about 11,000 and 19,000 newtons, roughly 15 kN in the middle of the range — near enough to a small car resting on a glass bead. Ordinary glass that size crushes in your hand. Sources: Aben, Anton, Ois, Viswanathan, Chandrasekar & Chaudhri, 'On the extraordinary strength of Prince Rupert's drops,' Applied Physics Letters 109, 231903 (2016); Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: In 1661 nobody could explain the glass drops: molten glass dripped into cold water sets into a tadpole whose head shrugs off a hammer, yet the whole thing bursts to powder when the thin tail is snapped. Sir Robert Moray went at the puzzle by changing one thing at a time, quenching the same melt in salad oil, in milk, in spirit of wine, in turpentine and in mercury. Reporting to the Royal Society that August, he named one bath that spoiled fewer drops than cold water did. Which one?
answer: Salad oil
choices: Salad oil
Milk
Spirit of wine
Mercury
context: Moray quenched the same molten glass in salad oil, milk, spirit of wine, turpentine and mercury in turn, and reported that in salad oil the drops 'do not miscarry so frequently as in cold water.' Hold everything constant, change one thing, compare the results: that is a controlled-variable experiment, run in 1661 on a curiosity nobody understood. Notice what Moray did NOT do — argue about it. He made batch after batch and looked. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, The Collation, on Prince Rupert's Drops.

question: Robert Hooke gave eleven pages of his Micrographia (1665) to the glass drops. His trouble was that the shattering ran far too fast for any eye to follow, and afterwards there was nothing left in one piece to examine. Hooke found a way to read the break anyway. What did he do to the drop first?
answer: Coated it in fish glue to hold the shards in place.
choices: Coated it in fish glue to hold the shards in place.
Sealed it in a bladder of water to slow the burst.
Blackened it with soot so the cracks would show up.
Bedded it in soft wax and snapped the tail beneath.
context: The glue was isinglass, made from fish swim bladders. Hooke coated the drop, snapped the tail, and the dried glue held the fragments roughly where they landed, so he could read the fault lines at leisure — a high-speed camera improvised out of fish glue, 250 years before high-speed cameras existed. The chapter is 'Observ. VII: Of some Phaenomena of Glass drops.' Hooke went on to reason from the mechanics of an arch and its keystone to an explanation that came remarkably close to the modern one, three and a half centuries before instruments could confirm it. Source: Folger Shakespeare Library, The Collation; Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: In a quartz crystal every silicon atom sits at the centre of a little pyramid of four oxygens. Take X-rays to a lump of fused quartz — glass made of silica alone — and you find the very same pyramids, the same bond lengths, joined corner to corner into a network. How are the pyramids arranged in that network?
answer: In rings of many different sizes, mixed together.
choices: In rings of many different sizes, mixed together.
In rings all of one size, six pyramids to a ring.
In flat sheets that slide across one another.
In rings, but with one corner in six left unlinked.
context: Glass is an amorphous solid: real order close up, no repeating order at a distance. W. H. Zachariasen named the picture in 1932 — the 'continuous random network,' silicon-oxygen tetrahedra (the pyramid's proper name) linked corner to corner into rings of many different sizes. The local geometry is nearly what quartz has; what is missing is the repeat. Ordinary window glass is not this pure — the sodium and calcium added to it break some of those corner links, which is why the question named fused quartz, silica alone. And a glass is a genuine solid, not a slow liquid: Zanotto (Am. J. Phys. 1998) estimated the structural relaxation time of window glass at room temperature at more than 10^32 years, revised in 1999 to about 10^23 years — against a universe roughly 1.4 x 10^10 years old. Gulbiten & Mauro (2018) put it more vividly still: medieval cathedral glass would flow about one nanometre in one billion years. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Glass' §Atomic and Molecular Structure; Zanotto, Am. J. Phys. 66, 392 (1998) and 67, 260 (1999); ceramics.org (2018).

question: Swing a hammer at the head of a Prince Rupert's drop and nothing happens: the outer skin is locked in compression — squeezed so hard no crack can open in it — while the glass underneath is stretched taut. Shine polarised light through the drop and both zones can be measured. How deep does that squeezed skin go?
answer: About a tenth of the head's width, half a millimetre.
choices: About a tenth of the head's width, half a millimetre.
About a third of the head's width, two millimetres.
About half the head's width, three millimetres.
A hundredth of the head's width, fifty micrometres.
context: Why the drop is built this way: its outside hits the cold water and sets hard first, and when the still-molten interior then cools and tries to shrink it cannot pull the rigid skin inward with it, so it hauls that skin into compression and leaves its own core in tension — stretched. Integrated photoelasticity, which reads stress from the way polarised light passes through the glass, puts the surface compression at roughly 400–700 MPa and the interior tension at roughly 225–400 MPa, in a compressed layer only about 0.5–0.85 mm thick — around 10% of the head's diameter. That thin squeezed skin is the whole trick: a crack cannot open in a surface being pressed shut, so the hammer accomplishes nothing. The tail is the exception — too thin ever to grow that protective skin, so its stretched interior lies almost at the surface, and snapping it gives a crack direct access to all the stored tension. The drop is solid glass throughout. Sources: Aben, Anton, Ois, Viswanathan, Chandrasekar & Chaudhri, Applied Physics Letters 109, 231903 (2016); '10% of the diameter of the head' via Wikipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'; Grokipedia, 'Prince Rupert's drop'.

question: The screen under your thumb was toughened in a bath. Sheets of aluminosilicate glass sit in molten potassium salt at about 400 degrees C for hours, and come out with a surface far harder to crack than the glass that went in — no hammer, no bucket of cold water. What happened to the glass in that bath?
answer: Potassium ions crowded into places sodium ions had left.
choices: Potassium ions crowded into places sodium ions had left.
A film of potassium salt fused onto it as a hard coating.
The heat drove out trapped water, closing tiny surface flaws.
Sodium ions drifted inward, leaving the surface pure silica.
context: This is ion exchange, and the point is size. A potassium ion is about 1.38 angstroms across; the sodium ion whose place it takes is about 1.02. Every incoming ion is wedged into a hole made for something smaller, and the jammed surface ends up in compression — reported up to about 900 MPa in a layer roughly 40–50 micrometres deep in early generations. That is Prince Rupert's trick performed with chemistry instead of quenching, and as of 2025 it is under the thumbs of users on more than 8 billion devices across 45+ brands. Keep the rival methods straight: annealing does the opposite (reheat, let viscous flow relax the stress out, cool slowly); thermal tempering gets there by blasting hot glass with high-pressure air, patented for flat glass by Francois Barthelemy Alfred Royer de la Bastie in 1874; lamination and wire mesh put nothing into compression at all — they just hold the fragments together. Source: Grokipedia, 'Gorilla Glass' §Chemical Strengthening Technique.

question: Snap the thin tail of a Prince Rupert's drop — a tadpole of glass frozen in cold water — and the destruction runs tail to head at something like 4,000 mph, splitting into fresh cracks as it goes. M. M. Chaudhri at Cambridge clocked that front with framing photography running up to about a million pictures a second, hardware almost no school will ever own. Physicists have since published a way to time the same crack with equipment a high school can afford. What does their rig use?
answer: A resistive grid glued to the drop, its lines cut one by one.
choices: A resistive grid glued to the drop, its lines cut one by one.
A microphone at each end, timing the crack's sound arrival.
A laser beam across the head, broken as the drop bursts open.
A strobe lamp pulsed at a known rate, stepping the crack forward.
context: The published method glues a resistive grid to the drop and watches a digital oscilloscope as the traces sever one by one, each break marking the crack front's arrival; the authors note it 'can therefore be widely used in high schools and universities.' The speed itself: reported values run roughly 1,450–1,900 metres per second (about 3,200–4,300 mph); Purdue renders it as 'more than 4,000 mph.' Treat every one of these as a measurement range across papers, not a constant. What is left afterward is just as striking: a single millimetre-sized drop breaks into more than 20,000 pieces, and the fragment sizes follow an exponential distribution rather than the power law ordinary brittle fracture gives, with two characteristic sizes around 0.31 mm and 0.064 mm — a coarse population and a dust population. Sources: Chaudhri's framing photography (from 1994); Purdue University News (2017); 'Explosive fragmentation of Prince Rupert's drops leads to well-defined fragment sizes' (PMC8097073); arXiv:1602.06801.

question: Cool a melt fast enough and it sets into glass without ever crystallising. Asked by Science in 1995 to name a problem worth the coming decade's attention, Philip W. Anderson picked this one — the nature of glass and the glass transition, 'the deepest and most interesting unsolved problem in solid state theory.' Thirty years on it is still open, and one camp holds that there is no genuine transition at all, only a liquid grown too sluggish to rearrange itself. Which measured oddity is that camp's best evidence?
answer: The temperature it sets at shifts when you cool it faster.
choices: The temperature it sets at shifts when you cool it faster.
The glass creeps back toward liquid over centuries of standing.
The same melt sets tens of degrees apart from run to run.
The transition fades away if the glass is reheated slowly.
context: The glass transition temperature moves roughly 3–5 K for every tenfold change in cooling rate — and a transition whose temperature moves when the experimenter changes speed is a very strange transition. That is the kinetic camp's best argument: nothing special happens thermodynamically, they say; relaxation just slows until the liquid can no longer keep up with the experiment. The thermodynamic camp answers with the Kauzmann paradox (Walter Kauzmann, 1948): extrapolate the supercooled liquid's configurational entropy downward and it would fall below the crystal's at a finite temperature, which is impossible — so something real must intervene. Note too that unlike freezing, glass formation releases no latent heat and shows no abrupt volume change, which is why glass has a softening range instead of a melting point. Nobody has settled it, thirty years after Anderson called it out in Science. Sources: Science 267, 1615 (1995); Grokipedia, 'Glass transition'.

question: In 2013 John Cook and colleagues published a study in Environmental Research Letters that read 11,944 climate paper abstracts from 1991 to 2011 and reported that 97.1 percent of them 'endorsed the consensus'. Before that percentage was computed, a share of the 11,944 was set aside for another reason. What roughly was that share?
answer: about 66 percent
choices: about 66 percent
about 3 percent
about 55 percent
about 70 percent
context: Cook 2013 reported that 66.4 percent of the abstracts - 7,930 papers - expressed no position on human causation at all. The famous 97.1 percent is a percentage of only the remaining third that did take a position. Source: iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/8/2/024024

question: Cook and colleagues 2013 sorted each climate abstract into seven levels. The largest 'endorsement' bucket by far was a category they labelled Level 3. What did a paper have to do to be scored Level 3?
answer: take a human contribution to warming for granted, without saying how much
choices: take a human contribution to warming for granted, without saying how much
state a specific percentage of warming caused by humans in its title or first line
recommend a specific climate policy such as a carbon tax or emissions cap
cite a named IPCC assessment report in its opening paragraph
context: Level 3 was called 'implicit endorsement': a paper about tree rings or Arctic sea ice that just assumed humans were part of the picture, with no number attached, landed in the same 97 percent as a paper explicitly saying humans are the dominant cause. Level 1 - the strictest 'explicit endorsement with quantification' - was a small minority. Source: iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/8/2/024024

question: The 97 percent slogan is really two figures pasted together. In 2009 Peter Doran and Maggie Zimmerman published a two-question survey in EOS: they emailed it to 10,257 earth scientists and got thousands of replies. Then they narrowed to a subgroup they called 'climate specialists': people who identified as climatologists AND had more than half of their recent publications on climate. How many people were in that subgroup?
context: Doran and Zimmerman's famous 97 percent is really 75 of the 77 climate specialists who answered the second question - out of a subgroup of 79 people. The 928 number is the abstract count from Naomi Oreskes's 2004 Science paper on the same question. Source: Doran & Zimmerman 2009, EOS, Transactions of the American Geophysical Union

question: The published pushback on Cook 2013 that is hardest to dismiss came from Richard Tol, an economist and IPCC contributing author who himself accepts that human activity is warming the planet. His comment in Energy Policy argued Cook's team had skipped a specific quality-control check that critics could not reconstruct from the paper. Which check?
answer: they never measured whether different raters agreed with each other
choices: they never measured whether different raters agreed with each other
they threw out papers written in languages other than English
they never trained their raters against a gold-standard subset before scoring
they refused to release their raw abstract ratings to critics
context: Tol argued that Cook's rating procedure lacked controls and any reported inter-rater reliability, so nobody could tell how consistently the same abstract would have been scored by different coders. Criticism from a working IPCC contributor on the same side of the physics is the strongest kind of published critique. Source: sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301421514002821
