context: A blue sky and a sunset in one piece of glass, 1869. Tyndall also found the scattered light was polarized, and it stayed 'perfectly polarized' for as long as the cloud remained distinctly blue; he called these hazes 'actinic clouds', an artificial sky. But his tube needed particles, so he assumed the real sky did too. Rayleigh's 1899 extension of the mathematics to individual molecules, swapping molecular polarizability for particle volume and refractive index, showed that the air's own molecules alone are enough. Dust is NOT required, and 'the sky is blue because of dust and pollution' is simply wrong. Sources: J. Tyndall, 'On the Blue Colour of the Sky, the Polarization of Skylight...', Proc. R. Soc. Lond. 17 (1868-69) 223-233; Wikipedia, 'Rayleigh scattering' ('1899: He extended the theory to individual molecules').

question: A cloud is made of nothing but water, lit by the very same sunlight that turns the sky around it blue, and it comes out brilliant white. Gustav Mie published the mathematics of it in 1908, with Ludvig Lorenz having reached it independently. What is it about a single cloud droplet that takes it out of Rayleigh's blue-making regime?
answer: It is far larger than a wavelength of light
choices: It is far larger than a wavelength of light
It is liquid water rather than a gas at all
It is much denser than the air around it
It carries a small charge picked up in the cloud
context: Size, not substance. Cloud droplets run roughly 1-20 micrometres across; visible light's wavelengths run 0.4-0.7 micrometres. Rayleigh himself left the dividing line behind as a size ratio, x = 2*pi*r/lambda: below about one-tenth of a wavelength his law rules, and at cloud-droplet sizes you are in the Mie regime, where all colours are scattered nearly identically. Big droplets play no favourites, so what comes back to you is white. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Mie scattering' ('water droplets... scatter all wavelengths of visible light approximately identically'); Wikipedia, 'Rayleigh scattering' (the 1881 derivation from Maxwell's 1865 electromagnetism, and the size criterion).

question: Almost everyone will tell you the sea is blue because it reflects the sky. Charles Braun and Sergei Smirnov tested that in 1993 by looking down instead of up: through a three-metre tube of pure water with white paper at the bottom, no sky involved at all. The water was blue. Something about the water molecule itself is taking the red out of the light. What is doing it?
answer: The O-H bonds of the molecule, vibrating
choices: The O-H bonds of the molecule, vibrating
The electrons of the molecule, jumping levels
The molecules themselves, scattering light
The molecules themselves, spinning end over end
context: An O-H bond is the link between the oxygen and each hydrogen in H2O. Water absorbs red through a four-quantum overtone (v1+3v3) of its O-H stretching vibrations at 698 nm, sitting right at the red edge of vision. Braun and Smirnov called it 'the only example from nature in which color originates from vibrational transitions'; every other colour you see is made by electrons. Water is most transparent at 418 nm, deep violet-blue, where its attenuation length is about 227 metres, which is why a glassful looks clear and a lake looks blue: you need metres of path before the absorption shows. Check it where no sky can reflect, in deep holes punched in fresh snow, in frozen waterfalls, in glacier ice. Sources: C. L. Braun & S. N. Smirnov, 'Why is water blue?', J. Chem. Educ. 70(8) 612 (1993); Wikipedia, 'Electromagnetic absorption by water'; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, 'Why is the ocean blue?'.

question: Heavy water is ordinary water with its hydrogen swapped for deuterium, hydrogen's heavier twin. The molecule keeps exactly the same shape and exactly the same electrons; only the nuclei are heavier, and heavier nuclei shift every one of the molecule's vibrations to lower energy. Ordinary water's key absorption band sits at 760 nanometres. What does heavy water look like?
answer: Colourless, with no tint at all
choices: Colourless, with no tint at all
Blue, just as ordinary water is
Blue, but deeper than ordinary water
Green, like the tint in thick glass
context: Lower energy means longer wavelength. Ordinary water's 760 nm band sits just at the far red edge of human sight, close enough to bite the red out of what you see; in D2O that band moves out to about 1000 nm, well past the edge of vision, and the blue is simply gone. Same molecular shape, same electrons, heavier nuclei, colour vanished. It is about as clean a confirmation as chemistry offers that water's colour is vibrational rather than electronic. Source: C. L. Braun & S. N. Smirnov, 'Why is water blue?', J. Chem. Educ. 70(8) 612 (1993) ('D2O is colorless because all of its corresponding vibrational transitions are shifted to lower energy by the increase in isotope mass').

question: Screw a polarizing filter onto a camera on a clear day, aim it at the sky and turn it. One stretch of sky goes dramatically darker while another barely changes: the sky's light is polarized, its waves lined up along one direction, and the effect is far from even across the sky. Where does the polarization peak, reaching about 80%?
answer: In a band right round the sky, 90 degrees from the Sun
choices: In a band right round the sky, 90 degrees from the Sun
In a tight ring within 10 degrees of the Sun itself
Straight overhead, within 20 degrees of the zenith
In a band within 20 degrees of the horizon, all round
context: The Rayleigh sky model puts maximum polarization in a circular band 90 degrees from the Sun, typically peaking near 80%. There are also three neutral points where the polarization vanishes entirely: the Arago point above the antisolar point, the Babinet point above the Sun, and the Brewster point below it. Test it yourself with one lens of a pair of polarized sunglasses: rotate it while sweeping across the sky, and the darkening bites hardest when you are looking at right angles to the Sun. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rayleigh sky model' ('The maximum degree of polarization occurs in a circular band 90 degrees from the Sun').

question: Albert Einstein spent 1910 working out why a gas scatters light at all. His answer arrived with a bonus nobody had gone looking for: the same equations would also yield a fundamental constant of nature, and it could be extracted from measurements of skylight itself. What was Einstein able to get out of the colour of the sky?
answer: Avogadro's number, how many molecules make a mole
choices: Avogadro's number, how many molecules make a mole
Planck's constant, the size of one quantum of energy
The electron's charge, the smallest unit of electricity
The speed of light, the fixed limit of the universe
context: The strangest part is the premise. Einstein showed that a PERFECTLY uniform gas would not scatter light at all; scattering exists only because molecules jostle and leave random density fluctuations behind. Marian Smoluchowski had pointed at fluctuations in 1908 without a formula, and Einstein supplied it in 'Theorie der Opaleszenz von homogenen Flussigkeiten'. The same mathematics gave a fresh, independent route to Avogadro's number (a mole being the chemist's standard counting unit for atoms and molecules). You can count the molecules of the air by looking at the colour of the sky. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Critical opalescence'; UCR Physics FAQ, 'Why is the sky blue?' ('Einstein (1911) calculated the scattering formula for molecules and verified Avogadro's number'; the paper itself is dated 1910).

question: Every night you spend a large fraction of your life unconscious, motionless, and completely defenceless in the dark. From an evolutionary point of view, that arrangement looks like a terrible idea -- and every animal with a brain does it anyway. How much of a human lifetime is typically spent asleep?
answer: about one third
choices: about one third
about one tenth
about one half
about one twentieth
context: Roughly eight hours out of every twenty-four -- about one-third of a life -- spent unconscious and vulnerable. Whatever sleep does for us, evolution keeps paying that steep cost, in humans and in essentially every animal with a nervous system. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0060106

question: University of Chicago, 1983. Allan Rechtschaffen and Bernard Bergmann needed to keep rats totally awake for weeks without shocks or drugs. What mechanical trick did their apparatus use?
answer: a divided disk over water slowly rotated whenever the rat fell asleep, forcing it to walk
choices: a divided disk over water slowly rotated whenever the rat fell asleep, forcing it to walk
bright overhead lamps flicked on whenever the rat closed its eyes for more than a few seconds
an automatic treadmill under the cage sped up whenever the rat's brain activity slowed
a technician on night shift pinched the rat's tail whenever it stopped moving
context: The famous 'disk-over-water' apparatus: two rats sat on halves of a divided disk above shallow water; when the experimental rat began to sleep, the disk rotated and it had to walk or drop in. The control rat could sleep whenever the experimental one was awake -- a yoked design that ruled out stress as the cause of what followed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disk-over-water_method

question: Allan Rechtschaffen summarised his own field's problem in a line still quoted decades later: if sleep does not serve an absolutely vital function, he said, then it is the biggest mistake this process has ever made. Which process was he talking about?
answer: the evolutionary process
choices: the evolutionary process
the digestive process
the industrial process
the metabolic process
context: Rechtschaffen's line -- 'If sleep does not serve an absolutely vital function, then it is the biggest mistake the evolutionary process has ever made' -- captures the mystery. The cost is obvious; the payoff is not. Source: Rechtschaffen 1971/1978, cited in Sleep Research Society retrospectives.

question: Sleep is one leading candidate for stabilising memory. In one influential experiment, a rat learned a maze while researchers recorded from its hippocampal place cells -- neurons that fire when the animal is at a particular spot. During the slow-wave sleep that followed, what did those same place cells do that made sleep a live theory of memory?
answer: fired again in the exact sequence they had used during the maze
choices: fired again in the exact sequence they had used during the maze
fell almost completely silent for the whole slow-wave phase
fired in the reverse of the maze sequence but far slower
fired at random with no relation to the maze at all
context: Neural replay in hippocampal place cells is one of the cleanest pieces of evidence for a memory role of sleep: the same firing sequences that ran during the day's task run again during subsequent slow-wave sleep, and sleep after learning beats an all-nighter on later memory tests. The mechanism is credible; that it is THE reason we sleep is not proven. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nrn2084

question: May 2024, Nature Neuroscience. Andawei Miao with Nick Franks and Bill Wisden at Imperial College London injected fluorescent tracer into mouse brains and measured how quickly it moved out in animals that were awake, asleep, or under anaesthesia. What did they report?
answer: clearance was slower during sleep and anaesthesia than during wakefulness
choices: clearance was slower during sleep and anaesthesia than during wakefulness
clearance was faster during sleep, matching the 2013 Rochester result
clearance was faster only during REM sleep, not slow-wave sleep
clearance stopped almost entirely under anaesthesia but was normal in sleep
context: Miao et al. reported the opposite of the Nedergaard 2013 result: clearance in their experiment was reduced -- not enhanced -- during sleep and anaesthesia. The glymphatic 'sleep cleans the brain' story is now openly contested rather than settled science. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-024-01638-y

question: December 2019: the independent writer Alexey Guzey published a line-by-line critique of Matthew Walker's bestseller 'Why We Sleep', documenting misrepresented studies and a bar removed from a reproduced graph. A well-known statistician then covered the critique on his own blog and largely backed Guzey up. Which one?
answer: Andrew Gelman
choices: Andrew Gelman
John Ioannidis
Uri Simonsohn
Nate Silver
context: Andrew Gelman's blog 'Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science' ran a detailed post in November 2019 walking through Guzey's claims and finding most held up. Ioannidis, Simonsohn and Silver are all serious living critics of published-science quality -- the point is that Gelman was the specific one who took the time. The episode is a Discovery-Pattern reminder: even bestselling popular science gets audited. Sources: https://guzey.com/books/why-we-sleep/ and https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2019/11/18/is-matthew-walkers-why-we-sleep-riddled-with-scientific-and-factual-errors/

question: The leading candidate answers to why we sleep -- memory consolidation, glymphatic clearance, synaptic downscaling, energy conservation, immune support -- each have real researchers behind them. How many of the five are currently backed by direct, uncontested experimental proof in humans?
answer: zero of them are proven
choices: zero of them are proven
only memory consolidation is proven
memory and glymphatic are both proven
all five are proven
context: There is no single accepted answer to why we sleep. Every candidate has supporting evidence, none has closed the case, and several may turn out to be simultaneously true. This is one of biology's most durable open questions. Source: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0060106

question: In the 1790s the young surveyor William Smith walked the fresh cuts of the Somerset Coal Canal near Bath. In cut after cut, the same rock bands appeared in the same ORDER -- and each band carried its own signature, so that even when two bands looked alike to the eye, Smith could still tell them apart. What was that signature?
answer: The fossils in the layer
choices: The fossils in the layer
The mineral hardness of the layer
The magnetic direction of the layer
The chemical smell of the layer
context: This is the principle of FAUNAL SUCCESSION -- each stratum has its own signature assemblage of fossils, so fossils identify the layer even when the rock type does not. It is still the way rock sequences on different continents are matched today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: In 1815 William Smith published the work of a life spent walking English hills: 15 sheets that, when assembled, measured more than eight feet by six feet at a scale of five miles to the inch, printed over the London mapmaker John Cary's base. Historians credit it as the first of its kind ever produced for a whole nation. What did the sheet show?
answer: The rocks and strata of England and Wales
choices: The rocks and strata of England and Wales
The soil fertility of the English counties
A gazetteer of mineral-ore locations
The canals and coalfields of the realm
context: The full title was 'A Delineation of the Strata of England and Wales, with part of Scotland'. Soil, mineral-locality, and canal maps had earlier precedents; what Smith produced -- rocks by kind and age across a whole country -- was new. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: Smith's colouring on the 1815 map was not decoration -- it was DATA. For each rock band he laid down the strongest tone right along one edge and let the pigment fade away as it crossed the band. That single trick let a flat sheet of paper convey a three-dimensional fact about the ground beneath. What did the graded shading reveal?
answer: Which way the strata dip underground
choices: Which way the strata dip underground
How deep coal seams reached
Where earthquakes had ruptured
The direction of past river currents
context: By making the base of each stratum darkest, Smith made the map read like a cutaway view: the reader could see at a glance which side of a band was on top and which way the layer slanted down into the earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: After a lifetime of surveying and one great map, Smith was ruined by a side venture -- a Bath stone quarry that failed, leaving him owing his co-investor Charles Conolly. To pay down the debt he sold his most personal scientific possession to the British Museum for GBP 700, and still came up short. What did he sell?
answer: His fossil collection
choices: His fossil collection
His original map plates
His country house
His surveying instruments
context: The collection was the physical evidence that had underwritten faunal succession -- Smith's hand-labelled specimens, tied to specific strata. The Museum bought it for GBP 700; the debt still swallowed him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: In June 1819 the man who had mapped a nation was locked up in London's King's Bench, a notorious debtors' prison. He served 11 weeks and was released on 31 August 1819, only to walk home and find one particular grim thing waiting for him. What had happened to Smith's house while he was inside?
answer: The bailiffs had cleared it out
choices: The bailiffs had cleared it out
It had burned to the ground
His wife had sold it and left
The Geological Society had bought it
context: Smith returned to a house stripped by bailiffs against his outstanding debts -- a genuinely ugly moment in the biography of the man who had just published England's geology. Source: scienceblog.com/n-twenty-eight-years-of-surveying-then-ten-weeks-in-prison.

question: A popular version of Smith's story blames the gentlemen of the Geological Society for plagiarism -- specifically George Bellas Greenough's rival map. Current scholarship pushes back: Greenough's rival did not appear until May 1820, AFTER Smith was already out of debtors' prison, and the drumbeat of accusation is now attributed largely to one particular figure sympathetic to Smith who ran the rivalry narrative. Who fuelled that narrative?
answer: John Farey Sr.
choices: John Farey Sr.
Robert Bakewell
Adam Sedgwick
William Buckland
context: Sedgwick would later crown Smith 'the Father of English Geology' with the first Wollaston Medal in 1831; Bakewell and Buckland were contemporary geological writers with their own agendas. Farey Sr., sympathetic to Smith, is now seen by historians as the main amplifier of the plagiarism story. Both maps, incidentally, sold badly. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smith_(geologist).

question: In 1775 a Birmingham physician named William Withering heard that a family in Shropshire had a herbal tea of more than twenty ingredients that reliably eased a terrifying disease -- a body ballooning with retained fluid until the skin was tight and the lungs drowned. Bleeding, purges, and mercury did nothing for it. What was that disease called in Withering's day?
answer: the dropsy
choices: the dropsy
the consumption
the ague
the falling sickness
context: The dropsy was the eighteenth-century name for the massive fluid retention (edema) we now most often trace to congestive heart failure. The consumption was tuberculosis, the ague was malarial fever, the falling sickness was epilepsy -- three real terrors of the era. Standard 1775 treatments for dropsy also included tapping (draining) the swollen abdomen with a hollow needle called a trocar -- none of it addressed the failing heart. Source: hektoen international -- Withering and the foxglove; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Withering.

question: Withering was a serious botanist as well as a physician. Instead of just brewing the Shropshire family's twenty-plus-ingredient tea, he set out to work out which single plant in the jumble was actually doing the work -- and then he threw the rest of the recipe away. Which plant did he keep?
answer: the purple foxglove
choices: the purple foxglove
the deadly nightshade
the meadow saffron
the corn poppy
context: Withering identified Digitalis purpurea, the tall spike of hanging bells found in English hedgerows and gardens. The distractors are all real herbal-medicine plants of the period: deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna, a pupil-dilator and heart poison), meadow saffron (Colchicum autumnale, still prescribed for gout), and corn poppy (Papaver rhoeas, cousin to the opium poppy). Withering learned the recipe from 'an old woman in Shropshire'; the folksy 'Mother Hutton' name was invented in a 1928 Parke-Davis advertisement and is a myth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Withering.

question: In 1785 Withering published An Account of the Foxglove, based on ten years of dosing patient after patient with dried, weighed leaf. The book made him the father of modern drug testing. What did the 163 case histories in it do that no earlier drug book had done?
answer: included every patient the drug did nothing for or harmed
choices: included every patient the drug did nothing for or harmed
compared the drug against an inert pill from the same jar
hid the identity of the plant to protect his practice
randomly assigned each patient to a different dose
context: Withering's 163 cases -- 156 from his private practice and 7 from the Birmingham Hospital -- included the ones where the leaf did nothing and the ones where it made the patient worse. Publishing your negative results is the move that separates a drug from a nostrum. The distractors are the real inventions that came later: the placebo-controlled trial (twentieth century), the trade-secret nostrum tradition Withering was consciously breaking with, and the randomised controlled trial (Bradford Hill, 1948). Source: hektoen international -- Withering and the foxglove.

question: Withering wrote that the same hedgerow flower that could rescue a swollen dying patient would also kill you a little further up the dose -- so he wrote a rule his readers must obey. Start small, use dried leaf so the strength is even, raise the dose slowly, and STOP AT ONCE at the first sign of what?
answer: sickness, giddiness, or objects appearing green or yellow
choices: sickness, giddiness, or objects appearing green or yellow
a nosebleed or bleeding from the gums
cold hands, cold feet, and blue lips
a rash spreading down the arms
context: The 1785 book puts it directly: 'Foxglove, when given in very large and repeated doses, occasions sickness, vomiting, purging, giddiness, confused vision, objects appearing green or yellow.' Withering had figured out digitalis toxicity from bedside notebooks alone; the yellow-green tint to vision is a distinctive modern clinical sign of glycoside overdose. The distractors are real early-warning signs of other drug toxicities (aspirin or warfarin bleeding, shock, allergic rash). Note: foxglove is a common garden plant and eating any part can kill -- this whole story is a look-don't-touch wonder, never a try-it-yourself one. Source: Withering 1785, Project Gutenberg 24886.

question: Withering was honest about his reasoning as well as his cases, and recorded in the 1785 book why he thought the leaf worked -- but chemistry a century later showed his explanation was WRONG. Which organ did Withering incorrectly identify as the leaf's real target?
answer: the kidneys
choices: the kidneys
the liver
the spleen
the lungs
context: Withering saw his patients pass enormous amounts of urine after taking the leaf and concluded it was a diuretic acting on the kidneys. In fact the leaf makes a failing heart contract harder and beat more slowly; only THEN does the returning blood flow reach the kidneys with enough pressure to drain the accumulated fluid. Right result, wrong mechanism -- honestly recorded. The distractors are the other Georgian go-to organs for fluid trouble (the liver was blamed for dropsy from cirrhosis; the spleen was blamed for almost anything obscure; the lungs were the seat of consumption). Source: cvpharmacology.com -- digitalis.

question: It took roughly a century and a half for chemistry to catch up with Withering's leaf. In modern heart-muscle cells, digitalis latches onto one specific membrane pump and jams it, letting calcium build up inside the cell so the muscle fibres pull harder. Which membrane pump does the drug jam?
answer: the sodium-potassium pump
choices: the sodium-potassium pump
the stomach acid proton pump
the muscle calcium reuptake pump
the sweat-gland chloride pump
context: Digitalis blocks Na+/K+-ATPase on the heart cell membrane. Sodium builds up inside the cell, which stalls a second exchanger that would normally pump calcium out in trade for sodium in; calcium therefore accumulates too, and calcium is what makes the muscle fibres contract harder. The distractors are all real membrane pumps: the proton pump is the target of omeprazole (heartburn); SERCA sequesters calcium after each beat (a mutation in it causes Darier disease); CFTR is the chloride channel broken in cystic fibrosis. Source: cvpharmacology.com -- digitalis.

question: Withering's flower is still on the pharmacy shelf -- but under a different name and from a different species. In 1930 Dr Sydney Smith at Burroughs Wellcome isolated a purified cardiac glycoside from the leaf of the woolly foxglove; the drug he isolated is still prescribed today for heart failure and for slowing certain irregular heartbeats. What is that drug called?
answer: digoxin
choices: digoxin
warfarin
quinidine
atropine
context: Digoxin comes from Digitalis lanata; the closely related digitoxin comes from Withering's purple foxglove (Digitalis purpurea). The distractors are all real heart-era drugs: warfarin (a blood thinner from spoiled sweet-clover), quinidine (an antiarrhythmic from cinchona bark, cousin to the malaria drug quinine), and atropine (from the deadly nightshade of rung 2, used to speed a dangerously slow heart). A hedgerow flower is on the modern drug list because one physician measured it instead of believing it. Source: American Chemical Society -- Molecule of the Week: Digoxin.

question: Munich, 21 April 1912: Walter Friedrich and Paul Knipping aimed a narrow beam of X-rays through a small copper sulphate crystal, with a photographic plate set behind it. Nobody knew what would come out the far side. What did the developed plate show?
answer: A pattern of sharp spots ringing the central beam
choices: A pattern of sharp spots ringing the central beam
An even grey fog spread across the whole plate
A single blurred smear the width of the beam
A row of straight dark bands across the plate
context: The plate came out covered in well-defined spots arranged in intersecting circles around the central beam spot — patterns still called 'Laue diagrams' today. Copper sulphate was chosen simply because large pieces were easy to come by; zinc blende, tried soon afterwards, gave the cleaner four-fold pattern usually reproduced in books. Max von Laue, Friedrich and Knipping announced the result to the Bavarian Academy of Sciences on 4 May 1912. Sources: Wikipedia 'X-ray crystallography'; Physics World, 'One amazing moment'; Grokipedia 'Max von Laue'.

question: William Lawrence Bragg was serving as an officer at British army headquarters in France when word came that the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics had gone to him and to his father, William Henry Bragg. As of 2025, what record does that prize still hold?
answer: The youngest laureate in any science category
choices: The youngest laureate in any science category
The first physics prize ever won by a Briton
The first Nobel Prize ever split between two people
The only physics prize awarded during the war
context: As of 2025 William Lawrence Bragg is still the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize in physics, or in any science category — he was 25, and the wording matters, because Malala Yousafzai was younger overall, at 17, for the 2014 Peace Prize. The 1915 citation reads 'for their services in the analysis of crystal structure by means of X-rays', and the Braggs remain the only parent and child ever to share a Nobel Prize in any field. It came in a bitter year: Lawrence's brother had been killed at Gallipoli on 2 September 1915, weeks before the announcement. Sources: Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'; nobelprize.org 1915 prize pages.

question: Dorothy Hodgkin was 24 and new to X-ray work when rheumatoid arthritis swelled and twisted her hands. She would not give up the machine, and went on solving crystal structures for the rest of her life, later from a wheelchair. What did she rig up so she could still start the X-ray machine herself?
answer: A lever fitted over the main switch
choices: A lever fitted over the main switch
A foot pedal wired to the main switch
A cord to the switch she pulled with her teeth
A clockwork timer wired to the switch
context: She made a lever to operate the main switch of her X-ray equipment. The disease eventually put her in a wheelchair and she kept working, taking the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 'for her determinations by X-ray techniques of the structures of important biochemical substances'. Sources: Wikipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'; Royal Society, 'Scientists with disabilities: Dorothy Hodgkin'; nobelprize.org 1964 chemistry prize.

question: Tilt an ordinary CD under a white lamp and colours fan out across its face. Stamped into the disc's silver surface is one long spiral of data tracks, packed hundreds of tracks to the millimetre — finer than any line you could scratch by hand. What splits white light into colours there?
answer: Waves bouncing off neighbouring tracks fall in and out of step
choices: Waves bouncing off neighbouring tracks fall in and out of step
The clear plastic above the tracks bends blue harder than red
A dye beneath the tracks soaks up one colour at each angle
The tracks are stamped in bands of slightly different metals
context: A CD's data tracks sit about 1.6 micrometres apart — roughly 600 to the millimetre, almost exactly the 1.667 micrometre line spacing of a standard laboratory diffraction grating. That is why a disc throws rainbows. TEST IT YOURSELF: shine a laser pointer of known wavelength at the disc, mark where the reflected spots land on the wall, measure the angles, and you can work out how far apart the tracks are without ever seeing one. Sources: Science Buddies, 'Using a Laser Pointer to Measure the Data Track Spacing on CDs and DVDs'; Phys. Rev. Phys. Educ. Res. CD diffraction guided-inquiry manual.

question: Dorothy Hodgkin solved penicillin in 1945, and vitamin B12 — a far bigger molecule, with a cobalt atom at its heart — took her about eight years from 1948. Insulin she was handed as a single crystal back in 1934, when she was a young researcher just starting out. How long before she had its structure?
answer: Thirty-five years
choices: Thirty-five years
Twenty-seven years
Nineteen years
Eleven years
context: She got the structure in 1969, thirty-five years after that first crystal: a two-chain, disulfide-linked molecule resolved at 2.8 angstroms. She simply never let the problem go. Lawrence Bragg said her vitamin B12 result, published in 1955-56, was as significant an achievement as breaking the sound barrier. Sources: Wikipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'; Grokipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'.

question: A diffraction grating is a plate scored with lines so fine that light striking it fans out into a spectrum. In 1912 no workshop could rule lines fine enough to do that to X-rays, and Max von Laue argued that nobody needed to — nature had already ruled one. What makes a crystal work as a grating for X-rays?
answer: Its atoms sit about as far apart as an X-ray wave is long
choices: Its atoms sit about as far apart as an X-ray wave is long
Its atoms are packed far more tightly than the wave is long
Its atoms swing in step with each passing X-ray wave
Its flat faces meet at the same exact angles again and again
context: X-rays have wavelengths of around an angstrom — about the size of the gaps between atoms in a crystal — so a crystal is already a three-dimensional diffraction grating, no ruling engine required. Friedrich and Knipping tested that reasoning in April 1912, and the 1914 Nobel Prize in Physics went to von Laue alone, 'for his discovery of the diffraction of X-rays by crystals'. The Braggs' prize, the following year, was for what they did with his spots — the discovery of diffraction itself is not theirs. Sources: Grokipedia 'Max von Laue'; nobelprize.org 1914 physics prize; Wikipedia 'X-ray crystallography'.

question: Laue's plates came out covered in spots, and at first nobody could say what a single spot actually was. Walking by the river at Cambridge, the young Lawrence Bragg worked it out — and his reading is the one crystallographers still use. What is one bright spot on the plate?
answer: A reflection off one stack of parallel atomic sheets
choices: A reflection off one stack of parallel atomic sheets
A shadow cast by one heavy atom in the crystal
A glow given off by atoms the beam has excited
A gap where the beam passed through untouched
context: Bragg's reading: each spot is a reflection off one family of parallel sheets of atoms, and reflections from successive sheets only stay in step — only add up into a bright spot — at particular angles. The crystal sorts the beam for you. He presented his rock-salt work to the Cambridge Philosophical Society on 11 November 1912. Sources: Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'; crystallography365, 'The structure that started it all: rock salt'.

question: The Braggs divided the work. William Henry Bragg, the father, built a new instrument he called an ionization spectrometer, and his son William Lawrence Bragg took it from there. What could the father's instrument do that a photographic plate could not?
answer: It read out each reflection's strength as a number
choices: It read out each reflection's strength as a number
It held the crystal steady while the beam swept past
It magnified the crystal until single atoms showed
It kept the crystal too cold for its atoms to shift
context: The reflected X-rays entered a gas-filled chamber, where they knocked electrons loose and produced a small electric current — so every reflection came out as a number, a measured strength, instead of a darker or fainter mark on film. Those numbers are what the son turned into atomic positions. The instrument is the ancestor of every diffractometer since. Sources: Grokipedia 'William Henry Bragg'; Grokipedia 'Diffractometer'.

question: Lawrence Bragg turned his reading of the spots into a rule anyone could compute with. Send in X-rays whose wavelength you already know, turn the crystal until one reflected beam flares bright, and read off the angle it came out at. What has that one angle just told you?
answer: The spacing between neighbouring sheets of atoms
choices: The spacing between neighbouring sheets of atoms
The spacing between neighbouring atoms within a sheet
The width of a single atom in the crystal
The thickness of the crystal along the beam
context: The rule is Bragg's law: n·λ = 2d·sin θ, where λ is the X-ray wavelength, d the distance between adjacent planes of atoms, θ the angle, and n a whole number. Angles in, architecture out — you measure something you can see and get back a distance you never could. Grokipedia dates the derivation to March 1913. Sources: Grokipedia "Bragg's law"; Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'.

question: In France during the First World War, Lawrence Bragg was put on a wave problem of a different kind. His crews spread microphones along a measured baseline; when a German gun fired, the same boom reached each microphone a fraction of a second apart, and those gaps in arrival time fixed where the gun stood. The method nearly died at birth: ordinary microphones could not hear the gun's low boom at all, only the sharper crack of the shell. What did Lance Corporal William Tucker rig up to catch the low wave?
answer: A heated platinum wire strung across a hole in a box
choices: A heated platinum wire strung across a hole in a box
A drumskin stretched over the mouth of a buried drum
A brass horn feeding a needle onto a wax cylinder
A tuning fork clamped to a field telephone earpiece
context: Tucker's hot-wire microphone was a heated platinum wire stretched across a hole cut in an ammunition box: the low-frequency pressure pulse from the gun cooled the wire and changed its electrical resistance, which the instruments could read. By September 1916 every British sound-ranging section in France and Belgium had one, and a gun could be fixed to within about 50 yards at a range of 10,000 yards — the same arithmetic of waves and spacing Bragg used on crystals, run on sound instead of X-rays. Sources: APS News, 'Bragg and sound ranging'; Royal Society Notes and Records, "Lawrence Bragg's role in the development of sound-ranging in World War I"; Wikipedia 'Lawrence Bragg'.

question: The Braggs' picture of table salt showed no NaCl molecules in it at all: sodium and chloride ions alternate endlessly, and the equal numbers of each come from the geometry of the stack rather than from atoms pairing off. Thirteen years later Henry Edward Armstrong, a past President of the Chemical Society, still would not have it. How did he register his objection?
answer: He printed a protest in Nature headed 'Poor Common Salt!'
choices: He printed a protest in Nature headed 'Poor Common Salt!'
He printed a rival picture of salt in the Society's journal
He had the Chemical Society strike Bragg from its rolls
He asked the Nobel committee to take the 1915 prize back
context: Armstrong quoted Bragg's own sentences back at readers and objected to them: 'In sodium chloride there appear to be no molecules represented by NaCl. The equality in number of sodium and chlorine atoms is arrived at by a chess-board pattern of these atoms; it is a result of geometry and not of a pairing-off of the atoms.' Secondary accounts report that he called the chess-board pattern 'repugnant to common sense' and retorted that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry; the Nature page is paywalled, so treat those particular words as reported rather than confirmed. The measurements stood. Source: H. E. Armstrong, 'Poor Common Salt!', Nature 120, 478 (1927); quotation database todayinsci.com; Grokipedia 'Chemical structure'.

question: By 1945 penicillin was saving lives in every Allied hospital and no chemist could say what its molecule looked like. Two Oxford camps had formed: Edward Abraham backed one arrangement of its atoms, and Sir Robert Robinson — the most eminent organic chemist in Britain and a future Nobel laureate — backed a rival one. Dorothy Hodgkin put a penicillin crystal in an X-ray beam and photographed what came out. Which structure did the pictures show?
answer: A four-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
choices: A four-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
A six-membered ring with a sulphur atom set in it
Two flat rings stacked face to face around a metal atom
A long unbranched chain with no ring along it at all
context: The pictures showed a beta-lactam ring — a strained four-membered ring, then unknown in any biological molecule, which is precisely why so many chemists had refused it — fused to a five-membered ring. That was Abraham's proposal; Robinson had championed a rival oxazolone-thiazolidine structure. Hodgkin had the answer in 1945 and published it in 1949. Sources: Wikipedia 'Dorothy Hodgkin'; EBSCO research starter, 'Hodgkin Solves the Structure of Penicillin'; biobasedpress.eu, 'Chemistry vs bacteria: the beta-lactam'.

question: A kid at the kitchen table dips a straw into a glass of milk and drinks. Cheeks and tongue thin the air inside the mouth - that is the only thing they do. So what actually raises the milk up the tube?
answer: The outside air, pressing down on the surface of the milk
choices: The outside air, pressing down on the surface of the milk
A pulling force generated by the tongue and cheeks
Surface tension between the milk and the straw wall
Capillary action wicking the milk up the narrow tube
context: Suction is not a pulling force. The chest expansion lowers the pressure inside the mouth; the atmosphere, still at full pressure on the rest of the glass, does the actual lifting. Source: chem.libretexts.org, Introduction to Chemistry, Chapter 9: Straws.

question: A ten-second test settles the whole straw question. Take a normal straw, poke a single pin-hole through its side well above the drink's surface, put the straw in the glass, and try to drink as hard as you can. What happens, and why?
answer: Nothing rises - air enters the hole, so the atmosphere no longer has to lift the drink
choices: Nothing rises - air enters the hole, so the atmosphere no longer has to lift the drink
The drink rises faster, because the hole gives an extra outlet for suction
The drink rises only as far as the pin-hole and then stops there
The drink rises briefly, then chokes off once the mouth pressure equalises
context: The pin-hole is the ten-second proof that YOU never pull the liquid - the atmosphere lifts it, and only when the tube is sealed above the liquid line. Source: tec-science.com, How does a drinking straw work.

question: A schoolteacher hands out plastic straws twelve metres long and tells the class to drink orange juice through them from a bucket on the floor. Every child fails, no matter how hard they suck. What ceiling has the teacher run them into?
answer: The atmosphere can only push water up about ten metres, even against a perfect vacuum
choices: The atmosphere can only push water up about ten metres, even against a perfect vacuum
Human lungs cannot generate more than half an atmosphere of pull
Juice viscosity is too high for a tube that long to conduct
Static electricity along a long plastic tube stalls the flow
context: At sea level, one atmosphere can balance a column of water roughly 10.33 metres tall - about a three-storey house. No lung, and no pump on Earth, can beat that ceiling by sucking. Source: scienceabc.com, How High Can A Pump Suck Water.

question: A pump salesman claims his new 20-horsepower pump can suck water up a 15-metre pipe. A physics teacher says the claim is impossible for any horsepower ever built. Which fixed quantities decide the ceiling, no matter how strong the pump?
answer: Atmospheric pressure, water density, and the strength of gravity
choices: Atmospheric pressure, water density, and the strength of gravity
Motor horsepower, pipe diameter, and pump-seal tightness
Water temperature, salinity, and the intake filter's mesh
Impeller speed, pipe material, and elevation above sea level
context: Only three ingredients set the limit - and a manufacturer controls none of them. h = P / (rho * g) gives 101,325 / 9,810 = 10.33 m. Real pumps do worse, around 6-7 m, because of cavitation and friction; the 20 HP claim is snake oil. Source: scienceabc.com.

question: In Florence in the 1630s, well-diggers reported to the Grand Duke of Tuscany that their suction pumps refused to lift water past about ten metres, however well built. Galileo took up the problem in his Two New Sciences of 1638 - and he got it wrong. What EXPLANATION did Galileo publish for the ten-metre ceiling?
answer: That water, like a rope, has a breaking strength and snaps under its own weight
choices: That water, like a rope, has a breaking strength and snaps under its own weight
That the atmosphere has weight and pushes down on the surface of the water
That the pump seals leak invisibly at any height above ten metres
That the sun's heat evaporates the water column before it reaches the top
context: Galileo put the limit near 18 braccia (~10.5 m) and treated the column as a self-hanging rope of water. It was a genius's wrong answer. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_New_Sciences; encyclopedia.com, Torricelli.

question: Aboard the ISS, where straws work fine because the cabin is pressurised, astronauts still prefer sealed squeeze-pouches for most drinks. For open coffee, NASA engineered a special rimmed cup with a narrow inner wedge that needs no lid and no straw at all. What physical effect climbs the drink up that wedge to the rim, on its own?
answer: Surface wetting along the narrow wedge, drawing the liquid up by capillary action
choices: Surface wetting along the narrow wedge, drawing the liquid up by capillary action
Centripetal spin from the station's rotation, throwing the drink outward
Electrostatic charge on the plastic cup, pulling the polar water molecules
A tiny suction pump built into the cup's base, lifting the coffee up
context: The ISS does not spin for gravity; in microgravity the atmosphere still pushes drinks up a straw, but stray droplets can float into electronics, so pouches rule. NASA's capillary 'space cup' uses the same wetting that pulls water up a paper towel - geometry, not suction, does the work. Source: chowhound.com, NASA Space Cup.
